1.title: Class 1 — Music Fundamentals
1.html:
The grammar everything else is written in.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. This is where the school starts.

What closes it

  • Theory Midterm 1 — sat after completes. Carries a listening section drawn from Class 4.

2.title: Class 2 — Reading & Rhythm
2.html:
The two literacies: reading the page, and feeling the grid.

What it assumes

  • — Course 04 leans on knowing key signatures and intervals cold.

What closes it

  • Theory Midterm 2 — sat after completes. Carries a listening section drawn from Class 4.

3.title: Class 3 — Songwriting: Harmony & Melody
3.html:
Where the theory turns into songs — the strands closest to the music you actually make.

What it assumes

  • , and Course 02 in particular. Every strand here is an application of chord function.

What closes it

  • Theory Final Exam — sat after completes. Cumulative over Classes 1–3. Carries a listening section drawn from Class 4.

4.title: Class 4 — Ear Training
4.html:
A ~10-minute daily routine, not a reading block. Runs from day one and never stops.

Standing class — load: routine

Not a scheduled block. It doesn't consume a track slot, it doesn't gate anything, and it keeps running after its last lesson completes — the skill it builds decays if you stop. Its material also appears as the listening section inside both theory midterms and the theory final.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Runs from day one alongside everything else.

What closes it

  • Nothing. It's standing — there's no exam and no finish line. Its material is examined inside the theory midterms and final instead.

5.title: Class 5 — Beat & Arrangement
5.html:
Build order: the beat, the line over it, the song around it.

What it assumes

  • Nothing on the theory side. Course 11 assumes Course 10 (finish the groove, then write the bass around it); Course 12 assumes both.

What closes it

  • Production Midterm 1 — sat after completes.

6.title: Class 6 — Sound Design
6.html:
What the sounds are made of, and how to control them.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Both courses stand alone.

What closes it

  • Production Midterm 2 — sat after completes.

7.title: Class 7 — Vocals & Release
7.html:
The front of the record and the last mile out the door.

What it assumes

  • Nothing formally. In practice Course 16 lands last because it's about releasing, and there has to be something to release.

What closes it

  • Production Final Exam — sat after completes. Cumulative over Classes 5–7.

8.title: Class 8 — Guitar Sight Reading
8.html:
An intensive daily block: work through Leavitt's A Modern Method for Guitar in order, playing the pages.

The four courses

Course Section Pages Lessons
One 3–29 2
One 30–59 2
Two 60–99 2
Two 100–123 2

They run in ID order and each depends on the one before it, so exactly one is ever open.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Leavitt starts from zero.

What closes it

  • Finishing . There is no written exam — the check is a performance rep, logged on the course note — but the class does now have a finish line, which it did not when it was standing.

9.title: Class 9 — Piano Technique
9.html:
Hanon's The Virtuoso Pianist in order, one course per stretch of the book and one lesson per exercise — 60 in all — building the hand facility to voice chords and play parts. Worked as a daily block: the facility decays if you stop.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Hanon starts from zero.

What closes it

  • Finishing . There is no written exam — the check is a performance rep, logged on the course note — but the class does now have a finish line, which it did not when it was standing.

10.title: Class 10 — Jazz Harmony
10.html:
The idiom, taught on top of the grammar. Jazz gets its own class because it is not fundamental — it is a shared vocabulary built over the harmony Classes 1–3 install, and it earns a block rather than a corner of somebody else's.

Why this class exists

School Config records that JAZ was expanded from "dip a toe" to comprehensive on 2026-08-09, Nate's own call, and seventeen notes were written to back it — The ii-V-I, Guide Tones, Rhythm Changes, Tritone Substitution, Bebop Vocabulary, Modal Jazz and the rest. The notes landed and the syllabus never followed. JAZ sat as a named strand with a full library, no course and no concepts, until 2026-09-01. This class is that decision finally carried out.

It came in at 7 lessons and 26 concepts — nearly triple the original 4/10 estimate, because the sizing rule lets the material decide and Theory/Jazz/ carries seventeen notes. That is the measure of how far the strand had outrun its syllabus.

It is deliberately not in — Nate's rule is that fundamentals go in Class 1, and jazz is an idiom rather than a fundamental. It is also not folded into , which would have widened Theory Final Exam to cover a subject that class was never about.

What it assumes

  • — specifically for function, and and , which is why Course 31 carries depends_on: ["29", "30"]. Jazz harmony is chord vocabulary moving fast; you cannot substitute a chord you cannot spell or voice.

What closes it

  • Jazz Exam — sat after completes, at exam_pass: 80.

Where it pays off outside jazz

Nate produces hip hop, trap, EDM and pop while studying a jazz-first library. The transfer is real and specific: tritone substitution and reharmonisation are how a four-chord loop stops sounding like four chords, guide tones are the minimum voicing that still states a change, and modal jazz is the theory behind a vamp that refuses to resolve. Where a device transfers, the course says so.

01.title: Course 01 — Derivation Rules
01.intro:
Key signatures, intervals and enharmonics as rules you can apply to any key, rather than facts to look up.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. This is where the school starts.

What this unlocks

  • — the high-leverage course, unteachable until interval quality and key derivation are in place. That's why this one goes first.
  • The harder chord material — figured bass, 13ths, third inversion — becomes drilling rather than teaching once letter-distance spelling is solid.
  • Scale construction: spelling a mode from a parallel root is interval arithmetic and nothing else.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Two Names for One Pitch

**Read**
- [ ] [[Notes & Pitches]] → *Sharps & flats*, *Half-steps & whole-steps*

**The material**
- Two spellings, one sound — that's what [[FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents|enharmonic]] means. C♯ and D♭ are the same key on a piano and the same fret on a guitar.
- Which name is *correct* depends on context: the key you're in, and which letter the music needs next. There is always a right answer; it just isn't a property of the sound.
- The edge cases are the whole trap. **F♭ is E** and **E♯ is F**, because there's no black key between E–F or B–C — the only two white-key pairs without one.
- Said the other way round: every white-key pair has a black key between it *except* E–F and B–C. Same fact, and it's the one worth being able to state from either direction.

**Concepts**
- [[FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the enharmonic of C♯, F♭, E♯, B♯, G♭, A♯. Then say which of the six are white keys.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — on guitar, play one pitch in two positions and name it both ways: 6th fret of the low E as A♯ and as B♭. Do six pitches up the neck. Then find E♯ and F♭ on a piano and confirm they land on F and E.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 01 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — The Order, and Reading It Backwards

**Read**
- [ ] [[Circle of Fifths]] → *Sharp/flat order mnemonic*
- [ ] [[Key Signatures]] → *Full table*, *The pattern*

**The material**
- Two sequences, and the second is the first reversed — that's [[FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats|the order of sharps and flats]]. **Sharps: F C G D A E B.** **Flats: B E A D G C F.**
- Knowing four of seven is the usual stopping point and it isn't enough, because the reading rules are indexed off the **end** of the list.
- [[FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharps)|Reading sharps]]: take the **last sharp** and go up a semitone. Last sharp G♯ → A major.
- [[FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats)|Reading flats]]: the **second-to-last flat names the key**. B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ → A♭ major.
- **One flat is the exception** and you just memorise it: F major. There's no second-to-last flat to point at.
- Both rules run in reverse too, once you have the full order — that's the half people miss. Knowing "four flats is A♭" is useless if you can't then produce B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭.

**Concepts**
- [[FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats]]
- [[FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharps)]]
- [[FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats)]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — given 2, 3, 4 and 5 sharps, name the key. Given 1, 2, 3 and 4 flats, name the key *and* list the flats.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play I–IV–V in E, A and B on guitar, naming each key's sharps aloud *before* you start. Then set an Ableton Scale device to A♭ major and name all four flats from the second-to-last-flat rule before you look at what it highlights.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 01 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Intervals as a System

**Read**
- [ ] [[Intervals]] → *Interval quality: Perfect/Major/Minor/Augmented/Diminished*

**The material**
- Three rules that turn interval questions from recall into arithmetic.
- **[[FND-C05 — Interval inversion|Inversion]]** — flip an interval and the numbers sum to 9 while the quality flips: major↔minor, augmented↔diminished, perfect stays perfect. A major 3rd inverts to a minor 6th, and 3 + 6 = 9. Derivable under pressure, which is the point.
- **[[FND-C06 — Interval quality names|Quality is not optional]]** — it's easy to name intervals by number alone and never say major or minor, because C→F is unambiguous either way. The cost lands in ear training, where "a 3rd" with no quality attached is half an answer. Number tells you *how far*; quality tells you *which colour*.
- **[[FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the interval number|Letter distance decides the number]]** — C→A♯ *sounds* like a minor 7th and *is* an augmented 6th, because C D E F G A spans six letters. Count letters first, then fix the quality.
- That last rule is the one that unlocks chord spelling. It's why a diminished 7th is spelled G B♭ D♭ F♭ and not with an E: the chord needs four alternating letters, and E would break the pattern.

**Concepts**
- [[FND-C05 — Interval inversion]]
- [[FND-C06 — Interval quality names]]
- [[FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the interval number]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — invert M3, m6, P5, M2, m7. Then name C→F♯, C→G♭, D→B, A→F, and for each say *why* the number is what it is.
- [ ] **Technique** (~5 min) — [[Interval Ladder]] · guitar · 60→120 bpm. Minor 2nd to the octave, one string then across strings — the same intervals under the hand instead of on paper.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take the opening vocal line of [[🎵 THE BEATLES - In My Life]] and label every leap by number **and** quality. For each leap:
  1. Play the two notes of the leap **in the order the melody actually goes** — ascending leaps play low-to-high, descending leaps play high-to-low. Direction doesn't change what the interval is; "bottom note" and "top note" are about which pitch is lower/higher, not which one you play first. To name it, always sort the two by pitch: whichever is lower is the bottom note for the shortcut in [[FND-C06 — Interval quality names]], regardless of play order.
  2. **Build the inversion**: take the bottom note (by pitch, not play order) and move it up one octave (12 frets on the same string, or the same pitch class an octave up on a different string) so it now sits *above* the original top note. The original top note is now the bottom note of a new interval.
  3. Play that new pair **ascending — low to high** (the original top note, then the original bottom note an octave up). This step doesn't follow the melody's direction from step 1; it's a fresh drill on the new interval, and ascending is just the clearest way to hear it. Name it — number and quality.
  4. Check: the two interval numbers add up to 9 (2nd↔7th, 3rd↔6th, 4th↔5th), and the quality flipped per [[FND-C05 — Interval inversion]] (major↔minor, augmented↔diminished; perfect stays perfect).
  Worked example: G up to B is a major 3rd. Move the G up an octave — now B sits on the bottom, G on top. B up to G is a minor 6th. 3 + 6 = 9, major flipped to minor. That's the check, every time.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 01 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Past the Octave

**Read**
- [ ] [[Intervals]] → the table, top to bottom

**The material**
- A 9th is a 2nd plus an octave, an 11th is a 4th, a 13th is a 6th. [[FND-C08 — Compound intervals|Subtract 7]] to get the simple interval.
- "A 2nd or a 9th" is a half-answer that's technically true — the useful skill is naming the *simple* interval underneath, because that's what tells you the colour.
- This is the bridge to [[Extended Chords]]. A B♭13 is only confusing until 13 reads as "the 6th, an octave up."
- The octave matters to the *sound* even though it doesn't change the name: the same note voiced up top is a colour and voiced in the middle is a clash. That's why extensions live at the top of a voicing.

**Concepts**
- [[FND-C08 — Compound intervals]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — give the simple interval for a major 9th, a perfect 11th, a major 13th, a minor 9th. Then spell each above C.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — on piano, voice Cmaj9, C7♯11 and Cm13 with the extension in the top voice. Name the compound interval you're playing and its simple equivalent, then drop that note an octave and hear the colour flatten.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 01 — Lesson 4 Test]]

02.title: Course 02 — Chord Function
02.intro:
Teaches what chords do, not how to spell them. Every diatonic chord has one of three jobs, and once you hear the job instead of the letter, a progression becomes a shape you can manipulate.

What it assumes

  • — interval quality and key derivation have to be in place before function means anything.

What this unlocks

  • Four other strands, each an application of this one. POP is harmony over loops and vamps · BLU is harmony with a non-functional grammar · JAZ is harmony with substitutions layered on · MEL is melody written against harmony. None is teachable before this.
  • The harder chord material stops being memorisation and becomes derivation.
  • Practically: deliberate harmonic decisions in a loop, instead of finding chords by ear and keeping whatever sounds good.

The gap this course closes

Spelling chords fluently while being unable to say what any of them does is the standard gap at this stage — the vocabulary without the grammar. It's also why the four strands above stay out of reach until this is done.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Function

**Read**
- [ ] [[Chord Progressions]] → *Roman numeral analysis*, *Harmonic function (T / SD / D)*
- [ ] [[Chords by Key]]

**The material**
- The idea the whole course rests on: **every diatonic chord does one of [[HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D|three jobs]]** — tonic, subdominant or dominant.
- **Tonic** is home: I, plus its substitutes vi and iii. **Subdominant** is departure: IV and ii. **Dominant** is tension that wants to resolve: V and vii°.
- The normal cycle is **T → SD → D → T** — most of Western popular music in four symbols.
- Hearing chords as *functions* rather than letters turns a progression from a list into a shape. It also makes substitution obvious: **chords sharing a function can stand in for each other**, which is why I → vi barely disturbs a loop while I → V transforms it.
- The payoff is transposition-proof. "vi" behaves the same way in every key; "Am" only tells you which key you happen to be in.

**Concepts**
- [[HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take four progressions you've written. Label every chord T, SD or D. Find the ones that don't follow T→SD→D→T and work out what they do instead.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play a four-chord loop you know on piano, then re-voice it so every T chord is root position and every D chord is first inversion. Hear how much of "function" your hands were already doing by ear.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 02 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Cadences

**Read**
- [ ] [[Cadences]] → *The four types*, in full — it's a short note

**The material**
- A cadence is how a phrase ends: the punctuation of harmony. Four of them, and they're the difference between a phrase that stops and one that lands.
- The [[HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence|authentic cadence]] (V–I) is maximum resolution, and the default ending of most Western phrases.
- The [[HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence|plagal cadence]] (IV–I) is gentler because IV has **no leading tone** — nothing pulls up by a semitone, so it settles rather than resolves. That's why it's everywhere in gospel and rock.
- The [[HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence|deceptive cadence]] (V–vi) swerves, and it's believable precisely because vi shares two of its three notes with I. The ear accepts a near-miss.
- **The [[HAR-C05 — Half cadence|half cadence]] is the one worth internalising.** It ends *on* the dominant rather than resolving to it, which makes an antecedent phrase demand an answer — and that's what builds 8- and 16-bar sections out of 4-bar ones.
- Underneath all four sits [[HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone|the tritone]]. G7 contains one between **B and F** — maximally unstable, and each note is a semitone from a tonic chord tone. B rises to C, F falls to E; both resolve by half step into consonance.
- That's *why* V–I feels inevitable rather than merely conventional. It's also the same fact that explains tritone substitution later.

**Concepts**
- [[HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence]]
- [[HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence]]
- [[HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence]]
- [[HAR-C05 — Half cadence]]
- [[HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — find one of each cadence in songs you know. Then take a progression ending V–I and replace it with V–vi. Listen to what that does to the phrase.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — on guitar, play the same eight-bar phrase four times, ending with an authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadence. Record all four to one Ableton track, play them back and name each one blind.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 02 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Leaving the Key

**Read**
- [ ] [[Secondary Dominants]] → *The idea*, *Why it works*, *The full dominant-function roster*
- [ ] [[Borrowed Chords]] → *The workhorses*
- [ ] [[Parallel Minor]]

**The material**
- Two ways to use a chord from outside the key, and they do opposite things.
- **[[HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants|Secondary dominants]] borrow tension.** Any diatonic chord can be treated as a temporary tonic by putting *its* dominant in front of it. In C major the chord on A is Am; raise its 3rd to C♯ and you get A7, which now points at Dm. That's **V/ii**, and the C♯ is a borrowed leading tone.
- **[[HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal interchange|Borrowed chords]] borrow colour.** Keep the tonic, raid the parallel minor: Fm (iv), A♭ (♭VI), B♭ (♭VII), E♭ (♭III) in C major. The key centre never moves, so it reads as shade rather than a key change. The classic move is **IV → iv → I**.
- The distinction is the whole lesson: **secondary dominants add pull, borrowed chords add colour.** One creates motion, the other creates mood.
- A useful tell: a secondary dominant is nearly always a *dominant 7th* that isn't diatonic, and it resolves down a fifth. A borrowed chord usually isn't a dominant at all, and it resolves to the tonic or simply sits there.

**Concepts**
- [[HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants]]
- [[HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal interchange]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — in a C major loop, put E7 before Am and hear it pull. Then swap an F for an Fm and hear it darken. Same one-chord change, completely different jobs.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — in a C major loop in Ableton, drop E7 in front of Am and print it as a clip. Then swap the F for Fm and print that. A/B both against the plain loop.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 02 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Melody Against Harmony

**Read**
- [ ] [[Non-Harmonic Tones]] → *The 9 types*
- [ ] [[Modulation (Key Change)]] → *Common types*, *How to hear/analyze it*

**The material**
- **[[HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones|Non-harmonic tones]]** are the melody notes that aren't in the chord underneath — and they're most of what makes a melody sound like a melody rather than an arpeggio.
- The one to know cold is the **passing tone**: approached by step, left by step, same direction. Most of the other eight are variations on how you arrive and how you leave.
- Then the distinction that closes the course: [[HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation|tonicization versus modulation]].
- **Tonicization** points at a chord for a moment — a secondary dominant leaning on ii — then leaves. **No new key.**
- **Modulation** relocates the tonic and *confirms* it with a cadence. The ear resets.
- It's a spectrum rather than a binary, set by **how long you stay and whether you cadence there**. Four bars of V/V–V is genuinely borderline.
- What makes a modulation smooth is the **pivot chord** — diatonic to both keys, so it can be heard either way. Approach it in the old key, reinterpret it, cadence in the new one. Am is vi in C and ii in G, which is why C→G is the easiest modulation there is.

**Concepts**
- [[HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones]]
- [[HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take a melody you've written and label every note chord-tone or non-harmonic. Then modulate a loop from C to G using Am as the pivot, and confirm with D7–G.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — write a four-bar melody over that C loop, then modulate to G using Am as the pivot and confirm with D7–G. Label every melody note chord-tone or non-harmonic as you play it back.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 02 — Lesson 4 Test]]

tasks.html: Chord Progressions → Roman numeral analysis, Harmonic function (T / SD / D)
Chords by Key

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The idea the whole course rests on: every diatonic chord does one of — tonic, subdominant or dominant.
  • Tonic is home: I, plus its substitutes vi and iii. Subdominant is departure: IV and ii. Dominant is tension that wants to resolve: V and vii°.
  • The normal cycle is T → SD → D → T — most of Western popular music in four symbols.
  • Hearing chords as functions rather than letters turns a progression from a list into a shape. It also makes substitution obvious: chords sharing a function can stand in for each other, which is why I → vi barely disturbs a loop while I → V transforms it.
  • The payoff is transposition-proof. "vi" behaves the same way in every key; "Am" only tells you which key you happen to be in.

ids: HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D

tasks.html: Review — take four progressions you've written. Label every chord T, SD or D. Find the ones that don't follow T→SD→D→T and work out what they do instead.

Apply (~15 min) — play a four-chord loop you know on piano, then re-voice it so every T chord is root position and every D chord is first inversion. Hear how much of "function" your hands were already doing by ear.
Test — Course 02 — Lesson 1 Test
Cadences → The four types, in full — it's a short note

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• A cadence is how a phrase ends: the punctuation of harmony. Four of them, and they're the difference between a phrase that stops and one that lands.
  • The (V–I) is maximum resolution, and the default ending of most Western phrases.
  • The (IV–I) is gentler because IV has no leading tone — nothing pulls up by a semitone, so it settles rather than resolves. That's why it's everywhere in gospel and rock.
  • The (V–vi) swerves, and it's believable precisely because vi shares two of its three notes with I. The ear accepts a near-miss.
  • The is the one worth internalising. It ends on the dominant rather than resolving to it, which makes an antecedent phrase demand an answer — and that's what builds 8- and 16-bar sections out of 4-bar ones.
  • Underneath all four sits . G7 contains one between B and F — maximally unstable, and each note is a semitone from a tonic chord tone. B rises to C, F falls to E; both resolve by half step into consonance.
  • That's why V–I feels inevitable rather than merely conventional. It's also the same fact that explains tritone substitution later.

Apply (~15 min) — on guitar, play the same eight-bar phrase four times, ending with an authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadence. Record all four to one Ableton track, play them back and name each one blind.

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Two ways to use a chord from outside the key, and they do opposite things.
  • borrow tension. Any diatonic chord can be treated as a temporary tonic by putting its dominant in front of it. In C major the chord on A is Am; raise its 3rd to C♯ and you get A7, which now points at Dm. That's V/ii, and the C♯ is a borrowed leading tone.
  • borrow colour. Keep the tonic, raid the parallel minor: Fm (iv), A♭ (♭VI), B♭ (♭VII), E♭ (♭III) in C major. The key centre never moves, so it reads as shade rather than a key change. The classic move is IV → iv → I.
  • The distinction is the whole lesson: secondary dominants add pull, borrowed chords add colour. One creates motion, the other creates mood.
  • A useful tell: a secondary dominant is nearly always a dominant 7th that isn't diatonic, and it resolves down a fifth. A borrowed chord usually isn't a dominant at all, and it resolves to the tonic or simply sits there.

03.title: Course 03 — Scale Construction
03.intro:
Turns scales from shapes you've memorised into things you can build from a formula on any root. Reciting the seven modes in order is a different skill from spelling one, and this course is about the second.

What it assumes

  • — spelling a mode is interval arithmetic.
  • — Lesson 3 matches scales to chords, which needs function first.

What this unlocks

  • and the POP course both assume you can spell what you're playing over.
  • Practically: soloing and topline writing stop being pattern-matching on the fretboard and start being choices.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Minor Family and the Pentatonics

**Read**
- [ ] [[Scales]] in full — it's 65 lines and covers everything in this lesson

**The material**
- **[[SCL-C01 — Natural minor|Natural minor]]** is the white notes from A — the same notes as C major with a different tonic. From the parallel side: major with **♭3, ♭6, ♭7**.
- **[[SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor|Harmonic minor]]** raises the 7th, and it exists for one reason: to give minor keys a real leading tone and therefore a functioning V chord. That's the direct link back to [[Course 02 — Chord Function]] — without the raised 7th, minor has no dominant.
- **Melodic minor** raises the 6th *and* 7th ascending, smoothing out the augmented 2nd that harmonic minor leaves between ♭6 and ♮7. That gap is the reason the third scale exists at all.
- **[[SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales|Pentatonics]]** are the major scale **minus the 4th and 7th**: C D E G A, no F. Those two are exactly the notes that create half-step tension against a major triad, which is why removing them makes the scale nearly impossible to play wrong.
- Minor pentatonic is the same five notes taken from the relative minor root — which is why one shape covers both and why guitarists learn it first.

**Concepts**
- [[SCL-C01 — Natural minor]]
- [[SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor]]
- [[SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — spell A natural minor, A harmonic minor and A melodic minor ascending. Then C and G major pentatonic, and A minor pentatonic. Say what got removed or raised, and why.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play all three A minor scales on guitar, one octave up and down, then A minor pentatonic over the same drone. Say aloud which note you changed at each step.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance)]] · guitar, Stage 1 only to start: major pentatonic around the cycle of fifths, ascending and descending. Stage 2 adds the change-key-mid-pattern twist once the shapes are automatic.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance)]] · guitar, Stage 1 only to start: major pentatonic around the cycle of fifths, ascending and descending. Stage 2 adds the change-key-mid-pattern twist once the shapes are automatic.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Improvising Over a Drone Track]] · any fretted/keyed instrument — freeform improv against a sustained root drone, first playing [[SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales|the pentatonic]] straight through, then breaking from strict order (or running scale-degree number sequences) to internalize the shape by ear rather than by rote recall.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 03 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Modes as Construction

**Read**
- [ ] [[Diatonic Modes]] in full

**The material**
- The shift this lesson exists to make: **stop thinking "white notes starting on D" and start thinking "D minor with a raised 6th."**
- Those are the two ways in, and [[SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode thinking|the distinction matters]]. **Derivative** treats a mode as a rotation of a parent scale — fast to find, but it keeps your ear anchored to the parent's tonic.
- **Parallel** treats it as an alteration of major or minor *from the same root* — slower to work out, but it puts the characteristic note in front of you and keeps the mode's own tonic as home.
- **Parallel is the useful one for playing**, and it's the only one that makes [[SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root|spelling from an arbitrary root]] possible.
- Each mode differs from its major or minor baseline by **one [[SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes|characteristic note]]** — Locrian is the single exception, carrying two — so memorise that degree rather than the whole formula:

| Mode | Baseline | Characteristic note |
|---|---|---|
| Ionian | major | — (it *is* the baseline) |
| Lydian | major | **♯4** |
| Mixolydian | major | **♭7** |
| Aeolian | minor | — (it *is* the baseline) |
| Dorian | minor | **♮6** |
| Phrygian | minor | **♭2** |
| Locrian | minor | **♭5** — plus a ♭2; the one mode with two |

- The ♭5 is what makes Locrian unusable as a home key — its tonic triad is diminished, so there's nothing stable to come home to.
- Sound the characteristic note or the mode doesn't exist. A loop in "D Dorian" that never plays B is just D minor.

**Concepts**
- [[SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode thinking]]
- [[SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes]]
- [[SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — spell D Dorian, E Phrygian, F Lydian and G Mixolydian, each **from its own root**, by altering the parallel major or minor. Then name each one's characteristic note without looking.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Full Scale Workout]] · guitar · 60→100 bpm. The modal runs are this lesson with the fretboard attached.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Parallel Scale Alternate-Picking Drill (One-Note Mode Switching)]] · guitar — the drill's whole point *is* [[SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode thinking|parallel mode thinking]]: alter one degree of a memorized scale shape live (E natural minor → E Phrygian by lowering the 2nd) instead of recalling a second shape from a different parent.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Beyond-Linear Scale Practice Progression]] · guitar — Rounds 2 and 4 (root-interpolation, say-the-note-names-aloud) build the [[SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes|characteristic-note]] recall this lesson needs past shape memorization.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Chord Scale Up Down]] · guitar · 50→120 bpm — the failure mode section is this lesson's own point restated: playing the same parent scale from seven roots isn't spelling a mode, and the fix is naming each [[SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes|characteristic note]] as you play it.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — over a droning D, play D Dorian then D Aeolian, changing only the 6th. Do the same pair for E Phrygian vs E Aeolian (the ♭2). Record both A/Bs so you can hear the one-note difference cold.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 03 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Scales Against Chords

**Read**
- [ ] [[Scale Modes Reference]] → the mode/chord sections
- [ ] re-read [[Borrowed Chords]] from Course 02

**The material**
- Two applications that turn all of the above from trivia into a tool.
- **[[SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales|Modal interchange, seen as scales]].** Borrowing from the parallel minor — Course 02's [[HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal interchange|borrowed chords]] — is the *chord* view of what this course does with *scales*: keep the tonic, change the collection. Fm, A♭, B♭ and E♭ in C major are just the triads you get from C natural minor.
- **[[SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord|Matching a scale to a chord]].** Over a **Cmaj7♯11** the chord is asking for a ♯11, and Lydian's raised 4th *is* that note. Plain C major gives you a natural F — a half step above the E, and the classic avoid note over a major chord.
- The general rule underneath: **the chord names the notes that must be there, and the scale supplies the rest.** Pick the scale whose characteristic note matches what the chord is asking for.
- The blues case is the honourable exception. Minor pentatonic works over dominant chords precisely *because* its ♭3 grinds against the chord's major 3rd — that friction is the blues sound — and because three of its five notes are the chord's own tones (root, 5th and ♭7).
- It does **not** sidestep the natural 4th: the 4th is in the scale (A minor pentatonic is A C **D** E G), and blues passes through it rather than resting on it.

**Concepts**
- [[SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales]]
- [[SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — for Cmaj7♯11, C7, Cm7 and Cm7♭5, name a scale that fits and say which note makes it fit.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Full Scale Workout]] · guitar · 60→100 bpm
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Chord Scale Up Down]] · guitar · 50→120 bpm — one scale per chord, up to the 7th and back down. This lesson's concept as finger work: [[SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord|picking the collection]] fast enough that it stops being analysis.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Beyond-Linear Scale Practice Progression]] · guitar — Rounds 1 and 5 only: solo the scale over its own diatonic chords, then harmonize it into moving voicings. Both are [[SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord|scale-against-chord]] work done with the hands rather than on paper.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build one-bar vamps in Ableton on Cmaj7♯11, C7, Cm7 and Cm7♭5. Improvise 30 seconds over each with the scale you picked in the drill, and land the phrase on the note that makes it fit.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 03 — Lesson 3 Test]]

04.title: Course 04 — Reading & Position Play
04.intro:
Notation as rules you can apply cold, and the reason a written line is harder to play on guitar than on piano. Reading is two skills wearing one name: a reference layer you can learn off a page, and a perceptual skill that only comes from reps.

What it assumes

  • — a chart opens with a key signature, so reading one has to be automatic before any of this is useful.

What this unlocks

  • — where the reading actually happens, one lesson a week through Leavitt. It runs on the reference layer this one installs; without it every unfamiliar sign stops the read.
  • The theory practice lane, which already points at Sight Reading's lesson plans. This course and that lane are the same project from two directions.
  • Practically: charts, lead sheets and other people's parts stop being a decoding problem and become something you can play from.

The one belief worth correcting early

Guitar sight reading is usually blamed on ledger lines. That's the wrong mechanism, and Lesson 2 replaces it — see . It matters because the real cause has a fix and the imagined one doesn't.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Reference Layer

**Read**
- [ ] [[Notation]] → *accidental scope rules*, *rhythm notation*, *ledger lines and octave signs*, *navigation signs*. Five rules, one note

**The material**
- Five rules that decide whether a chart plays back correctly. None of them are guessable from the page, and all five are in [[Notation]].
- **[[NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure|An accidental lasts for the rest of that measure only]]** — and only on that exact line or space. The bar line cancels it, and it does *not* carry to the same letter in another octave. The octave half is the one that catches people.
- **A [[NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs|tie]] joins two notes of the *same* pitch** — attack the first, hold through the second. **A slur joins *different* pitches** — play legato, which on guitar means a hammer-on or a pull-off. One curved line, two unrelated instructions.
- **A [[NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes|dot adds half the note's own value]]**, so a dotted half is 3 beats. **A second dot adds half of what the first dot added** — a double-dotted half is 2 + 1 + ½ = **3½ beats**. Not 4; the second dot doesn't repeat the first.
- **[[NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco|`8va` means play an octave higher than written]]**, cancelled by *loco* or by the end of the dotted bracket. `8vb` below the staff is the octave-lower version. Both exist to keep ledger lines off the page.
- **[[NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda|`D.S. al Coda` is three moves]]**: back to **the sign (𝄋)**, play from there to the *To Coda* mark, **then** jump to the Coda. Going straight to the Coda is the standard misread, and it's why the chart scan in Lesson 3 checks the roadmap first.

**Concepts**
- [[NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure]]
- [[NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs]]
- [[NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes]]
- [[NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco]]
- [[NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write out the beat values for a dotted half, a double-dotted half, a dotted quarter and a double-dotted quarter. Then find a bar with an accidental in any chart and say which later notes it does and doesn't affect.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a chart with a D.S. al Coda out of [[A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment|Modern Method]] and trace the whole route with your finger before playing a note. Play it twice following only the navigation signs, then find one tie and one slur in it and play each.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 04 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — The Guitar Problem

**Read**
- [ ] [[Reading Notation on Guitar]] in full, then [[Reading Bass Clef]]

**The material**
- Two facts explain why the same page is harder on guitar than on piano, and only one of them is the one usually named.
- **[[NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower|Guitar sounds an octave lower than written]].** It's a transposing instrument: written pitch sits an octave *above* sounding pitch, effectively a permanent 8vb. Direction is the entire content of the fact — the reverse is the common wrong answer — and it's why guitar parts fit in treble clef at all.
- **[[NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: position|The difficulty is position, not ledger lines]].** The same written pitch exists in five or six different places on the fretboard. Notation tells you *what*, not *where*. On a piano the mapping is one-to-one, so the decision never comes up.
- **The fix is the position system** — a fixed four-fret window, one finger per fret, which makes the mapping unambiguous again. That's why Leavitt holds Volume 1 of [[A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment|Modern Method]] in first position for 24 pages, and it's the reason [[Sight Reading]]'s lesson plans are built the way they are.
- Bass clef is the same skill on a different set of lines. Learn it here rather than in the moment you need to read a bass part — [[Reading Bass Clef]] is a short note and it removes a whole category of stall.

**Concepts**
- [[NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower]]
- [[NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: position]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — play written middle C on the guitar, find the same *sounding* pitch on a piano, and say which direction the octave went. Then take one written phrase and locate it in three different fretboard positions.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take one written phrase from Modern Method, play it in three positions, then commit to first position and read it again at tempo. Say which position made the reading easiest and why it did.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 04 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Reading as a Skill

**Read**
- [ ] [[Sight Reading]] in full — including the 15 session-sized lesson plans

**The material**
- **[[NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan|The 30-second scan]]** is what happens between being handed an unseen chart and playing the first note. Five steps, in order:
1. **Key and time signature**
2. **The roadmap** — repeats, 1st/2nd endings, D.S., Coda
3. **Range** — highest and lowest note, so you can pick a position that holds the whole phrase
4. **Rhythm hotspots** — tuplets, syncopation, dotted figures, counted silently first
5. **A tempo you can hold through the hardest bar**, not the easiest
- Step 1 is the one everybody does, and on its own it doesn't prevent the derailment. Steps 2 and 5 are what actually save the read: the roadmap stops you playing into a repeat you didn't see, and the hardest-bar tempo stops you outrunning yourself in bar 9.
- Then the rule that saves a performance: **[[NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall behind|when you fall behind, keep the pulse]].** Drop notes, thin the chord, play only the downbeats, rejoin at the next downbeat. Never stop and never go back — the continuity *is* the skill being trained. "Slow down until I can play it" turns the exercise into a different one and trains hesitation.

> [!warning] This lesson is reps, not reading
> Reading is a perceptual-motor skill and no note will close it. The lesson test measures the *reference* layer; the skill itself comes from the daily lesson plans in [[Sight Reading]] running through the `theory` practice lane. **Treat the test as the floor, not the goal.**

**Concepts**
- [[NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan]]
- [[NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall behind]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — run the five-step scan out loud, in 30 seconds, on a line you've never seen. Then play it once, no second pass.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — cold-read one new line from [[A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment|Modern Method]] in first position, metronome slow enough for the hardest bar, no stopping and no going back. Log it against the monthly cold-read in [[Sight Reading]].
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 04 — Lesson 3 Test]]

05.title: Course 05 — Subdivision, Feel & Genre
05.intro:
Rhythm as a set of nameable choices rather than a thing you find by feel: how a bar divides, where a part sits against the grid, and the three parameters that separate one genre's drums from another's.

What it assumes

  • — the floor the whole school stands on.
  • — Lesson 3 compares grooves under real material, which means being able to spell what's playing over them.

What this unlocks

  • — a melody is a rhythm before it's a set of pitches, and the course lists this one as a prerequisite for exactly that reason.
  • and — both are this vocabulary applied inside a clip. Bassline Writing and Bass Design assume you can name a subdivision and a feel.
  • Harmonic rhythm — how often chords change — is this material pointed at chords instead of drums.
  • Practically: being able to name a groove is what turns it into a decision you can repeat, rather than one you got lucky with.

Naming what you can already hear

Most of this strand is documented in Time Signatures & Note Values and Rhythm and Groove and takes almost nothing new to learn — it takes retrieval, which is what the spaced repetition is for. Expect the course to feel more like recognition than instruction. The exception is hemiola in Lesson 2, which is genuinely new ground.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Meter and Subdivision

**Read**
- [ ] [[Time Signatures & Note Values]] → *Note-value subdivision*, *Strong/weak beat hierarchy*, *Simple, compound & complex meter*
- [ ] [[Syncopation and Metric Displacement]] → *Syncopation*

**The material**
- Two ideas, and the second only exists because of the first: how a bar divides, and what it means to play against that division.
- **[[RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dotted beats|Compound time signatures name the division, not the beat]].** In 6/8 the top number counts eighths. Divide by 3 and the real answer appears: **two dotted-quarter beats.** Six eighths written, two beats felt — and the felt half is the one you play from.
- Under any meter sits a **[[RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position strong to weak|strong/weak hierarchy]]** — beat 1 strongest, then 3, then the backbeats, then the offbeats between them. That hierarchy is the thing that makes a placement sound "on" or "off" at all.
- **[[RHY-C02 — Syncopation|Syncopation]] is emphasis where the meter doesn't expect it.** Three forms of the same move: accent a weak position, place a note on a weak position and **tie it over** the strong one, or **rest** where the arrival is expected.
- The condition that's easy to skip: **the meter has to stay in the listener's head for syncopation to mean anything.** Remove the steady pulse and there's nothing left to play against — it just sounds arbitrary.

**Concepts**
- [[RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dotted beats]]
- [[RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position strong to weak]]
- [[RHY-C02 — Syncopation]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — count a 6/8 bar out loud in six, then in two. Then do the same for 9/8 and 12/8, naming the beat count and beat value before you start.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — program a straight 16th hi-hat pattern, then make three syncopated versions with velocity alone, not moving a single note. Then loop a 6/8 groove and count it out loud in six, and again in two, while it plays.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 05 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Feel and Microtiming

**Read**
- [ ] [[Rhythm and Groove]] → *Subdivision: swing vs triplets vs offbeat*
- [ ] [[Pocket and Microtiming]] in full
- [ ] [[Syncopation and Metric Displacement]] → *Hemiola*, *Polyrhythm*

**The material**
- Lesson 1 was where notes are allowed to land. This lesson is the gap between that grid and where they actually land — which is where almost all of "feel" lives.
- **[[RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone|Swing lengthens the first eighth of each pair and shortens the second]]**, leaning toward a triplet feel. A shuffle is that triplet with the middle note removed: long, short.
- Full triplet swing is exactly 2:1 — the long note takes two of the beat's three triplet parts, the short note one — while swing sits anywhere between straight (1:1) and that full triplet, which is why swing amount is a dial rather than a switch.
- **[[RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing|Pocket is where a part sits relative to the grid]]** — consistently, and on purpose. Late reads relaxed and heavy; early reads urgent and driving. The usable range is about **5–30 ms**, and past 40 it stops reading as feel and starts reading as a mistake.
- The move that actually creates pocket is elements **disagreeing**: kick and snare on the grid, hats behind. Everything equally late just sounds slow — pocket is a relationship, not an offset.
- **[[RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove templates|Quantize, humanize and groove templates]]** are the controls for that. Quantize snaps to the grid, for anything meant to be machine-tight. Humanize adds timing and velocity variation, for anything meant to read as played. Neither belongs at 100% — **50–75% strength** pulls a performance toward the grid while keeping its feel.
- A **groove template** stores the timing and velocity offsets of one piece of material so you can apply them to another. That's the payoff: lift the feel off a break you like and put it onto your own stiff MIDI.
- **[[RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola|Polyrhythm stacks subdivisions; hemiola regroups them]].** Polyrhythm is two conflicting divisions at once — classically three against two. Hemiola is three groups of two against two groups of three: the same pulse, reorganised so a different meter is implied. Count 3-against-2 with *"nice cup of tea."*

**Concepts**
- [[RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone]]
- [[RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola]]
- [[RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing]]
- [[RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove templates]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — set a swing preset to 0%, 50% and maximum on a hat pattern and name what changed. Then clap 3-against-2 with *"nice cup of tea"* until it locks without counting.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — a repeating dotted-quarter hit across a 4/4 loop three bars or longer. Let it drift out of phase and hear it realign on the downbeat every three bars — eight dotted quarters to twenty-four eighths — that's hemiola with a clock attached.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a hip hop loop and nudge only the weak-beat hits 10–15 ms late, leaving strong beats on the grid. Then extract the groove from a break you like and apply it to the same drums. Keep the one you'd actually use.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 05 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Genre as Three Parameters

**Read**
- [ ] [[Genre Drum Patterns]] in full

**The material**
- **Three parameters explain nearly every genre distinction in drums: tempo, backbeat placement and hi-hat subdivision.** Kit choice and processing come after — these three decide what the pattern *is*.
- **[[RHY-C05 — Half-time|Half-time moves the backbeat to beat 3]]** instead of 2 and 4, so the groove feels half as fast at the same tempo: written at 140, felt at ~70. One moved hit does that much because the ear judges groove speed almost entirely from snare placement.
- That's the whole trick behind trap — fast enough for busy hi-hats and slow enough to rap over, at the same time.
- **[[RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap|Boom-bap against trap]]** is the comparison worth knowing cold. **Boom-bap:** ~85–95 BPM, backbeat on 2 and 4, straight 8th hats with an offbeat open hat, swung and laid back, sampled drums. **Trap:** written ~130–145 but felt half-time, snare on 3, 16th hats with 32nd and triplet rolls, tight kit and loose hats.
- "Trap hats are triplets" is the usual shorthand and it misses the structure: the bed is 16ths, and the 32nds and triplets are **rolls layered on top**. And in trap the **808 is the kick and the bass at once** — one element doing two jobs, which is why it gets tuned to the key.

**Concepts**
- [[RHY-C05 — Half-time]]
- [[RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take any 140 BPM beat with a snare on 2 and 4 and move the snare to beat 3 only. Nothing else changes. Listen to the tempo appear to halve, then say what the backbeat is doing.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — program eight bars of boom-bap and eight of trap from one empty clip, same kit. Change only tempo, backbeat placement and hat subdivision, then play both and confirm nothing else was needed.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 05 — Lesson 3 Test]]

06.title: Course 06 — Loop Harmony & Modal Colour
06.intro:
Harmony as it actually behaves in loop-based music: four chords that repeat, and everything you can do to them without adding a fifth. Where teaches what chords do, this teaches what they do when they come around again.

What it assumes

  • — this course is that grammar applied. Functions, cadences, secondary dominants and borrowed chords all appear here as tools, not as new material.
  • — Lesson 4 is modal colour, which means spelling a mode from its own root.

What this unlocks

  • — a topline is written against a loop, and Lesson 2 of that course splits on whether the harmony underneath is moving or static. This course is where that context comes from.
  • and the jazz material — both are applied harmony with a different grammar, and both are easier once loop harmony is fluent.
  • Practically: the ability to fix a stale loop on purpose, with a named move, instead of replacing the chords and hoping.

Do Course 02 first

This is the largest theory strand in the school and the one that looks most immediately useful, which makes it tempting to jump to. Taking it before means learning the applications of a grammar you don't have yet — every move here is described in terms of function.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — How Loops Behave

**Read**
- [ ] [[Loop-Based Harmony]] → *Vamps and harmonic rhythm*, *Why four repeating chords is satisfying*, *What creates motion when harmony doesn't*

**The material**
- The lesson exists to establish one thing: in loop-based music the harmony is the floor, not the event.
- **[[POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm|Harmonic rhythm]] is how fast the chords change, independent of tempo.** A track at 140 BPM with one chord per four bars has slow harmonic rhythm; the same tempo with two chords per bar has fast harmonic rhythm.
- Loop production wants it **slow**. The loop repeats dozens of times, so the interest has to come from drums, sound design and the vocal — and fast changes keep pulling attention back to the chords. Over a two-bar loop that gets exhausting quickly.
- **[[POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying|Predictability is the feature]], not a compromise.** Once the ear stops tracking the harmony it attends to the topline and the groove instead, and the progression becomes a bed rather than a series of events.
- The corollary is the useful half: **if a loop is boring, the chords usually aren't the problem.** Motion in a loop comes from rhythm, melody, timbre and arrangement. Rewriting the progression is the fix people reach for first and it's rarely the one that works.

**Concepts**
- [[POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm]]
- [[POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take a loop that feels stale and list everything that changes across 8 bars *other than* the chords. If the list is empty, the diagnosis is done.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take that same 4-chord loop and add 8 bars of non-harmonic change: filter movement, an arrival hat, a doubled bass octave. Bounce before and after, and play them back to back without looking at which is which.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 06 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Motion Without Chord Changes

**Read**
- [ ] [[Loop-Based Harmony]] → *Pedal point*, *Four chords with a moving bass*, *Reharmonizing a repeated section*, *Voicing over a loop*
- [ ] [[Chromatic Bass Lines]]

**The material**
- Four ways to make a loop move while the progression stays where it is.
- **[[POP-C03 — Pedal point|A pedal point is a sustained bass note held while the chords above it change]]** — usually the tonic or the dominant. An EDM build *is* a **dominant pedal**: sitting on V, refusing to resolve, so the drop supplies the release. The technique is older than the genre by about four centuries.
- **[[POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass|A moving bass does the inverse]]** — hold the chords, walk the bass through inversions. `C – G/B – Am – F` reads as far more movement than plain I–V–vi–IV contains, because **the ear takes the lowest note as the root**.
- **[[POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop|Three harmonic fixes for a stale loop]]**: reharmonize the last bar so each pass resolves differently, insert a secondary dominant to pull harder into a chord (`Am` becomes `E7 Am`), or move the bass under static harmony.
- **[[POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal|Sus2, sus4 and add9 voicings remove or blur the 3rd]]** — the note that decides major or minor — so a pad stops colliding with the topline and lets the vocal define the harmony. A topline landing on the **9th** adds colour without changing function: it isn't in the triad, so it floats.

**Concepts**
- [[POP-C03 — Pedal point]]
- [[POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass]]
- [[POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop]]
- [[POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take one 4-chord loop and produce three versions: a tonic pedal, a walking bass under unchanged chords, and a reharmonized last bar. Name what each one did to the feel.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — keep all three versions in one Session row and audition them in order. Then re-voice the pad as sus2 or add9 and check whether the topline sits better against it.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 06 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — The Axis and Its Rotations

**Read**
- [ ] [[The Axis Progression]] in full

**The material**
- **[[POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotations|Four chords, four rotations, and whichever one the loop starts and returns to is heard as home.]]** I–V–vi–IV is bright and lifting — "Let It Be", "Don't Stop Believin'". vi–IV–I–V is the identical pitch content reading as darker and more yearning.
- That's a real tool, not a curiosity: a section's mood can be flipped without changing a single chord, only the point at which the bar line falls.
- Underneath it sits [[POP-C08 — Relative-key switching|the relative major/minor relationship]] — same key signature, same seven notes, different tonal centre.
- Which is why a chorus that moves from C to Am darkens **without any modulation machinery**. Nothing is borrowed and no note is new; only the centre of gravity moved.

**Concepts**
- [[POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotations]]
- [[POP-C08 — Relative-key switching]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write one 4-chord loop and play all four rotations. Name which you'd use for a verse and which for a chorus, and say what decided it.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — record each rotation as its own clip on piano. Label one "verse" and one "chorus", then build a two-section sketch that uses both and changes nothing else.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 06 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Colour From Outside the Key

**Read**
- [ ] [[Modal Pop]], then [[Chromatic Mediants and Pop Modulation]]

**The material**
- Three modes carry most of the modal colour in pop, and each one is defined by a single note that produces a single chord.
- **[[POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII|Mixolydian gives you ♭VII]].** In C that's B♭, as in `C–B♭–F`. There's no leading tone, so it lifts and drifts rather than pulling home — it reads equally as borrowing from the parallel minor. It's a Beatles signature, alongside descending chromatic bass under a held chord.
- **[[POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv|Dorian gives you a major IV]].** `Dm–G` is Dorian, because G major needs a B natural — Dorian's raised 6th. `Dm–Gm` is natural minor, with a B♭. **One note is the entire colour difference:** Dorian lifts, Aeolian stays dark.
- **Aeolian gives you ♭VI–♭VII–i** — F–G–Am in A minor, all diatonic to natural minor. It's the cadence under a great deal of trap and film scoring.
- Then two ways pop leaves the key. **[[POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop modulation|A chromatic mediant is a chord a 3rd away with a quality the key doesn't provide]]** — in C those are **E, A, E♭ and A♭ major**. It shares a common tone and has no dominant pull, so it reads as a scene change rather than a modulation.
- The **truck driver's modulation** shoves everything up a step for the last chorus, unprepared. It's a cliché because it announces itself. Subtler alternatives: shift mode instead of key, approach the new tonic through its own V, or pivot on a shared chord.

**Concepts**
- [[POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII]]
- [[POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv]]
- [[POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop modulation]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take a minor loop and play it Dorian, then Aeolian, changing only the 6th. Say which chord each version produced and name the mode from that chord alone.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — drop a chromatic mediant into bar 4 of a loop in C — try E major, then A♭ major — and keep whichever one surprised you. Then try the same lift as a mode shift instead and compare how loudly each announces itself.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 06 — Lesson 4 Test]]

07.title: Course 07 — Blues Form & Vocabulary
07.intro:
The 12-bar form, the vocabulary that goes over it, and the one idea that makes both make sense: blues doesn't obey major-key functional harmony. Everything strange about it follows from that.

What it assumes

  • — you need the functional rules before the course that breaks them means anything. Blues is interesting precisely because it declines to resolve the way Course 02 says chords want to.

What this unlocks

  • The jazz material. A jazz blues is this form with substitutions layered over it, so the substitutions are unreadable until the plain form is automatic.
  • Joe Pass Guitar Chords - Enrichment p.23 — a 12-bar in C with six progressively denser reharmonisations. Good material, and the second tier rather than the first.
  • Practically: blues is the shared ancestor of rock, soul, funk and — through sampling — most of hip hop. The ♭3/♭7 vocabulary is already in the music; this makes using it a choice.

Twelve bars is the easy half

Knowing a blues is twelve bars long is where most people stop. The form, the three dominant chords, the scale, the turnaround and the blue notes are five separate pieces of knowledge, and each one is doing a job the others can't.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Form

**Read**
- [ ] [[Blues Form and Harmony]] → *The 12-bar form*, *Why every chord is a dominant 7th*, *The variants worth knowing*

**The material**
- **[[BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form|Twelve bars, three chords, three four-bar phrases.]]** In A the chords are **A7, D7 and E7** — I7, IV7, V7.
- `A A A A / D D A A / E D A E` — bar 12 is the turnaround back to the top, which is Lesson 2's material.
- Then the shift the whole strand rests on: **[[BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant 7th|all three chords are dominant 7ths, including the tonic]]**, and the major scale doesn't give you that. Blues isn't operating in major-key functional harmony at all.
- **The dominant 7th is the home sound here, not a tension needing resolution.** The ♭7 is colour. That single idea explains why the blues scale works over everything, why the ♭3 isn't wrong, and why the form circles rather than resolving.
- **[[BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor blues|Three variants worth knowing]]:** a **quick change** moves bar 2 to the IV instead of holding I. An **8-bar blues** is a separate form in its own right, not a truncated 12-bar. A **minor blues** uses i7 iv7 v7, often with a ♭VI at bar 9 — but the **V usually stays dominant**, because the leading tone is still wanted.

**Concepts**
- [[BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form]]
- [[BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant 7th]]
- [[BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor blues]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write out a 12-bar in A, then E, then G. Then the quick-change version of each, and say which bar changed.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play all three to a click at 90 BPM, saying the bar number out loud at every chord change until you stop needing to count. Then play a minor blues in A and find the point where the V is still dominant.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 07 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Turnarounds and the Lyric Shape

**Read**
- [ ] [[Blues Form and Harmony]] → *Turnarounds*, *Call and response*, *Feel*, *Where it went*

**The material**
- **[[BLU-C04 — Turnarounds|A turnaround is the last two bars]]**, and its job is to *break* the resolution so the ear expects bar 1 again — usually by landing on V. In A: `A7 – F♯7 – B7 – E7`, or a chromatic line descending over an A pedal.
- Without it the form stops instead of circling, which is the difference between twelve bars and a loop.
- **[[BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form|The form is call and response — AAB.]]** Bars 1–4 state a line, bars 5–8 repeat it, bars 9–12 answer it. The repeat is the point, not padding.
- In performance it plays out between the voice and an instrument, in the gaps the form deliberately leaves. **The space is where the response lives**, which is why a blues arrangement that fills every bar sounds wrong.
- **Shuffle feel** is a triplet with the middle note removed, long–short — the same fact as [[RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone]], arriving from a different direction.
- **[[BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop|Where it went.]]** Rock took the form and the pentatonic vocabulary almost wholesale. **Hip hop inherited it through sampling** — soul and funk records built on blues harmony got sampled, so the ♭3/♭7 vocabulary and the call-and-response phrasing survive in the loops even where the 12-bar doesn't.

**Concepts**
- [[BLU-C04 — Turnarounds]]
- [[BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form]]
- [[BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — play a turnaround in A and in E at the end of a full chorus. Then take a blues lyric and mark its AAB, saying which bars carry the call, the repeat and the answer.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — record a 12-bar in A and leave the gaps empty. Sing the AAB over it, then go back and fill only the gaps with a guitar answer. Nothing in the called bars.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 07 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — The Vocabulary

**Read**
- [ ] [[Blues Scales and Blue Notes]] in full

**The material**
- **[[BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale|Blue notes are the ♭3, ♭5 and ♭7]]**, played against a major or dominant background. The **blues scale is minor pentatonic plus the ♭5** — in A: **A C D E♭ E G** — and the ♭5 is a passing tone, never a resting note.
- Which raises the question the strand hinges on: the scale has a ♭3, the chord has a major 3rd, and a semitone apart is normally a clash. **[[BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong|Three reasons it isn't an error]]:**
1. **The friction *is* the sound.** The grind between ♭3 and ♮3 is what "bluesy" names.
2. **Blues isn't functional major/minor** — the scale is imposed over the chords, not derived from them. Lesson 1's dominant-7th tonic is the same fact.
3. **The note is a region, not a pitch.** Players bend the ♭3 up toward the ♮3 and sit between them; the blues has microtonality built in, and notation can't show it.
- The underrated half: over a dominant, three of minor pentatonic's five notes are the chord's own tones — root, 5th and ♭7 — so the ♭3 is the only note in it that deliberately fights the chord.
- It does **not** dodge the natural 4th, which is the one note that genuinely clashes against a major 3rd: in A that's the **D** in A C D E G, and it gets treated the way the ♭5 is, passed through rather than landed on. The scale that leaves the 4th out altogether is **major** pentatonic.

**Concepts**
- [[BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale]]
- [[BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — spell the blues scale in A, E and G, and say which note is the ♭5 in each. Then name the three blue notes in A without looking.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — over an A7 vamp, play the A blues scale and bend the ♭3 toward the ♮3 until it sits right. Then play A Mixolydian over the same vamp. Record both so you can hear the difference cold rather than while your hands are busy.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 07 — Lesson 3 Test]]

08.title: Course 08 — Melody Writing
08.intro:
How a melodic line is built, what it does against the chords underneath it, and what to change when it isn't working. Most strong melodies are one short idea developed, not a long line invented — this course is mostly about that sentence.

What it assumes

  • — the harmony a melody is written against.
  • — the rhythmic vocabulary behind Lesson 3's "change the rhythm first" rule, which is the single highest-yield fix in the course.
  • — Lesson 2 splits on whether the harmony under the melody is moving or static, and that's loop harmony's territory.

What this unlocks

  • It closes , and with it the cumulative exam over Classes 1 to 3.
  • Toplines and hooks become a set of named moves with a triage order, rather than a rewrite-until-it-works loop.
  • Everything upstream cashes out here: chord function supplies the harmony to write against, loop harmony supplies the context, and rhythm supplies the first thing to change when a line is dull.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Line Itself

**Read**
- [ ] [[Melody Writing]] → *Contour, motion, and range*
- [ ] [[Motivic Development]] in full — a single table, and the highest-value page in the lesson

**The material**
- **[[MEL-C01 — Melodic contour|Contour is the melody's shape over time]]** — how it rises and falls, independent of the actual pitches.
- A strong contour is **balanced**: what goes up comes back down, producing an arc with **one clear peak** rather than a flat line or a wandering one. Balance the *motion* as well — after a run of stepwise movement, take a leap.
- **[[MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them|A motive is a short fragment used as raw material to generate much more music.]]** Two or three bars is plenty; the value is in what you do with it afterward.
- The nine named development techniques are **repetition · sequence · inversion · interval contraction · interval expansion · diminution · augmentation · rhythmic metamorphosis · imitation.** They are the mechanism behind "one idea developed" — each one produces new material without introducing a new idea.
- Worth noticing: several of them change *only the rhythm* (diminution, augmentation, rhythmic metamorphosis) and still read as new material. That's the same principle Lesson 3 uses to fix a boring melody.

**Concepts**
- [[MEL-C01 — Melodic contour]]
- [[MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write four bars you like, then generate sixteen more using only techniques from the [[Motivic Development]] table. Name the technique used on each.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — do the same in Ableton, one clip per variation, with the technique in the clip name. Then draw the contour of the original as a line on paper and check it has a single peak.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 08 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Melody Against Harmony

**Read**
- [ ] [[Melody Writing]] → *Melody against harmony*, *Writing to a loop vs writing to changes*
- [ ] [[Non-Harmonic Tones]]

**The material**
- The same note means something different depending on the chord underneath it. **The root sounds settled** — it's where a phrase goes to end. **[[MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root|The 3rd colours the chord]]**, brighter or sadder, without changing the harmony, and it's less conclusive. The **7th** leans and wants to move. The **9th** is open and floating.
- **Landing on the root constantly is the most common reason a melody sounds boring.** It agrees with the harmony on every downbeat, so nothing is ever held in tension long enough to want resolving.
- Then the distinction that decides how you write: **[[MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to changes|over moving changes the harmony supplies the motion]].** Hold one note and let the chords recontextualize it — 5th, then 3rd, then 9th — and it moves without moving.
- **Over a static loop nothing does that for you**, so the melody has to generate its own movement through rhythm, contour and phrasing. Static loops do tolerate more repetition, because the listener is already in a looped frame.
- This is the practical reason a topline written over changes often collapses when it's dropped onto a one-chord loop. Nothing was wrong with the line; the thing that was moving it went away.

**Concepts**
- [[MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root]]
- [[MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to changes]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — for one melody note held over four different chords, name what degree it is against each. Then say which of the four sounded most settled and why.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — write one melody over a moving progression, then play the same melody over a one-chord loop on the same tonic. Mark every note that stopped working and say what it had been doing before.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 08 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Melody as Arrangement

**Read**
- [ ] [[Melody Writing]] → *Register, range and intensity*, *Building tension across a section*, *What makes a hook*, *Fixing a boring melody*
- [ ] [[Arrangement and Song Form]]

**The material**
- **[[MEL-C05 — Register and intensity|Higher reads as more intense]]** — partly convention, partly physiology, since a singer audibly works harder up there. That's why verses sit lower and choruses lift, and why "move the chorus up a third" often beats rewriting it. Widening the range does similar work.
- **[[MEL-C06 — Building tension across a section|Building tension]]** across a verse: climb in register, shorten the note values so the line gets busier, repeat a fragment in ascending sequence so it gathers, and **withhold the tonic** so nothing resolves until the chorus does it.
- The counter-move works too — strip everything back right before the chorus so it arrives against space rather than against a peak.
- **[[MEL-C07 — What makes a hook|A hook needs three things, in order]]: repetition** — it must come back, and be short enough to hold after one pass, which outranks everything else. **Rhythmic distinctiveness** — identifiable when tapped, with the pitches stripped out. **A singable range with clear contour.** Then contrast against what surrounds it. Simplicity usually beats complexity.
- **[[MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody|Fixing a boring melody has a ranking, and the ranking is the content.]] Change the rhythm first** — most boring melodies are boring *rhythmically*, circling even note values on the beat. Then **widen it**: add a leap, push the top note higher. Then **move where it sits against the chord**, targeting 9ths and 7ths instead of roots and 5ths.

**Concepts**
- [[MEL-C05 — Register and intensity]]
- [[MEL-C06 — Building tension across a section]]
- [[MEL-C07 — What makes a hook]]
- [[MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — tap the rhythm of a hook you know, with no pitches, and see whether it's still identifiable. Do it with three hooks and one melody you find forgettable, then say what separated them.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a melody that isn't working, apply the triage list in order, and stop at the first fix that solves it. Bounce before and after side by side, and note which step it was.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 08 — Lesson 3 Test]]
