09.title: Course 09 — Ear Training Method
09.intro:
Recognising what you're hearing by its feeling against a tonic, rather than by measuring intervals as abstract distances. Scale degrees first, then chord qualities, then progressions, then transcribing a song without a chart.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Lesson 1 starts at singing back a note you just heard.

What this unlocks

  • Song Practice by ear — Transcribing and Playing by Ear is the method for learning a queued song with no chart in front of you.
  • stops being paper. Hearing function is what makes "what does this chord do" a real question rather than a naming exercise.
  • — "roots first, by ear" is step 2 of writing a bassline, and it's the one place a production course names an ear skill as the blocker.

Standing, not scheduled

This runs every day, alongside whatever else is active, and it doesn't take a scheduled slot the way a reading course does. Ear training is a daily drip rather than a course: three minutes a day beats an hour a month.

Each lesson installs a daily routine, not a body of reading — which is why the reading here is short on purpose and the homework block is called The routine.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
> [!tip] There is a listening lane in this course, not just a singing one
> Three hour-long **listen-along** drills from Max Konyi — whose method this whole course is built on — sit alongside the daily routines: [[Immersive Ear Training - Major Scale (1-Hour)|Major]], [[Immersive Ear Training - Minor Scale (1-Hour)|Minor]] and [[Immersive Ear Training - Chromatic Scale (1-Hour)|Chromatic]]. Each plays a tone against a drone, speaks the correct degree, then replays the tone so the feeling and the number bind. They are designed for a walk or a commute and ask for no concentration at all.
>
> **They do not replace the routines.** The daily blocks make you *produce* the feeling by singing it, which is what locks it in; these give you volume of exposure, which is what makes recognition automatic. Do both — the listening is free time you were not otherwise using.

### Lesson 1 — The Tonic, and Being Able to Sing It

**Read**
- [ ] [[Scale Degree Ear Training]] → *Foundation: pitch matching and tonic recognition*

**The material**
- Two prerequisites, worth being honest about before anything else.
- **[[EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on|Pitch matching]]** — can you sing back a heard note, find a heard pitch on the instrument, and sing a random pitch then locate it? Every later skill falls back on "sing it or find it" the moment recognition fails, so a shaky fallback means getting **stuck** rather than getting slower.
- **[[EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it|Tonic recognition]]** is the other, and the ear already does it automatically — that's what makes music sound structured rather than like noise. The training is becoming consciously aware of something already happening.
- Three escalating levels: stop a scale one note short and *sing* the resolution; stop a progression on a non-tonic chord and sing the resolution; then do it with a song you've never heard, stopped at random.
- **Singing the resolution trains it harder than listening for it.** Producing the feeling is what locks it in.

**Concepts**
- [[EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it]]
- [[EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on]]

**The routine** — this is the homework. ~10 minutes, daily, not a reading block.
- [ ] **Review** — stop a C major scale on B and sing the resolution before playing it. Then A minor. Then a key you don't play.
- [ ] **Daily routine** (~10 min) — one song you know: flag the tonic chord every time it recurs, including mid-phrase. Then one song you don't, paused at random, singing the resolution before you check.
- [ ] **Technique** (~5–10 min) — [[Improvising Over a Drone Track]] · bass or guitar. Hold a drone on the tonic and improvise against it, so the resolution you have been *singing* gets found under the fingers. Not the reading's vocal drone method — it trains [[EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it|the same recognition]] generatively.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance)]] · guitar, Stage 3 (resonance) — sing every note while playing the day's warm-up pattern. The note-with-your-voice check is [[EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on|pitch matching]] itself, folded into a physical routine instead of run as a standalone drill.
- [ ] **Listen** (background, ~1 hr) — [[Immersive Ear Training - Major Scale (1-Hour)]] · put it on during a walk or a commute. Passive exposure to the whole degree set against a drone, with the answer spoken after every tone. It asks nothing of you — that is the point, and it is the cheapest hour in this course.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 09 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — The Twelve Feeling States, Against a Drone

**Read**
- [ ] [[Scale Degree Ear Training]] → *The 12 scale-degree feeling states* — the table, and the four practical notes under it

**The material**
- The central claim of the method: **every scale degree has its own recognisable feeling state relative to the tonic**, and it's the same *type* of experience whether it arrives as a melody note, a chord, or a bass note.
- The table's labels are one person's words, offered as a starting vocabulary. Find your own, then discard the words and keep the recognition.
- **[[EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill|Start with 3 versus ♭3.]]** Not arbitrary: hearing *a 3rd* without hearing *which* 3rd is the most common starting gap, and quality is the half carrying the emotion.
- Two structural facts make the other twelve tractable. **[[EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis|Degrees group into two worlds]]** — 1-4-5-2 clean and neutral, 3-6-7 warm and glowing — and almost every confusion happens *within* a world rather than across them.
- And **[[EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in feeling|close in pitch is not close in feeling]]**: 5 and ♯4 sit one fret apart and are about as opposite as the system has.
- Always practise against a **sustained tonic drone** while learning. In real listening you won't need one — the mind holds a virtual tonic once it knows the key.

**Concepts**
- [[EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill]]
- [[EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis]]
- [[EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in feeling]]

**The routine** — this is the homework. ~10 minutes, daily, not a reading block.
- [ ] **Listen** (2 min) — [[Visual Ear Training - The Perfect Melody]] · the gentlest thing in this lane: a familiar melody with every degree labelled on screen as it sounds. Nothing to answer, nothing to identify. Run it a few times before the hour-long drills if twelve feeling states feels like a lot.
- [ ] **Review** — against a C drone, alternate E and E♭, saying the feeling word before the degree name. Twenty reps, then move the drone to A.
- [ ] **Daily routine** (~10 min) — drone practice with sustained tones on each degree. Familiarity over speed.
- [ ] **Listen** (background, ~1 hr) — [[Immersive Ear Training - Chromatic Scale (1-Hour)]] · all twelve feeling states against a drone, which is this lesson's title as an hour of audio. [[Immersive Ear Training - Minor Scale (1-Hour)]] is the gentler way in if twelve at once is too much. Key changes every few minutes, so a degree that only feels right in one key gets exposed.
- [ ] **Listen** (2 min) — [[Visual Ear Training - The Perfect Melody]] · the gentlest thing in this lane: a familiar melody with every degree labelled on screen as it sounds. Nothing to answer, nothing to identify. Run it a few times before the hour-long drills if twelve feeling states feels like a lot.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 09 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Chords as Meta Feeling States

**Read**
- [ ] [[Scale Degree Ear Training]] → *Chords, chord qualities and progressions as "meta feeling states"*
- [ ] [[Seventh Chords]] and [[Chord Inversions]]

**The material**
- The counter-intuitive part, and the one that unlocks chord recognition: **[[EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees|a chord is not the sum of its component degree feelings.]]** Combining them produces a genuinely new, higher-level experience — the way syllables fuse into a word you hear whole.
- So don't decompose chords into degrees in real time. Train **each quality × position combination as its own flavour.**
- That's the direct fix for confusing the sevenths. **[[EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished|Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7♭5 are three memorised flavours]]**, not one triad with three different arithmetic operations applied to it.
- **[[EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling|Inversions are their own feeling states too]]**, driven by the bass note's degree feeling. A 3rd in the bass doesn't feel like 1, so an inverted chord never feels landed — which is how you can call *inverted* before you can call *which chord*.
- One honest caveat from the source: hearing **inner voices** works against the ear's natural fusing instinct and stays effortful even when trained. The fallback for a genuinely hard voicing is brute force — outer notes first, then inward.

**Concepts**
- [[EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished]]
- [[EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees]]
- [[EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling]]

**The routine** — this is the homework. ~10 minutes, daily, not a reading block.
- [ ] **Review** — Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7♭5 back to back, naming the feeling of the top note in each. Then blind and shuffled, ten reps.
- [ ] **Daily routine** (~10 min) — the seven diatonic triads of C in random order against a drone, named by position-and-quality as one label ("minor-on-6"), never by spelling.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 09 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Progressions, Bass Motion, Cadences

**Read**
- [ ] [[Transcribing and Playing by Ear]] → *Working out chords by ear*, and the bass-motion bullets under *Real-time transcription workflow*
- [ ] [[Cadences]]

**The material**
- Progressions are where ear training usually stalls. **[[EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear|Start with the two most worth owning: I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I]]**, drilled as single fused gestures — a ii–V is eventually heard as one chunk, not two lookups.
- The five-step progression drill is the engine: bass notes alone with the degree numbers sung → chords back in, naming each quality out loud → **quality swap** (change one chord's quality, hold everything else) → **position swap** (hold the quality, move the degree) → transpose and repeat. The swaps are what isolate the variable.
- Then the landmarks that make real songs tractable. **[[EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark|Half-step bass motion]]** in a major key is almost always IV→iii or vii°→I — and a major chord dropping to a minor chord a half step below is IV→iii, the only diatonic place that happens.
- **♯4 in the bass** means a V/V with its 3rd in the bass (D7/F♯ in C) or a **♯iv half-diminished** (♯ivø7 — F♯ A C E in C), before you test anything. **[[EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear|Cadences by ear]]** are the same trick at phrase scale: the ending tells you where the harmony thought it was going.
- Three modes of working out a chord, escalating as familiarity runs out: **immediate recognition** → **deduction** (narrow with clues, then test candidates) → **brute force** (outer notes first). Label whatever you work out and drill it, so it moves permanently into the first category.

**Concepts**
- [[EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear]]
- [[EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark]]
- [[EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear]]

**The routine** — this is the homework. ~10 minutes, daily, not a reading block.
- [ ] **Review** — loop I–V–vi–IV in C and sing the bass degrees. Swap vi for VI and name what changed. Then move it to E.
- [ ] **Daily routine** (~10 min) — the full five-step progression drill on one progression, borrowed from a song you're learning in [[Song Practice]].
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 09 — Lesson 4 Test]]

### Lesson 5 — Transcription, and the Routine That Keeps It

**Read**
- [ ] [[Transcribing and Playing by Ear]] in full — *Finding the key*, *Playing a melody by ear*, *The daily practice routine*
- [ ] [[From Ear Training Apps to Real Music]] — why app skill does not transfer, and the five exercises that bridge it. **The one to take away:** melody wants the arrangement pushed to the background, chords want it left to fuse into a single quality. Opposite instructions, and mixing them up is why chord transcription stalls.

**The material**
- The move that makes all of this work without perfect pitch: **[[EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfect pitch|sing the note that feels like the tonic, play any random note, judge what degree *that* is against what you sang, and back-calculate.]]**
- "I played a G and it feels like 4, so the key is D." It recurs in every transcription example in the source, and it's the reason relative hearing is enough.
- **[[EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear process|The five-step melody process]]** — memorise, map the contour, sing slowly and pencil in the degrees you feel, deduce the rest, verify on the instrument.
- Step two is the one people skip: **contour before degrees.** Getting the shape first constrains the degrees you can't hear by the ones you can. And when you're wrong, the learning is in *which degree got confused for which*, not in the fact of being wrong.
- Finally the routine itself. **[[EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routine has to touch|Four skills any complete routine touches]]: melodic scale-degree, bass-note, chord-quality, and chord-number/position.** Keep the whole thing under five minutes. This is the piece that outlives the course.

**Concepts**
- [[EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfect pitch]]
- [[EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear process]]
- [[EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routine has to touch]]

**The routine** — this is the homework. ~10 minutes, daily, not a reading block.
- [ ] **Review** — unknown song: sing the tonic, play a random note, back-calculate the key, check against a tuner. Five songs.
- [ ] **Daily routine** (~10 min) — one melody transcribed end to end by the five steps, logged with the degree you got wrong.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[Steal Like a Bassist — Ear-Training from Known Melodies]] · bass or guitar. [[EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear process|The five steps]] run on a melody you can already sing cold, where the ear cannot be wrong — sing the root, sing the melody, then find it in the shape. Its stumbling block is the useful part: not every melody starts on degree 1.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 09 — Lesson 5 Test]]

blocks.html:
• Two prerequisites, worth being honest about before anything else.
  • — can you sing back a heard note, find a heard pitch on the instrument, and sing a random pitch then locate it? Every later skill falls back on "sing it or find it" the moment recognition fails, so a shaky fallback means getting stuck rather than getting slower.
  • is the other, and the ear already does it automatically — that's what makes music sound structured rather than like noise. The training is becoming consciously aware of something already happening.
  • Three escalating levels: stop a scale one note short and sing the resolution; stop a progression on a non-tonic chord and sing the resolution; then do it with a song you've never heard, stopped at random.
  • Singing the resolution trains it harder than listening for it. Producing the feeling is what locks it in.

ids: EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on

tasks.html: Review — stop a C major scale on B and sing the resolution before playing it. Then A minor. Then a key you don't play.
Daily routine (~10 min) — one song you know: flag the tonic chord every time it recurs, including mid-phrase. Then one song you don't, paused at random, singing the resolution before you check.

Technique (~5–10 min) — Improvising Over a Drone Track · bass or guitar. Hold a drone on the tonic and improvise against it, so the resolution you have been singing gets found under the fingers. Not the reading's vocal drone method — it trains generatively.

Technique (~10 min) — Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance) · guitar, Stage 3 (resonance) — sing every note while playing the day's warm-up pattern. The note-with-your-voice check is itself, folded into a physical routine instead of run as a standalone drill.

Listen (background, ~1 hr) — Immersive Ear Training - Major Scale (1-Hour) · put it on during a walk or a commute. Passive exposure to the whole degree set against a drone, with the answer spoken after every tone. It asks nothing of you — that is the point, and it is the cheapest hour in this course.
Test — Course 09 — Lesson 1 Test

lessons.title: The Twelve Feeling States, Against a Drone

tasks.html: Scale Degree Ear Training → The 12 scale-degree feeling states — the table, and the four practical notes under it

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The central claim of the method: every scale degree has its own recognisable feeling state relative to the tonic, and it's the same type of experience whether it arrives as a melody note, a chord, or a bass note.
  • The table's labels are one person's words, offered as a starting vocabulary. Find your own, then discard the words and keep the recognition.
  • Not arbitrary: hearing a 3rd without hearing which 3rd is the most common starting gap, and quality is the half carrying the emotion.
  • Two structural facts make the other twelve tractable. — 1-4-5-2 clean and neutral, 3-6-7 warm and glowing — and almost every confusion happens within a world rather than across them.
  • And : 5 and ♯4 sit one fret apart and are about as opposite as the system has.
  • Always practise against a sustained tonic drone while learning. In real listening you won't need one — the mind holds a virtual tonic once it knows the key.

ids: EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in feeling

tasks.html: Listen (2 min) — Visual Ear Training - The Perfect Melody · the gentlest thing in this lane: a familiar melody with every degree labelled on screen as it sounds. Nothing to answer, nothing to identify. Run it a few times before the hour-long drills if twelve feeling states feels like a lot.
Review — against a C drone, alternate E and E♭, saying the feeling word before the degree name. Twenty reps, then move the drone to A.
Daily routine (~10 min) — drone practice with sustained tones on each degree. Familiarity over speed.

Listen (background, ~1 hr) — Immersive Ear Training - Chromatic Scale (1-Hour) · all twelve feeling states against a drone, which is this lesson's title as an hour of audio. Immersive Ear Training - Minor Scale (1-Hour) is the gentler way in if twelve at once is too much. Key changes every few minutes, so a degree that only feels right in one key gets exposed.

Listen (2 min) — Visual Ear Training - The Perfect Melody · the gentlest thing in this lane: a familiar melody with every degree labelled on screen as it sounds. Nothing to answer, nothing to identify. Run it a few times before the hour-long drills if twelve feeling states feels like a lot.
Test — Course 09 — Lesson 2 Test
Scale Degree Ear Training → Chords, chord qualities and progressions as "meta feeling states"
Seventh Chords and Chord Inversions

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The counter-intuitive part, and the one that unlocks chord recognition: Combining them produces a genuinely new, higher-level experience — the way syllables fuse into a word you hear whole.
  • So don't decompose chords into degrees in real time. Train each quality × position combination as its own flavour.
  • That's the direct fix for confusing the sevenths. , not one triad with three different arithmetic operations applied to it.
  • , driven by the bass note's degree feeling. A 3rd in the bass doesn't feel like 1, so an inverted chord never feels landed — which is how you can call inverted before you can call which chord.
  • One honest caveat from the source: hearing inner voices works against the ear's natural fusing instinct and stays effortful even when trained. The fallback for a genuinely hard voicing is brute force — outer notes first, then inward.

ids: EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling

tasks.html: Review — Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7♭5 back to back, naming the feeling of the top note in each. Then blind and shuffled, ten reps.
Daily routine (~10 min) — the seven diatonic triads of C in random order against a drone, named by position-and-quality as one label ("minor-on-6"), never by spelling.
Test — Course 09 — Lesson 3 Test
Transcribing and Playing by Ear → Working out chords by ear, and the bass-motion bullets under Real-time transcription workflow
Cadences

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Progressions are where ear training usually stalls. , drilled as single fused gestures — a ii–V is eventually heard as one chunk, not two lookups.
  • The five-step progression drill is the engine: bass notes alone with the degree numbers sung → chords back in, naming each quality out loud → quality swap (change one chord's quality, hold everything else) → position swap (hold the quality, move the degree) → transpose and repeat. The swaps are what isolate the variable.
  • Then the landmarks that make real songs tractable. in a major key is almost always IV→iii or vii°→I — and a major chord dropping to a minor chord a half step below is IV→iii, the only diatonic place that happens.
  • ♯4 in the bass means a V/V with its 3rd in the bass (D7/F♯ in C) or a ♯iv half-diminished (♯ivø7 — F♯ A C E in C), before you test anything. are the same trick at phrase scale: the ending tells you where the harmony thought it was going.
  • Three modes of working out a chord, escalating as familiarity runs out: immediate recognition → deduction (narrow with clues, then test candidates) → brute force (outer notes first). Label whatever you work out and drill it, so it moves permanently into the first category.

ids: EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark
EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear

tasks.html: Review — loop I–V–vi–IV in C and sing the bass degrees. Swap vi for VI and name what changed. Then move it to E.
Daily routine (~10 min) — the full five-step progression drill on one progression, borrowed from a song you're learning in Song Practice.
Test — Course 09 — Lesson 4 Test

lessons.title: Transcription, and the Routine That Keeps It

tasks.html: Transcribing and Playing by Ear in full — Finding the key, Playing a melody by ear, The daily practice routine

From Ear Training Apps to Real Music — why app skill does not transfer, and the five exercises that bridge it. The one to take away: melody wants the arrangement pushed to the background, chords want it left to fuse into a single quality. Opposite instructions, and mixing them up is why chord transcription stalls.

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The move that makes all of this work without perfect pitch:
  • "I played a G and it feels like 4, so the key is D." It recurs in every transcription example in the source, and it's the reason relative hearing is enough.
  • — memorise, map the contour, sing slowly and pencil in the degrees you feel, deduce the rest, verify on the instrument.
  • Step two is the one people skip: contour before degrees. Getting the shape first constrains the degrees you can't hear by the ones you can. And when you're wrong, the learning is in which degree got confused for which, not in the fact of being wrong.
  • Finally the routine itself. : melodic scale-degree, bass-note, chord-quality, and chord-number/position. Keep the whole thing under five minutes. This is the piece that outlives the course.

ids: EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfect pitch
EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear process
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routine has to touch

Its stumbling block is the useful part: not every melody starts on degree 1.

10.title: Course 10 — Drum Programming & Beat Construction
10.intro:
Drum sound and drum programming: building the sounds instead of repairing them, making a quantized grid read as something a person played, and giving a loop internal form. covers the theory of time and stops where the DAW starts. This is the other side of that line.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Lesson 1 starts at the parts of a kick drum.

What this unlocks

  • — its first instruction is "groove first, bass second", which assumes the groove is finished. That's this course.
  • — the three-changes tier method in Lesson 3 is arrangement at loop scale; Course 12 runs the same idea at song scale.
  • Practically: drums stop being something you fix in the mix and start being right where they're made.

Taught from zero

This course assumes no prior knowledge and skips nothing. Lesson 1 begins at "what are the parts of a kick", not one rung above it. Some of it will be revision, and revision is the cheap error — skipping the thing you didn't actually know is the expensive one.

If a lesson turns out to be entirely known, run /school test 10 early rather than sitting through it. The test is the gate; the lessons are the route.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Sounds

**Read**
- [ ] [[Kick Design]] → *Why synthesize a kick*, *Anatomy of a synth kick*, *Layering + placement*
- [ ] [[Snare Design]] → *Anatomy of a synth snare*
- [ ] [[Sampling and Sound Selection]]

**The material**
- The habit to unlearn first: **[[DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processing is not|stacking processing on a kick that doesn't hit]].** Compressor after compressor, EQ after EQ, chasing something the sample was never going to do.
- The fix is almost always upstream — pull the sample, audition another, drop the chain back to nothing. **A chain fixes a close-but-not-quite sample; it doesn't rescue a wrong one.**
- Synthesising instead gives you [[DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick|four parts to control]]: **body** (a pitched sine or triangle, tuned to the root, 200–450 ms decay), **pitch envelope** (+12 to +36 semitones falling to zero over 15–40 ms — the "pew" that reads as punch), **click** (a sub-10 ms noise or HF layer), and light **saturation** so it survives a phone speaker.
- Add a **Hold stage of 30–50 ms** before Decay, so the decay only ever shapes the tail rather than eating the body.
- Then the decision that ties drums to harmony: **[[DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and what to do when the key is too low|tune the kick to the song's root]].** Latch's kick hits F every bar and establishes a key the track otherwise avoids. When the root is too low to be usable, tune to the fifth above and let it bend.

**Concepts**
- [[DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processing is not]]
- [[DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick]]
- [[DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and what to do when the key is too low]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the four parts of a synth kick and a starting value for each. Then say what you'd do with a kick in C minor that flaps speakers.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build a kick from a sine in Operator using only body, pitch envelope, click and saturation. Tune it to the root of a track in progress, then A/B it against the sample you were using.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 10 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Making a Grid Read as a Performance

**Read**
- [ ] [[Rhythm and Groove]] → *Humanization*, *Ghost notes and note length*
- [ ] [[Pocket and Microtiming]] in full

**The material**
- **[[DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails on drums|One-click humanize does not work on drums]]**, and the reason generalises: it scatters timing *randomly* within a threshold, while a real drummer's deviations are **informed** — by feel, by groove, by experience. A few hits land well by luck and the whole thing reads as badly played.
- What works instead is a rule about **metric role**. **[[DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondaries go late|Anchor hits stay exactly on-grid]]** at static velocity — primary kick, primary snare — because the groove needs something dependable underneath it.
- **Secondary hits take the variation** — ghost snares, offbeat claps — shifted **late, never early**, by a *different* amount each time, since uniform lateness reads as a setting rather than a player. The rule follows the role, not the instrument: a hi-hat marking a strong beat alone stays on-grid, because it has inherited the anchoring job.
- **[[DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass — and they are the push-pull|Ghost notes are a second pass]].** Finish kick, snare and hat completely, then go back and hunt the gaps. They aren't decoration — the ear leans toward an expected strong beat, gets a syncopated ghost instead, and that displaced anticipation *is* the pleasurable tension in a groove.
- **[[DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity value|Velocity is the one place randomisation genuinely models a player]]**: drag a **range**, not a value, so every pass differs. Keep the band narrow — too wide reads as inconsistent rather than natural.

**Concepts**
- [[DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails on drums]]
- [[DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondaries go late]]
- [[DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass — and they are the push-pull]]
- [[DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity value]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — say which hits get nudged late and by how much, and why velocity randomisation works where timing randomisation doesn't.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a quantized beat. Nudge only the off-8th hats late by varying amounts, leave the anchors alone, then add a ghost-snare pass. A/B against an auto-humanized copy of the same beat.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 10 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Loop Form and Energy Tiers

**Read**
- [ ] [[Rhythm and Groove]] → *Pattern-level form*
- [ ] [[Arrangement and Song Form]] → the energy-tier bullets
- [ ] [[Layering and Stacking]]

**The material**
- A 4-bar loop that reads as one bar is the commonest failure at this scale. The fix is **[[DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop|A-B-A-C inside the loop]]**: a simple kick pattern on the A bars and a syncopated one on B, each paired with the **inverse** hat treatment — strong-beat hats under the busy kick, syncopated hats under the simple one.
- The two elements keep trading who anchors and who plays around, so the pattern doesn't read as repetition until the full cycle completes.
- Then **[[DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier method|the three-changes tier method]]**, the concrete cure for loop-itis at clip level. Write the sparsest **Intro** that still works, duplicate it for **A**, and make exactly **three changes** — each either an existing element made more active or a new element added, each immediately obvious and present throughout. Three more for **B**.
- A *swap* counts as a change: jingle bell to ride, toms pitched up into a new voice. Past a point, thin out rather than stack. Crashes and tom fills are transitional and don't count toward the three.
- Starting a song with four energy-tiered clips already built means four jumping-off points instead of one basket to overfill.
- Last, physical plausibility. **[[DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can't do that|A real kit can't ring an open hat through a closed one]]**, so enable *cut itself* on the group. The same goes for overlapping bass tails, which are worse. The four-limb ceiling is that constraint applied to writing rather than to tails.

**Concepts**
- [[DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop]]
- [[DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier method]]
- [[DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can't do that]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the three changes from Intro to A on a beat you've built, and say what doesn't count as one.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a 1-bar loop and expand it to A-B-A-C with inverse hat treatments. Then build Intro/A/B/Outro at three changes per tier, writing down what the three were each time.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 10 — Lesson 3 Test]]

11.title: Course 11 — Bass Writing & Design
11.intro:
How a bassline relates to everything else, and how to write a good one. The line first, then what it does against the drums, the chords and the vocal, then the sound it comes out as — in that order, because the relationships are the subject and the tone is the smallest part of it.

What it assumes

  • — step 1 of the method is finish the drum groove, then write the bass around it. It's a real dependency, not an ordering preference.

What this unlocks

  • — Lesson 2's section-by-section bass writing is the arrangement question asked from the low end.
  • — "roots first, by ear" is the one place a production course names an ear skill as the blocker, and it runs alongside this one for that reason.
  • — a moving bass under static harmony is , approached from underneath.

Composition, not technique

This is a writing and arrangement course. It covers how bass lines relate to everything else and how to write a good one — no fretboard drills, no scale positions, no repertoire. Bass Design covers the sound in Lesson 3; everywhere else the notes are the subject.

Taught from zero

No prior knowledge assumed and nothing skipped — Lesson 1 starts at one root note per bar, which is genuinely the beginner rung. Some of it will be revision, and that's the cheaper error. Run /school test 11 early if a lesson turns out to be known.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Writing the Line

**Read**
- [ ] [[Bassline Writing]] → *The method*, steps 1–6 and 11

**The material**
- Two steps open the method, and almost every bad bassline is one of them skipped.
- **[[BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — roots first, by ear|Groove first, bass second.]]** Finish the drum groove, then write around it. The trap inside that is assuming the bass follows the kick map — it doesn't, it locks to the **pocket**. Rhythmic choices made with no drums playing are provisional, and a real loop will overrule them.
- **Roots first, by ear.** Land the roots before any decoration. The beginner rung is literally one root per bar on each chord change, and chord quality doesn't matter yet, because only the root is sounding.
- That step is diagnostic: not hearing the roots is an ear gap rather than a writing problem, which is what [[Course 09 — Ear Training Method]] is for. Register is the trap in the same breath — the identical line an octave too low goes from fine to undefined mud, and the fix is moving it up, not processing it.
- Then motion. **[[BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabulary|Octaves are the default vocabulary]]** — up and back, occasionally through a passing tone, the 5th above being the classic. Fills come from **stealing the melody's rhythm**, so the busyness hides inside phrasing that's already there.
- **Record busy and mute down:** play a too-busy line through the whole loop, then keep only the killer moments, never repeating a fill in consecutive phrases.
- Two constraints close the lesson. **[[BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two basslines at once|The band test]]** — imagine a bassist physically playing it, and rewrite it if no player would phrase it that way. And the hard rule: **never two genuinely different basslines at once.** Two distinct low melodic lines read as mud, not richness. Doubling the *same* line is a different thing and is fine.

**Concepts**
- [[BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — roots first, by ear]]
- [[BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabulary]]
- [[BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two basslines at once]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the first two steps of the method and the trap inside each. Then say what the band test is and what it rejects.
- [ ] **Technique** (~10 min) — [[One-Finger-Per-Fret 5-Level Daily Drill]] · bass · 100→200 bpm. Level 4's root-fifth-octave riff puts this lesson's roots-first-then-octave-motion method physically under the hand.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — write over C–Am–F–G as one root per bar. Add subdivision. Add the octave. Stop there. Then solo the low end of a current project and count the distinct melodic lines in it.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 11 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Bass Against Harmony, Melody and the Kick

**Read**
- [ ] [[Bassline Writing]] → *The method* steps 7–10, and the funk/disco and section-energy bullets
- [ ] [[Chromatic Bass Lines]]

**The material**
- "How busy should the bass be" isn't a taste question — it's a question about what else is moving. **[[BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under static harmony|Showcase basslines only work over static held chords.]]** When the harmony above is busy, only root notes work; with a vocal or a synth hook on top, the bass supports.
- The corollary is the useful half: **two chords means the riffs ARE the line.** Static harmony moves all the interest into the fills, and one perfectly placed fill can be the entire event.
- **[[BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversation|Bass and keys are a conversation]]**, which is this course's central question in one line: what story is the bass telling, what story are the keys telling, and do they talk to each other? Keep the harmony simple and let the exchange carry it.
- The polyphonic version is a bass patch playing its own upper voice a 3rd or 5th above the root, in **contrary motion** — genuine two-voice writing rather than a melodic line with a thicker patch.
- For groove, one move does most of the work: **[[BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make it funky|switch to a 16th grid and move some notes off the kick's strong beats]]** onto the weak spots in between. Layer octave uppers and downers for bounce. Between phrases, a **chromatic walk-up or walk-down** connects regardless of scale.
- **[[BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line, all of them share a root|Across sections]]**, write a genuinely new rhythm, register and contour for each — rising, peak, B section, wind-down — while every line keeps returning to the **same root as home.** That's what keeps four different basslines reading as one song.

- [[BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under static harmony]]

- [[BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make it funky]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — say when the bass gets to show off and when it can only play roots. Then name the single move that makes a line funky.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a line locked to the kick, move a third of its notes onto 16th offbeats, and connect two phrases with a chromatic walk-up. Then write a keys part that *answers* it rather than moving with it.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 11 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — The Low End as a Shared Resource

**Read**
- [ ] [[Bassline Writing]] → *808-specific* and step 10
- [ ] [[Bass Design]], then [[Kick Design]] → the kick/bass clash bullets
- [ ] [[Sidechaining]] and [[Masking and Carving]]

**The material**
- Kick and bass fight because they're both trying to own the same twenty hertz. **[[BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don't EQ both|The fix isn't EQ on both — it's deciding who owns the sub.]]**
- Put an analyser on each, play them together, find where each fundamental actually peaks, pick one to hold the low end, and high-pass the other until the clash stops. If high-passing the kick guts it, swap the kick and cut the new one instead. The same decision made in *time* rather than frequency is sidechaining, or automating kick length by section.
- **[[BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then drop it back|Tuning an 808: pitch it up an octave or more, tune it there, then drop it back.]]** Never guess at pitch down at 40 Hz — the ear genuinely can't do that job in place.
- Slides on an audio 808: pitch it with warp **off**, then set warp mode to **Tones**, then draw the slides in the clip's transposition envelope.
- When the part is right but the tone is wrong, **[[BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-not-compressor|walk the ladder]]** rather than processing your way out: synth patch → different synth → real or sampled bass guitar → DI plus amp sim.
- Then control it with a **limiter, not a compressor.** Bass wants a ceiling with its dynamics intact, not gain-riding that pumps. Saturate for body, and sidechain last.

**Concepts**
- [[BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don't EQ both]]
- [[BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then drop it back]]
- [[BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-not-compressor]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — kick and bass both peak at 55 Hz. Say what you do, in order. Then describe how to tune an 808 and why you can't do it in place.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — analyse the kick and bass fundamentals on a current track, decide ownership in writing, and high-pass the loser. Then detune an 808, try to tune it at sub, fail, and tune it an octave up instead.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 11 — Lesson 3 Test]]

tasks.html: Bassline Writing → The method, steps 1–6 and 11

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Two steps open the method, and almost every bad bassline is one of them skipped.
  • Finish the drum groove, then write around it. The trap inside that is assuming the bass follows the kick map — it doesn't, it locks to the pocket. Rhythmic choices made with no drums playing are provisional, and a real loop will overrule them.
  • Roots first, by ear. Land the roots before any decoration. The beginner rung is literally one root per bar on each chord change, and chord quality doesn't matter yet, because only the root is sounding.
  • That step is diagnostic: not hearing the roots is an ear gap rather than a writing problem, which is what is for. Register is the trap in the same breath — the identical line an octave too low goes from fine to undefined mud, and the fix is moving it up, not processing it.
  • Then motion. — up and back, occasionally through a passing tone, the 5th above being the classic. Fills come from stealing the melody's rhythm, so the busyness hides inside phrasing that's already there.
  • Record busy and mute down: play a too-busy line through the whole loop, then keep only the killer moments, never repeating a fill in consecutive phrases.
  • Two constraints close the lesson. — imagine a bassist physically playing it, and rewrite it if no player would phrase it that way. And the hard rule: never two genuinely different basslines at once. Two distinct low melodic lines read as mud, not richness. Doubling the same line is a different thing and is fine.

12.title: Course 12 — Arrangement & Song Form
12.intro:
How a loop becomes a song. The three things standing in the way, in the order they actually come up: the loop that stops being interesting, the decision about what leaves and when, and the joins between the pieces.

What it assumes

  • — the tier method in Lesson 2 is the song-scale version of what that course does at loop scale, and this course assumes there's a finished loop to arrange.

What this unlocks

  • — its Lesson 3 is melody as arrangement and reads Arrangement and Song Form directly. This course is the proper foundation under it.
  • The Song Seeds pipeline — going from seed to sections before any production starts is this course applied upstream.
  • Practically: it's the difference between a folder of loops and a finished track. Nothing else in the school addresses that gap.

Taught from zero

No prior knowledge assumed and nothing skipped. Some of it will be revision, which is the cheaper error. Run /school test 12 early if a lesson turns out to be known.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Loop-itis and the Second Idea

**Read**
- [ ] [[Arrangement and Song Form]] → *The loop-itis diagnosis*, *Writing the B section*
- [ ] [[Musical Form]]

**The material**
- The pattern is specific: make a loop, love it, and thirty to sixty minutes later it feels worthless. **[[ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B section, not a new idea|The idea was never bad — it was alone.]]** A loop that bores you isn't asking for a new idea; it's asking for a B section.
- **[[ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B section|The method is three steps.]]** Duplicate the drums and strip everything else. Write a **complementary** part — different chords, opposite density, different mood. Then test **the return**: playing out of B back into A should feel like *we're home*.
- That test is the step people skip, and it's the whole point. **The right B section makes the A section better** — if the return is flat, B isn't finished.
- **[[ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B section|Two harmonic routes in]]**, both solving the same problem of *new but not random*. The **relative key** — up three semitones from a minor root — gives a different centre with identical scale tones, so the return can't clash.
- The **withheld chord** — audit which diatonic chords the verse and chorus never used, then open the bridge on exactly that one, because the ear hasn't heard it yet in this song.
- One honest ceiling: no amount of subtractive variation on a single loop sustains a song. A genuinely second loop becomes unavoidable, and **most attempts at one will be discardable.** That's the cost of the method, not a sign it's going wrong.

**Concepts**
- [[ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B section, not a new idea]]
- [[ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B section]]
- [[ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B section]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — give the three steps and the test they end in. Then name the two ways to choose B-section chords and what each one guarantees.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — open an abandoned project. Duplicate the drums, strip everything else, and write a B section using the withheld-chord route. Loop B→A four times and rate the return honestly.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 12 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Scheduled Absence and the Energy Curve

**Read**
- [ ] [[Arrangement and Song Form]] → *Sequencing one idea (subtraction scheduling)*, *Jam long, cut the fat*, *The simplicity referee*, and the energy-curve and section-length bullets

**The material**
- "Let the Beat Build" is the masterclass: hi-hat → clap → clap+snares → kick → bass → everything at the hook. **One idea, minutes of interest, purely from when things enter.**
- The principle inverts the instinct: **[[ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is scheduled absence|arrangement interest is scheduled absence]], not added layers.** Schedule the absences — pull the kick, the 808, all the drums, the melody. A middle ground between gone and full is attenuating an element's top end rather than muting it outright.
- Then the shape of the whole thing. **[[ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, and pull back before the end|Start deliberately low so there's room, build to exactly one apex, then pull back after it.]]** Sustaining the peak through to the outro reads as exhausting rather than climactic.
- Change **3–4 elements simultaneously** at each major boundary so it reads as a jump rather than a drift, and punctuate it with a crash.
- **[[ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, and breaking them on purpose|Section lengths are conventions worth knowing precisely]]**, because breaking one only reads as deliberate against a known pattern. House is flat 16-bar. Pop holds a proportional template — roughly a 4-bar intro, with verse, pre and chorus about double that — and the specific move that **the chorus gets longer each time it returns.**
- And the referee: **[[ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, and the artist sets it|too busy is a relative term]].** Lil Baby cut Kenny Beats off at five to seven sounds. The extra perc layer always matters less than it feels like it does while you're producing.

**Concepts**
- [[ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is scheduled absence]]
- [[ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, and pull back before the end]]
- [[ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, and breaking them on purpose]]
- [[ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, and the artist sets it]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — say how many elements change at a major boundary and what kind. Then say where the apex goes and what has to happen after it.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a full 8-bar loop and stagger every element's first entrance across 32 bars without writing a single new note. Then draw the energy curve of a reference track next to your own and find where they diverge.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 12 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Transitions

**Read**
- [ ] [[Arrangement and Song Form]] → the transition bullets
- [ ] [[Automation]] and [[Ear Candy and Hiding Synths]]

**The material**
- The finding worth internalising: an analysis of roughly 100 reference tracks for what makes transitions cohesive found **most weren't leaning on risers, swooshes or reverse cymbals at all.**
- **[[ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition; risers are the last step|The real technique is automating existing devices across the section itself]]** — filters, detune, sends, wet/dry. Risers are fine as deliberate icing once the parts already connect; reaching for one first just papers over a join that doesn't work.
- Three usable shapes: a **micro drop** (an instant filter wet/dry snap plus a gradual percussion sweep), a **macro drop** (maximum contrast via kick filtering, bass removal, slight detune and a timbre shift), and a **wet/dry drop** (send automation contrasting wet against dry, wide against mono, instead of tone). Mine your own elements for a sweep before importing one.
- Two devices do most of the remaining work. **[[ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged across the boundary|Carry one element unchanged across the boundary]]** — a motif, a signature sound — so the listener has something to hold onto while everything else changes.
- And **[[ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before the payoff|strip every added layer right before the payoff]]**, leaving only the core element to carry through. The sudden reduction reads as tension release rather than as a mistake.
- Subtraction reads as suspense generally. A listener can't track many simultaneous parts, so less makes what remains read as more — and a big reverb over an emptied section sells it as intentional.

**Concepts**
- [[ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition; risers are the last step]]
- [[ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged across the boundary]]
- [[ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before the payoff]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the three automation-driven transition shapes and what each contrasts. Then say what the last thing to happen before a drop is.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take the worst transition in a current project. Delete every riser and impact in it. Rebuild it with filter and send automation, one carried element, and a strip before the payoff.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 12 — Lesson 3 Test]]

13.title: Course 13 — Signal Path & Synthesis Methods
13.intro:
What a synth is actually doing, from the three blocks every one of them shares to the four methods that distinguish them. The difference this course exists for: following a patch recipe versus knowing why it works well enough to write your own.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Lesson 1 starts at the three blocks on the panel.

What this unlocks

  • Patch design from scratch rather than preset selection. Instrument Preset Map stays the right tool under deadline; this is the other mode.
  • Bass Design, Kick Design and Snare Design stop being recipes and become derivations — which is what Lesson 1 asks for when it says to synthesise the kick.
  • pairs with it naturally. Both are the concept layer underneath a tool that's already in daily use.

Hands on the synth, not on the page

Every drill here is done at an instrument. This is the one subject in the school where reading alone provably doesn't work — the ear has to connect the knob to the change, and no note can do that for you.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Path

**Read**
- [ ] [[Signal Path]], then [[Oscillators and Waveforms]] and [[Filters and Resonance]]

**The material**
- **[[SYN-C01 — The signal path|Oscillator → filter → amplifier.]] Generate, remove, shape.** Every subtractive synth on the market is that chain with a different panel drawn around it.
- The amp envelope is why anything is audible at all. The filter envelope is where most of the character comes from. LFOs sit alongside and move whichever block you point them at.
- The corollary explains half the strand: **a filter can only remove harmonics the oscillator generated.** Start on a sine and nothing downstream can brighten it, because there's nothing there to uncover.
- That's why patches start from saws — the richest raw material — and it's the reason [[FM Synthesis]] had to be invented at all. Subtractive can only subtract.

**Concepts**
- [[SYN-C01 — The signal path]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — open [[Analog]] and identify the three blocks on the panel. Play all four waveforms through a wide-open filter, then set the same cutoff on each and hear how much of each one is left.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build a patch from an initialized [[Analog]], one oscillator with the filter wide open, then close the filter to taste on each of the four waveforms. Save all four, naming each preset after what the filter left behind. Then close the oscillator entirely and push resonance until the filter self-oscillates into a sine.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 13 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Envelopes

**Read**
- [ ] [[Envelopes and ADSR]]

**The material**
- **[[SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one level|Three times and one level.]]** Attack, decay and release are durations. **Sustain is the only level** in the whole envelope.
- Decay is a *journey* — from the peak down to the sustain level — which is why filing it as a level makes the knob seem broken. It isn't setting a volume; it's setting how long the fall takes.
- Four shapes cover most of what you'll build: **[[SYN-C03 — Building a pluck|pluck]]** (sustain at **0**, so the note is only its own decay), pad, organ and bass.
- The pairing that creates character is the **filter envelope plus envelope amount.** An amp envelope alone gives you a shape; the filter envelope gives you a sound that changes while it plays, which is what "snap" actually is.

**Concepts**
- [[SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one level]]
- [[SYN-C03 — Building a pluck]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — on [[Analog]], build all four shapes from an initialized patch using the amp envelope only. Say what sustain is set to in each, and why.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build a pluck, a pad, a stab and a swell from one initialized patch, then add a filter envelope to each and find the envelope amount that makes the pluck actually snap. Put all four in a single 8-bar clip and play it against a beat.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 13 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Movement and Thickness

**Read**
- [ ] [[LFOs and Modulation]], then [[Voice Architecture]]

**The material**
- **[[SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not audio|An LFO is an oscillator below hearing range wired to a *parameter* rather than to the output.]]** You never hear the LFO — you hear what it moves. Push it past about 20 Hz and it becomes FM; the only difference is speed.
- **[[SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evolve|To make something evolve, modulate its timbre rather than its level]]** — filter cutoff or wavetable position. Level changes read as volume automation; timbre changes read as alive.
- Then thickness. **[[SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune|Unison stacks copies, detune spreads them, and unison without detune does almost nothing]]** — identical copies at the same pitch just sum to a louder version of the same sound.
- The rule that matters in bass-heavy genres: **no detune on subs and 808s.** Detuning the low fundamental turns a defined pitch into a beating, undefined smear.

**Concepts**
- [[SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not audio]]
- [[SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evolve]]
- [[SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — on [[Serum 2]] or [[DUNE 3]], walk unison from 1 to 7 voices with detune at zero and confirm almost nothing happens. Then bring detune up and say what changed.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build a [[Wavetable]] pad with two LFOs at different rates, one on cutoff and one on position. Hold a chord for 16 bars and record it; it should never repeat. Then rebuild the same chord in [[Serum 2]] and record unison 1 → 7 with detune coming up.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 13 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — The Four Methods

**Read**
- [ ] [[Subtractive Synthesis]], [[FM Synthesis]], [[Wavetable Synthesis]], [[Granular Synthesis]]

**The material**
- Four ways to make a sound, each defined by what it can do that the others can't.
- **[[SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM|Subtractive starts rich and filters away]]** — predictable, cheap, and unable to make inharmonic content. **FM has one oscillator modulate another's frequency, *creating* sidebands** that weren't in either source.
- **[[SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells|Integer ratios give harmonic, pitched results; non-integer ratios give inharmonic ones]]** — which is what bells and struck metal physically are. That's why FM does bells and subtractive can't: the overtones of a bell aren't multiples of its fundamental.
- **[[SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at the source|Wavetable]]** is a scannable table of waveforms with the position modulatable — timbral movement generated at the source rather than imposed by a filter.
- **[[SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from pitch|Granular breaks audio into grains, decoupling time from pitch]].** Freeze a moment, stretch enormously without transposing, or build texture out of any recording at all.

**Concepts**
- [[SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM]]
- [[SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells]]
- [[SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at the source]]
- [[SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from pitch]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — on [[Operator]], take the simplest algorithm at ratio 1:1 and sweep the modulation index, hearing harmonics appear on a sine. Then try 1:2, still harmonic, then 1:1.41. The moment it turns metallic is the lesson.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — make the same two-bar riff four times: [[Operator]] for FM, [[Wavetable]], [[Analog]] for subtractive, and [[Granulator 3]] over a bounce of your own voice. Same notes, four methods, one clip each in a Session row.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 13 — Lesson 4 Test]]

tasks.html: Signal Path, then Oscillators and Waveforms and Filters and Resonance

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Generate, remove, shape. Every subtractive synth on the market is that chain with a different panel drawn around it.
  • The amp envelope is why anything is audible at all. The filter envelope is where most of the character comes from. LFOs sit alongside and move whichever block you point them at.
  • The corollary explains half the strand: a filter can only remove harmonics the oscillator generated. Start on a sine and nothing downstream can brighten it, because there's nothing there to uncover.
  • That's why patches start from saws — the richest raw material — and it's the reason FM Synthesis had to be invented at all. Subtractive can only subtract.

blocks.label: The material

• Attack, decay and release are durations. Sustain is the only level in the whole envelope.

14.title: Course 14 — Compressor Mechanics
14.intro:
What a compressor is doing under the presets, which one to reach for, and what order the chain goes in. The smallest course in the school and one of the highest-return, because every chain in the vault already contains a compressor.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. It starts at what the device is.

What this unlocks

  • Nothing formally depends on it, which is what makes it a good course to run alongside a long theory one — two lessons, and it doesn't compete for attention.
  • — its limiter rule is Lesson 1's first fact applied to the 2-bus, and it reads better once you know a limiter is a compressor.
  • Practically: the compressor settings written into the chain notes stop being recipes to follow and start being decisions you can change.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — What a Compressor Actually Is

**Read**
- [ ] [[Compression]] → *What it is*, and the "compression is a person" mnemonic in the note
- [ ] [[Limiting]]
- [ ] [[Parallel Processing]]

**The material**
- **[[FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor|A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio acting as a ceiling.]]** Same device, extreme setting — not a different category.
- That single fact reframes the whole master-chain conversation, and it connects straight to [[MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus]] in [[Course 16 — Handoff & Release Prep]].
- **[[FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee|Knee is how abruptly the ratio engages.]] Hard knee** switches the full ratio on the instant the signal crosses threshold. **Soft knee** eases it in over a window either side, so compression begins gently *before* the threshold is properly reached.
- Soft knee for transparent levelling on vocals and the mix bus; hard knee for catching peaks, or when you want to hear the compressor working.
- **[[FX-C03 — Parallel compression|Parallel compression]]** duplicates the signal, crushes one copy and blends it *under* the untouched one. The dry path keeps its transients, so you get density and sustained detail without losing punch.
- In effect it's **upward** compression: lifting the quiet parts rather than pushing the loud ones down. Ableton's stock Compressor has a Dry/Wet knob, so it needs no return track at all.

**Concepts**
- [[FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor]]
- [[FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee]]
- [[FX-C03 — Parallel compression]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — on one drum bus, A/B hard against soft knee at the same ratio and threshold, and say which one you can hear working.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build parallel compression twice on the same source: once on a return track, once with the device's Dry/Wet. Null-test that they match, then decide which you'd actually keep in a session.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 14 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Choosing and Ordering

**Read**
- [ ] [[Multiband Compression]], then [[Saturation and Distortion]], then [[Compression Staging]] and [[Masking and Carving]]

**The material**
- **[[FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband|Multiband compresses one range; broadband compresses the whole signal.]]** That's the easy half. The reason it matters: with broadband, **one bad band drags everything down with it.**
- If a vocal's low-mids bloom on certain notes, a broadband compressor ducks the entire vocal on exactly those notes — including the top end that was fine.
- **[[FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics|Saturation adds harmonics]]**, and which harmonics is the choice you're actually making. **Even-order (2nd) sit at octaves and read as warm and full; odd-order (3rd) add edge and grit.** It also rounds transient peaks, so a saturated signal reads louder at the same meter.
- **[[FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, de-ess|Chain order: subtractive EQ → compression → de-ess → tone-shaping EQ.]]** De-essing after compression is the step most people invert.
- Clean up **first**, so the compressor isn't reacting to rumble and mic bumps it was never meant to hear. **De-ess after compression**, because pulling the body down *raises* the esses. Boosts **last**, so a presence lift doesn't get immediately squashed.
- This is the applied form of the "compress first, EQ after" rule in [[Compression]] — with the one exception that note already flags: cut non-musical content *before* the compressor.

**Concepts**
- [[FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband]]
- [[FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics]]
- [[FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, de-ess]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — name the four stages of the chain in order and say what each one is protecting the next from. Then say which harmonics you'd want on a warm bass and which on an aggressive one.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build the full vocal chain in that order on a real take. Then deliberately move the de-esser in front of the compressor, listen to the sibilance come back, and put it where it belongs.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 14 — Lesson 2 Test]]

15.title: Course 15 — Vocal Method
15.intro:
Everything that happens to a vocal before the chain goes on it — the mic, the comp, the tuning decision, the stack — plus what changes when the vocal is rapped rather than sung. Processing a vocal is a separate subject; this is how you end up with one worth processing.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. It starts at where to stand in front of the microphone.

What this unlocks

  • The 22 vocal chains in the vault. They all assume a finished take and a decided stack; this course is what produces both.
  • — comping and tuning are on the commit side of that course's boundary, so the decisions made here are the ones that go out permanently.
  • Practically: the difference between a take that gets fixed in the mix and one that didn't need fixing.

Short lessons on purpose

The lessons here are shorter than elsewhere in the school. Vocals are a subject where most of the knowledge is procedural — the value is in having the procedure stated, in order, so it can be followed the same way twice.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Before the Chain

**Read**
- [ ] [[Vocal Mic Technique]], then [[Vocal Comping and Takes]]

**The material**
- **[[VOX-C01 — Proximity effect|Proximity effect: bass response rises as a directional mic gets closer.]]** It turns distance into a tone control — move in for weight and intimacy, back off to stop a vocal getting boomy.
- That's the same fix as an EQ cut, made at the source where it costs nothing. It only applies to **directional** mics, which is why an omni is sometimes the right call for a singer who moves.
- **[[VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllable|Comp by phrase, not by syllable.]]** The criteria, in order, are **delivery, then pitch, then timing** — delivery outranks timing, because timing is fixable afterwards and delivery isn't.
- Watch the seams: cut on a breath, **keep the breaths**, and crossfade every edit. The failure mode is a Frankenstein comp that's technically perfect on every syllable and worse than the best single take.

**Concepts**
- [[VOX-C01 — Proximity effect]]
- [[VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllable]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — record the same line at 4 inches and at 12 inches, then name what changed and which EQ move it replaces.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — record four takes of one verse on the TLM 102 at a consistent 6 inches. Comp it twice, once by syllable and once by phrase, then A/B both against the best single take.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 15 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Tuning and Stacks

**Read**
- [ ] [[Vocal Tuning]], then [[Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs]]

**The material**
- **[[VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic dial|Retune speed is a stylistic dial, not a correctness setting.]]** The hard-tuned end and the transparent end are both deliberate choices. What's easy to miss: **fast retune destroys vibrato**, which matters when the vibrato is the reason the take is good.
- **[[VOX-C03 — When not to tune|Don't tune when the deviation is the expression.]]** That's a sharper rule than "when it sounds bad" — blues and soul phrasing lives between the notes, and a scoop or a note leaned into slightly flat is doing the emotional work.
- Then the rule the lesson exists for:
> **The further a part is from delivering the lyric, the more it can become texture.**
- **[[VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy|That's the treatment hierarchy]]:** lead centre, present, least processed. Doubles wide and lower. Harmonies lower still with more processing. Ad-libs widest, furthest back, heaviest effects.
- And the mechanism underneath the stack: **[[VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicken|an identical copy doesn't thicken anything]]** — it just gets louder, or comb-filters if you nudge it. Real doubles work *because* the two performances differ.

**Concepts**
- [[VOX-C03 — When not to tune]]
- [[VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic dial]]
- [[VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy]]
- [[VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicken]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take one sung phrase with vibrato in it. Retune it fast, then slow, and say what the fast setting cost. Then find one note in the take that should stay untuned and justify it.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build a lead, double, harmony and ad-lib for one hook in a single session. Set level, pan and processing for each from the hierarchy alone, *then* check it against what instinct would have done.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 15 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Rap

**Read**
- [ ] [[Rap Vocal Production]] in full

**The material**
- **[[VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first|Rap is a rhythmic performance — you're producing pocket, not pitch.]]** Everything in the lesson follows from that one line.
- **Timing edits happen at the syllable level** — deliberately the opposite of Lesson 1's rule, and not a contradiction: you comp *performance* by phrase and fix *timing* by syllable.
- **Punch-ins line by line** are the normal workflow here rather than a fallback for a bad take.
- **Doubles go on bar-ends and key phrases**, not across the whole verse. The double is an accent, not a texture.
- **A dedicated ad-lib pass** is structural, not decoration — it's what fills the space the lead leaves.
- **Compress harder and faster**, choosing presence over beauty, because the lyric has to stay parseable over a loud beat. And **keep the breaths**: in a dense verse they're the punctuation.

**Concepts**
- [[VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — say which edits happen by syllable and which by phrase, and why that isn't a contradiction with Lesson 1.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a recorded rap verse, duplicate the track twice, and nudge one copy 15 ms late and one 15 ms early. Play all three against the beat and commit to one, then say what the pocket you chose is doing.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 15 — Lesson 3 Test]]

16.title: Course 16 — Handoff & Release Prep
16.intro:
What has to be settled before a track leaves your computer: which decisions get baked in, what files go out and in what state, and what has to be cleared before anyone can hear it. Two strands, one question.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. It's the one course in the school that can be taken at any point.

What this unlocks

  • Nothing downstream depends on it, which is exactly why it can run early and in parallel with a long theory course.
  • — comping and tuning both sit on the commit side of Lesson 1's boundary, so this course decides how permanent they are.
  • Practically: it's the difference between handing a mixing engineer a session they can work with and one they have to undo first.

The one mistake that can't be taken back

Every other gap in the school is a knowledge gap you can close at leisure. These nine concepts govern what leaves your computer, and several of them can't be reversed after the fact — a limiter printed onto the 2-bus, or an uncleared sample on a released track.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — The Commit Boundary

**Read**
- [ ] [[Mix Handoff]] → *The commit boundary*, *Multitracks vs stems*

**The material**
- The governing rule: **[[MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open|commit what defines what a part *is*; leave open everything about how parts *relate*.]]**
- **Commit:** character distortion, synthesis, creative effects, sample choice, tuning, timing edits. **Leave open:** track-to-track balance, corrective EQ, bus compression, reverb amounts, the 2-bus.
- The pair that gets reversed most often is **track-by-track EQ and compression** — those belong on the *leave open* side. They're relational, which makes them the engineer's decision rather than yours.
- The test for anything ambiguous: **if removing it would change what the part is, commit it. If removing it would only change how loud or bright it sits against its neighbours, leave it.**
- Then the file question. **[[MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems|Multitracks are every individual track]]** and they're what a mixing engineer wants. **Stems are grouped submixes**, for remixers and live playback. The words get used interchangeably and they aren't.

**Concepts**
- [[MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems]]
- [[MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — for ten elements in a current session, call each one commit or leave-open and say why. Include at least one you're unsure about, and apply the removal test to it.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — open your most recent session and freeze-and-flatten every element you called *commit*. Leave the open ones alone. Note how much faster the session loads afterwards.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 16 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Delivery

**Read**
- [ ] [[Mix Handoff]] → *Delivery spec*, *Session organization*, *What to send alongside*, *Using a reference track properly*, *Mastering prep*

**The material**
- The limiter rule first, because it's the expensive one. **[[MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus|Nothing on the 2-bus.]]** Peaks at **−6 to −3 dBFS**, reached with a gain move rather than a processor. A limiter that pulled 8 dB off the peaks is 8 dB the engineer never gets to see.
- **[[MIX-C04 — Delivery spec|The spec]]:** native sample rate, 24-bit, WAV, no dither, consolidated from a common start, every track named for what it is. Format and headroom are the easy part; knowing *why* each line is what it is, is the lesson.
- **[[MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalization|LUFS is integrated loudness over time]]**, and streaming platforms normalize to roughly **−14**. Mastering louder than that just gets turned down again — you lose dynamics and gain nothing.
- **[[MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference|Level-match your reference track.]]** Anything louder sounds better, so an unmatched reference only tells you that it's louder. Use it for specific questions — low end, vocal position, brightness — not as a target to clone wholesale.
- **[[MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer needs|What the mastering engineer needs]]** is the mix at that headroom, with the reference and a short note saying what you're after. What they can't do is put back dynamics you already printed away.

**Concepts**
- [[MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus]]
- [[MIX-C04 — Delivery spec]]
- [[MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalization]]
- [[MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference]]
- [[MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer needs]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — run the checklist at the bottom of [[Mix Handoff]] against your most recent bounce and note every line that fails. Then say what −14 LUFS means for how loud you master.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — bounce one finished song to the full delivery spec: consolidated from bar 1, named, at the session sample rate, plus the reference track and a one-paragraph note. Put it in a folder you could send today without touching it again.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 16 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Clearance

**Read**
- [ ] [[Sample Clearance]] — all of it; it's short

**The material**
- **[[SMP-C01 — The two rights|Two rights, not one.]]** The **master** is the recording; the **composition** is the song. Sampling uses both, and both have to be cleared separately, often by different owners.
- **Interpolation — replaying the part yourself — uses only the composition.** That's why it's the standard move on a recognizable hook: it halves the number of people who have to say yes.
- **[[SMP-C02 — Clear before release|Clear before release, never after.]]** Afterwards you're negotiating with no leverage, against someone who now knows the song is working.
- The consequences are concrete: takedown, frozen royalties, or a majority publishing share handed over. The musical difference between sampling and interpolation is obvious; the clearance difference is the one that costs money.

**Concepts**
- [[SMP-C01 — The two rights]]
- [[SMP-C02 — Clear before release]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — for one sample-based idea, name which of the two rights it uses and who would have to clear each. Then say what interpolating it instead would change.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — write that idea's clearance line into the session notes: source, which of the five routes in [[Sample Clearance]] applies, and the one action that would make it releasable. Then play it with the sample muted and decide whether the track survives.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 16 — Lesson 3 Test]]

19.title: Course 19 — Hanon I
19.intro:
The first ten exercises of Hanon's The Virtuoso Pianist — Part I's preparatory work on agility, finger independence and evenness, one exercise per lesson, hands an octave apart in C.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Hanon starts from zero, and Part I is where it starts.
  • A piano or keyboard, The Virtuoso Pianist - Hanon.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the exercise.

What this unlocks

  • — the next block of exercises, which assumes these are in the hand.
  • Independence between the 3rd, 4th and 5th fingers — the weak set, and the reason Part I spends ten exercises there before it does anything else.
  • Enough evenness at ♩=108 that the wider stretches in exercises 11–20 have something to stand on.

sections.name: How to run it
sections.raw:
These are Hanon's own instructions, printed in the book, and they are the method rather than preamble. They apply to every lesson below, so each lesson states only what is particular to its exercise.

- **The metronome mark is a range, not a target.** Start at the low number, get it clean and even, then move up. Arriving at the top number with an uneven hand is not a pass.
- ***"Lift the fingers high and with precision, playing each note very distinctly."***
- **Both hands carry the same difficulty throughout** — the figure the left hand plays ascending is copied by the same fingers of the right descending. That refusal to let the weak hand off is the whole design of the book.
- **Hanon is cumulative.** *"As soon as Ex. 1 is mastered"* means move on, not stop playing it. Finished exercises stay in the warm-up.
- Page numbers below are the PDF's own count, 1–116, matching the `pages` parameter — not the printed book-page numbers visible in the scan.

sections.name: Course final
sections.raw:
A **performance check**, not a test page. There are no `type: school-test` pages in this course and nothing here enters the spaced-repetition drip — finger facility is a motor skill, and the drip is for facts.

The check is a rep: play exercises 1 through 10 back to back, in order, at the tempo each one is marked for, fingers high and precise, both hands equal. Pass is your own honest read of whether it was clean and even. Nothing in the system can hear the piano, so nothing here pretends to grade it.
