20.title: Course 20 — Hanon II
20.intro:
The second half of Hanon's Part I — exercises 11 to 20, extending the finger-independence work into trill preparation and wider stretches, and closing the preparatory set.

What it assumes

  • — Hanon is cumulative and these exercises assume the ones before them are still in the warm-up.
  • A piano or keyboard, The Virtuoso Pianist - Hanon.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the exercise.

What this unlocks

  • — the next block of exercises, which assumes these are in the hand.
  • The trill preparation and the 1–5 stretch that Part II's transcendent series assumes from its first bar.
  • The whole of Part I in the hand, which is the normal daily warm-up set and the honest scope for keyboard facility aimed at voicing chords and playing parts in.

These are Hanon's own instructions, printed in the book, and they are the method rather than preamble. They apply to every lesson below, so each lesson states only what is particular to its exercise.

- **The metronome mark is a range, not a target.** Start at the low number, get it clean and even, then move up. Arriving at the top number with an uneven hand is not a pass.
- ***"Lift the fingers high and with precision, playing each note very distinctly."***

- **Hanon is cumulative.** *"As soon as Ex. 1 is mastered"* means move on, not stop playing it. Finished exercises stay in the warm-up.

sections.name: Course final
sections.raw:
A **performance check**, not a test page. There are no `type: school-test` pages in this course and nothing here enters the spaced-repetition drip — finger facility is a motor skill, and the drip is for facts.

The check is a rep: play exercises 11 through 20 back to back, in order, at the tempo each one is marked for, fingers high and precise, both hands equal. Pass is your own honest read of whether it was clean and even. Nothing in the system can hear the piano, so nothing here pretends to grade it.

21.title: Course 21 — Hanon III
21.intro:
The opening of Hanon's Part II, the transcendent series — exercises 21 to 31, where both hands trade the same figure across the bar and the writing leaves the single-page format.

What it assumes

  • — Hanon is cumulative and these exercises assume the ones before them are still in the warm-up.
  • A piano or keyboard, The Virtuoso Pianist - Hanon.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the exercise.

What this unlocks

  • — the next block of exercises, which assumes these are in the hand.
  • Both hands equally fluent on the same figure — the mirroring is what the transcendent series is for, and it is the last thing before the book stops being about fingers alone.
  • The evenness the thumb-under work in exercises 32–38 needs before scales are worth attempting.

22.title: Course 22 — Hanon IV
22.intro:
The rest of Hanon's Part II — turning the thumb under, then the scales, chromatic scales and arpeggios in every key. From exercise 32 on, every exercise prints its own metronome mark.

What it assumes

  • — Hanon is cumulative and these exercises assume the ones before them are still in the warm-up.
  • A piano or keyboard, The Virtuoso Pianist - Hanon.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the exercise.

What this unlocks

  • — the next block of exercises, which assumes these are in the hand.
  • Scales, chromatic scales and arpeggios in every key, under the hand rather than on paper.
  • The thumb-under motion, which is the single mechanic every scale and arpeggio in the book rests on.

sections.name: How to run it
sections.raw:
These are Hanon's own instructions, printed in the book, and they are the method rather than preamble. They apply to every lesson below, so each lesson states only what is particular to its exercise.

- **The metronome mark is a range, not a target.** Start at the low number, get it clean and even, then move up. Arriving at the top number with an uneven hand is not a pass.
- ***"Lift the fingers high and with precision, playing each note very distinctly."***
- **Both hands carry the same difficulty throughout** — the figure the left hand plays ascending is copied by the same fingers of the right descending. That refusal to let the weak hand off is the whole design of the book.
- **Hanon is cumulative.** *"As soon as Ex. 1 is mastered"* means move on, not stop playing it. Finished exercises stay in the warm-up.
- Page numbers below are the PDF's own count, 1–116, matching the `pages` parameter — not the printed book-page numbers visible in the scan.

23.title: Course 23 — Hanon V
23.intro:
The opening of Hanon's Part III, the virtuoso section — repeated notes, the trill for every finger, wrist work in detached thirds and sixths, and legato thirds.

24.title: Course 24 — Hanon VI
24.intro:
The last eight exercises of The Virtuoso Pianist — octaves and broken octaves in all 24 keys, the fourfold and threefold trills, and the tremolo that closes the book.

What it assumes

  • — Hanon is cumulative and these exercises assume the ones before them are still in the warm-up.
  • A piano or keyboard, The Virtuoso Pianist - Hanon.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the exercise.

What this unlocks

  • The end of the book. Exercises 1–60 in the hand, which is the whole of The Virtuoso Pianist.
  • Octave technique in all 24 keys, the fourfold and threefold trills, and the tremolo.
  • Nothing in the school assumes this course. Part III is available rather than expected — the writing-and-producing lane is served by Part I.

25.stem: Course 25 — Reading I — First Position, Part One
25.title: Course 25 — Reading I — First Position, Part One
25.short: Reading I — First Position, Part One
25.intro:
The first half of Section One of Leavitt's A Modern Method for Guitar, Volume 1 — pages 3 to 29, where the notation arrives and gets read in the open first position: the staff, the note values, the key of C in both registers, accidentals, eighth notes, rests, ties and dots, and the first two pieces the book calls solos.

What it assumes

  • Nothing. Leavitt starts from zero, and page 3 is where it starts.
  • A guitar, A Modern Method for Guitar - Volume 1.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the page.

What this unlocks

  • — pages 30 to 59, the rest of Section One: six more major keys, the relative minor, sixteenths and triplets, and the eleven movable chord forms the section ends on.
  • The complete first position in the key of C, upper register and lower, ledger lines included.
  • Accidentals and their scope, eighth notes, rests, ties and dotted notes — read at tempo rather than defined.
  • The rhythm-accompaniment track from its first chord symbols (p. 11) through bass notes and chords (p. 17) to its first chord diagrams (p. 24).

sections.name: How this course is different, on purpose
sections.raw:
Every other course in the school teaches *ideas* and tests them in words. This one teaches nothing new — it is the place you **play the page**.

| | [[Course 04 — Reading & Position Play]] (Class 2) | This course (Class 8) |
|---|---|---|
| Teaches | Notation *as concepts* — dots, `D.S. al Coda`, clefs, why guitar reading is hard | Nothing new; it is reps |
| You do | Read a note, answer a question | Open the book and *play the page* |
| Uses the book as | One cited source among several | The spine — worked through in order |

Same pages can appear in both. Course 04's ledger-lines lesson may *teach from* p. 12; this course has you *reading* p. 12 at tempo. Leave both.

sections.name: How to run it
sections.raw:
- **The book is four courses, two lessons each, one lesson a week.** Section One is this course and [[Course 26 — Reading I — First Position, Part Two]]; Section Two is [[Course 27 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part One]] and [[Course 28 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part Two]]. A lesson is twelve to twenty book pages and up to twenty pieces, which is a week of reading rather than an evening's.
- **It teaches reading through repertoire, not drills.** Concept pages are sparse — across pages 3 to 29 it is pp. 3, 4, 12, 15, 18 and 21, and that is the whole of it. The rest is melodies, duets and etudes you sight-read, and progress comes from playing them.
- **The duets need a second part.** Leavitt is explicit that there is no student/teacher division — both guitar parts are written to be studied, and almost all of them stand alone musically. A recording, a teacher, or DAW playback of the other line all work.
- **Review is not optional.** *"Regular review of all material is a must!"* is printed at p. 9, and again at the foot of p. 18 shortened to *"Review of all material is a must"*; the notices get more insistent later in the book — *"REVIEW ALL MATERIAL"* at pp. 37 and 52. Finished pages stay in rotation.
- **From the preface:** *"Do not skip or 'slight' anything, and also do not attempt to 'completely perfect' any one lesson before going on. Playing technique is an accumulative process."*
- **Page numbers below are the book's own printed numbers.** One of them is absent from the vault's scan — p. 15 (Sharps and Flats). It is named in the homework anyway, because it is part of the lesson; source it elsewhere or skip it knowingly.
- **Where the reading lane had reached, as of 2026-08-20: page 24** — mid-Lesson 2. Everything past it sits ahead of that on purpose; that is the point of having the whole book.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — First Position in the Key of C

**The material**

- **Pages 3–14.** The whole of the first position in C, upper register then lower, closing on a full review.
- **Concept pages** — p. 3 tuning, the staff, the clef sign and the common note values; p. 4 time signatures; p. 12 ledger lines. Chord symbols and the rhythm-accompaniment track open on p. 11.
- **The instruction that governs the fingering numbers**, printed on p. 5: *"'READ' the notes, NOT the fingering, as these numbers will eventually be omitted."*

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — Exercises 1–4, pp. 4–5. The first-position notes as the book introduces them, one string group at a time.
- [ ] **Play** — *Sea To Sea* (duet), pp. 6–7. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — Exercises 5–6, p. 8. The upper register, starting on C an octave above the 5th-string C.
- [ ] **Play** — Exercises 7–8, p. 9, the *Note And Chord Review*.
- [ ] **Play** — *One, Two, Three, Four* (duet), pp. 10–11. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Rhythm Accompaniment* introduction, p. 11. The first chord symbols, strummed in time.
- [ ] **Play** — Exercise 9, p. 12. The lower register, which is where the ledger lines arrive.
- [ ] **Play** — Exercise 10, p. 13. The review that closes the complete first position in the key of C.
- [ ] **Play** — *Imitation Duet*, p. 14. Both parts.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 14, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

### Lesson 2 — Accidentals, Eighths and the First Solos

**The material**

- **Pages 15–29.** Accidentals and their scope, dynamics, eighth notes, rests, ties and dots — and the first two pieces the book calls solos, where melody and accompaniment land in the same part.
- **Concept pages** — p. 15 sharps, flats and naturals; p. 18 eighth notes, counted and picked; p. 21 rests, tied notes and dotted notes. Rhythm accompaniment gains bass notes and chords on p. 17 and its first chord diagrams on p. 24.
- **What a solo means here**, from the heading on p. 23: a *"solo arrangement… with melody AND accompaniment"*, with the standing instruction to hold every note for its full time value.
- **Page 15 is missing from the vault's scan.** Sharps, flats and naturals are covered from another source or read in a physical copy — the pieces from p. 16 on assume them.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — *Here We Go Again* (duet), pp. 16–17. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Rhythm Accompaniment: Bass Notes and Chords*, p. 17.
- [ ] **Play** — the eighth-note exercises 1–3, pp. 18–19, counted aloud and picked as marked.
- [ ] **Play** — *Etude No. 1* (duet), p. 20. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the rests, ties and dotted notes exercises, p. 21.
- [ ] **Play** — *Etude No. 2* (duet), p. 22. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *First Solo*, p. 23. Melody and accompaniment together, every note held its full value.
- [ ] **Play** — *Rhythm Accompaniment: Chord Diagrams*, p. 24, and the exercises under it.
- [ ] **Play** — *Second Solo*, p. 25.
- [ ] **Play** — *Etude No. 3* (duet), p. 26. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Picking Etude No. 1*, p. 27, and the *Etude* below it on the same page.
- [ ] **Play** — *Two, Two* (duet), pp. 28–29. Both parts, and mind the `D.S. al Coda`.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 29, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

sections.name: Course final
sections.raw:
A **performance check**, not a test page. There are no `type: school-test` pages in this course and nothing here enters the spaced-repetition drip — sight reading is a motor skill, and the drip is for facts.

The check is a rep. Open the book at an unseen page at or below p. 29, play it **once, at tempo, with no practice run**, and keep an even tempo through the wrong notes rather than stopping to fix them. Pass is your own honest read of whether it held together. Nothing in the system can hear the guitar, so nothing here pretends to grade it.

Reading decays the way ear training does. The course closing is not a reason to stop reading — it is the point at which [[Course 26 — Reading I — First Position, Part Two]] takes over and these pages become review material.

26.stem: Course 26 — Reading I — First Position, Part Two
26.title: Course 26 — Reading I — First Position, Part Two
26.short: Reading I — First Position, Part Two
26.intro:
The second half of Section One of Leavitt's A Modern Method for Guitar, Volume 1 — pages 30 to 59, which finishes everything the book does without leaving the open first position: six more major keys, three minors in all three of their forms, sixteenths and triplets and dotted figures, three right-hand techniques, and the eleven movable chord forms the section ends on.

What it assumes

  • — pages 3 to 29 read at tempo: the first position in C, accidentals, eighth notes, rests, ties and dots. None of it is re-taught here.
  • A guitar, A Modern Method for Guitar - Volume 1.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the page.

What this unlocks

  • — Section Two, which drops open strings entirely and moves the hand up the neck. It assumes the first position is fluent, because everything after page 60 is the same reading skill relocated.
  • First-position reading in C, G, F, B♭, D, A and E♭, plus A minor, E minor and D minor in all three minor forms.
  • The eleven movable chord forms and the Chord Simplification and Substitution Chart (p. 58) — enough comping vocabulary to play the accompaniment to a song in any key.
  • Alternate picking, reverse alternate picking and the older down-stroke-per-string technique, each taught as its own etude rather than as a note in the margin.

- **The duets need a second part.** Leavitt is explicit that there is no student/teacher division — both guitar parts are written to be studied, and almost all of them stand alone musically. A recording, a teacher, or DAW playback of the other line all work.
- **Review is not optional.** *"REVIEW ALL MATERIAL"* is printed at pp. 37 and 52, after the milder *"Regular review of all material is a must!"* at p. 9 and *"Review of all material is a must"* at p. 18. Finished pages stay in rotation, and that includes everything from Part One.
- **From the preface:** *"Do not skip or 'slight' anything, and also do not attempt to 'completely perfect' any one lesson before going on. Playing technique is an accumulative process."*
- **Page numbers below are the book's own printed numbers.** One of them is absent from the vault's scan — p. 34 (Another Duet in G). It is named in the homework anyway, because it is part of the lesson; source it elsewhere or skip it knowingly.
- **The keys arrive one page at a time.** Each new key opens with its scale in the first position and its rhythm-accompaniment chord diagrams on the same page, then the duet or solo that reads it. Play the scale before the piece, every time.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Sixteenths, Triplets and the Relative Minor

**The material**

- **Pages 30–44.** Two new major keys, three new rhythmic figures, the relative minor in two keys, and four duets to read them in.
- **Concept pages** — p. 31 sixteenth notes; p. 37 the triplet, with both picking types to be practised separately; p. 42 the dotted eighth and sixteenth. The grand barre arrives with the key of F on p. 35.
- **The relative-minor rule**, stated in one paragraph on p. 39: *"The sixth degree of any major scale is the tonic of its relative minor key. The major and relative minor key signatures are the same. There are 3 different scales in each minor key."*
- **Page 34 is missing from the vault's scan.** *Another Duet in G* is listed in the book's own contents and named below; source it elsewhere or skip it knowingly.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of G Major* scale, 1st position, p. 30, and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* chord diagrams below it.
- [ ] **Play** — the sixteenth-note exercises, p. 31, counted carefully.
- [ ] **Play** — *Duet in G*, p. 32. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Picking Etude No. 2*, p. 33.
- [ ] **Play** — *Another Duet in G*, p. 34. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of F* scale, 1st position, p. 35, and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* chord diagrams and grand barre on the same page.
- [ ] **Play** — *Duet in F*, p. 36. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the triplet exercise, p. 37, twice through: once with picking Type 1, once with Type 2.
- [ ] **Play** — *Waltz in F* (solo), p. 38.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of A Minor* scales, 1st position, p. 39 — natural, harmonic and melodic — and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* chord diagrams below them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Pretty Pickin'* (duet), pp. 40–41. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the dotted eighth and sixteenth exercises 1–3, p. 42.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of E Minor* scales, 1st position, p. 43, and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* chord diagrams below them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Take Your Pick* (duet), pp. 44–45. Both parts.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 44, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

### Lesson 2 — Movable Forms and the Remaining Open Keys

**The material**

- **Pages 45–59.** The remaining open-position keys, the chromatic scale, three right-hand techniques taught as etudes, and the chord chapter the whole rhythm track has been building toward.
- **The principle of movable chord forms, p. 45** — a form with no open strings can be slid up the neck, which is what makes eleven shapes enough for any key. It is also the idea Section Two applies to scales from p. 60 on.
- **Page 58 collects all eleven movable forms** and adds the Chord Simplification and Substitution Chart. Leavitt's own caveat: *"having only eleven chord forms at your command will cause you to move up and down the fingerboard much more than is desirable… The more forms you know, the less distance you have to travel."*
- **Page 59 teaches a second picking technique** — attack each new string with a down stroke — and is explicit that it is an addition to alternate picking, not a replacement: *"THE MOST CONCENTRATED EFFORT MUST STILL BE PLACED ON ALTERNATE PICKING."*

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — *Rhythm Accompaniment: The Principle of Movable Chord Forms*, p. 45, and the exercises under it.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chromatic Scale*, 1st position, p. 46, and *Speed Studies* patterns 1–3 on the same page, in both octaves.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of D Minor* scales, 1st position, p. 47 — all three forms — and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* exercises below them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Endurance Etude* (*Picking Etude No. 3*), pp. 48–49. Observe the tempo changes and vary the dynamics.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of B♭* scales, 1st position, p. 50, and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* exercises below them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Duet in B♭*, p. 51. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Reverse Alternate Picking Study*, p. 52. Strict attention to the picking as marked.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of D Major* scale, 1st position, p. 53, and *Duet in D* below it. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Dynamic Etude* (*Etude No. 4*, duet), pp. 54–55. Both parts, and play the dynamics rather than reading past them.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of A* scale, 1st position, p. 56, *Duet in A* below it, and the *Rhythm Accompaniment* exercises on the same page.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Key of E♭* scale, 1st position, p. 57, and *Duet in E♭* below it. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Movable Chord Forms* compilation, p. 58 — all eleven, chromatically up and down the neck — and read the Chord Simplification and Substitution Chart under it.
- [ ] **Play** — *Picking – A Different Technique*, p. 59, then apply it at measure 20 of the *Endurance Etude*, p. 48, which is the example the book points to.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 59, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

lessons.title: Movable Forms and the Remaining Open Keys

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Pages 45–59. The remaining open-position keys, the chromatic scale, three right-hand techniques taught as etudes, and the chord chapter the whole rhythm track has been building toward.

27.stem: Course 27 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part One
27.title: Course 27 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part One
27.short: Reading II — Position Playing, Part One
27.intro:
The first half of Section Two of Leavitt's A Modern Method for Guitar, Volume 1 — pages 60 to 99, where the open strings drop out and the hand moves up the neck: the position system itself, four of the five movable major-scale fingerings, four of the five Reading Studies, and the derivative chord sequence of Rhythm Accompaniment Part Two.

What it assumes

  • — Section One finished, the first position fluent in seven major keys and three minors. Section Two is the same reading skill relocated, and it does not re-teach the notation.
  • A guitar, A Modern Method for Guitar - Volume 1.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the page.

What this unlocks

  • — fingering type 4, the review that plays all five types back to back, and the same shapes moved to positions III, I and IV.
  • Guitar Positions stops being inferred and starts being sourced. The position system it is built on is defined on p. 60.
  • Reading in C, F, G and D in the second position with no open strings — fingering types 1, 1A, 2 and 3, four of the five the volume teaches.
  • The first half of the derivative-fingering chord sequence of Rhythm Accompaniment Part Two, plus natural harmonics, the muffled effect and the Latin beat.

sections.name: The one rule that matters most
sections.raw:
Leavitt's own instruction for the **Reading Studies**, printed at the top of p. 64. It is a method rather than a suggestion, and it governs pp. 64–65, 74–75, 84–85 and 94–95 here — and pp. 102–103 in [[Course 28 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part Two]], which is the fifth and last of them.

> **DO NOT PRACTICE these two pages** — just READ them, but not more than twice through in any single practice session. Do not play them on two consecutive days. Do not go back over any particular section because of a wrong note. **DO KEEP AN EVEN TEMPO** and play the proper time values.

A Reading Study you have memorised is no longer a reading study. This is the one thing in the book destroyed by ordinary practice, and it is exactly the material this course exists to serve. Page 95 extends it: play the tonic chord first to set your ear, then try to *sing* the music to yourself as you play it.

Everything else in the course is practice material and should be practised. The Reading Studies are not.

sections.name: How to run it
sections.raw:
- **Position is defined on p. 60**, and it is the most load-bearing page in the book. Position is the fret the **first finger** plays, written as a Roman numeral, and a position occupies four adjacent frets. Notes outside that span are reached by **finger stretch (F.S.)** — stretching the 1st or 4th finger *without shifting the hand*.
- **F.S. has a rule, not a preference.** For a scale tone the stretch follows the fingering type — type I stretches the 1st finger, type IV the 4th. For a non-scale tone, moving upward use F.S. 1 and moving downward F.S. 4, regardless of type. Page 61 adds the exception: always move *back into* a position from a stretch, never away from it.
- **No open strings from here on**, which is what makes every scale fingering movable — the same principle p. 45 applied to chords.
- **The chord track is half the book.** Rhythm Accompaniment Part Two starts on p. 67 and its forms are deliberately ordered so each new shape is a preparation for the next: *"Memorize the fingering for all chord structures in the order of their appearance… Do not skip around."*
- **The duets need a second part** — a recording, a teacher, or DAW playback of the other line. Both guitar parts are written to be studied.
- **Section One stays in rotation.** The first position does not maintain itself while the hand is at the second, and the triplet picking types from p. 37 are used again on p. 77.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Fingering Types 1 and 1A in Second Position

**The material**

- **Pages 60–79.** Section Two opens. C major as fingering type 1 and F major as type 1A, both in the second position, each followed by its own eighth-note study, arpeggio study, chord etude and speed study.
- **The first two Reading Studies** arrive on pp. 64–65 and 74–75, under the rule above. The book's own safety net, p. 65: *"If unusual difficulty is encountered reading these pages, go back to page 60 and start again."*
- **Rhythm Accompaniment Part Two** begins on p. 67 with three basic forms, then runs derivatives off each of them across pp. 68, 71 and 77.
- **Right-hand technique for rhythm playing, p. 69** — a combined rotary forearm and loose wrist motion producing an *"explosive"* attack, with pressure release points and accents determining the beat.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — the *C Major* scale, fingering type 1, 2nd position, pp. 60–61. Watch the F.S. marks; they are the point of the page.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Eighth Note Study* in C, p. 61.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Arpeggio Study (Broken Chords)* in C, p. 61, as picked and again with strict alternate picking.
- [ ] **Play** — *Chord Etude No. 1*, p. 62. Slowly and evenly, connecting the chords so they flow with no silence between them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Etude No. 5* (duet), p. 63. Both parts.
- [ ] **Read** — the *Reading Studies* in C major, fingering type 1, pp. 64–65. Twice through at most, never two days running, no going back for wrong notes.
- [ ] **Play** — *Ballad* (duet), pp. 66–67. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — *Movable Chord Forms (Rhythm Accompaniment, Part Two)*, p. 67 — basic forms #1, #2 and #3, chromatically up and down the neck, naming the roots.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 68, basic form #1 plus its seven derivatives, and the exercise under them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Rhythm Accompaniment: Right Hand Technique*, p. 69.
- [ ] **Play** — *Picking Etude No. 4*, p. 69. Third finger held down throughout.
- [ ] **Play** — the *F Major* scale, fingering type 1A, 2nd position, p. 70.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Eighth Note Study* and *Arpeggio Study* in F, p. 71, and the *Chord Forms* under them.
- [ ] **Play** — *Chord Etude No. 2*, p. 72. Rubato, as freely as you like.
- [ ] **Play** — *Another Duet in F*, p. 73. Both parts.
- [ ] **Read** — the *Reading Studies* in F major, fingering type 1A, pp. 74–75. Same rule.
- [ ] **Play** — *Play It Pretty* (duet), p. 76. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 77 and the *Triplet Study* below them, using both picking types from p. 37.
- [ ] **Play** — *Speed Study – fingering type 1*, p. 78, as written and with a dotted-eighth feel, with and without repeats.
- [ ] **Play** — *Speed Study – fingering type 1A*, p. 79, the same way.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 79, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

### Lesson 2 — Types 2 and 3, Harmonics and the Latin Beat

**The material**

- **Pages 80–99.** G major as fingering type 2 and D major as type 3, both in the second position, plus the two guitar effects the volume teaches and its syncopation study.
- **Natural harmonics, pp. 82–83** — third finger laid lightly over the 12th fret, strings struck sharply, finger removed almost at the same instant. The 7th and 5th frets are the next most practical.
- **The muffled effect, p. 86** — right hand laid lightly along the top of the bridge, all sounding strings covered. It inhibits picking, so the part gets practised open first.
- **Syncopation, p. 92** — pick down on the beat and up on the "and" while it is still being counted; vary the picking for phrasing only once the off-beats are no longer a problem.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — the *G Major* scale, fingering type 2, 2nd position, p. 80, and the *Eighth Note Study* under it.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Arpeggio Study* in G, p. 81, and the *Dotted 8th and 16th Study* below it, both as written and as a triplet figure.
- [ ] **Play** — *Waltz for Two* (duet), pp. 82–83. Both parts, ending on the harmonic.
- [ ] **Play** — *Presenting Natural Harmonics*, pp. 82–83, and find the same harmonics at the 7th and 5th frets.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 83 — diminished 7th, major 7th, 6th, 13th, 9th — and both exercises under them.
- [ ] **Read** — the *Reading Studies* in G major, fingering type 2, pp. 84–85. Twice through at most, never two days running. The second study continues without stopping in waltz time.
- [ ] **Play** — *Blues in G* (duet), p. 86. Practise the 1st guitar part open first, then with the muffled effect.
- [ ] **Play** — *Chord Etude No. 3*, p. 87, observing the position marks, which are what make it playable.
- [ ] **Play** — *Rhythm Accompaniment: Right Hand Technique*, p. 88, and its basic Latin beat, both written versions.
- [ ] **Play** — *Picking Etude No. 5*, p. 88. Fourth finger held down throughout.
- [ ] **Play** — *Short and Sweet* (duet), p. 89. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *D Major* scale, fingering type 3, 2nd position, p. 90, and the *Eighth Note Study* under it.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Arpeggio Study* in D, p. 91, and the *Chord Forms* below it — sus 4, minor 7th, minor 7th♭5 — with the exercise.
- [ ] **Play** — *Melodic Rhythm Study No. 1* (syncopation), pp. 92–93, as the optional duet with rhythm guitar on a Latin beat. Count it until you can feel it.
- [ ] **Play** — *Chord Etude No. 4*, p. 93, holding every note its full value.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Staccato – Legato* exercise, p. 93.
- [ ] **Read** — the *Reading Studies* in D major, fingering type 3, pp. 94–95. Same rule, plus p. 95's addition: play the tonic chord first, then sing the line to yourself as you play it.
- [ ] **Play** — *Dee - Oo - Ett* (duet), pp. 96–97. Both parts, and play the dynamics.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 97 — 9th, diminished 7th, major 6th, minor 6th — and both exercises.
- [ ] **Play** — *Speed Study – fingering type 2*, p. 98, and *Speed Study – fingering type 3*, p. 99, with and without repeats.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 99, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

28.stem: Course 28 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part Two
28.title: Course 28 — Reading II — Position Playing, Part Two
28.short: Reading II — Position Playing, Part Two
28.intro:
The second half of Section Two of Leavitt's A Modern Method for Guitar, Volume 1 — pages 100 to 123, which closes the volume: the last of the five second-position fingerings, the last Reading Study, the review that plays all five fingerings back to back, and the same shapes moved to positions III, I and IV.

What it assumes

  • — pages 60 to 99: the position system, finger stretch, and fingering types 1, 1A, 2 and 3 read in the second position with no open strings.
  • A guitar, A Modern Method for Guitar - Volume 1.pdf open on a stand, and a metronome.
  • No theory. This course teaches no ideas and tests none — it is the place you play the page.

What this unlocks

  • The complete set of major-scale fingering types — 1, 1A, 2, 3, 4 — which are the foundation for every other kind of scale, and the direct on-ramp to A Modern Method for Guitar, Part II.
  • Reading the most-used keys in positions I, III and IV, with no new shapes to learn — only new notes to read.
  • The rest of the derivative-fingering chord sequence of Rhythm Accompaniment Part Two: roughly sixty forms across the two Reading II courses, each derived from the one before it by moving or removing a finger.
  • The end of Volume 1, and the outside-reading habit p. 123 prescribes — which outlives the book, the course and the class.

A Reading Study you have memorised is no longer a reading study. Everything else in this course is practice material and should be practised. That one page pair is not — and the way it is read is the way p. 123 asks you to read everything after the book runs out.

### Lesson 1 — Fingering Type 4 and the Second Position Review

**The material**

- **Pages 100–111.** The last of the five second-position keys, the last Reading Study of the volume, and the review that plays all five fingering types back to back.
- **The 2nd Position Review, pp. 108–109**, runs types 1, 1A, 2, 3 and 4 in sequence over chord symbols, and can be taken as a duet — melody as written against a Latin beat, or melody in a dotted-eighth feel against straight four.
- **Quarter-note triplets, p. 111**, taught as a physical trick rather than a count: play two sets of eighth-note triplets with alternate picking, then two more sets missing the string on the up strokes.
- **The box at the foot of p. 111** is the hinge into Lesson 2: the same five fingerings transpose to any position, so position III gives C♯/D♭, F♯/G♭, A♭, E♭ and B♭ with no new shapes to learn — only new notes to read.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — the *A Major* scale, fingering type 4, 2nd position, p. 100, and the *Eighth Note Study* under it.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Arpeggio Study* in A, p. 101.
- [ ] **Play** — *Chord Etude No. 5*, p. 101. Rubato.
- [ ] **Read** — the *Reading Studies* in A major, fingering type 4, pp. 102–103. Twice through at most, never two days running, even tempo through the wrong notes.
- [ ] **Play** — *Tres Sharp* (duet), pp. 104–105. Both parts.
- [ ] **Play** — the *16th Note Study*, p. 105, counted carefully against p. 31.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 105 and their exercise.
- [ ] **Play** — *Speed Study – fingering type 4*, p. 106, as written and with a dotted-eighth feel, with and without repeats.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 107 and all three exercises, then transpose and write out each one a key or more higher, as the page asks.
- [ ] **Play** — the *2nd Position Review*, pp. 108–109. All five fingering types in sequence, then again as a duet with a Latin-beat rhythm part.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 110 and both exercises. The third major 6th form is the one worth keeping — no first string, better rhythm sound.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Quarter Note Triplets* exercise, p. 111, foot tapping in four, until the figure is felt rather than counted.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 111, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

### Lesson 2 — Positions III, I and IV

**The material**

- **Pages 112–123.** The same five fingering types moved to three new positions, each block closed by its own review. Nothing new is taught here — it is reading the fingerboard with patterns the hand already knows.
- **Position III, pp. 112–113** — B♭ as type 4, E♭ as type 3, A♭ as type 2, D♭ as type 1. **Position I, p. 117** — A♭ as type 4, D♭ as type 3, with no open strings. **Position IV, pp. 119–120** — G as type 1A, D as type 1, A as type 2, E as type 3.
- **The three position reviews** (pp. 114–115, 118, 122–123) are all optional duets with rhythm guitar, and 118 and 122 are in waltz time.
- **Leavitt's closing note, p. 125:** *"I cannot over-emphasize the importance of learning the four major scale fingering types well as they are the foundation for other kinds of scales."* Volume 2 learns the whole fingerboard by running every type **in the same key**.

**Homework**

- [ ] **Play** — *Major Scales in 3rd Position*, p. 112 — B♭ major as fingering type 4, E♭ major as type 3.
- [ ] **Play** — *Major Scales in 3rd Position*, p. 113 — A♭ major as type 2, D♭ major as type 1.
- [ ] **Play** — the *3rd Position Review*, pp. 114–115. Types 4, 3, 2 and 1 in sequence, then again as a duet with a Latin-beat rhythm part.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 116 and both exercises.
- [ ] **Play** — *Major Scales in 1st Position*, p. 117 — A♭ major as type 4, D♭ major as type 3, both closed fingerings with no open strings.
- [ ] **Play** — the *1st Position Review*, p. 118. Types 3 and 4, as a waltz-time duet with rhythm guitar.
- [ ] **Play** — *Major Scales in 4th Position*, p. 119 — G major as fingering type 1A, D major as type 1.
- [ ] **Play** — *Major Scales in 4th Position*, p. 120 — A major as type 2, E major as type 3.
- [ ] **Play** — the *Chord Forms* on p. 121 and both exercises, including the minor sequences written with augmented substitutes.
- [ ] **Play** — the *4th Position Review*, pp. 122–123. Types 1A, 1, 2 and 3, as a waltz-time duet with rhythm guitar.
- [ ] **Read** — pp. 124–125, the chord-form caution about weak bass degrees and the author's closing notes. Once, and not as a lesson.
- [ ] **Check** — a cold read of an unseen page at or below p. 123, once, at tempo, with no practice run.

sections.name: Course final
sections.raw:
A **performance check**, not a test page. There are no `type: school-test` pages in this course and nothing here enters the spaced-repetition drip — sight reading is a motor skill, and the drip is for facts.

The check is the one the book itself prescribes on p. 123, and it outlives the course: *"Find additional reading material — be sure it is easy to execute — then read five or more pages every day. Play each page not more than twice through. Do not practice. Do not memorize. Do not use the same pages on consecutive days. Vary the material, and READ, READ, READ."*

So: an unseen page of outside material, played once at tempo with no practice run, keeping an even tempo through the wrong notes. Pass is your own honest read of whether it held together. Nothing in the system can hear the guitar, so nothing here pretends to grade it.

This is also the end of [[Class 8 — Guitar Sight Reading]]. The class has a finish line; the reading does not.

29.title: Course 29 — Chord Vocabulary
29.intro:
Teaches how to spell a chord, and how the naming system that spells it actually works. One rule builds the whole vocabulary; the rest of the course is what happens at the edges of that rule — extensions, removals, alterations, symmetry, and the point where a name stops being a fact and becomes a choice.

What it assumes

  • — chord spelling is interval arithmetic. Major and minor thirds have to be automatic before stacking them means anything. Function is not a prerequisite; this course is the vocabulary, is the grammar, and they can run in either order.

What this unlocks

  • — the other half of the same skill. This course is whether you can spell a chord; that one is whether you can arrange and play it.
  • — substitution, tritone subs and reharmonisation are all operations on chord names, and none of them is teachable before the names are secure.
  • Practically: reading a chart without stalling on a symbol you don't recognise, and writing down a chord you found by ear instead of losing it.

Taught from zero

No prior knowledge assumed and nothing skipped. Some of it will be revision, which is the cheaper error. Run /school test 29 1 early if a lesson turns out to be known.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Stacked Thirds, and Why the System Generalises

**Read**
- [ ] [[Chords]] → *Triads (3 notes)*, *Beyond thirds: non-tertial harmony*
- [ ] [[Chord Classification from 2 to 12 Notes]] → *The count*

**The material**
- One rule builds the entire vocabulary: [[CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds|stack thirds from the root]]. Skip a scale degree, take the next one, repeat.
- Two thirds is a triad, three is a seventh chord, and continuing gives the 9th, 11th and 13th. The name for the system is **tertian** harmony, and it is the common-practice default rather than a law of nature.
- [[CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of the two thirds|Quality is the order of the two thirds]], not a fact to memorise per chord: M3+m3 major, m3+M3 minor, m3+m3 diminished, M3+M3 augmented — in half steps 4+3, 3+4, 3+3, 4+4.
- **Only the middle note separates major from minor.** Raise it a half step and the chord flips, which is the cheapest mood change available and the reason the 3rd is the quality tone. The 5th is what decides diminished against augmented.
- The two symmetrical orders — 3+3 and 4+4 — are the two chords that cause trouble in Lesson 3. Everything else in the system has an unambiguous root; those two do not.
- The rule also has an edge, and knowing where it sits matters: [[CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops|stack something other than thirds and the names stop working]].
- **Secundal** stacks 2nds and gives tone clusters, which are timbral rather than harmonic. **Quartal** stacks 4ths. **Quintal** stacks 5ths and respells as the same notes as quartal, so it is not a separate system.
- Quartal harmony does not fit the tertian naming convention at all, which is why standard symbols keep mislabelling it as sus4. A chord name is a construct, and harmony happens whether or not a stack has an agreed label.
- The catalogue is finite, which is the reassuring part: from one root inside an octave there are 11 dyads, 19 triads, 43 tetrads and 66 pentads. The system generalises; it does not sprawl.

**Concepts**
- [[CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds]]
- [[CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of the two thirds]]
- [[CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — from C, stack thirds up to a 13th and name the chord at every stage. Then build all four triad qualities from the same root and say which single note moved each time.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play a minor triad on guitar or piano, raise only the middle note to hear major, then move only the 5th to reach diminished and augmented. Finish by playing a quartal voicing and trying to name it with a standard symbol.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 29 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Sevenths and Extensions

**Read**
- [ ] [[Seventh Chords]] → *The three you'll use constantly*, *The rest of the family*
- [ ] [[Extended Chords]] → *The dominant series (built on C7)*, *What to actually play (standard omissions)*
- [ ] [[Upper Structure Chords]] → *The idea*, *The six bass-note options*

**The material**
- One more third on top of the triad, and [[CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities|four qualities fall out of a two-by-two grid]] — {major or minor triad} × {♭7 or natural 7}.
- maj7 (1 3 5 7), dominant 7 (1 3 5 ♭7), minor 7 (1 ♭3 5 ♭7), minor-major 7 (1 ♭3 5 7). Two more sit on the diminished triad: half-diminished m7♭5 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7) and diminished 7 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7), which differ only in the seventh.
- **The diatonic placement is the part worth memorising.** Dominant 7 occurs on exactly one degree of a major key and half-diminished on exactly one, so either chord spotted out of context names its parent key. A bare maj7 is ambiguous, a bare m7 worse.
- Keep stacking and you reach 9, 11 and 13 — but [[CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath|an extension name needs a complete structure underneath it]].
- "9 = 2, 11 = 4, 13 = 6, an octave up" is usually true and is not the rule. The rule is a role test: full triad present → the 2 becomes a 9; full seventh chord present → the 6 becomes a 13. Pull the lower tone and the name reverts, whatever octave it is voiced in.
- Cadd9 against Csus2 is that one fact — is the 3rd there. And Cmaj7♯11 is never called ♯4, because it sits on a complete seventh chord.
- **What you play is smaller than what you spell.** Drop the 5th on a 9th chord, the 3rd on an 11th because it clashes with the 11, and the 5th, 9th and especially the 11th on a 13th.
- Then the move that turns three shapes into a vocabulary: [[CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass|an upper structure is a chord over a bass note that is not its own]].
- If that bass note is already in the upper chord you have an inversion and nothing new. If it isn't, the composite gets its own name, its own function and its own resolution. Home position is the ♭6 of a major key.
- The same E minor triad over six different bass notes reads as a ♭6 major 7♯11, a ♭7 dominant 13, a iv minor 6/9, an altered dominant, and two rarer suspended-dominant colours. One shape, six chords.

**Concepts**
- [[CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities]]
- [[CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath]]
- [[CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — spell all six seventh qualities from C. Then voice C9, Cadd9 and Csus2 and say which note is missing from each.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a diatonic triad loop in Ableton and convert every chord to its diatonic seventh, then thin each voicing by the omission rules and A/B it against the full stack.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 29 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Alteration and Colour

**Read**
- [ ] [[Altered Chords]] → *Single alterations*, *Usage*
- [ ] [[Suspended Chords]] → *Types*, *How sus4 chords get used (three patterns)*
- [ ] [[Add Chords]]
- [ ] [[Sixth Chords]]
- [ ] [[Augmented Chords]] → *Usage — transition/passing chords*
- [ ] [[Diminished Chords]] → *Where they live diatonically*, *Usage — passing chords*

**The material**
- Three operations get lumped together as "colour" and they are not the same thing. [[CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neither is an alteration|Sus removes and add adds]] — neither one alters anything.
- **sus replaces the 3rd** with the 2nd or the 4th, so the chord is neither major nor minor. **add keeps the triad** and adds one note with no 7th: Cadd9 is C E G D, while C9 is C E G B♭ D.
- sus4 carries a pull and usually resolves; sus2 pulls weakly and often just sits as an open colour. In practice only two see much use — sus4 on major triads and 7sus4 on dominants.
- [[CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones|Alteration is the third operation]]: a chord tone shifted a half step. It is a dominant-family device, and the movable tones are the 5th and the 9th — ♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, ♯11.
- One rule governs all of them: **do not alter a note the melody is sitting on.** The symbol names a scale as much as a note stack, which is why G7♭9 and G7♭13 are interchangeable in writing and 7♯11 and 7♭5 share one physical voicing.
- [[CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor-6 naming trap|The 6th chord]] is a triad plus the 6th degree and no 7th — a milder colour than a 7th. The trap: the added 6th is always the **major** 6th, even on a minor triad, so Bm6 is B D F♯ G♯.
- A 6th chord is note-for-note its relative minor 7th — C6 is Am7 — and with no bass to anchor a root, both names are defensible. Classical figured bass also writes a superscript 6 for first inversion, so "C6" means C/E in an analysis and C E G A on a chart.
- Then the two chords built from one interval repeated: [[CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and what symmetry costs them|the symmetrical chords]]. Diminished 7 is 3+3+3 and augmented is 4+4.
- Symmetry buys transposability — slide a diminished 7th shape up three frets and it is the same four pitches — and costs a root the ear can find, a true inversion, and any function of its own. One dim7 has four names, one augmented triad three.
- **The functional half, which the reference note leaves out.** Look at the notes of the diminished chord. Is any one of them the leading note of the chord that follows? **No → a passing chord**, colouring the line and driving nothing. **Yes → a dominant substitute**, and it will resolve.
- The same ♯iv° is passing on the way to I — the leading note of I is not in it — and a functioning dominant on the way to V, because ♯4̂ *is* the leading note of 5̂. One shape, two jobs, decided entirely by what comes next.

**Concepts**
- [[CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neither is an alteration]]
- [[CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones]]
- [[CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor-6 naming trap]]
- [[CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and what symmetry costs them]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — sort sus2, add9, 7♯9, 6 and dim7 into removals, additions and alterations. Then spell Bm6 and Bm♭6 and say which note differs.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — over a V7 in a loop, add one alteration at a time and hear each resolution. Then play a melody over it and drop whichever alteration collides with the melody note.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 29 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Naming, Inversion and the Slash

**Read**
- [ ] [[Chord Inversions]] → *The inversions of C major*, *Why invert*
- [ ] [[Slash Chords]] → *The interpretation method*, *All twelve major triads over a C bass note*
- [ ] [[Chord Naming by Context]]

**The material**
- [[CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, different bass|An inversion changes exactly one thing]] — which chord tone is in the bass. Two inversions for a triad, three for a seventh chord, and the notes never change.
- The bass note is the single most important note for a chord's feel, which makes inverting a compositional decision rather than a fingering convenience.
- Three reasons to do it: **voice leading** (keep common tones, move the least), **bass-line control** (walk the bass by step under static harmony, C → C/B → Am), and hand economy.
- On guitar the decision inverts itself: with four fingers and six strings the live question is which tones to **drop**. Keep the 3rd and 7th, drop the 5th first and the root second. Rootless is the default with a bass player present, not an exotic case.
- [[CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord|A slash symbol is a playing instruction]] — upper chord over bass note — and what the composite *is* is a separate question with a three-step method.
- Take the bass as the root, relate every upper note back to it as a degree, then name the result. B♭/C is ♭7-9-11 over C, so C7sus4(9). G/C is 9-5-maj7, a Cmaj9 with no 3rd. E/C is maj3-♯5-maj7, so Cmaj7♯5.
- Two stopping points. If the bass note is already a tone of the upper chord there is no new chord at all — A♭/C is first-inversion A♭. And with no 3rd and no 7th present the reading is genuinely ambiguous, so only the surrounding harmony decides.
- Which is the idea the whole course exists to install, and the one four Pedler chapters converge on: [[CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relationship, not a fact|a chord name is chosen to expose a relationship, not to state a fact]].
- The correct name is the one that reflects the sound you actually hear and the voice leading as it resolves — not the one with the fewest accidentals, and not the one a chart would print.
- The same four notes are Cmaj7/E in the key of C and Em(add♭6) with E as the centre. Em6 is a half-diminished a third away or a rootless dominant 9th a fourth up, and **each name predicts a different next chord**.
- A diminished 7th has four names and an augmented triad three. The collection of pitches never changes; only what you are claiming about it does. That is a licence, not a loophole — pick the name that gets you where you are going.

**Concepts**
- [[CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, different bass]]
- [[CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord]]
- [[CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relationship, not a fact]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — run the three-step method on B♭/C, A/C and G♭/C, name each composite, and say where each wants to go. Then find one chord of your own that needed a slash and name it two ways.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a four-chord loop and re-voice it so the bass walks by step, then play the same loop with 3rds and 7ths only and check nothing about its identity was lost.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 29 — Lesson 4 Test]]

sections.raw:
`/school final 29` when all four lessons are done. Twenty-four questions weighted to the material that actually trips people — the extension-naming rule, the three colour operations, symmetry and the leading-note test, and the naming argument. Pass at **80%**.

Passing completes the course and seeds its concepts to `maintenance`. Failing keeps it `active` and re-seeds only the concepts you missed.

→ [[Course 29 — Final Exam]]

• One rule builds the entire vocabulary: . Skip a scale degree, take the next one, repeat.
  • Two thirds is a triad, three is a seventh chord, and continuing gives the 9th, 11th and 13th. The name for the system is tertian harmony, and it is the common-practice default rather than a law of nature.
  • , not a fact to memorise per chord: M3+m3 major, m3+M3 minor, m3+m3 diminished, M3+M3 augmented — in half steps 4+3, 3+4, 3+3, 4+4.
  • Only the middle note separates major from minor. Raise it a half step and the chord flips, which is the cheapest mood change available and the reason the 3rd is the quality tone. The 5th is what decides diminished against augmented.
  • The two symmetrical orders — 3+3 and 4+4 — are the two chords that cause trouble in Lesson 3. Everything else in the system has an unambiguous root; those two do not.
  • The rule also has an edge, and knowing where it sits matters: .
  • Secundal stacks 2nds and gives tone clusters, which are timbral rather than harmonic. Quartal stacks 4ths. Quintal stacks 5ths and respells as the same notes as quartal, so it is not a separate system.
  • Quartal harmony does not fit the tertian naming convention at all, which is why standard symbols keep mislabelling it as sus4. A chord name is a construct, and harmony happens whether or not a stack has an agreed label.
  • The catalogue is finite, which is the reassuring part: from one root inside an octave there are 11 dyads, 19 triads, 43 tetrads and 66 pentads. The system generalises; it does not sprawl.

CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of the two thirds
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops

tasks.html: Review — from C, stack thirds up to a 13th and name the chord at every stage. Then build all four triad qualities from the same root and say which single note moved each time.

Apply (~15 min) — play a minor triad on guitar or piano, raise only the middle note to hear major, then move only the 5th to reach diminished and augmented. Finish by playing a quartal voicing and trying to name it with a standard symbol.

Seventh Chords → The three you'll use constantly, The rest of the family
Extended Chords → The dominant series (built on C7), What to actually play (standard omissions)

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• One more third on top of the triad, and — {major or minor triad} × {♭7 or natural 7}.
  • maj7 (1 3 5 7), dominant 7 (1 3 5 ♭7), minor 7 (1 ♭3 5 ♭7), minor-major 7 (1 ♭3 5 7). Two more sit on the diminished triad: half-diminished m7♭5 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7) and diminished 7 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7), which differ only in the seventh.
  • The diatonic placement is the part worth memorising. Dominant 7 occurs on exactly one degree of a major key and half-diminished on exactly one, so either chord spotted out of context names its parent key. A bare maj7 is ambiguous, a bare m7 worse.
  • Keep stacking and you reach 9, 11 and 13 — but .
  • "9 = 2, 11 = 4, 13 = 6, an octave up" is usually true and is not the rule. The rule is a role test: full triad present → the 2 becomes a 9; full seventh chord present → the 6 becomes a 13. Pull the lower tone and the name reverts, whatever octave it is voiced in.
  • Cadd9 against Csus2 is that one fact — is the 3rd there. And Cmaj7♯11 is never called ♯4, because it sits on a complete seventh chord.
  • What you play is smaller than what you spell. Drop the 5th on a 9th chord, the 3rd on an 11th because it clashes with the 11, and the 5th, 9th and especially the 11th on a 13th.
  • Then the move that turns three shapes into a vocabulary: .
  • If that bass note is already in the upper chord you have an inversion and nothing new. If it isn't, the composite gets its own name, its own function and its own resolution. Home position is the ♭6 of a major key.
  • The same E minor triad over six different bass notes reads as a ♭6 major 7♯11, a ♭7 dominant 13, a iv minor 6/9, an altered dominant, and two rarer suspended-dominant colours. One shape, six chords.

CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass

tasks.html: Review — spell all six seventh qualities from C. Then voice C9, Cadd9 and Csus2 and say which note is missing from each.
Apply (~15 min) — take a diatonic triad loop in Ableton and convert every chord to its diatonic seventh, then thin each voicing by the omission rules and A/B it against the full stack.

Altered Chords → Single alterations, Usage
Suspended Chords → Types, How sus4 chords get used (three patterns)
Add Chords
Sixth Chords
Augmented Chords → Usage — transition/passing chords
Diminished Chords → Where they live diatonically, Usage — passing chords

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Three operations get lumped together as "colour" and they are not the same thing. — neither one alters anything.
  • sus replaces the 3rd with the 2nd or the 4th, so the chord is neither major nor minor. add keeps the triad and adds one note with no 7th: Cadd9 is C E G D, while C9 is C E G B♭ D.
  • sus4 carries a pull and usually resolves; sus2 pulls weakly and often just sits as an open colour. In practice only two see much use — sus4 on major triads and 7sus4 on dominants.
  • : a chord tone shifted a half step. It is a dominant-family device, and the movable tones are the 5th and the 9th — ♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, ♯11.
  • One rule governs all of them: do not alter a note the melody is sitting on. The symbol names a scale as much as a note stack, which is why G7♭9 and G7♭13 are interchangeable in writing and 7♯11 and 7♭5 share one physical voicing.
  • is a triad plus the 6th degree and no 7th — a milder colour than a 7th. The trap: the added 6th is always the major 6th, even on a minor triad, so Bm6 is B D F♯ G♯.
  • A 6th chord is note-for-note its relative minor 7th — C6 is Am7 — and with no bass to anchor a root, both names are defensible. Classical figured bass also writes a superscript 6 for first inversion, so "C6" means C/E in an analysis and C E G A on a chart.
  • Then the two chords built from one interval repeated: . Diminished 7 is 3+3+3 and augmented is 4+4.
  • Symmetry buys transposability — slide a diminished 7th shape up three frets and it is the same four pitches — and costs a root the ear can find, a true inversion, and any function of its own. One dim7 has four names, one augmented triad three.
  • The functional half, which the reference note leaves out. Look at the notes of the diminished chord. Is any one of them the leading note of the chord that follows? No → a passing chord, colouring the line and driving nothing. Yes → a dominant substitute, and it will resolve.
  • The same ♯iv° is passing on the way to I — the leading note of I is not in it — and a functioning dominant on the way to V, because ♯4̂ is the leading note of 5̂. One shape, two jobs, decided entirely by what comes next.

CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones

Chord Naming by Context

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• — which chord tone is in the bass. Two inversions for a triad, three for a seventh chord, and the notes never change.
  • The bass note is the single most important note for a chord's feel, which makes inverting a compositional decision rather than a fingering convenience.
  • Three reasons to do it: voice leading (keep common tones, move the least), bass-line control (walk the bass by step under static harmony, C → C/B → Am), and hand economy.
  • On guitar the decision inverts itself: with four fingers and six strings the live question is which tones to drop. Keep the 3rd and 7th, drop the 5th first and the root second. Rootless is the default with a bass player present, not an exotic case.
  • — upper chord over bass note — and what the composite is is a separate question with a three-step method.
  • Take the bass as the root, relate every upper note back to it as a degree, then name the result. B♭/C is ♭7-9-11 over C, so C7sus4(9). G/C is 9-5-maj7, a Cmaj9 with no 3rd. E/C is maj3-♯5-maj7, so Cmaj7♯5.
  • Two stopping points. If the bass note is already a tone of the upper chord there is no new chord at all — A♭/C is first-inversion A♭. And with no 3rd and no 7th present the reading is genuinely ambiguous, so only the surrounding harmony decides.
  • Which is the idea the whole course exists to install, and the one four Pedler chapters converge on: .
  • The correct name is the one that reflects the sound you actually hear and the voice leading as it resolves — not the one with the fewest accidentals, and not the one a chart would print.
  • The same four notes are Cmaj7/E in the key of C and Em(add♭6) with E as the centre. Em6 is a half-diminished a third away or a rootless dominant 9th a fourth up, and each name predicts a different next chord.
  • A diminished 7th has four names and an augmented triad three. The collection of pitches never changes; only what you are claiming about it does. That is a licence, not a loophole — pick the name that gets you where you are going.
