30.title: Course 30 — Voicings & Comping
30.intro:
Teaches what to do with a chord once you can spell it — which notes to keep, where to put them, when to strike them, and how to stay out of the way of whoever else is playing. It is the playing half of harmony, and it happens entirely on the instrument.

What it assumes

  • — you have to be able to name the notes in a chord before deciding which of them to leave out.

What this unlocks

  • Playing with other people. Everything in Lessons 4 and 5 is a rule about how a part fits beside other parts. Nothing else in the school covers it.
  • The arrangement fix for what looks like a mix problem. A chord low on the neck under a vocal is mud; the same chord higher is fine. That decision is made here, not in the mixer.
  • Jazz harmony becomes playable rather than theoretical. Substitution and reharmonisation are voicing decisions before they are analytical ones.
  • Practically: sitting down with a chart and a guitar and getting through it, instead of getting through it by ear and hoping.

The gap this course closes

School Config created the VOI strand for a specific reason: "CHD covers whether you can spell a chord and nothing covered whether you can arrange and play one — the actual guitar skill." That reasoning was recorded on 2026-08-03 and no concepts were written against it. This is that gap closed. It is a playing course — every Apply item puts hands on an instrument.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — A Voicing Is a Choice, Not a Chord

**Read**
- [ ] [[Chord Voicings]] → *Chord vs. voicing vs. shape*, *Which notes actually matter*, *The named voicing families*
- [ ] [[Breaking Up Voicings]] → *The core method*
- [ ] [[Quartal Chord Voicings]] → *What it is*, *One shape, many chord identities*

> [!warning] Ch13 is vault-only reading — deliberately NOT on the Read list above
> **[[Ch13 — The A Hard Day's Night Chord — Rock's Holy Grail]] §1–§2 is the strongest case in the
> library for this lesson, and it must be read in Obsidian, not on the school page.** Every note on
> a `**Read**` line is parked into the published artifact as its own page by `build.py`'s
> `reading_for()`; Ch13 is an extraction from a scanned commercial book and its own header says
> *"nothing here travels into the published artifact."* Citing it in prose keeps the pointer and
> publishes nothing. Courses 29 and 31 handle Ch11 and Ch12 the same way.
>
> And read it for the **argument, not for a chord**: the fret diagrams, tablature and frequency
> tables were destroyed by the scan — two pages carry printed accuracy estimates near 20%. The note
> says so and refuses to guess. Do not try to reconstruct the voicing from it.

**The material**
- The idea the course rests on: [[VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape|chord, voicing and shape are three different things]]. A **chord** is pitch content — C major is C-E-G in any order. A **voicing** is the specific order, spacing and register. A **shape** is one fingering that realises a voicing.
- Slide a shape up a fret and the voicing is unchanged while the chord changes. That is the proof they are separate.
- Ch13 is the strongest case in the library for treating the voicing as harmony rather than decoration: the sonority everyone recognises is **an ensemble effect no single instrument can play**, built from a 12-string, a bass, an overdubbed piano and room bleed. Even the guitarist who played it did not think of it as a chord he was playing.
- A 12-string is not a 6-string with the same notes — four courses tuned in octaves means a pitch nobody fingered is one of the most audible things in the sound. **Register and doubling are chord identity.**
- Then the practical half: [[VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings|which notes you can drop]]. Guide tones first — 3rd and 7th define quality and function. Then the extension you want. Then the root, which the bass has. The 5th goes first unless it is altered.
- **Shell** is root, 3rd, 7th. **Rootless** is 3rd, 7th, extensions. **Drop 2** moves the 2nd-highest note of a close voicing down an octave and is the workhorse; **drop 3** moves the 3rd-highest and spaces it wider.
- And the one that is ambiguous on purpose: [[VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on purpose|quartal voicings]] stack 4ths, so they state a set of notes without committing to a quality — which is why nothing in them wants to resolve anywhere.
- One quartal grip reads as minor 11, sus4, 6/9 or major 13 depending only on which note the ear takes as the root. The fingers never move.
- Last piece of texture: a struck four-note chord is four notes you can deploy separately — outside pair then inside pair, every other note, or a held top note with a line moving underneath.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape]]
- [[VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings]]
- [[VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on purpose]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take one chord you play constantly and write down every note in it. Cross out the 5th. Cross out the root. Say what is left and whether it still names the chord.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — on guitar, comp one tune with shell voicings only. Then do the same tune again with guide tones alone, no root. Record both to one Ableton track and listen back for what actually went missing.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Finding the Other Voicings

**Read**
- [ ] [[Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery]] → *The method*, *Collision-resolution mechanic, generalized*
- [ ] [[Major Triads Across the Fretboard (String-Group Inversions)]] → in full, it is a short note
- [ ] [[Multifunctional Voicings]] → *The core mechanism*, *Three worked shapes, three functions each*

**The material**
- Three ways to end up with more voicings than you memorised, and none of them is a chord chart.
- The first is generative: [[VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collision fix|move one note of a shape up or down an octave]] and see what you land on. If two notes collide on a string, move the **newly-colliding** note to its own nearest octave and cascade until every note has a string of its own.
- That mechanic is what makes it terminate instead of dead-ending, and it is also the definition of open position: a close voicing becomes a spread one exactly by lifting an interior note an octave. Move the root of a close C major up and you get another close inversion; move the middle note up and you get the open 1-5-3.
- The second is inventory: [[VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group|one triad lives in twelve places]] — three inversions on each of four adjacent 3-string groups.
- Because the guitar is tuned in fourths except between G and B, the two groups crossing that pair reuse the E-A-D / A-D-G shapes with every note **above** the pair a fret higher — **D-G-B shifts the top note, G-B-E the top two**. Twelve locations, not twelve grips.
- The payoff is not "more shapes to know". It is that you pick each chord by **proximity to the previous one** rather than defaulting to root position, which cuts hand travel, raises the tempo you can play cleanly, and sounds less generic.
- The third is reinterpretation: [[VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords|one shape covers several chords]] depending on which chord tone you play it from. A min7♭5 or half-diminished grip played off the **♭7 of a dominant** reads as that dominant, altered; the same family off the **3rd** reads as a dominant 9.
- That is the efficiency argument for the whole strand. You are not finding a grip for G7alt mid-tune — you are re-pointing one you already own.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collision fix]]
- [[VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group]]
- [[VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take one chord shape and move each of its notes up an octave in turn, resolving collisions. Write down the two results you would actually use and name the family each landed in.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — pick one major triad and find all three inversions on all four string groups. Use [[FretFlip]] to check yourself when a position will not come, then play a four-chord progression choosing the nearest voicing every time instead of the root-position one.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Voice Leading Between Voicings

**Read**
- [ ] [[Voice Leading]] → *The algorithm*, *The bass exception*
- [ ] [[Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude]] → *Spread triad, defined*, *The construction rule*
- [ ] [[Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude]] → skim the comparison table

**The material**
- A voicing is only good relative to the one before it, and there is an algorithm: [[VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-tone pivot|hold the common tone and move the rest by the nearest step]].
- Find the note both chords share. Do not move it. Move everything else to the nearest available note of the next chord. Repeat through the progression. You never have to name the inversion you land on.
- **The bass is the exception.** The lowest voice stays on each chord's actual root while the upper voices invert above it, because the ear reads the chord's identity from the bass. Voice-leading it too would smooth the motion and lose the harmony.
- The test is audible: the same progression in strict root position throughout keeps every note and loses the character.
- Then the rule turned into a generator: [[VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note per change|chain triads by thirds and move exactly one voice]]. A **spread** triad is a close triad with the middle note up an octave — 1-5-3, with a string skip and a wider, harp-like spacing.
- Chain the diatonic triads a third at a time — I, iii, V, vii°, ii, IV, vi — moving one voice by a half or whole step at each change, always to the closest spread voicing of the next chord. Land it with a real cadence, V7 to I.
- **Coverage falls out as a side effect.** Because the closest-voicing rule forces a different inversion each time a quality recurs, the chain touches every diatonic triad of the key in every inversion without inversions ever being drilled separately.
- Watch the terminology: "open position" here means spread spacing, not playing near the nut. Same words, unrelated meanings.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-tone pivot]]
- [[VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note per change]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write out a four-chord loop and, for each change, circle the note the two chords share. Then say where every other note goes and by how far.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — on piano, play that loop twice: once all root position, once voice-led by common tone with the left hand still on the plain roots. Then move to guitar and run the spread-triad chain down the neck in C, one note moving per change.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 3 Test]]

### Lesson 4 — Comping — Rhythm, Motif and Fills

**Read**
- [ ] [[Jazz Comping]] → the five named comping rhythms
- [ ] [[Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline]] → *The core tip*, *Bonus: walking bassline with the chords*
- [ ] [[Comping Fills]] → *The core tip*, *A fill's job is to connect, not decorate*
- [ ] [[Six Devices for R&B Rhythm Guitar Fills]] → pick two devices, not all six

**The material**
- The sentence the lesson exists for: [[VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is harmony|rhythm matters more than the notes]].
- So the practice order is fixed. Drill the rhythm **alone, on one static shell voicing**, metronome on 2 and 4, until it is automatic. Only then move it through the changes with real voicings.
- Five rhythms cover most of it. **Charleston** — beat 1, then the "and" of 2; the reference groove, and static. **Push** — a sustained hit on the "and" of 3 that pulls into the next bar, which is the momentum Charleston lacks.
- **Downbeat-anchored** — straight, unsyncopated, safe behind a busy soloist. **Off-the-one** — the "and" of 1 and beat 3, skipping the downbeat. **Response** — a reply to a phrase the soloist has just finished.
- The commonest failure is playing too much. Chords on 2 and 4, or one per bar, nearly always sit better than constant strumming.
- Then the thing that makes a part sound deliberate: [[VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then vary it|hold one motif before you vary anything]]. Reinventing the rhythm bar to bar reads as scattered even when every individual choice is defensible.
- Lock the motif for a full pass through the form. *Then* depart from it and return — the return only lands because the baseline was established first. Scaled up, that is riff comping: one whole figure held for eight bars at a time.
- A stable pattern is also what lets everyone else interact with you. A drummer can catch a hit and double it; a soloist can build on a surface that stays put.
- Walking bass under the same rhythm: **root on beats 1 and 3, an approach note toward the next root on 2 and 4** — a half step below, half step above, or whole step above. Try more than one direction; the interval decides.
- Last, the space between: [[VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere|a fill only enters when the soloist stops]], and its job is to connect forward to the next bar, not to decorate the chord it starts on.
- Build one bottom-up — a plain diatonic or blues line first, colour added as a second pass. The R&B device catalogue is the what: butterfly hammer-ons, three-string triad groupings, diatonic 6ths, 4ths, 3rds, and single-note pentatonic lines.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is harmony]]
- [[VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then vary it]]
- [[VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — listen to one track and write down only where the comping instrument strikes. No pitches. Then say which of the five rhythms it is closest to.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — one shell voicing, metronome on 2 and 4, one minute per rhythm: Charleston, push, downbeats, off-the-one, response. Then pick the best one, hold it through a full chorus of a blues, and play a fill only in the bars where the melody rests.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 4 Test]]

### Lesson 5 — Sharing the Role

**Read**
- [ ] [[Jazz Comping — Sharing the Role with Another Comping Instrument]] → in full
- [ ] [[Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads]] → *The core idea*, *Why triads specifically*
- [ ] [[Bossa Nova Comping Pattern]] → skim, for the case where the guitar owns the groove

**The material**
- Two harmony instruments playing independently reads as clutter no matter how good each part is. So: [[VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide register and time|divide the role explicitly]].
- **Assign it out loud at the top of the tune** — you comp the head, I comp the first solo, you take the second. That removes the guesswork rather than negotiating it live. Unrehearsed, the default is that piano is primary and the guitarist behaves like a horn player until cued.
- **Comp in the holes.** When the soloist settles into a repeating motif, place your hits in the gaps it leaves rather than doubling it. By the second repetition you can hear where the holes will be.
- **Track register and move opposite.** Soloist goes up, you comp lower. Going higher than the soloist is the more delicate move — it pulls attention off them — so it is used sparingly.
- **Laying out is a real choice**, including for a whole tune. It also buys thinking time: leaving room lets the soloist define what is needed, so you come back in with something that fits.
- The exception proves the rule. A Freddie Green straight-quarter-note part sits under a comping piano precisely because it has stopped being comping and become a second drummer — completely predictable, harmonically unassertive.
- On a bossa the convention flips: the **guitar** owns the repeating groove and the piano answers it. Only one instrument carries the ostinato at a time.
- Same problem, recorded instead of live: [[VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay small|stacked rhythm parts have to stay lean]]. Closed triads — three notes, no doublings — are small on purpose, which is what lets three of them sit on top of each other.
- What separates the layers is **string group, neck position and tone**, not different material. One triad vocabulary relocated: a bed part low and arpeggiated, a backbeat part on the top three strings, a double-stop melody above.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide register and time]]
- [[VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay small]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — take a recording with both piano and guitar comping. Write down who is playing in each eight-bar stretch and what each one gave up to make room.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — play along with a track that already has a comping instrument. Comp only in its gaps for one chorus, then lay out completely for the next one and just listen to what changed.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 5 Test]]

### Lesson 6 — From Chart to Chord Melody

**Read**
- [ ] [[Reading and Interpreting a Jazz Lead Sheet]] → *The core method*, steps 1–5
- [ ] [[Chord Melody Arranging]] → *The core idea*, *Physical execution: don't harmonize every note*
- [ ] [[Guide-Tone Diads for Blues Rhythm Guitar]] → *The core shape*, *Drill*
- [ ] [[Playing Chord Charts]] → the tool, worked as reading rather than as a drill

**The material**
- The strand's thesis in one line, and the tool page states it: making music from a chord chart is like cooking from a recipe. [[VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an instruction|A chart is a framework]].
- **Read the form before a single chord.** AABA or ABAC, 32 bars — and an AABA tune with an 8-bar A is often only 16 bars of distinct harmony once the repeats are accounted for.
- **Use the form to predict.** In an AABA tune starting on the tonic, the last two bars of each A are a turnaround about ninety percent of the time. That is a chunk of the chart solved before it is read.
- **Reduce to named devices.** A secondary ii-V into the IV chord is "the IV chord". A four-bar reset is "a turnaround". The point is recognising the same device in the *next* tune.
- **The printed harmonisation is a starting point.** When a chord clashes with the melody, substituting is normal practice, not a liberty. Judge it against the melody, not the page.
- Then playing melody and harmony at once: [[VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not the key|read every melody note as a degree of the chord under it]], not of the parent key. The same pitch is "5 of C" under a C chord and "4 of D" a beat later under Dm.
- Index your voicings by **which chord tone the melody note is and which string it lands on** — that is the lookup you need mid-arrangement, and it is why the shape transfers to any chord of that quality by sliding to the new root.
- **Do not harmonise every note.** Landing the melody note alone with one finger and adding the rest only sometimes is both physically easier and better sounding; the space reads as phrasing rather than a wall of block chords.
- And the floor everything else is built on: [[VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum viable voicing|two notes, the 3rd and the ♭7]], state a dominant chord on their own. Change the 3rd and it flips major to minor; change the ♭7 and it stops being a dominant.
- Through a blues in A the identical shape moves **down a half step for the IV and up a half step for the V**. One grip, the whole form. The rootless 9ths and 13ths are this pair with colour stacked on top.

**Concepts**
- [[VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an instruction]]
- [[VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not the key]]
- [[VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum viable voicing]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — open a standard you do not know. Before touching an instrument, mark the form, circle every likely turnaround, and reduce every multi-chord passage to one named device.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — run one progression through [[Playing Chord Charts]] in three keys using its transposer, then play a 12-bar blues in A on guitar with nothing but the 3rd-♭7 diad, moving by half step for the IV and V.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 30 — Lesson 6 Test]]

lessons.title: A Voicing Is a Choice, Not a Chord

blocks.label: Read

tasks.html: Chord Voicings → Chord vs. voicing vs. shape, Which notes actually matter, The named voicing families
Breaking Up Voicings → The core method
Quartal Chord Voicings → What it is, One shape, many chord identities

blocks.html:
Ch13 is vault-only reading — deliberately NOT on the Read list above

Ch13 — The A Hard Day's Night Chord — Rock's Holy Grail §1–§2 is the strongest case in the library for this lesson, and it must be read in Obsidian, not on the school page. Every note on a **Read** line is parked into the published artifact as its own page by build.py's reading_for(); Ch13 is an extraction from a scanned commercial book and its own header says "nothing here travels into the published artifact." Citing it in prose keeps the pointer and publishes nothing. Courses 29 and 31 handle Ch11 and Ch12 the same way.

And read it for the argument, not for a chord: the fret diagrams, tablature and frequency tables were destroyed by the scan — two pages carry printed accuracy estimates near 20%. The note says so and refuses to guess. Do not try to reconstruct the voicing from it.

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The idea the course rests on: . A chord is pitch content — C major is C-E-G in any order. A voicing is the specific order, spacing and register. A shape is one fingering that realises a voicing.
  • Slide a shape up a fret and the voicing is unchanged while the chord changes. That is the proof they are separate.
  • Ch13 is the strongest case in the library for treating the voicing as harmony rather than decoration: the sonority everyone recognises is an ensemble effect no single instrument can play, built from a 12-string, a bass, an overdubbed piano and room bleed. Even the guitarist who played it did not think of it as a chord he was playing.
  • A 12-string is not a 6-string with the same notes — four courses tuned in octaves means a pitch nobody fingered is one of the most audible things in the sound. Register and doubling are chord identity.
  • Then the practical half: . Guide tones first — 3rd and 7th define quality and function. Then the extension you want. Then the root, which the bass has. The 5th goes first unless it is altered.
  • Shell is root, 3rd, 7th. Rootless is 3rd, 7th, extensions. Drop 2 moves the 2nd-highest note of a close voicing down an octave and is the workhorse; drop 3 moves the 3rd-highest and spaces it wider.
  • And the one that is ambiguous on purpose: stack 4ths, so they state a set of notes without committing to a quality — which is why nothing in them wants to resolve anywhere.
  • One quartal grip reads as minor 11, sus4, 6/9 or major 13 depending only on which note the ear takes as the root. The fingers never move.
  • Last piece of texture: a struck four-note chord is four notes you can deploy separately — outside pair then inside pair, every other note, or a held top note with a line moving underneath.

ids: VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on purpose

tasks.html: Review — take one chord you play constantly and write down every note in it. Cross out the 5th. Cross out the root. Say what is left and whether it still names the chord.

Apply (~15 min) — on guitar, comp one tune with shell voicings only. Then do the same tune again with guide tones alone, no root. Record both to one Ableton track and listen back for what actually went missing.
Test — Course 30 — Lesson 1 Test
Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery → The method, Collision-resolution mechanic, generalized
Major Triads Across the Fretboard (String-Group Inversions) → in full, it is a short note
Multifunctional Voicings → The core mechanism, Three worked shapes, three functions each

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Three ways to end up with more voicings than you memorised, and none of them is a chord chart.
  • The first is generative: and see what you land on. If two notes collide on a string, move the newly-colliding note to its own nearest octave and cascade until every note has a string of its own.
  • That mechanic is what makes it terminate instead of dead-ending, and it is also the definition of open position: a close voicing becomes a spread one exactly by lifting an interior note an octave. Move the root of a close C major up and you get another close inversion; move the middle note up and you get the open 1-5-3.
  • The second is inventory: — three inversions on each of four adjacent 3-string groups.
  • Because the guitar is tuned in fourths except between G and B, the two groups crossing that pair reuse the E-A-D / A-D-G shapes with every note above the pair a fret higher — D-G-B shifts the top note, G-B-E the top two. Twelve locations, not twelve grips.
  • The payoff is not "more shapes to know". It is that you pick each chord by proximity to the previous one rather than defaulting to root position, which cuts hand travel, raises the tempo you can play cleanly, and sounds less generic.
  • The third is reinterpretation: depending on which chord tone you play it from. A min7♭5 or half-diminished grip played off the ♭7 of a dominant reads as that dominant, altered; the same family off the 3rd reads as a dominant 9.
  • That is the efficiency argument for the whole strand. You are not finding a grip for G7alt mid-tune — you are re-pointing one you already own.

ids: VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collision fix
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group
VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords

tasks.html: Review — take one chord shape and move each of its notes up an octave in turn, resolving collisions. Write down the two results you would actually use and name the family each landed in.

Apply (~15 min) — pick one major triad and find all three inversions on all four string groups. Use FretFlip to check yourself when a position will not come, then play a four-chord progression choosing the nearest voicing every time instead of the root-position one.
Test — Course 30 — Lesson 2 Test
Voice Leading → The algorithm, The bass exception
Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude → Spread triad, defined, The construction rule
Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude → skim the comparison table

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• A voicing is only good relative to the one before it, and there is an algorithm: .
  • Find the note both chords share. Do not move it. Move everything else to the nearest available note of the next chord. Repeat through the progression. You never have to name the inversion you land on.
  • The bass is the exception. The lowest voice stays on each chord's actual root while the upper voices invert above it, because the ear reads the chord's identity from the bass. Voice-leading it too would smooth the motion and lose the harmony.
  • The test is audible: the same progression in strict root position throughout keeps every note and loses the character.
  • Then the rule turned into a generator: . A spread triad is a close triad with the middle note up an octave — 1-5-3, with a string skip and a wider, harp-like spacing.
  • Chain the diatonic triads a third at a time — I, iii, V, vii°, ii, IV, vi — moving one voice by a half or whole step at each change, always to the closest spread voicing of the next chord. Land it with a real cadence, V7 to I.
  • Coverage falls out as a side effect. Because the closest-voicing rule forces a different inversion each time a quality recurs, the chain touches every diatonic triad of the key in every inversion without inversions ever being drilled separately.
  • Watch the terminology: "open position" here means spread spacing, not playing near the nut. Same words, unrelated meanings.

ids: VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-tone pivot
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note per change

tasks.html: Review — write out a four-chord loop and, for each change, circle the note the two chords share. Then say where every other note goes and by how far.

Apply (~15 min) — on piano, play that loop twice: once all root position, once voice-led by common tone with the left hand still on the plain roots. Then move to guitar and run the spread-triad chain down the neck in C, one note moving per change.
Test — Course 30 — Lesson 3 Test
Jazz Comping → the five named comping rhythms
Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline → The core tip, Bonus: walking bassline with the chords
Comping Fills → The core tip, A fill's job is to connect, not decorate
Six Devices for R&B Rhythm Guitar Fills → pick two devices, not all six

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The sentence the lesson exists for: .
  • So the practice order is fixed. Drill the rhythm alone, on one static shell voicing, metronome on 2 and 4, until it is automatic. Only then move it through the changes with real voicings.
  • Five rhythms cover most of it. Charleston — beat 1, then the "and" of 2; the reference groove, and static. Push — a sustained hit on the "and" of 3 that pulls into the next bar, which is the momentum Charleston lacks.
  • Downbeat-anchored — straight, unsyncopated, safe behind a busy soloist. Off-the-one — the "and" of 1 and beat 3, skipping the downbeat. Response — a reply to a phrase the soloist has just finished.
  • The commonest failure is playing too much. Chords on 2 and 4, or one per bar, nearly always sit better than constant strumming.
  • Then the thing that makes a part sound deliberate: . Reinventing the rhythm bar to bar reads as scattered even when every individual choice is defensible.
  • Lock the motif for a full pass through the form. Then depart from it and return — the return only lands because the baseline was established first. Scaled up, that is riff comping: one whole figure held for eight bars at a time.
  • A stable pattern is also what lets everyone else interact with you. A drummer can catch a hit and double it; a soloist can build on a surface that stays put.
  • Walking bass under the same rhythm: root on beats 1 and 3, an approach note toward the next root on 2 and 4 — a half step below, half step above, or whole step above. Try more than one direction; the interval decides.
  • Last, the space between: , and its job is to connect forward to the next bar, not to decorate the chord it starts on.
  • Build one bottom-up — a plain diatonic or blues line first, colour added as a second pass. The R&B device catalogue is the what: butterfly hammer-ons, three-string triad groupings, diatonic 6ths, 4ths, 3rds, and single-note pentatonic lines.

ids: VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is harmony
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then vary it
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere

tasks.html: Review — listen to one track and write down only where the comping instrument strikes. No pitches. Then say which of the five rhythms it is closest to.

Apply (~15 min) — one shell voicing, metronome on 2 and 4, one minute per rhythm: Charleston, push, downbeats, off-the-one, response. Then pick the best one, hold it through a full chorus of a blues, and play a fill only in the bars where the melody rests.
Test — Course 30 — Lesson 4 Test
Jazz Comping — Sharing the Role with Another Comping Instrument → in full
Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads → The core idea, Why triads specifically
Bossa Nova Comping Pattern → skim, for the case where the guitar owns the groove

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Two harmony instruments playing independently reads as clutter no matter how good each part is. So: .
  • Assign it out loud at the top of the tune — you comp the head, I comp the first solo, you take the second. That removes the guesswork rather than negotiating it live. Unrehearsed, the default is that piano is primary and the guitarist behaves like a horn player until cued.
  • Comp in the holes. When the soloist settles into a repeating motif, place your hits in the gaps it leaves rather than doubling it. By the second repetition you can hear where the holes will be.
  • Track register and move opposite. Soloist goes up, you comp lower. Going higher than the soloist is the more delicate move — it pulls attention off them — so it is used sparingly.
  • Laying out is a real choice, including for a whole tune. It also buys thinking time: leaving room lets the soloist define what is needed, so you come back in with something that fits.
  • The exception proves the rule. A Freddie Green straight-quarter-note part sits under a comping piano precisely because it has stopped being comping and become a second drummer — completely predictable, harmonically unassertive.
  • On a bossa the convention flips: the guitar owns the repeating groove and the piano answers it. Only one instrument carries the ostinato at a time.
  • Same problem, recorded instead of live: . Closed triads — three notes, no doublings — are small on purpose, which is what lets three of them sit on top of each other.
  • What separates the layers is string group, neck position and tone, not different material. One triad vocabulary relocated: a bed part low and arpeggiated, a backbeat part on the top three strings, a double-stop melody above.

31.title: Course 31 — Jazz Harmony
31.intro:
Teaches the four ideas jazz harmony actually runs on — the ii–V–I as its basic sentence, guide tones as the two notes that carry a chord, substitution as an engine with rules rather than taste, and reharmonization as the payoff — then the forms, the modal alternative and the melodic vocabulary built on top of them.

School Config records that JAZ was expanded from "dip a toe" to comprehensive on 2026-08-09, Nate's own call, and seventeen notes were written to back it. The notes landed; the syllabus never followed, and the strand sat with a full library, no course and no concepts until 2026-09-01. This course is that decision carried out.

What it assumes

  • — jazz harmony is chord vocabulary moving fast. You cannot substitute a chord you cannot spell, and the sevenths, extensions and alterations that course installs are the raw material here.
  • — a guide tone is a voicing decision before it is a theory one, and half of this course is choosing which notes to leave out.
  • — substitution is defined in terms of function. Without tonic, subdominant and dominant, "shares the same function" is not a usable rule.

What this unlocks

  • The chords in the music you already make. Neo-soul, jazzy hip hop and a great deal of modern R&B are jazz harmony arriving second-hand. This is how to write those chords deliberately instead of finding them by accident.
  • Reharmonization, which is the fastest way to get a second section out of material you already have — the melody stays, the chords underneath change, and the repeat reads as development.
  • The library. Seventeen notes in Theory/Jazz/ stop being a reading list and become an ordered syllabus, with the tools shelf wired in: Auralia tests this material as listening, Teoria drills the chord qualities free.

Where this course transfers, and where it does not

Nate produces hip hop, trap, EDM and pop while studying a jazz-first library, so every lesson names the transfer where there is one — the tritone sub and the backdoor are already in the pop repertoire, guide tones are a mixing decision, and modal jazz is sixty years of solutions to the loop problem. What does not transfer is density: bebop's note rate is a genre convention, not a principle.

sections.name: The lessons
sections.raw:
### Lesson 1 — Sevenths and the Central Cadence

**Read**
- [ ] [[Jazz Harmony]] → *The four ideas the whole subject runs on*, *Numerals in jazz vs. the classical style used elsewhere here*
- [ ] [[The ii-V-I]] → *The major version*, *The minor version*, *Chains — the thing that makes it worth learning*, *When the I doesn't arrive*, *Practical use outside jazz*

**The material**
- The premise before any rule: **[[JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not a colour|a bare "C" on a jazz chart means Cmaj7 or C6]]**. In common-practice harmony the triad is the default and the 7th is a colour; here the 7th is the default and the triad is the special case.
- Everything downstream assumes four notes. Guide tones need a 7th to exist; a tritone substitution has nothing to preserve without one. Reading a jazz chart as triads is not a simpler reading, it is a wrong one.
- The cell the language is built from: **[[JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor|Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7]]**, and in minor **Dm7♭5 – G7♭9 – Cm7**. The roots fall a fifth twice — the circle of fifths in miniature, and the strongest root motion in tonal music stacked back to back.
- The three minor-key differences are forced rather than chosen. The ♭5 is simply the 6th degree of natural minor; the ♭9 comes from harmonic minor, whose raised leading tone is what makes the V a dominant at all; and the tonic is ambiguous on purpose between m7, m6 and mMaj7.
- **The units chain**, which is what makes them worth learning: make the I of one unit the ii of the next, or drop a ii–V in front of any chord you want to arrive at. `| Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 | Cm7 F7 | B♭maj7 |` is two of them, a whole step apart.
- The reading tip: **[[JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the I never arrives|scan for any m7 followed by a dominant 7th a fourth above it]]**. Whatever it points at is the intended I — even when the I never arrives.
- Two cases where it does not. The **deceptive** move goes to vi or ♭VI instead. The **unresolved** ii–V moves straight to the next one, which is why a bebop head can look like it changes key every two bars when it does not.
- Outside jazz it shows up three ways: as the whole loop, as a turnaround pushing back to the top of a plain pop verse, or stripped to guide tones so it survives an arrangement with almost no chordal instrument.

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not a colour]]
- [[JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor]]
- [[JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the I never arrives]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write the major ii–V–I in all twelve keys and the minor version in four. Then take a four-chord loop of your own and re-spell every chord as a seventh.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — build `Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 Cmaj7` as a four-bar loop in Ableton and let it run. Then rewrite the same four bars as triads and A/B them.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 1 Test]]

### Lesson 2 — Guide Tones

**Read**
- [ ] [[Guide Tones]] → *Why the 3rd and the 7th*, *Guide tones move by step — that's the whole trick*, *Shell voicings*, *Using it to write*, *The one exception*

**The material**
- The highest-leverage idea in the strand: **[[JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the chord|two notes state a chord's quality]]**. The 3rd says major or minor, the 7th says major, dominant or minor. Together they name the chord.
- The root tells you nothing about quality and the 5th tells you almost nothing, which is why the 5th is the first note dropped from a voicing. This is why a bass and a horn can imply a full progression with no chordal instrument present.
- **The one exception is m7♭5.** Cm7♭5 and Cm7 share E♭ and B♭, so only the ♭5 separates them — a m7♭5 voicing that drops its 5th states the wrong chord.
- Now the mechanism: **[[JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3rd of the next|run the guide tones through Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7]]** and the lines go C → B → B and F → F → E. One voice holds while the other moves a half step, then they swap.
- Nothing leaps, and it is not luck — that is what root motion by fifths does. It is also the concrete test for a substitution: one that keeps the guide-tone lines stepwise is a good one, which is exactly why the tritone sub works.
- **Write the two lines before you voice anything.** Fix any leap larger than a step by inverting the chord or choosing a different extension, then decide the full voicings. Solving the horizontal problem first is faster and it produces smoother results.
- The practical form is the **[[JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings|shell]]** — root, 3rd and 7th, no 5th and no extensions, usually with the 7th below the 3rd. Extensions stack on top: shell plus 9, shell plus 13.
- On a dense arrangement a shell is often the *right* voicing rather than the simple one. A full five-note chord under a busy vocal is usually the mistake, and cutting a crowded chordal instrument to shells frees mids without losing any harmony.

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the chord]]
- [[JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3rd of the next]]
- [[JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write out only the 3rds and 7ths of a tune's changes as two horizontal lines. Circle every leap larger than a step and re-voice that chord until the leap is gone.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — comp a ii–V–I as shells in root–7th–3rd order under a vocal or lead you already have, then again as full five-note chords. Keep one.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 2 Test]]

### Lesson 3 — Substitution

**Read**
- [ ] [[Chord Substitution]] → *The governing rule*, *1. Diatonic substitution — chords a third apart*, *2. Tritone substitution — the important one*, *3. Backdoor substitution*, *4. Interpolating a ii in front of any dominant*, *Choosing between them*
- [ ] [[Tritone Substitution]] → *The mechanism*, *Pop/rock examples — found by ear, not by theory*
- [ ] [[Backdoor Progression]] → *The progression*, *Pop/R&B examples*, *Jazz standard usage*

**The material**
- **[[JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule: function first|Two chords can substitute when they share enough tones and the same harmonic function]]** — and function comes first. A substitute sharing three notes that resolves the wrong way is worse than one sharing two that resolves right.
- Diatonic substitution falls straight out of it: two diatonic chords a third apart share two of three triad tones, so `Cmaj7 Cmaj7 Fmaj7 G7` becomes `Cmaj7 Am7 Fmaj7 G7`. vi is the strongest I-substitute; iii is the weakest, because it lacks the root and contains the leading tone.
- **The failure mode is substituting everything.** Against plain harmony a substitution reads as sophisticated; wall to wall it reads as directionless. The melody is the test — a substitution that clashes with the tune is wrong however good the voice leading.
- **[[JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shared tritone|G7 and D♭7 contain the same tritone]]** — B and F, with the 3rd and 7th swapping roles, since D♭7's C♭ is B. Same tension, same resolution, different bass note.
- Only dominants qualify, and the substitute always sits a semitone above the target of resolution. What it buys is chromatic bass: `Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7` walks D – D♭ – C, which is most of the sound of neo-soul.
- It is already in pop, found by ear. "Toxic" descends iii → ii → ♭II, readable as subs of a 6-2-5; "One Note Samba" stacks two of them to make a whole turnaround chromatic.
- The V is not the only dominant on a chart. **[[JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary dominant, and the minimum viable form|♭II-of-ii is the commonest flat-five substitution in pop]]**, precisely because it is undramatic — it reads as a chromatic step from iii down to ii.
- And it needs far less chord than it looks: **any major triad a semitone above the target will do it.** Not an altered dominant, not even a dominant 7th. That is a two-second edit to any progression, which is the form of the rule most likely to get used.
- **[[JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone sub|The same ♭II resolving to I can be two devices]]**, and the tell is how you arrive. Chromatically, with the roots stepping down a semitone at a time into it (`Dm7 → D♭7 → Cmaj7`), it is a tritone sub. From ♭VI by descending fifths, it is a borrowed Phrygian cadence.
- ♭II–I sounds complete with no dominant in it because **every note of the ♭II triad falls a semitone into a note of the tonic triad** — ♭2̂→1̂, 4̂→3̂, ♭6̂→5̂. Three semitone resolutions, no tritone, no leading tone. ♭II going to *V* instead is a third thing, the [[Neapolitan Sixth]].
- The softer arrival: **[[JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place of V7|Fm7 – B♭7 – Cmaj7]]** in place of `Dm7 G7 Cmaj7`. Both chords are borrowed from C minor, and B♭7's A♭ — the ♭6 — falls to G instead of a leading tone rising to it.
- Reach for it when V7 is too final or too bright. It is all over Rihanna's "Stay", Zero 7's "The Waiting Line" and Stevie Wonder; the shorthand version, ♭VII7 straight to I with no minor iv, carries "New York State of Mind" and "Layla".
- Two of these are extended by [[Ch12 — Tritone Substitution and Other Mystery Chords]], which is vault-only reading rather than assigned. It confirms the mechanism the library already teaches and adds only the secondary-dominant cases, the minimum viable form and the Phrygian distinction.

- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — in a loop in Ableton, slide a plain major triad a semitone above the ii into the gap before it. Print that clip, then print the same bar with a full altered dominant instead, and A/B them.

### Lesson 4 — Turnarounds, Rhythm Changes and Form

**Read**
- [ ] [[Turnarounds]] → *The base form*, *The standard variations*, *The two-bar and one-bar compressions*, *Using them outside jazz*
- [ ] [[Rhythm Changes]] → *The shape: AABA, 32 bars*, *Why it's worth your time*, *Common substitutions*
- [ ] [[32-Bar Song Form]] → *The 16+16 shape*, *The 8+8 (asymmetric) variant*, *Learning method: form first, chords second*
- [ ] [[The Montgomery-Ward Bridge]] → *The shape*, *Outside jazz*
- [ ] [[Memorizing Jazz Standards by Harmonic Chunking]] → *The core method: the phone-number analogy*, *Theory as language, not a dictionary*

**The material**
- **[[JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled reset|I – vi – ii – V]]**, and its only job is to end a section by pointing back at the top. The root falls a third, then rises a fourth twice, and it lands on V, which wants the next chorus's I.
- **Write the four-chord version first, then compress** — to two bars, to one bar (`| Dm7 G7 |`, the commonest ending in the repertoire), or to V alone on beats 3–4. Compressing a good turnaround gives a good short one; expanding a bare `Dm7 G7` gives you nothing.
- Every named variation — VI7, III7–VI7, tritone subs, ♭III7, backdoor, minor — is Lesson 3 applied to this one skeleton. Learn the base form and the rules and you can generate the rest.
- Loop-based music is *all* turnaround. Three moves that work in production: end on **V7 or ♭II7**; end on **the ii**, leaving the V implied so the loop never closes; or **change only the last bar between repeats** — two loops of material for one bar of writing.
- **[[JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turnaround, answered|Bars 1–4 of a Rhythm Changes A section are I–vi–ii–V twice]]** and nothing else. Bars 5–8 answer them: `I → I7 → IV → iv → I → V/ii → ii → V`, with the borrowed iv as the moment the section goes somewhere.
- Four bars of a static loop do not get boring because four bars of real movement answer them. That question-and-answer shape inside one eight-bar unit is directly transferable to a verse — and it is the answer to why a loop that is fine on its own tires over sixteen bars.
- **[[JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made from harmonic rhythm alone|The bridge is `D7 D7 G7 G7 C7 C7 F7 F7`]]** in B♭ — four dominants, each resolving down a fifth, and only the last, F7, is the key's own V7. A pure circle-of-fifths run that leaves the key and walks back in.
- What makes it feel like a new section is not a key change, a tempo change or new instrumentation. **Harmonic rhythm drops from two chords per bar to one per two bars — a 4× slowdown — and that alone does it.** Contrast does not require new material.
- The off-the-shelf cousin is [[The Montgomery-Ward Bridge]], `I7 – IV7 – II7 – V7`, which Tin Pan Alley writers used when two A sections were written and eight contrasting bars were needed. Three of its four root moves are fifths; `IV → II` is the seam, and only the V7 is diatonic — I7, IV7 and II7 each bring in one note from outside the key (in C: B♭, E♭ and F♯).
- **[[JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in predictable slots|The two containers are AABA and 16+16]]**, and the first half of a 16+16 must not resolve to I — it has to reach V so the second half has somewhere to launch from.
- The slots are the point. A secondary ii–V to vi early, one to IV soon after, IV → iv → I around the IV chord, V7/V in the last line of the first half, a turnaround in the final bars. A new chart becomes "which variant is this", not 32 arbitrary bars.
- That is also how to memorise one — chunk it the way a phone number is chunked. Name the form, then name the functional units: "a 2-5 to six", not "half-diminished, then dominant, then minor". Learn a chunk once and it is recognised everywhere it appears.

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled reset]]
- [[JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turnaround, answered]]
- [[JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made from harmonic rhythm alone]]
- [[JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in predictable slots]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write the four-chord turnaround, then compress it to two bars, one bar and half a bar. Then take a standard you do not know, mark the form before reading a single chord, and fill it in by chunk name.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a busy eight-bar section of yours and rewrite it with the harmonic rhythm halved, changing nothing else. Decide whether it now reads as a different section.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 4 Test]]

### Lesson 5 — Passing Chords and Reharmonization

**Read**
- [ ] [[Passing Chords]] → *1. Chromatic passing chords (dominant diminished)*, *3. Diatonic passing chords*, *4. Dominant passing chords*
- [ ] [[Reharmonization]] → *The one constraint*, *The techniques, roughly in order of cost*, *A worked example*, *When not to*

**The material**
- The distinction that decides who has to know: **[[JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a substitute replaces|a passing chord connects two chords already in the progression]]**, and the bass player can keep walking the original changes underneath it. A substitution replaces a chord, so everyone plays it.
- **Put the passing chord on the weak beat and the real chord on the heavy beat.** The ear then tracks the actual harmony and hears the insert as colour rather than as a competing change. The exception is a chromatic passing chord written into the harmony itself.
- Four families: a **dominant diminished** a half step below the target (C♯dim7 → Dm7, which is a rootless A7♭9); a **shape slid a fret** into the target, where you think about the destination and never name the passing chord; **diatonic** inserts for stepwise motion; and a **dominant**, plain or tritone-subbed.
- Then the payoff of the whole strand. **[[JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constraint|The melody note must be a usable tone of the new chord]]** — a chord tone or a functioning extension. Not a note the chord contradicts, like a natural 9 over a ♭9 or a natural 4 on the 3rd.
- Everything else is negotiable, which is why you work **melody-first**: write the tune out, decide what each note could be relative to a candidate chord, and choose from there. Choosing chords first and hoping the melody survives is how you get the clashes.
- The cheapest move is **[[JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords|recontextualising a held note]]**. A sustained C is the root of Cmaj7, the ♭3 of Am7, the 5th of Fmaj7, the ♭7 of Dm7, the 3rd of A♭maj7 or the ♭5 of F♯m7♭5 — six meanings, one note.
- The systematic version is **delayed resolution**: harmonise the expected tonic note with anything except the tonic chord and arrive home late. Cdim7, A♭maj7, Fmaj7, D♭maj7 and B♭9 all take the tonic note as a different chord tone, and they chain.
- The rest of the ladder, in order of cost: interpolate a ii in front of any dominant, tritone-sub the dominants, add secondary dominants, change only the bass, hold a pedal point, borrow from the parallel minor — or reharmonize the *rhythm* and leave every chord alone.
- And the discipline: **[[JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement|reharmonization competes with the melody for attention]]**. If the tune is the point, a dense rewrite pulls focus and the song gets worse.
- Let the listener learn the plain version, then change what is underneath it. It reads as development rather than confusion, and it hands you a second section for free — which for an arrangement means verse 1 plain, verse 2 reharmonised.

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a substitute replaces]]
- [[JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constraint]]
- [[JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords]]
- [[JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — fill every transition of a I–vi–ii–V with a diatonic passing chord on the weak beats, then move them onto the strong beats and hear the progression stop reading.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — take a song of yours with a repeated section. Leave the first statement alone and reharmonise only the repeat, checking every melody note is a legal tone of its new chord.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 5 Test]]

### Lesson 6 — Modal Jazz

**Read**
- [ ] [[Modal Jazz]] → *The reaction it was*, *What replaces functional harmony*, *Modal interchange is a different thing — don't confuse them*, *Why it matters for the music you actually make*, *Modal islands — treating each chord of a non-functional vamp as its own mode*

**The material**
- Modal jazz removed the changes almost entirely — *So What* is 16 bars of D Dorian, 8 of E♭ Dorian, 8 more of D Dorian. **When harmony stops moving, everything else has to carry the music**, and that constraint is the whole subject.
- **[[JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony|Four things replace functional motion]]**: the mode's own character as material, quartal voicings, pedal points and drones, and rhythm, dynamics and texture marking the form.
- **It is not modal interchange.** Modal jazz holds one mode for many bars — a static approach to form. Interchange borrows a chord from a parallel mode inside functional harmony and returns. They share a word and almost nothing else.
- This is the jazz idiom closest to how loop-based music works. A four-bar loop on Fmaj7 is exactly the situation *So What* is in, so the strand's most directly useful material is here rather than in the substitution lessons.
- **[[JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to be sounded|Dorian's natural 6, Lydian's ♯4, Mixolydian's ♭7, Phrygian's ♭2]]** — land on it and the mode is established, avoid it and the music collapses into plain major or minor. In D Dorian the note is B.
- A loop that never plays the ♯4 is not Lydian, it is major with a Lydian label. In a vamp of several chords that are not functionally connected, treat each chord as its own **modal island** with its own scale rather than hunting for one key that explains all of them.
- **[[JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode without naming a chord|The *So What* voicing is three fourths with a major third on top]]** — E A D G B from the bottom. A stack of thirds names a chord and so implies a function, which is what this music is avoiding.
- Fourths sound open and unassigned, which is where the hollow, floating sound comes from. They also sit beautifully under a vocal: sparse, with no strong 3rd fighting the topline. Over sixteen bars of one chord they remove the commitment that gets tiring.
- The arrangement consequence, and it is the transferable one: with no chord changes to signal a section, **one new element — a texture, a countermelody, a register shift — reads as a whole new section.**

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony]]
- [[JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to be sounded]]
- [[JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode without naming a chord]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — loop one chord and improvise over it without ever playing the characteristic note, then again landing on it deliberately. Name the mode you actually hear in each take.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — voice a static vamp as tertian chords and then as the *So What* stack, both under a melody you have. Then write four sections over it differing only in texture.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 6 Test]]

### Lesson 7 — Bebop Vocabulary

**Read**
- [ ] [[Bebop Vocabulary]] → *1. The bebop scales — why an eighth note*, *2. Enclosures — approach a note from both sides*, *3. Approach notes*, *8. CESH — chromatic embellishment of static harmony*, *Transferring this outside jazz*
- [ ] [[Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction]] → *The core method*, *Why this works*

**The material**
- The melodic side of the strand, and useful here mostly for writing — these devices are what make a MIDI lead sound played rather than programmed, and they transfer to horn lines, guitar fills and vocal runs.
- **[[JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note is rhythmic|A bebop scale is a seven-note scale with one chromatic passing tone added]]**, and the reason is rhythmic. Seven notes in straight eighths and the chord tones drift onto offbeats; the eighth note puts them back on the beat every bar.
- Bebop dominant on G is G A B C D E F F♯ G. The rule generalises: the extra note goes wherever it makes chord tones fall on strong beats, and if yours already do you do not need one. This is also what makes a walking-ish bassline land.
- **[[JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes|An enclosure surrounds a target before playing it]]** — for a target of C, D♭–B–C, or D–B–C, or B–D♭–C, or the four-note D–D♭–B–C. An approach note is the one-note cousin, strongest from a half step below because it borrows the leading-tone pull.
- Put them on the note you want heard, usually a chord tone on a downbeat — **and not on every note.** Enclosures are punctuation; wall to wall, a line stops having a shape. Enclose the second note of a two-note synth hook and it stops sounding quantised from scratch.
- **[[JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under static harmony|CESH walks one note by half step across several bars]]** while the harmony stays still. An approach note targets a single arrival; this is a sustained line, closer to a bass device borrowed into the melody.
- It is the direct answer to a vamp going static, which pairs it with Lesson 6 — when the harmony is deliberately refusing to move, this supplies motion without breaking that decision.
- The practice method underneath all of it: **[[JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick|learn the solo by ear, chunk it, analyse each chunk against its chord, reduce it to one named concept, then improvise your own lines from the concepts]]**.
- The fourth step is the one that gets skipped. What you need from a great solo is a nudge toward somewhere, not a part to reproduce — and a per-chord concept list is a template that yields a whole session of new lines rather than one memorised chorus.
- What does not transfer is density. Bebop's note rate is a genre convention rather than a principle, and importing it wholesale into a trap beat just sounds busy.

**Concepts**
- [[JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note is rhythmic]]
- [[JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes]]
- [[JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under static harmony]]
- [[JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick]]

**Homework**
- [ ] **Review** — write a one-bar eighth-note run on a seven-note scale and mark where the chord tones land, then add the passing tone and mark them again. Then enclose only the three notes that matter in a melody you have.
- [ ] **Apply** (~15 min) — hold one chord for four bars in Ableton and walk a single inner voice down chromatically underneath it. Then take eight bars of a solo you know and write one named concept per chord.
- [ ] **Test** — [[Course 31 — Lesson 7 Test]]

blocks.html:
• The premise before any rule: . In common-practice harmony the triad is the default and the 7th is a colour; here the 7th is the default and the triad is the special case.
  • Everything downstream assumes four notes. Guide tones need a 7th to exist; a tritone substitution has nothing to preserve without one. Reading a jazz chart as triads is not a simpler reading, it is a wrong one.
  • The cell the language is built from: , and in minor Dm7♭5 – G7♭9 – Cm7. The roots fall a fifth twice — the circle of fifths in miniature, and the strongest root motion in tonal music stacked back to back.
  • The three minor-key differences are forced rather than chosen. The ♭5 is simply the 6th degree of natural minor; the ♭9 comes from harmonic minor, whose raised leading tone is what makes the V a dominant at all; and the tonic is ambiguous on purpose between m7, m6 and mMaj7.
  • The units chain, which is what makes them worth learning: make the I of one unit the ii of the next, or drop a ii–V in front of any chord you want to arrive at. | Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 | Cm7 F7 | B♭maj7 | is two of them, a whole step apart.
  • The reading tip: . Whatever it points at is the intended I — even when the I never arrives.
  • Two cases where it does not. The deceptive move goes to vi or ♭VI instead. The unresolved ii–V moves straight to the next one, which is why a bebop head can look like it changes key every two bars when it does not.
  • Outside jazz it shows up three ways: as the whole loop, as a turnaround pushing back to the top of a plain pop verse, or stripped to guide tones so it survives an arrangement with almost no chordal instrument.

blocks.html:
• The highest-leverage idea in the strand: . The 3rd says major or minor, the 7th says major, dominant or minor. Together they name the chord.
  • The root tells you nothing about quality and the 5th tells you almost nothing, which is why the 5th is the first note dropped from a voicing. This is why a bass and a horn can imply a full progression with no chordal instrument present.
  • The one exception is m7♭5. Cm7♭5 and Cm7 share E♭ and B♭, so only the ♭5 separates them — a m7♭5 voicing that drops its 5th states the wrong chord.
  • Now the mechanism: and the lines go C → B → B and F → F → E. One voice holds while the other moves a half step, then they swap.
  • Nothing leaps, and it is not luck — that is what root motion by fifths does. It is also the concrete test for a substitution: one that keeps the guide-tone lines stepwise is a good one, which is exactly why the tritone sub works.
  • Write the two lines before you voice anything. Fix any leap larger than a step by inverting the chord or choosing a different extension, then decide the full voicings. Solving the horizontal problem first is faster and it produces smoother results.
  • The practical form is the — root, 3rd and 7th, no 5th and no extensions, usually with the 7th below the 3rd. Extensions stack on top: shell plus 9, shell plus 13.
  • On a dense arrangement a shell is often the right voicing rather than the simple one. A full five-note chord under a busy vocal is usually the mistake, and cutting a crowded chordal instrument to shells frees mids without losing any harmony.

  • Loop-based music is all turnaround. Three moves that work in production: end on V7 or ♭II7; end on the ii, leaving the V implied so the loop never closes; or change only the last bar between repeats — two loops of material for one bar of writing.

  • Four bars of a static loop do not get boring because four bars of real movement answer them. That question-and-answer shape inside one eight-bar unit is directly transferable to a verse — and it is the answer to why a loop that is fine on its own tires over sixteen bars.
  • in B♭ — four dominants, each resolving down a fifth, and only the last, F7, is the key's own V7. A pure circle-of-fifths run that leaves the key and walks back in.
  • What makes it feel like a new section is not a key change, a tempo change or new instrumentation. Harmonic rhythm drops from two chords per bar to one per two bars — a 4× slowdown — and that alone does it. Contrast does not require new material.
  • The off-the-shelf cousin is The Montgomery-Ward Bridge, I7 – IV7 – II7 – V7, which Tin Pan Alley writers used when two A sections were written and eight contrasting bars were needed. Three of its four root moves are fifths; IV → II is the seam, and only the V7 is diatonic — I7, IV7 and II7 each bring in one note from outside the key (in C: B♭, E♭ and F♯).
  • , and the first half of a 16+16 must not resolve to I — it has to reach V so the second half has somewhere to launch from.
  • The slots are the point. A secondary ii–V to vi early, one to IV soon after, IV → iv → I around the IV chord, V7/V in the last line of the first half, a turnaround in the final bars. A new chart becomes "which variant is this", not 32 arbitrary bars.
  • That is also how to memorise one — chunk it the way a phone number is chunked. Name the form, then name the functional units: "a 2-5 to six", not "half-diminished, then dominant, then minor". Learn a chunk once and it is recognised everywhere it appears.

Reharmonization → The one constraint, The techniques, roughly in order of cost, A worked example, When not to

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The distinction that decides who has to know: , and the bass player can keep walking the original changes underneath it. A substitution replaces a chord, so everyone plays it.
  • Put the passing chord on the weak beat and the real chord on the heavy beat. The ear then tracks the actual harmony and hears the insert as colour rather than as a competing change. The exception is a chromatic passing chord written into the harmony itself.
  • Four families: a dominant diminished a half step below the target (C♯dim7 → Dm7, which is a rootless A7♭9); a shape slid a fret into the target, where you think about the destination and never name the passing chord; diatonic inserts for stepwise motion; and a dominant, plain or tritone-subbed.
  • Then the payoff of the whole strand. — a chord tone or a functioning extension. Not a note the chord contradicts, like a natural 9 over a ♭9 or a natural 4 on the 3rd.
  • Everything else is negotiable, which is why you work melody-first: write the tune out, decide what each note could be relative to a candidate chord, and choose from there. Choosing chords first and hoping the melody survives is how you get the clashes.
  • The cheapest move is . A sustained C is the root of Cmaj7, the ♭3 of Am7, the 5th of Fmaj7, the ♭7 of Dm7, the 3rd of A♭maj7 or the ♭5 of F♯m7♭5 — six meanings, one note.
  • The systematic version is delayed resolution: harmonise the expected tonic note with anything except the tonic chord and arrive home late. Cdim7, A♭maj7, Fmaj7, D♭maj7 and B♭9 all take the tonic note as a different chord tone, and they chain.
  • The rest of the ladder, in order of cost: interpolate a ii in front of any dominant, tritone-sub the dominants, add secondary dominants, change only the bass, hold a pedal point, borrow from the parallel minor — or reharmonize the rhythm and leave every chord alone.
  • And the discipline: . If the tune is the point, a dense rewrite pulls focus and the song gets worse.
  • Let the listener learn the plain version, then change what is underneath it. It reads as development rather than confusion, and it hands you a second section for free — which for an arrangement means verse 1 plain, verse 2 reharmonised.

Modal Jazz → The reaction it was, What replaces functional harmony, Modal interchange is a different thing — don't confuse them, Why it matters for the music you actually make, Modal islands — treating each chord of a non-functional vamp as its own mode

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• Modal jazz removed the changes almost entirely — So What is 16 bars of D Dorian, 8 of E♭ Dorian, 8 more of D Dorian. When harmony stops moving, everything else has to carry the music, and that constraint is the whole subject.
  • : the mode's own character as material, quartal voicings, pedal points and drones, and rhythm, dynamics and texture marking the form.
  • It is not modal interchange. Modal jazz holds one mode for many bars — a static approach to form. Interchange borrows a chord from a parallel mode inside functional harmony and returns. They share a word and almost nothing else.
  • This is the jazz idiom closest to how loop-based music works. A four-bar loop on Fmaj7 is exactly the situation So What is in, so the strand's most directly useful material is here rather than in the substitution lessons.
  • — land on it and the mode is established, avoid it and the music collapses into plain major or minor. In D Dorian the note is B.
  • A loop that never plays the ♯4 is not Lydian, it is major with a Lydian label. In a vamp of several chords that are not functionally connected, treat each chord as its own modal island with its own scale rather than hunting for one key that explains all of them.
  • — E A D G B from the bottom. A stack of thirds names a chord and so implies a function, which is what this music is avoiding.
  • Fourths sound open and unassigned, which is where the hollow, floating sound comes from. They also sit beautifully under a vocal: sparse, with no strong 3rd fighting the topline. Over sixteen bars of one chord they remove the commitment that gets tiring.
  • The arrangement consequence, and it is the transferable one: with no chord changes to signal a section, one new element — a texture, a countermelody, a register shift — reads as a whole new section.

Bebop Vocabulary → 1. The bebop scales — why an eighth note, 2. Enclosures — approach a note from both sides, 3. Approach notes, 8. CESH — chromatic embellishment of static harmony, Transferring this outside jazz
Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction → The core method, Why this works

blocks.label: The material
blocks.html:
• The melodic side of the strand, and useful here mostly for writing — these devices are what make a MIDI lead sound played rather than programmed, and they transfer to horn lines, guitar fills and vocal runs.
  • , and the reason is rhythmic. Seven notes in straight eighths and the chord tones drift onto offbeats; the eighth note puts them back on the beat every bar.
  • Bebop dominant on G is G A B C D E F F♯ G. The rule generalises: the extra note goes wherever it makes chord tones fall on strong beats, and if yours already do you do not need one. This is also what makes a walking-ish bassline land.
  • — for a target of C, D♭–B–C, or D–B–C, or B–D♭–C, or the four-note D–D♭–B–C. An approach note is the one-note cousin, strongest from a half step below because it borrows the leading-tone pull.
  • Put them on the note you want heard, usually a chord tone on a downbeat — and not on every note. Enclosures are punctuation; wall to wall, a line stops having a shape. Enclose the second note of a two-note synth hook and it stops sounding quantised from scratch.
  • while the harmony stays still. An approach note targets a single arrival; this is a sustained line, closer to a bass device borrowed into the melody.
  • It is the direct answer to a vamp going static, which pairs it with Lesson 6 — when the harmony is deliberately refusing to move, this supplies motion without breaking that decision.
  • The practice method underneath all of it: .
  • The fourth step is the one that gets skipped. What you need from a great solo is a nudge toward somewhere, not a part to reproduce — and a per-chord concept list is a template that yields a whole session of new lines rather than one memorised chorus.
  • What does not transfer is density. Bebop's note rate is a genre convention rather than a principle, and importing it wholesale into a trap beat just sounds busy.
