ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.id: ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B section, not a new idea
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.title: ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B section, not a new idea
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.short: A boring loop needs a B section, not a new idea
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.q: You made a loop, loved it, and an hour later it feels worthless. What's the actual diagnosis?
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.a: The idea was never bad — it was alone. A loop that bores you isn't asking for a new idea, it's asking for a B section. Kenny Beats: "a lot of ideas you're throwing out are really good ideas missing one other little idea to point out what it is you're doing." There is also a hard ceiling here: no amount of subtractive variation on one loop sustains a full song — a genuinely second loop is eventually unavoidable, and most attempts at it will be discardable before one lands.
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.why: Loop-itis is the single biggest reason projects die in the folder, and it's a misdiagnosis rather than a skill gap. Expecting the mediocre second-loop attempts is part of the technique, not a sign something's wrong.
ARR-C01 — A boring loop needs a B sectio.drill: Open three abandoned projects. For each, write one sentence describing what a complementary B section would do. Don't build them yet.

ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.id: ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B section
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.title: ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B section
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.short: How to actually write the B section
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.q: Give the three-step method, and the test that tells you it worked.
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.a: 1. Duplicate the drums, strip everything else — bass, keys, melody out. 2. Write a complementary part over them: different chords, opposite density, different mood (a sad/loose/simple B under a full/happy/soulful A). 3. Test the return — playing out of B back into A should feel like oh my god, we're home. That coming-home lift is the whole point: the right B section makes the A section better.
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.why: The test is the part people skip. A B section that's merely different isn't working; it has to make the return land. Extend the same move and you get A-B-C form — verse chords, different pre-hook chords, different hook chords.
ARR-C02 — How to actually write the B se.drill: Take one loop. Duplicate the drums, strip everything, write a B. Then loop B→A four times and rate the return honestly.

ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.id: ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B section
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.title: ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B section
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.short: Two harmonic routes into a B section
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.q: Name two ways to pick B-section chords that guarantee contrast without breaking the song.
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.a: The relative key — find the relative major/minor (up three semitones from a minor root) and centre the B progression there. Identical scale tones, different centre, so contrast is guaranteed and the return resolves cleanly. The withheld chord — audit which diatonic chords the verse and chorus never used (say both used C, D, E, G, A but never F) and open the bridge on exactly that one; the ear has never heard it in this song, so its arrival alone signals somewhere new.
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.why: Both solve the same problem — new but not random — from opposite ends. The withheld-chord move costs nothing and works before any instrumentation change lands.
ARR-C03 — Two harmonic routes into a B s.drill: Take a finished song of yours. List every chord used in verse and chorus. Name the diatonic chords you never used. Start a bridge on one.

ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.id: ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is scheduled absence
ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.title: ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is scheduled absence
ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.q: What does "Let the Beat Build" demonstrate, and what's the general principle?
ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.a: Hi-hat → clap → clap+snares → kick → bass → everything in at the hook. One idea, minutes of interest, purely from when things enter. The general principle: arrangement interest is scheduled absence, not added layers. Schedule the absences deliberately — pull the kick for a section, the 808, all the drums, the melody. A middle ground between gone and full: temporarily attenuate an element's top end rather than muting it, then restore it later.
ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.why: It inverts the instinct. When a section feels flat the reflex is to add, and the move is almost always to decide what leaves and when it comes back.
ARR-C04 — Arrangement interest is schedu.drill: Take a full 8-bar loop. Stagger every element's first entrance across 32 bars without writing a single new note.

ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.id: ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, and pull back before the end
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.title: ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, and pull back before the end
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.short: The energy curve — one apex, and pull back before the end
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.q: Sketch the shape of a whole song's energy, and give the two rules about how energy changes at boundaries.
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.a: Start deliberately low so there's room to build; build to exactly one clear apex, not several equal peaks; then pull the energy back down a notch after the apex before the ending, because sustaining the peak to the outro reads as exhausting rather than climactic. At each major boundary, add or remove 3–4 elements simultaneously rather than gradually, so the transition reads as a felt jump — and punctuate it with a crash.
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.why: Both rules cut against instinct: gradual change reads as drift rather than transition, and refusing to come down after the peak flattens the peak retroactively.
ARR-C05 — The energy curve — one apex, a.drill: Draw the energy curve of a reference track you love, boundary by boundary. Then draw yours. Compare where the apex sits.

ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.id: ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, and breaking them on purpose
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.title: ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, and breaking them on purpose
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.short: Section-length conventions, and breaking them on purpose
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.q: Contrast the house and pop templates, and say what makes a broken structure read as deliberate.
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.a: House — a flat 16-bar-everywhere rule. Pop — a proportional template that holds across very different songs: a short ~4-bar intro with verse, pre-chorus and chorus each roughly double it (~8), plus the pop-specific move that the chorus gets longer each time it returns — teasing on first appearance, longest at the very end. Breaking it reads as considered rather than sloppy only because the convention is well established: a Billie Eilish-style verse→drop→verse→drop at speed, with a 3-bar buildup, violates a pattern the listener already knows.
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.why: You can't deliberately break a rule you can't state. And a 10-bar loop against a vocal written in 8-bar phrases just reads as off — trim to 8 rather than leaving the odd length in.
ARR-C06 — Section-length conventions, an.drill: Count the bars of every section in three reference tracks. Note where the chorus lengthens on repeat.

ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.id: ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition; risers are the last step
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.title: ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition; risers are the last step
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.short: Automation is the transition; risers are the last step
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.q: A transition sounds stitched together. Why is reaching for a riser the wrong first move?
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.a: Because it papers over a transition that doesn't work. An analysis of ~100 reference tracks found most weren't leaning on reverse cymbals, swooshes or snare rolls at all — those are icing once parts already connect. The real technique happens earlier: automating existing devices (filters, detune, sends, wet/dry) across the section so one part flows into the next. Three shapes: a micro drop (instant filter wet/dry snap plus a gradual percussion sweep), a macro drop (max-contrast section change via kick filtering, bass removal, slight detune, timbre shift), and a wet/dry drop (send automation contrasting wet-vs-dry and wide-vs-mono instead of tone).
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.why: It relocates the transition from an inserted object to a property of the two sections. Also worth mining your own elements — a bassline repurposed as a sweep — before importing a sample.
ARR-C07 — Automation is the transition;.drill: Take a transition that isn't working. Delete every riser and impact. Fix it with filter and send automation only.

ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.id: ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged across the boundary
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.title: ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged across the boundary
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.short: Carry one element unchanged across the boundary
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.q: Two sections either side of a transition sound very different. What stops it reading as an abrupt cut?
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.a: Keep one recognisable element — a melodic motif, a signature sound — playing continuously and unchanged straight through the boundary. It gives the listener something to hold while everything else changes underneath. The complementary device on the same axis: a theme restated later in a new key reads as development rather than repetition, so a returning idea can feel like it's moved without a full modulation plan.
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.why: Connective tissue is a separate job from contrast, and the two are easy to confuse. Maximum contrast plus one constant thread beats moderate contrast everywhere.
ARR-C08 — Carry one element unchanged ac.drill: Find your most abrupt section change. Pick one element and let it run unchanged across the boundary. A/B.

ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.id: ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before the payoff
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.title: ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before the payoff
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.short: Strip the layers right before the payoff
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.q: You've layered elements in across a build. What happens immediately before the drop?
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.a: Cut all of them — so only the most essential element carries through into the structural boundary. The sudden reduction reads as dramatic tension release rather than a mistake, and it reinforces whatever hits at the payoff. Related devices on the same principle: a big reverb wash sells an emptied section as intentional, and scheduled silence is legitimate material.
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.why: It's the counterintuitive half of building — the last gesture before maximum is minimum. Subtraction reads as suspense because a listener can't track many simultaneous parts, so less makes what remains read as more.
ARR-C09 — Strip the layers right before.drill: On a build you've written, mute everything but one element for the last two bars before the drop. Compare against the stacked version.

ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.id: ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, and the artist sets it
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.title: ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, and the artist sets it
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.short: Too busy is a relative term, and the artist sets it
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.q: Give the simplicity referee: the number, and the principle behind it.
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.a: Five to seven sounds — the extra perc layer always matters less than it feels like it does while you're producing. Lil Baby cut Kenny Beats off at that count on "Toes" and "Smack the Baby". The principle is that "too busy" is relative, so it needs a referee outside your own ears: let the performer or the vocal decide, because the artist is the best common denominator for what the record actually needs.
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.why: The bias only runs one way — nobody over-strips while producing, everyone over-adds, and each layer feels essential at the moment you place it. Naming a number gives you something to check against when the loop is still fun to build on. It's also the counterweight to the rest of this lesson: scheduled absence only works if there's a limit on what got scheduled in.
ARR-C10 — Too busy is a relative term, a.drill: Count the sounds in the beat you're on. Over seven, mute the one you added most recently and play it back.

BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.id: BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — roots first, by ear
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.title: BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — roots first, by ear
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.short: Groove first, bass second — roots first, by ear
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.q: What are the first two steps of writing a bassline, and what's the trap in each?
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.a: 1. Finish the drum groove, then write the bass around it. The trap: bass notes do not have to start on the kicks — lock to the pocket, not the kick map. Rhythmic choices made with no drums playing are provisional and a real loop will overrule them. 2. Land the root notes under the chords before any decoration — by ear. The trap: if you can't hear the roots, that's an ear-training gap, not a writing gap. The beginner-tier version is genuinely one root per bar on each chord change; quality doesn't matter yet because only the root is sounding.
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.why: Almost every bad bassline is one of these two steps skipped. Register is the third trap in the same breath: the identical root line an octave too low goes from fine to undefined mud — move it up rather than processing it.
BAS-C01 — Groove first, bass second — ro.drill: Write a bassline over C–Am–F–G as one root per bar. Then add subdivision. Then add the octave. Stop there.

BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.id: BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabulary
BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.title: BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabulary
BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.q: What's the default move for adding motion to a root-based line, and where do fills come from?
BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.a: Jump up the octave and back, occasionally through a passing tone — a 5th above is the classic. A strong bassline can be mainly octaves with the occasional tiny fill. For the fills: steal the melody's rhythm — mirror the rhythm of what the guitar or melody just played, not necessarily its notes, so the busyness hides inside existing phrasing. Then record busy and mute down — play a too-busy line through the whole loop and delete everything but the killer moments, never repeating the same fill in consecutive phrases.
BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.why: Octave motion is where a disco or funk line's bounce actually comes from — it mimics how a real player physically moves around the neck. And rhythm-stealing keeps added busyness cohesive instead of arbitrary.
BAS-C02 — Octaves are the default vocabu.drill: Take a root-per-bar line. Add octave jumps only. Then add exactly one fill, borrowed rhythmically from the keys part.

BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.id: BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two basslines at once
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.title: BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two basslines at once
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.short: The band test, and never two basslines at once
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.q: Give the sanity check on a written line, and the one hard rule about layering bass.
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.a: The band test — imagine a bassist physically playing it; if no player would phrase it that way, rewrite it (unless the unplayable line is the point, e.g. reversed audio). The hard rule: never run two genuinely different basslines simultaneously. Chords and melody tolerate multiple simultaneous parts; two distinct low-end melodic lines clash and read as mud rather than richness. Doubling the same line on two instruments is a different thing entirely and is fine.
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.why: The band test is the same four-limb constraint that governs realistic drum programming, applied to one player instead of a kit. The layering rule is where most muddy low ends actually come from — not EQ, arrangement.
BAS-C03 — The band test, and never two b.drill: Play your busiest bassline and try to physically play it, or air-play it. Then solo your low end and count how many distinct melodic lines are running.

BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.title: BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under static harmony
BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.short: Busy basslines only work under static harmony
BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.q: When can the bass show off, and when can it only play roots?
BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.a: Showcase basslines — Chris Brown "Fine China", Thundercat — work over static held chords. When the harmony above is busy, only root notes work. And with a vocal or a synth hook on top, the bass supports; it doesn't compete. The corollary is the useful half: two chords means the riffs ARE the line — static harmony moves all the interest into the fills between roots, and one perfectly placed fill can be the entire event.
BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.why: It reframes "how busy should the bass be" as a question about what else is moving, rather than a taste call. Most overwritten basslines are written against harmony that was already doing the work.
BAS-C04 — Busy basslines only work under.drill: Take a busy bassline. Freeze the harmony to two chords and hear it come alive. Then put a vocal on top and hear it stop working.

BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.id: BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversation
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.title: BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversation
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.short: Bass and keys as a conversation
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.q: State the soul formula for arranging bass against harmony.
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.a: Keep the harmony dead simple — Lophiile's Leon Thomas "Mutt" example is two chords — and make the arrangement carry it: what story is the bass telling, what story are the keys telling, and do they talk to each other? Three instruments going, arranged as a call and response rather than as stacked parts. The polyphonic version of the same instinct: a bass patch playing its own upper harmony voice a 3rd or 5th above the root, in contrary motion to the root line.
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.why: It's the difference between bass as root support and bass as a voice. Very Beatles — McCartney lines are melodic statements, which is the tradition closest to your own writing.
BAS-C05 — Bass and keys as a conversatio.drill: Take a two-chord loop. Write a keys part and a bass part that answer each other rather than moving together.

BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.id: BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make it funky
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.title: BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make it funky
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.short: Syncopate off the kick to make it funky
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.q: What single move makes a bassline funky, and what's the connective device between phrases?
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.a: Switch to a 16th-note grid and deliberately move some bass notes off the kick's strong beats (1, 2, 3, 4) onto the weaker in-between spots — named as "the key to making a bassline funky fresh". Layer octave uppers and downers on top for bounce. Between phrases: a chromatic walk-up or walk-down, stepping through out-of-scale passing tones toward the next section's starting note — it works independently of whatever scale the line is in.
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.why: Bass has three simultaneous jobs — rhythmic (locking with the kick), harmonic (playing the root) and melodic (carrying hooks and fills). Syncopation is where you deliberately loosen the first one without losing it.
BAS-C06 — Syncopate off the kick to make.drill: Take a line locked to the kick. Move a third of its notes onto 16th-note offbeats. Then connect two phrases with a chromatic walk-up.

BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.id: BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don't EQ both
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.title: BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don't EQ both
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.short: Decide who owns the sub — don't EQ both
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.q: Kick and bass are colliding in the low end. What's the diagnostic and the fix?
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.a: Diagnostic: put an analyser EQ on each and play them together to find where each fundamental actually peaks — a real case had the kick peaking ~55 Hz with a second bump at ~120 and the bass also at ~55, a direct collision. Fix: pick one to hold the sub (the source with more low-end content, if the kick is otherwise interchangeable) and high-pass the other up until the clash stops. If high-passing the kick guts it, swap in a kick with more inherent high-end character first, then cut that one.
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.why: Ownership is a decision, not a compromise. EQing both leaves you with two thin sources and the same collision. Sidechaining and kick-length automation by section are the same decision made in time rather than frequency.
BAS-C07 — Decide who owns the sub — don'.drill: Analyse your current kick and bass fundamentals. Write down which one owns the sub. High-pass the other until it stops fighting.

BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.id: BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then drop it back
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.title: BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then drop it back
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.short: Tune the 808 up high, then drop it back
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.q: How do you tune an 808, and how do you get slides on an audio 808?
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.a: Pitch it up an octave or more to hear the note centre, tune it there, then return it to the sub register. Never guess at pitch down at 40 Hz. Slides on audio 808s: pitch to the note with warp off (a clean stretch), then set warp mode to Tones — best for bass — and draw the slides with the clip's transposition envelope. Easier than MIDI slides. Grace notes clicked in just before a target read as bends when no wheel is handy.
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.why: Sub-register pitch is genuinely inaudible as pitch on most systems, so the ear can't do this job in place. It's also the same principle as tuning the kick — a low end on the wrong note fights the song.
BAS-C08 — Tune the 808 up high, then dro.drill: Detune an 808 deliberately, then tune it by ear at the sub octave. Fail. Then do it an octave up and drop it back. Compare with a tuner.

BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.id: BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-not-compressor
BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.title: BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-not-compressor
BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.q: The bass part is right but the tone is wrong. What's the escalation, and how do you control it?
BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.a: Walk the ladder: synth patch → a different synth → a real or sampled bass guitar (Scarbee Rickenbacker, NI Motown, Trilian) → DI plus amp sim. Then control the level with a limiter, not a compressor, saturate for body, and sidechain last. Don't skip rungs by processing a patch that was never going to get there.
BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.why: Same lesson as swapping a kick sample rather than stacking chains — the fix is upstream. The limiter choice matters because bass needs a hard ceiling with its dynamics intact, not gain-riding that pumps the low end.
BAS-C09 — The sound ladder, and limiter-.drill: Take a bass part whose tone you dislike. Walk one full rung up the ladder before touching a device. Then add limiter → saturation → sidechain, in that order.

BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.id: BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line, all of them share a root
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.title: BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line, all of them share a root
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.short: Every section gets a new line, all of them share a root
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.q: Writing bass across a whole song: what changes section to section, and what stays the same?
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.a: A genuinely new rhythm, register and contour for each section — while every line keeps returning to the same root as home. Rising section, peak, B section, wind-down: four different lines, matched to each section's energy rather than the same pattern played louder or busier. The shared tonal center is what keeps all four reading as one song instead of four sketches.
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.why: It's a different scale of decision from the groove-level moves. Syncopating off the kick makes one bar funky; this is what stops a four-minute record sounding like one loop with the faders moved. It also gives you a concrete test for a section that isn't working: if the line is only louder or busier than the last one, it hasn't changed, and if it has wandered off the root, the song has come apart.
BAS-C10 — Every section gets a new line,.drill: Name the four sections of a track you're on and say what rhythm, register and contour the bass takes in each. Then check they land on the same root.

BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form.title: BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form
BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form.q: Write out a standard 12-bar blues in A. What are the three chords?
BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form.a: A7, D7, E7 — I7, IV7, V7. A A A A / D D A A / E D A E — three four-bar phrases, with bar 12 as the turnaround back to the top.
BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form.why: This is the foundation the whole strand sits on, and it's transposable — the same shape in any key, which is why blues is the standard first improvising form.
BLU-C01 — The 12-bar form.drill: Write it out in A, E and G from memory. Then play each.

BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.id: BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant 7th
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.title: BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant 7th
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.short: Why every chord is a dominant 7th
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.q: In a blues all three chords are usually dominant 7ths — including the tonic. Why, when the major scale doesn't give you that?
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.a: Because blues doesn't follow major-key functional harmony. The dominant 7th is the home sound, not a chord that needs resolving. The ♭7 is colour, not tension.
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.why: This is the single most important idea in the strand. It explains why one scale works over all three chords, why the ♭3 isn't an error, and why the form circles rather than resolving. Without it, every other blues fact looks like a violation of the rules.
BLU-C02 — Why every chord is a dominant.drill: Play I–IV–V in A as plain triads, then as A7–D7–E7. Name what changed.

BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.id: BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor blues
BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.title: BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor blues
BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.q: What's a quick change? How does an 8-bar blues differ? How does a minor blues differ harmonically?
BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.a: Quick change — bar 2 moves to the IV instead of staying on I. 8-bar blues is a real, separate form ("Key to the Highway"), not a truncation. Minor blues uses i7 iv7 v7, often with a ♭VI at bar 9 — but the V frequently stays dominant, because you still want the leading tone pulling home.
BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.why: Quick change and 8-bar both blank; minor blues got half credit for 'minor 3rd instead of major 3rd', which is the right core idea. The V-stays-dominant detail is the part that's easy to get wrong.
BLU-C03 — Quick change, 8-bar and minor.drill: Write a quick-change 12-bar in A and a minor blues in Am. Note where the V differs.

BLU-C04 — Turnarounds.title: BLU-C04 — Turnarounds
BLU-C04 — Turnarounds.q: What is a turnaround, where does it happen, and give one in A.
BLU-C04 — Turnarounds.a: The last two bars (11–12) — a figure that leads back to the top of the form. Its job is to break the resolution and usually land on V, so the ear expects bar 1 again. In A: A7 – F♯7 – B7 – E7, or a chromatic line descending over an A pedal.
BLU-C04 — Turnarounds.why: Both blank. Without a turnaround the form sounds finished every twelve bars — ending on V is what makes it circular. Any short sequence that creates motion and lands on V will do the job.
BLU-C04 — Turnarounds.drill: Play the A7–F♯7–B7–E7 turnaround, then loop back to bar 1. Then find one in E.

BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.id: BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.title: BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.short: Call and response is the form
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.q: How is call and response built into the 12-bar form, and how does it show up in performance?
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.a: The form is call and response: AAB. Bars 1–4 state a line (call), 5–8 repeat it, 9–12 answer it. In performance the vocal states a phrase and the guitar or horn answers in the gaps — the space in the form is where the response lives.
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.why: The repeat in bars 5–8 is the structural point — it gives the listener the line twice before resolving, and gives the singer time to land the answer. It's also why blues arrangements leave so much room.
BLU-C05 — Call and response is the form.drill: Take any blues lyric and mark its A / A / B sections against the twelve bars.

BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.id: BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.title: BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.short: Blue notes and the blues scale
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.q: What are the blue notes? Name the notes of the A blues scale.
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.a: Blue notes are the ♭3, ♭5 and ♭7, played against a major or dominant background. A blues scale: A C D E♭ E G — minor pentatonic plus the ♭5, where the ♭5 is a passing tone, never a resting note.
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.why: A common confusion: the ♭5 forms a tritone with the root, but blue notes are the three flattened degrees, not an interval. Sitting on the ♭5 sounds wrong; passing through it between the 4th and 5th is the most characteristic sound in the vocabulary.
BLU-C06 — Blue notes and the blues scale.drill: Play the A blues scale ascending and descending. Then stop on the E♭ — hear why it's a passing note.

BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong.title: BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong
BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong.q: The blues scale has a ♭3 but the chords have major 3rds. Why isn't that just wrong?
BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong.a: Three reasons. 1) The friction IS the sound — the grind between ♭3 and ♮3 is what 'bluesy' means. 2) Blues isn't functional major/minor — the scale is imposed over the chords, not derived from them. 3) The note is a region, not a pitch — players bend the ♭3 up toward the ♮3 and sit between them. The blues has microtonality built in.
BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong.why: Point 3 is what actually resolves the apparent contradiction — notation can only approximate what's played. It's also why pitch-correction software struggles with blues vocals (Vocal Tuning). And the underrated half: over a dominant, three of minor pentatonic's five notes are the chord's own tones (root, 5th, ♭7), so the ♭3 is the only note in it that deliberately fights the chord. It does not avoid the natural 4th — in A that's the D in A C D E G — which is the one note that genuinely clashes against a major 3rd; blues passes through it rather than resting on it, the same way it treats the ♭5. Major pentatonic is the scale that leaves the 4th out.
BLU-C07 — Why the ♭3 isn't wrong.drill: Over an A7 vamp, play the ♭3 (C), then bend it toward C♯ and sit between them.

BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.id: BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.title: BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.short: Blues into rock and hip hop
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.q: Name a way blues harmony or form shows up in rock or hip hop, and trace how it got there.
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.a: Rock took the 12-bar form and the pentatonic vocabulary almost wholesale — early Beatles and Stones material is blues form with different production. Hip hop inherited it through sampling: soul and funk records built on blues harmony got sampled, so the ♭3/♭7 vocabulary and call-and-response phrasing survive in the loops even where the 12-bar form doesn't.
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.why: It's the question that explains why this strand matters to the music you actually make. The dominant-7th-as-home-sound and the blue-note melodic language are still present in genres that essentially never play a 12-bar.
BLU-C08 — Blues into rock and hip hop.drill: Find the blues vocabulary in one hip hop track and one Beatles track you know.

CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds.title: CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds
CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds.q: What single rule builds every chord in the standard system, and what do you get after two, three and four applications of it?
CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds.a: Stack thirds from the root — skip a scale degree, take the next one, repeat. Two thirds gives a triad (1-3-5), three gives a seventh chord (1-3-5-7), and continuing gives the 9th, 11th and 13th. The system is called tertian harmony.
CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds.why: The whole chord vocabulary is one rule applied repeatedly, which is the difference between deriving a chord and memorising a table. Every chart in Chords is the same skip-a-note operation started on a different quality. It also sets the ceiling: six applications of the rule exhaust the diatonic notes, which is why 13 is the largest ordinary extension.
CHD-C01 — Chords are stacked thirds.drill: From C, stack thirds all the way to a 13th and name the chord at each stage. Then start on A with a minor 3rd on the bottom and do it again.

CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.id: CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of the two thirds
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.title: CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of the two thirds
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.short: Triad quality is the order of the two thirds
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.q: Give the four triad qualities as an ordered pair of thirds, with half-step counts and a C example each.
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.a: Major — M3 then m3 (4+3) — C E G. Minor — m3 then M3 (3+4) — C E♭ G. Diminished — m3 then m3 (3+3) — C E♭ G♭. Augmented — M3 then M3 (4+4) — C E G♯.
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.why: Quality is not a fact to memorise chord by chord; it is two intervals in an order. Only the middle note separates major from minor, so raising it a half step flips the chord — the fastest way to change a chord's mood without rebuilding it. The 3rd decides major versus minor, the 5th decides diminished versus augmented, and the two symmetrical orders (3+3 and 4+4) are the two chords that will cause trouble later.
CHD-C02 — Triad quality is the order of.drill: Play a minor triad, raise only the middle note, hear it turn major. Then hold the outer notes and move the 5th instead to reach diminished and augmented from the same root.

CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.id: CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.title: CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.short: Stack something other than thirds and the naming system stops
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.q: Name the three non-tertian stacking families, and say what happens to chord names when you leave thirds behind.
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.a: Secundal — stacked 2nds, i.e. tone clusters, timbral rather than harmonic. Quartal — stacked 4ths. Quintal — stacked 5ths, which respell as the same notes as quartal chords, so it is not a separate system. Quartal harmony does not fit the tertian naming convention at all — the standard symbols frequently mislabel it as sus4.
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.why: The naming system is not a description of harmony, it is a description of harmony built in thirds. Once you know where the assumption sits you can tell a chord that has an awkward name from a chord that has no honest name at all — and stop hunting for a symbol that was never going to exist. Chord names are a human construct; harmony happens whether or not a stack has an agreed label.
CHD-C03 — Stack something other than thi.drill: Play a quartal voicing and try to name it with a standard symbol. Notice which reading the symbol forces on you, and what it hides.

CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities.title: CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities
CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities.q: Build the four core seventh chords as a grid, and name the two more that come off a diminished triad.
CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities.a: The grid is {major or minor triad} × {♭7 or natural 7}: maj7 (1 3 5 7) · dominant 7 (1 3 5 ♭7) · minor 7 (1 ♭3 5 ♭7) · minor-major 7 (1 ♭3 5 7). On a diminished triad: half-diminished, m7♭5 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7) and diminished 7 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7).
CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities.why: The grid is the triad rule with one more third on top, so nothing here is new machinery — but the diatonic placement is worth memorising. Dominant 7 occurs on exactly one degree of a major key (V) and half-diminished on exactly one (vii), so either chord spotted out of context names its parent key. A bare maj7 is ambiguous (I or IV), and a bare m7 worse (ii, iii or vi). Minor-major 7 occurs in neither major nor natural minor — it is the tonic seventh of harmonic and melodic minor — which is why it reads as chromatic and turns up mostly inside a line cliché.
CHD-C04 — The four seventh qualities.drill: Spell all six qualities from C. Then take a diatonic triad progression and convert every chord to its diatonic seventh — the instant jazz version — and name what each one turned into.

CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.id: CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.title: CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.short: 9, 11 and 13 need a complete structure underneath
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.q: What makes an added 2, 4 or 6 count as a 9th, 11th or 13th — and what is the test not about?
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.a: It counts as an extension only when a complete lower structure is present: a full triad (1-3-5) for the 9 and 11, a full seventh chord (1-3-5-7) for the 13. Pull the 3rd and the added 2 stays a 2; pull the 7th and the added 6 stays a 6. It is not about octave placement — an extension voiced right next to the root is still called a 9.
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.why: The common shorthand "9 = 2, 11 = 4, 13 = 6, an octave up" is usually true and is not the rule. The real test settles the cases that actually come up: Cadd9 versus Csus2 is one fact — is the 3rd there — and Cmaj7♯11 is never called ♯4 because it sits on a complete seventh chord. The standard omissions fall out of the same logic: drop the 5th on a 9th chord, drop the 3rd on an 11th because it clashes with the 11, and drop the 5th, 9th and especially the 11th on a 13th.
CHD-C05 — 9, 11 and 13 need a complete s.drill: Voice C9, Cadd9 and Csus2 back to back and say which note is missing in each. Then play a full seven-note C13 and remove notes until it stops sounding muddy — check what you kept against the omission list.

CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.id: CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.title: CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.short: Upper structures: a chord over a foreign bass
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.q: What is an upper structure, and what decides whether it produces a genuinely new chord or just an inversion?
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.a: A chord — usually a triad — played over a bass note that is not its own root. If the bass note is already a tone of the upper chord you have an inversion and nothing new. If it isn't, you get a new composite chord with its own name, function and resolution. The reliable home position is the upper structure's root on the ♭6 of a major key (the natural 7 of a minor key).
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.why: One memorised triad becomes six different chords depending on which bass note goes under it — a ♭6 major (maj7♯11), a ♭7 dominant 13, a iv minor 6/9, an altered dominant, and two rarer suspended-dominant readings. That is the fastest route from "I know three shapes" to a large chord vocabulary, and it is the same mechanism as a slash chord pushed further, because here the bass note need not be a chord tone at all. The real skill is the bass motion that connects two readings, not the names.
CHD-C06 — Upper structures: a chord over.drill: Pick one minor triad, place it on the ♭6 of a major key, and write a progression that uses at least two of the six bass-note options, connected by smooth bass motion.

CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.id: CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neither is an alteration
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.title: CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neither is an alteration
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.short: Sus removes, add adds — neither is an alteration
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.q: What does a sus chord remove, what does an add chord add, and what single test tells an add chord from a sus chord?
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.a: Sus replaces the 3rd — with the 2nd (sus2) or the 4th (sus4) — so the chord is neither major nor minor. Add keeps the whole triad and adds one note with no 7th: Cadd9 = C E G D, while C9 = C E G B♭ D. The test is is the 3rd still there? Present → the added note is the 9 (add9). Absent → it is the 2 (sus2).
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.why: Neither device alters anything — nothing is sharpened or flattened — which is exactly what separates both from Altered Chords. Removing the 3rd costs the chord its quality, and that is the point: sus4 carries a pull and usually resolves, sus2 has a weaker pull and often just sits as an open colour. In practice only two get real use, sus4 on major triads and 7sus4 on dominants, and add9 is the pop and acoustic workhorse because it shimmers without the tension a 7th brings.
CHD-C07 — Sus removes, add adds — neithe.drill: Play Csus4 → C and hear the 4th fall to the 3rd. Then play Cadd9 and Csus2 back to back and name which note is missing. Finally hold a sus4 while adding the 3rd underneath it, and hear a resolution that keeps its residue.

CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.id: CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.title: CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.short: Alteration proper: the dominant's movable tones
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.q: What does "altered" actually mean, which tones can be altered, and what is the one rule about the melody?
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.a: An alteration is a chord tone shifted a half step, not a note added or removed. It is a dominant-family device, and the movable tones are the 5th and the 9th (sometimes the 11th): ♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, ♯11. The rule: do not alter a note the melody is sitting on.
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.why: This is the third of the three colour operations and the one the other two get confused with — sus removes, add adds, altered moves. Alterations are free substitutions for any dominant 7th, especially the V7 going to I: more tension in, stronger resolution out. Worth knowing that the symbol names a scale as much as a note stack, which is why G7♭9 and G7♭13 are interchangeable as written symbols, and why 7♯11 and 7♭5 share one physical voicing — the spelling only changes which note is implied absent.
CHD-C08 — Alteration proper: the dominan.drill: Take a V7 in a loop and add one alteration at a time — ♭9, then ♯9, then ♭5, then ♯5 — and hear how each changes the resolution. Then play the melody over it and drop whichever alteration collides.

CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.id: CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor-6 naming trap
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.title: CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor-6 naming trap
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.short: The sixth chord, and the minor-6 naming trap
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.q: How is a 6th chord built, what is the minor-6 naming trap, and which other chord shares its notes?
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.a: A major or minor triad with the 6th degree added on top and no 7th — a milder colour than a 7th. The trap: the added 6th is always the major 6th, even on a minor triad — Bm6 = B D F♯ G♯, never G natural. The "minor" names only the triad. A minor triad with the actual flat 6 is a different chord, written m♭6. And a 6th chord is note-for-note its relative minor 7th: C6 = Am7, B♭6 = Gm7.
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.why: The 6th is where colour and naming collide, and the collision is real rather than pedantic. When there is no bass to anchor a root, C6 and Am7 are genuinely undecidable and either name is defensible — the opening a cappella chord of "Bohemian Rhapsody" is the standing example. There is also a notation collision worth carrying: classical figured bass writes a superscript 6 for first inversion, so "C6" in a harmonic analysis means C/E, while "C6" on a jazz chart means C E G A. Which tradition you are reading disambiguates it; nothing in the symbol does.
CHD-C09 — The sixth chord, and the minor.drill: Spell Bm6 and Bm♭6 and hear the difference. Then play B♭6 and Gm7 back to back and find a bass note that makes each one unambiguous.

CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.id: CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and what symmetry costs them
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.title: CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and what symmetry costs them
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.short: The symmetrical chords, and what symmetry costs them
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.q: What makes the diminished 7th and the augmented triad symmetrical, how many names does each have, and what does symmetry take away?
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.a: Diminished 7 is three stacked minor 3rds (3+3+3), four notes; augmented is two stacked major 3rds (4+4). The pattern repeats, so any note can be read as the root — four names for one diminished 7th (and only three distinct dim7 chords exist), three for one augmented triad. What symmetry costs: no root the ear can pick out, no true inversion, and no function of its own — the chord's job has to be read off what follows it.
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.why: That last cost is the useful half, and it reduces to one binary test: is any note of the diminished chord the leading note of the chord that follows? No → a passing chord, colouring the line and driving nothing. Yes → a dominant substitute, and it will resolve. The same ♯iv° is passing on the way to I (I's leading tone is not in it) and a functioning dominant on the way to V (♯4̂ is 5̂'s leading tone). One shape, two jobs, decided entirely by context — see Ch11 — Diminished: Songwriting Sleight-of-Hand, since Diminished Chords teaches only the passing half.
CHD-C10 — The symmetrical chords, and wh.drill: Slide one diminished 7th shape up three frets and confirm it is the same four pitches under a new name. Then find a diminished chord in a song you know, look at what follows it, and apply the leading-note test.

CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.id: CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, different bass
CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.title: CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, different bass
CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.q: What does inverting a chord change, how many inversions does a chord have, and what are the reasons to invert?
CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.a: Only which chord tone is in the bass — the notes themselves are unchanged, and the bass note is the single most important note for a chord's feel. A triad has two inversions, a seventh chord three. Reasons: voice leading (keep common tones, move the least), bass-line control (walk the bass by step under static harmony — C → C/B → Am), and hand economy (nearby shapes instead of jumps).
CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.why: On a piano this is a choice about which note goes lowest. On guitar it usually is not: with four fingers and six strings the live decision is which tones to drop, and the bass note follows from that. Keep the 3rd and 7th — the guide tones carry quality and function — drop the 5th first, then the root. A rootless voicing is the default when a bass player is present, not an exotic case. An altered 5th is a colour tone rather than a 5th, so it stays when a plain 5th would go.
CHD-C11 — Inversion: same notes, differe.drill: Take a four-chord loop and re-voice it so the bass walks by step. Then play the same loop with 3rds and 7ths only, and check that nothing about the progression's identity was lost.

CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord.title: CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord
CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord.q: Give the method for reading a slash chord you do not recognise, and the two cases where the method stops short of an answer.
CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord.a: 1. Take the bass note as the root. 2. Relate every note of the upper chord back to it as a scale degree or extension. 3. Name the chord from those degrees — which tells you whether it is behaving as a dominant, a major-7 type or a minor-7 type, and therefore how it wants to resolve. It stops in two cases: if the bass note is a tone of the upper chord there is no new chord, only an inversion (A♭/C is first-inversion A♭); and if the composite has no 3rd and no 7th (D/C) the reading is genuinely ambiguous and only the surrounding harmony decides.
CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord.why: A slash symbol is a playing instruction — upper chord over bass note — and it looks mysterious only because it refuses to sort into a familiar category at a glance. It has to be decoded rather than read off a symbol chart. Worked: B♭/C is ♭7-9-11 over C, i.e. C7sus4(9). G/C is 9-5-maj7, a Cmaj9 with no 3rd. E/C is maj3-♯5-maj7, i.e. Cmaj7♯5. The method works identically on minor, diminished and augmented upper triads, and on four-note upper chords too.
CHD-C12 — Decoding a slash chord.drill: Run the three steps on B♭/C, A/C and G♭/C. Name each composite and say where each one wants to go.

CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.id: CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relationship, not a fact
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.title: CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relationship, not a fact
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.short: A chord name exposes a relationship, not a fact
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.q: When one sonority admits several valid names, what decides which name is correct?
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.a: The name is chosen to expose a relationship, not to state a fact. The right name is the one that reflects the sound you actually hear and the voice leading as it resolves — not the one with the fewest accidentals, and not the one a chord chart would print. Where a shape has several valid names, the choice is an analytical convenience, so pick the one that predicts where you are going.
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.why: The same four notes are Cmaj7/E in the key of C and Em(add♭6) with E as the tonal centre. C-E-G-A is C6 or Am7. Em6 is a half-diminished a third away or a rootless dominant 9th a fourth up — and each name implies a different resolution, which is the whole payload. A diminished 7th has four names, an augmented triad three, and neither collection changes. Chord quality comes from the actual intervals, not from the case of a Roman numeral: an uppercase or lowercase symbol signals position and function, and the stacked intervals decide major, minor or dominant.
CHD-C13 — A chord name exposes a relatio.drill: Take a chord of your own that needed a slash to write down. Name it two different ways, and for each name say what it predicts about the chord that follows.

DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.id: DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processing is not
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.title: DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processing is not
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.short: Selection is the fix; processing is not
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.q: A kick doesn't hit right. You've added a compressor and two EQs and it's still wrong. What's the actual move?
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.a: Swap the sample. Pull it out, audition a different one, and drop the processing back to near-nothing. A chain fixes a close-but-not-quite sample; it does not rescue a wrong one. Same logic downstream: if high-passing a kick to resolve a bass clash guts its punch, don't keep EQing it thinner — find a kick with more inherent high-end character and cut that one instead.
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.why: It's the single most expensive habit in drum production — chasing upstream problems with downstream tools. Selection is the recording step for programmed drums.
DRM-C01 — Selection is the fix; processi.drill: Take a beat where the kick feels weak. Bypass every device on it and audition six replacements before touching a single parameter.

DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.id: DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick
DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.title: DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick
DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.q: Name the four parts of a synthesised kick and a starting point for each.
DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.a: Body/tone — the pitched sine or triangle fundamental, tuned to the song root, amp decay ~200–450 ms. Pitch envelope — the downward "pew" that reads as punch, +12 to +36 semitones falling to zero over 15–40 ms. Click/beater — the attack transient, a short noise or HF layer under 10 ms. Saturation — light, so it reads on small speakers. Add a Hold stage (~30–50 ms) before Decay so the decay curve only ever shapes the tail and never eats the body.
DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.why: Every one of the four is a separate decision you lose access to with a fixed sample. Knowing which part is failing is what turns "this kick is weak" into a specific fix.
DRM-C02 — Anatomy of a synth kick.drill: Build a kick from a sine in Operator using only those four stages. Then A/B it against a sample you like and name which of the four differs.

DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.id: DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and what to do when the key is too low
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.title: DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and what to do when the key is too low
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.short: Tune the kick to the key — and what to do when the key is too low
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.q: Why tune a kick at all, and what's the move in a very low key?
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.a: A kick on the wrong note fights the song; tuned to the root it reinforces the key (Latch's kick hits F every bar and establishes an F minor the track otherwise avoids). In a very low key the root is unusable — a C sub-kick flaps speakers and vanishes outside a club — so tune it to the fifth above and let it bend. Related: a knock kick that lives around 100 Hz with nothing at 50 leaves the low end entirely to the sub or 808.
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.why: This is the decision that connects drum design to harmony, and it's the one most people never make. It also determines whether you need a separate sub layer at all.
DRM-C03 — Tune the kick to the key — and.drill: Take a track in C minor. Tune the kick to C, then to G, then A/B on headphones and on a phone speaker. Note which register disappears where.

DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.id: DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails on drums
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.title: DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails on drums
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.short: Why one-click humanize fails on drums
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.q: What does an algorithmic humanize actually do, and why does it read as worse than a quantized part?
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.a: It scatters timing randomly within a threshold. A few hits land well by luck, but the whole reads as badly played, because a real drummer's deviations are informed — by feel, by groove, by experience — not statistically random. Work instead by playing the part by hand and adjusting after, or quantizing first and nudging manually.
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.why: Random ≠ human is the core insight of the whole realism topic. It also explains why velocity randomisation within a narrow band works while timing randomisation doesn't: velocity variance really is close to random, timing variance is structural.
DRM-C04 — Why one-click humanize fails o.drill: Take a quantized 2-bar beat. Make a copy, run auto-humanize on it, hand-nudge the other. A/B blind and describe the difference in one sentence.

DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.id: DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondaries go late
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.title: DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondaries go late
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.short: Anchors stay on-grid; secondaries go late
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.q: Which hits get timing variation, which don't, and in which direction?
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.a: Anchor hits — primary kick, primary snare — stay exactly on-grid at full, static velocity; softening them loses the dependable strength the groove needs. Secondary hits — ghost snares, offbeat claps, secondary kicks — take the variation, shifted deliberately late, never early, by a different amount each occurrence (uniform lateness reads as a setting, not a performance). The rule tracks metric role, not instrument: a hi-hat marking a strong beat alone stays on-grid because it has inherited the anchoring job.
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.why: This is the rule that makes hip-hop swing read as pocket instead of sloppiness. Late-only is a stylistic law here — loose-and-late is the genre, loose-and-early is a mistake.
DRM-C05 — Anchors stay on-grid; secondar.drill: On a lo-fi beat, nudge only the off-8th hats late by varying small amounts. Leave kick and snare untouched. Then try nudging them early and hear it fail.

DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.id: DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass — and they are the push-pull
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.title: DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass — and they are the push-pull
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.short: Ghost notes are a second pass — and they are the push-pull
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.q: When do you write ghost notes, and what do they actually do to a listener?
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.a: After the main pattern is finished — kick, snare and basic hat complete, then a distinct second pass hunting for the gaps where nothing is hitting. Mechanically: the ear leans toward an expected strong beat, gets a syncopated ghost hit instead, and that displaced anticipation is the pleasurable tension of groove. Not decoration — the mechanism.
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.why: Writing them simultaneously with the main pattern produces clutter, because you can't see the gaps until the anchors exist. And knowing why they work tells you where to put them: at the point of maximum expectation, not evenly.
DRM-C06 — Ghost notes are a second pass.drill: Finish a plain kick/snare/hat pattern. Second pass only: add very-low-velocity ghost snares in the gaps. Count how many you deleted again.

DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.id: DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity value
DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.title: DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity value
DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.q: What does dragging a velocity range do in Ableton, and when does it stop helping?
DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.a: Each hit plays back at a random velocity within the band on every loop pass, so no two passes are identical. Keep the band narrow — too wide reads as inconsistent playing rather than natural playing. It pays off far more on multi-sampled/round-robin kits, where a wider band also swaps articulation rather than just changing volume. Cheapest version with no randomisation at all: alternate hat velocity high/low/high/low.
DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.why: It's the one place randomisation genuinely models what a player does, which is why it works where random timing doesn't. The narrow-band constraint is the whole difference between the two.
DRM-C07 — Velocity range, not velocity v.drill: Set a narrow velocity range on a hi-hat line, loop it eight times, and listen for whether any pass sounds wrong. Widen until one does — that's your ceiling.

DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.id: DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop
DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.title: DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop
DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.q: Why does a 4-bar loop often read as shorter than four bars, and what's the fix?
DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.a: Because it's one bar repeated with tiny variations, so the ear registers the repeat length rather than the bar count. Fix: structure the loop A-B-A-C — a simple kick pattern for A bars, a syncopated one for B, each paired with the inverse hi-hat treatment (strong-beat hats under the busy kick, syncopated hats under the simple kick) so the two elements constantly trade who's anchoring and who's playing around.
DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.why: It's the loop-scale version of the song-scale "give it real length" principle. The pattern doesn't feel like repetition until the full cycle completes — which buys you real bars for free.
DRM-C08 — A-B-A-C inside a single loop.drill: Take a 1-bar loop you like. Expand it to 4 bars as A-B-A-C with inverse hat treatments. Time how long before it bores you, versus before.

DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.id: DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier method
DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.title: DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier method
DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.q: How do you build Intro / A / B / Outro drum clips, and what counts as a change?
DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.a: Write the sparsest Intro clip that still works, duplicate it for A, and make exactly three changes, each of which is either an existing element made more active or a new element added — every change immediately obvious and present throughout the whole loop. Then three more for B. A swap counts too (jingle bell → ride, toms transposed up into a new voice). Past a point, thin out rather than stack: delete the closed hats sitting under a new open hat. Crashes at the start and tom fills at the end are transitional and don't count as one of the three.
DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.why: It's the concrete cure for loop-itis at the clip level: start a song with four energy-tiered clips already built and you have four jumping-off points instead of one basket to overfill.
DRM-C09 — The three-changes energy tier.drill: Build Intro → A → B → Outro from one pattern using exactly three changes per tier. Write down what the three were each time.

DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.id: DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can't do that
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.title: DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can't do that
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.short: Choke groups — a real kit can't do that
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.q: An open hi-hat rings through the following closed-hat hit. Why is that wrong, and what fixes it?
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.a: A physical kit can't do it — one hand, one hat. Enable "cut itself" on the sampler channel or group so a new hit truncates the previous tail; a zero-velocity note at the cutoff point is an alternative or a stack. Watch the same problem in the low end, where overlapping tails are far uglier — bass sample tracks have it too.
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.why: Part of a family of physical-plausibility constraints that make programmed drums read as played — the four-limb ceiling (a real drummer has two hands and two feet) is the same idea applied to pattern writing rather than tails.
DRM-C10 — Choke groups — a real kit can'.drill: Find an open-hat into closed-hat transition in an existing beat. Enable choke. A/B it. Then check your 808 track for the same overlap.

EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.id: EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.title: EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.short: Tonic recognition, and the three levels of practising it
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.q: What is the tonic as a feeling, and what are the three escalating ways to practise finding it?
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.a: Home — rest, completion, stability, independent of the absolute pitch. The same physical C feels nothing like itself as tonic of C major vs as scale degree 5 of F major. Practise it: (1) scale-based — play a scale and stop one note short, then sing the resolution before playing it. (2) progression-based — play a progression that stays in one key, stop on a non-tonic chord, sing the resolution. (3) real-music-based — flag the tonic chord every time it recurs in a song you know, then stop an unheard song at a random moment and sing the resolution before checking.
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.why: Every one of your six progression questions came back blank, and all six of them start here. The ear already infers a tonic automatically — the training is becoming consciously aware of what it already does. Singing the resolution trains it harder than only listening for it, because producing the feeling locks it in.
EAR-C01 — Tonic recognition, and the thr.drill: Play a C major scale and stop on B. Sing the resolution before you play it. Repeat in A minor, then in a key you don't normally play. Then do it once with a song you've never heard.

EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.id: EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.title: EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.short: Pitch matching is the fallback the whole method rests on
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.q: What three pitch-matching abilities are the prerequisite for scale-degree work, and why do they matter more than they look?
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.a: (1) Sing back a note you just heard, in any octave. (2) Find a heard pitch on your instrument. (3) Sing a random pitch, then find that on the instrument. They matter because every later skill — degrees, chords, transcription — falls back on "sing it or find it on the instrument" the moment recognition fails. Without the fallback you're simply stuck.
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.why: This is the diagnosis step, not a warm-up. If any of the three is shaky, that's your actual starting point and no amount of drone drilling will substitute for it.
EAR-C02 — Pitch matching is the fallback.drill: Play three random notes. Sing each back. Then sing a note cold and find it on the guitar within five seconds.

EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.id: EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.title: EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.short: Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the first drill
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.q: Describe the 3 and the ♭3 as feeling states, and say why this specific pair is your named starting line.
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.a: 3 — sweetness, warmth, glow, vitality; a whole extra dimension that 5 doesn't have. ♭3 — the thing that defines minorness: dark, serious, gloomy, a bit of sorrow. Number tells you how far; quality tells you which colour. Hearing "a 3rd" without hearing which 3rd is the standard gap at this stage, and quality is the half that does the emotional work.
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.why: The results note names this pair as literally the first drill: you're hearing that there's a third and not which one. Every chord-quality question downstream is the same failure at a larger scale.
EAR-C03 — Major 3rd vs minor 3rd — the f.drill: Against a C drone, alternate E and E♭. Say the feeling word out loud before you name the degree. Twenty reps, then switch the drone to A.

EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.id: EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.title: EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.short: The two worlds — the 5-axis and the 3-axis
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.q: Which scale degrees group into the "5 world" and which into the "3 world", and what does the split predict?
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.a: 5 world: 1, 4, 5, 2 — clean, neutral, pure. 3 world: 3, 6, 7 — warm, glowing, sweet. The split predicts where your mistakes will be: most confusions happen within one family, not across it. Mishearing 3 for 6 is normal; mishearing 3 for 4 is not.
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.why: It turns the 12 feeling states from a flat list into two shortlists. When you can't name a degree, you can usually still name its world — which halves the guess before you start deducing.
EAR-C04 — The two worlds — the 5-axis an.drill: Against a drone, play a random diatonic degree. Before naming it, say only "5 world" or "3 world". Check. Ten reps — score the world call, not the degree.

EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.id: EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in feeling
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.title: EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in feeling
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.short: Close in pitch is not close in feeling
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.q: Arrange the degrees by feeling rather than by pitch. What does adjacency on that circle tell you, and what's the counter-intuitive case?
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.a: Degrees next to each other on the feeling-circle are the ones you'll mistake for one another — 3/6, 3/7, ♭3/♭7. The counter-intuitive case: degrees a half-step apart melodically are usually maximally far apart by feeling. 5 (pure, stable, expansive) and ♯4 (bright, strange, alien, spiky) are one fret apart and about as opposite as the system gets.
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.why: It's why interval-distance training doesn't transfer. The ear isn't measuring distance, it's recognising a role — so a training system organised by semitone count is organised on the wrong axis.
EAR-C05 — Close in pitch is not close in.drill: Against a C drone, alternate G and F♯ and say what makes them opposite. Then alternate E and A and say what makes them easy to confuse.

EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.id: EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.title: EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.short: Which seventh is it — dominant, major, or half-diminished
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.q: You heard a dominant 7th and answered "major 7", then heard a half-diminished 7th and answered "dominant 7". What is the actual gap, and how do the three qualities differ?
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.a: The gap is that you're hearing that there's a seventh but not which one — the two answers were swapped relative to what played, which is the signature of a size-not-quality read. Major 7 — the 7 feeling on top: melancholy/bittersweet, sharpened by the half-step rub against the root. Dominant 7 — ♭7 on top: light, powerful, playful, wants to move. Half-diminished — a diminished triad carrying that same ♭7; unstable underneath and unresolved on top.
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.why: Every seventh-chord question is one distinction, asked three ways. Train each quality as its own whole flavour rather than assembling it from a triad plus an interval.
EAR-C06 — Which seventh is it — dominant.drill: Play Cmaj7, C7 and Cm7♭5 back to back. Name the feeling of the top note in each. Then shuffle and identify blind, ten reps.

EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.id: EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.title: EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.short: A chord is a gestalt, not a stack of degrees
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.q: Why shouldn't you decompose a chord into its component scale degrees in real time, and what should you train instead?
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.a: Because combining feeling states produces a genuinely new, higher-level experience — the way syllables combine into a word you hear whole rather than as separate sounds. Train each chord type × quality × position as its own feeling state directly (major-on-4, minor-on-6, dominant-on-♭7), the same way you trained the twelve single degrees. Reserve conscious decomposition for the cases that actually need it, like an unfamiliar voicing you're transcribing.
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.why: It's the reason chord recognition doesn't get faster by getting better at intervals. The recursion runs degree → chord → progression → whole song, and each level is recognised as a gestalt rather than reconstructed from the one below.
EAR-C07 — A chord is a gestalt, not a st.drill: Play the seven diatonic triads of C in random order against a C drone. Name each by position and quality as one label ("minor-on-6"), not by spelling it.

EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.id: EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.title: EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.short: Inversions are heard from the bass note's own degree feeling
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.q: How do you tell root position from an inversion by ear, without identifying the full chord first?
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.a: By the bass note's own scale-degree feeling. A root-position bass note carries the "1" feeling — solid, landed, this is it. An inverted bass note carries whatever that degree feels like: a 3rd in the bass feels like 3, a 5th feels like 5. So you can know a chord is inverted before you know which chord it is, purely from the bass not feeling like home.
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.why: Inversions are their own feeling states, not the root chord plus a formula applied afterward. This is also the doorway into bass-motion tracking, which is the main landmark in real transcription.
EAR-C08 — Inversions are heard from the.drill: Play C/E, C/G and C in random order. Call inverted-or-not from the bass alone before naming the inversion. Ten reps.

EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.id: EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear
EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.title: EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear
EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.q: You spelled both of these correctly on paper and answered "idk" when they played. What's the training move that closes that specific gap?
EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.a: Drill them as single fused gestures, not as chains of chords to identify one at a time. A ii–V is eventually heard as one chunk. Run the progression drill sequence: play the bass notes alone and sing the degree numbers → add the chords back and name each quality out loud → quality-swap (change one chord's quality, hold everything else) → position-swap (hold the quality, move the degree) → transpose the whole thing and repeat.
EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.why: Written, heard and named are three separate skills, and right now only the first is connected. These two progressions are the highest-value pair to connect first because you already own the written half of both.
EAR-C09 — I–V–vi–IV and ii–V–I by ear.drill: Loop I–V–vi–IV in C. Sing the bass degrees. Then swap the vi for VI and hear what changed. Then move it to E and do it again.

EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.id: EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.title: EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.short: Half-step bass motion is a diatonic landmark
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.q: You hear the bass move by a half step inside a major key. What are the only two likely places, and what narrows it further?
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.a: IV→iii (4→3) or vii°→I (7→1). If you also hear a major chord moving to a minor chord a half step below, there's only one diatonic spot that happens: IV→iii in major (♭VI→v in minor).
