Related landmark: a ♯4 in the bass almost always signals either a secondary dominant of V (V/V with its 3rd in the bass — in C, D7/F♯) or a ♯iv half-diminished (♯ivø7 — in C, F♯ A C E).
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.why: Bass motion is the primary chord-to-chord landmark in real transcription — you read it first and confirm the quality on top second. One recognised half step can collapse a whole progression's candidate set.
EAR-C10 — Half-step bass motion is a dia.drill: Play IV→iii and vii°→I in C. Then play both in A♭ without looking. Name which one you're hearing from the bass move alone.

EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear.title: EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear
EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear.q: Name the four cadences by the feeling of their landing, not by their Roman numerals.
EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear.a: Authentic (V–I) — full arrival, the door closing. Plagal (IV–I) — arrival without the pull; softer, already-home rather than coming-home. Half (…–V) — suspended, a question left open, the sentence stopping mid-breath. Deceptive (V–vi) — the pull of an authentic cadence resolving somewhere that isn't home; the specific feeling is surprise plus incompleteness.
EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear.why: EAR-18 gave you four chords and asked for the cadence in the last two. Cadence recognition is where degree-feeling and progression-feeling meet, and it's the cheapest way to start hearing form rather than chords.
EAR-C11 — Cadences by ear.drill: Play all four in C, then in G, then have them shuffled. Call each one before the last chord finishes ringing.

EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.id: EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfect pitch
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.title: EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfect pitch
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.short: Finding the key with no perfect pitch
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.q: You can hear where the music resolves but you don't know what note it is. What's the move?
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.a: Sing the note that feels like the tonic (you don't need to know its pitch), then play any random note on your instrument and judge what scale degree that note feels like relative to what you sang. Back-calculate: "I played a G and it feels like 4, so the key is D." This single move is the one that recurs in every real-time transcription example.
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.why: It removes the perfect-pitch dependency entirely — you only ever need relative hearing plus one reference note you can produce on demand. Backups when it's murky: the last melody note, or the bass of the most stable chord.
EAR-C12 — Finding the key with no perfec.drill: Put on a song you don't know. Sing the tonic, play one random note, name its degree, back-calculate the key. Check against a tuner. Five songs.

EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear pr.title: EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear process
EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear pr.q: List the five steps for playing a melody back by ear.
EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear pr.a: 1. Memorise — sing or hum it back until it's internalised. 2. Map the contour — up/down and roughly how far (step, leap, big leap); no degree numbers yet, just the shape. 3. Sing it slowly and pencil in whichever degrees you can genuinely feel. 4. Deduce the rest from the contour plus theory, then sing it back and check the felt states actually match. 5. Verify on the instrument — and when you're wrong, work out which degree got confused for which. That last part is where the learning is.
EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear pr.why: Contour before degrees is the step people skip. Getting the shape down first means the degrees you can't hear are constrained by the ones you can, instead of being twelve-way guesses.
EAR-C13 — The five-step melody-by-ear pr.drill: Take a nursery rhyme. Run all five steps without touching the instrument until step 5. Log which degree you got wrong.

EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.id: EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routine has to touch
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.title: EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routine has to touch
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.short: The four skills a daily routine has to touch
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.q: What four recognition skills does a complete ear-training routine cover, and what's the daily shape?
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.a: Melodic scale-degree · bass-note · chord-quality · chord-number/position. Daily shape: drone practice on sustained degrees · a melody-transcription rep on something simple · improvisation over a drone with conscious degree-tracking · the five-step chord/progression drill (bass alone → add chords → quality swap → position swap → transpose).
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.why: Three minutes a day beats an hour a month here — this is a perceptual skill, and it's the reason EAR runs as a standing daily drill rather than a course you finish.
EAR-C14 — The four skills a daily routin.drill: Run one rep of each of the four, timed. If it takes more than five minutes you're doing too much per day.

FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents.title: FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents
FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents.q: What does enharmonic mean? Give the enharmonic equivalent of C♯, F♭ and E♯.
FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents.a: Two different names for the same pitch — same key, same fret, different spelling. C♯ = D♭. F♭ = E. E♯ = F.
FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents.why: Which spelling is correct depends on the key and on which letter name the music needs next. F♭ and E♯ look wrong because there is no black key between E–F or B–C — those two pairs are the only white-key half steps, which is the same fact behind FND-17.
FND-C01 — Enharmonic equivalents.drill: Name the enharmonic of: C♯ · F♭ · E♯ · B♯ · G♭ · A♯. Which of those are white keys? D♭, E, F, C, F♯, B♭. white: E, F, C

FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.id: FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats
FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.title: FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats
FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.q: Give the order of sharps as they appear in key signatures, and the order of flats.
FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.a: Sharps: F C G D A E B. Flats: B E A D G C F — the sharp order reversed.
FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.why: Both sequences run all seven, and stopping short is the usual mistake. It matters because the key-reading rules are indexed off the end of the list — the last sharp, the second-to-last flat — so a truncated list can't be read backwards.
FND-C02 — Order of sharps and flats.drill: Write both orders from memory. Then: which sharps does E major take? Which flats does A♭ major take?

FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharp.title: FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharps)
FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharp.q: How do you work out the major key from a key signature with sharps?
FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharp.a: Take the last sharp and go up a half step. Last sharp G♯ → A major.
FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharp.why: This is half of FND-18, where you knew the count mattered but not the method. It works because the last sharp is always the leading tone — scale degree 7 — which sits a semitone below the tonic.
FND-C03 — Reading a key signature (sharp.drill: Name the key: 2 sharps · 3 sharps · 4 sharps · 5 sharps. Then work backwards — how many sharps in B major?

FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats.title: FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats)
FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats.q: How do you work out the major key from a key signature with flats? What's the exception?
FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats.a: The second-to-last flat names the key. B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ → A♭ major. The exception is one flat = F major, which you memorize because there's no second-to-last.
FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats.why: The other half of FND-18, and the rule that would have completed FND-08 — you knew four flats is A♭ major but couldn't produce the flats. With the order memorized (FND-C02) this rule runs in both directions.
FND-C04 — Reading a key signature (flats.drill: Name the key: 1 flat · 2 flats · 3 flats · 5 flats. Then: list the flats in E♭ major.

FND-C05 — Interval inversion.title: FND-C05 — Interval inversion
FND-C05 — Interval inversion.q: What happens to an interval when you invert it? Invert a major 3rd.
FND-C05 — Interval inversion.a: The numbers sum to 9 and the quality flips. Major↔minor, augmented↔diminished, perfect stays perfect. A major 3rd inverts to a minor 6th (3 + 6 = 9).
FND-C05 — Interval inversion.why: This converts a recall question into arithmetic you can do under pressure. It's also why a shell voicing works — inverting guide tones keeps the quality readable.
FND-C05 — Interval inversion.drill: Invert: M3 · m6 · P5 · M2 · m7 · P4 · A4.

FND-C06 — Interval quality names.title: FND-C06 — Interval quality names
FND-C06 — Interval quality names.q: Why isn't "a 4th" or "a 3rd" a complete interval name?
FND-C06 — Interval quality names.a: The number says how far (how many letter names). The quality says which colour — perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished. C→F is a perfect 4th; C→E is a major 3rd, C→E♭ a minor 3rd.
FND-C06 — Interval quality names.why: It is easy to get by on interval numbers alone — C→F is unambiguous whether or not you can name its quality. The cost only shows up in ear training, where "a 3rd" with no major or minor attached is half an answer. Quality is the distinction ear training is built on.
FND-C06 — Interval quality names.drill: Name fully: C→F · C→F♯ · C→E♭ · D→A · D→A♭ · E→C · E→C♯.

FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.id: FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the interval number
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.title: FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the interval number
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.short: Letter distance decides the interval number
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.q: C→A♯ sounds identical to a minor 7th. Why isn't it called one?
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.a: Because the interval number comes from letter distance, not from sound. C D E F G A spans six letter names, so C→A♯ is a sixth — an augmented 6th. C→B♭ spans seven letters, so that's the m7.
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.why: The rule underneath all correct spelling. It's why a fully diminished 7th on G is spelled G B♭ D♭ F♭ rather than using E — the chord needs a 7th, so it needs an F of some kind.
FND-C07 — Letter distance decides the in.drill: Name and explain: C→A♯ vs C→B♭ · C→D♯ vs C→E♭ · G→F♭ vs G→E.

FND-C08 — Compound intervals.title: FND-C08 — Compound intervals
FND-C08 — Compound intervals.q: What simple interval is a major 9th equivalent to? What's the general rule?
FND-C08 — Compound intervals.why: You half-had this — "2nd or 9th" were both true and the question wanted the simple one. It's the bridge into extended chords: a B♭13 stops being confusing once 13 reads as "the 6th, an octave up."
FND-C08 — Compound intervals.drill: Reduce: major 9th · perfect 11th · major 13th · minor 9th · ♯11. Then spell each above C.

FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.id: FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor
FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.title: FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor
FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.q: What's the practical difference between a limiter and a compressor?
FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.a: A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio, acting as a ceiling. Same device, extreme setting — not a different category of tool.
FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.why: Reframing it this way makes the master-chain conversation obvious, and it connects directly to — a limiter isn't a special mastering object, it's a compressor squashing so hard there's nothing left for the engineer.
FX-C01 — A limiter is a compressor.drill: Take a compressor, set the ratio to 20:1 with a fast attack, and compare it to a limiter on the same source.

FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.id: FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee
FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.title: FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee
FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.q: What's the difference between a hard knee and a soft knee, and when is each appropriate?
FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.a: Hard knee applies the full ratio the instant the signal crosses threshold. Soft knee eases the ratio in over a window either side, so compression starts gently before threshold. Soft for transparent levelling (vocals, mix bus); hard for catching peaks or when you want it audible.
FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.why: Knee is routinely confused with ratio — "how extreme the compression is" describes ratio, not knee. Knee is about how abruptly the ratio engages, and it's most of why two compressors at identical settings sound different.
FX-C02 — Hard knee vs soft knee.drill: A/B hard vs soft knee on a vocal at the same ratio and threshold. Then on a drum bus.

FX-C03 — Parallel compression.title: FX-C03 — Parallel compression
FX-C03 — Parallel compression.q: What is parallel compression, and why does it work?
FX-C03 — Parallel compression.a: Blend a heavily compressed copy underneath the dry signal. The dry path keeps its transients, so you get density and sustained detail without losing punch — it behaves like upward compression, lifting the quiet parts rather than pushing the loud ones down.
FX-C03 — Parallel compression.why: And you don't need a return track: Ableton's stock Compressor has a Dry/Wet knob that does it in one device — already noted in Compression.
FX-C03 — Parallel compression.drill: Set it up both ways on drums — a return track, and stock Dry/Wet at ~50%. Confirm they behave the same.

FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband.title: FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband
FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband.q: When would you reach for multiband compression instead of broadband?
FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband.a: When only part of the spectrum has the dynamic problem. Broadband sees one band's peaks and pulls the whole signal down with them — a vocal whose low-mids bloom on certain notes gets ducked entirely on those notes. Multiband compresses just that range.
FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband.why: Knowing the trigger is the easy half; the failure mode is the useful one. The 'whole signal ducks' part is what makes the choice obvious in practice.
FX-C04 — Multiband vs broadband.drill: Find a source where one band misbehaves. Fix it broadband, then multiband. Listen to what broadband costs.

FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics.title: FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics
FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics.q: Beyond "warmth" — what does saturation do to a signal, in terms of harmonics?
FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics.a: It generates new harmonic content that wasn't in the source. Even-order (2nd) sit at octaves and read warm and full; odd-order (3rd) add edge and grit. It also rounds transient peaks, so a saturated signal reads louder and denser at the same meter reading.
FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics.why: 'Adds harmonics and distortion' is the core of it. The even/odd split is the half that turns it into a choice rather than a texture you either like or don't.
FX-C05 — Saturation adds harmonics.drill: On one source, find a saturator with a tone or bias control. Push it toward even, then odd. Name the difference.

FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.id: FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, de-ess
FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.title: FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, de-ess
FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.q: A vocal is dull, inconsistent in level and sibilant. In what order do EQ, compression and de-essing go — and why?
FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.a: Subtractive EQ → compression → de-ess → tone-shaping EQ. Clean up first so the compressor isn't reacting to rumble. De-ess after compression, because pulling the body down raises the esses. Boosts last, so a presence lift doesn't get immediately squashed.
FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.why: 1.5/5 — you put de-ess after compression, which is right and is the part most people get wrong. What's missing is corrective EQ first and tone-shaping last. This is the applied form of the 'compress first, EQ after' rule already in Compression.
FX-C06 — Chain order: EQ, compression, d.drill: Build the chain in that order on a real take. Then move the de-esser before the compressor and hear the sibilance return.

HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.id: HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.title: HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.short: The three functions: T, SD, D
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.q: What are the three harmonic functions, which chords carry each in a major key, and what's the normal cycle?
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.a: Tonic (T) — I, vi, iii — home, at rest. Subdominant (SD) — IV, ii — departure. Dominant (D) — V, vii° — tension wanting to resolve. The normal cycle is T → SD → D → T.
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.why: The idea the whole course rests on. It is almost never tested directly, which is why its absence shows up everywhere else instead. Once chords are functions rather than letters, a progression becomes a shape, and substitution becomes obvious: chords sharing a function can stand in for each other.
HAR-C01 — The three functions: T, SD, D.drill: Label every chord in four of your own progressions T, SD or D. Find the ones that break T→SD→D→T.

HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence.title: HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence
HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence.q: Which two chords make an authentic cadence, and what does it do?
HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence.a: V → I. Dominant to tonic — a full stop. The strongest closure in tonal harmony.
HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence.why: This is the default ending of most phrases in most Western music; not having the name means not having a way to think about why a phrase feels finished.
HAR-C02 — Authentic cadence.drill: Find the authentic cadence in three songs you know. Then remove it — end on V instead — and hear what changes.

HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence.title: HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence
HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence.q: What chord movement makes a plagal cadence, and how does it differ from an authentic one?
HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence.a: IV → I — the "amen" cadence. Softer than V–I because there's no leading tone, so there's no semitone pull into the tonic.
HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence.why: The missing-leading-tone point is the whole reason it sounds gentler and more modal — and it's why IV–I is everywhere in rock and gospel where V–I would sound too formal.
HAR-C03 — Plagal cadence.drill: Play IV–I and V–I back to back in the same key. Name the difference in your own words.

HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence.title: HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence
HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence.q: In a deceptive cadence, V resolves to what instead of I — and why use it?
HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence.a: vi. The dominant sets up a resolution to I and lands on the submediant instead — so the phrase stays open when the ear expected closure.
HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence.why: It's the cheapest way to extend a phrase that was about to end, and vi shares two notes with I, which is exactly why the swerve is believable rather than jarring.
HAR-C04 — Deceptive cadence.drill: Take a progression ending V–I and change it to V–vi. Then continue the phrase from there.

HAR-C05 — Half cadence.title: HAR-C05 — Half cadence
HAR-C05 — Half cadence.q: How is a half cadence different from an authentic cadence, and when would you use one?
HAR-C05 — Half cadence.a: A half cadence ends ON V, unresolved — a question mark. An authentic cadence goes V→I and closes. Use the half cadence at the end of an antecedent phrase so the consequent has something to answer.
HAR-C05 — Half cadence.why: The question/answer phrase structure it creates is the backbone of how 8- and 16-bar sections are built — this is a form tool as much as a harmony one.
HAR-C05 — Half cadence.drill: Write an 8-bar phrase: 4 bars ending on V, 4 bars ending V–I. Hear the question and the answer.

HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.id: HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone
HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.title: HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone
HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.q: Explain why V–I feels resolved, in terms of the tritone.
HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.a: V7 contains a tritone — in G7, between the 3rd (B) and the ♭7 (F). That interval is maximally unstable, and each note has a half-step target in the tonic triad: B rises to C, F falls to E. Both voices resolve by semitone into consonance, so the resolution feels inevitable.
HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.why: It's the mechanism under every cadence. It also explains tritone substitution — D♭7 works in place of G7 because it contains the same tritone.
HAR-C06 — Why V–I resolves: the tritone.drill: Play G7 and find the B and the F. Resolve just those two notes to C and E. That's the cadence, in two voices.

HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants.title: HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants
HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants.q: What is a secondary dominant? Spell V/V in C major, and say what A7 is doing in | Cmaj7 | A7 | Dm7 | G7 |.
HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants.a: A dominant chord built on the V of a chord other than the tonic, temporarily treating that chord as a tonic. V/V in C = D7 (V of G). In that progression A7 is V/ii — diatonically the chord on A is Am; raising the 3rd to C♯ makes it a dominant pointing at Dm, tonicizing it before the fall through G7 to C.
HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants.why: Both questions blank. This is the single most common way popular music leaves the key for a moment, and the tell is always a chromatic leading tone — the C♯ that isn't in C major.
HAR-C07 — Secondary dominants.drill: In a C major loop, put E7 before Am. Then D7 before G. Name the borrowed leading tone in each.

HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.id: HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal interchange
HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.title: HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal interchange
HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.q: What is modal interchange? Name the four workhorse borrowed chords in C major.
HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.a: Keep the tonic, raid the parallel mode. In C major you borrow from C minor: iv (Fm), ♭VI (A♭), ♭VII (B♭), ♭III (E♭). The key centre never moves, so it reads as colour rather than a key change. The classic move is IV → iv → I.
HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.why: Both blank. Contrast with secondary dominants (HAR-C07): secondary dominants add pull, borrowed chords add colour. One creates motion, the other creates mood. IV→iv→I works because the A♭ in Fm falls a half step to G as the tonic returns.
HAR-C08 — Borrowed chords and modal inte.drill: In a C major loop, swap one F for an Fm. Then try A♭ and B♭. Say what each one does to the mood.

HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones.title: HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones
HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones.q: What is a non-harmonic tone? Name the one approached by step and left by step in the same direction.
HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones.a: A melody note not in the chord underneath it. The one approached and left by step in the same direction is a passing tone.
HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones.why: Non-harmonic tones are most of what makes a melody sound like a melody rather than an arpeggio — the notes between the chord tones are where the line lives. Directly relevant to the MEL strand (20%).
HAR-C09 — Non-harmonic tones.drill: Take a melody you've written. Label every note chord-tone or non-harmonic. Count the ratio.

HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation.title: HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation
HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation.q: What's the difference between tonicization and modulation, and what does a pivot chord do?
HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation.a: Tonicization points at a chord briefly — a secondary dominant leaning on ii, then back. No new key. Modulation relocates the tonic and confirms it with a cadence, so the ear resets. It's a spectrum set by duration and whether you cadence. A pivot chord is diatonic to both keys — approach it in the old key, reinterpret it, cadence in the new one. Am is vi in C and ii in G.
HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation.why: HAR-16 blank; HAR-13 got 'shared chord' and missed the reinterpretation and the confirming cadence — which are the two things that make it a modulation rather than just a chord both keys happen to own.
HAR-C10 — Tonicization vs modulation.drill: Modulate a loop from C to G using Am as the pivot, confirmed with D7–G. Then do the same move but leave immediately — that's tonicization.

JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.id: JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not a colour
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.title: JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not a colour
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.short: Sevenths are the baseline, not a colour
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.q: In a jazz context, what does a bare chord symbol like "C" actually mean, and why does that assumption have to be settled before any other rule?
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.a: Cmaj7 or C6 — a four-note chord. In common-practice harmony the triad is the default and the 7th is a colour added on top. In jazz the 7th is the default, and a triad is the special case. Every rule that follows — substitution, voice leading, guide tones — assumes four notes.
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.why:
First of the four ideas Jazz Harmony says the whole subject runs on, and the one that silently breaks the other three if it is missed. Guide tones cannot exist without a 7th; tritone substitution has nothing to preserve without one. Reading a jazz chart as triads is not a simpler reading, it is a wrong one.

It also transfers straight into pop and R&B writing: swapping the triads of a loop for sevenths is the single cheapest way to move a progression from bright-and-generic toward the neo-soul end of the dial.
JAZ-C01 — Sevenths are the baseline, not.drill: Take a four-chord loop you have already written and re-spell every chord as a seventh — maj7 on I and IV, m7 on ii, iii and vi, dominant 7 on V. Play both versions back to back and name what changed.

JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.id: JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor
JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.title: JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor
JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.q: Spell the ii–V–I in C major and in C minor, and say why these three chords rather than any others.
JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.a:
Major: Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7. Minor: Dm7♭5 – G7♭9 – Cm7 (Cm6 and CmMaj7 are equally in use).

The reason is root motion. D → G → C is the circle of fifths in miniature — each root falls a fifth, which is the strongest progression in tonal music, and the cell stacks two of them back to back.
JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.why:
The sentence jazz is written in. Nearly all standard-repertoire harmony is ii–V–I units chained, transposed and disguised, so seeing them is what stops a lead sheet looking arbitrary.

The three minor-key differences are all forced by the scale rather than chosen: the ii goes half-diminished because the ♭5 is simply the 6th degree of natural minor; the V keeps its major 3rd because the raised leading tone is what makes it a dominant at all, and picks up a ♭9 from harmonic minor; and the tonic is deliberately ambiguous between m7, m6 and mMaj7.
JAZ-C02 — The ii-V-I, major and minor.drill: Write the major ii–V–I in all twelve keys from memory, then the minor version in four. Then play Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 Cmaj7 as a four-bar loop and notice that it is already a complete, loopable progression with nothing added.

JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.id: JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the I never arrives
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.title: JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the I never arrives
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.short: Spotting a ii-V, and when the I never arrives
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.q: What is the scan that finds a ii–V on an unfamiliar chart, and what are the two common cases where the promised I never turns up?
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.a:
Scan for any m7 chord followed by a dominant 7th a fourth above it. That is a ii–V, and whatever it points at is the intended I — even when the I never actually sounds.

The two cases: the deceptive move, where the ii–V lands on vi or ♭VI instead (Dm7 G7 Am7); and the unresolved ii–V, which moves straight to the next ii–V without resolving at all.
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.why:
This is the reading tip that pays for itself. It is also the fix for the commonest misreading of a bebop head — an unresolved chain of ii–Vs makes a chart look like it changes key every two bars when it does not.

The chaining device behind it is worth having as a writing tool, not just an analysis one: make the I of one unit into the ii of the next, or simply drop a ii–V in front of any chord you want to arrive at.
JAZ-C03 — Spotting a ii-V, and when the.drill: Take a standard's chart and bracket every m7 followed by a dominant a fourth up. Write in the I each one implies, then mark which of those I chords actually arrive, which are deceptive, and which never resolve at all.

JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.id: JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the chord
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.title: JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the chord
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.short: The 3rd and the 7th carry the chord
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.q: Which two notes state a chord's quality, why those two rather than the root and the 5th, and what is the one exception?
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.a:
The 3rd and the 7th. The 3rd says major or minor; the 7th says major, dominant or minor. Together they name the chord.

The root tells you nothing about quality and the 5th tells you almost nothing, which is why the 5th is the first note dropped from a voicing. The exception is m7♭5 — Cm7♭5 and Cm7 share E♭ and B♭, so only the ♭5 separates them, and a voicing that drops it states the wrong chord.
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.why:
The highest-leverage idea in the strand. Two notes per chord are enough to state a whole progression, which is why a bass player and a horn can imply the harmony with no chordal instrument present at all.

It is also a mix tool. When the mids are crowded, cutting the chordal instrument down to guide tones frees space without losing any harmony — the 5th and the doubled root were the notes doing the crowding.
JAZ-C04 — The 3rd and the 7th carry the.drill: Write out only the 3rds and 7ths of a tune's changes as two horizontal lines, before voicing anything. Then play just those two lines and check the progression is still recognisable.

JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.id: JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3rd of the next
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.title: JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3rd of the next
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.short: The 7th of one chord is the 3rd of the next
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.q: Run the guide tones through Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7 and say what the two lines do.
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.a:
Dm7 is F and C · G7 is B and F · Cmaj7 is E and B. One line runs C → B → B, the other F → F → E.

Nothing leaps. One voice holds while the other moves a half step, then they swap. Each chord's 3rd is held over as the next chord's 7th, and each chord's 7th falls a half step onto the next chord's 3rd — that is not a coincidence, it is what root motion by fifths does, and it is the mechanical reason the cell sounds inevitable rather than merely conventional.
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.why:
It turns voice leading into a procedure instead of a judgement call: solve the horizontal problem first, fix any leap bigger than a step by inverting the chord or choosing a different extension, and only then decide the full voicings.

It also gives the concrete test for a substitution. A substitute that keeps the guide-tone lines stepwise is a good one — which is exactly why the tritone sub works, since it swaps the guide tones rather than disturbing them.
JAZ-C05 — The 7th of one chord is the 3r.drill: Write the 3rd and 7th of every chord in a tune as two lines. Circle every leap larger than a step and re-voice that chord until the leap is gone.

JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings.title: JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings
JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings.q: What is a shell voicing, which of its two orderings usually sounds better, and when is it the right voicing rather than the cheap one?
JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings.a:
Root + 3rd + 7th — three notes, no 5th, no extensions. Root–7th–3rd, with the 7th below the 3rd, is usually the better-sounding of the two orderings.

It is the right voicing, not the lazy one, whenever something else needs the register: under a busy vocal, or with a second chordal instrument in the arrangement. A full five-note chord in that spot is the mistake. Extensions stack on top of it — shell plus 9th, shell plus 13th — which is the whole vocabulary.
JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings.why:
Shells are the practical form of guide-tone thinking. They are easy to grab on guitar or piano, they never sound muddy, and they leave the entire register above free for melody or for another player.

For Nate's own tracks that is the direct payoff: a shell under a vocal leaves the topline alone, and it is the same fix as cutting a pad's low mids, done at the writing stage instead of the mix stage.
JAZ-C06 — Shell voicings.drill: Play a ii–V–I as shells in root–7th–3rd order, then again as full five-note chords, both under a vocal or lead you already have. Decide which one you would actually keep.

JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.id: JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule: function first
JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.title: JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule: function first
JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.q: State the rule that decides whether one chord can replace another, say which half of it settles ties, and name the failure mode.
JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.a:
Two chords can substitute for each other when they share enough tones and the same harmonic function — and function comes first, tones second. A substitute sharing three notes that resolves the wrong way is a worse choice than one sharing two that resolves right.

The test on top of that is the melody: a substitution must be completely compatible with what it replaces, so one that clashes with the tune is wrong however good the voice leading. The failure mode is substituting everything — against plain harmony a substitution reads as sophisticated, wall to wall it reads as directionless.
JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.why:
This is what makes substitution a set of rules rather than a matter of taste, and it is the rule the rest of the lesson is applications of. Diatonic substitution falls straight out of it: two diatonic chords a third apart share two of their three triad tones, which is why Cmaj7 Cmaj7 Fmaj7 G7 becomes Cmaj7 Am7 Fmaj7 G7 — the I–vi–IV–V that half of popular music runs on.

The caution attached is worth as much as the rule: vi is the strongest I-substitute and iii the weakest, because iii lacks the root and contains B, which drags it toward dominant function.
JAZ-C07 — Substitution's governing rule:.drill: Take a loop of yours and replace one I with vi, then with iii. Sing the melody over both and decide which one the tune survives.

JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.id: JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shared tritone
JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.title: JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shared tritone
JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.q: Why can D♭7 stand in for G7, which chords qualify for this treatment, and what does the swap buy you?
JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.a:
Both chords contain the same tritone. G7's is B and F; D♭7 contains F and C♭, and C♭ is B. The 3rd and 7th simply swap roles, so the tension and the resolution are unchanged.

Only dominant chords qualify — the tritone is what is being preserved, and only a dominant 7th has one. The substitute always sits a semitone above the target of resolution. What it buys is chromatic bass motion: Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 becomes Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7, roots walking D – D♭ – C.
JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.why:
That descending chromatic bass is one of the most recognisable sounds in jazz and neo-soul, and it is available for the price of one chord. Substituting the V of a ii–V–I gives the very common IIm7 – ♭II7 – Imaj7.

It is already in pop, found by ear rather than by theory — the chromatic iii → ii → ♭II descent in "Toxic" reads as tritone subs of a 6-2-5, and "One Note Samba" stacks two subs to turn a whole turnaround into a chromatic descending bassline. Worth remembering that the theory is a lens applied after the fact, not necessarily the writer's own model.
JAZ-C08 — Tritone substitution: the shar.drill: Take a 3-6-2-5 turnaround and tritone-sub every dominant in it. Play the resulting bassline on its own and confirm every root drops a single semitone.

JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.id: JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary dominant, and the minimum viable form
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.title: JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary dominant, and the minimum viable form
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.short: Substituting a secondary dominant, and the minimum viable form
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.q: The V is not the only dominant on a chart. Which tritone substitution is commonest in pop, and what is the smallest chord that will do the job?
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.a:
♭II-of-ii — the substitute for VI7 on the way to ii — is the commonest flat-five substitution in rock and pop, precisely because it is undramatic. It sits inside a progression as a chromatic passing step from iii down to ii, and most listeners never register it as a substitution at all.

And the minimum viable form is any major triad a semitone above the target. It does not have to be altered, and it does not have to be a dominant 7th at all.
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.why:
Any dominant on a chart is a candidate, not just the V — the substitute is labelled relative to the chord it resolves to, as ♭II of that chord, which is why V/ii, V/V and V/vi can all be swapped the same way.

The minimum viable form is the part most likely to actually get used: a plain major triad a semitone above where you are going is a two-second edit to any progression, on guitar or in a piano roll, and it needs no altered-chord vocabulary to pull off.

This material comes from Ch12 — Tritone Substitution and Other Mystery Chords, which extends the vault's own Tritone Substitution note rather than repeating it — the mechanism and the bossa-nova case studies were already covered there.
JAZ-C09 — Substituting a secondary domin.drill: Find a iii → ii move in one of your own progressions and slide a major triad a semitone above the ii into the gap. Then do the same in front of a V and a vi and compare how obvious each one sounds.

JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.id: JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone sub
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.title: JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone sub
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.short: ♭II–I is not always a tritone sub
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.q: The same ♭II chord resolving to I can be two different devices. What separates them, and why does ♭II–I sound so complete with no dominant in it?
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.a:
How you arrive at it. Dropping into ♭II chromatically — the roots stepping down a semitone at a time into it, as in Dm7 → D♭7 → Cmaj7 — it is a tritone substitution, standing in for a dominant that never appears. Arriving at it from ♭VI by descending fifths on the flat side (♭III → ♭VI → ♭II) it is a borrowed chord, a Phrygian cadence. The audible difference is whether the roots move chromatically or by fifths on the way in.

It sounds complete because every note of a major triad on ♭II falls a semitone into a note of the tonic triad — ♭2̂→1̂, 4̂→3̂, ♭6̂→5̂. Three simultaneous semitone resolutions, no tritone and no leading tone.
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.why:
It is a counter-case to : a strong cadence built by a completely different mechanism from the one that card explains.

It also sharpens the ear test. A half-step bass drop that is not one of the diatonic landmarks in is very often a flat-five substitute arriving at the end of a chromatic run. And ♭II going to V rather than to I is a third thing again — the Neapolitan Sixth, the same chord with a different destination.
JAZ-C10 — ♭II–I is not always a tritone.drill: Play ♭II–I twice: once approached chromatically from ii, once approached from ♭VI. Name which is which by ear from the bass motion alone, with the chords voiced identically.

JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.id: JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place of V7
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.title: JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place of V7
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.short: The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place of V7
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.q: Give the backdoor cadence in C, say where its chords come from, and say when you would reach for it instead of V7.
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.a:
Fm7 – B♭7 – Cmaj7 — iv7 – ♭VII7 – I, often landing on Cmaj9 rather than a plain triad.

Both borrowed chords come from C minor. B♭7 contains A♭, the ♭6 of C, which resolves down to G, and D, which is already in the tonic chord once you land on Cmaj9. Reach for it when V7 sounds too final or too bright — it is warmer, plagal-flavoured and more ambiguous. The lighter shorthand is the backdoor dominant: ♭VII7 straight to I with no minor iv in front.
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.why:
This is the substitution that already lives in the music Nate makes. Rihanna's "Stay" is Am7 → D in E; the whole chorus of "No Such Thing" is one long backdoor; Zero 7's "The Waiting Line" uses it as the main progression; and "Lights Up" resolves an A♭ minor song to A♭ major through it. Stevie Wonder used it twice on one record, each time set up by a ii–V aimed at IV that gets redirected onto the minor iv instead.

The backdoor dominant on its own — no minor iv — is even more common: "New York State of Mind", "Layla", "You Are So Beautiful".
JAZ-C11 — The backdoor: ♭VII7 in place o.drill: Take a loop that ends V–I and replace the cadence with iv7–♭VII7–I. Then strip the iv and use ♭VII7 alone. Decide which of the three endings the track wants.

JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.id: JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled reset
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.title: JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled reset
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.short: A turnaround is a controlled reset
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.q: Give the base turnaround, say what job it does, and give the writing habit that goes with it.
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.a:
I – vi – ii – V — in C, Cmaj7 Am7 Dm7 G7. Its only job is to end a section by pointing back at the top: the root falls a third, then rises a fourth twice, and it ends on V, which wants the I of the next chorus.

The habit: write the four-chord version first, then compress. Two bars (| Cmaj7 A7 | Dm7 G7 |), one bar (| Dm7 G7 |, the commonest ending in the repertoire), or V alone on beats 3–4. Compressing a good turnaround gives a good short one; expanding a bare Dm7 G7 gives you nothing to work with.
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.why:
Loop-based music is all turnaround — a four-bar loop that repeats is a turnaround by definition, and getting the last bar right is what makes a loop feel circular rather than merely repeated.

Three moves that work directly in production: end on V7 or ♭II7 for the classic pull; end on the ii, softer and very common in neo-soul, leaving the V implied and the loop never fully closed; or change only the last bar between repeats — two loops of material for one bar of writing, which is the cheapest arrangement variation available.

Every named variation — VI7, III7–VI7, tritone subs, ♭III7, backdoor, minor — is Lesson 3's substitution rules applied to this one four-chord skeleton, so they can be generated rather than memorised.
JAZ-C12 — A turnaround is a controlled r.drill: Write the four-chord turnaround, then compress it to two bars, one bar and half a bar. Then take a loop of yours that ends on I and re-end it on V, on ii, and on ♭II7.

JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.id: JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turnaround, answered
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.title: JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turnaround, answered
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.short: Rhythm Changes: a looped turnaround, answered
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.q: What happens in bars 1–4 and bars 5–8 of a Rhythm Changes A section, and what makes the pair worth stealing for a verse?
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.a:
Bars 1–4 are I–vi–ii–V twice — a turnaround, looped, and nothing else. Bars 5–8 answer it by going to the subdominant and back: I → I7 → IV → iv → I → V/ii → ii → V, with the borrowed iv (in B♭, E♭ → E♭m6) as the moment the section actually goes somewhere.

Four bars of a static loop do not get boring because four bars of real harmonic movement answer them. That question-and-answer structure inside one eight-bar unit is the transferable part.
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.why:
It is a masterclass in loop writing, and the answer to why a four-bar loop that is fine on its own gets tiring over sixteen bars: it was never given anything to answer it.

The form is also a substitution playground — tritone subs on the bridge dominants, an interpolated ii in front of every dominant, diminished passing chords in the A section — so it is where Lesson 3's rules get exercised on real repertoire rather than on an abstract turnaround.
JAZ-C13 — Rhythm Changes: a looped turna.drill: Write eight bars where the first four are one loop repeated and the second four move to IV, borrow the minor iv, and come home. Then try the same eight bars with the loop repeated four times instead and hear the difference.

JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.id: JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made from harmonic rhythm alone
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.title: JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made from harmonic rhythm alone
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.short: A bridge can be contrast made from harmonic rhythm alone
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.q: Give the Rhythm Changes bridge, and say what makes it feel like a different section given that it introduces no new material.
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.a:
| D7 | D7 | G7 | G7 | C7 | C7 | F7 | F7 | in B♭ — III7–VI7–II7–V7, four dominants two bars each, each resolving down a fifth into the next, and only the last of them — F7, the key's own V7 — diatonic.

What makes it feel new is not a key change, a tempo change or new instrumentation. It is a switch from diatonic and busy to chromatic and slow: harmonic rhythm drops from two chords per bar to one chord per two bars — a 4× slowdown — and that alone reads as a different section.
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.why:
This is the cheapest bridge available in production. Contrast does not require new material: halve the harmonic rhythm, leave everything else alone, and the section changes.

The bridge is also a self-contained lesson in dominant motion by fifths — playing the eight-bar loop teaches it faster than any explanation. Its off-the-shelf cousin is The Montgomery-Ward Bridge, the stock I7–IV7–II7–V7 Tin Pan Alley writers reached for when they had two A sections and needed eight contrasting bars; three of its four root moves are fifths and the fourth, IV → II, is the seam.
JAZ-C14 — A bridge can be contrast made.drill: Take a busy eight-bar section of your own and rewrite it with the harmonic rhythm halved and then halved again, changing nothing else. Decide at which point it stops sounding like the same section.

JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.id: JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in predictable slots
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.title: JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in predictable slots
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.short: Standard forms put devices in predictable slots
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.q: Name the two 32-bar containers, say what the first half of a 16+16 tune must not do, and say what knowing the form buys you before you read a single chord.
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.a:
AABA — four 8-bar sections, the same A three times around a contrasting bridge, as in Rhythm Changes. And 16+16 — two halves, the second repeating most of the first with a different ending.

The first half of a 16+16 must not resolve to I. It has to reach V, or a V-substitute, so the second half has somewhere to launch from; the second half's ending is the tune's real cadence.

Knowing the shape tells you how much of the chart is genuinely new material, and puts the recurring devices in known slots: a secondary ii–V to vi early, one to IV soon after, IV → iv → I around the IV chord, V7/V in the last line of the first half, and a turnaround in the final bars.
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.why:
The point is not memorising one chart. It is that unrelated standards by different composers keep reusing the same device in the same position, so a new chart in a known form reduces to "which variant of the usual devices is this one" rather than 32 bars of arbitrary chords.

That is also how to memorise one: chunk it the way a phone number is chunked. Name the form first, then name the cadences and functional units — "a 2-5 to six", not "half-diminished, then dominant, then minor" — and once a chunk is learned once it is recognised everywhere else it appears.
JAZ-C15 — Standard forms put devices in.drill: Take a standard you do not know, mark the form and the section boundaries before reading a single chord, then fill in the chunks by name rather than by chord symbol. Count how many distinct things you actually had to remember.

JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.id: JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a substitute replaces
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.title: JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a substitute replaces
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.short: A passing chord connects; a substitute replaces
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.q: What separates a passing chord from a substitution, and what is the placement rule that keeps the real progression audible?
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.a:
A passing chord connects two chords that are already in the progression, and is usually optional decoration — the bass player can keep walking the original changes underneath it and it still works. A substitution replaces a chord of the chart, so everyone has to play it.

The rule: put the passing chord on the weak beat and keep the real chord on the heavy beat. The ear then tracks the actual harmony and hears the passing chord as colour rather than as a competing chord change.

The exception is a chromatic passing chord written into the harmony itself, which changes the bass motion and does need the whole band.
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.why:
It settles the question of who has to know. Decoration you can add alone while comping; a substitution has to be agreed, or the bass and the chords will disagree about what the tune is.

The four families are worth having by name: a dominant diminished a half step below the target (C♯dim7 → Dm7, which is a rootless A7♭9); a chord shape slid a fret into the target, where you think about the target and not about naming the passing chord; diatonic chords inserted for stepwise motion (Dm7 → Em7 → Fmaj7 → G7); and a dominant, either a plain secondary dominant or its tritone sub.
JAZ-C16 — A passing chord connects; a su.drill: Take a I–vi–ii–V and fill every transition with a diatonic passing chord, keeping the real chords on the heavy beats. Then play the same passage with the passing chords on the strong beats instead and hear the progression stop reading.

JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constrai.title: JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constraint
JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constrai.q: What is the only rule reharmonization has to obey, and what does it imply about the order you work in?
JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constrai.a:
The melody note must be a usable tone of the new chord — a chord tone (1, 3, 5, 7) or a functioning extension (9, 11, 13, or an altered version of those). What it must not be is a note the new chord actively contradicts: a natural 9 over a ♭9 chord, or a natural 4 sitting on the 3rd.

Everything else — function, bass motion, density — is negotiable. So you work melody-first: write out the melody, decide what each note could be relative to a candidate chord, and choose from there. Choosing chords first and hoping the tune survives is how you get the clashes.
JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constrai.why:
Reharmonization is the practical payoff of the whole strand — it is what turns a plain loop into something that sounds composed, and it is the fastest way to get a second section out of material you already have.

The constraint is also what makes it checkable. Every technique in the note — interpolating ii chords, tritone-subbing the dominants, adding secondary dominants, changing only the bass, a pedal point, modal interchange, or reharmonising the rhythm instead of the chords — is legal exactly when the melody still fits.
JAZ-C17 — Reharmonization's one constrai.drill: Take a four-bar melody of yours, write each melody note above a blank bar, and list three chords that make each note a legal chord tone or extension. Pick a path through them and play it against the original harmony.

JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.id: JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords
JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.title: JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords
JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.q: A vocal is holding a C. Name several chords that can sit under it, and say what each one turns the C into.
JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.a:
Cmaj7 — C is the root, neutral and home · Am7 — the ♭3, softer, relative minor · Fmaj7 — the 5th, plagal and warm · Dm7 — the ♭7, suspended and unresolved · A♭maj7 — the 3rd, borrowed and cinematic · F♯m7♭5 — the ♭5, tense and needing to move.

Same melody note, six different meanings. It is the cheapest reharmonization move there is. The systematic version is delayed resolution: hold the melody on its expected tonic note but harmonise it with anything except the tonic chord, and arrive home late.
JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.why:
Cycling chords under a sustained vocal is most of the neo-soul trick, and it costs nothing but the chord choice — the topline does not change, so nothing has to be re-sung or re-recorded.

It is also the cheapest way to get a second section: run the same held note through a different set of chords on the repeat and the passage reads as development rather than as a loop going round again.
JAZ-C18 — One melody note, many chords.drill: Record or program a single sustained note, then move six different chords underneath it without changing the note. Name what the note is in each chord as it goes past.

JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.id: JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.title: JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.short: Reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.q: When does reharmonization make a song worse, and what is the rule of thumb that prevents it?
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.a:
It competes with the melody for attention. If the tune is the point — a strong vocal hook, a memorable lead line — dense reharmonization pulls focus and the song gets worse.

The rule: reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement. Let the listener learn the plain version, then change what is underneath it. It then reads as development rather than as confusion, and it hands you a second section for free.
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.why:
It is the discipline that keeps every technique in this lesson from becoming the failure mode Lesson 3 already warned about — a substitution reads as sophisticated against plain harmony and as directionless wall to wall, and the same is true of reharmonization across a song.

For Nate's own arrangements it is a scheduling rule as much as a harmonic one: verse 1 plain, verse 2 reharmonised, and the change lands as an arrangement event rather than as harmonic noise.
JAZ-C19 — Reharmonize the repeats, not t.drill: Take a song of yours with a repeated section. Leave the first statement exactly as written and reharmonise only the repeat. Then listen once through and check the change registers as an event rather than as a mistake.

JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.id: JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony
JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.title: JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony
JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.q: What does modal jazz put in place of functional harmony, and which similarly-named thing is it not?
JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.a:
Four things carry the music once the chords stop moving: the mode's own character as the melodic material, quartal voicings, pedal points and drones, and rhythm, dynamics and texture marking the form.

It is not modal interchange. Modal jazz holds one mode for many bars — a static approach to form. Modal interchange borrows a chord from a parallel mode inside functional harmony and returns — a chromatic spice. They share a word and almost nothing else.
JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.why:
This is the jazz idiom closest to how modern loop-based music actually works. A four-bar loop on Fmaj7, or a two-chord vamp, is exactly the situation So What is in: the harmony is not going anywhere and the interest has to come from somewhere else. Modal jazz is sixty years of worked solutions to that problem.

The practical consequence for arrangement: with no chord changes to signal a section, one new element — a texture, a countermelody, a register shift — reads as a whole new section.
JAZ-C20 — A loop is modal harmony.drill: Take a two-chord vamp of yours and write four sections over it that differ only in texture and density, with the harmony untouched. Check whether the sections still read as sections.

JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.id: JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to be sounded
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.title: JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to be sounded
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.short: The characteristic note has to be sounded
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.q: Give the characteristic note of Dorian, Lydian, Mixolydian and Phrygian, and say what happens if you avoid it.
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.a:
Dorian — the natural 6 (against natural minor) · Lydian — the ♯4 (against major) · Mixolydian — the ♭7 (against major) · Phrygian — the ♭2 (against natural minor).

Land on it and the mode is established; avoid it and the music collapses into plain major or minor. In D Dorian the note is B: hit B and it is Dorian, dodge B and it is D minor.
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.why:
A loop that never plays the ♯4 is not Lydian, it is major with a Lydian label. The colour has to be sounded, not declared — which is the single commonest way a modal idea fails to arrive in a finished track.

The advanced case is the same rule applied in miniature: in a short vamp of several chords that are not functionally connected, treat each chord as its own modal island with its own scale, rather than hunting for one key that explains the whole progression.
JAZ-C21 — The characteristic note has to.drill: Loop one chord and improvise over it for a minute without ever playing the characteristic note, then again while landing on it deliberately. Name the mode you actually hear in each take.

JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.id: JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode without naming a chord
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.title: JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode without naming a chord
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.short: Quartal voicings state a mode without naming a chord
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.q: What is the So What voicing, and why fourths rather than thirds?
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.a:
Three perfect fourths with a major third on top — from the bottom, E A D G B.

A stack of thirds names a chord, and naming a chord implies a function — which is exactly what modal music is trying to avoid. Fourths sound open and unassigned, so they state the mode without committing to a chord. That is where the hollow, floating sound comes from.
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.why:
It transfers straight into production: quartal voicings sit beautifully under a vocal because they are sparse and have no strong 3rd fighting the topline. This is the same problem solves, answered a different way — the shell keeps the 3rd and drops the 5th, the quartal voicing avoids the 3rd altogether.

Over sixteen bars of one chord it also removes the harmonic commitment that gets tiring, which is why it is the default answer to a long static section.
JAZ-C22 — Quartal voicings state a mode.drill: Voice a static Dm7 vamp as a tertian chord and then as the So What stack, and A/B them under a melody. Then move the same quartal shape in parallel across a two-chord vamp and hear it hold the two chords together.

JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.id: JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note is rhythmic
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.title: JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note is rhythmic
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.short: Bebop scales: the extra note is rhythmic
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.q: What makes a scale a bebop scale, and what problem does the added note solve?
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.a:
A normal seven-note scale with one chromatic passing tone added, making eight notes.

The reason is rhythmic, not harmonic. Play a seven-note scale in straight eighths from a downbeat and by the next bar the chord tones have shifted onto offbeats. The eighth note puts them back on the beat, every bar. Bebop dominant on G is G A B C D E F F♯ G — the F♯ is the addition, and running it down from the root lands G, F, D and B on downbeats — the four chord tones of G7.

The rule: the extra note goes wherever it makes chord tones fall on strong beats. If yours already do, you do not need one.
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.why:
It reframes a scale as a rhythmic object rather than a pitch collection, which is the useful half.

The transfer is to basslines: the added eighth is exactly what makes a walking-ish line land its chord tones on the beat instead of drifting off it. What does not transfer is the note rate — bebop's density is a genre convention, not a principle, and importing it wholesale into a trap beat just sounds busy.
JAZ-C23 — Bebop scales: the extra note i.drill: Write a one-bar eighth-note run using the seven-note scale and mark where the chord tones land. Add the passing tone and mark them again.

JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes.title: JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes
JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes.q: What is an enclosure, where does it belong, and how does an approach note differ?
JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes.a:
An enclosure surrounds a target note before playing it. For a target of C: D♭ – B – C (chromatic both sides, classic bebop), D – B – C (diatonic above, chromatic below, smoother), B – D♭ – C (more angular), D – D♭ – B – C (longest and most obviously jazz).

An approach note is the one-note cousin: precede the chord tone with the note a half step below (the default and the strongest, because it borrows the leading-tone pull), a half step above (softer), or a scale step away (most neutral, most usable outside jazz).

Both belong on the note you actually want heard — usually a chord tone on a downbeat. Not on every note. Enclosures are punctuation; wall to wall, a line stops having a shape.
JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes.why:
The most transferable device in the whole vocabulary, and it works in any genre. Take a two-note synth hook and enclose the second note: it costs two 16ths and stops the line sounding quantised from scratch.

A single chromatic approach into the downbeat of a chorus is the cheapest lift available anywhere in an arrangement.
JAZ-C24 — Enclosures and approach notes.drill: Take a melody you have already written, pick the three notes that matter most, and enclose only those. Leave everything else alone and check the line still has a shape.

JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.id: JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under static harmony
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.title: JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under static harmony
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.short: CESH: a chromatic line under static harmony
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.q: What is CESH, and how does it differ from an approach note or an enclosure?
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.a:
Chromatic embellishment of static harmony — take one note that matters (a chord root, a guide tone) and walk it by half step across several beats or bars, while the harmony underneath stays still or moves more slowly.

The difference is scale. An approach note or an enclosure targets a single arrival on a single chord tone. CESH is a sustained chromatic line, closer to a bass-line device borrowed into the melody than to a one-note ornament. The term names the chromatic line, not the chord.
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.why:
It is the direct answer to a vamp or a held chord going static — forward motion generated without changing the chord itself, which is exactly the standing problem in loop-based writing.

It pairs with the modal material from Lesson 6: when the harmony is deliberately refusing to move, this is one of the few devices that supplies motion without breaking that decision.
JAZ-C25 — CESH: a chromatic line under s.drill: Hold one chord for four bars and walk a single inner voice down chromatically underneath it. Then do the same over a two-bar vamp you already have and decide whether it needs any other change at all.

JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.id: JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.title: JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.short: Keep the concept, not the lick
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.q: Give the steps that turn a transcribed solo into your own vocabulary, and say which one gets skipped.
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.a:
Learn the solo by ear in full · chunk it into small sections, a phrase or a chord at a time · analyse each chunk against the chord underneath it for the scale, arpeggio or device being used · reduce each chunk to one named concept — a scale choice, an arpeggio substitution, a target note · then improvise your own solo over the same changes applying the concepts rather than the licks.

The skipped step is the fourth. Learning a solo by ear is not enough on its own — the concept, not the lick, is the thing worth keeping.
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.why:
What you actually need from a great solo is a nudge toward somewhere, not a part to reproduce. A set of per-chord concepts is a template you can play through repeatedly, which turns one transcription into a whole practice session's worth of new lines rather than one memorised chorus.

The same logic generalises past soloing: it is the melodic twin of , where a chart is chunked into named functional units instead of chord symbols.
JAZ-C26 — Keep the concept, not the lick.drill: Take eight bars of a solo you already know by ear. Write one named concept per chord, put the original away, and improvise three different choruses from the concept list alone.

MEL-C01 — Melodic contour.title: MEL-C01 — Melodic contour
MEL-C01 — Melodic contour.q: What is melodic contour, and what makes it strong?
MEL-C01 — Melodic contour.a: The melody's overall shape over time — how it rises and falls. A strong contour is balanced: what goes up comes back down, producing an arc with one clear peak rather than a flat or wandering line. Balance the motion too — after stepwise movement, take a leap.
MEL-C01 — Melodic contour.why: Melody Writing already defined it and covered balancing it. This was a retention gap, not a teaching gap. Constraining the range with an explicit top and bottom note before writing does most of the work of producing a shape at all.
MEL-C01 — Melodic contour.drill: Draw the contour of three melodies you like as a single line. Find the peak in each.

MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.id: MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.title: MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.short: Landing on the 3rd vs the root
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.q: A melody lands on the 3rd of the chord instead of the root. What changes?
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.a: The root sounds settled and final — where a phrase goes to end. The 3rd is more melodic and colours the chord (brighter or sadder) without changing the harmony, and it's less conclusive. Other tones: 7th leans and wants to move; 9th is open and floating, colour without changing function.
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.why: And the consequence is the practical part: landing on the root constantly is the single most common reason a melody sounds boring — it agrees with the harmony on every downbeat, so nothing is ever in tension. Target 3rds and 7ths on strong beats.
MEL-C02 — Landing on the 3rd vs the root.drill: Take a melody. Move every phrase-ending from the root to the 3rd, then the 7th. Name what each does.

MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.id: MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.title: MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.short: Motifs and how to develop them
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.q: What is a motif, and name at least two ways to develop one.
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.a: A short musical fragment used as raw material to generate much more music. Nine named techniques: repetition · sequence · inversion · interval contraction · interval expansion · diminution · augmentation · rhythmic metamorphosis · imitation.
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.why: Motivic Development has had a table of all nine in the vault the whole time. The point that generalizes: most strong melodies are one short idea developed, not a long line invented.
MEL-C03 — Motifs and how to develop them.drill: Write four bars. Generate sixteen more using only techniques from the table. Name each one you used.

MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.id: MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to changes
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.title: MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to changes
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.short: Writing to a loop vs to changes
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.q: How does writing a melody over a static one-chord loop differ from writing over moving changes?
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.a: Over changes the harmony supplies the motion — hold one note and the chords recontextualize it (5th, then 3rd, then 9th), so it moves without moving. Over a static loop nothing does that, so the melody must generate its own movement through rhythm, contour and phrasing. Static loops also tolerate more repetition, since the listener is already in a looped frame.
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.why: It's the distinction that matters most in loop-based production. It's why rhythm-first writing suits your workflow: over a static loop, rhythm is the only source of motion you fully control.
MEL-C04 — Writing to a loop vs to change.drill: Write one melody over a moving progression, then play it over a one-chord loop. Note what stops working.

MEL-C05 — Register and intensity.title: MEL-C05 — Register and intensity
MEL-C05 — Register and intensity.q: What's the relationship between a melody's register/range and a section's emotional intensity?
MEL-C05 — Register and intensity.a: Higher reads as more intense — partly convention, partly physiology, since a singer audibly works harder up there. So verses sit lower and choruses lift, and the lift is much of what makes a chorus feel like one. Widening the range does similar work: bigger leaps and a wider span feel more dramatic than a melody circling three notes.
MEL-C05 — Register and intensity.why: The practical payoff: if a chorus isn't landing, check where it sits relative to the verse before rewriting it. Moving it up a third often does more than new notes.
MEL-C05 — Register and intensity.drill: Take a chorus that isn't landing. Move it up a third without changing anything else.

MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.id: MEL-C06 — Building tension across a section
MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.title: MEL-C06 — Building tension across a section
MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.q: Melodically, how do you build tension across a verse so the chorus lands?
MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.a: Climb — rise in register, shorten the note values so the line gets busier, and repeat a fragment in ascending sequence so it gathers. Withhold the tonic so nothing resolves until the chorus does it. The counter-move also works: strip everything back right before the chorus so it arrives against space.
MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.why: The counter-move is the one worth remembering for your genres — in loop-based production the drop is the arrival, so subtraction before it often beats building into it.
MEL-C06 — Building tension across a sect.drill: Take a verse. Build one version that climbs into the chorus, one that strips back. Pick the better.

MEL-C07 — What makes a hook.title: MEL-C07 — What makes a hook
MEL-C07 — What makes a hook.q: What makes a hook memorable? Name at least three factors.
MEL-C07 — What makes a hook.a: 1) Repetition — it has to come back, and be short enough to hold after one pass. This outranks everything. 2) Rhythmic distinctiveness — identifiable from its rhythm alone, with the pitches stripped out. 3) Singable range and clear contour. Then: contrast against what surrounds it. Simplicity usually beats complexity.
MEL-C07 — What makes a hook.why: The test for factor 2 is concrete — tap the hook with no pitches. If it's still recognisable, it's rhythmically distinct. A hook has to survive being remembered badly.
MEL-C07 — What makes a hook.drill: Tap three hooks you know, no pitches. Which are still identifiable?

MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody.title: MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody
MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody.q: A melody you've written feels boring. Name three things you'd change, and which usually matters most.
MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody.a: Change the rhythm first — most boring melodies are boring rhythmically, circling even note values on the beat. Then widen it (add a leap, push the top note higher). Then move where it sits against the chord — target 9ths and 7ths instead of roots and 5ths. Also: add space, displace it off the downbeat, or reharmonize underneath it.
MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody.why: The ranking is the answer, not the list — rhythm is the highest-leverage fix by a wide margin, and it's the one people reach for last because pitch feels like where melody lives.
MEL-C08 — Fixing a boring melody.drill: Take a melody that isn't working. Apply the triage in order and stop at the first fix that solves it.

MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus.title: MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus
MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus.q: Should you leave a limiter on the master bus when sending a mix to be mastered?
MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus.a: No — take it off. Deliver peaks at roughly −6 to −3 dBFS, reached with a gain move rather than a limiter. If you want them to hear your loudness intent, send both versions clearly labelled.
MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus.why: A brick-wall limiter that pulled 8 dB off your peaks isn't headroom you saved — it's 8 dB of information deleted before the engineer ever sees the file, and there's no undoing it. This is the most consequential mistake in the whole MIX strand, and it is live because you actually hand off.
MIX-C01 — No limiter on the 2-bus.drill: Open your most recent bounce. Is anything on the 2-bus? What are the peaks? Fix both.

MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems.title: MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems
MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems.q: What's the difference between multitracks and stems, and which does a mixing engineer want?
MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems.a: Multitracks are every individual track, unbundled — each mic, each synth, each vocal layer. Stems are grouped submixes (drums, bass, music, vocals) bounced to a handful of files. Send multitracks unless they've specifically asked otherwise.
MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems.why: Stems are for remixers, live playback and sync licensing. An engineer handed stems can't touch the snare without also touching the kick.
MIX-C02 — Multitracks vs stems.drill: For a current session: how many multitracks would you deliver, and what would the four stems be?

MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open.title: MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open
MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open.q: Before handing off, what should you commit and what should you leave open?
MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open.a: Commit what defines what a part is — character distortion, synthesis, creative effects, sample choice, tuning and timing edits. Leave open everything relational — track-to-track balance, corrective EQ, bus compression, reverb amounts, and the 2-bus entirely.
MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open.why: The governing rule of the whole handoff. You couldn't answer this at MIX-07, then answered it backwards at MIX-11 by putting track-by-track EQ and compression on the commit side — those are relational, so they're the engineer's. Over-commit and they work around you; under-commit and they mix somebody else's record.
MIX-C03 — Commit vs leave open.drill: Take ten elements in a current session. Call each commit or leave-open and say why. The test: would removing it change what the part is, or only how it sits?

MIX-C04 — Delivery spec.title: MIX-C04 — Delivery spec
MIX-C04 — Delivery spec.q: What format, sample rate, bit depth and headroom do you deliver?
MIX-C04 — Delivery spec.a: WAV or AIFF (never MP3), at the session's native sample rate with no conversion, 24-bit minimum, no dither, peaks −6 to −3 dBFS, every file consolidated from the same timeline zero, every track descriptively named.
MIX-C04 — Delivery spec.why: Format, bit depth and headroom are the easy three. The two that get missed are native rate (don't convert — conversion artifacts are permanent) and no dither (dither is the last step of the last process, and that isn't you).
