MIX-C04 — Delivery spec.drill: Recite the spec without looking. Then check your last export against it.

MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalizati.title: MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalization
MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalizati.q: What does LUFS measure, and why does it matter for streaming?
MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalizati.a: Integrated perceived loudness over time — not peak level. Streaming services normalize playback to a target near −14 LUFS, so a master pushed to −7 simply gets turned down on playback.
MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalizati.why: 'Perceived loudness' is where most people stop. The commercial half is the normalization: pushing past the target costs dynamics and buys nothing, because the platform undoes the loudness and keeps the damage.
MIX-C05 — LUFS and streaming normalizati.drill: What happens to a −7 LUFS master on Spotify versus a −14 one? Which sounds better, and why?

MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference.title: MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference
MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference.q: What is a reference track for, and what's the one step that makes it work?
MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference.a: A finished commercial record in the same lane, used as an external anchor for tone and balance. Level-match it. Anything louder sounds better, so an unmatched reference only tells you it's louder.
MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference.why: The target-sound framing is the well-known half; level matching is the one that gets skipped. Without it you chase a loudness difference with EQ and compression, which is how references make mixes worse. Use it for specific questions — low end, vocal position, brightness — not as something to clone.
MIX-C06 — Level-matching a reference.drill: Pick a reference for a current track. Match its loudness to yours, then answer three specific questions about the difference.

MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.id: MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer needs
MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.title: MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer needs
MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.q: What does a mastering engineer need from you, and what makes their job harder?
MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.a: Needs: a full-resolution WAV at native rate, 24-bit, real headroom, nothing on the 2-bus, plus a reference and a note on intent — and the running order and gaps if it's a release. Harder: an already-limited mix, sample-rate conversion, an MP3 anywhere in the lineage, or a problem buried in the mix that mastering can only make louder rather than fix.
MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.why: The summary concept — it's every other MIX concept applied at once.
MIX-C07 — What a mastering engineer need.drill: Write the two-line email you'd send with a mix. What's attached, and what does the note say?

NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure.title: NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure
NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure.q: An accidental not in the key signature applies for how long, and to which notes?
NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure.a: For the rest of that measure only, and only on that exact line or space (that octave). The bar line cancels it. It does not apply to the same letter in other octaves.
NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure.why: Both halves missed. The octave restriction is the part that catches people — a ♯ on the third-space C doesn't sharpen the C an octave up.
NOT-C01 — Accidentals last one measure.drill: Find a bar with an accidental in any chart. Say which later notes it does and doesn't affect.

NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs.title: NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs
NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs.q: A curved line joins two noteheads. What's it called when the pitches are the same, and when they differ?
NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs.a: Same pitch = a tie — attack only the first, hold through the second. Different pitches = a slur — play legato; on guitar that's a hammer-on or pull-off.
NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs.why: The guitar-specific half matters: a slur is an instruction about technique, not just phrasing.
NOT-C02 — Ties vs slurs.drill: Find both in a chart. Play a tied pair and a slurred pair and confirm you're doing different things.

NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes.title: NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes
NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes.q: In 4/4, how many beats does a dotted half get? A double-dotted half?
NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes.a: 3 and 3½. A dot adds half the note's own value (2 + 1 = 3). The second dot adds half of what the first dot added (+ ½), not half the original again.
NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes.why: The single dot is straightforward; the double dot is where it breaks down. Answering '3 and 4' is the classic error — it assumes the second dot repeats the first.
NOT-C03 — Dotted and double-dotted notes.drill: Write beat values for dotted and double-dotted half, quarter and eighth notes.

NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco.title: NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco
NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco.q: What does 8va above a passage mean, and what cancels it?
NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco.a: Play an octave higher than written. Cancelled by loco (or by the end of the dotted bracket). 8vb below the staff means an octave lower.
NOT-C04 — Octave signs: 8va and loco.why: These exist to keep ledger lines readable — worth knowing, because ledger lines are commonly blamed for guitar reading being hard when they aren't the reason (see ).

NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda.title: NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda
NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda.q: You reach "D.S. al Coda" in a chart. Walk through exactly what you do.
NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda.a: Three moves. 1) Go back to the sign (𝄋 / segno). 2) Play from there until the To Coda mark. 3) Jump to the Coda section.
NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda.why: 'Go to the coda and play it' is the usual half-answer — it skips the first two steps. The jump is precisely where people get lost, and it's the reason the 30-second scan checks the roadmap before anything else.
NOT-C05 — Navigation: D.S. al Coda.drill: Find a chart with a D.S. and trace the whole route with your finger before playing a note.

NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.id: NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower
NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.title: NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower
NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.q: Guitar is written in treble clef but doesn't sound at the written pitch. What's the relationship?
NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.a: It sounds an octave LOWER than written. Guitar is a transposing instrument — written pitch sits an octave above sounding pitch (effectively 8vb).
NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.why: Direction matters — 'an octave higher' is the reverse and is wrong. Directly relevant to reading anything written for you, and to writing parts for other instruments.
NOT-C06 — Guitar sounds an octave lower.drill: Play written middle C on the guitar. Find the same sounding pitch on a piano. Note the octave difference.

NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.id: NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: position
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.title: NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: position
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.short: Why guitar reading is hard: position
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.q: Sight reading is harder on guitar than piano. What's the actual mechanism, and what's the standard solution?
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.a: The same written pitch exists in five or six different places on the fretboard. Notation says what, not where — on piano the mapping is one-to-one, so the decision doesn't exist. The fix is the position system: a fixed four-fret window, one finger per fret, making the mapping unambiguous.
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.why: There's a confident wrong model in wide circulation here — that it's ledger lines. It isn't, and a wrong belief is more useful than a blank because it can be corrected directly. It's also why Leavitt keeps Volume 1 in first position for 24 pages.
NOT-C07 — Why guitar reading is hard: po.drill: Find one written phrase in three different fretboard positions. Then commit to first position and read it again.

NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan.title: NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan
NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan.q: You get 30 seconds with an unseen chart before you play it. What do you look at, and why?
NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan.a: 1) Key and time signature. 2) The roadmap — repeats, endings, D.S., Coda. 3) Range — highest and lowest note, so you can pick a position containing the whole phrase. 4) Rhythm hotspots — tuplets, syncopation, dotted figures, counted silently. 5) A tempo you can hold through the HARDEST bar.
NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan.why: 1/5 — key signature counts, BPM isn't the time signature. Naming only key and time is the half everyone does and the half that doesn't prevent the derailment. The roadmap and the hardest-bar tempo are what actually save the read.
NOT-C08 — The 30-second chart scan.drill: Take an unseen line. Run the five-step scan out loud in 30 seconds, then play it once.

NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.id: NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall behind
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.title: NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall behind
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.short: Keep the pulse when you fall behind
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.q: You fall behind mid-piece. What do you do, and what are the two things you never do?
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.a: Keep the pulse — thin it out and rejoin at the next downbeat. Drop notes, thin the chord, or play only the downbeats until you catch up. Never stop and never go back. A wrong note is a wrong note; a stop is a failure of the skill itself, because the continuity is what the exercise trains. "Slow down until I can play it" is the third trap — it turns the rep into a different exercise and rehearses hesitation.
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.why: It's the rule that saves a performance, and the hardest habit to build. Sight reading exists for the situation where you can't fully play what's in front of you, so dropping the tempo until everything is playable removes the exact condition being trained — and builds the stop-and-fix reflex that ends a live read when there's a band who won't wait.
NOT-C09 — Keep the pulse when you fall b.drill: Cold-read a line too fast for you, once. When it falls apart, play downbeats only and rejoin — no stopping, no second pass.

POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm.title: POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm
POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm.q: What is harmonic rhythm, and why does slow harmonic rhythm suit loop-based production?
POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm.a: How fast the chords change, independent of tempo. Loop-based production wants it slow — one or two chords over several bars — because the loop repeats dozens of times and the interest comes from drums, sound design and vocals. Fast harmonic rhythm pulls attention to the changes and makes a 2-bar loop exhausting.
POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm.why: It's the most important harmonic parameter in the music you make and the classical library doesn't cover it — harmonic rhythm appears in the vault only in Part-Writing and 20th-Century Harmony.
POP-C01 — Harmonic rhythm.drill: Take a loop. Double its harmonic rhythm, then halve it. Which version survives 16 bars?

POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.id: POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying
POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.title: POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying
POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.q: Why are so many successful pop songs built on four repeating chords? And if the harmony isn't moving, what creates motion?
POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.a: Predictability is the feature. Once the ear stops tracking the harmony it attends to the vocal and the groove instead — the progression becomes a bed rather than a series of events. Motion comes from rhythm, melody/topline, timbre and arrangement, not harmony.
POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.why: POP-26 blank; POP-05 half credit (you said 'drums', which is one of four sources). The corollary is the useful part: if a loop is boring, the chords usually aren't the problem — nothing above them is changing.
POP-C02 — Why four chords is satisfying.drill: List everything that changes across 8 bars of one of your loops, other than the chords. If it's nothing, that's the diagnosis.

POP-C03 — Pedal point.title: POP-C03 — Pedal point
POP-C03 — Pedal point.q: What is a pedal point, and what is an EDM build doing harmonically?
POP-C03 — Pedal point.a: A sustained bass note held while the chords above it change — usually the tonic or dominant. An EDM build is a dominant pedal: sitting on V and refusing to resolve, so the drop provides the release.
POP-C03 — Pedal point.why: It had zero coverage anywhere in the vault before 2026-08-04, despite being everywhere in the music — the EDM build that sits on V and resolves at the drop is a pedal point. The application usually arrives long before the name does.
POP-C03 — Pedal point.drill: Build 8 bars over a held tonic pedal, changing chords above it. Then do the same over a dominant pedal and hear the tension build.

POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.id: POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.title: POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.short: Four chords with a moving bass
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.q: What does "four chords with a moving bass" mean, and why does it feel like more movement than it is?
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.a: The chords stay the same; the bass walks through inversions underneath them. C – G/B – Am – F gives a descending bass line over plain I–V–vi–IV. It reads as more harmonic movement because the ear takes the lowest note as the root, so changing the bass changes the perceived chord.
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.why: It's the cheapest way to make four chords feel like eight, and it pairs with the inverse move — hold the bass, move the chords () — and with Chromatic Bass Lines, which the vault already covered.
POP-C04 — Four chords with a moving bass.drill: Take a 4-chord loop and write a descending bass line under it using inversions only. Change no chords.

POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop.title: POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop
POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop.q: Name three harmonic ways to create movement in a stale 8-bar loop — not arrangement or mixing moves.
POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop.a: 1) Reharmonize the last bar so the loop resolves differently each pass. 2) Insert a secondary dominant in front of a chord to pull harder into it (Am → E7 Am). 3) Move the bass under static harmony with inversions or a pedal. Also: swap a chord for its parallel, or open voicings into sus/add9.
POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop.why: The question deliberately excluded arrangement and mixing — the fixes you'd reach for by instinct. These three are the harmonic toolkit, and the first one is the highest-leverage single change.
POP-C05 — Reharmonizing a loop.drill: Take one loop and make three versions, one per technique. Keep the arrangement identical.

POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.id: POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.title: POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.short: Sus and add9 under a vocal
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.q: Why voice pads as sus2/sus4/add9 rather than plain triads under a vocal? And what does a topline landing on the 9th add?
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.a: Sus and add9 voicings remove or blur the 3rd — the note defining major or minor — so the pad stops colliding with the topline and lets the vocal define the harmony. A topline on the 9th adds colour without changing function: the 9th isn't in the triad, so it sounds open and floating rather than settled.
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.why: Both blank. These are the two voicing decisions that matter most in loop-based music, because the same voicing is heard dozens of times. A plain triad under a busy vocal fights it.
POP-C06 — Sus and add9 under a vocal.drill: Take a pad under a vocal. Voice it as a triad, then sus2, then add9. Note which one you stop noticing.

POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.id: POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotations
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.title: POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotations
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.short: The Axis family and its rotations
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.q: Name the Axis progression and a song that uses it. I–V–vi–IV and vi–IV–I–V contain the same four chords — what actually changes?
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.a: I–V–vi–IV (or any rotation) — "Let It Be", "Don't Stop Believin'", "With or Without You". Between rotations the chords are identical; what changes is which one the ear hears as home. I–V–vi–IV feels bright and lifting; vi–IV–I–V reads as darker and more yearning.
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.why: POP-02 blank immediately after you spelled the progression correctly at POP-01 — you could build it and couldn't name it. POP-13 blank too. Whichever chord the loop starts and returns to becomes the tonic, which means you can flip a section's mood without changing a single chord.
POP-C07 — The Axis family and its rotati.drill: Write one 4-chord loop and play all four rotations. Pick one for a verse and one for a chorus.

POP-C08 — Relative-key switching.title: POP-C08 — Relative-key switching
POP-C08 — Relative-key switching.q: A chorus switches from C major to A minor. What's the relationship, and what does the switch do?
POP-C08 — Relative-key switching.a: Relative major and minor — they share a key signature. Same seven notes, different tonal centre. So the section darkens without changing the available notes and without any modulation machinery.
POP-C08 — Relative-key switching.why: 'Relative minor' and 'happy to sad' are the easy half; the mechanism is the one that makes it usable. The same-notes point is what makes it a free move: no pivot chord, no new material, just a different resolution target.
POP-C08 — Relative-key switching.drill: Take a loop in C. Restart it on Am and end it there. Nothing else changes — name what happened.

POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII.title: POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII
POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII.q: In I–♭VII–IV (C–B♭–F in C), where does the ♭VII come from — and what Beatles device does this describe?
POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII.a: Mixolydian (major with a ♭7), or equivalently borrowed from the parallel minor — both readings are valid. It has no leading tone, so it lifts and drifts rather than pulling home. It's a Beatles signature, alongside descending chromatic bass under a held chord ("Michelle", "Something").
POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII.why: POP-03 blank, and POP-18 — the Beatles question — blank in your core lane. ♭VII is the single most common non-diatonic chord in rock and pop, and the missing-leading-tone point is why it sounds modal rather than functional.
POP-C09 — Mixolydian ♭VII.drill: Play C–B♭–F and C–G–F back to back. Name why one pulls home and the other doesn't.

POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.id: POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv
POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.title: POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv
POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.q: Compare Dm–G and Dm–Gm. What note differs, what mode does each imply? And what's ♭VI–♭VII–i called?
POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.a: Dm–G is Dorian — G major needs a B natural, Dorian's raised 6th. Dm–Gm is natural minor (B♭). One note is the entire colour difference — Dorian lifts, Aeolian stays dark. ♭VI–♭VII–i is the Aeolian cadence (F–G–Am in A minor), all diatonic to natural minor.
POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.why: All three blank. Dorian vamps are everywhere in neo-soul, house and modern R&B precisely because they're minor without being bleak; the Aeolian cadence is the harmonic bed under a large amount of trap.
POP-C10 — Dorian IV vs Aeolian iv.drill: Loop Dm–G for 8 bars, then Dm–Gm. Change nothing else. Name the feeling difference.

POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.id: POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop modulation
POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.title: POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop modulation
POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.q: What is a chromatic mediant? What is a truck driver's modulation, why is it a cliché, and what's subtler?
POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.a: A chromatic mediant is a chord a 3rd from the tonic with a quality the key doesn't provide — from C: E, A, E♭, A♭ major. Shares a common tone, has no dominant pull, so it reads as a lift or scene change. A truck driver's modulation shoves everything up a step for the final chorus, unprepared — a cliché because it announces itself. Subtler: shift mode instead of key, approach the new tonic through its own V, or pivot on a shared chord.
POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.why: Both blank, and both had zero vault coverage before 2026-08-04. Note ♭VI and ♭III are simultaneously borrowed chords and chromatic mediants — same chord, two framings.
POP-C11 — Chromatic mediants and pop mod.drill: Drop an E major into a C major loop and let it sit. Then try A♭. Name what each does to the section.

RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.id: RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dotted beats
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.title: RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dotted beats
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.short: Compound meter is felt in dotted beats
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.q: In 6/8, how many beats are in a bar and what note value gets the beat?
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.a: Two beats, and the dotted quarter gets the beat. Six eighth notes are written; they group into two dotted-quarter pulses.
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.why: Compound time signatures lie: the top number is the division count, not the beat count. Divide by 3 for the real beat count, and the beat unit is always a dotted note. The written half (six eighths) is the easy one; the felt half is what matters when you're playing it.
RHY-C01 — Compound meter is felt in dott.drill: Count a 6/8 bar out loud in six, then in two. Then do 9/8 and 12/8.

RHY-C02 — Syncopation.title: RHY-C02 — Syncopation
RHY-C02 — Syncopation.a: Accenting a weak beat or an offbeat — putting emphasis where the meter doesn't expect it. Three forms: accent a weak position, place a note on a weak position and tie it over the strong one, or rest on the strong beat.
RHY-C02 — Syncopation.why: The single most important rhythmic device in every genre you make. The key insight: the meter has to stay in the listener's head for syncopation to mean anything — remove the steady pulse and there's nothing to syncopate against.
RHY-C02 — Syncopation.drill: Take a straight 16th hat pattern. Make it syncopated three ways using velocity only, no note moves.

RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.id: RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.title: RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.short: Swing is a triplet with the middle note gone
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.q: What does swing do to a pair of eighth notes, and how is a shuffle different from a triplet?
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.a: Swing lengthens the first eighth of each pair and shortens the second, toward a triplet feel. A triplet divides the beat into three equal parts; a shuffle is that triplet with the middle note removed (long–short). Full triplet swing is exactly 2:1 — the long note takes two of the beat's three triplet parts and the short note takes one; swing sits anywhere between straight (1:1) and that.
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.why: 'Makes them late on the grid' describes the audible result of the second note only. The mechanism is the uneven long-short division — and the triplet relationship is what makes swing amount a continuous dial rather than an on/off switch.
RHY-C03 — Swing is a triplet with the mi.drill: Set a swing preset to 0%, 50%, then maximum on a hat pattern. Then program an actual triplet and delete the middle note of each.

RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola.title: RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola
RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola.q: What is a polyrhythm? What is a hemiola? How do they differ?
RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola.a: Polyrhythm = two conflicting subdivisions at once — classically 3 against 2, three evenly spaced notes in the span of two. Hemiola = a pattern implying a different meter over the prevailing one — three groups of two against two groups of three. Polyrhythm stacks subdivisions; hemiola reorganizes the grouping.
RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola.why: Both blank, and hemiola appeared nowhere in the vault before 2026-08-03. Count 3-against-2 with "nice cup of tea" — 'nice' and 'of' are the 2; 'nice', 'cup', 'tea' are the 3. Practical hemiola: a dotted-quarter pulse over 4/4 — three eighths against a bar of eight — cycles out of phase and realigns on the downbeat every 3 bars (8 dotted quarters = 24 eighths = 3 bars).
RHY-C04 — Polyrhythm and hemiola.drill: Clap 3-against-2 with the phrase until it locks. Then program a repeating dotted-quarter hit over a 4/4 loop at least 3 bars long and hear it drift, then land back on the downbeat of bar 4.

RHY-C05 — Half-time.title: RHY-C05 — Half-time
RHY-C05 — Half-time.q: What is a half-time feel, and what happens to the backbeat?
RHY-C05 — Half-time.a: The backbeat moves to beat 3 instead of 2 and 4, so the groove feels half as fast at the same tempo. A track written at 140 feels like ~70.
RHY-C05 — Half-time.why: It's the defining rhythmic fact of your primary genre. The ear judges groove speed almost entirely from snare placement, which is why this works. It's the trick that lets trap be fast enough for busy hi-hats and slow enough to rap over, simultaneously.
RHY-C05 — Half-time.drill: Take any 140 BPM beat with a snare on 2 and 4. Move the snare to beat 3 only. Nothing else changes — listen to the tempo appear to halve.

RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.id: RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing
RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.title: RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing
RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.q: What does it mean to play "in the pocket", and what's the difference between laying back and pushing?
RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.a: Pocket is where a part sits relative to the grid — consistently, on purpose. Laying back = slightly late → relaxed, heavy (hip hop, soul). Pushing = slightly early → urgent, driving. Roughly 5–30 ms; past ~40 ms it reads as a mistake.
RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.why: Pocket isn't the same as 'tight' — a part can be perfectly consistent and sit 15 ms behind. The move that actually creates pocket is elements disagreeing: kick and snare on the grid, hats late. Everything equally late just sounds slow.
RHY-C06 — Pocket: laying back vs pushing.drill: On a hip hop loop, leave strong beats on the grid and nudge only the weak-beat hits late. Then try pushing the hats early instead and hear the energy change.

RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap.title: RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap
RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap.q: Rhythmically, what distinguishes a boom-bap drum pattern from a trap one?
RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap.a: Boom-bap: ~85–95 BPM, backbeat on 2 and 4, straight 8th hats with an offbeat open hat, swung and laid back, sampled drums. Trap: written ~130–145 but felt half-time, snare on beat 3, hats in 16ths with 32nd and triplet rolls, tight kit and loose hats, and the 808 is the kick and the bass at once. The giveaways are hi-hat activity and the half-time backbeat.
RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap.why: 'Triplets' is the usual shorthand for trap hats, and it misses the structure: the bed is 16ths, with 32nds and triplets layered as rolls on top. Three parameters explain nearly every genre distinction: tempo, backbeat placement, hat subdivision.
RHY-C07 — Boom-bap vs trap.drill: Program 8 bars of boom-bap and 8 of trap from an empty clip using the same kit. Change only tempo, backbeat and hat subdivision.

RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove tem.title: RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove templates
RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove tem.q: When do you quantize, when do you humanize, and what is a groove template actually storing?
RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove tem.a: Quantize snaps to the grid — for anything machine-tight (808s, sidechained elements). Humanize adds controlled timing and velocity variation — for anything meant to read as played. Neither at 100%: partial quantize strength (50–75%) pulls a performance toward the grid while keeping its feel. A groove template stores timing and velocity offsets extracted from one piece of material and applies them to another.
RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove tem.why: Your best two answers in the strand, and both were the ones with an Ableton control surface — you knew when and not what. The groove-template payoff is extraction: pull the feel off a break you like and put it on your own stiff MIDI.
RHY-C08 — Quantize, humanize, groove tem.drill: Extract the groove from a break you like and apply it to your own drums. Then re-do it at 50% quantize strength instead and compare.

RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.id: RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position strong to weak
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.title: RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position strong to weak
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.short: Meter ranks every position strong to weak
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.q: Give the strong/weak hierarchy in a 4/4 bar, strongest first — and say what it's responsible for.
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.a: Beat 1 strongest, then 3, then the backbeats 2 and 4, then the offbeats between them — and the ranking continues inside the beat: on the beat, then the "and", then the "e" and "a" weakest. Meter is what creates that ranking; an undifferentiated stream of identical beats has no structure until it's grouped, and quadruple grouping is what makes 1 and 3 strong in the first place. The hierarchy is then the thing that makes any placement sound "on" or "off" at all.
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.why: It's the reference everything rhythmic is measured against — syncopation, half-time and pocket are all defined as departures from it, so none of them mean anything without it. The standard backbeat falls straight out of it too: kick on the strong 1 and 3, snare on the weak 2 and 4. Matching velocity to the ranking is also most of what makes a programmed part read as played rather than gridded.
RHY-C09 — Meter ranks every position str.drill: Say a 4/4 bar's eight eighth-note positions out loud, ranking each one strong or weak as you go.

SCL-C01 — Natural minor.title: SCL-C01 — Natural minor
SCL-C01 — Natural minor.q: Name the notes of A natural minor. What's the parallel-view formula?
SCL-C01 — Natural minor.a: A B C D E F G — the white notes from A. Parallel view: major with ♭3, ♭6 and ♭7.
SCL-C01 — Natural minor.why: Two ways in: derivative (same notes as C major, different tonic) and parallel (alter the major from the same root). The parallel formula is the one that lets you spell it from any root.
SCL-C01 — Natural minor.drill: Spell natural minor from A, D, E and C — using the ♭3/♭6/♭7 formula, not the relative-major shortcut.

SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor.title: SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor
SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor.q: What single note changes between natural and harmonic minor? What does melodic minor do ascending?
SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor.a: Harmonic minor raises the 7th. Melodic minor ascending raises both the 6th and the 7th — A melodic minor asc = A B C D E F♯ G♯.
SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor.why: Both blank. Harmonic minor exists for a reason worth knowing: raising the 7th creates a real leading tone, which gives a minor key a functioning V chord. Melodic minor raises the 6th too, to smooth out the augmented 2nd that harmonic minor leaves between ♭6 and ♮7. Direct link to .
SCL-C02 — Harmonic and melodic minor.drill: Spell A natural, harmonic and melodic minor side by side. Then build the V chord in each and say which works.

SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales.title: SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales
SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales.q: Name the notes of C major pentatonic. Which degrees were removed, and why those two?
SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales.a: C D E G A. The 4th and 7th are removed. Those are exactly the notes that create half-step tension against the major triad — take them out and the scale is very hard to play wrong.
SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales.why: You included an F. This matters more than one question: the major pentatonic is the most-played scale on guitar, and getting it wrong means it's been learned as a fretboard shape rather than as a set of notes.
SCL-C03 — Pentatonic scales.drill: Spell major pentatonic from C, G and A. Then minor pentatonic from A and E. Name what was removed each time.

SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.id: SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode thinking
SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.title: SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode thinking
SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.q: Two ways to think about D Dorian: "white notes from D" or "D minor with a raised 6th." What's the difference, and which is more useful when playing?
SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.a: Derivative = the mode as a rotation of a parent scale — fast, but keeps your ear anchored to the parent's tonic. Parallel = the mode as an alteration of major/minor from the same root — puts the characteristic note in front of you and keeps D as home. Parallel is more useful for playing.
SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.why: You described both views accurately without the vocabulary and couldn't say which to prefer. Parallel is also the view that makes spelling possible from any root, which is what the rest of this strand failed on.
SCL-C04 — Parallel vs derivative mode th.drill: Describe G Mixolydian both ways. Then E Phrygian. Say which one you'd actually use mid-solo.

SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes.title: SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes
SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes.q: Which mode has a raised 4th? Which interval makes Locrian unusable as a tonic?
SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes.a: Lydian has the ♯4. Locrian's ♭5 makes it unstable — the tonic triad is diminished, so there's nothing stable to resolve home to. Characteristics: Dorian ♮6 · Phrygian ♭2 · Lydian ♯4 · Mixolydian ♭7 · Locrian ♭2 and ♭5.
SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes.why: Both blank. The characteristic note is the mode — it's the one note distinguishing it from plain major or minor, and it's what your ear should be listening for.
SCL-C05 — Characteristic notes.drill: For each of the seven modes, name its characteristic note without looking. Then play each one and hear it.

SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.id: SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.title: SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.short: Spelling a mode from its root
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.q: Spell D Dorian and E Phrygian — from the root, using the parallel method.
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.a: D Dorian: D E F G A B C (D natural minor with a raised 6th — B♮ not B♭). E Phrygian: E F G A B C D (E natural minor with a flattened 2nd — F♮ not F♯).
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.why: Both blank, and this is the strand's core skill. Reciting the mode list is recall; spelling from a root is construction, and only the second one is usable while playing.
SCL-C06 — Spelling a mode from its root.drill: Spell all seven modes from D. Then all seven from A. Parallel method only — no rotating a parent scale.

SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales.title: SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales
SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales.q: What does borrowing from the parallel minor actually mean, in terms of scales?
SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales.a: Keep the tonic, swap the collection. In C major you pull from C minor — Fm (iv), A♭ (♭VI), B♭ (♭VII), E♭ (♭III). The key centre never moves, so it reads as colour rather than modulation.
SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales.why: This is the scale view of what covers as chords — those four chords are just the triads you get building on C natural minor. Same idea, two lenses.
SCL-C07 — Modal interchange as scales.drill: Build every triad on C natural minor. Compare to C major's. The differences are your borrowed chords.

SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.id: SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.title: SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.short: Matching a scale to a chord
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.q: Which mode fits a Cmaj7♯11, and why doesn't plain C major work? Why does minor pentatonic work over a dominant?
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.a: C Lydian — its ♯4 is the ♯11 the chord asks for. Ionian's natural F sits a half step above the E, the avoid note over a major chord. Minor pentatonic works over dominants because its ♭3 grinding against the chord's major 3rd is the blues sound, and because three of its five notes are the chord's own tones (root, 5th and ♭7). It does not sidestep the natural 4th — the 4th is in the scale (A minor pentatonic: A C D E G) — blues passes through it rather than resting on it.
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.why: Both blank. This is where the strand stops being trivia — the chord tells you which scale, and the characteristic note is the reason.
SCL-C08 — Matching a scale to a chord.drill: For Cmaj7♯11, C7, Cm7 and Cm7♭5, name a fitting scale and the specific note that makes it fit.

SMP-C01 — The two rights.title: SMP-C01 — The two rights
SMP-C01 — The two rights.q: In clearance terms, what's the difference between sampling a record and interpolating it?
SMP-C01 — The two rights.a: A recording is two properties. Sampling uses the actual audio, so it needs the master (label) and the composition/publishing (songwriters). Interpolation — replaying the part yourself — uses only the composition, so it needs publishing only.
SMP-C01 — The two rights.why: The musical difference is the obvious one; the clearance difference is the one that costs money. This distinction is why interpolation is the standard move on a recognizable hook — it removes the label from the conversation entirely and halves the negotiation.
SMP-C01 — The two rights.drill: For a sample you've used: who owns the master, who owns the composition, and would interpolating it be workable?

SMP-C02 — Clear before release.title: SMP-C02 — Clear before release
SMP-C02 — Clear before release.q: When do you clear a sample, and what happens if you don't?
SMP-C02 — Clear before release.a: Before release. Always. Clearing afterwards means negotiating with no leverage against someone who now knows the song is working. Uncleared can mean takedown, frozen royalties, a majority publishing share, or the track's entire income.
SMP-C02 — Clear before release.why: You sample — so this is the shortest distance between a knowledge gap and a real cost. The routes that avoid the problem: licensed libraries, royalty-free packs, interpolation, replay-and-rewrite, or full clearance through a service.
SMP-C02 — Clear before release.drill: Take one sample-based idea you've made. Which of the five routes applies, and what would you actually do to release it?

SYN-C01 — The signal path.title: SYN-C01 — The signal path
SYN-C01 — The signal path.q: Describe the signal path of a basic subtractive synth voice, and say where envelopes and LFOs act.
SYN-C01 — The signal path.a: Oscillator → Filter → Amplifier. Oscillators generate the raw waveform (optionally mixed with a sub and noise); the filter removes harmonics; the amplifier controls level over time. An envelope drives the amp — nothing is audible without it. A second envelope usually drives the filter cutoff, which is where character comes from. LFOs modulate whatever you route them to — pitch for vibrato, cutoff for movement, amp for tremolo.
SYN-C01 — The signal path.why: The single most load-bearing fact in synthesis. Every subtractive synth you own is these three blocks in this order — learn it once and every synth becomes the same instrument with a different skin. It also explains the three classic problems: no attack (amp envelope), dull no matter what (wrong waveform), doesn't evolve (nothing modulating).
SYN-C01 — The signal path.drill: Open Analog and point at each of the three blocks on the panel. Then say which envelope is doing what.

SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.id: SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one level
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.title: SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one level
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.short: ADSR: three times and one level
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.q: In ADSR, which parameters are times and which are levels?
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.a: Sustain is the only level. Attack, decay and release are all times.
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.why: Filing decay as a level is the classic ADSR misread, and the reason decay knobs never behave the way people expect. Decay is a time because it describes a journey: how long to fall from the attack peak down to the sustain level. Sustain is a destination, not a duration, and it lasts exactly as long as you hold the key.
SYN-C02 — ADSR: three times and one leve.drill: Say out loud: rise over A, fall over D until you reach S, hold, then fall to zero over R. Then set sustain to 100% and explain why decay now does nothing.

SYN-C03 — Building a pluck.title: SYN-C03 — Building a pluck
SYN-C03 — Building a pluck.q: What ADSR settings make a plucky bass, and why does that produce a "pluck"?
SYN-C03 — Building a pluck.a: Attack near zero, short decay, sustain at or near ZERO, short release. All the energy is front-loaded and then gone — that's what 'pluck' means. Put the same envelope on the filter with a healthy envelope amount for the bright-then-dark snap that sells it.
SYN-C03 — Building a pluck.why: Attack and decay are the intuitive two; the other two matter more. Sustain 0 is the pluck — with sustain up, the note holds and it's a bass, not a pluck. And the filter-envelope half is what separates a synth patch from a volume shape.
SYN-C03 — Building a pluck.drill: Build it on Analog from an initialized patch. Then raise sustain and hear it stop being a pluck.

SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.id: SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not audio
SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.title: SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not audio
SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.q: What is an LFO, and how does it differ from an audio-rate oscillator?
SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.a: A Low Frequency Oscillator runs below the hearing range (~under 20 Hz) and is wired to modulate a parameter rather than be heard as a tone. Same circuit as an audio oscillator — just slow, and routed to a knob instead of the output. You never hear the LFO; you hear what it moves.
SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.why: The name is common knowledge; the distinction isn't. The payoff: push an LFO past ~20 Hz and it stops sounding like movement and starts sounding like tone — at which point you've built FM. The line between modulation and audio is only speed, which is why FM Synthesis and this are the same idea.
SYN-C04 — LFOs modulate parameters, not.drill: Name five things worth routing an LFO to, and what each produces.

SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.id: SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evolve
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.title: SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evolve
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.short: Modulate timbre to make it evolve
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.q: You want a pad that evolves over eight bars. What do you modulate, and with what?
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.a: A slow LFO or a long envelope on filter cutoff or wavetable position — the timbre, not the level. Layer modulators at different rates (an 8-bar LFO on cutoff, a 1–2 bar one on position) so nothing repeats obviously.
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.why: 'Use an LFO' with no target is the incomplete version. The rule: modulate timbre, not level. Level changes read as volume automation; timbre changes read as the sound being alive. Mixing envelopes with LFOs matters too — an LFO is periodic and eventually reveals its loop; an envelope fires once per note.
SYN-C05 — Modulate timbre to make it evo.drill: On Wavetable, hold one chord for 16 bars with two LFOs at different rates. Then remove the position LFO and hear how much deader it gets.

SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune.title: SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune
SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune.q: What do unison and detune do to a sound — and what happens with unison but no detune?
SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune.a: Unison stacks multiple copies of the same oscillator; detune spreads them slightly apart in pitch. Unison without detune does almost nothing — identical copies just sum louder. The thickening comes entirely from the copies beating against each other.
SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune.why: Detune gets the credit; unison is the one doing the work. Two costs worth remembering: wide detuned voices can partially cancel in mono, and detune below ~150 Hz makes low end wobbly — keep subs and 808s mono with no detune, and layer if you want width.
SYN-C06 — Unison needs detune.drill: On Serum 2 or DUNE 3: unison 1 → 7 with detune at zero (nothing), then bring detune up. Then check it in mono.

SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM.title: SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM
SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM.q: What's the fundamental difference between subtractive and FM synthesis?
SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM.a: Subtractive starts with a harmonically rich waveform and filters harmonics away. FM uses one oscillator to modulate another's frequency, generating new sidebands that weren't there. One removes; the other creates.
SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM.why: The organizing distinction of the whole strand. The consequence: a subtractive filter can only remove what the oscillator produced — start on a sine and nothing can brighten it. That limitation is precisely what FM exists to escape.
SYN-C07 — Subtractive vs FM.drill: Explain why you can't make a bright lead starting from a sine wave in a subtractive synth.

SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells.title: SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells
SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells.q: Why is FM good at metallic and bell-like tones that subtractive struggles with?
SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells.a: FM's sidebands land at positions set by the carrier-to-modulator ratio. Integer ratios give harmonic sidebands (pitched — basses, e-pianos). Non-integer ratios give inharmonic sidebands that fall between the harmonics, so the ear can't fuse them into one pitch — metallic and clangorous. Bells and metal are physically inharmonic, so FM matches them naturally.
SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells.why: Subtractive can't get there: its oscillators are harmonic by construction and a filter can only attenuate existing partials — it can't relocate one to a non-integer position.
SYN-C08 — Why FM does bells.drill: On Operator, one modulator into one carrier: sweep the index at ratio 1:1, then 1:2, then 1:1.41. Name the moment it turns metallic and say why.

SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.id: SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from pitch
SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.title: SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from pitch
SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.q: What is granular synthesis, and what's its defining property?
SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.a: It chops audio into very short grains (~1–100 ms) and replays them with independent control over position, size, density and pitch. The defining property: playback position and pitch are decoupled, so you can freeze a moment indefinitely or stretch enormously without transposing.
SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.why: 'Glitchy stuff' is a real use but undersells it badly. The decoupling is what makes everything else possible — texture, pads, extreme stretching, clouds from a half-second source. Its best use is as a resampling target: print something, granulate it, print again.
SYN-C09 — Granular decouples time from p.drill: Load one second of a bounce into Granulator 3. Find three different instruments in it at 5 ms, 40 ms and 150 ms grain size.

SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.id: SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at the source
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.title: SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at the source
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.short: Wavetable moves the timbre at the source
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.q: Where does a wavetable synth's timbral movement come from, compared with a subtractive one's?
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.a: From the source — a scannable table of single-cycle waveforms whose position is modulatable. Subtractive imposes its movement downstream by filtering harmonics away; wavetable generates it at the oscillator, so the harmonic content itself changes while the pitch stays put. Set position statically and it's just an ordinary oscillator on an unusual waveform — modulating position is the entire reason the method exists. Slow LFO gives an evolving pad, an envelope gives a bright attack into a mellow body, velocity makes harder playing select a more aggressive waveform.
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.why: It tells you which control to reach for when a sound needs to move. Position modulation changes what harmonics are there rather than filtering existing ones, which is why it usually beats a cutoff sweep for a pad. Two cautions: most tables hold a few useful waveforms and a lot of transitional material, so modulate between the good positions rather than sweeping the whole table — and on bass, sweeping position shifts the fundamental's level and reads as inconsistent volume.
SYN-C10 — Wavetable moves the timbre at.drill: Hold one note on Wavetable with the amp envelope at full sustain and drag the position marker across the table by hand. No filter movement at all.

VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape.title: VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape
VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape.q: What is the difference between a chord, a voicing and a shape — and why is the choice of voicing harmonic rather than cosmetic?
VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape.a: A chord is the abstract pitch content (C major = C-E-G, any order, any octave). A voicing is the specific order, spacing and register those notes are put in. A shape is one physical fingering that realises a voicing. The voicing is harmonic because register, spacing and doubling change what the ear hears the chord doing — the same pitch classes, arranged differently, can stop functioning the same way.
VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape.why: This is the distinction the whole strand rests on, and it is the one a chord chart hides. A chart says "C" and stops; everything after that is a decision, and it is the decision that determines whether the chord supports a vocal or buries it. Pedler's forty pages on one Beatles chord land here: the sonority is an ensemble effect no single instrument can play, so no chord symbol can name it and no guitarist can reproduce it.
VOI-C01 — Chord, voicing, shape.drill: Play one chord three ways on guitar — close and low, spread across the neck, and up on the top three strings. Same chord every time. Say out loud what each one is now fit for.

VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.id: VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.title: VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.short: Which notes to drop: shell and rootless voicings
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.q: Six strings, two hands, four notes wanted. What is the priority order for which notes stay, and what are a shell voicing and a rootless voicing?
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.a: Keep, in this order: the 3rd and the 7th (the guide tones — they define quality and function), then the extension you actually want, then the root (the bass has it), then the 5th — which is the first thing to go, unless it is altered. Shell = root + 3rd + 7th. Rootless = 3rd + 7th + extensions.
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.why: The interesting decision on guitar is not which notes to play but which to leave out, and this order answers it every time without recalculating. It is also why the named families exist: drop 2 takes a close voicing and moves the 2nd-highest note down an octave, drop 3 the 3rd-highest — both are ways of making four notes reachable and spaced rather than clustered.
VOI-C02 — Which notes to drop: shell and.drill: Comp a tune you know with shell voicings only, then again with guide tones alone — 3rds and 7ths, no root, no extension. Notice how little you actually needed.

VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.id: VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on purpose
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.title: VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on purpose
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.q: What is a quartal voicing, and why does stacking 4ths sound ambiguous where stacking 3rds does not?
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.a: A quartal voicing stacks 4ths instead of 3rds — 1-4-7 off any scale degree rather than 1-3-5. A stack of 3rds names a quality (major, minor, dominant) and therefore implies a function; a stack of 4ths states a set of notes without committing to a quality, so nothing resolves anywhere. That is the point, not a side effect.
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.why: It is the clearest case of a voicing carrying harmonic meaning on its own. One fixed quartal grip reads as minor 11, ♭maj7♯11, sus4, 6/9 or major 13 depending purely on which note the ear takes as the root — the fingers never move. That is why quartal voicings are the natural vocabulary for modal playing, where re-implying a key centre is the failure mode.
VOI-C03 — Quartal voicings: ambiguity on.drill: Build 3-note quartal shapes up one scale on strings 2-3-4, hold a low D drone, and play them over it. Then move the drone to another note and play the identical shapes again.

VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.id: VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collision fix
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.title: VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collision fix
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.short: Octave shift, and the collision fix
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.q: Give the method for turning one chord shape you already know into new voicings of the same chord, and the rule that keeps it from dead-ending.
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.a: Move one note of the shape up or down an octave. If that lands two notes on the same string, move the newly-colliding note to its own nearest octave — and cascade that fix until every note has its own string. Repeat from the shape you land on. Some results are unplayable; discard those and move a different note.
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.why: It is the mechanism behind close and open position rather than a name for them: a close voicing becomes an open one exactly by lifting an interior note an octave and leaving the gap. So instead of memorising a voicing chart you can generate the chart. Moving the root of a close C major up an octave gives another close inversion; moving the middle note up instead gives the open 1-5-3.
VOI-C04 — Octave shift, and the collisio.drill: 15 min: take one chord shape you play automatically, move each note in turn up an octave, resolve every collision, and keep the two results you like. Name what family each one landed in.

VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.id: VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.title: VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.source: Major Triads Across the Fretboard (String-Group Inversions)
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.q: How many places does one major triad live on the fretboard, how are they organised, and what is the practical payoff of knowing them all?
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.a: Four adjacent 3-string groups — E-A-D, A-D-G, D-G-B, G-B-E — each holding three inversions (root, 3rd or 5th on the bottom): twelve locations for one chord. The payoff is that you pick each chord's voicing by proximity to the previous chord instead of defaulting to the root-position shape, which cuts hand travel, raises the playable tempo and sounds less generic.
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.why: This is the fretboard half of voice leading: the rule says move the least, and this is the inventory that makes moving the least possible. The two groups that cross the G–B string pair reuse the same shapes with the notes above that pair shifted up one fret, to compensate for its major-3rd tuning: D-G-B needs the top note a fret higher, G-B-E the top two — so it is genuinely three shapes in three fingerings, not twelve unrelated grips.
VOI-C05 — One triad, every string group.drill: 15 min: pick one major triad and find all three inversions on all four string groups. Then play a four-chord progression choosing, each time, the nearest voicing rather than the root-position one.

VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords.title: VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords
VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords.q: What is a multifunctional voicing, and give the repeatable rule that turns a min7♭5 or half-diminished grip into an altered dominant?
VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords.a: One memorised shape played off a different chord tone of the target chord each time — the fingering never changes, only which note you treat as the root. The rule: play a min7♭5 or half-diminished shape off the ♭7 of a dominant and it reads as that dominant, altered. Play the same family off the 3rd of a dominant instead and it reads as a dominant 9.
VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords.why: It is the efficiency argument for the whole strand: fewer shapes memorised, more chords covered. It is also what makes new voicings affordable mid-tune — you are not finding a grip for G7alt, you are re-pointing a grip you already own. The tritone-substitution version is the same move with the new root chosen a tritone away.
VOI-C06 — One shape, several chords.drill: 15 min: take one min7♭5 shape. Play it as itself, then off the ♭7 of a dominant a minor 7th below (Dm7♭5 read as E7alt, say), then resolve to the I. Say out loud which chord it is each time.

VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.id: VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-tone pivot
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.title: VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-tone pivot
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.short: Move the least: the common-tone pivot
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.q: Give the algorithm for choosing which voicing of the next chord to play — and name the one voice it does not apply to.
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.a: Find the note the two chords share, hold it exactly where it is, and move every remaining note to the nearest note of the next chord. Repeat chord to chord. The exception is the lowest voice — the bass, or a piano left hand — which usually stays on each chord's actual root, because the bass is what the ear reads the chord's identity from.
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.why: It is the difference between comping that sounds like a list of chords and comping that sounds like music: the same progression in strict root position loses its character while keeping every note. You never have to name the resulting inversion — the rule is about minimising motion, not about labelling the result.
VOI-C07 — Move the least: the common-ton.drill: 15 min: play a four-chord loop on piano twice — once all root position, once voice-led by common tone with the left hand still on the roots. Same chords. Hear the difference.

VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.id: VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note per change
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.title: VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note per change
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.short: Spread triads, and one note per change
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.q: What is a spread triad, and what construction rule generates every diatonic triad of a key in every inversion?
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.a: A spread (open-position) triad is a close triad with the middle note moved up an octave — the same three notes reordered 1-5-3, with a string skip and a wider, harp-like spacing. The rule: chain the diatonic triads a third at a time and move exactly one voice, by a half or whole step, at every change. Full coverage of the key falls out as a side effect.
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.why: It is voice leading turned into a generator instead of a lookup. Because the one-note rule always lands you on the closest voicing of the next chord, each triad quality comes back in a different inversion each time — so you cover the key without drilling inversions as a separate exercise. Watch the terminology trap: "open position" here means spread spacing, not playing near the nut.
VOI-C08 — Spread triads, and one note pe.drill: 15 min: start on a tonic spread triad high on the neck and chain down by thirds — I, iii, V, vii°, ii, IV, vi — moving one voice per change. Close with V7 to I.

VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.id: VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is harmony
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.title: VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is harmony
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.short: Comping is rhythm before it is harmony
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.q: What is a comping part judged on first, what practice order follows from that, and what is the commonest failure?
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.a: The rhythm, not the notes. So drill the rhythm alone on one static shell voicing, metronome on 2 and 4, until it is automatic — then move it through real changes with real voicings. The commonest failure is playing too much: chords on 2 and 4, or one per bar, nearly always sit better than constant strumming.
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.why: Five rhythms cover most situations — Charleston (beat 1 and the "and" of 2), push (a sustained hit on the "and" of 3 that pulls into the next bar), downbeat-anchored (unobtrusive, safe behind a soloist), off-the-one (the "and" of 1 and beat 3), and response (a reply to a phrase the soloist just finished). Separating rhythm from harmony is also what makes new voicings usable: changing only the top note of a shape you own doubles what you can do with it.
VOI-C09 — Comping is rhythm before it is.drill: 15 min: one shell voicing, metronome on 2 and 4, one minute per rhythm — Charleston, push, downbeats, off-the-one, response. Then run the best one through a ii-V-I.

VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.id: VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then vary it
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.title: VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then vary it
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.short: One repeatable motif, then vary it
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.source: Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.q: Why does repeating one rhythmic idea beat inventing a new one every bar — and in what order do you introduce variation?
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.a: Repetition is what makes comping read as cohesive and intentional. Reinventing the rhythm bar to bar reads as scattered even when every individual choice is correct. So lock one motif first — hold it for a full pass through the form — then depart from it and return. The return only lands because the motif was established as the baseline.
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.why: A stable comping pattern is also what lets everyone else in the rhythm section interact with you: a drummer can catch a hit and double it, a soloist can build on a surface that stays put. Scaled up, the same idea is riff comping — hold one whole melodic-rhythmic figure for eight bars at a time and let the tune's own repetitions tell you when to change it.
VOI-C10 — One repeatable motif, then var.drill: 15 min: pick one two-hit-per-bar motif — say the "and" of 1 and beat 3 — and hold it through a whole chorus. Then add a walking bass: root on beats 1 and 3, an approach note toward the next root on 2 and 4.

VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.id: VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.title: VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.short: A fill waits for the rest, and it goes somewhere
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.q: When does a fill belong in a comping part, and what is the first design question to ask about one?
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.a: Only when the soloist or singer has actually stopped. Check whether anyone else is playing before reaching for one — a fill layered under an active melody is not a fill, it is clutter. And the first question is where does this lead: a fill's job is to connect forward to the next bar or the next section, not to decorate the chord it starts on.
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.why: It converts a fill from a melodic flourish into a structural device, which is what makes it worth practising. Length follows from the same rule — read how much space the form actually gives you and take a few notes or a whole bar accordingly. Build one bottom-up: a plain diatonic or blues line first, colour added as a second pass, not composed dense from the first note.
VOI-C11 — A fill waits for the rest, and.drill: 15 min: comp a blues and play a fill only in the bars where the melody rests. Every fill has to land on a chord tone of the next chord.

VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.id: VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide register and time
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.title: VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide register and time
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.short: Two comping instruments divide register and time
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.source: Jazz Comping — Sharing the Role with Another Comping Instrument
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.q: Guitar and piano are both in the band. Name the three things that keep them from colliding.
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.a: Assign roles out loud at the top of the tune — who comps the head, who comps each solo. Comp in the holes the other player and the soloist leave, rather than on top of them. Track register and move opposite the soloist: they go up, you go lower. And the fourth answer that is always available — lay out. Not playing is a legitimate choice, not a cop-out.
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.why: Two harmony instruments playing independently reads as clutter to a listener no matter how good each part is. The unrehearsed default is that piano is primary and the guitarist behaves like a horn player until cued. The exception proves the rule: a Freddie Green straight-quarter-note part works under a comping piano precisely because it has stopped being comping and become a second drummer.
VOI-C12 — Two comping instruments divide.drill: 15 min: play along with a recording that already has a comping instrument. Comp only in its gaps, and lay out entirely for one chorus.

VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.id: VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay small
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.title: VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay small
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.source: Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.q: You are stacking three rhythm guitar parts on one progression. What keeps them from turning into mud, and what actually separates them?
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.a: Closed triads — three notes, no doublings, no six-string chords. They are lean on purpose, which is what lets three of them sit on top of each other. What separates the layers is string group, neck position and tone, not writing different material for each: one triad vocabulary, relocated. A bed part low and arpeggiated, a backbeat part on the top three strings, a melodic double-stop part above that.
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.why: It is the same "which notes do I leave out" economy as a shell voicing, applied for a production reason instead of a voice-leading one — you are buying headroom to layer. It is also the arranging version of the two-compers problem: the division is by register and role either way, whether the other player is in the room or on another track.
VOI-C13 — Layered rhythm parts stay smal.drill: 15 min: record three passes of one four-chord loop — closed triads on the D-G-B strings arpeggiated, the same chords on the top three strings on the backbeat, and a double-stop line above. Change the tone between passes, not the chords.

VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.id: VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an instruction
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.title: VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an instruction
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.short: A chart is a framework, not an instruction
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.source: Reading and Interpreting a Jazz Lead Sheet
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.q: You are handed an unfamiliar standard ten seconds before the count-off. What do you read first, and what do you do with the chords printed on the page?
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.a: Read the form first, before a single chord — AABA or ABAC, and how much of the chart is therefore actually new material. Then reduce the chords to recurring named devices: a secondary ii-V into the IV chord is "the IV chord", four bars of motion is "a turnaround". The printed harmonisation is a starting point, not gospel — when a chord clashes with the melody, substitute.
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.why: Thirty-two bars cannot be understood as thirty-two independent decoding problems in the time available. Form plus device-matching turns an unfamiliar chart into a known shape with a few details filled in. A concrete prediction that comes free: in an AABA tune starting on the tonic, the last two bars of each A are a turnaround about ninety percent of the time.
VOI-C14 — A chart is a framework, not an.drill: 15 min: open a standard you do not know. Before playing anything, mark the form, circle every turnaround, and name every multi-chord passage as one device. Then comp it.

VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.id: VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not the key
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.title: VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not the key
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.short: Renumber off the chord, not the key
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.q: In chord melody you play the tune on top and the harmony underneath. What do you read each melody note as, and how should the voicings you reach for be indexed?
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.a: Read every melody note as a scale degree of whichever chord is sounding right now, not of the parent key — the same pitch is "5 of C" under a C chord and "4 of D" a beat later under Dm. Index your go-to voicings by which chord tone the melody note is, and which string it lands on — that is the lookup you actually need mid-arrangement.
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.why: Thinking in the parent key hides the relationship that tells you which shape fits; renumbering off the current chord reveals it, and the shape then transfers to any chord of that quality by sliding to the new root. The other half is physical: do not harmonise every note. Playing single melody notes between chord grabs is easier and sounds better — space reads as phrasing.
VOI-C15 — Renumber off the chord, not th.drill: 15 min: take eight bars of a tune you know. Say each melody note's degree relative to the chord under it, out loud, as you play. Harmonise only the notes that start a phrase.

VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.id: VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum viable voicing
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.title: VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum viable voicing
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.short: Guide-tone diads: the minimum viable voicing
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.source: Guide-Tone Diads for Blues Rhythm Guitar
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.q: What is the smallest thing you can play that still states a dominant chord, and how does it move through a blues?
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.a: Two notes — the 3rd and the ♭7. They alone fix the quality: change the 3rd and the chord flips major to minor, change the ♭7 to a major 7 and it stops being a dominant. With a bass player covering the root, that is all the guitar owes the chord. Through a blues in A the identical shape moves by half step — down a half step for the IV, up a half step for the V.
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.why: It is the floor of the whole strand, and everything larger is built on it: the rootless 9ths and 13ths are this pair with colour added on top. It is also the arrangement fix for a crowded track — two notes leave room for a vocal where a barre chord does not. The sus4 raise and the low-diad-against-high-stab alternation are embellishments of the same two notes.
VOI-C16 — Guide-tone diads: the minimum.drill: 15 min: play a 12-bar blues in A with nothing but the 3rd-♭7 diad, moving by half step for the IV and V. Then add the raise of the 3rd to the 4th and back.

VOX-C01 — Proximity effect.title: VOX-C01 — Proximity effect
VOX-C01 — Proximity effect.q: What is proximity effect, and how do you use it?
VOX-C01 — Proximity effect.a: Bass response rises as a directional mic gets closer to the source. Use it as a tone control: move in (2–6 in) for weight and intimacy; back off to stop a vocal getting boomy — the same fix as a low-end EQ cut, applied at the source. Only applies to directional mics; omni has essentially none.
VOX-C01 — Proximity effect.why: The most useful mic fact there is, because it turns distance into a knob. Directly relevant to the TLM 102 and SM57. It's also why a pop filter helps twice — it blocks plosives and sets a minimum distance, which keeps tone consistent.
VOX-C01 — Proximity effect.drill: Record the same line at 3, 8 and 14 inches. Name the tonal difference without looking at a meter.

VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.id: VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllable
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.title: VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllable
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.short: Comp by phrase, not by syllable
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.q: How do you comp a vocal — what are you listening for, and where do comps go wrong?
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.a: Comp by phrase, not by syllable. Listen for delivery first (which take means it), then pitch, timing, tone. Watch the seams — cut on a breath, keep the breaths, crossfade every edit. The failure mode is a Frankenstein comp: technically perfect, assembled from the best fragment of every word, and worse than your best single take because the performance stops being continuous.
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.why: 1.5/5 — you named pitch, timing and delivery, but ranked timing above delivery and had no method. The check that matters: a comp should beat your best single take. If it doesn't, use the single take.
VOX-C02 — Comp by phrase, not by syllabl.drill: Comp one vocal twice — by syllable, then by phrase. A/B both against the best full pass.

VOX-C03 — When not to tune.title: VOX-C03 — When not to tune
VOX-C03 — When not to tune.a: When the deviation is the expression — blues and soul phrasing lives between the notes; bends, scoops and a note leaned into slightly flat are doing the emotional work. Also when the genre's identity is a human voice, when the singer is strong (fix the two wrong notes, not the take), and when it's already meant to be an effect. Correct genuine mistakes, leave the rest.
VOX-C03 — When not to tune.why: 2.5/5 — genre dependence was right; the core reason wasn't. Over-tuning is far more common and more damaging than under-tuning, because it's invisible while you're doing it and obvious a week later. Fast retune also flattens vibrato, which is often why the take was good.

VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.id: VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic dial
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.title: VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic dial
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.short: Retune speed is a stylistic dial
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.q: What does retune speed control, and how is it a stylistic choice?
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.a: How fast correction pulls a note to pitch. Slow preserves scoops, slides and vibrato — inaudible, transparent tuning. Fast/zero snaps instantly, killing scoops and stepping the vibrato — the hard Auto-Tune sound. No correct setting: a genre at each end.
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.why: The reference points are widely known. The addition worth keeping: fast retune destroys vibrato, and the real mistake isn't picking either end — it's reaching for fast retune to fix a pitch problem and getting the effect by accident.
VOX-C04 — Retune speed is a stylistic di.drill: Take one phrase. Tune it at slow, medium and zero retune speed. Name where the vibrato disappears.

VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy.title: VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy
VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy.q: How does treatment change from a lead vocal to a double to a harmony to an ad-lib?
VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy.a: The further a part is from delivering the lyric, the more it can become texture. Lead — centre, most present, least processed. Doubles — wide, well under the lead, not heard as separate. Harmonies — lower still, more processing, colour not content. Ad-libs — widest, furthest back, heaviest effects.
VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy.why: 0.5/5 — you knew there were different chains and couldn't state the principle. You have 22 vocal chains that already implement this, so it's purely a naming gap. The rule works because the lead needs every word parseable and an ad-lib doesn't.
VOX-C05 — The treatment hierarchy.drill: Set level, pan and processing for a lead/double/harmony/ad-lib from the hierarchy alone. Then compare to what instinct would have done.

VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.id: VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicken
VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.title: VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicken
VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.q: What's the difference between a real double and a copied-and-delayed one, and why does it matter?
