VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.a: A real double is a second performance — timing, pitch and tone differ naturally, and that variation is the thickening. A copy is identical, so summing it just makes the signal louder; delay or pitch it and you get comb filtering or slapback, not width.
VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.why: A copied-and-pasted double is the same performance twice, so it sums like one louder track rather than two voices — the Lennon-era fix for exactly that is ADT. Kept as a concept because it's the reason the whole stack section works, and because Artificial Double Tracking (ADT) is the deliberate exception: a sound, not a substitute.
VOX-C06 — A copied double doesn't thicke.drill: Duplicate a vocal and sum it — note it only gets louder. Now delay the copy 20 ms. Then compare both to a genuinely re-sung double.

VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first.title: VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first
VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first.q: What's different about recording and producing a rap vocal versus a sung one?
VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first.a: Rap is a rhythmic performance — you're producing pocket, not pitch. Workflow follows: punch-ins line by line, timing edits at the syllable level, doubles on bar-ends and key phrases rather than the whole verse, and a dedicated ad-lib pass. Processing leans on compression and presence for intelligibility; pitch correction is absent or an obvious effect. Keep the breaths — in a dense verse they're punctuation.
VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first.why: It's your core lane. The syllable-level timing rule is deliberately the opposite of the phrase-level comping rule (): comp performance by phrase, fix timing by syllable. Doubling a whole verse flattens it — the double is an accent, not a texture.
VOX-C07 — Rap is rhythm-first.drill: Take a rap verse you've recorded. Nudge it 15 ms late, then 15 ms early. Pick one and say why.

notes-pitches--sharps-flats.title: Sharps & flats
notes-pitches--sharps-flats.html:
• ♯ = raise a half-step · ♭ = lower a half-step
  • Every black key has two names (enharmonic equivalents): C♯ = D♭, D♯ = E♭, F♯ = G♭, G♯ = A♭, A♯ = B♭
  • Which name to use depends on the key — each scale uses each letter exactly once
  • B♯, E♯, C♭, and F♭ are real, not a simplification some teachers skip — B♯ = C (raise B by a half-step) and E♯ = F (raise E by a half-step); C♭ = B and F♭ = E (lower by a half-step) the other way. They're not optional/wrong spellings — a major scale MUST use every letter A–G exactly once (Scales), so any key that lands on the "wrong" natural for its 7th or 4th degree has to rename it: e.g. F♯ major's 7th degree is enharmonically F but has to be spelled E♯ to keep E as the letter used once; G♭ major's 3rd degree is enharmonically B but has to be spelled C♭ to keep C as the letter used once. Skipping these notes because "they're basically the same as a natural" breaks the one-of-each-letter rule and makes the resulting triads/7th chords misspelled. → Scales (spelling rules + C♯/C♭ major worked examples) — Daniel Seriff, BIGGEST Music Theory MYTH That Will RUIN Your Understanding
notes-pitches--sharps-flats.lede: ♯ = raise a half-step · ♭ = lower a half-step

notes-pitches--half-steps-whole-steps.title: Half-steps & whole-steps
notes-pitches--half-steps-whole-steps.html:
• Half-step (semitone) = smallest distance; two pitches with nothing between them — including black keys
    • E→F and B→C are the natural half-steps (no black key between)
    • A→B is NOT a half-step (A♯/B♭ sits between) — it's a whole-step
  • Whole-step = 2 half-steps (C→D, A→B, B♭→C)
  • All chord and scale formulas are built from these units — see Intervals for the full interval names

circle-of-fifths--sharp-flat-order-mnemo.title: Sharp/flat order mnemonic

key-signatures--the-pattern.title: The pattern
key-signatures--the-pattern.html:
• Sharps are always added in the same order: F C G D A E B (each new sharp key adds one)
  • Flats are added in the order: B E A D G C F (sharps order reversed)
  • Each step around the Circle of Fifths adds exactly one sharp (clockwise) or flat (counterclockwise)
  • Memory hook: last sharp = one half-step below the major tonic; second-to-last flat = the major key name
key-signatures--the-pattern.lede: Sharps are always added in the same order: F C G D A E B (each new sharp key adds one)

intervals--interval-quality-perfect-majo.title: Interval quality: Perfect/Major/Minor/Augmented/Diminished
intervals--interval-quality-perfect-majo.html:
• Counting the number — count scale degrees (lines/spaces) from the bottom note as 1, ignoring accidentals, up to the top note: a 3rd, a 6th, etc.
  • Perfect intervals — unisons, 4ths, 5ths, and octaves are "perfect" when built from only the white keys, except F–B (that pair is a half-step off from every other 4th/5th — it's the tritone, aug 4th/dim 5th). A half-step larger than perfect = augmented; a half-step smaller = diminished. There's no such thing as a diminished unison.
  • Imperfect intervals — 2nds, 3rds, 6ths, 7ths are never "perfect," only major or minor (still augmented/diminished a half-step beyond that). Shortcut: an interval is major if the top note is in the bottom note's major key; minor if the bottom note is in the top note's major key. Work it out with accidentals stripped first, then re-add them one at a time and track how each shift changes the size.
  • The Rule of Nines — inverting an interval (moving the lower note up an octave above the upper) swaps its number to whatever completes a sum of 9: 2nd↔7th, 3rd↔6th, 4th↔5th. Quality flips too: major↔minor, augmented↔diminished, perfect stays perfect. — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.10–13

Related: Music Theory · Notes & Pitches (half/whole steps) · Chords (intervals stacked into chords) · Scales · Set Theory (interval content of non-tertial pitch collections) · Scale Degree Ear Training (why scale-degree hearing transfers to real music better than isolated-interval drilling)

chord-progressions--roman-numeral-analys.title: Roman numeral analysis
chord-progressions--roman-numeral-analys.html:
• Replace each chord's root letter with its scale degree in the song's key: in C, C Dm F G → I ii IV V
  • Same numerals describe the progression in every key — instant transposition (Circle of Fifths)
  • Only label chords that ARE diatonic; a D major chord in the key of C isn't "II", it's non-diatonic (borrowed/secondary)
  • Two systems: classical (lowercase = minor: ii, vi) vs Berklee/pop (always uppercase + suffix: IIm, VIm; minor keys numbered from the major scale: ♭III not III). See Chords by Key
chord-progressions--roman-numeral-analys.lede: Replace each chord's root letter with its scale degree in the song's key: in C, C Dm F G → I ii IV V

chord-progressions--harmonic-function-t-.title: Harmonic function (T / SD / D)
chord-progressions--harmonic-function-t-.html:
Every diatonic chord has a job:

Function Chords (major key) Feel Tension
T Tonic I home, at rest lowest
(T) Substitute tonic vi, iii semi at-rest low
SD Subdominant IV, ii moved away from home medium
D Dominant V (vii°) wants to resolve home highest
  • vi & iii substitute for I because they share 2 of its 3 notes; vi is stronger (contains the tonic note, and = the relative minor's home chord — Keys)
  • ii ≈ IV (share degrees 4 & 6): jazz prefers ii (as ii7), rock/folk/country prefer IV, blues IV7
  • Minor keys: i = T, ♭III = (T), iv & ♭VI = SD, V/v = D, ♭VII = (D)
  • The archetypal cycle: T → SD → D → T ("advancing"); reversing it feels like retreating
  • Analyze songs by graphing the tension story: start at rest → climb → peak on D → resolve. (Dylan's Like a Rolling Stone chorus = I IV V = T SD D, 2 bars, repeated 6×. Gnarls Barkley's Crazy = Im ♭III ♭VI Vsus4 V = T (T) SD D, with a sus4 resolution)

cadences--the-four-types.title: The four types
cadences--the-four-types.html:
Cadence Chords "Perfect" requires Feel
Authentic V (or vii°) → I V→I only (not vii°→I), both root position, soprano ends on tonic by step full resolution, "home"
Plagal IV (or ii) → I IV→I only (not ii→I), both root position, soprano keeps the common tone, ends on tonic the "amen" cadence — softer landing than authentic
Half anything → V — (half cadences don't have a "perfect" variant) stops on the dominant, deliberately unresolved
Deceptive V → anything but I (almost always vi) — the "psych-out" — sets up a resolution, then dodges it
  • Any of the above that misses its "perfect" criteria is labeled imperfect (imperfect authentic, imperfect plagal).
  • Phrygian half cadence — a specific minor-key half cadence: iv6 → V, with soprano and bass moving stepwise in contrary motion, both landing on scale degree 5.
  • A deceptive cadence shows up more often mid-phrase than as a true ending — in that context it's sometimes called a "cadence-like structure" rather than a true cadence.
  • The three ways an authentic cadence can fail to be "Perfect" and become Imperfect (IAC) instead, US voicing-strictness terms: (1) both chords root position, but the top voice of I isn't the tonic note; (2) either chord is inverted; (3) V is substituted for the leading-tone (vii°) chord — a rootless dominant 7th standing in for V.
  • Minor plagal cadence ≠ plagal cadence in a minor key — two different things that sound similar by name. The minor plagal cadence is a chromatic borrowing INSIDE a major-key song: iv→I (not IV→I), introducing a ♭6 that pulls strongly down into the tonic chord's 5th — a bittersweet color, arguably more resolving than the plain major plagal despite the "wrong" chord quality. The actual plagal cadence in the minor key is just iv→i, no chromaticism, both chords minor as expected.
  • The minor-key perfect/authentic cadence keeps V major. Diatonically the v chord in a minor key is minor, but a true minor-key perfect cadence borrows the major V from the harmonic minor scale (v→i with both minor is still a real resolving cadence, just not a formally-named classical one).
  • The Super Mario cadence — ♭VI→♭VII→I (in C: A♭→B♭→C) — a "slang" cadence with no classical pedigree, functionally resolving the same way the named ones do; worth keeping as a case study in how a cadence name gets coined and spreads (a shared cultural reference point standing in for formal terminology). — David Bennett Music Theory, Every type of Cadence EXPLAINED
cadences--the-four-types.lede: Any of the above that misses its "perfect" criteria is labeled imperfect (imperfect authentic, imperfect plagal).

secondary-dominants--the-idea.title: The idea
secondary-dominants--the-idea.html:
• Any major or minor chord can be treated, for a moment, as a temporary "I" — and you approach it with its own V7.
  • Notation: V7/x ("five-seven of x") = the dominant of the chord x. E.g. V7/vi = the dominant that resolves to the vi chord.
  • In C major, the diatonic chords are C Dm Em F G Am Bdim (I ii iii IV V vi vii°). The secondary dominants are the V7 of each:
  • V7/ii = A7 → Dm
  • V7/iii = B7 → Em
  • V7/IV = C7 → F
  • V7/V = D7 → G
  • V7/vi = E7 → Am
  • Each one contains a note outside the key (its leading-tone), which is the "lift" you hear — e.g. E7 → Am borrows G♯, the leading tone of A.
secondary-dominants--the-idea.lede: Any major or minor chord can be treated, for a moment, as a temporary "I" — and you approach it with its own V7.

secondary-dominants--why-it-works.title: Why it works
secondary-dominants--why-it-works.html:
• A dominant 7th has a tritone (3rd ↔ ♭7) that strongly wants to resolve. Aiming that pull at a non-tonic chord makes that chord feel, briefly, like home — then the progression moves on. Instant forward motion + a splash of chromatic color.
  • The most common by far is V7/vi, which pulls a major-key loop toward its relative minor (Keys) — the source of a lot of mellow/introspective R&B and pop feels.
secondary-dominants--why-it-works.lede: A dominant 7th has a tritone (3rd ↔ ♭7) that strongly wants to resolve. Aiming that pull at a non-tonic chord makes that chord feel, briefly, like home — t…

secondary-dominants--the-full-dominant-f.title: The full dominant-function roster
secondary-dominants--the-full-dominant-f.html: V7/x is only the most common case — there are actually 5 dominant-function chords usable as secondary dominants: V/x, V7/x, vii°/x, vii°ø7/x, vii°7/x, all approached/resolved with the same root-movement rules as any other chord. In major keys, "x" can be any diatonic chord except tonic and the leading-tone triad itself; in minor keys, composers generally restricted secondary dominants to only "of iv" and "of V." — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.42

borrowed-chords--the-workhorses-borrowed.title: The workhorses (borrowed from parallel minor, in a MAJOR key)
borrowed-chords--the-workhorses-borrowed.html:
Borrowed chord In C major Sound
iv (minor four) Fm the "heartbreak" chord — IV → iv → I
♭VI A♭ epic, cinematic lift
♭VII B♭ rock/Mixolydian move (I–♭VII–IV)
♭III E♭ darker, bluesy
♭II (Neapolitan) D♭ dramatic pre-dominant
iiø7 (half-dim) Dø7 minor-key ii, jazzy pre-dominant
  • The most emotionally reliable is IV → iv → I: the major subdominant brightening, then its minor version darkening, then home. Instant bittersweetness.
  • From a major key you can also borrow the whole Mixolydian ♭VII (rock) or Dorian color.
  • ♭II isn't actually borrowed from the parallel minor despite the naming pattern — see Neapolitan Sixth for the classical convention it almost always follows in practice: near-exclusive use in first inversion (hence "Neapolitan 6th," not "the Neapolitan sixth chord"), resolving to a dominant 7th in 3rd inversion or a cadential 6/4.
  • Borrowed ii° is always used in first inversion (it's diminished — same rule as diminished triads generally, see Part-Writing). The two altered-root chords (♭III, ♭VI) resolve better with contrary motion than strict alteration-direction resolution, to avoid parallel octaves.
borrowed-chords--the-workhorses-borrowed.lede: The most emotionally reliable is IV → iv → I: the major subdominant brightening, then its minor version darkening, then home. Instant bittersweetness.

parallel-minor.title: Parallel Minor
parallel-minor.html:
Part of Music Theory → Keys. The parallel minor of a major key is the minor key that shares the same tonic note (C major ↔ C minor). Distinct from the relative minor, which shares the same notes but a different tonic (C major ↔ A minor — see Keys).

Parallel vs. relative — don't confuse them

Shares Example (from C major)
Relative minor the same notes/key signature A minor (no sharps/flats)
Parallel minor the same tonic, different notes C minor (3 flats)
  • Relative = same neighborhood, different home. Parallel = same home, different mood.

Why it matters

  • The parallel minor is the source pool for Borrowed Chords (modal interchange): iv, ♭III, ♭VI, ♭VII borrowed into a major key all come from the parallel minor.
  • Parallel-minor modulation (a whole section moving to the parallel minor) is a classic contrast move: keep the tonic anchored so the change reads as a mood shift (bright → dark) rather than a full key change — the ear stays oriented because "home" hasn't moved.
  • Flipping the tonic triad major↔minor (picardy third the other way, or a minor-key song ending on the major tonic) is the smallest version of this.

Hear it

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Here There and Everywhere — G major verse, middle 8 to G minor, back to G major.

non-harmonic-tones--the-9-types.title: The 9 types
non-harmonic-tones--the-9-types.html:
Name Abbr. Approach Resolution Notes
Passing tone PT step step (same direction) fills the gap between two chord tones a 3rd apart
Neighboring tone NT step step (returns to origin) steps away and immediately back
Appoggiatura APP leap step (opposite direction) leap-then-step-back — the classic "leaning" ornament
Escape tone ET step leap (opposite direction) step-then-leap-away
Changing tones CT any step a pair of NHTs flanking the resolution note on either side
Anticipation ANT any common tone a chord tone from the next chord, sounded early
Suspension SUS common tone step (down) held over from the previous chord, resolves down
Retardation RET common tone step (up) held over from the previous chord, resolves up
Pedal tone PED common tone common tone a chord tone that becomes non-harmonic under moving harmony above it, then becomes a chord tone again

modulation-key-change--common-types.title: Common types
modulation-key-change--common-types.html:
• Parallel — to the parallel key (same tonic, major↔minor): a mood flip that keeps the ear oriented. (Beatles "Here There and Everywhere" bridge.)
  • Relative — to the relative major/minor (shares notes; see Keys): the smoothest change, often barely noticed.
  • Pivot-chord — use a chord common to both keys as the hinge, then reinterpret it (the classical/jazz-smooth way).
  • Secondary-dominant / tonicization — a V7/x that briefly makes x feel like home; string several together to travel around the Circle of Fifths.
  • Direct ("truck-driver") modulation — just jump up a step (semitone/whole-tone) with no preparation, usually for a final-chorus lift (the classic pop key change).
  • Common-tone — hold one note and rebuild a new key's chord around it.
modulation-key-change--common-types.lede: Parallel — to the parallel key (same tonic, major↔minor): a mood flip that keeps the ear oriented. (Beatles "Here There and Everywhere" bridge.)

modulation-key-change--how-to-hear-analy.title: How to hear/analyze it
modulation-key-change--how-to-hear-analy.html:
• Watch for new accidentals that persist (not just passing color) and a chord that behaves like a new V → I.
  • Map both sections in Roman numerals (Chord Progressions) and find the pivot: where does the same chord get two names?

scales.title: Scales
scales.html:
Part of Music Theory. A scale = a sequence of pitches in order, defined by its pattern of half/whole steps (see Notes & Pitches). The scale's starting pitch is the tonic; its numbered pitches are degrees.

Major scale

Step pattern: W W H W W W H

Key 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
C C D E F G A B
G G A B C D E F♯
D D E F♯ G A B C♯
A A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯
E E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯
B B C♯ D♯ E F♯ G♯ A♯
F♯ F♯ G♯ A♯ B C♯ D♯ E♯
G♭ G♭ A♭ B♭ C♭ D♭ E♭ F
D♭ D♭ E♭ F G♭ A♭ B♭ C
A♭ A♭ B♭ C D♭ E♭ F G
E♭ E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D
B♭ B♭ C D E♭ F G A
F F G A B♭ C D E
C♯ C♯ D♯ E♯ F♯ G♯ A♯ B♯
C♭ C♭ D♭ E♭ F♭ G♭ A♭ B♭
  • Each scale uses each letter name exactly once — that's why C♯ vs D♭ spelling matters (Notes & Pitches)
  • Ordered by sharps/flats added = the Circle of Fifths; the accidentals per key = Key Signatures
  • C♯ major and C♭ major are the two "all-accidental" major keys — 7 sharps and 7 flats respectively, so every degree of C major (C D E F G A B) just gets sharped or flatted straight across: C♯ major = C♯ D♯ E♯ F♯ G♯ A♯ B♯ (needs E♯ and B♯, not F/C); C♭ major = C♭ D♭ E♭ F♭ G♭ A♭ B♭ (needs F♭, not E). Both are real, usable keys even though they're less common — a capo'd guitarist ends up in C♯ major from C major shapes at the 1st fret, and a horn player who thinks in flats may prefer C♭ major over its enharmonic twin B major. → Notes & Pitches (why E♯/B♯/C♭/F♭ exist), Key Signatures (7-sharp/7-flat rows) — Daniel Seriff, BIGGEST Music Theory MYTH That Will RUIN Your Understanding

Spelling rules — building a valid major scale

Four rules that guarantee a major scale/key is spelled correctly (and explain why keys like F♯, C♯, G♭, and C♭ need "funny" accidentals like E♯, B♯, C♭, F♭ — see Notes & Pitches):

  1. No mixing sharps and flats in one key — a key is all-sharp or all-flat, never both.
  2. All seven letters (A–G) must appear, one of each — never skip a letter or double one up.
  3. Never use two different accidental versions of the same letter in one key — no G and G♭ together, no A and A♯ together.
  4. The next scale degree is always the next letter of the musical alphabet (wrapping G → A) — never restate the same letter for the next note even if it's enharmonically simpler to think that way. Applying these forces the "funny" spellings: e.g. F♯ major's raised 6th-to-7th step lands on the pitch also known as F, but rule 2 already used F♯ for the tonic and rule 4 demands the letter after D♯ is E — so it has to be spelled E♯, not F. Same logic gives G♭ major its C♭ (the pitch also known as B) and C♯/C♭ major their full sharp/flat sets above. — Daniel Seriff, BIGGEST Music Theory MYTH That Will RUIN Your Understanding

Natural minor scale

Formula vs. major: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 (lower degrees 3, 6, 7 a half-step)

  • Every minor scale shares its pitches with one major scale = its relative major (Keys)
  • Find relative minor: go DOWN two scale degrees from the major tonic (C → A minor)
  • Find relative major: go UP two degrees from the minor tonic (B minor → D major)
  • For harmonic & melodic minor (and their modes/chords): Scale Modes Reference
  • For the 7 modes generated by starting the major scale on each of its own degrees (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian…) and the mood each one carries: Diatonic Modes

Extended scale degrees (above 8)

Degrees keep counting past the octave and repeat pitch names: 9 = 2 · 10 = 3 · 11 = 4 · 12 = 5 · 13 = 6 This is where 9th/11th/13th chord names come from — see Extended Chords and Chords by Key (chords are stacked from every-other degree: 1-3-5, 2-4-6, 5-7-9…).

Pentatonic scales

  • Major pentatonic: 1 2 3 5 6 (major scale minus 4 and 7). Feel: simple/folk/rock. Contains all the notes of the key's I chord; all pitches adjacent on the Circle of Fifths
  • Minor pentatonic: 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7. Used over minor keys/chords — and over major-key blues, where the key-based minor pentatonic is played against major chords
  • Two ways to use either one:
    • Key-based — one pentatonic scale for the whole progression
    • Chord-based — switch to each chord's own pentatonic as the chords change
  • Bonus: major hexatonic (1 2 3 4 5 6) — rarer 6-note pitch palette (Bruce Hornsby-style)

diatonic-modes.title: Diatonic Modes
diatonic-modes.html:
Part of Music Theory → Scales. The 7 modes generated by starting the major scale on each of its own scale degrees — same 7 pitches, different tonic, different mood. For the modes of melodic/harmonic minor and other non-diatonic scales, see Scale Modes Reference (that page assumes these seven as the baseline "anchor" set).

The seven modes (built from C major / the white keys)

# Mode Starts on (of C major) Formula vs. major Character
1 Ionian C 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 (= the major scale) Happy, bright, resolved — the "default" major sound
2 Dorian D 1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 ♭7 Melancholy but hopeful — minor with a brighter natural 6th
3 Phrygian E 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 Dark, tense, exotic — the ♭2 gives a flamenco/metal edge
4 Lydian F 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7 Dreamy, floating, fantastical — the raised 4th is the signature note
5 Mixolydian G 1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7 Bright but unresolved — major with a bluesy/rock ♭7; reads as dreamy/romantic
6 Aeolian A 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 (= natural minor) Sad, serious, cinematic — the default "minor" sound
7 Locrian B 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 ♭5 ♭6 ♭7 Unstable, unresolved — the only mode with a diminished tonic triad; rarely used as a true home key

Modal ambiguity — when the tonic itself is genuinely disputed

All 7 modes above share the exact same 7 notes (the white keys) — they differ only in which of those notes is treated as the tonic. That means the same seven-note collection can plausibly be heard as any of its 7 modes, and real songs sometimes leave the choice genuinely unresolved rather than settled: different listeners latch onto different notes as "home," and there's no single objectively correct answer — it isn't listener error on either side.

Three factors that create or resolve the ambiguity:

  1. A repeating chord loop with no resolution. A song built on a 4-bar (or similar) rotating chord cycle that never breaks out into a resolving cadence gives the ear no moment of arrival to lock onto — different chords in the loop can each sound like "home" to different listeners, because the loop just keeps resetting instead of concluding.
  2. The melody's own tonic pull, independent of the chords. A melody has its own implied tonic even unaccompanied — and the SAME chord loop, set to two different melodies, can point the ear toward two different tonic notes, because it's the melody, not just the harmony, doing a large share of the work.
  3. Whether all 7 notes of the shared collection actually get used. Some of the 7 candidate modes differ from each other by only one note (e.g. E♭ major vs. A♭ major differ only in D natural vs. D♭) — if a song's melody happens to avoid that one distinguishing note entirely, there's no evidence left to settle which of two neighboring modes is "really" the key.

The first chord has outsized influence, independent of all three factors above: whatever chord opens the loop gets a "home-field advantage" simply by being the first thing the ear hears with zero prior context — even when it isn't the strongest candidate by the other criteria.

A resolvability test, generalizable: check whether any passage in the song states the ONE note that would distinguish the competing readings. If it does, the ambiguity resolves; if the song systematically avoids that note (deliberately or not), the dispute stays genuinely open. A companion song by the same artist, on the same chord loop, that eventually breaks out and resolves demonstrates the mechanism directly — the resolving version removes the ambiguity the looping version has.

This is a perceptual switch, not a blend — like an optical illusion (duck/rabbit). A trained listener can consciously shift which note they hear as tonic, but can't hear two readings simultaneously; recontextualizing lets you flip between them, not hold both at once.

Two ways to find/build any mode

  • Relative approach — play the same 7 notes as a known major scale, just start (and center the phrase) on a different degree: e.g. D Dorian = the white keys, but centered on D instead of C. Same pitch collection as C major, different tonic → completely different mood. Fastest way to answer "what mode am I already implying with these notes?"
  • Parallel/formula approach — build the mode off any root directly, by altering the major-scale formula on that root: e.g. Aeolian = major scale with ♭3 ♭6 ♭7 (exactly the natural minor formula in Scales). Fastest way to answer "I want THIS mood, starting on THIS specific note."

Aeolian in depth (it's the one you'll use most)

  • Build it from its parallel Ionian: take the major scale on the same root and flatten scale degrees 3, 6, and 7 a half-step (C Ionian → C Aeolian: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7). This is the natural minor formula.
  • Find it from a relative Ionian: every major scale's Aeolian relative starts on that scale's own 6th degree (G Ionian → E Aeolian; C Ionian → A Aeolian) — same notes as finding the relative minor.
  • The i–♭VI move is the essence of the sound. Build the full diatonic harmony off any Aeolian tonic — i ii° ♭III iv v ♭VI ♭VII (the natural-minor pattern in Chords by Key) — but the two-chord fragment that instantly reads as "Aeolian" regardless of genre is the tonic moving to its ♭VI (often voiced as an inversion for a smoother top line): i → ♭VI. Cited as the backbone of somber cinematic scoring and also common in EDM as ♭VI–♭VII–i. → Chord Progressions
  • Ear-training the minor scale by drone: drill exactly the 3 degrees that differ from major (♭3, ♭6, ♭7), one at a time against a sustained tonic drone, since those are the only new feeling-states minor adds beyond what major-scale degree training already covers. Comparing adjacent pairs (5 vs. ♭6, 6 vs. ♭6, ♭3 vs. ♭6) sharpens the contrast — ♭3 reads as the degree that most defines "minorness" itself, while ♭6 and ♭7 are each their own distinct flavor rather than interchangeable "flat" degrees. The feeling-state of any given degree is octave-invariant and (for most listeners without perfect pitch) transfers unchanged to a new key. → Scale Degree Ear Training — Max Konyi, Essential Ear Training - Feeling the Minor Scale

Telling natural minor (Aeolian) apart from harmonic minor by ear/eye

The two most common minor scales in pop/rock differ by exactly one degree — the 7th — but that one note changes the whole character and gives two reliable tests:

  • Check the v chord: in natural minor (Aeolian) the 5th-degree chord is minor (v); in harmonic minor it's major (V) — because the raised 7th becomes that chord's 3rd. "Ain't No Sunshine" (Bill Withers, A minor) uses Em (v) → confirms Aeolian.
  • Check the 7th scale degree directly in the melody: unaltered (G♮ in A minor) → Aeolian; raised (G♯) → harmonic minor. "Jolene" (Dolly Parton, C♯ minor) uses an unaltered 7th (B♮) → Aeolian. "Back to Black" (Amy Winehouse, D minor) uses a raised 7th (C♯), both in the melody and via major-A chords → harmonic minor.
  • A song can genuinely use both within itself — "Sultans of Swing" (Dire Straits) switches between the raised and unaltered 7th at different points, and further mixing (Dorian, melodic minor) is common enough that "just describe it as being in the minor key" without committing to one variant is sometimes the more honest label than forcing a single scale name onto the whole song.
  • Character difference: harmonic minor's raised 7th (a semitone from the octave) creates strong upward pull/resolution — directional, "wants to move." Aeolian's unaltered 7th has much weaker pull — laid-back, less resolved, more purely "sorrowful" than harmonic minor's brighter/stricter/more dramatic color. A/B comparison: "Losing My Religion" (R.E.M.) recomposed in harmonic minor loses its laid-back sorrow and gains a stricter, almost sinister edge.

Dorian in depth

  • Build it from the parallel natural minor: Dorian = natural minor (Aeolian) with the 6th degree raised a half-step (E Aeolian ♭6 = C natural → E Dorian ♮6 = C♯). That single raised 6th is the ONE note that distinguishes Dorian from plain natural minor — everything else about the two scales is identical, which makes it the note to listen/write for when deliberately invoking Dorian over Aeolian. Described as "a less sad minor scale" — brighter, more mystical/uplifting than Aeolian, without becoming major.
  • The Dorian vamp — i–IV — a minor tonic moving to a major IV chord (the major IV is only possible in Dorian; Aeolian's iv is minor) is the fastest way to state Dorian in two chords: the minor i sets a minor key, the major IV introduces the raised 6th. Extremely common in funk (arguably more common there than plain Aeolian) and vamped for extended stretches in Pink Floyd. An alternative to the major IV: a minor ii chord built on the 2nd degree also carries the raised 6th (it's minor rather than diminished specifically because of that raised 6th) and gives the same Dorian color from a different chord. → Chord Progressions
  • Placement of the raised 6th signals intent. Several songs deliberately withhold Dorian's 6th from the melody until a structurally important moment (the chorus) even when the chords have carried it from the start — "Blue Jeans" (Lana Del Rey), "Mad World" (Tears for Fears/Gary Jules, chords Dorian from the verse, vocal only touches the raised 6th in the chorus) — the delayed payoff lifts the chorus and sets it apart from the verse. Some songs never touch the 6th in the melody at all and stay Dorian purely via the chords ("Drive," R.E.M. — a major IV chord recontextualizes an otherwise ambiguous minor vocal melody as Dorian for the whole song). And some songs sit on an ambiguous pentatonic minor (touching neither Dorian's raised 6th nor Aeolian's flat 6th) until a specific structural moment resolves the ambiguity — "Woodstock" (Joni Mitchell) stays pentatonic until the end of the first chorus, when the vocal finally lands on the Dorian 6th.
  • Direct Dorian↔Aeolian contrast within one song is a deliberate mood device, not just modal drift: "Eleanor Rigby" shifts from E Dorian (raised 6th) to E Aeolian (natural 6th) line to line, contributing to its unsettled, eerie mood; "Thriller" (Michael Jackson, written by Rod Temperton) sits mostly in C♯ Dorian but briefly dips a chord to the Aeolian minor iv for the same bright/bleak contrast effect.
  • Modal jazz vs. functional harmony: "So What" (Miles Davis) doesn't use a chord progression at all — 16 bars of D Dorian, 8 bars of E♭ Dorian, 8 bars back to D Dorian. Even though the underlying chords could be spelled Dm7→E♭m7→Dm7, these are genuinely mode changes, not chord changes — closer to a key change than a ii-related chord substitution — with the soloist exploring each Dorian scale over a static tonal center rather than resolving through functional harmony. → Modal Jazz
  • Other Dorian song examples: "Riders on the Storm" (The Doors, textbook intro — the descending keyboard line walks straight down E Dorian), "Scarborough Fair" (traditional, the "rosemary and thyme" melodic line lands on the Dorian raised 6th).

Phrygian in depth

  • Build it from the parallel natural minor: Phrygian = natural minor (Aeolian) with the 2nd degree lowered a half-step. That's the one note that separates it from Aeolian, and it's what gives Phrygian its dark, unnerving, exotic edge on top of Aeolian's plain minor bleakness — described as "all the bleakness of the minor scale, plus an extra streak of darkness." Doesn't suit typical pop music, but is a natural home in metal (Metallica's "Wherever I May Roam," "Harvester of Sorrow" — both feature the lowered 2nd directly in the riff) and hip-hop (Snoop Dogg's "Gin and Juice" — a two-chord i–♭II Phrygian vamp between the minor tonic and a chord built on the lowered 2nd; Kendrick Lamar's "Humble" — a single altered scale degree in an otherwise minimal piano riff carries the whole dark quality).
  • A song can state Phrygian in the chords/melody without the tonic note being unambiguous — because modal ambiguity is about which note reads as "home," not which notes are used. Modes sharing a parent scale share every note; "New Person, Same Old Mistakes" (Tame Impala) uses only the notes of A♭ major, but different listeners genuinely hear different tonics (C, giving C Phrygian, vs. A♭, giving A♭ major) — the song sounds identical either way, only the felt tonal context changes, and the ambiguity itself is part of what reads as "modal."
  • A i(Phrygian)→major-V chord substitution resolves a Phrygian cadence far more strongly than staying diatonic — "London Calling" (The Clash) sits mostly in E Phrygian, but resolves its chorus hook via a D major chord (borrowed from outside Phrygian, which would diatonically give D minor) moving to E minor. The borrowed major D's F♯ pulls up a single semitone to the E minor tonic's 3rd (G); the diatonic D minor's F♮ would have to travel a whole step to reach the same target, giving a visibly weaker pull. Generalizes: substituting a major chord for the mode's own diatonic minor chord one step below the tonic strengthens the cadence, at the cost of stepping outside the pure mode for that one chord.
  • Not every "exotic ♭2" scale outside the West is really Phrygian — in Arabic/Middle Eastern music the equivalent lowered 2nd is often a genuine quarter-tone (roughly half a semitone, a "half-flat"), not the West's fixed semitone-lowered 2nd, so mapping it onto 12-tone Phrygian is an approximation, not a match (example: "Hadi Kedra" by Nass El Ghiwane, later sampled by The Chemical Brothers for "Galvanize"). See Harmonic Minor Modes § From videos for the closely-related-but-distinct Phrygian dominant (major 3rd) and double harmonic/Hijaz (major 3rd + raised 7th) scales, both frequently confused with plain Phrygian.

Lydian in depth

  • Build it from the parallel major: Lydian = major (Ionian) with the 4th degree raised a half-step. That raised 4th gives Lydian its bright, ethereal, "magical" quality — the standard color for film-score wonder/magic (Yoda's Theme, John Williams; the flying theme from E.T., John Williams — both introduce the raised 4th mid-theme as the moment magic enters the music; Back to the Future, Alan Silvestri, transposes a Lydian motif upward for escalating awe). Rare in pop/rock but real: "Waltz No. 2" (Elliott Smith), "When We Dance" (Sting), "Possibly Maybe" (Björk), "Dancing Days" (Led Zeppelin — Lydian with an added blues ♭3, "a Lydian blues scale"), "Oceans" (Pearl Jam, shifts between two different Lydian keys section to section).
  • The i–II vamp — tonic chord to a major II chord (only possible in Lydian; Ionian's ii is minor) is the efficient two-chord way to state Lydian: the tonic establishes the key center, the major II supplies the raised 4th. Seen in Yoda's Theme and other film-score Lydian passages.
  • Lydian is harmonically the LEAST stable mode, despite being called the "most stable" in some contexts — the apparent contradiction resolves once you separate melodic stability (George Russell's Lydian Chromatic Concept, which the video sets aside) from harmonic stability (the concern here). Every major-scale mode contains one tritone; in Ionian it sits between the 4th and 7th degrees and resolves outward onto the two most consonant scale tones (3 and 1), which is exactly what makes the major scale feel so resolved. In Lydian the tritone sits between the root and the 4th degree itself — its most natural resolution (root held, 4th rising to 5th) only weakly implies the Lydian tonic; in practice a I→V move in Lydian tends to get re-heard as a IV→I move in the plain major scale a 4th below, collapsing the Lydian color back into ordinary Ionian. This is why almost no song commits to Lydian for its entire duration — it usually surfaces for one section, then resolves back to major.
  • Tonic ambiguity is common and demonstrable mid-song — "Here Comes My Girl" (Tom Petty): verse vamps A(I)–B(II), A unambiguously reads as tonic (A Lydian); the chorus uses the identical seven notes but now E reads as tonic, since A Lydian and E major share every note — the song audibly shifts from Lydian to plain major without changing a single pitch, only which note the ear crowns "home." "Man on the Moon" (R.E.M.) does the same shift, C Lydian in the verse to G major in the chorus.
  • Pedaling the tonic note stabilizes an otherwise-unstable Lydian passage — sustaining/repeating the root underneath the chords keeps the ear anchored despite Lydian's weak tritone resolution. "Sara" (Fleetwood Mac, Stevie Nicks) uses the identical chord progression to "Dreams" but pedals F throughout, which is what actually makes it F Lydian — whereas "Dreams" itself is commonly misidentified as F Lydian from its F–G vamp, but the melody clearly resolves to A, making it A Aeolian (chords vi–♭VII of C, not I–II of F Lydian).
  • Lydian dominant is a distinct, closely related scale — Lydian's raised 4th plus a lowered 7th (plain Lydian keeps the natural 7th). Commonly confused with plain Lydian: The Simpsons theme (Danny Elfman) is often cited as Lydian for its raised 4th but is actually Lydian dominant, confirmed by its lowered 7th; "Pretty Ballerina" (The Left Banke) is a second real example.
  • A borderline case, useful as a "how strict is the label" test: "Blue Jay Way" (The Beatles) uses all of C Lydian's notes but routinely swaps in a minor 3rd alongside the major 3rd — since the major 3rd is essential to Lydian's identity, the song only reads as Lydian in the moments it uses it, and isn't a clean single-scale example.

Mixolydian in depth

  • Build it from the parallel major: Mixolydian = major (Ionian) with the 7th degree lowered a half-step — "the major scale's cooler younger brother." Mellow/relaxed but still bold; probably MORE common than plain major in rock. Fully-committed examples: "Clocks" (Coldplay), "Bittersweet Symphony" (The Verve), "Royals" (Lorde). Chord-only (melody stays diatonic, the ♭7 chord alone carries the color): "Sweet Child O' Mine" (Guns N' Roses — a ♭VII chord does the work even though neither riff nor vocal touches the ♭7 note itself).
  • Why the lowered 7th softens resolution: the major scale's 7th degree is a leading tone (a half-step below the tonic) that strongly pulls upward — the mechanism behind a perfect cadence's tension. Mixolydian's lowered 7th is now a whole step from the tonic (closer to the 6th degree than the root), so that pull weakens dramatically — tension/release still exist, but read as patient and laid-back rather than urgent. This is the harmonic reason Mixolydian riffs can loop indefinitely without feeling like they need to resolve (Gary Numan's "Cars" — the ♭7 riff never completes a cadence, so it "can just continue rolling forward forever"; the equivalent major-scale version of the same riff sounds finished after one pass).
  • The i–♭VII–IV–i vamp — the signature efficient Mixolydian progression: tonic establishes the key, ♭VII makes the lowered-7th color unambiguous, then a perfect-4th descent to IV and back home to I. Heard in "Royals," "Sweet Child O' Mine," "It's a Long Way to the Top (If You Wanna Rock 'n' Roll)" (AC/DC). → Chord Progressions
  • Mixolydian sits halfway between major and the blues scale — it shares the blues scale's lowered 7th but keeps major's natural 3rd and 5th (no minor 3rd, no ♭5), giving blues-adjacent songs a brighter edge than a full minor-blues scale would. "All Blues" (Miles Davis, Kind of Blue) is a modal-jazz example built on G Mixolydian.
  • Key-signature confusion is common because Mixolydian shares a key signature with the major scale a 4th below it — "All Night Long" (Lionel Richie, fully A♭ Mixolydian) is frequently mislabeled D♭ major on sheet-music sites because both use the same 5-flat key signature; the signature only fixes which notes are in play, never which one is the tonic.
  • Mixing Mixolydian with a nearby mode mid-song as a light↔dark shift: "Norwegian Wood" (Beatles) opens in E Mixolydian, then shifts to E Dorian (one degree darker — only the 3rd flattens) for the middle eight. "Burn the Witch" (Radiohead) opens vamping F♯ Mixolydian (tonic to ♭VII), then shifts at the chorus to F♯ Aeolian/minor (two degrees darker — both the 3rd and 6th flatten) for a much more pronounced bright-to-dark contrast than the Mixolydian→Dorian shift.

Ionian in depth: triad quality per degree

Stacking every-other note of any Ionian scale (root, skip a note, add a note, skip, add) gives the same quality pattern in every major key:

Degree I ii iii IV V vi vii°
Quality Major minor minor Major Major minor diminished
  • The quality is decided purely by counting half-steps inside the stacked triad: 4 + 3 half-steps = major, 3 + 4 = minor, 3 + 3 = diminished (major/minor both total 7 half-steps root-to-top; diminished totals only 6 — the "odd one out," which is why vii° sounds unresolved and gets avoided/used only as a passing chord). Matches Chords; the full per-key table already lives in Chords by Key.

scale-modes-reference--opening.title: Scale Modes Reference
scale-modes-reference--opening.html:
Mode descriptions use the "anchor + alteration" format: each mode is named by the familiar diatonic mode it most resembles, plus what's different. This matches the logic of the major/minor chart — Natural Minor is just Major starting on the 6th degree, so the mode order inherits naturally. These non-diatonic scales don't have that shortcut, so each degree is described independently.

This page is the mode-by-mode catalog — looked up, not derived. For the reusable technique behind it (deriving any mode's formula by hand, finding its parent scale by chart, building a polychord substitute for a big chord), see Mode Derivation and Polychords.

Chord symbol key: Δ = major 7th · mΔ = minor-major 7th · m7 = minor 7th · ø = half-diminished · ° = full diminished · 7 = dominant 7th

borrowed-chords.title: Borrowed Chords
borrowed-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords / Chord Progressions. A borrowed chord is a chord taken from a parallel key/mode (same tonic, different scale) and dropped into an otherwise-diatonic progression for color. Also called modal interchange. It's the single biggest source of "sophisticated pop" harmony — the Beatles, Radiohead, and film music live here.

The idea

  • Every major key has a Parallel Minor (same tonic — C major ↔ C minor). Modal interchange borrows chords from that parallel minor (or other parallel modes: Dorian, Mixolydian…) without fully changing key.
  • The borrowed chord contains a note outside the home scale — that chromatic note is the "color."

The workhorses (borrowed from parallel minor, in a MAJOR key)

Borrowed chord In C major Sound
iv (minor four) Fm the "heartbreak" chord — IV → iv → I
♭VI A♭ epic, cinematic lift
♭VII B♭ rock/Mixolydian move (I–♭VII–IV)
♭III E♭ darker, bluesy
♭II (Neapolitan) D♭ dramatic pre-dominant
iiø7 (half-dim) Dø7 minor-key ii, jazzy pre-dominant
  • The most emotionally reliable is IV → iv → I: the major subdominant brightening, then its minor version darkening, then home. Instant bittersweetness.
  • From a major key you can also borrow the whole Mixolydian ♭VII (rock) or Dorian color.
  • ♭II isn't actually borrowed from the parallel minor despite the naming pattern — see Neapolitan Sixth for the classical convention it almost always follows in practice: near-exclusive use in first inversion (hence "Neapolitan 6th," not "the Neapolitan sixth chord"), resolving to a dominant 7th in 3rd inversion or a cadential 6/4.
  • Borrowed ii° is always used in first inversion (it's diminished — same rule as diminished triads generally, see Part-Writing). The two altered-root chords (♭III, ♭VI) resolve better with contrary motion than strict alteration-direction resolution, to avoid parallel octaves.

Related: parallel-minor modulation

When a section stays in the parallel minor for a while (not just one chord), that's parallel-minor modulation — e.g. a bright major verse dropping to the parallel minor for the bridge, then returning (🎵 THE BEATLES - Here There and Everywhere).

Hear it

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Here There and Everywhere — middle 8 drops to G minor (parallel minor) then slides home.
  • iv chord ("heartbreak"): countless Beatles endings and pop ballads use IV → iv → I.

notation--4-accidentals-and-key-signatur.title: 4. Accidentals and key signatures
notation--4-accidentals-and-key-signatur.html:
Sign Effect
♯ sharp Raise a half step — one fret
♭ flat Lower a half step — one fret
♮ natural Cancel a previous sharp or flat
𝄪 double sharp Raise a whole step
𝄫 double flat Lower a whole step

The scope rules, which are the actual content of this section:

  • A sharp or flat in the key signature applies for the whole piece, in every octave, until the key signature changes.
  • An accidental not in the key signature applies only for the rest of that measure, and only on that exact line or space — not the same letter in another octave.
  • The bar line cancels it. A natural at the start of the next measure is a courtesy accidental — technically redundant, printed to stop you second-guessing.
  • A natural cancelling a key-signature sharp or flat is likewise good only to the end of the measure.
  • A tie carries an accidental across the bar line for that one held note.

Enharmonic = same pitch, different spelling (F♯ = G♭, B♯ = C, F♭ = E). The spelling is not arbitrary — it encodes function. See Key Signatures and Chord Naming by Context.

notation--5-rhythm-notation.title: 5. Rhythm notation
notation--5-rhythm-notation.html:
Each value is exactly half the one before:

double whole → whole → half → quarter → eighth → 16th → 32nd → 64th → 128th

(128th notes are vanishingly rare in practice — the textbook example is the intro of Beethoven's "Pathétique" Sonata, Op. 13, 1st mvt.) Each value has a matching rest; rests are proportional to each other the same way. Eighths and shorter carry flags when alone and beams when grouped; beaming is not decorative — it groups notes into beats, and correct beaming is half of what makes a rhythm readable at a glance.

  • Slash/tremolo shorthand — a diagonal slash through a stem (or below a stemless note) reads one of two ways depending on context: a literal tremolo (rapidly repeat the note), or a notational shorthand for smaller embedded values — e.g. a half note with two slashes means "eighth notes in the space of a half note." The mark alone doesn't disambiguate; the surrounding context does. — The Elements of Rhythm, p.12
  • Augmentation dot — three interpretations, not just one: 1. Addition reading (the one most players know): adds half the note's own value. A second dot adds half of the first dot's addition, not half the original again (double-dotted half = 2 + 1 + ½ = 3½ beats). 2. Divides into three non-dotted values — a dotted half → three quarter notes. 3. Divides into two smaller dotted values — a dotted half → two dotted quarter notes. Reading (2) — that a dotted value's natural division is into three — is the specific fact that makes compound meter make sense: a compound pulse is written as a dotted note precisely because dotted values divide in threes. See the Time Signature Table for how this plays out in practice. — The Elements of Rhythm, p.12–13, 18
  • Tie — joins two noteheads of the same pitch into one sustained sound, most often across a bar line when a duration exceeds what a measure can hold. Only the first is attacked. For three or more, tie between each adjacent pair; never draw one long tie spanning several noteheads.
  • Slur — a curved line connecting different pitches, telling the performer to play them fluidly connected (no re-articulation for winds/voice, one bow stroke for strings, legato for piano; on guitar, hammer-on/pull-off). Drawn connecting noteheads, not stems — the standard student mistake is drawing it stem-to-stem; the one exception is a slur crossing a passage where stems change direction.
  • Phrase marking — visually a slur (a curved line), but a different job: marks off a complete musical idea/statement, drawn above the staff, and carries no articulation instruction of its own. A slur can sit nested inside a phrase marking without conflict — don't conflate the two just because they look identical.
  • Tuplets ("artificial division") — a bracketed number divides a beat against the prevailing meter: triplet = a compound (3-part) division inserted into a simple-meter beat; duplet = the mirror image, a simple (2-part) division inserted into a compound-meter beat. A super-triplet (or other larger tuplet) is the same device spanning multiple beats instead of one. Full treatment: Tuplets.

Rests are read, not skipped. Whole rest hangs below line 4 and means "the whole measure" in any meter; half rest sits on top of line 3. The rhythm-first principle: when reading breaks down, it is almost always rhythm rather than pitch — see Sight Reading.

notation--3-ledger-lines.title: 3. Ledger lines
notation--3-ledger-lines.html:
Short lines extending the staff for notes above or below it. They continue the same alternating line/space pattern — the staff simply keeps going, invisibly.

Ledger lines are where most readers stall, because the anchor is far away and they revert to counting from the top line every time. The fix is more anchors (middle C above the bass staff, middle C below the treble staff), not more counting.

Octave signs avoid stacks of ledger lines: 8va = play an octave higher than written, 8vb = an octave lower, 15ma = two octaves higher. The dotted bracket shows how far the instruction runs; loco cancels it.

notation--7-navigation-signs.title: 7. Navigation signs
notation--7-navigation-signs.html:
The part of notation that has nothing to do with pitch and stops a reader dead when unfamiliar. Charts and lead sheets lean on these heavily.

Sign Means
𝄆 … 𝄇 repeat bars Play the enclosed section twice
1st / 2nd endings (volta brackets) Take bracket 1 the first time, skip to bracket 2 on the repeat
D.C. (da capo) Go back to the beginning
D.S. (dal segno) Go back to the sign 𝄋
al Fine …and stop at the word Fine
al Coda / To Coda ⊕ …then jump to the Coda section
Coda ⊕ The tail section jumped to
Simile / % Repeat the previous measure (or two) as written

Read the roadmap before playing a chart. Working out a D.S. al Coda mid-performance is the single most common way a competent reader gets lost.

reading-notation-on-guitar.title: Reading Notation on Guitar
reading-notation-on-guitar.html:
Part of Music Theory → Notation. Why guitar is genuinely harder to read on than piano, and what the notation actually asks of you. The symbol system itself is in Notation; this is the instrument-specific layer.

1. Guitar sounds an octave below what's written

Guitar is a transposing instrument. Written middle C sounds as the C an octave below middle C. The whole instrument is printed an octave high so it fits comfortably on a treble staff instead of crawling all over the grand staff.

Engravers sometimes mark this with a small 8 beneath the treble clef (the 8vb clef). Modern scores usually leave it off and assume the player knows — so the absence of the 8 tells you nothing. Bass guitar works the same way in bass clef.

This only bites when you're reading against something — matching a written piano part, checking a DAW's score view, or writing a part for someone else. Playing solo from a guitar chart, it's invisible.

Guitar's written range in standard tuning runs from E below the treble staff (open 6th string) up past the staff into 8va territory at the top of the neck. Anything above about the 12th fret on the 1st string is printed with 8va to keep the ledger lines sane.

2. The real problem: one pitch, five places

On piano, middle C is one key. On guitar, the same written pitch exists in up to five or six places on the fretboard, each with a different fingering, a different tone, and a different set of notes reachable next.

That means reading on guitar is not a pitch→note problem, it's a pitch→position problem. The notation does not tell you where to play it. You decide, and you decide ahead of the notes.

This is exactly what the position system exists to solve. Guitar Positions and the twelve Position NN pages define a fixed four-fret window with a fixed finger-per-fret assignment. Inside a position, every written note has one answer. Reading becomes possible because the ambiguity is removed before you start.

Leavitt's whole Volume 1 is first position and nothing else for 24 pages, for exactly this reason — see A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment.

3. Position and fingering marks

Mark Means
Roman numeral (V, VII, IX…) Play in that position — index finger at that fret
Circled number ①–④ Fretting-hand finger: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 pinky
Plain number beside a notehead Same thing in most guitar engraving
p i m a c Picking-hand fingers (classical): thumb, index, middle, ring, pinky
Circled number on a string ⑥–① Which string to play it on — 6 is low E
⊓ / ∨ Pick downstroke / upstroke
C / CVII Full barre at that fret (half-barre often ½C)
Roman numeral, no C/B prefix (e.g. V2) Pure position marker, not a barre instruction — tells you which of several playable positions/fret-locations the tab assumes for that shape (useful when the same chord is reachable in more than one place on the neck)
8va Play an octave higher than printed

String numbering runs 6 → 1, low to high: E A D G B E. Fret numbering starts at the nut. The two systems get confused constantly — a "3" could be third finger, third string or third fret depending on where it's printed, so read its position on the page, not the digit.

Why p-i-m-a-c doesn't map 1:1 onto English finger names: the letters come from the Spanish names for the picking-hand fingers — pulgar (thumb), índice (index), medio (middle), anular (ring), meñique (pinky) — so index/middle happen to line up with their English initials (i, m) but thumb and ring don't (p, a), and the pinky is c, not "p" for pinky. A printed "c" above a note in a chord frame or tab means the pinky plays it.

A bracket over specific strings (not always the top or bottom half) marks a partial/half barre — e.g. "half CV" over strings 4-3-2 rather than the full 6-string barre implied by a plain "CV." The bracket shows exactly which strings are covered; don't assume it's a literal top-half or bottom-half split. — Jared, Georgia on My Mind Fingerstyle Guitar Tutorial (With Sheet Music & Tab)

4. Chord frames (chord boxes)

The grid diagram above a chord symbol. Joe Pass states the convention plainly on p.2 of Guitar Chords, and it's near-universal:

  • Vertical lines = strings, low E on the left. Horizontal lines = frets.
  • A heavy line across the top = the nut (open position). No heavy line + a Roman numeral to the right = start at that fret instead.
  • x above a string = muted, not played. o = played open.
  • Numbers in circles = fingering. A curved line across several strings = a barre with that finger.
  • Note names printed under the diagram spell the actual voicing, low to high — this is the most useful part of a chord box and the most ignored.

Play only the strings indicated. Joe Pass is explicit that some of his voicings sound wrong if you fill in the muted strings. A chord box is a precise instruction, not a suggestion of a region.

5. Slash / rhythm notation

Diagonal slashes on the staff with chord symbols above: play the chord, one strum per slash, rhythm as written, voicing up to you. This is how comping and rhythm-guitar parts are notated, and it's what most real-world charts hand you.

Leavitt introduces it on p.11 of Volume 1 and keeps a "Rhythm Accompaniment" thread running alongside the reading thread the whole way through (p.11, p.17, p.24) — chord symbols, then bass-note-and-chord patterns, then chord diagrams.

A rhythmic slash with a stem and flags specifies the rhythm exactly. A plain slash means "keep time, your call."

6. Tab vs standard notation

Tab Standard
Tells you Where to put your fingers What pitch, and how long
Rhythm Often absent or approximate Exact
Transposes No — it's tied to one tuning Yes, freely
Readable by Guitarists Everyone
Teaches you the fretboard No Yes, forced

Tab is faster to use and teaches you nothing. Standard notation is slower to learn and is the only one that makes you know where the notes are. Combined tab+standard systems (the modern default in published guitar books) let you take the rhythm from the top staff and the position from the bottom — useful, but it's also the easiest way to never actually learn to read, because the eye drops to the tab under pressure.

None of the three method books in this vault use tab. Joe Pass Guitar Chords gives standard notation and a chord box for every voicing; Guitar Style and A Modern Method are standard-notation only.

7. What makes guitar reading break down

  • Position choice, not note recognition. Scan a phrase for its highest and lowest note before playing, and pick a position that contains both. Deciding mid-phrase is what causes the stall.
  • Looking at the fretboard. Guitar tempts you to look down in a way piano doesn't. Reading requires eyes on the page, which means the position window has to be secure by feel.
  • Chords read vertically. A four-note stack is one object, not four notes — recognise the shape against the chord symbol rather than spelling it out.
  • Rhythm, as always. The most common failure point in reading of any kind. See Sight Reading.

7a. The one-spot-per-note drill (a training shortcut)

A deliberately narrower training method for the exact problem in §2 — worth running alongside (not instead of) the full position system. Piano removes the pitch→position decision entirely: one written pitch, one key. Guitar doesn't have that luxury, but you can manufacture it: pick one specific fret/string location for each note name, in one working register, and commit to playing that note there every single time it shows up in any piece of sheet music — even when it's reachable elsewhere (an open string, a different position). No exceptions, so there's zero decision-making left when the note appears mid-phrase.

  • Sequence pitch before rhythm, strictly. First pass: ignore rhythm completely, just quiz yourself — "where's that note, where's that note" — jumping from notehead straight to the fixed fretboard spot as fast as possible, like a flashcard drill. Only once the pitch-jump feels automatic, go back and layer rhythm on top. Don't try to solve both at once while the pitch map is still new.
  • Starts in the middle of the neck, not open position, on purpose. Most method books start you in open/first position and work outward — which can take years to reach fluent reading further up the neck (Leavitt's own Volume 1 alone is 24 pages of first position only, see §2 above). This drill skips that ladder: build the one-spot map anywhere on the neck you like, the point is committing to a single fixed answer per pitch, not which register you pick.
  • Practice on real lead sheets, not exercises — actual real-book melodies (demoed on Pat Metheny's "Bright Size Life" and "What a Wonderful World"), and for a denser workout once the basic drill is easy, the Charlie Parker Omnibook (dense, chromatic, transcribed improvised lines, not just heads).
  • Claimed payoff: ~2 weeks of this drilling to go from stuck to "grab any tune and start plunking out the melody," versus a much longer position-by-position method-book trajectory to reach the same point in the middle of the neck.

— Jared Borkowski, Shortcut to Reading Sheet Music for Guitar - Read Guitar Lead Sheets

reading-bass-clef.title: Reading Bass Clef
reading-bass-clef.html:
Part of Music Theory → Notation. The clef guitar never made you learn. Every guitar method in this vault is treble-only by design — A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment included — so bass clef is a real hole rather than a review. It matters for three things Nate actually does: reading piano music (the left hand lives here, and 11 of the vault's piano song pages are Satie), writing and reading bass lines, and reading a full score or a string/horn arrangement without guessing.

Why it exists at all

One staff can't hold the range of music without burying everything in ledger lines. Bass clef is the F clef: the two dots straddle the line that is F below middle C (line 4). Treble is the G clef: its spiral wraps G above middle C (line 2).

Together they form the grand staff, and the two clefs are positioned so that middle C sits exactly between them — one ledger line below the treble staff, one ledger line above the bass staff. That is the same note, printed two different ways. Internalising that one fact is most of the battle.

treble ═══════════════════
       ─── middle C (1 ledger below treble)
       ─── middle C (1 ledger above bass)
bass   ═══════════════════

The landmark method

Do not learn nine positions. Learn three anchors and step to everything else. This is the standard approach in modern method books and it is faster than mnemonics because it keeps working once you leave the staff.

Anchor Where Why this one
F Line 4 — between the clef's two dots The clef literally points at it
Middle C One ledger line above the staff The bridge to everything you already read
G Line 1 (bottom line) The bottom anchor; also the guitar's low open-ish register

From an anchor, move by step = adjacent line/space and skip = line-to-line or space-to-space (a 3rd). Read intervals, not letters.

Mnemonics as a backstop, not a method:

  • Lines, bottom to top — G B D F A ("Good Burritos Don't Fall Apart")
  • Spaces, bottom to top — A C E G ("All Cows Eat Grass")

They break the instant you hit a ledger line, which is why they're the fallback.

The trap: it is not "treble moved down"

The most common wrong shortcut is "read it as treble and shift." The line/space letters differ by a 2nd, not a clean octave — a note on the bottom line is E in treble and G in bass. Any rule you build on "shift it" will be right sometimes and wrong the rest of the time, which is worse than counting.

Learn it as its own alphabet anchored to F. It takes days, not weeks.

Bass clef on the instruments Nate plays

Piano. The left hand normally reads bass clef, the right treble — but not always. Composers freely put the right hand in bass clef for low passages, and the left hand in treble for high ones; look for the clef change at the start of a system or mid-measure. Satie does this. So does anything with hands crossing.

Bass guitar. Notated in bass clef and, like guitar, sounds an octave lower than written. Low E on a 4-string is written on the bottom space+ledger territory of the bass staff.

Guitar in bass clef. Rare on its own, but you meet it constantly in piano/vocal/guitar charts, full scores and horn arrangements — anything where you're reading someone else's part to know what's going on. Also relevant when writing a bass line in a DAW score view.

Getting fluent, concretely

The method is the same as any reading skill — see Sight Reading for the full version — but bass clef specifically responds to:

  1. Naming drills away from the instrument. 2 minutes, name notes aloud from a random page of piano music. Cheap and it works because the bottleneck is recognition speed, not fingers.
  2. Play the left hand alone. Take a piano piece already in the repertoire (a Satie) and read only the bass staff, slowly. Known music removes the pitch guessing so the clef is the only new variable.
  3. Read intervals off the anchors. "F, up a 3rd, up a step" beats "G-B-D-F-A… fourth line… F."
  4. Write in it. Notating a bass line by hand forces the mapping in the opposite direction, which is where it sticks.

sight-reading.title: Sight Reading
sight-reading.html:
Part of Music Theory → Notation. The skill, not the symbol system. Notation is what the marks mean; this is how you turn them into sound at tempo, on the first pass. It's the backing note for the theory lane in Practice System Config ("Theory & Sight Reading").

The central reframe: sight reading is not "reading fast." It is prediction. Fluent readers are two to four beats ahead of what their hands are playing, recognising groups — a scale fragment, an arpeggio, a familiar rhythm — rather than decoding note by note. Everything below is in service of moving the eye ahead of the hands.

The five rules that do most of the work

  1. Read below your playing level. Sight-reading material should look easier than what you can perform. If decoding takes all your attention there's nothing left over to look ahead with, and looking ahead is the entire skill being trained. Playing hard music slowly is a different exercise.
  2. Never stop, never go back. The pulse is the one thing you may not break. A wrong note is a wrong note; a stop is a failure of the actual skill. If you fall behind, drop notes — keep the beat and rejoin. This is the hardest habit to build and the most important.
  3. Frequency beats intensity. 5–10 minutes daily beats an hour on Sunday. Short, low-stakes, frequent exposure is what the pedagogy research consistently supports; a 30-second read at the top of a session is worth more than an occasional high-pressure test.
  4. Rhythm first. Reading breaks down at rhythm far more often than at pitch. Drill rhythm on its own — clap or count a line before playing it, and give it dedicated minutes rather than hoping it comes along for free.
  5. Interleave, don't repeat. Alternate short reads of several different pieces rather than repeating one. Repeating a passage stops being sight reading on the second attempt — by definition you're no longer reading at sight.

The 30-second pre-scan

Before the first note, every time. Costs half a minute, prevents most derailments:

Look at Ask
Key signature Which sharps/flats, and where do they fall in this position?
Time signature What's the beat unit? Where does the pulse sit?
Roadmap Repeats, 1st/2nd endings, D.S., Coda — where does this actually go?
Range Highest and lowest note → which position covers both? (guitar-specific and load-bearing — see Reading Notation on Guitar)
Rhythm hotspots Any tuplets, syncopation, dotted figures? Count them silently now.
Accidentals Circle the ones that will surprise you.
Tempo Pick one you can hold through the hardest bar, not the easiest.

Then set the pulse — count a full bar in, out loud or with a metronome — and start.

Practice modes

Rotate these; they train different halves of the skill.

  • Cold reads. New material, once through, no stopping. The core exercise. A duet part, an etude, a page you've never opened.
  • Rhythm-only. Clap or tap the line while counting aloud. Removes pitch entirely so the rhythm is the only variable. Leavitt's own instruction on p.21 is blunt about this: count aloud as you play.
  • Away from the instrument. Read a page and hear it, or name notes aloud, with no guitar in hand. Trains recognition speed, which is the actual bottleneck.
  • Slow-motion reading. Half tempo, but strictly in time and eyes always ahead. Not the same as playing slowly to get notes right.
  • Position drills. Same short line, read in three different positions. Attacks guitar's one-pitch-many-places problem directly. A more aggressive variant of this same idea: instead of reading in several positions, freeze one fret/string spot per note name in one register and commit to it with zero exceptions — trades flexibility for speed while the pitch map is new, then you can always widen back out to multiple positions later. Claimed payoff: ~2 weeks to fluent melody-plunking vs. years working out from open position book by book. — Jared Borkowski, Shortcut to Reading Sheet Music for Guitar - Read Guitar Lead Sheets, see Reading Notation on Guitar §7a
  • Metronome on 2 and 4. Once basic reading is steady — keeps time honest without spoon-feeding the downbeat.

Where the material comes from

Source What it's good for
A Modern Method for Guitar - Enrichment The spine. Volume 1 teaches reading through repertoire — melodies, duets and etudes, with sparse concept pages. Pages 3–24 are in the vault as page images.
The duets Sea to Sea (p.6), One Two Three Four (p.10), Imitation Duet (p.14), Here We Go Again (p.16), Etude No. 1 (p.20), Etude No. 2 (p.22). These are the sight-reading workout the book is known for — they need a second part (recording, teacher, or a DAW playing the other line).
The Whole Enchilada fake book Melodies + chord symbols. Good cold-read material and it doubles as ear/harmony work.
Joe Pass Guitar Chords - Enrichment Standard-notation chord stacks read vertically — a different reading skill from single-line melody.
Piano repertoire Forces Reading Bass Clef. Read the left hand of a Satie already in the repertoire.

Lesson plans for the theory lane

Session-sized blocks for Practice System Config's Theory & Sight Reading lane. Each is ~10–15 minutes and cites exact pages, so /practice can serve one without inventing content. Ordered by the book's own progression; the concept half of each is in Notation.

# Focus Do this Book pages
1 First position, key of C Pre-scan, then cold-read Exercises 1–4 once through at a tempo you can hold. Then Ex. 2 again at 2/3 tempo, eyes ahead. p.4–5
2 Upper register of first position Ex. 5–6, focusing on the C above the 5th string — the notes most likely to stall you. p.8
3 Note + chord review Ex. 7–8 cold. Then name every note on p.9 aloud without the guitar. p.9
4 First duet Sea to Sea — record the second part, then read the first against it. Do not stop. p.6
5 Rhythm accompaniment / slash notation Read the chord-symbol line as comping: one strum per slash, chords your choice of voicing. p.11
6 Ledger lines Ex. 9, then a rhythm-only clap-through of the same line. p.12
7 Complete first position Ex. 10, the key-of-C review. This is the checkpoint for Section One. p.13
8 Sharps and flats Read p.15's examples, then re-read Ex. 10 transposed in your head to F (one flat). p.15
9 Duet + dynamics Here We Go Again, then the dynamics/bass-note-and-chord material. p.16–17
10 Eighth notes Ex. 1–2 with alternate picking marked. Count "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &" aloud. p.18–19
11 Etude No. 1 Full cold read of the duet, then rhythm-only pass of the trickiest four bars. p.20
12 Rests, ties, dots Read p.21's paired examples — the same phrase written with dots and with ties. Clap both. p.21
13 Etude No. 2 Cold read. By here the pre-scan should be automatic. p.22
14 Melody + accompaniment First Solo — the first page where you're reading two things at once. p.23
15 Chord diagrams Read the chord-frame page as voicings, cross-referenced to Reading Notation on Guitar §4. p.24

Bass-clef lessons run in parallel and are not in the book — see Reading Bass Clef for the drill set.

Measuring it

Sight reading improves invisibly, so track something. Once a month, cold-read a page you've never opened at a fixed tempo and note: did you keep the pulse, how many stops, how far ahead were your eyes.

One finding worth knowing: a Psychology of Music study found students given growth-mindset training improved their sight reading significantly more than those who weren't. The skill has an unusually large "I'm just not a reader" self-belief component, and it isn't true.

time-signatures-note-values--strong-weak.title: Strong/weak beat hierarchy — and why it matters for production
time-signatures-note-values--strong-weak.html:
Not all rhythmic positions carry equal weight, and matching velocity to that hierarchy is most of what makes a programmed pattern read as "played" rather than "gridded":

  • Meter is what CREATES the strong/weak hierarchy in the first place — an undifferentiated stream of identical beats has no structure until it's grouped: duple (groups of 2, "ONE-two") gives strong-weak; triple (groups of 3, "ONE-two-three") gives strong-weak-weak, uncommon in electronic music, somewhat common in rock; quadruple (groups of 4, "ONE-two-THREE-four" — effectively two duples stacked) is by far the dominant organization in modern music (~90% of it), with beat 1 strongest, beat 3 next-strongest, beats 2 and 4 weak. → Max Konyi, Essentials of Rhythm - Organizing Beats and Bars (Meter)
  • The standard kick/snare backbeat falls directly out of quadruple meter's strong/weak hierarchy: kick on the strong beats (1 and 3, low/"boom" sound), snare on the weak beats (2 and 4, higher/upper-accent sound) — not an arbitrary convention, a direct application of which beats are metrically strong. → Rhythm and Groove — Max Konyi, Essentials of Rhythm - Organizing Beats and Bars (Meter)
  • A drum pattern needs internal variation across its full bar length or it collapses back to feeling like a shorter meter — a 4-beat pattern where beats 1–2 sound identical to beats 3–4 risks reading as a repeated 2-beat (duple) idea instead of a genuine 4-beat one; a single differentiating hit (e.g. one extra 16th-note hit at the very end of the bar) is enough to make the ear register the full cycle. → Max Konyi, Essentials of Rhythm - Organizing Beats and Bars (Meter)
  • "A whole note = one bar" is a quadruple-meter-specific shortcut, not a universal rule. A whole note is always 4 beats — in quadruple meter that happens to equal one full bar, but in triple meter a bar is only 3 beats long, so a 4-beat whole note can't fit inside one triple-meter bar at all (the note that fills a triple-meter bar is a dotted half note instead). Keep "beats" and "bar" as separate units when reasoning about note values outside 4/4. → Max Konyi, Essentials of Rhythm - Organizing Beats and Bars (Meter)
  • Strongest: on the beat (the numbered positions — 1, 2, 3, 4).
  • Weaker: the "and" (the off-beat eighth-note midpoint between beats).
  • Weakest: the "e" and "a" (the sixteenth-note subdivisions flanking the "and").
  • A hit landing in a weak spot should generally carry lower velocity than a hit landing on the beat — this single rule does a lot of the "lifelike" work before reaching for any humanize plugin. → Rhythm and Groove (the full humanization treatment) — You Suck at Producing, Writing Your First Drum Beats in Ableton

time-signatures-note-values--simple-comp.title: Simple, compound & complex meter
time-signatures-note-values--simple-comp.html:
• Simple beat unit divides in 2 (undotted note gets the beat); compound beat unit divides in 3 (dotted note gets the beat) — compound time signatures (6/8, 9/8, 12/8) are "lying": the top number is actually the division count, divide by 3 to get the real beat count, and the beat unit is always a dotted note.
  • Why 6/8 feels different from 3/4 despite having the same 6 eighth notes per bar: the grouping. 6/8 groups its six eighth notes into two groups of three (felt "ONE-two-three-FOUR-five-six" → 2 felt beats/bar, each subdividing into 3 like a built-in triplet — the compound feel); 3/4 groups the identical six eighth notes into three groups of two (felt "ONE-and-TWO-and-THREE-and" → 3 felt beats/bar). Same note count, different accent grouping = the entire source of 6/8's rolling/lilting feel versus 3/4's more waltz-like three-count. When a piece doesn't feel locked into a clear pulse, explicitly test which grouping (4/4, 6/8, or 3/4) the material actually wants — the same raw material can genuinely support more than one valid reading until a grouping is committed to. → Max Konyi, The Magic of 6/8 Time
  • Complex meter — simple and compound meter almost never combined within one measure in common practice (only as mixed meter, alternating whole measures — written with two stacked time signatures, e.g. 6/8 + 3/4). 20th-century primitivist composers (see 20th-Century Harmony) broke this: complex meter has BOTH simple and compound beats in the same measure.
  • Odd-meter groupings (5/8, 7/8, 9/8, 10/8, 11/8…) can each be split multiple valid ways: 5 = 2+3 or 3+2; 7 = 2+2+3, 2+3+2, or 3+2+2; the underlying eighth-note division stays the same length throughout even though the beats it groups into are uneven — matches this page's existing polyrhythm section from the production side. — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.5, 17
  • Asymmetrical meter graphs onto the Time Signature Table the same way compound meter does — the written signature is the First Division row, and Pulse is found by summing groups. Groupings can also be built irregularly out of meters that aren't inherently odd: 8/8 as 3+3+2, 10/8 as 3+3+2+2, and so on — the same "sum the groups to find Pulse" logic applies regardless of whether the top number is odd. Named real-world examples: Tchaikovsky's Symphony No. 6 ("Pathétique"), 2nd movement, in 5 — one of the few pre-20th-century asymmetrical examples; Pink Floyd's "Money" in 7 (4+3); Peter Gabriel's "Solsbury Hill," mostly in 7 (4+3); Genesis's "Back in New York City," mostly in 7 (2+2+3); Bartók's Concerto for Orchestra IV (Intermezzo), alternating simple duple with 5; Stravinsky's The Firebird closing and The Rite of Spring; jazz big-band composer/arranger Hank Levy's odd-meter body of work. Asymmetrical meter was rare before the 20th century and became a hallmark of it, in both classical and vernacular genres. — The Elements of Rhythm, p.47–49
