mix-handoff--the-commit-boundary.title: The commit boundary
mix-handoff--the-commit-boundary.html:
The single decision that governs everything else. Commit what defines what a part is. Leave open everything about how parts relate.

Commit it Leave it open
Character distortion — the thing that makes that guitar that guitar Track-to-track balance
Synthesis and patch design Corrective EQ
Creative effects that are part of the writing (the stutter, the reverse, the filtered break) Bus and glue compression
Sample choice and chops Reverb and delay amounts
Tuning and timing edits on vocals Stereo width decisions on the mix as a whole
Arrangement — what plays when The 2-bus, entirely

The test: if removing it would change what the part is, commit it. If removing it would only change how loud or bright it sits against its neighbours, leave it.

The failure mode runs in both directions. Over-commit and the engineer works around your decisions instead of through them — a printed reverb can't be pulled back when the arrangement changes underneath it. Under-commit and you've handed over a pile of raw tracks with none of the intent that made the demo good, and they'll mix somebody else's record.

Print a safety. When you commit something destructive, keep the unprocessed version alongside it, muted and named. Costs nothing, and it's the difference between "can you undo that" and "no."
mix-handoff--the-commit-boundary.lede: The single decision that governs everything else. Commit what defines what a part is. Leave open everything about how parts relate.

mix-handoff--multitracks-vs-stems.title: Multitracks vs stems
mix-handoff--multitracks-vs-stems.html:
Not interchangeable, and the wrong one wastes a round trip.

  • Multitracks — every individual track, unbundled. Each mic, each synth, each vocal layer. This is what a mixing engineer wants.
  • Stems — grouped submixes bounced to a handful of files: drums, bass, music, vocals. These are for remixers, live playback, and sync licensing. A mixing engineer handed stems can't fix a snare without also touching the kick.

Send multitracks unless they've specifically asked for stems.
mix-handoff--multitracks-vs-stems.lede: Not interchangeable, and the wrong one wastes a round trip.

mix-handoff--delivery-spec.title: Delivery spec
mix-handoff--delivery-spec.html:
Format WAV or AIFF. Never MP3, never a lossy source anywhere in the chain.
Sample rate The session's native rate. Do not convert. If you tracked at 48 kHz, deliver 48 kHz.
Bit depth 24-bit minimum. 32-bit float is fine if they'll take it.
Headroom Peaks around −6 to −3 dBFS. Achieve it with a gain move on the 2-bus, not with a limiter.
Dither None. Dither is the last step of the last process, and that isn't you.
Start point Every file consolidated from the same timeline zero, so nothing can drift on import.
Naming Descriptive. Lead Vox Double L, not Audio 12.

Headroom is the one people get wrong in the harmless direction — there's no prize for −18, and no penalty either. What matters is that nothing is clipping and nothing is limited. (Sonarworks)
mix-handoff--delivery-spec.lede: Headroom is the one people get wrong in the harmless direction — there's no prize for −18, and no penalty either. What matters is that nothing is clipping…

mix-handoff--session-organization.title: Session organization
mix-handoff--session-organization.html:
Do this before the export, not after they ask.

  1. Name every track for what it is. The engineer shouldn't have to solo anything to find out what it is.
  2. Order and group logically — drums, bass, music, vocals. Colour-code if the DAW supports it.
  3. Consolidate each track across the full song length from a common start. No floating regions.
  4. Delete unused tracks. Twelve muted alternates aren't helpful, they're twelve questions.
  5. Flag anything deliberate that looks like a mistake — a part that's intentionally out of tune, a sound that's meant to clip, an effect that has to stay.
mix-handoff--session-organization.lede: Do this before the export, not after they ask.

mix-handoff--what-to-send-alongside.title: What to send alongside
mix-handoff--what-to-send-alongside.html:
Audio alone is an incomplete handoff. Three things travel with it:

  • Your rough mix, as a reference. This is the balance you were hearing when you made every arrangement decision. It's the most useful single file in the package and the one most often left out.
  • A reference track — a finished commercial record in the same lane, for tone and balance target.
  • Written notes on intent. Short. What the song is doing, what you want louder or darker, what you're unsure about, anything that must not change.
mix-handoff--what-to-send-alongside.lede: Audio alone is an incomplete handoff. Three things travel with it:

mix-handoff--using-a-reference-track-pro.title: Using a reference track properly
mix-handoff--using-a-reference-track-pro.html:
The step that makes references work and almost everyone skips: level-match it.

Anything louder sounds better. An unmatched commercial reference is mastered 6–10 dB hotter than your mix, so A/B-ing against it tells you nothing except that it's louder — and you'll chase that difference with the wrong tools.

Match the loudness first, then use it for specific questions, not a general vibe check:

  • Is my low end bigger or smaller than theirs?
  • Is the vocal further forward or further back?
  • Am I duller or brighter above 8k?
  • Is my stereo image wider or narrower?

A reference is a measuring stick, not a target to clone. Switch often, on the same system, at matched level.
mix-handoff--using-a-reference-track-pro.lede: The step that makes references work and almost everyone skips: level-match it.

mix-handoff--mastering-prep.title: Mastering prep
mix-handoff--mastering-prep.html:
Deliberately light — mastering isn't an interest, and prep is the only part that's yours.

  • Everything in the Delivery spec above applies.
  • Nothing on the 2-bus. No limiter, no clipper, no "just a little" glue compression you'd miss.
  • LUFS is context, not a target. It measures integrated perceived loudness over the whole track. Streaming services normalize playback to roughly −14 LUFS, so a master pushed to −7 gets turned down on playback and arrives quieter-sounding and flatter than one that wasn't. Chasing loudness past the normalization target costs dynamics and buys nothing.
  • If it's a release rather than a single, send the running order and the gaps you want between tracks.
  • Turn temporal effects (reverb, delay, modulation) down before sending, not just off the 2-bus. Reverb/mod content sits lower in amplitude than the dry signal almost always, so the mastering engineer's own compression/limiting will lift those quiet tails more than the reference mix ever showed — leaving them at mix-reference level hands over a track that gets brighter/wetter-sounding than intended once it's processed. (Sage Audio)

What makes their job harder: an already-limited mix (nothing left to work with), sample-rate conversion, an MP3 anywhere in the lineage, and a problem buried in the mix that mastering can only make louder rather than fix.
mix-handoff--mastering-prep.lede: Deliberately light — mastering isn't an interest, and prep is the only part that's yours.

sample-clearance.title: Sample Clearance
sample-clearance.html:
Not a craft note — a release-blocker note. Sampling and Sound Selection covers choosing sounds and flipping them. This covers whether you're allowed to put the result out.

Not legal advice

This is a working producer's summary of how clearance operates. For an actual release with an actual sample in it, a music attorney or a clearance service is the right call — the cost of asking is far below the cost of not.

The thing to know: there are two rights

A recorded song is two separate pieces of intellectual property, owned by different people, cleared separately.

Right What it is Usually held by
Master The specific recording — the actual audio The label, or whoever paid for the session
Composition (publishing) The underlying song — melody, lyrics, chords, structure The songwriters and their publishers

Sampling uses both. Lifting audio from a record means you're using their recording and the song inside it. Two clearances, two negotiations, two sets of fees.

This is the distinction the placement asked about and the one worth internalizing, because it's what makes the alternative below work.

The one clean exception: public domain

Composition copyright expires 70 years after the composer's death in most countries — after that, the underlying song needs no clearance at all, from anyone, for any use. This is why so much classical-derived pop material (Pachelbel's Canon in D under Maroon 5's "Memories"; Leoncavallo's Pagliacci under Queen's "It's a Hard Life"; Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 3 under Procol Harum's "A Whiter Shade of Pale," see Songs Inspired By Bach) never triggers a lawsuit even when the melodic lift is note-for-note close — the pieces have been in the public domain for centuries. The recording itself is still a separate right: a specific performance/recording of a public-domain piece can still carry its own master-rights clearance requirement even though the composition underneath it is free to use — public domain status applies to the composition, never automatically to any given recording of it. — David Bennett Music Theory, 14 Songs That 'Rip Off' Classical Music

Sampling vs interpolation

Interpolation is replaying or re-recording the part yourself so it sounds like the original without using the original audio.

  • Sample → master + publishing. Two rights.
  • Interpolation → publishing only. One right.

That's why interpolation is the standard move on a recognizable hook: it removes the label from the conversation entirely and leaves you negotiating with the publisher. It's usually faster, usually cheaper, and always fewer parties.

It is not a loophole. Re-playing a melody is still using the composition, and "I played it myself" is not a defence. What it does is halve the problem.

Clear before release, never after

The rule with the least ambiguity and the highest cost when broken.

Clearing after a track has traction means negotiating with no leverage — the rights holder knows the song is working and prices accordingly. Before release you're one of many requests; after release you're a party who already infringed and needs a fix.

What an uncleared sample can cost:

  • Takedown from streaming and distribution
  • Frozen royalties — income accrues but doesn't pay out
  • The whole track's income, if the settlement is a majority publishing share
  • Delayed release while it gets sorted, usually at the worst moment

On a recognizable sample, holders routinely ask for a significant publishing share — sometimes a majority — plus a percentage of the master and an upfront fee. That's the trade to weigh before building a song around it. (Symphonic, Tracklib)

The practical routes

Roughly in order of how much friction each carries.

  1. Licensed libraries — Tracklib and similar clear both rights up front for a fee and a defined split. Zero negotiation. The catalogue is the constraint, not the paperwork.
  2. Royalty-free / one-stop sample packs — cleared by definition. Check the licence covers commercial release and not just personal use.
  3. Interpolation — replay it. One right instead of two.
  4. Replay and rewrite — change enough that it's your composition. There is no bar-count or note-count safe harbour; "how much is enough" is a legal question, not a rule of thumb, and producers who rely on a supposed threshold are the ones who end up settling.
  5. Full clearance — a clearance service or attorney approaches both sides. Slowest and most expensive, and the only route for a specific famous recording.

Before you build a song around a sample

  • Do I know what the source recording actually is? (An unidentified sample can't be cleared.)
  • Is it from a licensed library — already handled?
  • Could I interpolate it instead and drop the master side?
  • If this needs full clearance, is the song worth a possible majority publishing split?
  • Am I prepared to clear it before release, or to shelve it?

The last one is the real question. A great flip you can't release is a beat, not a song — deciding that early is cheaper than deciding it after the mix.

What this doesn't cover

Broader music-business material — splits, PRO registration, royalties, distribution, sync — is still unwritten in the vault. Flagged as parked in Coverage Review 2026-08-09 §3 and genuinely live given the releases in Originals/.

Three other named families, by stack interval: secundal (stacked 2nds → tone clusters, timbral rather than harmonic), quartal (stacked 4ths — an early-1900s sound, used deliberately in Stravinsky's neoclassicism; guitar fretboard shapes + the So What voicing on Quartal Chord Voicings), quintal (stacked 5ths — respells as the same notes as quartal chords, so it doesn't form a separate system). — Toby W. chord-classification-from-2-to-12-notes-.title: The count
chord-classification-from-2-to-12-notes-.html:
Combinations from one fixed root inside an octave, with inversions folded together:

Notes Raw combinations Symmetry adjustment Unique types
2 — dyads 11 — 11 intervals
3 — triads 55 1 symmetrical (augmented) → (55−1)/3 = 18 19
4 — tetrads 165 1 fully symmetrical (º7) + 2 partly symmetrical pairs → (165−5)/4 = 40 43
5 — pentads 330 none symmetrical → 330/5 = 66 66
6 — 11th chords not enumerated
7 — 13th chords — "most extended 13th chords can be matched with their respective 7-note scale" —
12 — he has one, and it spans nearly 4½ octaves 1

Dyads. Each of the 11 tempered intervals stands for at least two named intervals. He colour-codes provenance: 12 of the names occur in the major scale and its modes, 4 more in harmonic minor, 2 in Neapolitan minor — 18 that cover "the vast majority of music." The last 4, including the augmented third and diminished sixth, need a scale with both ♭2 and ♯4 — which points straight at Raag Todi. All 20 exist inside the thaat system; see The 32 Thaats (32 Modes), which reaches the same 20 from the other direction.

Triads (19). The four named ones (major, minor, diminished, augmented) plus the suspended family (sus4, sus♯4, sus♭2 — sus2 is treated as an inversion of sus4). The other eleven are all "no 5" chords — extended triads with the fifth removed. He excludes "no 3" chords outright, on the grounds that every one is an inverted "no 5."

Tetrads (43). Method: take each named triad, add every remaining note one at a time. What each tetrad reads as, in each key it could belong to. His two rules for what will actually attach:

  • To a major or augmented triad: ♯1, ♭2, 2, ♯2, ♭3, 4, ♯4, ♯5, ♭6, 6, ♯6, ♭7, 7.
  • To a minor or diminished triad: ♭1, ♭2, 2, 3, ♭4, 4, ♯4, ♭5, ♭6, 6, 𝄫7, ♭7, 7.
  • Suspended chords sit in between. The ♯9/♭10 only attaches to major; the ♭9/♯8 to anything.

Pentads. Three framings, and the third is the practical one: "think of a tetrad played over an additional bass note. For me, this is the easiest way to think of 5-note chords." Which is the Slash Chords and Upper Structure Chords view, arrived at by counting.

extended-chords--what-to-actually-play-s.title: What to actually play (standard omissions)
extended-chords--what-to-actually-play-s.html:
Full stacks get muddy — omit freely:

  • 9th chords: drop the 5th
  • 11th chords: drop the 3rd (the 3rd clashes with the 11) → sounds like C9sus4 (Suspended Chords)
  • 13th chords: drop the 5th, 9th, and especially the 11th
  • Drop the root too if a bass player has it
extended-chords--what-to-actually-play-s.lede: Full stacks get muddy — omit freely:

upper-structure-chords--the-idea.title: The idea
upper-structure-chords--the-idea.html:
• Pick any chord as the "upper structure" (triads are typical, but 7th chords and beyond work too).
  • Put a bass note underneath it. If that bass note is already a tone of the upper chord, you just get an inversion. If it isn't, you get a genuinely new composite chord — a different name, a different function, sometimes a different key implication entirely.
  • Where to place it: the most common, most reliably useful placement is the ♭6 degree of a major key (or the natural 7 of a minor key) — put the upper structure's root there and build out from that home position.
upper-structure-chords--the-idea.lede: Pick any chord as the "upper structure" (triads are typical, but 7th chords and beyond work too).

upper-structure-chords--the-six-bass-not.title: The six bass-note options (worked from an E-minor upper structure on the ♭6 of E major = C)
upper-structure-chords--the-six-bass-not.html:
Bass note relationship to the upper structure's root Resulting chord (in E major, upper structure = Em, bass on C) Function / typical resolution
Same as the upper structure's root ♭6 major chord — Cmaj7♯11 (= maj7♭5) No fixed resolution; can sit unresolved. Optional smooth move: ♭6 → 5 (half step down)
A 4th below the root (upper structure read as the bass note's ♭7) ♭7 dominant 13 — D13 Dominant function: backdoor resolution to I, tritone sub into the chord a half-step up, straight V7 into a new key/modal chord
A major 3rd below the root (upper structure read as the bass note's ♭3) iv minor6/9 — Am6add9 Dramatic, tension/tragedy color; commonly resolves to I but forgiving — works resolving almost anywhere
A major 3rd above the root, enharmonically (upper structure read as an altered dominant's upper triad) Altered dominant ♭7♯5♯9 — G♯7♯5♯9 (= V7alt/vi) Classic jazz altered-dominant sound; typically resolves down a 5th into a minor chord, but can target IV, ii, ♭III (as a tritone sub), or the relative/parallel major
A ♯4 above the root (rarer) "Spanish dominant" — 7sus4♭9-type (F♯7sus4♭9) Suspended-dominant color, resolves similarly to a plain V7sus
A ♭9/♭2 above the root (rarer) Same shape a half-step away (B7sus4♭9) Functions similarly to the ♯4 option above

• Jazz: free substitutions for any dominant 7th, especially the V7 resolving to I (Chord Progressions) — extra tension → stronger resolution
  • Rule of thumb: don't alter a note the melody is sitting on (the clash)
  • ♯9 in funk/rock: E7♯9 is the James Brown / Hendrix stab

suspended-chords--how-sus4-chords-get-us.title: How sus4 chords get used (three patterns)
suspended-chords--how-sus4-chords-get-us.html:
1. Suspension → resolution: sus4 chord then its normal version — Csus4 → C (F falls to E), G7sus4 → G7. Usually on the V or I chord. Classic "special effect" — e.g. the Gsus4 → G in Gnarls Barkley's Crazy (Chord Progressions)
  2. V chord under a tonic melody: melody sits on the tonic note while the V plays → tonic clashes with the V's 3rd. Vsus4 swaps that 3rd for the tonic note itself. (Key of C: melody on C over G → Gsus4 instead.)
  3. Keep the suspension AND add the resolution, for tension that never fully releases — instead of dropping the suspended 4th when the chord "resolves," hold it while adding the resolved 3rd underneath/alongside it (e.g. a sus4 chord's D held together with the C♯ it would normally resolve to). Reads as resolving while a residue of the original tension stays audible on top — a way to color a resolution instead of fully releasing it. → You Suck at Producing, You Suck at Music Theory No. 2: Creating Tension
suspended-chords--how-sus4-chords-get-us.lede: Suspension → resolution: sus4 chord then its normal version — Csus4 → C (F falls to E), G7sus4 → G7. Usually on the V or I chord. Classic "special effect"…

add-chords.title: Add Chords
add-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. A triad + one extra note, no 7th — that's what separates add chords from Extended Chords (Cadd9 = C E G D; C9 = C E G B♭ D).

Types

Chord Notes (C) Note
Cadd9 C E G D 9th on top — the common one
Cadd2 C D E G same pitch class as add9, packed inside the triad
Cadd11 C E G F rare
Cadd4 C E F G add11's inside voicing
Cadd6 (= C6) C E G A usually just written C6
C6/9 C E G A D 6th + 9th; common ending chord (a.k.a. "6add9")
  • add9 vs add2: same added pitch, different octave placement
  • Minor versions work identically: Cmadd9 = C E♭ G D; Cmadd2 = C D E♭ G

Usage

  • Pop/acoustic color chords — add9 keeps a triad's stability but shimmers (no 7th tension, unlike Seventh Chords)
  • 6/9 = classic jazz/soul final-I chord
  • If the 3rd is replaced rather than added → that's a sus chord
add-chords.lede: Part of Music Theory → Chords. A triad + one extra note, no 7th — that's what separates add chords from Extended Chords (Cadd9 = C E G D; C9 = C E G B♭ D).

sixth-chords.title: Sixth Chords
sixth-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. A 6th chord (e.g. C6) is a major (or minor) triad with the 6th scale degree added on top — milder color/tension than adding a 7th. Common in jazz/swing and has an "old-fashioned" association, though it shows up across pop and rock too.

The minor-6th naming trap

The added 6th in a minor 6th chord is still the major 6th degree, never the minor scale's 6th — Bm6 = B minor triad (B-D-F♯) + G♯ (NOT G natural). The "minor" in the chord name describes only the underlying triad, not the added note. A minor triad + the actual flat-6 is a different chord, written m♭6 (or "add ♭6").

Enharmonic identity with minor 7th chords

Any 6th chord is identical, note-for-note, to the minor 7th chord built a minor 3rd lower — its relative minor (B♭6 = Gm7; C6 = Am7) — the same phenomenon Chord Inversions documents for sus4/sus2 pairs. Which name is "correct" depends on context (which note reads as the root); when context is genuinely ambiguous (an unaccompanied vocal chord, no bass to anchor it), either name is defensible.

Classical vs. modern "6" — a real notation collision

Classical figured-bass notation uses a superscript 6 to mean first inversion (the outer-note interval of an inverted triad is a 6th) — completely different from modern pop/jazz "6," which means an added 6th degree. "C6" in a classical harmonic analysis = C/E; "C6" on a jazz chart = C major + A. Context (which tradition you're reading) disambiguates.

augmented-chords--usage-transition-passi.html:
Small chromatic shift from a plain triad creates movement between unrelated chords:

  • C → Caug → Am (5th walks G → G♯ → A)
  • G → Gaug → Em
  • Classic move: I → Iaug → VIm (or → IV6). The rising line is the hook

diminished-chords--where-they-live-diato.html:
• vii° is the 7th-degree triad of every major key; ii° in minor keys (Chords by Key)
  • ø is the ii in the minor-key jazz ii–V–i (Chord Progressions)

diminished-chords--usage-passing-chords.html:
Mostly "in-between" chords creating tension between stronger chords:

  • I → ♭iii° → V7
  • Imaj7 → ♭ii°7 → ii7 (chromatic connector)
  • i7 → iiø7 → V7

chord-inversions--the-inversions-of-c-ma.title: The inversions of C major
chord-inversions--the-inversions-of-c-ma.html:
Position Notes Slash symbol
Root position C E G C
1st inversion E G C C/E
2nd inversion G C E C/G
  • Triads have 2 inversions; 4-note chords (Seventh Chords) have 3 (Cmaj7/B etc.)
  • Read "C/E" as "C over E"
  • Alternate letter system: Ca = root, Cb = 1st inv, Cc = 2nd inv, Cmaj7d = Cmaj7/B
  • Worked 4-note example with feels per inversion: Chord Naming by Context

chord-inversions--why-invert.title: Why invert
chord-inversions--why-invert.html:
1. Less hand movement — faster changes, less looking down
  2. Voice leading — keep common tones between chords; smoother progressions (Chord Progressions)
  3. Bass line control — walk the bass stepwise under static chords (C → C/B → Am…)
  4. Comfort — nearby shapes instead of jumps
chord-inversions--why-invert.lede: Less hand movement — faster changes, less looking down

slash-chords--the-interpretation-method.title: The interpretation method
slash-chords--the-interpretation-method.html:
1. Take the bass note as the root, whether or not it's actually a tone of the upper triad.
  2. Relate every note of the upper triad back to that root as a scale degree/extension (3rd, ♭7, 9, ♯11, ♭13…).
  3. Name the resulting chord from those degrees — this tells you whether it's functioning as a dominant, a major-7-type, a minor-7-type, or an ambiguous/diminished-adjacent color, and therefore how it wants to resolve.
  4. If the bass note is a chord tone of the upper triad, there's no new chord at all — it's just an inversion (e.g. Ab/C is 1st-inversion Ab major, F/C is 2nd-inversion F major).
  5. Chords with no 3rd and no 7th present (e.g. D/C, built from 9-♯11/♭5-13) are genuinely ambiguous between a major-7-type (lydian) and dominant-type (lydian dominant) reading — the surrounding harmony decides which; you can't tell from the voicing alone.
  6. This same take-the-bass-as-root method works identically on minor, diminished, and augmented upper triads, not just major (only major triads are catalogued below) — and generalizes to any 4-note upper chord over a bass note too (see below).
slash-chords--the-interpretation-method.lede: Take the bass note as the root, whether or not it's actually a tone of the upper triad.

slash-chords--all-twelve-major-triads-ov.title: All twelve major triads over a C bass note
slash-chords--all-twelve-major-triads-ov.html:
Worked chromatically from Jens Larsen's lesson — every possible major triad stacked over the same static C bass, analyzed by the method above:

Upper triad / C bass Notes relative to C Reads as Notes
C/C 1-3-5 C major Bass note is the root — just a plain C chord, no slash needed
B/C ♭3(enh. D♯), ♭5(enh. F♯), maj7 C diminished with a major 7 Sounds like a sus4-diminished suspension device — a "2-5-1" where the diminished chord suspends the I. See Diminished Chords
Bb/C ♭7, 9, 11 C7sus4(9) Same voicing as the classic textbook slash-chord example (B♭ triad/C bass)
A/C maj3, ♭9, 13 C7(♭9, 13) — "diminished harmony" flavor Ambiguous ♭7-vs-maj7 chord in isolation; in practice almost always heard as dominant
Ab/C ♭3(enh.), 5, root Ab major, 1st inversion C is already a chord tone (the 3rd of Ab) — not a new chord, just an inversion
G/C 9, 5, maj7 C major-7-type, rootless (Cmaj9 no 3rd) No 3rd present so quality is technically ambiguous, but reads as major in most contexts — this is Jens's own go-to voicing for a Cmaj7 sound
Gb/C ♭9, ♭5(♯11), ♭7 C7(♭9, ♭5) — dissonant, wants to resolve Ambiguous major/minor in isolation, clearly a tension chord in context
F/C 5, root, 3rd F major, 2nd inversion C is the 5th of F — not a new chord, just an inversion
E/C maj3, ♯5, maj7 Cmaj7♯5
Eb/C ♭3, 5, ♭7 C minor 7 Recognize this one on sight — it's just Cm7 spelled as a slash chord
D/C 9, ♯11/♭5, 13 Ambiguous: Cmaj7♯11 (lydian) or C7♯11 (lydian dominant) No 3rd, no 7th present — context alone decides which reading applies
Db/C ♭9, ♯4/sus4, ♭13 C7sus(♭9, ♭13) — "phrygian" sound Heard as a susb9/phrygian-dominant color

chord-naming-by-context.title: Chord Naming by Context
chord-naming-by-context.html:
The same notes can have different names depending on the tonal center you're in. This is where slash chords and inversion analysis matter.

Example: E, G, B, C

These four notes are a Cmaj7 chord — C, E, G, B reordered with E in the bass.

Cmaj7 Inversions
Inversion Notes Feel
Root position C, E, G, B Grounded home base
1st inversion E, G, B, C Lighter, open — E in bass
2nd inversion G, B, C, E Tension, common as passing chord
3rd inversion B, C, E, G Most unstable — half-step B→C pulls to resolve
Same notes, different tonal center
Context Name
Key of C Cmaj7 (1st inversion)
E as tonal center Cmaj7/E or Em(add♭6)
Jazz/modal Could read as Asus or Am9 depending on surrounding chords

Key principle: Chord quality is determined by the actual intervals, not the roman numeral case. An uppercase or lowercase numeral signals position/function — the stacked intervals determine major/minor/dominant.
chord-naming-by-context.lede: The same notes can have different names depending on the tonal center you're in. This is where slash chords and inversion analysis matter.

chord-voicings--chord-vs-voicing-vs-shap.title: Chord vs. voicing vs. shape
chord-voicings--chord-vs-voicing-vs-shap.html:
Three genuinely separate things, named explicitly by Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) but implicit in every section of this page: a chord is the abstract pitch content — "C major" means C-E-G, any order, any octave, no fretboard involved yet. A voicing is the specific order and interval spacing those notes are arranged in — root-3rd-5th stacked as close together as possible is a different voicing from 3rd-5th-root-with-the-root-an-octave-up, even though both are still "C major." A shape is the specific physical fretboard fingering used to realize a given voicing — the same voicing can be fingered as an open-position shape, a shape at the 5th fret, or a shape rooted off a different string, all genuinely different shapes playing the identical voicing; a piano player can play that same voicing with zero relationship to any guitar shape at all. Slide a whole shape up or down the neck by a fret and the voicing stays identical while the chord it's voicing changes. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Chord voicings guitar lesson - Unlimited Chord Options!

How to move between them — octave-shift voicing discovery. Take a known chord shape, move one note up or down an octave (to another instance of the same pitch elsewhere on the neck), and if that lands two notes on the same string, cascade the fix by moving the newly-colliding note to its own nearest octave too. This is the concrete mechanism behind this page's close-position/open-position distinction below — a close voicing becomes an open one exactly by moving an interior note up an octave and leaving a gap. Full method, the collision-resolution mechanic, and four worked chord examples (C major, A major, B7, D minor 7) with three song ties → Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery.

chord-voicings--which-notes-actually-mat.title: Which notes actually matter
chord-voicings--which-notes-actually-mat.html:
For a four-note chord you have six strings and two hands. Something has to go. The priority order:

  1. The 3rd and the 7th — the guide tones. These define quality and function: 3rd says major or minor, 7th says dominant or major-7th. Lose either and the chord stops being itself. Everything else is optional.
  2. The extension you actually want to hear — the 9th, 13th, ♯11, ♭9, whatever the colour of the moment is.
  3. The root — droppable. In a band the bass has it. Dropping it is what makes a rootless voicing, and it frees a finger for colour.
  4. The 5th — the first thing to go, almost always. It adds nothing to identity. (Exception: an altered 5th — ♭5 or ♯5 — is a colour tone, not a 5th, and stays.)

Shell voicing = root + 3rd + 7th only. Three notes, unambiguous, works anywhere, and it's the fastest way to comp through a tune you don't know. Rootless = 3rd + 7th + extensions. Guide-tone comping — playing only 3rds and 7ths through the changes — is the standard first exercise, and it's worth doing on its own before adding anything.

Concrete way to build a rootless voicing without recalculating from a rule table: replace the root with the diatonic neighbor tone a whole step away — the 9th above, or the 7th below. Both destinations are notes you probably want to hear anyway (the 9th is a colour extension; the 7th turns a triad into a 7th-chord voicing), so the swap does double duty. Worked examples: an F major triad with its root replaced by the major 7th (whole step below) → a rootless F major 7 — and the resulting shape is physically identical to an A minor triad, the same Fmaj7/Am relationship Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords derives from the rule table; a G7, first inversion with its (open-string) root replaced by the 9th (whole step above) → the shape becomes a half-diminished chord shape in root position, reread as a rootless G9. Stacks with this page's own "the 5th is the first thing to go" rule: take that rootless G9 (3-♭7-9-5) and replace its 5th with the 13th (another whole step up) for a rootless G13 (3-♭7-9-13, no root, no 5th) — playable an octave up on the top four strings too. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

Pass's book demonstrates this constantly without naming it: E B D G printed under a diagram is a Cmaj9 with no C in it — 3rd, 7th, 9th, 5th.
chord-voicings--which-notes-actually-mat.lede: For a four-note chord you have six strings and two hands. Something has to go. The priority order:

chord-voicings--the-named-voicing-famili.title: The named voicing families
chord-voicings--the-named-voicing-famili.html:
Family What it is Sounds like
Close All notes inside one octave Dense, cluttered on guitar, mostly impractical
Drop 2 Take a close voicing, move the 2nd-highest note down an octave The workhorse. Sits on strings 5-4-3-2 (warm) or 4-3-2-1 (bright)
Drop 3 Move the 3rd-highest down an octave Wider, bass note + a gap. Strings 6-4-3-2
Shell Root, 3rd, 7th Lean, unambiguous, leaves room
Rootless 3rd, 7th, extensions The bass has the root; you have the colour
Quartal Stacked 4ths Modal, ambiguous, modern — not in the Pass book (fretboard shapes on Quartal Chord Voicings)

Drop 2 is the one worth systematising first: it's the most common jazz-guitar voicing family and its four inversions across two string sets covers most comping situations.

breaking-up-voicings--the-core-method.title: The core method
breaking-up-voicings--the-core-method.html:
Take any known chord voicing — worked here on a C major 7 drop-2 voicing rooted on the A string (see Chord Voicings for the drop-2 family) — and instead of always striking all four notes at once, play subsets or orderings of them:

  • Outside notes, then inside notes (or reversed) — split the voicing into its outer pair and inner pair, play one pair then the other.
  • Every other note — skip through the voicing rather than reading it top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top.
  • Hold the top note as a pedal, play the remaining notes below it as a line — turns a static chord into a moving inner-voice line under a sustained top note, a related idea to Chord Voicings's common-tone-threading entry (Jack Ruch) but generated from breaking a single voicing apart rather than choosing extensions across a progression.

Once one drop-2 inversion is exhausted, repeat the whole process on the chord's other inversions — each inversion has its own four notes to recombine, multiplying the available material. This generalizes to any voicing family, not just drop-2 (shell, drop-3, quartal — see Chord Voicings, Quartal Chord Voicings) — and is described as especially effective on larger/denser chords, where there are more notes and therefore more combinations to draw fragments from.

quartal-chord-voicings--what-it-is.title: What it is
quartal-chord-voicings--what-it-is.html: Where a normal ("tertiary"/tertial) chord takes 1-3-5(-7) of a scale, a quartal chord takes 1-4-7(-…) — stack 4ths instead of 3rds, off any scale degree, and keep stacking as far as you want. Building through the scale of C major on the 5th-4th-3rd strings gives 3-note quartal chords; extend the stack across the middle 4 strings and you get 4-note quartal chords. Sound: open, ambiguous, "less traditional" than tertiary harmony — because a stack of 3rds names a chord quality and therefore implies a function, while a stack of 4ths states a set of notes without committing to major/minor/dominant. That's also why it reads as more dissonant/modern to the ear trained on common-practice harmony.

quartal-chord-voicings--one-shape-many-c.title: One shape, many chord identities (rootless-voicing crossover)
quartal-chord-voicings--one-shape-many-c.html:
The same 3-note quartal shape reharmonizes to a different named tertian chord depending purely on which note you're mentally treating as the root — a direct crossover with the rootless-voicing logic on Chord Voicings ("one physical shape, several harmonic identities depending on context"). Worked off one fixed 3-note quartal shape:

Treated as root Resulting chord
bottom note minor 11
next note up (4th fret in the worked example) ♭ major 7♯11
next sus4
next 6/9
next major 13
next 7sus4 (or minor 11)
next sus2
next 6/9 (an octave/register up from the earlier one)

The physical grip never changes — only the ear's assumption about which note is the root does. Stringing several of these root-reinterpretations together in sequence reads as a legitimate ambiguous-but-coherent chord progression, and is exactly the quality that makes quartal shapes so at-home in a modal context: the chord never insists on one specific identity.

octave-shift-voicing-discovery--the-meth.title: The method
octave-shift-voicing-discovery--the-meth.html:
1. Start from a chord shape you already know — root position is the natural starting point since it's usually the one already memorized.
  2. Pick one note in the chord and move it up or down an octave, using the octave/unison-shape skill above to find where that same pitch lands elsewhere on the neck.
  3. If the moved note now collides with another note already on that string (you can't play two notes on one string at once), move the colliding note to its own nearest available octave too — cascading as many times as needed until every note in the chord has a distinct playable string.
  4. Repeat with a different note, or repeat the whole cycle from the new shape, treating each result as a fresh starting point for the next move.
  5. Some results will be physically unplayable or just bad — that's a normal, expected outcome of moving things around blind, not a sign the method is broken. Discard and try a different note.

There's no fixed order, no target voicing, and no guarantee of what you'll land on — that's the point. Jared frames it explicitly against his own more "systematic and heavy duty" prior lessons (memorize a fixed set of shapes in a set order): this is loose, playful, puzzle-solving exploration, closer to noodling with intent than a drill. "If teaching you a chord by giving you a chord shape diagram is giving you a fish, this lesson is teaching you how to fish."
octave-shift-voicing-discovery--the-meth.lede: Start from a chord shape you already know — root position is the natural starting point since it's usually the one already memorized.

octave-shift-voicing-discovery--collisio.title: Collision-resolution mechanic, generalized
octave-shift-voicing-discovery--collisio.html: The one piece of real mechanical rigor inside an otherwise loose method: whenever an octave shift lands two notes on the same string, the fix is always the same — move the newly-colliding note (not the one you were originally moving) to its own nearest available octave, and repeat if that triggers another collision. This cascading fix is what turns "randomly move notes around" into something that reliably terminates in a playable four-or-fewer-note voicing rather than a dead end.

major-triads-across-the-fretboard-string.title: Major Triads Across the Fretboard (String-Group Inversions)
major-triads-across-the-fretboard-string.html: Learn one major triad's three inversions (root-position, 1st inversion, 2nd inversion) on each of the four 3-string groups, so any major chord is playable from at least a dozen fretboard locations rather than one memorized open-position shape. Companion to Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude and Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude (composed voice-leading studies) — this page is the raw shape-inventory those etudes assume, plus the practical spacing payoff for riff-writing.

multifunctional-voicings--the-core-mecha.title: The core mechanism
multifunctional-voicings--the-core-mecha.html: Take a single chord-voicing shape (any of the standard families — min7♭5, half-diminished, maj7♯5, dominant 9 — see Chord Voicings) and play it starting from a different chord tone of the target chord each time. The shape's fingering never changes; only which note you're mentally treating as the root shifts — same underlying logic as Chord Voicings's rootless-voicing reinterpretation and Quartal Chord Voicings's root-reassignment table, but the destination here is always "which dominant/target chord does this shape become," not just "which chord symbol could this be."

multifunctional-voicings--three-worked-s.title: Three worked shapes, three functions each
multifunctional-voicings--three-worked-s.html:
1. A minor7♭5 shape → three separate roles, from Galbraith's Tangerine etude (a ii-V-I comping line):

  • Played off its own root → a plain minor 7♭5 (e.g. F m7♭5).
  • Played off the ♭7 of a dominant chord → a highly altered voicing for that dominant (worked example: the F m7♭5 shape used under a G7, since F is G7's ♭7 — reads as G7alt).
  • Played off the 3rd of a dominant chord → a dominant 9 voicing (general starting point — stated as a recurring move throughout the book, not tied to one specific root in the source).

2. A half-diminished shape → root, then altered-dominant ♭7 role, resolving to I:

  • Played off its own root → a plain half-diminished chord.
  • Played off the ♭7 of the dominant → an altered voicing for that dominant (worked example: played from A♭, the ♭7 of B♭7, to produce a B♭7-altered sound) — then resolves to the I chord. This is the same "shape reused off the ♭7 of the V chord" move as shape 1's second function, confirming it as a repeatable rule for any min7♭5/half-diminished-family shape, not a one-off.

3. An A♭ major7♯5 shape → root role, then altered-dominant 3rd role:

  • Played off its own root → a plain maj7♯5 chord.
  • Played off the 3rd of a dominant chord → another altered-dominant color (worked in a 2-5-1 line: the same shape used off the 3rd of the V7 to color it altered before resolving).
multifunctional-voicings--three-worked-s.lede: 1. A minor7♭5 shape → three separate roles, from Galbraith's Tangerine etude (a ii-V-I comping line):

voice-leading--the-algorithm.title: The algorithm
voice-leading--the-algorithm.html:
1. Find the note(s) shared between the current chord and the next chord in the progression — a note common to both.
  2. Keep that shared note exactly where it is (don't move it at all) — it becomes the pivot the hand/voicing rotates around.
  3. Move the remaining notes to the nearest available note of the next chord — by the smallest possible interval, usually a step, not a leap.
  4. Repeat chord-to-chord through the whole progression.

You don't need to identify which inversion results (root position, first inversion, etc.) to do this — the method is entirely about minimizing motion between chords, not about naming the resulting voicing. Worked example: Am → F, sharing the note C — keep C fixed, move A→A (already shared) note stays, and the remaining note moves by step (E→F) rather than leaping down to the next chord's root.
voice-leading--the-algorithm.lede: Find the note(s) shared between the current chord and the next chord in the progression — a note common to both.

voice-leading--the-bass-exception.title: The bass exception
voice-leading--the-bass-exception.html: The lowest voice in an arrangement (the piano left hand, a bass part) is usually NOT voice-led — it stays on each chord's actual root note throughout, even while the upper voices are inverted and voice-led above it. Voice-leading the bass too would smooth out the bass motion but lose the harmonic clarity and character the root-motion bassline provides — a full arrangement's overall chord identity (root position vs. inversion) is usually judged from the bass note regardless of how the upper voices are voiced.

spread-triad-voice-leading-etude--spread.title: Spread triad, defined
spread-triad-voice-leading-etude--spread.html: A close-position triad stacks its three notes on adjacent strings/scale-tones (e.g. D minor root position: root-♭3-5 = D-F-A). A spread (a.k.a. "open position voicing") triad takes that same three-note chord and moves the middle note up an octave, reordering the stack to 1-5-♭3 — same notes, same chord, wider interval spacing with a string skip in the middle, an "open," harp-like sound. Worked example: D minor close position frets pinky-5th-fret/A-string (root), middle-finger-3rd-fret/D-string (♭3), index-2nd-fret/G-string (5th); moving the middle note (the ♭3, on the D string) up an octave produces the spread voicing 1-5-♭3. Terminology trap: "open position" in this sense is music-theory/composition jargon for spread voicing — it has nothing to do with the guitar-specific meaning of "open position" (playing near the nut using open strings). Same term, two unrelated meanings; don't conflate them.

spread-triad-voice-leading-etude--the-co.title: The construction rule (this is the whole etude)
spread-triad-voice-leading-etude--the-co.html:
1. Start on the tonic triad (worked in C major) in a spread voicing, high up the neck.
  2. Chain through the diatonic triads a third at a time: C → E minor → G major → B diminished → D minor → F major → A minor → back to C — the full seven diatonic triads of the key, taken in ascending-third order, repeating the cycle.
  3. Every chord change moves exactly one note of the three-note spread voicing, by a half step or a whole step — never more than one voice moves, never more than a step. Which of the three voices (top/middle/bottom of the spread shape) moves next rotates through the voicing in a repeating sequence as the chain proceeds.
  4. The whole etude is one continuous descent down the fretboard, chord by chord, using the single-voice-move rule to always land on the closest spread voicing of the next chord in the third-chain, until it reaches the lowest playable position on the neck.
  5. Close with a real cadence, not another triad: the etude ends G7 → C — the only point where an actual dominant-7th chord (not a bare triad) appears, a deliberate "how to land a triad study" move rather than just fading out on another spread triad.
  6. Coverage is a side effect, not a separate drill: because the third-chain touches every diatonic triad of the key, and the closest-voicing rule forces a different inversion each time a given triad quality recurs, the etude ends up covering every diatonic triad of the key in every one of its inversions — full spread-triad vocabulary for the key, generated by the voice-leading rule alone.
spread-triad-voice-leading-etude--the-co.lede: Start on the tonic triad (worked in C major) in a spread voicing, high up the neck.

close-position-triad-voice-leading-etude.title: Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude

A composed practice etude for internalizing close-position triad inversions across the diatonic key of C major, by the same "move exactly one note, exactly one half/whole step, every chord change" voice-leading rule as Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude — but worked on ordinary close-position triad shapes on strings 2-3-4 (B-G-D) instead of spread/open voicings, and walking up the fretboard rather than down. Labeled "#1"/"ASCENDING" by its author because it's the first half of a planned two-part series — a "part two" descending version is announced but not yet published (nothing to extract from it yet). jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.note: Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline
jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.title: The core tip: one repeatable rhythmic motif, not constant variety
jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.html:
Pick a simple, single rhythmic idea — a specific pair or handful of beats where the chord lands — and repeat it consistently before reaching for anything fancier. A demonstrated starting motif: hit on the "and" of beat 1, and on beat 3. Repetition is what makes comping read as cohesive and intentional; constantly reinventing the rhythm bar-to-bar reads as scattered, even if each individual choice is "correct." (General starting point — pick any two-hit-per-bar pattern and hold it for a full pass through the form before varying.)

Sequencing matters: lock the motif in first, then introduce variation or departures from it. A deliberate detour away from the motif, followed by a return to it, reads as "grounded" — the return only lands because the motif was established as the baseline first. This mirrors the "overuse a device to internalize it, then use it tastefully" practice logic already documented on Chord-Tone Soloing.

jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.note: Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline
jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.title: Bonus: walking bassline with the chords
jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.html:
Layer a moving bass note under the same comping rhythm:

  • Beats 1 and 3: play the current chord's root as the bass note.
  • Beats 2 and 4: pass toward the next chord's root with a chromatic or scale-step approach note — a half step below, a half step above, or a whole step above the target. Which approach direction sounds best depends on the specific interval between the two roots; try more than one.
  • Works best on progressions where chords change every two beats — there's a clean "root, approach-note, new root, approach-note" cycle available. On a chord that lasts a full bar, apply the same beats-1-and-3 root logic "passing to itself" (root, [passing tone], root, approach-to-next).
  • Once the bassline is solid, the chord voicing itself can be freed from a fixed grid — e.g. moved to beat 1 + the "and" of beat 3 instead of a rigid every-beat pattern — for a less mechanical feel. Same "vary only after the base pattern is locked" sequencing as the primary motif tip above.

comping-fills--the-core-tip-fills-only-h.title: The core tip: fills only happen when the soloist rests
comping-fills--the-core-tip-fills-only-h.html: Joe Pass never fills over the top of a vocalist or soloist who's still singing/playing — a fill only enters the texture when there's genuine space, i.e. call-and-response spacing rather than decoration layered underneath an active melody. Before reaching for a fill, check: is anyone else actually playing right now? If yes, hold the comp; if the space is genuinely open, that's the cue.

comping-fills--a-fill-s-job-is-to-connec.title: A fill's job is to connect, not decorate
comping-fills--a-fill-s-job-is-to-connec.html: Quoted directly from Pass himself: a fill has "gotta go... with the melody... to the next bar." A fill that just sits on top of the current chord and doesn't lead anywhere is doing it wrong, by Pass's own framing — the fill's function is to move the music forward to the next chord or the next section of the form, the same forward-motion logic that drives a bebop line. (This reframes a fill as a harmonic/structural device, not a purely melodic flourish — treat "where does this fill lead" as the first design question, before "what notes sound good here.")

layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.note: Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads
layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.title: The core idea: one triad vocabulary, four string groupings, three positions
layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.html:
A four-chord progression — worked in A major – E major – F♯ minor – D major (I–V–vi–IV in A) — gets played as three different guitar parts, and all three are built from the same triad shapes, just relocated:

Part String group Position Role
1 — Bed D, G, B strings One position, jumps to a second higher position for the verse Arpeggiated harmonic floor
2 — Backbeat Top three strings Two positions (a "close-by" pair), used across sections for a flavor change R&B accent, rhythmic punctuation
3 — Melody Top three / top two strings Built from Parts 1–2's own shapes plus two double-stop devices Melodic double-stop line

The stated general lesson: the same handful of chords lives in four different string groupings and three different neck positions, and once those shapes are under your fingers you can freely recombine them — this is the arranging equivalent of Triads as a Fretboard Map's "one triad, three zones" soloing method.

layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.note: Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads
layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.title: Why triads specifically: they're small on purpose
layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.html: Closed triad shapes (root-3rd-5th, no doubled notes, no full six-string chords) are deliberately lean — "these little morsels... don't take up too much space, don't fill up too much sound." That leanness is why three of them can stack on top of each other in a mix without collapsing into noise — the same "which notes to leave out" economy Chord Voicings argues for on the jazz-comping side, applied here for a production reason (headroom to layer) rather than a voice-leading one.

reading-and-interpreting-a-jazz-lead-she.note: Reading and Interpreting a Jazz Lead Sheet
reading-and-interpreting-a-jazz-lead-she.title: The core method
reading-and-interpreting-a-jazz-lead-she.html:
1. Establish the form first, before looking at a single chord. Most standards played chorus-only run some flavor of 32 bars in one of two shapes: AABA (one 8-bar idea repeated three times around a contrasting 8-bar bridge) or ABAC (effectively two 16-bar halves). Read it mechanically off the page — a repeat sign after 8 bars with two different endings signals AABA even when the book doesn't spell it out. Knowing the shape tells you how much of the chart is actually new material — an AABA tune with an 8-bar A and 8-bar bridge is often only 16 bars of distinct harmony, not 32, once repeats are accounted for. A tag (extra bars appended to the last A so the tune can close) is common and worth spotting early. → Musical Form, Rhythm Changes
  2. Use the form to predict, not just describe. The stated goal is being able to expect how a passage will sound before you play it, rather than reacting cold to an unfamiliar chord symbol. A concrete, reusable rule: in an AABA tune where the first chord is the tonic, the last two bars of each A are very likely (~90%) some kind of turnaround — meaning a chunk of the chart is already "solved" by pattern-matching before it's been individually analyzed. → Turnarounds
  3. Reduce the chart to recurring, nameable devices — and generalize across tunes, not just within one. Chunk multi-chord passages into single concepts: a secondary ii–V into the IV chord reduces to "the IV chord," a full turnaround reduces to "a turnaround," a ♯4-diminished cadence reduces to "the sharp-4 sound." The real payoff is recognizing the same device recurring across different standards — once one instance is internalized, a new tune reusing it is already half-analyzed rather than a cold read. Two devices worth having pattern-matched on sight: the ♯4-diminished cadence resolving to I (also documented in "Embraceable You" and "You Do Something to Me") → Diminished Chords; and turning a major chord into its own parallel minor to pivot key, the same modulation trick used in "How High the Moon," "Afternoon in Paris," and "Solar." → Modulation (Key Change), Parallel Minor
  4. Treat a printed real-book harmonization as a starting point, not gospel. When a chord clashes visibly with the melody — a common failure mode in stock tag harmonizations especially — swapping in a better-fitting substitution is normal, expected practice among players who actually know the tune, not a liberty that needs permission. Judge it against the melody, not the page.
  5. Read the melody just well enough to comp without clashing — not full sight-singing. Lead sheets are concert pitch; account for your instrument's actual sounding register before judging where the melody sits. You usually don't need to play the melody note-for-note if someone else is stating the head, but you do need a working sense of where it sits so your own voicings don't land a half-step from a long melody note. Concrete clash rule: check which chord tone/extension the melody is actually voicing at that moment, and don't stack your own voicing a half-step away from it unless the clash is a deliberate effect (e.g., an 11th in the melody against a chord voicing that includes the natural 4th/11th right next to it; a 9th sitting above a chromatically adjacent chord tone reads fine, the same interval with the 9th underneath does not). → Guide Tones, Chord Voicings
  6. Comp in service of the soloist, not on a fixed density plan. Play less when the soloist is busy, get more active in the gaps where they lay out. Comping can be stripped down to almost nothing (root motion, or chords only on strong beats) and still read as complete — density is a choice made in response to what's happening, not an obligation to fill every bar. → Ensemble Listening and Comping Restraint
  7. Solo by reducing to function, not by decoding chord-by-chord. Apply the same chunking used for reading: instead of tracking every chord symbol individually, identify the note you're moving from and the note you're targeting for a passage, and let that arc drive the line. Know which chord in a reduced unit is actually structurally important — in a turnaround built on a I–vi–ii–V-family shape, the tonic-substitute chord (not the dominant that follows it) is often the one actually worth targeting; collapsing the whole unit down to "just play off the final V7" loses that. Reharmonizing mid-solo (e.g., substituting a plain minor-7–dominant-7 pair for the expected half-diminished–altered-dominant pair, deliberately choosing the more surprising color) is legitimate once the underlying function is understood — it's a controlled departure from a known baseline, not guesswork.
  8. Use chord-scale theory as a fast first guess, not the final answer. Matching one scale to one chord symbol ("it's a minor 7, play Dorian") gets you in the ballpark but ignores that a chord's actual character depends on the surrounding harmony and key — a minor 7 chord isn't always the same kind of minor-7 sound in context. Refine the first guess with the functional/contextual read from steps 2–3 rather than trusting the chord symbol in isolation. → Scale Modes Reference

chord-melody-arranging--the-core-idea-re.title: The core idea: renumber off the chord, not the key
chord-melody-arranging--the-core-idea-re.html: Read every melody note as a scale degree of whichever chord is sounding right now, not as a scale degree of the parent key. This is Diatonic Modes's "relative approach" (same 7 notes, different tonic) applied live, beat to beat: the same physical note can be "2 of C" while a C chord is under it, then "4 of D" a beat later once the harmony moves to Dm — same pitch, different functional meaning, different go-to shape to reach for. Thinking "1-2 of the C scale" when a Dm chord (the ii chord) is actually sounding hides the real relationship; thinking "4-5 of the current chord's root" reveals it, and it's that revealed relationship that tells you which memorized shape fits.

chord-melody-arranging--physical-executi.title: Physical execution: don't harmonize every note
chord-melody-arranging--physical-executi.html: The single highest-leverage habit for actually playing a chord melody smoothly (as opposed to arranging it on paper) is choosing, note by note, when to play a full chord shape and when to just play the single melody note and let the previous harmony (or nothing) carry through. This is a deliberate artistic choice, re-decidable every time you play the piece — not a rule to solve once. Two real payoffs, not just one: it's physically easier (fewer full-hand jumps between shapes, since you're often landing the melody note alone with one finger before adding the rest) and it sounds better (space between chord grabs reads as phrasing rather than a wall of block chords; even solo/unaccompanied, mostly-single-notes-with-occasional-chords still sounds fully harmonized). A concrete glide move for a sustained/repeated melody note across a chord change: play the first chord shape, glide the fretting finger (often the 4th) down to the next melody note while it holds, sound that note alone, then land the next full chord shape from the same position — smoother than jumping cold into the next shape. Demonstrated across "What Is This Thing Called Love" with rootless dim7-as-C7♭9 and rootless G7-altered voicings (guide-tones-non-optional / root-and-extension-interchangeable logic — see Guide Tones, Diminished Chords, Altered Chords) and a one-note half-step voice-leading link between a half-diminished ii shape and its rootless V7♭9, described as a "piano left-hand comping" effect. → Chord Melody Arranging is Miserable (Until You Do It This Way) — Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared, Chord Melody Arranging is Miserable (Until You Do It This Way)

guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.note: Guide-Tone Diads for Blues Rhythm Guitar
guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.title: The core shape: 3rd + ♭7, nothing else
guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.html:
A dominant 7 chord is root-3rd-5th-♭7, but only the 3rd and ♭7 determine the chord's quality (major/minor/dominant) — change just the 3rd and the chord's whole character flips; change just the ♭7 to a major 7 and it becomes a maj7 sound. In a band context with a bass player covering the root, the guitar only needs those two notes to outline the chord.

Worked in a 12-bar blues in A (A7-D7-E7):

  • A7: the two notes just outside the bar-chord shape — ♭7 = G, major 3rd = C♯.
  • D7 (IV): the identical two-note shape slides down a half step from the A7 grip — now sounding D7's 3rd (F♯) and ♭7 (C).
  • E7 (V): the identical shape slides up a half step from the A7 grip — now sounding E7's 3rd and ♭7.
  • The whole I-IV-V cycle uses one movable shape, relocated by half steps only — no new grip to learn per chord, just A7 → down ½ step → D7 → up ½ step → A7 → up ½ step → E7 → down ½ step → D7 → A7.

guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.note: Guide-Tone Diads for Blues Rhythm Guitar
guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.title: Drill — the video's own build order
guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.html:
1. Bare guide-tone diads only — 3rd+♭7 shape through the full 12-bar A7-D7-E7 form, moving by half steps, no embellishment. Lock this in first against a backing track.
  2. Add the sus4 slide-and-raise on top of step 1, across all three chords (remembering the 3rd's position flips between chords). Optionally add the D-triad-hammer-on variant on the A chord.
  3. Add the high/low register alternation — top-two-string root/5th chord stab against the low guide-tone diad, thumb-wrapped bass notes underneath. Swap in the full D9 grip (with raised-4th embellishment) over the IV chord.
  4. Play the full assembled part through the whole form against a backing track, listening for lock with the drums.
  5. Learn the second (5th + major 3rd) diad vocabulary separately, up around the 9th/10th fret — down a string set for IV, up a whole step for V — as an alternate higher-register part.
  6. Free-application stage: apply the guide-tone-diad-plus-embellishment approach to other progressions and genres by ear — listen to the track and the other musicians in the room to find the rhythmic spaces where a small fragment fits, rather than reusing this exact arrangement verbatim.

(General starting-point structuring of the 6-step order — the video demonstrates each layer in sequence but the explicit "practice it built up this way" framing is the standard way to internalize a layered comping part like this.)

jazz-harmony--the-four-ideas-the-whole-s.title: The four ideas the whole subject runs on
jazz-harmony--the-four-ideas-the-whole-s.html:
Jazz harmony looks complicated and is mostly four ideas applied repeatedly.

1. Sevenths are the baseline, not an extension. In common-practice harmony a triad is the default and a seventh is a colour. In jazz the seventh is the default — a "C chord" means Cmaj7 or C6 unless something says otherwise. Every rule below assumes four-note chords. → Seventh Chords

2. The ii–V–I is the sentence. Nearly all standard-repertoire harmony is ii–V–I units, chained, transposed and disguised. Learn to see them and most lead sheets stop looking arbitrary. → The ii-V-I

3. Any chord can be replaced by another sharing its function. Substitution is the engine of variety, and it follows rules rather than taste. → Chord Substitution

4. The 3rd and the 7th carry the harmony; everything else is colour. Two notes are enough to state a chord's identity and to voice-lead a whole progression. → Guide Tones

Get those four and the rest — reharmonization, bebop line construction, modal playing — are applications.

jazz-harmony--numerals-in-jazz-vs-the-cl.title: Numerals in jazz vs. the classical style used elsewhere here
jazz-harmony--numerals-in-jazz-vs-the-cl.html:
Worth flagging because the vault mixes them and it causes real confusion.

  • Classical style (used in most of this vault): case shows quality. ii is minor, V is major, vii° is diminished. See Chord Naming by Context.
  • Jazz/Berklee style: always uppercase, quality shown by suffix. IIm7, V7, Imaj7, ♭VII7.

Both name the same chords. Jazz style wins on lead sheets because chord qualities get altered constantly and case stops being able to carry the information — a V7♯9♭13 has no lowercase equivalent.

This vault uses classical style in theory notes and jazz style when quoting a jazz source. Intervals decide quality, not numeral case.

the-ii-v-i--the-major-version.title: The major version
the-ii-v-i--the-major-version.html:
In C major: Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7.

  • Dm7 = D F A C — subdominant function, the setup
  • G7 = G B D F — dominant function, the tension
  • Cmaj7 = C E G B — tonic, the resolution

Why these three and not others: it's the circle of fifths in miniature. D → G → C, each root falling a fifth. Root motion down a fifth is the strongest progression in tonal music, and ii–V–I stacks two of them back to back. → Circle of Fifths

The voice leading is the other half of the reason. Between Dm7 and G7, two notes stay put and two move by a step. Between G7 and Cmaj7, the tritone resolves: G7's B and F are a tritone apart, B pulls up to C and F pulls down to E. That's Guide Tones, and it's why the progression feels inevitable rather than merely conventional.
the-ii-v-i--the-major-version.lede: In C major: Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7.

the-ii-v-i--the-minor-version.title: The minor version
the-ii-v-i--the-minor-version.html:
In C minor: Dm7♭5 → G7♭9 → Cm7 (or Cm6, or CmMaj7).

Three differences from the major, all forced by the minor scale:

  • ii becomes half-diminished. Dm7♭5 = D F A♭ C. The ♭5 is simply the 6th degree of C natural minor.
  • V keeps its major 3rd but usually gains a ♭9. G7♭9 borrows from harmonic minor — the raised leading tone is what makes it a functioning dominant at all, and the ♭9 (A♭) is the minor 6th of the key.
  • The tonic is ambiguous on purpose. Cm7, Cm6 and CmMaj7 are all in use and pick different flavours. Cm7 is the modal/pop choice; CmMaj7 is the classical-sounding one.
the-ii-v-i--the-minor-version.lede: In C minor: Dm7♭5 → G7♭9 → Cm7 (or Cm6, or CmMaj7).

the-ii-v-i--chains-the-thing-that-makes-.title: Chains — the thing that makes it worth learning
the-ii-v-i--chains-the-thing-that-makes-.html:
ii–V–I units chain, and standards are largely built by chaining them through different keys. The most common device: make the I of one unit into the ii of the next, or drop a ii–V in front of any chord you want to arrive at.

  • Descending in whole steps: | Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 | Cm7 F7 | B♭maj7 | — a ii–V–I in C, then one in B♭.
  • Turnaround chains: | Cmaj7 A7 | Dm7 G7 | — the A7 is a secondary dominant setting up Dm7. → Secondary Dominants · Turnarounds

Reading tip that pays for itself: scan a lead sheet for any m7 chord followed by a dominant 7th a fourth above it. That's a ii–V, and whatever follows is the intended I — even when the I never actually arrives.
the-ii-v-i--chains-the-thing-that-makes-.lede: ii–V–I units chain, and standards are largely built by chaining them through different keys. The most common device: make the I of one unit into the ii of…

the-ii-v-i--when-the-i-doesn-t-arrive.title: When the I doesn't arrive
the-ii-v-i--when-the-i-doesn-t-arrive.html:
Two very common cases, both worth recognising rather than mis-analysing:

  • The deceptive move — ii–V goes somewhere other than I, usually vi or ♭VI. Dm7 G7 Am7 instead of Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.
  • The unresolved ii–V — a ii–V that just moves to the next ii–V without resolving at all. Extremely common in bebop heads and the reason a chart can look like it changes key every two bars when it doesn't.
the-ii-v-i--when-the-i-doesn-t-arrive.lede: Two very common cases, both worth recognising rather than mis-analysing:

the-ii-v-i--practical-use-outside-jazz.title: Practical use outside jazz
the-ii-v-i--practical-use-outside-jazz.html:
The ii–V–I is why so much neo-soul and jazzy hip hop sounds the way it does. Three ways it shows up in modern writing:

  • As the whole loop. Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 Cmaj7 over four bars is a complete, endlessly loopable progression.
  • As the turnaround only. Straight-ahead pop verse, then a ii–V at the end of the section to push back to the top.
  • Stripped to guide tones. Play only the 3rds and 7ths and the progression still reads — which is how it survives in arrangements with almost no chordal instrument. → Guide Tones
the-ii-v-i--practical-use-outside-jazz.lede: The ii–V–I is why so much neo-soul and jazzy hip hop sounds the way it does. Three ways it shows up in modern writing:

guide-tones--why-the-3rd-and-the-7th.title: Why the 3rd and the 7th
guide-tones--why-the-3rd-and-the-7th.html:
Take the four chord types you meet most:

Chord Notes 3rd 7th What the pair tells you
Cmaj7 C E G B E B major 3rd + major 7th → major
C7 C E G B♭ E B♭ major 3rd + minor 7th → dominant
Cm7 C E♭ G B♭ E♭ B♭ minor 3rd + minor 7th → minor
Cm7♭5 C E♭ G♭ B♭ E♭ B♭ needs the ♭5 too — the exception

The root tells you nothing about quality. The 5th tells you almost nothing — it's the first note dropped from a voicing precisely because it's the least informative. The 3rd says major or minor; the 7th says major, dominant or minor. Together they name the chord.

That's why a bass player and a horn can imply a full progression with no chordal instrument present at all.
guide-tones--why-the-3rd-and-the-7th.lede: Take the four chord types you meet most:

guide-tones--guide-tones-move-by-step-th.title: Guide tones move by step — that's the whole trick
guide-tones--guide-tones-move-by-step-th.html:
Run the guide tones through a ii–V–I in C:

Chord 3rd 7th
Dm7 F C
G7 B F
Cmaj7 E B

Follow one line: C → B → B. Follow the other: F → F → E.

Nothing leaps. One voice holds while the other moves a half-step, then they swap. The 7th of each chord becomes the 3rd of the next — that's not a coincidence, it's what root motion by fifths does, and it's the mechanical reason ii–V–I sounds inevitable. → The ii-V-I
guide-tones--guide-tones-move-by-step-th.lede: Run the guide tones through a ii–V–I in C:

guide-tones--shell-voicings.title: Shell voicings
guide-tones--shell-voicings.html:
Play only the guide tones plus a root and you have a shell voicing — three notes, no 5th, no extensions:

  • Root – 3rd – 7th, or
  • Root – 7th – 3rd (7th below the 3rd; usually the better-sounding of the two)

Shells are the practical form of this idea. On guitar or piano they're easy to grab, they never sound muddy, and they leave the entire register above free for melody or for another player. On a dense arrangement they're often the right voicing rather than the simple one — a full 5-note chord under a busy vocal is usually the mistake.

Add extensions on top of a shell and you have the whole vocabulary: shell + 9th, shell + 13th. → Extended Chords · Chord Voicings
guide-tones--shell-voicings.lede: Play only the guide tones plus a root and you have a shell voicing — three notes, no 5th, no extensions:

guide-tones--using-it-to-write.title: Using it to write
guide-tones--using-it-to-write.html:
To voice-lead a progression: write out the 3rds and 7ths of every chord first, as two horizontal lines. Fix any leap larger than a step by inverting the chord or choosing a different extension. Only then decide the full voicings. This is faster than voicing chord-by-chord and it produces smoother results, because you've solved the horizontal problem before the vertical one.

To test a substitution: a substitute chord that keeps the guide-tone lines stepwise is a good one. This is the concrete test behind Chord Substitution — the tritone sub works precisely because it swaps the guide tones rather than disturbing them.

To thin an arrangement: when a mix is crowded in the mids, cutting the chordal instrument to shells frees space without losing the harmony. The 5th and the doubled root were the notes doing the crowding. → Masking and Carving

guide-tones--the-one-exception.title: The one exception
guide-tones--the-one-exception.html: Half-diminished and diminished chords need the 5th. Cm7♭5 and Cm7 have the same 3rd and 7th (E♭ and B♭); only the G♭ distinguishes them. Any voicing of a m7♭5 that drops the 5th states the wrong chord. → Diminished Chords

chord-substitution--the-governing-rule.title: The governing rule
chord-substitution--the-governing-rule.html:
Two chords can substitute for each other when they share enough tones and the same harmonic function.

Function first, tones second. A substitute that shares three notes but resolves the wrong way is a worse choice than one sharing two notes that resolves right. Functions are tonic, subdominant and dominant — see Chord Progressions § Harmonic function.
chord-substitution--the-governing-rule.lede: Function first, tones second. A substitute that shares three notes but resolves the wrong way is a worse choice than one sharing two notes that resolves ri…

chord-substitution--1-diatonic-substitut.title: 1. Diatonic substitution — chords a third apart
chord-substitution--1-diatonic-substitut.html:
Any two diatonic chords a third apart share two of their three triad tones, so they can often stand in for each other.

In C major:

Original Substitute Shared tones
C (C E G) Am (A C E) C, E
C (C E G) Em (E G B) E, G
F (F A C) Dm (D F A) F, A
G (G B D) Em (E G B) G, B

The classic application: replace I with vi or iii to keep a loop moving without changing where it sits harmonically. Cmaj7 Cmaj7 Fmaj7 G7 becomes Cmaj7 Am7 Fmaj7 G7 — the I–vi–IV–V that half of popular music runs on.

Caution: vi is the strongest I-substitute, iii the weakest. iii shares E and G with C but lacks the root and contains B, which drags it toward dominant function. Substituting iii for I at a final cadence usually sounds unresolved — which is sometimes the point.
chord-substitution--1-diatonic-substitut.lede: Any two diatonic chords a third apart share two of their three triad tones, so they can often stand in for each other.

chord-substitution--2-tritone-substituti.title: 2. Tritone substitution — the important one
chord-substitution--2-tritone-substituti.html:
Replace any dominant 7th with the dominant 7th a tritone away.

The reason it works is exact rather than approximate. Take G7 and D♭7:

  • G7 = G B D F
  • D♭7 = D♭ F A♭ C♭

The B and F of G7 are a tritone apart — that pair is what makes it a dominant chord. D♭7 contains F and C♭, and C♭ is enharmonically B. So the two chords share the same tritone, with the 3rd and 7th swapping roles: G7's 3rd (B) is D♭7's 7th (C♭), and G7's 7th (F) is D♭7's 3rd.

Same tension, same resolution, different bass note. →

What it buys you: chromatic bass motion. Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 has roots D → G → C. Substitute and you get Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7 — roots D → D♭ → C, walking down by half-step. That descending chromatic bass is one of the most recognisable sounds in jazz and neo-soul. → Chromatic Bass Lines

Rules of thumb:

  • Only substitute dominant chords. The tritone is what's being preserved, and only dominant 7ths have one.
  • The substitute is always a half-step above the target of resolution. Resolving to C? The sub is D♭7.
  • It pairs naturally with the ♯11: D♭7♯11 is the fullest-sounding version, because the ♯11 of D♭ is G — the root of the chord being replaced.
  • Substituting the V of a ii–V–I gives you the extremely common IIm7 – ♭II7 – Imaj7.
chord-substitution--2-tritone-substituti.lede: Replace any dominant 7th with the dominant 7th a tritone away.

chord-substitution--3-backdoor-substitut.title: 3. Backdoor substitution
chord-substitution--3-backdoor-substitut.html:
Approach the tonic from ♭VII7 instead of V7. In C major: Fm7 B♭7 Cmaj7 in place of Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.

B♭7 = B♭ D F A♭. It contains A♭, the ♭6 of C, which resolves down to G, and D, which is already in the tonic. It's borrowed from C minor — a plagal-flavoured, softer arrival than a real V7.

When to use it: when V7 sounds too final or too bright. The backdoor is warmer and more ambiguous, which is why it shows up constantly in gospel, soul and Steely Dan-adjacent writing. → Borrowed Chords · Parallel Minor
chord-substitution--3-backdoor-substitut.lede: Approach the tonic from ♭VII7 instead of V7. In C major: Fm7 B♭7 Cmaj7 in place of Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.

chord-substitution--4-interpolating-a-ii.title: 4. Interpolating a ii in front of any dominant
chord-substitution--4-interpolating-a-ii.html:
Any dominant 7th can be preceded by its own related ii chord — the m7 a fourth below it. This doesn't replace a chord so much as expand one.

Cmaj7 A7 Dm7 G7 becomes Cmaj7 Em7 A7 Dm7 G7 — the Em7 is A7's ii.

This is how a sparse progression becomes a dense one without changing its harmonic path at all, and it's the single most useful reharmonization move. → Reharmonization
chord-substitution--4-interpolating-a-ii.lede: Any dominant 7th can be preceded by its own related ii chord — the m7 a fourth below it. This doesn't replace a chord so much as expand one.

chord-substitution--choosing-between-the.title: Choosing between them
chord-substitution--choosing-between-the.html:
You want Reach for
Keep the loop harmonically still but add motion Diatonic sub (I → vi)
Chromatic descending bass Tritone sub
A softer, less final arrival Backdoor
More chords without changing the path Interpolate a ii
A brighter, more urgent push to a chord Secondary dominant → Secondary Dominants

The failure mode to avoid: substituting everything. Substitution reads as sophisticated against a background of plain harmony; wall-to-wall, it reads as directionless. Bowman's own framing is that substitutions must be "completely compatible" with what they replace — the test is whether the melody still fits, and a substitution that clashes with the tune is wrong no matter how good the voice leading is.

tritone-substitution--the-mechanism.title: The mechanism
tritone-substitution--the-mechanism.html:
If a progression is C – G7 – C, the tritone sub swaps G7 for D♭7 (a tritone from G): C – D♭7 – C. It still resolves convincingly because of what the two chords have in common, not what's different.

Every dominant 7th chord's tension comes from its internal tritone — G7's tritone is between F and B (the ♭7 and the 3rd). A dominant chord built a tritone away from the original root contains that exact same tritone: D♭7 also spans F and B (spelled/functioning differently, but the same two pitches). So the pull-to-resolution is fully preserved even though the bass now moves chromatically (D♭→C, a semitone) instead of by a falling fifth (G→C).

Practical effect: tritone-subbing a chain of dominants (e.g., a 3-6-2-5 turnaround, Dm7–G7–Cm7–F7) turns fifth-based root motion into a smooth, entirely chromatic descending bassline — every root drops a single semitone from chord to chord instead of jumping around the circle of fifths.
