tritone-substitution--pop-rock-examples-.title: Pop/rock examples — found by ear, not by theory
tritone-substitution--pop-rock-examples-.html:
Several songwriters land on the tritone-sub sound without ever encountering the term — worth remembering when analyzing pop material: the theory is a useful lens after the fact, not necessarily the writer's own mental model.

  • "It Keeps You Runnin'" (The Doobie Brothers) — same tritone-sub-of-a-3-6-2-5 device as "One Note Samba."
  • "Toxic" (Britney Spears) — minor-key iii→ii→♭II chromatic descent, readable as tritone subs of a 6-2-5.
  • "Things We Said Today" (The Beatles) — the middle-eight's second rotation swaps the plain V (E) for B♭.
tritone-substitution--pop-rock-examples-.lede: Several songwriters land on the tritone-sub sound without ever encountering the term — worth remembering when analyzing pop material: the theory is a usefu…

backdoor-progression--the-progression.title: The progression
backdoor-progression--the-progression.html: iv7 – ♭VII7 – I (in C: Fm7 – B♭7 – C, often voiced Cmaj9 for a soulful, "flavorsome" landing). A borrowed/modal-interchange move rather than a secondary dominant proper — see Secondary Dominants for the related-but-distinct device.
backdoor-progression--the-progression.lede: iv7 – ♭VII7 – I (in C: Fm7 – B♭7 – C, often voiced Cmaj9 for a soulful, "flavorsome" landing). A borrowed/modal-interchange move rather than a secondary do…

backdoor-progression--pop-r-b-examples.title: Pop/R&B examples
backdoor-progression--pop-r-b-examples.html:
• "Stay" (Rihanna) — Am7 (minor iv) → D (♭VII), key of E.
  • "No Such Thing" (John Mayer) — the entire chorus is essentially one long backdoor progression.
  • "Underground" (Ben Folds Five) — quick backdoor progression, key of B.
  • "I Want to Be Where You Are" (The Jackson 5) — Gm7–C7–Dmaj7, key of D.
  • "The Waiting Line" (Zero 7) — the song's main progression is a backdoor progression in full, key of C.
  • "Lights Up" (Harry Styles) — the chorus resolves an otherwise A♭-minor song to A♭ major via the backdoor move — a minor-key song deliberately resolving major.
backdoor-progression--pop-r-b-examples.lede: "Stay" (Rihanna) — Am7 (minor iv) → D (♭VII), key of E.

backdoor-progression--jazz-standard-usag.title: Jazz standard usage
backdoor-progression--jazz-standard-usag.html:
• "Misty" — backdoor progression under the lyric "clinging to a cloud."
  • "Just Friends" — Cm7→F7→Gmaj7, key of G.
  • "Stella by Starlight" — an unusual case: the backdoor move resolves not to the piece's ultimate tonic (C) but to a local, temporarily-tonicized G (the tune has modulated to G at that point in the form, common in older jazz standards) — a "backdoor progression of five" rather than of the true I.
backdoor-progression--jazz-standard-usag.lede: "Misty" — backdoor progression under the lyric "clinging to a cloud."

turnarounds--the-base-form.title: The base form
turnarounds--the-base-form.html:
I – vi – ii – V, in C: Cmaj7 – Am7 – Dm7 – G7

Every other turnaround below is this one modified. It works because the roots walk down in thirds then jump a fourth, and because it ends on V, which wants the I at the top of the next chorus.
turnarounds--the-base-form.lede: I – vi – ii – V, in C: Cmaj7 – Am7 – Dm7 – G7

turnarounds--the-standard-variations.title: The standard variations
turnarounds--the-standard-variations.html:
Name In C What changed Sound
Plain Cmaj7 Am7 Dm7 G7 — Neutral, endlessly usable
VI7 Cmaj7 A7 Dm7 G7 vi → secondary dominant Brighter, stronger pull to Dm7
III7–VI7 Cmaj7 E7 A7 Dm7 G7 two secondary dominants Very strong forward motion
Tritone subs Cmaj7 E♭7 Dm7 D♭7 subs on the dominants Chromatic descending bass
♭III7 Cmaj7 E♭7 Dm7 G7 one tritone sub The cheapest way to sound "jazz"
Backdoor Cmaj7 Am7 Fm7 B♭7 ii–V → backdoor Softer, gospel-flavoured return
Minor Cm7 A♭maj7 Dm7♭5 G7♭9 minor key throughout Darker; the ii is half-diminished

All of these are applications of Chord Substitution to the same four-chord skeleton. Learn the base form and the substitution rules and you can generate the rest rather than memorising them.

turnarounds--the-two-bar-and-one-bar-com.title: The two-bar and one-bar compressions
turnarounds--the-two-bar-and-one-bar-com.html:
Turnarounds compress to fit the space available:

  • Two bars: | Cmaj7 A7 | Dm7 G7 | — two chords per bar
  • One bar: | Dm7 G7 | — just the ii–V, the most common ending in the repertoire
  • Half bar: | ... G7 | — V alone on beats 3–4

A useful writing habit: write the four-chord version first, then compress. Compressing a good turnaround gives a good short one; expanding a Dm7 G7 gives you nothing to work with.
turnarounds--the-two-bar-and-one-bar-com.lede: Turnarounds compress to fit the space available:

turnarounds--using-them-outside-jazz.title: Using them outside jazz
turnarounds--using-them-outside-jazz.html:
The last bar of a loop is the whole game. A four-bar loop that ends on I feels closed and gets boring on repeat. The same loop ending on V, or on a chord a half-step above the downbeat chord, pulls back to the top and can run indefinitely.

Three moves that work in modern production:

  • End on V7 or ♭II7. The classic pull. Cmaj7 | Am7 | Fmaj7 | G7 | or ... | D♭7 |.
  • End on the ii. Softer, very common in neo-soul — leaves the V implied and unresolved so the loop never fully closes.
  • Change only the last bar between repeats. Loop A ends plain, loop B ends with the turnaround. Two loops of material, one bar of writing. This is the cheapest arrangement variation available and it's underused. → Arrangement and Song Form

rhythm-changes--the-shape-aaba-32-bars.title: The shape: AABA, 32 bars
rhythm-changes--the-shape-aaba-32-bars.html:
Four 8-bar sections. The A sections are the same; the B section (the bridge) is completely different in method.

The A section — I–vi–ii–V, twice

In B♭ (the standard key), two bars compressed to two chords each:

| B♭  G7  | Cm7  F7  | B♭  G7  | Cm7  F7  |
| B♭  B♭7 | E♭  E♭m6 | B♭/F G7 | Cm7  F7  |

Bars 1–4 are I–vi–ii–V twice — a turnaround, looped. That's it. → Turnarounds

Bars 5–8 move to the subdominant and back: I → I7 → IV → iv → I → V/ii → ii → V. The E♭ → E♭m6 is a borrowed iv, and it's the moment the A section actually goes somewhere. → Borrowed Chords

The last A gets a different ending (an ending rather than a turnaround) so the tune can stop.

The B section — the bridge, a cycle of dominants

| D7  | D7  | G7  | G7  | C7  | C7  | F7  | F7  |

Four dominant chords, two bars each, each resolving down a fifth to the next: D7 → G7 → C7 → F7 → (B♭). This is a pure circle-of-fifths run, and it's usually described as III7 – VI7 – II7 – V7.

Every chord is dominant, and none of them is diatonic to B♭. That's the point — the bridge leaves the key entirely and walks back in by fifths. → Circle of Fifths · Secondary Dominants

This bridge is a self-contained lesson. If you want to internalise how dominant motion by fifths works, playing this eight-bar loop teaches it faster than any explanation.
rhythm-changes--the-shape-aaba-32-bars.lede: Four 8-bar sections. The A sections are the same; the B section (the bridge) is completely different in method.

rhythm-changes--why-it-s-worth-your-time.title: Why it's worth your time
rhythm-changes--why-it-s-worth-your-time.html:
The A section is a masterclass in loop writing. Four bars of nothing but I–vi–ii–V that don't get boring, because bars 5–8 answer them with actual harmonic movement. That question-and-answer structure inside an eight-bar unit is directly transferable to a verse. → Loop-Based Harmony

The bridge is a masterclass in contrast. Not a key change, not a tempo change, not new instrumentation — just a switch from diatonic and busy to chromatic and slow. Harmonic rhythm drops from two chords per bar to one chord per two bars, a 4× slowdown. That alone makes it feel like a different section.

The lesson for production: contrast doesn't require new material. Halving the harmonic rhythm and leaving everything else alone is a legitimate way to build a bridge, and it's cheaper than writing new parts. → Arrangement and Song Form
rhythm-changes--why-it-s-worth-your-time.lede: The A section is a masterclass in loop writing. Four bars of nothing but I–vi–ii–V that don't get boring, because bars 5–8 answer them with actual harmonic…

rhythm-changes--common-substitutions.title: Common substitutions
rhythm-changes--common-substitutions.html:
The form is a substitution playground, and every move is from Chord Substitution:

  • Tritone subs on the bridge dominants: D7 → A♭7, G7 → D♭7, giving chromatic descending roots
  • Interpolated ii chords: | Am7 D7 | Dm7 G7 | Gm7 C7 | Cm7 F7 | — the bridge with a ii in front of every dominant
  • Diminished passing chords in the A section: B♭ → B°7 → Cm7 in place of B♭ → G7 → Cm7 → Diminished Chords
rhythm-changes--common-substitutions.lede: The form is a substitution playground, and every move is from Chord Substitution:

32-bar-song-form--the-16-16-shape.title: The 16+16 shape
32-bar-song-form--the-16-16-shape.html:
• Two 16-bar halves. The second half repeats most of the first half's material, changing mainly the ending so the tune can actually close instead of looping forever.
  • The first chord of each half is usually — not always — the tonic. "Just Friends" is a documented counter-example: it opens on IV.
  • The first half's ending doesn't resolve to I. It needs to reach V (or a V-substitute) so the second half has somewhere to launch from; the second half's ending is the tune's real cadence.

Recurring devices, by structural slot

The practical value of this form isn't memorizing any one chart — it's recognizing that unrelated standards by different composers keep reusing the same move in the same position. Once the slot is familiar, a new chart in this form reduces to "which variant of the usual devices is this one using," not 32 bars of arbitrary chords.

Slot Device Notes
Early first half Secondary ii–V to vi Grouped and thought of as one unit, "a 2-5 to six" — never as two separate chords → The ii-V-I, Secondary Dominants
Early-to-mid first half Secondary ii–V to IV Same chunking logic, "a 2-5 to four" → The ii-V-I, Secondary Dominants
On/around the IV chord IV → IV-minor → I The same functional shape as Borrowed Chords's "heartbreak cadence" (IV→iv→I), confirmed as a real, positionally-predictable device in the jazz standard repertoire, not just a pop/Beatles move. Realized differently tune to tune — sometimes a literal minor IV chord with the minor 3rd audible in the melody, sometimes a backdoor-flavored dominant a half step below the eventual target, sometimes a ♭VII7-ish move. Statistically the most likely single bar to carry this device across the form.
Last line of the first half V7/V ("the dominant of the dominant") Very common in major-key standards specifically in this slot. Can appear plain, as a full ii–V into it, or tritone-substituted and still functionally read as the same device → Secondary Dominants
End of first half → top of second half No resolution to I The whole reason the form needs two halves — the first half's job is to arrive back at V, not I.
Near the very end A diminished/half-diminished reharmonization Common in the closing bars of the second half, often feeding a chain back through a secondary dominant into the final turnaround → Diminished Chords
Final 1–2 bars A turnaround Length isn't fixed — most tunes in this form use a 2-bar turnaround, but at least one documented tune ("It Could Happen to You") compresses to a 1-bar turnaround instead → Turnarounds

32-bar-song-form--the-8-8-asymmetric-var.title: The 8+8 (asymmetric) variant
32-bar-song-form--the-8-8-asymmetric-var.html:
Not every tune in this family splits its 16-bar half evenly. Some ("Out of Nowhere," "Just Friends") read more like an 8-bar phrase followed by a contrasting 8-bar phrase, rather than one continuous 16-bar idea — and the slot-devices above show up inconsistently in these looser tunes: the IV-minor cadence or the dominant-of-the-dominant may be missing from a slot where the strict 16+16 tunes would place it.

The reason traces to the melody, not an independent harmonic rule. In the documented examples, the harmony moves less in the phrase where the melody itself is more static, and moves more where the melody is more active — the harmonic slot devices above are really a description of what tends to happen under a certain kind of melodic phrase, and a tune whose melody is built differently legitimately skips them. Practical implication: learn the melody alongside the harmony — the "why" behind a form deviation is usually sitting in the tune, not a harmony rule being broken.

32-bar-song-form--learning-method-form-f.title: Learning method: form first, chords second
32-bar-song-form--learning-method-form-f.html:
The efficient way to internalize a tune in this form (or transcribe one by ear) is top-down, not chord-by-chord:

  1. Establish the form first — how many bars, how many sections, where the halves/phrases split. No chords yet.
  2. Note the key if it's already clear.
  3. Fill in chords while listening, leaving anything unclear open rather than guessing.
  4. Exploit repetition — once a section has been worked out, a later repeat of the same section (or a whole standard sharing this form's shape) usually confirms rather than re-derives.

Directly analogous to the 12-bar blues shortcut: knowing just one binary fact ("does it go to IV in bar 2 or not") is often enough to play a new blues immediately, because the rest is shared vocabulary. The same logic scales up to the 32-bar standard form via the slot table above. → Transcribing and Playing by Ear
32-bar-song-form--learning-method-form-f.lede: The efficient way to internalize a tune in this form (or transcribe one by ear) is top-down, not chord-by-chord:

the-montgomery-ward-bridge--the-shape.title: The shape
the-montgomery-ward-bridge--the-shape.html:
I7 – IV7 – II7 – V7, in C: C7 – F7 – D7 – G7, two bars each across eight bars.

Every chord is a dominant 7, which is the whole point — none of them is functioning as a stable tonic. In the key of C, C7 is not home; it's V7-of-IV, already leaning. → Secondary Dominants

The expanded eight-bar version puts a ii in front of the last two dominants:

v7 | I7 | IV | IV | vi m7 | II7 | ii m7 | V7

which is the same skeleton with ii–V pairs substituted in — the standard dressing-up move. → The ii-V-I, Chord Substitution
the-montgomery-ward-bridge--the-shape.lede: I7 – IV7 – II7 – V7, in C: C7 – F7 – D7 – G7, two bars each across eight bars.

the-montgomery-ward-bridge--outside-jazz.title: Outside jazz
the-montgomery-ward-bridge--outside-jazz.html:
Rare as a loop, common as a lift. The progression's defining feature — a non-diatonic II chord a whole step above the tonic, approached from IV — is the same move behind a lot of pre-chorus writing that needs to raise the temperature before a chorus without changing key.

The diatonic softening, I – IV – ii7 – V7 (minor ii instead of II7), loses the F♯ and with it most of the character. It's smoother, more neo-soul, and much less distinctive. Worth knowing as the alternative but it's a different progression emotionally. → Loop-Based Harmony

memorizing-jazz-standards-by-harmonic-ch.note: Memorizing Jazz Standards by Harmonic Chunking
memorizing-jazz-standards-by-harmonic-ch.title: The core method: the phone-number analogy
memorizing-jazz-standards-by-harmonic-ch.html:
A phone number isn't memorized digit by digit — it's memorized as country code + area code + the rest, because that structure means there's genuinely less to hold in memory. Apply the identical idea to a chord chart:

  1. Identify the form first. How many bars, how many sections, where sections repeat. AABA, ABAC, a 2×16-bar form, whatever it is — see 32-Bar Song Form, Musical Form. Once the form is known, material that repeats (a whole A section, or even just the first few bars of two different sections) only has to be memorized once.
  2. Within each section, name the cadences and small functional units rather than the individual chords — a secondary ii–V, a IV-minor-to-I move, a turnaround, "the dominant of the dominant." Chunk each of those into a single mental "thing" ("a 2-5 to six," not "half-diminished, then dominant, then minor").
  3. Group chords by function on the strong beats, treat the rest as embellishment. When a stretch of the chart looks dense (several chord symbols per bar), check which chords actually land on the strong beats and carry the real harmonic motion — the others are frequently passing/auxiliary color that doesn't need to be remembered as its own event, just as a decoration on the chunk it sits inside.
  4. Cross-reference against tunes you already know. The real payoff isn't chunking one chart — it's recognizing that the same chunk (secondary ii–V to the vi, IV-minor-to-I, V7/V at the end of a first half or a bridge) shows up in the same structural slot across dozens of unrelated standards. Once a chunk is chunked once, it's recognized instantly everywhere else it appears — "when you've learned one, you've almost learned ten already."

The chunk vocabulary is built the same way vocabulary in a spoken language is: by encountering it in context, over and over, inside real tunes, until it's recognized by ear before it's ever consciously labeled.

passing-chords--1-chromatic-passing-chor.title: 1. Chromatic passing chords (dominant diminished)
passing-chords--1-chromatic-passing-chor.html:
A diminished 7th a half step below the target, functioning as that target's dominant. C♯dim7 → Dm7 works because C♯dim7 sounds like a rootless A7 (A7's 3rd–5th–♭7–♭9 traces a diminished-7 shape — the same "7♭9 = rootless dim7 + root a major 3rd below" relationship already on Diminished Chords), and A7 is Dm7's own V7.

  • Resolves up a half step, always — that's the simplest way to think about it: whichever note you're tracking moves up a semitone into the target.
  • The payoff is the chromatic bass line it creates: C → C♯ → D. → Chromatic Bass Lines
  • Because it changes the bass motion of the actual progression, this type is usually written INTO the chart, not left as optional comping decoration — everyone in the band needs to play it.
  • Also usable as a whole embellishing device stacked through a 3-6-2-5-1 as an intro.
  • Same-root diminished neighbor tone — a distinct variant, embellishing a STATIC chord instead of approaching the NEXT one. Rather than building the diminished a half step below the upcoming target, build it on the current chord's own root and resolve straight back to that same chord — works over both a major and a dominant chord: Cmaj7 → Cdim → Cmaj7, or G7 → Gdim → G7 (functions like the chord's own suspension, pure color/movement, no chord change actually happening). → Diminished Chords — Jens Larsen, Passing Chords And How To Sound Amazing With Them

passing-chords--3-diatonic-passing-chord.title: 3. Diatonic passing chords
passing-chords--3-diatonic-passing-chord.html:
The stepwise-bass cousin of type 2, using chords that stay inside the key instead of chromatic ones. Core definition: any chord already present in the parent scale's diatonic set (in C major: Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bø7) can be inserted between two chords of the real progression to create stepwise connective motion — no theory beyond "is it in the scale" is required.

  • Stepwise diatonic bass, harmonized: e.g. connecting C down to Am7 via a G triad over a B bass note (G/B) — the bass walks C → B → A while the chord stays diatonic.
  • Walking a ii up to its V: instead of sitting still on Dm7 before G7, walk Dm7 → Em7 → Fmaj7 → G7 — diatonic passing chords filling the space, melody kept moving independently of the chord roots for an extra layer of motion.
  • Sound: often reads as gospel-flavored when stacked into a turnaround.
  • Like type 2, these are usually optional embellishments, not written into the chart — and they still work even if the bass player just plays the original unembellished changes underneath.

Full worked example: every transition of a 1-6-2-5 in C (Cmaj7 – Am7 – Dm7 – G7)

The same I–vi–ii–V skeleton documented on Turnarounds, embellished with diatonic passing chords at every step. Rhythm placement rule that keeps it sounding like the original progression: put the passing chord on the weak beat, keep the real progression chord on the heavy beat — the ear tracks the real harmony while the passing chord reads as color rather than a competing chord change.

  • Cmaj7 → Am7 (I→vi): stepwise-between (Cmaj7 → Bø7 → Am7, the direct scale-tone in between — same B half-diminished this page already used above, here reached diatonically instead of chromatically); triad-inversion variant of the same slot (G/B in place of Bø7, brighter/more consonant); approach from below (C → G7 → Am7, borrowing a dominant move into a diatonic vi target); full walk (C → F → G → Am, skip down to F then step up through G).
  • Am7 → Dm7 (vi→ii): chord-below approach (Am7 → Cmaj7 → Dm7 — Am7/Cmaj7 share enough tones that the insert "does no harm" and tends to sit under whatever the melody/solo is doing); full walk-up (Am7 → Bø7 → Cmaj7 → Dm7); approach from above (Am7 → Em7 → Dm7); extended walk-down adding one more diatonic step for a fuller descending line into Dm7.
  • Dm7 → G7 (ii→V): whole-step-below approach (Dm7 → Fmaj7 → G7 — Fmaj7 functions almost like a "G sus" substitute since the two sound close); stepwise walk-up (Dm7 → Em7 → Fmaj7 → G7); beat-displacement move (the distinctive one): because Fmaj7 and G7 sound so similar, push G7 itself off the strong beat and put Fmaj7 on the downbeat instead, landing G7 right after — the passing chord temporarily takes over the harmonic-rhythm slot that "belongs" to the real V chord and it still reads as sensible; full stepwise walk-down mirrors the same idea the other direction.
  • G7 → Cmaj7 (V→I): full walk-up through the ii-V (Dm7 → G7 → Am7 → Bø7 → Cmaj7) — reuses Am7/Bø7 as passing motion approaching the final I rather than resolving G7 directly; specific rhythm placement: because G7 and Bø7 sound so close (Bø7 functions almost like a rootless G9), put both on the heavy beats with Am7 slotted on the offbeat between them (on-beat G7 → off-beat Am7 → on-beat Bø7 → I); full stepwise walk-down (G → F → E → D → C), one passing chord per scale step.

Practice method: sit with a simple progression (a 2-5-1 or 1-6-2-5) and try inserting different diatonic passing chords by ear, testing each by playing it as chords first — the fastest way to check a substitution actually makes sense — before moving the same vocabulary into single-note improvised lines. Where it earns its keep: especially valuable comping in a duo setting behind a horn player or singer, where reharmonizing a static chord with inversions of itself rarely sounds convincing — more distinct chords via passing motion beats voicing-shuffling the same chord. → Turnarounds, The ii-V-I — Jens Larsen, How To Use Diatonic Passing Chords With Easy Practical Examples

passing-chords--4-dominant-passing-chord.title: 4. Dominant passing chords
passing-chords--4-dominant-passing-chord.html:
Use a functioning dominant — the strongest resolution in harmony — as connective tissue between two chords, exactly like a secondary dominant but framed as decorative/optional rather than a fixed part of the progression.

Two variants, both resolving into the same target:

  • Regular 5–1 — a plain secondary dominant a 5th above the target.
  • Tritone substitute — the same dominant, transposed a tritone, so it resolves down a half step into the target instead of down a 5th. → Chord Substitution § Tritone substitution

Worked turnaround (targeting a ... A7 – G7 – Cmaj7-shaped skeleton): an all-tritone-sub pass (B♭7→A7, A♭7→G7, D♭7→Cmaj7) versus a mixed pass using plain secondary dominants where a tritone sub isn't wanted (E7→A7, D7→G7 — the D7 sits over a static melody note — then still closing on D♭7→Cmaj7, a tritone sub, since going straight V7 there sounds weaker). Underlying principle: Barry Harris's sixth-diminished-scale system is built on exactly this same tonic-chord-plus-dominant-diminished relationship, generalized into a full scale. → Diminished Chords § Usage — passing chords

reharmonization--the-one-constraint.title: The one constraint
reharmonization--the-one-constraint.html:
The melody note must be a usable tone of the new chord.

Usable means a chord tone (1, 3, 5, 7) or a functioning extension (9, 11, 13, or an altered version of those). What it must not be is a note the new chord actively contradicts — a natural 9 over a ♭9 chord, or a natural 4 sitting on the 3rd.

Everything else is negotiable. Function, bass motion, density — all of it can change, as long as the tune still fits.

This is why you reharmonize melody-first. Write out the melody notes, decide what each one could be relative to a new chord, and choose from there. Choosing chords first and hoping the melody survives is how you get the clashes.

reharmonization--the-techniques-roughly-.title: The techniques, roughly in order of cost
reharmonization--the-techniques-roughly-.html:
1. Change the chord's function under a held note

The cheapest move. A melody sitting on C can be harmonized as:

Chord C becomes its… Effect
Cmaj7 root Neutral, home
Am7 ♭3 Softer, relative minor
Fmaj7 5th Plagal, warm
Dm7 ♭7 Suspended, unresolved
A♭maj7 ♯5 / ♭6 Borrowed, cinematic
F♯m7♭5 ♭5 Tense, needs to move

Same melody note, six different meanings. Cycling through these under a sustained vocal is the entire trick behind a lot of neo-soul.

1b. Delayed resolution

A named special case of technique #1, worth its own entry because it's a full systematic device rather than a one-off swap: hold the melody on its expected tonic note, but harmonize that note with anything except the expected tonic chord, and only arrive at the real tonic later — letting the tension hang longer than expected before the actual resolution. Works over a plain ii–V–I; the tonic note (say C, over a I chord of C major) gets reharmonized as a different chord tone each time:

Substitute for the tonic chord Tonic note becomes its… Notes
Cdim7 root The classic — early pop/classical/jazz go-to; resolve to Cmaj7 or C triad
A♭maj7 (or A♭dom7♯11) 3rd Borrowed/cinematic color, same as technique #1's row
Fmaj7 5th Reads as a plagal (IV–I) cadence
Fm6 5th (upgraded) Jazzier version of the Fmaj7 row above
D♭maj7 major 7th "Major seven a half step up, then a half step down" — very common jazz move; guitaristic voicing: 3rd inversion with the tonic note in the bass (D♭maj7/C-shape), top three notes walk down on the resolve
D half-diminished (Dø7) ♭7 (of the relevant Dm) Same notes as Fm6, different inversion (Dm6 and Dø7 share a structure) — best voicing: 3rd inversion, Dø7/C (tonic note stays in the bass through the resolution, only the upper chord moves)
B♭9 (B♭dom7 add 9) 9th One physical shape, dominant color

Delaying progressions (chain two or more of the rows above before resolving):

  • A♭maj7 → B♭9 → C (3rd-row then 9th-row, played slowly)
  • A♭maj7 → G7sus4 → C (holds the tonic note inside the V chord's suspension for a second layer of delay)
  • E♭m6 → A♭7 → D♭maj7 → C (a full ii–V–I in D♭ major — a half step up from the real key — substituted ahead of the drop back down a half step to the true tonic)
  • F half-diminished → Fm6 → E7♯5 → E♭13 → Dm7 → D♭maj7 → C (chromatic bass line walking all the way down to the root before the final half-step resolution — the biggest version of the device)

Applies to single-note lines too, not just full harmony: over a plain ii–V heading to the tonic, superimpose/outline a substitute chord's arpeggio in the lead line (e.g. outline D♭maj7 over the V chord) before resolving the melodic line to the real target — same logic purely melodically, so it works even when the rhythm section keeps playing the plain changes.

Live example in the vault: 🎵 HOAGY CARMICHAEL - Georgia on My Mind's arrangement substitutes E minor for the expected C major tonic, twice, at phrase-ending cadences. Full worked-example video → Delayed Resolution - A Gorgeous Reharmonization Technique (10 Examples). → Diminished Chords, Slash Chords, Chromatic Bass Lines, Suspended Chords.

2. Interpolate ii chords

Put a ii in front of any dominant. Doubles the chord count without changing the harmonic path. Detailed in Chord Substitution § 4. The safest reharmonization there is — it can't clash, because it doesn't change where the progression goes.

3. Tritone-substitute the dominants

Turns diatonic bass motion into chromatic descending motion. Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 → Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7. Detailed in Chord Substitution § 2.

Check the melody: over D♭7, the melody notes that work well are F (3rd), C♭ (7th), G (♯11) and E♭ (9th). A melody sitting on D natural will fight it.

4. Add secondary dominants

Precede any diatonic chord with the dominant a fifth above it. Brightens and adds urgency. → Secondary Dominants

5. Change the bass, keep the chord

A slash chord reharmonizes without touching the upper structure. Cmaj7 → Cmaj7/E → Cmaj7/G → Cmaj7/A (which is Am9). Cheapest possible variation and it costs one note. → Upper Structure Chords · Chord Inversions

6. Pedal point

Hold one bass note and move everything above it. The tension between static bass and moving harmony does the work, and it's very forgiving of clashes because the ear attributes them to the pedal. Common on a tonic or dominant pedal.

7. Modal interchange

Borrow chords from the parallel minor (or any parallel mode). Cmaj7 Fmaj7 → Cmaj7 Fm7. The single most reliable way to make a bright progression turn bittersweet. → Borrowed Chords · Parallel Minor

8. Reharmonize the rhythm, not the chords

Underrated. Keep every chord and change only where they land — push a chord an eighth early, or hold one an extra bar. Harmonic rhythm is a separate dial from harmonic content and changing it alone can transform a section. → Syncopation and Metric Displacement

reharmonization--when-not-to.title: When not to
reharmonization--when-not-to.html:
Reharmonization competes with the melody for attention. If the tune is the point — a strong vocal hook, a memorable lead line — dense reharmonization pulls focus and the song gets worse.

The rule of thumb: reharmonize the repeats, not the first statement. Let the listener learn the plain version, then change what's underneath it. That way the reharmonization reads as development rather than as confusion, and it gives you a second section for free. → Arrangement and Song Form · Motivic Development

modal-jazz--the-reaction-it-was.title: The reaction it was
modal-jazz--the-reaction-it-was.html:
Bebop had reached a point where tunes changed chords every two beats and improvisation was largely about navigating them. Modal jazz (from the late 1950s — Kind of Blue is the reference recording) removed the changes almost entirely: So What is 16 bars of D Dorian, 8 of E♭ Dorian, 8 more of D Dorian.

When harmony stops moving, everything else has to carry the music. That constraint is the whole subject.

modal-jazz--what-replaces-functional-har.title: What replaces functional harmony
modal-jazz--what-replaces-functional-har.html:
1. The mode is the material

There's no ii–V to outline, so the line is built from the mode's own character — specifically its characteristic note, the one degree that distinguishes it from the plain major or minor:

Mode Characteristic note Against
Dorian natural 6 natural minor
Lydian ♯4 major
Mixolydian ♭7 major
Phrygian ♭2 natural minor

Land on it and the mode is established; avoid it and the music collapses into plain major or minor. In D Dorian the note is B — hit B and it's Dorian, avoid B and it's D minor. →

2. Quartal voicings

Stacking fourths instead of thirds. The classic So What voicing is three perfect fourths with a major third on top: E A D G B from the bottom.

Why fourths: a stack of thirds names a chord and therefore implies a function, and function is the thing modal music is trying to avoid. Fourths sound open and unassigned — they state the mode without committing to a chord. They're also why modal jazz has its particular hollow, floating sound.

Transfers directly: quartal voicings under a vocal sit in a mix beautifully because they're sparse and have no strong 3rd fighting the melody. → Chord Voicings, Quartal Chord Voicings (fretboard shapes, the So What voicing fully derived, and a reharmonization trick for using quartal shapes over ordinary tertian chords)

3. Pedal points and drones

With no root motion, a held bass note costs nothing and anchors everything. Move the upper voices freely above it.

4. Rhythm and space carry the form

When harmony can't signal a section change, dynamics, density and texture have to. This is the same problem loop-based production has, solved the same way. → Arrangement and Song Form

modal-jazz--modal-interchange-is-a-diffe.title: Modal interchange is a different thing — don't confuse them
modal-jazz--modal-interchange-is-a-diffe.html:
• Modal jazz — the harmony stays on one mode for a long time.
  • Modal interchange / borrowed chords — you borrow a chord from a parallel mode and return. → Borrowed Chords ·

They share a word and almost nothing else. The first is a static approach to form; the second is a chromatic spice within functional harmony.
modal-jazz--modal-interchange-is-a-diffe.lede: Modal jazz — the harmony stays on one mode for a long time.

modal-jazz--why-it-matters-for-the-music.title: Why it matters for the music you actually make
modal-jazz--why-it-matters-for-the-music.html:
A loop is modal harmony. A four-bar loop on Fmaj7 or a two-chord vamp is exactly the situation So What is in — the harmony isn't going anywhere and the interest has to come from somewhere else. Modal jazz is 60 years of worked solutions to that problem.

The three that transfer cleanest:

  • Commit to a characteristic note. A loop that never plays the ♯4 isn't Lydian, it's major with a Lydian label. The colour has to be sounded.
  • Voice in fourths when the chord is static. Removes the harmonic commitment that gets tiring over sixteen bars of the same chord.
  • Change one thing per section. With no chord changes, one new element — a texture, a countermelody, a register shift — reads as a whole new section.

modal-jazz--modal-islands-treating-each-.title: Modal islands — treating each chord of a non-functional vamp as its own mode
modal-jazz--modal-islands-treating-each-.html:
A different application of "harmony stays still" than the rest of this page: instead of one static mode for a long stretch, a short vamp with several different chords, none of them functionally connected to each other, each held long enough to be its own local tonal center. Rather than searching for one key that explains the whole progression, treat each chord as a small island — pick its scale independently, and don't worry about how it connects to its neighbours.

A private tool for choosing notes on an island chord that doesn't sit in any obvious key: invent a small, admittedly fictional fragment of functional harmony between two adjacent chords — hear this move "as if" it were a ii–V, or "as if" it were a IV→iv, in some key that doesn't actually govern the rest of the progression — purely to have a reference for scale choice and target notes. Never claimed as the real analysis, just a usable one — the same method applies to genuinely non-functional written tunes (Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock), not only to a composer's own vamps.

Two supporting devices that make islands cohere without functional glue:

  • Place the actual scale/tonal shift on a weak bar rather than a strong one, when the goal is to obscure the tonal center rather than clarify it — keep the strong internal move scale-static and let the shift happen somewhere the ear isn't watching.
  • A single voicing shape moved chromatically/in parallel across different roots can be the real thread holding a set of otherwise-unrelated island chords together, even when it wasn't planned that way going in — worth checking for after the fact, not just before writing.

Why this differs from the "static mode" case above: So What holds one mode for many bars; a modal-islands vamp changes chord (and mode) every bar or two, but each chord still gets treated with the same "commit to its own material, don't chase a global key" logic — the island is just shorter-lived.

bebop-vocabulary--1-the-bebop-scales-why.title: 1. The bebop scales — why an eighth note
bebop-vocabulary--1-the-bebop-scales-why.html:
A bebop scale is a normal seven-note scale with one chromatic passing tone added, making eight notes.

That's the entire idea, and the reason is rhythmic rather than harmonic. Play a seven-note scale in straight eighths starting on the downbeat and by the next bar you've shifted: chord tones start landing on offbeats. Add an eighth note and the chord tones land on the beat again, every bar.

Scale Formula Added note
Bebop dominant Mixolydian + natural 7 passing tone between ♭7 and root
Bebop major Major + ♯5 passing tone between 5 and 6
Bebop dorian Dorian + natural 3 passing tone between ♭3 and 4
Bebop melodic minor Melodic minor + ♯5 passing tone between 5 and 6

Bebop dominant on G: G A B C D E F F♯ G. The F♯ is the added tone. Run it descending from the root in eighths and G, E, D and B — the chord tones of G7 — all land on downbeats.

The practical rule: the extra note goes wherever it makes chord tones fall on strong beats. If your line's chord tones are landing on offbeats, you need a passing tone; if they're already on the beat, you don't. → Scale Modes Reference
bebop-vocabulary--1-the-bebop-scales-why.lede: A bebop scale is a normal seven-note scale with one chromatic passing tone added, making eight notes.

bebop-vocabulary--2-enclosures-approach-.title: 2. Enclosures — approach a note from both sides
bebop-vocabulary--2-enclosures-approach-.html:
Surround a target note before playing it. This is the most transferable device in the whole vocabulary and it works in any genre.

Target: C

Type Notes Character
Chromatic above/below D♭ – B – C Tight, classic bebop
Diatonic above, chromatic below D – B – C Smoother
Below then above B – D♭ – C Slightly more angular
Double chromatic D – D♭ – B – C Longest, most obviously "jazz"

Where to use them: on the note you actually want the listener to hear — usually a chord tone on a downbeat. An enclosure delays arrival by two or three notes and makes the arrival feel intentional. Applied to a plain melody it instantly reads as improvised.

Where not to: on every note. Enclosures are punctuation. Wall-to-wall, a line stops having a shape.

A chord-tone-independent drilling variant exists: apply enclosures systematically to every note of a scale form in descending order, with no regard for which notes are chord tones — a simpler entry point than targeting chord tones directly, worked out step by step on Enclosures Through the Scale.

A beat-driven sizing rule also exists, orthogonal to the shape table above: which of the two/three-note enclosure types to use is decided purely by which beat the target lands on (downbeat → two notes, upbeat → three), reused to drill diatonic arpeggios and to build ii–V connective lines — full rule on Downbeat and Upbeat Enclosures.
bebop-vocabulary--2-enclosures-approach-.lede: Surround a target note before playing it. This is the most transferable device in the whole vocabulary and it works in any genre.

bebop-vocabulary--3-approach-notes.title: 3. Approach notes
bebop-vocabulary--3-approach-notes.html:
The simpler cousin. Precede a chord tone with the note a half-step below (or above, or a scale step away). One note, not three.

  • Chromatic from below is the default and the strongest — it borrows the leading-tone pull.
  • Chromatic from above is softer and slightly melancholy.
  • Scale step is the most neutral and the most usable in non-jazz contexts.

A pivot-tone variant pedals (repeats) one tone and uses it as the launch point for a chromatic approach to a second tone, rather than approaching from a static position — minor chords pivot the 5th into the 6th (which becomes the 3rd of the following V7 in a 2-5-1), major/dominant chords pivot the root into the 5th (approached from the 3rd, or the reverse). Also covers applying the half-step-approach idea to every tone of an arpeggio (not just one target), and to comping voicings treated as single-note-line targets. Full device → Pivot Tone Lines.
bebop-vocabulary--3-approach-notes.lede: The simpler cousin. Precede a chord tone with the note a half-step below (or above, or a scale step away). One note, not three.

bebop-vocabulary--8-cesh-chromatic-embel.title: 8. CESH — chromatic embellishment of static harmony
bebop-vocabulary--8-cesh-chromatic-embel.html:
Take one note — usually the root of a chord that's about to sound, or that's currently sitting still — and move it chromatically up or down through the changes, independent of the underlying harmonic rhythm. The harmony can be genuinely static (one chord held for a while) or just slower-moving than the chromatic line riding underneath it; either way the term describes the chromatic line, not the chord.

Where it differs from an approach note or an enclosure (§2–3): those target a single arrival on a single chord tone. CESH is a sustained chromatic line across several beats or bars, more like a bass-line device borrowed into the melody than a one-note ornament.

Practical use: pick a note that matters (a chord root, a guide tone) and walk it by half step under or against otherwise-static harmony — it's a way to generate forward motion without changing the chord itself, useful anywhere a vamp or a held chord risks going static. → Chromatic Bass Lines, Non-Harmonic Tones

bebop-vocabulary--transferring-this-outs.title: Transferring this outside jazz
bebop-vocabulary--transferring-this-outs.html:
Three things here earn their place in modern production:

  • Enclosures on a lead melody. Take a two-note synth hook, enclose the second note. Costs two 16ths and stops the line sounding quantized-from-scratch.
  • Chromatic approach into a section. A single half-step approach into the downbeat of a chorus is the cheapest lift available.
  • Bebop-scale passing tones in a bass line. The added eighth is exactly what makes a walking-ish bass line land its chord tones on the beat. → Bassline Writing

What doesn't transfer well is density. Bebop's note rate is a genre convention, not a principle, and importing it wholesale into a trap beat just sounds busy.

solo-analysis-and-concept-extraction--th.title: The core method
solo-analysis-and-concept-extraction--th.html:
1. Learn the solo by ear, in full, first — chords and melody/solo line, all by ear. This alone builds vocabulary and ear, but on its own isn't enough — "it's not enough to just simply learn a solo by ear, you've got to get under the hood."
  2. Chunk it — break the solo into small, manageable sections (a phrase, a chord or two at a time), rather than analyzing it as one continuous line.
  3. Analyze each chunk against the chord underneath it — work out which scale, arpeggio, or harmonic device the original player is drawing from over that specific chord.
  4. Reduce each chunk to one named "concept" — a single reusable idea (a scale choice, an arpeggio substitution, a target note) rather than the literal notes played. The concept, not the lick, is the thing worth keeping.
  5. Use the set of per-chord concepts as a template — improvise a new solo of your own over the same changes, applying the concepts (not the original licks) at each chord. Comping distinct concepts to the same underlying chords is what turns a single transcription into a whole practice session's worth of new lines.
  6. Layer alternate concepts over the same changes — Ruch demonstrates two (sometimes three) different valid concepts for the same chord across repeats of the form (e.g. blues/flat-5 phrasing vs. melodic-minor vocabulary over the same i chord — see below), reinforcing that a chord doesn't have one "correct" scale, just a menu of concepts worth having ready. — Jack Ruch, How I Approach Practicing

12-level-chromatic-alternate-picking-spe.title: How to run it
12-level-chromatic-alternate-picking-spe.html:
• Play through all 12 levels in one sitting, back to back — the workout is the ladder, not one isolated tempo.
  • Goal, every note, at every tempo: one continuous unbroken stream — no hesitation or unwanted noise at string transitions. A clean lower tempo beats a sloppy higher one.
  • Log the date and the BPM level you got stuck at, then return the next day and try to beat it — the drill is explicitly designed as a day-over-day progression tracker, not a one-and-done exercise.
  • If a specific tempo step feels technically wrong (not just "hard," but genuinely uncontrolled), that's a signal to drop back and drill string-transition mechanics specifically rather than muscling through at that tempo.

• Play all six blocks back to back in one 15-minute sitting — the shape is the point, not any single block in isolation.
  • Left-hand fingers stay close to the fretboard throughout; picking motion stays relaxed and economical, not full-arm.
  • Log the tempo/point you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.

2-note-per-string-arpeggio-picking-exerc.note: 2-Note-Per-String Arpeggio Picking Exercise (C Minor Scale-Degree Chords)
2-note-per-string-arpeggio-picking-exerc.title: How to run it
2-note-per-string-arpeggio-picking-exerc.html:
• One 4-note chord shape per scale degree of C minor, picked 2 notes per string.
  • Consistent picking angle (even grouping) — pick should clear the strings after each down-up pair, not get trapped between them.
  • Total picking-hand relaxation is required, not optional — tension collapses the exercise (multiple strings ring together) rather than just degrading it.
  • Curled (not flat) fretting fingers keep each arpeggiated note cleanly separated — this is the single biggest factor in how clean it sounds.
  • Doubles as a fretting-hand independence exercise: one fretted note per string against two picking strokes.

30-day-sweep-picking-speed-burst-challen.html:
• Play E minor shape → E major shape → alternate between them, tempo climbing session to session.
  • Add a fast burst of sweep picking on each repetition — meant to push past the comfort zone, not to be played clean immediately. Failing to complete the full workout on day one is expected.
  • Log the tempo you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.

4-minute-alternate-picking-shred-challen.note: 4-Minute Alternate Picking Shred Challenge (200 BPM Ladder)
4-minute-alternate-picking-shred-challen.title: How to run it
4-minute-alternate-picking-shred-challen.html:
• Strict alternate picking throughout (no economy shortcuts) — down/up/down/up regardless of string change.
  • Stay relaxed; a fully locked/tensed wrist is both a speed ceiling and an injury risk at this tempo.
  • Log the tempo where you get stuck plus the date, come back the next day, and try to push past it — day-over-day overload, not a one-off run.
  • Good finisher once basic wrist-unlocking work (see Directional Alternate Picking System) is already in place — this drill is pure speed ladder, no technique-building content of its own.

4-notes-per-string-stretch-workout--how-.title: How to run it
4-notes-per-string-stretch-workout--how-.html:
• Support the thumb from behind the neck, never draped over the top — that's what makes the stretch reachable.
  • Keep the picking wrist relaxed and moving even above 200 BPM; avoid locking into a stiff full-arm motion.
  • Log the tempo you got stuck at and try to beat it next session (daily morning routine, per the source).
  • Getting stuck at a plateau here is a signal to check underlying picking technique, not just to push harder.

downstroke-workout--how-to-run-it.html:
• Start at tempo_current, not at 60 every time. Move up a rung only when the current one is clean for the full page.
  • The failure mode is tension, not speed. If the forearm locks up, drop two rungs rather than pushing — downstroke stamina is built by staying relaxed under load, and practising tense just trains tension.
  • Short and frequent beats long and occasional. Five minutes daily moves the ladder faster than half an hour on Sunday.

  • Best used as the thing you do when the answer to "am I practising today" is otherwise no. A five-minute page beats a missed session, and the guitar drills only work on frequency.

• When the pinky isn't fretting, hover it close over the strings rather than letting it bend away — the concrete self-check this drill trains.
  • Resist widening the motion as tempo increases; stay small and relaxed even under speed pressure.
  • Prioritize control and independent finger feel over raw speed — work through the 3 levels slowly before attempting a faster pass.

  • Go slow enough to actually clear each level before adding tempo — the source video is explicit that rushing costs you the flying-fingers fix, the plucking pattern, and the theory layer all at once, not just speed.

backward-chaining-practice.title: Backward Chaining Practice
backward-chaining-practice.html:
A practice-order method: instead of always starting a piece (or a hard passage) from the beginning, work it from the end backward — nail the last measure alone, then add the measure before it, then the one before that, and so on until the whole passage is chained back together. Instrument-agnostic — demonstrated on classical guitar but applies to any piece on any instrument.

Why backward beats forward

  • Forward-only practice front-loads confidence in the wrong place. Starting every rep at bar 1 means the opening gets played far more times than the ending, so a piece gets less secure as it goes — by the time you reach the hardest, least-rehearsed material (the ending), you're also the most fatigued and the least warmed into it. Working backward inverts that: the newest, least-familiar material becomes the most-drilled, so confidence builds as you play through instead of draining away — you finish a piece on your most secure material rather than your shakiest. — Jared, Piece #6 of 7 Easy Classical Guitar Songs for Beginners
  • Chunking: start with just the final measure, then the final 2, then the final 4 (Jared's own worked example) — expand backward in whatever chunk size suits the passage, not necessarily one measure at a time.
  • Source: Jared traces this to watching a David Russell (classical guitar virtuoso) masterclass, where Russell had a student work a piece backward from its last measure rather than from the top — he calls it a "tried and true" method he didn't invent but adopted after seeing it demonstrated live. — Jared, Piece #6 of 7 Easy Classical Guitar Songs for Beginners

Pair it with a deliberate-practice token system

Backward chaining answers what order to drill in; this answers how to know a chunk is actually done before expanding it.

  • Line up physical tokens (guitar picks, coins, anything) on the desk. Play the current chunk once. Only slide a token over if that take actually satisfies you — a hesitant entrance, a scraped nail, a tone/timing wobble all disqualify the take and the token stays put; a genuinely clean take earns moving one token.
  • Require several clean takes in a row before expanding the chunk, not just one. Jared's baseline is 3 in a row; 5 is better if you have the time. The count resets on any take that doesn't meet the bar — he describes rejecting takes back-to-back ("nope, nope, nope") before one finally satisfies him.
  • The real payoff is the listening standard, not the tally. Counting clean reps forces active critical listening on every single take (tone, timing, note clarity) rather than passive repetition — Jared notes his own standards have risen over time from "I played the right notes" to catching small velocity/tone inconsistencies, and that this heightened attention is what actually accelerates the relearning, not just the rep count.
  • Once a chunk hits its clean-in-a-row target, expand it (one more measure, chained backward) and reset the token count for the new, larger chunk.

— Jared, Piece #6 of 7 Easy Classical Guitar Songs for Beginners

bebop-vocabulary-practice-joe-pass-metho.title: Bebop Vocabulary Practice (Joe Pass Method)
bebop-vocabulary-practice-joe-pass-metho.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material. Where Etude-Based Vocabulary Practice documents how to absorb a composed comping etude (Galbraith), this page documents the sibling method for Joe Pass's Guitar Style (Alfred/Pacific Jazz) — a graded sequence of blues, minor blues, modern blues, rhythm-changes, and 3/4-blues solo studies (p.33–54) that culminates in a full, chord-symbol-free transcription of Pass's own solo on "For Django" (p.55–58, Pacific Jazz PJ-85). Full book synopsis on Joe Pass Guitar Style - Enrichment; the melodic devices this material trains (enclosures, approach notes, guide tones, line closers, CESH) are catalogued on Bebop Vocabulary.

1. Take the "For Django" solo apart phrase by phrase (p.55–58)

The solo is printed with no chord symbols at all — the book states this outright: "so you must do your own analysis" (p.55). A separate chart on the same page shows "some of the basic chordal thinking used in the solo," but explicitly frames it as a skeleton, not the full picture: "with chord embellishment/substitution, variations are almost limitless" (p.55). Treat that chart as a starting point for your own analysis, not the answer key.

Work it in the chunks the book itself gives you, rather than top-to-bottom in one pass:

  • The notation is broken into rehearsal letters (A, B, C, D) across the four pages — use each lettered section as one practice unit.
  • A Tacet marking partway through (end of the first page) shows where the recorded guitar drops out — worth noting as a natural section break, and a reminder that the transcription follows an actual performance, not a composed study.
  • Several passages are marked 8va (with a dashed continuation line back down to loco) — get the octave placement right before working the phrase into a line at all; an 8va passage played in the wrong register won't line up with the guide tones underneath it.
  • A Bridge label appears partway through the transcription — "For Django" has its own bridge-shaped harmonic motion, so treat that stretch as its own vocabulary chunk rather than folding it into the surrounding blues-adjacent material.

For each rehearsal-letter chunk:

  1. Play it exactly as written first — no analysis, no chord symbols filled in yet. Same play-before-analyze order as Etude-Based Vocabulary Practice's step 1.
  2. Go back and write your own chord symbols underneath the notes, phrase by phrase, checking your reading against the book's own partial chordal-thinking chart.
  3. Once the harmony is nailed down, name the devices already tracked on Bebop Vocabulary as they show up: enclosures (§2), approach notes (§3), guide-tone targets (§4), line closers (§7), CESH (§8). File short extracted phrases into those buckets rather than keeping the whole page as one long memorized block — the same "collection-first" filing method documented on Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction.
  4. Move to the next lettered section only once the current one is clean at a real tempo.

2. What the graded study sequence is teaching, in order (p.33–54)

The sequence isn't just "more reps" — each stage removes a different piece of scaffolding. Read it as training-wheels removal, in this order:

Blues (p.35–36) — rhythmic density first. The first chorus is written in straight 8th notes, then the identical form is rewritten in 16th notes: "This one is in 16th notes. It gives you more to play on each chord" (p.36). The book's own stated reason for starting with straight 8ths: eliminating rhythmic variety forces the ear to build better melodic lines and "avoids the practice of playing memorized licks" (p.35) — chord symbols are given "for your analysis, not necessarily for accompaniment" (p.35), i.e. read them, don't assume they're the comping part.

Minor Blues (p.37–39) — same drill, new tonic. Identical progressive-difficulty approach (straight 8ths → denser lines) reapplied over a 12-bar minor blues in C minor. Nothing new mechanically — the point is proving the method transfers to a different tonal center before the harmony itself gets harder.

Modern Blues (p.39–44) — the harmony gets harder, the line stays put. A single 12-bar blues form is given as three parallel reharmonizations: Basic (plain blues changes), Optional B (adds ii–V motion and secondary dominants over what were static chords), Optional C (a heavily altered/chromatic reharmonization — passing diminished chords, ♭9/♯5 dominants, chromatic ii–V insertions). The solo studies that follow are written to be playable against any of the three — the teaching point is that one melodic line can sit under multiple harmonizations, and that a line's "correctness" depends on how aggressively the accompaniment reharmonizes underneath it. This section also introduces blank measures with only chord symbols given ("Improvise in the blank measures," p.42) — the first place in the book where notation is deliberately withheld and you supply the line yourself.

Rhythm Changes (p.43–48) — fast tempo, then withheld notation on the bridge. AABA "I Got Rhythm" changes, given as two BASIC rhythm-pattern chord charts (p.43) that every player varies from. The bridge (starting bar 17) is a single two-bar phrase repeated through a descending cycle of dominant 7ths a fourth apart (p.46–49) — and instead of notating it out, the book gives two example two-bar phrases and an instruction: "Finish the chorus with something of your own" (p.48). This is the sequence's clearest scaffolding-removal moment: you're handed the harmonic device (a two-bar cell recycled through a dominant cycle) and two worked examples, then told to generate your own.

3/4 Blues (p.49–54) — the same method in waltz time, run as a continuous performance. Two different 12-bar blues chord-change sets in 3/4, each preceded by an INTRO vamp and followed by six labeled passes — Improvising, Harmony, 2nd Chorus, 2nd Solo, 3rd Chorus, 3rd Solo (p.49–51) — written so the last measure of one chorus feeds directly into the pickup of the next. Nothing here is conceptually new; the point is stamina and continuity — playing multiple choruses back-to-back as one performance rather than isolated 12-bar excerpts, in an unfamiliar meter.

What makes it "graded," stated plainly: the time signature and form stay fixed within each section while (1) rhythmic density escalates (8th → 16th notes), (2) harmonic density escalates (Basic → Optional B → Optional C), (3) written notation is progressively withheld (full notation → blank "improvise here" measures → "finish this yourself" prompts with only two worked examples), until the sequence culminates in the fully chord-symbol-free, fully unnotated-analysis "For Django" solo — the graded studies are rehearsal for exactly the skill the capstone solo demands cold.

3. Working it as practice material

  1. Pick one stage — a single 12-bar blues chorus, one Modern Blues reharm level, one rhythm-changes chorus — and play it exactly as written before analyzing anything.
  2. Fill in what the book withholds. For the Modern Blues blank measures and the Rhythm Changes bridge, write your own two-bar phrase before checking it against the book's worked examples. For "For Django," write your own chord analysis under each rehearsal-letter chunk (see §1).
  3. Transpose. The book states its own intent directly: every study is "written to be transposed to all keys and analyzed by ear, not memorized as licks" (synopsis, Joe Pass Guitar Style - Enrichment). Move a cleaned-up stage to at least two or three other keys before calling it done — a phrase that only survives in its original key hasn't actually been internalized as vocabulary.
  4. Extract and file. Pull two or three short phrases per stage and file them into Bebop Vocabulary's device buckets (enclosure, approach note, guide-tone line, closer, CESH) rather than keeping the whole page as one long memorized unit.
  5. Advance stages only when clean. Move Blues → Minor Blues → Modern Blues → Rhythm Changes → 3/4 Blues → For Django only once the current stage is comfortable at tempo in the original key and at least one transposed key — the sequence is ordered for a reason; skipping ahead skips the scaffolding.
  6. Work "For Django" last, one rehearsal-letter section at a time (§1), since it's the sequence's own capstone — everything upstream of it (rhythmic density, reharm density, withheld notation) is rehearsal for reading and playing over changes with no chord symbols at all.

chord-scale-up-down--how-to-run-it.title: How to run it
chord-scale-up-down--how-to-run-it.html:
• Take a progression you already know. Start with a diatonic one — ii–V–I in G: Am7 · D7 · Gmaj7 — before anything that borrows.
  • One chord per bar. Ascend the chord's scale from its root to its 7th; on the next chord, descend from the 7th back to the root. Alternate direction chord to chord so you are never restarting from the same place.
  • Play it against the harmony. Record the progression first and loop it. Without chords underneath, a descending A Dorian starting on G just sounds like G major, and the whole exercise collapses into "one scale, seven starting notes" — which is exactly the misunderstanding it exists to break.
  • Once diatonic is automatic, use a progression where the answer is not the parent key — a Cmaj7♯11 (Lydian, for the ♯11) or a borrowed Fm in C. That is where this stops being finger work and starts being .

etude-based-vocabulary-practice.title: Etude-Based Vocabulary Practice
etude-based-vocabulary-practice.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — a four-part method for absorbing vocabulary from a written comping/soloing etude book (Barry Galbraith's Comping Etudes is the source here, but the method generalizes to any notated jazz etude collection), distinct from Internalizing a Tune Through Repetition (which is about learning a song, not a composed practice etude) and a cousin of Backward Chaining Practice and Hub-Latching Approach (other named practice-order methodologies in this strand).

1. Treat the etude like a transcription — play first, deconstruct after

Don't read the chord symbols. Play the etude precisely and memorize it entirely before doing any harmonic analysis — treat it as "a comprehensive comping solo," the same discipline applied to soloing transcriptions. Only after it's under the fingers and memorized do you go back and pick it apart: analyze the voicings, the rhythms, the overall feel. Same play-before-analyze sequencing already documented on Internalizing a Tune Through Repetition (steps 1-2 there: play the tune off the page before noticing/naming what's happening in it) — this is the etude-specific version of that same ordering principle.

2. Play along with the recording, not just the page

A method book with audio (Galbraith's comes with recordings of Galbraith himself comping the etudes alongside bassist Milt Hinton) is a resource beyond the notation — play along with the recording until you're completely locked in with the rhythm section. The stated payoff is feel and time, not just correct notes: hearing (and playing against) two masters at work teaches pocket and rhythmic confidence that reading the page alone can't. Don't underestimate this step or treat it as optional polish.

3. One etude at a time, worked for months — patience over pace

Only work on one etude at a time. Dedicate real time to it — described as often months per etude in the source's own practice — absorbing its nuances daily until the etude's vocabulary genuinely becomes "what professional jazz comping feels and sounds like," not just something you can play through once. Explicitly not a race: the framing is deep assimilation over coverage. This is a patience/depth instruction, not a pacing suggestion — resist the urge to move to the next etude before the current one is fully internalized.

4. Drill rhythmic precision with a rhythm app, not a plain metronome

Practice the etude against a dedicated rhythm/groove app (named tools: Drum Genius, Pro Metronome) rather than a bare click — these let you isolate and reinforce the specific rhythmic concepts the etude is built on (e.g. Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline's Charleston-rhythm placements), sharpening timing precision so the comping "feels solid and grooving" rather than merely rhythmically correct on paper.

Why this order

Steps 1-2 build the etude into the hands and ears (play it right, then play it with real time-feel from the recording) before step 3 asks for sustained months-long depth on that material — front-loading correctness and feel before committing the long-haul repetition, the same "get it right before you drill it in" logic underlying Backward Chaining Practice's clean-takes-before-expanding rule. Step 4's rhythm-app work can run alongside any of the other three steps rather than as a separate final stage — it's a precision tool applied throughout, not a capstone.

full-scale-workout--how-to-run-it.title: How to run it
full-scale-workout--how-to-run-it.html:
• Say the mode name out loud as you start each one. Fingers learn the shape either way; naming it is what connects the shape to Diatonic Modes.
  • Listen for the characteristic note of each mode as it goes by — the ♯4 in Lydian, the ♭2 in Phrygian (). If they all sound the same, the drill is being played as exercise rather than as music, and slowing down fixes it.
  • Alternate picking is strict. A missed alternation is a repeat.
