interleaved-practice-chunking-and-delibe.note: Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills
interleaved-practice-chunking-and-delibe.title: Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills
interleaved-practice-chunking-and-delibe.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — Daniel Seriff's general-purpose deliberate-practice toolkit for how to structure any practice session, instrument-agnostic in application even though demonstrated on guitar. Where The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice answers what a complete jazz-guitar practice system needs to cover (ear skills, vocabulary, technique, theory, repertoire) and Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance) (same channel, Daniel Seriff) answers how to warm up before a session, this note answers how to drill any single piece of material once you've decided to work on it — the mechanics of interleaving, chunking, hands-separate isolation, trouble-spot targeting, edge-of-ability loading, and mental rehearsal. Several pieces here overlap in spirit with The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice's "long-term mindset" (spaced short reps beat cramming) and Backward Chaining Practice's clean-reps-before-expanding logic — cross-linked below rather than duplicated.

Interleaved practice, not massed practice

Massed practice — repeating the same thing over and over trying to perfect it — is named as the single biggest mistake guitar players make. It feels productive (fingers moving, time being logged) but the brain checks out and you stop actually learning; you're going through the motions, not learning.

The fix: interleaved practice — rotate between several different things within one session instead of drilling one thing for 20 minutes straight. (Worked example: 2–3 minutes each on five different things, then cycle back through all five again next session.) Why it works: the act of cycling back to something forces recall/retrieval practice — every time you return to an item you're quizzing yourself on it, and that retrieval attempt is what builds deeper learning than uninterrupted repetition. It will feel harder and less immediately satisfying than massed drilling ("feeds your ego a little less") — that discomfort is explicitly framed as the signal you're in the zone where the learning is actually happening, not a reason to retreat to something comfortable. Sourced to Make It Stick and Peak (Anders Ericsson). — Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

Cited research numbers for exactly how much this costs/pays off (a second, independent source converging on the same mechanism): interleaved practice roughly tripled subsequent test performance vs. blocked practice — 63% vs. 20% in one study cited — but at a real short-term cost: accuracy during interleaved practice itself dropped to ~60% vs. ~89% for blocked practice. In other words interleaving makes the practice session visibly messier and more mistake-prone while it's happening, and that's precisely what makes the later test/performance better — this is the concrete number behind "feeds your ego a little less" above. Researchers also checked whether interleaving's benefit was just spaced repetition in disguise and found it isn't — interleaving (mixing the order) carries a separate, additional benefit on top of spacing (widening the gap between touches). Much of the underlying research is on motor skills specifically (directly relevant to an instrument) — cited example: interleaved batting practice (mixed pitch types) outperformed blocked batting practice (all fastballs, then all curveballs) on later hitting performance. — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

Interleaving the order itself, not just which items rotate: with three items (Song/exercise A, B, C), don't settle into a fixed cycle A→B→C→A→B→C — change the permutation each pass (A-B-C, then B-C-A, then C-A-B…), which scales to real variety once you have a real batch of material (12 songs → many possible orderings). The opposite, block practice (AAA, then BBB, then CCC, even within one sitting), is the same failure mode as massed practice above, just applied across multiple items instead of one.

A remembered (unverified by the source, flagged as such) fighter-pilot training anecdote illustrates the same practice-vs-performance tradeoff vividly: pilots trained with heavy context-switching/chaos/surprise did far worse in training than pilots trained on a clean linear curriculum — but dominated when the two groups then competed against each other, because the linear group had over-optimized for one fixed context and hadn't built the skill of handling the unfamiliar. — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

Interleaving degrades when it silently turns into a fixed autopilot path — a named failure mode from teaching improv specifically: a student settles on one arpeggio-through-the-changes approach that "works," runs it identically every time, and stops actually improvising — the path becomes a drilled lick rather than real-time decision-making, and flexibility to jump to a different note or recall why it's the right chord tone is lost. Fix: interleave the approach, not just the material — vary which technique/lens is applied to the same changes, not only which song is being played. — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

Spaced repetition — the forgetting-curve schedule

Definition: "gradually increase the time between review sessions, reinforcing the material just as you're about to forget it." Also called spaced learning, distributed practice, spaced practice — same mechanism, several names — and it's the mechanism underneath this note's Rotation principle and this note's own 15–20 minute session-chunking rule above.

The forgetting-curve shape (illustrative, not a strict prescription — the source is explicit he doesn't personally chase exact intervals):

  • Learn something new → ~100% retention immediately, then it drops off fast.
  • Review again quickly (before it's gone) → back to ~100%, and the next safe gap is a little longer (illustrative: ~2 days).
  • Each successful review widens the gap needed before the next one — illustratively 2 days → ~7 days → longer again — the curve flattens more each cycle.
  • After roughly the 5th review cycle, a piece can go ~2 months between touches and still hold — treated as the point it's genuinely in long-term memory. (General starting shape, not a fixed schedule — adapt freely.)
  • Real-world use counts as review — if a piece gets played in a gig, taught, or referenced in a jam, that's a review cycle without a dedicated practice slot, and it extends how long the piece can go untouched afterward.

— Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

Independent convergence from a bass-side channel, same core spacing claim, plus a motor-learning/sleep mechanism not detailed above: frequent distributed practice sessions beat rare "mega" sessions — cited mechanisms are the rest between sessions helping consolidate memories, and sleep specifically helping the brain finish learning new motor skills (qualitative claim from the source, not a cited study — treat as a general spaced-practice/motor-learning finding rather than a sourced statistic). The source's own comparison: his bass practice stayed frequent ("rare that I don't pick it up at least a few times a week") for years, while his guitar practice — tied to an unrealistic "mega session or nothing" standard — went weeks or months untouched. The practical rule stated directly: "put in the time you have, not the time you wish you had, and just show up as often as you can" — the same "consistency over intensity" conclusion as this note's own spacing/chunking material, arrived at from a bass-practice angle rather than guitar. — BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

Case study for spacing at the extreme — biweekly-only, zero practice between sessions, ~1 year: a private student who never practiced between lessons, seen only every two weeks, picked apart a technically demanding Steely Dan solo ("Bodhisattva") in ~30-minute chunks purely during lesson time, with neither teacher nor student touching the material in between. After ~6 months to a year of this, both could play the entire solo — despite each session opening with near-total forgetting of the last one. The mechanism: every cold re-encounter forced a genuine re-learn, and each of those forced re-learns reinforced the material more deeply than the same total time spent unbroken would have. — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

The batch/collection scheduling method (concrete "how" for spacing + interleaving together)

Don't work one piece to completion before starting the next — turn a single target song into a batch of ~10–12 items (6 is fine too) and treat the whole batch as one project (a "concept album," not "a single"). Work a little on item 1, move to item 2, work a little, move on, and so on; when rotation brings you back to item 1, expect to have mostly forgotten it and treat that as the intended review moment, not a setback, before adding anything new to it.

Worked scheduling contrast — "learn 12 songs, one per month": the wrong version is literally finishing song 1 in month 1, then starting song 2 in month 2, etc. The right version under this method: treat all 12 as one rotating batch from day one, spacing and interleaving the touches across all of them from the start — claimed to converge on all 12 solid in less total time than the sequential version, because each piece gets ongoing spaced review instead of being learned once and abandoned. Progress feels slower moment-to-moment than "finishing" one thing fast (a "candy" satisfaction) — that's the expected, correct-feeling tradeoff, the same shape as the practice-vs-test accuracy tradeoff above. Generalizes past repertoire to techniques, exercises, and multi-course curricula — rotate between courses rather than finishing one before starting the next (same guidance given independently in How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop)).

Choose material worth reviewing forever. Since anything not actively used eventually needs a cold-start review regardless, the compounding payoff of this method only accrues on pieces you actually want to keep returning to — material picked purely to "check off a list" doesn't get the same benefit because there's no pull to revisit it. Worked examples of pieces the source has cold-started and relearned dozens of times over years, each time baking deeper into long-term memory: Bach's Cello Suite No. 1 Prelude, Tárrega's "Lágrima" and "Recuerdos de la Alhambra," Jerry Reed's "The Claw," "Autumn Leaves," "Georgia on My Mind."

— Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

The "principle of added stress" (context-variation beyond just item order)

Credited to a classical piano professor's lecture: deliberately add controlled stress/distraction into practice sessions so real performance conditions (nerves, an unfamiliar room, an audience) feel less foreign when they happen for real — concrete examples the professor used on himself: friends vacuuming around him or physically getting in his way while he practiced, background noise, changed lighting. Framed as the same underlying principle as interleaving applied more broadly than item order: a fixed, always-identical practice context creates an efficient but brittle "autopilot" — the same reason you recognize your dentist at the office but might not on the street. (Flagged by the source himself as a tangent — concrete but not deeply developed; a starting point for varying practice environment, not a worked system.) — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!

The practice journal — plan forward, don't log backward

A plain notebook or a document is enough; the discipline that matters is writing down what you're going to work on before the session, not logging what you did after. You'll typically be revisiting the same items tomorrow and the day after to bring them to an adequate level, so the journal is a rolling forward plan, not a diary.

  • Track concrete parameters in it: tempos, keys, tracks/material played over.
  • Interleaved practice only works if you actually know what you're rotating between — without a journal you sit down and "pick around," which defaults you back to whatever's already comfortable (the material you've played for years).
  • Two payoffs of writing it down in advance: (1) you show up with a plan instead of improvising your session on the spot; (2) you start to notice patterns — which things keep coming up as challenging, which you've been avoiding, which you thought you knew but keep getting wrong when you come back to them.
  • Rotate across roughly five categories per session: skills and technique, theory and ears, creative application, and tunes/tracks/licks/lines (the source names four cleanly and references "five different categories" without fully separating the fifth in the transcript — treat the fifth as likely a split between "tunes/tracks" and "licks/lines," and adjust the category list to fit your own instrument/style rather than trying to force an exact five-way split).

— Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

Session length: 15–20 minute chunks, enforced with a hard timer

You should not practice in long unbroken stretches — 15 to 20 minutes per chunk is about the maximum before focus drops off completely and you're "just spinning your wheels." Multiple shorter sessions spread across the day will always beat one long marathon.

  • Use a physical timer, hard cutoff, not a soft "when it feels done" stopping point. Seriff uses a cheap kitchen timer and moves on the instant it goes off, no exceptions — block sizes named: 30 seconds, 1 minute, 2 minutes, 3 minutes, 5 minutes (pick a size per item, not one fixed size for everything).
  • Traced to The Musician's Way by Gerald Klickstein (the transcript's auto-captions garble the name as "Jeroen Klijsen," but Seriff separately credits Gerald Klickstein by name later in the same video for the hands-separate method below, and both references describe the same teacher, so this is very likely one person the captions rendered two different ways — treat "Jeroen Klijsen" as a caption artifact for Gerald Klickstein).
  • This is the same underlying rule as The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice's day-to-day spaced-vs-massed guidance ("spaced daily reps beat one long cram session" — 30 min/day beats one 2-hour block, with the same hard-timer mechanic) — two different teachers converging on the identical mechanism and even a similar timer-based enforcement method.

— Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

The additive approach (chunking)

Anders Ericsson's Peak calls this chunking; Seriff's practical name for it is the additive approach, and frames it as one of the most practical applications of deliberate practice there is. Generalizes to any material — a chord progression, a lick, anything being learned — regardless of difficulty.

Method, worked on a 4-chord progression (G, Em, D, C):

  1. Don't try to play the whole thing first. Start with just the first piece alone — here, the G chord. Don't play through it, just play the one chord, 3–5 times, with a small pause between reps, until it's solid.
  2. Add the next piece and drill the pair, still without playing through the rest. G then D — not the full progression, just the two-piece unit, pausing between reps.
  3. Add the third piece the same way. G, Em (as the third addition in the demonstrated order) — stop, repeat, pause between reps.
  4. Add the final piece, arriving at the complete progression only after each smaller piece was already solid on its own.

(general starting point: 3–5 clean reps per addition before adding the next piece, with a deliberate pause between each rep — the source doesn't give a stricter numeric bar than this)

— Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

Independent convergence, bass side — chunking applied to fixing a fretting-hand fingering rather than a chord progression. BassBuzz's "chunk it" tip for de-overwhelming a flying-fingers fix on a one-finger-per-fret bass exercise: work a small handful of notes (e.g. just the first five of the riff) in slow motion, as much as needed, until it feels smooth and comfortable, then move on to the next chunk, then the next, then start piecing them together — same core shape as Seriff's method above (small solid pieces first, whole thing last), applied to a fretting-hand coordination fix rather than a chord-progression memorization task. Full exercise: One-Finger-Per-Fret 5-Level Daily Drill. — BassBuzz, Practice THIS Daily (10 Mins)

Hands-separate practice

For anything technically demanding, credited to studying classical guitar with Gerald Klickstein:

  1. Work the fretting-hand shape alone first, with no picking/strumming at all, until it feels solid.
  2. Mute the strings and drill the picking/strum pattern alone, isolated from the fretting hand entirely. (Worked example strum pattern: down-down-up-up-down-up.)
  3. Combine without sounding it yet: fret the chord shapes with the left hand while miming the strum pattern in the air with the right hand — full coordination rehearsal before the two hands are actually allowed to make sound together.
  4. Only after that does the actual playing happen.

Aim for 3–5 clean repetitions at each stage before moving to the next one. Seriff still uses this himself, not just with students, whenever something is proving genuinely challenging.

— Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

Independent convergence, different instrument and channel — bass-specific worked example, applied to speed rather than a new coordination skill: BassBuzz recommends the same hands-separate isolation specifically for recovering technique that backslides under tempo ("death by speed") — solid slow-tempo technique commonly falls apart once a line speeds up, and working each hand alone first is offered as the fix rather than just "practice slower." Mechanics: mute the strings with the plucking hand and drill fretting alone, humming the bassline's pitches rather than relying on audible confirmation from actually sounding the notes — this isolates and trains flying-fingers control and fretting pressure without the plucking hand's timing demands competing for attention; then flip it — mute with the fretting hand and drill plucking alone, again humming along, reading the tab to confirm which string each note falls on and noting which plucking transitions feel hardest; only recombine once each hand is independently solid. Named payoff: with both hands "not sucking by themselves," ramping up to full speed afterward is a much smoother process than going in cold on both hands at once. — BassBuzz, Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix)

Target the trouble spot directly — don't restart from the top

The average player, on a mistake mid-passage, either restarts from the beginning or glazes over the error — which means the opening of a piece/progression/song gets drilled far more than the actual problem material, and the real trouble spot never gets fixed. Result: players get very good at the first section of a piece specifically because they always restart there.

Instead: the instant something breaks down, go directly to that specific spot — "every time you hit the C chord, you botch it → go straight to the C" — and isolate and drill just that trouble spot rather than replaying the whole passage around it hoping it smooths out.

— Daniel Seriff, How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)

Independent convergence, different channel, same source material: Jared (Sound Guitar Lessons) arrives at the identical principle citing the same Ericsson/Peak material directly — "push yourself well outside your comfort zone and see what breaks down first, then design a practice technique aimed at improving that particular weakness" — plus a case study (research subject "Steve," extending digit-span memory) showing an apparent hard ceiling was really just one or two specific problem components, not the whole skill maxing out; also cites a doctor-performance study showing skill can decline, not just plateau, once a task stops being challenging. Full extraction on Repetition with Manipulation (Getting Past a Plateau). — Jared, How to Get Better at Guitar - The science of getting past a plateau

internalizing-a-tune-through-repetition.title: Internalizing a Tune Through Repetition
internalizing-a-tune-through-repetition.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — a process for learning a new tune (a jazz standard from a fake book, or any song) that leans on sustained repetition over analysis-first study, with harmonic analysis and lyric-driven feel folded in as later passes rather than the starting point.

The core process, in order

  1. Play the melody with the chords, off the page, over and over until basic comfort sets in. No shortcuts — this is the same "melody + chords" starting point Chord Melody Arranging and Chord-Tone Soloing both assume as prerequisite knowledge of a tune.
  2. As comfort grows, start noticing different ways to play it — alternate voicings, and where the passing chords in the tune actually are (the same passing-chord vocabulary Melodic-Harmonic Blending (Comping While Soloing)'s every-beat drill surfaces deliberately; here it emerges naturally from repetition instead).
  3. Listen to as many recorded versions of the tune as possible. The stated payoff is specific: different versions carry a rough sense of the tune's own history/lineage, can be radically different from each other and genuinely inspiring, and are a real source of passing chords and rhythmic approaches that repetition alone won't surface — this step feeds back directly into step 2.
  4. Play it over and over until it becomes meditative — described as needing an hour or more of sustained repetition before a tune genuinely "opens up." The framing is explicit: you have to unlock a tune's secrets, and the only way to do that is to actually internalize it through time spent, not through faster analysis.
  5. Once memorized (eyes off the page), bring in the lyrics as a separate, later pass. Looking at the lyrics' phrasing and meaning is flagged as a genuine tangent away from harmonic thinking — it pulls attention from chords/notes toward the lyric's emotional content, which is a different creative source, not a distraction to avoid. A concrete effect: if the lyric's meaning calls for "opening up," that can translate directly into a musical choice — e.g. reaching for a more open-voiced chord at that moment — a vibe-driven harmonic decision arrived at through the words rather than through substitution theory. → Reharmonization, Chord Substitution

Why this order, not analysis-first

The process deliberately front-loads raw repetition (steps 1–2, mostly mechanical) before the two research-heavy inputs (recordings, lyrics) that require the tune to already be somewhat under the hands — comparing other versions or following lyric phrasing against a tune you can't yet play smoothly just adds cognitive load without payoff. Repetition itself is treated as the primary internalization mechanism; recordings and lyrics are additive color layered on afterward, not competing starting points.

interval-ladder--how-to-run-it.title: How to run it
interval-ladder--how-to-run-it.html:
• Say the interval name out loud as you play it. The point is connecting three things — the name, the semitone count, and the shape — and the name is the one that falls off if you don't voice it.
  • Do it in a second key. Starting from the 5th fret of the low E is comfortable and therefore memorisable as a picture rather than a system. Move it to the A string and the B-string offset changes everything, which is the real lesson.
  • The B string breaks the pattern. Guitar is tuned in fourths except G→B, which is a major 3rd. Every cross-string interval shape shifts by one fret once the B string is involved. Running the ladder in order is what makes that a known quantity instead of a recurring surprise. → Guitar Positions
  • Five minutes. This is a warm-up, not a workout.

learning-theory-on-the-fretboard-not-on-.note: Learning Theory on the Fretboard, Not on Paper
learning-theory-on-the-fretboard-not-on-.title: Learning Theory on the Fretboard, Not on Paper
learning-theory-on-the-fretboard-not-on-.html:
A methodology principle, not a specific exercise: any music theory concept has to be translated into a fretboard-specific practice exercise before it actually becomes usable, or it stays inert knowledge that never shows up in real playing. Complements Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills (how to structure a session once you've decided what to work on) — this note is about how to convert an abstract theory concept into something worth putting in that rotation in the first place.

The core claim

Studying theory abstractly (a theory book, a chart, the musical staff) doesn't transfer to playing until it's been re-derived on the actual instrument. Recognizing a rule intellectually ("I know the 2 chord in a major key is minor") is not the same skill as being able to produce it under your fingers on demand — the abstract version and the instrument-specific version are treated as genuinely separate pieces of knowledge that don't automatically link. Analogy given directly: studying theory on paper without applying it to guitar is like learning to swim by reading about swimming, or learning music theory "on a tuba" and hoping it transfers to guitar without a second translation step.

Why abstract study specifically fails to click: a theory book presents concepts in the composer's/notation domain (the staff), which is its own separate "instrument" with its own fluency requirement — studying theory there is legitimate but doesn't by itself buy fretboard fluency, any more than fluency on a different physical instrument would.

The method: translate every concept into your own guitar-specific exercise

Given any theory concept, the practice task is to design a fretboard exercise for it yourself — not to look one up and drill it, but to work out how this specific idea maps onto strings and frets as part of the learning. Four worked examples given as templates for the pattern, not as an exhaustive list:

  1. Modes, worked one string at a time. Once you know the major scale's own half-step/whole-step skeleton (3-4 and 7-1 are half steps, everything else whole steps), each mode's formula ("Mixolydian = major scale with a flat 7") gets played out on a single string, so the sound of the altered degree is heard immediately rather than just named.
  2. The circle of fourths, mapped as a physical guitar shape: from any root, the note a fourth up sits on the identical fret, one string higher — walking straight up the string set reproduces the whole circle of fourths as one continuous physical motion rather than a memorized chart.
  3. Interval identification ("what's a fifth above this note"), done live on random notes anywhere on the neck instead of on paper — play any note, find its fifth, and use the ear to confirm before checking, so an error is caught by sound rather than just by rule.
  4. The diatonic chords of a key, played straight through — for each scale degree, play its chord and say its quality out loud (I: major, ii: minor, iii: minor, IV: major, V: major, vi: minor, vii°: diminished) ascending then descending through the full seven, physically pattern-matching the major-minor-minor-major-major-minor-diminished sequence to the fretboard rather than memorizing it as a list.

When a concept doesn't have a design-your-own answer yet (the source's own example: chord substitutions, for a player not yet equipped to invent a fretboard exercise for it) — that's a legitimate temporary limit, not a failure; the guidance is to keep reaching toward being able to design one, not to force a premature exercise.

Why this compounds: one exercise covers many songs at once

Working a theory structure on the fretboard (rather than memorizing it per-song) generalizes across the whole repertoire that structure appears in — recognizing "this progression is a I-vi-IV-V, moved around" replaces memorizing that same shape separately for every song that happens to use it. Framed as the actual payoff of doing the translation work: tonal music runs on a small, closed set of underlying relationships (12 notes, 7-note diatonic scales), so one well-internalized fretboard structure is doing double duty across "thousands of songs at once" rather than being single-use knowledge.

"Scratching your head" is real practice time

A direct counter to the instinct that practice only counts when notes are being played fast and continuously: pausing, being stuck, and consciously working out how a concept fits under your hands is named explicitly as good practice time for theory specifically — the opposite habit (repeating something fluidly without that friction) is called out as often not good practice. This is scoped to theory/conceptual work; for pure technique, the source draws the line the other way — sitting and thinking without playing is not the useful mode there.

parallel-scale-alternate-picking-drill-o.note: Parallel Scale Alternate-Picking Drill (One-Note Mode Switching)
parallel-scale-alternate-picking-drill-o.title: How to run it
parallel-scale-alternate-picking-drill-o.html:
• 10-15 minutes daily. Change the scale/mode pairing weekly (e.g. next week: major → Lydian; the week after: natural minor → Dorian or melodic minor).
  • Rotate which string pair you use (low E/A, B/high E, etc.) once the D/G pair is comfortable, so the horizontal-visualization skill generalizes across the neck.
  • Think the actual note names while playing, not just finger positions — the drill is explicitly framed as failing its purpose if you memorize "where fingers go" for each variant instead of "which note I'm altering."

practice-mindset-hard-truths-and-realist.note: Practice Mindset — Hard Truths and Realistic Expectations
practice-mindset-hard-truths-and-realist.title: Practice Mindset — Hard Truths and Realistic Expectations
practice-mindset-hard-truths-and-realist.html:
Eight practice-relevant observations from Brandon D'Eon's "25 Hard Truths About Guitar," extracted from a much longer, mostly-comedic list of mindset/industry commentary. Grouped here as realistic-expectation-setting rather than technique instruction.

  • Your rhythm playing is probably worse than you think. "Rhythm" here means literally playing in time with a metronome, not comping chords. Diagnostic: play a simple strum pattern against a metronome — many experienced players fail this cleanly regardless of years played.
  • Most practice isn't practice — it's just playing. Intentional, goal-directed work on a specific weakness is a different activity from noodling on material you already know, not a lesser version of the same thing.
  • You aren't as good as you sound to yourself. Self-perceived skill runs reliably inflated (the "most drivers rate themselves above average" bias, applied to playing). Fix: record yourself playing your best material and listen back. See Recording Yourself for Self-Diagnosis for the fuller method.
  • Performance conditions cost real, measurable skill. Playing for someone else in real time can cost roughly half your practiced skill level (one reported student estimate: closer to 80%) — a function of the changed environment/judgment context, not a loss of underlying ability. Practice performance conditions deliberately (playing for others, recording live) rather than assuming solo fluency transfers automatically.
  • Fixing an ingrained bad habit feels like temporary regression — expect it, don't read it as failure. A real technique correction (e.g. changing pick grip) typically dips performance for weeks to months before recovering past the prior level.
  • "Finding your own voice" too early is usually avoidance of studying established players. The actual sequence: study the language first (transcription, vocabulary from players you admire), and an original voice follows from having material to draw on — not from deliberately avoiding influence.
  • "I just play by ear" as an exclusive claim is often theory-avoidance dressed as a virtue. Playing by ear is a legitimate skill on its own; treating it as the only legitimate approach is usually a coping frame for skipped or abandoned theory study, not a real methodological stance.
  • Splitting practice across many instruments at once dilutes skill on all of them. Build real depth on one instrument before adding the next, rather than developing several simultaneously.

recording-yourself-for-self-diagnosis.title: Recording Yourself for Self-Diagnosis
recording-yourself-for-self-diagnosis.html:
A self-teaching process — how to use recordings of your own playing to do the job a teacher would otherwise do: listen to your playing, identify what to work on, and evaluate whether it's actually improving. Complementary to The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice rather than a slice of it — the Five Pillars framework says what categories a complete practice system covers; this note answers how you find out what needs work inside any of those pillars without a teacher in the room. Also a natural partner to Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction (which analyzes other people's recorded playing) and Woodshedding Changes with a Looper (which uses recording/looping as a rehearsal tool, not a diagnostic one) — this note is specifically about turning a recording of yourself into an accurate, actionable diagnosis.

Why recording beats live self-assessment

While you're playing, your attention is on performing — you can't simultaneously give full analytical focus to how it actually sounds. Recording splits the two tasks apart in time: play now, evaluate later, each with full attention. Recording is specifically good at catching things that are hard to hear in the moment: swing feel (triplet-feel eighths vs. straight/even), general phrasing habits, staying stuck in one octave/register of the instrument, and other phrasing tendencies that only become obvious from the outside. — Jens Larsen, Guitar Practice - How To Be Your Own Teacher

Setup

  • Video, not just audio — a smartphone is sufficient; get clear enough framing to actually see your hands if you're checking technique.
  • Protect the audio signal. If the recording distorts, you lose the ability to judge timing/phrasing detail and some notes drop out entirely — a bad recording defeats the exercise before you even listen back. Basic mic distance/level care matters more than gear quality; "a phone and a coffee mug on the table" is explicitly enough.
  • Dedicated technique-review use: point the camera specifically at your picking hand (or fretting hand) for a session focused purely on mechanics, independent of how the notes sound.
  • Metronome before backing track when starting out. A metronome is the harder, more honest test — it forces you to generate and hold your own sense of time/groove rather than riding a backing track's built-in feel. Once your own time is solid, move to a backing track or a groove app (Drum Genius named) to test whether you actually lock in with a real rhythm-section feel. — Jens Larsen, Guitar Practice - How To Be Your Own Teacher

The obstacle: nobody likes hearing themselves back

Near-universal, not a personal flaw — even Allan Holdsworth and Michael Brecker were famously uncomfortable listening to their own recordings. Everything you play already sounds like a cliché to you because you've already practiced it, even when it sounds fresh to a listener. It gets easier with repetition — push through the discomfort rather than avoiding the recordings. Two concrete counter-moves:

  • Keep a running list of three things you're working on and three things you already do well, side by side — stops the process from turning into pure self-criticism.
  • Don't listen back immediately — let time pass first. Right after playing you still remember what you meant to play and where you flinched, and that memory biases how you hear the take. Waiting (same logic labels use when deciding which take makes an album — distance first, then judge) removes the bias so you're hearing what's actually on the recording. — Jens Larsen, Guitar Practice - How To Be Your Own Teacher

The evaluation checklist — three rules, applied every time you review a recording

  1. Don't get distracted from the one thing you're evaluating. If the recording is for checking eighth-note swing feel, play long eighth-note lines and listen only for that — don't get pulled into judging melodic content, phrase interest, or any other flaw you happen to notice in the same take. Note other issues for their own dedicated pass; evaluating everything at once evaluates nothing well.
  2. Name the gap specifically — never just "good" or "bad." "That was bad, make it better" is the worst feedback a teacher can give because it's not actionable. Turn a vague reaction into a specific, exercise-able target: "I need to play more evenly on a swing groove," "I need to play more laid-back." This requires already knowing what the target sound is and being able to hear the difference between that and your take — if you can't yet hear the target, that's the actual gap to close first (see Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction for building that reference).
  3. Measure progress over multiple sessions, and keep each recording short. One day's take-and-review won't show change — improvement shows up across several sessions, so record regularly (daily is a good habit) but keep each clip to a few choruses or a single chorus of a standard — long recordings turn the review itself into wasted practice time. Archive clips and periodically compare old against new; hearing real improvement is what sustains the motivation to keep doing this. — Jens Larsen, Guitar Practice - How To Be Your Own Teacher

A ready-to-use self-diagnosis session structure

Combine the above into a repeatable loop, usable as a drop-in stage inside any The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice session block:

  1. Pick one specific thing to check this session (a swing-feel question, a technique/hand-motion question, a "does this line lock with the band" question) — don't record a diagnostic session with no target.
  2. Set a metronome (or backing track, once time is solid) and record a short take — a chorus or two, not a long session.
  3. Let it sit — don't review immediately; come back after a break (hours, or the next day).
  4. Review against the single target only, and write down a specific, exercise-able gap (rule 2) — plus one thing that's already working, to balance the self-critical instinct.
  5. File the clip (with date + target) so it can be compared against a later take on the same target — this is what turns individual reviews into a visible progress trend.

Why bad technique has to be faced eventually (the case for feedback at all)

Bad technique has real consequences whether or not anyone corrects it — the correction isn't optional, only its source is a choice. Illustrated with a vivid personal anecdote: while studying upright bass, the source's teacher (Karen Zimmerman, Santa Rosa Symphony) placed a sharp pencil just below where his elbow should sit, because dropping the elbow ruins upright strength and intonation — not to stab him, but so that he would stab himself the instant he reverted to the bad habit. "Bad technique has consequences. Sometimes that's your teacher [with a pencil], but most of the time it's that you have to struggle way harder to play anything." The broader point: at some stage you have to actually face and fix a bad-technique habit rather than route around it indefinitely — a teacher's correction (however memorable) is just one source of the feedback that forces that reckoning; self-recording (below) is presented as the accessible substitute when a teacher isn't available. — BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

A concrete worked example of what real expert technique feedback looks like, given as a short on-camera cameo from guitar teacher Alex Leach: (1) when gripping a chord, already be thinking about the next chord shape rather than reacting to it after landing the current one; (2) tighten up excess picking-hand movement; (3) find a fixed anchor point on the guitar for the picking hand rather than leaving it floating. Useful less for the specific guitar content than as a template for what "concrete, actionable feedback" sounds like — three short, specific, checkable notes, not a vague "sounds a bit off." The source then used exactly these three criteria as the review checklist for his own self-recorded practice sessions (see below) — a direct worked example of turning one-time expert feedback into a repeatable self-assessment target. — BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

Self-assessment as a real substitute for a teacher, not just a stopgap

The case against treating a private teacher as unconditionally "the gold standard": most people don't have a teacher's access, time, or budget — but more importantly, self-taught musicians with no teacher at all still reach elite technique, which means the self-assessment skill is learnable on its own, not just a workaround. Named examples: Billy Sheehan ("king of all shredders," self-taught playing in bars and clubs), Paul McCartney (self-taught on bass), and Tina Weymouth (Talking Heads, self-taught in "just a few months"). The logic stated directly: those players must have had some self-feedback method, or they'd still be stuck with bad technique and rhythm — meaning "assess your own playing critically and improve it" is one underlying skill everyone eventually needs, whether or not a teacher is in the room. Reframing of a teacher's actual value, worth keeping alongside this note's own framing above: a good teacher's real contribution is helping a student build their self-assessment skill and giving them criteria to assess with — not fixing the playing directly. This is the same conclusion this note already reaches independently (see "The evaluation checklist" above) from a different channel and instrument, now with a second, independent argument for it. — BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

Named companion principle for what to actually record for — don't just repeat blindly: mindless, unfocused repetition of something already being played badly doesn't fix it — "if you practice playing crappily... you just get better at playing crappily." This is the reason a self-recording session needs a specific target (rule 1 in this note's evaluation checklist) rather than just capturing more reps of the same unexamined habit — repetition alone isn't deliberate practice, and recording without a specific question to check against just documents the bad habit instead of fixing it. — BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

repetition-with-manipulation-getting-pas.note: Repetition with Manipulation (Getting Past a Plateau)
repetition-with-manipulation-getting-pas.title: Repetition with Manipulation (Getting Past a Plateau)
repetition-with-manipulation-getting-pas.html:
Jared's (Sound Guitar Lessons) own named practice method, distilled from Anders Ericsson's Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise — the research-backed answer to why progress stalls at all and the concrete discipline for preventing/breaking through it. This is the theory layer underneath two notes already in the vault built on the same underlying mechanism from a different angle: Technique Is Part of the Path (The Red-Flag Repair Loop) (Jared's own "go directly to the exact spot" mid-session method — this note supplies the Ericsson research citation for exactly that move) and Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills (Daniel Seriff's "target the trouble spot directly, don't restart from the top," arrived at independently on a different channel, also citing Peak). Where those two notes are session-mechanics toolkits, this note is closer to The Practice Priority Pyramid's Stage 5 (Deliberate/challenging practice) — it's the research case for why that stage is the hardest one and why almost everyone avoids it.

Why plateaus happen

Improvement is driven by challenge, not by repetition volume. When you first attempt something new, you're forced to think — genuinely challenged — and that's what produces rapid early gains. The instant a skill reaches a "functional/acceptable" level, the brain (evolved to conserve effort and shortcut anything solved) stops treating it as a problem to think through — it becomes a formula, a routine, a habit — and progress halts at that exact moment, not gradually afterward. Doing more reps past that point doesn't help, because volume was never the variable driving the gains; novelty/challenge was. Ericsson's own supporting data point: doctors 20–30 years into practice score worse on objective performance measures than doctors 2–3 years out of school, because day-to-day practice of medicine mostly doesn't challenge them anymore — a skill can decline, not just stall, once it stops being pushed.

Don't mistake a plateau for a real skill ceiling. Ericsson: "When you first start learning something new it is normal to see rapid or at least steady improvement, and when that improvement stops it is natural to believe you've hit some sort of implacable limit... This is the major reason that people in every area stop improving." Jared's gloss: this is the actual mechanism behind "fixed mindset" — not an inherent hard ceiling, but a belief that becomes self-fulfilling the moment you stop pushing because of it. Treat every plateau as "task stopped being challenging," never as "this is my limit."

Find the actual weak component, not the whole passage

Ericsson's "Steve" case study (a research subject extending digit-span memory): what looked like a hard ceiling turned out to be one or two specific problem groups within the string, not overall capacity maxing out — fixing exactly those groups freed up the rest. Same shape in guitar practice: "any reasonably complex skill will involve a variety of components... when you reach a point at which you are having difficulty getting better, it will be just one or two of the components... not all of them."

Diagnostic method: push a little past your current comfort/ability and watch for what breaks down first — that's the real bottleneck. Worked example: speed up tempo past clean and note which spot goes wrong first, not the whole passage. Then go one level deeper than "that spot is hard" — is it a specific finger's technique, a pull-off, picking-hand tone, or time feel? Per Jared, correctly isolating the actual cause (rather than the felt/assumed one) is "the biggest thing" private teaching does — worked anecdote: a student was convinced a hard passage was a left-hand problem; the actual cause was the right hand missing a string, and once that got fixed the passage cleared immediately.

Ericsson's full recipe, stated directly: "First figure out exactly what is holding you back, what mistakes are you making and when. Push yourself well outside your comfort zone and see what breaks down first. Then design a practice technique aimed at improving that particular weakness." — and this is explicitly not the default: "trying this and that and hoping something works" is named as the common failure mode, even among experienced teachers.

The method: repetition with manipulation

Repetition is necessary to internalize anything, but identical repetition stops driving improvement once it stops being challenging — so repeat the material while deliberately varying it: a different spot on the fretboard, a different string set, a different position, a different key. This is the same underlying idea as The Practice Priority Pyramid's Rotation/Variation mechanic and Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's interleaving, but framed at the level of a single piece of material rather than a whole session's item rotation — "how else can I know this, where else can I play this."

  • Stated personal motivation, not just plateau-avoidance: Jared is explicitly wary of anything becoming a fully automatic habit — he feels it disconnects him from intentional, expressive playing. Automaticity is treated as a risk to guard against, not only a plateau symptom.
  • It's supposed to feel uncomfortable. Manipulation works precisely because it keeps you out of the comfort zone that causes plateaus — nobody finds it naturally pleasant, though it can become exciting/stimulating. Stated payoff over time: a genuine craving for the challenge, where a session with nothing to strive for starts to feel wrong.

Design exercises with strict, specific, pass/fail parameters

A self-designed exercise only works as a diagnostic if success/failure is unambiguous:

  • Concrete examples: "play this three times in a row at this tempo without buzzing a single note" (one buzz = fail, three clean at tempo = pass — no gray area); "improvise over this progression using only chord tones 3 and 5" (won't produce a great solo — that's not the point — it isolates one specific musicianship muscle, same logic as a weighted exercise targeting one muscle group).
  • Manipulate the rule once the current version is solid, to keep generating fresh challenge instead of re-running a drill that's already stopped teaching anything — swap chord tones 3/5 for 7/1, change the time signature from 4/4 to 3/4 on the same material, etc. (General starting point — no fixed rep count given; the constraint is what matters, not a specific number.)
  • Worked example — scale patterns instead of "just run the scale." Running a scale straight up and down produces solos that sound like "playing a scale." Fix: a written melodic pattern that forces jumping around inside the scale shape rather than moving linearly. Jared's own free resource for this specifically: a downloadable PDF of his top 3 pentatonic scale patterns for more melodic soloing (off-platform link in the video description, not captured here).

Self-diagnosis prompt (usable as a standing practice-journal question)

Three-part audit, directly mirroring Ericsson's recipe above: (1) where in your playing have you hit a plateau or felt stale, (2) what do you actually think the weak spot causing it is, (3) what specific exercise could you design to target exactly that. Pairs well with Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's forward-planning practice journal — this question is a good one to answer before a session rather than after.

resolving-seven-common-guitar-practice-d.title: Resolving Seven Common Guitar-Practice Debates
resolving-seven-common-guitar-practice-d.html:
Brandon D'Eon's resolved positions on seven commonly-contradicted pieces of guitar advice — mostly "both sides are right depending on your goal" rather than a single winner, but concrete enough to act on.

  1. Scales needed for soloing? Goal-dependent. Simple fills/riffs with a strong ear → not strictly required. Full-fretboard, any-key improvisation → required.
  2. Clean vs. distorted practice tone. Split by hand: clean tone for left-hand technique (legato, trills — distortion masks sloppiness a clean signal exposes). Distorted tone for right-hand technique (alternate/sweep picking — distortion amplifies muting and noise mistakes far more harshly than clean).
  3. Slow-gradual metronome climbs vs. short fast speed bursts. Use both, in sequence: push straight to a target tempo beyond your current plateau to break it (recruits different hand/forearm muscle patterns a comfortable tempo never activates), then grind for accuracy at that new tempo until it's clean.
  4. Learn technique through songs vs. dedicated exercises. Technique-dependent, judged by how musical isolated reps can be. Bending → songs (few bending exercises are musical enough to sustain engagement). Sweep picking → dedicated exercises (too many specific failure modes — ringing notes, pick angle, muting, spacing, hand-sync — for incidental song-learning to catch reliably).
  5. CAGED system: tool or crutch? His position: mostly a crutch beyond beginner level — it teaches memorized shapes rather than the underlying notes/scale-degree construction, and breaks down for voicings/positions outside the five shapes (worked example: a given Phrygian position ambiguously "fits" two different CAGED shapes at once). Useful for beginners specifically; the alternative is learning notes/construction directly. (Note: this vault's own material — CAGE System Scale Shapes, Positional CAGED Soloing with Matched Modes and Arpeggios — uses CAGED as a practical organizing tool; this is a real pedagogical disagreement worth knowing about, not an error to reconcile.)
  6. Does theory help or hurt creativity? Helps, with the same goal-dependent carve-out as #1 — pure-entertainment/song-playing goals don't strictly need it. "Theory kills creativity" is treated as usually post-hoc justification rather than a real trade-off.
  7. What does "phrasing" mean? (Definitional, not a real disagreement.) Two incompatible definitions circulate: content (which notes/phrases you choose) vs. delivery (dynamics/timing/articulation of the same notes — like saying the same sentence several different ways). Worth clarifying explicitly whenever the word shows up in feedback, since the two definitions imply different practice actions.

technique-is-part-of-the-path-the-red-fl.note: Technique Is Part of the Path (The Red-Flag Repair Loop)
technique-is-part-of-the-path-the-red-fl.title: Technique Is Part of the Path (The Red-Flag Repair Loop)
technique-is-part-of-the-path-the-red-fl.html:
Jared's (Sound Guitar Lessons) direct answer to a trap that shows up constantly once you have a real goal and a real path toward it (see The Practice Priority Pyramid): technique breaking down mid-session gets mentally filed as a separate, competing problem — "I should be working on my goal, but instead I have to go fix my technique" — which produces the feeling of getting derailed off the real path. His correction: technique isn't a fifth category alongside scales/positions/ear-training, it's the thing that lets any of those actually come out of your hands — so it belongs on the same path, targeted exactly as specifically as everything else on the checklist, not siphoned off into generic, unrelated drilling. Where The Practice Priority Pyramid and Vision-Driven Practice and the Overwhelm Reflex operate at the goal/vision level (what belongs on a practice list and why), this note operates one level down, in the middle of an actual session: what do you do the instant something on that list breaks. Companion practice-diagnosis note to Recording Yourself for Self-Diagnosis (Jens Larsen's parallel "find the gap, name it specifically" method) and shares its core spaced-return logic with Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's trouble-spot targeting.

The reframe: don't reach for the wrong ingredient

Burger analogy. Missing a bun for a burger and grabbing a baguette or croutons instead "solves" the shape of the gap (something bread-like) without solving the actual gap — the burger still isn't right. On guitar: when a passage breaks down technically, reaching for a generic, unrelated technique exercise is the baguette. The fix is always the exact missing ingredient — the exact flub, the exact arpeggio, the exact scale slur — not an adjacent substitute that feels productive.

Golf-fitness analogy. A golf-specific fitness trainer builds exercises (e.g. weighted medicine-ball rotations) targeted at the precise muscles/motions a golf swing uses — not generic advice like "get fit, go hiking on weekends," which improves cardio without making anyone a better golfer. Same logic for guitar technique: general technique drilling has real value, but targeted work aimed at the exact motion your goal requires is what actually closes the gap.

The red-flag repair loop (the core reusable method)

The general-purpose loop, demonstrated live across two case studies below:

  1. Play the real thing — the actual goal material (the piece, the improvisation, the passage), not a generic exercise.
  2. When something breaks down, treat it as a "red flag" — a data point, not a failure. "That was a problem" is useful information, not a reason to feel behind.
  3. Go directly to the exact spot, not the general area. Identify precisely what broke — which two fingers, which string transition, which tempo — rather than a vague sense that "the fast part" or "the sweep section" is hard. 🎬 Research backing (same channel, a separate video): Anders Ericsson's Peak gives this exact recipe — "push yourself well outside your comfort zone and see what breaks down first, then design a practice technique aimed at improving that particular weakness" — and a case study (a memory-research subject, "Steve") showing an apparent hard ceiling was actually just one or two specific problem components, not the whole skill maxing out. Full extraction on Repetition with Manipulation (Getting Past a Plateau). — Jared, How to Get Better at Guitar - The science of getting past a plateau
  4. Build or reach for the most direct, targeted fix for that exact flub — a "speed burst" (see below), a cross-string transfer (see below), or an isolated-tempo workshop against a backing track — whatever actually targets the specific mechanical gap.
  5. Test it small and fast — don't commit to a long, unverified detour. Explicit warning against going "off on a monthlong practice of this thing that you think was the solution" before confirming it's actually the right fix.
  6. Return to real playing as soon as possible. The isolated drill is a brief repair stop, not a new destination — the point is always to get back to the goal material, where the next red flag surfaces naturally.
  7. Repeat continuously — alternate between real playing and short targeted technique detours rather than doing either exclusively; expect to cycle through this many times in one session, not just once.
  8. Use your own red flags as your practice curriculum, not someone else's generic list. Direct paraphrase: instead of treating what a teacher or a book says to practice as the practice item, treat your own real, felt limitations from your own actual playing as the practice item — framed as the mechanism for becoming "your own best teacher."

Two named repair techniques

The "speed burst" (slow → fast → slow)

For a spot that's breaking down on synchronization specifically (e.g. two fingers not landing at exactly the same instant, not a raw-speed problem): repeat the exact transition slow, then fast, then slow again, as a repeated set. (General starting point — no fixed rep count or tempo ratio given; adjust to the spot.) Worked example: a Super Mario Bros. theme arrangement where fingers 1–2 and 4–3 weren't landing together — the speed burst measurably improved it across two practice days.

Cross-string transfer

Take any lick, arrangement passage, or fragment (named use case: classical/solo-guitar arrangement material) and deliberately move it to a different set of strings, without regard for whether it sounds musically "weird" there — the goal isn't a usable musical result on the new strings, it's that displacing a familiar shape from its comfortable position builds strength/flexibility/dexterity that transfers back to the original spot. Can be combined with the speed burst on the same passage.

Worked case study — 12-bar blues improv (the loop demonstrated live, start to finish)

Working "alternate hybrid picking" (alternate picking combined with the middle and ring/annular fingers simultaneously) applied to playing in octaves, over a 12-bar blues loop (four bars B♭7, two bars E♭7, back to B♭7, then a V–IV–I–V turnaround):

  1. Improvise for real over the loop while bringing in the octave/hybrid-picking technique — comes out sloppy (red flag).
  2. Don't default to a generic technique exercise. Workshop the exact motion against the backing track instead: strip away note/improvisation content entirely, focus purely on staying clean and relaxed at the current tempo.
  3. Once clean at that tempo, push the tempo up on the isolated technique, still ignoring note content.
  4. Recombine incrementally with real musical content — once the technique holds up, layer it back onto actual improvisation (e.g. outlining the chord tones of each change using the technique, mapping the next chord the same way), testing it inside real harmonic movement rather than in isolation.
  5. When it breaks again, that's expected — go back to the isolated drill, not backward through the whole practice plan. Loop steps 2–5 repeatedly within the session.

Why technique gains feel slower than conceptual gains — set expectations accordingly

Technique (strength, flexibility, dexterity) is physically slow to build: "watering a plant" analogy — growth is invisible while you're doing the work and only shows up after repeated sessions with recovery time between them (adaptation needs rest, not just repetition, so one long session doesn't substitute for several shorter ones spread out). This is contrasted with conceptual/vocabulary learning (a new scale, song, or chord shape), which can feel like visible same-session progress precisely because the underlying technique is usually already in place — you're just layering new information on top of existing physical capability. Practical implication: don't judge a technique fix by same-session results, and don't be discouraged when a fix takes days or weeks rather than one sitting — that's the expected shape of technique gains, not a sign the approach is wrong. Ear training is named as sharing this same slow-gain shape.

General conditioning still matters separately. This targeted-repair loop supplements, not replaces, a standing general technique routine — Jared references his own daily warm-up ritual (a free PDF, not detailed in this video — see Vision-Driven Practice and the Overwhelm Reflex's note on the same undetailed-but-consistent habit).

the-check-off-method-for-repertoire-prac.note: The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice
the-check-off-method-for-repertoire-prac.title: The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice
the-check-off-method-for-repertoire-prac.html:
A named practice-order method for learning written repertoire (a classical piece, a fingerstyle arrangement, solo guitar, any fully-notated melody) — Jared's own name for it is the "check-off method." Same channel/author as Backward Chaining Practice and shares that note's clean-reps-in-a-row gating mechanic, but a different combination order: Backward Chaining works end-to-beginning, one measure at a time; the check-off method builds a piece forward in pairs, deliberately alternating between drilling small units alone and drilling them combined, in a fixed pyramid pattern. Best suited to through-composed/written material rather than looser improvisational playing — Jared is explicit that this is for "something that is just written," not a looser or more improvised context.

The pyramid combination order

Worked example on an 8-measure passage (the opening of Bach's Bourrée in E minor from the Lute Suite, BWV 996, Jared's own solo-guitar arrangement):

  1. Measure 1 alone.
  2. Measure 2 alone.
  3. Measures 1+2 together.
  4. Measure 3 alone.
  5. Measure 4 alone.
  6. Measures 3+4 together.
  7. Measures 1–4 all together.
  8. Measure 5 alone.
  9. Measure 6 alone.
  10. Measures 5+6 together.
  11. Measure 7 alone.
  12. Measure 8 alone.
  13. Measures 7+8 together.
  14. Measures 5–8 together.
  15. Measures 1–8 (the whole passage) together.

The shape is: drill each single unit → drill the pair combined → once two pairs are both solid, combine the pair-of-pairs into a group of 4 → once two groups of 4 are solid, combine into a group of 8. This doubling structure generalizes to any passage length by continuing the same pattern (groups of 8 combine into 16, and so on) rather than being fixed at 8 measures. Segment boundaries follow phrasing, not always a literal barline — where a segment starts with a pickup beat, Jared always lands the segment on beat 1 of the following measure rather than cutting it exactly at the bar line.

(general starting point on segment size: single measures is "the most broken-down version you can do," explicitly recommended especially for classical material — but Jared says he often skips straight to a larger first unit, e.g. starting at 2 or 4 measures at once, when the material allows it, rather than always starting at 1 measure)

The gate: N clean reps in a row, not N reps total

Each segment isn't "checked off" until it's played correctly a set number of times consecutively — a genuine unbroken streak, not an accumulated tally. A single wrong note resets the count to zero, even if you were on the last rep of the target count.

  • Baseline demoed: 3 correct in a row. For anything higher-stakes or where real certainty is needed, push the target count well above 3 — Jared references wanting counts as high as 10 in a row for real assurance.
  • Why push the count up rather than stopping at 3: at a low count you risk "accidentally" getting it right three times without the passage actually being secure. At a high count (e.g. approaching 10), a slip becomes useful information rather than a setback — Jared describes an almost paradoxical relief at failing near the top of a high count ("Oh, good... that means I don't have it") because it confirms the segment genuinely isn't locked in yet, rather than letting a lucky streak create false confidence. The goal is explicitly not to minimize mistakes but to eliminate the possibility of them — over-program the segment so execution requires no conscious thought when it counts, freeing full attention for musical expression (dynamics, phrasing) instead.
  • Judge each rep at your own standard of strictness — a technically-correct rep with one small tone issue can still count if you decide it does; the point is a real, honest streak against whatever bar you set, not a rigid note-perfect requirement.

Tracking mechanism

Two interchangeable versions of the same system, either works:

  • On the printed sheet music itself, in pencil: bracket the measure groupings directly on the score (a bracket over measure 1, over measure 2, over measures 1+2, etc.) with a checkbox next to each bracket, checked off once that segment hits its clean-rep target. This was Jared's method "for years" — print the piece, draw brackets and checkboxes by hand.
  • A spreadsheet, one row per segment — lists every segment (measure 1, measure 2, measures 1+2, measure 3…) down the piece, with a column to track completion; scales to holding an entire repertoire list (multiple pieces) in one place rather than loose marked-up sheet music per piece.
  • Rep counter app: Jared uses an app called Multi Timer as a simple tap-counter for tracking reps toward the target streak in real time, especially once the target count goes past 3 or 4 and becomes hard to track by feel; the same app also runs his overall practice-session timer and a break timer (to cap how long a rest between segments runs).
  • No metronome for classical/expressive material — deliberately not used here, even though the demoed Bach passage is fairly metronomic by nature; the point is to leave room for expressive timing rather than mechanical timing, which a metronome would suppress during this drilling phase.

Why it beats normal "practice until it feels done"

The "shiny spot" bias: left unstructured, players default to replaying whatever is already comfortable, because it feels good and low-risk — Jared's analogy is cleaning a bathroom and gravitating back to the one spot that's already sparkling instead of the genuinely dirty one. The result (without a system) is a passage with a few measures drilled a hundred times and others drilled four times — an uneven "heat map" of security across the piece, with the real trouble spots the least rehearsed. Checking a segment off removes it from what you keep re-drilling, forcing attention onto whatever's still unchecked — i.e., onto the actual weak material — instead of onto the parts that already feel good.

Refresh is built in, not a separate maintenance step. Because later stages recombine already-checked-off smaller units (playing measures 1–4 together necessarily replays measures 1, 2, 3, and 4 again), the early segments get naturally re-exposed as the piece is built up, without needing a dedicated spaced-repetition pass bolted on afterward. If a checked-off segment later proves shaky when it resurfaces inside a bigger combination, the fix is simple: drill it again, at a higher rep count than before, rather than reworking the whole tracking system.

Origin and use case

Developed under real time pressure: Jared traces the method back roughly 10 years to being called, with only a few weeks' notice, to play a technically demanding new guitar/orchestra score (Stuart Copeland's re-imagined score for Ben Hur, performed with the Seattle Rock Orchestra and Copeland himself on drums) while already overcommitted elsewhere. The check-off method — used exclusively to prepare that part — is credited as the specific reason the performance came together in time and went well. Framed explicitly as a "secret weapon" for compressed prep time, but usable for any written piece regardless of deadline pressure.

the-five-essentials-of-guitar-practice.note: The Five Essentials of Guitar Practice
the-five-essentials-of-guitar-practice.title: The Five Essentials of Guitar Practice
the-five-essentials-of-guitar-practice.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — Daniel Seriff's answer, after 27 years of playing and 25,000 lessons taught, to "what would I focus on exclusively if I were starting over." Genre-agnostic (rock/blues examples throughout — Gilmour, Beck, Hendrix, Eric Johnson — rather than jazz), and organized around backing-track-driven improvisation as the delivery mechanism for all five, not scale-running in isolation. Compare The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice — Nathan Borton's five-pillar framework (ear/vocabulary/technique/theory/repertoire) covers similar ground from a jazz-vocabulary angle; Seriff's five are more execution-and-feel-focused (rhythm, immersive listening, non-verbatim scale practice, fretboard/theory in short bursts, and embellishment/expression) and slot in as a complementary, non-jazz-specific layer — his rhythm work overlaps Borton's Pillar 3 (technique), his immersive-listening step overlaps Pillar 1 (ear skills), and his fretboard/theory step overlaps Pillar 4, but the "never play scales straight up and down" rule and the five-embellishments rule have no equivalent in the Pillars note.

1. Rhythm — picking hand + groove, not just chords

Most players ignore the picking hand and rhythm generally, associating "rhythm" only with chords/comping — but it shapes every note played, lead lines included. Two drills, both run over a backing track, both improvised (not scale-run up/down):

  • Consistent Rhythms drill. Pick a backing track (Seriff demos a D minor one-chord vamp — D Dorian or D minor pentatonic both fit) and a subdivision — start with quarter notes, then build to eighth notes, triplets, then 16ths. Improvise, locking every note to that subdivision the whole time. "Slowing the rate of change" tool for when a subdivision is too fast to improvise cleanly at: repeat each note 4 times at that subdivision before moving to the next note, then thin to 2 times, then to 1 (full speed) as it gets comfortable — a graduated on-ramp rather than dropping straight into unbroken 16ths. Push tempo over time and work at "the edge of your ability" — Seriff uses Ableton Live to gradually speed up the backing track, but any backing-track player works.
  • Targeted Rhythms drill. Same backing track, still improvising, but instead of playing on every beat of the chosen subdivision, restrict yourself to one specific beat only — e.g. only on beat 2 (repeating "1-2, 1-2…" and making music out of just that hit), or only on "3-and" in eighth notes. Cycle through different target beats and subdivisions. Explicitly hard to make musical at first, but named as excellent for beat recognition and groove awareness — the payoff is a felt sense of where you are in the groove at all times, not just correct rhythm.

2. Immersive listening — absorb before you transcribe

Deliberately expose yourself to the most exciting playing you can find, then live inside a short piece of it before trying to reproduce any of it:

  • Pick a genuinely inspiring performance — classic (Gilmour, Beck, Hendrix) or something modern found on Instagram/YouTube.
  • Screen-record or audio-record the clip on your phone, then load it into a slow-down/looping app — Amazing Slow Downer or Transcriber named specifically — to isolate the part that inspires you.
  • Listen to that isolated fragment on repeat, as many times as possible, before attempting to play any of it. The mechanism (citing the book Decoding Greatness): mere presence around great work makes you better — you start to audiate it (hear it internally) before you're technically able to play it; passive listening alone absorbs the language.
  • Go deep on a few favorites rather than wide across many recordings — depth over breadth, same logic as vocabulary quality-over-quantity elsewhere in this vault's practice notes.
  • Only once ready, start picking notes out by ear, or fall back to learning them from the video if the ear isn't there yet — that's expected and fine.
  • Ear-training app named: Functional Ear Trainer — use it to build ear skill ahead of being able to physically locate notes on the guitar.

3. Scales and arpeggios — learn once, then never run them straight again

The core rule: once a scale, arpeggio, or pattern is learned well enough to visualize and play decently, stop practicing it verbatim up and down immediately. Verbatim up/down repetition — even a lot of it — will never translate into musical playing (Seriff calls out the classical-pedagogy assumption that it does as false).

  • "Limitation exercise" drill, concrete example — three-note-groups in D minor: once the pattern is under the fingers, don't run it top-to-bottom; apply it over a backing track in the same key. Don't start on the root/bottom note — start in the middle of the pattern. Mix up the note order (not just strict ascending/descending). Insert hammer-ons and pull-offs. Play short musical fragments rather than the whole pattern in sequence. Mistakes are explicitly okay — the goal is music, not accuracy.
  • Same treatment applies to two-string-group exercises (cites the shapes baked into Eric Johnson-style licks) — great for building speed, but running them straight up/down adds little; apply the same limitation-exercise treatment (backing track, broken order, fragments) to get real playing value from them.
  • Metronome vs. backing track: metronome practice is not the recommendation here — it's fine for advanced players but gives no real rhythmic feel feedback, only a click. Prefer practicing scale/arpeggio material against real backing tracks or downloaded drummer loops (cheap/free online) so the ear trains simultaneously with the fingers, feeling a real human groove rather than a click.

4. Fretboard knowledge and core theory — short daily bursts, not marathons

  • Do this work in short bursts of a few minutes a day, not long single sessions — Seriff explicitly regrets doing it "ad nauseam" (long sessions, all at once) early in his own playing and says the research favors short/frequent over long/occasional.
  • Foundation: master the major scale first — "all music theory comes from the major scale; if you don't understand the major scale, you don't understand music." Concrete goal: learn all 15 major scales (every key, including enharmonic spellings), both forwards and backwards, both said or sung aloud and played on the fretboard.
  • Concrete starting drill: in the key of C, spend a few minutes a day saying (or better, singing) the natural note names on each string while playing them, ascending string by string up to the 12th fret and back, then continuing as high as you can go and back down. Repeat/expand the same drill key by key as C becomes solid.

5. Embellishment — the "mojo" that makes correct notes sound musical

The insight that took Seriff years to land on: technically-correct, in-key playing that still sounds "vanilla"/bland isn't a vocabulary problem — the great players are often playing the same notes, just embellished. A friend (Ben Forehand) diagnosed this in him directly as "needing more vibe."

  • Five core embellishments to apply to essentially every note, layered on top of clean plucking: 1. Slides — into a note from another scale tone, or from just a half step below. 2. Hammer-ons. 3. Pull-offs. 4. Bends — e.g. bending up into a target note from a half step below. 5. Vibrato.
  • Drill: take existing licks/lines (including material from Essentials 1–3 above) and deliberately re-play them inserting one or more of the five embellishments on notes that were previously just plucked clean — the goal stated explicitly is maximum "sauce" in every moment, not just correct pitches and rhythm.
