blues-scales-and-blue-notes.title: Blues Scales and Blue Notes
blues-scales-and-blue-notes.html:
The melodic half of the blues — what to play, and why notes that should clash don't.

Companion to Blues Form and Harmony, which covers the form and the chords.

Blue notes

The ♭3, ♭5 and ♭7, played against a major or dominant background.

That's the definition (BLU-05, where you answered "tritone" — the ♭5 is part of a tritone with the root, but blue notes are the three flattened degrees, not an interval).

They're "blue" because they sit against the harmony rather than inside it. The ♭3 rubs against the chord's major 3rd, the ♭7 against the major 7th you'd expect in a major key, the ♭5 against nothing at all — it's pure passing colour.

The blues scale

Minor pentatonic plus the ♭5.

In A: A C D E♭ E G — six notes.

Built from A minor pentatonic (A C D E G) with the E♭ added as a chromatic passing note between the 4th and 5th.

The ♭5 is a passing tone, not a resting note. Sit on it and it sounds wrong; pass through it between D and E and it's the most characteristic sound in the vocabulary.

Why the ♭3 isn't just wrong

The question the whole strand hinges on (BLU-14).

The blues scale has a ♭3 (C in A). The I7 chord has a major 3rd (C♯ in A7). Played together those are a semitone apart — in functional harmony, an error.

Three reasons it isn't:

  1. The friction is the sound. The grind between ♭3 and ♮3 is what "bluesy" means. Remove it and you have a major-key melody over dominant chords, which is something else entirely.
  2. Blues isn't functional major/minor. As Blues Form and Harmony covers, the dominant 7th is the home sound here, not a tension. The scale is imposed over the chords rather than derived from them, so "belonging to the key" isn't the test.
  3. The note is a region, not a pitch. Players bend the ♭3 up toward the natural 3rd and sit between them. On a guitar that's a quarter-tone bend; on a voice it's just where the note lands. What's notated as a ♭3 is played as somewhere between the two.

That third point is the one that resolves the apparent contradiction. The blues has microtonality built in, and notation can only approximate it — which is also why tuning software struggles with blues vocals (see Vocal Tuning).

What to play over the I7

Mixolydian, the blues scale, or a blend — usually the blend.

  • Mixolydian (major with a ♭7) matches the chord exactly. It has the major 3rd, so it sounds "correct" and sweet.
  • The blues scale has the ♭3 and the ♭5, so it grinds.
  • The blend is what most players actually do: blues scale for the grit, Mixolydian's major 3rd and 6th for the sweetness, moving between them.

Why minor pentatonic works over dominants at all (SCL-14, also missed): besides the blue-note friction, it avoids the natural 4th — which genuinely clashes with the chord's major 3rd and is the one note that sounds like a mistake rather than a choice.

That's the underrated half. The minor pentatonic isn't "wrong notes that happen to work" — it's a set that keeps the productive friction and removes the destructive one.

Kansas City blues scale

A named, guitaristic five-note distillation of the blues scale, sourced from a Nathan Borton breakdown of Grant Green's playing — captured here as a distinct, named blues-vocabulary variant even though the exact interval formula wasn't given in the free source material (gated to the creator's paid lesson).

  • Five notes, not six — trims the six-note blues scale (minor pentatonic + ♭5) down further, described as distilling "the sound of the blues scale."
  • Emphasizes the 6th degree specifically — called out as the note the scale "really focuses on," distinguishing it from a plain minor-pentatonic-plus-♭5 reading.
  • Movable, guitaristic pattern — designed to be repositioned around the fretboard rather than tied to one box shape, used for riffing and generating melodic ideas rather than outlining a fixed lick.
  • Flag: exact scale-degree spelling not confirmed from the source captions — treat as a named device to revisit if a fuller breakdown surfaces, not a verified formula. → 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Cool Blues

Practical

  • One scale over all three chords works. A blues scale in A covers A7, D7 and E7. That's unusual and it's why blues is a good first improvising vocabulary.
  • Following the changes sounds different. Switching scale with each chord (A Mixolydian over A7, D Mixolydian over D7) is more "correct" and less bluesy. Both are valid; know which you're doing.
  • Target the chord tones on the strong beats, pass through the blue notes. The same principle as Non-Harmonic Tones — the colour notes live between the structural ones.
  • The ♭7 is in the chord, so it's not really a blue note against a dominant — it only reads as blue against a major context.
secs: What to play over the I7

melody-writing.title: Melody Writing
melody-writing.html:
Writing a single strong melody (contour, motion, range, phrase structure), and writing more than one melodic line that plays well together — giving each melody a distinct job (rhythmic vs. harmonic) rather than writing two lines that compete for the same role. Companion to Bassline Writing (the low-end equivalent of "give it one job") and Arrangement and Song Form (where multiple melodic layers get introduced/removed across sections). Motif development is Motivic Development; the harmony a melody is written against is Loop-Based Harmony and Non-Harmonic Tones.

Expanded 2026-08-04

Six sections added to back the MEL strand — melody against harmony, loop vs changes, register and intensity, tension building, hooks, and boring-melody triage. The strand scored 20%.

Two complementary roles for simultaneous melodies

  • Rhythm-first melody: pick ONE note (typically the scale's root) and write an interesting rhythm/groove using just that single repeated note — establish the groove before worrying about pitch at all. Only afterward, shift some of those notes up or down the scale for melodic interest, so the rhythm stays the anchor and pitch variation is layered on top of an already-solid groove, not the other way around.
  • Harmony-first melody: build a second, contrasting line from longer, more sustained notes, spending the most time on the STRONGEST scale degrees (the root and the fifth), and using weaker scale tones (2nd, 4th, etc.) as brief stepping-stones connecting one strong note to the next. This line's job is harmonic weight, not rhythmic interest — long notes, strong intervals, minimal rhythmic complexity.
  • Played together, a rhythm-first melody and a harmony-first melody read as two independent, complementary parts rather than two lines competing for the same "job" — one carries groove, the other carries harmonic identity.

Contour, motion, and range (writing ONE strong melody)

Section sourced from You Suck at Producing, You Suck at Producing: Melody

  • Constrain the range with an explicit top and bottom note before writing anything — pick an upper bound and a lower bound (roughly an octave-plus-a-third apart is a reasonable starting range) and never go outside that band while improvising — this single constraint does most of the work of preventing an aimless, directionless melody; without it, a melody written with "no constraints" tends to wander unpredictably in both pitch and phrase length rather than developing a shape.
  • Balance melodic contour: what goes up should come back down, and vice versa — contour is the melody's overall shape over time (rising, falling, sitting still); a strong melody has a sense of balance in that shape — after traveling upward for a while, bring it back down rather than letting it drift indefinitely in one direction, and the reverse. This balance, combined with the range constraint above, naturally produces an "arc" shape with a single clear peak note rather than a flat or erratic line.
  • Balance melodic motion: after stepwise movement, take a leap (and vice versa) — contour also has a type of motion, not just a direction: stepwise motion (moving between adjacent scale degrees) reads as smooth/connected, while leaps (larger intervals) read as more dramatic. A strong melody balances the two — after a stretch of stepwise movement in one direction, a leap (often back the other way) keeps the line from feeling monotonous; a melody that's all steps or all leaps reads as one-dimensional.
  • Antecedent/consequent phrasing: repeat the first half of a phrase exactly, vary the second half — write a melodic phrase, then write a second phrase whose FIRST half is identical to the first phrase's first half (the "antecedent," a question), but whose SECOND half is different (the "consequent," the answer) — same opening, different close, across a pair of phrases. This call-and-response repetition-with-variation structure is what makes a melody read as cohesive and "groovy" rather than as an unstructured stream of notes, and is a much stronger default than either exact repetition (boring) or constant variation (aimless, the "no constraints" failure mode above).

Melody against harmony

Added 2026-08-04 — the MEL strand's biggest gap.

The section above treats melody in isolation: contour, motion, range. But the same melody note means something different depending on the chord underneath it, and choosing that relationship deliberately is most of what separates a written melody from a hummed one.

Which chord tone you land on changes the feeling, not the harmony:

Landing note Effect
Root Settled, final, safe. Where a phrase goes to end.
3rd Colours the chord — brighter or sadder. More melodic than the root, less final.
5th Stable but neutral. Strong without being conclusive.
7th Leaning, unresolved, wants to move.
9th Open and floating. Colour without changing the chord's function.

Landing on the root constantly is the single most common reason a melody sounds boring — it agrees with the harmony on every downbeat, so nothing is ever in tension. Target 3rds and 7ths on strong beats and the same notes suddenly read as a melody rather than an arpeggio.

The 9th deserves special mention because it's the pop move: it isn't in the triad, so it adds colour without redefining the chord — which is why toplines landing on the 9th feel emotive and unresolved. See Loop-Based Harmony.

Non-chord tones are where the line lives. The notes between the chord tones — passing tones, neighbours, suspensions — are most of what makes a melody sound composed. See Non-Harmonic Tones.

Singability, range, and climax

Added 2026-08-05, sourced from Max Konyi, What Makes a Good Melody? | Musical Warp Drive - Part 2.

  • Design for singability, and test it by asking whether the melody could be hummed from memory. Steps (movement to the next scale tone) are easy to sing; leaps (a third or bigger) are hard. A good melody usually blends both, but when singability specifically matters (writing for a vocalist), shrink oversized leaps down to steps and keep only one or two moderate leaps — a demonstrated revision kept just a single 6th at the very end of an otherwise stepwise line and was audibly easier to sing without losing the melody's identity.
  • Range: an octave to an octave-and-a-half is the practical ceiling most strong, singable melodies actually use. Past roughly two octaves most melodies start losing singability and listeners start losing track of the contour — wide-range melodies can absolutely work, but treat octave-and-a-half as the default unless there's a reason to go wider.
  • A strong melody usually has one climax — a single high point it rises to and falls from, occurring only once. It doesn't have to sit in the middle of the phrase (start, end, and anywhere between all work) — the point is a melody that repeatedly revisits its own top note reads as weaker than one with a single clear peak.
  • Outlining chord changes: build the melody substantially from the underlying chords' own tones so it implies the harmony even with zero chords sounding. Tested directly against a control: a melody built from arpeggiated chord tones still clearly implied the chord progression when isolated with no chords playing, while a melody with constant pitch repetition, static/repetitive rhythm, and arbitrarily-placed notes implied none of the underlying harmony at all in isolation — one of the clearest structural tells of a strong vs. weak melody. See the landing-note table above for which chord tone to target; this is the same idea applied across a full arpeggiated line rather than single landing notes. → Non-Harmonic Tones, Chord Progressions

Order of operations: chords first vs. melody first

Added 2026-08-05, sourced from Max Konyi, What Makes a Good Melody? | Musical Warp Drive - Part 2.

  • Chords first (the majority approach, especially in modern/pop music): write the full progression, then compose the melody on top of the already-sounding chords. The resulting melody is naturally well-integrated with the harmony because it was written in direct response to it.
  • Melody first: write the melody with zero chords sounding, from an internal/felt sense of harmony only, then compose new chords underneath it afterward. Produces a genuinely different, sometimes more original line, precisely because it isn't pre-shaped by existing harmony — but it commits you to writing fresh chords for it. Recycling old chords under a melody-first line, even in the same key, tends to clash; a melody written free of harmony generally needs harmony written specifically to fit it.
  • Practical takeaway: pick the order deliberately rather than by default. Chords-first is faster and produces tighter harmonic integration; melody-first is slower but a reliable way to break out of chord-progression-driven melodic habits when writing feels formulaic.
  • A third order, distinct from both above: rhythmic-track-first, where the beat/bass/synth groove is built before any vocal melody exists, rather than starting on a chord instrument at all. Finneas contrasts his earlier process — sit at a piano, write the song, THEN migrate into a DAW and record vocals/piano/drums/bass around it (Billie Eilish's "My Future" was written exactly that way) — against building from a track's rhythmic components first. His stated conclusion, after a sparse Trilian bass patch reset a stalled verse's whole rhythmic feel and pulled a new vocal groove out of Billie: starting rhythmic-track-first surfaced songwriting choices "that would never have been true" if they'd started on acoustic guitar — the starting instrument/approach actively shapes what the song can become, not just how fast it gets written. → Arrangement and Song Form, Bassline Writing — Mix with the Masters (Finneas), Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas

Writing to a loop vs writing to changes

These are genuinely different problems and the same melody rarely works for both.

Over moving changes, the harmony supplies the motion. You can hold one note and let the chords recontextualize it underneath — the same pitch becomes the 5th, then the 3rd, then the 9th, and it sounds like it's moving without moving. Long notes work. The melody can afford to be simple because something else is changing.

Over a static loop, nothing does that for you. The melody has to generate its own movement — through rhythm, contour and phrasing. A held note over one chord for eight bars is just a held note.

Two consequences:

  • Static loops demand more rhythmic interest from the topline. This is why rhythm-first writing (above) suits loop-based production so well.
  • Static loops tolerate more repetition. The listener is already in a looped frame, so a repeating melodic figure reads as a hook rather than as laziness.

See Loop-Based Harmony for the harmony side of the same distinction.

Register, range and intensity

Higher reads as more intense. Partly convention, partly physiology — a singer audibly works harder at the top of their range, and the ear hears the effort.

That's why the standard arrangement shape works: verses sit lower, choruses lift. A large part of what makes a chorus feel like a chorus is simply that it's higher than what came before it.

Widening the range does similar work. A melody circling three notes feels contained; one with bigger leaps and a wider span feels dramatic, independent of how high it goes.

Practical: if a chorus isn't landing, check where it sits relative to the verse before rewriting it. Moving it up a third often does more than new notes.

Building tension across a section

How to make a verse arrive at a chorus rather than just stop.

Climb. Raise the register toward the end of the verse, shorten the note values so the line gets busier, and repeat a fragment in ascending sequence so it gathers.

Withhold the tonic. If the melody never lands on the root, nothing feels resolved — so the chorus doing it becomes the release.

The counter-move works too. Strip everything back right before the chorus so it arrives against space rather than against a wall. In loop-based production this is often more effective than building, because the drop is the arrival.

Pairs with Arrangement and Song Form — melodic tension and arrangement density should agree, not fight.

What makes a hook

At minimum three things, in rough order of importance:

  1. Repetition. A hook has to come back, and be short enough to hold after one pass. This outranks everything else.
  2. Rhythmic distinctiveness. A good hook is identifiable from its rhythm alone, with the pitches stripped out. Test it by tapping it.
  3. Singable range and clear contour. If it can't be sung back, it isn't a hook.

Then: contrast against what surrounds it. If the verse is busy and low, a sparse high hook lands harder. And simplicity usually beats complexity — the hook is the part that has to survive being remembered badly.

Developing a motif

A motive is a short fragment used as raw material to generate much more music. Motivic Development already documents eight named ways to develop one — repetition, sequence, inversion, interval contraction and expansion, diminution, augmentation, rhythmic metamorphosis, imitation.

That note is the reference; the practical point here is that most strong melodies are one short idea developed, not a long line invented. Write four bars you like, then generate the rest by transforming it.

Fixing a boring melody

Triage, most-effective first:

  1. Change the rhythm. Most boring melodies are boring rhythmically — even note values, everything on the beat. This is the highest-leverage fix by a wide margin.
  2. Widen it. Add a leap, push the top note higher, break out of the three-note orbit.
  3. Move where it sits against the chord. Target 9ths and 7ths instead of roots and 5ths (see above).
  4. Add space. Rests make what surrounds them land — see the existing note on breathing.
  5. Displace it rhythmically. Start the phrase off the downbeat.
  6. Reharmonize underneath it. Same melody, different chords, completely different meaning.

If you only do one, do the rhythm.

motivic-development.title: Motivic Development
motivic-development.html:
Part of Music Theory → Musical Form. A motive is a short musical fragment used as the raw material to generate a much larger amount of music. 8 named ways to develop one:

Technique What it does
Repetition Repeat the phrase immediately — the simplest form, doubles the material instantly
Sequence Repeat the motive starting at a different pitch level; intervals within it don't have to match exactly
Inversion Flip the motive upside-down — a downward leap in the original becomes an upward leap
Interval contraction Shrink the intervals within the motive
Interval expansion Widen the intervals within the motive
Diminution Play the motive faster
Augmentation Play the motive slower
Rhythmic metamorphosis Change the motive's rhythm in any way other than tempo
Imitation An "echo" of the motive between different voices (different instruments in an ensemble, or different registers on one instrument)

arrangement-and-song-form.title: Arrangement and Song Form
arrangement-and-song-form.html:
Why good loops die in the project folder, and how to turn one idea into a song. (composition — companion to Automation's mute-as-arrangement and the Song Seeds pipeline)

The loop-itis diagnosis

The pattern: make a loop → love it → 30–60 minutes later it feels boring/worthless → close or delete the project. The idea was never bad — it was alone. A loop that bores you isn't asking for a new idea; it's asking for a B section. (Kenny Beats: "a lot of ideas you're throwing out are really good ideas missing one other little idea to point out what it is you're doing.")

Writing the B section

  1. Duplicate the drums, strip everything else (bass/keys/melody out).
  2. Write a complementary part over them — different chords, opposite density (sparse vs full), different mood (his Leon Michaels example: sad/loose/simple B section under a full/happy/soulful A).
  3. Test the return: playing out of B back into A should feel like "oh my god, we're home." That coming-home lift is the whole point — the right B section makes the A section better.

Extend when ready: verse chords → different pre-hook chords → different hook chords = A-B-C form (extendable to A-B-C-D…). You don't need three-beats-in-one (Sicko Mode) every time — just more than one section.

Sequencing one idea (subtraction scheduling)

  • "Let the Beat Build" (Lil Wayne) is the masterclass: hi-hat → clap → clap+snares → kick → bass → everything in at the hook. One idea, minutes of interest, purely from when things enter.
  • Schedule absences: take the kick out for a section, the 808, ALL drums, the melody; drop the claps in sections; drop everything at the end of a bar. Arrangement interest = scheduled absence, not added layers.
  • The filtered-intro trick: run the main loop filtered / an octave off / reversed as the intro; when the real version drops it "feels big" because the ear was primed by the lesser twin.
  • Multiple bass sections — a synth-bass ("Mike Dean") section vs an 808 section, or live bass answering between 808 hits; the low end can be an arrangement dimension too.

Jam long, cut the fat

Record the whole exploration (Dahi jammed ~6 minutes for "Used," kept the best ~90 seconds): "what makes a great producer is someone who can listen and go — THAT's the moment." Arrange from the keeper moment outward. Same philosophy as comping takes; applies to beats.

The simplicity referee

Artists are the best common denominator: Lil Baby cut Kenny off at 5–7 sounds ("Toes," "Smack the Baby"). The extra perc layer matters less than it feels while producing. "Too busy is a relative term" — let the performer (or the vocal) decide.

Chains/workflows that apply it

Song Seeds (seed → sections before production) · Automation (mute-as-arrangement) · Hip Hop - Trap (drum drops, multi-section beats) · Drums Group

scale-degree-ear-training.title: Scale Degree Ear Training
scale-degree-ear-training.html:
Part of Music Theory → Intervals. A method (Max Konyi / Mind of Max, creator of the Sonop ear-training app) for training the ear on scale degrees as feeling states relative to a tonic, rather than on intervals as abstract pitch-distances. The core claim: every scale degree, chord quality, chord position, and rhythm/meter has its own recognizable "feeling state" — a subjective, non-verbal quality that's the same TYPE of experience whether it shows up as a melody note, a chord, or a bass note — and ear training is the practice of consciously labeling those feeling states until recognition becomes instant.

Why scale degrees over raw intervals

Training melodic intervals in isolation (an app playing two disembodied pitches) teaches a distance, not a musical feeling — and that distance changes character completely once it's placed in a tonal context. A minor 6th floating in free space sounds "dark," but the identical interval as the 3rd-to-root of a major chord (E→G inside C major) sounds nothing like that — it sounds like a major chord. The brain cannot hear pitches without context; it will always assign a root/tonic to whatever it's given and hear everything relative to that. This is why scale-degree training (which builds the tonic-relationship in from the start) transfers to real listening far better than pure interval training — a lesson both Max Konyi and David Bennett (interviewed on the channel, see David Bennett on Music Theory, Composition & the YouTube Life Sonic Sorcery Podcast No. 04) converged on independently: Bennett says explicitly that scale-degree hearing ("that's the fifth moving to the sixth") is the ear-training skill he actually uses day to day, more than named-interval recognition.

Foundation: pitch matching and tonic recognition, before scale degrees

Two prerequisite skills, worth diagnosing first:

  1. Pitch matching — can you sing back a note you just heard (any octave)? Find a heard pitch on your instrument? Sing a random pitch and then find it on the instrument? If any of these are shaky, that's the actual starting point — scale-degree/chord work all falls back on "sing it or find it on the instrument" whenever recognition fails, so without this fallback you're stuck when you don't instantly know what you're hearing.
  2. Tonic recognition — the ear constantly, automatically infers a tonic from the notes it's hearing, the same way vision resolves a blurry/low-res image into a recognizable shape as more information arrives. Every new note either reinforces or breaks the current tonic assumption; enough broken assumptions and the ear drops the old tonic for a new one — that switch IS the subjective experience of a key change/modulation. You don't need to consciously do anything to make this happen — if music sounds pleasurable/structured to you at all, your ear is already doing it; ear training is about becoming consciously aware of what it already knows.

Three levels of deliberate tonic-recognition practice, easy to hard (the tonic is "home" — rest, completion, stability, independent of the specific absolute pitch; the same physical note feels completely different depending on its role — C as the tonic of C major feels nothing like the same C as scale degree 5 of F major):

  1. Scale-based — play a scale up or down and stop one note short of the tonic; let the feeling of near-completion build, then sing the resolving note before playing it (producing the feeling, not just perceiving it, is what locks it in).
  2. Chord-progression-based — play any progression that stays in one key (start with something simple and familiar, e.g. I–IV–I–V), stop on a non-tonic chord, and sing the resolution. Escalate to progressions you don't already know, even improvised ones.
  3. Real-music-based, two variants: (a) with a song whose chords you already know, consciously flag the tonic chord every time it recurs — including mid-phrase, not just at the start/end; (b) with a song you've never heard, stop playback at a random moment and try to sing the resolution note before checking — an active test of whether the tonic feeling has actually been internalized, not just recognized in the abstract.

Singing (producing) the tonic trains it more effectively than only listening for it. — Max Konyi, The Secret of Ear Training

The 12 scale-degree feeling states

Trained against a drone (the tonic held underneath), each of the 12 chromatic scale degrees has a distinct, describable feeling state. These are one person's subjective labels — offered as a starting vocabulary, not gospel; the point is to find your own words, then discard the words and keep only the felt recognition:

Degree Feeling state Most easily confused with
1 (tonic) Perfect, complete, whole, resolved, stable — the minimum-energy state —
5 Pure, stable, consonant, smooth, but active — open, expansive, outward 1, 4
4 Neutral/pure like 5, but contractive, inward-curling, "square," flat-in-shape 1, ♭7
3 Sweetness, warmth, glow, vitality — a whole extra dimension 5 doesn't have 6, 7
2 Clean, crystalline, placid, "5 multiplied" — sharper/more amped than 5 5, 6
6 3's warmth mixed with 4's neutrality — softer, more pastel/muted than 3 2, 3
7 Melancholy/bittersweet — combines the 5-feeling and 3-feeling, sharpened by the half-step dissonance against the tonic 3, ♯4
♯4 One of the strongest/most energized states — bright, strange, "alien," spiky; maximally opposite of 1 on the circle 7, ♭2
♭7 Lightest of the "flat"/minor-leaning degrees — powerful, playful, "fun minor," not dark 4, ♭3
♭3 Defines "minorness" itself — dark, serious, gloomy; a bit of sorrow ♭7, ♭6
♭6 More intense than ♭3, less than ♭2 — desperate, hopeless, no-joy, high negative emotional valence ♭3, ♭2
♭2 The most extreme/dissonant — in-your-face, bitter, "the world's going to end," strongest tension ♭6, ♯4

Practical notes on the table:

  • Circle-adjacency predicts confusions. Arrange the 12 degrees in a circle by feeling-similarity (not pitch order) and degrees next to each other are the ones people mistake for one another (3/6, 3/7) — degrees a half-step apart melodically (5 and ♯4) are usually maximally far apart on this feeling-circle, which is the whole point: close in pitch ≠ close in feeling.
  • Two "worlds": the 5-axis and the 3-axis. 1-4-5-2 share a clean/neutral/pure quality (the "5 world"); 3-6-7 share a warm/glowing/sweet quality (the "3 world"). Most confusions happen within one of these two families, not across them.
  • Drone practice, not free-floating. Always train against a sustained tonic drone — it's the reference the brain uses to build these relationships explicitly while learning; in real listening you don't need the drone because the mind holds a "virtual tonic" automatically once it's familiar with a piece's key.
  • The transfer test: play a descending major scale and just focus attention on landing on 1 — that felt sense of arrival/completion IS the degree-1 feeling state, and it's the easiest one to bootstrap the whole method from.

Bridging from drone training to real music

The single biggest gap ear-training apps leave: they train degrees against an isolated drone or a single chord, but real music has a constantly shifting harmonic context underneath the melody, which recontextualizes what a melody note "sounds like" (a C over a C chord sounds like 1; the same C over an F chord sounds like 5; over a Dm chord it sounds like ♭7). Two skills, and they're different:

  • Chord-relative hearing — the melody note's feeling relative to the CURRENT chord underneath it (useful for voicings/comping).
  • Key-relative hearing — the melody note's feeling relative to the overall TONIC of the song, independent of which chord is under it at the moment (this is the scale-degree skill, and it transfers to being able to play back what you hear).
  • The bridging drill: take a song you know, try to hear/label the scale degrees of the melody as they go by from the key-center perspective, stop and check by singing/playing it out to confirm, then relisten with the confirmed answer in mind. Repeat on new material. Over time this becomes simultaneous — you can hear that a note is "the 7 of the current chord AND the 3 of the key" at once — but it starts as this slow stop-check-relisten loop.
  • Non-diatonic/modulating passages will always be harder — there's no shortcut past more repetition once the harmonic context gets genuinely ambiguous (key changes, non-diatonic chords).

Chords, chord qualities, and progressions as "meta feeling states"

  • Chords are not the sum of their component scale-degree feelings — combining feeling-states produces a genuinely NEW, higher-level ("meta") experience, the same way syllables combine into a word you hear as a whole rather than as separate sounds. Practical implication: don't try to consciously decompose every chord into its individual scale degrees in real time (unless you specifically need to, e.g. transcribing a tricky voicing) — instead train each chord type/quality/position combination as its own feeling state directly (major-on-4, minor-on-6, dominant-7-on-♭7, etc.), the same way you trained the 12 single-degree feelings.
  • This stacks recursively: individual degrees → chord (quality × position) → progression → whole-song feeling, each level its own holistic "meta" experience, recognized as a gestalt rather than reconstructed from parts (same as the harmonic-series point below: even a single note is technically a "chord" of overtones, and you don't consciously parse that either).
  • Chord inversions are their own feeling states, not calculated from the chord + a formula. Root position has a distinct "bang, solid, this is IT" landed feeling; each inversion has its own equally-distinct-but-different feeling, driven by the bass note's own scale-degree feeling (a 3rd or 5th or 7th in the bass doesn't feel like "1," so an inverted chord never feels like a landed root-position chord even before you consciously identify which inversion it is). See Chord Inversions.
  • Extended chords (9/11/13) blur major/minor identity and read as their own distinct "pastel," softened meta-experience rather than as [base chord] + [extension] stacked consciously — train major-9, major-add9, major-6/9, major-9-♯11 etc. as individually memorized flavors the same way, rather than trying to hear the 9th/11th/13th as a separately-identified scale degree layered on top. See Extended Chords.
  • Hearing inner voices (the notes buried inside a chord) works against a natural integrating instinct — the ear/brain actively fuses simultaneous notes into one gestalt (same mechanism that fuses a word's syllables, or that fuses a single note's own harmonic overtones into "one sound"). Pulling a chord apart into its individual voices is going against that fusion instinct, not extending it — it CAN be trained (with enough repetition it gets much faster), but for most people it needs deliberate, repeated, conscious effort, and even then it stays effortful compared to top/bottom-note recognition. Practical fallback for transcribing a genuinely hard voicing: brute-force it — play it back repeatedly, match individual pitches on the instrument/voice one at a time, then name what you found.
  • Telling root position from an inversion by ear = recognizing the bass note's own scale-degree feeling. A root-position bass note has the "1" feeling (solid, landed); an inverted bass note has whatever THAT degree's feeling is (a 3rd sounds like "3" in the bass, a 5th like "5") — you can know a chord is inverted without yet knowing the full chord, purely from the bass note's feeling not matching "1."

Practice routine, roughly in order

  1. Pitch matching (sing back / find on instrument) if that's not already solid.
  2. Tonic recognition — learn to consciously notice what your ear is already doing automatically.
  3. Scale degrees against a drone — one degree at a time, compare/contrast against its most-confused neighbors (the table above), then in short melodies.
  4. Melodic intervals — worth doing, but Konyi ranks this below scale-degree training in priority; do both, they reinforce each other in real playing (a leap "up a 5th" and "landing on scale degree 3" can be recognized simultaneously, not sequentially).
  5. Chord qualities and positions — same drone-and-drill method, chord by chord, extending into progressions.
  6. Real-music bridging drill — the stop/sing/confirm/relisten loop on songs you know, moving from drone-isolated training into full harmonic context.
  7. Extensions and altered chords — last, since they take the longest and blur identity the most; isolate one extension type at a time on one chord type at a time before mixing them.

This is explicitly a years-long, not weeks-long process — Konyi is candid that even after extensive training he still regularly hits sounds he can't immediately identify and has to brute-force. Progress is measured by how often that happens, not by ever reaching zero.

Listen-along hours (Max Konyi)

Three 68-minute drills that run this note's method as continuous audio, from the same source the method itself came from. Each plays a tone against a drone, speaks the correct scale degree, then replays the tone so the feeling and the number bind on the second hearing. The key changes every few minutes, so degrees are learned rather than pitches. Recorded from his app Sonofield in "Pocket Mode" — built for walking and commuting, and explicitly not something to sit and concentrate on.

His own instruction for beginners is worth repeating: do not try to guess. Just listen and relax. Guessing wrong for an hour trains anxiety, not recognition.

  • Immersive Ear Training - Major Scale (1-Hour) — start here; the reference set — ▶ listen-along, 1:07:50

- Immersive Ear Training - Minor Scale (1-Hour) — ♭3, ♭6 and ♭7 as their own feelings, not "major but sad" — ▶ listen-along, 1:07:50

- Immersive Ear Training - Chromatic Scale (1-Hour) — all twelve; pairs with Lesson 2 — ▶ listen-along, 1:07:50

seventh-chords.title: Seventh Chords
seventh-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. A 7th chord = triad + the 7th, making 4 notes. The 7th usually adds tension that wants to resolve — the engine of blues and jazz harmony.

The three you'll use constantly

Type Symbol Formula C example
Dominant 7th C7 1 3 5 ♭7 C E G B♭
Major 7th Cmaj7 1 3 5 7 C E G B
Minor 7th Cm7 1 ♭3 5 ♭7 C E♭ G B♭
  • Dominant 7 = most common; major triad + minor 7th. THE blues chord, and the V7 in every key (Chords by Key)
  • Major 7 = major scale degrees 1-3-5-7; dreamy/jazzy color (not used in blues)
  • Minor 7 = minor triad + minor 7th; the ii and vi chords in jazz progressions

The rest of the family

Type Symbol Formula C example
Minor-major 7th CmM7 1 ♭3 5 7 C E♭ G B
Half-diminished (m7♭5) Cm7♭5 / Cø 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 C E♭ G♭ B♭
Diminished 7th Cdim7 / C°7 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7 C E♭ G♭ A
Augmented 7th Caug7 / C7♯5 1 3 ♯5 ♭7 C E G♯ B♭
  • m7♭5 = minor 7th with lowered 5th; the ii chord in minor-key jazz ii–V–i (Chord Progressions)
  • dim7 vs m7♭5 differ only in the 7th (♭♭7 vs ♭7) — see Diminished Chords
  • 7♭5, 7♯9 etc. live in Altered Chords; mM7 as the i of melodic/harmonic minor: Scale Modes Reference

Usage

  • Diatonic 7ths per key (Imaj7, ii7… pattern): Chords by Key
  • Swap all triads → diatonic 7ths for an instant "jazzy version" of a progression
  • A lone 7th chord in a pop song usually exists to create a stepwise melodic line (in melody, bass, or an inner voice)
  • Voicing: split root (left hand) from upper structure (right hand); see Chord Inversions for slash-chord readings

Classical usage: which 7ths, and resolving the 7th

  • Building a 7th on every scale degree gives 8 theoretical seventh-chord types, but common practice only actually used 5: major 7th, dominant/major-minor 7th, minor 7th, half-diminished (ø7), fully-diminished (°7) — the table above.
  • Root movement for 7th chords follows the same up-2nd/down-3rd/down-5th pattern as triads (Chord Progressions), PLUS a 4th option unique to 7ths: common root (V7→V7 is fine, but V7→V as a plain triad is NOT — a 7th chord can't "downgrade" to a triad on the same root).
  • The 7th of ANY seventh chord must always resolve down by step — approach by common tone, step, or downward leap; never approach it with an upward leap.
  • Dominant 7th's four non-standard resolution detours: ornamental (decorative detour before the down-step landing), transferred ("hot potato" — the 7th passes to another voice in a later V-chord before finally resolving down by step), delayed (motion to IV holds the 7th out until V7 returns, then it resolves normally), bass resolution (the 7th still resolves down by step but lands in the bass via V7→I6, while the voice that had it resolves up). → Part-Writing — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.32–33
secs: Classical usage: which 7ths, and resolving the 7th

chord-inversions.title: Chord Inversions
chord-inversions.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. Same notes, reordered so a chord tone other than the root is in the bass. The bass note is the single most important note for a chord's feel.

The inversions of C major

Position Notes Slash symbol
Root position C E G C
1st inversion E G C C/E
2nd inversion G C E C/G
  • Triads have 2 inversions; 4-note chords (Seventh Chords) have 3 (Cmaj7/B etc.)
  • Read "C/E" as "C over E"
  • Alternate letter system: Ca = root, Cb = 1st inv, Cc = 2nd inv, Cmaj7d = Cmaj7/B
  • Worked 4-note example with feels per inversion: Chord Naming by Context

Slash chords: inversion vs non-chord bass

  • Inversion — bass note IS a chord tone (C/E)
  • Non-chord bass — bass note isn't in the chord (C/D). More specialized; works in fewer contexts
  • A slash chord often analyzes as a root-position chord: F/D sounds as Dm7; C/D ≈ D7sus4(9). One symbol for playing, another for analysis (Chord Naming by Context)
  • Full non-chord-bass catalog: all twelve major triads over a fixed bass note, worked and named one by one (which ones are just inversions vs. genuinely new chords, and how to decode each) → Slash Chords

Why invert

  1. Less hand movement — faster changes, less looking down
  2. Voice leading — keep common tones between chords; smoother progressions (Chord Progressions)
  3. Bass line control — walk the bass stepwise under static chords (C → C/B → Am…)
  4. Comfort — nearby shapes instead of jumps

On guitar, inversion is mostly omission

Everything above assumes you play all the notes and choose which goes lowest — true at a piano. On guitar you have four fingers and six strings, so the live decision is usually which tones to drop, and the bass note follows from that rather than driving it.

  • Keep the 3rd and 7th (the guide tones) — they carry quality and function. Drop the 5th first, then the root. A rootless voicing is not an exotic case, it's the default when a bass player is present.
  • E B D G under a chord diagram is a Cmaj9 with no C in it — 3rd, 7th, 9th, 5th. Nothing about that reads as "inversion" in the classical sense, but it is the same underlying choice.
  • An altered 5th (♭5/♯5) is a colour tone, not a 5th — it stays when a plain 5th would go.
  • Because a written pitch exists in several places on the neck, the same "inversion" has multiple grips with different tone and different reachable next chords — see Reading Notation on Guitar.

Full treatment, the six-category system it comes from, and drop 2 / shell / rootless families: Chord Voicings, built from Joe Pass Guitar Chords p.2–13.

Shape-level vs. functional inversion

A guitar voicing can be labeled an inversion (some chord tone other than the root sits under your fingers) while functioning as plain root position — because function depends on the lowest note of the whole ensemble/song, not on the guitarist's own voicing. If the bass player (or another instrument) is still holding the root underneath, an "inverted" guitar shape isn't actually inverting anything musically — it's just a rootless-sounding voicing of the same root-position chord. Two separate practices follow from this:

  • Shape practice — cycling through a chord's inversion fingerings purely as fretboard mapping (e.g. jumping around a D7 chord's inversion shapes while still "just thinking of D," with no intention that a bass instrument actually sound each one).
  • Functional use — a specific moment in a real piece where the bass line itself has an inversion happening, driving genuinely different low-end motion. This is the sense that actually produces the "why invert" benefits above (voice leading, stepwise bass control). Both are worth practicing, but they are not the same skill — a guitarist can be fluent in inversion shapes without ever using a functional inversion in a real arrangement, and vice versa. → Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared, Inverted Guitar Chords - Guitar chord inversions explained

Classical context: doubling & the restricted 2nd inversion

In strict 4-voice writing, WHICH note gets doubled depends on the inversion (root position doubles the root; 1st inversion doubles soprano for major, bass-or-soprano for minor, bass for diminished; 2nd inversion always doubles the bass/5th) — full table and the three narrow contexts where 2nd inversion is actually allowed (cadential 6/4, passing 6/4, pedal 6/4) live on Part-Writing. Diminished triads are always used in first inversion in this style.

transcribing-and-playing-by-ear.title: Transcribing and Playing by Ear
transcribing-and-playing-by-ear.html:
Part of Music Theory → Scale Degree Ear Training. Where Scale Degree Ear Training builds the perceptual foundation (the 12-degree feeling-state vocabulary, chords as meta feeling-states, drone drilling), this note is the applied workflow — Max Konyi's (Mind of Max) step-by-step process for actually finding the key of a real song, working out its chords, playing back a melody, and transcribing a full arrangement in real time, plus the daily practice routine that trains all of it. Ties into Song Practice — this is the literal method for learning a queued song by ear rather than from a chart.

Finding the key of a song by ear

A key = tonic (the home note) + tonality (major or minor). See Keys for the theory; this is the ear-only workflow:

  • Finding the tonic — listen to enough of the song to get its context (10–15 seconds, or one loop), then pause and imagine the music resolving to a single note; sing or find that note. Backup: check the last note of the melody — a common but not guaranteed place for the tonic to land, so treat it as a place to look, not a rule. Second backup: find the tonic chord (the most stable-feeling chord, the one the song could end on) and sing its bass note — on a root-position tonic chord, the bass note IS the tonic. For the underlying skill (why the ear does this automatically), see Scale Degree Ear Training § tonic recognition.
  • Advanced shortcut — if you can already recognize any scale degree by ear, you don't need the tonic directly: identify any note you recognize (e.g. "that's scale degree 5") and back-calculate the tonic from it.
  • Finding the tonality — the ideal is pure vibe: listen to the isolated tonic note itself and ask whether it feels bright/warm/major or dark/melancholy/minor — with practice the whole song's color becomes audible in that one note. Backup/check method: once you have a candidate tonic, play the minor 3rd and the major 3rd above it against the track and hear which one actually fits — whichever third sounds "correct" tells you major vs. minor. Second backup: find the tonic chord and read its quality directly.
  • Common mistakes: (1) confusing relative major and minor — many progressions can genuinely be heard tilted either way (e.g. hearing D minor vs. its relative F major), and sometimes both answers are legitimately defensible depending on framing — know relative major/minor cold so you recognize when this is happening rather than treating it as a wrong answer. (2) Assuming the first or last chord of a song is the tonic — sometimes true, often not, especially in modern music; it's a place to check, never a rule to rely on. — Max Konyi, Find the Key of Any Song in 30 Seconds (By Ear)

Physical alternative for finding the tonic — chromatic single-string search. Instead of singing/imagining the target note first, play chromatically up one string (low E is a natural default) against the track until a note sounds like "home" — a direct brute-force search, useful as a fallback for anyone who can't yet reliably sing or imagine the tonic. Works reasonably well even on a rough guess since any key uses 7 of the 12 available notes, so the odds already favor landing in-key. Confirming minor quality by playability, not just by ear-feel: play the minor pentatonic scale rooted on the candidate tonic against the track — if it fits cleanly, the key is very likely minor (with the caveat that minor keys don't always read as sad by feel — can read as funky or other moods depending on genre). — Brandon D'Eon, How to hear the key of a song INSTANTLY

Working out chords by ear

Every chord has three aspects to determine — the root/degree (which scale degree is the root), the quality (major, minor, sus2, dominant 9, diminished 7…), and the bass note (usually the root, but not if the chord is inverted). Each has its own feeling; together they form a holistic meta-feeling that immediate recognition eventually catches as a single gestalt rather than three separate lookups.

Three modes of working out a chord, escalating as familiarity runs out:

  1. Immediate recognition — the chord's identity is instinctively obvious the moment it's heard, no thinking or guessing. This is the target state ear training builds toward, one chord type at a time.
  2. Deduction — when a chord doesn't resolve instantly, narrow the (effectively infinite) possibility space using perceptual clues: a recognized quality ("sounds major"), a recognized bass degree, a recognized bass motion between chords, or genre-specific harmonic conventions (jazz vs. blues vs. classical vs. R&B each imply different vocabularies). Combine clues with music theory to shrink the candidate set to a handful, then test each candidate — either by playing it on an instrument and comparing, or by imagining it (the imagined version doesn't need to be perfectly clear, just close enough to judge a match). Worked example: an unfamiliar major-sounding chord in a major key narrows to I, IV, or V; the tonic is already established so I is ruled out; hearing the chord's bass sits a half-step above the previous chord's bass rules out V (no diatonic half-step approach) and confirms IV (which has one, from iii).
  3. Brute force note-finding — the last resort for a chord that gives no usable clues at all: listen to it repeatedly and pick out individual pitches one at a time. Grab the outer notes first (lowest and highest) since they immediately constrain the possibility space, then work inward guessing inner tones; a solid theory background (e.g. recognizing "this must be a flat-9 over a flat-7") lets brute force converge much faster than picking notes with no framework at all. Even a rough guess at a "cluster" of close inner tones (without resolving each pitch individually) is useful evidence.

Once a chord's full identity is worked out, label it and drill it (listen, play, name) so it moves permanently into the immediate-recognition category rather than needing deduction again next time. → Chords, Chord Inversions — Max Konyi, Chords by Ear: The Real Process

Playing a melody by ear — the 5-step process

  1. Memorize the melody — sing/hum it back until it's internalized; if singing pitches back is difficult, that's a skill worth training on its own (Konyi calls it something he uses "in every facet of my musical life" despite not being a singer).
  2. Map the melodic contour — for each note, note only whether it moves up or down from the previous one and by roughly how much (step / leap / large leap); no scale-degree numbers yet, just the shape. Drawing the contour on paper helps.
  3. Sing it slowly, one note at a time, feeling for the tonic and any other recognizable degrees — pencil in whichever degrees you can confidently feel as candidates on the contour map (the tonic is usually, but not guaranteed to be, present in the melody).
  4. Deduce the rest — use the contour's shape relative to the degrees you already have, plus music theory, to work out what the remaining degrees must be; sing the whole thing back and check that the felt states actually match your guesses (some degrees are easy to confuse — see Scale Degree Ear Training's confusion table).
  5. Verify on an instrument — sing the tonic you believe you've found, play a random note, and identify which scale degree that random note is; back-calculate the tonic's real pitch from there (e.g. "if A is scale degree 2, then G must be 1"). Apply the full contour map to the real tonic pitch and play it against the source — if it's wrong, analyze exactly which degree got confused for which; that's where the actual learning happens.

Finish by alternating between listening to the real recording with the scale degrees in mind, singing the melody solo with degrees in mind, and singing along with the recording — repetition across all three modes fuses the sound, the label, and the instrument together until the melody can be heard and identified in real time with no pausing or singing required. — Max Konyi, How to Play Any Melody by Ear - Step by Step Guide

Real-time transcription workflow

The full pipeline for transcribing a song cold, demonstrated live across country, pop, deep-house, video-game (Crosscode, Genshin Impact), and jazz-fusion-adjacent K-pop tracks:

  • The mental map — an abstracted, key-agnostic chromatic scale (1, ♭2, 2, ♭3, 3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭6, 6, ♭7, 7) held in mind around an unknown "1," filled in with real letter names only once the actual key is worked out. Every bit of harmonic/melodic vocabulary built through practice slots into this map.
  • No-perfect-pitch trick for finding "1": sing the note that feels like the tonic (you don't need to know its pitch), then play any random note on your instrument and judge what scale degree that note feels like relative to the note you sang; back-calculate the tonic's real pitch from the relationship (e.g. "I played a G and it sounds like scale degree 4 relative to what I sang, so the key must be D"). This is the single most-repeated move across every transcription example. — Max Konyi, Transcribing Music by Ear in Real-Time | Ep.01, Ep.02
  • Track bass motion continuously as the primary chord-to-chord landmark — half-step bass drops, a descending diatonic bass line harmonizing a scale (a very common device: I, V/vi(inverted), vi, V/IV, IV, V/ii, ii, V…), and inversions (signaled by a bass note that isn't the chord's root) are all read off the bass first, then confirmed against the chord quality on top.
  • Half-step bass motion is a strong diatonic landmark — in a major key it's almost always IV→iii (4→3) or vii°→I (7→1); combined with hearing "major chord moving to a minor chord a half-step below," there's only one diatonic spot that happens (IV→iii in major; ♭VI→v in minor) — narrows the whole progression fast.
  • Chord quality and chord function ("fourness," "twoness," "fiveness") are each their own trained perception, built specifically from having transcribed "hundreds and hundreds" of songs — matches Scale Degree Ear Training's point that chords are recognized as holistic meta-feelings, not reconstructed live. A ii–V is eventually heard as one fused gesture ("a chunk") rather than two separate chords once this is trained.
  • Sharp-4 in the bass is a specific, learnable landmark — very commonly signals either a secondary dominant of V ("two-chord," V/V, a Baroque-era-common move) or a ii∅7 (half-diminished ii); hearing sharp-4 narrows the guess to one of those two before any testing starts. Related: the sharp-4-half-diminished chord native to the 4th degree of Lydian mode is a distinct, recognizable "flavor" chord worth training on its own. → Diatonic Modes, Secondary Dominants
  • A minor ii–V doesn't always resolve to minor — real songs frequently set up a minor ii–V (which strongly implies a minor destination) and then land on the major I instead (and vice versa); keep the ear open to both outcomes rather than assuming the implied resolution is the actual one. Common in jazz and jazz-adjacent pop writing.
  • Expanding chord vocabulary from real music: when an unfamiliar-but-appealing sound shows up repeatedly across different songs, isolate it, work it out (in one case: a ii chord voiced as a minor 9 whose implied major-3rd-of-the-key color makes it sound almost major), and deliberately drill it until it's a recognized vocabulary item for next time — this is literally how the immediate-recognition category grows over years.
  • First-pass triage: on a genuinely dense arrangement, it's fine to capture a lead-sheet-level chord+melody sketch on the first pass and leave inner voicing details for a dedicated re-listen later, rather than stalling out trying to catch every note at once.
  • Real songs can feel genuinely ambiguous between relative major and minor in the moment — the ear can "flip-flop" on which key center it's hearing depending on which chord just played; acknowledge that instability as a real perceptual phenomenon rather than forcing a single premature answer. — Max Konyi, Transcribing Music by Ear in Real-Time | Ep.01, Transcribing Complex Music by Ear in Real-Time | Ep.02, Ep.03

The daily practice routine

Four core skills every routine needs to touch: melodic scale-degree recognition, bass-note recognition, chord-quality recognition, and chord-number/position recognition.

  • Drone practice — sing or play long, sustained tones of each scale degree against a held drone; pure familiarity over speed. See Scale Degree Ear Training for the full 12-degree feeling vocabulary this drills.
  • Melody transcription drill — pick a simple, familiar song (a nursery rhyme is fine); sing along with the recording, then sing it from memory alone; find the tonic and work out the remaining degrees by feel; verify on an instrument; alternate between listening and singing with the degrees held in mind until it "clicks" — matches the 5-step melody process above almost exactly.
  • Melodic improvisation with conscious degree-tracking — improvise over a drone or backing track in a known key, but stay consciously aware of which scale degree is being played at every moment, rather than free-noodling; builds the subconscious sound↔label↔finger association during an otherwise fun, low-pressure activity.
  • Chord/progression drill sequence, run in order on a chosen progression (own or borrowed from a song): 1. Play just the bass notes of the progression and sing along, holding the scale-degree numbers in mind. 2. Add the full chords back in; keep singing the bass notes while now also attending to each chord's quality (major/minor/etc.), naming each one out loud as it passes. 3. Quality-swap drill — keep every chord's position/number the same, but change ONE chord's quality (e.g. turn a minor iii major) and compare against the original; isolates what a quality change alone sounds like with everything else held constant. 4. Position-swap drill — the inverse: keep a chord's quality the same but move it to a different scale-degree position (e.g. swap a minor chord at position 3 for a different minor chord at position 2 or 6); isolates what a position change alone sounds like. 5. Transpose the whole exercise to a new key and repeat it — the point is to notice what stays constant (the numbers, the relationships) versus what changes (the actual pitches), since the numbers are the actual translation layer being trained. — Max Konyi, The Perfect Ear Training Routine
secs: Finding the key of a song by ear
Playing a melody by ear — the 5-step process

from-ear-training-apps-to-real-music.title: From Ear Training Apps to Real Music
from-ear-training-apps-to-real-music.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The missing half of every ear-training method: why app skill does not transfer to real music, and what to do about it. Max is blunt about his own product — "being good at an ear training app is not really worth anything… you can get all the gold gems and everybody thinks you're the man. But if you can't do it in real music, does it really matter?" His answer is that the premise of a path from app to real music is itself the bug: real music belongs in the routine from day one, running alongside the app, not waiting at the end of it. Split cleanly into a melody half and a chords half, and the two halves end on opposite instructions — which is the most useful thing in the video.

What's taught

Melody

  • Contextual over intervallic. Apps teach melody one of two ways: absolute distances between notes ("it went up a fifth, then down a second") or scale degrees against a key centre. He is not neutral — "real music is contextual and your training should be contextual too. Melodic intervals are a support to that. They're not the main event."
  • Three reasons app skill fails in the wild. (1) Changing harmony — chords move underneath a held melody note and change every relationship it has; he flags this as worth a video of its own. (2) Arbitrary instrumentation — an app gives you a piano or one drone timbre; real music gives you a voice inside a full arrangement. (3) A mindset gap — in the app you are training; with music you are just enjoying it, and those are different mental postures that have to be deliberately bridged.
  • Get the pure feeling states perfect in the app first. The app is "training wheels" — a simplified ground where a degree can be learned unobscured, so that in real music you know what you are even listening for.
  • Exercise 1 — listen with the answers already in hand. Transcribe (or look up) a melody, know the key, then listen to the actual record with the degrees consciously in mind: "you know the melody goes 3 4 3 2 3 1… you keep that in mind and you repeat, you pause, you sing, you listen again with the knowledge in mind." He calls what this feeds the brain an "information soup" — sound, label, and feeling arriving together until the brain synthesises the link itself.
  • Exercise 2 — produce melodies while naming their degrees. Improvise or write over a drone, backing track or band, staying conscious that you are playing 1 5 6 5 1 7 1 5 ♯4 5 2 3 2 1. Degrees of the key, not of the chord. Aimed straight at a habit guitarists have: running scale shapes with no idea what any note is.
  • Exercise 3 — one degree, held under everything. Pick a single scale degree, and over music whose key you know, sing or play that degree continuously while the harmony moves under it. His analogy is the whole point: you know an object well, then see it "in broad daylight… in shadow… under a strobe light… under blue light" — confusing at first, then you learn to see through the lighting to the object. The "twoness" of 2 survives every chord it sits over.
  • Three closing tips. Push the rest of the music to the background and keep the melody in front — "parting the waters." Aim for immediate recognition, not calculation — no melodic resolutions, interval math or theory derivation unless you genuinely have to. And ignore the pitch: be with the feeling of each note, since that is what stays constant across octave and key.

Chords

  • The same three problems, sharpened. Arbitrary instrumentation — the chord is "distributed across the whole arrangement," not played by one piano. Arbitrary voicings — C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are all C major but land differently. Distractions — drums, bass, melody, second harmony instrument, none of it holding still.
  • Learn qualities and degrees in isolation, then take them out. Chord qualities as vertical entities (major, minor, suspended, minor 9, diminished 7…) and chord degrees (the 4 chord, the 5 chord, ♭2, ♭3) drilled in the app or on the instrument — then fed the same information soup across a wide range of genres and arrangement styles, so the mind can work out what the common thread is and what to discard.
  • Exercise — guess before you check. Transcribing chords starts as soon as you can stand it. For each chord going past, call it without touching an instrument — major? minor? something else? sus? diminished? — then do whatever it takes to verify: listen for the bass note, fumble at the instrument, use what theory you have. "Get dirty and make mistakes… you kind of need to fall in every hole."
  • Exercise — narrate your own playing. Whenever you play, stay conscious of key, chord number and quality: "I'm on a one chord, it's major. I'm on a six chord, it's minor." Even in trivial songs. Varied input plus correct labels, repeatedly.
  • What he actually did: no method at all — brute-force transcribed "hundreds and hundreds of songs," whole playlists of pop and folk, chorus by chorus, one to two hours every day. He is openly unsure whether to recommend it, which is why the exercises above exist.

The one contrast worth remembering

Melody and chords ask for opposite listening. For a melody you block out the arrangement and keep one line in the foreground. For chords you do the reverse — a chord's identity is "the sum total of all tonal harmonic interaction between all the instruments," so you stay open and let everything fuse into one quality. Trying to isolate an instrument while chasing chords is working against the thing you are trying to hear. (The exception: chasing one player's specific voicing, which is a different job.)

Routed to

  • Scale Degree Ear Training — § Bridging from drone training to real music, which is exactly this video's subject
  • Transcribing and Playing by Ear — the guess-then-verify chord method and the brute-force account
  • Harmonic Ear Training — the chords half
  • — added to Lesson 5's reading, the transcription-and-routine lesson

kick-design.title: Kick Design
kick-design.html:
Building and shaping a kick from a synth/kick-synth instead of relying on a sample — a recurring Disclosure habit (Latch's kick is a synth note; "No Cap" layers a tuned knock over a loop). The kick straddles two Palette slots: its body lives in SUB Slot (20–60 Hz) and its click/beater in TRANSIENT Slot / low BASS Slot. Companion to Drums Kick Track (the processing chain), Sidechaining, and the Sound Palette.

Why synthesize a kick

  • Tune it to the song. A synth kick's fundamental can be set to the track's root so it reinforces the key (Latch: the kick hits F every bar to establish an F-minor that otherwise avoids its root).
  • Shape any envelope. You decide the pitch drop, the click, and the decay — impossible with a fixed sample. Guy learned kick-shaping on Logic's Ultrabeat; the modern tools are Big Kick and Kick 2 (Nicky Romero).

Anatomy of a synth kick (general starting points — tune by ear)

Part What it is Starting point
Body / tone The pitched sine/tri fundamental → SUB Slot Tune to the song root (e.g. F1); amp decay 200–450 ms
Pitch envelope The downward "pew" that reads as punch +12 to +36 st → 0 over 15–40 ms
Click / beater The attack transient → TRANSIENT Slot Short noise/HF layer < 10 ms, or a click sample
Saturation Harmonics so it reads on small speakers Decapitator / Softube / tape — light

The Disclosure "knock" kick

All punch, no sub — ~100 Hz, "nothing at 50 Hz" (old UK-garage). Used when a bendy sub loop or an SUB Slot bass already owns the low end, so the kick only needs to knock through the BASS Slot without clashing (see "No Cap"). Pair with a real sub layer or an 808 for weight.

Layering + placement

  • Two-kick layering: a short punchy sub kick + a kick with a hat/click baked in; nudge the punchy one a hair ahead so its transient leads (see the fake-compression move in Compression).
  • Small-speaker check: if the kick is sub-only it vanishes on phones — add an octave-up layer for 100–200 Hz warmth (Referencing and Translation).
  • vs bass: kick and BASS Slot must not fight — sidechain or offset (Sidechaining).

From books

  • Four-move kick EQ starting point, and where it disagrees with the vault's existing advice. Low cut 40–60 Hz (remove rumble — clears the SUB Slot of everything under the fundamental; note 1 Drums Kick Track runs a lower 25–30 Hz HPF because that kick keeps its own sub weight, so 40–60 Hz is really the trap/808 setting where the 808 owns the sub) · low shelf 80–100 Hz for thump (the low BASS Slot — what phones and small speakers actually reproduce as "kick") · boost 2–4 kHz for snap (top of the MIDS Slot into the LEAD Slot; a TRANSIENT Slot job by role — matching the chain's existing "click +1–2 dB @ 3–5 kHz") · a band at 8–10 kHz for click. ⚠️ That last one is printed as a NOTCH with "for click" as its reason — self-contradictory, since a notch there removes click; read it as a boost for click, or as a genuine narrow notch for a clicky resonance. Cross-check against Lophiile's opposing rule already on 1 Drums Kick Track: don't low-pass a kick's top off ("a kick under a pillow"), shelf the lower-highs down and filter only the extreme highs, plus a ~1 kHz dip on boxy kicks. → EQ, Pro-Q 4, Masking and Carving — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
secs: Anatomy of a synth kick (general starting points — tune by ear)

snare-design.title: Snare Design
snare-design.html:
Building a snare/clap from scratch out of synths and layered effects instead of only auditioning samples — the snare-specific sibling of Kick Design. A snare (or clapper) is really just "any somewhat tonal sound with a punchy or snappy transient" — tonal dubstep-style snares that emulate a real drum sit at one end, pitched-up percussion sounds at the other, and real percussion one-shots (found or foleyed) in between. Straddles MIDS Slot (body, ~160–250 Hz) and TRANSIENT Slot (click/crack). Companion to Drums Snare-Clap Track (the mixing chain for a chosen/finished snare), Layering and Stacking, and the Sound Palette.

Anatomy of a synth snare (general starting points — tune by ear)

Part What it is Starting point
Body A fixed-frequency oscillator (Operator) → MIDS Slot Frequency macro-mapped ~160–250 Hz; Re-trigger on, Voices = 1; Sustain + Decay down, Initial + Attack up
Punch A pitch envelope on the body oscillator Peak ≈ 48, Decay brought down — reads as percussive rather than a pitch-sweep; FM the oscillator for a "perky" character
Tail A noise oscillator (Operator) + reverb, EQ'd to stay out of the body's way Map the reverb's Decay (kept short) and Size to macros; EQ out the low end + trim harmonics so the body still punches through
Extra transient / click A second noise layer, harmonics pushed up, often with an initial click before the main hit for tension (the Jack Ü habit) Short, bright, < 10 ms read
Texture Shifter (chorus/frequency-shift or fine-tune, macro-mapped) and/or Corpus (physical-modeling resonance) layered under or over the built snare Cap decay so texture layers don't ring out too long
Punchy resonance A narrow EQ peak around ~200 Hz Narrow Q = more ring; map Gain + Q to a macro (floor at 0) for controlled variation

Building the "snare starter" rack

  • Build body → tail → extra-transient → texture as described above, group the whole thing into a rack, and save it as a reusable "snare starter." Keep macro-mapping every stage (frequency, pitch-envelope peak, reverb decay/size, EQ gain/Q, texture dry/wet) so the saved rack is a combinatorial starting point, not a single fixed sound — every future snare becomes a variation on the rack instead of a from-scratch build. → Randomized Rack Design
  • Resample to lock in a keeper. Because a macro-mapped rack like this is randomizable, highlight a short section (roughly half a bar), Command+L to loop it, add a new audio track, and continuously resample the snare rack while nudging macros — Live 12.2's take-lane dropdown (or Enter on a stacked take) makes it fast to audition and keep the best pass. → Randomized Rack Design

Layering and texture options

  • Metallic (SOPHIE/umu-style) snares via Grain Delay. Grain Delay samples small snippets of the incoming signal (snippet size set by its Frequency knob); with Time at zero, turning up Spray randomly and differently offsets the left/right timing on every grain cycle — the result reads as metallic, and the effect gets more varied (and "cooler") the more Feedback and Frequency get pushed. This is a texture layer over an existing plain snare, not a replacement for the body/tail build above.
  • Foley/percussion browser layering. Filter the Samples browser for One-Shot + Foley or Percussion tags and save the search for reuse — a fast way to build a personal library of raw layering material (clicks, snaps, splashes) instead of hunting fresh each time. → Sampling and Sound Selection
  • A pitched-up impact one-shot as a percussive layer. Filter Samples → One-Shot → "impact" for something big and booming, then pitch it up ~4 octaves (same logic as pitching a dubstep snare up into percussion territory) via Simpler; chain Drum Bus → Pro-Q 4 (light expansion/compression using its dynamic-band Attack/Release) for a perky, boomy hit. Some results read closer to a hi-hat than a snare — keep that in mind and pick accordingly.
  • Spectral transient shaping (unowned). Kilohearts Spiff (see Plugin Wishlist) is a spectral transient shaper with a Delta mode (hear only what's being boosted vs. dry) — another route to a perky snare; layering its noisier results under a plain snare can make good clap/snare hybrids.
  • Reverb-based tails don't have to be noise — a short, tight reverb (small Size) can stand in for the tail layer entirely, e.g. a "water splash" character instead of a noise burst.

From books

  • Four-move snare EQ starting point — and the 200 Hz conflict worth resolving by ear. Low cut 100–200 Hz ("more if necessary") to get the snare out of the BASS Slot and off the kick · low shelf 200–300 Hz for "umph"/body (top of the BASS Slot into the BED Slot) · boost 5–7 kHz for crisp/crack (upper LEAD Slot into the AIR Slot) · high cut 15–20 kHz ("remove harsh freq"). Note the first two moves butt directly against each other: the HPF's upper bound (200 Hz) is the shelf boost's lower bound, and 1 Drums Snare-Clap Track actually boosts +1–3 dB @ 200–250 Hz for exactly that thwack — so high-pass below wherever this snare's body actually sits rather than at a fixed 200 Hz, or you cut the body you're about to boost. The 5–7 kHz crack is the brighter half of the chain's existing "crack/presence 3–6 kHz." The 15–20 kHz high cut is a headroom move, not a harshness fix — real snare harshness is 2–5 kHz and is better handled dynamically (Soothe2, De-essing); compare Lophiile's "EQ out the papery top of a saturated snare" already noted on the track chain. → EQ, Pro-Q 4, Masking and Carving, TRANSIENT Slot — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
secs: Anatomy of a synth snare (general starting points — tune by ear)

sampling-and-sound-selection.title: Sampling and Sound Selection
sampling-and-sound-selection.html:
How Disclosure actually build tracks: not from scratch synths, but by auditioning and re-pitching a pile of samples until a vibe assembles — and choosing sounds for the feeling they evoke, not the literal thing they are. This note is the method; for specific "good sound for X" picks by role (drum hits, bass, guitar, synths) see the Sound Selection Guide. Companions: Sound Palette, TEXTURE Slot, Ambient Texture and Field Recording, RC-20 Retro Color.

Speed-up sampling

  • Slow source → sped up is a signature: a slow (e.g. 87 BPM) R&B/soul sample run at the track tempo (136 BPM) gets a fluttery, bright, "chipmunk-adjacent" character that's hard to get any other way. The speed-up is the sound.
  • Always key-match. Pitch every sample to the song key with a key-match sampler (ADSR Sample, Splice Bridge, Ableton warp) so a collage of unrelated sources sits together.
  • Ableton's warping is the tool of choice for sample-heavy tracks (better than Logic's for this).

Evocative, not literal

  • Build a mood from sound choice, not sound effects — Disclosure's "Deeper" feels underwater with no water SFX at all (ancient flute, reverse vocals, plucks, distorted reverse-reverb pads). Pick each layer for how it feels against the hook; spend the hours auditioning "what sits with this without covering it." → fill the Sound Palette slots with feeling, then carve.

Where to actually get samples

  • Trade in the community (Discord swaps) beats trawling YouTube — you get more interesting material, and pack-makers who nail a sound tend to keep making them (find one you like and depend on them).
  • Movies via PlayPhrase.me — type a phrase, get clips of people saying it across thousands of films (e.g. an intro vocal hook of the same line said many ways).
  • Keep your ears open in life — the "When a Fire Starts to Burn" hook was found by accident watching a video, not sample-hunting.
  • Make your own from a great singer — give a vocalist chords and ask for oohs/ahs (or their favourite song a cappella) and sample that (Lianne La Havas → "Simulation"). The most original samples are ones you created.

Using loops without sounding like everyone

  • Prefer top-loops (shakers, tambourines, hats) over full kick-hat-snare loops — drums are the most recognisable giveaway of a stock loop.
  • Play your own kick/rhythm in under a borrowed loop, or chop one-shots out and program your own groove, so the backbone is yours.
  • Layer several small textures (an Ambient Texture and Field Recording bed, a pluck, a reverse hit) under the main element rather than one busy loop.
secs: Using loops without sounding like everyone

layering-and-stacking.title: Layering and Stacking
layering-and-stacking.html:
Building one perceived sound out of many hidden layers — the listener hears "a synth" or "a snare," never the 8 or 2 sources under it. This is the through-line of Ian Kirkpatrick's pop production: every hook element is a stack where each layer does exactly one job, and pulling any one degrades the whole. Companion to Kick Design, Sampling and Sound Selection, Sound Palette, and the per-slot notes (SUB Slot … AIR Slot).

The core idea

  • Each layer has a single job. In New Rules' 8-layer main synth, one layer exists only for sustain — "without this bottom layer I don't get as much sustain… all of a sudden I can hear more of the notes in the midst of everything." Name each layer's job (body, sustain, attack, air, grit, movement) before adding it.
  • The listener doesn't know it's layered. A two-layer snare (a "bamboo" body + a tonal/transient top) is heard as one snare. Complexity is invisible and in service of one impression — see Ian Kirkpatrick - New Rules (25 Big Tips in 13 Min).
  • Print the stack to one stem. Ian combines all the layers of the chorus synth into a single audio stem and mixes that, so downstream processing (OTT, LFO Tool) hits the composite, not each part.
  • Assign layers across the Sound Palette. A full stack usually spans slots: body in SUB Slot/BASS Slot, harmony in BED Slot, the defining timbre in MIDS Slot/LEAD Slot, sparkle in AIR Slot. If two layers fight for the same slot, one is redundant — cut it or filter it out of the zone.

Recurring stacks (from the streams)

  • Main synth from a pitched 808 tom — layer 1 of New Rules' hook synth is an 808 tom with heavy OTT, over a clean sine 808 for body, glued with Sausage Fattener. A drum becomes the fundamental of a synth. → Roland TR-808, SUB Slot
  • Two-layer snare: body + transient — a famous "bamboo" snare (heavy upward OTT) + a tonal transient layer. Split so you can EQ/compress each role independently. → TRANSIENT Slot
  • Kick as multiple layers — hook: a big kick + a smaller kick; chorus: the layers + a room-mic'd "roomie." Splitting lets you raise just the transient late in the song to keep the kick present without turning the whole kick up (see Kick Design and Ian Kirkpatrick - Make Your Kick Stand Out). → TRANSIENT Slot
  • Plucks + pads stacked to one lead — New Rules' lead is stacked pluck/synth layers filling different octaves; see Ian Kirkpatrick - New Rules Plucks and Synths Layers.
  • Bass = main patch + sub sine + slap layer — Don't Start Now: NI Scarbee patch (no low end) + a sine sub for weight + a separate "slap" from Trilian's Atmosphere patch. Three sources, one bass. → Bassline Writing, Ian Kirkpatrick - Don't Start Now Bassline

Discipline

  • Bright, defining layer sets the identity; the rest support it. Build around the one layer that makes the sound recognizable; everything else fills gaps under it.
