  • Mono/narrow the low layers, widen the top. Keep sub/body layers mono; reserve width for the air/texture layers (Width and Stereo, Stereo Field).
  • If a layer isn't missed when muted, delete it. Layers should be load-bearing, not decoration — this is the flip side of rate of information.

bassline-writing.title: Bassline Writing
bassline-writing.html:
How to write the bass part — note choice, fills, and restraint. Companion to the bass sound chains (Digital Bass Track, Electric Bass DI Track, Bass Group), Bass Design (the synthesis/sound-design side — tuning saturators/Corpus to the note), and the low-end slot pages (BASS Slot, SUB Slot). Seeded from Lophiile's 3-hour basslines focus stream; grow it with every bass breakdown.

The method

  1. Groove first, bass second. Finish the drum groove, then write the bassline around it. Bass notes do not have to start on the kicks — lock to the pocket, not the kick map.
  2. Roots first, by ear. Land the root notes under the chords before any decoration. If you can't hear the roots, that's the ear-training gap to close (Song Practice).
  3. Octaves are the default vocabulary. Jump up the octave and back, occasionally through a passing tone (a 5th above is the classic); a strong bassline can be "mainly octaves with the occasional tiny fill."
  4. Steal the melody's rhythm for fills. Mirror the rhythm of what the guitar/melody just played (not necessarily its notes) — the busyness hides inside existing phrasing and stays cohesive.
  5. Record busy, mute down. Play a too-busy line through the whole loop, then delete everything but the killer moments; never repeat the exact same fill in consecutive phrases.
  6. The band test. Imagine a bassist in the band physically playing it — if no player would phrase it that way, rewrite it (unless the unplayable line IS the point, e.g. reversed audio).
  7. Don't get in the way. With vocals or a synth hook on top, the bass supports. Busy showcase basslines (Chris Brown "Fine China," Thundercat) only work over static held chords — when the harmony above is busy, only root notes work.
  8. Two chords = the riffs ARE the line. Static harmony moves all the interest into the fills between roots; conversely, one perfectly-placed fill can be the entire event (Arrangement and Song Form).
  9. Bass and keys should talk. Arrange them as a conversation — "what story is the bass telling, what story are the keys telling, and do they talk to each other?" (Lophiile's soul formula.)
  10. Walk the sound ladder when the part is right but the tone is wrong: synth patch → different synth → real/VST bass guitar (Kontakt 7 Scarbee Rickenbacker Pure Neck DI, NI Motown bass, Trilian) → DI + amp sim. Then control with a limiter, not a compressor (Limiting), saturate for body (Saturator "A Bit Warmer"), and sidechain last (Sidechaining).
  11. Never run two genuinely different basslines simultaneously. Chords and melody tolerate multiple simultaneous instruments fairly well (doubling the same part, or even two different melodic lines at once, can work), but two distinct low-end melodic lines competing at once clashes and reads as mud rather than richness — commit to one bassline per section. Doubling the SAME bassline on two instruments is fine and different from this (that's a unison/doubling move, not two basslines). → Layering and Stacking (the doubling case) — Max Konyi, Beat Making 101 - Primary Elements (Bass)

Riff ideation — borrow, don't copy (BassBuzz's 7 "steal" methods)

When the block is "what should I even play," turn to an existing bass line you love as raw material rather than starting from nothing — the difference between a lawsuit and a legitimate "inspired by" is how much survives the transfer and which dimension changes. Ordered from most-to-least of the original kept intact:

  1. Steal half — take a riff's first half (notes + rhythm) verbatim, then write an original second half from the halfway point on. Easiest of the seven; the shared opening still reads as connective tissue to the ear. Real chain: Kool & the Gang "Hollywood Swinging" → Chic "Good Times" → Queen "Another One Bites the Dust," all sharing one low-E opening, diverging halfway. (general starting point: snip the first half of a line you love, keep noodling the second half on the same underlying scale.)
  2. Steal the rhythm, change the notes — keep the exact rhythmic pattern, write new pitches. Rhythm carries more of a groove's identity than pitch does, so this is close to undetectable. Demo: turn any known rhythm (e.g. "Express Yourself") into a totally different-feeling line just by swapping the notes over it.
  3. Steal the notes, change the rhythm — the riskiest of the seven when under-cooked (this is the Zeppelin "Stairway to Heaven" vs. Spirit "Taurus" lawsuit mechanism). On generic note sets (roots + fifths) it's nearly untraceable; on a distinctive note set (e.g. "Iron Man"'s riff) even a rhythm-only change still reads as a genuinely different riff — distinctiveness of the source, not just note count, sets how much rhythmic change is needed.
  4. Steal notes AND rhythm, but rearrange them — reorder the notes, shift octave placement, or otherwise restructure, while keeping both pitch and rhythm content. Needs real tastefulness (a lazy rearrangement — same key, ~75% of the rhythm intact — reads as an obvious copy). Cleanest worked example: The Killers (Mark Stoermer) rearranging The Smiths' "Barbarism Begins at Home" (Andy Rourke) — moves the ending tag up an octave, borrows partial rhythmic vibe, then diverges into new chords for the remaining bars, which is the actual transformative move.
  5. Change the feel — keep anchor notes/rhythm close to identical, change tempo, drum beat, tone, or key instead. Recognizability is context-dependent, not purely note-dependent. What NOT to do: Ray Parker Jr. "Ghostbusters" vs. Huey Lewis "I Want a New Drug" — same notes, same bass tone, similar beat, same intro FX = no context change = lawsuit. What works: Jane's Addiction "Mountain Song" (Eric Avery) vs. Iron Maiden "Wrathchild" (Steve Harris) — same key/pattern/plucking, but 20+ BPM slower with a different beat = enough context shift to avoid the same fate. (general starting point: try any known riff faster or slower — the new tempo naturally pulls toward a different drum beat.)
  6. Steal from other instruments — port a rhythmic idea from a non-bass part (guitar, vocal) onto bass rather than only borrowing from other bass lines; needs a genuinely rhythmic source part, since a smooth melody "isn't much of a bass line" ported unchanged. Worked example: ABC "Poison Arrow" (Mark Lickley) borrows from the guitar part in Chic "Le Freak" (Nile Rodgers), not from Chic's own bass line. (general starting point: take a vocal hook, drop it an octave, add grit.)
  7. Steal from a different genre — the genre shift itself does most of the transformation work, so this needs the least direct copying to still feel original. Weak version: same-genre "borrowing" (no genre shift = no transformation, reads as a straight lift). Strong version: Black Sabbath's foundational riff reportedly grew from Geezer Butler's fondness for Holst's The Planets ("Mars") — classical → metal, stacked with method 1 (only half the theme taken) and method 4 (rearranged) at once.

They stack. Run one source riff through several methods in sequence/combination rather than picking just one — demonstrated live on Megadeth's "Peace Sells": half → rhythm-kept/notes-changed → notes-kept/rhythm-changed → reordered → feel+genre-changed, each pass a usable new idea from the same seed. Complements step 4 above ("steal the melody's rhythm for fills") — that's method 2 applied specifically to fill-writing rather than whole-riff writing. Parallels the formal composition vocabulary in Motivic Development (rearrange ≈ inversion/permutation, change-the-feel ≈ augmentation/diminution, genre-swap ≈ imitation across a different "voice") — same underlying idea, ear-trained pop-songwriting version vs. music-theory-textbook version. → BassBuzz, 7 Stupidly Simple Methods for Killer Bass Lines

See also: both worked examples above — Chic "Good Times" (method 1) and "Express Yourself" (method 2) — also appear as riffs #4 and #17 in the BassBuzz performance reel Top 30 Most Iconic FUNK Bass Riffs, a third BassBuzz appearance of each riff (no new technique content there — it's a non-narrated montage).

808-specific

  • Tune it up high, then drop it back — pitch the 808 up an octave+ to hear the note center, tune, return. Never guess at sub pitch.
  • Slides on audio 808s: pitch to the note with warp OFF (clean stretch) → warp mode Tones ("best for bass") → clip transposition envelope → draw the slides. Easier than MIDI slides. → Digital Bass Track, SUB Slot
  • Fake pitch-bends by clicking in grace notes — short approach notes before targets read as bends when no wheel is handy (Paradise).
  • 808 glides via Simpler/Sampler's MIDI tab: Pitch Bend Range to 24 semitones, then MIDI Control mapped to Pitch Bend. On the instrument's MIDI tab, push Pitch Bend Range all the way up (two full octaves), then assign Pitch Bend under MIDI Control so the pitch-bend lane drives Ableton's pitch modulation directly — more continuous, controllable glides than a hand-drawn pitch envelope. → Simpler, Sampler — Decap (Sol State), 9 Producer Tips From "Drums That Knock" Creator Decap
  • Two 808s in one trap beat: a subby/long main 808 as the primary low end, plus a second 808 reversed and layered in purely for flavor. The reversed second 808 is a texture add on top of the main sub, not a competing rhythmic line — Ozzy's (Drake/21 Savage "No BS") regular dark-trap recipe. → SUB Slot — loner, the secrets behind OZ's 'her loss' production!?
  • Audition-then-isolate 808-slide workflow: stretch the 808 across the whole beat first, THEN play it back and chop wherever a slide feels right by ear — rather than writing slides in up front, loner stretches the 808 across the full beat, listens through, and at any point where "I want an 808 slide in here," uses the chop tool to cut the pattern there and right-clicks → Make Unique to detach that one segment into its own independent instance, so only that isolated hit gets slid/edited without touching the rest of the pattern. Pairs directly with this section's audio-808-slide mechanics above (warp OFF → Tones mode → clip transposition envelope) — same end result, different starting point (find-by-ear first, then isolate, vs. planning the slide in advance). → Genre Drum Patterns (UK Drill build order) — loner, how to make hard drill beats with synths from scratch (headie one, drake etc.)
secs: Riff ideation — borrow, don't copy (BassBuzz's 7 "steal" methods)

bass-design.title: Bass Design
bass-design.html:
Reinforcing a bass patch's fundamental and harmonic body with tuned devices — saturators and resonators dialed to the note being played, not just broadband drive — instead of only reaching for EQ after the fact. The sound-design sibling of Kick Design and Snare Design for the low end, and the synthesis-side companion to Bassline Writing (which covers the composition/arrangement side: grooves, octave patterns, 808 slides). A bass patch straddles SUB Slot (20–60 Hz, the felt fundamental) and BASS Slot (60–250 Hz, the harmonic body/growl that reads on small speakers). See also Operator's "FM bass growl" Patch Recipe and Wavetable's Reese-bass technique for the synthesis side of this same territory.

Tune supporting devices to the note, not just the patch

The core idea from the source video below: instead of driving a generic saturator or resonator across the whole signal and hoping it lands somewhere useful, tune each supporting device to the actual note being played so its harmonic reinforcement lines up with the bass's own fundamental instead of fighting it.

  • Two (or three) Saturators, each tuned to the note — on an Operator/Serum/Wavetable bass note, add a Saturator and set its tunable pre-filter/tone stage to the note's fundamental frequency (e.g. ~156 Hz for D♯), then add a second Saturator tuned an octave up, and optionally a third a further step above that — each one reinforcing a different harmonic of the same note rather than one saturator doing everything broadband.
  • Corpus tuned to the same sub frequency — set Corpus's resonator type and tuning to match the same note (the sub frequency, D♯ in the source example) so its physically-modeled resonance reinforces the fundamental the Saturators are already emphasizing, rather than adding an unrelated ringing pitch. → Corpus
  • A free, pre-tuned rack version exists — the source video's creator built this exact dual-Saturator + Corpus recipe as a downloadable rack with each note pre-tuned, released free in the video's description — worth grabbing directly rather than rebuilding the tuning-per-note manually every time.

Escalation ladder for extra thickness (from the same source — diminishing returns past a point)

Each further rung adds more density; the video's own conclusion is that the later steps stack into "too much" fast, so treat this as a menu to sample from, not a checklist to always run in full.

  1. Resample, then add a parallel high-passed harmonic layer — bounce the tuned bass to a new audio track, run it through another Saturator into an EQ Eight high-pass set somewhere around 150–300 Hz, so this new layer keeps only the driven upper harmonics — blend it back under/over the clean tuned bass without muddying the actual sub. → EQ
  2. Multiband compression + a notch EQ, fine-tuned by ear — a multiband-compression pass (built from the Multiband Dynamics device) glues the stacked layers together; add a narrow notch EQ cut wherever the stack has built up too much resonance, then fine-tune every EQ in the chain to taste. → Multiband Dynamics, EQ
  3. Tune a phase-disperser to a harmonic multiple of the note (unowned: Kilohearts Disperser) — calculate a harmonic multiple of the bass note's fundamental (roughly 1244 Hz off a ~156 Hz D♯ — an ~8th-harmonic multiple) and tune an all-pass phase-disperser device to that frequency for further metallic motion/smear on top of the stack. → Plugin Wishlist
  4. Add grit (unowned: iZotope Trash), then duplicate the whole chain — a lo-fi/distortion plugin stacked right after the disperser for extra grit, then duplicate the entire processing chain for even more density if the sound can take it. → Plugin Wishlist
  5. A Limiter as a safety net — once the stack gets this dense, add a Limiter before going further so the result doesn't clip/blow out unpredictably — explicitly framed as ear protection, not a mix decision.
  6. Optional extreme layer: OTT and/or Vocoder for a longer tail/texture — reached for only when chasing an especially long, wild tail; both are explicitly called out as "feeling really wild" territory rather than a standard step. → OTT, Vocoder
secs: Tune supporting devices to the note, not just the patch
Escalation ladder for extra thickness (from the same source — diminishing returns past a point)

sidechaining.title: Sidechaining
sidechaining.html:
What it is: any processor whose detector listens to a different signal than the one it processes. The classic use: a compressor on the bass keyed from the kick — every kick hit ducks the bass, so both feel loud in the same octave.

Why it exists

Kick and bass occupy the same frequencies. Played together they mask each other, eat headroom, and mud the low end. Ducking one when the other hits makes space in time instead of in frequency — and the pumping itself became a compositional device (modern dance basslines are written into the duck).

The three flavors

  1. Compressor sidechain (Pro-C 2 external SC, Glue Compressor, Duck_Buddy): reactive — louder trigger = more duck. Organic, but limited curve control and can click on subby material.
  2. Volume-shaper LFO (Kickstart 2): draws the duck curve directly; consistent every hit, can reach silence, anti-click smoothing built in. Trigger it from the kick (audio/MIDI) when patterns vary. Curve position is the groove: early ramp-up = urgent, late = lazy. Mix knob = duck depth — back it off until the pump stops being audible.
  3. Frequency-domain sidechain (Soothe2 external SC, Pro-Q 4 dynamic node keyed externally): ducks only the colliding frequencies, not the level — invisible unmasking. The modern default for vocal-vs-instruments (see Masking and Carving).

Recipes

  • Kick vs 808: Digital Bass Track stage 4. Trap counter-school (Mixed by Ali): don't duck at all — EQ pockets + gate the kick tail; sidechain "pulls the punch out."
  • Stealth duck: multiband — duck only <150 Hz of the bass. Full mix benefit, zero audible pump.
  • Ghost trigger: a muted click track feeds the compressor SC — duck patterns independent of the actual kick (works through kickless breakdowns).
  • Vocal priority ducks: backups −1–2 dB under the lead (Backup Vocals Group), FX bus under the vocal (FX Bus), delay/reverb tails under the dry vocal (Delay Send Other, Reverb Send Long), pads under everything (Synth Bed Track).
  • Click fixes: raise the synth's own amp release slightly, use anti-click smoothing, or soften the curve corner.

Rule of thumb: duck the lower-priority element, keyed from the higher-priority one — see the masking hierarchy in FX Chain System.

  • "Bow tying" — a whole-signal amplitude sidechain (LFO Tool-style) on a bass/sub carves a pinched, bow-tie-shaped envelope into the low end: the sub gets ducked out right at the kick hit, exactly when it's needed. Fix: sidechain only the top end of the bass (just above the sub), not the whole signal — you rarely hear sub, you feel it, so ducking it costs low-end energy for zero perceived-pump benefit. This is the inverse of the sub-only multiband duck documented above from Disclosure (duck only the sub, protect the top) — here the strategy flips: duck the top, protect the sub. Defaults to multiband sidechaining on the kick as a habit. → LFO Tool, Multiband Compression — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), New Sidechain Trick (Bow Tie, Pump & Subs)
  • Advanced alternative to sidechaining entirely: bus the kick and sub together and clip them, forcing their transients to lock together. Route both to a shared group and drive a clipper across it — clipping forces them to share headroom and align tightly, getting closer to a "perfect" kick/sub relationship than sidechain compression alone; clean up the resulting kick distortion with a fast, soft-knee multiband move sidechained to the kick's own low end (only active while the kick and sub overlap), then blend dry kick back in to restore its level. Use an oscilloscope to see exactly which harmonics got clipped away and re-EQ them back into the dry kick — a supplement to your ears, not a substitute. → ClipGain, jo.Oscilloscope, Clipping and Loudness — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), New Sidechain Trick (Bow Tie, Pump & Subs)
  • Low end is binary, high end is to taste — a philosophy for splitting the multiband sidechain. Below the low-end crossover, duck essentially all-or-nothing (fully ducked out or full volume) so only one element ever occupies that register at a time — mute everything else on the low band and the kick alone fills the gap on its own; above the crossover, dial duck depth to taste since more of the mix can coexist there without masking. "You don't really want layers in your low end, you want just one thing." → Multiband Compression — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), Advanced Sidechain for MORE BASS (Rare Tips)
  • A spectrum of high-end pump styles, not just one setting. On the top end: a genuinely subtle duck-plus-tiny-pump that clears space exactly where needed and leaves a little room for the hi-hat transient on the next eighth, a more aggressive and audibly pumped version, and the fully obvious "Daft Punk"-style pump that a lot of producers still reach for — not a personal favorite, but it can work for the right aesthetic/genre. → Kickstart 2 — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), Advanced Sidechain for MORE BASS (Rare Tips)
  • Give the snare its own, lighter low-end sidechain than the kick's. A snare is shorter and pitched higher than a kick, so it doesn't need nearly as much low end taken out — run a separate, gentler duck on the snare's low end rather than reusing the kick's aggressive binary settings. — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), Advanced Sidechain for MORE BASS (Rare Tips)
  • "Adaptive sidechaining" — at mixdown/mastering, consolidate every instrument's low-end duck onto one shared trigger instead of a bespoke sidechain per instrument. Once flipping the master, you don't want to be managing a different low-end sidechain per element — keep top-end ducks separate/per-instrument (subtle and to-taste anyway), but swap all low-end ducking onto one shared low-end trigger. The payoff isn't just simpler routing — it recovers low-end sustain: swapping the snare off its own dedicated low-end duck and onto the shared trigger let several more oscillations of low end survive under the snare's tail instead of getting cut off. → Multiband Compression — Fox Stevenson (Sol State), Advanced Sidechain for MORE BASS (Rare Tips)

masking-and-carving.title: Masking and Carving
masking-and-carving.html:
What it is: frequency masking = two elements sharing a band at similar levels; the ear picks one and the other vanishes. Carving = deciding who owns each band and cutting the loser there. Most "my mix is muddy/cluttered/vocal is buried" problems are masking problems.

The hierarchy (who wins a collision)

Lead vocal → kick/snare backbeat → bass → hooks/leads → everything else. When two elements collide, the lower-ranked one moves: dip, duck, pan apart, octave change, or arrangement edit. Cut the loser, don't boost the winner (boosting into a masked band just escalates the war).

Diagnosis before surgery

  • Mute test: mute the suspect group — whatever suddenly gets clearer is what it was masking (and vice versa: turn it up and hear what disappears).
  • Pro-Q collision detection: Pro-Q 4 on both buses, analyzer sidechained — colliding frequencies light up red while both play. Cut the red on the lower-priority bus. (Workflow in Inst-Synth Group.)
  • Solo lies: piano/guitar boosts at 1–2 kHz sound honky solo and correct in the mix — always judge carves in context.

The carving toolkit (gentlest first)

  1. Arrangement — two parts in the same register are an arrangement problem no EQ fixes. Change the octave/voicing.
  2. Panning — elements can share a band if they don't share a position (guitar L, keys R).
  3. Static carve — the loser gives up 1–3 dB where the winner lives (guitars dip 2–4 kHz for vocal; everything HPFs above what it needs — see each group note).
  4. Mid/side carve — cut the loser's low-mids in the mid channel only (can go deep, −6–9 dB): the center clears for vocal/snare/bass while the sides keep the body. The element even gets wider. (Acoustic Piano Track, Synth Bed Track.)
  5. Dynamic carve — Pro-Q 4 dynamic node keyed from the winner: the dip exists only while the winner plays. Full sound in the gaps.
  6. Sidechained soothe2 — the surgical endgame: ducks exactly the colliding resonances, exactly when they collide (Guitar Group, Inst-Synth Group).

Standing lane assignments (this template)

  • Sub <100 Hz: 808/bass only, mono · kick vs bass pocket: pick per song (50–60 vs 80–120 Hz) · pads/FX/hats never below 150–300 Hz · vocal air 10 kHz+ beats hat sparkle · repeats/reverbs always duller and narrower than their source.

From books

  • The drum kit's own internal lane ladder — four ascending high-passes that keep each drum out of the zone below it. Kick 40–60 Hz · toms 60–200 Hz (per drum — floor toms low, rack toms high, "stop clashing" is the stated reason) · snare 100–200 Hz ("more if necessary") · hats 200–300 Hz or higher. This is the standing-lane-assignments rule above applied inside the kit rather than across the mix, and it pairs with a second rule: cut below the fundamental, boost at it — kick shelf 80–100 Hz, snare shelf 200–300 Hz, toms boost 100–300 Hz. Collision points to watch: the snare's 100–200 Hz HPF sits directly under its own 200–300 Hz body shelf (cut too high and the "thwack" goes with it — 1 Drums Snare-Clap Track actually boosts +1–3 dB @ 200–250 Hz there), and the toms' 60–200 Hz cut overlaps their own 100–300 Hz power boost, which only resolves if the cut sits under that specific drum's fundamental. Presence lanes stay separated the same way: kick 2–4 kHz snap · snare 5–7 kHz crisp · toms 5–10 kHz punch · hats 7–10 kHz+ sizzle, with a tom boxiness cut at 300–800 Hz (sweep a narrow boost to find the honk first). → EQ, Pro-Q 4, Kick Design, Snare Design, SUB Slot, BASS Slot, BED Slot, MIDS Slot, LEAD Slot, AIR Slot — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

musical-form.title: Musical Form
musical-form.html:
Part of Music Theory. Form is the large-scale layout of a piece — how sections are arranged/repeated and what keys they're in. Covers the common-practice-period forms; not the same axis as a pop song's verse/chorus arrangement, though the same "sections that contrast and return" logic applies.

Binary form (A B)

Two contrasting sections. Contrast can be mood, tempo, key, or a combination.

  • Baroque dance form — a specific binary usage: both sections repeated; the A section starts in the tonic and modulates to the dominant; the B section starts in that new key and modulates back home. Used across the full Baroque dance-suite repertoire (allemande, gavotte, bourrée, courante, sarabande, loure, gigue…), written for solo keyboard, chamber groups, or full orchestra; performers of the era improvised ornamentation on the repeats. When theorists/musicologists say "binary form" about Baroque music, they usually mean this specific variant.
  • Rounded binary (A B A′) — the A section returns after B, but the reprised A′ is notably shortened — distinct from full ternary form below, where the reprised A is full length.

Ternary form (A B A)

Three-part form, though really two contrasting sections with the first reprised. Both A sections are full-length and similar in character; B is contrasting.

  • Minuet & trio — instrumental ternary form; instead of writing out the reprised A, the score marks "Da Capo al Fine" after the B section (return to the beginning, play through, end at "Fine"). Repeats inside either section are skipped during the reprise.
  • Da capo aria — the vocal/operatic equivalent of minuet & trio, same "Da Capo al Fine" convention.
  • Military march form — descended from minuet & trio (John Philip Sousa's lineage): the A section itself splits into a first strain and second strain, usually preceded by a short fanfare; the trio section modulates to the subdominant key (adds a flat/drops a sharp from the signature); most marches include a dramatic contrasting passage between trio repeats, called the dogfight or breakstrain.

Sonata-allegro form (A B A)

Descends from ternary form; first used by early Classical composers in opening movements of multi-movement works, adopted through the Classical and early Romantic eras.

  • Exposition — states two contrasting themes. Major key: theme 1 in tonic, theme 2 in the dominant. Minor key: theme 1 in tonic, theme 2 in the relative major.
  • Development — reworks the exposition's themes (often introduces new material too).
  • Recapitulation — restates both themes, but now both in tonic — this is the form's key-resolution moment; the earlier theme-1/theme-2 key contrast collapses back together.
  • Optional elements: an introduction before the exposition; a transition between the exposition's two themes; a codetta closing the exposition; a coda closing the whole piece.
  • Composers frequently broke these "rules" deliberately, even within works considered canonical examples of the form.

Pop/rock forms without a chorus

The common-practice forms above cover through most instrumental repertoire; pop/rock songwriting has its own small set of chorus-free layouts, distinct from the standard verse/pre-chorus/chorus template.

  • Through-composed — never returns to a previous section once it's complete (contrast with all the return-based forms above). Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" is the canonical pop example: five distinct sections, none repeated, each borrowing a chorus-like role (the rock section supplies the dynamic peak/release, the operatic section supplies the memorable hooks) without any of them qualifying as an actual chorus.
  • AABA (pop variant) — same skeleton as 32-Bar Song Form's jazz-standard shape, but functioning as a chorus-substitute in rock/pop: the dynamic arc comes from A/B contrast rather than a verse→chorus energy build ("a swinging ship" vs. "a rollercoaster"). Modern examples are rare post-1970s but real: "Make You Feel My Love" (Dylan/Adele), "Don't Know Why" (Norah Jones), "Yesterday" and "The Long and Winding Road" (Beatles).
  • Instrumental chorus — a wordless section (a riff, a sax line) fills the chorus's structural slot (energetic peak, the part you anticipate during the verse) without carrying lyrics. "Seven Nation Army" (White Stripes) and "Baker Street" (Gerry Rafferty) both build the whole song from a repeating verse plus this device. In modern electronic pop the same slot becomes the drop: muted verse → pre-chorus-like buildup → an all-tension-released instrumental peak in place of a sung chorus.
  • Strophic form — one repeating verse section, AAA…, each verse with new lyrics over identical music (as opposed to AABA's internal contrast). Common wherever a group needs to sing along without rehearsal: national anthems, hymns/spirituals, nursery rhymes, folk songs, 12-bar blues (which often doubles down by repeating the same lyric line twice within each verse). Structural contrast still gets built in even without a second section — subdividing the one verse into sub-phrases ("God Save the Queen": 6 bars + 8 bars), or fixing the final lyric line/title across every verse. Rock examples exist but are rare: Beatles' "Tomorrow Never Knows" (near-strophic, broken up by an instrumental section), Tame Impala's "Elephant" (same device).
  • No chorus, no clean label — some songs just have multiple contrasting sections where none is repeated/prominent enough to call a chorus. The Stranglers' "Golden Brown" functions like an instrumental-chorus song (the harpsichord riff fills the role); Squeeze's "Up the Junction" uses a long repeating verse + bridge specifically because it's a storytelling song and a repeating chorus would eat narrative time.

automation.title: Automation
automation.html:
What it is: the fourth dimension of mixing — a static mix is a photograph; automation makes it a film. Every playbook in Genres Index leans on it: the chorus that "opens up" is almost never new plugins, it's automated sends, width, and level.

The hierarchy of what to automate (most value first)

  1. Vocal level rides — ±1–2 dB phrase-by-phrase so every word sits (use a Utility before the wet sends, not the fader, so the fader stays free for balance). The single highest-leverage automation in any mix.
  2. Send levels per section — verse dry/intimate → chorus blooms (Reverb Send Long, Width Send, Delay Send Other up). This IS the verse/chorus contrast in Modern Pop and the wet/dry drama in Travis Scott Vocal Chain.
  3. The crush return +1 dB in choruses (Parallel Comp Send) — energy without level.
  4. Filter/macro moves across sections — one LPF opening over 8 bars beats three new parts (House - EDM, EDM Subgenres).
  5. Single-word events — delay throws on line-ends, one distorted word, a formant flip (Charli XCX Vocal Chain), the reverb-drenched word. Small, surgical, memorable.
  6. Mute automation as arrangement — A.G. Cook / trap school: the arrangement is which elements are off (Hip Hop - Trap, Dance Pop (Dua Lipa, Charli XCX)).

Craft rules

  • Automate late: balance → then automate. Automating a bad static mix bakes the badness in.
  • Draw section-level moves in blocks (bar-aligned), performance-level rides by hand/controller — different tools for different resolutions.
  • Automate sends and inserts' parameters, not track faders, wherever possible — keeps the mix re-balanceable afterward.
  • Effects with musical time (delay feedback, phaser rate, RC-20 wobble) reward being ridden like instruments — the psych moves in Psych-Pop (Tame Impala) are literally knob performances (automate EchoBoy's time knob for the detune-warble).
  • Name a pass: one playthrough automating ONE thing (vocal rides pass, send pass, mute pass) — passes beat noodling.

Quick recipes

  • Chorus lift without level: width send +, long verb send +, crush return +1 dB, hat/air shelf +0.5 dB — reads as "bigger," measures the same.
  • Verse intimacy: kill the width send, halve the room send, vocal up 0.5 dB.
  • The last-chorus trick: everything from the chorus lift plus a key element you've been muting since intro (saved for last).
  • Transitions: riser send into the downbeat, then cut ALL sends for beat 1 (the dry slam — Drums FX Track).
secs: The hierarchy of what to automate (most value first)

ear-candy-and-hiding-synths.title: Ear Candy and Hiding Synths
ear-candy-and-hiding-synths.html:
Small, often-subliminal details that reward attention and accentuate the vocal without competing with it — Ian Kirkpatrick's signature obsession. The rule that governs all of it: candy serves the song and the story, and it lives just at the point of perception — present, but never enough to distract. Companion to Arrangement and Song Form, Depth and Space, rate of information, and Automation.

Hiding synths in / behind vocals

  • A synth playing the note, buried behind a vocal word, to make that word "pop." Instead of a reverb throw on a standout word, put a synth on the same note underneath it — loud enough to feel, low enough that "you don't even know." His current obsession. → Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals, Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals (pt 2)
  • Build the synth patch from the vocal itself. Drag a word (e.g. "move," "me") into PadShop and make a patch from it, so the pad sounds like the vowel — the "ooh" of move, the "ee" of me. The synth and the word are the same timbre, so it fuses. → PadShop, Pitch and Formant
  • Sidechain mode (iZotope VocalSynth 2): route a synth loop into VocalSynth's sidechain so the synth modulates the vocal — combinations "that don't exist anywhere." → Ian Kirkpatrick - Creating Vocal FX (VocalSynth 2)

Vocal candy

  • Tiny vocal fragments on their own track — chop little pieces of the lead to a dedicated track for scoop/echo candy (one of Ian's "favorite echoes ever"). → Delay, EchoBoy Jr
  • Pitched "altar-boy" vocal — pitch a vocal snippet up (Little AlterBoy / Output Exhale) as a pre-drop excitement source. → Little AlterBoy, Exhale, Pitch and Formant
  • A chop that stops before the snare — cut a vocal so it ends before the downbeat instead of clipping it on the beat, so you hear it stop ("a little oh what the—"). Automate the LFO Tool duck to switch on exactly when the chorus drops. → LFO Tool, Automation
  • Lower/upper octave doubles — add an octave under a vocal (VocalSynth Compuvox / Polyvox / Biovox in auto mode) to fatten it or reach notes the singer can't. → Ian Kirkpatrick - Pitch Shifted Vocals (VocalSynth 2)

Found-sound & texture candy

  • Keep the room talk in. Tapping a guitar/desk for percussion with friends chatting left in the recording ("the more talking the better, it sounds natural"), gated. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording, TEXTURE Slot
  • Reverse-reverb swell into the "one" — resolves attention onto the downbeat. → Reverb
  • A texture "just at the point of perception" — a low chorus layer kept barely audible on purpose; felt, not heard. → Depth and Space

Discipline

  • Candy must survive the "does it distract from the vocal?" test. If a rhythmic or melodic detail pulls the ear off the story, it's over-produced — cut it (rate of information).
  • The reason is the candy. New Rules' "everything stops" moment came from an idea, not a plugin — chase the inspiration, then build the detail to serve it.

signal-path.title: Signal Path
signal-path.html:
The single most load-bearing fact in synthesis, and the one the placement found missing (SYN-11, blank). Every subtractive synth you own is the same three blocks in the same order. Learn this and every synth stops being a wall of knobs and becomes the same instrument with a different skin.

Oscillator → Filter → Amplifier.

Generate a raw tone. Remove some of it. Control how loud it is over time.

That's it. Everything else — envelopes, LFOs, modulation matrices, macros — exists to move those three blocks while a note is held.

The three blocks

Block Job The question it answers
Oscillator (VCO/DCO) Generates a raw, harmonically rich waveform What is the sound made of?
Filter (VCF) Removes harmonics — usually the highs What is the tone?
Amplifier (VCA) Controls level over time What is the shape?

Optionally the oscillator stage mixes several sources: two or three oscillators, a sub oscillator, and a noise generator. They sum before the filter.

Where the modulators act

This is the half that makes it a synth rather than a tone generator. Envelopes and LFOs don't sit in the audio path — they sit alongside it and move the blocks.

          ┌──────────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌───────────┐
  NOTE →  │ OSC(s)   │ → │ FILTER │ → │ AMPLIFIER │ → OUT
          └──────────┘   └────────┘   └───────────┘
                ↑             ↑             ↑
             LFO/ENV      FILTER ENV     AMP ENV
             (pitch)      (cutoff)       (level)
  • The amp envelope is mandatory. Without it nothing sounds at all — a VCA at zero is silence. This is why every synth has an ADSR wired to the amp by default and why "why can't I hear anything" is almost always a dead amp envelope.
  • The filter envelope is where the character lives. A second envelope on cutoff, with an envelope amount control, is what produces the bright-then-dark snap of a pluck, the slow open of a pad, the wub of a bass.
  • LFOs go anywhere. On pitch → vibrato. On filter cutoff → movement. On amp → tremolo. On pulse width → the classic chorusy thickening. On wavetable position → morphing timbre.

Reading it on your own synths

The same three blocks, differently dressed:

Synth Oscillator Filter Amp
Analog OSC1/OSC2 + noise Filter section Amp with its own ADSR
Wavetable Osc 1/2 (wavetable + position) Filter 1/2 Amp envelope
Drift Osc 1/2 + noise Filter (with its own env) Amp env
Serum 2 Osc A/B + sub + noise Filter (routable per osc) Env 1 → amp by default
Model 84 Saw + sub + pulse The Juno filter Amp ADSR
Operator Four operators (FM — see FM Synthesis) Optional filter Operator A's envelope

Operator is the informative exception: it's FM, so its "oscillators" modulate each other rather than summing. The filter and amp stages still behave the same way.

Why the order matters

The blocks are in that order for a reason, and reversing them in your head causes real mistakes.

Filter before amp means the filter shapes tone while the note is still at full level, and the amp then shapes the result. If the amp came first, a fast amp decay would leave the filter nothing to work on.

The filter is subtractive — it can only remove what the oscillator generated. A sine wave has one harmonic; no filter can make it brighter, because there's nothing above the fundamental to let through. This is why patches start from saws and squares: you can't carve what isn't there. It's also the core limitation that FM Synthesis exists to escape.

What this unlocks

Once the path is internalized, three common problems become obvious rather than mysterious:

  • "The patch has no attack." The amp envelope's attack is too slow, or the filter envelope is opening slower than the amp.
  • "It sounds dull no matter what I do with the filter." The oscillator isn't generating enough harmonic content — wrong waveform, or a sine.
  • "It doesn't evolve." Nothing is modulating the filter or the wavetable position. A held note with static blocks is a static sound. (SYN-10: the answer is a slow LFO or long envelope on cutoff or wavetable position — the timbre, not the level.)
secs: Reading it on your own synths

oscillators-and-waveforms.title: Oscillators and Waveforms
oscillators-and-waveforms.html:
The first block in the Signal Path. The oscillator generates the raw tone; everything downstream can only shape what it produces.

The governing rule: a subtractive filter can only remove harmonics. It can never add them. So the waveform you start on sets the ceiling on how bright the patch can ever be. Start on a sine and no amount of filter tweaking will give you a lead.

The four basic waveforms

Wave Harmonics Sounds like Use for
Sine Fundamental only — no harmonics at all Pure, hollow, flute-ish Subs, 808s, bells (via FM Synthesis), layering under anything
Triangle Odd harmonics, falling off fast Soft, slightly reedy Gentle leads, softer subs, flute-like pads
Square / pulse Odd harmonics only Hollow, woody, clarinet-ish Basses, chiptune leads, retro anything
Sawtooth All harmonics, falling off gradually Bright, buzzy, full Supersaws, brass, strings, the default for pads and leads

Saw is the workhorse precisely because it has the most harmonic content — the most raw material for the filter to carve. When in doubt, start there.

The square-vs-saw difference is worth hearing rather than reading: square omits every even harmonic, which is what produces its hollow character. That's the same reason a clarinet sounds hollow — it behaves like a closed pipe and suppresses even harmonics too.

Pulse width

A square wave is a pulse at exactly 50% width. Move that width away from 50% and the harmonic content changes — thinner, more nasal as it narrows.

Pulse width modulation (PWM) — a slow LFO on pulse width — is one of the oldest and best thickening tricks in synthesis. It makes a single oscillator sound like several slightly detuned ones without the CPU cost or the phase issues. The classic string-machine and Juno pad sound is PWM.

Stacking oscillators

Most patches use more than one source, summed before the filter.

  • Two oscillators detuned slightly — the fundamental thickening move. See Voice Architecture.
  • An octave apart — adds weight below or sparkle above without muddying.
  • A fifth apart — instant power-chord character. Locks the patch to one harmonic function, so use deliberately.
  • Sub oscillator — usually a sine or square one or two octaves down, dedicated to low-end weight. Keep it clean: no detune, no drive. In a mix the sub is doing a job the ear reads as level, not tone.
  • Noise — not a pitched oscillator at all. White noise is flat across the spectrum; pink noise falls off with frequency. A short burst of filtered noise on the attack is what gives a patch its "breath" or its pick attack, and it's the cheapest way to make a synth sound less synthetic.

Phase and retrigger

Whether an oscillator restarts its waveform at the same point on every note (retrigger / phase reset) or runs freely matters more than it sounds like it should:

  • Retriggered — every note attacks identically. Essential for basses and 808s, where a consistent transient is the whole point.
  • Free-running — every note is slightly different. Good for pads and anything that should feel organic.

An 808 or sub bass with a free-running oscillator will have inconsistent attack level note-to-note. That's a real and commonly misdiagnosed problem — it gets blamed on the compressor.

On your synths

  • Analog · Model 84 — two oscillators plus sub and noise, the classic layout, nothing hidden.
  • Drift — two oscillators with a genuinely good noise source and its "drift" control, which slightly randomizes pitch and is what makes it sound analogue.
  • Wavetable · Serum 2 — the waveform itself is scannable rather than fixed. See Wavetable Synthesis.
  • Operator — sine oscillators only, because in FM you build harmonics rather than filtering them away. See FM Synthesis.

Drill

On Analog, listen to all four waveforms through a wide-open filter, then close the filter to the same cutoff on each. Note how much each one still has left. That difference is the harmonic content, and it's why saw is the default.

filters-and-resonance.title: Filters and Resonance
filters-and-resonance.html:
The second block in the Signal Path, and the one that gives subtractive synthesis its name. The filter removes harmonics the oscillator generated. It cannot add any.

Filter types

Type Passes Removes Use for
Low-pass (LPF) Below cutoff Highs The default. Warmth, distance, closing a pad down
High-pass (HPF) Above cutoff Lows Thinning a pad out of the bass's way, telephone effects
Band-pass (BPF) A band around cutoff Both ends Nasal, radio, focused mids — good for ear candy
Notch Everything except a band A narrow band Phaser-adjacent movement, removing a resonance

Low-pass is the one you'll use 80% of the time, because it maps onto how real sound behaves: distance, absorption and dullness all read as fewer highs.

Cutoff and slope

Cutoff is the frequency the filter acts around. Everything else is relative to it.

Slope is how steeply it acts, in dB per octave:

  • 12 dB/oct (2-pole) — gentle. Leaves some of the removed material audible. Warmer, more "analogue."
  • 24 dB/oct (4-pole) — steep. The Moog ladder sound; more dramatic sweeps, more obviously synthetic.

A 12 dB filter closed all the way still lets some brightness through; a 24 dB one really shuts the door. Neither is better — 12 for warmth, 24 for drama.

Resonance

Resonance boosts a narrow band right at the cutoff frequency. It doesn't change what's removed; it emphasizes the edge of the removal.

Musically this is what makes a filter sweep sing rather than just get dull. Low resonance = a tonal change. High resonance = a pitched, vocal quality that follows the cutoff as it moves.

Push it far enough and the filter self-oscillates — it starts generating a pure sine tone at the cutoff frequency, with no oscillator input at all. That's the half the placement (SYN-05) missed, and it's genuinely useful: a self-oscillating filter is a free sine oscillator you can play with the cutoff knob. Many classic laser, zap and kick-drum sounds are exactly this.

Resonance and level

High resonance adds real energy at the cutoff. Sweeping a resonant filter can produce sudden loud peaks — especially in the low end, where a resonant sweep through 60 Hz will slam a limiter. Watch levels when automating cutoff with resonance up.

Filter drive

Most modern filters have a drive or saturation stage. This is not a bonus feature — analogue filters distorted as a matter of physics, and that distortion is a large part of why they sound "warm." Driving a digital filter puts some of that back. Small amounts are almost always an improvement on basses and leads.

The filter envelope

Covered in Envelopes and ADSR, but the essential pairing lives here: cutoff + envelope amount is where character comes from.

  • Pluck — filter envelope with fast decay, sustain 0, high envelope amount. Bright on the attack, dark immediately after.
  • Pad swell — slow attack on the filter envelope so the patch opens over seconds.
  • Wub / bass movement — an LFO on cutoff, tempo-synced.
  • Negative envelope amount — the filter closes on attack. Uncommon and distinctive.

Key tracking is the other control worth knowing: it makes cutoff follow the note pitch, so high notes stay proportionally as bright as low ones. Without it, a patch that sounds right in one octave sounds muffled two octaves up.

The mix-context rule

The most common filter mistake isn't technical. A patch soloed with the filter wide open sounds impressive; in a mix it eats the same space as the vocal and the hats.

Filter to fit, not to impress. Most synth parts in a finished record are duller in isolation than you'd expect. Closing the filter is usually a better fix than EQ, because it removes the harmonics at the source rather than carving them out afterwards — see Masking and Carving.

On your synths

Model 84 has the Juno filter — a 24 dB low-pass with the resonance character the whole bedroom-pop and synthwave lane is built on. Analog and Drift both offer switchable 12/24 dB. Serum 2 and Wavetable carry large filter menus including comb and formant types worth exploring once the basics are automatic.

Drill

On Analog with a saw: sweep cutoff with resonance at zero, then at 50%, then near maximum until it self-oscillates. Then kill the oscillator entirely and play the self-oscillating filter as a sine. Five minutes and resonance stops being abstract.

envelopes-and-adsr.title: Envelopes and ADSR
envelopes-and-adsr.html:
An envelope is a shape drawn over time, triggered by a note, applied to a parameter. It is not a sound — it's a controller.

The one to fix first

Three of the four ADSR controls are times. Only sustain is a level. The placement (SYN-06) had decay filed as a level, which is the single most common ADSR misread and the reason decay controls never behave the way people expect.

The four stages

Stage Type What it does
Attack Time How long to rise from silence to full level after the key goes down
Decay Time How long to fall from full level down to the sustain level
Sustain Level The level it holds at while the key stays down
Release Time How long to fall from the sustain level to silence after the key comes up

Read as a sentence: rise over A, fall over D until you reach S, hold there, then fall to zero over R.

Decay is a time because it describes a journey — from peak down to sustain. Sustain is a level because it's a destination, not a duration. Sustain is also the only stage with no time of its own: it lasts exactly as long as you hold the key.

 level
   │      ╱╲
   │     ╱  ╲______________          ← sustain LEVEL (held)
   │    ╱                   ╲
   │   ╱                     ╲
   └──┴────┴──────────────────┴──── time
      A    D                  R
      ↑    ↑                  ↑
    time  time              time

Two envelopes, two jobs

Every subtractive patch uses at least two, and knowing which is which solves most "why does it sound wrong" questions.

  • Amp envelope → the amplifier. Controls loudness over time. Mandatory — with no amp envelope there's no sound at all.
  • Filter envelope → the filter cutoff. Controls brightness over time. This is where character comes from.

The filter envelope has an extra control the amp envelope doesn't: envelope amount (sometimes "env depth" or a bipolar knob). It scales how far the envelope pushes the cutoff, and it can be negative — a negative amount makes the filter close on attack instead of opening, which is a distinctly different and underused sound.

The four shapes worth knowing

Most patches are a variation on one of these.

Pluck / percussive — attack 0, short decay, sustain 0, short release. All the energy is in the first fraction of a second and then it's gone. That's what "pluck" means, and the sustain-at-zero is the part people miss (SYN-12). Copy the same shape onto the filter envelope with a healthy envelope amount and you get the bright-then-dark snap that sells it.

Pad — slow attack, long decay, high sustain, long release. The note swells in and lingers. A pad with a fast attack isn't a pad, it's an organ.

Organ / stab — attack 0, decay irrelevant, sustain 100%, release 0. Fully on while held, fully off when released. Decay does nothing here because sustain is already at maximum — there's nowhere to fall to. Useful to understand: it's why the decay knob sometimes appears broken.

Bass — attack 0, medium decay, sustain moderate, short release. Instant, some front-weight, controlled tail. Short release matters — a long release on a bass smears every note into the next and is the most common cause of muddy low end.

Beyond ADSR

  • DAHDSR (Serum 2, Wavetable) adds delay before the attack and hold at the peak. Delay is genuinely useful for staggering layers so they don't all hit at once.
  • Envelope curves. Most modern synths let you bend each segment from linear to exponential. Real acoustic decay is exponential — a linear decay reads as synthetic, which is sometimes exactly what you want.
  • Free envelopes / mod envelopes. Any spare envelope can be routed anywhere via the modulation matrix — wavetable position, FM amount, pan, effect depth. See LFOs and Modulation.
  • Velocity → envelope. Routing velocity to the filter envelope amount is what makes a patch feel played rather than typed: hit harder, it opens brighter.

On your synths

Analog and Model 84 give you the classic pair, amp and filter, and nothing else — the best place to learn the shapes. Drift has one envelope hard-wired to the amp plus a flexible second. Wavetable and Serum 2 give three or more, freely routable. Operator gives each of its four operators its own multi-stage envelope, which is the whole reason FM can produce evolving timbres — see FM Synthesis.

Drill

Load Analog on a saw wave and build all four shapes above from scratch, amp envelope only. Then add the filter envelope to each and find the envelope amount that makes the pluck snap. Ten minutes, and the ADSR misread stops being possible.

lfos-and-modulation.title: LFOs and Modulation
lfos-and-modulation.html:
Modulation is what separates a synth from a tone generator. A patch with nothing moving is a static sound no matter how good the oscillator is.

What an LFO actually is

A Low Frequency Oscillator is an oscillator running below the hearing range — roughly under 20 Hz — used to modulate a parameter rather than be heard as a tone.

The placement (SYN-04) got "low frequency oscillator" and stopped there. The distinction that matters is the second half: it's the same circuit as an audio oscillator, just slow, and it's wired to a knob instead of to the output. You never hear the LFO. You hear what it's moving.

Push an LFO up past ~20 Hz and it stops sounding like movement and starts sounding like tone — at which point you've built FM Synthesis. The line between "modulation" and "audio" is only speed.

LFO controls

Control What it does
Rate How fast. Free-running in Hz, or tempo-synced to note values
Shape Sine (smooth), triangle, square (on/off jumps), saw (ramp + snap back), random/S&H (stepped chaos)
Depth / amount How far it pushes the target. Often bipolar
Phase / offset Where in its cycle it starts
Retrigger Restart on each note, or run free
Fade in Ramp the depth up over time — how you get delayed vibrato

Tempo-sync is the single most useful setting. An LFO at 1/8 or 1/4 locks movement to the groove; the same LFO free-running at an arbitrary Hz fights it. For anything rhythmic, sync it.

What to modulate

Same LFO, entirely different results depending on destination:

Target Result
Pitch Vibrato (subtle, with fade-in) or a warble/siren (extreme)
Filter cutoff Movement, the wub, sweeping pads
Amplitude Tremolo; square-wave LFO gives gated/stutter
Pulse width The classic thickening — see Oscillators and Waveforms
Wavetable position Morphing timbre — see Wavetable Synthesis
Pan Auto-pan; use sparingly, check mono
FM amount Evolving harmonic content
Effect depth Movement without touching the synth voice

Making a pad actually evolve

This was SYN-10 — you had "use an LFO" and no target. The answer is filter cutoff or wavetable position, modulated slowly.

The rule: to make a sound evolve, modulate its timbre, not its level. Level changes read as volume automation; timbre changes read as the sound being alive.

For a genuinely evolving eight-bar pad, layer modulators at different rates so nothing repeats obviously:

  1. A very slow LFO (8 or 16 bars) on filter cutoff — the broad sweep.
  2. A second, faster LFO (1–2 bars) on wavetable position or a second filter — detail.
  3. A long envelope (not LFO) on something, so the first pass differs from later ones.
  4. Slight random/drift on pitch, if the synth offers it — Drift's "drift" control does exactly this.

The reason to mix envelopes with LFOs: an LFO is periodic and eventually reveals its loop. An envelope fires once per note and doesn't.

The modulation matrix

Beyond the hard-wired routings, most modern synths give you a matrix: pick a source, pick a destination, set an amount.

Sources aren't just LFOs — velocity, aftertouch, mod wheel, note number, random-per-note, and envelopes are all modulators. Some of the most useful routings have nothing to do with LFOs:

  • Velocity → filter envelope amount — hit harder, sound brighter. The single biggest "feels played" upgrade.
  • Note number → cutoff (key tracking) — keeps high notes from sounding muffled.
  • Mod wheel → LFO depth — vibrato under your control instead of always-on.
  • Random per note → pitch (tiny amount) — subtle humanization, kills the machine-gun effect on repeated notes.

Modulate the modulator. An LFO whose depth is controlled by an envelope gives vibrato that fades in — much more musical than vibrato from note one. Most synths allow this; almost nobody uses it.

On your synths

Serum 2 has the most flexible matrix, with drag-and-drop routing and drawable LFO shapes. Wavetable gives two LFOs plus a matrix and is the most direct place to hear position modulation. Drift is deliberately simple — one LFO, a few destinations — which makes it a good place to learn. Operator routes modulation per-operator, which is the entire point of FM.

Drill

On Wavetable: build a pad, then add a 4-bar LFO to filter cutoff and an 8-bar LFO to wavetable position at different rates. Hold one chord for 16 bars and listen to it not repeat. Then remove the position LFO and hear how much deader it gets.

voice-architecture.title: Voice Architecture
voice-architecture.html:
How a synth allocates notes — and how many copies of the Signal Path run at once. This is where thickness comes from, and where CPU goes.

Unison and detune

The placement (SYN-09) had detune and not unison. They only work together, and unison is the one doing the work.

  • Unison stacks multiple copies of the same oscillator on the same note.
  • Detune spreads those copies slightly apart in pitch.

Unison without detune does almost nothing — identical copies just sum to the same waveform, louder. The thickening comes entirely from the copies being slightly out of tune with each other, so they drift in and out of phase and produce slow beating. That beating is what the ear reads as "big."

Control Effect
Voices How many copies. 3–5 for warmth; 7–16 for the supersaw wall
Detune How far apart. Small = warm; large = seasick
Blend / stack Balance between the centre voice and the outer ones
Spread / width Pans the copies across the stereo field

The supersaw is exactly this: many detuned saws, spread wide. DUNE 3's Leads/Supersaw banks have it pre-engineered; Serum 2 builds it from unison voices on a saw.

Two costs

Mono compatibility. Detuned voices spread wide can partially cancel in mono. Always check — see Width and Stereo.

Bass. Detune below about 150 Hz produces beating that reads as wobbly, unstable low end. Keep subs and 808s in mono with no detune. If you want a wide bass, layer: clean mono sub + detuned wide upper layer. See Bass Design.

Polyphony modes

Mode Behaviour Use for
Poly Many notes at once, each its own voice Pads, chords, keys
Mono One note at a time, retriggers envelopes Basses, leads
Legato One note; overlapping notes don't retrigger envelopes Expressive leads, 808 glides

Legato is the one worth understanding. In mono, every new note restarts the envelopes — a fresh attack each time. In legato, if you hold one note and play another before releasing, the pitch changes but the envelope keeps running. The result is a smooth, connected phrase.

Combined with glide/portamento — the time taken to slide between pitches — legato is how you get the 808 slide that defines trap low end. Glide with retrigger off, short glide time, and the note bends into the next rather than restarting.

Voice count and CPU

Each voice is a full signal path. A 16-voice unison patch played as a four-note chord is 64 simultaneous oscillator-filter-amp chains, before effects.

This is the main CPU cost in most projects. Practical responses:

  • Drop unison voices on parts that don't need the width — a bass rarely does.
  • Freeze or resample. Printing the part to audio removes the cost entirely and forces a commitment, which is usually good anyway. See Committing and Printing.
  • Watch voice stealing — when a synth hits its voice limit it kills the oldest note, which on a pad with a long release is audible as tails cutting off abruptly.

Voice-level randomization

The subtle thing that makes hardware sound alive: on a real analogue synth, every voice is a slightly different physical circuit, so no two notes are identical.

Digital synths emulate this deliberately:

  • Drift's drift control randomizes pitch and filter slightly per voice — the reason it sounds analogue.
  • Analog and Model 84 apply small per-voice variation by design.
  • In Serum 2 or Wavetable, route random-per-note to pitch at a tiny depth for the same effect.

Without it, repeated notes are byte-identical and the ear notices — the machine-gun effect. This is the synth equivalent of the humanization discussion in Rhythm and Groove.

Drill

On Serum 2 or DUNE 3: take a saw lead, set unison to 1 voice, then walk it up to 7 with detune at zero — note that nothing much happens. Now bring detune up. That's the whole mechanism. Then check the result in mono.

subtractive-synthesis.title: Subtractive Synthesis
subtractive-synthesis.html:
Start with more than you need, then take away. The oldest and most common approach, and the one the Signal Path describes.

Generate a harmonically rich waveform — a saw or a square — then use a filter to remove harmonics until what's left is the sound you wanted. Sculpture, not construction.

Why it dominates

  • It maps onto how hearing works. Removing highs reads as further away, duller, warmer — the same cues real acoustics produce. Filter moves feel musical without you having to think about spectra.
  • It's cheap. A few oscillators and a filter, which is why it existed in analogue hardware decades before digital synthesis.
  • It's predictable. Turn cutoff down, it gets darker. Every time. Compare FM Synthesis, where a small parameter change can transform the timbre unrecognizably.

The limitation that defines it

A subtractive filter can only remove harmonics the oscillator already generated.

That's not a criticism, it's the definition, and it's the answer to SYN-07 — what actually separates subtractive from FM. Start on a sine, which has no harmonics above the fundamental, and no filter on earth will brighten it. There's nothing there to let through.

It also means inharmonic content is essentially unreachable. Saw and square waves have harmonics at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, and filtering can only attenuate those — never move them to non-integer positions. Bells, metal and glass are inharmonic, which is precisely why subtractive synths are bad at them and FM Synthesis is good at them.

The standard patch recipe

Almost every subtractive sound is this, with different numbers:

  1. Pick the waveform for harmonic content. Saw for bright and full, square for hollow, triangle/sine for soft. Oscillators and Waveforms
  2. Add a second oscillator — detuned for thickness, an octave down for weight, or a sub. Voice Architecture
  3. Set the filter type and cutoff. Low-pass, roughly where you want the brightness ceiling.
  4. Shape the amp envelope — the loudness contour. Envelopes and ADSR
  5. Shape the filter envelope with envelope amount — the character. This is the step that separates a patch from a tone.
  6. Add modulation — an LFO on cutoff for movement, PWM for thickness, velocity to filter for playability. LFOs and Modulation
  7. Then, and only then, effects.

Steps 4 and 5 are where beginners stop early and where the sound actually lives.

Four patches worth being able to build cold

Patch Recipe
Sub bass Sine or triangle, mono, no detune, fast attack, short release. Nothing clever.
Pluck Saw, filter env fast decay + sustain 0 + high env amount, amp env matching.
Pad Two detuned saws, slow amp attack, high sustain, long release, slow LFO on cutoff.
Supersaw lead Saw, unison 7+, moderate detune, wide spread, filter mostly open, mono/legato with glide.

Build all four from an initialized patch and subtractive synthesis stops being mysterious.

On your synths

The purest ones are Analog, Model 84 and Drift — two oscillators, one filter, two envelopes, an LFO. Nothing hidden, everything on one panel. Learn on these.

Serum 2, Wavetable and DUNE 3 are subtractive at heart with a more complex oscillator stage — the filter and amp behave identically, the source is just richer. Omnisphere is subtractive processing over sampled sources rather than generated ones.

The habit worth building

Initialize the patch and build it yourself. Preset-browsing teaches sound selection; building teaches sound design, and only the second one generalizes. This is exactly the gap the placement found — Instrument Preset Map shows fluent preset navigation, and SYN-11 showed the signal path underneath was blank.

The Instrument Preset Map advice still holds for working fast under deadline. This is the other mode, for when you're learning.
secs: Four patches worth being able to build cold

fm-synthesis.title: FM Synthesis
fm-synthesis.html:
Frequency Modulation: one oscillator modulates another's frequency, generating harmonics that weren't there before.

This is the fundamental split from Subtractive Synthesis, and the answer to SYN-07. Subtractive starts rich and removes. FM starts with sine waves — the simplest possible source — and creates harmonic content through modulation. Additive by mechanism, subtractive's opposite by philosophy.

Carriers and modulators

Two roles, and any operator can play either:

  • Carrier — the oscillator you actually hear.
  • Modulator — an oscillator wired to the carrier's frequency, which you don't hear directly.

Wire a modulator to a carrier and the carrier's pitch wobbles at the modulator's rate. Slow, that's vibrato — an LFO. Speed the modulator into the audio range and the wobble stops being heard as pitch movement and starts being heard as new harmonic content: sidebands appearing above and below the carrier frequency.

FM is just an LFO running too fast to hear as movement. That's the whole trick, and it's why LFOs and Modulation and this page are the same idea at different speeds.

Two controls govern everything:

Control Effect
Ratio (modulator freq ÷ carrier freq) Where the sidebands land — decides harmonic vs inharmonic
Index / amount (modulation depth) How many sidebands and how loud — decides brightness and aggression

Modulation index is FM's brightness knob. Envelope it and you get the DX7 electric piano — bright bell-like attack decaying into a soft sine body — which is one envelope on one parameter.

Why FM does bells and metal

The question the placement asked (SYN-13, blank), and the mechanism is worth knowing exactly.

  • Integer ratios (1:1, 2:1, 1:3) → harmonic sidebands. They land on whole-number multiples of the fundamental, right on the overtone series. Your ear fuses them into one clear pitch. Result: basses, electric pianos, organs, plucks.
  • Non-integer ratios (1:1.41, 3:2.7) → inharmonic sidebands. They land between the harmonics. The ear can't fuse them into a single pitch, so the sound turns clangorous and metallic. Result: bells, mallets, metal, glass, aggressive digital leads.

Real bells are physically inharmonic — a struck metal object vibrates in modes that aren't whole-number multiples of any fundamental. FM reproduces that naturally because non-integer ratios put partials in exactly those non-integer positions. (MusicTech, Synth Basics)

Subtractive can't get there. Its oscillators are harmonic by construction and the filter can only attenuate what exists — it can't relocate a partial to a non-integer position. That's the complete answer to why subtractive struggles with bells and FM doesn't.

Algorithms

More than two operators, and the wiring matters. An algorithm is a preset routing: which operators modulate which, and which reach the output.

  • Stacked (A modulates B modulates C) — modulating a modulator, spectra get complex fast. Aggressive, digital, hard to predict.
  • Parallel (several carriers side by side) — closer to additive; each carrier contributes its own partial set. Smoother, more organ-like.
  • Mixed — most useful algorithms, some modulation depth plus a clean carrier for body.

Operator gives four operators and eleven algorithms, displayed as a diagram in the top-left. That diagram is the patch's architecture — read it first, before touching anything.

Why it has a reputation for being hard

Honest framing, because it explains why the placement found this blank and that's normal:

  • Parameters aren't perceptual. Cutoff maps to "brightness" intuitively. "Ratio 1.41 at index 6" maps to nothing until you've heard it.
  • It's non-linear. Small ratio changes can transform a patch completely. Subtractive degrades gracefully; FM jumps.
  • Tweaking randomly rarely converges. Subtractive rewards fiddling. FM mostly rewards understanding.

The practical route in: don't build from scratch first. Load an Operator preset, look at its algorithm, then change one thing — one ratio, or one operator's envelope — and listen. Ratios first, index second, envelopes third.

Where it earns its place in your music

FM isn't a niche curiosity for the genres you work in:

  • Bells, mallets and glassy plucks — the ear-candy melodic layer. Operator and Collision both cover this.
  • Electric pianos — the DX7 lane, all over 80s pop and modern R&B.
  • Hard digital basses — FM basses have a bite subtractive can't produce. Relevant to EDM Subgenres.
  • Clean sine subs — Operator with modulation at zero is a pure sine generator, which is a perfectly good 808 source.

Drill

On Operator: pick the simplest algorithm (one modulator into one carrier). Set ratio 1:1 and sweep the modulation index from 0 up — hear harmonics appear on a sine. Then move the ratio to 1:2 (still harmonic), then to 1:1.41 (inharmonic). The moment it turns metallic is the whole lesson.
