wavetable-synthesis.title: Wavetable Synthesis
wavetable-synthesis.html:
A table of single-cycle waveforms, scanned through by a movable position — and the position is modulatable, so the timbre morphs over time.

The placement had this one right (SYN-08). The refinement worth adding is the precision: it isn't just "lots of waveforms available," it's that scanning between them is a continuously modulatable parameter, which is the entire reason the method exists.

How it works

A wavetable is an ordered array of single-cycle waveforms — often 64 or 256 of them. The oscillator plays one at a time. Position (or "index") selects which.

Set position statically and it's an ordinary oscillator on an unusual waveform. Modulate position and you get timbral movement no fixed oscillator can produce — the sound changes character while the pitch stays put.

That's the distinction from Subtractive Synthesis, where timbre change comes from filtering harmonics away. Here the source itself changes.

Position is the whole instrument

The single most important routing in wavetable synthesis:

Modulator on position Result
Slow LFO Evolving pad — the classic use
Envelope Timbre that changes across the note's life (bright attack → mellow body)
Velocity Harder playing selects a more aggressive waveform
Mod wheel Hands-on timbral control while playing
Fast LFO / audio-rate Harsh, digital, FM-adjacent territory

This is also the correct answer to the evolving-pad question (SYN-10): filter cutoff or wavetable position, modulated slowly. Position is often the better choice because it changes the harmonic content rather than just filtering it, so the movement is more interesting than a sweep.

Interpolation

How the oscillator gets between adjacent waveforms in the table:

  • Interpolated / morphing — smoothly crossfades. Fluid, natural, the default.
  • Stepped — jumps discretely. Glitchy, digital, rhythmic when synced.

Most synths default to interpolation. Stepped is worth knowing for hard electronic textures.

Where wavetables come from

  • Factory tables — the fastest way in. Wavetable ships with a well-organized set; Serum 2's library is enormous.
  • Analogue-style tables — tables that sweep saw→square→pulse, giving a subtractive-flavoured sound with morphing built in.
  • Imported audio. Serum 2 will slice any audio file into a wavetable. Drop in a vocal, a field recording, a drum loop — the result is usually unusable as-is and occasionally extraordinary. This is a genuine sound-design lane and it connects to Sampling and Sound Selection.
  • Drawn by hand — for the patient.

Practical notes

Not every position sounds good. Tables often contain a few genuinely useful waveforms and a lot of transitional material. Find the two or three positions that sound right, then modulate between those rather than sweeping the whole table.

Position modulation can wreck low end. On a bass, sweeping position changes the fundamental's relative level, which reads as inconsistent volume. Keep bass positions static or modulate narrowly, and see Bass Design.

It stacks with everything. A wavetable oscillator still runs into a filter and an amp envelope — the Signal Path is unchanged. Wavetable replaces the oscillator block only.

On your synths

Wavetable (Ableton stock) is the best learning tool — the table is drawn on screen and you watch the position marker move as you modulate it. That visual feedback is what makes the concept click.

Serum 2 is the deeper version: two wavetable oscillators, imports, wavetable editing, warp modes per oscillator. DUNE 3 and Massive both use wavetable oscillators under a more traditional interface.

Per Instrument Preset Map, the Pads folder in Wavetable with position-LFO movement is already your established starting point — this note explains why that works.

Drill

On Wavetable: hold one note, set the amp envelope to full sustain, and slowly drag the position marker by hand across the whole table. Listen to how much the sound changes with no filter movement at all. Then assign an 8-bar LFO to position and stop touching it.

granular-synthesis.title: Granular Synthesis
granular-synthesis.html:
Chop audio into very short grains — typically 1–100 ms — and replay them with independent control over position, size, density and pitch.

The placement (SYN-14) had "samples a specific part of a waveform, good for glitchy stuff." Glitch is a real use, but it undersells it: the defining property is that playback position and pitch become independent, which is what makes everything else possible.

The decoupling

In normal sample playback, time and pitch are locked. Play a sample at half speed and it drops an octave — tape behaviour, and what re-pitching does.

Granular breaks that link. Because the synth is re-triggering tiny grains rather than playing the file linearly, it can:

  • Freeze — hold the position still and repeat the same grain indefinitely. An infinite sustain from a half-second source.
  • Stretch enormously — move the position slowly while grains fire at their own rate. Ten-second stretches of a one-second sample, with no transposition.
  • Transpose without changing duration — pitch the grains, leave position speed alone.
  • Scatter — randomize position and get a cloud rather than a line.

That decoupling is the concept. Glitch is one thing you can do with it.

The four controls

Control What it does Typical range
Position Where in the source file grains are taken from The main performance control
Grain size How long each grain is ~1–10 ms = buzzy/pitched · 20–50 ms = smooth · 100 ms+ = recognizable fragments
Density / rate How many grains fire per second Sparse = stuttery · dense = continuous texture
Spray / jitter Randomization of position per grain A little = organic · a lot = cloud

Grain size is the character control. Very short grains stop sounding like the source at all and start producing tone from the grain rate itself — the source becomes raw material rather than something you recognize. Longer grains keep the source's identity.

Spray is the "make it sound less like a machine" control. Zero spray with high density produces a periodic buzz; a small amount breaks up the regularity into texture.

What it's genuinely for

  • Pads and textures from anything. Take half a second of a vocal, a room recording, a guitar note — get an evolving bed. This is the highest-value use and it costs almost nothing.
  • Ambient beds and drones — see Ambient Texture and Field Recording.
  • Time-stretching as sound design rather than tempo-matching. Stretching something 20× produces material that doesn't sound like a stretch, it sounds like a new instrument.
  • Reverb-like tails without a reverb — dense, sprayed grains from a decaying source behave like a diffuse tail with a different character than any algorithm.
  • Glitch and stutter — sparse, low-density grains at rhythmic intervals.

The workflow that matters most

Granular's best use in your workflow is as a resampling target, not a live instrument:

  1. Print or bounce something — a chord, a vocal phrase, a drum fill.
  2. Load it into Granulator 3.
  3. Freeze on an interesting moment, find a grain size and spray that sounds good.
  4. Print the result and treat it as new source material.

That's the print → mangle → reprint loop, and it connects directly to the resampling gap the placement found (SMP-09). See Committing and Printing and Sample Clearance if the source isn't yours.

Practical notes

It is CPU-hungry. Many grains, each with its own envelope. Print early.

Mono-check dense granular. Grains scattered in stereo can partially cancel — see Width and Stereo.

Source quality is everything. Granular magnifies whatever's there. Noise, hum and clipping in the source become features of the texture, sometimes usefully and usually not.

It's rarely a foreground sound. Granular textures sit under things. A granular pad at 20% in the background does more for a track than one at the front.

On your synths

Granulator 3 (Max for Live) is the main tool — drop in a sample, position knob, grain controls, done. Also Granulator II and its Follow/Input variants for live-input granulation.

Omnisphere has granular modes inside its oscillator section, useful when you want granular character with a full synth architecture around it. Simpler in its own way overlaps — its warp modes do related work at a coarser grain (see Sampling and Sound Selection).

Drill

Take one second of any sustained sound you've made. Load Granulator 3, freeze the position, and find grain sizes at 5 ms, 40 ms and 150 ms — three completely different instruments from one source. Add spray to the smoothest one, print it, and use it as a pad.

compression.title: Compression
compression.html:
General, tool-agnostic best practice for compression — the why behind the moves, independent of any one plugin. Specific-plugin settings live on the plugin notes (Solid Bus Comp, Glue Compressor, Pro-C 2, OTT, API-2500); reusable lessons live here. See also Compression Staging, Limiting, Multiband Compression.

What it is

Turning down the loud bits so the quiet bits can come up — control, glue, and (used as an effect) color. The art is matching gain so you judge the processing, not just the level jump.

Owned (first-call)

Glue Compressor · Solid Bus Comp (SSL-style bus glue) · Pro-C 2 / Pro-C 2 · OTT (multiband, upward) · API-2500 · Compressor (Ableton) · Ghz Vulf Compressor 3 · TL EasyComp

limiting.title: Limiting
limiting.html:
General best practice for limiting and the mix→master handoff. Specific tools: Pro-L 2 / Pro-L 2, Oxford Inflator, Ozone 9 Maximizer. See also Clipping and Loudness, Compression.

What it is

The ceiling — catching the last peaks for loudness. The recurring lesson: it's what you do leading up to the limiter that matters, and often the limiter comes off before you hand the mix to mastering.

Owned (first-call)

Pro-L 2 / Pro-L 2 · Oxford Inflator · Ozone 9 Maximizer · Limiter (Ableton) · Ghz Faraday Limiter 3

parallel-processing.title: Parallel Processing
parallel-processing.html:
What it is: blend a heavily-processed copy under the untouched original, instead of processing the original. The dry path keeps everything you love (transients, tone, dynamics); the wet path contributes only the quality you wanted more of (density, dirt, width, sustain).

Why it beats serial

Serial processing always trades: compression trades transients for control, distortion trades cleanliness for harmonics. Parallel sidesteps the trade — you add the processed quality instead of converting the signal into it. This is why you can crush a parallel path absurdly hard ("it's supposed to sound ugly soloed") and the blend still sounds natural.

Mechanics (Ableton)

  • Return track, 100% wet chain, feed it with post-fader sends — per-track send levels become per-source "amount" knobs into one shared flavor.
  • Send selectively: drums crush gets kick/snare/toms, never cymbals/hats (splatty). That selectivity is the whole reason it's a send, not a group insert.
  • Blend the return up from silence until the effect is felt, then back off 1 dB. Mute-test: you should miss it, not hear it.
  • Watch latency/phase: Live compensates plugin delay automatically, but never duplicate a path through different manual routes.
  • Alternative for one source: a plugin's own mix knob (Pro-C 2 dry knob, API-2500 mix, Decapitator mix) = parallel-in-place.

The house parallel returns

  • Parallel Comp Send — 1176 all-buttons crush (density, sustain, room)
  • Saturation Send — Decapitator dirt (attitude, phone-speaker audibility)
  • Width Send — MicroShift micro-pitch (size without losing the mono center)
  • Automation trick: ride the return up +1 dB in choruses — energy lift without level lift.

Other parallel recipes

  • Parallel dirty bass: amp-sim copy bandpassed 160 Hz–1.2 kHz under the clean DI (Electric Bass DI Track)
  • Parallel wide vocal: HPF a copy until it's all air, chorus/flange it, tuck it under (Main Vocal Track hooks)
  • Upward parallel (OTT-style): bring up quiet detail rather than crushing loud detail (OTT at low depth is this in one plugin)

multiband-compression.title: Multiband Compression
multiband-compression.html:
General best practice for band-split dynamics — compressing, ducking, or sidechaining one frequency range without touching the rest. Specific tools: Pro-MB, OTT, Saturn 2 (dynamic bands). See also Compression, Sidechaining, Masking and Carving.

What it is

Dynamics per frequency band — so you can duck only the sub, tame only the low-mids, or glue with a gentle upward multiband, instead of clamping the whole signal.

Owned (first-call)

Pro-MB · OTT (upward/downward multiband) · Pro-Q 4 (dynamic bands) · Ozone 9 Vintage Compressor

saturation-and-distortion.title: Saturation and Distortion
saturation-and-distortion.html:
General best practice for adding harmonics — from subtle glue to violent destruction. Specific tools: Decapitator, Saturn 2, Oxford Inflator, RC-20 Retro Color, Kramer Tape. See also Compression, Clipping and Loudness.

What it is

Generating harmonics that make a sound bigger, warmer, or nastier — and, across a whole mix, a loudness/density tool that lets you clip cleanly.

Owned (first-call)

Decapitator · Saturn 2 (multiband) · Roar (Ableton, multi-stage: serial/parallel/multiband/mid-side/feedback) · Oxford Inflator (perceived-loudness/upward) · Kramer Tape · RC-20 Retro Color · Decimort 2 (bit-crush/sampler grunge)

compression-staging.title: Compression Staging
compression-staging.html:
What it is: splitting dynamic control across several gentle compressors (tracking → track → group → bus → master) instead of one deep one. Every serious chain in this template compresses in stages.

Why stages beat one big squash

One compressor doing 10 dB has to have its threshold low enough that peaks slam it — deep GR, audible pumping, dead transients. Three compressors doing 2–4 dB each barely work individually; the signal arrives at each stage already controlled, so each can be transparent. Total control is the same; the sound is dramatically better.

The classic pair: 1176 → LA-2A

  • 1176 first (peaks): fastest attack in the business (50 μs at full clockwise — knobs run backward). 4:1 safe, 8:1/12:1 for surgical peaks-only (higher ratio = steeper knee). 3–7 dB GR only on peaks. No threshold — drive the input, match the output.
  • LA-2A second (program): one knob, slow optical. 1–5 dB riding the whole phrase like a fader.
  • Why they pair: mirror-image release curves. The 1176 releases faster as it approaches zero GR; the LA-2A "stomps on the brakes" — fast at first, slower near zero. Each covers the other's blind spot. (Vocal Bus, Main Vocal Track.)

The full vocal staging in this template

  1. Clip-gain by hand (±∞:1, free) → 2. UAD 1176 at tracking, 2–4 dB peaks → 3. Pro-C 2 on the track, 3–5 dB shape → 4. LALA/Glue at group, 1–2 dB → 5. LA-2A on the bus, 1–3 dB → 6. Glue on the master, 1–2 dB. ~15 dB of total control; no stage audible.

Stage-tuning rules

  • Each stage gentler than the last (big GR early, whispers late).
  • Attack decides punch: slow attack (20–30 ms+) = transients pass = punch; fast = control/density.
  • Release decides groove: time it so the meter breathes with the tempo (or use auto/variable release — the API-2500's variable mode recovers faster after light hits).
  • If any single stage regularly exceeds ~4 dB in a mix context, the problem is upstream (level, arrangement, or a hotter earlier stage needed).
  • Cap safety: Pro-C 2's range slider hard-limits GR per stage.

The full vocal staging in this template

vocal-mic-technique.title: Vocal Mic Technique
vocal-mic-technique.html:
The part of the vocal sound that's decided before any plugin loads. Distance, angle and what the singer hears — none of which can be fixed later.

Scoped to what's actually owned: the TLM 102 (large-diaphragm condenser) and the SM57 (dynamic), usually through the UAD Neve 1073.

Proximity effect

Bass response rises as a directional microphone gets closer to the source. This is the placement's blank (VOX-06) and it's the most useful mic fact there is, because it turns distance into a tone control.

  • Close (2–6 in) — noticeably more low end. Intimate, thick, "radio voice". Also more plosive risk and more mouth noise.
  • Mid (8–12 in) — the neutral working range for most vocals.
  • Far (12 in+) — thinner, more room in the sound, more natural dynamics.

Use it deliberately:

  • Want weight and intimacy on a quiet verse → move in.
  • Vocal getting boomy or muddy → back the singer off before reaching for an EQ cut. It's the same fix at the source rather than after the fact.
  • Want a consistent tone → keep distance consistent, which is what a pop filter doubles as (it sets a minimum distance).

It only applies to directional mics — cardioid and its relatives. An omni pattern has essentially none, which is exactly why omni is sometimes the right choice for a singer who moves.

Distance and angle

Off-axis — angling the mic slightly rather than pointing it straight at the mouth:

  • Reduces plosives (the blast of air from p/b sounds misses the capsule)
  • Reduces sibilance slightly, since high frequencies are more directional
  • Softens the top end a little — useful on a bright voice

The standard move is to have the singer address the mic slightly off-centre, or tilt the mic a few degrees. Combined with a pop filter it removes most plosive problems at the source rather than with the 100 Hz surgical cut described in Rap Vocal Production.

Consistency is the real skill. A singer who moves 6 inches during a take produces level and tone swings that no compressor fully fixes. For a mover: back them off slightly, or accept it and ride the fader.

TLM 102 vs SM57

TLM 102 SM57
Type Large-diaphragm condenser Dynamic
Detail High — captures air and nuance Lower — rounder, more limited top
Room sensitivity High — picks up the room Low — rejects room, forgiving
Handles loud Fine, but can get harsh Extremely well
Best for Sung leads, quiet/intimate takes, anything wanting air Loud/aggressive delivery, untreated rooms, a deliberately grittier sound

The room decides more than the mic does. In an untreated space the SM57's rejection is often the better result, because a detailed condenser capturing a bad room gives you a detailed bad room. That's a real and underrated reason to reach for the dynamic on rap vocals.

The headphone mix

Singers pitch and phrase against what they hear — so the monitor mix is part of the performance, not a convenience (VOX-08, which you got).

  • Enough vocal to hear pitch, not so much that they under-sing. Too loud in the cans and singers pull back; too quiet and they push and go sharp.
  • A little reverb helps almost everyone. It makes singing feel easier and encourages a more confident take. Print dry, monitor wet.
  • Keep the low end controlled — a bass-heavy mix makes pitch hard to hear.
  • Ask. "More or less of yourself?" costs ten seconds and improves every subsequent take.

One headphone off is common for pitch reference and is fine — expect a little bleed.

vocal-comping-and-takes.title: Vocal Comping and Takes
vocal-comping-and-takes.html:
Everything that happens before the vocal chain. Production/Chains/1 Vocals/ has 22 chains and every one of them describes processing a vocal that already exists — this is the part that decides whether there's a good performance to process.

How many passes

There's no correct number, but there is a wrong shape: too few and you have no options; too many and the singer is worn out and you're comping fatigue.

A workable default:

  1. Two or three full passes while the voice is fresh, top to bottom, no stopping. These usually carry the performance.
  2. A pass for the sections that aren't landing — chorus only, or the bridge.
  3. Punch-ins for specific lines that are close but not right.

Track the full passes first, always. A vocal assembled entirely from punch-ins never has a through-line, because the singer never had one.

Label as you go. Vox T1, Vox T2, Vox chorus T4. Ten unnamed takes an hour later is a comping session that starts with archaeology.

Comping

Comp by phrase, not by syllable.

The instinct is to take the technically best fragment of every word. That produces a take that's perfect and dead — a Frankenstein comp that's measurably better than any single pass and worse to listen to, because the performance stops being continuous. A phrase carries intention; a syllable doesn't.

What you're listening for, in order:

  1. Delivery — which take actually means it. This outranks everything below.
  2. Pitch — but see Vocal Tuning; some of what sounds off is expression.
  3. Timing — where it sits against the beat. Often fixable by nudging (see Pocket and Microtiming).
  4. Tone — brightness and weight, which drift as the voice warms up and tires.

Where comps give themselves away: the seams. Breaths and consonants at edit points are audible if you cut carelessly.

  • Cut on a breath wherever you can — it masks the join.
  • Keep breaths. Removing every breath sounds unnatural and unsettling; a vocal with no breathing reads as inhuman. Ride them down if they're loud, don't delete them.
  • Watch consonant collisions — cutting mid-word leaves a doubled or clipped consonant.
  • Crossfade every edit. Short, but present.

The rule worth remembering

A comp should be better than the best single take. If it isn't, use the best single take.

That's a real check, not a platitude — assemble the comp, then A/B it against your strongest full pass. If the single take feels more alive, you over-comped, and the fix is to comp in longer chunks.

Punch-ins

Recording over a specific section rather than re-taking the whole part.

  • Give a run-up. Start playback several bars early so the singer arrives in the phrase rather than starting cold on it.
  • Match the energy, not just the notes. A punch-in recorded at a different intensity to the surrounding lines is more obvious than a pitch problem.
  • Watch the room and the mic position — if the session resumes another day, a moved mic or a different distance makes the punch obvious. Photograph the setup.
  • Central to rap workflow, where the whole verse is often built line by line. See Rap Vocal Production.

vocal-tuning.title: Vocal Tuning
vocal-tuning.html:
Tuning as a workflow, not as an effect. Auto-Tune-as-a-sound is Pitch and Formant. This is the decision layer: what to correct, what to leave, and how hard.

The two modes

Automatic Graphical
What it does Snaps everything to a scale in real time Note-by-note editing of the pitch curve
Speed Instant Slow — minutes per phrase
Sound Audible when fast; the modern pop/rap sound Transparent when done well
Use for Stylized effect, rough comps, live Preserving a performance

Automatic needs a key and scale, and it will confidently retune a passing note or a blue note into something you didn't want. Graphical lets you fix the two notes that are actually wrong and leave everything else — which is usually what you want on a sung lead.

The practical answer is often both: automatic at a gentle setting to catch drift, graphical for the handful of notes that still stand out.

Retune speed

The single most consequential control. It sets how fast correction pulls a note to pitch.

  • Slow (long) — the note's natural scoop, slide and vibrato survive. Correction is inaudible. This is transparent tuning.
  • Fast (short/zero) — the pitch snaps instantly, killing scoops and flattening vibrato into a stepped line. This is the T-Pain / hard Auto-Tune sound, and it's a creative choice, not a mistake.

There is no "correct" setting — it's a stylistic dial with a genre on each end. What is a mistake is reaching for fast retune to fix a pitch problem and getting the effect by accident.

Fast retune destroys vibrato. If a singer's vibrato is part of why the take is good, a fast setting will remove exactly that.

When not to tune

The question the placement asked (VOX-10), and the one worth having a real answer to.

When the deviation is the expression. Blues, soul, gospel and a lot of rock live between the notes. A bend, a scoop into a note, a phrase leaned into slightly flat — these are doing the emotional work. Snap them to the grid and you remove precisely what made the take good.

When the genre's identity is a human voice. Folk, soul, live-feel material, singer-songwriter. Audible correction in these contexts reads as a mistake even when it's subtle.

When the singer is good. A strong performance with two off notes needs two notes fixed, not a tuning pass.

When it's already the sound. If the vocal is meant to be obviously processed, correct pitch is beside the point.

The general rule: correct the genuine mistakes, leave the rest. Over-tuning is far more common and far more damaging than under-tuning, because it's invisible while you're doing it and obvious a week later.

Practical order

  1. Comp first. Tuning a take you'll later replace is wasted work. See Vocal Comping and Takes.
  2. Fix timing before pitch — a note that's late often reads as out of tune when it isn't.
  3. Tune the lead, then decide about the stacks. Doubles and harmonies usually want more correction than the lead, because tuning discrepancies between layers are much more audible than a single voice being slightly off. See Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs.
  4. Listen in the mix, not soloed. Tuning decisions made in solo are almost always too aggressive.

vocal-stacks-and-ad-libs.title: Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs
vocal-stacks-and-ad-libs.html:
Everything around the lead — doubles, harmonies, ad-libs — and the rule that decides how each one gets treated.

The governing rule

The further a part is from delivering the lyric, the more it can become texture.

That single sentence answers most stack questions, and it's the one the placement asked for (VOX-11).

Part Position Level Processing Job
Lead Centre Loudest Least Carry the lyric
Double Wide L/R Well under lead Moderate Thicken — not heard as separate
Harmony Wide, often narrower than doubles Lower still More Colour
Ad-lib Widest, furthest back Varies Heaviest Energy, answer, texture

The lead stays present and relatively dry because every word has to be parseable. An ad-lib doesn't — nobody needs to catch every syllable — so it can take heavy delay, reverb, filtering and pitching.

Doubles

A real double is a second performance of the same line, layered with the first.

A copied-and-delayed double is not the same thing. An identical copy summed with itself just gets louder — it can't thicken, because there's no variation to create the effect. Delay or pitch it and you get comb filtering or a slapback, not a double.

What makes a real double work is that the two takes differ slightly in timing, pitch and tone. That variation is the thickening.

Practical:

  • Track doubles, don't fake them. Ask for the same delivery, not a different interpretation.
  • Tighten timing on the consonants — doubles that disagree on where a word ends read as sloppy rather than wide.
  • Tune doubles harder than the lead. Pitch disagreement between layers is far more audible than one voice being slightly off.
  • Pan hard and drop the level. A double you can consciously hear as a separate voice is too loud.

A counter-perspective on the "tune doubles harder" rule above — Kevin Parker (Tame Impala) argues the opposite is what makes his signature double read as a double at all. On "The Less I Know The Better," the only vocal layer is a single double (no harmony) — Parker states his own pitch isn't razor-precise take-to-take, and that's why the double is audibly perceived as two voices rather than one. Counter-example cited: Stevie Wonder's famously exact pitch meant his own doubled vocals reportedly didn't read as doubled at all — just louder, since there was no audible disagreement between the takes for the ear to latch onto. Reconciling with this page's own rule: both are describing the same mechanism (pitch variation between layers is what the ear perceives as "doubled" vs. "loud") — the difference is intent. Tune hard for a clean, controlled double; leave natural pitch drift in for a looser, more audibly-doubled character. → Kevin Parker, Behind the Track - 'The Less I Know The Better' by Tame Impala

Artificial Double Tracking (ADT) is the deliberate fake — the Abbey Road technique, a delayed and modulated copy. It's a sound (very Lennon), not a substitute for a real double. Worth knowing as the exception that proves the rule.

Harmony stacks

  • Fewer, louder beats more, quieter — three well-sung harmony parts beat eight mushy ones.
  • Double the harmonies too if they need to compete with a doubled lead.
  • Keep them below the lead even in the chorus. A harmony at lead level turns the lyric into a chord.
  • Watch the top voice — the highest harmony is what the ear tracks, so it needs to be the most accurate.

Ad-libs

Secondary vocal responses layered around the lead — the strand's other strong answer on the placement (VOX-07).

What they do:

  • Fill the gaps at the ends of phrases, where the lead has stopped
  • Answer the main line — call and response
  • Add energy without adding words
  • Widen the stereo picture, since they usually sit off-centre

Arranging them:

  • Space, not density. Ad-libs go where the lead isn't. An ad-lib on top of a lyric fights it.
  • Pan them off-centre, keeping the lead centred. Kenny Beats' point about aux percussion applies here identically — see Width and Stereo.
  • Vary the treatment across the track — a filtered one, a heavily delayed one, a dry close one. They don't all need the same chain.
  • Print the good accidents. Ad-libs are often the best thing on the record and are almost always improvised.
  • A chopped, repeated ad-lib can work as a continuous background texture, not just a phrase-gap filler — dial it down in level rather than removing it once its role becomes clear. A rhythmic "so-so-so-so" vocal chop, originated as an unplanned improvised ad-lib on an original demo vocal, was kept running throughout the whole track as a textural bed layer; an early mix had it much louder before it became clear its job was texture, not a lead element — pulled down in level, not cut. → Arrangement and Song Form — Ryan Tedder, Behind the Track - 'greedy' by Tate McRae
  • A naturally quiet good accident doesn't need a louder retake — automate it up instead. Billie Eilish did a genuinely quiet, natural laugh on a verse take that Finneas and the engineer liked; rather than asking for a louder take, they rode the gain up +27 dB on that single moment so it would pop out in the mix — a concrete, quantified version of "print the good accidents," where automation (not performance) does the rescuing. → Automation, Billie Eilish Vocal Chain, Gain Staging — Mix with the Masters (Finneas), Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas

rap-vocal-production.title: Rap Vocal Production
rap-vocal-production.html:
The strand's most conspicuous gap — VOX-12 asked what's different about producing a rap vocal versus a sung one and came back blank, in a core lane.

The one difference everything follows from

Rap is a rhythmic performance. The thing you're producing is pocket, not pitch.

Where a sung vocal is judged on intonation, tone and phrasing, a rap vocal is judged on where the syllables land against the beat. That single shift changes the workflow, the editing, the processing and what "a good take" even means.

Corollary: the tools you reach for are the rhythm tools. Pocket and Microtiming is more relevant to a rap vocal than Vocal Tuning is.

Pocket and delivery

  • Laying back vs pushing applies to voices too. A verse delivered slightly behind the beat reads as relaxed and authoritative; pushing ahead reads as urgent and aggressive. Both are choices.
  • Nudge, don't re-record. A take that's rushing or dragging but otherwise good gets dragged left or right in the timeline until it locks. This is the most basic and most-used rap vocal fix — already noted in YouTube Notes/You Suck at Producing - Rap Vocals.md.
  • Edit at the syllable level for timing — which is the opposite of the comping advice in Vocal Comping and Takes, and deliberately so. Comp performance by phrase; fix timing by syllable.
  • Consistency of pocket matters more than perfection of any line. A verse where every bar sits the same distance behind the beat sounds intentional. One where it varies sounds sloppy.

Workflow differences

Sung Rap
Tracking Full passes, then punch-ins Line by line punch-ins are normal, not a fallback
Comping By phrase, for delivery By phrase for delivery, by syllable for timing
Doubles Often the whole part On bar-ends and key phrases, not the whole verse
Ad-libs Optional colour A separate pass, structurally essential
Tuning Transparent correction Absent, or pushed into obvious effect

Doubling conventions. Doubling an entire rap verse flattens it — it removes the dynamic contrast between a plain line and an emphasized one. The convention is to double the last few words of a bar, the hook line, and anything you want to hit harder. The double is an accent, not a texture.

The ad-lib pass is not optional. In most modern rap the ad-libs carry a large part of the energy and the personality. Track them as a dedicated pass after the main verse, with the artist reacting to their own take. See Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs.

Breath and space. Rap fills more of the bar than singing does, so the gaps are load-bearing. Don't remove breaths — they're punctuation, and in a dense verse they're often the only thing separating two ideas.

Processing emphasis

Different weighting to a sung vocal, not different tools.

  • Compression harder and faster. Rapid-fire delivery has wide level swings between syllables. Fast attack and fast release, threshold under the loud outlier words, then makeup gain — the result reads as tighter and more powerful, not quieter. See Compression.
  • Presence and intelligibility over beauty. The lyric has to be parseable over a loud beat. That usually means more upper-mid than you'd put on a sung vocal.
  • De-essing matters more, because the compression that buys intelligibility also raises sibilance. See De-essing and the chain order in Compression Staging.
  • High-pass around 100 Hz to kill plosives and mic pops — surgical, not a broad sweep. See EQ and Vocal Mic Technique.
  • Pitch correction is either absent or an effect. There's no transparent middle ground in most rap.
secs: The one difference everything follows from

mix-handoff.title: Mix Handoff
mix-handoff.html:
The connective tissue, not a mixing curriculum. You mix as you go, get it to your own version, then hand off to a mixing engineer. Everything here is about that transfer — what to commit, what to leave alone, what to send, and what makes the next person's job harder.

The nine Production/Techniques/ component notes already cover the how of mixing (Gain Staging, Masking and Carving, Phase Alignment, Depth and Space, Width and Stereo, Parallel Processing, Compression Staging, Clipping and Loudness, Referencing and Translation). This is what happens after them.

The one that costs the most

Take the limiter off the 2-bus before you send. A brick-wall limiter that pulled 8 dB off your peaks is 8 dB the engineer will never see — it's not headroom you saved, it's information you deleted. If you want them to hear your loudness intent, send both versions clearly labelled. (Mat Leffler-Schulman, Sage Audio)

The commit boundary

The single decision that governs everything else. Commit what defines what a part is. Leave open everything about how parts relate.

Commit it Leave it open
Character distortion — the thing that makes that guitar that guitar Track-to-track balance
Synthesis and patch design Corrective EQ
Creative effects that are part of the writing (the stutter, the reverse, the filtered break) Bus and glue compression
Sample choice and chops Reverb and delay amounts
Tuning and timing edits on vocals Stereo width decisions on the mix as a whole
Arrangement — what plays when The 2-bus, entirely

The test: if removing it would change what the part is, commit it. If removing it would only change how loud or bright it sits against its neighbours, leave it.

The failure mode runs in both directions. Over-commit and the engineer works around your decisions instead of through them — a printed reverb can't be pulled back when the arrangement changes underneath it. Under-commit and you've handed over a pile of raw tracks with none of the intent that made the demo good, and they'll mix somebody else's record.

Print a safety. When you commit something destructive, keep the unprocessed version alongside it, muted and named. Costs nothing, and it's the difference between "can you undo that" and "no."

Multitracks vs stems

Not interchangeable, and the wrong one wastes a round trip.

  • Multitracks — every individual track, unbundled. Each mic, each synth, each vocal layer. This is what a mixing engineer wants.
  • Stems — grouped submixes bounced to a handful of files: drums, bass, music, vocals. These are for remixers, live playback, and sync licensing. A mixing engineer handed stems can't fix a snare without also touching the kick.

Send multitracks unless they've specifically asked for stems.

Delivery spec
Format WAV or AIFF. Never MP3, never a lossy source anywhere in the chain.
Sample rate The session's native rate. Do not convert. If you tracked at 48 kHz, deliver 48 kHz.
Bit depth 24-bit minimum. 32-bit float is fine if they'll take it.
Headroom Peaks around −6 to −3 dBFS. Achieve it with a gain move on the 2-bus, not with a limiter.
Dither None. Dither is the last step of the last process, and that isn't you.
Start point Every file consolidated from the same timeline zero, so nothing can drift on import.
Naming Descriptive. Lead Vox Double L, not Audio 12.

Headroom is the one people get wrong in the harmless direction — there's no prize for −18, and no penalty either. What matters is that nothing is clipping and nothing is limited. (Sonarworks)

Session organization

Do this before the export, not after they ask.

  1. Name every track for what it is. The engineer shouldn't have to solo anything to find out what it is.
  2. Order and group logically — drums, bass, music, vocals. Colour-code if the DAW supports it.
  3. Consolidate each track across the full song length from a common start. No floating regions.
  4. Delete unused tracks. Twelve muted alternates aren't helpful, they're twelve questions.
  5. Flag anything deliberate that looks like a mistake — a part that's intentionally out of tune, a sound that's meant to clip, an effect that has to stay.

What to send alongside

Audio alone is an incomplete handoff. Three things travel with it:

  • Your rough mix, as a reference. This is the balance you were hearing when you made every arrangement decision. It's the most useful single file in the package and the one most often left out.
  • A reference track — a finished commercial record in the same lane, for tone and balance target.
  • Written notes on intent. Short. What the song is doing, what you want louder or darker, what you're unsure about, anything that must not change.

Using a reference track properly

The step that makes references work and almost everyone skips: level-match it.

Anything louder sounds better. An unmatched commercial reference is mastered 6–10 dB hotter than your mix, so A/B-ing against it tells you nothing except that it's louder — and you'll chase that difference with the wrong tools.

Match the loudness first, then use it for specific questions, not a general vibe check:

  • Is my low end bigger or smaller than theirs?
  • Is the vocal further forward or further back?
  • Am I duller or brighter above 8k?
  • Is my stereo image wider or narrower?

A reference is a measuring stick, not a target to clone. Switch often, on the same system, at matched level.

Mastering prep

Deliberately light — mastering isn't an interest, and prep is the only part that's yours.

  • Everything in the Delivery spec above applies.
  • Nothing on the 2-bus. No limiter, no clipper, no "just a little" glue compression you'd miss.
  • LUFS is context, not a target. It measures integrated perceived loudness over the whole track. Streaming services normalize playback to roughly −14 LUFS, so a master pushed to −7 gets turned down on playback and arrives quieter-sounding and flatter than one that wasn't. Chasing loudness past the normalization target costs dynamics and buys nothing.
  • If it's a release rather than a single, send the running order and the gaps you want between tracks.
  • Turn temporal effects (reverb, delay, modulation) down before sending, not just off the 2-bus. Reverb/mod content sits lower in amplitude than the dry signal almost always, so the mastering engineer's own compression/limiting will lift those quiet tails more than the reference mix ever showed — leaving them at mix-reference level hands over a track that gets brighter/wetter-sounding than intended once it's processed. (Sage Audio)

What makes their job harder: an already-limited mix (nothing left to work with), sample-rate conversion, an MP3 anywhere in the lineage, and a problem buried in the mix that mastering can only make louder rather than fix.

Checklist

  • Limiter and clipper off the 2-bus
  • Peaks −6 to −3 dBFS, achieved with gain
  • Multitracks (not stems), unless asked otherwise
  • Native sample rate, 24-bit, WAV, no dither
  • Every file consolidated from a common start
  • Every track descriptively named
  • Unused tracks deleted, deliberate oddities flagged
  • Rough mix included
  • Reference track included
  • Written notes on intent
  • Safety copies of anything destructively printed

sample-clearance.title: Sample Clearance
sample-clearance.html:
Not a craft note — a release-blocker note. Sampling and Sound Selection covers choosing sounds and flipping them. This covers whether you're allowed to put the result out.

Not legal advice

This is a working producer's summary of how clearance operates. For an actual release with an actual sample in it, a music attorney or a clearance service is the right call — the cost of asking is far below the cost of not.

The thing to know: there are two rights

A recorded song is two separate pieces of intellectual property, owned by different people, cleared separately.

Right What it is Usually held by
Master The specific recording — the actual audio The label, or whoever paid for the session
Composition (publishing) The underlying song — melody, lyrics, chords, structure The songwriters and their publishers

Sampling uses both. Lifting audio from a record means you're using their recording and the song inside it. Two clearances, two negotiations, two sets of fees.

This is the distinction the placement asked about and the one worth internalizing, because it's what makes the alternative below work.

The one clean exception: public domain

Composition copyright expires 70 years after the composer's death in most countries — after that, the underlying song needs no clearance at all, from anyone, for any use. This is why so much classical-derived pop material (Pachelbel's Canon in D under Maroon 5's "Memories"; Leoncavallo's Pagliacci under Queen's "It's a Hard Life"; Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 3 under Procol Harum's "A Whiter Shade of Pale," see Songs Inspired By Bach) never triggers a lawsuit even when the melodic lift is note-for-note close — the pieces have been in the public domain for centuries. The recording itself is still a separate right: a specific performance/recording of a public-domain piece can still carry its own master-rights clearance requirement even though the composition underneath it is free to use — public domain status applies to the composition, never automatically to any given recording of it. — David Bennett Music Theory, 14 Songs That 'Rip Off' Classical Music

Sampling vs interpolation

Interpolation is replaying or re-recording the part yourself so it sounds like the original without using the original audio.

  • Sample → master + publishing. Two rights.
  • Interpolation → publishing only. One right.

That's why interpolation is the standard move on a recognizable hook: it removes the label from the conversation entirely and leaves you negotiating with the publisher. It's usually faster, usually cheaper, and always fewer parties.

It is not a loophole. Re-playing a melody is still using the composition, and "I played it myself" is not a defence. What it does is halve the problem.

Clear before release, never after

The rule with the least ambiguity and the highest cost when broken.

Clearing after a track has traction means negotiating with no leverage — the rights holder knows the song is working and prices accordingly. Before release you're one of many requests; after release you're a party who already infringed and needs a fix.

What an uncleared sample can cost:

  • Takedown from streaming and distribution
  • Frozen royalties — income accrues but doesn't pay out
  • The whole track's income, if the settlement is a majority publishing share
  • Delayed release while it gets sorted, usually at the worst moment

On a recognizable sample, holders routinely ask for a significant publishing share — sometimes a majority — plus a percentage of the master and an upfront fee. That's the trade to weigh before building a song around it. (Symphonic, Tracklib)

The practical routes

Roughly in order of how much friction each carries.

  1. Licensed libraries — Tracklib and similar clear both rights up front for a fee and a defined split. Zero negotiation. The catalogue is the constraint, not the paperwork.
  2. Royalty-free / one-stop sample packs — cleared by definition. Check the licence covers commercial release and not just personal use.
  3. Interpolation — replay it. One right instead of two.
  4. Replay and rewrite — change enough that it's your composition. There is no bar-count or note-count safe harbour; "how much is enough" is a legal question, not a rule of thumb, and producers who rely on a supposed threshold are the ones who end up settling.
  5. Full clearance — a clearance service or attorney approaches both sides. Slowest and most expensive, and the only route for a specific famous recording.

Before you build a song around a sample

  • Do I know what the source recording actually is? (An unidentified sample can't be cleared.)
  • Is it from a licensed library — already handled?
  • Could I interpolate it instead and drop the master side?
  • If this needs full clearance, is the song worth a possible majority publishing split?
  • Am I prepared to clear it before release, or to shelve it?

The last one is the real question. A great flip you can't release is a beat, not a song — deciding that early is cheaper than deciding it after the mix.

What this doesn't cover

Broader music-business material — splits, PRO registration, royalties, distribution, sync — is still unwritten in the vault. Flagged as parked in Coverage Review 2026-08-09 §3 and genuinely live given the releases in Originals/.

chords.title: Chords
chords.html:
Part of Music Theory. Construction hub for every chord family. A chord = several pitches sounded together; its notes are named root, 3rd, 5th (+ 7th, 9th… for bigger chords). All formulas below are in half-steps from the root (see Notes & Pitches, Intervals).

Triads (3 notes)

Type Symbol Scale formula Half-steps C example
Major C 1 3 5 4 + 3 C E G
Minor Cm 1 ♭3 5 3 + 4 C E♭ G
Diminished C° / Cdim 1 ♭3 ♭5 3 + 3 C E♭ G♭
Augmented C+ / Caug 1 3 ♯5 4 + 4 C E G♯
  • Major = degrees 1-3-5 of the major scale; minor lowers the 3rd a half-step
  • The 3rd decides major vs minor; the 5th decides dim/aug — details: Diminished Chords, Augmented Chords, Unlimited Minor Chords

Seventh chords (4 notes) — full page: Seventh Chords

Type Symbol Half-steps C example
Major 7 Cmaj7 4+3+4 C E G B
Dominant 7 C7 4+3+3 C E G B♭
Minor 7 Cm7 3+4+3 C E♭ G B♭
Minor-major 7 CmM7 3+4+4 C E♭ G B
Half-diminished Cm7♭5 / Cø 3+3+4 C E♭ G♭ B♭
Diminished 7 Cdim7 3+3+3 C E♭ G♭ A
Augmented 7 Caug7 4+4+2 C E G♯ A♯(B♭)

Beyond thirds: non-tertial harmony

Everything above stacks 3rds ("tertial" harmony — the common-practice default). Three other named families, by stack interval: secundal (stacked 2nds → tone clusters, timbral rather than harmonic), quartal (stacked 4ths — an early-1900s sound, used deliberately in Stravinsky's neoclassicism; guitar fretboard shapes + the So What voicing on Quartal Chord Voicings), quintal (stacked 5ths — respells as the same notes as quartal chords, so it doesn't form a separate system). — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.18

Beyond sevenths

  • Extended Chords — 9ths, 11ths, 13ths (keep stacking 3rds; extensions = 2nd/4th/6th an octave up)
  • Suspended Chords — sus2/sus4 replace the 3rd
  • Add Chords — add9/add2/6/9: triad + one extra note, no 7th
  • Altered Chords — dominant chords with ♭5/♯5/♭9/♯9/♯11
  • Chord Inversions — same notes, different bass (slash chords)

Working with chords

  • Diatonic chords per key: Chords by Key · how they move: Chord Progressions
  • Ambiguous stacks (is it Cmaj7/E or Em(add♭6)?): Chord Naming by Context
  • Chord-per-scale-degree for exotic scales: Scale Modes Reference

Lookup tools

  • Piano diagrams for every chord/root: pianochord.org · reverse lookup: chord converter
  • Guitar shapes + audio (2,700+): all-guitar-chords.com · notes → name: chord identifier

Ear training

Hearing chord quality/position combinations by ear is its own skill, trained as a "meta feeling state" above the individual scale degrees rather than reconstructed from them in real time — see Scale Degree Ear Training.
secs: Seventh chords (4 notes) — full page: Seventh Chords

chord-classification-from-2-to-12-notes.title: Chord Classification from 2 to 12 Notes
chord-classification-from-2-to-12-notes.html:
Part of Music Theory. Chords, Seventh Chords, Extended Chords and Chord Naming by Context each teach a slice. This is the complete enumeration — how many distinct chords exist at each size, and what governs whether a name is honest. From Nick Clark's ~153,000-character "Chord Theory."

The count

Combinations from one fixed root inside an octave, with inversions folded together:

Notes Raw combinations Symmetry adjustment Unique types
2 — dyads 11 — 11 intervals
3 — triads 55 1 symmetrical (augmented) → (55−1)/3 = 18 19
4 — tetrads 165 1 fully symmetrical (º7) + 2 partly symmetrical pairs → (165−5)/4 = 40 43
5 — pentads 330 none symmetrical → 330/5 = 66 66
6 — 11th chords not enumerated
7 — 13th chords — "most extended 13th chords can be matched with their respective 7-note scale" —
12 — he has one, and it spans nearly 4½ octaves 1

Dyads. Each of the 11 tempered intervals stands for at least two named intervals. He colour-codes provenance: 12 of the names occur in the major scale and its modes, 4 more in harmonic minor, 2 in Neapolitan minor — 18 that cover "the vast majority of music." The last 4, including the augmented third and diminished sixth, need a scale with both ♭2 and ♯4 — which points straight at Raag Todi. All 20 exist inside the thaat system; see The 32 Thaats (32 Modes), which reaches the same 20 from the other direction.

Triads (19). The four named ones (major, minor, diminished, augmented) plus the suspended family (sus4, sus♯4, sus♭2 — sus2 is treated as an inversion of sus4). The other eleven are all "no 5" chords — extended triads with the fifth removed. He excludes "no 3" chords outright, on the grounds that every one is an inverted "no 5."

Tetrads (43). Method: take each named triad, add every remaining note one at a time. What each tetrad reads as, in each key it could belong to. His two rules for what will actually attach:

  • To a major or augmented triad: ♯1, ♭2, 2, ♯2, ♭3, 4, ♯4, ♯5, ♭6, 6, ♯6, ♭7, 7.
  • To a minor or diminished triad: ♭1, ♭2, 2, 3, ♭4, 4, ♯4, ♭5, ♭6, 6, 𝄫7, ♭7, 7.
  • Suspended chords sit in between. The ♯9/♭10 only attaches to major; the ♭9/♯8 to anything.

Pentads. Three framings, and the third is the practical one: "think of a tetrad played over an additional bass note. For me, this is the easiest way to think of 5-note chords." Which is the Slash Chords and Upper Structure Chords view, arrived at by counting.

The seventh-chord availability chart

His most directly usable artifact. Rows are chord quality — maj7, 7, (♯6), 6, m(maj7), m7, m6, ºmaj7, m7♭5, º7, +maj7, +7, +(♯6), 7♭5. Columns are scale degree — I, ♭II, II, ♭III, III, IV, ♭V, ♯IV, V, ♭VI, VI, ♭VII, VII. Each cell names the scale in which that quality occurs on that degree, filled in a stated priority order: Ionian → Aeolian → the other church modes → harmonic minor → melodic minor → harmonic major → Neapolitan minor → Neapolitan major → Hungarian minor → Todi.

It deliberately keeps ♭V and ♯IV as separate columns, and 7 vs ♯6 and +7 vs +(♯6) as separate rows — enharmonically identical, harmonically not.

What falls out of it:

  • Diminished and augmented chords are harmonically scarce (m7♭5 excepted). That scarcity, not taste, is why they are rare in mainstream writing (Diminished Chords, Augmented Chords).
  • 7♭5 is only available on II and V.
  • ºmaj7 requires an augmented third, so it needs a ♭2+♯4 scale — essentially Raag Todi only. Which is why, he argues, "in most cases a Cºmaj7 chord is more accurately a Cº(♭8) chord."

The naming argument

This is the through-line of every document he has written, and it is worth engaging with even where the school won't adopt the notation.

"The ♭ in ♭3 stands for minor third, not flattened third. Flats and sharps are used to describe notes and pitches… minor, major, perfect, augmented, diminished are used to describe intervals."

From which: ♭10 not ♯9 wherever the pitch is genuinely a minor third over a major third; ♯8 (augmented unison) and ♭8 (diminished unison) as real chord tones; (♯6) written into a symbol to separate a true augmented sixth from a ♭7. See Augmented Sixth Chords and Chord Naming by Context.

Where the school lands: keep standard names on charts and in concept notes — his own conclusion concedes the point ("it is easier to write it as D13… this also gives each musician the room to use their own favorite 13th chord voicings"). Reach for his spelling when an analysis has stopped making sense, which is precisely when the distinction earns its keep.

Five claims a textbook wouldn't make

  1. Identity comes from the root you pick, not the notes. Imagine a chord's notes repeating up and down forever: …C, E♭, G, B♭, C, E♭, G, B♭… From that one sequence you can build Cm7, E♭6, Cm/B♭ or Cm7/G. The pitches decide nothing on their own (Chord Inversions).
  2. Voicing decides quality. "If the ♯9 is voiced above the major 3 then it feels more like a C(♯9/♭10) chord, but if the 3 is voiced above the ♯9 then it might start to sound like a minor chord with an added 10th." And ordering can flip function outright: G, B♭, D, F♯ reads as Gm(maj7); put the F♯ on the bottom and it reads as F♯+(♭9).
  3. The instrument's own overtones fight altered fifths. Because the 5th sounds anyway as an overtone, "chords with a ♭5 or ♯5 have the risk of sounding more like an added ♯11 or ♭13 chord." Cmaj7♭5 becomes Cmaj7(♯11); C+7 becomes C7(♭13).
  4. You have to convince the listener. "You can't just play the notes and call it a chord, you have to convince the listener that that is what they're hearing." Some intervals are essentially unsellable — a Cm(♭4) will be heard as a major third, a Cm(𝄫7) as a 6.
  5. 7sus4 chords are disguised. There are four in a major key (on II, III, V, VI); only the V reads as dominant. The others get heard as minor sevenths purely because of expected function (Suspended Chords).

He is honest about where the obsession came from, which is a nice piece of context: the ukulele has four strings. He worked out fingerings for 30 of the 43 tetrads in all 12 keys — 360 four-note voicings.

And the closing frame, borrowed from the Tao Te Ching: one → two → three → ten thousand. One is the root; two is major/minor (Ernst Levy) or bright/dark (George Russell); three is T/SD/D () or relating every chord to one of the three fully diminished sevenths (Barry Harris — the mechanism behind Dominant Chord Movement and Flexibility).

"There are 10,000 different ways to categorize chords… but at the end of the day they can all be simplified into at most 3 categories."

"Interesting Chords" — no separate note

The eighth document in his collection, "Interesting Chords," is a republication of this document's own chapter — he says so himself in the hub. It is a flat sequence of ~21 song vignettes, each a prose analysis plus stacked multi-key Roman numerals. It gets no note of its own; the only material unique to the standalone is a spelling convention (aug6) where the parent writes (♯6), and one Roman-numeral typo that differs between the two. The parent adds a Louis Cole "Everytime" citation the standalone lacks.

The catalogue itself, since it is the useful part:

Chord What it really is Song
E/E♯ not E/F, not a ºmaj7 — E is the ♭VII of the coming F♯m7 and E♯ is the bass leading tone The 1975, "Sincerity is Scary"
F/D♭ D♭+maj7 = ♭III+maj7 from harmonic minor, embellishing D♭maj7 Mac Miller, "Cinderella"
D/C Cmaj13(♯11) no 3/5/7 — "a sort of lydian tonic chord," or an inverted D7 Thundercat, "What Is Left to Say"
IV6sus♯4 "the only sus♯4 chord diatonic to a major key" Thundercat, "What Is Left to Say"
Gm/F♯ contains a B♭+; he weighs and rejects F♯+(♭9), B♭+(13)/F♯, Gm(maj7) inverted, D+7(11) James Blake, "Unluck"
A7♭5 usually really A7(♯11) no 5 — here he argues both readings are live at once "Fly Me to the Moon" (Charles Cornell)
Dadd4/C Csus♯4(9,13) — and the melody sings the ♯4, which is what makes it a sus♯4 rather than an inverted D7. "Two identical chords can sound completely different depending on context" Billy Joel, "Lullabye"
Cm(♭8) normally written Cm(maj7); he hears C→C♭ vs C→B as genuinely undecidable in 12-TET Knower, "Same Smile Different Face"
E♭7♯9 (Hendrix) his reading: E♭(♯6,♯9), the ♭V augmented sixth of A major Mac Miller, "God Is Fair, Sexy Nasty"
A13(♯11) play it as Gmaj7♭5/A. True spelling in A♭: a B𝄫 triad + augmented sixth = the ♭II augmented sixth, i.e. the tritone sub Michael Jackson, "I Can't Help It"
six maj7♭5 shapes down the whole-tone scale over an E pedal only one of the six actually contains a B; the constant structure creates "the illusion that these chords are simply moving down by whole step" Stevie Wonder, "Too High"
Cm(maj7)(10) a minor chord with an added major third — the mirror of 7♯9 Matt Maltese, "As the World Caves In"
Dm7(9,11,13) → G7(♭9,11,13) → Cmaj7(9,♯11,13)+♯8 his own cadence, 7+7+8 notes, given four ways at once: chord names, note lists, polychords, and scales Nick Clark

extended-chords.title: Extended Chords
extended-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. Extended chords keep stacking 3rds past the 7th: 9th, 11th, 13th. The common shorthand — 9 = 2, 11 = 4, 13 = 6, an octave up — is a usually-true simplification, not the actual rule. The real rule (chord-tone role, not octave distance): a 2/4/6 only gets renamed 9/11/13 when it's stacked on top of a complete lower structure — a full triad (1-3-5) for the 9/11 case, a full seventh chord (1-3-5-7) for the 13 case. If the corresponding lower tone is missing (no 3 present, or no 7 present), the added note keeps its plain scale-degree name instead, regardless of what octave it's actually voiced in — extensions don't have to be an octave-plus away from the root at all; they can sit right next to the root and still be labeled 9/11/13. Full breakdown → From videos below.

The dominant series (built on C7)

Chord Notes Built from
C7 C E G B♭ dominant 7th
C9 C E G B♭ D C7 + major 3rd on top
C11 C E G B♭ D F C9 + minor 3rd
C13 C E G B♭ D F A C11 + major 3rd

Major and minor versions exist too (Cmaj9 = C E G B D; Cm9 = C E♭ G B♭ D) — full half-step formulas in Chords. Alternative names: Cdom9/Cdom11/Cdom13.

What to actually play (standard omissions)

Full stacks get muddy — omit freely:

  • 9th chords: drop the 5th
  • 11th chords: drop the 3rd (the 3rd clashes with the 11) → sounds like C9sus4 (Suspended Chords)
  • 13th chords: drop the 5th, 9th, and especially the 11th
  • Drop the root too if a bass player has it

Voicing (two-hand / polychord approach)

  • C11: LH E G B♭ + RH B♭ D F
  • C13: LH E B♭ D + RH A D G — or LH B♭ E A + RH C E A
  • More on stacking hands: Chord Inversions

Usage

  • Jazz substitutions for plain triads and dom 7ths (Chord Progressions)
  • Altered extensions (♭9, ♯11…) → Altered Chords
  • add9/6/9 chords are NOT extended chords (no 7th) → Add Chords

Classical usage note

Common practice used extended harmonies (9ths/11ths/13ths) almost exclusively as diatonic chords built on the dominant (V9/V11/V13) — the 11th/13th barely appear before the Romantic era. The 4-part voicing logic matches the omission rules above: keep root + 3rd (tertial identity) + 7th (bridges to the extension, keeps it reading as one chord instead of two stacked triads), drop the 5th — the extension itself is the one note that's actually required. Almost always found in root position; inverted extended chords aren't really a thing in this style. — Toby W. Rush, Music Theory for Musicians and Normal People, p.34

upper-structure-chords.title: Upper Structure Chords
upper-structure-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords / Chord Naming by Context. An upper structure is a chord (usually a triad, but any chord type works) played over a different bass note. The same upper voicing gets a completely different name, function, and color depending purely on which bass note sits underneath it — the jazz/jazz-fusion cousin of a slash chord, pushed further: the bass note isn't necessarily even a tone from the upper chord.

The idea

  • Pick any chord as the "upper structure" (triads are typical, but 7th chords and beyond work too).
  • Put a bass note underneath it. If that bass note is already a tone of the upper chord, you just get an inversion. If it isn't, you get a genuinely new composite chord — a different name, a different function, sometimes a different key implication entirely.
  • Where to place it: the most common, most reliably useful placement is the ♭6 degree of a major key (or the natural 7 of a minor key) — put the upper structure's root there and build out from that home position.

The six bass-note options (worked from an E-minor upper structure on the ♭6 of E major = C)

Bass note relationship to the upper structure's root Resulting chord (in E major, upper structure = Em, bass on C) Function / typical resolution
Same as the upper structure's root ♭6 major chord — Cmaj7♯11 (= maj7♭5) No fixed resolution; can sit unresolved. Optional smooth move: ♭6 → 5 (half step down)
A 4th below the root (upper structure read as the bass note's ♭7) ♭7 dominant 13 — D13 Dominant function: backdoor resolution to I, tritone sub into the chord a half-step up, straight V7 into a new key/modal chord
A major 3rd below the root (upper structure read as the bass note's ♭3) iv minor6/9 — Am6add9 Dramatic, tension/tragedy color; commonly resolves to I but forgiving — works resolving almost anywhere
A major 3rd above the root, enharmonically (upper structure read as an altered dominant's upper triad) Altered dominant ♭7♯5♯9 — G♯7♯5♯9 (= V7alt/vi) Classic jazz altered-dominant sound; typically resolves down a 5th into a minor chord, but can target IV, ii, ♭III (as a tritone sub), or the relative/parallel major
A ♯4 above the root (rarer) "Spanish dominant" — 7sus4♭9-type (F♯7sus4♭9) Suspended-dominant color, resolves similarly to a plain V7sus
A ♭9/♭2 above the root (rarer) Same shape a half-step away (B7sus4♭9) Functions similarly to the ♯4 option above

Using it

  • Chain multiple bass-note readings of the same upper triad through one progression — alternate a plain diatonic chord with an upper-structure reading, cycling through 2+ of the six options above, connected by smooth bass motion/voice-leading between the bass notes. This is how a full upper-structure progression gets built rather than using just one option in isolation.
  • Not every dominant-function upper structure needs to resolve where you'd expect — especially in fusion, deliberately NOT resolving an unstable-sounding upper structure (or resolving it somewhere unexpected) is a stylistic choice, not an error.
  • Practice method: pick one upper-structure triad, place it on the ♭6 (major) or natural 7 (minor) of a key, and write a progression using at least two of the six bass-note options above — the real skill is the voice-leading/bass-motion connecting them, not just knowing the chord names.

Two different "upper structure" devices — don't conflate them

This page's upper structure is a different chord dropped over a foreign bass note (a reharmonization/polychord device). Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords uses the same term for something narrower and more literal: the triad already sitting inside a seventh chord's own 3rd-5th-7th, extracted as a lighter-weight stand-in for the full chord. Same word, two jazz devices.
secs: The six bass-note options (worked from an E-minor upper structure on the ♭6 of E major = C)

altered-chords.title: Altered Chords
altered-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. Dominant-family chords with the 5th and/or 9th (sometimes 11th) shifted a half-step. Notation: ♭/♯ and −/+ are interchangeable (C7♭5 = C7-5).

Single alterations

Chord Notes
C7♭5 C E G♭ B♭
C7♯5 (= Caug7) C E G♯ B♭
C7♭9 C E G B♭ D♭
C7♯9 ("Hendrix chord") C E G B♭ D♯
C7♯11 C E G B♭ F♯

Bigger / multiple alterations

Chord Notes
C9♯11 C E G B♭ D F♯
C13♭9 C E G B♭ D♭ F A
C13♯11 C E G B♭ D F♯ A
C7(♯5♯9) C E G♯ B♭ D♯
C13(♭9♯11) C E G B♭ D♭ F♯ A

Non-dominant alterations exist too: maj7♭5 (C E G♭ B), maj7♯5 (C E G♯ B) — see Seventh Chords.

Usage

  • Jazz: free substitutions for any dominant 7th, especially the V7 resolving to I (Chord Progressions) — extra tension → stronger resolution
  • Rule of thumb: don't alter a note the melody is sitting on (the clash)
  • ♯9 in funk/rock: E7♯9 is the James Brown / Hendrix stab
  • Chord-scale source for fully-altered sounds: the altered scale (melodic minor mode) — Scale Modes Reference

suspended-chords.title: Suspended Chords
suspended-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. "Sus" = suspension: the 3rd is replaced by the 2nd (sus2) or 4th (sus4). No 3rd = neither major nor minor — open, unresolved sound.

Types

Chord Formula C example
Csus2 1 2 5 C D G
Csus4 (or just Csus) 1 4 5 C F G
C7sus2 1 2 5 ♭7 C D G B♭
C7sus4 1 4 5 ♭7 C F G B♭
C9sus4 1 4 5 ♭7 9 C F G B♭ D
Csus2/4 (rare) 1 2 4 5 C D F G
  • C9sus4 ≈ C11 without the 3rd — see Extended Chords
  • In practice only two get used much: sus4 on major triads and 7sus4 on dominants (Seventh Chords)
  • Old chart notation: C4 = Csus4

How sus4 chords get used (three patterns)

  1. Suspension → resolution: sus4 chord then its normal version — Csus4 → C (F falls to E), G7sus4 → G7. Usually on the V or I chord. Classic "special effect" — e.g. the Gsus4 → G in Gnarls Barkley's Crazy (Chord Progressions)
  2. V chord under a tonic melody: melody sits on the tonic note while the V plays → tonic clashes with the V's 3rd. Vsus4 swaps that 3rd for the tonic note itself. (Key of C: melody on C over G → Gsus4 instead.)
  3. Keep the suspension AND add the resolution, for tension that never fully releases — instead of dropping the suspended 4th when the chord "resolves," hold it while adding the resolved 3rd underneath/alongside it (e.g. a sus4 chord's D held together with the C♯ it would normally resolve to). Reads as resolving while a residue of the original tension stays audible on top — a way to color a resolution instead of fully releasing it. → You Suck at Producing, You Suck at Music Theory No. 2: Creating Tension
secs: How sus4 chords get used (three patterns)

add-chords.title: Add Chords
add-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. A triad + one extra note, no 7th — that's what separates add chords from Extended Chords (Cadd9 = C E G D; C9 = C E G B♭ D).

Types

Chord Notes (C) Note
Cadd9 C E G D 9th on top — the common one
Cadd2 C D E G same pitch class as add9, packed inside the triad
Cadd11 C E G F rare
Cadd4 C E F G add11's inside voicing
Cadd6 (= C6) C E G A usually just written C6
C6/9 C E G A D 6th + 9th; common ending chord (a.k.a. "6add9")
  • add9 vs add2: same added pitch, different octave placement
  • Minor versions work identically: Cmadd9 = C E♭ G D; Cmadd2 = C D E♭ G

Usage

  • Pop/acoustic color chords — add9 keeps a triad's stability but shimmers (no 7th tension, unlike Seventh Chords)
  • 6/9 = classic jazz/soul final-I chord
  • If the 3rd is replaced rather than added → that's a sus chord

sixth-chords.title: Sixth Chords
sixth-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. A 6th chord (e.g. C6) is a major (or minor) triad with the 6th scale degree added on top — milder color/tension than adding a 7th. Common in jazz/swing and has an "old-fashioned" association, though it shows up across pop and rock too.

The minor-6th naming trap

The added 6th in a minor 6th chord is still the major 6th degree, never the minor scale's 6th — Bm6 = B minor triad (B-D-F♯) + G♯ (NOT G natural). The "minor" in the chord name describes only the underlying triad, not the added note. A minor triad + the actual flat-6 is a different chord, written m♭6 (or "add ♭6").

Enharmonic identity with minor 7th chords

Any 6th chord is identical, note-for-note, to the minor 7th chord built a minor 3rd lower — its relative minor (B♭6 = Gm7; C6 = Am7) — the same phenomenon Chord Inversions documents for sus4/sus2 pairs. Which name is "correct" depends on context (which note reads as the root); when context is genuinely ambiguous (an unaccompanied vocal chord, no bass to anchor it), either name is defensible.

Classical vs. modern "6" — a real notation collision

Classical figured-bass notation uses a superscript 6 to mean first inversion (the outer-note interval of an inverted triad is a 6th) — completely different from modern pop/jazz "6," which means an added 6th degree. "C6" in a classical harmonic analysis = C/E; "C6" on a jazz chart = C major + A. Context (which tradition you're reading) disambiguates.
secs: Classical vs. modern "6" — a real notation collision

augmented-chords.title: Augmented Chords
augmented-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. Major triad with the 5th raised a half-step — root + two stacked major 3rds (4+4 half-steps). Symmetrical like dim, so it repeats every 4 half-steps.

Chord Symbols Formula C example
Augmented triad Caug / C+ / C(♯5) 1 3 ♯5 C E G♯
Augmented 7th Caug7 / C7♯5 / C7+ 1 3 ♯5 ♭7 C E G♯ B♭ (site spells A♯)
  • Sounds dissonant because the ♯5 falls outside the root's major scale (Gaug = G B D♯ — D♯ isn't in G major)
  • 7♯5 with more alterations → Altered Chords; the Δ♯5 chord from melodic/harmonic minor → Scale Modes Reference

Usage — transition/passing chords

Small chromatic shift from a plain triad creates movement between unrelated chords:

  • C → Caug → Am (5th walks G → G♯ → A)
  • G → Gaug → Em
  • Classic move: I → Iaug → VIm (or → IV6). The rising line is the hook

diminished-chords.title: Diminished Chords
diminished-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords. Minor 3rd + flatted 5th — the ♭5 gives the tense, non-diatonic sound. Three flavors:

Chord Symbol Formula C example
Diminished triad Cdim / C° 1 ♭3 ♭5 C E♭ G♭
Diminished 7th Cdim7 / C°7 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭♭7 C E♭ G♭ A (B♭♭)
Half-diminished Cm7♭5 / Cø 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 C E♭ G♭ B♭
  • Triad = stacked minor 3rds (3+3 half-steps); dim7 = all minor 3rds (3+3+3) — perfectly symmetrical, so any note can be the root and it repeats every 3 frets/keys
  • dim7 vs ø differ only in the 7th: ♭♭7 (= 6th enharmonically) vs ♭7
  • ø can also be read as a minor 7th chord with lowered 5th (Seventh Chords)

Where they live diatonically

  • vii° is the 7th-degree triad of every major key; ii° in minor keys (Chords by Key)
  • ø is the ii in the minor-key jazz ii–V–i (Chord Progressions)
  • Chord-scale sources (Locrian etc.): Scale Modes Reference

Usage — passing chords

Mostly "in-between" chords creating tension between stronger chords:

  • I → ♭iii° → V7
  • Imaj7 → ♭ii°7 → ii7 (chromatic connector)
  • i7 → iiø7 → V7

slash-chords.title: Slash Chords
slash-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords / Chord Naming by Context. A slash chord as written on a jazz/fusion chart (Bb/C, A/C, D/C…) is almost always a triad or seventh chord voiced over a bass note, not a true two-key polychord (though the polychord reading exists and is occasionally the intent) — the upper letter is a normal chord, the lower letter is what's in the bass, and "read" it as "\ over \." The symbol looks mysterious mainly because it refuses to sort into a familiar category (m7, dominant 7, maj7) at a glance — it has to be decoded rather than read off a symbol chart.

The interpretation method

  1. Take the bass note as the root, whether or not it's actually a tone of the upper triad.
  2. Relate every note of the upper triad back to that root as a scale degree/extension (3rd, ♭7, 9, ♯11, ♭13…).
  3. Name the resulting chord from those degrees — this tells you whether it's functioning as a dominant, a major-7-type, a minor-7-type, or an ambiguous/diminished-adjacent color, and therefore how it wants to resolve.
  4. If the bass note is a chord tone of the upper triad, there's no new chord at all — it's just an inversion (e.g. Ab/C is 1st-inversion Ab major, F/C is 2nd-inversion F major).
  5. Chords with no 3rd and no 7th present (e.g. D/C, built from 9-♯11/♭5-13) are genuinely ambiguous between a major-7-type (lydian) and dominant-type (lydian dominant) reading — the surrounding harmony decides which; you can't tell from the voicing alone.
  6. This same take-the-bass-as-root method works identically on minor, diminished, and augmented upper triads, not just major (only major triads are catalogued below) — and generalizes to any 4-note upper chord over a bass note too (see below).

All twelve major triads over a C bass note

Worked chromatically from Jens Larsen's lesson — every possible major triad stacked over the same static C bass, analyzed by the method above:

Upper triad / C bass Notes relative to C Reads as Notes
C/C 1-3-5 C major Bass note is the root — just a plain C chord, no slash needed
B/C ♭3(enh. D♯), ♭5(enh. F♯), maj7 C diminished with a major 7 Sounds like a sus4-diminished suspension device — a "2-5-1" where the diminished chord suspends the I. See Diminished Chords
Bb/C ♭7, 9, 11 C7sus4(9) Same voicing as the classic textbook slash-chord example (B♭ triad/C bass)
A/C maj3, ♭9, 13 C7(♭9, 13) — "diminished harmony" flavor Ambiguous ♭7-vs-maj7 chord in isolation; in practice almost always heard as dominant
Ab/C ♭3(enh.), 5, root Ab major, 1st inversion C is already a chord tone (the 3rd of Ab) — not a new chord, just an inversion
G/C 9, 5, maj7 C major-7-type, rootless (Cmaj9 no 3rd) No 3rd present so quality is technically ambiguous, but reads as major in most contexts — this is Jens's own go-to voicing for a Cmaj7 sound
Gb/C ♭9, ♭5(♯11), ♭7 C7(♭9, ♭5) — dissonant, wants to resolve Ambiguous major/minor in isolation, clearly a tension chord in context
F/C 5, root, 3rd F major, 2nd inversion C is the 5th of F — not a new chord, just an inversion
E/C maj3, ♯5, maj7 Cmaj7♯5
Eb/C ♭3, 5, ♭7 C minor 7 Recognize this one on sight — it's just Cm7 spelled as a slash chord
D/C 9, ♯11/♭5, 13 Ambiguous: Cmaj7♯11 (lydian) or C7♯11 (lydian dominant) No 3rd, no 7th present — context alone decides which reading applies
Db/C ♭9, ♯4/sus4, ♭13 C7sus(♭9, ♭13) — "phrygian" sound Heard as a susb9/phrygian-dominant color

Worked ii–V–I examples using these voicings

All three from the same lesson, chosen to show the slash chords in real progressions — written on the chart as their functional names (a ii–V–I), not as slash symbols; the slash reading is just how you find the voicing:

  • ii–V–I in F: Gm7(11) → A/C [reads as C7(♭9,13)] → Fmaj6/9. The A-major-triad-over-C voicing supplies the dominant's alterations.
  • Minor ii–V into a lydian I: Dm7 → G7(♭13/♯5) → D/C [reads as Cmaj7♯11] used as the tonic voicing, resolving with a lydian color instead of plain maj7.
  • ii–V–I in F (2nd pass): Gm11 → Gb/C [reads as C7(♭9,♭5)] → straightforward drop-2 Fmaj7. Same dissonant Gb/C from the table above used as the dominant right before resolution.

Beyond triads, and comping without the bass note

  • Four-note chords over a bass note work the same way but usually carry a functional meaning beyond "here's a color" — e.g. Dm7/C is really a bass-motion device standing in for a known chord (here, a half-diminished-adjacent sound); the slash is describing a bass line move more than a new harmony.
  • When comping (not playing the bass note yourself), the "extra" note that would have been the bass can instead be voiced as a color tone on TOP of the triad — e.g. taking the Gb/C voicing above and putting the C on top of the Gb triad instead of underneath it produces a different, unexplored color. Flagged in the video as a follow-up-lesson candidate; not worked out in detail here.
  • The takeaway framing: don't treat slash chords as their own scary category — think of each one as another way to voice a chord type you already know, evaluate whether you like the sound, and use it as a voicing choice rather than trying to memorize the symbol itself.
