chord-naming-by-context.title: Chord Naming by Context
chord-naming-by-context.html:
The same notes can have different names depending on the tonal center you're in. This is where slash chords and inversion analysis matter.

Example: E, G, B, C

These four notes are a Cmaj7 chord — C, E, G, B reordered with E in the bass.

Cmaj7 Inversions

Inversion Notes Feel
Root position C, E, G, B Grounded home base
1st inversion E, G, B, C Lighter, open — E in bass
2nd inversion G, B, C, E Tension, common as passing chord
3rd inversion B, C, E, G Most unstable — half-step B→C pulls to resolve

Same notes, different tonal center

Context Name
Key of C Cmaj7 (1st inversion)
E as tonal center Cmaj7/E or Em(add♭6)
Jazz/modal Could read as Asus or Am9 depending on surrounding chords

Key principle: Chord quality is determined by the actual intervals, not the roman numeral case. An uppercase or lowercase numeral signals position/function — the stacked intervals determine major/minor/dominant.

chord-voicings.title: Chord Voicings
chord-voicings.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords, guitar side. Same chord, different arrangement of its notes — and on guitar that choice is most of the sound. Chord Inversions covers which note goes in the bass, mostly from a piano angle; this covers the guitar reality, which is that you rarely play all the notes and the interesting decision is which ones to leave out.

Built largely from Joe Pass Guitar Chords - Enrichment, which is a 24-page dictionary of exactly this.

Chord vs. voicing vs. shape

Three genuinely separate things, named explicitly by Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) but implicit in every section of this page: a chord is the abstract pitch content — "C major" means C-E-G, any order, any octave, no fretboard involved yet. A voicing is the specific order and interval spacing those notes are arranged in — root-3rd-5th stacked as close together as possible is a different voicing from 3rd-5th-root-with-the-root-an-octave-up, even though both are still "C major." A shape is the specific physical fretboard fingering used to realize a given voicing — the same voicing can be fingered as an open-position shape, a shape at the 5th fret, or a shape rooted off a different string, all genuinely different shapes playing the identical voicing; a piano player can play that same voicing with zero relationship to any guitar shape at all. Slide a whole shape up or down the neck by a fret and the voicing stays identical while the chord it's voicing changes. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Chord voicings guitar lesson - Unlimited Chord Options!

How to move between them — octave-shift voicing discovery. Take a known chord shape, move one note up or down an octave (to another instance of the same pitch elsewhere on the neck), and if that lands two notes on the same string, cascade the fix by moving the newly-colliding note to its own nearest octave too. This is the concrete mechanism behind this page's close-position/open-position distinction below — a close voicing becomes an open one exactly by moving an interior note up an octave and leaving a gap. Full method, the collision-resolution mechanic, and four worked chord examples (C major, A major, B7, D minor 7) with three song ties → Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery.

The core idea: chords are sounds, not spellings

Joe Pass files every chord into six categories of sound: Major · Seventh · Augmented · Minor · Diminished · Minor 7th ♭5. Any symbol you meet reduces to one of them, and the substitutes available to you come from that category's pool.

Symbol you see Reduces to Category
C, C6, Cma7, Cma9, C6/9 C major Major
C7, C9, C11, C13, C7♯5, C7♭9 C7 Seventh
Cm, Cm6, Cm7, Cm9, Cm11 Cm Minor
C°, C°7 C° Diminished
C+, C7♯5 (as a colour) C+ Augmented
Cm7♭5, Cø7 Cm7♭5 m7♭5

That reduction is the practical skill. Faced with E♭ma9♯11 at speed, you need "it's a major sound" in under a second, not a spelling.

Which notes actually matter

For a four-note chord you have six strings and two hands. Something has to go. The priority order:

  1. The 3rd and the 7th — the guide tones. These define quality and function: 3rd says major or minor, 7th says dominant or major-7th. Lose either and the chord stops being itself. Everything else is optional.
  2. The extension you actually want to hear — the 9th, 13th, ♯11, ♭9, whatever the colour of the moment is.
  3. The root — droppable. In a band the bass has it. Dropping it is what makes a rootless voicing, and it frees a finger for colour.
  4. The 5th — the first thing to go, almost always. It adds nothing to identity. (Exception: an altered 5th — ♭5 or ♯5 — is a colour tone, not a 5th, and stays.)

Shell voicing = root + 3rd + 7th only. Three notes, unambiguous, works anywhere, and it's the fastest way to comp through a tune you don't know. Rootless = 3rd + 7th + extensions. Guide-tone comping — playing only 3rds and 7ths through the changes — is the standard first exercise, and it's worth doing on its own before adding anything.

Concrete way to build a rootless voicing without recalculating from a rule table: replace the root with the diatonic neighbor tone a whole step away — the 9th above, or the 7th below. Both destinations are notes you probably want to hear anyway (the 9th is a colour extension; the 7th turns a triad into a 7th-chord voicing), so the swap does double duty. Worked examples: an F major triad with its root replaced by the major 7th (whole step below) → a rootless F major 7 — and the resulting shape is physically identical to an A minor triad, the same Fmaj7/Am relationship Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords derives from the rule table; a G7, first inversion with its (open-string) root replaced by the 9th (whole step above) → the shape becomes a half-diminished chord shape in root position, reread as a rootless G9. Stacks with this page's own "the 5th is the first thing to go" rule: take that rootless G9 (3-♭7-9-5) and replace its 5th with the 13th (another whole step up) for a rootless G13 (3-♭7-9-13, no root, no 5th) — playable an octave up on the top four strings too. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

Pass's book demonstrates this constantly without naming it: E B D G printed under a diagram is a Cmaj9 with no C in it — 3rd, 7th, 9th, 5th.

The named voicing families

Family What it is Sounds like
Close All notes inside one octave Dense, cluttered on guitar, mostly impractical
Drop 2 Take a close voicing, move the 2nd-highest note down an octave The workhorse. Sits on strings 5-4-3-2 (warm) or 4-3-2-1 (bright)
Drop 3 Move the 3rd-highest down an octave Wider, bass note + a gap. Strings 6-4-3-2
Shell Root, 3rd, 7th Lean, unambiguous, leaves room
Rootless 3rd, 7th, extensions The bass has the root; you have the colour
Quartal Stacked 4ths Modal, ambiguous, modern — not in the Pass book (fretboard shapes on Quartal Chord Voicings)

Drop 2 is the one worth systematising first: it's the most common jazz-guitar voicing family and its four inversions across two string sets covers most comping situations.

Voice leading is the actual point

A voicing choice is only good relative to the one before it. Three rules that carry almost everything:

  1. Move the least. Between two chords, hold every common tone and move the rest by step. Dm7 → G7: keep the F and C, move A→B and D→D. Two fingers.
  2. The top note is a melody. Pass says it flatly in the blues section: "Try to sustain lead notes from one chord to the next. For example, C9 to F13, sustain the G on top." Reharmonise underneath a held top note. This is the difference between comping that sounds like a progression and comping that sounds like a piece of music.
  3. Approach chromatically. Any chord can be entered from a half step above or below — slide the whole shape in. Pass builds a 12-bar blues out of one fingering moved in half steps. Whole steps work too, and diminished/augmented shapes connect dominants because they're symmetric.
  4. A rigid shape works too — voice-lead a whole voicing as one unit through an entire cadence. Take one close-interval, incomplete 3-note voicing and move every note the SAME direction by the SAME interval to land on the next chord — e.g. raise a Dm-family voicing a whole step to get a usable G7♭9, then raise it a whole step again for a usable Cmaj7 — covering a full ii-V-I from one mechanically-transposed shape rather than deriving three unrelated voicings. Pairs naturally with incompleteness: the higher the register or the more altered the dominant, the less a voicing needs to spell every chord tone, since the tensions/alterations already signal the chord's identity. — Gilad Hekselman / Lage Lund / Nelson Veras-style voicings, via Jens Larsen, Modern 3 note voicings and voice leading - How to find new jazz chords

Comping, practically

  • Leave space. The most common failure is playing too much. Chords on beats 2 and 4, or one chord per bar, will nearly always sit better than constant strumming.
  • Play only the strings indicated. Pass is explicit that several of his voicings sound wrong if you fill in the muted strings. Muted strings are part of the voicing.
  • Register matters more than you think. The same chord low on the neck is mud under a vocal and fine as a solo statement. When something else occupies the low mids, comp higher. This is an arrangement fix for what would otherwise show up as a mix problem — see Masking and Carving.
  • Hybrid picking — pick plus 2nd and 3rd fingers — makes the open-voiced shapes (skipped strings) playable. Pass calls it common practice. For a full drill system on the mechanics (planting, finger order, block-chord evenness) see Hybrid Picking Exercises.
  • Two-chord-per-bar reharmonisation is the highest-value trick: a static bar of Dm7 becomes Dm7 | Em7 A7, Dm7 | B♭7 E♭9, Dm7 | G°… Full menus in Joe Pass Guitar Chords - Enrichment §Standard Pattern Chord Substitutions.

When there's no answer: ambiguous chords

Not every incomplete voicing resolves to one clear chord label, and that's a legitimate stopping point, not a failure. Most often it's a missing 3rd that causes this — without it, major/minor can't be determined no matter which note is assumed to be the root. Worked example: a shape where the bottom note as root gives ♭9+5 with no 3rd; a different note as root gives major-7+♭5; the unplayed note as root (rootless) gives ♭9, 5, and ♯11 — three readings, none a complete, unambiguous chord. Context (key, direction of resolution) can sometimes narrow an ambiguous shape down, but in a vacuum it's fine to just note the tensions present and call it "ambiguous" rather than force a label onto it. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

Getting these under the fingers

The book's own method — and it is a good one — is ear-first, not name-first: learn a grip exactly as written, play it in context against the category it belongs to, and only then break it into partials or transpose it. Everything is written in C and meant to be moved to all twelve keys.

A workable order:

  1. Shell voicings for all six categories, two string sets. Comp a tune with nothing else.
  2. Guide tones only through a set of changes — 3rds and 7ths, no root, no extensions.
  3. Drop 2, one string set, all inversions, one chord quality at a time.
  4. Add one colour tone — the 9th on major and minor, the 13th on dominants.
  5. Altered dominants last: ♭9, ♯9, ♭5, ♯5. G7♯5♯9 is the endpoint and it's four notes.
  6. Then the Pass dictionary as vocabulary to raid, category by category.

Ear-training add-on for rootless voicings specifically: hold a rootless voicing and try to sing the unplayed root. There's no reference pitch to latch onto, so it forces hearing the root purely in relationship to the sounding notes — a stated route to actually internalizing a harmonic progression rather than just memorizing shapes. — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

Voice leading is the actual point
When there's no answer: ambiguous chords

breaking-up-voicings.title: Breaking Up Voicings
breaking-up-voicings.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — a comping-texture device that sits next to Chord Voicings (which shapes to grab) and Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline (when to strike them): once you've got a voicing, don't treat "strum all four notes together" as the only option. A struck 4-note chord is really four separate notes you can deploy in any combination or order — treating the voicing as raw material for fragments and lines, not a single fixed event, opens up a lot of comping texture from shapes you already know.

The core method

Take any known chord voicing — worked here on a C major 7 drop-2 voicing rooted on the A string (see Chord Voicings for the drop-2 family) — and instead of always striking all four notes at once, play subsets or orderings of them:

  • Outside notes, then inside notes (or reversed) — split the voicing into its outer pair and inner pair, play one pair then the other.
  • Every other note — skip through the voicing rather than reading it top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top.
  • Hold the top note as a pedal, play the remaining notes below it as a line — turns a static chord into a moving inner-voice line under a sustained top note, a related idea to Chord Voicings's common-tone-threading entry (Jack Ruch) but generated from breaking a single voicing apart rather than choosing extensions across a progression.

Once one drop-2 inversion is exhausted, repeat the whole process on the chord's other inversions — each inversion has its own four notes to recombine, multiplying the available material. This generalizes to any voicing family, not just drop-2 (shell, drop-3, quartal — see Chord Voicings, Quartal Chord Voicings) — and is described as especially effective on larger/denser chords, where there are more notes and therefore more combinations to draw fragments from.

Applying it to a progression

Run this over a basic progression — a 2-5-1 is given as the starting ground (see The ii-V-I) — in two stages:

  1. First pass: pick the chord shapes for the whole progression, then find ways to break up every chord.
  2. Second pass: dial it back — break up only a couple of the chords in the progression rather than all of them, which increases the impact of the broken voicings by contrast against chords still struck normally. Treat "which chords stay struck vs. which get broken" as its own arranging decision, not an all-or-nothing setting.

Practice note: apply it to a narrow target, not everywhere at once

Rather than trying to internalize every combination across every voicing, pick one small fragment to drill — e.g. one specific way of breaking up chords, or one area of the neck — and hyperfocus on it for an extended stretch (a couple of months, sometimes closer to a year) until it starts coming out naturally in real playing, then move to the next fragment. A personal example given: applying the breaking-up idea specifically to diminished chord inversions (playing off each inversion of a diminished shape rather than always the same one) as a current focus area — same "isolate one narrow thing and grind it until it's automatic" logic as Etude-Based Vocabulary Practice.
secs: Practice note: apply it to a narrow target, not everywhere at once

quartal-chord-voicings.title: Quartal Chord Voicings
quartal-chord-voicings.html:
Chords built by stacking 4ths instead of 3rds — the guitar-fretboard companion to the theory-side Chords tertial/quartal/quintal breakdown and 20th-Century Harmony's Stravinsky entry, and the concrete fingerings behind Modal Jazz's "quartal voicings" section (the So What chord). Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) devotes a full lesson to defining the sound, mapping shapes to the fretboard, and — the most reusable part — using quartal shapes as a reharmonization tool over ordinary tertian chords, not just in modal contexts.

What it is

Where a normal ("tertiary"/tertial) chord takes 1-3-5(-7) of a scale, a quartal chord takes 1-4-7(-…) — stack 4ths instead of 3rds, off any scale degree, and keep stacking as far as you want. Building through the scale of C major on the 5th-4th-3rd strings gives 3-note quartal chords; extend the stack across the middle 4 strings and you get 4-note quartal chords. Sound: open, ambiguous, "less traditional" than tertiary harmony — because a stack of 3rds names a chord quality and therefore implies a function, while a stack of 4ths states a set of notes without committing to major/minor/dominant. That's also why it reads as more dissonant/modern to the ear trained on common-practice harmony.

Why it pairs with modal harmony

In Modal Jazz's terms: modal harmony has a tonal center (the root) but treats every other scale degree as equal — nothing resolves anywhere, there's no harmonic motion to track, which is what makes a mode "jammable" indefinitely. Tertiary chords built from that scale start to smuggle back in a sense of function/resolution; quartal chords stay neutral and nebulous, so they're the natural harmonic vocabulary for staying inside a mode without accidentally re-implying a key center. Historical note: tertiary/functional harmony dominated Western classical music through the 19th century; in the 20th century, Stravinsky, Ravel, Debussy, Schoenberg and others deliberately stacked voices in 4ths to escape the sense of a traditional key center — see 20th-Century Harmony for the fuller Stravinsky/Hindemith split.

The So What voicing (Miles Davis, Kind of Blue, 1959)

The best-known real-world example, and the birth of the term "modal jazz." "So What" sits in D Dorian — D is the tonal center, every other note of D Dorian is equally fair game to improvise with, no note besides the root carries extra weight. Bill Evans's signature comping chord between melody phrases: a stack of four perfect 4ths with a major 3rd on top — from the bottom, E-A-D-G-B — so it's not purely quartal (that top major-3rd breaks the pure-4ths stack), but close enough that it's the standard reference "quartal chord" in jazz vocabulary. Move the top note (B, on the high E string) down an octave to the low E string at the same fret and the five notes reorder into pure perfect-4th stacks all the way up — a genuine 5-note quartal chord, same pitches, different voicing.

On a lead sheet, "So What" is usually written as a static Dm11 for 16 bars — that's the closest a chord symbol (built from tertiary-harmony vocabulary) can get to naming a Dorian modal sound. Derivation: take Dm7, replace the 5th with the 11 (= the 4, a whole step above the 5) → the resulting shape is one of the stacked-perfect-4ths quartal voicings above. The more accurate framing is "playing in D Dorian," not "playing over Dm11" — the chord symbol is a functional-harmony approximation of a modal sound, not the actual thing being played.

Fretboard shapes

  • 3-note quartal chords through D Dorian on strings 2-3-4 — map one shape per scale degree of D Dorian along the top three strings; these are the practical comping/improvising vocabulary for playing over "So What"-style modal vamps. Use the top note of each shape as a melody note (arpeggiate the shapes for melodic lines), or comp with them under a soloist.
  • 3-note quartal chords through C major on strings 5-4-3 and 4-note quartal chords through C major on the middle 4 strings — the general fretboard-mapping drill: build the shape at every scale degree, same "climb the whole scale in one voicing type" logic as the Chords by Key tonic-to-tonic triad/7th-chord mapping drill, just with quartal stacks instead of tertian ones.

Reharmonizing tertian chords with quartal shapes (the reusable trick)

Quartal shapes aren't only for modal tunes — they're a genuine reharmonization/color tool over ordinary minor chords, tertian or not:

  1. Harmonize the minor pentatonic scale with 4ths. Take the minor pentatonic scale along one string (e.g. E minor pentatonic on the 2nd string) and stack two perfect 4ths below each scale tone — same physical shape repeats at every scale degree. This introduces a natural 6 into the sound, which is the same thing as treating the minor chord as Dorian even when the underlying chord isn't officially Dorian — described as "totally okay" to do regardless. Slide the same shape to any root to reharmonize any minor or minor-7 chord (worked over both E minor and A minor in the video). → pairs directly with the natural-6 "characteristic note" logic already on Modal Jazz.
  2. Connect shapes chromatically through the blues note. The same quartal shape, built off the ♭5/blues note of the pentatonic scale, works as a passing/connecting voicing between the diatonic shapes — and the whole set arpeggiates into melodic lines as well as chordal stabs.
  3. Drone/pedal the root underneath while playing the moving quartal shapes above — a low root note (played or implied by a bassist) keeps the ear anchored while the quartal voicings float ambiguously on top. → Modal Jazz §Pedal points and drones.
  4. Any chord type, not just minor — map quartal shapes off the scale a chord actually comes from (e.g. quartal shapes over a G7 pull from the C major scale G7 belongs to), then apply the same reharmonization logic.

One shape, many chord identities (rootless-voicing crossover)

The same 3-note quartal shape reharmonizes to a different named tertian chord depending purely on which note you're mentally treating as the root — a direct crossover with the rootless-voicing logic on Chord Voicings ("one physical shape, several harmonic identities depending on context"). Worked off one fixed 3-note quartal shape:

Treated as root Resulting chord
bottom note minor 11
next note up (4th fret in the worked example) ♭ major 7♯11
next sus4
next 6/9
next major 13
next 7sus4 (or minor 11)
next sus2
next 6/9 (an octave/register up from the earlier one)

The physical grip never changes — only the ear's assumption about which note is the root does. Stringing several of these root-reinterpretations together in sequence reads as a legitimate ambiguous-but-coherent chord progression, and is exactly the quality that makes quartal shapes so at-home in a modal context: the chord never insists on one specific identity.

Inverting quartal shapes for new colors

Take a quartal shape (e.g. the E-minor-pentatonic-harmonized-in-4ths shape above) and invert it two ways:

  • Bottom note up an octave → produces a genuinely new shape (no longer a pure quartal stack) built from the same pitch classes — still usable in exactly the same context (same scale, same chord) since the note content is identical. Following the E minor pentatonic scale along the 2nd string with this inversion gives a whole-step interval on top — a distinct, "beautiful" color from the plain stacked-4ths version.
  • Top note down an octave → another new shape from the same notes; following the scale along the 5th string instead gives yet another usable voicing, called out as a favorite.

Both inversions are worth cycling through as a deliberate variation set once the plain quartal shape is comfortable — same "same notes, new physical shape, new usable color" principle that Chord Voicings documents for altered-dominant and dim7 shapes elsewhere on the fretboard.

Practice method (pedal points, melody-first, avoid-note handling)

Jens Larsen's practice-focused companion lesson to the definitional material above — less about what quartal chords are, more about how to actually get them into your hands and ears in a usable order.

  1. Voicings first, on a couple of string sets. Get the 3-note quartal shapes under the fingers before doing anything else with them — Larsen says he personally reaches for the top two string sets the most, though drilling every string set is worth it for thoroughness.
  2. Then drill over a pedal point, starting with the ii chord. Hold a static root (drone, backing track, or looper — see below) and practice the quartal voicings over it, beginning with the ii chord (D minor in a C-major context) because it's the most forgiving entry point. Of the seven diatonic 3-note quartal voicings, only one actually spells a "normal"-sounding Dm7 on its own — the rest are intentionally incomplete and work by accumulation: stack several of them in sequence and let the sum of the notes convey the chord, rather than expecting any single grip to sound complete. Move to the V chord next (G — the plain major-scale quartal voicing there already reads as a "G7 with a 13"), then the I chord last (see the avoid-note problem below). Scope the whole drill to a plain 2-5-1, not all seven scale degrees at once.
  3. Melody-first practice technique: improvise a one-string single-note melody, then drop a quartal chord underneath it. The natural next step once the harmonized-scale voicings are comfortable — you've already practiced playing the scale harmonized on one string, so picking a melody note there and adding a quartal voicing under it is a small step. This is the bridge from "I know the shapes" to actually using them expressively, and it's also how several of the worked ii–V–I examples below are built (a melody line doing more of the harmonic-identity work than any single chord grip).
  4. Practice against a drone/loop, not a self-played root. On camera the root gets played by hand to demonstrate the sound, but the recommended practice setup is a backing track or a loop pedal holding the pedal tone, freeing both hands for the quartal voicings and melody.

The tonic (I) chord is the hardest of the three — the "avoid note" problem. Over C major 7, any quartal voicing containing F (the 4th/11th) clashes with the major 3rd (E) and stops reading as a resting tonic sound — three of the seven diatonic 3-note quartal voicings contain F and work mainly as passing chords, not landing points. Explicit advice: don't reach for a Lydian sound to dodge this at the start — raising the 4th to a ♯11 (Lydian) does remove the clash and is common advice for quartal-tonic voicings, but it's framed here as unnecessary complexity for a beginner; stay inside the plain major scale first, add Lydian later once the basic vocabulary is comfortable. → Modal Jazz (Lydian as the natural "easier tonic" mode for quartal/modal playing generally)

Quartal voicings for altered dominants (melodic-minor harmonization)

Same harmonize-every-scale-degree-in-4ths method used for the major scale, applied to the melodic minor scale instead, to get quartal voicings usable over an altered dominant. For a G7alt sound, harmonize Ab melodic minor — a half step above the dominant root ("a flat melodic minor, which is the same as G7 altered") — in stacked 3-note 4th-voicings. Stated as a repeatable template: cover other dominant colors the same way later (Lydian dominant, tonic-minor chords, etc.) by harmonizing the matching parent scale in 4ths. → Altered Chords, Jens Larsen - Melodic Minor - Altered Scale

Worked ii–V–I application (four examples, Dm7 → G7alt → C69 in C major). The core device: make the altered dominant audible by voicing G7alt with notes absent from the preceding Dm7 voicing, not by nailing one textbook-correct chord shape. Open on a quartal Dm7-area voicing chosen to sound unambiguously like D minor 7 (or a one-string melody line doing the same job — examples 3 and 4 lean on this instead of a fixed grip), then move to a quartal G7alt voicing built from the Ab-melodic-minor harmonization — the ♭9/♯9-family notes (Ab, Eb, Bb) weren't present in the Dm7 voicing, so the ear registers "something changed, this is altered" even without any single voicing spelling G7alt cleanly. Example 4 goes furthest: it avoids the major 3rd of G7 entirely and still reads as altered purely from the ♭9/♯9-family color notes. All four resolve to a C69 tonic voicing (not a plain Cmaj7) — consistent with the plain-major-scale (not Lydian) tonic voicings from the practice method above. → The ii-V-I — Jens Larsen, Jazz Chord Essentials 3 part Quartal Harmony

Two extensions named but not developed in the source lesson (flag for a future enrichment pass if covered elsewhere): using quartal voicings melodically inside improvised lines, not just as chords; and building quartal harmony by harmonizing pentatonic scales instead of the full major/melodic-minor scale — "another way to approach this and get some other sounds." The pentatonic-harmonization extension is now covered — Pentatonic Scale Harmonized in Thirds does the tertian (3rds) sibling of this technique: stacking the pentatonic scale's own notes in scale-step thirds rather than 4ths, cycled through every scale degree for a second, differently-colored family of voicings from the same five notes — Nathan Borton, Joe Henderson's Pentatonic Secrets.

octave-shift-voicing-discovery.title: Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery
octave-shift-voicing-discovery.html:
A deliberately unsystematic method for turning up new voicings of any chord shape you already know — Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) exploratory counterpart to the more rigorous drilling in Hub-Latching Approach and Chord Inversions. Where those work a chord's voicings by known theory (four inversions per chord tone, a fixed practice path), this method finds them by playful trial and error: move one note of a shape up or down an octave, see what turns up, and keep going. Directly demonstrates the mechanism behind Chord Voicings's existing "close position" and "open position" rows and its chord/voicing/shape distinction — this page supplies how to move between them, not just what they're called.

Prerequisite: seeing a note in other places

Assumes the ability to locate the same pitch class in other fretboard positions via octave and unison interval shapes — see Octave and Unison Shapes for Fretboard Navigation. Concretely, this means being able to answer "where else on the neck is this exact note" fast enough to move a chord tone without stopping to calculate — the same fretboard fluency Triads as a Fretboard Map and Guitar Positions build toward from other angles.

The method

  1. Start from a chord shape you already know — root position is the natural starting point since it's usually the one already memorized.
  2. Pick one note in the chord and move it up or down an octave, using the octave/unison-shape skill above to find where that same pitch lands elsewhere on the neck.
  3. If the moved note now collides with another note already on that string (you can't play two notes on one string at once), move the colliding note to its own nearest available octave too — cascading as many times as needed until every note in the chord has a distinct playable string.
  4. Repeat with a different note, or repeat the whole cycle from the new shape, treating each result as a fresh starting point for the next move.
  5. Some results will be physically unplayable or just bad — that's a normal, expected outcome of moving things around blind, not a sign the method is broken. Discard and try a different note.

There's no fixed order, no target voicing, and no guarantee of what you'll land on — that's the point. Jared frames it explicitly against his own more "systematic and heavy duty" prior lessons (memorize a fixed set of shapes in a set order): this is loose, playful, puzzle-solving exploration, closer to noodling with intent than a drill. "If teaching you a chord by giving you a chord shape diagram is giving you a fish, this lesson is teaching you how to fish."

Worked examples

C major triad (the from-scratch demo). Root position C-E-G, close position. Move the root (C) up an octave → E-G-C — still close position, a different inversion of the same voicing family. From the original root position instead, move the middle note (E) up an octave → C-G-E, this time with real space between the C and the G — an open position voicing, specifically the 1-5-3 voicing. That 1-5-3 voicing is then shown realized as three different physical shapes (open position, a shape at the 5th fret, a shape rooted off the 6th string) — same voicing, three shapes, directly demonstrating Chord Voicings's voicing-vs-shape distinction. Sliding any one of those shapes up a half step keeps the voicing (1-5-3) intact while changing which chord it is.

A major, open chord → movable first-inversion 3-1-5. Starting triad: 5th-root-3rd. Move the 5th up an octave (resolve the resulting collision), move the 3rd down an octave, relocate the root via a "find the 5th below" fretboard move → 3-1-5, first inversion, no open strings, fully movable to any major chord. Named as the I → V(1st inv.) → vi voice-leading move used in "Tears in Heaven" (Eric Clapton), "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right" (Bob Dylan), and "Somebody to Love" (Queen) — full song ties on Chord voicings guitar lesson - Unlimited Chord Options!.

B7, dominant 7th → four usable inversions from one shape. Starting shape: root-3rd-♭7-5th. Sequential octave shifts turn up, in order: (1) root-♭7-3-5 (barred, standard root-position dominant-7 shape); (2) ♭7-3-5-root, third inversion, ♭7 on the bottom — the opening chord of "Águas de Março" (Jobim); (3) 3-♭7-1-5, first inversion, resolves naturally to a I chord; (4) 3-♭7-5-root — the shape used for the intro to "Wave" (Jobim/Sinatra).

D minor 7, the "Wave" companion chord. Starting shape: root-5th-♭7-♭3. One pass turns up an unplayable shape — discarded, a normal outcome. A further shift → root-♭3-5-♭7, third inversion, ♭7 on the bottom — the functional partner to the B7 third-inversion shape above (resolves the same way, to I). A second, separate shift → ♭3-♭7-root-5, first inversion, 3rd in the bass — noted to sound like a major 6 chord (a first-inversion m7 and a major-6 chord share overlapping pitch content), usable as a general-purpose colorful substitute for any plain Dm(7).

Collision-resolution mechanic, generalized

The one piece of real mechanical rigor inside an otherwise loose method: whenever an octave shift lands two notes on the same string, the fix is always the same — move the newly-colliding note (not the one you were originally moving) to its own nearest available octave, and repeat if that triggers another collision. This cascading fix is what turns "randomly move notes around" into something that reliably terminates in a playable four-or-fewer-note voicing rather than a dead end.

Why this differs from the hub-latching approach

Hub-Latching Approach and this method solve adjacent problems from opposite directions. Hub-latching starts from known theory (a chord has N inversions, defined by which chord tone is lowest) and drills a fixed path through all of them systematically, always anchored back to a "hub." This method has no theory prerequisite and no anchor — it's a way to discover voicings you didn't already know existed by physically moving notes and listening, useful specifically when you already have a shape memorized and want more options from it without deriving them analytically first. Both feed the same destination: more voicings under the fingers, reachable from different starting skill levels.

Practice framing

Feed it with any root-position shape you already know — Jared's own free "Chords with Color" chart supplies deliberately limited, single-position root-position voicings specifically as raw material for this method to multiply. Treat each session as exploratory rather than comprehensive: work one chord shape at a time, keep what sounds good, discard what's unplayable, and don't expect (or need) to exhaust every possible octave permutation.

— Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Chord voicings guitar lesson - Unlimited Chord Options!

major-triads-across-the-fretboard-string.title: Major Triads Across the Fretboard (String-Group Inversions)
major-triads-across-the-fretboard-string.html:
Learn one major triad's three inversions (root-position, 1st inversion, 2nd inversion) on each of the four 3-string groups, so any major chord is playable from at least a dozen fretboard locations rather than one memorized open-position shape. Companion to Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude and Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude (composed voice-leading studies) — this page is the raw shape-inventory those etudes assume, plus the practical spacing payoff for riff-writing.

The four string groups, three voicings each

Worked on A major (A-C♯-E) across all four adjacent 3-string groups — E-A-D · A-D-G · D-G-B · G-B-E:

  • On each group, find the root in three different octave locations, and at each one a different note ends up on the bottom of the stack: root-on-bottom (root-3rd-5th), 3rd-on-bottom (3rd-5th-root), and 5th-on-bottom (5th-root-3rd).
  • Because the guitar is tuned in fourths except for the B string, the D-G-B and G-B-E groups reuse the same three voicing shapes as E-A-D/A-D-G but with the top note shifted one fret to compensate for the B string's major-3rd tuning interval — same notes, same octave, same voicing type, different fingering.
  • Finding the root in every position first is the prerequisite step — use the octave-shape relationships already covered in the vault's note-location material (open string ↔ 12th fret, and the string-pair octave shapes) rather than searching blind.

Why this matters beyond "more shapes to know"

  • Extends directly to bigger chords. Once a triad inversion is solid, adding the 7th (or further tensions) on top doesn't require learning a whole new chord — it's the same triad shape plus one note, matching the extension-on-a-known-shape method in Chord Voicings and Best DARK Metal Chord - Spice Up Your Evil Chords Now!.
  • Non-root-position voicings sound less generic. Defaulting to root-on-bottom voicings (the easiest to find) is the common habit; deliberately reaching for 3rd-on-bottom or 5th-on-bottom voicings of the same chord produces a noticeably different, more interesting color from identical notes.

Practical payoff — spacing a chord riff for speed and interest

A riff written using only root-position triads anchored to the low E string forces the fretting hand to travel the full neck between chords, capping how fast it can be played cleanly. Fix: pick each chord's voicing based on proximity to the previous chord, not by defaulting to the root-position shape — worked on a G-B♭-F-C-G progression, chaining voicings so each new chord's nearest available inversion (root/3rd/5th-on-bottom, on whichever string group is closest) is chosen over the "obvious" root-anchored one. Result: dramatically smaller hand movement between chords, faster playable tempo, and a more interesting sound than repeating the same voicing shape transposed up and down one string.

Practice recommendation

10-15 minutes/day finding all inversions of one triad across the neck, rotating the root note daily.

multifunctional-voicings.title: Multifunctional Voicings
multifunctional-voicings.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — a reharmonization concept sitting alongside Chord Voicings's "one physical shape, several harmonic identities" rootless-voicing principle and Quartal Chord Voicings's "one shape, eight identities," but framed here as a deliberate comping strategy rather than an analytical curiosity: one memorized voicing, played off different chord tones of a target chord, does the work of several separate shapes. Nathan Borton's name for a device he draws from Barry Galbraith's Comping Etudes — a book of comping-focused jazz-guitar etudes (with audio recordings featuring Galbraith and bassist Milt Hinton) built around exactly this kind of practical, playable vocabulary rather than abstract theory. The payoff is efficiency: fewer shapes to memorize, more harmonic mileage from each one — "it's not about memorizing endless chord shapes, but rather understanding how many different chords you can imply with just one versatile shape."

The core mechanism

Take a single chord-voicing shape (any of the standard families — min7♭5, half-diminished, maj7♯5, dominant 9 — see Chord Voicings) and play it starting from a different chord tone of the target chord each time. The shape's fingering never changes; only which note you're mentally treating as the root shifts — same underlying logic as Chord Voicings's rootless-voicing reinterpretation and Quartal Chord Voicings's root-reassignment table, but the destination here is always "which dominant/target chord does this shape become," not just "which chord symbol could this be."

Three worked shapes, three functions each

1. A minor7♭5 shape → three separate roles, from Galbraith's Tangerine etude (a ii-V-I comping line):

  • Played off its own root → a plain minor 7♭5 (e.g. F m7♭5).
  • Played off the ♭7 of a dominant chord → a highly altered voicing for that dominant (worked example: the F m7♭5 shape used under a G7, since F is G7's ♭7 — reads as G7alt).
  • Played off the 3rd of a dominant chord → a dominant 9 voicing (general starting point — stated as a recurring move throughout the book, not tied to one specific root in the source).

2. A half-diminished shape → root, then altered-dominant ♭7 role, resolving to I:

  • Played off its own root → a plain half-diminished chord.
  • Played off the ♭7 of the dominant → an altered voicing for that dominant (worked example: played from A♭, the ♭7 of B♭7, to produce a B♭7-altered sound) — then resolves to the I chord. This is the same "shape reused off the ♭7 of the V chord" move as shape 1's second function, confirming it as a repeatable rule for any min7♭5/half-diminished-family shape, not a one-off.

3. An A♭ major7♯5 shape → root role, then altered-dominant 3rd role:

  • Played off its own root → a plain maj7♯5 chord.
  • Played off the 3rd of a dominant chord → another altered-dominant color (worked in a 2-5-1 line: the same shape used off the 3rd of the V7 to color it altered before resolving).

A fourth device: reusing a dominant-9 shape at its tritone substitute root

From Galbraith's minor-blues etude: a familiar dominant 9 shape (the kind you'd normally finger as, e.g., a B♭ dominant 9) is instead played rooted a tritone away, functioning as an altered voicing of the "real" dominant — here a B♭ dominant-9 grip used to voice an E7♯9♯5, because B♭ is E7's tritone substitute (same guide tones, shared altered tensions — see Chord Substitution for the underlying tritone-sub theory). This is the same "one shape, reused at a different root, new function" logic as the three shapes above, but the destination root is chosen via tritone substitution specifically rather than "the same chord's own chord tone."

Worked 2-5-1 lines that chain these together

Three full comping lines from the book layer this device on top of Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline's Charleston rhythm (see that note's "Charleston off different beats" addition, same video):

  1. A Charleston starting on beat 3, D7 voiced via the half-diminished-off-the-♭7 trick (shape rooted a half step below D, i.e. off C — the ♭7 of D7 — to sound altered), resolving to a quartal voicing off G major built off the 3rd (→ Quartal Chord Voicings).
  2. A 5-1 line mixing Charleston with quarter and half notes: the dominant chord first voiced with the half-diminished-off-♭7 trick (shape 2 above), then the new A♭maj7♯5-off-the-3rd trick (shape 3 above), resolving to a A minor 9 voicing using open strings — a specific fingerboard-knowledge move worth remembering as a go-to open-position A minor 9 shape.
  3. The minor-blues etude's two V-I ideas: the first uses one of the multifunctional shapes above voiced as an E7; the second is the tritone-substitute dominant-9-as-altered-E7 device described above; the phrase again resolves to the same open-string A minor 9 voicing as line 2 — confirming it as Galbraith's recurring resolution shape, not a one-off.

A fifth device: the "magic chord" — one voicing, five identities via melodic minor

A different construction route to the same "one shape, several harmonic identities" payoff, this time built from a scale rather than derived from a chord-tone family: voice the notes of C melodic minor into a single chord shape (nicknamed "the magic chord") and the same physical voicing reads as five different chords depending purely on which note the bass plays underneath it:

  • Bass on C → C minor(major7) 6/9 (Cm(maj7)69) — the tonic reading.
  • Bass on F → F13(♯11,9) — a Lydian-dominant-flavored reading a 4th up.
  • Bass on B → B altered (B7alt) — the melodic-minor-up-a-half-step-from-the-7th-degree altered-dominant reading.
  • Bass on A → A minor7♭5(natural 9) — a half-diminished reading with a natural 9 (from being drawn straight out of the parent melodic minor rather than a "pure" locrian ♮2 chord).
  • Bass on E♭ → E♭ major7♯5(♯11) — a lydian-augmented reading. This is the same underlying mechanism as the four devices above (fix the notes, change what the bass implies as root), just entered from "harmonize a melodic minor scale into one grip" instead of "start a min7♭5/half-diminished/maj7♯5/dominant-9 shape off a different chord tone." Worked as a full 2-5-1: the one C-melodic-minor voicing covers the ii (via its A m7♭5(♮9) reading), the V (via its B altered reading, or combined with a tritone-substitute-flavored bass choice), and resolves — the whole progression playable off one memorized shape by changing only the bass note under it. Also explicitly stacked with Breaking Up Voicings (fragment the magic-chord voicing itself instead of striking it whole) and Counterpoint Line Generation (generate a two-voice line first, then harmonize it with the magic chord's five readings) — see those notes for the companion devices from the same lesson.

Why this matters for comping efficiency

The whole point is vocabulary compression: instead of memorizing a distinct shape for every altered-dominant color you might need, memorize a handful of core 4-note shapes (min7♭5, half-diminished, maj7♯5, dominant 9) and learn which chord tone to start each one from to get a different, usable harmonic result. That's fewer total shapes under the fingers with more comping mileage per shape — directly analogous to Chord Voicings's rootless-voicing reuse and Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords's one-triad-many-chords logic, just applied specifically to altered-dominant sounds.

A sixth device: chromatic-slide reharmonization of a rootless 9 chord (blues rhythm-guitar version)

A guitar-mechanical, blues-specific route to the same "one grip, several identities" payoff, from a different channel/lineage than the Galbraith devices above: take a rootless dominant 9 shape (3rd–♭7–9th–5th, no root — the same base grip documented on Rootless 9th Chords and Chromatic Movement in Blues Rhythm Guitar) and slide the whole shape up a half step. Because the four notes don't change, only which root they're heard against does, so the identical grip reads as any of:

  • Its own dominant 9 (unmoved).
  • A dominant 9 a half step up (the moved position's most literal reading).
  • A half-diminished (m7♭5) chord, off a different root again.
  • A minor 6 chord, off yet another root.
  • An altered dominant a half step below the moved position (reading the moved shape's ♭7/major 3rd/♭13/♭9 against that root instead). Worked example (rootless G9 slid up a half step): reads as A♭9 (A♭ mixolydian), Cm7♭5 (C locrian), E♭m6 (E♭ dorian-family), or D7alt (D altered — the source's own favorite reading, and the one demonstrated in the solo). One chromatic slide, four to five usable harmonic destinations depending on how the soloist/comper chooses to hear it — the same economy-of-shapes payoff as the Galbraith devices above, reached here from a half-step chromatic slide rather than "start the same shape off a different chord tone."

A seventh device: the half-diminished shape's six-way ambiguity, worked into a full progression

A single root-position half-diminished shape (top four strings: root-♭5-♭7-♭3) is the richest example of this page's whole theme found yet — the source calls it his "favorite example" of one-shape-many-identities specifically because it supports six distinct chord readings depending purely on which of its four notes is treated as the (possibly unplayed) root:

  • Its own root → plain half-diminished (m7♭5).
  • A different note as root → minor 6.
  • Another note as root → dominant 9.
  • Another note as root → dominant 7 ♭13 ♭9.
  • The same root as the previous reading, but reinterpreting the "♭13" note as a ♯5 instead → dominant 7 ♯5 ♭9 — identical notes, identical assumed root, different scale/label (stated as an important distinction because it changes which scale a soloist would draw from, even though nothing physically changes in the grip).
  • The remaining note as root → major 13 ♯11 (= maj7♯11).

Worked as a full held-voicing progression (the payoff move — the same top shape reused across an entire chord progression rather than one chord at a time): shell voicings first, D major 7 → B minor 6 → E7 → B♭7 → resolve to A major 7; then the identical top-note shape held throughout, only the assumed root/bass moving underneath — D major 13♯11 → B minor 6 → E9 → B♭7(♭13,♭9) → A major 7. Demonstrates a chord progression that sounds like genuine harmonic motion in the bass while the guitar's rootless voicing on top never physically moves; explicitly not framed as a sound to sit on constantly, but as a deliberate static-color option to have on tap. → Chord Voicings, Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

An eighth device: a static triad held over a moving chord progression (songwriting application)

The same "one shape, many identities" mechanism run in the opposite direction and toward composition rather than jazz comping: instead of picking a different root for the same fixed voicing chord to chord, pick a fixed small triad shape and find a sequence of different underlying chords that each legitimately contain it, so a genuinely moving progression can carry one repeating melodic/harmonic idea on top. Worked on an arpeggiated A minor triad held constant against five different underlying chords, each one shown to actually contain the Am triad: Am (plain) → F♯ half-diminished (contains Am) → F major 7 (contains Am, via this page's own root-replaced-with-7th mechanism) → C major 6 (this specific voicing of C6 contains Am) → D minor, reasoned chord-tone by chord-tone: Am's root becomes Dm's ♭7 (→ Dm7), Am's 5th becomes Dm's 9th (→ Dm9). Arrangement-simplification move layered on top: rather than playing each full chord underneath, play only the 1st and 3rd of each chord in the sequence — a repeating two-note fragment under a moving progression, described as producing a deliberate "energy build" from the repetition. A concrete demonstration that this page's whole device family applies to writing a part, not just comping a jazz standard. → Chord Voicings — Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), Rootless Voicings - WOW!

voice-leading.title: Voice Leading
voice-leading.html:
Choosing WHICH inversion/voicing of each chord in a progression to play, rather than defaulting to root position, so the individual notes move by the smallest possible steps from one chord to the next. Companion to Species Counterpoint (the same melodic-line-independence discipline, applied here to chord voicing rather than free counterpoint) and Part-Writing (the four-voice chorale-writing tradition this technique generalizes from).

The algorithm

  1. Find the note(s) shared between the current chord and the next chord in the progression — a note common to both.
  2. Keep that shared note exactly where it is (don't move it at all) — it becomes the pivot the hand/voicing rotates around.
  3. Move the remaining notes to the nearest available note of the next chord — by the smallest possible interval, usually a step, not a leap.
  4. Repeat chord-to-chord through the whole progression.

You don't need to identify which inversion results (root position, first inversion, etc.) to do this — the method is entirely about minimizing motion between chords, not about naming the resulting voicing. Worked example: Am → F, sharing the note C — keep C fixed, move A→A (already shared) note stays, and the remaining note moves by step (E→F) rather than leaping down to the next chord's root.

Why it works — the choir analogy

Give each note of a chord to a different singer in a choir. If every chord is played in root position, each singer has to leap around unpredictably from chord to chord (root-position-to-root-position motion can be a large jump even between closely related chords). Voice-led inversions let most singers hold their note or move by a single step, which is both easier to sing/play AND reads as smoother, more melodic motion to the ear — the individual voices stop sounding like they're "randomly jumping around the scale."

The bass exception

The lowest voice in an arrangement (the piano left hand, a bass part) is usually NOT voice-led — it stays on each chord's actual root note throughout, even while the upper voices are inverted and voice-led above it. Voice-leading the bass too would smooth out the bass motion but lose the harmonic clarity and character the root-motion bassline provides — a full arrangement's overall chord identity (root position vs. inversion) is usually judged from the bass note regardless of how the upper voices are voiced.
secs: Why it works — the choir analogy

spread-triad-voice-leading-etude.title: Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude
spread-triad-voice-leading-etude.html:
Part of Chord Inversions and Song Practice. A composed practice etude for internalizing spread-triad ("open position") voicings across an entire diatonic key by voice-leading rule rather than by drilling shapes in isolation. Distinct from Open Voice Triads for Soloing — that page's Jens Larsen material uses the same physical spread/open-voice triad shapes as soloing vocabulary over jazz changes; this etude uses them as a fretboard-mapping and voice-leading study, walking the whole key rather than improvising over a progression. Also distinct from Triads as a Fretboard Map and Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing, both of which use close-position triads — this page's triads are spread/open voicings throughout (see below for the difference).

Spread triad, defined

A close-position triad stacks its three notes on adjacent strings/scale-tones (e.g. D minor root position: root-♭3-5 = D-F-A). A spread (a.k.a. "open position voicing") triad takes that same three-note chord and moves the middle note up an octave, reordering the stack to 1-5-♭3 — same notes, same chord, wider interval spacing with a string skip in the middle, an "open," harp-like sound. Worked example: D minor close position frets pinky-5th-fret/A-string (root), middle-finger-3rd-fret/D-string (♭3), index-2nd-fret/G-string (5th); moving the middle note (the ♭3, on the D string) up an octave produces the spread voicing 1-5-♭3. Terminology trap: "open position" in this sense is music-theory/composition jargon for spread voicing — it has nothing to do with the guitar-specific meaning of "open position" (playing near the nut using open strings). Same term, two unrelated meanings; don't conflate them.

The construction rule (this is the whole etude)

  1. Start on the tonic triad (worked in C major) in a spread voicing, high up the neck.
  2. Chain through the diatonic triads a third at a time: C → E minor → G major → B diminished → D minor → F major → A minor → back to C — the full seven diatonic triads of the key, taken in ascending-third order, repeating the cycle.
  3. Every chord change moves exactly one note of the three-note spread voicing, by a half step or a whole step — never more than one voice moves, never more than a step. Which of the three voices (top/middle/bottom of the spread shape) moves next rotates through the voicing in a repeating sequence as the chain proceeds.
  4. The whole etude is one continuous descent down the fretboard, chord by chord, using the single-voice-move rule to always land on the closest spread voicing of the next chord in the third-chain, until it reaches the lowest playable position on the neck.
  5. Close with a real cadence, not another triad: the etude ends G7 → C — the only point where an actual dominant-7th chord (not a bare triad) appears, a deliberate "how to land a triad study" move rather than just fading out on another spread triad.
  6. Coverage is a side effect, not a separate drill: because the third-chain touches every diatonic triad of the key, and the closest-voicing rule forces a different inversion each time a given triad quality recurs, the etude ends up covering every diatonic triad of the key in every one of its inversions — full spread-triad vocabulary for the key, generated by the voice-leading rule alone.

Figured-bass / Roman-numeral reading (taught alongside the etude)

Classical figured-bass shorthand, used on the etude's own analysis: plain Roman numeral = root position (root in the bass); "6/4" = second inversion (5th in the bass — the "6" and "4" are the interval sizes up from the bass note once the chord is collapsed to close position: a 6th and a 4th); "6" (short for "6/3," the 3 dropped by convention) = first inversion (3rd in the bass). Applied to the etude's own third-chain: C = root position → E minor = 6/4 (5th in bass) → G = 6 (3rd in bass) → the pattern repeats every three chords (root → 6/4 → 6, root → 6/4 → 6…), cycling against the seven-chord third-chain — a 3-against-7 relationship, so the pairing of "which triad" with "which inversion" shifts phase each time the chain repeats through the full key. See Chord Inversions for the general inversion/figured-bass framework this is a worked instance of.

How to practice it

  1. Play it off the page first. Read the tab/notation as written and get it under the fingers and into the ear before attempting any theoretical analysis — don't try to reason through it cold.
  2. Then name the anatomy of every voicing. For each chord in the chain: which chord tone is in the bass (root/3rd/5th)? What inversion does that make it? What single note is about to move to reach the next chord, and by how much?
  3. Internalize it structurally, not by rote. Target state: land on any chord in the chain (e.g. D minor) and reason it out live — "up a third in the key is F major, and I know the middle voice moves here, so that gives me this shape" — rather than a memorized finger sequence with no theory underneath it.
  4. A standalone drill this etude's logic generates, usable on any spread-triad material: grab any spread-triad voicing at random and work out, by ear and by theory, the single note that has to move a half or whole step to reach the next diatonic chord a third up. This is literally how the etude was composed — noticing the one-note connection between two spread triads and extending it through the whole diatonic key.

Practice-philosophy point worth generalizing beyond this etude: this kind of slow, low-note-count, analytical "why is this the voicing" practice is flagged explicitly as some of the most potent practice available for building theoretical/fretboard structural understanding — distinct from the high-repetition technical practice needed for playing tunes or building chops. Match the practice mode to the goal: reps for technique, slow analysis for internalized structure. Complements Etude-Based Vocabulary Practice's play-first-then-analyze sequencing (same ordering principle, applied there to a comping-vocabulary method book rather than a self-contained theory etude) and Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's broader deliberate-practice framing.

Caveat — exact tab not fully captured

The source video's on-screen notation carries the complete voicing/fret data for the whole ~20-chord descent; the spoken track narrates which voice moves and by how much at each step but doesn't verbalize every fret number. The construction rule above (third-chain order, one-note-per-change rule, rotating voice, root→6/4→6 inversion pattern, G7-C cadence ending) is fully captured and is enough to reconstruct or freely generate the etude on the fretboard by following the rule, even without the exact original fingering — start on any spread triad, chain up by thirds, move one note per change. The exact original tab/PDF is sold separately via the creator's paid weekly-lesson membership (soundguitarlessons.com/join), not reproduced here.

close-position-triad-voice-leading-etude.title: Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude
close-position-triad-voice-leading-etude.html:
Part of Chord Inversions and Song Practice. A composed practice etude for internalizing close-position triad inversions across the diatonic key of C major, by the same "move exactly one note, exactly one half/whole step, every chord change" voice-leading rule as Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude — but worked on ordinary close-position triad shapes on strings 2-3-4 (B-G-D) instead of spread/open voicings, and walking up the fretboard rather than down. Labeled "#1"/"ASCENDING" by its author because it's the first half of a planned two-part series — a "part two" descending version is announced but not yet published (nothing to extract from it yet). Distinct from Triads as a Fretboard Map and Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing, which use close-position triads as soloing landmarks/motifs rather than a composed voice-leading study.

Prerequisites (drill these before the etude)

  1. Major scale as scale-degree numbers, not the whole/half-step mnemonic: 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-1, half steps only between 3-4 and 7-1, everything else a whole step.
  2. Lay that number structure out along one string at a time, on the three strings this etude uses (worked in the key of C): - String 2 (B string): fret 1 = C = "1." Practice 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-1 ascending and 1-7-6-5-4-3-2-1-7-1 descending. - String 3 (G string): open = G = "5." Practice the same shape starting from 5. - String 4 (D string): open = D = "2." Practice the same shape starting from 2.
  3. Map numbers to letters by the alphabet from the tonic: C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D up, D-C-B-A-G-F-E-D-C-B down.
  4. Two practice levels: play the shapes only, or (recommended) actively name the chord at every step.

The construction rule

  1. Start on an E minor close-position triad on strings 2-3-4 (exact starting fret not captured in the source — see caveat).
  2. Move exactly one note per chord change, by a half or whole step, whichever keeps it inside the C major scale.
  3. Which voice moves rotates in a fixed order: top (string 2) → middle (string 3) → bottom (string 4) → repeat. Unlike the spread-triad etude (whose rotation order isn't stated explicitly in its own source video), this video states the rotation order plainly.
  4. The note that just moved always becomes the new chord's ROOT — the load-bearing rule that makes every landing chord mechanically nameable rather than a guess. This rule is stated explicitly in this video; it isn't stated on the spread-triad etude's page, so treat it as specific to this close-position construction unless/until confirmed otherwise for the spread version.
  5. Chord chain (descending by a third each change): E minor → C major → A minor → F major → D minor → B diminished → G major → cycle repeats. Every step moves down a third in the key (E→C, C→A, A→F, F→D, D→B, B→G, G→E), even though the shapes physically climb up the neck.
  6. Diatonic triad qualities (standard C-major harmonization): I major, ii minor, iii minor, IV major, V major, vi minor, vii° diminished.
  7. Ends on a plain C major triad high up the neck — no dominant-7 cadence (contrast with the spread-triad etude's G7→C close). Stop wherever the guitar's range runs out (nylon-string players won't reach the top); don't reverse direction.

How it compares to the spread-triad sibling

Close Position Triad Voice-Leading Etude (this page) Spread Triad Voice-Leading Etude
Voicing type Close-position (adjacent-string stack) Spread/open-position (middle note moved up an octave)
Fretboard direction Ascending (climbs up the neck) Descending (walks down the neck)
Chord-chain direction Down a third each change (E→C→Am→F→Dm→Bdim→G) Up a third each change (C→Em→G→Bdim→Dm→F→Am)
Starting chord E minor C major (the tonic)
Rotating-voice order Explicitly stated: top → middle → bottom, repeating Not explicitly stated in the source
"Moved note = new root" rule Explicitly stated Not stated (not confirmed either way)
Ending Plain C major triad, no cadence Real cadence: G7 → C
Companion piece "Part two" (descending version) announced, not yet published —

Same generative idea (chain the diatonic triads a third at a time, move exactly one voice per change, land on the closest voicing), applied to the two different triad-voicing families guitarists actually use, in opposite directions on both axes (voicing type and neck direction). Treat them as a matched pair rather than duplicates.

How to practice it

  1. Drill the four prerequisites above until the scale-degree/string layout is automatic.
  2. Play the etude off the page/by ear first, shapes only.
  3. Then re-run it naming every chord as you land on it, using the "moved note = new root" shortcut rather than reasoning out each triad from scratch.
  4. Standalone drill this etude's logic generates: from any close-position triad, work out which single note has to move (and by how much) to land on the triad a third below in the key, with that moved note becoming the new root — the exact move-by-move logic used to construct this etude, usable as a cold drill on any close-position shape.
  5. When "part two" (the descending version) is published, work it as the companion drill — same logic, opposite fretboard direction, "slightly different" rules per the author's own teaser.

Caveat — exact tab not fully captured

As with the spread-triad sibling, the spoken track narrates which voice moves, by how much, and what chord results at each step, but doesn't verbalize starting fret numbers — no on-screen notation data reached the transcript. The construction rule above (starting chord, rotation order, root rule, third-chain direction, ending) is fully captured and is enough to reconstruct or freely generate the etude on the fretboard.

jazz-comping.title: Jazz Comping
jazz-comping.html: Part of Music Theory → Chord Voicings, the rhythm/accompaniment side. Comping = accompanying, not soloing — the goal on every idea below is something solid and cohesive that supports whatever else is happening, not the flashiest thing playable in the moment. No home existed yet for comping-specific technique (as opposed to voicing vocabulary, which lives on Chord Voicings) — created from three concrete comping moves surfaced across Body and Soul and Someday My Prince Will Come.

jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.title: Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline
jazz-comping-rhythmic-motif-and-walking-.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — a rhythm-first comping method, deliberately separate from Chord Voicings (which shapes to grip) and Chord-Tone Soloing (soloing over the changes). This note is about when to strike the chord and what the bass note underneath it is doing, applicable to any tune regardless of its harmony.

The core tip: one repeatable rhythmic motif, not constant variety

Pick a simple, single rhythmic idea — a specific pair or handful of beats where the chord lands — and repeat it consistently before reaching for anything fancier. A demonstrated starting motif: hit on the "and" of beat 1, and on beat 3. Repetition is what makes comping read as cohesive and intentional; constantly reinventing the rhythm bar-to-bar reads as scattered, even if each individual choice is "correct." (General starting point — pick any two-hit-per-bar pattern and hold it for a full pass through the form before varying.)

Sequencing matters: lock the motif in first, then introduce variation or departures from it. A deliberate detour away from the motif, followed by a return to it, reads as "grounded" — the return only lands because the motif was established as the baseline first. This mirrors the "overuse a device to internalize it, then use it tastefully" practice logic already documented on Chord-Tone Soloing.

Riff comping — a named, larger-scale sibling of the core motif idea

Instead of a repeatable one- or two-beat rhythmic hit, stick with a whole melodic/rhythmic riff for a stretch of the form — demonstrated at roughly 8 bars per idea, tracked to a tune's own internal repetition (an AABA-shaped tune's first static-feeling 8 bars get one riff, its more harmonically-moving 8 bars get a second, the repeated A section brings the first riff back, and a different tag/ending idea closes it out). Two reasons to reach for it:

  • Repetition itself builds energy and sits well in a groove — especially valuable over a static feel (Latin/bossa/samba are the clearest case, where the guitar part usually has to lock to one distinct repeating pattern regardless of what's being soloed over).
  • Riff comping is the practice on-ramp to genuinely open/free comping, not a separate, lesser approach. Even "open" playing with almost no audible groove still requires the whole band to have silently agreed on what groove they're not playing — riff-based practice through a tune's changes builds the vocabulary and rhythmic habits that make later free playing sound intentional instead of aimless, rather than skipping straight to open playing without that foundation.
  • Doubles as ear-training for absorbing an unfamiliar rhythm into your default vocabulary — take a rhythm you don't already reach for, force it through a whole tune's changes a few times, and by the source's account it tends to "stick" as usable material afterward. (General starting point: pick one riff, run it through a full chorus of a tune before switching, then repeat with a second, different rhythm.)

Bonus: walking bassline with the chords

Layer a moving bass note under the same comping rhythm:

  • Beats 1 and 3: play the current chord's root as the bass note.
  • Beats 2 and 4: pass toward the next chord's root with a chromatic or scale-step approach note — a half step below, a half step above, or a whole step above the target. Which approach direction sounds best depends on the specific interval between the two roots; try more than one.
  • Works best on progressions where chords change every two beats — there's a clean "root, approach-note, new root, approach-note" cycle available. On a chord that lasts a full bar, apply the same beats-1-and-3 root logic "passing to itself" (root, [passing tone], root, approach-to-next).
  • Once the bassline is solid, the chord voicing itself can be freed from a fixed grid — e.g. moved to beat 1 + the "and" of beat 3 instead of a rigid every-beat pattern — for a less mechanical feel. Same "vary only after the base pattern is locked" sequencing as the primary motif tip above.

Worked example

Demonstrated over "Softly As in a Morning Sunrise"'s minor-2-5-1-heavy A section (Cm – Dm7♭5 – G7♭9, minor 2-5-1): root-on-1-and-3 walking bass under the shell-voicing/full-voicing chords from Chord Voicings, with the C-to-D and D-to-G root motions given as the clean two-beat-per-chord approach-note cases. → 🎵 SIGMUND ROMBERG - Softly As in a Morning Sunrise

comping-fills.title: Comping Fills
comping-fills.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — the melodic-fill counterpart to Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline (which covers when to strike a chord and what the bass is doing) and Chord Voicings (which covers which notes to voice a chord with). This note is about the third comping element: the short melodic phrases played between or on top of the chords, and specifically when and why to reach for one — sourced from a breakdown of Joe Pass comping behind Ella Fitzgerald.

The core tip: fills only happen when the soloist rests

Joe Pass never fills over the top of a vocalist or soloist who's still singing/playing — a fill only enters the texture when there's genuine space, i.e. call-and-response spacing rather than decoration layered underneath an active melody. Before reaching for a fill, check: is anyone else actually playing right now? If yes, hold the comp; if the space is genuinely open, that's the cue.

A fill's job is to connect, not decorate

Quoted directly from Pass himself: a fill has "gotta go... with the melody... to the next bar." A fill that just sits on top of the current chord and doesn't lead anywhere is doing it wrong, by Pass's own framing — the fill's function is to move the music forward to the next chord or the next section of the form, the same forward-motion logic that drives a bebop line. (This reframes a fill as a harmonic/structural device, not a purely melodic flourish — treat "where does this fill lead" as the first design question, before "what notes sound good here.")

Short vs. long: let the form decide

Don't default to one fill length. Read how much open space the form actually gives you at that moment:

  • Short fill — a few notes, e.g. filling the tail end of a bar while the vocal phrase is between lines. Functions almost like a passing tone at the phrase level.
  • Long fill — used when there's genuinely more room (a longer instrumental gap, a turnaround, a full bar or more open). A long fill can stand on its own as a real melody, or be woven directly into the chords rather than staying purely single-note.

Build the fill bottom-up: simple line first, color added after

Same "staying practical" logic documented on Chord Voicings for building a chord bottom-up: start a fill from a simple, recognizable base — e.g. a plain major blues melody — and only then layer color on top (a major 7th slid into, a ii-V-ish passing move, a run of dominant chords down to a rootless target). This keeps the fill playable and musical in real time instead of trying to compose something harmonically dense from the first note. (General starting point: sketch the fill as a simple diatonic or blues line first; add alterations/passing chords as a second pass, not simultaneously.)

A fill can carry real harmonic motion, not just melody

A fill isn't restricted to single notes over a static chord — it can itself move the harmony, e.g. inserting a passing chord mid-fill to walk from one chord to the next (C6 → [G7 passing chord] → C7), or landing on a rootless voicing of the destination chord to keep the texture consistent with the rest of the comp. Treat a fill as a compressed version of the full "chord + bass + melody" comping toolkit, deployed in miniature during the open space.

Worked example

Over "Gee Baby, Ain't I Good to You" (blues-inflected standard, bigger/more colorful chords than a typical shell-voicing comp): a short fill closes bar two of the A section — a simple melodic fragment on the A7 (13 → ♭13 → 9th on the D7) — after which the vocal returns to finish the phrase. A longer fill later in the form mixes blues and jazz vocabulary, doubles as a turnaround back toward the A7 that opens the next A section, and — going into the bridge — extends into a full chord-solo-style passage: simple major blues melody first, then a major 7th (slid into), a D♭7 → C7 move, and a run of C7 chords down to a rootless F7 to keep the phrase moving into the next section. → The Secret Jazz Chord System of Joe Pass

Approaching a chord shape like it's a single note in a line

A different device from the fills above — this decorates the chord voicing itself, not the space between chords. Treat a comping voicing as if it were one note in a melodic line, then apply the same approach-note/enclosure vocabulary (Bebop Vocabulary §2–3) directly to the shape:

  1. Start with basic, fundamental voicings over the progression (worked over a plain 2-5-1).
  2. Add approach notes/enclosures into the shape the same way you'd chromatically approach a single target tone — e.g. the half-step-per-arpeggio-tone device reused from soloing, applied to comping shapes instead.
  3. Once that's comfortable, swap in richer voicing color for the same targets — a minor 9, a major 6, a major 6/9 shape — each one just another approachable target.
  4. Know the inversions of each shape, not just the root-position grip — inversions are what make the approach-into-a-voicing device usable across a full progression rather than jumping around the neck. Stated payoff: once chord shapes are treated as single-note-line targets, comping opens up the same expressive range melodic soloing gets from the same vocabulary. Full device (plus the pivot-tone and arpeggio-approach devices it's paired with in the source video) → Pivot Tone Lines.

A fill's job is to connect, not decorate
Short vs. long: let the form decide
Build the fill bottom-up: simple line first, color added after
A fill can carry real harmonic motion, not just melody
