six-devices-for-r-b-rhythm-guitar-fills.title: Six Devices for R&B Rhythm Guitar Fills
six-devices-for-r-b-rhythm-guitar-fills.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. Six concrete, genre-specific tools for filling the gaps between a lead vocal/melody's phrases with rhythm-guitar fills, worked over a three-chord R&B backing track (A major – B minor – F♯ minor, all diatonic to A major — I–ii–vi). Where Comping Fills gives the jazz-comping philosophy of fills (fill only when the soloist rests, connect forward to the next chord/section, build simple-then-color) and 9th and 13th Chord Voicings for Blues Rhythm gives two specific fill licks for a blues 9th/13th-chord comping part, this page is the R&B/gospel-lineage device catalog — six distinct interval/shape vocabularies (not fill placement theory) any of which can decorate a chord voicing or bridge two chords. The theory-of-when framing from Comping Fills still applies here (fill in the space the vocal/melody leaves); this page is the theory-of-what.

The setup

All six devices are demonstrated over the same progression, so the harmonic groundwork is shared: A – Bm – F♯m, all three chords diatonic to A major. That means the A major scale / A major pentatonic supplies every note for every device below — over the A chord it sounds like plain A major; over F♯m the same A-major-pentatonic notes are heard as F♯ minor pentatonic (its relative-minor reframing), which is what gives that chord its different color despite using identical fingerings/notes to the A-major fills.

1 — Butterfly fills (fast hammer-on/pull-off licks)

Named for the style's gospel/early-R&B origin — cited players Curtis Mayfield and Bobby Womack. Fast hammer-on/pull-off licks pulled from the A major pentatonic scale, played around the current chord voicing rather than as a standalone lead line — worked directly into the chord shape you're already fretting.

  • Over A major: hammer from the 5th degree up to the 6th while letting the open high A ring; separately, hammer from the 9th degree up to the major 3rd with the 5th ringing underneath.
  • Over B minor and F♯ minor: the same hammer-on/pull-off device applied around each chord's own voicing shape — same technique, relocated to the new chord grip, still pulling only from the shared A major pentatonic pool.
  • Drill: loop one chord at a time (A only, then Bm, then F♯m) against a static drone/backing track; find the hammer-on/pull-off inside that one chord shape first (don't chase new fingerings — the notes are already under your fretting hand in the chord grip) before switching chords.

2 — Triad-grouping fills

Uses the three-string triad groupings (top three strings / upper-middle three strings / lower-middle three strings — the same close-position triad system as Triads as a Fretboard Map and Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads) as fill material, either decorating one chord or alternating between two different triads for a mini-progression-within-the-fill.

  • Worked moves: A major triad → E major triad (I → V, a fourth/fifth relationship), and A major → D major (I → IV).
  • Each chord in the progression (A, Bm, F♯m) has its own set of these three-string triad shapes available in the same neck area — the fill vocabulary is "which triad grouping, which string set," not a fixed lick.
  • Drill: isolate one triad grouping (e.g., top three strings) across all three chords first, then practice alternating pairs (A→E, A→D) purely as a rhythmic chop, before mixing groupings.

3 — Sixths (double stops a 6th apart)

Two notes separated by a 6th (in A major: A up to F♯ is a 6th), diatonically harmonized and moved through the A major scale under the chord progression. Cited as the classic Steve Cropper / Memphis Soul sound. Because the shapes are diatonic 6th intervals inside A major, the same double-stop shape slides scale-degree to scale-degree and stays in key without any per-chord adjustment — move it under A, Bm, or F♯m and it still fits.

  • Drill: play the 6th-interval shape as a straight ascending/descending run through the A major scale first (no rhythm, just the shapes), then apply it as fills on beats/subdivisions that land in the gaps of the vocal melody.

4 — Fourths (double stops a 4th apart)

Two notes separated by a 4th (E up to A is a 4th in this key). Also a defining R&B double-stop sound. Two named grip pairs slide diatonically:

  • 9th+5th → 3rd+6th: starting on B with E on top (9th + 5th of A), slide up to C♯ with F♯ on top (3rd + 6th of A).
  • 5th+root → 6th+9th(-ish): E + A (5th + root) slides a whole step up to F♯ + B (6th + 2nd/9th).
  • Over the minor chords (Bm): play the ♭7 + minor 3rd above the chord, then slide that up a whole step to land on root + 4th — same shape family, minor-chord-specific starting interval.
  • Drill: learn the major-chord pair (9th+5th → 3rd+6th) first against the A chord alone, then the minor-chord variant against Bm, before combining both into fills across the full progression.

5 — Thirds (double stops a 3rd apart)

Two notes separated by a 3rd (A up to C♯ is a 3rd), moved diatonically through the A major scale and across different string sets. Framed as a general-purpose device: any scale (or any scale that fits a chord progression) can be harmonized in 3rds to generate fills and counter-melodies — this video's R&B application is one instance of a broadly reusable idea (cf. the jazz-side analogue in Pentatonic Scale Harmonized in Thirds, which stacks pentatonic-scale-degree "3rds" rather than diatonic 3rds — same family of device, different scale source).

  • Drill: pick one string-set for the 3rds shape and run it straight through the A major scale (root to root) before trying to place any of it rhythmically as a fill; then try the same shape on a second string set to compare the fingering.

6 — Single-note pentatonic lines

Straight single-note lines from the A major pentatonic scale (reframed as F♯ minor pentatonic over the F♯m chord) played in the gaps between rhythmic chord "chunks" — the chord jabs implying the backbeat/snare groove, with single-note fills threaded between them. Three named uses:

  • Call and response with the melody (echo/answer the vocal's phrase).
  • Counter-melody running against the melody rather than echoing it.
  • Muted fills — the same pentatonic material played palm-muted for a percussive texture rather than a melodic one, adding rhythmic color without competing tonally with the vocal.
  • Drill: first play just the chunked backbeat chord pattern alone (lock the groove), then add pentatonic single notes only in the silences, starting with simple call-and-response (echo a short vocal-melody fragment) before trying counter-melody or muted textures.

Practice order across all six

The video's own progression is device-by-device, not simultaneous — the natural drill order: (1) loop the A-Bm-F♯m backing track (or any I-ii-vi/I-IV-V diatonic progression) at a slow tempo; (2) work one device at a time until it's comfortable over all three chords; (3) once 2–3 devices are solid, mix them freely within one pass through the form — e.g., a butterfly fill on the A chord, a 6th-interval fill into the Bm, a pentatonic call-and-response line answering the melody over F♯m — since all six draw from the same A-major-scale pool, they combine without needing separate vocabulary per device.

jazz-comping-sharing-the-role-with-anoth.title: Jazz Comping — Sharing the Role with Another Comping Instrument
jazz-comping-sharing-the-role-with-anoth.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — the ensemble-etiquette companion to Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline (which is about what to play once it's your turn to comp). This note is about whose turn it is — how two harmony instruments (typically guitar and piano, but the same logic covers vibes or a second guitar) share the comping role in a small group without colliding. Two comping instruments playing fully independently almost always reads as clutter to the listener, so the two players need an explicit or implicit division of labor.

Assign roles out loud, before playing

The single most reliable fix: call it at the top of the tune, the same way a bandleader calls a form. A concrete script: "you comp the head, I'll comp the first solo, you take the second solo, I'll comp the head out, and you can add fills." This removes the guesswork entirely rather than leaving it to be negotiated in real time. (General starting point — assign by section: head / solo 1 / solo 2 / head out, alternating or splitting however the tune calls for.)

  • Default hierarchy in an unrehearsed jam session: if there's no time to negotiate, piano is the default primary comping instrument and the guitarist defaults to functioning like a horn player — solo when cued, otherwise lay out rather than comp — until/unless the guitarist gets an explicit cue to comp. This isn't a rule about instrument hierarchy in general, just a practical default for a jam session with no rehearsal time.
  • With musicians you know well, the explicit call can shrink to a nonverbal cue: one player just starts comping (plays one or two chords), the other player catches on within a bar or two and drops out/switches roles — same negotiation, compressed to real time because the trust is already there.

Comp in the holes, not on top

When the soloist establishes a repeating, predictable rhythmic motif, don't double it — place your comping hits in the gaps the motif leaves open. A predictable, repeated idea from the soloist is exactly what makes this possible: by the second or third repetition you can hear where the holes will be and land there instead of on top of the line. This is also framed as the more generally useful comping instinct even outside a two-comper situation: playing something repetitive and a little predictable gives the soloist a stable surface to build on and interact with — it reads as more supportive than constantly varying what you play, and a stable comping pattern is also what lets a drummer catch a hit and double it (see below). This pairs directly with the "one repeatable motif, not constant variety" principle already on Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline — here it's a listening skill (finding the other player's holes) rather than a producing one (holding your own motif).

  • Big-band horn kicks as the mental model for these comping hits/fills — think of the rhythms a horn section would punch in behind a soloist, not a constant harmonic wash. Named explicitly as where these rhythmic ideas come from.
  • The interaction runs both ways through the whole rhythm section, not just soloist↔comper. A comping hit can be picked up and doubled by the drummer (or vice versa — the drummer originates a hit and the comper catches it), and a bass player or a second comping instrument (vibes was named as an example) can join the same call-and-response. This is why an unplanned second comping instrument is described as "a disaster" — it turns a two-way conversation the whole rhythm section can plug into into an uncoordinated crowd.

Stay out of each other's register ("canceling each other out")

When there's a soloist plus a single comping instrument plus rhythm section, actively track the soloist's register and move opposite it: soloist goes up → comp lower; soloist goes down → comp higher. Concretely: watch the neck/hands, and react. This is much easier when a bass player is covering the low end and the comper's only job is comping (not also supplying a bass line) — trying to do both (full harmony + implied bass + register-tracking) at once, e.g. solo guitar comping without a bassist, is harder and gets deprioritized first.

  • Going higher than the soloist is flagged as the more delicate move of the two — it risks visibly pulling listener attention off the soloist, so it's used more sparingly than dropping lower.
  • Extension awareness is part of the same "stay out of the way" skill, but harmonic rather than registral: if the other comping voice is playing a specific alteration (e.g. a natural 13), don't simultaneously play a clashing alteration of the same extension (e.g. a ♭13) — track what alteration the other harmony instrument has committed to and don't step on it.

It's always OK to not play

Laying out is a legitimate, valued choice, not a cop-out — including laying out for an entire tune once roles are assigned at the top (e.g. sitting out completely through another player's solo chorus). Framed explicitly through a conversation analogy: in a group conversation, staying quiet for a while while others talk is a sign of confidence, not insecurity; comping works the same way. Not playing also buys thinking time — leaving room lets the soloist define what's actually needed moment to moment, which makes it easier to come back in with something that actually fits, rather than reflexively filling every gap. Named reference points for comping-optional/no-piano playing: McCoy Tyner-less late Coltrane, and Jim Hall laying out extensively in duo playing (the Jim Hall / Bill Evans duo album is cited as the model for two harmony players making constant room for each other rather than both filling space).

  • This is a practiced skill, not just a preference — comping habitually makes laying out feel effortful. A player who mostly performs without a second harmony instrument (piano-less trio, for example) gets so used to filling all the harmonic space alone that deliberately laying out in a different context (with a comper present) can feel unnatural at first — the adjustment is staying locked to the form (still tracking where you are) while consciously not filling it.

Fills as the "other" role

When one player is assigned to comp, the other player's job in the gaps is often fills, not silence and not full comping — think of it as the horn-section fill role again (see the big-band mental model above), placed in the space the comping player leaves open.

  • Octaves are a solid default texture for guitar fills when you're not comping full chords underneath — a simple, clean way to state a melodic fill line without it reading as competing harmony.

The exception: a rhythm role can run under someone else's comping

Two ways two harmony instruments can sound at the same time without colliding, both because one part stops behaving like "comping" and starts behaving like a rhythm-section pulse instead:

  • Freddie Green–style straight-quarter-note guitar rhythm. All-quarter-note strummed guitar (the Freddie Green big-band rhythm-guitar role) is low-profile and metronomically predictable enough that it functions like a second drummer laying down the pulse, not a harmonically assertive comping voice — so the piano is free to comp on top of it without stepping on anything. The style is sometimes looked down on as "just sitting there strumming," and in a big band it's often nearly inaudible in the mix, but it locks the rhythm section together and is described as "the best thing in the world" when it's working. Because the shapes involved are simple, almost any chord fits, and the rhythmic role is completely predictable — the same "very defined, predictable role" logic that makes comping-in-the-holes possible above.
  • Pre-arranged unison hits instead of improvised comping. Write the hit ahead of time so both instruments land it together — an arrangement decision, not a real-time comping negotiation. Diana Krall's band is cited as using arranged hits regularly; besides solving the two-comper collision problem, it's also just a general way to make an arrangement feel tight.

Groove-carrying instrument depends on the style — don't assume guitar always sits back

For a straight-eighth-note tune (bossa nova given as the example, e.g. "Corcovado"/"Quiet Nights"), the convention flips from a swing tune: the guitar carries the recognizable rhythmic groove pattern, and the piano deliberately stays out of that pulse-carrying role, instead laying down sparser harmony and fills that answer the guitar rather than doubling its rhythm (mirrors what's already documented on the production side for this genre — see Bossa Nova (João Gilberto)'s "Keys — Jobim's answers" pillar: piano/keys comping in the same syncopation as the guitar's stabs, answering rather than doubling). Only one instrument should carry the groove ostinato at a time — if the guitar is playing the pattern, the piano shouldn't also try to play it.

  • Contrast explicitly drawn with swing/Freddie Green tunes, where the rhythm-carrying role (predictable quarter notes) more often falls to guitar while piano comps more freely on top — same principle (one instrument owns the predictable pulse, the other is free to comp), different genre convention for which instrument owns which role.

layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.title: Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads
layering-rhythm-guitar-parts-with-triads.html:
Part of Guitar Positions, the arranging-side counterpart to Triads as a Fretboard Map (which applies the same triad-shape/position-relocation idea to soloing). This page is about stacking multiple rhythm-guitar parts on the same chord progression without them turning into mud — the core move is reusing one small set of closed-position triad shapes across a handful of string groupings and neck positions, then separating the resulting layers by tone/pickup selection, not by writing genuinely different material for each layer.

The core idea: one triad vocabulary, four string groupings, three positions

A four-chord progression — worked in A major – E major – F♯ minor – D major (I–V–vi–IV in A) — gets played as three different guitar parts, and all three are built from the same triad shapes, just relocated:

Part String group Position Role
1 — Bed D, G, B strings One position, jumps to a second higher position for the verse Arpeggiated harmonic floor
2 — Backbeat Top three strings Two positions (a "close-by" pair), used across sections for a flavor change R&B accent, rhythmic punctuation
3 — Melody Top three / top two strings Built from Parts 1–2's own shapes plus two double-stop devices Melodic double-stop line

The stated general lesson: the same handful of chords lives in four different string groupings and three different neck positions, and once those shapes are under your fingers you can freely recombine them — this is the arranging equivalent of Triads as a Fretboard Map's "one triad, three zones" soloing method.

Why triads specifically: they're small on purpose

Closed triad shapes (root-3rd-5th, no doubled notes, no full six-string chords) are deliberately lean — "these little morsels... don't take up too much space, don't fill up too much sound." That leanness is why three of them can stack on top of each other in a mix without collapsing into noise — the same "which notes to leave out" economy Chord Voicings argues for on the jazz-comping side, applied here for a production reason (headroom to layer) rather than a voice-leading one.

Voicing sources for each part

  • Part 1 (bed): plain closed triads on the D-G-B string set, arpeggiated. 🎬 From video: a companion lesson on the same channel maps this exact bed layer in full over the same I-V-vi-IV-in-A progression (A-E-F♯m-D): on the D, G, B strings, each of the three usable neck positions uses one consistent triad-inversion shape family carried across all four chords — position 1 = 5th-root-3rd, position 2 = root-3rd-5th, position 3 = 3rd-5th-root — which is why the four chords fall right next to each other in any given position (learn one hand-shape per position, not four). Glue technique for turning the bare triads into a moving part: since all four chords are diatonic to A major, connect any two adjacent triads with a short 2-4 note passing-tone run pulled from the A-major-scale fingering that sits in that same position — no separate lick vocabulary needed per chord change. Practice order: drill one position's four triads bare, then again with scale-tone fills between changes, before moving to the next position; only string positions together once each is solid alone. Full position-by-position voicings and the drill sequence → Learn These Simple Triads to Improve Your Rhythm Guitar Skills! — Jack Ruch, Learn These Simple Triads to Improve Your Rhythm Guitar Skills!
  • Part 2 (backbeat accents), all derived from full chord shapes you already know, sliced to the top three strings:
  • A major = an open D-major-chord shape moved up the neck, root on the 10th fret of the B string.
  • E major = the top three strings of the standard E-shape bar chord.
  • F♯ minor = the top three strings of the F♯m bar chord.
  • D major = the top three strings of the D-shape bar chord.
  • The trick generalizes: instead of inventing new triad grips, take the top slice of a bar chord you already play.
  • Part 3 (melody), built from the same shapes plus two double-stop devices off a root-3rd-5th triad: 1. Add the 6th above the 5th — from a held triad, move the 5th up to the 6th/13th (worked as fret 5 → fret 7 on the B string) — a melodic extension layered on top of the triad, not a new shape. 2. Drop the 3rd to the 9th — from the same root-3rd-5th grip, drop the 3rd down a whole step to the 9th (2nd) — a contrasting color move off the identical hand position. Both are named directly as common R&B double-stop devices in this style (cited lineage: Curtis Mayfield, Jimi Hendrix).
  • A leaner top-two-strings variation reuses the same triads with hammer-ons/slides inside the shape itself (e.g. hammering within the A-major triad's top two notes) rather than fretting a new pitch — one more textural pass through the same four chords.

The separation move: pickup/tone, not different material

The part that makes this a genuine production/arranging technique rather than just a guitar lesson: each of the three layers gets a deliberately different pickup + effect setting, stated explicitly as the reason each part gets "its own sonic space":

  • Part 1 (bed): middle pickup position (both pickups blended) + a light tremolo from the pedalboard — suits the arpeggiated feel.
  • Part 2 (backbeat): switch to the bridge pickup, tremolo off — brighter/more percussive for accents.
  • Part 3 (melody): switch to the neck pickup — warmer/rounder for the lead-ish double-stop line.

This is the guitar-specific version of the same rule the Sound Palette states generally — give each simultaneous occupant its own space rather than stacking identical timbres and fixing the collision with EQ afterward (Masking and Carving is the repair shop for when this isn't done up front). Here the separation tool is pickup selection + a modulation effect, decided before tracking, not carved in afterward.

bossa-nova-comping-pattern.title: Bossa Nova Comping Pattern
bossa-nova-comping-pattern.html:
The classic two-bar bossa nova right-hand accompaniment figure, played fingerstyle: a thumb keeping a steady half-note bass (the surdo drum's role) against fingers stabbing syncopated chord tones on top (the tamborim's role) — one guitar doing the job of a whole rhythm section. This is the guitar engine documented at the top of Bossa Nova (João Gilberto)'s genre pillars, worked here as its own standalone right-hand-pattern drill rather than folded into a full genre write-up.

Hand setup

  • Thumb (p): bass notes only — root of the current chord (upgrade: alternating root/5th, see below).
  • Index/middle/ring (i/m/a): the upper chord tones, on the top 3 strings of whatever voicing is in use. No pinky.
  • Works over any chord voicing that separates cleanly into "a bass string" + "a 3-string chord above it" — a 4-string subset of the full chord shape. A fretted bass note (not an open string) is preferred so the bass line has full independent control rather than being locked to one open pitch — e.g. for D major 7, fret the root at the 5th fret/A string instead of relying on open low D.

Worked example — D major 7, fretted-bass voicing (from How to Play a Bossa Nova Guitar Rhythm):

  • Index: 5th fret, A string (root, D)
  • Ring: 7th fret, D string (5th, A)
  • Middle: 6th fret, G string (7th, C♯)
  • Pinky: 7th fret, B string (3rd, F♯)
  • Spelling low-to-high: 1–5–7–3

The two-bar rhythm

Bass (thumb): half notes on beats 1 and 3 of every bar, unchanging — the fixed reference the whole pattern is measured against.

Chord (fingers):

  • Bar 1 — chord lands with the bass on beat 1 (the only point in the whole cycle where bass and chord attack together), alone on beat 2, on the offbeat after beat 3 ("&" of 3), and on the offbeat anticipating the next bar ("&" of 4).
  • Bar 2 — further offbeat hits through the bar, landing back on the beat only once more, on beat 4 — the last beat of the two-bar cycle, before it loops.
  • Net result: only 2 of the pattern's roughly 6 chord attacks land on the beat (bar 1 beat 1, bar 2 beat 4) — everything else is syncopated onto the "&"s. That heavy offbeat weighting is what reads as the bossa "bounce."

This lines up with Bossa Nova (João Gilberto)'s existing Level 1/Level 2 description (bass on 1 & 3, chords on 2 and the "& of 3," with the anticipation push into the next bar) — same underlying rhythm, this page's version adds the full two-bar hit list and a build-it-yourself practice method rather than just the finished grid.

How to learn it (incremental-build method)

Don't try to play the finished 2-bar pattern from a chart — build it note by note, always re-anchored to the bass:

  1. Bass alone — half notes on 1 and 3, rock steady, both bars.
  2. Add exactly one chord attack at a time, in the order it actually occurs in the pattern (beat 1 together → beat 2 → the offbeats), replaying from the top after each addition — never skip ahead to the full pattern before each single addition feels secure.
  3. If the offbeats are the sticking point, isolate them: tap your foot on the quarter-note beat and pluck only the offbeat 8th notes, skipping every downbeat — compared directly to a ska/reggae accent feel. Re-add the bass once the offbeat feel alone is solid.
  4. Metronome with a distinct offbeat click (a different tone on the "&"s) locks the ear onto the offbeat grid directly.

Right-hand touch

  • Planting — pre-place the plucking fingers on the strings just before the attack; this produces the pattern's characteristic rhythmic "bounce" rather than a flat pluck. Same core habit as Right-Hand Pinky Fingerstyle Technique's calibration exercises.
  • Optional damping — briefly muting the ringing notes before the next pluck for a more clipped, percussive color; a stylistic layer on top of the pattern, not required to play it correctly.

Next level — alternating root/5th bass

Once the static-root version is solid, upgrade the thumb to alternate root and 5th on the two bass hits per bar instead of repeating the same note. Worth the extra coordination mainly when sustaining one chord for a longer stretch — moving through a fast chord progression, the plain repeated-root version reads cleaner and is what most players actually use in practice.

Comping adaptation (playing with others, not drilling alone)

When accompanying a melody, vocal, or soloist rather than practicing solo, the strict pattern loosens: on a chord change it's common to play just the root instead of the full root+upper-voicing hit, purely to keep the timing smooth, while never breaking the underlying pulse to nail every note of the drilled pattern. Treat the strict two-bar pattern as the practice target — internalize it fully — then let live playing be a natural adaptation of it, the same way jazz comping in general trades strict pattern execution for feel once the vocabulary is internalized (see Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline).

Applied — "Wave" (Jobim)

Demonstrated over the A section of "Wave," starting on the D major 7 voicing above (stated to be the tune's actual opening chord and "the exact voicings" used on well-known recordings, incl. a popular Frank Sinatra version and multiple Jobim versions), moving through Dm7 → G7 as part of the progression. See Bossa Nova Chords - Wave (Dylan Torrance) for the earlier (chord-less) stub on this same tune — this page is now the vault's first real chord source for it.
secs: Comping adaptation (playing with others, not drilling alone)

reading-and-interpreting-a-jazz-lead-she.title: Reading and Interpreting a Jazz Lead Sheet
reading-and-interpreting-a-jazz-lead-she.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. The applied workflow for the specific situation of getting handed a jazz standard's lead sheet cold — at a jam, a gig, or when woodshedding a new tune — and needing to understand it fast enough to comp and solo convincingly. Distinct from Sight Reading (the pitch-decoding skill — turning noteheads into sounds at tempo) and from Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction (reverse-engineering vocabulary from a recorded solo): this page is about harmonic triage of a written chart — reducing 32 unfamiliar bars to a small set of recognizable, predictable devices before you ever have to play a note.

The core method

  1. Establish the form first, before looking at a single chord. Most standards played chorus-only run some flavor of 32 bars in one of two shapes: AABA (one 8-bar idea repeated three times around a contrasting 8-bar bridge) or ABAC (effectively two 16-bar halves). Read it mechanically off the page — a repeat sign after 8 bars with two different endings signals AABA even when the book doesn't spell it out. Knowing the shape tells you how much of the chart is actually new material — an AABA tune with an 8-bar A and 8-bar bridge is often only 16 bars of distinct harmony, not 32, once repeats are accounted for. A tag (extra bars appended to the last A so the tune can close) is common and worth spotting early. → Musical Form, Rhythm Changes
  2. Use the form to predict, not just describe. The stated goal is being able to expect how a passage will sound before you play it, rather than reacting cold to an unfamiliar chord symbol. A concrete, reusable rule: in an AABA tune where the first chord is the tonic, the last two bars of each A are very likely (~90%) some kind of turnaround — meaning a chunk of the chart is already "solved" by pattern-matching before it's been individually analyzed. → Turnarounds
  3. Reduce the chart to recurring, nameable devices — and generalize across tunes, not just within one. Chunk multi-chord passages into single concepts: a secondary ii–V into the IV chord reduces to "the IV chord," a full turnaround reduces to "a turnaround," a ♯4-diminished cadence reduces to "the sharp-4 sound." The real payoff is recognizing the same device recurring across different standards — once one instance is internalized, a new tune reusing it is already half-analyzed rather than a cold read. Two devices worth having pattern-matched on sight: the ♯4-diminished cadence resolving to I (also documented in "Embraceable You" and "You Do Something to Me") → Diminished Chords; and turning a major chord into its own parallel minor to pivot key, the same modulation trick used in "How High the Moon," "Afternoon in Paris," and "Solar." → Modulation (Key Change), Parallel Minor
  4. Treat a printed real-book harmonization as a starting point, not gospel. When a chord clashes visibly with the melody — a common failure mode in stock tag harmonizations especially — swapping in a better-fitting substitution is normal, expected practice among players who actually know the tune, not a liberty that needs permission. Judge it against the melody, not the page.
  5. Read the melody just well enough to comp without clashing — not full sight-singing. Lead sheets are concert pitch; account for your instrument's actual sounding register before judging where the melody sits. You usually don't need to play the melody note-for-note if someone else is stating the head, but you do need a working sense of where it sits so your own voicings don't land a half-step from a long melody note. Concrete clash rule: check which chord tone/extension the melody is actually voicing at that moment, and don't stack your own voicing a half-step away from it unless the clash is a deliberate effect (e.g., an 11th in the melody against a chord voicing that includes the natural 4th/11th right next to it; a 9th sitting above a chromatically adjacent chord tone reads fine, the same interval with the 9th underneath does not). → Guide Tones, Chord Voicings
  6. Comp in service of the soloist, not on a fixed density plan. Play less when the soloist is busy, get more active in the gaps where they lay out. Comping can be stripped down to almost nothing (root motion, or chords only on strong beats) and still read as complete — density is a choice made in response to what's happening, not an obligation to fill every bar. → Ensemble Listening and Comping Restraint
  7. Solo by reducing to function, not by decoding chord-by-chord. Apply the same chunking used for reading: instead of tracking every chord symbol individually, identify the note you're moving from and the note you're targeting for a passage, and let that arc drive the line. Know which chord in a reduced unit is actually structurally important — in a turnaround built on a I–vi–ii–V-family shape, the tonic-substitute chord (not the dominant that follows it) is often the one actually worth targeting; collapsing the whole unit down to "just play off the final V7" loses that. Reharmonizing mid-solo (e.g., substituting a plain minor-7–dominant-7 pair for the expected half-diminished–altered-dominant pair, deliberately choosing the more surprising color) is legitimate once the underlying function is understood — it's a controlled departure from a known baseline, not guesswork.
  8. Use chord-scale theory as a fast first guess, not the final answer. Matching one scale to one chord symbol ("it's a minor 7, play Dorian") gets you in the ballpark but ignores that a chord's actual character depends on the surrounding harmony and key — a minor 7 chord isn't always the same kind of minor-7 sound in context. Refine the first guess with the functional/contextual read from steps 2–3 rather than trusting the chord symbol in isolation. → Scale Modes Reference

Why this works

The whole approach is triage under time pressure: a lead sheet handed to you at a gig has to be understood in roughly the ten seconds before the count-off, and the only way that's possible is by not treating 32 bars as 32 independent decoding problems. Form-recognition + device-pattern-matching + melody-aware voicing turns an unfamiliar chart into "a known shape with a couple of tune-specific details filled in," which is the same reduction principle 32-Bar Song Form documents from the analysis side and Turnarounds's chunking approach documents from the vocabulary side — this page is the reading-under-pressure application of both.

chord-melody-arranging.title: Chord Melody Arranging
chord-melody-arranging.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and the guitar side of Chord Voicings — chord melody (aka solo guitar arrangement) is playing the melody on top while filling in harmony underneath it, one instrument covering both parts, usually with rootless chord shapes (the melody note stands in for the top voice, so the shape only needs the rest of the chord's color). The analytical trick that makes this workable in real time, rather than a slow puzzle, is modal renumbering applied note-by-note as the harmony moves.

The core idea: renumber off the chord, not the key

Read every melody note as a scale degree of whichever chord is sounding right now, not as a scale degree of the parent key. This is Diatonic Modes's "relative approach" (same 7 notes, different tonic) applied live, beat to beat: the same physical note can be "2 of C" while a C chord is under it, then "4 of D" a beat later once the harmony moves to Dm — same pitch, different functional meaning, different go-to shape to reach for. Thinking "1-2 of the C scale" when a Dm chord (the ii chord) is actually sounding hides the real relationship; thinking "4-5 of the current chord's root" reveals it, and it's that revealed relationship that tells you which memorized shape fits.

Memorized "go-to" shapes, moved across roots

Build a small vocabulary of chord shapes tagged by which scale degree of the current chord's root the melody note lands on, then reuse the exact same physical shape over any chord of that quality just by sliding it to the new root — the shape doesn't change, only which chord root it's being renumbered against. Demonstrated over a Let It Be-style G→Am→F→C→G→F passage: a single memorized rootless minor-7 shape (melody note on the 4th, no root voiced — the open A string is available as an optional root if wanted) gets reused as the harmony walks through F ("6-5-5"), C ("4-3-4-3"), and G ("6-5-6-5") — full worked-out passage on Chord Melody Made Simple (Part 5): Modes of the C Major Scale. This is the direct payoff of the renumbering habit: once you can instantly say "that's the 4th of whatever chord I'm on," you already know which go-to shape covers it, so arranging speeds way up and the choice sticks in memory longer.

The drill: run every mode of the key, saying the numbers out loud

Homework, done in the open position in the key of C: play up and down the C major scale, but say the scale-degree numbers relative to whichever chord/mode you're currently drilling, not relative to C. Same 7 notes each time, renumbered off a different chord tone:

Chord (degree) Mode Ascending Descending
C (I) Ionian 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 1 1 7 6 5 4 3 2 1
Dm (ii) Dorian 1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 ♭7 1 1 ♭7 6 5 4 ♭3 2 1
Em (iii) Phrygian 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 1 1 ♭7 ♭6 5 4 ♭3 ♭2 1
F (IV) Lydian 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7 1 1 7 6 5 ♯4 3 2 1
G (V) Mixolydian 1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7 1 1 ♭7 6 5 4 3 2 1
Am (vi) Aeolian 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 1 1 ♭7 ♭6 5 4 ♭3 2 1
B° (vii°) Locrian 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 ♭5 ♭6 ♭7 1 1 ♭7 ♭6 ♭5 4 ♭3 ♭2 1

Formulas match Diatonic Modes's table exactly (same modes, same parent scale) — this drill is that table converted into a spoken, played exercise rather than a lookup. Mastery bar: get each mode's spoken-numbers-while-playing pass correct three times in a row before moving to the next one; no metronome required to start (add timing later once the numbers come without a struggle).

Baby-step variant: note, then root

Before attempting a full up-and-down run in a new mode, alternate melody note → chord root, back and forth, to hear the actual interval rather than only reciting its name — e.g. play a note, then immediately play/sound the Dm root, to internalize what "that specific distance" sounds like before trying to name every degree in sequence. Useful specifically as the on-ramp into a mode that still feels unfamiliar (worked example: getting the Dorian sound under your ear before drilling the full Dorian run).

Lock your view onto the closest root, not always the lowest

Rather than computing every interval against one fixed low root on the neck, mentally re-anchor to whichever instance of the current chord's root is physically closest to the note you're on, wherever that falls on the fretboard — recomputes intervals faster and transfers regardless of which octave or string the phrase sits in. Worked example over a mid-neck D (Dorian root, the ii chord): reading a run of notes around it as 4, ♭3, 2, 1 (root), ♭7, 6, 5 by treating that specific D as "home," not the open low D.

Two valid ways in — fretboard-first or name-first

Either on-ramp is fine and they converge with repetition: fretboard-first — you already feel/see the shape and interval (e.g. "that's a 4th") and only then attach the scale-degree name to it; or name-first — drill the spoken number sequence until you know it cold, and the fretboard association builds from repeating it. Which one is faster depends entirely on what you already know well (an interval you already recognize easily is a shortcut; one you don't, isn't) — don't force one approach if the other is working.

Practice mindset: practice perfectly, don't demand perfect playing

Set the goal as getting each mode's drill correct three times in a row, not flawless execution on the first pass. Reframe "I didn't play it perfectly" (a bad outcome to dread) into "I practiced with full focus and followed the drill's own rules" (a good outcome, achievable every time) — this removes the perfectionism block that otherwise stalls repetitive drilling. The drilling itself can feel genuinely unpleasant while you're still weak at a mode — that's expected and not a sign to stop.

Step-by-step lead-sheet method (the deliberate, on-paper counterpart to the live method above)

Where the section above is the real-time method (renumber on the fly, reach for a memorized shape), this is the slow, working-it-out method for arranging a full lead sheet ahead of time — four repeatable steps per melody note:

  1. Root of the chord — just the chord symbol's letter name (G half-diminished → G; C7♭9 → C; Fm6 → F).
  2. Letter name of the melody note — read it off the staff with the "FACE in the spaces" shortcut (the spaces of a treble-clef staff spell F-A-C-E bottom to top; everything else is alphabetical around them), then apply the key's sharps/flats.
  3. Chord-tone number of the melody note relative to the root — the hard step. Two ways in: a visual interval-number chart anchored on the current root (e.g. guitarcientist.com generates one per root), or counting the major-scale formula (whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half) up from the root by ear/hand. Counting straight up gets you close ("some kind of 3") but not exact — you still need the letter name from step 2 to know major vs. flat.
  4. Find/build a voicing with that chord tone as the top note. A hand-built reference works better indexed by which string the melody note lands on (string 1 / string 2 / string 3), not just by chord type — that's the actual lookup you need mid-arrangement. Keep a 3-note and a 4-note version per slot, plus a 2-note fallback for when the melody note isn't a chord tone at all.

No-chart fretboard-only variant: memorize the natural half-steps (E–F, B–C; every other adjacent natural note is a whole step), walk the alphabet from any known note to find any other note by ear/hand, then apply the major-scale interval formula from the root to get the chord-tone number without a chart — you still need each chord type's own spelling (e.g. half-diminished = root ♭3 ♭5 ♭7) to build the voicing itself. Deriving inversions the same way: from a known voicing, find the next-closest chord tone on the same string, moving down, for every note simultaneously — repeat and you walk the shape down through its inversions without a reference at all.

Physical execution: don't harmonize every note

The single highest-leverage habit for actually playing a chord melody smoothly (as opposed to arranging it on paper) is choosing, note by note, when to play a full chord shape and when to just play the single melody note and let the previous harmony (or nothing) carry through. This is a deliberate artistic choice, re-decidable every time you play the piece — not a rule to solve once. Two real payoffs, not just one: it's physically easier (fewer full-hand jumps between shapes, since you're often landing the melody note alone with one finger before adding the rest) and it sounds better (space between chord grabs reads as phrasing rather than a wall of block chords; even solo/unaccompanied, mostly-single-notes-with-occasional-chords still sounds fully harmonized). A concrete glide move for a sustained/repeated melody note across a chord change: play the first chord shape, glide the fretting finger (often the 4th) down to the next melody note while it holds, sound that note alone, then land the next full chord shape from the same position — smoother than jumping cold into the next shape. Demonstrated across "What Is This Thing Called Love" with rootless dim7-as-C7♭9 and rootless G7-altered voicings (guide-tones-non-optional / root-and-extension-interchangeable logic — see Guide Tones, Diminished Chords, Altered Chords) and a one-note half-step voice-leading link between a half-diminished ii shape and its rootless V7♭9, described as a "piano left-hand comping" effect. → Chord Melody Arranging is Miserable (Until You Do It This Way) — Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared, Chord Melody Arranging is Miserable (Until You Do It This Way)

guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.title: Guide-Tone Diads for Blues Rhythm Guitar
guide-tone-diads-for-blues-rhythm-guitar.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. The smallest-footprint rhythm-guitar comping vocabulary in this collection: a single 2-note "diad" — just the 3rd and ♭7 of a dominant chord — carries the whole harmonic identity, with everything else (root, 5th) left for the bassist to cover. Where 9th and 13th Chord Voicings for Blues Rhythm and Rootless 9th Chords and Chromatic Movement in Blues Rhythm Guitar work from bigger 4-note rootless grips, this page starts one layer below that — the guide-tone core those bigger voicings are built on top of — and builds it up in stages with sus4 embellishment, a kick/snare-style register-alternation technique, and a second, higher-position diad vocabulary. Same author, same "reduce the chord to its essential notes so it doesn't crowd the mix" instinct as Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads, but that page stacks three separate parts for production; this page builds one comping part for playing live in a band.

The core shape: 3rd + ♭7, nothing else

A dominant 7 chord is root-3rd-5th-♭7, but only the 3rd and ♭7 determine the chord's quality (major/minor/dominant) — change just the 3rd and the chord's whole character flips; change just the ♭7 to a major 7 and it becomes a maj7 sound. In a band context with a bass player covering the root, the guitar only needs those two notes to outline the chord.

Worked in a 12-bar blues in A (A7-D7-E7):

  • A7: the two notes just outside the bar-chord shape — ♭7 = G, major 3rd = C♯.
  • D7 (IV): the identical two-note shape slides down a half step from the A7 grip — now sounding D7's 3rd (F♯) and ♭7 (C).
  • E7 (V): the identical shape slides up a half step from the A7 grip — now sounding E7's 3rd and ♭7.
  • The whole I-IV-V cycle uses one movable shape, relocated by half steps only — no new grip to learn per chord, just A7 → down ½ step → D7 → up ½ step → A7 → up ½ step → E7 → down ½ step → D7 → A7.

Embellishment 1 — sus4 slide-and-raise

Layered on the core diad: slide into the shape rhythmically, then raise the 3rd up a half step to the 4th for a sus4 color before it resolves back. Works across all three chords with the same physical move, but the 3rd's string position isn't fixed — on D7 the 3rd sits on the bottom of the grip rather than the top, so the raise-to-4th motion has to be adapted to whichever string the 3rd is actually on for that chord. Alternative on the A chord: instead of the plain sus4 hit, grab a full D-triad fragment and hammer on from a lower note up into the 3rd — one more embellishment option on the same base shape, not a different chord choice.

Embellishment 2 — high/low register alternation ("kick and snare")

A technique the source calls out as one he uses constantly: alternate low-register notes against high chord stabs on the top two strings, mimicking a kick drum (low) and snare (high) rhythmically within the same comping part.

  • Low: the guide-tone diad in its low-register position, fretted with the thumb wrapped over the neck (or a plain bar-chord-shape fingering as an alternative).
  • High: just the top two strings of the bar-chord shape — concretely, 5th fret of the high E and B strings = the chord's root and 5th.
  • Over the IV chord specifically, substitute a full D9 chord for the plain diad: the same dominant-7 "C-shape" grip barred up a whole step, with the 9th added on top — called out directly as "a super common chord to use in blues rhythm stuff." The sus4-style raised-4th embellishment layers onto this D9 grip too, same as on the plain diad.
  • Build order: slide into the low A7 diad → jump to the high root/5th stab → back down to thumb-wrapped bass notes → repeat the D-triad hammer-on → another high chord jab → slide into the IV chord (D9 with raised-4th) → up to V → back down.

A second diad vocabulary — 5th + major 3rd, higher position

A distinct shape used deliberately in a different neck area from everything above: the A major triad up around the 9th/10th fret, playing only its two outside notes — 5th and major 3rd (skipping the middle/root note in that particular voicing). Same rhythmic slide-in treatment as the core diad.

  • A chord: 5th + major 3rd of A, in this higher position.
  • D chord: the identical interval relationship, moved down one string set (not a fret-distance relocation like the core diad — a string-set shift).
  • E chord: the identical shape moved up a whole step from the A-chord position.
  • Same underlying logic as the core diad (one small movable shape relocated across I-IV-V) but a second vocabulary built from a different pair of chord tones (5th-3rd instead of 3rd-♭7), giving a genuinely different register/sound option for the same progression rather than a variation on the first shape.

Drill — the video's own build order

  1. Bare guide-tone diads only — 3rd+♭7 shape through the full 12-bar A7-D7-E7 form, moving by half steps, no embellishment. Lock this in first against a backing track.
  2. Add the sus4 slide-and-raise on top of step 1, across all three chords (remembering the 3rd's position flips between chords). Optionally add the D-triad-hammer-on variant on the A chord.
  3. Add the high/low register alternation — top-two-string root/5th chord stab against the low guide-tone diad, thumb-wrapped bass notes underneath. Swap in the full D9 grip (with raised-4th embellishment) over the IV chord.
  4. Play the full assembled part through the whole form against a backing track, listening for lock with the drums.
  5. Learn the second (5th + major 3rd) diad vocabulary separately, up around the 9th/10th fret — down a string set for IV, up a whole step for V — as an alternate higher-register part.
  6. Free-application stage: apply the guide-tone-diad-plus-embellishment approach to other progressions and genres by ear — listen to the track and the other musicians in the room to find the rhythmic spaces where a small fragment fits, rather than reusing this exact arrangement verbatim.

(General starting-point structuring of the 6-step order — the video demonstrates each layer in sequence but the explicit "practice it built up this way" framing is the standard way to internalize a layered comping part like this.)

jazz-harmony.title: Jazz Harmony
jazz-harmony.html:
Part of Music Theory. The hub for the JAZ strand.

Jazz was deliberately shallow in this vault until 2026-08-09 — "dip a toe." That was reversed: the strand is now built out properly. The reason is practical rather than stylistic. Almost everything that makes modern hip hop, neo-soul, R&B and jazzy pop sound the way it does is jazz harmony arriving second-hand, and the fastest way to write those chords deliberately instead of by accident is to learn where they came from.

You do not need to want to play jazz to need this.

The four ideas the whole subject runs on

Jazz harmony looks complicated and is mostly four ideas applied repeatedly.

1. Sevenths are the baseline, not an extension. In common-practice harmony a triad is the default and a seventh is a colour. In jazz the seventh is the default — a "C chord" means Cmaj7 or C6 unless something says otherwise. Every rule below assumes four-note chords. → Seventh Chords

2. The ii–V–I is the sentence. Nearly all standard-repertoire harmony is ii–V–I units, chained, transposed and disguised. Learn to see them and most lead sheets stop looking arbitrary. → The ii-V-I

3. Any chord can be replaced by another sharing its function. Substitution is the engine of variety, and it follows rules rather than taste. → Chord Substitution

4. The 3rd and the 7th carry the harmony; everything else is colour. Two notes are enough to state a chord's identity and to voice-lead a whole progression. → Guide Tones

Get those four and the rest — reharmonization, bebop line construction, modal playing — are applications.

Where the vault covers it

V/V, V/vi and the rest Secondary Dominants
Blending an improvised line with self-comped harmony Melodic-Harmonic Blending (Comping While Soloing)

Reusing one voicing off different chord tones for multiple functions Multifunctional Voicings
Connective chords between two changes — the taxonomy Passing Chords
Portable numeric scale-degree cells for connecting licks and reaching substitutions Digital Patterns

Numerals in jazz vs. the classical style used elsewhere here

Worth flagging because the vault mixes them and it causes real confusion.

  • Classical style (used in most of this vault): case shows quality. ii is minor, V is major, vii° is diminished. See Chord Naming by Context.
  • Jazz/Berklee style: always uppercase, quality shown by suffix. IIm7, V7, Imaj7, ♭VII7.

Both name the same chords. Jazz style wins on lead sheets because chord qualities get altered constantly and case stops being able to carry the information — a V7♯9♭13 has no lowercase equivalent.

This vault uses classical style in theory notes and jazz style when quoting a jazz source. Intervals decide quality, not numeral case.

What "comprehensive" means here, and what it doesn't

Now covered properly: functional harmony, substitution, voice leading, reharmonization, the two standard forms, modal playing, and the melodic vocabulary.

Deliberately not covered, because they're performance disciplines rather than writing tools and nothing in the school needs them:

  • Solo transcription practice as a discipline (the technique is in Transcribing and Playing by Ear)
  • Chord-tone-targeting practice drills over changes as a performance skill (the technique is in Chord-Tone Soloing)
  • Big-band arranging and section writing
  • Walking bass line construction as a bass-player skill — Bassline Writing covers what's needed for writing
  • Free jazz and post-1960 avant-garde — 20th-Century Harmony covers the adjacent material

If any of those become relevant, they're additive and nothing here blocks them.

the-ii-v-i.title: The ii-V-I
the-ii-v-i.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. The sentence jazz is written in. Learn to see it and most lead sheets stop looking arbitrary.

The major version

In C major: Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7.

  • Dm7 = D F A C — subdominant function, the setup
  • G7 = G B D F — dominant function, the tension
  • Cmaj7 = C E G B — tonic, the resolution

Why these three and not others: it's the circle of fifths in miniature. D → G → C, each root falling a fifth. Root motion down a fifth is the strongest progression in tonal music, and ii–V–I stacks two of them back to back. → Circle of Fifths

The voice leading is the other half of the reason. Between Dm7 and G7, two notes stay put and two move by a step. Between G7 and Cmaj7, the tritone resolves: G7's B and F are a tritone apart, B pulls up to C and F pulls down to E. That's Guide Tones, and it's why the progression feels inevitable rather than merely conventional.

The minor version

In C minor: Dm7♭5 → G7♭9 → Cm7 (or Cm6, or CmMaj7).

Three differences from the major, all forced by the minor scale:

  • ii becomes half-diminished. Dm7♭5 = D F A♭ C. The ♭5 is simply the 6th degree of C natural minor.
  • V keeps its major 3rd but usually gains a ♭9. G7♭9 borrows from harmonic minor — the raised leading tone is what makes it a functioning dominant at all, and the ♭9 (A♭) is the minor 6th of the key.
  • The tonic is ambiguous on purpose. Cm7, Cm6 and CmMaj7 are all in use and pick different flavours. Cm7 is the modal/pop choice; CmMaj7 is the classical-sounding one.

Chains — the thing that makes it worth learning

ii–V–I units chain, and standards are largely built by chaining them through different keys. The most common device: make the I of one unit into the ii of the next, or drop a ii–V in front of any chord you want to arrive at.

  • Descending in whole steps: | Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 | Cm7 F7 | B♭maj7 | — a ii–V–I in C, then one in B♭.
  • Turnaround chains: | Cmaj7 A7 | Dm7 G7 | — the A7 is a secondary dominant setting up Dm7. → Secondary Dominants · Turnarounds

Reading tip that pays for itself: scan a lead sheet for any m7 chord followed by a dominant 7th a fourth above it. That's a ii–V, and whatever follows is the intended I — even when the I never actually arrives.

When the I doesn't arrive

Two very common cases, both worth recognising rather than mis-analysing:

  • The deceptive move — ii–V goes somewhere other than I, usually vi or ♭VI. Dm7 G7 Am7 instead of Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.
  • The unresolved ii–V — a ii–V that just moves to the next ii–V without resolving at all. Extremely common in bebop heads and the reason a chart can look like it changes key every two bars when it doesn't.

Guitar shortcut: the power-chord finder

A fast, no-math way to find both halves of a ii–V using nothing but a two-note power-chord shape on the low two strings — the same physical shape used both directions:

  • Chord → its V (or secondary dominant): fret the power chord with the bottom note on the root of the chord you're starting from. The top note of that shape is its V. Example: bottom note A (for Am, the vi of C) → top note E, so E7 is V7/vi in C. → Secondary Dominants
  • Dominant 7th → its related ii: same shape, read the other way. Bottom note = the dominant chord's root, top note = the root of its related ii. Example: bottom note C (for C7) → top note G, so C7's related ii is Gm7 (the pair resolves to Fmaj7: Gm7 C7 Fmaj7).
  • Same trick derives a backdoor ii from its dominant: bottom note B♭ (for B♭7, the backdoor dominant of C) → top note F, so B♭7's related ii is Fm7 — the backdoor 2–5 Fm7 B♭7 Cmaj7. → Turnarounds § Backdoor

Practical use outside jazz

The ii–V–I is why so much neo-soul and jazzy hip hop sounds the way it does. Three ways it shows up in modern writing:

  • As the whole loop. Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 Cmaj7 over four bars is a complete, endlessly loopable progression.
  • As the turnaround only. Straight-ahead pop verse, then a ii–V at the end of the section to push back to the top.
  • Stripped to guide tones. Play only the 3rds and 7ths and the progression still reads — which is how it survives in arrangements with almost no chordal instrument. → Guide Tones
secs: Chains — the thing that makes it worth learning

guide-tones.title: Guide Tones
guide-tones.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. The 3rd and the 7th carry the harmony. Everything else is bass, colour or doubling.

This is the highest-leverage idea in the whole strand: two notes per chord are enough to state a progression, and following those two notes is how you voice-lead anything.

Why the 3rd and the 7th

Take the four chord types you meet most:

Chord Notes 3rd 7th What the pair tells you
Cmaj7 C E G B E B major 3rd + major 7th → major
C7 C E G B♭ E B♭ major 3rd + minor 7th → dominant
Cm7 C E♭ G B♭ E♭ B♭ minor 3rd + minor 7th → minor
Cm7♭5 C E♭ G♭ B♭ E♭ B♭ needs the ♭5 too — the exception

The root tells you nothing about quality. The 5th tells you almost nothing — it's the first note dropped from a voicing precisely because it's the least informative. The 3rd says major or minor; the 7th says major, dominant or minor. Together they name the chord.

That's why a bass player and a horn can imply a full progression with no chordal instrument present at all.

Guide tones move by step — that's the whole trick

Run the guide tones through a ii–V–I in C:

Chord 3rd 7th
Dm7 F C
G7 B F
Cmaj7 E B

Follow one line: C → B → B. Follow the other: F → F → E.

Nothing leaps. One voice holds while the other moves a half-step, then they swap. The 7th of each chord becomes the 3rd of the next — that's not a coincidence, it's what root motion by fifths does, and it's the mechanical reason ii–V–I sounds inevitable. → The ii-V-I

Shell voicings

Play only the guide tones plus a root and you have a shell voicing — three notes, no 5th, no extensions:

  • Root – 3rd – 7th, or
  • Root – 7th – 3rd (7th below the 3rd; usually the better-sounding of the two)

Shells are the practical form of this idea. On guitar or piano they're easy to grab, they never sound muddy, and they leave the entire register above free for melody or for another player. On a dense arrangement they're often the right voicing rather than the simple one — a full 5-note chord under a busy vocal is usually the mistake.

Add extensions on top of a shell and you have the whole vocabulary: shell + 9th, shell + 13th. → Extended Chords · Chord Voicings

Using it to write

To voice-lead a progression: write out the 3rds and 7ths of every chord first, as two horizontal lines. Fix any leap larger than a step by inverting the chord or choosing a different extension. Only then decide the full voicings. This is faster than voicing chord-by-chord and it produces smoother results, because you've solved the horizontal problem before the vertical one.

To test a substitution: a substitute chord that keeps the guide-tone lines stepwise is a good one. This is the concrete test behind Chord Substitution — the tritone sub works precisely because it swaps the guide tones rather than disturbing them.

To thin an arrangement: when a mix is crowded in the mids, cutting the chordal instrument to shells frees space without losing the harmony. The 5th and the doubled root were the notes doing the crowding. → Masking and Carving

The one exception

Half-diminished and diminished chords need the 5th. Cm7♭5 and Cm7 have the same 3rd and 7th (E♭ and B♭); only the G♭ distinguishes them. Any voicing of a m7♭5 that drops the 5th states the wrong chord. → Diminished Chords
secs: Guide tones move by step — that's the whole trick

chord-substitution.title: Chord Substitution
chord-substitution.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. Replacing a chord with a different one that does the same job. This is the engine of variety in jazz harmony, and it follows rules rather than taste.

Bowman's §D is the vault's source for the rules; the worked examples here are original.

The governing rule

Two chords can substitute for each other when they share enough tones and the same harmonic function.

Function first, tones second. A substitute that shares three notes but resolves the wrong way is a worse choice than one sharing two notes that resolves right. Functions are tonic, subdominant and dominant — see Chord Progressions § Harmonic function.

1. Diatonic substitution — chords a third apart

Any two diatonic chords a third apart share two of their three triad tones, so they can often stand in for each other.

In C major:

Original Substitute Shared tones
C (C E G) Am (A C E) C, E
C (C E G) Em (E G B) E, G
F (F A C) Dm (D F A) F, A
G (G B D) Em (E G B) G, B

The classic application: replace I with vi or iii to keep a loop moving without changing where it sits harmonically. Cmaj7 Cmaj7 Fmaj7 G7 becomes Cmaj7 Am7 Fmaj7 G7 — the I–vi–IV–V that half of popular music runs on.

Caution: vi is the strongest I-substitute, iii the weakest. iii shares E and G with C but lacks the root and contains B, which drags it toward dominant function. Substituting iii for I at a final cadence usually sounds unresolved — which is sometimes the point.

2. Tritone substitution — the important one

Replace any dominant 7th with the dominant 7th a tritone away.

The reason it works is exact rather than approximate. Take G7 and D♭7:

  • G7 = G B D F
  • D♭7 = D♭ F A♭ C♭

The B and F of G7 are a tritone apart — that pair is what makes it a dominant chord. D♭7 contains F and C♭, and C♭ is enharmonically B. So the two chords share the same tritone, with the 3rd and 7th swapping roles: G7's 3rd (B) is D♭7's 7th (C♭), and G7's 7th (F) is D♭7's 3rd.

Same tension, same resolution, different bass note. →

What it buys you: chromatic bass motion. Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 has roots D → G → C. Substitute and you get Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7 — roots D → D♭ → C, walking down by half-step. That descending chromatic bass is one of the most recognisable sounds in jazz and neo-soul. → Chromatic Bass Lines

Rules of thumb:

  • Only substitute dominant chords. The tritone is what's being preserved, and only dominant 7ths have one.
  • The substitute is always a half-step above the target of resolution. Resolving to C? The sub is D♭7.
  • It pairs naturally with the ♯11: D♭7♯11 is the fullest-sounding version, because the ♯11 of D♭ is G — the root of the chord being replaced.
  • Substituting the V of a ii–V–I gives you the extremely common IIm7 – ♭II7 – Imaj7.

3. Backdoor substitution

Approach the tonic from ♭VII7 instead of V7. In C major: Fm7 B♭7 Cmaj7 in place of Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.

B♭7 = B♭ D F A♭. It contains A♭, the ♭6 of C, which resolves down to G, and D, which is already in the tonic. It's borrowed from C minor — a plagal-flavoured, softer arrival than a real V7.

When to use it: when V7 sounds too final or too bright. The backdoor is warmer and more ambiguous, which is why it shows up constantly in gospel, soul and Steely Dan-adjacent writing. → Borrowed Chords · Parallel Minor

4. Interpolating a ii in front of any dominant

Any dominant 7th can be preceded by its own related ii chord — the m7 a fourth below it. This doesn't replace a chord so much as expand one.

Cmaj7 A7 Dm7 G7 becomes Cmaj7 Em7 A7 Dm7 G7 — the Em7 is A7's ii.

This is how a sparse progression becomes a dense one without changing its harmonic path at all, and it's the single most useful reharmonization move. → Reharmonization

5. Coltrane changes — worth recognising, rarely worth writing

Substituting a chain of ii–Vs moving in major thirds (three key centres dividing the octave evenly), as on Giant Steps. Named here so it's recognisable on a chart; it's a virtuoso device and almost never the right answer for the writing this vault serves.

Choosing between them

You want Reach for
Keep the loop harmonically still but add motion Diatonic sub (I → vi)
Chromatic descending bass Tritone sub
A softer, less final arrival Backdoor
More chords without changing the path Interpolate a ii
A brighter, more urgent push to a chord Secondary dominant → Secondary Dominants

The failure mode to avoid: substituting everything. Substitution reads as sophisticated against a background of plain harmony; wall-to-wall, it reads as directionless. Bowman's own framing is that substitutions must be "completely compatible" with what they replace — the test is whether the melody still fits, and a substitution that clashes with the tune is wrong no matter how good the voice leading is.

4. Interpolating a ii in front of any dominant
5. Coltrane changes — worth recognising, rarely worth writing

tritone-substitution.title: Tritone Substitution
tritone-substitution.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. A tritone substitution ("tritone sub") swaps a dominant chord for the dominant chord built a tritone (6 semitones) away — same resolving pull, completely different root motion and color.

The mechanism

If a progression is C – G7 – C, the tritone sub swaps G7 for D♭7 (a tritone from G): C – D♭7 – C. It still resolves convincingly because of what the two chords have in common, not what's different.

Every dominant 7th chord's tension comes from its internal tritone — G7's tritone is between F and B (the ♭7 and the 3rd). A dominant chord built a tritone away from the original root contains that exact same tritone: D♭7 also spans F and B (spelled/functioning differently, but the same two pitches). So the pull-to-resolution is fully preserved even though the bass now moves chromatically (D♭→C, a semitone) instead of by a falling fifth (G→C).

Practical effect: tritone-subbing a chain of dominants (e.g., a 3-6-2-5 turnaround, Dm7–G7–Cm7–F7) turns fifth-based root motion into a smooth, entirely chromatic descending bassline — every root drops a single semitone from chord to chord instead of jumping around the circle of fifths.

Origin case study — "Garota de Ipanema" / "The Girl from Ipanema"

The original recording (Pery Ribeiro) uses a plain, un-subbed ii–V–I; nearly every subsequent cover/arrangement tritone-subs the V chord, to the point that most published lead sheets today show the substituted version rather than Jobim's original. This use is the likely direct influence behind the tritone sub in the Wii Shop Channel theme, itself an explicit bossa nova homage to Jobim's writing.

"One Note Samba" — a double sub

Also Jobim (earliest recording João Gilberto): two separate tritone subs in the same tune — the V chord (F7, key of B♭) is subbed to B7; the vi chord's own dominant (which would normally set up a 3-6-2-5, Dm7–G7–Cm7–F7) is instead subbed to D♭7. Stacking both subs turns the whole turnaround into a fully chromatic-descending bassline.

Pop/rock examples — found by ear, not by theory

Several songwriters land on the tritone-sub sound without ever encountering the term — worth remembering when analyzing pop material: the theory is a useful lens after the fact, not necessarily the writer's own mental model.

  • "It Keeps You Runnin'" (The Doobie Brothers) — same tritone-sub-of-a-3-6-2-5 device as "One Note Samba."
  • "Toxic" (Britney Spears) — minor-key iii→ii→♭II chromatic descent, readable as tritone subs of a 6-2-5.
  • "Things We Said Today" (The Beatles) — the middle-eight's second rotation swaps the plain V (E) for B♭.
