bebop-vocabulary.title: Bebop Vocabulary
bebop-vocabulary.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. The melodic side of the strand — how jazz lines are built, as opposed to how the chords underneath them work.

Useful here mostly for writing: these devices are what make a MIDI lead sound played rather than programmed, and they transfer directly to writing horn lines, guitar fills and vocal runs.

For hands-on practice rather than reading, Bebop Vocabulary Practice (Joe Pass Method) works this material against Joe Pass's Guitar Style — a graded blues/rhythm-changes/3-4-blues solo sequence capped by a full, chord-symbol-free transcription of Pass's own "For Django" solo.

1. The bebop scales — why an eighth note

A bebop scale is a normal seven-note scale with one chromatic passing tone added, making eight notes.

That's the entire idea, and the reason is rhythmic rather than harmonic. Play a seven-note scale in straight eighths starting on the downbeat and by the next bar you've shifted: chord tones start landing on offbeats. Add an eighth note and the chord tones land on the beat again, every bar.

Scale Formula Added note
Bebop dominant Mixolydian + natural 7 passing tone between ♭7 and root
Bebop major Major + ♯5 passing tone between 5 and 6
Bebop dorian Dorian + natural 3 passing tone between ♭3 and 4
Bebop melodic minor Melodic minor + ♯5 passing tone between 5 and 6

Bebop dominant on G: G A B C D E F F♯ G. The F♯ is the added tone. Run it descending from the root in eighths and G, E, D and B — the chord tones of G7 — all land on downbeats.

The practical rule: the extra note goes wherever it makes chord tones fall on strong beats. If your line's chord tones are landing on offbeats, you need a passing tone; if they're already on the beat, you don't. → Scale Modes Reference

2. Enclosures — approach a note from both sides

Surround a target note before playing it. This is the most transferable device in the whole vocabulary and it works in any genre.

Target: C

Type Notes Character
Chromatic above/below D♭ – B – C Tight, classic bebop
Diatonic above, chromatic below D – B – C Smoother
Below then above B – D♭ – C Slightly more angular
Double chromatic D – D♭ – B – C Longest, most obviously "jazz"

Where to use them: on the note you actually want the listener to hear — usually a chord tone on a downbeat. An enclosure delays arrival by two or three notes and makes the arrival feel intentional. Applied to a plain melody it instantly reads as improvised.

Where not to: on every note. Enclosures are punctuation. Wall-to-wall, a line stops having a shape.

A chord-tone-independent drilling variant exists: apply enclosures systematically to every note of a scale form in descending order, with no regard for which notes are chord tones — a simpler entry point than targeting chord tones directly, worked out step by step on Enclosures Through the Scale.

A beat-driven sizing rule also exists, orthogonal to the shape table above: which of the two/three-note enclosure types to use is decided purely by which beat the target lands on (downbeat → two notes, upbeat → three), reused to drill diatonic arpeggios and to build ii–V connective lines — full rule on Downbeat and Upbeat Enclosures.

3. Approach notes

The simpler cousin. Precede a chord tone with the note a half-step below (or above, or a scale step away). One note, not three.

  • Chromatic from below is the default and the strongest — it borrows the leading-tone pull.
  • Chromatic from above is softer and slightly melancholy.
  • Scale step is the most neutral and the most usable in non-jazz contexts.

A pivot-tone variant pedals (repeats) one tone and uses it as the launch point for a chromatic approach to a second tone, rather than approaching from a static position — minor chords pivot the 5th into the 6th (which becomes the 3rd of the following V7 in a 2-5-1), major/dominant chords pivot the root into the 5th (approached from the 3rd, or the reverse). Also covers applying the half-step-approach idea to every tone of an arpeggio (not just one target), and to comping voicings treated as single-note-line targets. Full device → Pivot Tone Lines.

4. Target the guide tones

The structural principle underneath all of the above: good lines aim at 3rds and 7ths, not roots.

Landing on the root of each chord states the obvious and sounds like an exercise. Landing on the 3rd or 7th states the chord's quality, and because guide tones move by step between chords, a line built on them is automatically smooth across changes. → Guide Tones

Over Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, a line landing on F, B, E on the three downbeats is already a good line before any decoration.

5. Digital patterns

Numbered scale-degree cells transposed through the changes — 1-2-3-5, 1-3-5-7, 3-5-7-9, 5-3-2-1. Mechanical to generate, which makes them good raw material and bad finished writing.

Their real use is as a grid to decorate: generate a 1-2-3-5 through the changes, then enclose the strong notes and add passing tones. That's a workable method for writing a horn line from nothing.

7. Line closers — stock cadential tails

A line closer is a short, largely fixed phrase kept in memory purely to end a line — the mirror image of the freely-built middle of a phrase. New device for the vault (not previously named here, though several ## From videos bullets above describe cadence-shaped tags without naming the category).

The default shape: arpeggio up, line closer down. Start on a chord tone (often the 3rd) of the dominant, walk up its arpeggio (with extensions optionally thrown in — 9th/11th, a sound Grant Green and Wes Montgomery lean on), then drop into a memorized closer that resolves down into the target chord — worked example: start on the 3rd of F7 (A), walk up the F7 arpeggio, then a closer starting on F7's ♭9 (G♭) walking down to the 3rd of the I chord (B♭). This is the textbook 5–1 bebop shape.

The arpeggio doesn't have to hand off smoothly. You can jump straight from wherever the arpeggio lands to the closer's own starting note — the closer is a fixed unit, not something that has to be voice-led into.

Flipped: closer first, arpeggio second. The same closer that normally ends a phrase can instead open it, with the arpeggio then extending the line outward rather than resolving it. This reads as tonic dominant language — a dominant chord treated as its own stable sound rather than tension wanting to resolve — useful for stretching a dominant line before an eventual resolution, or for soloing over a static dominant that isn't moving (the B section of Rhythm Changes).

Practice loop: memorize a small bank of closers, then combine them freely with any arpeggio/enclosure pattern from §1–2 and finish every combination with one of the closers — a fast way to generate "correct-sounding" lines without composing a full cadence from scratch each time.

8. CESH — chromatic embellishment of static harmony

Take one note — usually the root of a chord that's about to sound, or that's currently sitting still — and move it chromatically up or down through the changes, independent of the underlying harmonic rhythm. The harmony can be genuinely static (one chord held for a while) or just slower-moving than the chromatic line riding underneath it; either way the term describes the chromatic line, not the chord.

Where it differs from an approach note or an enclosure (§2–3): those target a single arrival on a single chord tone. CESH is a sustained chromatic line across several beats or bars, more like a bass-line device borrowed into the melody than a one-note ornament.

Practical use: pick a note that matters (a chord root, a guide tone) and walk it by half step under or against otherwise-static harmony — it's a way to generate forward motion without changing the chord itself, useful anywhere a vamp or a held chord risks going static. → Chromatic Bass Lines, Non-Harmonic Tones

Transferring this outside jazz

Three things here earn their place in modern production:

  • Enclosures on a lead melody. Take a two-note synth hook, enclose the second note. Costs two 16ths and stops the line sounding quantized-from-scratch.
  • Chromatic approach into a section. A single half-step approach into the downbeat of a chorus is the cheapest lift available.
  • Bebop-scale passing tones in a bass line. The added eighth is exactly what makes a walking-ish bass line land its chord tones on the beat. → Bassline Writing

What doesn't transfer well is density. Bebop's note rate is a genre convention, not a principle, and importing it wholesale into a trap beat just sounds busy.
secs: 1. The bebop scales — why an eighth note
2. Enclosures — approach a note from both sides
8. CESH — chromatic embellishment of static harmony

solo-analysis-and-concept-extraction.title: Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction
solo-analysis-and-concept-extraction.html:
Part of Music Theory → Jazz Harmony. Jack Ruch's practice method for turning a transcribed solo into reusable improvisation vocabulary rather than a memorized part — the applied use of a transcription, as opposed to Transcribing and Playing by Ear's note on the ear-only mechanics of getting the notes off the record in the first place. Ties into Song Practice as a concrete workflow for the "learn a solo by ear" stage of practice.

The core method

  1. Learn the solo by ear, in full, first — chords and melody/solo line, all by ear. This alone builds vocabulary and ear, but on its own isn't enough — "it's not enough to just simply learn a solo by ear, you've got to get under the hood."
  2. Chunk it — break the solo into small, manageable sections (a phrase, a chord or two at a time), rather than analyzing it as one continuous line.
  3. Analyze each chunk against the chord underneath it — work out which scale, arpeggio, or harmonic device the original player is drawing from over that specific chord.
  4. Reduce each chunk to one named "concept" — a single reusable idea (a scale choice, an arpeggio substitution, a target note) rather than the literal notes played. The concept, not the lick, is the thing worth keeping.
  5. Use the set of per-chord concepts as a template — improvise a new solo of your own over the same changes, applying the concepts (not the original licks) at each chord. Comping distinct concepts to the same underlying chords is what turns a single transcription into a whole practice session's worth of new lines.
  6. Layer alternate concepts over the same changes — Ruch demonstrates two (sometimes three) different valid concepts for the same chord across repeats of the form (e.g. blues/flat-5 phrasing vs. melodic-minor vocabulary over the same i chord — see below), reinforcing that a chord doesn't have one "correct" scale, just a menu of concepts worth having ready. — Jack Ruch, How I Approach Practicing

Why this works

Once fundamental vocabulary is under the fingers, what's actually needed from a great solo isn't the transcription itself but "a push, a nudge, a suggestion of where to go with something" — a seed concept that plants an idea you can then run with in your own direction, rather than a part to reproduce verbatim. — Jack Ruch, How I Approach Practicing

A more literal alternative — verbatim transcription and stitching

Not every video in this vein reduces a transcription all the way to a named concept first. How to Add Bebop Jazz Vocabulary to the Blues teaches three real bebop saxophone licks (Cannonball Adderley, Charlie Parker, Jimmy Forrest) essentially verbatim — mapped to a matching structural chunk of a jazz-blues 12-bar form — then stitches all three together into one continuous chorus, seamlessly transitioning between them. Stated method: "transcribe different players, then pull the solos apart and combine them with other things you know." A useful complementary entry point before enough vocabulary exists to abstract into concepts — full breakdown on Bebop Vocabulary § From videos. → Bebop Vocabulary, Blues Form and Harmony — Jack Ruch, How to Add Bebop Jazz Vocabulary to the Blues

A second, even more direct instance of the same non-abstracted method. How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues transcribes two Grant Green solo excerpts (over the same B♭ jazz-blues form) and teaches the licks essentially as-played, without reducing them to named concepts first — but states the same underlying payoff as this page's core method: "over time it starts to blend in and become a part of your playing and starts to pop out in your improvising." A recommended prerequisite is stated too — learn the arpeggios of the underlying chords first, and this style of vocabulary turns up naturally inside them (→ Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes). Full breakdowns on 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo and 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Number One Green Street. → Bebop Vocabulary, Turnarounds, Chord Substitution, Blues Form and Harmony — Jack Ruch, How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues

A third instance, this one making the "and make them your own" step explicit and demonstrated live rather than just implied. Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own is a direct methodology companion to the entry above — same channel, same two Grant Green tunes, overlapping excerpts — but its focus flips: instead of teaching the licks as-played, Ruch names the harmonic device behind each phrase (an altered scale, a Lydian-dominant color, a diminished-7 arpeggio for a ♭9 sound, a 2-5-1-of-the-target-chord shape) and then plays his own reworked version of it live, closing the loop this page's core method describes in the abstract. Two concrete "make it your own" devices come out of it that aren't named elsewhere on this page: resolving the same lick to different chord tones than the original, and transposing a fragment by a fixed interval (a half step or a minor third) to a related chord, the latter identified as a genuine recurring Grant Green habit, not just a Ruch teaching trick — new device added to Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines. Also states the same "learn the chord progression first, for context" principle as Transcribing and Playing by Ear's real-time transcription workflow. → Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines, The ii-V-I, Diminished Chords, Turnarounds — Jack Ruch, Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own

Worked example — "Delilah" (Clifford Brown / Max Roach)

Applied to a bluesy AABA jazz solo over F♯ minor — full chord-by-chord concept map on 🎵 CLIFFORD BROWN & MAX ROACH - Delilah. The concepts pulled out (each usable independently of this tune): blues/flat-5 phrasing over a minor i (Blues Scales and Blue Notes), a relative-major arpeggio over a minor chord for a minor-9 color, an upper-structure diminished-7 arpeggio off the 3rd of an altered dominant, melodic-minor-family substitutions (melodic minor over the i, the altered scale over V, harmonic minor as a "major-7-over-minor" color, Lydian dominant on a half-step-above approach chord) — see Scale Modes Reference § From videos and Altered Chords § From videos for the transferable, tune-agnostic versions of these devices.

Worked example — "D Natural Blues" (Wes Montgomery)

A second, shorter application of the same method — this time applied to a jazz icon's playing rather than Ruch's own transcription-derived variation, and restricted to just the I (D7) and IV (G7) chords of a 12-bar jazz blues rather than a full AABA form. Full passage-by-passage concept map on 🎵 WES MONTGOMERY - D Natural Blues. Concepts pulled out: D7 (Mixolydian) scale into direct chord-tone targeting on the IV change, a chromatic walk-down (5th→3rd) into a D7♭9 arpeggio, the whole-half (tonic) diminished scale used as connective tissue bridging IV back to I (not a static "correct scale"), a C major 7 arpeggio over D7 for its upper-extension stack (♭7-9-11-13) followed by D minor pentatonic as a bluesy cadential move into the IV, and an A minor 7 ("v-minor") arpeggio over D7 for its own extended-color stack (5-♭7-9-11). Same step-5 payoff as the Delilah example: after naming each concept, Ruch immediately plays his own line built from it. → Scale Modes Reference, Diminished Chords, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Chord-Tone Soloing, Blues Scales and Blue Notes — Jack Ruch, Wes Montgomery Blues Lesson D Natural Blues

Worked example — "Work Song" (Nat Adderley, Wes Montgomery guitar solo)

A fourth, compact instance of the same underlying goal — reduce a short real solo to reusable devices rather than a part to memorize — this time from Nathan Borton, over a Nat Adderley original (Work Song, 1960, key of A♭) rather than a blues. Distinct from the Ruch and Larsen examples above: Borton doesn't run the full "chunk → analyze → name → replay as your own line" pipeline explicitly, but the shape is the same — three short excerpts (bars 2, 8, 12) each reduced to one portable device. Full passage-by-passage breakdown on 🎵 NAT ADDERLEY - Work Song. Devices pulled out: a relative-major/relative-minor arpeggio swap (an A♭ major 7 arpeggio over F minor 7 implies a 9th; reversed, an F minor 9 arpeggio over A♭ major 7 implies a 13th — one shape, either direction, because the two chords are relative major/minor), a passing-tone-legitimized "wrong" shape over a V-I resolution (an F minor(major7) arpeggio that "doesn't technically work" over E♭7 until its ♭3 is reframed as a passing tone resolving to the 9th — stacking a 9th, a 13th, and a ♭9 into one short phrase), and a movable 4-note guitar shape (C-B♭-G-F), shared with Grant Green, portable across any diatonic chord in the key. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Extended Chords — Nathan Borton, How To Use Chord Extensions In Your Solos!

Worked example — "Take the Coltrane" (John McLaughlin, F blues)

A sixth instance, Jens Larsen. Full breakdown → John McLaughlin - This Is Not Like Other Approaches. Distinct focus: an improviser whose lines are built mostly from scale fragments and chromatic connectors rather than arpeggios, analyzed for HOW he stays musical without leaning on chord-tone-outlining vocabulary. Devices: harmonic pull-ahead — playing content belonging to the next chord before the bar line arrives (e.g. an F7 bar already sounding like G7 Lydian dominant), offered as an alternate reading of an apparently-outside note as an anticipated resolution instead; triad-for-sus substitution — an F major triad over G7, or B♭ major triad over C7, both spelling that root's 7sus4 sound without naming it that way; motif displacement — restating an identical short motif shifted to a different beat than its first statement, varying rhythm without varying melodic content; and a tritone-substitution ii-V reading (F♯7→B7 heard as the tritone-sub ii-V resolving to B♭, not named in F). → Pentatonic Superimposition and Side-Slipping — Jens Larsen, John McLaughlin - This Is Not Like Other Approaches

Worked example — "Blackbird" (Kenny Burrell, on Jimmy Smith's Standards)

A fifth instance, Jens Larsen again, distinct from the others in isolating tension sources other than harmony/note-choice. Full breakdown → Kenny Burrell - How to Make the Blues Sound Outside. Two devices not covered by the other worked examples on this page: rhythmic-feel contrast as an independent tension axis — a phrase shifts from straight/medium swing eighths to a noticeably harder shuffled swing feel with the exact same notes, generating surprise purely from rhythmic character rather than pitch content ("not about altered dominants or extra chords... it's really about other aspects of music"); and one-note, one-rhythm motif development — a single repeated pitch (the 9th) played with a simple 16th-note rhythmic motif creates contrast against a medium-swing backdrop with zero harmonic movement at all. Also reinforces this page's general standing point about long-arc phrasing: ideas stretched and developed across several bars rather than resolved quickly, framed as a mark of a strong improviser independent of any specific vocabulary device. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes, Groove and Microtiming — Jens Larsen, Kenny Burrell - How to Make the Blues Sound Outside

Worked example — "Billie's Bounce" (George Benson)

A third instance of the same chunk-analyze-name-the-device method, this time from a different teacher (Jens Larsen rather than Jack Ruch) applied to a 12-bar jazz blues in F. Full passage-by-passage concept map on 🎵 GEORGE BENSON - Billie's Bounce. The concepts pulled out: mixing bebop-arpeggio language and blues-double-stop language inside a single unbroken phrase (no seam between vocabularies), a half-diminished (not full dim7) arpeggio off a dominant chord's own 3rd as a recurring signature device (Diminished Chords § From videos), treating a ii-chord as a plain triad plus chromatic leading notes rather than thinking in a parent scale — explicitly named as what produces bigger, less-predictable interval jumps while still always landing on a chord tone (Chord-Tone Soloing § From videos) — a bar-1 bebop cliché answered by its own melodic inverse on the next chord (call-and-response), and a well-worn F-minor blues cliché kept fresh by resequencing its notes rather than retiring it. Distinct from the Wes Montgomery and Clifford Brown/Max Roach examples above in not reducing every passage to a single named "concept" before replaying it — Larsen narrates the device in place on the recording rather than performing Step 5's "play it back as your own line" step explicitly, closer in that respect to the "more literal" verbatim-transcription approach described above. → Chord-Tone Soloing, Diminished Chords, Bebop Vocabulary, Blues Scales and Blue Notes — Jens Larsen, George Benson - This is The Best Jazz Blues Solo I know

A composing-focused variant — Jens Larsen's analyze-then-compose pipeline

A second, independently-arrived-at version of this page's core method, from a different teacher (Jens Larsen). Same two-stage shape — break a source line into small reusable fragments, then deliberately reuse them — but two things differ from Ruch's method above: Larsen doesn't reduce each chunk to one named "concept," he stays closer to the literal fragment and composes transposed/modified variants of it directly; and he adds a from-scratch composing mode with no source lick at all — start from a bare diatonic arpeggio (no transcription to analyze first) and compose original lines with it, which Ruch's concept-extraction method doesn't cover.

  1. Analyze a source phrase into its small melodic building blocks — worked over a Charlie Parker Omnibook rhythm-changes fragment, chunked into five pieces and judged individually rather than treated as equally useful: a chromatic passing run (judged least interesting), a four-note pentatonic fragment (flagged as exactly the kind of small, high-frequency fragment worth hunting for), a plain scale run (flagged as the least useful piece in the whole line), a chromatic enclosure into the next bar's downbeat, and a descending arpeggio + 6th-interval leap (see Bebop Vocabulary § From videos for the full breakdown of that last fragment). Stated principle: a small bag of small pieces beats either a large bag of small pieces or a small bag of large pieces — small, recombinable fragments are what actually pay off live, where long memorized licks don't.
  2. Compose new lines by transplanting a fragment onto a new context and asking "what's the next thing I hear?" — rather than planning a full line up front, play the borrowed fragment into the new progression and let the ear supply the next note-choice at a time. Recommends writing early attempts down on paper specifically so a line that doesn't work can be diagnosed afterward, the same diagnostic step used when analyzing the source line itself.
  3. A from-scratch composing mode with no source lick — starting only from a bare diatonic arpeggio (the arpeggio off the 3rd of a ii chord, over a 2-5-1), compose several original lines from it: straight descending arpeggio into existing altered vocabulary; the same arpeggio approached via a pedal point instead of starting cold; the same idea with the rhythm changed (straight eighths → a triplet); and the same idea combined with a retargeted enclosure (an enclosure originally built for one target note reworked to approach a different one — the generalizable move named explicitly: "you've taken one idea and made it into another idea").
  4. The composed lines are disposable — the process is the point. Stated directly: none of the composed 2-5-1 lines are meant to be played verbatim while soloing. The goal is rehearsing the act of finding a good way to use a small fragment, so the same searching-and-evaluating process is already trained and available live, rather than only ever meeting a new idea for the first time mid-solo. Follow-up step once a fragment feels solid: take it to a slow/medium-tempo turnaround or a known standard and work it in time.
  5. Analyzing + composing is framed explicitly as a taste-development tool, not just a vocabulary-acquisition one — judging "does this work, do I like this" on every composed attempt is what builds a personal sound. Worked example: on the Parker fragment's flat-13→3rd resolution, Larsen states his own taste diverges from what Parker actually plays (a plain scale-step resolution) and he'd substitute a fully altered line instead (flat-13 → sharp-9 → flat-9 → root) — noticing the source, then consciously choosing a different color rather than treating the transcription as gospel. — Jens Larsen, Jens Larsen - Overlooked SKILLS for Learning Jazz - CREATIVITY is in your Brain

A style-trait variant — extracting identity traits rather than per-chord concepts

Not every solo-analysis video reduces the material to a chord-by-chord concept map. 🎵 KURT ROSENWINKEL - Nefertiti (Ballad Session) takes a different cut through the same underlying goal (reverse-engineer reusable vocabulary from a real solo): instead of naming one concept per chord, Jens Larsen pulls out a small set of recurring style traits across four excerpts of a Kurt Rosenwinkel solo — very wide range inside a short phrase, a melodic idea that survives a chord change instead of resetting, lines built from stacked arpeggios/triads rather than one scale, and tight motivic restraint (a small note pool developed without sounding obvious). The chord-by-chord concept map still applies within each excerpt, but the headline takeaway is a player identity checklist rather than a per-chord substitution menu — a useful complementary lens when the goal is "sound more like this player" rather than "solve this specific turnaround." Rosenwinkel's own stated practice method behind the "melody survives the chord change" trait is documented separately on Never-Ending Scale Exercise. → Solo Dynamics and Arc, Motivic Development, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing — Kurt Rosenwinkel via Jens Larsen, Kurt Rosenwinkel - This Is What Makes His Style Unique

A collection-first variant — sort every phrase into a lick journal by device type, then plug and chug

A simpler entry point than the per-chunk concept-naming methods above: rather than analyzing each chunk against its specific underlying chord (Ruch's step 3), just sort every extracted phrase into a "lick journal" by which device it is, independent of which tune or chord it came from — all the 5-1 phrases together, all the CESH phrases together, all the altered phrases together, and so on. Stated reasoning: organized-by-function vocabulary is dramatically easier to digest and easier to get into the fingers than vocabulary still tangled up inside one transcribed melody, because a whole category can be "plugged and chugged" over any changes that call for it rather than searched for one phrase at a time. Demonstrated on a full phrase-by-phrase breakdown of Charlie Parker's "Confirmation" head melody — full breakdown → 🎵 CHARLIE PARKER - Confirmation, Bebop Vocabulary §From videos. Complementary rather than competing with the per-chord concept method above: the two-stage version (concept-name each chunk, then file it into a category bucket) combines both. → Bebop Vocabulary, 🎵 CHARLIE PARKER - Confirmation — Nathan Borton, Learn Charlie Parker's Phrasing Secrets... with CONFIRMATION!

A practice-routine variant — turn the extracted techniques into timed drills, not just concepts

Every other variant on this page ends the extraction with a named concept or trait; this one (from a live master class, not a per-tune video breakdown) is distinct in going one step further — it's a complete workflow for turning a listening session into an actual daily practice schedule, extracted from Nathan Borton's own teacher, Randy Napoleon, rather than Borton's own transcribed solos.

  1. Play the model recording and have the target-technique observations be concrete and nameable, not vague. Explicitly ruled out: "he plays fast, I want to play fast." Ruled in: specific, breakdown-able qualities — in the worked session, a room of students named movement (the phrasing "moved forward and back," never sitting in one rhythmic spot), harmonic motion (passing chords), and melody harmonization (chording the tune the way a piano player would).
  2. Design one concrete, systematic drill per named technique — an extreme, "do it on everything" version first, a selective/musical version second. Two worked drills, both following the same two-stage shape: (a) melody harmonization — first harmonize every single note of the melody, deliberately unmusical ("junk-junk-junk"), to prove you can do it at all; then narrow to a specific harmonic target — only the ii–V's, only ♯IV walk-downs, only dominant-to-tonic resolutions, only the backdoor dominants — leaving the rest as a single line. (b) passing chords — chromatically side-slip (half-step above or below) into every chord change as the extreme pass, then narrow the same side-slip to just specific slots (e.g. only the ii–V's). A third drill for a technique that isn't chord-shaped at all: movement — alternate 2 bars of the melody played strictly to a metronome with 2 bars of free improvisation, forcing the "never sitting still" rhythmic-freedom quality to be practiced deliberately instead of left to feel.
  3. Time-box each technique against your actual daily practice budget, rather than working all of them unstructured. Worked example: a student with 4 hours/day splits time across the extracted techniques — e.g. 2 hours on melody harmonization (1 hour harmonize-everything, 1 hour harmonize-selectively), with the remaining time going to the next technique (movement) — and reallocates hours toward the next technique as comfort with the first one increases.
  4. Write the plan down — the explicit closing instruction, so a session is executed from a written allocation rather than improvised from scratch each day.

This differs from Ruch's/Larsen's per-chord "concept" methods above in scope: instead of reducing a solo to a chord-by-chord vocabulary menu, it extracts whole-performance-level techniques (harmonization, chromatic passing motion, rhythmic freedom) and answers the scheduling question ("how many hours on which technique today") that the other variants leave implicit. Full drill mechanics and the harmonization/passing-chord specifics also live on Chord Melody Arranging § From videos; the day-to-day spaced-practice rule this same video teaches lives on The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice. → Chord Melody Arranging, Passing Chords, The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice, Song Practice — Nathan Borton, Master Class: "How To Get The Most Out Of Your Practice Time"

A self-analysis variant — practicing by contrasting two solos over the same tune, and the "listen → predict what comes next" loop

Every other variant on this page analyzes someone else's recorded solo. This one, from Jens Larsen, turns the same underlying discipline (reduce playing to reusable, nameable devices rather than raw noodling) onto your own live playing, and answers a different problem than the other variants — not "how do I extract vocabulary from a great solo" but "how do I even practice soloing in a way that isn't just unstructured noodling with no visible progress," the way scales/exercises practice visibly is. Diagnosed failure state, named directly: if every chord gets its own disconnected idea with nothing threading them together, "that's not a solo, that's just a bunch of licks next to each other."

  1. Give soloing practice an explicit, nameable goal before you start — Larsen's is melodicism, narrowed immediately to one drillable mechanism: motivic development. A vague goal ("play more melodic") doesn't work as a practice target; a named mechanism does.
  2. Play two full solos back-to-back over the same tune and let the contrast do the teaching. Solo 1 is the honest baseline — competently connect the harmony (arpeggios, target notes — see the Chord-Tone Soloing cross-reference below) but with no larger melodic thread linking one chord's idea to the next. Solo 2 is the fix applied: state one short motif (2–3 notes is plenty — an 8–10 note melody is "just a lot of calculating" to move through changes) and develop it continuously through a whole section, varying its rhythm and its ending rather than starting fresh on every chord, before deliberately pivoting to a new idea when it's run its course ("you don't want to stick to a motif too long"). → full bar-by-bar breakdown of both solos on Is Your Improvisation Practice a Waste of Time? (And How to Fix That).
  3. The transferable daily drill: after playing a phrase, listen back and ask "what should come next?" — explicitly not a note-name or scale-name decision (Larsen rules out "now I want to hear F♯ diminished" as the wrong mental model). Think in terms of the sound/shape wanted next, then find it on the instrument. Concrete exercise version: take just the first few bars of a tune, state a simple motif, then keep changing how the phrase ends and the order of its notes — repeat until the listen-predict-play loop itself starts to feel automatic, independent of which tune it's practiced on.
  4. Have a strong harmonic overview of the tune before soloing on it, even one you've never played — analyze it as functional devices (ii–V, turnaround, backdoor dominant) rather than a flat chord list; this is what let Larsen improvise convincingly on a jazz standard called on a gig that he'd never played before, cold, at tempo. Same "devices not isolated chords" principle as The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice Pillar 4.
  5. A concrete harmonic-connection device usable inside either solo (baseline or motif-developed): target only the notes that actually change between adjacent chords. F major7 → F♯ diminished moves only two notes (F→F♯, E→E♭) — play exactly those two on the diminished chord to make the chord change audible without recalculating a whole new arpeggio; G minor7 → C7 moves only one note (F→E). Full worked instances → Chord-Tone Soloing § From videos.

This differs from every other variant on this page in what it analyzes (your own real-time playing, not a transcription) and in what problem it solves (structuring practice time itself, not extracting vocabulary from a source solo) — but shares the page's core thesis that a solo should reduce to a small number of nameable, reusable devices rather than be treated as an unrepeatable, un-analyzable performance. → Motivic Development, Chord-Tone Soloing, The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice, Song Practice — Jens Larsen, Is Your Improvisation Practice a Waste of Time? (And How to Fix That)

12-level-chromatic-alternate-picking-spe.title: 12-Level Chromatic Alternate-Picking Speed Workout
12-level-chromatic-alternate-picking-spe.html:
A 12-tempo-level daily picking play-along, chromatic-scale-based (all four fretting fingers, one note per fret) so there's no scale/theory content to learn — the drill is pure right-hand speed and clean string transitions. Starts at 50 BPM (Level 1) and climbs through all 12 levels in one sitting.

How to run it

  • Play through all 12 levels in one sitting, back to back — the workout is the ladder, not one isolated tempo.
  • Goal, every note, at every tempo: one continuous unbroken stream — no hesitation or unwanted noise at string transitions. A clean lower tempo beats a sloppy higher one.
  • Log the date and the BPM level you got stuck at, then return the next day and try to beat it — the drill is explicitly designed as a day-over-day progression tracker, not a one-and-done exercise.
  • If a specific tempo step feels technically wrong (not just "hard," but genuinely uncontrolled), that's a signal to drop back and drill string-transition mechanics specifically rather than muscling through at that tempo.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure right-hand dexterity on the chromatic scale — no scale, mode, or chord-tone knowledge being applied or tested. reinforces: [] per the Drill Index's own drill-vs-routine test (a drill you can run while thinking about literally anything else).

Variation — asymmetric 4-notes-per-string chromatic run in groups of 10

A more advanced, musically-shaped chromatic exercise (distinct from this drill's plain linear ladder): a 4-notes-per-string chromatic pattern across a chosen fretboard section, not symmetrical because of the B string's different tuning interval from its neighbors — you have to actually track the fingering rather than just repeat one shape across every string. Phrased in groups of 10 (a group of 6 combined with a group of 4, repeating) instead of the usual groups of 2/3/4 — the odd grouping puts accents in more interesting places than a standard chromatic warmup. Picked with continuous alternate picking throughout (no exceptions), which also makes it a solid wrist-loosening warmup on top of the note-spacing/hand-synchronization work. Practiced at 3 tempos in the source video. Reusable takeaway beyond this specific exercise: build note groupings deliberately into licks/solos for more original rhythmic phrasing, not just even 2s/3s/4s. → Chromatic Shred Challenge - Can You Play This? — BERNTH, Chromatic Shred Challenge - Can You Play This?

15-minute-play-along-guitar-workout.title: 15-Minute Play-Along Guitar Workout
15-minute-play-along-guitar-workout.html:
A six-block daily play-along session (scrolling on-screen tabs, no fixed BPM ladder): Warm-up → Left-Hand Technique → Stretching → 3-Notes-Per-String Patterns → Hand Synchronization 1 → Hand Synchronization 2 → Speed Exercise.

How to run it

  • Play all six blocks back to back in one 15-minute sitting — the shape is the point, not any single block in isolation.
  • Left-hand fingers stay close to the fretboard throughout; picking motion stays relaxed and economical, not full-arm.
  • Log the tempo/point you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure warm-up/synchronization mechanics — no scale, mode, or chord-tone knowledge applied. Motor skill only.

2-note-per-string-arpeggio-picking-exerc.title: 2-Note-Per-String Arpeggio Picking Exercise (C Minor Scale-Degree Chords)
2-note-per-string-arpeggio-picking-exerc.html:
Four-note chord arpeggios (2 notes per string), one built on every scale degree of the C minor scale, targeting the often-neglected mid-tempo (120–130 BPM) alternate-picking range.

How to run it

  • One 4-note chord shape per scale degree of C minor, picked 2 notes per string.
  • Consistent picking angle (even grouping) — pick should clear the strings after each down-up pair, not get trapped between them.
  • Total picking-hand relaxation is required, not optional — tension collapses the exercise (multiple strings ring together) rather than just degrading it.
  • Curled (not flat) fretting fingers keep each arpeggiated note cleanly separated — this is the single biggest factor in how clean it sounds.
  • Doubles as a fretting-hand independence exercise: one fretted note per string against two picking strokes.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Picking-hand/fretting-hand coordination and relaxation at a specific tempo range — the C minor scale-degree shapes are a vehicle for the technique, not a theory concept being tested.

2-week-full-technique-workout-6-block-da.title: 2-Week Full Technique Workout (6-Block Daily Routine)
2-week-full-technique-workout-6-block-da.html:
A six-block daily workout meant to be run in one 10-minute sitting for two weeks, touching every major technique family in sequence.

The six blocks

  1. Alternate-picking ascending arpeggios in 5/8 (Bb major) — warmup, tempo climbs each rep.
  2. Legato/stretching — hammer-on/pull-off with the fretting thumb positioned behind the index finger for reach; a hybrid-picked note before the last note of each sequence.
  3. Sweep/economy picking through common arpeggio shapes, following a specific picking pattern.
  4. Alternate-picking string transitions across mixed 6/8–7/8 measures — both up- and down-escape motions needed.
  5. Tapping lick with multi-finger tapping and tapping slides — pick held between index and thumb throughout.
  6. Hybrid picking — pick plus middle/ring fingers on D/G/B strings for string-skipping lines.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

A mixed-technique physical routine — no scale/mode/chord-tone knowledge being taught or tested, just running each hand-technique family through its motions daily.

30-day-sweep-picking-speed-burst-challen.title: 30-Day Sweep Picking Speed-Burst Challenge
30-day-sweep-picking-speed-burst-challen.html:
A 30-day daily sweep-picking ladder on just two shapes — E minor and E major — alternated, with an escalating fast speed-burst added on top of each repetition as tempo climbs.

How to run it

  • Play E minor shape → E major shape → alternate between them, tempo climbing session to session.
  • Add a fast burst of sweep picking on each repetition — meant to push past the comfort zone, not to be played clean immediately. Failing to complete the full workout on day one is expected.
  • Log the tempo you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Two fixed shapes, pure speed/burst mechanics — no scale/mode/chord-tone decision-making involved.

4-minute-alternate-picking-shred-challen.title: 4-Minute Alternate Picking Shred Challenge (200 BPM Ladder)
4-minute-alternate-picking-shred-challen.html:
A short daily play-along: an ascending 3-note pattern (×4) then a descending 3-note pattern (×4), then alternating between the two, run through tempo blocks climbing toward 200 BPM in straight 16th notes.

How to run it

  • Strict alternate picking throughout (no economy shortcuts) — down/up/down/up regardless of string change.
  • Stay relaxed; a fully locked/tensed wrist is both a speed ceiling and an injury risk at this tempo.
  • Log the tempo where you get stuck plus the date, come back the next day, and try to push past it — day-over-day overload, not a one-off run.
  • Good finisher once basic wrist-unlocking work (see Directional Alternate Picking System) is already in place — this drill is pure speed ladder, no technique-building content of its own.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure alternate-picking speed on a fixed pattern — no scale, mode, or chord-tone knowledge involved. Per the Drill Index's drill-vs-routine test, this is a drill you can run on autopilot once the pattern is memorized.

4-notes-per-string-stretch-workout.title: 4-Notes-Per-String Stretch Workout
4-notes-per-string-stretch-workout.html:
A daily 5-minute alternate-picking lick built on a deliberately wide 4-notes-per-string fretting-hand stretch — the stretch is the point: you can't fake correct fretting-hand form and still reach the notes.

How to run it

  • Support the thumb from behind the neck, never draped over the top — that's what makes the stretch reachable.
  • Keep the picking wrist relaxed and moving even above 200 BPM; avoid locking into a stiff full-arm motion.
  • Log the tempo you got stuck at and try to beat it next session (daily morning routine, per the source).
  • Getting stuck at a plateau here is a signal to check underlying picking technique, not just to push harder.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure alternate-picking speed + fretting-hand stretch mechanics — no scale/mode/chord-tone knowledge applied.

5-minute-alternate-picking-workouts-bern.title: 5-Minute Alternate Picking Workouts (BERNTH)
5-minute-alternate-picking-workouts-bern.html:
Two paired 5-minute daily play-alongs covering two distinct alternate-picking sub-skills:

  • Hand synchronization — a scale pattern with open strings woven in, moved to four fretboard positions. The open strings expose sync errors a fretted note would hide.
  • Endurance — sustaining fast picking over a longer passage rather than a short burst, with a specifically lighter/relaxed attack (a hard "burst" attack doesn't hold up over a sustained passage).

How to run it

  • Run either (or both) daily; log the tempo/point you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.
  • For the endurance workout specifically, keep picking attack light — resist the urge to attack harder as fatigue sets in.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure right-hand mechanics (sync and endurance) — no theory content applied.

5-minute-legato-workout.title: 5-Minute Legato Workout
5-minute-legato-workout.html:
A 5-minute daily play-along drill: hammer-ons and pull-offs, switching note-value groupings while climbing a BPM ladder.

How to run it

  • Play through the 5-minute climb daily; log the BPM you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.
  • Focus on hammer-on/pull-off consistency and volume as the note grouping changes, not raw speed alone.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure legato mechanics (hammer-on/pull-off dexterity) — no theory content applied.

5-minute-multi-finger-tapping-workout.title: 5-Minute Multi-Finger Tapping Workout
5-minute-multi-finger-tapping-workout.html:
A single tapping riff (multi-finger tapping plus tapping slides) played along at a progressive tempo ladder starting at 30 BPM. Doubles as a fretting-hand technique workout, since tapping demands very precise fretting-hand control.

How to run it

  • Play along at each tempo step; log the date and tempo you get stuck at, come back the next day and try to beat it.
  • If genuinely stuck (not just "hard," but uncontrolled) well below a reasonable target, that's a signal to work tapping fundamentals in isolation before returning to this workout.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure tapping-hand/fretting-hand coordination on a fixed riff — no scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge involved.

beginner-sweep-picking-play-along-workou.title: Beginner Sweep Picking Play-Along Workout
beginner-sweep-picking-play-along-workou.html:
A 10-minute daily beginner sweep-picking play-along (scrolling on-screen tabs, no fixed BPM ladder).

How to run it

  • Apply the two beginner sweep-picking fundamentals while running through this: the chord-strum motor-pattern reframe (Best Beginner Sweeping Exercise - Master Sweep Picking TODAY!) and the first/last-note metronome anchor (SWEEP PICKING for Beginners - The 5 BEST Exercises!).
  • Play daily; log the tempo/point you got stuck at and try to beat it next session.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure sweep-picking motion mechanics — no scale/mode/chord-tone decision-making applied.

downstroke-workout.title: Downstroke Workout
downstroke-workout.html:
Right-hand stamina. All downstrokes, no upstrokes — the picking hand never recovers on the way back up, which is what makes it a conditioning drill rather than a speed drill.

  • 18 pages, standard tuning
  • A tempo ladder in 10 BPM steps from 60 to 210 — the whole structure of the drill is the ladder. Each rung is the same figure at the next tempo.
  • Play through Downstroke Workout.pdf

How to run it

  • Start at tempo_current, not at 60 every time. Move up a rung only when the current one is clean for the full page.
  • The failure mode is tension, not speed. If the forearm locks up, drop two rungs rather than pushing — downstroke stamina is built by staying relaxed under load, and practising tense just trains tension.
  • Short and frequent beats long and occasional. Five minutes daily moves the ladder faster than half an hour on Sunday.

Progress

Track by tempo. Update tempo_current when a rung is genuinely clean; don't rate it, and don't run it through spaced repetition — this wants daily reps at a rising tempo, which is the opposite of a widening SR interval.

essential-patterns.html:
A single-page pattern sheet at ♩=40 — the shortest thing in the drill library and the easiest to actually do on a bad day.

  • 1 page, written slow on purpose
  • Play through Essential Patterns.pdf

How to run it

  • Five minutes, no ladder. This one isn't built around climbing tempo; it's built around being short enough that there's no excuse to skip it.
  • Best used as the thing you do when the answer to "am I practising today" is otherwise no. A five-minute page beats a missed session, and the guitar drills only work on frequency.

finger-independence-harmonic-minor-exerc.title: Finger Independence Harmonic Minor Exercise
finger-independence-harmonic-minor-exerc.html:
A 3-level fretting-hand exercise on a harmonic minor shape, targeting finger independence and the "flying pinky" problem.

How to run it

  • When the pinky isn't fretting, hover it close over the strings rather than letting it bend away — the concrete self-check this drill trains.
  • Resist widening the motion as tempo increases; stay small and relaxed even under speed pressure.
  • Prioritize control and independent finger feel over raw speed — work through the 3 levels slowly before attempting a faster pass.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure fretting-hand dexterity/economy-of-motion — no scale/mode/chord-tone decision-making applied (the harmonic minor shape is a vehicle, not the point).

finger-independence-and-grip-control-thr.title: Finger Independence and Grip Control (Three Fixes)
finger-independence-and-grip-control-thr.html:
Three short fretting-hand fixes targeting index-finger over-anchoring and excess grip tension.

The three exercises

  1. Open-string finger workout — incorporate open strings into a chromatic pattern so every finger must lift off between notes; run it with no wrist assistance, isolating the motion to the fingers alone.
  2. Non-anchored lick — play a lick where the index finger deliberately can't stay planted on one string, forcing the other fingers to work without its support.
  3. Decreasing-grip chromatic workout — the open-string pattern from exercise 1, this time deliberately reducing grip pressure rep by rep until notes start to die, to find the real minimum-pressure sweet spot by feel.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure fretting-hand finger-independence and grip-tension calibration — no scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge involved.

finger-technique-exercises.title: Finger Technique Exercises
finger-technique-exercises.html:
Four exercises for finger independence. The instruction printed on page 1 is the whole design:

Only use your fretting hand for all exercises.

No picking at all — every note is hammered on or pulled off. That isolates the left hand completely, so weakness shows up immediately instead of being masked by the pick.

  • 11 pages, standard tuning, written at ♩=120 but start well under that
  • Four numbered exercises, each drilling a different finger pairing
  • Written for distorted guitar (dist. guit.) — the compression makes uneven notes audible, which is the point. Playing it clean hides exactly the flaws it's trying to surface.
  • Play through Finger Technique Exercises.pdf

How to run it

  • This is the warm-up of the guitar set, not the workout. Six minutes before anything else.
  • One exercise per session is fine. Rotating through all four across a week beats grinding all four daily.
  • Because there's no picking, it can be done quietly on an unplugged electric — useful when a full practice session isn't possible.

five-painful-finger-and-picking-exercise.title: Five Painful Finger and Picking Exercises
five-painful-finger-and-picking-exercise.html:
Five drills, ranked worst-to-best by the source teacher for actual playing transfer (5 = least valuable, 1 = most valuable).

1. Three-notes-per-string modes (rank: best, "10/5")

Play through all seven modal shapes using a three-notes-per-string fingering, worked in the key of G (chosen because it lays out cleanly for this fingering). Trains both hands, covers key/fretboard layout, and is musical — the source's top-ranked exercise for that reason. See CAGE System Scale Shapes / Diatonic Modes for the underlying shapes.

2. Odd/even finger-pair pattern (rank: 4/5)

Number the fretting fingers 1–4. Only ever use fingers 1+3 together or 2+4 together — never mix an odd-numbered finger with an even-numbered one. Play a fixed pattern down the strings using only those two-finger pairings, then turn around and play it back. To increase difficulty, let notes ring longer instead of damping them. Ranked "tricky but not too musical."

3. Anchor-finger exercise (rank: 3/5)

Anchor one finger (ring finger recommended as the hardest, though any finger works) on a fixed fret — the 7th fret in the demo — and keep it planted there for the entire exercise while the other fingers move. Good for left-hand independence and works at any skill level by adjusting the metronome. Ranked above the fan drill below because it functions closer to real playing (a static reference finger while the hand moves around it).

4. 3-minute continuous chromatic picking (rank: 2/5)

Play a simple chromatic exercise continuously for 3 minutes without stopping, metronome around 130 BPM. The goal is sustaining tempo, not perfection — occasional mistakes are fine as long as speed doesn't drop. Track pick slips as a data point: more than ~4 slips means the tempo is too fast, dial it back. The "3-minute rule" generalizes to any exercise — pick one, run it continuously for 3 minutes, repeat up to 3 sets a day, with rest between sets since this is physically demanding.

5. One-finger-per-string fan exercise (rank: worst, 5/5)

Plant all four fingers on the G string, then alternate the first finger between the G and E strings 20–30 times while the other three fingers stay completely still; repeat for each finger in turn (ring finger is typically hardest, pinky close behind). Move to a higher, tighter-fret position to make it harder, or a lower, wider-fret position to make it easier. Attributed to Scott Tennant's Pumping Nylon. Good for pure finger independence but ranked lowest here for being the least musical of the five.

funk-inspired-right-hand-rhythm-and-muti.title: Funk-Inspired Right-Hand Rhythm and Muting Workout
funk-inspired-right-hand-rhythm-and-muti.html:
Three chord-strumming rhythm exercises on a single E7♯9 ("Hendrix chord") voicing, aimed at picking-hand wrist looseness and timing rather than fretting-hand technique.

The chord

Root E (A string, 7th fret), ♯3 G♯, ♭7 D, ♭3 G — low E string blocked with the fretting thumb.

The three exercises

  1. Alternating open chord stabs and fully-muted dead notes (percussive picking-hand mute at the bridge, plus the fretting block) — big tonal contrast between the two, no blur.
  2. Same vocabulary with a syncopated group-of-3 rhythm, 32nd notes (not 16th-note triplets — a deliberately different feel).
  3. Triplet feel with a downstroke placed on every strong-beat accent (two downstrokes in a row where needed), rather than continuous alternation.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Right-hand rhythm/muting/wrist looseness on one fixed chord shape — no new scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge, just physical timing and mute control.

legato-finger-strength-workout.title: Legato Finger Strength Workout
legato-finger-strength-workout.html:
Fretting-hand strength and evenness. Hammer-ons and pull-offs carry the notes; the pick starts a phrase and then gets out of the way.

  • 9 pages, standard tuning
  • Tempo ladder in 10 BPM steps from 40 to 130 — starts deliberately slow, because the point is even volume between picked and unpicked notes, which only shows up when it's slow enough to hear.
  • Play through Legato Finger Strength Workout.pdf

How to run it

  • The measure of success is whether a hammered note is as loud as a picked one. Speed is a by-product. Record a phrase and listen back rather than trusting the hand.
  • Four-finger patterns across positions (7-9-10-11 shapes and their reverses) — the 3rd-to-4th finger transition is where it falls apart first, and that's the rung to sit on.
  • Complements Downstroke Workout: one loads the picking hand, this one loads the fretting hand. Running both in a session covers each hand.

pinky-finger-control-ladder-chromatic-ha.title: Pinky-Finger Control Ladder (Chromatic Hammer_Pull-off Progression)
pinky-finger-control-ladder-chromatic-ha.html:
A 4-note A minor pattern (frets 5-7-8 on the low E string, 5-7 on the A string), moved chromatically across all six strings, layered up in three stages to fix pinky "flying" between string changes.

The ladder

  1. Picked, slow — focus purely on keeping the pinky close to the fretboard after each string change rather than letting it drift.
  2. Add a hammer-on — only one picking stroke per string, the rest hammered.
  3. Add a pull-off after the hammer-on — start in one position (E/A strings only) before moving across the neck; avoid a large pull-off motion that grazes neighboring strings.
  4. Hardest variation — add one more hammer-on to fill the remaining 8th-note rest, producing a continuous gapless eighth-note stream.

Every note (picked or legato'd) should be equally audible and articulated — the target is that a listener can't tell which notes were picked.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure fretting-hand finger-independence/control drilling on a fixed chromatic shape — no scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge involved.

semi-chromatic-no-lift-finger-angle-dril.title: Semi-Chromatic No-Lift Finger-Angle Drill
semi-chromatic-no-lift-finger-angle-dril.html:
A basic and an advanced fretting-angle exercise.

Basic

Semi-chromatic pattern, frets 5-8 on every string, alternate picked, 4 notes per string. Don't lift a finger until it's needed again on the next string — this forces a proper perpendicular fretting angle, since a bad angle blocks/mutes the next string's note. Listen for unwanted note-overlap dissonance as the mistake signal, not just watching the hand. 5-15 minutes daily.

Advanced

Two repeating one-note-per-string shapes, moved across neck positions, sweep-picked (some pull-offs). Not meant to sound musical — pure finger/angle refinement at speed. Nearly impossible to execute with a flying pinky or bad angle, so it self-corrects both.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure fretting-hand angle and finger-independence mechanics — no scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge involved.

six-step-legato-fretting-hand-workout.title: Six-Step Legato Fretting-Hand Workout
six-step-legato-fretting-hand-workout.html:
Six short fretting-hand exercises, each targeting one legato mistake, ending in applying the fixed mechanics to a real lick/backing track.

The six steps

  1. Finger-independence pattern with a twist: lift each finger the instant it isn't hammering/pulling — don't leave unused fingers pressed down.
  2. Same pattern moved to a "sandwiched" middle string (e.g. G) to force silence on both neighboring strings, not just the outer strings.
  3. A two-shape connecting exercise — practice the transition between two legato shapes until the seam disappears.
  4. A B/E-string exercise specifically training fretting near the fingernail rather than the fleshy fingertip pad.
  5. A full six-string legato scale run, focused entirely on holding one constant wrist angle rather than rotating it per string.
  6. Apply the fixed technique to a real lick or improv over a backing track — not another isolated drill rep.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure fretting-hand mechanics (finger independence, muting, contact point, wrist angle) — no scale/mode/chord-tone knowledge being applied. Per the Drill Index's drill-vs-routine test, this is motor skill, not concept application.

speed-burst-tension-release-picking-dril.title: Speed-Burst Tension-Release Picking Drill
speed-burst-tension-release-picking-dril.html:
A short-burst-then-rest alternate-picking drill, consolidated from three separate BERNTH videos that independently teach the same drill shape on different scale material — a chromatic two-string burst, a one-string 16th/16th-triplet burst, and a 7-note odd-grouping chromatic burst against a drum backing track. All three share the same core mechanism and are one drill with three worked variations, not three separate near-duplicate notes.

The shared mechanism

  • A brief fast burst (4-8 notes) followed by a short rest, repeated. The comparison between the burst and the rest is the actual training signal — it teaches how little picking-attack force a fast burst needs by contrasting it against the felt relaxation of the following rest.
  • Target tension curve is flat, not spiky. Don't alternate between fully tense (during the burst) and fully relaxed (during the rest) — the goal is staying close to relaxed through the burst too, using the rest only as a comparison reference, not a recovery period.
  • Progression: once the burst-then-rest version is controlled, remove the rests and chain the bursts back to back for a pure-speed variant.

Three worked variations

  1. Two-string chromatic, 4+1 grouping. 4 notes on one string (down-up-down-up), 1 downstroke on the next string, chromatic. Trains the specific string-switch of ending a group on an upstroke and immediately needing a downstroke on the next string. Self-check: if the first note on the new string ever lands as anything but a downstroke, hand sync is off.
  2. One-string, straight-16ths-into-16th-triplets. A comfortable mid-tempo run of straight 16th notes (e.g. ascending A minor on one string) with a short burst of 16th-note triplets inserted, then back to the comfortable tempo. Prerequisite: don't start below ~80-90 BPM continuous straight 16ths — this is a speed-extension drill, not a beginner exercise.
  3. Odd 7-note chromatic grouping against a drum backing track. 6 sixteenth notes + 1 eighth note + 1 eighth rest, repeated — the odd count against 4/4 constantly shifts the accent measure to measure, forcing active note-spacing awareness rather than muscle-memory autopilot. A double-bass drum backing track (not just a click) gives continuous feedback on whether the burst lands early/late/exactly on the grid.

How to run it

  • Pick any one variation, or rotate through all three across a week.
  • Keep the picking motion the same physical size at high tempo as at low tempo — a growing motion signals tension and wastes energy/creates noise.
  • Left hand: fingers stay close to the fretboard through the burst, worst-case check is the pattern's highest-to-lowest-finger reversal (pinky-down-to-index).

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure right-hand speed/relaxation and note-spacing dexterity — no scale, mode, or chord-tone knowledge being applied. The school has no concept for motor skill.

ten-daily-fretboard-gliding-exercises.title: Ten Daily Fretboard-Gliding Exercises
ten-daily-fretboard-gliding-exercises.html:
Ten short daily exercises for fretting-hand strength/coordination, picking-hand speed, chord-shape stretching, sweep picking, and away-from-the-guitar rhythm counting. Progress criterion for the sequential ones: once a run can be played 3 times through without stopping, increase the tempo.

1. 1-2-3-4 finger combinations (baseline)

The classic four-fret, one-finger-per-fret ascending/descending exercise. Trains finger strength and hand synchronization. Common mistakes: lifting fingers too high while ascending, letting open strings ring, not staying smooth/connected. Once the basic 1-2-3-4 order gets easy, vary the finger order (2-4-1-3, 3-2-4-1, 4-3-1-2, etc.) to keep it challenging.

2. Anchored-finger version of exercise 1

Same four-fret span, but anchor one finger down for the whole pattern (the ring finger is named as the hardest choice) while the others move. A harder variant of exercise 1 — same benefit, more hand stretch.

3. Right-hand-only 16th-note string-crossing speed drill

Left hand not used at all. Play a full bar of 16th notes on the high E string, then two groups of 16ths alternating E and B strings, then two more groups alternating E and G strings. The catch: the pattern starts on an upstroke on the downbeat, the reverse of the usual downstroke-on-downbeat default — deliberately trains picking-hand speed and string-crossing independent of fretting-hand demands.

4. The "Macroclin" two-string interval pattern

Named after Thomas Macroclin (source of exposure, not necessarily the exercise's originator). Two interleaved patterns at once: the high E string repeats the same four notes throughout, while the string underneath it cycles a 3-2-1-4 finger order using only fingers 1+3 or 2+4 (never both pairs together) — forming either a minor 3rd or a perfect 5th interval shape (exact interval only strictly true on the B/E string pair; treated loosely elsewhere for organizational purposes). A genuine hand-stretch exercise.

5. Satriani's staircase chord-shape drill

Build a "staircase"-shaped chord voicing, invert it, and repeat — a chord-shape/voicing exercise (not a scale run) credited to Joe Satriani, aimed at players who want musical/melodic material rather than pure shred technique. Works across different string sets too.

6. Paul Davids' major-7 arpeggiated chord + fixed-finger reach drill

Two parts, credited to Paul Davids. Part 1: form the same "staircase" chord shape as exercise 5 (a major 7th chord), then pick the notes individually while keeping all fingers planted on their frets — notes should sound picked one at a time, not rung together like a strum (a lighter-touch analogue of sweep picking). Part 2 (much harder): keep all fingers anchored in their original chord-shape position while only the middle and ring fingers are allowed to move to reach the exercise's other notes — genuinely difficult to keep the anchored fingers, especially the middle finger, from drifting.

7. Away-from-the-guitar rhythm counting

No guitar needed — just a metronome app. Practice counting "1-2-3-4" out loud in time. Easy at faster tempos (demoed ~75 BPM); much harder as the tempo drops (demoed down to 50 BPM, then 30 BPM — the metronome's floor). At very slow tempos, count the 16th-note subdivisions between beats out loud ("1-e-and-uh, 2-e-and-uh...") to stay anchored — removes "I don't have my guitar" as an excuse to skip rhythm practice.

8. Sweep-picked version of the Satriani staircase chord

Credited to John Petrucci's Rock Discipline. Take the same staircase chord shapes from exercise 5, but sweep-pick through them instead of arpeggiating with individual picking — see Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes for the general sweep mechanic. Caution: don't tense the shoulder to power the sweep motion — it should come from the wrist/forearm, not the shoulder.

9. Two-finger micro version of exercise 1, playable as trills

A reduced version of exercise 1 using only two fingers at a time instead of all four, playable either as picked notes or as trills (rapid hammer-on/pull-off alternation between the two fretted notes) — likened to a flute player's trilling technique.

10. Pre-playing warm-up routine

Run hands under hot water to increase blood flow before playing. Massage and squeeze the fingers. Stretch fingers backward, then make a grabbing/fist motion, repeated in both directions, for all fingers — recommended 10–15 minutes total (not rushed) to properly condition the hands and reduce injury risk. Optional callus maintenance: trim excess finger-tip skin (not the nail itself) with nail clippers on all fingers that contact the strings.

three-tempo-zone-string-jumping-ladder.title: Three-Tempo-Zone String-Jumping Ladder
three-tempo-zone-string-jumping-ladder.html:
Four progressively harder string-jumping/wrist-independence exercises, built around the idea that picking motion has to adapt across three tempo zones (slow <~90 BPM, mid ~90–160 BPM, fast >~160 BPM) even though grip stays fixed.

The four exercises

  1. Classical-style pattern jumping between non-adjacent strings, always returning to one repeating "dominant string" phrase — wrist-unlocking foundation.
  2. One measure of single-string tremolo picking alternated with one measure of a harder 2-string phrase, aiming to make both feel identical in hand motion.
  3. Switch strings after almost every single stroke — the hardest exercise of the set; brute force fails, precision and relaxation are required.
  4. A fast burst and a mid-tempo phrase chained with no rest between them — requires instant, automatic switching between the two motions.

Why reinforces: [] is correct here

Pure wrist/string-transition mechanics across tempo zones — no scale, mode or chord-tone knowledge involved, just picking-hand motor control.

flea-slap-speed-drill.title: Flea Slap Speed Drill
flea-slap-speed-drill.html:
A single two-bar octave pattern, chromatically walked up the neck to the 12th fret and back down, taught by BassBuzz as the speed drill Flea himself uses — Flea's own on-camera explanation of his slap/pop technique opens the video, then BassBuzz breaks the drill down and adds a tempo ladder and three composition recipes for turning it into original basslines. Distinct from — and a good speed-focused companion to — Slap Bass 5-Level Daily Drill: that drill layers new technique elements (pops, ghosts, hammer-ons, phrasing) one at a time; this one holds the technique constant (pure octave slap-pop) and drills pure speed and endurance by walking one fixed pattern chromatically across the whole neck.

(Minutes is a general starting point, not from the source — the video explicitly does not play the full drill on camera "because it takes forever," so treat 10 minutes as a starting session length and extend once endurance allows.)

Flea's own technique, in his words

Before teaching the drill, BassBuzz cuts to Flea explaining his own slap/pop mechanics directly (from a separate clip): "strike the low string with your thumb with the bone that's in the middle of your thumb," then pop by hooking the middle finger underneath the string and pulling up — Flea's own phrasing: "I will slap down with my thumb and then with my middle finger it will go underneath the D string and pull up." Full general mechanics (angle, anchoring, muting) are already covered in Slap Thumb Technique — Angle, Anchoring, and Muting — this is Flea's own worked description of the same slap-then-pop motion that note's "Fix 1–3" break down mechanically, plus BassBuzz's own "lightning round" refresher layered on top: fresh round-wound strings, low-to-medium action, tone knob up, rotate the forearm at the elbow to strike with the side of the thumb, set a finger under the target string, rotate the forearm back up to pop. That refresher motion — rotate down, strike, set finger, rotate up — is the same single-cycle idea as Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique, described here in Flea-specific language.

The pattern

A repeating two-bar phrase, all notes played as octaves (the same note name, one octave apart):

  • Ignoring the very first note, the pattern is a simple repeating cell: pop–thumb–thumb, pop–thumb–thumb, pop–thumb–thumb..., ending on pop–thumb, where that final thumb doubles as the first note of the next two-bar repeat — so mechanically it's really one repeating cell played continuously, not two distinct bars.
  • Every note is an octave — the low note plus its higher repeat, found by going up two strings and up two frets from the low note (or, working the other direction, down two strings and down two frets). This is the same octave-shape fact documented in Octave Technique — Split-Finger Fretting and Duck-Wrist Prevention; see that note for the wrist/finger-split mechanics of jumping between the two notes.
  • Fretting rule: use index and pinky, not index and ring, once you're past the open string (the open-E starting position obviously needs no fretting-hand octave note yet). BassBuzz flags this explicitly because some students default to index-ring — it "wastes energy" for this shape; index-pinky is the efficient choice. (Not yet documented elsewhere in the vault — new detail from this video, distinct from the low/high split-finger anchoring in Octave Technique — Split-Finger Fretting and Duck-Wrist Prevention, which is about alternating between two anchored fingers across a scale run rather than which two fingers hold a single stationary octave shape.)
  • Chromatic walk: play the two-bar cell twice starting on the open E-string octave, then move the whole shape up one fret and play it twice again, and so on — Flea takes this all the way up to the 12th fret, then works his way back down the same way.

Tempo ladder

Level Tempo Notes
Beginner starting point ~70 BPM Explicit starting tempo from the video for anyone new to slap
Progression +2–3 BPM at a time Small, gradual increments — not big jumps
Intermediate target ~140 BPM Named milestone before pushing toward Flea's own tempo
"Flea tempo" ~218 BPM The tempo of the octave pattern as Flea actually plays it in the source clip — the video's explicit ceiling target ("if you can go faster than that, you get to replace Flea in the Chili Peppers")

Four things to watch while drilling

  1. Accuracy — are you hitting only the strings you mean to hit?
  2. Consistency — are all the notes ringing out clearly for their full duration, not getting choked/muted short?
  3. Breathing — by the halfway point of a full pass most players have stopped breathing normally; a genuine practice reminder, not a joke aside.
  4. (A fourth "watch-for" in the source video is a plug for BassBuzz's paid course — not a technique point, skipped here.)

Why this exact pattern — it's a real Flea line, not just an exercise

BassBuzz points out the drill isn't an arbitrary made-up shape — it's lifted straight from real Red Hot Chili Peppers basslines:

  • "Get Up and Jump" (from the Chili Peppers' 1984 self-titled debut) uses almost exactly this pop-thumb-thumb pattern, minus a small hammer-on at the end of the line.
  • A related variant — the same thumb-thumb-pop cell, just starting on the thumb instead of the pop — shows up in "Dark Necessities" and in the Chili Peppers' cover of "Higher Ground."
  • These are name-checked as pattern matches only (no tab/settings given in this video) — general reference for ear-training/pattern-recognition in the spirit of Steal Like a Bassist — Ear-Training from Known Melodies, not full song breakdowns; no dedicated song notes created from this alone.

Turning the drill into original basslines — three recipes

Once the pattern and tempo ladder are solid, BassBuzz gives three ways to use the same rhythmic cell to write actual lines/solos rather than just drilling the fixed octave shape. All three keep the same pop-thumb-thumb rhythm and swap what pitches go where — a sibling approach to the recipe-driven composition methods in Bass Pentatonic Riff-Writing Recipe and The Bingo Method — Number-Pattern Riff Generation, but built specifically on the slap/pop rhythmic skeleton rather than a plain scale walk or number sequence.

  1. Static bass. Leave every slap (thumb note) on the open E string — that's the fixed "static" bass note — and move only the pops around a scale of choice. Worked example: E minor pentatonic (E, G, A, B, D), one simple shape to frame the notes in, popping a randomly-chosen scale note on each pop while the thumb stays locked to open E.
  2. Moving octaves. Instead of anchoring the slap to one fixed note, move the whole octave shape (both the slap note and its pop octave) around the scale — grab a lower-register run of the same E minor pentatonic scale for the slap notes, then use the same two-strings-up/two-frets-up shape to find each note's higher octave for the corresponding pop. Same rhythm throughout, just a moving root instead of a static one.
  3. Be the Flea. The bigger lesson under the first two recipes: come up with your own one-or-two-bar combination of slaps and pops that sounds good to you, and drill that up to speed the same way — moving it around the bass the same way Flea's original pattern gets moved. The real takeaway isn't copying Flea's exact notes, it's copying the mindset he used to invent the drill in the first place — that's what actually transfers into being able to write original speed drills and slap lines later.

How to run it

  • Nail the mechanical fundamentals first — this drill assumes the Slap Thumb Technique — Angle, Anchoring, and Muting and Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique basics are already in hand; it's a speed/endurance drill layered on top of clean technique, not a substitute for building it.
  • Start at ~70 BPM, walk the full chromatic range (open through 12th fret and back) at that tempo before pushing the metronome up in small 2–3 BPM steps.
  • Once the chromatic walk feels solid, spend separate reps on recipe 1 and 2 above using a scale relevant to whatever you're working on (Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues for shape reference), then try recipe 3 with an original 1–2 bar cell of your own.
  • A free PDF with sheet music/tab for the drill is named in the source video's description — not yet pulled into the vault; grab it from the video description if working from tab rather than by ear.
