Routine 2 — Sweep arpeggio shape through all 12 keys (technique + rhythm + fretboard + theory)
Routine 3 — Backing-track position/subdivision improv (all five categories — the most complete of the four)
Routine 4 — Spoken major scale in every key (theory + rhythm + fretboard, weakest of the four for technique)

the-practice-priority-pyramid.title: The Practice Priority Pyramid
the-practice-priority-pyramid.html:
Jared's (Sound Guitar Lessons) top-level framework for what order practice fundamentals need to be established in, plus the three-part discipline he runs within it — the connective philosophy behind the concrete category/spreadsheet system he walks through in How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop), the payoff video that Practice Log #1 first previewed and Practice Log #5 partially demonstrated. Jared's dedicated deep-dive on Stage 1 specifically — the "cut it in half" minimum-commitment rule, the missed-day quota system, and the "runner's itch" framing — lives on "how much should i practice guitar?" (the surprising answer that will keep you going), folded into the Stage 1 bullet below. Same channel/author as The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice and Backward Chaining Practice, both of which are applied instances of the "milestone" mechanic below. Where The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice answers what topics a complete practice system needs to cover, and Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills answers how to drill a single piece of material, this note answers a third, earlier question: what has to be true before "hard practice" is even a good idea, and in what order do you build it.

The five stages

Presented explicitly as a pyramid — each stage is a precondition for the next, not a parallel option to pick from:

  1. Consistency. Show up, any amount of time — Jared's own baseline example: "5 minutes a day, 10 minutes a day, whatever... I don't care if it's 20 minutes three times a week." Content doesn't matter yet at this stage; showing up does. The concrete mechanism for actually hitting this stage — deliberately explained as the "surprising answer" in Jared's dedicated deep-dive on the question "how much should I practice": take whatever amount of time you think you want to practice, then cut it in half, and commit to that half as your daily minimum (2 hrs you want → 1 hr commitment; 1 hr wanted → 30 min commitment; 30 min wanted → 15 min commitment). The reasoning ties directly back to this stage's priority ordering: an ambitious target is easy to blow past on a good day but easy to break on a hard one, and breaking the streak costs more than an ambitious number is worth, since Consistency outranks everything else in the pyramid. Critically, the minimum is a floor, not a ceiling — you can always do more when you have time or energy (Jared's own current minimum is 1 hour/day of jazz guitar, despite training in an 8-hrs/day conservatory environment, and he regularly plays well past it). A missed-day "quota" system pairs with the halved minimum: if a day is missed, make it up by roughly doubling on a later day rather than treating the gap as a failure — flagged by Jared himself as optional/"a little hardcore," not a requirement. Sustained enough, consistency produces a "runner's itch" — it starts to feel wrong not to practice, the signal the habit has taken hold independent of willpower. — Jared, "how much should i practice guitar?" (the surprising answer that will keep you going)
  2. Enjoyment. Once you're consistent, optimize for what you'll actually enjoy doing — without this, consistency won't hold, because you won't want to come back tomorrow. (general starting point on how to find it: ask directly "what's going to make this fun/nourishing" — e.g. working with recordings you love, or sight-reading fresh material if that's what's satisfying)
  3. Goals. Once you're consistently enjoying it, get real clarity on outcomes — what music you want to play, why, and where/how you want to play it (a specific piece finished and recorded, a repertoire list, a technical benchmark). Framed as often "tricky" and genuinely personal — Jared's own goals split into technique goals (pursued partly as their own game, independent of any specific piece) and repertoire goals (get this piece down, played all the way through, recorded).
  4. Design/definition. Once goals exist, build the literal bridge from where you are to each one — the actual curriculum, exercise list, and rules. Explicitly counts as real, productive practice time, not procrastination — Jared describes deliberately allowing himself to spend a chunk of official practice time just designing/refining the system itself ("even if it takes me half an hour... that is when things really shifted for me"). The one hard boundary he draws against this becoming avoidance: it has to be honest, ongoing work that's actually moving you toward practicing, not a permanent substitute for practicing (see also the "finish the system, then practice it" rule on Practice Log #1, which is the same discipline stated as a hard rule rather than a guideline).
  5. Deliberate/challenging practice. Practice genuinely at the edge of your ability — the stage most people never actually reach, per Jared, precisely because they try to jump straight to it without stages 1–4 in place first. His claim: with the other four stages solid, deliberate practice stops feeling like grinding and starts feeling like "an endorphin workout" you can't wait to repeat, because every session has clear direction and a known target. Without the earlier stages, hard practice with no visible destination just produces quitting. The research case for why this stage matters at all — Anders Ericsson's Peak, cited directly: progress halts the instant a skill stops being challenging (not gradually — right at that point), and a doctor-performance study showing skill can decline, not just plateau, once a task stops demanding anything new. Full extraction, plus the named "repetition with manipulation" method and parameter-locked exercise design, on Repetition with Manipulation (Getting Past a Plateau). — Jared, How to Get Better at Guitar - The science of getting past a plateau

Milestones, Rotation, Variation — the operating mechanic

The three-part discipline that runs inside stage 5, applied uniformly across every exercise in his system (and, per Jared, "imagine that with every exercise and every category of practicing" — this is meant to generalize, not stay confined to guitar technique):

  • Milestones. Every exercise needs an explicit "done" condition before you can know when to move on — without one, "we're truly just flying blind." The gate itself varies by exercise: sometimes a single perfect pass (Angular Reach Exercise, the finger-permutation warm-up), sometimes a clean-streak count (The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice's escalating rep target, Backward Chaining Practice's 3-or-5-in-a-row token system), sometimes a checked-tempo-then-required-increase rule (Circle-of-Fourths One-Position Scale Drill). The common thread across all of them: a real, defined bar, not "practice until it feels done."
  • Rotation. Cycle between multiple exercises and categories — within a single session, across days, or across the whole system — instead of grinding one thing to full completion before ever coming back to anything else. This is the same underlying idea as interleaving on Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills (Daniel Seriff, same "don't mass-practice one thing" logic, different channel), and it's what keeps a large system's early material fresh without a separate spaced-repetition pass bolted on — later-stage rotation naturally re-exposes earlier-checked-off items (documented concretely on The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice's "refresh is built in" section). Jared's own dedicated deep-dive on why this works names the mechanism directly: interleaving (mixing item order) plus spaced repetition (widening review gaps on a forgetting curve) — cited research on Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills puts interleaved practice at roughly triple the test performance of blocked practice (63% vs. 20%), at the cost of visibly messier in-the-moment accuracy (60% vs. 89%) — and gives the concrete scheduling form of Rotation as a 10–12 item "batch/collection" rotated as one project rather than finished item-by-item, worked out fully on Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills. — Jared, Spaced Repetition Method & Interleaving Practice: Boost Your Music Retention 2-3x!
  • Variation. When something checked-off comes back around in rotation, don't repeat it identically — vary it so the return visit still pushes growth instead of just reconfirming what's already secure. Simplest form named: faster tempo (matches Circle-of-Fourths One-Position Scale Drill's "never repeat a checked-off tempo" rule exactly), but Jared is explicit there are "so many variations" beyond just speed — a different pick, a different right-hand pattern, a different fingering approach (Angular Reach Exercise's chord/sweep variants of the same base shape are a concrete example of this in practice).

Why the "video game" framing matters

Jared repeatedly describes a fully-designed system (stages 1–4 solid) as feeling like "my video game" — not because the practice gets easier, but because ambiguity disappears: sit down, see the highlighted cell/next item, and dive straight in with zero decision-making overhead. The claimed payoff is emotional as much as technical — showing up becomes something you crave rather than something you have to talk yourself into (his own anecdote: not missing a single practice day through two consecutive colds, purely because he didn't want to miss it, not out of discipline).

Applying this to scattered material across multiple courses/books

For anyone with many disconnected courses, books, or loosely-taught YouTube exercises rather than one coherent curriculum:

  • Don't finish one course before starting the next. Treat each course/book as its own rotation category (same logic as the categories above) — work a bit on one, check off whatever gets checked off, then rotate to the next course/category next session, rather than working straight through one course front-to-back before touching another.
  • Exception: true sequenced-beginner material should still be finished in order — a ground-up beginner foundation course is the one case where linear completion is still correct; skill-specific courses (chord melody, single-note improvisation, a technique deep-dive) have no required order relative to each other and should rotate.
  • A good exercise is one someone already designed for a specific result — don't reinvent it. Cites Giuliani's 120 Right-Hand Studies (worked through as part of the Warm-up & Technique category, see How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop)) as the model: someone already solved "what are the useful permutations here," so use the existing resource instead of re-deriving it from scratch.
  • Minimal tracking is enough. A stack of PDF books plus a plain checklist, or literally pencil-and-paper checkmarks, does the same job as a spreadsheet — the tracking tool is incidental, the milestone/rotation/variation structure is what matters.

three-stage-warm-up-physical-mental-reso.title: Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance)
three-stage-warm-up-physical-mental-reso.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — a warm-up framework built on three named principles rather than a fixed exercise list, each principle mapped to one of the three underlying components of music itself: physical mechanism → rhythm, mental faculty → harmony, resonance principle → melody. The exercises below are the worked examples, but the framework is meant to be regenerated with new exercises once the three principles are understood — "I can just make up exercises" once the categories are internalized.

Stage 1 — Physical: right-hand/left-hand coordination

Warms the physical mechanism that produces rhythm. Worked exercises:

  • Chromatic scale the full length of the neck, ascending and descending, shifting position by moving up a fret with the first finger each time (one-finger-per-fret, moving the whole hand up the neck rather than staying in one box).
  • A full major scale, same up-the-neck approach, shifting through positions the same way as the chromatic run above.
  • Major pentatonic through the cycle of fifths, ascending and descending — start on one key's pentatonic box, move to the next key up a fifth, and so on around the cycle.

Stage 2 — Mental: speed up the thinking process

Same drills as Stage 1, but with a deliberate twist that forces faster real-time decision-making rather than rote repetition: instead of always running a full pattern all the way up then all the way down in one key, change key partway through — e.g. start the pentatonic-cycle-of-fifths exercise on G, ascend, then switch to the next key mid-pattern on the way back down rather than completing the full descent in the original key. The mental faculty being trained is the same one Continuous Scale Exercise drills for tune-specific key changes — find the closest correct note in the new key and keep moving — but here it's practiced as a warm-up in the abstract, not tied to a specific tune's chord-scale map. → Continuous Scale Exercise

Stage 3 — Resonance: singing as its own intelligence

Activated by singing while playing — described as a principle with "its own intelligence," independent of the mental/harmonic faculty. The strongest evidence for treating it as genuinely separate: after deliberately scrambling all conscious harmonic knowledge (see the retuning experiment below), singing every note stayed intact and accurate even though naming or predicting those same notes intellectually was no longer possible — the resonance principle kept working when the mental faculty had nothing to contribute. → Vocal Harmony

Practice discipline: cycle all three, all the time — not just at the start of a session

The three stages aren't a fixed warm-up sequence to run once and then abandon; the discipline is to keep jumping between all three principles throughout playing, not only during warm-up: always singing while playing (resonance), always attending to touch and tone, and always keeping a mental overview a step ahead of the current moment (thinking ahead, tracking harmonic integrity) rather than only reacting in real time. Framed explicitly as a defense of the "mental"/intellectual faculty in music — a commonly distrusted faculty, but only a liability when it dominates the other two rather than working alongside them (see the retuning story below, where the mental faculty had become too dominant and needed deliberate suppression, not elimination).

Retuning as a mental-pattern reset (an extreme Stage-2/Stage-3 rebalancing move)

A concrete story of what happens when the mental faculty gets too dominant relative to the other two: reached a point where seeing a chord symbol (e.g. G7) meant already knowing exactly what it would sound like before playing it — no surprise left, described as feeling "dry" and boring, a sign the mental/pattern-recognition layer had crowded out the physical and resonance layers. The fix was to retune the guitar to an unfamiliar tuning, which "obliterates" all of the accumulated mental/pattern knowledge at once (a known chord shape no longer produces the known sound) while leaving the physical connection to the instrument intact. The genuinely surprising result: singing (Stage 3, resonance) remained completely unaffected — every note could still be sung accurately even with zero conscious knowledge of what the retuned strings would produce, which is offered as direct evidence that the resonance principle really is independent of, not downstream of, the mental/harmonic faculty. After a period of relying on retuned exploration, the mental faculty was deliberately rebuilt for the new tuning (learning the shapes in the new tuning explicitly) before eventually returning to standard tuning — the point of the exercise wasn't the alternate tuning itself, but the deliberate, temporary rebalancing of which of the three principles was allowed to lead.

Stage 3 — Resonance: singing as its own intelligence
Practice discipline: cycle all three, all the time — not just at the start of a session

vision-driven-practice-and-the-overwhelm.title: Vision-Driven Practice and the Overwhelm Reflex
vision-driven-practice-and-the-overwhelm.html:
Part of Song Practice's practice-methodology material — Jared Borkowski's answer, spread across four separate Q&A answers in the same video, to "how do I stay organized when there's infinite guitar material to practice." The throughline: there is no objectively required practice material — only material in service of a genuinely felt, specific goal ("vision") — and managing the resulting overwhelm is itself a skill to deliberately train, not a one-time organizational fix. Complements Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills (Daniel Seriff's session-structuring mechanics) and The Five Essentials of Guitar Practice (Seriff's what-to-cover framework) — this note is closer to the why layer underneath those how layers: it doesn't prescribe a session structure, it prescribes a way of choosing what belongs in one at all.

Nothing is objectively required — only conditional on a stated goal

Core rule, stated directly: "there's nothing you need to practice, unless you have a big if." No single skill — reading music, playing chords, single-note lines, sight-reading — is mandatory to be a great or successful musician; cites Paul McCartney (doesn't read music, arguably as successful as a musician gets) as the counter-proof to "you have to learn to read." The "if" is always a specific, named goal: if you want to join a guitar quartet that requires reading, then practice reading. Before adding anything to a practice list, name the "if" it's actually in service of — a piece of material with no attached goal is exactly the kind of thing that produces the "lots of jazz chords, but I'm not making music" disorganized feeling this note starts from.

Disorganized practice is usually a vision problem, not a discipline problem

Diagnosed directly against a self-described case (lots of teachers, lots of Santana riffs, lots of jazz chords, but "not making music," feeling disorganized): the fix isn't more material or more discipline, it's a genuinely clear end point. Concrete framing questions to actually answer, not just consider:

  • What kind of music do you want to play? What inspires you the most?
  • What's a specific, finished, start-to-finish piece of music you want to be able to play?
  • What does "done" mean for it — comfortable performance level? A rough take recorded on your phone? Just understanding the theory of it? All are legitimate, but pick one on purpose.

Once the goal is rock-solid clear, the steps in between either become obvious or can be deliberately invented. Practicing whatever material an outside source (a teacher, a video, "someone online") recommended, with no felt personal connection to why, is what produces the hectic/disorganized feeling — the fix is reconnecting each practice item to a real, personally-held goal, not abandoning structure altogether.

"Directness" — learn what you can apply right now, not what seems generically useful

Named concept, credited to Scott Young's book Ultra Learning: directness. Don't learn something because it seems like a good thing to know in the abstract — learn something you have a direct, immediate application for. The mechanism: applying a skill right away is what makes it actually stick as learning rather than sitting as inert, stockpiled information. Practical filter for any new practice item: can I use this for something I actually want to do soon? If not, it may not be worth the practice slot right now even if it's "good to know" in general.

Start the hard goal now, adapted down — don't wait to "be ready"

Answering whether to chase an ambitious goal immediately (a full solo chord-melody arrangement of a jazz standard) or wait until finishing prerequisite material first: go toward the exciting, inspiring goal right away — don't wait. The one caveat is to adapt it down to your current skill level rather than attempting the full difficult version cold: play just the melody, play it much slower, learn just the roots of the chords running through it, and build up from there. "You can manipulate anything difficult to make it easier" — and getting practice specifically at doing that adaptation (watering a hard goal down into something currently playable) is a transferable skill in its own right, separate from the piece itself. The trap this avoids: practicing prerequisite material for a long stretch ("a year") before ever touching the actual goal, by which point the goal-connection and motivation that made it worth doing in the first place has usually faded.

Rotate practice material — and come back right before you'd forget it

A second, independent piece of the same answer: rotate through multiple practice items rather than finishing one before starting the next. Could be as few as three things or as many as a hundred — your call, and it can be either loosely inspiration-driven (jump around by feel) or strict (a set rotation order). The discipline that actually matters: come back to each item right before you'd have forgotten it — that's framed as the single highest-leverage timing for a return rep, far better than either over-massing one item to full mastery before moving on, or leaving something so long between touches that it has to be relearned from scratch. The alternative (nail something once, then don't touch it again for a long stretch) reliably loses the material. (This is the same underlying spaced-return mechanism as Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's interleaving/retrieval-practice logic from a different channel — two teachers converging on "rotate and return before forgetting" as the core lever, independent of session-length or timer mechanics.)

Overwhelm itself is a skill to practice, not a problem to solve once

The final, capstone answer in the video, framed as the big question saved for last on purpose: the amount of available guitar material is functionally infinite, so feeling overwhelmed by it is the default state, not a sign something is wrong with your organization. "You're never going to practice everything ever" — the reframe on offer is to treat not-getting-overwhelmed as its own muscle to deliberately train, the same way you'd train a scale or a technique, rather than as a one-time checklist or planning problem to be solved and closed out.

  • Practical, moment-to-moment gauge (not a comprehensive plan): if a practice session — even a short one, 20 minutes — makes time slip away and leaves you feeling nourished/excited rather than dutiful, that's the right material for right now. This is a felt check, run per-session, not a long-range curriculum decision.
  • Framing: close to a meditative practice — quiet the noise of "everything there is to do" and narrow to the one thing in front of you. The target feeling is described as "this is exactly where I'm supposed to be right now," explicitly contrasted with the stress-feeling of being pulled in many directions simultaneously; landing on the former is treated as evidence the overwhelm-management is working, independent of how much material got covered.
  • Standing personal habit as an anchor: Jared runs the identical specific warm-up every single time he sits down to play, without skipping it — offered as one concrete way to give a session a stable, low-decision starting point before the "what should I even work on" question has to be answered at all. (Warm-up content itself not detailed in this video; a free PDF + video demo is offered at soundguitarlessons.com/warmup — not yet pulled into the vault.)

woodshedding-changes-with-a-looper.title: Woodshedding Changes with a Looper
woodshedding-changes-with-a-looper.html:
A practice-order method for working out lines over a chord progression using a hardware looper pedal with a built-in drum machine (or a DAW backing track doing the same job) as the rhythmic/harmonic anchor, rather than practicing free of any groove. Sibling to Backward Chaining Practice (a different practice-order methodology, same channel) and the physical-practice half of Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes's chunk-then-connect strategy.

Why loop the chords instead of playing free

Playing ideas with no backing reference lets you invent nice-sounding lines, but you can't tell whether they'll actually fit the pocket of the groove — timing and phrasing only prove out against a real rhythmic/harmonic bed. Looping the chord progression with a drum groove underneath keeps you "rhythmically and harmonically accountable" while you work out phrasing, so what you land on is something you know will sit correctly, not just something that sounds fine in isolation. — Jack Ruch, How using the TELEPORT can IMPROVE your PRACTICE routine!

The loop-and-work routine

  1. Record 2–4 bars of the chord chunk you're targeting into the looper, with the built-in drum machine running underneath for rhythmic support — a one-measure count-in before recording makes it easy to lock the chunk in cleanly on the first take. A dedicated record button with no secondary functions and no latency (as opposed to loopers where record shares a footswitch with other functions) matters here — any lag or mis-hit while trying to nail the chunk's start breaks the whole loop and forces a redo.
  2. Stop the loop and work out ideas against silence first — look at the chord shapes and their corresponding arpeggios in position, without the groove running, to plan targets and connecting tones before trying to execute them in time (mirrors the out-of-time stage of Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes's two-stage drill).
  3. Start the loop and test the idea against the groove — play the planned line over the looped chunk to hear whether the phrasing actually locks with the drum machine's rhythm; expect flubs and ugly note choices early on, and use the loop's low-pressure repetition to iterate rather than aiming for a clean take immediately.
  4. Chunk long progressions into 2–4-chord units, work each in isolation, then expand. A long, twisty chord progression gets broken into small pieces (e.g. the first 3 chords, then the next 2–5–1 unit, then the turnaround) — each chunk is looped and worked separately until it's comfortable, then adjacent chunks are combined, and finally the whole progression is looped so the connected phrasing can be run start to finish. Same "chunk-then-connect" logic as Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes § Chunk-then-connect, here driven by the looper's per-section record/clear workflow instead of just mental sectioning.
  5. Swap drum grooves/tempos to match the tune's feel before looping — e.g. an eighth-note rock groove at 86 BPM for one progression, a slower 128-ballad-feel groove for a gospel-style progression — so the chunk being drilled is practiced against a rhythmic context that actually matches the target song, not a generic click.

Worked example: a Ray Charles–style gospel progression

Looped in chunks over a slowed 128-ballad drum groove: E♭maj → G7 → Cm (targeted first, chord tones addressed individually per chord since the move isn't a simple diatonic run), then B♭m7 → E♭9 → A♭7 (a secondary ii–V resolving to the ♭IV rather than the I — see The ii-V-I for the general "251 as a landing-spot device" framing), each chunk looped and soloed over individually before being tied into the full progression. — Jack Ruch, How using the TELEPORT can IMPROVE your PRACTICE routine!

The gear behind it: what makes a looper good for this

Reviewing the Teleport (a new looper pedal with an app for sharing recorded loops/performances with other players): the features that actually matter for this practice use are a built-in drum machine (locks parts in rhythmically without a separate backing track), a one-measure count-in on record, and a dedicated, single-function record button with virtually no latency — avoiding the sync problems that come from loopers where record shares a button with other functions, especially when layering multiple rhythm parts. Nate's own looper, the Line 6 DL4, is a comparable class of tool for this exact routine — pair the drum-groove-and-count-in workflow above with it, or with a DAW backing track (Jack Ruch notes he mostly uses his own DAW and pre-made backing tracks nowadays rather than a pedal looper day to day). — Jack Ruch, How using the TELEPORT can IMPROVE your PRACTICE routine!

goal-tiered-practice-and-the-self-taught.title: Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments
goal-tiered-practice-and-the-self-taught.html:
BassBuzz's framework for structuring self-taught bass practice without a teacher — six "commandments," delivered as a comedy bit (a self-serious "bass ghost" narrator) wrapped around a genuinely concrete practice-design system. The throughline: a self-taught player's biggest failure mode isn't lack of material, it's picking the wrong material with no way to check whether it's actually useful — the video's opening cautionary examples are a player stuck at "barely progressed beyond 6 months" after two years, and one stuck unable to play a single full song after 14 years. The fix is a three-tier goal ladder (long/medium/short) that turns "what should I practice today" from a guess into a derived answer, plus four practice categories (songs, technique, fretboard, theory) to check the ladder's short-term goals against so nothing gets skipped. This is the same underlying problem — and largely the same answer, "clarify the goal, then let the goal choose the material" — that Vision-Driven Practice and the Overwhelm Reflex documents from a guitar channel; the two notes are companions from different instruments converging on the same fix, worth reading together.

Commandment 1 — Set thy goals: the long/medium/short-term ladder

Core mechanism: without goals you can't judge whether any given exercise or theory topic is useful for you — a routine that's great for one player (e.g. jazz walking-bass drills) is a waste of time for another (e.g. a beginner who just wants a Chili Peppers bassline). The fix is three linked goal tiers, each solving a different failure mode of the tier above it:

  • Long-term goal — the destination, months out (e.g. "play in my friend's bar band," or "learn Hysteria by Muse"). Motivating, but if it's the only goal you set, you'll feel like a failure for the entire stretch before you're actually close to it — a beginner aiming straight at a hard song like Hysteria won't get meaningfully near it for months, and will "feel like a failure the whole time" with only the long goal to check progress against.
  • Medium-term goal — a process commitment, not an outcome: what you do, not where you get. (examples given) "Practice 20 minutes a day, 4x/week for the next 3 months" for a moderate long-term goal; "an hour a day, 5x/week for 6 months" for an ambitious one. Named as the fix for demotivation specifically because it's something you fully control — you either showed up today or you didn't, independent of how far off the long-term goal still feels. Every session is a checked box, which is concrete progress even when the long-term goal itself hasn't moved yet.
  • Short-term goal — the actual day-to-day practice material, derived by breaking the long-term goal down into its component skills. (worked examples) For a "play in a bar band" long goal: daily focus on solid rhythm-with-a-drummer and building simple basslines over a chord chart. For a "learn an advanced song right out of the gate" long goal: daily plucking-speed practice and fretting-hand coordination work.

The catch the video names directly: handing you those two worked examples above is a shortcut — as a self-taught player without a teacher's expertise, you have to do the long→short breakdown yourself for your own goal, which is exactly where self-taught players "flounder, practice the wrong stuff, and rage-post on Reddit years later." Commandments 2–4 exist specifically to give the four categories to break any long-term goal down against, so the breakdown step isn't a total guess.

Commandment 2 — Learn thy songs early (motivation as fuel, not a reward)

Songs, not drills, are what make people want to keep playing bass — cited stat: per Fender's own data, 90% of new guitarists quit within a year (BassBuzz applies this to bass as the same cautionary number). The claim: skipping songs in favor of "earning" them after enough exercise-grinding starves the exact motivation that keeps a self-taught player showing up, so songs belong in the rotation from early on, not gated behind a technique threshold. Secondary benefits beyond motivation: playing real songs naturally trains rhythm, technique, and ear at the same time, rather than needing separate isolated drills for each. No-theory alternative also offered: if learning existing songs isn't the draw, freeform noodling/making up your own parts by ear is a legitimate substitute for staying inspired — but the video is explicit this only works in combination with Commandment 3 (technique), since without coordination you can't execute either a learned song or your own noodled ideas.

Commandment 3 — Suffer not poor technique: the exercise-quality checklist

Technique = the physical skills (fretting, plucking, muting) — named as the usual answer to "why can't I play my goal song yet." Since there's effectively an infinite pool of possible exercises and no teacher to pick for you, the video gives a checklist that makes almost any exercise effective, rather than trying to name "the right" exercises:

  1. Focus on how you play, not what you play — the exercise choice matters less than the quality of attention on your own execution while doing it.
  2. Practice with a metronome or drum track — timing discipline built into every rep, not bolted on later.
  3. Start slower than you think you should.
  4. Don't speed up until you can play it decently at least 5 times in a row (explicit clean-reps gate before advancing tempo) — the same clean-reps-before-progression logic as the guitar-side Backward Chaining Practice and The Check-Off Method for Repertoire Practice gating mechanics, applied here as a bass-agnostic exercise rule rather than a specific combination order.
  5. Track progress in a simple journal.

Applies to BassBuzz's own catalog of fretting/plucking/muting drills already in the vault — see Fretting-Hand Strength, Stretch, Stamina, and Finger Control, String Crossing and Plucking Patterns, Bass Note Muting Technique, and Fretting-Hand Finger Independence Drill — this checklist is the meta-layer for running any of them well, not a replacement for them.

Commandment 4 — Make thy life easier: fretboard knowledge + theory as force multipliers

Framed as optional-but-much-harder-without: you can become a solid bassist without either, but both remove a specific tax on every song you try to learn:

  • Fretboard knowledge (note names + where they live on the neck, plus recognizing reusable shapes/patterns) — the payoff is turning a tab into chunked, familiar information instead of "random meaningless numbers" you have to memorize one at a time. See Bass Fretboard Note Memorization System for the vault's existing note-naming drill this feeds directly into.
  • Theory — not framed as mandatory for everyone, but named as accelerating three things specifically: understanding what you're playing, memorizing songs faster, and coming up with your own original parts. Points at BassBuzz's own dedicated theory video (see Music Theory for Bass) rather than teaching theory content in this video.

The four-category checklist, assembled: songs (Commandment 2) + technique (Commandment 3) + fretboard + theory (Commandment 4) = the full beginner coverage map. Worked example applying it (goal: learn "Hysteria" by Muse): songs — covered by definition; technique — will need heavy practice, this is the hard part of that particular song; fretboard/theory — not strictly critical if you're willing to just memorize the tab number-by-number, but knowing the note names and which scale they come from makes memorization faster and keeps the other categories from going neglected while all the practice time pours into technique. Sample short-term daily routine given for an ambitious (1 hr/day) medium goal: warm-up 5 min, scales 5 min, fretting exercises 10 min, plucking exercises 10 min, song practice in small chunks 15 min, free/fun playing for decompression 5 min — offered as (general starting point), scaled to however ambitious the medium-term goal actually is.

Commandment 5 — Avoid common self-taught pitfalls (quickfire list)

A named grab-bag of mistakes the video calls out as chronic and progress-killing, each with a one-line fix:

Problem Solution
Buying the wrong bass Get a 4-string fretted bass you actually enjoy playing, and get it professionally set up.
Pressing way too hard with the fretting fingers/thumb Do minimum-viable-pressure (MVP) exercises — now detailed in a later BassBuzz video: rest a finger on the string with zero pressure (confirm via a silent pluck, no note sounds), add pressure gradually until the string just starts to rattle against the fret, then add only a tiny bit more until the note goes clean, and hold exactly that pressure — no harder. Named as something to actively re-check even by experienced players, since pressure creeps back up the longer a session runs. Compare Fretting-Hand Strength, Stretch, Stamina, and Finger Control's Exercise 1, which covers the opposite failure — not pressing hard/close enough — so the two notes bracket the correct pressure range from both sides. → BassBuzz, Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix)
Putting stickers on the frets to mark note names Never do this — named as a hard no, no nuance given.
Learning bass only through Musician/Guitar Hero/Rocksmith-style games Treat those as dessert, not dinner — supplement real lessons/practice with them, don't substitute.
Practicing unplugged Use an amp or headphones — you need to hear the instrument the way it actually sounds, and it's more fun/motivating.
Leaving the bass in its case or closet between sessions Keep it out on a stand (or on the couch) so it's always ready to pick up on impulse.
Learning entirely alone and feeling isolated Build musical community — jam with friends, or engage on bass-focused online forums.

Commandment 6 — Thou shalt be patient (the actual #1 failure cause)

Named directly as the single biggest cause of self-taught bassists failing — explicitly contrasted against marketing claims of "magic 30-day transformation." Self-teaching a skill is a long game: not a perfect routine, not unbroken daily consistency, but showing up repeatedly past the point the initial excitement has worn off, with progress that's gradual rather than dramatic. The video's closing move ties patience back to Commandment 1's short-term goal problem: since picking the right day-to-day material only gets harder to sustain as months pass, it points to a companion "what order to learn everything on bass" curriculum video as a way to keep short-term goals fresh over a 6–12 month horizon — that companion video is now in the vault: What to Learn on Bass (in Order), distilled into The BassBuzz 55-Step Bass Learning Roadmap. Its own Level 2 (Step 21) independently names "notice your progress" as the single most-missed self-taught habit — the same diagnosis as this commandment, from the opposite direction (patience vs. progress-blindness are two faces of the same failure to see gradual movement).

Commandment 2 — Learn thy songs early (motivation as fuel, not a reward)
Commandment 3 — Suffer not poor technique: the exercise-quality checklist

improvising-over-a-drone-track.title: Improvising Over a Drone Track
improvising-over-a-drone-track.html:
BassBuzz's answer to "how do you actually get a scale in your bones" beyond memorizing a shape or copying a written riff — freeform improvisation against a sustained drone note. Framed explicitly as low-stakes ("there's really no way to go wrong") and positioned as the deepest of the three internalization steps in its source lesson (shape drilling, then riff-copying, then this) because it forces the mind-to-finger connection to work generatively — hearing an idea and finding it — instead of only recalling a memorized pattern. Taught here on the bass scale shapes in Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues, but the method itself is instrument-agnostic — any fretted or keyed instrument with a scale shape under the fingers can use the same drone-improv approach. Distinct from Scale Degree Ear Training's drone method, which drills singing/labeling each degree's feeling-state by ear — this is instrumental free-play against the drone, not a vocal/labeling exercise, though both use a sustained drone as the reference tone.

Setup

Get a drone track — any sustained note matching the scale's root/starting note (a held tone, pad, or looped bass note underneath). The drone removes the need for a fixed groove or chord progression, so rhythm stays completely open while pitch stays anchored to one center.

Method 1 — reorder the scale by ear

Start by playing the scale straight through in order (works for any of the shapes — major or major pentatonic first, minor or minor pentatonic later), then deliberately break from the in-order pattern and follow curiosity note to note ("I wonder if I went from this note to this note... oh, that sounded like that"). No wrong answers — every note in the scale is, by definition, guaranteed to work against the drone.

Method 2 — scale-degree number sequences

A more structured, analytical alternative to pure ear-following: play sequences of scale-degree numbers rather than free-following the ear — e.g. the 1st note, then the 3rd note, or longer runs like 2-4-3-5-4-6-5-7-6-8. A way to systematically explore combinations of scale degrees instead of relying purely on instinct. Either method — or anything in between — counts; the point is deliberately playing the notes out of their default order, not picking the "correct" one of the two.

Rhythm stays flexible

Because the drone imposes no groove, rhythm is free — play a loose, flowing melody, or lock into your own stuck-in groove. Neither is more correct; both count as valid practice reps.

Why it works

Doing any version of this drills the scale at a deeper level than shape-memorization or riff-copying alone (called out directly as going deeper than most "shape regurgitators" ever get) — it's simultaneously ear training (recognizing what a degree/interval sounds like before playing it) and finger-coordination training, because the player has to generate a sound in their head and then execute it, rather than recall a pre-learned pattern.

Applying it

Warm up on the scale shape(s) being drilled that day first, then spend 5–10 minutes on the improv itself. Its source lesson schedules two dedicated sessions across a 7-day routine — one for major/major pentatonic, one for minor/minor pentatonic — see Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues § The 7-day practice structure for the full week.
secs: Method 1 — reorder the scale by ear

noodling-as-a-scheduled-reward-the-peak-.title: Noodling as a Scheduled Reward (The Peak-End Rule)
noodling-as-a-scheduled-reward-the-peak-.html:
A session-structuring rule for where unstructured, no-agenda "noodling" belongs in a practice session — not whether to do it at all. BassBuzz's Josh reframes noodling (aimless, exploratory playing with no goal) from a guilty pleasure or a waste of time into a deliberate, scheduled tool, on the strength of one simple placement rule: do the structured work first, and save noodling for the very end of the session. This is a companion to the vault's other session-structuring notes (Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's session-length/timer rules, The Practice Priority Pyramid's ordering logic) but answers a different question than any of them: not what to practice or how long, but how a session should feel by the time it ends, and why that matters for whether you come back tomorrow.

The core mechanism: the peak-end rule

People's memory and evaluation of an experience is disproportionately shaped by its peak moment and, especially, by how it ends — not by an accurate average of the whole thing. Illustrated with a movie analogy: a mediocre film with a great ending is remembered fondly; a good film with a bad ending leaves you feeling bad walking out, even though more of the actual runtime was enjoyable. Applied to practice: your felt memory of "practicing today" is set largely by the last few minutes of the session, regardless of how the middle of it went.

The practical rule this produces: structured/hard practice work first, unstructured noodling last. You still get the productive work done — nothing about this delays or skips the actual exercises, drills, or repertoire — but the session's last impression, and therefore the memory you form of "what practicing feels like," is the fun, pressure-free part. That positive last impression is what pulls you back to the instrument again tomorrow, which is the actual leverage point: this is a motivation/retention technique, not a skill-acquisition technique.

Noodling placed carelessly (e.g., at the start, or scattered with no rule at all) doesn't get this benefit — Josh names this directly as his own guitar-practice mistake vs. his bass practice, where he applied the end-of-session placement consistently. The noodling itself isn't the variable; where in the session it lands is.

Why noodling itself is worth defending (not just where to put it)

Before the placement rule, the video makes the case that noodling is not wasted time to begin with — worth keeping on the page since the placement rule only matters if noodling stays in the rotation at all:

  • Slash wrote the "Sweet Child O' Mine" riff from a random noodle — a genuine hit, not a discarded warm-up.
  • Jam bands (Phish, the Grateful Dead) built entire careers on noodling — extended improvisation is the art form, not a departure from it.
  • The Offspring's guitarist performs under the stage name "Noodles" — a direct nod to the same idea as an identity, not just a technique.

A ready-to-use application

  1. Run the actual planned session first — drills, trouble-spot work, repertoire, whatever the day's plan calls for (pairs naturally with Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills's rotation/timer structure for that portion).
  2. When the planned work is done, switch to fully unstructured noodling with no goal — no metronome, no checklist, no correctness bar — for the last stretch of the session, however long feels natural.
  3. Don't front-load noodling as a warm-up instead of this closing slot — a warm-up is a different function (see Three-Stage Warm-Up (Physical, Mental, Resonance)); the peak-end effect specifically needs the fun part to be last.
  4. Let the session end there, on the noodling, rather than closing with one more "serious" repetition — the last thing you play is the thing that colors how the whole session gets remembered.

— BassBuzz, 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes
secs: The core mechanism: the peak-end rule
Why noodling itself is worth defending (not just where to put it)

steal-like-a-bassist-ear-training-from-k.title: Steal Like a Bassist — Ear-Training from Known Melodies
steal-like-a-bassist-ear-training-from-k.html:
BassBuzz's fix for "the rookie scale mistake" that happens right after a beginner has drilled a scale shape and can transpose/extend it: they still think of the scale as a memorized pattern rather than as music, because they never connected it to melodies already living "deep in your bones" from a lifetime of hearing them (children's songs, holiday music, pub sing-alongs). Named after the "good artists copy, great artists steal" line, applied literally: shamelessly copy and play existing melodies that use the scale you already know, using your own ear as the bridge between the shape your fingers know and the sound your ear already knows. Taught on Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues's major scale shape, but the process is scale-agnostic — it works on any shape you've already memorized.

The four-step process

  1. Pick a melody that's deep in your bones and ears already. Doesn't need to be "cool" — familiarity beats coolness for this exercise, since the whole point is exploiting a melody your ear already fully knows. Worked twice in the source video: "When the Saints Go Marching In" (useful repertoire for jazz/New Orleans-style gigs) and "The Sound of Music"'s "The Hills Are Alive" (picked as an archetypal, near-universally-known major-scale melody). A companion PDF from the source video supplies a "mega list" of simple, mostly-memorized melodies to draw from.
  2. Pick any starting note and play the scale shape starting on that note, purely to get your ear oriented to that key before singing anything — the specific starting note doesn't matter (demonstrated on both B♭ and E). This is Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues's transposability step, reused here as an ear-orientation step rather than a fretboard-coverage one.
  3. Play the root note again, then sing it out loud (bad singing explicitly encouraged — the point is pitch reference, not vocal quality), then sing the melody starting on that note.
  4. Find those notes on the bass, inside the scale shape, starting from the correct scale degree of the melody's first note. This is the step that actually links ear to fingers — the process is iterative-by-ear in practice ("oh when... no, too far... oh when the saints... there we go"), not an instant lookup.

The hidden stumbling block: not every melody starts on scale degree 1

"When the Saints Go Marching In" is an easy first example specifically because its melody starts on the scale's root note (degree 1) — step 4 gets a guaranteed win locating the starting note, since it's the same note the scale shape starts on. Most melodies aren't this convenient. "The Hills Are Alive" starts on the 5th scale degree instead — worked in the video by counting up the shape (1-2-3-4-5) to find where the melody actually begins before singing/searching from there. This is named directly as the single biggest beginner stumbling block in the whole process — without knowing which degree a melody starts on, step 4 has no anchor point to search from. The companion PDF solves this by listing each melody's starting scale degree alongside the melody itself, so a beginner doesn't have to derive it by ear alone (a skill the video says comes with time).

Payoff: this is also an improvisation/soloing method

The same four steps double as a cure for solo-panic: when a bandleader calls for a solo, "find your scale shape, find the melodies you know... and then you can just doodle around those" — using a known melody as a starting anchor for improvisation rather than freezing or noodling randomly. Explicitly framed as not just a beginner-teacher trick but how working musicians actually think — demonstrated with Jaco Pastorius quoting "The Hills Are Alive" mid-solo in a live recording.
secs: The hidden stumbling block: not every melody starts on scale degree 1
Payoff: this is also an improvisation/soloing method

the-bass-inner-game-comparison-your-why-.title: The Bass Inner Game — Comparison, Your Why, and Embracing the Suck
the-bass-inner-game-comparison-your-why-.html:
BassBuzz's Josh, reflecting on what he'd change if he restarted learning bass, names four inner-game mechanisms — not scales, fretting technique, gear, or metronome work (the video opens by explicitly ruling those "outer game" answers out) — as the actual difference between the players who quietly quit and the ones who are still playing decades in. His framing for why this matters at all: technique and theory "will only get you halfway there" — if the inner game is neglected the outcome is years of plateau, frustration, and stagnation rather than steady visible progress, and it's offered as the explanation for why so many more people used to play an instrument than currently play one, and so few people are still playing into their 50s and 60s. The four keys, in the order given (the video's own numbering skips from "key number one" to "key number two" to an unlabeled third movement to an explicitly-flagged "final key," so the third isn't verbally numbered in the source — treated here as key 3 for continuity): (1) don't let comparison run your life, (2) know your why, (3) don't wait for inspiration — just show up, (4) embrace the suck. This is the direct mindset/motivation counterpart to Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments's Commandment 6 (patience as the #1 self-taught failure cause) and Noodling as a Scheduled Reward (The Peak-End Rule)'s motivation-as-a-resource framing — all three are BassBuzz videos converging on the same underlying claim, that staying a bassist is a psychology problem at least as much as a technique problem.

Key 1 — Don't let comparison run your life

The trap, named concretely: you're feeling good about your playing, you had a good week, then you see a nine-year-old shredding harder than you ever have and want to quit — one bad comparison erases real progress you'd actually made. Personal case study offered as the extreme version: moving to LA "overconfident," having his ego crushed comparing himself to the city's musicians, and — rather than connecting with the new players, being shown his weaknesses, and working through them — fleeing to Phoenix instead of meeting the challenge. Framed as the textbook bad outcome of unmanaged comparison: discouragement, deterioration, giving up.

The reframe — comparison itself isn't the problem, the kind of comparison is:

  • Helpful comparison — "I love how tastefully she chose her bass fills, I'm inspired to improve" — comparison used as a specific, actionable model to move toward.
  • Unhelpful comparison — "she's so much better than me, I quit" — comparison collapsed into a global, hopeless verdict on yourself.
  • Named cause of why the unhelpful version wins by default: brains are wired to focus on the negative — the helpful framing takes deliberate redirection, not just "not comparing."

The mechanism underneath both outcomes — fixed vs. growth mindset (drawn from mindset research, not named on-camera but described directly): a fixed mindset treats talent/ability as a static trait you either have or don't, which makes comparison inherently discouraging — if you don't believe you can improve, you don't act to improve, which means you don't improve, a self-fulfilling prophecy. A growth mindset treats talent/ability as something built through hard work, strategy, and mentoring, which makes comparison inspiring instead — believing you can improve makes you want to practice, which makes you actually get better, which reinforces the belief. Everyone runs a mix of both beliefs across different areas of life — this isn't a switch you flip once, and nobody has a clean growth mindset everywhere.

The concrete tool: the "question-markify" technique. Take a limiting belief stated as flat fact and turn it into a question — "I can't get better" → "Can I get better?"; "I'm too old to learn bass" → "Am I too old to learn bass?" The question form leaves an open blank where the statement had a closed verdict, which prompts you to actually go check the belief against reality instead of accepting it unexamined. (General starting point — apply it to any fixed-mindset belief that shows up around comparison, not just the two named examples.)

Key 2 — Know your why

Core claim: no clear why → aimless drift. Named directly as his own 20s — "stumble aimlessly, forget to practice for years at a time, and just generally suck." Your why is simply what you actually want out of learning bass — examples given run from grand to trivial on purpose (be famous, play with friends, play along with favorite songs) specifically to establish that a small, personal why counts exactly as much as an ambitious one.

Two named ways people get this wrong:

  1. Thinking the why has to be grandiose. A modest why — "I just want to play music and have fun" — is a completely legitimate why if it's actually true for you. A clear why, however simple, does two concrete things: it keeps you connected to whatever originally inspired you to start, and it gives you a practice agenda — you can now deliberately work on whatever boosts your enjoyment, rather than a generic curriculum.
  2. Forgetting that your why changes over time. Treated as natural, and possibly a sign of maturing rather than a failure to stay consistent. Worked personal example: at 14 his why was "become a world-renowned virtuoso like Victor Wooten" — and he did the matching work (heavy practice, music study, gigging). Over time the why quietly shifted — he cared more about groove and musical communication, less about shredding, and no longer wanted to spend five hours a day practicing — but he didn't notice the shift and kept running the old virtuoso-practice regimen against a why that no longer existed, which led to abandoning practice altogether for a long stretch. The actionable lesson: periodically check whether your why has moved, and update what you practice to match the current why, not the one you started with — a stalled-out practice habit can be a why mismatch rather than a discipline failure.

Finding your current why: no universal answer given — "hunt for the one that lights you up the most" among the range of reasons players actually have (the transcript doesn't itemize BassBuzz's specific list on-screen, so treat this as an open self-check rather than a fixed catalog).

Key 3 — Don't wait for inspiration; just show up

Names the failure mode directly: "the inspiration myth" — the belief that you'll consistently feel like practicing, and that feeling is what should trigger picking up the bass. Reality, per the video: it doesn't work like that, and believing it does keeps you "stuck passively waiting for lightning to strike before you actually take any action."

Two outside references used to back this up:

  • Stephen King (65+ novels) — "amateurs sit and wait for inspiration, the rest of us just get up and go to work."
  • Flea (Red Hot Chili Peppers) — "it's not always fun, but if you want to be good at something, you have to do it when it's not fun."

Self-honesty beat: Josh admits he still loses to this himself — money spent on pedals and a looper for a "cool bass looping idea" he'd made zero progress on in six months at time of filming. The point isn't that this gets solved once; it's an ongoing practice.

The actual fix, stated plainly: show up and do the work regardless of whether you feel like it or feel inspired — inspiration is not a precondition for practicing. This is where Key 2 pays off directly: a clear why is what carries you through the moments resistance shows up ("I don't feel like it, I'm tired, the economy...") — without a why, that resistance wins.

Practical lever named for making "just show up" easier: remove the daily decision-making overhead. A structured course (his own "Beginner to Badass" is the named example, but the mechanism generalizes) works specifically because you don't have to invent a practice routine from scratch each session — you just execute the next bite-size lesson. This is the same lever as Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments's Commandment 1 short-term-goal ladder — both are ways of pre-deciding what to practice so "should I practice today" never has to become "what would I even practice," which is where a lot of no-shows actually originate.

Key 4 (the final key) — Embrace the suck

Reframe: skill acquisition isn't a smooth climb — there's suck woven through the whole process, and the fix isn't tolerating it passively, it's leaning into it intentionally. Named instances of "the suck": feeling discouraged after a bad comparison, feeling uninspired during scale practice, not feeling like practicing at all next week — Keys 1–3 are, in effect, three specific flavors of the suck this key is the general answer to.

Worked case study — "Forget Me Not" (the Patrice Rushen bassline later sampled in Will Smith's "Men in Black"): after 15 years of playing, Josh found himself embarrassed he couldn't play a fast passage in it cleanly. He was tempted to permanently fake it with hammer-ons (an easier substitute technique that dodges the actual skill gap) rather than build the real thing. Instead he spent weeks practicing the one specific weak-point movement (a thumb technique) every day, slow, at his own actual speed until he could genuinely play it — and demonstrated the result on camera in a later video. The reframe that made this sustainable: the fact that something sucks that much is itself a signpost you're moving in the right direction, not a signal to quit or route around it.

Failure-based learning, backed by Michael Jordan: "I've missed more than 9,000 shots in my career... I have failed over and over and over again in my life, and that is why I succeed." Named claim: people who fail and learn from the failure improve faster than people who avoid failing/risking failure in the first place — avoidance isn't actually the safer path for progress, it's the slower one.

A concrete drill for training the "grit muscle" itself (not a substitute for embracing the suck generally — a specific exercise to build the capacity for it):

  1. Flip the bass over and play it "opposite-handed" — mirror the way you normally hold it; the actual string order doesn't matter, the point is guaranteed incompetence on your own instrument.
  2. Try something simple in that reversed configuration (his own example: "some Pink Floyd").
  3. The target isn't the music — it's your relationship to the mistakes. Normal playing + a mistake tends to produce "I shouldn't have made that mistake" (resisting the suck). This drill is deliberately unplayable enough that the mistakes become funny instead of shameful — "these are funny horrible noises we're making, this is how I sounded on day one."
  4. Repeat this kind of exposure regularly — one session of the reversed-bass drill doesn't rewire the mindset by itself; the grit-building effect comes from doing it, or things like it, "day after day."

Closing pointer: names a "10-minute daily practice exercise" as a way to both embrace the suck and build real technique/groove gains through repetition — this is BassBuzz's Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix), already in the vault with the actual exercise (minimum-viable-pressure fretting, flying-finger control, octave technique) worked out in full.
secs: Key 1 — Don't let comparison run your life
Key 3 — Don't wait for inspiration; just show up
Key 4 (the final key) — Embrace the suck

the-bassbuzz-55-step-bass-learning-roadm.title: The BassBuzz 55-Step Bass Learning Roadmap
the-bassbuzz-55-step-bass-learning-roadm.html:
The master "what to learn next" reference for self-taught bass, distilled from BassBuzz's curriculum-overview video What to Learn on Bass (in Order). Six levels (0 through 5), 55 numbered steps, each linked to the vault's existing dedicated technique/theory note where one already exists — this note is the connective index between the roadmap's sequencing and the vault's much deeper individual notes, not a re-teaching of any of them. Use it as a checklist: find your current level, confirm the steps below it are solid, and use the linked notes to actually go learn the next step rather than treating this page itself as the lesson.

Companion framework, not a duplicate of it: The Five-Tier Bass Theory Curriculum also ladders material into five levels, but by a different axis — that note sorts theory topics by which player goal needs them (Bedroom Player → Extreme Jazz-Fusion Shredder); this note sorts the entire skill curriculum (technique, rhythm, theory, and style all mixed together) by the order BassBuzz recommends learning it in. They overlap in content (both cover scales, keys, chord progressions, modes, etc.) but are genuinely different cuts through the same material — cross-reference both when planning what's next, don't treat one as a superset of the other.

the-five-tier-bass-theory-curriculum.title: The Five-Tier Bass Theory Curriculum
the-five-tier-bass-theory-curriculum.html:
BassBuzz's answer to "how much music theory do I actually need to learn bass?" — a five-level goal ladder that maps how much and which theory to learn directly onto what you actually want to do with the instrument, rather than a fixed syllabus everyone is supposed to work through in order. Core thesis, stated as the video's real complaint about most bass/theory teaching: teachers routinely dump theoretical jargon on beginners without ever asking where the student is trying to get to — the video's own analogy is a gym coach putting a client who "just wants to lose eight pounds and not have back pain" on an Olympic-weightlifting program (300g of protein a day, TRT, max squat). The fix isn't "skip theory" (the video is explicit that's also wrong) — it's matching the theory dose to the goal tier, and each tier is defined by what it unlocks, not by difficulty for its own sake. The universal filter, given directly as the closing takeaway and the thing to apply to every item in every tier below: "will learning this make me play closer to my goals? If you or your teacher can't answer that question, don't learn that thing." This is a companion framework to Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments — that note's long/medium/short-term goal ladder is the general self-teaching structure; this note is the theory-specific instance of the same idea, answering "which theory is the short-term goal material" rather than practice scheduling generally. The two are meant to be read together.

The five levels

Level 1 — The Bedroom Player

Goal: play favorite songs for yourself, low-pressure, no ambition to perform or jam with others. Framed as a fully legitimate, common goal on its own — "very common... and totally legit" — not a lesser stopping point on the way to something else.

  • Minimum theory required: effectively zero. "You can mostly say f*k theory and learn intuitively" — theory answers why*, and a bedroom player doesn't need the why to enjoy playing. Explicitly: "even with zero theory you can get all the way from your bedroom to Wembley Stadium."
  • What actually unblocks a bedroom player instead of theory: tab, not sheet music. Sheet music takes months to read fluently; tab ("Tabanese") is learnable in minutes and tells you exactly which fret to play. The one real gap tab leaves: it shows what notes, not when — so pair tab with basic rhythm theory (see Time Signatures & Note Values) once a riff's timing won't click by ear alone.
  • Technique outranks theory at this level. Good basic fretting/plucking technique is named as the thing that actually turns a "home run riff" into a playable one; a bedroom player with strong technique and zero theory "can get pretty far."
  • No home team needed — level one is explicitly where most working teachers are least useful ("you don't really need us unless your favorite songs are crazy jazz fusion, in which case stick around for level five").

Level 2 — The Casual Jammer

Goal: play music with friends, hold your own showing up to an informal jam without embarrassing yourself.

  • Note names on the neck — the first real theory requirement. Communicating by fret number alone ("three, five?") breaks down the moment other musicians are involved; knowing note names lets you follow a chord/note called out verbally. → Bass Fretboard Note Memorization System is the vault's existing drill for exactly this.
  • Basic drum/rhythm-section awareness — "the first thing I ever learned about bass was that when the bass drum hits a note, you play with it... the rhythm section is the master of the universe." Framed as more urgent than melodic theory once a real drummer is in the room — losing the pocket, not playing a wrong note, is the failure mode named.
  • Common bass line shapes, used without necessarily knowing the underlying theory. Named explicitly as the "minimum theory way" to stop playing boring root notes: "you can fully fake it as a level two casual jammer by using shapes... watch any pro bassist play, you'll see them using these common bass line shapes, whether they know the theory or not." Scales/triads/major-minor theory would help build these shapes from first principles, but the video's point is the shapes are learnable and usable as pattern-recognition alone, no formal theory required — the practical version of this is BassBuzz's own movable scale-shape teaching, see Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues and Scales § From videos.

Level 3 — The Bar Band Bassist

Goal: learn a real setlist fast (the video's framing device: a Saturday jam goes well, Sunday the band calls wanting a gig booked "maybe in a week" — 10 songs, one week, an audience).

  • Intervals and ear training — named as what turns "learn a bar's worth of songs in a week" from panic into a repeatable skill: "you'd learn those same songs with less scrambling and sweating if you learned intervals and ear training." → Intervals, Harmonic Ear Training, Scale Degree Ear Training.
  • Chord progressions — called "the biggest key to understanding the why of modern music." Positioned as the fix for a specific failure mode: memorizing a song by rote (which fret, in what order) without understanding why the notes go in that order, which is what makes memory fail under gig pressure. → Chord Progressions.
  • Major/minor chords, arpeggios, diatonic chord progressions, Nashville numbers — bundled together as "the kind of theory that makes people quit," explicitly flagged as needing to be taught piece-by-piece with real musical examples rather than absorbed as classroom abstraction. → Chord Naming by Context, Chords by Key.
  • The minimum-theory shortcut for this tier: three named scales cover 90%+ of common riffs, each tied to a concrete listening example — major pentatonic (cited: Queen), minor pentatonic (cited: Audioslave), and the blues scale (cited: "Sunshine of Your Love," already the internalization riff BassBuzz uses for the blues scale elsewhere in the vault — see Blues Scales and Blue Notes § From videos). → Scales § From videos.
  • Explicit, load-bearing caveat — read this before treating level three as mandatory: "I know many gigging bass players who probably don't know half the theory I mentioned in level three, or at least they don't know that they know it... just like you can speak English without thinking 'ah yes, prepositional phrases.' So once again, the minimum theory you need to play bars is actually still zero." Level three theory's actual job is speed — learning the why makes memorizing a 10-song setlist in a week faster and steadier under pressure, not gatekeeping whether you can gig at all.

Level 4 — The Working Pro

Goal: take any gig, with any band, without the specific-repertoire safety net of "the same songs every time" — the threshold where theory stops being optional because the material itself keeps changing out from under you.

  • Major and minor scales (not just pentatonics) — named as the foundation the pentatonics sit on top of, needed once you're generalizing across arbitrary songs rather than working from a fixed vocabulary of shapes. → Scales.
  • Reading music — called "the most hotly contested topic in all of music theory." The stated payoff is narrow and concrete, not general musicianship: reading opens specific gig categories that are otherwise closed (musicals, cruise ships, session work) rather than making you a better player in the abstract. Named counter-caveat: famous musicians who can't read "usually got famous playing with one band" — reading's value is specifically about gig flexibility across many different projects, which is exactly the level-four definition above. Quoted authority, with the specific reading skill named: session legend Lee Sklar, in a Music Radar interview — "You have to be able to read on many levels, Nashville number charts, chord charts, notated music and so on." → Reading Bass Clef § From videos, Sight Reading.
  • The circle of fifths — deliberately downgraded from its usual billing. Explicitly contrasted against "theory book authors" who call it "the Rosetta Stone of music theory": "for the modern musician, the circle of fifths is like, kind of useful for memorizing key signatures, but it's not the frigging Rosetta Stone. It's just a map of how different keys are related." Direct prioritization advice for this tier, credentialed by the speaker's own background (undergrad theory + 15 years teaching): "if you want to be a working pro, skip the circle and work on your groove" — i.e. at this tier, marginal practice time is better spent on rhythm-section feel than on a reference tool. → Circle of Fifths § From videos.

Level 5 — The Extreme Jazz-Fusion Shredder

Goal: play anything, with anyone, at any shred level — named as only worth pursuing if you specifically "love going ooh at abstract theory," crave "the completionist dopamine rush of knowing every theory fact ever," and want to walk in the footsteps of Jaco Pastorius and Stanley Clarke. Framed as the level most teachers push on students who never asked for it — the video's explicit reason for including this tier's full list even for a casual jammer is so the viewer can recognize over-scoped teaching and opt out of it.

The list, given rapid-fire ("60 seconds on the clock"):

  • All seven major modes (Ionian through Locrian) — see Diatonic Modes.
  • Odd time signatures (5, 7, 9) — named use case: playing along with Snarky Puppy and Rush. See Time Signatures & Note Values, Syncopation and Metric Displacement.
  • The whole-tone scale — named use case: sounding like Thelonious Monk.
  • Harmonic minor and its modes; melodic minor and its modes — see Scale Modes Reference.
  • Upper chord extensions — 9ths, 11ths, 13ths and their alterations, plus sus/diminished/augmented chords — see Extended Chords, Suspended Chords, Diminished Chords, Augmented Chords.
  • Common polyrhythms — named, only half-jokingly, as necessary "or Dennis Chambers will eat you for breakfast."
  • Harmonics — named use case: sounding like Jaco Pastorius.
  • Non-diatonic chord changes — tritone substitutions, secondary dominants, borrowed chords ("modal interchange"). See Chord Substitution, Secondary Dominants, Borrowed Chords.

Not detailed here on purpose — this level is presented as a checklist of topics to go find dedicated instruction on, not something the video itself teaches; the vault's existing theory library above already covers every item at real depth. The point of listing it in full is tier-recognition (see below), not curriculum content.

A sixth data point: the ear-driven exception (Billy Sheehan)

A "rules of bass" breakdown states the standard version of this note's core thesis directly, then names its own counter-example: teachers want you to learn theory so you understand why things sound good — but Billy Sheehan is offered as a pro who "seems to do just fine without it." Sheehan quoted directly: "I have patterns and notes and melodies and moves that I do — I don't know what scale they are, I don't know what notes they are, I flunked rudiments of music in high school." The verdict lands exactly on this note's own universal filter, applied to the theory-or-not question itself rather than to a specific topic within theory: yes, you can skip theory if you have an amazing ear (Sheehan's case) — but without one, theory is the more reliable path to build a better ear, on top of the practical payoffs of being able to talk about music, understand what's happening in a song, and analyze other players' parts. Sheehan's case maps closest to Level 1 — The Bedroom Player's "minimum theory required: effectively zero" territory above, but by a different route than that tier describes: not a deliberately low-theory goal, but an exceptional, unusually well-developed ear substituting for formal theory entirely — the video's closing point is that this substitution is real but rare, not a general permission slip to skip theory. → BassBuzz, The 10 Rules of Bass Playing (That Pros Break)

The load-bearing move: tier-recognition, not tier-completion

The video's real payoff, stated directly, isn't "here's level five" — it's teaching the viewer to recognize which tier a given piece of theory actually belongs to, so they can tell when a teacher (or a book, or a YouTube algorithm) is teaching them level-four or level-five material for a level-one or level-two goal. Applied test for any theory topic, from any source: would learning this make me play closer to my actual goal? If the answer is no, or if nobody can answer the question, it's the wrong material for right now — not wrong material, period. This is the same underlying diagnostic as Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments's Commandment 1 (set a goal before judging any exercise/topic as useful), applied specifically to theory topic selection rather than practice material generally.
