rhythm-notation-meter-reading-practice.title: Rhythm Notation & Meter-Reading Practice
rhythm-notation-meter-reading-practice.html:
Five short written/analytical drills, lifted directly from The Elements of Rhythm's own end-of-section exercise sets (Ch. 1, a college theory textbook). That book was mined as a source, not split into a linear practice unit — every fact it teaches now lives on Time Signatures & Note Values and Notation — but its exercises themselves had no home. This is that home: a hands-on set for actually doing rhythm notation and meter identification, not just reading about it. Instrument-independent (pencil-and-paper, or a metronome and a clock), which is why it sits in the Theory lane rather than under Guitar or Bass.

Unlike the tempo-progressed drills in the instrument Practice Method folders, none of this is a motor skill you ramp up over weeks — it's closer to a worksheet plus two physical/aural drills. Run all five in one sitting (30–45 min) when you want a rhythm-reading refresher, or pull one section at a time. No tempo targets, no status tracking — work it, check it against the book, move on.

1. Hand-draw durational values, rests, and their divisions

What the book is testing (pp. 17–19): that you can produce the proportional durational-value chain by hand, not just recognize it. The chain is a strict halving: double-whole → whole → half → quarter → eighth → 16th → 32nd → 64th, each exactly half the one before it (see Notation for the full chain and the tremolo/slash shorthand reading of it). Rests are the exact durational equivalents for silence — same chain, same dotting rules, different symbol.

The harder part is dotted values, which the book insists have three separate, simultaneously-true readings, not one:

  1. Addition — the dot adds half the note's own value again (dotted half = half + quarter). This is the reading everyone already knows.
  2. Divides into three non-dotted values — a dotted half splits into three quarter notes.
  3. Divides into two smaller dotted values — a dotted half splits into two dotted quarters.

Reading 2 is the one that matters most: it's why a compound-meter pulse is written as a dotted note in the first place — a dotted value's natural division is threes, not twos, which is the entire mechanical basis for section 2 below. See Notation for the full walkthrough of this.

Drill (on paper):

  • Pick any durational value (start with a half note). Draw its next three lower divisions with correct beaming.
  • Draw that same value's equivalent rest.
  • Pick a dotted value (dotted half, then dotted quarter). Draw: (a) its dotted lower divisions [dotted half → two dotted quarters], (b) its non-dotted lower divisions [dotted half → three quarters], (c) its addition-form equivalent [dotted half → half tied to quarter].
  • Draw an incomplete beat (e.g. a dotted quarter sitting alone in a bar that needs a full measure) and add the durational value that completes it. Do this for 4/4, 3/4, and 6/8 bars.

Check yourself: if the dotted half's three readings don't all land on the same total duration, the error is almost always in reading 2 (dividing into three) — that's the one that isn't muscle memory yet.

2. Fill out the Time Signature Table — simple, compound, and asymmetrical

This is the book's single most load-bearing idea, already ported to the Time Signature Table section — but reading about the method and actually filling the table from a blank sheet are different skills. This drill is the second one.

The table, as a reminder: three rows — Pulse (the felt beat), First Division (does the pulse split into 2 or 3?), Subdivisions (one more split down). For simple meter, every row just halves, and the written time signature is the Pulse row. For compound and asymmetrical meter, the written time signature is actually the First Division row — you have to derive Pulse by grouping First Division into sets of three (compound) or a mix of twos and threes (asymmetrical) and summing each group into one dotted value.

Worked walkthrough, 6/8 (compound duple), to run before drilling:

  1. Write the six eighth notes of 6/8 into the First Division row, grouped as two sets of three: ♪♪♪ | ♪♪♪.
  2. Sum each group of three eighths into one dotted quarter. Write two dotted quarters into the Pulse row. That's why 6/8 is Compound Duple — two pulses — not "compound sextuple": six is the First Division count, not the pulse count.
  3. Split each First Division eighth note into two 16ths for the Subdivisions row.

Drill — fill a blank three-row table (Pulse / First Division / Subdivisions) for each of the following, on paper, before checking against Time Signatures & Note Values:

  • Simple vs. compound pairs, from scratch: Simple Duple + Compound Duple (e.g. 2/4 and 6/8), Simple Triple + Compound Triple (3/4 and 9/8), Simple Quadruple + Compound Quadruple (4/4 and 12/8). One layer of subdivisions is enough.
  • Dual readings — graph each of these as both simple and compound: 3/16, 3/8, 6/8, 9/8. (3/16, 3/8, and 3/4 are the specific simple-triple signatures that can flip to being heard as compound depending on tempo — see the tempo-perception note on Time Signatures & Note Values. 6/8 and 9/8 are naturally compound but the exercise is worth doing "as simple" anyway, to feel why it reads wrong.)
  • Asymmetrical meter, from scratch: 5/16, 5/8, 7/8, 11/8. Same procedure as compound — list the written signature in First Division, but this time group it as a mix of 2s and 3s (5/8 as 2+3 or 3+2; 7/8 as 2+2+3, 2+3+2, or 3+2+2; 11/8 pick any valid grouping), sum each group to a Pulse-row value, then add one Subdivision layer. Note that the grouping is genuinely ambiguous — there's no single correct answer, only valid ones. See Time Signatures & Note Values for real-song examples of specific groupings (Pink Floyd's "Money" in 7 as 4+3, Genesis's "Back in New York City" in 7 as 2+2+3).
  • Grouping-only drill (no full table needed): for 7/8, 9/8, 10/8, 11/8, and 13/8, list three different valid division groupings for each (e.g. 7/8 → 2+2+3, 2+3+2, 3+2+2), then sum each grouping to confirm it actually produces a valid pulse count for that meter.

3. Two-hand/two-foot pulse-vs-division tapping

Where section 2 is written, this one is physical — a felt demonstration of the same simple-vs-compound distinction, straight from the book's own exercise (p. 30).

The drill:

  1. Tap a slow, steady pulse with your left foot only. This is the background beat — don't let it waver.
  2. Against that same foot pulse, tap two even divisions per beat with your right hand (simple division — the beat splits in 2).
  3. Keeping the same foot pulse running, switch to tapping three even divisions per beat with your right hand (compound division — the beat splits in 3).
  4. Switch hands and feet and repeat both divisions.

The point isn't coordination for its own sake — it's making the Pulse/First-Division relationship from section 2 something you can feel in your limbs, not just fill into a table. If the right-hand division keeps creeping toward the left-foot's tempo (2 collapsing toward 3 or vice versa), slow the pulse down until they separate cleanly, then speed back up.

Extension, if it's still shaky: the book's companion notated drill (its Figure 1.26, p. 31) alternates bars of simple duple and compound duple over one constant background pulse — practice each bar type separately first, then run them in sequence, switching from simple to compound as you go without losing the pulse.

4. Conduct 2/3/4/6 patterns against a metronome

The conducting patterns are documented as reference on Time Signatures & Note Values (credited to Michael Paolantonio, pp. 33–37) — this is the drill that makes them a physical habit rather than trivia. Even non-conductors get value here: each gesture is a physical trace of exactly where the strong beat falls, which is the same strong/weak hierarchy describes in words.

The patterns:

  • Two-pattern (simple/compound duple) — "away–up."
  • Three-pattern (simple/compound triple) — "down–away–up."
  • Four-pattern (simple/compound quadruple) — "down–across–away–up."
  • One-pattern — fast triple meters conducted as a single gesture per bar.
  • Six-pattern — compound duple at a tempo too slow to comfortably conduct in two.

Drill (the book's own exercise, p. 41): set a metronome and conduct the 2-, 3-, 4-, and 6-patterns against it in turn, varying the tempo each pass. Deliberately push the tempo slow enough on a duple/quadruple meter that the six-pattern starts to feel more natural than the two- or four-pattern, and fast enough on a triple meter that the one-pattern takes over from the three-pattern — that's the same tempo-dependent-perception effect documented on Time Signatures & Note Values, felt in the arm instead of just heard.

5. Identify meter from a rhythm with a missing time signature

The book's own reverse-engineering exercise (p. 41, worked examples on p. 42): given a notated rhythm with no time signature, work out what it must be and label it correctly (e.g. Simple Duple, Compound Triple).

Method:

  1. Find the beat grouping. Look for where the rhythm's beaming and bar-line spacing implies a repeating pulse — beamed groups of two eighth notes suggest a simple beat unit; beamed groups of three suggest a compound beat unit (this is the direct inverse of the Time Signature Table's First Division logic from section 2).
  2. Count how many pulses are in the bar to get the top number, using the same "how many... of what kind?" two-question method the book uses for reading a written signature.
  3. Determine simple vs. compound from whether those beamed groups split in two or three.
  4. Name it: (Simple | Compound) + (Duple | Triple | Quadruple), from steps 2–3.

Drill: without access to your own compositions or a lead sheet handy, the fastest version of this exercise is to take a rhythm you already know by ear (a groove you can clap, a phrase from a song you produce with) and notate it without deciding the time signature first — let the beaming fall out of how the note groups actually feel, then label the meter after the fact from what you drew. That's the same skill the book's blank-signature worksheet is testing, run in reverse from sound instead of from a printed page.

How to run this

Work sections 1 and 2 first — they're the written foundation everything else depends on. Sections 3 and 4 are short physical breaks that reinforce what you just wrote down. Section 5 is the synthesis: it only works once 1–4 are solid, since it asks you to reconstruct the notation system from a rhythm instead of following it. If you only have ten minutes, do section 2's simple/compound pairs and section 4's metronome conducting — that combination covers both halves of the book's core idea (the mechanical table method and the felt-in-the-body version of it) fastest.
secs: 1. Hand-draw durational values, rests, and their divisions
2. Fill out the Time Signature Table — simple, compound, and asymmetrical

song-reference-interval-recognition.title: Song-Reference Interval Recognition
song-reference-interval-recognition.html:
A song-anchor method for identifying intervals by ear: memorize one famous melody per interval (its opening two notes ARE that interval), ascending and descending separately, then compare an unknown interval against the anchor set until one matches. Instrument-independent — pure listening/singing, no fretboard or keyboard needed — which is why it sits in Theory/Practice Method/ rather than under Guitar/Piano/Bass.

The anchor set

Interval Ascending Descending
Minor 2nd Jaws theme "I Am the Walrus" (Beatles)
Major 2nd "Ferrari" (opening) "Mamma Mia" chorus (ABBA)
Minor 3rd "Mad World" "Come Together" bass line close (Beatles)
Major 3rd "Sir Duke" (Stevie Wonder) "The National Anthem" bass line (Radiohead)
Perfect 4th "Summer Nights" bass line "Under Pressure"/"Ice Ice Baby" bass riff
Tritone "YYZ" intro vamp (Rush) "Black Sabbath" bass line (Black Sabbath)
Perfect 5th Star Wars main theme "My Girl" bass line (The Temptations)
Minor 6th "Baker Street" sax line "One of Us" (Joan Osborne)
Major 6th "The Holly and the Ivy" "No Surprises" opening riff (Radiohead)
Minor 7th "Somewhere" (West Side Story) "Watermelon Man" trumpet (Herbie Hancock)
Major 7th "Take On Me" chorus leap "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" closing line
Octave "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" "Bulls on Parade" guitar riff (RATM)
Minor 9th (bonus, beyond the octave) "Killing in the Name" bass line (RATM) —

How to run it

  • Drill format: play (or imagine) an interval, run through the anchor list until one matches by ear, name the interval. Do both directions — ascending and descending sets are genuinely different sounds for the same interval, not mirror images.
  • Sing, don't just recognize: hum the anchor melody's first two notes before checking the answer — connects the sound to a physical/vocal memory, not just a label.
  • Weak anchors are still useful: a couple of the descending examples (minor 6th, major 7th) are flagged by the source as imperfect — use them anyway until a better one is found; a weak-but-memorized anchor beats no anchor.
  • No tempo target, no gear needed — a few minutes any time, ideally spread across days rather than crammed once.

Synopsis

Six voicings of a single chord — Cm7 — in under a minute. The description keeps it to one line: one guitar chord played multiple different ways. This is the most directly practiceable video in the batch, because the target is fixed and only the grip changes, which makes it a voicing drill rather than a lesson.

What to watch for

  • Where each voicing sits on the neck and which string set it uses. Six Cm7 grips will span drop-2, drop-3, rootless and shell shapes — sort them by string group as you collect them. Chord Voicings.
  • Which are rootless. A rootless Cm7 is really an E♭maj7 shape doing double duty — that is the idea behind Multifunctional Voicings and it is worth spotting live.
  • The top note of each. Six voicings of one chord are six different melody notes; that is the whole basis of chord-melody. Chord Melody Arranging.
  • Run it as a drill. Cycle all six on Cm7, then move the set to Fm7 and B♭m7 around the cycle of fourths. See Chord Quality Cycle Exercise.

Routed to

  • Chord Voicings — the six grips
  • Multifunctional Voicings — rootless shapes serving two chords
  • Chord Quality Cycle Exercise — how to drill the set
  • Octave-Shift Voicing Discovery — finding more of the same chord

A joke-framed but genuinely useful minute on Em11. The description carries the actual theory and is worth reading before watching: a full E minor 11 is 1–♭3–5–♭7–9–11, six notes; the guitar has six strings and jazz voicings are typically four notes or fewer, so the 9 gets dropped and the chord is still Em11 — not, he argues at length, "Em7(add11)". The point underneath the joke is that extended-chord names describe the highest extension reached, not a requirement to voice every degree below it.

  • Which degrees he keeps. With the 9 dropped you are hearing 1–♭3–5–♭7–11; note which string carries the 11 and whether the root is even present.
  • Why it is 'the easiest chord ever' — Em11 has an open-position voicing that is close to no fingers at all. Watch for that shape specifically, since it is the payoff of the joke.
  • The naming argument itself, which is real theory: Chord Naming by Context and Extended Chords both cover why an extension name does not obligate every lower degree.
  • Then move it. The open shape is only free in E — see what it costs to take it up the neck.

how-basic-chords-work-music-theory-lesso.title: How Basic Chords Work - Music Theory Lesson 1
how-basic-chords-work-music-theory-lesso.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Watch-only page — chords built from intervals, from the ground up

Michael New's first lesson, and the one that made the channel. It teaches chords as a consequence of interval arithmetic rather than as shapes to memorise: learn the third, and every triad and seventh chord follows. He is a music graduate and full-time teacher, and it shows in the pacing.

What to watch for

The claim, in his words: learning the theory under chords

…will not only allow you to find any chord you want, anywhere you want, it will also give you a solid foundation to build your entire understanding of music theory on.

That is exactly Course 01's premise — derivation rules, not memorised tables — which is why this sits at the front of Class 1.

What it actually teaches:

  • Major and minor thirds as the only building material. Stack M3 + m3 and you have a major triad; m3 + M3 gives minor. This is doing real work rather than being a naming quiz.
  • Counting the letter distance first, quality second — . He counts inclusively and out loud, which is the habit worth stealing.
  • Why the pattern generalises — once thirds are the unit, diminished, augmented and seventh chords need no new rule, which is what is pointing at from the other side.

The famous correction — read it before you watch. Present-day Michael pinned an update to his own description:

Past Michael chose his words poorly when he said "this chord doesn't work" … What he SHOULD have said was "by moving notes closer together than a minor third or farther apart than a major third, you're creating an entirely new chord that you're almost definitely not expecting."

This is the more useful lesson of the two. Nothing in harmony "doesn't work" — stacking something other than thirds gives you quartal, cluster or added-tone harmony, all of which are real and all of which show up in the music this vault is actually about. Hold that alongside Making Sense of Rock's Tonal Systems, which makes the same argument at article length: a rule that says a sound is wrong is usually a rule that only describes one system.

Where it plugs in

Class 1, Course 01 — watch before or during Lesson 1. His follow-ups (rhythm, keys, more on chords) are linked from the video description and are worth the same treatment if they earn it.

immersive-ear-training-chromatic-scale-1.title: Immersive Ear Training - Chromatic Scale (1-Hour)
immersive-ear-training-chromatic-scale-1.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Listen-along page — this one is used, not read

Sixty-eight minutes of ear training you put on and listen to. There is no transcript and there should not be one: the answers are spoken aloud two seconds after each tone, so a transcript would be an hour of "…that was 3… that was 5…" — an answer key for an exercise that already gives you the answer. The value is in playing it. Everything below is grounded in Max's own description of the exercise.

What it is

A continuous drill on all twelve chromatic degrees, heard against a drone. The loop is always the same three moves: a tone is played → the correct scale degree is spoken → the same tone is played again, so you get to feel the degree a second time now knowing what it was. That second hearing is the part that does the work — it is where the feeling and the number get welded together. The key changes every few minutes, which is what stops you memorising pitches instead of learning degrees.

It is a direct recording of Max's app Sonofield running in "Pocket Mode" — built for hands-free training while walking, commuting, or doing nothing in particular.

Hardest, and the one that pairs with Course 09 Lesson 2. Twelve feeling states against one drone is the full set — every note in the octave given its own identity rather than being sorted into in-key and out-of-key.

How to use it

  • Do not sit down and concentrate on this. It is designed for the background — a walk, a commute, the washing up. An hour of relaxed exposure beats ten minutes of straining.
  • Focus on the feeling state of each tone, not the pitch. Max's core claim, and the one the vault has already adopted: a degree's feeling is the same in every octave and every key. That is the thing being learned — see .
  • If you are starting out, do not try to guess. His explicit instruction: just listen and relax. Guessing wrong repeatedly trains anxiety, not recognition.
  • When the tone repeats after the answer, that is the rep. Connect the number you just heard to the feeling you are having. Everything else is setup.
  • The key change every few minutes is a feature — if a degree only feels right in C, it has not been learned yet.

Where it fits in the school

Backs — this is the listening counterpart to the course's singing work. Lesson 1 has you produce the tonic feeling by singing it; this has you receive the whole set, passively, for an hour. Different modality, same target.

  • — the drone is a held tonic; everything is heard against it
  • · — the feeling-state framing this drill runs on
  • Scale Degree Ear Training — the vault note that already carries Max's method in prose

learn-music-theory-in-half-an-hour.title: Learn music theory in half an hour
learn-music-theory-in-half-an-hour.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Watch-only page — the whole syllabus in 31 minutes, from a producer

Andrew Huang compresses notes, chords, keys, the number system, inversions, melody and rhythm into one sitting. It is not a substitute for Class 1 — it is the map you watch before Class 1, so the courses arrive as detail on a shape you have already seen rather than as a list of new things.

What to watch for

Chapters, and where each lands on this syllabus (his own timestamps):

Time Topic Concept it previews
2:36 Notes — why the same pitch has two names
10:12 Chords stacked thirds, the ground under Course 02
11:58 Major and Minor
15:36 The Number System — chords as numbers, which is what makes a progression portable between keys
20:29 Inversions the voicing question CHD/VOI splits apart
23:59 Melodies ·
27:26 Rhythm ·

He gets one term wrong on purpose-ish, and says so. From his own description:

It will forever haunt me that in this video I misremembered one bit of terminology — the chord voicings begin with "root position" before moving onto "first inversion" and so on.

Worth knowing before the inversions chapter, so the error does not get learned. But the sentence he draws out of it is the reason this video is on the shelf at all:

…understanding music — how it works and how you can use these tools to express yourself — is a separate and more important thing than knowing all the technical terms.

That is the correct framing for the whole school. The concept cards test terminology because terminology is testable, not because it is the point.

The number system is the half-hour's real payload. Everything else here is covered better and slower elsewhere on the shelf; thinking in numbers rather than letters is the shift that makes Basics of Classical Harmony & Counterpoint, the POP concepts and Course 09's scale-degree ear work all turn out to be the same idea.

Where it plugs in

Class 1, before Course 01 — a one-time orientation pass. Pairs with 12tone — Building Blocks, which covers the same ground far more slowly and from first principles.

visual-ear-training-the-perfect-melody.html:

What it is

Two minutes and twenty-two seconds of Somewhere Over the Rainbow with a visualizer showing the scale degree of every note as you hear it. No commentary. You watch the numbers and listen.

His analogy for why it works is the good part: it is subtitles in a foreign language. You are not translating — you are receiving sound and correct label simultaneously, over and over, until the pairing stops needing conscious effort. That is the same "information soup" mechanism he describes at length in From Ear Training Apps to Real Music, reduced to its smallest possible form.

Max's stated prerequisite: if scale degrees are new, watch the opening of his Sonofield User Guide first. His production note is worth honouring — watch in 4K, since YouTube's compression can smear the numbers.

How to use it

  • Watch, don't test yourself. There is nothing to answer. Stay conscious of the number on screen as its note sounds; that is the whole exercise.
  • Repeat it. At 2:22 it costs nothing to run several times, and the melody is deliberately one of the most familiar in existence — the ear brings no confusion of its own, so all the attention lands on the degree labels.
  • It is the gentlest thing in the ear-training lane — the hour-long drone drills ask you to identify from feeling alone; this hands you the answer in advance and simply asks you to notice it.

ant-nio-carlos-jobim-the-girl-from-ipane.title: 🎵 ANTÔNIO CARLOS JOBIM - The Girl from Ipanema
ant-nio-carlos-jobim-the-girl-from-ipane.html:
Bossa nova standard, 32-bar AABA, typically played in F major (the famous Getz/Gilberto recording is in D♭) — a melody built on sustained chord extensions and a notoriously tricky bridge.

Chords (as taught for guitar)

Key: F major. A section: Fmaj7 (I) → G7 (II7, often with ♯11) → turned minor, ii–V–I back to F — the exact same relative shape as the A section of Ellington's "Take the A Train" (reportedly an intentional Jobim homage). Then a direct half-step-up modulation into the bridge with no ii–V approach.

Bridge (the confusing part): minor9 → dominant-7-off-the-♭6, repeated at two more pitch levels, then a plain 2-5-5 back home. Unlocks with a reinterpretation trick: read the "confusing" chord's implied major-6 partner as its relative minor (a major-6 chord and its relative-minor-7 chord share every note) — reveals all four opening bridge chords as the same relationship repeated three times, not four unrelated grabs. → Chord Naming by Context

Scales (for improvising)

A section: F major over Fmaj7 → G Mixolydian (= C major, upgrade to G Lydian dominant if the ♯11 is voiced) over G7 → back to F major. Bridge: G♭ Lydian (= D♭ major) over the maj7-type chords, Mixolydian (or Lydian dominant) over the dominant 7ths, Dorian over the minor chords (preserves the same relative-major/minor relationships as the chord analysis above), altered scale over the closing ii-V-ii-V's dominants. Default to plain Mixolydian/Dorian first — save the altered scale for once the basic changes are comfortable, since jumping straight to "what's the tritone sub" slows down real-time playing. → Scale Modes Reference

Steal this

  • Reinterpret a puzzling chord as its relative major/minor to reveal a hidden repeating sequence — turns "four chords that don't seem related" into one pattern moved three times. Works as a general reharmonization-reading trick, not just on this tune. → Chord Naming by Context
  • A rootless m9 voicing and a first-inversion maj7 voicing, one string set apart, are the same physical shape — memorize one shape, reuse it as either chord depending on what root you're thinking against. → Chord Voicings
  • Sustain a melody's extensions (9ths) as main tones, not passing ones, to get a floaty/soft feel rather than a plain chord-tone melody.

Why I like it

  • Getz/Gilberto (1964) — Grammy Album of the Year 1965
  • Guitar listening recommendation from the lesson: Baden Powell's version

baby-keem-16.title: 🎵 BABY KEEM - 16
baby-keem-16.html:
Short, melodic cut from Baby Keem's debut studio album The Melodic Blue (2021).

Chords

Key: C major (relative A minor) · 94 BPM · 4/4

Main loop: Fmaj7 – C – E7 – Am → IVmaj7 – I – V7/vi – vi

The E7 is a secondary dominant (V7/vi) that tonicizes the Am, pulling the loop toward its minor relative before landing there — that pull is where the mellow, introspective feel comes from. The whole loop lives on 7th chords (Fmaj7 → E7), which is what gives it the jazzy, Frank-Ocean softness rather than a plain pop-major feel. See Chord Progressions · Chords by Key.

User-verified chords (corrects an earlier unverified Hooktheory/Ultimate Guitar reading).

Production & Arrangement

The album's cinematic closer — shimmery, soaring synths, an earworm chorus over quick verses. Critics note that without the drums it reads like a Frank Ocean record, and James Blake appears (uncredited) on the track — which explains the lush, gospel-leaning chord voicings and the airy, processed vocal aesthetic (Line of Best Fit · Wikipedia).

  • Palette: the maj7/dom7 loop on a warm pad/synth = the harmonic bed; sparse 808 + light trap kit sits under it rather than driving it (subtract the drums → ambient R&B).
  • Vocal treatment: airy, layered, lightly-tuned lead — the James-Blake-adjacent "processed but intimate" sound (soft tune, air, wide doubles), not hard trap tune.
  • Space: reverb-forward, wide — the synths and vocal stacks carry the width; drums stay narrow/centered.

Steal this

  • Maj7 → secondary-dominant loop for instant mellow-introspective R&B: build the 4-chord loop in Operator or Keyscape, voice it with 7ths, and let one chord be a V7/vi to pull toward the relative minor.
  • "Ambient R&B" arrangement test: mute the drums — if the synth+vocal bed still stands alone (like this track), the harmony is doing the work. Then add a sparse 808 + light kit under it, not over it.
  • Vocal: soft Auto-Tune Pro (Retune ~45), Gem Dopamine for air, wide doubles, generous Reverb Send Long → the James-Blake intimacy. → 1 Main Vocal Track.
  • Bass: sub-forward, felt-not-heard 808 with only light mid harmonics (this is a bed, not a knock track) → 1 Digital Bass Track §2 restraint.

Why I like it

bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.title: 🎵 BEE GEES - How Deep Is Your Love
bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.html:
Written by Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb; from the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack (1977).

Chords

Key: E♭ major · ~104 BPM.

Verse: E♭ – Gm7 – Fm7 – C7 – Fm7 – G7 – A♭9/B♭, then repeats with a substitution: E♭ – Gm7 – Cm7 – Fm7 – A♭9/B♭ → I – iii7 – ii7 – V7/ii – ii7 – V7/vi – IVadd9/V — the C7 and G7 are both secondary dominants slipping in and out around the diatonic ii7 (Fm7), pulling the ear forward without ever fully tonicizing anywhere else → Secondary Dominants

Pre-chorus: A♭maj7 – Gm7 – Fm7 – D♭7(9) – Gm7 – A♭9/B♭ → IVmaj7 – iii7 – ii7 – ♭VII7(9) – iii7 – IVadd9/V — the D♭7 is a borrowed ♭VII7, a soulful ballad color chord lifted from E♭ Mixolydian rather than the parent major scale → Borrowed Chords

Chorus: E♭ – E♭maj7 – A♭maj7 – A♭m6 – E♭maj7 – D♭6(9) – C7 – Fm7 – A♭m6 → I – Imaj7 – IVmaj7 – iv(m6) – Imaj7 – ♭VII6(9) – V7/ii – ii7 – iv(m6) — built on the classic "major-IV-to-minor-iv" cliché plus a second borrowed ♭VI/♭VII color chord.

Worth checking directly against the reputation this kind of soft-rock ballad has: this is not the plain I–vi–IV–V doo-wop loop or the axis progression — the actual changes are denser, leaning on secondary dominants (C7, G7) and borrowed minor/♭VII chords throughout, and never settle into that 4-chord shape.

billy-joel-vienna.title: 🎵 BILLY JOEL - Vienna
billy-joel-vienna.html:
From The Stranger (1977, prod. Phil Ramone). The "slow down, you crazy child" ballad — patience and mortality over jazzy, chord-nerd piano.

Chords

Key: B♭ major. Unverified (AI analysis) — to confirm: Vienna is a chord-nerd song — dense with 7th and extended voicings and secondary dominants that briefly tonicize non-tonic chords (the source of its restless, jazzy pull), plus a signature descending bass line under the verses. Fill the verified Roman-numeral read against a chart; the analytic point is function (T → SD → D with chromatic secondary-dominant detours), not just letters. See Chord Progressions · Chords by Key.

Production & Arrangement

Phil Ramone's clean, uncluttered late-'70s production — the arrangement is built around Billy Joel's solo piano, which does most of the harmonic and rhythmic work; everything else supports it:

  • Piano front-and-center: virtuosic, stride/jazz-inflected, wide dynamic range — recorded warm and close, minimal processing (let the performance carry it).
  • Accordion (Dominic Cortese) is the signature color on the intro/verses — the "old-world Vienna" cue that makes the arrangement instantly identifiable.
  • Restraint: bass + light drums enter to lift sections, not to drive — a lot of the song is nearly solo piano + voice. Dynamics come from arrangement (adding/removing parts), not from a loud mix.
  • Vocal: intimate, upfront, lightly compressed — a storytelling vocal, not a belted one.

Steal this

  • Let one instrument carry the song: arrange around a single expressive part (Keyscape grand / 1 Acoustic Piano Track) and add supporting parts only to lift sections — dynamics from arrangement, not fader pushes.
  • Chord-nerd harmony: voice a progression in 7ths/extensions and drop in a secondary dominant to tonicize a non-tonic chord for restless, sophisticated motion → Secondary Dominants · Seventh Chords.
  • A signature "color" instrument (here, accordion) makes an arrangement identifiable — pick one unexpected timbre and feature it.
  • Descending bass line under a static-ish top for gentle forward pull.

bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.title: 🎵 BON JOVI - Livin' on a Prayer
bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.html:
Slippery When Wet (1986). This note is a bass-focused breakdown — pedal point on the iconic main riff, three worked bass-run/fill examples (including a target-note run that spans three chords across a bar line), and a bassline that deliberately tracks the song's overall intensity arc — as taught by BassBuzz. Bass credit is genuinely disputed in the source video: either Alec John Such or Hugh McDonald.

Chords

Key: E minor, though (as flagged above) the song reads just as naturally as G major — verse, pre-chorus, and chorus all draw from the exact same four chords, just entered at a different point each time, which is precisely why the "is it Em or is it G" debate exists.

Verse (the pedal-point riff, bass holding E under all of it): Em – C – D – Em → i – ♭VI – ♭VII – i (read against G major instead: vi – IV – V – vi)

Pre-chorus / bridge build: C – G – D – Em → IV – I – V – vi (in G)

Chorus ("Whoa, we're halfway there"): D – G – C, folding back to Em on the way out → V – I – IV (– vi) (in G)

→ All four sections share the same four chords — G, Em, C, D (I, vi, IV, V) — just started from a different point in the cycle each time: verse = vi-♭VI/vi-♭VII-i, pre-chorus = IV-I-V-vi, chorus = V-I-IV. That's the axis progression family by definition, not a coincidence — this is one case where the doo-wop-adjacent 4-chord loop really does hold up under scrutiny. → The Axis Progression

The key change: for the final chorus, the whole song transposes up a minor third, E minor → G minor — Wikipedia's composition notes state this plainly, which resolves the ambiguity flagged above (some fan transcriptions instead claim a whole-step E minor→F♯ minor change). The chart backs up the minor-third reading directly: Gm–E♭–F mirrors Em–C–D exactly, and B♭–E♭–F mirrors D–G–C, both transposed up the same minor third. One of rock's most-cited "truck driver's gear change" moments, landing the last chorus a whole register higher. → Modulation (Key Change)

The main riff: pedal point against the changing keys

The iconic main riff (doubled by guitar) uses pedal point: the bass holds E minor while the keyboards move through E minor → C major → D major → back to E minor above it. The held bass note disagrees with the keyboard chords it doesn't match, building tension that resolves when everyone lands back on E minor together. A/B'd directly against a version where the bass instead follows the keyboard's chord changes — that version reads noticeably flatter. How to apply it: simply don't move your bass note when the other instruments change chords underneath you. Full device (tonic vs. dominant pedal, why it works, the loop-based-harmony framing) → Loop-Based Harmony, and the spaced-rep flashcard version → .

Verse → pre-chorus: a scale run instead of a flat chord jump

Chord change: E minor → C major. Two flatter alternatives demoed first (straight E→C jump, or sit on the root until the section changes) before the actual run: climbing the E minor scale using scale degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, then 6 to melodically connect E to C — creating forward momentum into the pre-chorus rather than a static handoff.

Pre-chorus bar 4: a run that copies the vocal's rhythm

Rather than the plain D→E motion the guitar chords themselves spell out, this fill instead mimics the rhythm of the vocal line at "make it or not" — bass and vocal move together rhythmically at that exact moment, one of BassBuzz's own favorite melodic moments in the song.

The chorus run: target notes and playing over the bar line

The song's biggest fill connects three chords (D, G, C) in a single continuous run rather than resetting at each chord's downbeat — a worked example of playing over the bar line: most fills start and end squarely on beat one, but this one runs straight through a bar line instead. The trick to doing this without sounding lost is picking target notes first: this run needs to hit D on the first beat one, G on the next beat one, and C on the "and of two" (the run's final target deliberately copies an accent in the vocal line at that same "and of two"). Once the targets are locked, the notes in between are fair game — demonstrated twice with different filler-note choices, both drawn from the E minor/G major scale, both hitting the same three targets. Full general method (not just this song's example) → Bass Runs and Target Notes; the "spans a bar line" framing itself → Syncopation and Metric Displacement.

Whole song: bassline density tracks the song's intensity arc

Intro vs. outro is the bluntest data point — a huge jump in busyness. Zoomed in further, first chorus vs. last chorus: the first chorus stays mostly scripted eighth notes with one fill (a 16th-note "hiccup") at the phrase end; by the last chorus — after the song modulates up a key — the same four bars carry a slide at the end of bar 1, an extended version of the scale-run fill, and a bar 4 packed with 16th notes. General lesson: read a song's felt intensity arc first, then decide how much space to fill at the start vs. the end (or verse vs. chorus), saving runs/fills/fast notes for the more intense sections — without going overboard. Full note, more cross-song examples → Bassline Writing.

Steal this

  • Hold your bass note through a chord change on purpose — pedal point trades a moment of tension for a stronger release when the harmony resolves back.
  • A scale run using non-adjacent scale degrees (1-2-3-5-6, not every note) can still read as smooth, forward-moving connective tissue between two chords.
  • A bass fill doesn't have to invent new rhythm — copying the vocal's own rhythm at a transition point is a legitimate, cohesive fill source.
  • Pick target notes before improvising a run that spans a bar line — nail the notes that have to land where the chords actually change, and treat everything else as free choice.
  • Chart a song's intro-to-outro intensity arc and make sure the bassline's busyness (fills, run complexity) actually tracks it — don't hold a static level of activity across a song that's building.

brockhampton-sugar.title: 🎵 BROCKHAMPTON - Sugar
brockhampton-sugar.html:
Second track from BROCKHAMPTON's fifth studio album Ginger (2019), featuring Ryan Beatty; a hip hop/pop/R&B slow jam built on a looped acoustic-guitar figure with folk and funk textures under bubbling drum programming.

Chords

Key: C# major (though the tonic barely shows up) · ~123 BPM

Chorus and verses both ride the same four-chord loop: D#m – F# – B – A#m → ii – IV – ♭VII – vi. The tonic C# is nowhere in it — the ♭VII (B major, borrowed off C# Mixolydian) does the "pulling back around" work a dominant would normally do, but it never actually resolves. That's the source of the floaty, unresolved, breezy quality — a loop that circles rather than lands.

The pre-chorus is where the tonic finally arrives: D#m – F# – B – C# – D#m – F# – B – A#m – D#m – C# – F# – B – A#m – G#m → ii – IV – ♭VII – I – ii – IV – ♭VII – vi …, landing on I (C#) for the first time, then sliding into a borrowed minor v (G#m, not the diatonic major V) as a pivot chord into the next chorus — which reharmonizes the same loop, swapping G#m and C# in for the usual D#m (v – IV – ♭VII – vi … IV – I – ♭VII – vi), a brighter recoloring of the identical four-chord shape.

The bridge/outro tighten the same material into B – G#m – D#m – F# → ♭VII – v – ii – IV, the same color chords reshuffled, still never touching a real V–I cadence.

No progression here matches a named form in the vocabulary — it's a genuinely tonic-avoiding loop, not a turnaround, blues, or vamp. progressions: [] is accurate, not a placeholder.

broken-bells-the-high-road.title: 🎵 BROKEN BELLS - The High Road
broken-bells-the-high-road.html:
Lead single (Dec 2009) off Broken Bells' self-titled 2010 debut album — a collaboration between James Mercer (The Shins) and Danger Mouse.

Chords

Key: D Dorian · 80 BPM · 4/4

Main loop (intro/verse/chorus): Dm – C – G → i – VII – IV (in D Dorian)

Centered on Dm rather than resolving to a major tonic — the C and G major chords are both diatonic to D Dorian (D E F G A B C), which is what gives the loop its moody, modal (rather than straightforwardly minor) color. Outro moves to C – F – Dm – G.

Unverified — chart-derived reading, not yet user-confirmed.

Production & Arrangement

Danger Mouse (Brian Burton) + James Mercer, 2010 — warm, psychedelic indie-pop production: vintage drum-machine + live kit blended, hazy analog keys, and Mercer's high falsetto floated in reverb. Danger Mouse's signature dusty-but-lush sonics.

Steal this

  • Blend a drum machine with a live kit for a hybrid, slightly-lo-fi groove (Drum Rack + played fills).
  • Hazy analog keys + tape warmth (Cassette/Kramer Tape) for the dusty-lush vibe.
  • Falsetto floated in reverb over a mid-tempo pulse → Reverb Send Long.

cedar-walton-bolivia.title: 🎵 CEDAR WALTON - Bolivia
cedar-walton-bolivia.html:
Jazz standard, changes-only breakdown (no melody — the source video skips it for copyright reasons). Nathan Borton's approach: reduce the tune's four sections to a small set of already-known vocabulary buckets (5-1s, a tritone-sub 5-1, one long static-minor stretch, short closing 2-5s) rather than treating each chord change as a unique event. → How To SOLO Over Bolivia! (Cedar Walton)

Chords

Key: no single tonic — a four-section form threading through several key centers, framed front and back by a static dominant vamp (Wikipedia describes the tune as composed "in G major" around a 16-bar G7(13) vamp).

A section (16 bars): a modal vamp — the whole section sits on G7(13), Mixolydian, no chord change, no cadence.

B section (16 bars), by function (section numbers below match Nathan Borton's own breakdown, referenced in Solo concepts further down):

Section 1: E♭ major (tonic) → A7 → D (a 5-1 into the key of D)

Section 2: A♭7 → G — a tritone substitution standing in for the diatonic D7 → G (D7 is a tritone from A♭7)

Section 3 (the long stretch, reduces almost entirely to B minor): Bm7 → C Lydian → Bm7 → Bm7/A → A♭m7♭5 (half-diminished)

Section 4 (closing run): a 2-5 into F major → a tritone sub into B♭ major (also playable as a plain 2-5) → a 5-1 into Dm7

Turnback into the closing vamp: A7 → G7 (see Solo concepts below — this is the tune's trickiest single move)

The literal chord symbols behind the above: E♭maj7 → A13 (V7 of the next key) → Dmaj7 (I, a clean 5–1) → A♭7 (tritone sub standing in for D7, itself V of the next key) → Gmaj7 (I) → F♯7♯9 → Bm7 → C7♯11 → Bm7 → Bm7/A → A♭m7♭5 → Gm7 → C7 (a genuine ii–V into F) → Fmaj7 (I) → B7 (tritone sub setting up B♭) → B♭maj7 → A7 (V7, turning the form back around into the top G7 vamp). This lines up with the vault's own key-center summary above (E♭ → D → G → B minor → F/B♭/D minor). See The ii-V-I, Chord Substitution.

Solo concepts by chord (Nathan Borton's breakdown)

  • Over A7 → D (section 1): either (a) play the two key centers — E♭ major ideas, then D♭ major ideas over both the A7 and the D (keep the same color running through the dominant); or (b) engage the 5-1 directly — A7 ideas resolving to D major 7 ideas. → The ii-V-I
  • Over A♭7 → G (section 2): either (a) play the actual tritone-sub progression — A♭7 ideas resolving to G major 7; or (b) ignore the sub and just play a plain 5-1 (as if it were D7 → G) — still works, since the sub shares the same V-to-I pull. → Chord Substitution § 2. Tritone substitution
  • Over the section-3 stretch: think B minor almost the whole way through — Bm7 (straight); the C Lydian chord with B minor 7 pentatonic (the two sounds overlap because B minor pentatonic sits diatonically inside the C Lydian/G major collection); Bm7 again; Bm7/A ("the exact same sound" as plain Bm7, just a different bass note — no vocabulary change needed); and the A♭m7♭5 with B melodic minor — rule given: go up to the chord's own ♭3 (A♭'s ♭3 is B) and play melodic minor rooted there. Matches Scale Modes Reference § Melodic Minor's own table exactly: the vi degree of a melodic-minor scale is a half-diminished chord, so "melodic minor off the ♭3" and "play the vi-chord's parent melodic minor" are the same fact. → Scale Modes Reference
  • Over the section-4 closing run: short 2-5 licks and short minor-2-5 licks dropped straight in across the 2-5-into-F, the tritone-sub-into-B♭ (or its plain-2-5 fallback), and the final 5-1 into Dm7. → The ii-V-I, Chord Substitution
  • Over the A7 → G7 turnback (the payoff move of the lesson): since G7 is the V of a 2-5-1 in the key of C, its related ii is Dm7, and a ii chord and its V are functionally the same sound — so the whole A7 → G7 move can be reheard as A7 → D minor, i.e. a plain 5-1, folding an awkward-looking dominant-to-dominant move into vocabulary already built for a 5-1. → The ii-V-I § Guitar shortcut: the power-chord finder, Chord Substitution § From videos

Steal this

  • Reduce a scary-looking tune to a handful of known sound-buckets before trying to solo it. Four separately-intimidating sections collapse to "5-1 lines and static-minor sounds" once you stop treating every chord change as its own unique event.
  • A ii chord and its V are interchangeable soloing material — recognizing a tricky dominant-to-dominant move (A7 → G7 here) as secretly "dominant → [V's related ii]" turns it into ordinary 5-1 vocabulary. → The ii-V-I
  • Melodic minor off a half-diminished chord's own ♭3 as a quick, no-counting way to find the extension-rich scale for a min7♭5 chord. → Scale Modes Reference
  • Categorize transcribed licks by type as you learn them (5-1 / 2-5-1 / static-minor) so you have a ready bucket to reach into instead of re-deriving vocabulary tune-by-tune. → Bebop Vocabulary

charlie-parker-confirmation.title: 🎵 CHARLIE PARKER - Confirmation
charlie-parker-confirmation.html:
A 32-bar AABA bebop standard in F major. Nathan Borton pulls the melody apart phrase by phrase into named, reusable devices — framed the same way as his other Parker-melody breakdowns in this vault — rather than teaching the tune as a fixed thing to memorize. See Learn Charlie Parker's Phrasing Secrets... with CONFIRMATION! for the source video, full routing, and confidence notes. A follow-up in Borton's Parker-melody series (an earlier video on the same topic is referenced but not yet in the vault).

Chords

Key: F major · Form: 32-bar AABA.

A section: opens on Fmaj7 (I), then drops straight into a minor ii–V starting a half step below the tonic — Em7♭5 → A7♭9 (ii–V of D minor, the tune's signature "Bird changes" move) resolving toward Dm7. The line keeps cascading down in secondary ii–V pairs — Cm7 → F7 (ii–V of B♭) landing on B♭7 (IV7) — continuing the cycle back toward G7 → C7 (ii–V home). Each A section closes on a turnaround built from secondary dominants — Am7 → D7 → Gm7 → C7 — back to Fmaj7.

Bridge: breaks from the A material — the A sections are a partial contrafact of "Twilight Time," but Parker wrote the bridge's harmony himself — modulating briefly to ♭VI (D♭maj7) via its own ii–V (E♭m7–A♭7) before the CESH device (chromatic root motion under held harmony, see the melody breakdown below) walks it back to a plain ii7–V7–I cadence home to F.

Real book editions vary slightly bar to bar (Confirmation is notorious for that); this is the commonly cited skeleton. Note the source transcript itself isn't spelled out chord-by-chord — Borton narrates by function (our ii chord, our dominant 7 chord, the B♭7, our A7) rather than a full lead sheet, so the skeleton above reconstructs concrete chords from his functional labels rather than inventing bar numbers he didn't give. See The ii-V-I, Turnarounds, Bebop Vocabulary.

Melody breakdown (Nathan Borton's phrase-by-phrase breakdown)

A section:

  • Opening phrase: a 6th-interval leap right off the top of the melody — the interval Borton calls out as a Parker signature worth training in isolation. → Bebop Vocabulary, Intervals
  • A minor ii–V lick (E half-diminished → A7, resolving toward D minor) built from a triad plus the 6th. Walks the root and 3rd of Em7♭5, descends a G minor triad (the chord's own ♭3-♭5-♭7 spelled as a triad), then jumps a 6th from A7's root to its 3rd. → The ii-V-I, Guide Tones
  • Blues mixed into the line over B♭7 — the F blues scale (rooted on B♭7's own 5th), not B♭'s. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • A dominant line resolvable two ways — a plain 5–1, or the same idea stretched into a full ii–V–I by prepending a short line. → The ii-V-I
  • A 5–1 phrase layering the 6th with two guide-tone connective lines — ♭9 of the dominant down to the root, and the 4th of the dominant resolving to the 3rd. → Guide Tones
  • The 4th-to-3rd tension-and-release device, extended into a jump to an altered tone. Start on the 4th (an "avoid" tone against the chord), resolve to the 3rd, then leap to an altered extension — worked here as the ♭5 of A7; other options named (♯9, ♭9, ♯5). → Altered Chords, Bebop Vocabulary
  • More blues-over-dominant variation, then the A section closes on a strong 5–1 phrase Borton recommends as a general line-ending device.

B section:

  • CESH (chromatic embellishment of static harmony) opens the B section — the root of the ii chord moved chromatically up or down through the changes while the harmony sits still. → Bebop Vocabulary §6
  • A closing phrase Borton says he "uses all the time" to end a line — demonstrated in isolation, then in context.
  • The B section closes on another 5–1 line, "super cool" — the same closer logic as the A section.

Steal this

  • Leap a 6th to open or close a line, or drop a random 6th into a straight scale run to see what falls out — the cheapest way to get the interval into your ear and your fingers before trying to place it deliberately.
  • Over any dominant chord, try the blues scale rooted on its 5th, not its own root — the F-blues-over-B♭7 device, transposes to any dominant.
  • When you want a tension-and-release move on a major or dominant chord: start on the 4th, resolve down to the 3rd, then jump to an altered extension (♭9/♯9/♭5/♯5). Works even though the 4th "shouldn't" be there — the resolution is what earns it.
  • CESH: pick one note (often a chord root) and walk it chromatically underneath otherwise-static harmony — a way to generate motion without changing the underlying chord.
  • Keep a "lick journal" categorized by device type (5–1s, CESH, altered, etc.), not by tune — makes vocabulary reusable across changes instead of stuck to this one melody. → Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction §A collection-first variant

charlie-parker-donna-lee.title: 🎵 CHARLIE PARKER - Donna Lee
charlie-parker-donna-lee.html:
A bebop standard — one of the "aural transcription" tunes named directly on The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice § Pillar 2 as a canon solo worth transcribing by ear, alongside Miles Davis's "So What" and Grant Green's "Cool Blues." First given its own page here from How To Improve Your BEBOP LINES and Phrases with DONNA LEE - The Ultimate Bebop Guide... (Nathan Borton), which teaches the head melody itself plus a "DNA" breakdown of the four devices Parker leans on throughout — arpeggios, chromaticism, the major bebop scale, and line closers. The tune's own harmonic quirks (a non-functional B♭7 and a backdoor dominant) were already logged on Modal Jazz and Turnarounds/Diminished Chords from a separate, companion Borton video ("THIS Song Turns Students Into BEBOP Pros...") — both video sources are consolidated here.

Chords

Key: A♭ major · Form: 32-bar contrafact of "(Back Home Again in) Indiana," transposed down a whole step from Indiana's usual key of B♭.

A section (×2): a turnaround shape reused across the section — A♭maj7 (I) → F7 (VI7, a secondary dominant standing in for the diatonic vi) → B♭m7 (ii) → E♭7 (V7) — the same I–VI7–ii–V skeleton that underlies rhythm changes' own A section (hence this page's "rhythm-changes-adjacent" structure tag, despite not sharing Gershwin's actual changes). One pass swaps the diatonic ii chord for a static, non-resolving B♭7 in its place instead — Nathan Borton's "tonic dominant" reading, logged above.

Bridge: cascades through a rapid chain of secondary ii–V's outside the home key — Gm7 → C7 → Fm7 → B♭7-type motion, touching several key centers two bars at a time — before a backdoor dominant, D♭maj7 → G♭7 (♭VII7), pulls it back toward home, landing the form on A♭maj7 via a final ii–V–I.

Extremely fast harmonic rhythm (Parker's original recording sits around 220–225 BPM) is as much the tune's identity as the changes themselves. See Bebop Vocabulary, Turnarounds, The ii-V-I.

Additional harmony logged from a companion source video (also working example-by-example off named chord targets rather than a full re-derived lead sheet):

  • Fm6 – C7 – Fm6 – B°, where the B° is read as a rootless G7♭9 resolving up a half step into Cm7 — the general spotting rule stated directly: "when you see a diminished chord moving up a half step below a chord, it usually acts as the five of that next chord." → Diminished Chords
  • A non-diatonic B♭7 sitting where a diatonic ii chord (Bbm7) would normally go — flagged as "weird" because it doesn't belong to the key, then reframed as a static tonic dominant: its own bebop-dominant scale, or the melodic minor built on its own 5th (F melodic minor over B♭7). → Modal Jazz
  • D♭maj7 → G♭7, a backdoor dominant (♭VII7→I) resolving back to D♭maj7 — soloed either as another static tonic dominant, or by substituting D♭ minor 6 and borrowing minor-key language over it. → Turnarounds § Backdoor

Melody & line-building breakdown (Nathan Borton)

  • Learn the melody first, by ear, before touching the analysis. Stated explicitly as the priority: sing it, memorize it away from the page — the eighth-note feel and phrasing are the point, and reading it defeats the purpose. Borton notes a couple of corrected notes he plays (matching Parker's actual recording) that differ from the standard real-book lead sheet.
  • Arpeggio → line closer, the default 5–1 shape. Start on the 3rd of the dominant (F7's 3rd, A), walk up the arpeggio, then drop into a fixed line closer — a short, largely memorized cadential tail — that resolves down into the target chord: this example starts the closer on F7's ♭9 (G♭) and walks down to the 3rd of the I chord (B♭). The arpeggio doesn't have to voice-lead smoothly into the closer; you can jump straight to wherever the closer starts. New device for the vault, full writeup → Bebop Vocabulary §7.
  • The same shape decorated with extensions. A second line uses an arpeggio with the 9th and 11th thrown in — named directly as "a sound that Wes Montgomery and Grant Green like to use a lot" — before its own line closer. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • The formula flipped — closer opens, arpeggio extends. The same closer Parker usually uses to end phrases opens this one instead, with the arpeggio then extending the line rather than resolving it — named directly as tonic dominant language ("a dominant chord that doesn't resolve to the one chord... it just kind of stays in the sound of the dominant"), useful for stretching a dominant line before an eventual resolution or over a static dominant section like the B section of Rhythm Changes. A fourth independent confirmation of the tonic-dominant concept already logged three times on Bebop Vocabulary. → Modal Jazz
  • Chromatic enclosures around chord tones AND extensions, generalized into a repeatable pattern. One line encloses the root of the dominant chord; a second part of the same line encloses the ♭5. Both are shown to generalize: the root-enclosure pattern can be walked up or down through the whole arpeggio (enclose the 3rd, jump down to the ♭7, repeat the pattern from there), and the ♭5-enclosure pattern extends to every other altered chord tone in turn — ♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9. Stated payoff: combine different combinations of these enclosure patterns, close with a line closer, and "you have some really great sounding [lines]." → Bebop Vocabulary §2
  • The major bebop scale, right out of the gate in the melody itself. Major scale plus one added note (the ♯5), which lets a line start on any chord tone and land back on the same chord tone one measure later. The caveat stated directly: don't count the 7th as a chord tone when using this scale — move it to the 6th, so the "arpeggio" in play is root–3rd–5th–6th, not root–3rd–5th–7th. Matches Bebop Vocabulary §1's bebop-major row (Mixolydian... wait, major + ♯5, passing tone between 5 and 6) exactly. → Bebop Vocabulary §1
  • A worked 3-6-2-5-1 line in the key of A♭, built from the bebop-major rule above. Starting on C over A♭maj7 (I, one measure) — because the rule guarantees landing back on C a measure later — then into Cm7 (the 3, leading to the 6, then the 2-5-1). Stated shortcut: if you already know short 2-5 vocabulary that starts on the root, you can "plug and chug" it straight in at that point. The line finishes over the final 2-5-1 by pulling directly from Donna Lee's own melody. → Bebop Vocabulary §1, The ii-V-I
  • A short etude over the first half of the tune, deliberately combining melody licks with the newly-built vocabulary above, closing the lesson.
  • Practice recommendation, stated directly: take this melody further than just learning it — go through line by line, extract the licks you like, and move each one through all 12 keys. Framed as a transcription "everybody knows," dense enough with reusable material to be worth this treatment on its own.

Steal this

  • Build a phrase from just two pieces: an arpeggio (with or without extensions) and a memorized line closer — you don't need to compose a fresh cadence every time, just chain a chord-outlining half into a fixed cadential tail.
  • Flip any closer to open a phrase instead of ending one whenever you want a tonic-dominant, non-resolving feel rather than a cadence.
  • When using the major bebop scale, remember the 6th-not-7th swap — the "arpeggio" underneath the scale is root-3rd-5th-6th, not the usual 7th-chord shape.
  • Move a favorite lick through all 12 keys once it's under your fingers — the stated payoff for treating a well-known transcription (this tune, or any other) as a genuine practice resource rather than a one-time listen.

clifford-brown-max-roach-delilah.title: 🎵 CLIFFORD BROWN & MAX ROACH - Delilah
clifford-brown-max-roach-delilah.html:
Old jazz standard covered by Clifford Brown & Max Roach — a bluesy AABA solo used by Jack Ruch as the worked example for Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction. Key noted in the source video as "F minor" but every chord in the analysis (i, iv, V) is consistent with F♯ minor as tonic — flagged as a likely captioning slip, not corrected in the quote below.

Chords

Key: F♯ minor · Form: AABA, 8 bars per section.

A section (i–iv–V): F♯m (i) → Bm7 (iv) → C♯7alt (V) — a straightforward minor-key cadential shape, the altered dominant setting up the pull back to F♯m at the top of the next section. Not a ii–V (there's no ii chord present — iv stands in its place), so this doesn't map onto the vault's ii-V-I tag; it's closer to a plain minor i–iv–V turn.

Bridge: Bm7 (iv) → C♯7 (V) → D7/D9 (♭VI7, a half-step-above approach chord) → C♯7 (V) — the ♭VI7 works as a chromatic approach into the dominant rather than a real modulation, resolving back to the V before the final A section.

Full solo vocabulary mapped onto these changes (two full passes — blues-based, then melodic-minor-based, one different solo concept per A-section pass) is below. See Blues Scales and Blue Notes, Scale Modes Reference.

Solo concepts by chord (Jack Ruch's analysis)

Two full passes through the same AABA changes, each pass using a different vocabulary set — see Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction for the general method these came from.

Pass 1 (bluesy):

  • Over F♯m (i): bluesy phrasing leaning hard on the ♭5 (blue note) — repetitive, signature minor-blues phrasing. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • Over Bm7 (iv): a D major 7 arpeggio (the relative major of Bm) — outlining the relative-major triad/7th over a minor chord gives a minor-9 color without naming it directly. → Chord Substitution, Scale Modes Reference
  • Over C♯7alt (V): an upper-structure diminished-7 arpeggio built off the 3rd of the altered dominant (3rd–5th–♭7–♭9 stack) — a classic bebop device; because a diminished 7th chord is symmetrical, the same shape slides up in minor thirds anywhere over the chord. → Altered Chords, Diminished Chords

Pass 2 (melodic-minor):

  • Over F♯m (i): F♯ melodic minor — the natural 7 (major 7th) over a minor tonic is the ear-catching move (vs. the expected ♭7 of a plain minor 7 chord). → Scale Modes Reference
  • Over Bm7 (iv) and C♯7alt (V): C♯ altered scale (the 7th mode of D melodic minor / built as a mode of F♯ melodic minor's relative material) pushed hard for an "outside" sound. → Altered Chords, Scale Modes Reference

Bridge:

  • Over Bm7 (iv): same D major 7 arpeggio device as the A section.
  • Over C♯7 (V): F♯ harmonic minor — reached for as an alternate way of conceiving the same territory as a C♯ Phrygian-dominant scale; the natural (major) 7th against the ♭6 gives a dramatic, "Spanish" color. → Scale Modes Reference
  • Over D7/D9 (♭VI dominant, half-step above the eventual V): Lydian dominant (a mode of melodic minor: dominant scale with a ♯11/♯4 and ♭7) — Ruch's own favorite scale sound, used specifically as a half-step-above approach into the following V/target. → Scale Modes Reference

Steal this

  • Two solos, one form: run the exact same changes twice with two deliberately different concept sets (blues vocabulary, then melodic-minor vocabulary) — a fast way to double a practice session's output from one transcription.
  • Relative-major arpeggio over a minor chord as a quick, ear-friendly minor-9 substitution — works on guitar or any comping instrument, not jazz-specific.
  • Half-step-above dominant as an approach chord (D7/D9 → C♯7) — a reusable target/approach shape, see Secondary Dominants.

Why I like it

  • Search "Clifford Brown Max Roach — Delilah"

djo-end-of-beginning.title: 🎵 DJO - End of Beginning
djo-end-of-beginning.html:
Sixth track from Joe Keery's (Djo) second album Decide (2022); reissued as a single in 2024 after going viral on TikTok, later hitting #6 on the Billboard Hot 100 following the Stranger Things series finale.

Chords

Key: D major · 80 BPM

The verses ride a simple D – Bm – A loop → I – vi – V, with Em stepping in as a passing ii chord (Em – A, ii – V) on the way back around each time — pleasant, unresolved pop motion, no hard cadence.

The chorus opens it up into G – D – A – Bm → IV – I – V – vi — one of the four rotations of the axis progression (the I–V–vi–IV family), entered on the IV instead of the I. Same four core pop chords as the verse (D, A, Bm) plus G, just reordered into the classic axis shape for the hook, before dropping back to the verse's I–vi–V loop.

elani-karaindrou-eternity-and-a-day-ii-b.title: 🎵 ELANI KARAINDROU - Eternity and a Day II. By The Sea 1
elani-karaindrou-eternity-and-a-day-ii-b.html:
Film score for Theo Angelopoulos' 1998 Palme d'Or–winning film. Sparse and impressionistic. A recurring melodic motif builds and dissolves. Slow harmonic movement creates a timeless, suspended quality.

Chords

Key: B♭ minor · 3/4 · slow, suspended

Core: B♭m – E♭m – F7 – B♭m → i – iv – V7 – i (the F7 is the harmonic-minor dominant — the one bright pull in an otherwise dark, static field)

Color: D♭ (♭III) and A♭ (♭VII) drift through as the melody rises and dissolves.

From your sheet: Songs/Files/Elani Karaindrou - Eternity and a Day II. By The Sea.pdf; harmony cross-checked online.

Production & Arrangement

Greek film composer Eleni Karaindrou (ECM / Theo Angelopoulos films) — minimalist, mournful cinematic chamber music: a slow, aching melody carried by strings/oboe/accordion over sparse harmony, with vast space and long tones. Sorrow as atmosphere.

Steal this

  • Cinematic melancholy: one aching melodic line (oboe/violin/accordion patch) over held, sparse strings (Omnisphere + strings) with lots of space.
  • Long tones + silence — let a theme breathe across bars.
  • Modal/minor sorrow → Scale Modes Reference; interpolate as a film-score-style intro.

Why I like it

Listen

erik-satie-gnossienne-no-1.title: 🎵 ERIK SATIE - Gnossienne No. 1
erik-satie-gnossienne-no-1.html:
Chords

Key: F minor (with Dorian / "Satie scale" color) · free time, no bar lines

A theme (over the repeating left-hand vamp): Fm – Cm – Fm → i – v – i

Contrasting phrase: B♭m – Fm, with passing B♭ and a Picardy F major at cadences → iv – i (color tones: B♭ = IV major / Dorian shimmer, F = I major Picardy)

The whole piece lives on just three minor chords — Fm (i), B♭m (iv), Cm (v) — with the major-IV and major-I inflections giving it the mystical, modal feel.

Verified via Hooktheory / theory analyses.

Production & Arrangement

Erik Satie's proto-ambient piano — sparse, modal, and harmonically unresolved. Satie stripped Romantic drama away: slow tempo, lots of space, gentle dissonances that hang without resolving (he pioneered the idea of music as atmosphere — 'furniture music,' a century before ambient). The Gnossiennes famously have no bar lines or time signatures and quirky written directions; the Gymnopédies are gentle 3/4 melancholies over a rocking left-hand ostinato.

  • Gnossienne No. 1 — free-time (no bar lines), an exotic/modal minor melody over a steady left-hand vamp; hypnotic and unresolved.

Steal this

  • Space as an instrument: slow the tempo, leave silence, let single notes ring — atmosphere over motion (the drumless idea at its origin).

  • Left-hand ostinato + floating melody: a simple rocking accompaniment under a sparse tune (Keyscape felt piano + long Reverb Send Long).

fats-waller-honeysuckle-rose.title: 🎵 FATS WALLER - Honeysuckle Rose
fats-waller-honeysuckle-rose.html:
The flagship Montgomery-Ward tune — Wikipedia names it "particularly" as the example. Its A section is a ii–V vamp that refuses to resolve for four full bars, which makes it a genuinely odd tune to walk over.

Chords

Key: F major. 32-bar AABA, up-tempo swing.

A section (bars 1–8)

Two published charts, differing only in harmonic rhythm and one connector:

Source bars 1–4 bars 5–8
Learn Jazz Standards Gm7 \| C7 \| Gm7 \| C7 Fmaj7 A♭°7 \| Gm7 C7 \| Fmaj7 B♭7 \| Am7 D7
iGigBook / realbook.us Gm7 C7 \| Gm7 C7 \| Gm7 C7 \| Gm7 C7 F6 F7/A \| B♭6 C7 \| F6 B♭7 \| Am7 D7

The whole first half is a ii–V on Gm7–C7 that never lands — four bars of it — before bar 5 finally reaches the I. Both charts agree exactly on F6/Fmaj7 – B♭7 – Am7 – D7 to close. → The ii-V-I

Bridge (bars 17–24) — the Montgomery-Ward

  • Bare (iGigBook): F7 | F7 | B♭6 | B♭6 | G7 | G7 | C7 | C7
  • ii–V substituted (LJS): Cm7 | F7 | B♭maj7 | B♭maj7 | G7 | G7 | C7 | C7

In F: I7 – IV – II7 – V7, two bars each. Learn Jazz Standards states outright that this is not a rhythm-changes release (III7–VI7–II7–V7) — it's the commercial bridge. → The Montgomery-Ward Bridge

For bass

  • The A section is the hard part, not the bridge. Only two roots — G and C — across four bars. There is no root motion to lean on, so the line has to generate its own interest through approach notes and chromatics. Good tune for exactly that problem. → Chromatic Bass Lines
  • Bridge root motion breaks once: F → B♭ (down a 5th), then B♭ → G (down a m3 — the hinge), then G → C → F (fifths home). That third-drop is the fingerprint of this bridge, and the thing that distinguishes it by ear from the rhythm-changes release, which is an unbroken fifths chain.
  • Oscar Pettiford on Thelonious Monk's version is the cited bass reference — his line mirrors Monk's left-hand Gm7/C7 and transposes it up a minor third. (Single-sourced, Reverb "Bass Walk of the Week.")

Related repertoire

Charlie Parker's "Scrapple from the Apple" (also in F) is built on this tune's A section, with a rhythm-changes bridge swapped in for the Montgomery-Ward. → Rhythm Changes

Why I like it

Listen

  • Fats Waller, 1934 (Grammy Hall of Fame)
  • Fats Waller, 1937 all-star jam with Tommy Dorsey and Bunny Berigan
  • Django Reinhardt with Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter, 1937

frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.title: 🎵 FRANK CHURCHILL - Someday My Prince Will Come
frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.html:
A 3/4 jazz waltz in B♭ major — one of the few standards in a waltz feel, built around a signature dominant 7♯5 as its 2nd chord.

Chords (as taught for guitar)

Key: B♭ major, 3/4 time. B♭6/maj7 tonic; E♭maj7 (IV) carries an available ♯11 (true of any major IV chord — the 4th mode of a major scale is Lydian); the tune's signature 2nd chord is a dominant 7♯5, voiced in practice as a flat-13 shape (from C harmonic minor). Slash chords create deliberate chromatic bass motion; a C♯dim7 with the melody note A functions in practice as a rootless A7♭9.

Steal this

  • A go-to jazz-waltz comping backdrop: bass note on beat 1, chord stabs on "and" of 2 and on 3 — a reliable fallback pattern for 3/4, which most jazz vocabulary (built mostly in 4/4) doesn't cover by default. → Jazz Comping
  • Any inversion of a half-diminished shape on a dominant's ♭7 also voices that dominant's ♭9/♭13 — one fretboard-study target (half-diminished inversions), two usable voicing vocabularies. → Chord Voicings
  • Whole-tone vs. altered scale over a dominant 7♯5 — both contain the chord's tones; altered adds ♭9/♯9 for more tension. Pick one by ear, not by rule.
  • Practice arpeggios starting from every note in the shape, not just the root — closes the gap between "knowing the chord" and finding it live mid-improvisation. → Chord-Tone Soloing

Why I like it

Listen

  • Miles Davis, 1961 (the canonical recording)
  • Guitar listening recommendation from the lesson: Emily Remler, "Cookin' at the Queens"

frank-ocean-ivy.title: 🎵 FRANK OCEAN - Ivy
frank-ocean-ivy.html:
From Blonde (2016). Built around a detuned guitar riff, produced with Rostam Batmanglij and Om'Mas Keith.

Chords

Chart on file: !<span class="xlink xlink-vault" data-note="Frank Ocean - Ivy - Chords.pdf" title="Vault note — not in this page">Frank Ocean - Ivy - Chords.pdf</span>. Unverified (AI analysis) — to confirm against the chart: an A-minor-centered loop where the bright, slightly-detuned guitar arpeggiates the changes rather than strumming block chords; the wistful pull comes from major-chord color over the minor tonic (a IV/♭VI brightness against the Am). Fill the verified Roman-numeral read here. See Chord Progressions · Keys.

Production & Arrangement

The blueprint of Blonde's anti-drums aesthetic: no drum kit at all — the entire groove is carried by one bright, doubled, slightly detuned/chorused electric guitar + Frank's layered vocals. That "wrong on purpose" detune is the whole mood.

  • Vocal layering (the Blonde signature): stacked lead + harmonies with varispeed/pitch-shifted layers (some sped-up/brighter, some pitched-down/darker) sitting under the main take — intimate, minimally-tuned, human.
  • The ending is the point: the mix deliberately breaks up / distorts as Frank pushes into the emotional climax — a printed lo-fi degradation, not a clean fade. Contrast (pristine → falling apart) is the arrangement's payoff.
  • Space: reverb-forward, wide guitar, dry-ish intimate vocal in front — depth from the guitar's width, not from drums.

Steal this

  • Drumless arrangement: build a whole song on one detuned/chorused guitar (Chorus-Ensemble low mix + a few cents of pitch via Little AlterBoy/MicroShift) + vocal stacks. Mute-the-drums test (see 🎵 BABY KEEM - 16).
  • Varispeed vocal layers: pitch a double up and down under the lead (Little AlterBoy / kHs Pitch Shifter) for the Blonde texture — 1 Double Vocal Track / 1 Harmony Vocal Track.
  • Print the breakdown: automate distortion/lo-fi (Decapitator Punch, RC-20 Retro Color) to bloom at the last chorus and print it — commit to the fall-apart.
  • Detune as mood: a deliberately-detuned lead instrument is an emotional cue, not a mistake.

frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.title: 🎵 FRANK SINATRA - Fly Me to the Moon
frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.html:
Jazz standard written by Bart Howard (1954); Sinatra's 1964 recording with the Count Basie Orchestra (arr. Quincy Jones) is the definitive version.

Chords

Key: C major. The A section is a real book-standard descending circle-of-fifths chain: Am7 (vi) → Dm7 (ii) → G7 (V) → Cmaj7 (I) → Fmaj7 (IV) → Bm7♭5 (iiø) → E7 (V7) → Am7 (vi) — the first four chords are a plain vi-ii-V-I, and the tune keeps the same descending-by-fifths root motion straight through the turnaround by reinterpreting the IV chord's arrival as the launchpad for a minor ii-V-i landing back on vi (Bm7♭5-E7-Am7, treating Am momentarily as a local tonic) rather than resolving home to Cmaj7. Each root drops a fifth in turn except the Fmaj7→Bm7♭5 step, which is a tritone jump rather than a true fifth — the one deliberate "break" in an otherwise unbroken circle-of-fifths run.

The B section continues the same ii-V-I engine (per the tune's well-documented chart), consistent with this page's own "the whole tune walks around the Circle of Fifths" framing below. Only the A-section changes above are verified against a specific published chart here; the full AABA lead sheet isn't reproduced bar-for-bar.

Production & Arrangement

Sinatra's 1964 version — Quincy Jones arrangement with the Count Basie band, a swinging big-band 4/4 that rides a descending circle-of-fifths progression (the whole tune walks around the Circle of Fifths — a jazz-standard hallmark). Effortless swing, tight horn section.

Steal this

  • Circle-of-fifths progression: a chain of ii-V motion walking around the circle for that jazz-standard inevitability → Circle of Fifths · Secondary Dominants.
  • Big-band swing feel + tight horn stabs.
  • Crooner vocal upfront, dry and intimate against a full band.

fr-d-ric-chopin-nocturne-op-9-no-1.title: 🎵 FRÉDÉRIC CHOPIN - Nocturne Op. 9 No. 1
fr-d-ric-chopin-nocturne-op-9-no-1.html:
Performer: Arthur Rubinstein Reference recording: YouTube — Rubinstein

Key of B♭ minor. One of Chopin's most lyrical nocturnes — slow, expressive, wide left-hand arpeggios under a singing right-hand melody.

Chords

Classical piano, not a jazz/pop chord-changes tune — no progressions: tag applies here (tagged progressions: [] deliberately), and this is a harmonic outline rather than a chord-symbol chart.

Ternary (ABA) form, 85 measures in 6/4: the primary theme opens and closes the piece, flanking a contrasting secondary theme starting at measure 19, with a varied, more ornamented reprise of the primary theme from measure 70. The opening measures oscillate between the tonic (i, B♭ minor) and the submediant (VI, C♭ major) — a chromatic-mediant-adjacent color relationship (B♭ minor and C♭ major share no diatonic function but sit a half step apart at the root) that gives the opening its wistful, harmonically "floating" character before the phrase resolves back to B♭ minor. The piece is a well-known example of Chopin's habit of stretching functional harmony with chromatic passing motion under a long-breathed melodic line — treat any full Roman-numeral reduction as secondary to just hearing where the tonic pulls resolve.

Why I like it
