george-benson-billie-s-bounce.title: 🎵 GEORGE BENSON - Billie's Bounce
george-benson-billie-s-bounce.html:
A 12-bar jazz blues in F (Charlie Parker's tune). Jens Larsen calls George Benson's solo on this recording probably the best jazz blues solo he knows, and spends a full video chunk-analyzing four passages of it — the same transcribe → chunk → name-the-device → replay-your-own-version method as Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction. Transcript confidence: auto-captions garbled jazz terminology heavily; read through context, not verbatim — see George Benson - This is The Best Jazz Blues Solo I know for the full caveat.

Chords

Key: F · Form: 12-bar bebop blues (the "Parker blues" reharmonization of a plain 12-bar).

Bars 1–4: F7 (I7) held, sometimes reharmonized in bar 4 with a secondary Cm7 → F7 (ii–V of B♭) to set up the move to IV. Bars 5–6: B♭7 (IV7). Bars 7–8: back to F7 (I7), often with a secondary Am7 → D7 (iii7–VI7) landing the turnaround on ii. Bars 9–12 (the turnaround): Gm7 (ii) → C7 (V7) → F7 (I7) → C7 — closing on the dominant rather than resolving home, the Parker trademark that keeps the chorus rolling into the next one.

Exact substitutions (a diminished passing chord in bar 6, extra ii–V's in bars 4/8) vary chart to chart — this is the commonly cited skeleton. Benson's solo (analyzed below) treats every dominant as a launchpad for the same handful of arpeggio/enclosure devices regardless of which secondary chord is passing underneath. See Blues Form and Harmony, The ii-V-I, Turnarounds.

Solo concepts by passage (Jens Larsen's analysis)

Four passages, each reduced to a device Benson leans on repeatedly across the whole solo — full write-up on George Benson - This is The Best Jazz Blues Solo I know.

  • Turnaround, C7 → F7 (early in the solo): a B♭-major-9-type arpeggio/pentatonic idea built off C7's own ♭7 (upper extensions rather than the plain triad), sliding up into an enclosure around the B♭ — then resolving onto F7 with a blues double-stop (sustained D over G-A♭-F, "almost Dorian over F7") possibly borrowed from Wes Montgomery's playing on "No Blues" — then a plain F-major-pentatonic phrase (3rd-5th-6th-root). Bebop language into blues language into major-pentatonic language, back to back in one short passage. → Bebop Vocabulary, Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • Minor ii-V turnaround into G minor: rather than a parent scale, Benson treats G minor 7 as a plain G-B♭-D triad and decorates it entirely with chromatic leading (approach) notes into each chord tone — producing wide, unpredictable interval skips that still resolve correctly because the target is always a chord tone. Two variations of the same idea are played back a chorus apart. → Chord-Tone Soloing (Shapes 1–3), Bebop Vocabulary
  • His recurring dominant-chord device — half-diminished arpeggio off the chord's own 3rd: over C7, an E half-diminished-shaped arpeggio (E-G-B♭-D = 3-5-♭7-9 of C7) skipping down to the 3rd and back up to the 7th before resolving — called out as recurring "again and again" across the whole solo whenever a dominant chord passes. A more "inside"/consonant cousin of the full-dim7-off-the-3rd device already documented on Diminished Chords. → Diminished Chords, Chord-Tone Soloing, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • Bar 1 bebop cliché + call-and-response, then an F-minor blues cliché reordered: the 13th/6th-up-to-root cliché, a long chromatic climb from the ♭3 to the 5th, a bebop-scale-style descent to the root — then B♭7 answers with the melodic inverse of that same shape (call-and-response). Later, on B♭7, a standard F-minor blues cliché (A♭-C-G-F, off the chord's 5th) is played with the note order rearranged from how it's usually voiced — the same lick, kept fresh by resequencing. → Bebop Vocabulary, Blues Scales and Blue Notes

Steal this

  • Half-diminished (not full dim7) arpeggio off a dominant's own 3rd — a more "inside" alternative to the altered/full-dim7 version of the same "arpeggio off the 3rd" trick, worth having both colors ready. → Diminished Chords
  • Treat a ii-chord as a plain triad and decorate purely with chromatic leading notes, skip the scale entirely — bigger, more surprising interval jumps than scalar playing, while still resolving correctly every time because the target is always a chord tone. → Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Reorder a well-worn blues cliché's notes rather than retiring it — same underlying lick, same harmonic logic, different sequencing keeps it sounding fresh.
  • Call-and-response across a chord change — answer one chord's phrase with the melodic inverse of it on the next chord.

george-harrison-beware-of-darkness.title: 🎵 GEORGE HARRISON - Beware of Darkness
george-harrison-beware-of-darkness.html:
From All Things Must Pass (1970), produced by Phil Spector. Devotional warning against illusion, maya, and negative thought. Possibly Pete Drake on pedal steel. Slow, hymn-like progression.

Chords

Key: E major (the vault's C♯ minor is its relative minor) · slow, hymn-like

Verse: B – B/A – G7 – G♯m – C♯m – E – A → V – V/♭7 – ♭III7 – iii – vi – I – IV (the G7 is a chromatic borrowed chord — that haunting, gospel sideways turn)

Bridge ("Watch out now…"): E – D – A – F♯m – Bm (passing G7) → I – ♭VII – IV – ii – v

Verified via Ultimate Guitar / Hooktheory.

Production & Arrangement

All Things Must Pass (1970) — Phil Spector's Wall of Sound: layered acoustics, slide guitar, lush reverb, and a huge, cavernous production around Harrison's spiritual ballad. Grand and reverby.

Steal this

  • Slide guitar as the singing lead voice (Harrison's signature).
  • Dynamic lift from intimate verse to grand chorus.

gorillaz-feel-good-inc.title: 🎵 GORILLAZ - Feel Good Inc
gorillaz-feel-good-inc.html:
Demon Days (2005), lead single. This note is a bass-focused breakdown of the main riff, its slide, and the short bass solo, as taught by BassBuzz's Josh and cross-checked against Gorillaz's real touring/session bassist Shay Adelican, who contributed a voice note on feel and tuning. Named by the video as "the riff that sold a million bass guitars" — Murdoc's own DVD commentary on the music video credits the riff's syncopation for why it hits so hard.

Chords

Key: E♭ minor (natural/Aeolian) — the same handful of chords do double duty across the main riff, the "Windmill" hook, and the De La Soul rap verse, just in slightly different orders.

Main riff: E♭m – B♭m7 – A♭m7 – E♭m → i – v7 – iv7 – i

"Windmill, windmill for the land" hook: E♭m – B♭m → i – v, resolving down into Dm – Am under the De La Soul verse entry (the same i–v shape, a whole step lower)

De La Soul rap verse: Dm – Am – Gm – Am → i – v – iv – v (concert pitch: E♭m – B♭m – A♭m – B♭m)

→ Everything here is minor i–v–iv in one order or another — a natural-minor loop with no raised leading tone anywhere, so that "v" never actually functions as a real dominant (it's a plain minor v, not a V7). Worth checking directly against the brief's hunch: this is not the axis progression or the I–vi–IV–V doo-wop loop — both are major-key devices built on a leading-tone V7, and this track never leaves E♭ natural minor. It reads more like a repeating modal loop, though at three chords deep it's a shade busier than the "static one/two-chord vamp" the vault's modal-vamp tag is defined around, so it's left untagged here rather than stretched to fit.

The riff: fretting and plucking as two independent systems

The riff mixes open strings (0) with fretted notes (2nd and 3rd fret) — the beginner trap is "finger syncing": matching plucking-hand finger choice to fretting-hand finger choice (fret-with-index → pluck-with-index, fret-with-middle → pluck-with-middle). Never do this — it's inflexible and collapses the moment a line needs to pluck the same note twice or fret with the ring/pinky, which happens constantly in real basslines. Treat the two hands as unrelated systems:

  • Fretting: index on every 2nd-fret note, middle on every 3rd-fret note — open, open, index, middle, middle, index, open, open, middle, index, middle, open.
  • Plucking: straight alternating regardless of what the fretting hand is doing — index, middle, index, middle, index, middle for the full 12-note riff, twice through.

Rhythm: syncopated, felt via the drum part

The riff's notes mix on-beat and off-beat hits — genuine syncopation, not a straight pulse. (The exact beat-by-beat count is only approximately captured from the source transcript — treat the specific subdivision below as a general sketch, not a verified chart.) Rough shape: on, off, on, off, off, off, continuing through the bar. The riff has a rest on beat 2 and beat 4 before landing on the next beat 1.

Internalizing it — hum the drum part instead of counting numbers: the drum track has a snare on beat 2, snare on beat 4, kick on beat 1 — hum "bum-snare, bum-bum-bum-snare, bum-kick, bum" in place of the bassline's own silences, locking your feel to what the drums are actually doing rather than trying to count blank space. See Syncopation and Metric Displacement for the general beat-ruler method this is a worked example of.

Shay Adelican on the feel: "it can be quite wobbly cuz it's a funky one — so have some fun" — the wobble is expected, not a sign you're playing it wrong.

Note length / muting

Right notes + right rhythm still sounds wrong if the notes don't end on time — a held note has to be actively stopped (touch the string with the fretting hand or the plucking hand), it won't stop on its own. For this riff's rest on beat 4: release the fretting pressure on the last note before the rest, adding a safety mute if needed so the silence is actually silent. Full technique → Bass Note Muting Technique.

The slide

Written with a scoop mark and no note leading into it — it's about the destination, not the starting fret. Slide up to the 7th fret, starting a few frets below (a middle distance — one fret away reads as anticlimactic, the max distance is excessive). Use the pinky (least shifting required afterward). Press down for the full slide but don't over-press or the hand sticks partway through; keep your eyes on where you're going, not where you started. Full method → Bass Slide Technique.

The bass solo

Short, and explicitly a synthesis of everything above rather than new material:

  • Fretting: pinky, index, pinky, shift, index, open.
  • Plucking: alternating index-middle-index-middle-index, then free choice for the last two notes after the phrase break.
  • Rhythm (beat-ruler shape): on, off, off, off, off, on, on.

Tuning

The riff is in E♭. Retune only the E string down a half step to E♭ — this riff stays entirely on the E and A strings, so the D and G strings can be left standard. Confirmed by Gorillaz's own bassist Shay Adelican: "the riff is E flat, so I detune my E string to E flat... yeah, the song is in E flat."

Advanced variant (Shay's actual live approach): rather than crossing from the low string to the A string the way BassBuzz teaches it to beginners, Shay plays the entire main riff on the single detuned low string — notes read fatter on the thicker string, and it means less retuning to manage on stage. BassBuzz teaches the cross-string version first because it's easier to learn, but flags the single-string version as the "cooler" thing to graduate to once the basic riff is solid.

Steal this

  • Never sync a fretting-hand fingering choice to a plucking-hand fingering choice — work out each hand's pattern independently; a plucking pattern that mirrors the fretting pattern will force inefficient same-finger repeats the moment the two hands' shapes diverge (they almost always do). → String Crossing and Plucking Patterns
  • Borrow the actual drum hits as your rhythm-counting syllables when a line is syncopated enough that blank counting breaks down — hum the kick/snare pattern that's really driving the groove instead of numbers. → Syncopation and Metric Displacement
  • A slide with no note leading into it is about the landing fret, not the starting fret — pick a starting distance that reads as a real gesture (not one fret, not the whole neck) and let the ear register the destination.
  • When a real player's live version differs from the record you're emulating, default to matching the record unless you're deliberately reinterpreting the part — that's the version a listener will actually recognize.

Why I like it

-

grant-green-blues-for-willarine.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Blues for Willarine
grant-green-blues-for-willarine.html:
A swing blues in B♭. Only one line — the closing 6-2-5-1 turnaround phrase — is transcribed here, so this is a stub rather than a full-chorus breakdown; see 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo and 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Number One Green Street for the fuller companion excerpts from the same lesson family. First vault documentation of this tune.

Chords

Key: B♭ · Form: 12-bar jazz blues. Only the closing turnaround is transcribed in the source lesson — the rest of the chorus isn't spelled out bar-by-bar for this specific tune, so treat the skeleton below as confirmed for bars 9–12 only:

Turnaround (bars 9–12): G7 – Cm7 – F7 – B♭ → VI7 – ii7 – V7 – I — the classic jazz-blues "6-2-5-1," the same shape documented in full (all 12 bars) on the companion tunes 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo and 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Number One Green Street from the same Jack Ruch lesson family. → Blues Form and Harmony, Turnarounds § VI7, The ii-V-I

Solo breakdown (Jack Ruch's transcription, excerpted 6-2-5-1 line)

  • A "classic 6-2-5-1 line" — Ruch's own description — that outlines the turnaround's chord changes primarily with chord tones plus a few altered notes, rather than leaning on one dense device the way the other two Green excerpts do. → Chord-Tone Soloing, Bebop Vocabulary
  • Reworked by Ruch using the minor-third-transposition device first demonstrated on the "Number One Green Street" excerpt: starts the line identically to Green's original, then takes one fragment of it and moves it up a minor third, before tying the result into his own existing vocabulary to close out the last few chords of the progression. → Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines § Transposition device

Steal this

  • A 6-2-5-1 turnaround line built mostly from chord tones with light alteration — a good "floor" line for the turnaround before reaching for the denser diminished-arpeggio/altered-scale vocabulary documented on the other two Green excerpts.
  • The minor-third-transposition move, confirmed a third time — same device Green uses in "Number One Green Street," now also shown as something Ruch deliberately reapplies when reworking a transcribed line into his own — i.e. it's both an analysis finding (something Green does) and a usable composing tool (something you can do to any lick).

Why I like it

grant-green-cool-blues.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Cool Blues
grant-green-cool-blues.html:
A B♭ jazz blues from Born to Be Blue. Nathan Borton pulls three named "essential sounds" plus a fourth umbrella of blues-language devices out of Green's solo, framed as a complete, generalizable toolkit for jazz improvisation rather than tune-specific licks — see Unlock Jazz Improv with ONE Grant Green Solo?! Honestly, Yes. 🙌 for the source video and full routing. A third Grant Green solo breakdown now in the vault, alongside 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo and 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Trace and Tracy — this one is the most abstract/concept-forward of the three.

Chords

Key: B♭ · Form: 12-bar blues. "Cool Blues" is a Charlie Parker composition (a "Bird blues" head) — Nathan Borton's breakdown of Green's Born to Be Blue solo works off three named chord targets rather than a bar-by-bar chart: B♭7 (I) → E♭7 (IV) → F7 (V), i.e. the standard I7 – IV7 – V7 blues skeleton. → Blues Form and Harmony

Solo breakdown (Nathan Borton's concept breakdown)

  • 5-to-1 lines at the I→IV move. Single-note lines outlining a V→I pull, used at the B♭7→E♭ transition to create forward momentum rather than static chord-to-chord playing. → Guide Tones, Blues Form and Harmony
  • Altered 5-to-1 lines (9, ♭9, ♯9) for a stronger pull. Two further phrases lean on altered dominant tensions specifically because they pull harder to the target than the plain version. → Altered Chords
  • 2-equals-5/5-equals-2 over F7: soloing C minor (F7's related ii) straight over the sounding F7. Up the C Dorian scale, then a descending 5-3-2-1 pattern — no F7 arpeggio played at all, just C minor language, and it "sounds awesome" over the dominant. → Chord Substitution § 4, The ii-V-I
  • 5-to-1 mixed into its related ii, recurring at bar 8 nearly every chorus. A form-anchored combination move, not a one-off. → Turnarounds
  • Tonic dominant over a sitting E♭7 — the 9th and 13th as stable, resolved-sounding melodic content. Treats the static dominant as "home," not tension. Two techniques: a D♭ major 7 arpeggio (the maj7 arpeggio starting on the ♭7 of E♭7, spelling its own ♭7-9-11-13), and the dominant bebop scale (landing the added chromatic passing tone into the 13th). → Bebop Vocabulary § 1, Extended Chords, Blues Form and Harmony § Why every chord is a dominant 7th
  • Walk-ups/walk-downs — chromatic connectors between chord tones. Anchored root, chromatic walk-down from the ♭7 to the 5th (reversible: 5th→♭7 ascending); also a 3rd→5th walk-up elsewhere in the solo. → Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch
  • Classic, movable blues-opening vocabulary. The solo's own opening phrase, stated to work over any dominant or major chord in the form (B♭7, E♭7, or F7) unmodified.
  • The Kansas City blues scale. A named five-note distillation of the blues scale, guitaristic and movable, with an emphasis on the 6th degree — used to riff and generate melodic ideas. Exact interval formula gated to the creator's paid lesson, not in the free captions. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes § Kansas City blues scale

Steal this

  • Alter a 5-to-1 line (9/♭9/♯9) any time you want the resolution to feel harder-earned — the same device as a plain guide-tone line, just with more pull.
  • Solo a dominant chord's related ii minor straight over the dominant itself — no ii chord has to actually sound; it's purely a soloing-vocabulary reframe of any V7.
  • On a static dominant that isn't resolving, reach for its 9th/13th (or the maj7-arpeggio-off-the-♭7 shortcut) instead of running its Mixolydian scale plain — the extensions are what make an unmoving dominant sound settled rather than stuck.
  • Any classic blues opening phrase is worth testing over all three chords of the form, not just the one it was first played over — dominant/major vocabulary transfers more freely than it seems like it should.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Search "Grant Green — Cool Blues" (Born to Be Blue)

Learning

grant-green-grant-s-tune.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Grant's Tune
grant-green-grant-s-tune.html:
A Grant Green original from Solid, picked by audience poll. Nathan Borton's approach: rename the A section's two-chord vamp as a disguised 1-5-1 (D♭7 is G7's tritone sub), lay out four interchangeable soloing systems for it, then treat the B section's slash chords as ordinary E♭-rooted qualities once fingered with E♭ in the bass. → How To Solo Over Grant's Tune! (Grant Green)

Chords

Key: C minor, modulating to E♭ major for the bridge — confirmed independently by jazzleadsheets.com's own analysis of the tune: chords "pivot between a tonic and a fifth in each measure," C minor in the A section (D♭7 alternating with G7) and E♭ major in the bridge.

A-section vamp: Cm7 – D♭7 (repeated) → i – ♭II7 — a disguised i–V–i, since D♭7 is the tritone substitute for G7 (V of C minor). A-section tag: E♭ major → plain ♭III (relative major), no substitution.

B section (slash chords over a held E♭ bass): E♭ | G♭/E♭ | E♭ | D♭/E♭ → finger the upper triads with E♭ underneath and they resolve to ordinary E♭ major – E♭ minor7 – E♭ major – E♭sus9. → Chord Substitution

Solo concepts by section (Nathan Borton's breakdown)

  • Over the Cm7–D♭7 vamp — four interchangeable systems, pick one and keep its partner sound consistent on the dominant: 1. C blues scale, hitting E♭, F, or G specifically over the dominant (D♭7/G7) — those three notes are chord/color tones of the dominant that also sit inside the C blues scale, so the line's shape doesn't change, it just resolves through those three notes as the harmony turns over. 2. C Dorian (natural 6, ♭7) over the minor, paired with A♭ melodic minor over the dominant — A♭ melodic minor is G7's altered scale (melodic minor a half step above the dominant root), so the whole vamp reduces to just two key centers: C minor and A♭ minor. 3. C "minor diminished" (the whole-half diminished scale off C), usable over both chords — caveat: the scale's A natural and D natural sound a little weird against the D♭7/G7. Fix: start on E♭ or A and walk straight up — works over either chord, best used as a transition device between the two or extra "scalier language," not a full-time solution. 4. Ignore the Cm7 and play G7♭9 the whole vamp — the reduced/static "easy mode": treat the loop as one dominant sound rather than two chords.
  • 5-to-1 motifs to open, close, or connect lines through the turnaround back into Cm7. → Turnarounds, Guide Tones
  • Over the A-section tag (E♭ major): plain tonic language — E♭ major vocabulary or enclosed chord tones of E♭maj7, no reharmonization.
  • Over the B section (E♭ major → E♭m7 → E♭ major → E♭sus9): either (a) modally — treat each chord as its own brief key center and match the sound to each; or (b) blend E♭ blues throughout, swapping only the 3rd — flat 3rd over the E♭m7, major 3rd everywhere else. Recommended: combine both, moving between the modal and blues readings phrase to phrase rather than committing to one.

Steal this

  • Rename a scary two-chord vamp before soloing over it. "Minor to an unrelated dominant a half step away" hides a plain 1-5-1 once the tritone sub is spotted — the rename, not new vocabulary, is what unlocks it. → Chord Substitution
  • When a scale doesn't cleanly fit every chord in a short loop, use it as connective tissue between the chords instead of a full-time solution — the C minor-diminished walk-up (from E♭ or A) is explicitly a transition device here, not the main system.
  • On slash chords over one held bass note, finger the upper triad with the bass underneath before assuming the progression is exotic — E♭ | G♭/E♭ | E♭ | D♭/E♭ is just E♭ major/minor7/major/sus9 in ordinary clothes.
  • Practice both halves of the same skill inside one tune — sitting on a single static sound over a long stretch, and moving one sound fluently across several chord qualities, are different muscles; this tune drills both in eight bars.

Why I like it

  • Search "Grant Green — Grant's Tune" (Solid)

grant-green-miss-ann-s-tempo.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo
grant-green-miss-ann-s-tempo.html:
A swing blues in B♭. Jack Ruch transcribes the opening chorus of Green's solo, phrase by phrase, as concrete jazz-blues vocabulary — see How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues for the source video and the broader routing. For the underlying 12-bar jazz-blues form and its 6-2-5-1 turnaround, see Blues Form and Harmony and The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues, which analyzes the identical turnaround in the abstract. A second Jack Ruch video, Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own, transcribes the tune's opening five bars with a different framing — a 2-5-1-of-the-IV cadence — and demonstrates moving that exact line to fit the tune's other 2-5-1 (inside the main 6-2-5-1 turnaround).

Chords

Key: B♭ · Form: 12-bar jazz blues, swing feel (from Grant's First Stand, 1961). Bars 1–4: B♭7 (I). Bars 5–8: E♭7 (IV) back to B♭7 (I). Bars 9–12: the jazz-blues turnaround — G7 – Cm7 – F7 – B♭7 → VI7 – ii7 – V7 – I (the "6-2-5-1"). → Blues Form and Harmony, Turnarounds § VI7

A second reading of bars 1–5 (from Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own) frames the approach into the IV chord as its own ii–V–I of E♭: Fm7 – B♭7 – E♭, resolving to the local tonic before the form's own IV arrives — the same ii–V–I shape that reappears at the turnaround's Cm7 – F7 – B♭7. → The ii-V-I

Solo breakdown (Jack Ruch's transcription, opening chorus)

  • Bars 1–4 (I, B♭): opens with a slide-based lick out of a chord-shape fingering — minor 3rd up to major 3rd (D♭→D), then 5th up to 6th up to root (F→G→B♭) — then descends into B♭ minor pentatonic/blues-scale territory: ♭7 down to the 5th (A♭→F), a slide from the 4th up to the ♭5 (E♭→E), back down to the ♭7. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • Bars 5–8 (IV, E♭): the I→IV chromatic pivot — the major 3rd of B♭ (D) drops a half step to D♭, which is the plain scale tone over I but becomes the ♭7 of E♭7 the instant the harmony changes. → Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Bars 9–12 (6-2-5-1 turnaround, G7–Cm7–F7–B♭7): lands the VI chord (G7) on nothing more than its root, G, then plays a signature line targeting the ♭9 of G7 (A♭), dense with enclosures and chromatic pedal tones — the same altered/bebop device The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues extracted from Green's style in the abstract. Followed by a related "common Grant Green / bebop phrase" bridging back from the IV-chord material into the G7 line, taught slow then at tempo. → Turnarounds § VI7, Bebop Vocabulary § Target the guide tones
  • Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own's reading of bars 1–5: frames the same opening material as B♭ major triad → G minor triad (with chromatic passing notes) → F minor 7 → B♭7 → resolving to the 3rd of E♭ — an explicit 2-5-1 of the IV chord (F minor 7 = ii of E♭, B♭7 = V of E♭, E♭ = local I). Stated method behind this reading: "always learn the chord progression first — that gives you context for what's happening in the solo." Ruch then reuses this exact line over the tune's other 2-5-1 — the C minor 7 → F7 → B♭7 inside the main 6-2-5-1 turnaround — adjusting the phrasing to fit the new chord tones. A concrete demonstration that a 2-5-1 lick learned in one spot in a tune is directly reusable at any other 2-5-1 in the same key. → The ii-V-I, Chord Substitution

Steal this

  • The I→IV half-step pivot (major 3rd of I drops to become the ♭7 of IV) — cheap, guitar-idiomatic reharmonization-by-reinterpretation of a single held note, no scale change required.
  • Land the VI chord on the plain root before spending your vocabulary on the denser 2-5-1 that follows — not every chord needs decoration, especially right before one that will get plenty.
  • Target the ♭9 over a VI7/secondary-dominant for the altered bebop color, confirmed here as genuine Green vocabulary (not just a Ruch teaching example) since it recurs almost identically in 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Number One Green Street.
  • Learn a 2-5-1 line once, then reuse it at every other 2-5-1 in the same key — the opening bars' F minor 7 - B♭7 - E♭ line reappears, adjusted, over the turnaround's own C minor 7 - F7 - B♭7 later in the same chorus. → The ii-V-I

Why I like it

grant-green-number-one-green-street.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Number One Green Street
grant-green-number-one-green-street.html:
A swing blues in B♭, the second of two Grant Green solos Jack Ruch transcribes to build jazz-blues vocabulary — see How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues for the source video, and 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo for the companion excerpt over the same key/form, several devices shared between the two. A second Jack Ruch video, Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own, transcribes an overlapping I→IV→VI→ii passage from this same solo with a methodology focus (how to rework a transcribed line into your own), adding the minor-third-transposition device and a diminished-7-arpeggio reading of the VI7 color not covered in the first video.

Chords

Key: B♭ · Form: 12-bar jazz blues, swing feel (from Green Street, 1961 — track listed as "No. 1 Green Street"). Bars 1–4: B♭7 (I). Bars 5–8: a ii–V–I into IV — Fm7 – B♭7 – E♭ → ii7 – V7 – I (of E♭) — before working back toward the top. Bars 9–12: the jazz-blues turnaround — G7 – Cm7 – F7 – B♭7 → VI7 – ii7 – V7 – I, the same "6-2-5-1" as 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo. → Blues Form and Harmony, Turnarounds § VI7, The ii-V-I

Solo breakdown (Jack Ruch's transcription, first chorus)

  • Pickup into bar 1: a rhythmic pickup phrase plays into the top of the form rather than starting cold on the downbeat. → Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch
  • Bars 1–4 (I, B♭): plain blues vocabulary — root, major 3rd, 4th, 5th, root, ♭7 — called out as "pretty standard blues stuff," the floor beneath the denser material elsewhere in the chorus. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • Bars 5–6 (2-5-1 into IV): a lick built directly out of the ii chord of the target — F minor 7 – B♭7 – E♭, played "right out of an F minor seven" arpeggio rather than a scale run across the two bars. → Chord Substitution § 4. Interpolating a ii in front of any dominant, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • Landing on IV (E♭): the same I→IV chromatic pivot as 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Miss Ann's Tempo — hitting the ♭7 of E♭7 (D♭), confirming it's genuine recurring Green vocabulary rather than a one-off. → Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Back to I: more minor-pentatonic blues vocabulary bridging back to the top of the form. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes
  • Bars 9–12 (6-2-5-1 turnaround): the same signature move as the companion tune — target the ♭9 of G7 (A♭) for the altered/bebop color — followed by a C minor arpeggio/triad over Cm7, then F7, back to B♭7. Closes the turnaround with a chromatic walk up to the 3rd of the I chord (B♭7), a guide-tone-targeting resolution mirroring the ♭9-then-chromatic-walk device used on the VI7. → Turnarounds § VI7, Bebop Vocabulary § Target the guide tones / Approach notes
  • Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own's reading of the same I→IV→VI→ii stretch: the I→IV move is described as the B♭ altered scale over B♭7, shifted down a half step over E♭7 to outline an E♭♯11 (Lydian dominant) color — a slightly different framing of the same chromatic pivot documented above. Going into the VI chord (G7), the ♭9 color is attributed to a diminished-7th arpeggio device (stated rule: dim7 built a half step above the dominant's root — standard half-whole-diminished; the specific worked instance named in that video is ambiguous between that and a same-root G-dim7-over-G7 reading — confirm by ear). Over the ii chord (Cm7), Green plays a short phrase and then immediately transposes it up a minor third and repeats it — called out as "a really common theme in a lot of Grant's phrasing," and not documented from the first video. → Diminished Chords, Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines § Transposition device

Steal this

  • Approach a IV chord with a 2-5-1 built from its own ii-chord arpeggio (F minor 7 into B♭7 into E♭) rather than running a scale across the transition — a small, self-contained harmonic unit worth having ready any time a IV chord is a bar or two away.
  • Chromatic walk-up to the tonic's 3rd as a turnaround-closing device — the mirror image of the ♭9-then-chromatic-walk approach used on the VI7 earlier in the same chorus, now landing the whole form instead of coloring one chord.
  • "Learn the arpeggios to the underlying chords first" — Ruch's own stated on-ramp for finding lines like these, aimed at players newer to this vocabulary. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • Transpose a short phrase up a minor third and replay it immediately — a genuine recurring Grant Green habit (confirmed here over the ii chord), and a free way to generate a second phrase from one idea without composing anything new. → Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

  • Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own (Jack Ruch — methodology-focused re-transcription of the I-IV-VI-ii stretch of this same solo, adding the minor-third-transposition device)

grant-green-trace-and-tracy.title: 🎵 GRANT GREEN - Trace and Tracy
grant-green-trace-and-tracy.html:
A minor blues in B♭ minor. Nathan Borton pulls four foundational concepts out of Green's solo over this tune — tonic minor soloing, color-tone emphasis, a named rhythmic embellishment ("the dilla rhythm"), and classic blues-language vocabulary — see Why Grant Green's Minor Blues Soloing Is PERFECT (Jazz 101) for the source video and the broader routing. For the minor-blues form itself, see Blues Form and Harmony § Minor blues, which documents the same "the V frequently stays a dominant" rule this solo's tonic-minor devices are built on.

Chords

Key: B♭ minor · Form: minor blues (i–iv–V family, per Blues Form and Harmony § Minor blues: i7 – iv7 – … – V7 – i7, V typically staying a dominant rather than resolving to minor). The source breakdown names only the two chords it solos over directly — B♭m7 (i) and E♭m7 (iv) — matching that skeleton; a full bar-by-bar chart isn't given in the lesson, and independent listings for this tune (recorded as "Tracin' Tracy," from the Sunday Morning session) only confirm the same i–iv minor-blues relationship, not the complete 12-bar sequence. → Tonic Minor Soloing

Solo breakdown (Nathan Borton's transcription)

  • Tonic minor — implied 5–1 inside a static chord. Two phrases from the same line: D natural → E♭ over the E♭ minor (iv) chord (D is the major 3rd of B♭7, V7 of E♭ minor — an implied 5-1 compressed into two notes), and A natural → B♭ over the B♭ minor (i) chord (A is the major 3rd of F7, V7 of B♭ minor), the identical device transposed to the other chord. → Tonic Minor Soloing
  • A full 5–1 line played straight over a static chord. A complete phrase outlining F7 moving to B♭ minor, played in its entirety over an unmoving B♭m vamp (the V chord isn't actually sounding), with a plain minor phrase tagged onto the end to land back in blues/pentatonic language. → Tonic Minor Soloing
  • Color tones over B♭ minor. Deliberately lands on and emphasizes the 9th (C natural), the natural 13th (G), and (named as a further option) the 11th (E♭) of B♭ minor — chord extensions used as a conscious melodic feature of the tonic-minor and blues lines rather than incidental passing tones. → Extended Chords
  • The "dilla rhythm." A named rhythmic embellishment cell that interrupts a straight eighth-note line to move through scale or arpeggio tones — demonstrated walking down the tonic minor scale, and separately embellishing a B♭ minor 6 arpeggio. Part of Green's broader habit in this solo of constantly shifting between eighth notes, quarter notes, and triplets. → Dilla Rhythm Ornamentation
  • Blues language, end of chorus 1. A phrase built from a small, one-octave blues box — moved around the neck rather than parked in a single position, the same "many small boxes over the whole neck" idea documented on String-Group Pentatonic Bursts and Diagonal Pentatonic Blues Soloing. → Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch
  • Blues language, start of chorus 2. The blues scale played vertically, up and down the neck rather than horizontally within one box — milking the high register — and again landing on the minor 11th extension (part of the blues scale itself), tying the color-tone habit above directly into blues-scale vocabulary. → Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch, Extended Chords

Steal this

  • Compress a V7→i cadence into a single outside note (the V7's major 3rd, resolved down a half step into a chord tone) any time you're stuck on a static minor chord — cheap, immediate harmonic motion with no change to the actual changes.
  • Play the whole 5-1 line, not just the outside-note shortcut, when there's room — a complete dominant-to-tonic phrase over a chord that never moves reads as far more sophisticated than pentatonic alone, and it still resolves cleanly because the line itself supplies the resolution.
  • Consciously target the 9/11/13 of a static minor chord as a feature, not a byproduct — the same extensions that make comping voicings interesting (see Extended Chords) work as melodic landing points in a solo too.
  • Break up a straight eighth-note run with one syncopated embellishment cell rather than a whole new subdivision — variety from placement, not from switching feels.

Why I like it

harry-warren-there-will-never-be-another.title: 🎵 HARRY WARREN - There Will Never Be Another You
harry-warren-there-will-never-be-another.html:
A 32-bar ABAC standard in E♭ major, used by Jens Larsen as the full worked example for a chord-memorization-by-chunking method — the same slot-devices (32-Bar Song Form's table) that recur across "It Could Happen to You," "But Not for Me," and other tunes in this form. Full breakdown: Memorizing Chord Progressions and Jazz Standards - Jazz Theory and Analysis put to use!.

Chords

As analyzed, chunked.

A (8 bars) — E♭maj7 (2 bars) | Dø7 – G7 → Cm7 (2-5 to vi) | B♭m7 – E♭7 → A♭maj7 (2-5 to IV) B (8 bars) — A♭maj7 (IV) | A♭m6/D♭7 (IV-minor) → E♭maj7 (I) | F7 – B♭7 (V7/V, "5 of 5," 2 bars) | Fm7(ii, opens back to A) A (8 bars) — repeat of the first A C (8 bars) — A♭maj7 (IV) | A♭m6/D♭7 (IV-minor) → E♭maj7 (I) | Dø7 → Gm7 (♯4°-reharmonized-as-ii, cadencing to ii) | E♭maj7 – A♭7 – Gm7 – C7 (closing turnaround-flavored progression) | B♭7 (tag, back to top)

Chunk map (the memorization payoff)

Chunk Bars Reads as
Tonic A, bar 1–2 I, 2 bars
2-5 to vi A, bar 3–4 Dø7–G7→Cm7, one unit
2-5 to IV A, bar 5–6 B♭m7–E♭7→A♭maj7, one unit
IV → IV-minor → I B/C opening Reused verbatim between B and C
V7/V B, late 2-bar "5 of 5," a very common ABAC-form first-half-ending device
♯4°→ii minor cadence C, mid Historically a bare ♯4-diminished, reharmonized post-bebop into a minor ii–V — see Diminished Chords
Cadence to C minor C, closing (4 bars) Bracket-grouped as one chunk
2-5-1 to the 6th degree C, closing (4 bars) Bracket-grouped as one chunk
"4-minor back to 1" C, closing (4 bars) Reusable shape across many standards in this form
"5-of-5 to 2-5" C, closing (4 bars) Also common at the END OF A BRIDGE in AABA tunes (Ellington-style), not unique to this form

Steal this

  • Chunk a chart the same way you'd memorize a phone number — country code / area code / rest, i.e. form → cadences → small functional units — rather than a flat row of chord symbols. → Memorizing Jazz Standards by Harmonic Chunking
  • Once B and C share their opening bars, that material only needs to be learned once — check any ABAC-shaped tune for this before assuming the second half is all-new material. → 32-Bar Song Form
  • Cadences to the IV degree at the start of the B section, and IV→IV-minor→I shortly after, are recurring, position-predictable devices across this whole family of 32-bar standards — recognize the slot, not just the one tune's chords. → 32-Bar Song Form
  • A ♯4-diminished chord resolving into a minor cadence is very often a reharmonized bebop-era substitution for what used to be a bare diminished chord — "Embraceable You" is (possibly) one of the earliest examples of this specific move. → Diminished Chords
  • When a passage looks harmonically dense, check what's on the strong beats — here the closing turnaround reads as just I→ii with A♭7/C7 as passing embellishments, not four equally-important chords.

Why I like it

hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.title: 🎵 HOAGY CARMICHAEL - Georgia on My Mind
hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.html:
1930 standard (Carmichael/Gorrell); Ray Charles' 1960 recording (key of G) is the definitive version and Georgia's official state song. Chord chart below is Jared Borowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons with Jared) open-position arrangement — deliberately "the REAL chords" (jazz-informed harmony, not a simplified 3-chord version) fingered so any guitarist with basic open chords can play it. A companion video from the same channel, Georgia on My Mind Fingerstyle Guitar Tutorial (With Sheet Music & Tab), builds the same harmony (also transposed to the key of C) into a full solo fingerstyle chord-melody arrangement — see the Fingerstyle arrangement section below and 🎵 HOAGY CARMICHAEL - Georgia on My Mind (Guitar) for the measure-by-measure breakdown. Jared's own recommended order is chords first (this note), then the fingerstyle arrangement.

Chords

Taught key: open-position shapes in the key of C. Capo 5 to play along with sheet music (usually published in F, the most common key). Capo 7 to play along with the Ray Charles recording (key of G).

A section — "Georgia, Georgia, the whole day through, just an old sweet song keeps Georgia on my mind":

Chord (C-shape) Lyric anchor Alt / color options
C "Geor-gia" Cmaj7 (lift one finger, jazzier)
E7 "Geor-gia" open E7 (melody on pinky, 2nd string/3rd fret) preferred → std. E7 shape (can read muddy); jazz option: Bm7♭5 → E7 (insert the half-diminished as a passing chord in front of E7)
Am "song of you" —
Am/G (bass walk) A minor stays the chord; G forced as the bass note — deliberate descending bassline
D/F♯ (bass walk) D7/F♯ (more spice, melody note included) → D9/F♯ (root omitted from the shape, singer supplies it)
F minor 6 "the whole day through" Jared's favorite chord in the arrangement
E minor 7 — plain Em, fully interchangeable
A7 "old sweet song keeps" only option, no alternates
D minor 7 "Georgia" plain Dm
G13 — G7 w/ open high-E on top preferred → std. open G7
E minor 7 → E minor — deliberate double voicing back to back
C major → (delayed) E minor "on my mind" expected cadence delayed — see Delayed resolution below
Em → Em7 → C → A7 → Dm "old sweet song keeps Georgia on my mind" Em→A7 functions like a ii–V pulling toward the coming Dm
D minor (resolution) "my [mind]" Dm7 / plain Dm simple → G7♯5 (chromatic pre-chord, "spicy," ♯5 outside the key) jazzier → G+ (augmented triad, no 7th) alt to the dominant version, same color, lower register

A section repeats with the same chord menu (2nd verse).

Bridge into pre-chorus — "through the Pines...":

  • F7 (leaves the tonic) → alt F minor 6 (reused favorite) → alt B♭9 (near-identical voicing to Fm6, bottom note on a different string; B♭9→C is another delayed-resolution move)
  • Strumming note: avoid the top two strings on the F7 shape, mute if strumming through
  • Back to C (or Cmaj7)

B section — "The arms that reach out to me...":

  • E7 (any voicing) → Am (or Am7 for a floatier/jazzier sound)
  • E7 again OR D minor 6 ("more traditional") — both work, melody note fits either
  • 3rd alt at same spot: F minor 6 again (open D = melody note here too)
  • Am7 — physically the same shape as the E7 voicing on a different string set, so Am7→E7→Am7 is one repeated shape shifted across string groups
  • F7 again (same strum caution)
  • B section repeats ("the eyes smile...")
  • E7 — no alternates here — "still in peaceful dreams I see"
  • C6 — Jared's own arrangement choice (C shape + added note, 3rd string/2nd fret); steps down a half step for smooth bass motion
  • B7 — hard fingering (pinky on the 5th string), give it extra practice time. Many charts insert a chord before it (same device as Bm7♭5→E7); this arrangement goes straight to B7.
  • E minor → A7 — a ii–V in the key
  • D minor 7 — deliberately correct even though it does not contain the sung melody note (E) — stated exception to the "melody note should be in the chord" rule. Alt: plain Dm. Alt: D minor 9 (adds open high-E, restores the melody note to the voicing)
  • G13 (preferred) or plain G7

A section repeats to the end.

Turnaround (cycling back to repeat the form — solos, repeats): E♭ diminished 7 preferred, "more jazz" or plain A minor more classic.

Ending (last time through): land on C major (or Cmaj7), arrived at via any of the leave-and-return pre-chords above (F7 / F minor 6 / B♭9).

Reharmonization devices used throughout

  • Delayed resolution — the expected tonic (C) is deferred by substituting a chord that shares the melody note (e.g. C → Em instead of landing on C, B♭9 → C) → Reharmonization.
  • Passing-chord insertion — a chord placed in front of the "real" chord for extra harmonic motion (Bm7♭5 before E7; a chord before B7) → Passing Chords.
  • Chromatic altered pre-chord — G7♯5 / G augmented before Dm, an out-of-key color tone resolving into the target → Passing Chords · Altered Chords.
  • Slash-chord bass walks — Am/G and D/F♯ keep the chord identity fixed while the bass descends stepwise underneath → Slash Chords.
  • Melody-note-in-the-chord substitution rule — any chord containing the sung melody note is a legal reharmonization at that spot, whether or not it's the "obvious" chord (stated explicitly, then also shown broken once on purpose at the D minor 7 in the B section) → Reharmonization.
  • Turnaround color choice — E♭dim7 (jazz) vs. Am (classic) at the repeat point → Turnarounds.

Fingerstyle arrangement

Jared Borowski also built a full solo fingerstyle chord-melody arrangement of the tune (same channel, also key of C) — melody, harmony and a moving bass line all fingerpicked at once on one guitar, rather than strummed chords. Full measure-by-measure breakdown lives on 🎵 HOAGY CARMICHAEL - Georgia on My Mind (Guitar) and the source video is Georgia on My Mind Fingerstyle Guitar Tutorial (With Sheet Music & Tab). Highlights:

  • Opens with a Travis-picking/Chet-Atkins-style alternating bass under a plain C chord, then a chromatic walking bassline carries the harmony down toward E major — at one point there's no chord at all, just a moving bass note doing the harmonic work.
  • Structure: A section (measures 1–5) repeats with a 1st/2nd ending, into a B section, then DC al Coda (repeat to the top, jump to the Coda after measure 5 the second time) — a compact, through-composed AABA-shaped form matching this note's structure field.
  • The song's signature "Georgia... on my mind" hook is voiced with a "haunting," out-of-key neighbor chord rearticulated multiple times (fingering forces the re-strike) rather than sustained once — an intentional ornamentation device, not a limitation.
  • Ends on a genuine ii–V voice-leading move into the Coda, singled out by Jared as one of his favorite moments in the arrangement.

Production & Arrangement

Not covered in either lesson (guitar chord chart / solo fingerstyle arrangement only, no production breakdown) — see the Ray Charles 1960 recording separately if a production pass is wanted later.

Steal this

  • "Chord in front of a chord" as a general jazz-harmony move — insert a related chord (often the ii or a half-diminished) immediately before a target chord to add motion without changing the underlying changes → Passing Chords · Reharmonization.
  • Delayed resolution as a phrase-ending device — substitute at the expected cadence point instead of landing, then land later → Reharmonization.
  • Slash chords for intentional bass motion under a static chord identity (Am/G, D/F♯) → Slash Chords.
  • Walking chromatic bass notes between chord changes (5th of the current chord → passing tone → root/bass note of the next chord) — full detail on the video page.

Why I like it

-

Listen

  • Ray Charles — "Georgia on My Mind" (1960, key of G) · search "Georgia on My Mind Ray Charles"

jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.title: 🎵 JAMIROQUAI - Emergency on Planet Earth
jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.html:
Title track, Emergency on Planet Earth (1993), bassist Stuart Zender. This note is a bass-focused breakdown of just the intro riff — a simple slap-and-pop roots-and-octaves pattern — as taught by BassBuzz as the real-music payoff for its Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique lesson.

Chords

The only stretch of this song with a chord chart consistent enough across sources to trust: the intro, in (likely) G minor: Gm9 – B♭7/F – E♭maj9 – D7♯5♭9 → i9 – III7 (1st inv.) – ♭VImaj9 – V7♯5♭9 — a genuinely jazz-funk intro voicing: extended 9ths throughout and an altered dominant (D7♯5♭9) resolving back to the Gm9 tonic, consistent with the acid-jazz genre and keyboardist Toby Smith's Rhodes writing across the album.

The rest of the song does not have a chord chart I could verify with confidence. The handful of tab sites offering a full verse/chorus breakdown disagree with each other on both the chords and their order — one lists a chromatically-walking Gm–Am–B♭m–Cm chorus that doesn't fit the intro's harmonic language at all, and reads like an unreliable auto-generated chart. Rather than pick one arbitrarily, this section stays scoped to the intro only, matching this page's existing "intro riff only" framing above.

The riff

Roots and octaves throughout — a deliberately simple pattern chosen specifically as a slap-and-pop workout, not a virtuoso line. Fretting given as index (slap) + pinky (pop) unless noted:

  1. Index, 3rd fret E string (slap) → pinky, 5th fret D string (pop). The D-string pop here is the harder popping-finger placement flagged throughout Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique and Popping Technique — Thumb Up vs Thumb Down, Hook, and Minimum Viable Pressure — no G string to tuck against as a guide.
  2. Slide the same shape down: index, 1st fret E string (slap) → pinky, 3rd fret D string (pop).
  3. Move up: index, 6th fret A string (slap) → pinky, 8th fret G string (pop) — the easier G-string pop.
  4. A root-only note: pinky, 5th fret A string — sets up the next phrase.
  5. Index, 3rd fret A string (slap) → pinky, 5th fret G string (pop).
  6. Up two frets: index, 5th fret A string (slap) → pinky, 7th fret G string (pop).
  7. Up one more fret: index, 6th fret A string (slap) → pinky, 8th fret G string (pop).
  8. Closing notes: middle finger, 4th fret E string — resolves back into the top of the riff for the repeat.

Why BassBuzz uses this riff

Picked specifically as a real-song teeter-totter workout: it's simple (roots and octaves, no fancy fills) but still forces the popping finger onto the trickier D string early on (step 1 above), then eases into the more forgiving G-string pop for the rest of the phrase — good sequencing for a player who's just drilled the open-string E/G and E/D teeter-totter patterns and is ready to apply the motion to fretted notes in a real riff.

Steal this

  • A roots-and-octaves riff is a legitimate slap-and-pop workout in its own right — not every slap line needs to be flashy to be a useful drill or a useful part.
  • Sequence the harder D-string pop early in a phrase, before easing into the easier G-string pop — mirrors how BassBuzz builds up drills generally (see Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique's open-string progression).

Why I like it

jerome-kern-all-the-things-you-are.title: 🎵 JEROME KERN - All The Things You Are
jerome-kern-all-the-things-you-are.html:
A 36-bar AABA-shaped jazz standard that modulates through four key centers (A♭ → C → E♭/G → E → back to A♭) — more modulation than almost any other tune in the standard repertoire, which makes it the canonical teaching vehicle for pivot-chord analysis and for the "modulate up a major 3rd" device. Full worked breakdown: Jens Larsen - All The Things You Are - Harmonic Analysis.

Form and key map

Section Bars Key center What happens
A1 8 A♭ major → C major 1-6-2-5-style turnaround, then a G7 pivot resolves UP to C major instead of down to the expected Cm
A2 8 E♭ major → G major Same shape as A1, transposed up a step; C7 pivots up to G major
Bridge 8 G major → E major 2-5-1 in G, then a deceptive ii-V that resolves to E major instead of the expected vi (E minor)
A3 12 E major → A♭ major (stays) One-bar pivot (E major → C7alt) drops back into F minor/A♭ major; extended +4 bars into a tag/coda ending, no further modulation

Chords

As analyzed, not the literal real-book voicings — see note below on triads.

A1 — Fm7 – B♭m7 – E♭7 – A♭maj7 – G7(pivot) – Cmaj7 A2 — A♭m7 – D♭m7 – G♭7 – B♭maj7 – C7(pivot) – E♭maj7 (→ hints Cm) Bridge — Am7 – D7 – Gmaj7 – F♯ø7 – E major (deceptive resolution) – [Emaj7 → C7alt, one-bar pivot] A3 (coda, extended) — Fm7 – B♭m7 – E♭7 – A♭maj7 – D♭maj7(IV) – D♭m6/G♭7(iv-minor) – Cm7(iii) – ♭3°/♯4° dim – B♭m7♭5(ii) – E♭7alt(V) – A♭maj7(I)

Chord-scale map for soloing (from the video, A♭-major reading)

Chord Scale
A♭ tonic material (Fm7-B♭m7-E♭7-A♭maj7) A♭ major throughout
G7 / C7 (pivot chords) C / G harmonic minor (♭9/♭13, "smooth" reading) — or Lydian-then-half-step-down as an alternate color on the landing major chord
Bridge (G major, then F♯ø7-E) G major scale; F♯ half-diminished as a straight minor ii-V
C7alt → Fm (bridge's one-bar pivot) F harmonic minor
D♭m6/G♭7 (iv-minor in the coda) D♭ melodic minor
♭3°/♯4° diminished (coda) C harmonic minor, derived by ear from A♭ major (swap B♭→B, D♭→D) — enharmonically ≈ A♭ harmonic major

Steal this

  • Confirm the key from the ENDING (final cadence + final melody note), never from the opening chord — the tune opens on what sounds like a tonic-minor (Fm7) but the real key is A♭ major, confirmed only by where it actually resolves. → Keys, Cadences
  • "Modulate up a major 3rd" is a reusable, recognizable device — worth having in the toolkit for both analysis (spot it fast in other tunes) and composition/reharmonization. → Modulation (Key Change)
  • When a pivot chord is genuinely ambiguous, pick the reading that puts the surprise at the resolution, not at the dominant — an altered dominant already signals "modulating," so save the "aha" for the landing chord. → Modulation (Key Change)
  • A single altered chord tone can flip a stable tonic triad into a functioning altered dominant for a fast one-bar key exit (E major → lower the 5th → functions as C7alt → resolves to F minor). → Chord Substitution § Tritone substitution
  • The ♭3°/♯4° diminished before a final ii-V is a recurring, teachable device, not a one-off — same chord/melody-note relationship also appears in "Stella by Starlight" and "I Remember You." → Diminished Chords
  • Bare triad voicings (not extended chords) can be a deliberate ambiguity tool — Kern's own coda opens in plain triads specifically so the F-minor/A♭-major ambiguity survives a couple of bars before resolving; voicing the tonic minor as a m6 chord (the "normal" jazz habit) would kill that ambiguity outright. → Chord Voicings

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

Full chord-by-chord and bar-by-bar breakdown (modulation reasoning, chord-scale choices, the diminished-chord derivation, the triad-voicing ambiguity device) → Jens Larsen - All The Things You Are - Harmonic Analysis. Tie into Song Practice if/when queued for active learning (not auto-queued by this enrichment pass).

jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.title: 🎵 JEROME KERN - Nobody Else But Me
jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.html:
Framed by the source video as an unusually dense teaching vehicle — one standard containing seven distinct, frequently-recurring jazz harmonic devices, so it works as a compressed survey of the wider standards repertoire rather than a one-off tune to memorize. Full worked breakdown: The Jazz Standard That Turns Students Into Pro Players.

Devices found in this tune (by location)

Location Device What's happening
Measures 6–9 Two 5–1 modulations 5–1 in B, then 5–1 in E — signals a key change each time
Home key (ii chord) Dominant two chord D7 in place of the expected Dm7/Dm7♭5 — a static lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant color, not a functioning V
End of tune Passing diminished chords C°7 (read as rootless A7, resolving to Dm) and E♭° (resolving downward to D, read as triads from the diminished scale)
Measure 26 Backdoor dominant B♭7 → Cmaj7 — the ♭VII7→I backdoor cadence, treated with the same lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant sound as the dominant-two chord
Last 3 bars Chord walkup progression ii chord walks up to the V chord instead of sitting static
Closing turnaround Tadd Dameron turnaround A dense chromatic turnaround, simplified via C minor pentatonic or the "Coltrane pattern" (1-2-3-5 chord tones per chord)
Measures 9–12 Non-functional changes (melody-driven reharmonization) D♭ then E♭7 chords exist only because Kern is harmonizing the top melody note, not moving through real function

Chords

Chord-scale / vocabulary map, from the video.

Spot Scale / approach
Dominant two chord (D7 in C) Melodic minor built off the dominant's own 5th (A melodic minor over D7) — the lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant sound
Passing diminished, dominant read (C°7 → Dm) Standard 5–1 vocabulary treating C°7 as A7
Passing diminished, downward-resolving (E♭° → D) Triads pulled from the diminished scale (F triad over E♭°, transposable in minor 3rds)
Backdoor dominant (B♭7 → Cmaj7) Same D7 grips/lines, moved to B♭7; target treated as F minor
Chord walkup (last 3 bars) Three options: outline the key center (Cmaj7 language) / one long substituted ii–V / the literal walkup chords
Tadd Dameron turnaround C minor pentatonic straight through, or the "Coltrane pattern" (1-2-3-5 per chord)
D♭ chord (measures 9-12) C-major language transposed to D♭
E♭7 chord (measures 9-12) E♭ lydian dominant, or B♭ melodic minor (E♭7's own 5th)

Steal this

  • Pick one standard that happens to be harmonically dense and drill it as a survey of the whole vocabulary, rather than sampling one device per tune across many tunes. → Song Practice
  • A diminished chord's resolution DIRECTION decides how to play it — resolving up a half step into a dominant target → read it as a rootless dominant a half step below; resolving DOWN → read it as triads out of the diminished scale instead. A clean, generalizable rule, not tune-specific. → Diminished Chords
  • "Dominant two chord" and "backdoor dominant" are the same underlying sound wearing two different chord-symbol hats — both get the lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant treatment (melodic minor off the 5th), so learning one grip vocabulary covers both. → Modal Jazz § Tonic dominant, Turnarounds § Backdoor
  • When a passage looks harmonically overwhelming, there's almost always a cheaper legal read available — outline the key center instead of chasing every chord (walkup progressions), or lean on a single pentatonic scale across a dense turnaround (Tadd Dameron) — reserve the literal chord-by-chord read for when you actually want that level of detail. → Chord Progressions, Turnarounds
  • Some chord changes exist to harmonize the melody, not to move through function — check whether the "chord progression" is actually just voicing a static or repeating melody note before analyzing it as real harmonic motion. → Reharmonization

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

Full chord-by-chord and device-by-device breakdown → The Jazz Standard That Turns Students Into Pro Players. Tie into Song Practice if/when queued for active learning (not auto-queued by this enrichment pass).

joe-pass-little-darlin.title: 🎵 JOE PASS - Little Darlin'
joe-pass-little-darlin.html:
Jens Larsen transcribes and breaks down the opening ~20 bars of Joe Pass's chord-melody arrangement of this standard from Intercontinental — see This is How Joe Pass Plays Amazing Solos for the source video and the full routing. Caption quality flag: the source captions are garbled/auto-generated-style throughout (labeled "en" but reading like an auto-translated track); chord names below are Larsen's reconstructed reading, not verbatim caption text — treat as medium confidence.

Chords

Key: C major (this arrangement) · Form: 32-bar-family swing standard — Neal Hefti's "Li'l Darlin'," famous from the Count Basie Orchestra's 1958 recording at a notoriously slow ~64 BPM ("an object lesson in how to swing at a slow tempo"); this page covers Joe Pass's solo-guitar chord-melody reading of it, in C.

The arrangement never opens on the tonic — D7 → G7 → Cmaj7 (V7/V → V7 → I) — before the same phrase recurs twice more, reharmonized differently each time (see the arrangement breakdown below). Recurring devices across the excerpt: the diatonic iii (Em) turned into its own dominant, E7, a Joe Pass trademark that doesn't need to resolve anywhere; a basic I–IV–I passage under the F6–B♭7–C6 phrase (IV7 borrowed as a color, not a real modulation); and, by bars 17–20, the same opening phrase harmonized a third time as a straight ii–V throughout (a Dm11-type ii moving to G7) — denser than the V7/V opening, the clearest ii–V–I stretch in the excerpt.

This is one specific arrangement's harmonization, not "the" one published chart for the tune — Pass reharmonizes the same phrase differently every time it returns, by design (see Steal this below). The analyzed excerpt covers roughly the first 20 bars (opening through the approach to the bridge), harmonized as chord melody (block chords under the melody, fills in the sustained-note gaps). See Secondary Dominants, The ii-V-I, Chord Melody Arranging.

Arrangement breakdown (Jens Larsen's transcription, opening ~20 bars)

  • Bars 1–2 (D7–G7–Cmaj7): block-chord melody harmonization opens on V7/V rather than I; the D7 bar reads equally as a rootless D9 or an F♯ half-diminished voicing (same notes, root-dependent identity); a ♭9 color lands on G7 immediately before the Cmaj7 resolution. → Chord Voicings, Secondary Dominants
  • Bars 3–4 (fill, Cmaj7–F7–E7–A7–D7): the first sustained-note fill, built by moving through one voicing rather than a scale run; the diatonic iii (Em) is reharmonized as E7, the Joe Pass "turn a diatonic chord into a dominant" trademark documented in full on Secondary Dominants § From videos. A ♭9→♯9 slide colors the same E7 mid-fill. → Secondary Dominants, Altered Chords
  • Bars 5–8 (phrase repeated, reharmonized): the same melodic phrase returns with different harmonization — a rootless D7 voice-led by a 3rd interval, a shape-shift-by-two-frets converting F-triad material into C7, and a stripped-down G7-to-rootless-C7 fill (root, tritone, resolve) with a concrete fingering for adding the ♭9. → Chord Voicings
  • Bars 9–12 (IV-chord passage, F6–B♭7–C6): a fuller melodic statement over basic I-IV-I harmony, voiced partly in 4ths rather than tertian stacks; the video's clearest worked example of "arpeggiate a complete chord voicing instead of harmonizing note by note" appears here (an F7-flavored fill). → Chord Melody Arranging, Chord Voicings
  • Bars 13–16 (phrase repeated again): the trademark dominant-substitution recurs (E7♯9 standing in for the diatonic chord, possibly Pass's own addition per Larsen), plus a ♭13-to-natural-13 A7 reharmonization Larsen associates with bossa nova, bridging into D7. → Secondary Dominants, Altered Chords
  • Bars 17–20 (approach to the bridge): the opening phrase returns a third time, now harmonized as a straight ii-V throughout (denser than the V7/V opening); a Dm11 (ii-7/11) voicing arpeggiated as a triplet is the fullest worked "voicing-as-fill" example in the video; a repeated "circling the tritone of A7" figure is named as a recurring, genuinely typical Pass device beyond this one tune. → Chord Melody Arranging, Bebop Vocabulary

Steal this

  • Harmonize a repeated melodic phrase differently each time it recurs rather than reusing the same voicings — Pass reharmonizes the same opening phrase three separate times across this short excerpt.
  • Use the tune's sustained/held melody notes as the designated slot for chord-derived fills — look for where a melody holds before deciding where a fill belongs, rather than filling everywhere.
  • Turn a diatonic minor chord (especially the iii) into its own dominant seventh as a standing color, without needing it to resolve anywhere — a genuine, repeatable Joe Pass trademark, not tune-specific; full harmonic detail on Secondary Dominants.
  • Arpeggiate a chord voicing you already know instead of harmonizing a fill note by note — the single biggest reusable idea in the whole video; full writeup on Chord Melody Arranging.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Joe Pass, Intercontinental — "Little Darlin'"

Learning

  • This is How Joe Pass Plays Amazing Solos (Jens Larsen's bar-by-bar breakdown of this exact arrangement)

john-klenner-just-friends.title: 🎵 JOHN KLENNER - Just Friends
john-klenner-just-friends.html:
A 32-bar standard that starts on the IV chord, not the I — and whose two halves are close enough to identical that the whole tune reduces to a small handful of repeating harmonic units. Well suited as a comping study tune because the ♯IV° diminished, a chromatic-2-5 substitute reading of it, and a tritone-substitution option on the return to IV all show up inside one repeating shape.

Chords

  • A (bars 1-8): IV(B♭maj7) | IV | iv-minor(B♭m7-E♭7) | iv-minor | I(F, often 3rd in bass) | ♯IV°(B°/A♭, or read as A♭m7-D♭7, a chromatic 2-5) | ii-V(Gm7-C7) | I(F, or read as iii/Am). Larsen collapses bars 3-4 into one mental unit — "just B♭ minor to F," not two separate chords — and treats the ♯IV° bar the same way, as one category rather than a fresh analytical problem each time through.
  • Bridge-ish 8 (bars 9-16): dominant-of-the-dominant (D7, 2 bars — a common Lydian-dominant spot) resolving through ii-V(Gm7-C7) back toward IV, reached either by a straight cadence or the tritone substitution Fm-B7 → B♭.
  • Second half (bars 17-24): repeats bars 1-8 exactly (same IV / iv-minor / I / ♯IV° / ii-V shape).
  • Turnaround/tag (bars 25-32): ends with Cm7-F7 resolving home; because the tune itself starts on IV rather than I, the classic "I-VI" turnaround becomes a ii-V-to-IV shape instead: F(I) → Dm7(vi) → [D♭m, chromatic passing minor] → Cm7(ii/V-of-IV) → F7(V7/IV). The D♭m bar is a comper's-liberty embellishment — it can clash a beat against the melody and resolve immediately, something you can add as an accompanist that would be much harder to justify soloing over yourself.

♯IV° diminished — two usable chord-scales

The diminished chord in bars 6 and 22 (spelled B° with A♭ in the bass, an inversion) is the harmonic focal point of the tune for comping purposes. Rather than the symmetric whole-half diminished scale (Larsen's stated default avoidance on diminished chords generally — it's a theoretical/mathematical construct, not what's naturally happening in most standards' written harmony), derive a usable scale by changing exactly one note of the parent F major scale:

Derivation Change from F major Result
Raise the 4th (for the ♯4), then also raise the 5th to cover A♭ B♭→B, G→G♯ F harmonic minor
Raise the 4th, then lower the 6th instead (Larsen's actual working choice) B♭→B, A→A♭ C harmonic major

Practical rule: check the diminished chord against the tune's actual melody to see which of these (or neither) fits — don't default to the diminished scale by habit. Full derivation and general theory → Diminished Chords.

Comping approaches (all three demonstrated on this tune)

  1. Drop-2, chord by chord — superimposed-shape thinking throughout (Dm7 grip = B♭maj9, E♭7 thought of as E♭m6, F major voiced as Am). Full worked voicing choices → Chord Voicings, Jazz Comping - Jazz Chords and Approaches - Just Friends - Jazz Guitar Lesson.
  2. Bare triads (same chord, bass note dropped) — B♭maj7 → D minor triad; B♭m7 → D♭ major triad; discipline rule: keep thinking the real chord's name even while playing only 3 notes, so the harmonic reasoning doesn't drift into a progression that isn't actually there. → Chord Voicings
  3. Open comping — arpeggiation, sustain-a-note-plus-moving-inner-melody, and riff comping (stick with one idea for ~8 bars, tracking the tune's own AABA-shaped repetition) as the practice on-ramp to genuinely free playing. → Melodic-Harmonic Blending (Comping While Soloing), Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline

Steal this

  • Collapse a chord run into "one word." Any time a stretch of the progression reduces to a single recognizable sound (iv-minor for 2 bars, ♯IV° treated as one category regardless of how it's spelled), learn it as that one thing rather than as separately-memorized individual chords — directly reduces how much there is to actively think about while comping.
  • The D♭m chromatic-passing-minor turnaround trick generalizes beyond this tune: any I-VI-ii-V-shaped turnaround can take a chromatic passing minor chord between the vi and the ii, added specifically as a comper's embellishment (not something a soloist is expected to navigate). → Turnarounds
  • Riff comping as a deliberate practice stage, not just a performance choice — locking to one repeating idea for a chunk of the form before opening up to free playing. → Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline

Why I like it

Listen

  • Wes Montgomery with Wynton Kelly's trio (behind Cannonball Adderley) — busy-but-not-in-the-way comping reference
  • Bill Frisell with Paul Motian and Charlie Haden, "On Broadway" record series (behind Joe Lovano) — minimal, harmony-only comping reference, Larsen's closer personal touchstone
  • Herbie Hancock with Tony Williams behind Miles Davis — highly interactive rhythm-section comping
  • Wynton Kelly — Smokin' at the Half Note
  • John Scofield on Joe Henderson's So Near, So Far

Learning

Full lesson (harmonic analysis, ♯IV° chord-scale derivation, drop-2 chorus, triad chorus, open/riff-comping chorus, ensemble-listening philosophy) → Jazz Comping - Jazz Chords and Approaches - Just Friends - Jazz Guitar Lesson

john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.title: 🎵 JOHN MAYER - Slow Dancing in a Burning Room
john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.html:
Continuum (2006). This note is a stub focused on one small, recurring arrangement detail — the IV→I (A→E) triad move and John Mayer's hammer-on ornament over it — as broken down by Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared, not a full chord chart for the song. Jared picked this exact fragment because it's the recurring question from his students: "what is he doing when he does this thing?"

Chords

Key: E major. This gives the whole-song chart the A→E fragment above sits inside.

Verse: C♯m7 – A – E, looping → vi7 – IV – I

Chorus: B11 – C♯m7 – A – B11 – C♯m7 – F♯m7 – C♯m7 – A – E → V11 – vi7 – IV – V11 – vi7 – ii7 – vi7 – IV – I

→ The chorus's tail end (C♯m7–A–E, i.e. vi–IV–I) is the same core cell as the verse, just arrived at from the dominant (B11) instead of repeated cold, and the section touches all four of the "axis" chords (I, V, vi, IV) at some point. It doesn't cleanly rotate the same four chords in a fixed loop the way a true axis-progression song does, though — the inserted ii7 (F♯m7) and the verse's omission of the V chord keep it a looser, more idiosyncratic phrase than a clean rotation, so it's left untagged below rather than forced into the axis family.

The recurring A→E (IV→I) fragment broken down below — with its voice-leading and signature hammer-on ornament — is the harmonic backbone both the verse and the chorus's ending keep landing on.

The move: A→E plagal cadence with hammer-on

Harmony: key of E major. The chord move is A → E, a plagal cadence (IV → I) — the "amen cadence," softer than a V→I authentic cadence because there's no leading tone pulling into the tonic. → Cadences

Core voicing (strings D-G-B / 4-3-2), 5th position: | Chord | D string | G string | B string | Chord tones | |---|---|---|---|---| | A (root position) | fret 7 (A) | fret 6 (C♯) | fret 5 (E) | 1-3-5 | | E (2nd inversion) | fret 6 (G♯) | fret 4 (B) | fret 5 (E) | 3-5-1 |

Voice leading between them (why it sounds so smooth): the B-string note (E) stays exactly the same, the D-string note moves A→G♯ (half step down), the G-string note moves C♯→B (whole step down) — one voice held, one half-step move, one whole-step move: the smallest possible per-voice motion between the two triads.

The hammer-on (the "unique John Mayer thing"): just before resolving A→E, Mayer hammers on to the chord's 3rd (C♯) from the major 2nd (B) a whole step below it, on the triad's middle voice — in this voicing, the G string, fret 4 → fret 6 — then continues into the voice-led E chord. Described in the lesson as "2 hammering onto 3." This ornament, layered on top of the plain voice-led A→E move, is what gives the phrase its identity.

Bass-note mute (critical, easy to miss): playing the triads with their open bass strings underneath (open low A under the A triad), the right-hand thumb must hop over and mute the open A string the instant you move to E — otherwise the low A rings against the E harmony and sounds muddy. Mute by hopping the thumb clear or laying its side across the string.

The same move recurs in at least three neck positions, found each time by voice-leading to the nearest E triad and locating the 3rd→2 hammer-on spot on whichever string carries the 3rd in that voicing:

  • Strings 4-3-2 — the 5th-position voicing tabbed above.
  • Strings 5-4-3 — a second A→E pairing; here E is kept as a constant pedal bass note under both chords (E is already the 5th of A and the root of E, so one bass note works under both harmonies) — the "neighbor IV chord" variant of the same plagal cadence.
  • Strings 3-2-1 (top three strings) — a third A→E pairing at the top of the neck, same voice-leading-then-hammer-on method.

Telecaster vibrato aside (general technique, not specific to this song's own gear): a slight pull on the guitar's neck (bending the neck, not a string) gives a subtle vibrato that "breathes life" into sustaining notes — called out as common on Telecaster.

Steal this

  • Find the closest triad voicing between two chords before anything else — voice-lead the plain chord change first (smallest per-voice motion, using inversions), THEN add ornamentation on top; ornamenting an un-voice-led move loses the smoothness that makes it sound intentional. → Chord Inversions
  • The "2 hammering onto 3" embellishment is portable — any major triad's 3rd can be preceded by a hammer-on from the major 2nd a whole step below, on whichever string carries that voice; not specific to A or E, works on any triad shape once you can identify the 3rd.
  • Mute the outgoing bass note on a IV→I move that keeps open strings — the classic "muddy plagal cadence" failure mode is an un-muted IV bass note ringing into the I chord; thumb-mute it, don't just trust the new chord to mask it.
  • Package a small discovery into a timed, in-tempo, ordered exercise — chord, then embellished chord, repeated up each string set (5-4-3 → 4-3-2 → 3-2-1) — turns a one-off lick into a testable milestone ("can I do this in time, cleanly, through every position") rather than open-ended noodling.

Why I like it
