johnny-green-body-and-soul.title: 🎵 JOHNNY GREEN - Body and Soul
johnny-green-body-and-soul.html:
Dense jazz ballad, 32-bar AABA in D♭ major, full of 2-5-1s and a bridge key change — a study piece for tritone substitution, chromatic bass motion, and default scale choices on altered dominants.

Chords (as taught for guitar)

Key: D♭ major. Frequent 2-5-1s, chromatic descending bass under slash chords, a bridge key change into D major, and a backdoor dominant moment (D natural minor, read as "a 2-5 in the key of D"). The 2nd chord ("5 of 2") is treated as coming from harmonic minor with an implied ♭9/♭13 by default, even where the lead sheet only states a plain dominant symbol. → Chord Substitution · Altered Chords

Steal this

  • Insert a dominant a half-step above any chord, freely, as decoration — the tritone-sub logic applied as a comping/reharmonization habit rather than a fixed arranger's choice. → Jazz Comping
  • Default any dominant-to-minor resolution to harmonic minor with an implied ♭9/♭13, regardless of the written symbol — one reliable choice instead of agonizing over "the" correct reading.
  • Voice a chromatic descending bass line explicitly, even solo — the composed slash-chord bass motion is part of the tune's character, not incidental.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Coleman Hawkins, 1939 (the landmark recording)
  • Guitar listening recommendation from the lesson: Mary Osborne, "A Girl and Her Guitar"

Learning

Full chords/scales/voicing breakdown → BODY AND SOUL Guitar Lesson (chords, tab, scales, melody) No. 18 of Top 25 Jazz Standards for Guitar

johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.title: 🎵 JOHNNY GREEN - Out of Nowhere
johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.html:
A tune whose real subject, per Jens Larsen's analysis, is how the "outside" sound of E♭7 works inside G major — it shows up twice, for two different structural reasons, and both times it's the same sharp-4 double-diminished / German augmented sixth sound. Two static two-bar zones (the opening G major7, and the A minor cadence chord later on) are loose enough at a medium tempo to support real modal/upper-structure triad exploration, which is what makes this tune a good vehicle for triad-based soloing practice specifically.

Chords

  • Bars 1–2: G major7 (I), static — first of two loose, modal-feeling zones in the form.
  • Bars 3–4: B♭m7 → E♭7, a 2-5 into A♭, resolving back to G major7. The E♭7 here is a sharp-4 double-diminished chord — Larsen's term, equivalent to the German augmented sixth chord — closely related to C♯ diminished (double-diminish the 3rd, E→E♭, and the same voicing an octave up reads as E♭7). → Augmented Sixth Chords
  • Bars 5–6: B minor → E7 altered, a minor-cadence secondary dominant.
  • Bars 7–8: A minor (ii) — the cadence target, and the second static/loose zone in the form.
  • Bars 9–10: E♭7 again — this time functioning as the tritone substitute of A7 (the "dominant of the dominant" spot). Same chord symbol as bars 3–4, different function — described by Larsen as the tune's whole point: E♭7 working two different ways in the same key.
  • Bars 11–12: effectively a D-sub → D7 turnaround, closing the first half's dominant motion.
  • Second half: repeats the same shape — G major7, the same B♭m7-E♭7 double-diminished turnaround, then G major → B minor → dominant → A minor cadence again — except the final turnaround uses a flat-3 diminished chord (another inversion of the same sharp-4-diminished sound) into a final 2-5 that actually resolves to the tonic this time (the first half only reached a half cadence).

Chord-scale / triad map (as taught for guitar improvisation over the first half)

Chord Base triads "Outside" triads available Notes
G major7 (I, static) G major, B minor, D major, E minor Lydian: A major, F♯ minor, (C♯ dim, less useful) · Lydian augmented (=E melodic minor): B major, G augmented · Augmented scale: G major + E♭ major combined A minor/C major/F♯ dim deliberately left out of the base set (all contain the "weak" C against a major7)
B♭m7 (ii of the 2-5 into A♭) B♭ minor, D♭ major (3rd), F minor (5th) — Basic diatonic triads only
E♭7 (bars 3-4, sharp-4 double-diminished) Played Lydian dominant since it doesn't resolve as a normal dominant B♭ minor, F major, D♭ augmented, C minor (3rd below root) Transcript garbled through this exact passage — captured qualitatively
G major (sometimes reharmonized as C7 tritone dominant) — C, E diminished, G minor, B♭ augmented, D major Same Lydian-dominant family as the E♭7 above
B minor (iii, brief) B minor — Not enough duration for a fuller set
E7 altered (secondary dominant → A minor) — B♭ major, D diminished, F minor, A♭ augmented, C major Must still land the G♯ (the 3rd) somewhere in the line
A minor (ii/cadence target, tonic-minor treatment) A minor, F major (3rd below root) A augmented, E major (both usable) · G♯ augmented, B minor (both weaker) Melodic minor palette; melody itself suggests Aeolian/Dorian, bop convention favors melodic minor
A minor (2nd-half cadence, non-tonic, suspending D7) A minor, C major, E minor — Dorian here, not melodic minor — avoids clashing with the coming D7
D7 (V, resolving the 2nd-half ii-V) — Tritone-sub/Lydian-dominant (as A♭7): A♭ major, C diminished, E♭ minor, F♯/G♭ augmented, B♭ major (+ minor-quality cousins D minor, F minor, A♭ minor, B minor) · Diminished scale: D major, F major, A♭ major, B major Diminished-triad options also exist from this scale but are downplayed — "might as well just play diminished arpeggios"

Full derivation and reasoning for every row → Advanced Jazz Guitar: Triads and Spread Triads on Out Of Nowhere - Modern Jazz Guitar Licks.

Steal this

  • A dominant chord's function can change on repeat — same chord symbol, different job. E♭7 appears twice in the form: once as a sharp-4 double-diminished predominant resolving straight back to I, once as a tritone substitute for A7 (dominant of the dominant). Same sound, different structural role — worth checking for on any tune with a repeated "unusual" chord. → Augmented Sixth Chords · Chord Substitution
  • Static two-bar chords are an invitation to go modal, at a medium tempo — the tonic G major7 and the A minor cadence chord both get the full Lydian/Lydian-augmented/augmented-scale (or melodic-minor) treatment specifically because there's time to establish the color before moving on. A fast-moving 2-5 doesn't need the same treatment — it's already interesting on its own.
  • Cross-chord half-step motif: a triad idea built on G major7 (the B minor triad) is directly reusable a half step down on the following B♭m7-E♭7 — using a shape as a transposable motif rather than inventing new material per chord creates continuity across a phrase. → Triad Melodic Devices for Jazz Soloing
  • One-note scale-connection trick: G major7's own scale and the G melodic minor used over the following (Lydian-dominant) C7 differ by exactly one note (B → B♭) — swap that one note in an existing line to bridge the chord change almost for free. → Triad Melodic Devices for Jazz Soloing

Why I like it

Listen

  • Jonathan Kreisberg's recording — the direct inspiration for Jens Larsen's analysis, credited with the tune's "almost modal vibe"; also reportedly uses the augmented scale in his solo. Linked in the source video's description (not pulled into this vault).
  • Charlie Parker, Clifford Brown, and many others across the standard jazz repertoire.

Learning

Full harmonic analysis (form, function, the E♭7 double-diminished/German-6th chord) plus the complete chord-by-chord triad map, worked lines (single-triad-as-reference + inversions, triad pairs on the altered dominants, spread/open-voice triads), and the closing angularity/dwell-time principles → Advanced Jazz Guitar: Triads and Spread Triads on Out Of Nowhere - Modern Jazz Guitar Licks

joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.title: 🎵 JOSEPH KOSMA - Autumn Leaves
joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.html:
A G-minor standard whose first 8 bars are the canonical teaching progression for jazz-guitar comping — one pass through Cm7–F7–B♭maj7–E♭maj7–Aø7–D7–Gm(i)–G7 touches all four common seventh-chord qualities (minor 7, dominant 7, major 7, half-diminished), which is why it shows up repeatedly across the vault as the worked example for upper-structure triads, extension substitution, and reharmonization. Full extension-by-extension breakdown: Autumn Leaves Chords - 5 Useful ways to unlock Extensions. The same 7 chords, derived from the opposite direction (root-position 7th chords → their upper-structure triads), are worked in Upper structure triads for comping and soloing and documented on Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords.

Chords (first 8 bars, basic Drop 2 — no extensions)

Cm7 – F7 – B♭maj7 – E♭maj7 – Aø7 – D7 – Gm6(i) – G7

  • All bare Drop 2, top string set (keeps room to add extensions later without muddying the lower "basic power" of the chord).
  • The tonic minor chord (Gm, bar 7) is voiced as a minor 6, not minor-major — a deliberate resolution-vs-color choice: minor 6 reads more consonant/resolved, minor-major reads more like unresolved color. Worth choosing per context (a slow bossa nova version calls for less color here than a burning swing version).

The extension-substitution system

Same skeleton, five increasingly colored passes — the reusable mechanism, not just this tune's specific voicings:

  1. Bare Drop 2 (above) — the reference set everything else is built from.
  2. Root → 9th on every chord (one substitution each): Cm9, F9, B♭maj9, E♭maj9 (= a rootless Gm7 shape — same notes), Aø11 (3rd→11th instead, to dodge a clashing diatonic 9), D7♭9♭13, Gm6/9, G7♭9♭13.
  3. Root AND 5th substituted (keep 3rd + 7th fixed as the anchor): Cm11, B♭maj7(9,13), E♭maj9, Aø(nat9, from C melodic minor), D7♭9♭5 (altered/diminished-scale color), Gm(maj6/13), G7♯9♭5.
  4. Drop 2 shapes re-derived from upper-structure triads: Cm9(11) via a B♭-major-triad upper structure over the 3rd, F7♭13♭9, B♭maj7♯11 (Lydian color), E♭maj7(9,13), Aø(nat9,11), D7alt(♭5,♯9), Gm(maj7) with no extension (deliberate close-voiced dissonance instead), G7♭9♭5 (≈ D♭7 tritone sub).
  5. Modal/color-first pass (chords treated as isolated sounds, not functional steps — the late-Miles-Davis-Quintet treatment): Cm(11,13), F7alt (3rd omitted to delay the ii→V function signal), incomplete B♭maj7♯11(9) resolving to a C7(13)/B♭ slash chord, plain E♭maj9, an inserted extra ii-V (B♭m7(11)→E♭7(9)) that reharmonizes the cadence toward Aø7, Am9 substituted outright for Aø7 ("doesn't belong in G minor" — kept on purpose), D7♭13♯9, Gm6/9♯11 (from D harmonic minor — an unusual tonic-minor color), G7♯9(nat5) via a B♭-triad-over-B-bass upper structure (diminished-family color, not altered).

Full worked chord names, reasoning, and the one caption-uncertain spot → Autumn Leaves Chords - 5 Useful ways to unlock Extensions.

Upper-structure triad reading (all seven chords, from a separate video)

Chord Quality Upper structure triad
Cm7 minor 7 E♭ major
F7 dominant 7 A diminished
B♭maj7 major 7 D minor
E♭maj7 major 7 G minor
Aø7 half-diminished C minor
D7 dominant 7 F♯ diminished
Gm7 minor 7 B♭ major

Full derivation and the four chord-quality rules behind this table → Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords.

Steal this

  • The root→9th / 5th→11th-13th substitution system, generalizable to any tune's changes, not just this one — always keep the 3rd and 7th (the guide tones) fixed, and treat the root and 5th as the two "free" slots for color. → Extended Chords
  • Which extension is "correct" isn't fixed by the chord symbol — check it against function. The Aø7 in bars 5/6 gets an 11th instead of the diatonic 9 specifically because that 9 (B♭) clashes with the cadence into G minor. → Chord Substitution
  • A chord-tone can be deliberately omitted to delay a functional signal, not just added to for color — dropping F7's own 3rd (A natural) in the modal pass keeps the ear from immediately hearing "we've arrived at the V" while the alterations still carry forward motion. → Chord Substitution
  • A tune survives heavy reharmonization when its bones are strong enough — Kosma's chord progression stays recognizable even under the video's most heavily altered pass (inserted extra ii-V, substituted Am9, upper-structure G7), which is explicitly why it was picked as the demo vehicle. Useful test for choosing which of Nate's own tunes tolerate deep reharmonization practice.

kurt-rosenwinkel-nefertiti-ballad-sessio.title: 🎵 KURT ROSENWINKEL - Nefertiti (Ballad Session)
kurt-rosenwinkel-nefertiti-ballad-sessio.html:
A Wayne Shorter composition — famous from the second Miles Davis Quintet — reharmonized/reinterpreted on Mark Turner's album Ballad Session, featuring Kurt Rosenwinkel on guitar. This page is not a chord chart or a chart to learn the tune from; it's Jens Larsen's style-trait analysis of four short excerpts from Rosenwinkel's solo, used to reverse-engineer what makes his melodic language distinct rather than to transcribe the tune itself. Full breakdown video: Kurt Rosenwinkel - This Is What Makes His Style Unique. Rosenwinkel's own stated practice method behind the "melody survives the chord change" idea below is documented in full on Never-Ending Scale Exercise.

Why Nefertiti is the right vehicle for this analysis

Shorter's tunes have "strong melodies and beautiful harmonies but the chords don't really move in the way that we're used to" if you're used to functional standards — the chords sit as distinct colors next to each other rather than resolving into one another. That non-functional harmony is exactly why the video can isolate melody-first playing: there's no strong functional pull to lean on, so whatever coherence the line has has to come from the melody's own logic (direction, range, motif), not from outlining a ii-V.

Solo excerpts by section (Jens Larsen's analysis)

  • Opening phrase — A sus4 → D7alt(♭9)/B♭ → F♯sus4: starts on a low D, climbs to a high F within one bar — a large fraction of guitar range covered fast, flagged as a Rosenwinkel signature. D major scale (no G) over the A-sus color → up to F, F♯, skip to B♭, play around a B♭ major triad shape for the altered sound → back to F → chromatic half-step descent down to D♯ to land the F♯sus4. The ascending scale run that opens the phrase doesn't reset direction when the chord changes — it keeps climbing straight through the barline into the D7alt, "free of the changes." → Solo Dynamics and Arc, Never-Ending Scale Exercise
  • End-of-first-chorus phrase — E sus4 → E♭7♯11 → A7alt (2 bars) → A♭maj7: a reharmonization Larsen notes differs from Nefertiti's usual changes — resolves more functionally here (real V–I motion back to the top of the form). Rosenwinkel is noted to consistently emphasize the ♯11 on E♭7 every time it recurs across the whole solo, not just here — a deliberate recurring color choice. Line: E7sus4 pickup → down to A → ♯11 on E♭7 → a long ascending run from A up to a high F built from a D♭maj7♯5 arpeggio, then a leap down a fifth to B♭ instead of the "expected" scale-wise contrary-motion resolution — direction of the melody outranks counterpoint-style resolution rules here. Continuing into the two bars of A7alt: pickup scale run → up, C♯, down an augmented triad → G, skip to C for a descending C♯maj7 arpeggio → back to G → ascending B♭ major triad → descending diminished triad (source material read as B♭ melodic minor) → resolves down from C to B♭. Large range, non-sequential, "different arpeggios tied together" rather than one scale run — what keeps it vocal-like instead of mechanical. → Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • E major7♯11 excerpt: E major triad, 2nd inversion, from a low B → up to a C♯ minor triad → up to the ♯11 (A♯) → a pentatonic-flavored fragment (A♯, C♯, D) landing back on the major 7 to close the line. Fast, wide-range motion from low B to D♯, then down to C♯ and up to F♯ to set up a chromatic half-step descent into the 5th of the next chord (A). → Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords
  • Motif excerpt — B♭m7 → Amaj7♯11 → E♭7 (Lydian dominant): motif stated as an F minor7 arpeggio, deliberately restricted to only those notes, over B♭m7. Same shape then developed across the next two chords: a descending arpeggio → fifth interval into a descending Amaj7♭5 arpeggio on the Amaj7♯11 → further development on the E♭7 (Lydian dominant) re-emphasizing the ♯11/Lydian color → closes on a descending augmented triad back to A. Rosenwinkel's stated tendency: stick to a small pool of notes for a motif rather than immediately spreading across the whole scale — done here without the motif reading as obvious or repetitive, the harder half of the skill. → Motivic Development

Steal this

  • Let an ascending (or descending) line keep going through a chord change instead of resetting direction at the barline — treat the melodic idea, not the chord grid, as the thing generating the next few notes. → Never-Ending Scale Exercise
  • Cover more of the instrument's range inside a single short phrase than feels "safe" — low-to-high-and-back within a bar or two, used as a deliberate identity trait, not an accident. → Solo Dynamics and Arc
  • Build a line from adjacent arpeggios/triads stitched together rather than one scale stretched over the whole passage — non-sequential, large-interval movement that still reads as coherent because the arpeggios share close voice-leading, not because they're diatonic to one scale. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing
  • Restrict a motif to a genuinely small note pool (e.g. one arpeggio) and develop it across two or three chord changes without telegraphing "this is the motif." → Motivic Development
  • When a chord's color tone (e.g. a ♯11) is available, come back to it deliberately every time that chord recurs across a whole solo — a repeated color choice, not incidental.

lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.title: 🎵 LANA DEL REY - Let The Light In
lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.html:
Duet with Father John Misty from Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd (2023); a warm, acoustic-leaning love song.

Chords

Key: A major · 132 BPM

Nearly every section — intro, verses, pre-chorus, chorus — rides the same five-chord cell: Bm – E – A – A7 – D → ii – V – I – I7 – IV. The heart of it is a clean, textbook ii–V–I (Bm–E–A) that actually resolves to the tonic; the A7 that immediately follows turns that arrival into a bluesy passing chord, pulling forward into the IV (D) before the whole cell loops back to the top — a real cadence used as a launchpad rather than a place to rest.

The bridge darkens the same shape with a chromatic ii–V7–I (Bm – E7 – A instead of plain E), and the outro closes it out on Dm – A – E – A — a borrowed iv (D minor in place of the major IV used everywhere else), a brief flash of modal-mixture melancholy resolving up into the dominant before the fade.

lana-del-rey-video-games.title: 🎵 LANA DEL REY - Video Games
lana-del-rey-video-games.html:
Breakout single from Lana Del Rey's major-label debut Born to Die (2012); a stripped, string-laden ballad built around a descending piano/harp figure.

Chords

Key: F# minor · 122 BPM

The verses vamp on a repeating natural-minor loop: F#m – A – F#m – A – C#m – D → i – III – i – III – v – VI. There's no dominant anywhere in it — the v chord (C#m) stays minor instead of resolving as a real dominant, so the loop just circulates rather than arriving, which is exactly the hazy, drifting quality the verses need.

The chorus moves further from home: E – D – A – F#m – D → VII – VI – III – i – VI, a descending, subtonic-led progression (again, no functional V anywhere), closing each pass on a chromatic F augmented chord — a half-step below the tonic — that slides back up into F#m (i) at the top of the next verse, a chromatic voice-leading approach rather than a cadence.

Nothing here matches a controlled-vocabulary progression: the moving four-chord verse loop isn't a static vamp (it's not modal-vamp, which requires one/two chords), and there's no ii–V–I, I–vi–IV–V, axis rotation, blues, or turnaround anywhere in the harmony. progressions: [] is the honest tag.

Verified via Hooktheory / Ultimate Guitar.

miles-davis-solar.title: 🎵 MILES DAVIS - Solar
miles-davis-solar.html:
Jazz standard, 12 bars, moving through five key centers in that span — a compact, fast-changing form that makes it a go-to for practicing scale/key-change navigation.

Chords

Chord-scale map, as taught for guitar improvisation. Five zones, mapped as close together as possible in a single fretboard position (four of the five sit in the very same position; only the D♭ zone needs a small shift):

Measures Scale / key center
2 C melodic minor
4 F major
3 E♭ major
2 D♭ major
1 C harmonic minor

12 measures total, then the form repeats. Some zones have more than one workable scale option — the choices above are one workable path, not the only one.

Steal this

  • A 12-bar form that changes key center five times — an efficient way to drill fast key-change navigation without a long tune to sit through. → Modulation (Key Change)
  • Melodic minor and harmonic minor both appear as the "home" scale for the C-minor zones (not just natural minor) — worth having both minor-scale colors ready over a minor tonic, not just one.

nat-adderley-work-song.title: 🎵 NAT ADDERLEY - Work Song
nat-adderley-work-song.html:
A Nat Adderley original from his 1960 album Work Song, in the key of A♭. Nathan Borton transcribes and breaks down Wes Montgomery's short guitar solo on the tune — not the whole form, just three excerpted licks (bars 2, 8, and 12) — to teach reusable devices for landing 9th/11th/13th chord extensions melodically rather than as isolated color notes. Distinct from the vault's other Wes Montgomery solo breakdown, 🎵 WES MONTGOMERY - D Natural Blues (Jack Ruch's chunk-analyze-template method over Wes's own 12-bar blues) — this one is a single-teacher, three-device lesson over a Nat Adderley sideman date rather than a full chunk-by-chunk concept map, and see Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction for how the two compare as methods.

Chords

Key: A♭ (as tagged) — but the tune's actual tonal center is its relative minor, F minor; this is a 16-bar minor-blues variant, not the standard 12-bar form. Commonly published changes (Real Book / widely-cited transcriptions):

Fm7 – Fm7 – Fm7 – Fm7 / Fm7 – Fm7 – Cm7 – C7 / Fm7 – Fm7 – Fm7 – Fm7 / Fm7 – B♭7 – G7 – C7 (then back to the top)

Relative to the page's stated key of A♭ major: Fm7 reads as vi7 (the chord the tune actually treats as "home"), C7 as V7/vi (the dominant of that F-minor tonic), B♭7 as a dominantized ii7, and G7 as a passing secondary dominant (V7/V of vi) that walks the turnaround down to C7 before resolving back to Fm7. Nat Adderley's own recording reportedly plays F7 throughout rather than a clean Fm7/F minor split — the same "every chord can be a dominant 7th, the ♭7 is a color not a tension" convention documented on Blues Form and Harmony § Why every chord is a dominant 7th, blurring the line between a minor blues and a straight dominant blues.

Doesn't map cleanly onto this vault's progressions: controlled vocabulary — 16 bars rather than a 12-bar form, and the closing B♭7-G7-C7 turnaround is a descending secondary-dominant chain rather than a clean I-vi-ii-V shape — so it's tagged progressions: [] rather than forced onto the closest-sounding label.

What the source video actually covers (a subset of the full form above): only three short excerpts of the solo are analyzed (bar 2, bar 8, bar 12); the full 12-bar/chorus form isn't transcribed in the video itself. Bar 2 sits over an F minor 7 (the relative minor within A♭ major), bar 8 sits over a V-I dominant resolution (E♭7 → A♭), and bar 12 is played against a stretch of diatonic A♭-major chords.

Solo devices by passage (Nathan Borton's analysis)

Three short excerpts, each reduced to one reusable device — see Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction for the general chunk-analyze-name-concept method this lesson loosely follows (without Jack Ruch's explicit "replay it as your own line" step).

  • Bar 2, over F minor 7: an A♭ major 7 arpeggio played over Fm7 — three shared notes plus a G that reads as the 9th of Fm9 — reversible (Fm9 arpeggio over A♭maj7 → A♭ major 13 sound), since A♭maj7 and Fm9 are relative major/minor. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Extended Chords
  • Bar 8, resolving E♭7 → A♭ (V-I): a line that hits the 9th, jumps to the 13th, then uses the ♭9 resolving down to the 5th of the A♭ tonic — read on guitar as an F minor(major7) shape arpeggio that only "works" over the E♭7 if its ♭3 (A♭) is treated as a passing tone resolving to the 9th (G) rather than a static chord tone; sounds like plain F minor without the backing chords underneath it. → Extended Chords, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Bar 12, over a diatonic A♭ stretch: a movable 4-note guitar shape (C-B♭-G-F) shared with Grant Green, transposable in octaves down the neck and portable across any diatonic chord in the key for an instant extension color — no single "correct" target chord prescribed. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes

Steal this

  • Relative-major/relative-minor arpeggio swap as a one-shape way to imply a 9th (major arpeggio over the relative minor chord) or a 13th (minor arpeggio over the relative major chord) — reusable any time a minor chord's relative major (or vice versa) is already comfortable under the fingers.
  • A shape that "doesn't work" over its chord in isolation can still work once one note is reframed as a passing tone resolving into a real chord tone — always test an extension-heavy line against the actual backing progression before judging it, not a cappella.
  • A single 4-note shape (C-B♭-G-F) portable across every diatonic chord in a key, octave-transposable — a low-overhead "extension color" tool to reach for without re-deriving an arpeggio per chord.

nathan-borton-all-of-me.title: 🎵 NATHAN BORTON - All of Me
nathan-borton-all-of-me.html:
A 1931 Gerald Marks/Seymour Simons standard, featured in the 1932 film Careless Lady, used as the full worked example for a step-by-step solo-guitar chord-melody build process: melody → in-time-with-metronome → chord roots in the gaps → full chords → chromatic passing chords → melody harmonized by top-note voicing lookup → connective lines. Full process breakdown: THIS Simple Process Creates Successful Solo Guitar Playing.

Chords

Key: C major. The 1931 Gerald Marks/Seymour Simons standard's commonly published changes (Real Book):
Cmaj7 E7 A7 Dm7
E7 Am7 D7 Dm7 – G7
Cmaj7 E7 A7 Dm7
F Fm C – Em7 A7
Dm7 G7 C6

→ I – VI7 – II7 – ii (a 1-6-2 "turnaround" shape opening the tune, the dominant VI7/II7 pair working as secondary dominants that keep circling back to the ii chord rather than resolving straight home) – VI7 – vi – II7 – ii-V (repeats, then closes) – IV – iv (borrowed) – I/iii – V7 – ii – V7 – I, a genuine ii-V-I (Dm7-G7-C6) closing out the final phrase. Both the opening 1-6-2 shape and the closing ii-V-I are why this page is tagged progressions: [ii-V-I, turnaround].

The opening phrase's harmonization below (Borton's actual arrangement) voices bar 4 as F major13 rather than the Real Book's plain Dm7 — not a different chord, just a different bass/root choice: Dm7 and F6 share every pitch (D-F-A-C = the same four notes read from either root), the identical relative-major/relative-minor overlap already logged on this vault's 🎵 ANTÔNIO CARLOS JOBIM - The Girl from Ipanema page. → Chord Naming by Context

Opening phrase — as harmonized

Phrase Chord Melody-note harmonization
1 C major (triad melody) Phrase-ending E harmonized with a C6 shape (E on top)
2 E7 Common E7 voicing with E on top
3 A7 Standard A7 drop 3 voicing, continuing E on top
4 (tricky spot) F (melody note D) F major 13 voicing (= F major 7 drop 3 with the top note moved from C to D)

Learning notes

  • Learned from a period source, not a lead sheet — Borton traces the tune back to its 1932 film appearance (Careless Lady) and learns the melody from a recording of that era rather than reading it off a chart, deliberately keeping it "in the ears and hands," not "in the eyes."
  • Metronome discipline used while building the arrangement: accent beat 1 only (not 2-and-4) until the downbeat feel is solid on its own — see THIS Simple Process Creates Successful Solo Guitar Playing for the full reasoning.
  • Chromatic passing chords worked over the C major voicing in this tune's opening — slide the same shape up or down a half step (or two) as connective color. → Passing Chords § 2. Chromatic passing/approach chords
  • Connective line between phrases: an enclosure to the 3rd of the current chord, then down to the 5th — worked over both E7 and A7 in this tune's opening progression, used interchangeably with the chord-in-the-gap option from the same slot.
  • Full step-by-step build order (this is the primary worked example for the whole method) → THIS Simple Process Creates Successful Solo Guitar Playing, generalized method → Chord Melody Arranging.

paul-mccartney-every-night.title: 🎵 PAUL MCCARTNEY - Every Night
paul-mccartney-every-night.html:
Simple acoustic ballad from Paul McCartney's 1970 solo debut — about wanting to stay in with a loved one instead of going out.

Chords

Key: G major (chord charts commonly tab it in open E-shapes with a capo at the 3rd fret — E-position chords there sound as G) · 100 BPM

The verses sit on a single droning chord — E7 alternating with E7sus2, sounding as I7 — a static vamp under the "every night / every day" lines, all rhythm and no harmonic motion.

The pre-chorus is where it finally moves: A – F#m – Bm – F#7 – B – E, sounding as C – Am – Dm – A7 – D – G → IV – ii – v – V7/V – V – I. The Bm/Dm is a borrowed minor v (not the diatonic major V), used as a passing chord into a proper secondary dominant (F#7/A7, "V7 of V") that resolves correctly to B/D (V) and on home to E/G (I).

The chorus is the tightest cadence in the song: F#m – B7 – E, sounding as Am – D7 – G → ii – V7 – I — a clean, textbook two-five-one right under "But tonight I just wanna stay in / And be with you."

progressions: [ii-V-I]

Production & Arrangement

From McCartney (1970) — his first solo album, recorded mostly at home on a Studer 4-track (plus some Abbey Road time) with McCartney playing every instrument himself. A deliberate reaction to Beatles polish and the breakup: loose, intimate, lo-fi, unfinished-on-purpose.

  • Gentle acoustic-led multitrack, warm and close; the charm is the homemade intimacy, not perfection.
  • One man overdubbing guitar, bass, harmony vocals — a whole arrangement from a single player.

Steal this

  • DIY home multitracking: build a full arrangement yourself, part by part (Drum Rack/Simpler + one-take instruments), and keep the homemade looseness.
  • Intimacy over polish: minimal processing, close and warm — imperfections are the sound.
  • One-person arrangement: layer guitar/bass/harmony from a single performer → double your own harmonies (Artificial Double Tracking (ADT)).

paul-mccartney-junk.title: 🎵 PAUL MCCARTNEY - Junk
paul-mccartney-junk.html:
Tender fingerpicked ballad about abandoned objects finding new owners. Written during the Rishikesh retreat with the Maharishi. An instrumental version, 'Singalong Junk,' also appeared on McCartney (1970).

Chords

Key: A major (leans on its relative F♯ minor) · gentle 4/4 ballad

Verse: F♯m – C♯7 – D – A → vi – V7/vi – IV – I (the C♯7 is a secondary dominant pointing at F♯m before the line falls to IV–I)

"Buy, buy…" chorus: D7sus4 – Dm – A – E → IV(sus) – iv – I – V (the Dm is the borrowed minor-iv — the bittersweet McCartney signature)

Harder than it sounds — lots of extended/suspended voicings. Verified via Ultimate Guitar / Hooktheory.

Production & Arrangement

From McCartney (1970) — his first solo album, recorded mostly at home on a Studer 4-track (plus some Abbey Road time) with McCartney playing every instrument himself. A deliberate reaction to Beatles polish and the breakup: loose, intimate, lo-fi, unfinished-on-purpose.

  • Sparse and wistful — a home-demo feel with lightly-strummed guitar, bass, and a fragile lead vocal; even has an instrumental reprise ('Singalong Junk').
  • Nostalgic waltz-y lilt; the emptiness is the emotion.

Steal this

  • Home-demo aesthetic: leave a song sparse and unfinished-sounding when the fragility is the point.
  • Instrumental reprise: re-use the same changes as a wordless version for a second emotional pass.
  • Waltz lilt + wistful 7ths for nostalgia.

paul-mccartney-teddy-boy.title: 🎵 PAUL MCCARTNEY - TEDDY BOY
paul-mccartney-teddy-boy.html:
Lighthearted story song about a boy caring for his widowed mother. Started during the Get Back sessions; Lennon famously improvised mockery over it during rehearsals. Released on McCartney (1970).

Chords

Key: D major · ~83 BPM · 4/4

Verse: D – A – Am – Em – G – A → I – V – v – ii – IV – V (the Am is a borrowed Mixolydian minor-v — the signature color of the verse)

Chorus: F♯ – B – E – A – D – A → III – VI – II – V – I (a descending circle-of-fifths chain of secondary dominants resolving home to D)

Bridge (lifts toward F♯): F♯ – C♯ – C♯m – G♯m – B – C♯ → tonicizes F♯ before dropping back to the verse.

Verified via Ultimate Guitar / Hooktheory.

Production & Arrangement

From McCartney (1970) — his first solo album, recorded mostly at home on a Studer 4-track (plus some Abbey Road time) with McCartney playing every instrument himself. A deliberate reaction to Beatles polish and the breakup: loose, intimate, lo-fi, unfinished-on-purpose.

  • Folky, narrative — originally worked up during the Get Back/Let It Be sessions, then finished solo at home.
  • Acoustic-driven, loose, storytelling delivery.

Steal this

  • Rescue a band idea solo: a song that didn't fit the group can become an intimate solo cut.
  • Loose feel: don't grid-tighten a storytelling folk take.

ray-charles-hard-times.title: 🎵 RAY CHARLES - Hard Times
ray-charles-hard-times.html:
A slow blues Jack Ruch's organ trio plays regularly, used as the vehicle for a layered soloing lesson: the same tune, played three times, each pass adding a harder layer of theory over the last. See Soloing Over Changes in 3 LEVELS! for the full breakdown.

Chords

Key: E♭ major — a 12-bar-family jazz-blues dressed up with several embellishments layered onto the plain I-IV-V skeleton: a 1-6 move into the relative minor (E♭ → G7 → Cm7, I → V7/vi → vi), a full major ii-V-I landing on the IV chord instead of the I (B♭m7 → E♭7 → A♭7, ii-V-I of A♭), a passing diminished chord between IV and I (♯IV°), and a chromatically-walked VI7 turnaround (C7 sliding down in half steps) before the closing V (B♭7) sends the form back to the top.

→ I – V7/vi – vi – (ii-V-I of IV) – IV – ♯IV°(passing) – I – VI7(turnaround) – V — the same jazz-blues 1-6-2-5 family already documented on Blues Form and Harmony and Turnarounds, just with the "6" reached via a secondary dominant (G7) rather than a plain vi chord, and the "2-5" landing on the IV rather than the I. Full bar-by-bar reconstruction (from Jack Ruch's spoken-changes video, not a verified lead sheet) below.

Reconstructed from the video's spoken chord names (Ruch shows chord names on screen against a backing track rather than reciting a lead sheet — treat this as best-effort, not a verified transcription, and check against the video or a real lead sheet before relying on it for performance):

Chord Function
E♭ (maj / 7) I
G7 V7/vi, moving to Cm7
Cm7 (or Cm(maj7)) vi
B♭m7 ii of A♭ — first chord of a 251 into the IV
E♭7 V7 of A♭ — second chord of that 251, altered-scale spot
E♭ I, briefly
A♭7 IV
♯IV°(passing) diminished passing chord between IV and I
E♭ I
C7 VI7 turnaround, walked down chromatically in half steps
B♭7 V, at the very end of the form, heading back to the top

The three-level soloing map (Jack Ruch's lesson)

Same tune, same solo skeleton, three passes with increasing harmonic sophistication — see Soloing Over Changes in 3 LEVELS! for full detail on each level.

  • Level 1 — pentatonic blues foundation. E♭ major pentatonic (two CAGED-adjacent shapes, C-shape and A-shape, rooted 6th fret/A string) for the bright/sweet sound, switching to E♭ minor pentatonic specifically at the C→B→B♭ walk-down over the passing diminished chord. Phrasing/dynamics/touch over theory. → Diagonal Pentatonic Blues Soloing
  • Level 2 — chord-tone/arpeggio outlining. Each chord's root-3rd-5th-♭7 arpeggio, fingered with CAGED-adjacent shapes kept in one small position (the whole E♭-G7-Cm7-B♭m7 stretch stays in one ~5-fret zone), stitched together with chromatic connecting tones and blended back into Level 1's pentatonic phrasing. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Level 3 — the altered scale over the three functioning dominants. G altered (over G7→Cm), E♭ altered (over the E♭7 in the 251 to A♭), and B♭ altered (over the closing V7) — same shape relocated to each root, always resolved onto a chord tone of the next chord on the downbeat. → Scale Modes Reference, Altered Chords

Steal this

  • Practice a new tune in exactly this order — plain pentatonic/blues phrasing first (touch and space, no theory pressure), then chord-tone/arpeggio precision, then altered/outside color — rather than trying to sound "advanced" on the first pass.
  • The walk-down (C-B-B♭) over the passing diminished chord is where the minor pentatonic switch belongs — a concrete, transposable rule: lean minor-pentatonic-bluesy specifically at a chromatic passing/diminished moment, not just "sometimes."
  • The altered scale as "dominant shell + four extensions," relocated by root — one mental model (root-3rd-♭7 shell, add ♭9/♯9/♯11/♭13) covers all three altered-scale spots in this tune (G7, E♭7, B♭7) without re-deriving the scale each time.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Ray Charles, "Hard Times" — organ-trio slow blues in E♭

ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.title: 🎵 RAY CHARLES - You Don't Know Me
ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.html:
A classic Eddy Arnold/Cindy Walker song, taught here in Ray Charles's arrangement (key of E♭ major) by Jack Ruch as a real-tune vehicle for functioning dominant chords — the primary V7 (B♭7) and three secondary dominants (E♭7 → A♭, C7 → Fm, G7 → Cm) — plus a diminished-passing-chord move (A♭ → A°). Full breakdown of the lick/soloing method → A Classic Tune for Learning About Secondary Dominants.

Chords

Key: E♭ major. The portion of the tune covered here is a chain of secondary dominants, not a stock progression: E♭ (I) → B♭7 (V7) → E♭ (I) → E♭7 (V7/IV) → A♭ (IV) → C7 (V7/ii) → Fm (ii) → G7 (V7/vi) → Cm (vi) → A♭ (IV) → A° (passing diminished). Every secondary dominant resolves down a fifth into its target exactly as expected (E♭7→A♭, C7→Fm, G7→Cm), which is what makes it a clean teaching vehicle for Secondary Dominants — but because the ii chord itself never gets its own dominant (no true ii-V-I pair), and the sequence isn't a stock turnaround/axis/1-6-2-5 shape, it doesn't map onto any single entry in this vault's progressions: controlled vocabulary. Tagged progressions: [] rather than forced onto the nearest-sounding label — only the primary V7-I at the very top (B♭7→E♭) is a "real" dominant-tonic cadence in the classic sense.

Progression (as walked through in the source video, not the full lead sheet — this is what's covered):

  • E♭ → B♭7 → E♭ → E♭7 — opens on the tonic, moves to the primary dominant (B♭7 = V7) and back, then to E♭7, a secondary dominant (V7/IV) that resolves to the next chord, A♭ major.
  • … → A♭ — target of the E♭7 secondary dominant; adding the ♭7 (D♭) to the E♭ chord voice-leads down and resolves to G, the 3rd of A♭.
  • … → C7 → F minor — C7 is V7/ii (F minor is the ii of E♭ major); still functions as a dominant even though it resolves to a minor chord.
  • … → G7 → C minor — G7 is V7/vi (C minor is the vi of E♭ major); same minor-target dominant logic.
  • … → A♭ → A° (diminished passing chord) — not a functioning dominant, but a diminished sound with enough space in the form to address it with a version of the same diminished lick.

Soloing devices worked over this tune

  • Movable diminished-7 arpeggio lick off the chord's own 3rd — start on the 3rd of whichever dominant is sounding, ascend a dim7 arpeggio (3rd–5th–♭7–upper tone), then resolve down into the 3rd of the target chord. Same shape relocated to all five spots above (B♭7→E♭, E♭7→A♭, C7→Fm, G7→Cm, A♭→A°). → Diminished Chords, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • E♭ major pentatonic as the base solo template through the whole form, into which the diminished lick gets substituted one spot at a time, then blended with "minor-y bluesy" phrasing for a full solo. → Blues Scales and Blue Notes

red-hot-chili-peppers-funky-monks.title: 🎵 RED HOT CHILI PEPPERS - Funky Monks
red-hot-chili-peppers-funky-monks.html:
Funk-rock track from Blood Sugar Sex Magik (1991). Targeted for funk/blues feel and hammer-on/pull-off skill building.

Chords

Key: E · 92 BPM

The verse/intro is genuinely a one-chord funk vamp, not a progression — Frusciante's signature lick is a hammer-on/pull-off riff (A♯ and D hammered together on the G and B strings) worked around a single center, colored with the E blues scale and E minor pentatonic's ♭3 (the riff sits melodically on G, the ♭3 of E). No chord changes happen under it — it's rhythm and scale-tone bending doing all the work, the classic funk move of never resolving because there's nothing to resolve from.

The hook/chorus is where actual chord motion shows up: A5 – C5 – D♯5 – D5 – F7 – E → IV – ♭VI – vii – ♭VII – ♭II7 – I, a chromatic, non-diatonic power-chord slide (not a functional cadence — ♭II7 sliding into I is a tritone-flavored rock move, not a real Neapolitan resolution) that finally lands the riff back on the tonic E before the vamp resumes.

progressions: [modal-vamp]

Production & Arrangement

From Blood Sugar Sex Magik (1991) — Rick Rubin moved the band into a reputedly-haunted mansion and recorded them live as a band in the room for raw, spontaneous energy (the antithesis of grid-perfect production).

  • Flea's slap/funk bass and Frusciante's guitar interlock live — the groove is a band performance, not a stacked arrangement.
  • Roomy, live drum sound; minimal overdubs; the vibe of four people playing at once.

Steal this

  • Track the rhythm section live in one room for feel/interplay you can't program — commit to a band take.
  • Slap-bass as the lead groove — let bass + drums be the hook, guitar answers.
  • Roomy, minimally-processed drums (UAD Pure Plate Reverb/room verb, light comp) for live energy.
  • Vibe/environment matters: an inspiring room can be the whole production.

sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.title: 🎵 SIGMUND ROMBERG - Softly As in a Morning Sunrise
sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.html:
A minor-key jazz standard that's almost a minor 2-5-1 study — the A sections are essentially nothing but Cm(i) – Dm7♭5(ii°) – G7♭9(V7) chained over and over, with a bridge that escapes to the relative major (E♭) before a final 2-5 walks back home. Learning it well transfers directly to any tune built from the same shape.

Chords

  • A section: i – ii° – V7 repeated (Cm – Dm7♭5 – G7♭9), connected by a passing diminished chord a half step above the ii and a half step below the V (step-wise tension into G7). Second ending resolves via a 2-5 into the bridge.
  • Bridge: modulates to E♭ major, the relative major of C minor (same key signature, three flats — E♭ sits a minor 3rd / three frets above the C-minor tonic). Runs iv(Fm) – V7(B♭7) – I(E♭maj) (a 2-5-1 into the relative major), then VI7(C7) – iv° – V7(G7) walking back to the top of the form. C7 is reached "off the major 6" of E♭ (a dominant 7th built on E♭'s 6th degree).
  • G7♭9 carries an implied ♭13 as well — a ♭9 dominant borrowed from harmonic minor conventionally carries the ♭13 too, even when the lead sheet only shows "♭9." → The ii-V-I (minor version) · Extended Chords

Chord-scale map (as taught for guitar improvisation)

Two levels, presented as equally valid (not beginner vs. advanced):

Complete — a scale per harmonic zone:

Zone Scale
i (Cm7) C natural minor
minor 2-5-1's dominant-tension zone C harmonic minor
Bridge ii-V (E♭ major zone) E♭ major
Passing F measure F Dorian (same notes as E♭ major/C natural minor, re-rooted)
Passing diminished chord F♯ diminished
V7 (C7♭9/♭13, the minor-2-5-1's dominant) F harmonic minor, rooted C-to-C = C Phrygian dominant (harmonic minor's 5th mode)

Simplified — three big regions: "basically C natural minor" for most of the A section (the ear adds the chromatic major-7 tone from harmonic minor by feel, not by mechanically switching scales), a real F harmonic minor region for the 2-bar zone that can't be faked as anything else, and E♭ major for the bridge.

The melody itself never plays the ♭7 (no B♭ anywhere) — since the only difference between C harmonic minor and C natural minor is B♭ vs. B♮, avoiding B♭ keeps the melody safely in C natural minor throughout. → Scale Modes Reference · Diatonic Modes

Steal this

  • Prolongation across a whole tune, not just a turnaround. The entire A section can be heard as one prolonged C-minor sonority — the ii-V motion is just "tension and back," not a real key change. Same device as Chord-Tone Soloing's prolongation section, scaled up from a 4-chord turnaround to a full song section. → Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Circle-of-fourths distance-thinking instead of chord names, worked through the entire form including the bridge's modulation to the relative major — full writeup on the video page. → The ii-V-I · Circle of Fifths
  • A comping rhythmic-motif + walking-bassline pairing, demonstrated directly on this tune's A section. → Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline

Why I like it

Listen

  • Barney Kessel — Live at Sometime (Jared's recommended version for learning this tune)

steely-dan-deacon-blues.title: 🎵 STEELY DAN - Deacon Blues
steely-dan-deacon-blues.html:
Becker and Fagen's meditation on romantic losers and alternate lives. Pete Christlieb's saxophone solo is widely considered one of the greatest in rock. Extended multi-section structure over jazz harmony. From Aja (1977).

Chords

Key: C major, but with shifting jazz tonal centers (C / G / F) and dense extended voicings · ~115 BPM

Intro (the signature chromatic maj7 "planing"): Cmaj7 – Gsus2/B – B♭maj7 – Fsus2/A – Dmaj7 – Asus2/C♯ – Cmaj7 – Gsus2/B – E♭maj7 – E7♯9 → Imaj7 … ♭VIImaj7 … IImaj7 … ♭IIImaj7 … V7♯9 — parallel maj7 chords sliding by whole/half steps, a Steely Dan trademark.

Verse (drifts into F major): Fmaj7 – Am7 – E7 – Em7 – A7 … → IVmaj7 – vi7 – III7 – iii7 – VI7 (relative to C) — chains of ii–V motion.

Chorus ("…they call me Deacon Blues"): built on a G7sus → C / ii–V pull back to the C tonic.

Harmonically dense — these are the skeleton changes. See Ultimate Guitar (ver 2) / Hooktheory for full extended voicings.

Production & Arrangement

The peak of Steely Dan's obsessive studio perfectionism (Aja, 1977) — Fagen & Becker famously auditioned dozens of the best LA/NY session players and comped from countless takes to get a "perfect," effortless-sounding record. Pristine, high-fidelity jazz-rock.

  • Jazz harmony in a pop song: lush maj7 / min9 / dominant-with-extensions voicings (Extended Chords / Seventh Chords) — sophisticated, "wrong-but-right" changes.
  • The famous tenor sax solo (Pete Christlieb) was cut in a couple of takes late at night — a hired virtuoso as the hook.
  • Immaculate, wide, clean mix — every element in its own space, tons of headroom.

Steal this

  • Comp for "effortless": the relaxed feel comes from meticulous take selection — comp hard, hide the effort.
  • Jazz voicings in pop: replace plain triads with maj7/9/13 extensions for that Steely Dan sophistication → Extended Chords · Seventh Chords.
  • Hire/feature one virtuoso solo as the centerpiece (sax here) — record it fresh, keep it short.
  • Pristine hi-fi mix: everything clean, wide, and separated; lean on Pro-Q 4 carving + generous headroom.

Why I like it

steely-dan-only-a-fool-would-say-that.title: 🎵 STEELY DAN - Only a fool would say that
steely-dan-only-a-fool-would-say-that.html:

Fuller motion across sections: C – Am – F – G – Dm → I – vi – IV – V – ii — major-key diatonic with the soft bossa sway; seventh and sixth extensions throughout.

Can't Buy a Thrill (1972) — a breezy, bossa-inflected jazz-rock cut: relaxed Latin groove, clean electric guitars, and sophisticated but easygoing changes. Early-Dan warmth before the later hi-fi obsession.

Steal this

  • Sophisticated jazz voicings kept light and airy.

tadd-dameron-lady-bird.title: 🎵 TADD DAMERON - Lady Bird
tadd-dameron-lady-bird.html:
A 16-bar C-major standard whose turnaround (Cmaj7–Fm7–B♭7-ish, substituting iv-minor for the expected ii chord, with the ♭VI7 resolving directly by descending major third instead of acting as a tritone sub) is the tune's most-cited feature — and, per Jens Larsen, plausibly one of the harmonic seeds behind Coltrane's "Giant Steps" major-third cycle. Full harmonic breakdown and per-chord soloing vocabulary: Analysis and Jazz Guitar Solo ideas for a Jazz Standard - Lady Bird - Pentatonic, Lydian Dominant.

Chords (16-bar form, key of C)

Cmaj7 | Fm7 B♭7 | E♭maj7(ish, read as borrowed ♭VI rather than a true modulation) | Am7 D7 | Dm7 G7 | Cmaj7 | (turnaround:) Fm7 B♭7(→A♭7, resolving down by major 3rd, not as a tritone sub) | ...back to Cmaj7

  • Read from a spoken chord-by-chord walkthrough (captions garbled, several chord identities reconstructed from context) — treat the exact bar-by-bar spelling above as best-effort, not a verified lead sheet; verify against a real book before performance use.
  • A♭maj7 is deliberately read as a borrowed ♭VI chord (from C minor), not a modulation — Larsen's stated position in an ongoing disagreement with other analysts who do hear it as a key change. Either reading is defensible; the practical payoff of the borrowed-chord reading is that it keeps the whole form anchored in one key center rather than juggling a short-lived tonicization. → Borrowed Chords
  • The turnaround substitutes Fm7 (iv minor) for the expected ii chord of a base 1-6-2-5 — Larsen notes the vi slot (here effectively covered by the A-minor-family material earlier in the form) is freely interchangeable with A7 or an altered/diminished A7 with the same function, and the same interchangeability holds for G7 in the closing ii-V.
  • The A♭7 in the turnaround does NOT function as a tritone substitute of D7 (its "expected" role sitting a half step above the target) — instead it resolves directly by descending major third, the same interval-cycle engine that drives "Giant Steps." Flagged explicitly as good, low-stakes preparation vocabulary before tackling Coltrane changes.

Soloing vocabulary (chord by chord)

  • Cmaj7 (tonic): straight C major, kept simple — avoid reaching for outside color this early in a solo. Occasional full-chorus Lydian pass as a deliberate exception, not the default.
  • Cmaj7 → Fm7: E minor pentatonic over the Cmaj7 (its "10th line scale"), shifted up a half step to F minor pentatonic the instant Fm7 lands — the same movable box slides one fret, no new shape. → Half-Step Pentatonic Shift Over Moving Changes
  • B♭7 (turnaround dominant, off the iv-minor): Lydian dominant as the default color (heard as "Fm6 with a B♭ bass," not an independent dominant); alternate device — plane a D♭maj7 arpeggio a half step above the target and resolve down into Cmaj7. → Scale Modes Reference § Lydian Dominant
  • A♭maj7 → Am7: work out the individual guide-tone voice leading by hand rather than reaching for a scale; also colored with diminished-family and altered-scale material because the turnaround's own half-step-up-diminished character recurs through the tune. → Guide Tones, Diminished Chords
  • Confined-position practice take on this exact transition: when the A♭maj7 arpeggio itself is awkward to finger in whatever area you're soloing in, sub in the F minor or C minor arpeggio instead (both relative-minor-family substitutes for the same Maj7 sound — F minor is A♭'s relative minor, C minor is its iii chord); pick whichever actually sits better under the hand locally rather than defaulting to "practice the A♭maj7 arpeggio more." Full four-step drill this is worked from → One-Position Fretboard Overview Drill — Jens Larsen, Fretboard Visualization - How To Develop A Complete Overview
  • Am7: treated identically to the Cmaj7 tonic material — functionally a rootless/related tonic extension, no separate vocabulary needed.
  • Am7 → D7: target notes NOT present in the previous chord, avoiding the bare root over the bass; the 9th of D7 is a smooth landing target.
  • D7 (V7/V): Lydian dominant as default (matches the general "long-sitting V7/V" rule); melodic-minor pass also demonstrated (a G♯7♭5-type shape from the same parent scale). → Scale Modes Reference § Lydian Dominant
  • D7: the D and E major triad pair, deliberately mixed/alternated rather than run low-to-high. → Triad Pairs
  • E7 (later in the form): a shell voicing rooted on the 3rd (an F major-7 shell shape) as the line's orientation anchor, plus an altered-dominant pass. → Chord Voicings
  • G7 (closing turnaround dominant): a diminished-family triad pair (not the augmented/major type used earlier) drawn from the whole-tone-adjacent dominant/diminished scale. → Triad Pairs, Diminished Chords
  • Closing turnaround (C→A♭7): the same half-step-planing device reused from the B♭7 spot — practiced by playing the line slowly in tempo, targeting one note per chord first, then filling connective material once the skeleton holds. → Half-Step Pentatonic Shift Over Moving Changes

Steal this

  • A "10th line" pentatonic that's a half step below the next chord's own tonic pentatonic is a free half-step-shift device — pick the color pentatonic specifically because its relative sits one fret from where you're headed, not just because it sounds good in isolation. → Half-Step Pentatonic Shift Over Moving Changes
  • Target-note practice generalizes to any unfamiliar tune: pick reachable notes in the NEXT chord and build backward, rather than reacting to the chord you're currently on. → Chord-Tone Soloing
  • A turnaround's "surprising" chord (here, ♭VI7 resolving by descending major third instead of as a tritone sub) is worth naming as a small dose of a bigger system (Giant Steps) — learn the small version first. → Chord Progressions

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

Full lesson (harmonic analysis + chord-by-chord soloing vocabulary) → Analysis and Jazz Guitar Solo ideas for a Jazz Standard - Lady Bird - Pentatonic, Lydian Dominant

the-beatles-a-hard-day-s-night.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - A Hard Day's Night
the-beatles-a-hard-day-s-night.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack hears this as the record where the blues finally recedes. Compared with "Can't Buy Me Love" (blues in form, changes and tune) and "You Can't Do That" (blues form, wavering third), what survives here is only the 12-bar length, the AAB phrasing and a trace of minor-third flavour — the rest is Lennon and McCartney ().

Form. A 2-bar intro in tempo; a 12-bar verse that borrows the blues' proportions (three equal 4-bar phrases) but not its progression; an 8-bar bridge in two parallel phrases; a half-instrumental "semi-solo" verse that hands the last phrase back to the voice; and an outro that triple-repeats the closing half-phrase before fading on the opening chord.

Harmony. Solidly G, with the verse's ♭VII an early instance of a habit that becomes theirs (). The verse withholds a formal V–I until its third phrase, having already confirmed the tonic by the gentler route of IV and ♭VII — closed-sounding without ever cadencing. The bridge feints at B minor for a phrase but never supplies its dominant, so it stays tonicization rather than modulation ().

The famous opening sonority works as a surrogate V into G: roughly D minor, F and G stacked, with G sitting as a suspended 4th over a low D and no B anywhere. Beginning and ending a rock record on a non-tonic chord was close to unheard of.

Arrangement. George's 12-string arrives as an identity here. Ringo plays essentially one figure the whole way with cowbell added in the bridges — the absence of fills and texture changes is what makes the track a steamroller.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-across-the-universe.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Across the Universe
the-beatles-across-the-universe.html:
Lennon's mantra-inspired ballad. Two fans (Lizzie Bravo and Gayleen Pease) provided backing vocals on the original. George Martin added Hammond organ. Phil Spector added orchestration for the Let It Be release.

Chords

Key: D major (the Let It Be recording is tuned down a semitone, so it sounds in D♭) · slow 4/4

Verse: D – Bm – F♯m – Em7 – A7 …then… D – Bm – F♯m – Em7 – Gm → I – vi – iii – ii7 – V7 … I – vi – iii – ii7 – iv (the Gm is a borrowed minor-iv — the line's aching turn)

Chorus ("Jai guru deva om / Nothing's gonna change my world"): D – A7sus4 – A – A7 – G – D → I – V7sus4 – V – V7 – IV – I

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-across-the-universe-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A floating, meditative drone-song built on a tanpura/tambura drone and Lennon's stream-of-consciousness "Jai guru deva om" refrain. The released Let It Be version (Spector) added lush orchestra + choir and slowed the tape; an earlier version had bird sounds and backing "aahs" — either way, the arrangement is atmosphere over motion.

  • Modal, drone-anchored harmony — the tonic never really leaves, so it feels suspended.
  • Heavily reverbed, slowed, dreamy vocal.

Steal this

  • Drone anchor: hold a tonic pad/tanpura under the whole song (Omnisphere / a sustained synth) so it floats → Scale Modes Reference.
  • Mantra refrain: a repeated sung phrase as the emotional center.
  • Slow the tape + heavy reverb for a suspended, dreamy lead (Little AlterBoy pitch-down, ValhallaVintageVerb long).
  • Atmosphere over chord motion — let texture, not changes, carry a section.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — Across the Universe"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Across the Universe (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Across The Universe — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #169.

Form. A flat folk-ballad shape whose repeated group is two verses → Mantra → Refrain, run three times. The interpolated "Mantra" section before every refrain is the unorthodox part, and the two near-identical verse variants are reordered each time round (V/V′, then V/V, then V′/V) so the listener registers freshness without being able to name what changed (). Almost nothing is four-square: intro 6 bars, verse 8 (with an extra half bar in the later verse of the first two pairs), verse′ 7, Mantra 6, refrain 16.

Harmony. Verse: I – vi – iii · ii – V · Verse′: I – vi – iii · ii – iv · Mantra: I (4) – V (2) · Refrain: V (4) – IV (2) – I (2), ×4. Diatonic apart from the minor iv, a Lennon staple (). His argument is that the interest is entirely in where sections stop: only the refrain closes, everything else opens out to V, and verse′ is aimed at minor iv purely to break the monotony of a repeated target. The refrain's V–IV–I is the blues trope, and he flags how differently it reads from IV–V–I.

Notable. Every section gets its own contour () — a patter-syllabic inverted arch, then a descending syllabic verse, then the Mantra as a rising triadic fanfare, then sixth-leaps in the refrain. The outro shortens the Mantra so its two-bar move to V disappears, leaving it over a drone into the fade.

Against this page. Same key reading (D). His form is finer-grained than the structure: field: what the page counts as a chorus he splits into Mantra plus Refrain.

the-beatles-all-i-ve-got-to-do.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - All I've Got To Do
the-beatles-all-i-ve-got-to-do.html:
Pollack's analysis

Three things stacked make this sound exotic on an otherwise plain 1963 record: a near-entirely pentatonic tune, constant major/minor byplay, and a belly-dance syncopation that never lets up. Pollack's claim is that the refusal to commit to a key is deliberate.

Form. Two bridges with a single verse between them — the harmonic rhythm is sparse enough that a third verse there would sag. The verse is an odd 11 bars (4 + 2 + 5), stretched by repeating its own material right where the hard syncopation eases off. Two quiet experiments sit on the plain shape: an opening chord that isn't quite an intro, and a wordless hummed final verse that fades out mid-section.

Harmony. The key is genuinely undecided between E major and C♯ minor (): verse phrases start on vi, no firm V–I ever lands, and the only V chord in the whole song is the B in the bridge's last bar. Working the vi/I pair this way was a standing habit of the period. Late in the verse the major IV gives way to a borrowed minor iv, and the cause is a chromatic inner voice sliding down rather than a colour choice (). The opening sonority resists labelling — an augmented triad on C♯ over an E bass — but it functions as a surprise IV-substitute into the minor.

Melody and arrangement. Almost pure pentatonic (), broken only by a couple of D♯ appoggiaturas. Paul's countermelody starts in parallel thirds and converts to parallel fourths simply by holding one note while John keeps moving; his bass plays double stops across the c♯/E alternation, keeping the common tone G♯ on top of both.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-all-my-loving.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - All My Loving
the-beatles-all-my-loving.html:
Pollack's analysis

This is the essay where Pollack sets out his working distinction between bridge and refrain — hook inside the verse means the middle section is a bridge (contrast and respite); hook elsewhere means that elsewhere is a refrain (the payoff, with key-confirming harmony) (). The song is the awkward case that has both.

Form. No intro, no downbeat to give Paul his pitch, and a non-tonic first chord — a device they liked enough to reuse repeatedly. A 16-bar verse in two parallel 8-bar phrases (first open on V, second closed on I), an 8-bar refrain built from one 4-bar phrase twice, an 8-bar bridge for the guitar solo, and an outro extending the refrain.

Harmony. Chords change almost every bar and never sit longer than two — hyperactive by their 1963 standards (). Verse bars 3–8 run a chain of descending thirds instead of a circle of fifths, and the ♭VII in bar 7 acts as a connector between ii and V, motivated by a rising inner line (). The refrain's best detail is a rootless augmented chord — a line cliché falling out of an inner voice descending C♯–C♮–B — held a full bar so you can't miss it. The outro repeats the refrain's vi–I but strips the augmented chord out, and that subtraction is what reads as an ending.

Why both sections. Pollack's thought experiment: delete the refrain and there's no hook; delete the bridge and the refrain is exposed as giving no harmonic confirmation, no textural contrast and no change of pace. The bridge supplies all three, above all a slower harmonic rhythm — which is why the solo needed its own changes rather than the verse's ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-all-together-now.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - All Together Now
the-beatles-all-together-now.html:
Pollack's analysis

A children's song with adult joinery inside it: I–IV–V harmony, a melody spanning about four notes, and a form that quietly refuses to settle. The improvised feel is faked — the execution is far too clean.

Form. The sophistication is structural, and it matches neither the pop nor the folk template (). It opens orthodoxly (verse, verse, bridge, refrain), then runs a verse, two refrains with no bridge between them, a bridge with no verse in front of it, and very nearly three refrains back to back. The verse and refrain are both harmonically closed 8-bar shapes on two chords; the bridge is an asymmetrical 10 bars because its last phrase is rhetorically stretched.

Harmony. The bridge is the only section open at both ends — it starts on IV and finishes on V, which is also where the melodic climax lands, and it's the only place all three chords appear. That single difference does all the sectional contrast work. The outro turns an unexpected third refrain into a full V–I ending, and while the tempo pushes forward the harmonic rhythm abruptly slows to one chord every four bars; that slowdown against an accelerating backbeat is what tells you the record is landing ().

Melody and arrangement. Syllabic, patter-like, and still describing a real arch on four notes; the verse's syncopation is placed to coincide with the tune's apex rather than scattered (). The build is strictly choreographed — one element added per section, acoustic guitar alone up to a full chorus with horns and handclaps — and the sharpest move is dropping the lead vocal at the first bridge instead of adding to it.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-all-you-need-is-love.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - All You Need Is Love
the-beatles-all-you-need-is-love.html:
Pollack's analysis

The verses breathe unevenly — 4/4 with 3/4 bars folded in on a pattern that's regular without being predictable — and that is exactly what keeps an anthem-march from sounding like one. Pollack's structural claim is that the song opens with three consecutive verses of which the first is really the intro: it carries no tune, it installs the "love, love, love" backing figure everything later rides on.

Form. Three bars of deliberately misquoted "Marseillaise" to open, trilled to read as vaguely Baroque. Verses phrase four-square even though their bar lengths don't. The refrain is a near-square 8 bars with only its last bar dropping to 3/4. The final refrain and outro take roughly 1:40 of a 3:52 record — an unusual amount of structural weight on an ending — and the outro settles fully into 4/4, giving the fade a different underlying pattern from everything before it.

Harmony. The verse's real motion is only I ↔ V; the chords between are voice leading, outer parts in parallel tenths over a bass stepping G–F♯–E–D and back, which is why so many of them are inversions rather than root positions (). The song keeps sagging out of G major toward E minor. In the refrain the B major is a secondary dominant to vi (), but the section's fingerprint is the backing vocals sounding A and G a major 2nd apart while the tune holds D above them.

Melody. The strongest unifier isn't in the tune: it's the dotted bass figure D–E–G rising at the end of every phrase, the same shape as the misquoted intro, and it persists straight through the fade.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-and-i-love-her.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - And I Love Her
the-beatles-and-i-love-her.html:
Pollack's analysis

Paul's first released straight love song, and the essay Pollack uses to define pivot chords and relative-key modulation properly. The bittersweetness is a tonal ambiguity that never resolves — the song flip-flops continually between C♯ minor and E major — and the second event is a modulation up a half step at the guitar solo, entered on the new key's IV.

Form. One bridge only, with two verses before it and three after, the middle of those three given to the solo. A 4-bar intro, an odd 10-bar verse phrased across five short units, a four-square 8-bar bridge, then a complete ending.

Harmony. The vocabulary is just the six chords shared by E major and C♯ minor, which is what makes the pivoting frictionless — a chord is heard first in the old key and re-heard a bar or two later in the new one (, ). The intro's ii → I is a weak cadence toward the major that establishes nothing; the verse then repeats a IV → I plagal cadence in the relative minor three times to ground you in C♯ minor () before walking IV–V–I back to E. The bridge converges on the major's V, and that V is then denied its resolution — the next verse simply restarts with its minor plagal cadence. The final chord is a Picardy third.

The half-step upshift is a fifties staple made strange by entering on IV of the new key — a G minor triad with no notes in common with the four-sharp world it interrupts. All the shock is in that first chord; a few bars later the new plane is unremarkable.

Arrangement. Sparse by design: acoustic lead and rhythm guitars, bass, claves. Resting on beat one is a motif — the opening hook and every vocal phrase begin with a rest.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-and-your-bird-can-sing.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - And Your Bird Can Sing
the-beatles-and-your-bird-can-sing.html:
Interlocking twin guitar riff between Lennon and Harrison is the defining feature. McCartney's bass lines are unusually melodic. Hard-driving Revolver track.

Chords

Key: E major · ~130 BPM, driving

Verse: E – F♯m – A – E → I – ii – IV – I

Bridge ("When your prize possessions…"): G♯m – B – E – F♯m – B7 → iii – V – I – ii – V7

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-and-your-bird-can-sing-chords.pdf (charted in E; the chart also lists Capo II / Capo IV transpositions).

Production & Arrangement

Revolver — famous for its dual harmonized lead-guitar line (Harrison + McCartney playing interlocking parts in harmony), bright and jangly, driving the whole song.

Steal this

  • Harmonized twin-guitar lead: write a melodic line and double it a 3rd/6th above for a bright, interlocking hook (Morgan Amps Suite, double-track it).
  • Guitar riff as the song's identity, not just the vocal.
  • Jangly, bright electric tone.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Revolver · search "The Beatles — And Your Bird Can Sing"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - And Your Bird Can Sing (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — And Your Bird Can Sing — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #98.

Form. A two-bridge model with a single verse between the bridges, plus a full repeat of the guitar-solo verse just before the outro. Intro 4 bars (one chord, and deliberately only the first half of what later becomes the complete solo); verse 8 as 4+4 AB, the two phrases separated partly by harmonic rhythm — the first four bars sit on one chord, the second four move; bridge 8 over a chromatic bass descent; outro the obbligato again, with a complete ending rather than a fade.

Harmony. Verse: I (4 bars) | ii | IV | I (2) in E — closed, and the key is established plagally, with the dominant withheld from the entire song until the bridge (). In the solo verses bar 6's IV is swapped for V, partly because IV clashes with the solo line but mainly because V makes the climax land. Bridge: iii (4) | I | ii (2) | V over a bass walking G♯ – G♮ – F♯ – F♮ – E; it sets up as though modulating to G♯ minor and the leisurely chromatic descent quietly deposits it back home instead. The song ends on IV in second inversion — rarer than an unresolved ending on V, and unprepared by anything else in the arrangement.

Notable. He reads the guitar obbligato as Baroque-shaped — perpetual even eighths, embellished stepwise content, ritornello-style cyclic return — dropped into a deliberately dirty mix, with the pentatonic touches typical of John over it (). John's vocal is artificially double-tracked and split hard left/right; the rhythm section is clunky on purpose, so nearly all the syncopation comes from the guitar lick and the voice.

Against this page. Same key (E major). He hears no chorus at all — verse/bridge only — where this page's structure: reads I-V-C-V-C-B-C.

the-beatles-another-girl.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Another Girl
the-beatles-another-girl.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack treats this less as a career highlight than as a catalogue of every Beatles device in circulation by early 1965 — and as evidence of John's influence running back onto Paul, since the opening gambit, the refrain habit and the modulation scheme all come from "You're Going To Lose That Girl".

Form. A standard two-verse / two-bridge layout that sounds stranger than it is, because the verse's last phrase behaves like a refrain and doubles as the intro. Parse that phrase as part of the verse and the shape snaps into place. The intro runs closer to five bars than four — it lands on the downbeat of bar 5 — so every appearance elides into whatever follows. The verse is 16 bars phrased AABC, close to a non-traditional 12-bar plus a short refrain.

Harmony. Verses stay inside I, IV, V and ♭VII, with ♭VII used only as a neighbour between two statements of I (). The IV is then held for four bars that deliberately don't line up with the phrase divisions — harmonic rhythm working subliminally (). The bridge is a genuine modulation to C major, the relative major of the parallel minor (, ). Two pivots earn attention: going in, the verse's final D chord puns as IV at home and V-of-V in C, unresolved until two bars into the bridge; coming out, C is re-read as III in A minor and cadences V–i, except the "i" arrives major.

Melody. Descending chromatic fragments circling a narrow range, leaning on ♭3 and ♭7 hard enough to read bluesy over harmony that is nothing like a blues — and hard enough to leave the mode of the home key genuinely ambiguous ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-any-time-at-all.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Any Time At All
the-beatles-any-time-at-all.html:
Pollack's analysis

Formulaic-looking and not: the form belongs to neither the one- nor the two-bridge model. A frequently recurring refrain dominates folk-ballad style, there are only two verses, the bridge is held back to near the end, and it brings genuinely new material rather than recycling.

Form. An 8-bar closed refrain opens the record on a drum thwack landing on beat 2 — you can't place it in the meter until the second refrain. The verse is an unusual 14 bars, its lopsided 6 + 8 really the same 6-bar phrase twice with the second's first bar elided onto the first's last. The bridge runs 10 bars; the outro is a petit reprise of the refrain's tail.

Harmony. A small chord set close to home, carrying two Lennon–McCartney trademarks: the vi → I cadence that opens the refrain, and a nearly fully chromatic walking bass under the verse (). The minor iv in a major key isn't a colour chosen for itself — the bass walking B down to B♭ to A is what puts it there (). The bridge builds tension by approaching V and backing off repeatedly before releasing, and its opening phrase is built from contrary motion in the outer voices, which is why ordinary seventh chords land in unusual inversions.

Melody. Arch-shaped, somewhat pentatonic, and stuffed with appoggiaturas (); bluesy F naturals cross-relate with the F♯s underneath and make the leaning tones bite. The tune is short interjections with gaps, and the guitar and bass figures filling those gaps are real motifs — one returns quietly at the end of the verse and comes back transformed at the bridge's climax ().

Arrangement. John's double-tracked lead carries almost everything, except that Paul takes the refrain's second line in hocket — a texture change and a range fix at once. The whole track rides one flavour of syncopation, the harder "4-and" kind where the following downbeat isn't explicitly marked ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-ask-me-why.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Ask Me Why
the-beatles-ask-me-why.html:
Pollack's analysis

The most over-engineered form in the early catalogue. It's a mutated two-bridge model in which the verse exists in three versions, each cut for a different structural job, and Pollack's argument is that the corny Latin backbeat makes the craft easy to miss.

Form. The initial verse runs 13 bars and ends open on V, so it can only lead to another verse. A first variant is identical until its last three bars, then rewritten to close and hand off to the bridge — it appears exactly once. A much shorter second variant alludes to the verse rather than restating it, carries the title phrase and functions as a refrain, appearing three times and altered each time. Everything enters on a pickup from the middle of the previous bar.

Harmony. Solidly E major, leaning toward the relative minor mid-verse. The engine is stepwise streams of parallel sevenths rather than plain triads. The build works by the harmony changing character: streams give way to root motion, the harmonic rhythm broadens, and a V⁹ lands just before the melodic peak (). Secondary dominants do the lifting — V-of-vi, V-of-V and an augmented tonic acting as V♯5-of-IV (). The first variant swaps a borrowed minor iv in where the initial verse had major IV (). The refrain variant is deliberately weak — streams plus a plagal IV–I () — so it powers the song down instead of climbing, and on its second pass its final bar is swapped for the augmented tonic, buying a clean run into the second bridge without replaying the whole first variant.

Melody. Almost everything sits inside one octave; only the initial verse's last phrase breaks out to a falsetto peak. First pass John descends from high G♯; on the repeat he goes up to high B — a small masterclass in holding something back.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-baby-you-re-a-rich-man.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Baby You're A Rich Man
the-beatles-baby-you-re-a-rich-man.html:
Pollack's analysis

Written and cut fast, and the interest is almost entirely modal. Pollack calls the key G Mixolydian major on literal evidence: the D major V chord never appears anywhere in the song, and F♯ never appears in the tune. What holds the key together is a tonic pedal plus a three-chord vocabulary () — the same drone logic as "Rain".

Form. An 8-bar I–IV vamp states the whole harmonic idea up front. The verse is three phrases (ABB) across an odd 11 bars, because its A phrase runs three; the refrain is also three phrases but ABA across an even 12, squaring off against the lopsided verse. The verse's B phrases open toward IV rather than V, so the section has no forward pull — with two verses back to back at the top it is genuinely hard to hear where one ends.

Harmony. Three chords: I, IV and ♭VII, the last reading here as IV-of-IV (). Because so many phrases close on the IV, the centre of gravity sits high for a song supposedly in G. The one outside chord is ♭III in the refrain, reached by a chromatic bass climb, and the reason it works across the catalogue is the cross-relation it strikes against the chords either side () — so it should not be voiced smoothly.

Arrangement. A crowded track, but the craft is in the intro entrances: bass arrives halfway through bar 3 and the clavioline immediately after, rather than on the downbeat of bar 4. That single mid-bar choice is what keeps the vamp from feeling boxy.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-baby-s-in-black.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Baby's In Black
the-beatles-baby-s-in-black.html:
Pollack's analysis

Formally verbose by their standards — refrain, verse, bridge and a solo section — a shape Pollack notes turns up almost exclusively in John's songs. Stylistically it's a mishmash: bluesy tune and chords over a near-hillbilly vocal arrangement, with drone open fifths under the final verse. John called it a waltz, but the tempo and agitation don't fit the dance.

Form. Very few sections are square (). The 4-bar intro is engineered so you feel you walked in mid-song, coming out of a refrain. The refrain is 12 bars in three equal phrases, melodically an inverted arch and harmonically closed. The verse is 14 bars phrased asymmetrically 4 + 4 + 6. The bridge is nominally 8 but runs into the downbeat of bar 9 and elides directly into the next refrain — the words elide too, one section's syllable landing on the other's downbeat.

Harmony. Almost nothing but I, IV and V, firmly in A, with the bridge adding vi and V-of-V ().
