The trademark is that V-of-V resolves to IV rather than V — the same move as "She Loves You" and "Eight Days A Week". The refrain uses blues chords in a decidedly non-blues order, and in the verse the chords deliberately don't change on the phrase boundaries, which loosens an otherwise closed section ().

Melody. Range is managed across the whole song rather than inside a section (): the recurring refrain holds the lowest note and hammers a constricted ceiling, the verse opens the top a little, and the true peak is withheld until the downbeat of the bridge.

Arrangement. An unbroken end-to-end vocal duet, John below and Paul above — the absence of textural relief is what keeps the tension up. The band texture is likewise constant, with one calculated exception: a radical change of backing for the final verse only, then straight back for the closing refrain.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-back-in-the-ussr.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Back In The USSR
the-beatles-back-in-the-ussr.html:
Pollack's analysis

An album opener built as a palate cleanser — straight hard rock after two years of studio experiments — stacked with deliberate references (the Beach Boys everywhere, Chuck Berry underneath the conceit). The analytically useful claim is that it is neither a twelve-bar blues nor four-square: it takes the blues chord budget and none of the blues form.

Form. The intro pounds four bars on V with mounting pressure to resolve, and pointedly declines to repeat its own syncopated whack in the last two bars. Verses are four-square 8s; the refrain is an unusual 6 bars whose last phrase exists in two versions depending on what follows; the bridge is the loosest section, always carrying a two-bar extension. The 6-bar refrain and the elastic bridge are what keep a three-chord rocker from sounding like a grid ().

Harmony. I, IV and V, with ♭III carrying more weight than any of them. The harmonic rhythm is slow enough that you can hear ♭III play two different roles (, ): parked between two statements of IV in the verse, so it reads as hesitation; and in the refrain a sub-subdominant creeping up on IV from below. The recurring chromatic bass fills work as a motif in their own right and the bridge backing vocals double them.

Melody. Very bluesy, leaning hard on the flattened third against A major harmony so a cross-relation sounds most of the time (). The melodic seventh is avoided completely in the vocal and handed to the sawtooth guitar riff instead — the note is in the song without ever being in the tune.

Arrangement. A thick overdubbed patchwork choreographed section by section, one element added at a time. Handclaps exist from the first refrain but are only pushed forward at the end, which is cheaper than adding a new part.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-because.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Because
the-beatles-because.html:
Pollack's analysis

Three-part vocal harmony overdubbed three times over arpeggiated electric harpsichord, and a home key that never quite settles. Pollack's structural point is the two-bar mini bridge: it keeps steering toward D major — a ♭II Neapolitan behaving like a new tonic — and then a diminished seventh melts it back to i. The song establishes C♯ minor by ordinary i–ii–V–i means over and over precisely because that interlude keeps undermining it ().

Form. Underneath, an ordinary verse–verse–bridge–verse, blurred by the recurring mini bridge. The full bridge is built as an extension of the mini bridge. The outro looks on paper like a verse plus a mini bridge, but the vocals go wordless throughout, which binds the preceding mini bridge to the outro into a symmetrical ABA — inverting the separation the song has drilled every previous time.

Harmony. Stock is i, half-diminished ii, V and VI, plus IV in major form borrowed from melodic minor (, ). The demonstration piece is the pair of diminished sevenths: enharmonically the same four pitches, sounding identical, but the voice leading roots them differently so one melts back to i and the other functions as vii-of-IV. Same chord, two functions, one song.

Arrangement. A layered intro — harpsichord alone, then guitar doubling it plucked near the bridge so the attacks match, then voices and bass, then a brass-voiced Moog. The arpeggio figuration groups 3 + 3 + 2. The track ends on the diminished seventh, unresolved: since that chord has resolved to i every previous time, verse-plus-mini-bridge is a loop with no exit and breaking it is the only available ending.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-being-for-the-benefit-of-mr-.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Being for the Benefit of Mr Kite
the-beatles-being-for-the-benefit-of-mr-.html:
Lennon transcribed the lyrics from a Victorian circus poster. George Martin created the surreal middle section by cutting up and randomly splicing steam organ tape recordings. Calliope-driven carnival atmosphere.

Chords

Key: D minor · circus waltz (drops to 3/4 in the middle) · deliberately chromatic

Verse: Cm – Gaug – B♭ – Dm – G → loosely ♭vii – V+ – VI – i – IV (the augmented G and the C-minor color make it woozy on purpose)

"Mr. K. will challenge the world" turnaround: Dm – Dm/C – B♭ – A7 – Dm → i – i/♭7 – VI – V7 – i (a descending bass line D–C–B♭–A under the chords)

Instrumental break: modulates through Dm–F–C and Em–C–B before snapping back.

Harmonically wild by design (Lennon wanted a steam-organ fairground). From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-being-for-the-benefit-of-mr-kite-c.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

The Victorian-circus swirl is a chance-based tape collage: Martin and engineer Geoff Emerick recorded steam-organ/calliope and harmonica tape loops, cut the tape into pieces, threw them in the air, and spliced them back together at random to get an unplayable, disorienting fairground wash. Chaos by design.

  • Heavy tape manipulation, varispeed, and swirling organ atmosphere over a straight-ish waltz feel.
  • The "atmosphere" is entirely a studio construction, not a played part.

Steal this

  • Chance-based sample collage: chop a loop into fragments, randomize/reassemble them (kHs Reverser / granular Granulator II / manual slicing) for a chaotic atmospheric bed.
  • Period-instrument pastiche (calliope/organ) for instant era/atmosphere.
  • Build an "impossible" texture out of many tiny spliced pieces rather than one performance.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band · search "The Beatles — Being for the Benefit of Mr. Kite!"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Being for the Benefit of Mr Kite (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Being For The Benefit Of Mr. Kite — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #112.

Form. Every section sits on the same fourteen-bar chord plan. The two instrumental interludes read as contrast but run the identical progression transposed up a whole step, disguised by having no vocal, a pile of tape loops and (the first time) a waltz meter. He reads that as deliberate economy: if one department goes berserk, the backbone underneath has to stay simple. Intro 3 bars; verse an unusual 14 bars phrased AA′BB′ as 4+3+4+3, the uneven phrases giving the whole thing a limp; the second interlude returns to 4/4 and simply ends the song, so there is no outro at all.

Harmony. Intro: (d) ♭VI – V – i, that i re-read as (c) ii – V · Verse A: (c) i – V♯5 · vi-of-ii – ii · V · V♯5 · Verse B: (d) i – iv – V, ×3, final G re-read as (c) V. Two things do the work: the augmented dominant (V♯5) as a recurring colour, and a modulation engine where each section starts a step below where the last one ended, so verse runs C minor → D minor and the interlude D minor → E minor (). These are real modulations, not tonicisations, and the ladder would ratchet upward forever — which is why the first interlude ends with an abrupt call to attention that kills the waltz and yanks the music back to C minor.

Against this page. A real disagreement on key. Pollack reads the song as arriving in E minor — "three keys" is a dodge, in his view, and the D-minor opening and C-minor verse starts are a ruse designed to leave you off balance, because the ear awards "home" to where you land. This page's frontmatter says C minor and the Chords section says D minor. Both are readings; nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-birthday.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Birthday
the-beatles-birthday.html:
Pollack's analysis

One of very few Lennon/McCartney originals built on a strict twelve-bar frame () — for all the blues they covered early on, they used the actual form sparingly, as a colour rather than a home idiom. But the best lesson in the essay is not the blues: it's the pair of connector sections that do the same structural job by opposite means.

Form. Effectively the standard two-bridge model, disguised by a long instrumental opening (the entire verse played through as an anticipation) and by the connectors introducing each bridge. Excluding the long connector, the sung sections form a near-palindrome. Throughout, the lead vocal enters after the downbeat; the only vocals landing on a downbeat are the female backing singers in the bridges.

Harmony. Every verse chord is a dominant seventh, with one deviation from the textbook: bar 10 sustains V instead of dropping to IV. The long connector's payoff is a deceptive resolution () — eight hammered bars of V going not to I but to ♭III, which is less remote than it sounds, being the relative major of the parallel minor (). The bridge bassline is the detail worth copying: a chromatic climb that simply keeps going past its target so the chord lands in second inversion, momentarily keyless, until the bass drops to the root and reveals it as V again.

Arrangement. Antiphony is the unifying device and it's in every section () — only the responder changes: lead guitar, then the vocal, then a processed tack piano, then the backing singers. The two connectors are the teaching point: the long one prolongs V for sixteen bars and resolves deceptively; the short one is four bars of guitars in plain octaves sliding over in the parallel natural minor, and it's the only place in the song the drums stop. The second time round the listener needs relief, not another build.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-blackbird.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Blackbird
the-beatles-blackbird.html:
Pollack's analysis

Very few raw materials, recombined so economically that the song sounds far richer than its parts. Two things to take away: the guitar part is a chain of parallel tenths, and the melodic motion of those tenths — not root progression — is what the ear follows, so many bars simply do not contain an analysable chord; and the phrasing is free-verse uneven almost everywhere.

Form. Verse phrases run 3½ + 4 + 3 + 4 bars; the refrain is 4 + 5 despite a plainly parallel AA' shape (). A 4-bar instrumental C phrase compresses the previous six bars and appears after the first verse only. The back half is intricate: refrain into a full instrumental verse, back into a second refrain, then an extension that halts like an ending, then a pseudo-intro made of two phrases elided together — at which point the birdsong enters and the last verse begins.

Harmony. Roman numerals are deliberately sparse here. You can name a chord in every bar if you insist, but the motion is carried by stepwise, partly chromatic bass under parallel tenths, and naming the passing sonorities misrepresents what you hear (, ). Structurally, the refrain's first phrase is a long prolongation of IV that pulls back at the last moment; the second phrase goes ahead and reaches V-of-V (). Verses are plain major, refrains shift to a bluesy Dorian.

Melody. The song's peak is a high G in the middle of the refrain landing on that V-of-V — highest note and strongest harmonic goal in the same instant.

Arrangement. Acoustic guitar and a metronome tick, and that is all. The birdsong is a lesson in effect placement: held back for the second half only, and allowed to run a second or two past the last note.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-blue-jay-way.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Blue Jay Way
the-beatles-blue-jay-way.html:
Pollack's analysis

Indian influence at one remove — no Indian instruments and no metric fireworks, just a drone bass and a raga-like modal tune. The mode is the event: a major scale with both the second and fourth degrees raised (). Folk-ballad form, the same shape as "The Fool On The Hill", which makes the two an instructive pair on one record.

Form. Intro, then verse–refrain three times, a fourth refrain, and a long outro. The intro is ad libitum with no meter but about eight measures' worth of duration. The verse is one beat short of eight measures, which renders the impatience of waiting structurally rather than lyrically (); the refrain is a full eight plus a pickup measure, more than paying the beat back.

Harmony. Effectively two chords for the whole song over a bass that never moves (). The ♯ii°7 is worth separating from the familiar vii°7: vii°7 is a dominant surrogate whose four notes all resolve stepwise into I, while ♯ii°7 is a subdominant surrogate where three resolve and the fourth is sustained across the change. George reaches it by outlining the diminished seventh already sitting inside his chosen scale, so the progression is implied by the tune as much as played.

Melody. The refrain is where the raga flavour actually lands, taking its pathos from leaning on the seventh and the raised fourth over the drone, the ♯4 supplying an appoggiatura the solo cello previews in the intro ().

Arrangement. A kitchen sink of every effect accumulated across Revolver and Pepper, thickening steadily. The outro only sounds improvised: each successive refrain is shorter and plainer, and the apparently new tune the last ones carry had already been slipped into a backing vocal several sections earlier — a composed ending disguised as a fader move.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-can-you-take-me-back.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Can You Take Me Back
the-beatles-can-you-take-me-back.html:
Pollack's analysis

A 28-second fragment over one static chord, not even listed on the album sleeve. Two things make it worth studying: prose-like phrasing that refuses to line up with the bar grid, and the fact that the released version is an act of editing — it was excerpted from a longer take at the "I Will" session, and the haunting mid-verse fade is, in the source performance, a plain complete coda. The crop made the song.

Form. One verse plus a second fading out. The verse is 12 bars counted internally as 3 × 4, but the three sung phrases straddle that division rather than sitting inside it. The first starts on a downbeat and ends on a hard accent just before the downbeat of bar 4, with the guitar vamp filling the rest. The second starts on a downbeat but plants its sustained high note in exactly the rhythmic slot where the first ended, tying across into the next four-bar group. The third is squeezed onto the tail of the second and melismas out to bar 12.

Harmony. One chord — a dominant seventh on the tonic, held throughout. The ♭3s in the tune grind against its major third, so a cross-relation runs continuously ().

Melody. Strictly pentatonic (), but spread across a tenth. Wide range on five notes is what gives a one-chord fragment any shape at all.

Arrangement. Paul on acoustic guitar, Ringo and John on light percussion. Nothing else. The lesson: over a static chord, phrasing is the only structure you have.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-can-t-buy-me-love.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Can't Buy Me Love
the-beatles-can-t-buy-me-love.html:
Pollack's analysis

A standard long form carrying something that isn't standard at all — the verse is a strict twelve-bar blues and the intro, outro and refrain are pointedly not (). The verse uses only I, IV and V with a melody restricted to ♭3 and ♭7; the intro and outro lean on iii and vi with a melody that insists on the natural third. The refrain then sets the two worlds against each other in alternation.

Form. The intro is an unusual 6 bars because the verse arrives early and elides it — the two bars that would square it off are simply cut, and they do get played, in the outro. Verses are strict 12-bar frames. The refrain is a square 8, four 2-bar phrases, with the lyric in an AB-AC pattern the music mirrors. An extra bar is inserted before the guitar-solo verse — the reverse of the elision gambit, flagging the solo and throwing the count off.

Harmony. The intro is in medias res and audacious about it: the home key isn't confirmed until bar 6, and every chord before it is minor, while the melody spells the tonic triad as literally as a bugle call. Blue-note cross-relations carry the verse () and appoggiaturas supply most of the remaining spice over otherwise bare triads (). The single most distinctive detail is the bluesy ♭3 dropped into bar 3 of the refrain, surrounded by natural thirds on both sides.

Arrangement. Sizzling cymbals everywhere except the intro and outro — texture used purely to articulate form. The ensemble cuts out for an instant right after the downbeat of verse bar 10, and the silence reads as an accent. George's solo sounds improvised and isn't; the live versions prove it was worked out.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-carry-that-weight.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Carry That Weight
the-beatles-carry-that-weight.html:
Reprises the harmonic and melodic themes from 'You Never Give Me Your Money.' George Martin orchestral arrangement. Closing movement of the Abbey Road medley.

Chords

Key: C major

Chorus ("Boy, you're gonna carry that weight"): C – G – C → I – V – I

Verse / "You Never Give Me Your Money" reprise: Am – Dm7 – G – C – Fmaj7 – Dm – E7 – Am → vi – ii7 – V – I – IVmaj7 – ii – III7 (V/vi) – vi

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-carry-that-weight-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Abbey Road medley — famous for the all-four-Beatles gang vocal on the title line (a rare unison of the whole band) and its reprise of 'You Never Give Me Your Money' (theme recall across the medley). Big, communal, orchestral.

Steal this

  • Gang vocal: everyone sings the hook in unison for communal weight (2 Ensemble Stack Group, Hand Clap Studio).
  • Theme recall: reprise an earlier section's melody/changes later for a suite payoff → 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Never Give Me Your Money.
  • Orchestral doubling of the chords for scale.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Carry That Weight"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Carry That Weight (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Carry That Weight — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #190.

Form. He calls it the most symphonic thing in the catalogue, built as an A-B-A arch — except that both the B section and the outro are lifted wholesale from "You Never Give Me Your Money". The reprise is transformed twice over: functionally, because an opening verse is re-cast as a mid-flight bridge, and rhetorically, because the massed orchestration realises heroic potential only latent in the original. There is no real intro; the last bar of "Golden Slumbers" is filled with a drum figure that launches this one without dropping a beat. Refrain is a square 16 (an 8-bar phrase repeated almost literally) whose poetic pattern is ABBC — phrase two opens by restating how phrase one closed, which is what makes a symmetrical section sound syncopated at the phrase level. Where "Golden Slumbers" runs on uneven phrases, this track is deliberately four-square.

Harmony. Refrain: I – V | V – I across eight bars, twice, with the bass walking down to B in the final bar. Bridge: the complete diatonic circle of fifths in A minor, i – iv – ♭VII – ♭III – ♭VI – ii° – V – i, then G13; the pivot both directions is C, read as III in A minor and I in C major (). Outro: I – V(6/3) | A – (held). That last chord is the interesting one — the same progression slid into A major at the end of "... Money," but with C as home here the identical chords sound like drifting away, and only resolve retroactively once "The End" opens in A.

Notable. The bridge tune keeps one triadic outline that is a literal inversion of the refrain's (), and chord changes land squarely on downbeats while the tune repeatedly anticipates them (). The handoff into "The End" is the album's one inexact metric shift.

Against this page. Agrees on C major.

the-beatles-come-together.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Come Together
the-beatles-come-together.html:
Pollack's analysis

Four and a half minutes of extremely little material, proportioned to feel unhurried over a driving tempo: the first refrain doesn't arrive until 1:10, the harmonically frozen outro eats about the same span at the other end, and the four-bar intro keeps returning in between. Pollack's stylistic point is evocation rather than imitation — an old style updated so knowingly the antecedents stop mattering.

Form. Intro 4 bars, verse 8, refrain just 2 bars, outro just under 24. The craft is editorial: two of the later intro reprises are cut in half to stop the second half sagging, and the full-length intro returns right before the closing section specifically to telegraph the ending.

Harmony. Only i, IV and V, plus one vi in the refrain. The verse is open on IV rather than V — Pollack reads it as a twelve-bar frame with its middle four bars deleted. The two-bar refrain is the only place in the song where the harmonic rhythm speeds up at all (), which is enough to make it the hook by contrast alone. The best analytical catch: the track sounds full of minor/major collision and almost never actually is — the friction is a side effect of using major IV under a minor tonic where the diatonic iv would be expected (), with the major third kept out of the tonic chord entirely.

Melody. Verse tune is pentatonic Dorian: minor third, minor seventh, sixth degree avoided outright.

Arrangement. Produced to sound larger than life rather than stranger than life — the technology is spent on weight, not weirdness. The vocal staging is almost entirely a schedule of absences (): verse 1 is John alone; later verses bring Paul in late in the first phrase and drop him before the end, so John is exposed at both edges.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-cry-baby-cry.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Cry Baby Cry
the-beatles-cry-baby-cry.html:
Lennon's fairy-tale verse structure inspired by nursery rhymes. George Martin plays harmonium. Eerie, minor-key atmosphere with each verse presenting a different royal character.

Chords

Key: G major / E minor

Verse ("The king of Marigold…"): Em – Emmaj7 – Em7 – Em6 – C – C7 – G → i – i(maj7) – i7 – i6 – VI – VI7 – III (the Em→Emmaj7→Em7→Em6 is a chromatic inner descent E–D♯–D–C♯)

Chorus ("Cry baby cry"): G – Am – F – G – Em7 – A7 – F → I – ii – ♭VII – I – vi7 – V7/V – ♭VII (the F is a borrowed ♭VII, A7 a secondary dominant)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-cry-baby-cry-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Lennon's minor-key nursery-rhyme/fairy-tale song (White Album) — harpsichord, storybook imagery, and a spooky, sing-song melody. Ends with McCartney's unrelated 'Can you take me back' fragment tacked on.

Steal this

  • Fairy-tale minor melody + harpsichord (Keyscape) for a storybook mood.
  • Tack an unrelated fragment to the end as a haunting coda.
  • Sing-song, circular melody over descending changes → Chord Progressions.

Why I like it

Listen

  • The Beatles (White Album) · search "The Beatles — Cry Baby Cry"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Cry Baby Cry (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Cry Baby Cry — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #154.

Form. A standard folk-song shape opened by a refrain, then four verse/refrain cycles, then an outro — note that he starts the form on the refrain, not the verse. Refrain 8 bars in two loosely parallel phrases; verse 12, better heard as a 4-bar sung phrase plus a 2-bar instrumental flourish, stated twice; outro the refrain three times over. The structural interest is elision: the opening refrain ends on E minor and runs into verse 1, bar 12 of every verse elides into the following refrain, and the first two outro refrains overlap the next. Without that the folk frame would sit square and dead.

Harmony. Refrain (8): I – ii – ♭VII – I · vi – V-of-V – ♭VII – I · Verse (12): vi held 4 bars over a descending bass E – E♭ – D – D♭ · C7 (IV) – I, ×2. There is no V chord anywhere in the song — ♭VII carries the whole cadential load (), which produces an implied cross-relation against the key signature's F♯, made explicit by the A major chord in the refrain and again by the C7's blue B♭ against the G chord.

Notable. The verse's first four bars are his object lesson in when not to use Roman numerals: E minor, E♭ augmented, G in 6/4 and a half-diminished seventh on D♭ are not a progression, they are a line (), and the only reason they read as chords is the time scale — one bar each. The tune is mostly pentatonic on G–A–B–D–E (), and the track ends on E minor, not G, with an unresolved 4th hanging over it ().

Against this page. The frontmatter key: here reads A major; Pollack reads G major / E minor, deliberately unresolved between the two — which is what this page's own Chords section says as well. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-day-tripper.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Day Tripper
the-beatles-day-tripper.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack's set-piece essay on harmonic rhythm (): the whole song runs on tension between a fast tempo and chords that refuse to move. Ten bars of intro on a single chord, a verse managing three changes in its first twelve, and a "middle eight" that is twelve bars of prolonged V.

Form. The intro is five repeats of the riff — not four, not six. Four would be square, six too long, and an odd count means the verse arrives before you've finished counting the pattern out. Verse 16 bars in four phrases; the bridge is nominally a middle eight and actually 12 bars. Ostinato reprises sit between verses 1 and 2 and between bridge and final verse, acting as a brake on accumulated momentum. There's a single bridge where the period norm was to repeat it — but this one is a total climax, so a second pass would be an anti-climax.

Harmony. I, IV and V matched one for one by three altered chords: V-of-V, V-of-vi and major VI. Another way to see it: there isn't a single minor chord in the song. The pacing is the substance — after a ten-bar single-chord intro the verse still can't get off the ground, and the V-of-V is held four full bars and then still not allowed to resolve until the end of the following phrase ().

Melody. More rap-like and jagged than tuneful, and genuinely hard to sing without the chords underneath — one reason the record reads as instrumental. Riff and vocal syncopate at different points and mostly don't coincide (); writing out the composite rhythm is the exercise, because that misalignment is what the groove actually is.

Arrangement. The intro thickens by increments — guitar, then bass, then rhythm guitar and tambourine, then nothing new at all on the fourth repeat, then drums on the fifth. Holding one repeat back is what keeps the build from sounding mechanical.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-dear-prudence.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Dear Prudence
the-beatles-dear-prudence.html:
Pollack's analysis

A song built on near-total stasis — one chord under almost everything and a floor plan that's just a chain of identical verses with one short bridge at the midpoint — that nonetheless produces a genuine build and release. Since neither harmony nor melody can supply the arc, the job goes entirely to texture and a long dynamic crescendo.

Form. The intro is really an intro to the intro: four bars of drone while the lead guitar walks down a scale, before the ostinato proper begins. The verse is 14 bars phrased AA'B, rounded off by a two-bar instrumental washer; the bridge is an odd 5½ bars — the verse in miniature. The outro returns abruptly to the quiet intro texture, and unlike the "Hey Jude" coda it turns the corner and is gone.

Harmony. Nearly everything sits over a D pedal (). What you could label as a chord progression is better heard as upper voices harmonising a semi-chromatic tenor line descending D–C–B–B♭–A, and that reading holds even when the bass later takes the descent over. The one explicit harmonic move in the verse is a single bar where the bass abruptly gets busy — it registers as an event precisely because nothing else has moved. ♭VII harmony plus a melody that never touches the seventh is what makes the mode read Mixolydian ().

Melody. Pentatonic — the fourth and seventh avoided outright () — and assembled from short repeated motifs rather than a spun-out arch.

Arrangement. One continuous crescendo from near-silence, then a hard reset (). Each section gets exactly one new element. The bass outlines both the pedal and the walking tenor at once, a Baroque trick executed on one instrument. The climax is marked by stretching the crux phrase to double length rather than by more volume.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-dig-it.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Dig It
the-beatles-dig-it.html:
Pollack's analysis

Barely a song — a 50-second window cut out of an eight-minute jam, faded in at one end and out at the other, with a spoken tag lifted from a different arrangement recorded two days earlier. Pollack's angle is that the value here is editorial rather than compositional: the musical content is thin, the edit is what makes it a gesture, and it exists largely to set up the album's next track.

Form. Circular and undifferentiated — one four-bar pattern looping in pairs, with no sections to speak of. The fade-in does structural work: it announces you're hearing a slice of something much longer, and the circularity reinforces the illusion of open-ended duration. Pollack is explicit that this is not the complete-but-tiny "bonsai" form he assigns to "Wild Honey Pie" — those are whole songs in miniature, this is a crop.

Harmony. Three chords and nothing else: I – IV – V – IV. The V doesn't resolve down to I; it falls back to IV and the loop restarts, which is part of why it never closes. A vamp whose dominant retreats instead of resolving will run indefinitely without ever asking to end.

Melody. Pinned to the tonic note in talking-blues fashion — more chanted than sung — with intermittent ♭3 and ♭7 colouring against the major harmony.

Arrangement. A deliberately muddy everything-in-the-room backing track with organ, piano and drums out front. The released excerpt sits in a syncopated 3/4, though across the full take the meter drifts toward a 4/4 march. The spoken bit is spliced so its beginning overlaps the band's fade-out while its ending is left completely bare — the exposure is the point.

Provenance. The official track misrepresents it as a solo turn; the idea goes back to a January 1969 Twickenham improvisation over a twelve-bar vamp with names traded antiphonally.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-dig-a-pony.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Dig a Pony
the-beatles-dig-a-pony.html:
Performed live on the Apple rooftop. Lennon's stream-of-consciousness lyrics. Billy Preston's electric piano adds a gospel texture beneath the hard rock groove.

Chords

Key: A major · 3/4

Intro / Chorus ("All I want is you"): G – D – A → ♭VII – IV – I

Verse: A – F♯m – Bm – G7 – Bm – G7 – E → I – vi – ii – ♭VII7 – ii – ♭VII7 – V (the G7 is a bluesy ♭VII)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-dig-a-pony-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Rooftop/Let It Be — a bluesy, loose Lennon jam with irregular phrase lengths (extra beats that keep you off-balance) and a live-band feel. Ragged on purpose.

Steal this

  • Irregular phrasing: add/drop a beat in a phrase for a lurching, human feel → Chord Progressions.
  • Live take energy over precision.
  • Bluesy, riff-anchored arrangement.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — Dig a Pony"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Dig a Pony (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Dig A Pony — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #168.

Form. Far more detailed writing than the deliberately rough performance suggests, and one of very few Beatles tracks with a genuine ternary backbeat (company: "Baby's In Black," "I Me Mine"). Verse/refrain like a folk ballad, but with doubled verses and a half-time instrumental break borrowed from pop. Intro 11 bars, AAB — it would be 12 except the last bar overlaps the start of verse 1, and its first two phrases preview the refrain instrumentally. Verse an odd 13 bars, ABB′, all three phrases different lengths. Refrain AA′, roughly 10 bars, uncountable exactly because a dramatic pause stretches A′. Outro is the intro again as a bookend — and he argues Spector's cut of one phrase from both bookends damages the design, since they are what make the song a struggle between John's two personae rather than a tidy alternation of moods.

Harmony. Intro: ♭VII – IV – I (×2) · ♭VII – viiø7 – I · Verse: I held 4 – vi (6) · ii – ♭VII (3) · ii – ♭VII – V (4) · Refrain: ♭VII – IV – I (×2), plus the pause. Six of the seven diatonic chords appear — only iii is missing — and ♭VII gets an enormous share of the airtime, most of it inside the double plagal ♭VII – IV – I (, ). Because all three intro phrases approach home from ♭VII rather than V, the tonic arrives without authority, which is exactly the unsettled footing the song wants.

Notable. The verse tune strains to stay pentatonic and cannot, because ♭VII carries both degree 4 and ♭7 (). Contour is the engine (): the verse leaves its second upswing hanging, the refrain takes over from that exact pitch and immediately posts a higher ceiling. The riff's third iteration is broken on purpose, and the drums reset the tempo before the verse downbeat rather than on it.

Against this page. Agrees on A major and 3/4. He hears no bridge — verse and refrain only — where the structure: field reads I-V-C-V-C-B-C.

the-beatles-do-you-want-to-know-a-secret.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Do You Want To Know A Secret
the-beatles-do-you-want-to-know-a-secret.html:
Pollack's analysis

A song built almost entirely from repetition and chromatic three- and four-note fragments, which sounds like lazy craft and is the point — Pollack reads the mantra-like restatement as supplying the emotional realism the lyric can't. Formally lopsided on purpose: slow ad-lib intro, long verse, unusually short bridge.

Form. The compact single-bridge model. The lyric is identical across all three verses; intro and bridge carry the only new words. Entry rhythms are deliberately differentiated — the intro sings after the downbeat, the verses are led in by a long guitar pickup ahead of the beat, the bridge attacks on the beat. Verse 14 bars as a couplet of 6 + 8; bridge 6 bars as 4 + 2.

Harmony. Home key is major, but the intro is in the parallel minor, and the switch at the first verse is the song's best cheap trick — smooth because the keys are parallel, still startling. A ♭II Neapolitan appears in both intro and verse, acting there as a dominant substitute back to I (). The recurring chromatic chord stream in the odd bars is coloristic rather than functional; the ear tracks only the endpoints. The verse's second phrase broadens its harmonic rhythm and lands a deceptive cadence on vi before cycling back to V (). The bridge is a real modulation, not a tonicisation (), and coming out of it is textbook: the ear retroactively rehears the bridge's tonic as ii of the home key.

Pollack's added-sixth argument is worth the essay: an outtake ends cold on an added-sixth chord where the release fades, and much of the song already implies it — every deceptive cadence where you expect I and get vi. I with an added sixth is I and vi superimposed, so that chord summarises the song's ambiguity, and the fade masks it.

Arrangement. George takes the lead — his first on a Lennon–McCartney song — with doo-wop backing that pointedly enters at verse 2; an outtake has it from the top, which breaks the layering habit.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-doctor-robert.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Doctor Robert
the-beatles-doctor-robert.html:
Pollack's analysis

The interesting thing here is a home-key trick. The song opens on A and sits there unbothered for eight bars, long enough that you take A for the tonic. Then the first real cadence lands on B, and in retrospect that A was ♭VII the whole time (). Pollack rates it among John's more daring harmonic experiments short of "Strawberry Fields Forever", and uses it to make a general point: the song feels slight, and that comes from its short form, absent instrumental break and static arrangement — not from its running time.

Form. A 4-bar intro vamping on ♭VII. The verse reads as four square phrases but a rhetorical extension in the third pushes the real length to 18 bars. The refrain reads as a standard 8 and rounds itself out to 10, its last two bars eliding into the next verse. No instrumental break, and nothing new enters the arrangement after the first refrain.

Harmony. Those opening eight bars establish A by drone, not by progression — which is exactly why the key stays equivocal. Tonal music normally establishes a key through chord motion, and the first genuine cadence doesn't arrive until the end of the verse. In the moment it feels like a modulation up a step; the honest reading is retroactive relabelling. In the refrain, the same E chord that is unambiguously IV in the first phrase begins behaving like V-of-♭VII in the second.

Melody. The intro's lead guitar plants a 4–3 appoggiatura that becomes the song's connective motif (), reappearing in the verse's third phrase and again in the refrain.

Arrangement. Rich but recorded plainly, with staggered layering: backing vocals from the second verse, guitar overdubs just before the refrain, and a harmonium plus stacked vocals giving the refrain an incongruously carol-like texture. The ending is mastered as a fade but appears to be covering a breakdown.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-don-t-bother-me.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Don't Bother Me
the-beatles-don-t-bother-me.html:
Pollack's analysis

George's first solo composition on a Beatles record, and Pollack's point is that it is not an imitation of his bandmates — it already contains what George would spend a decade on: minor key, sensual modal melody, sad-angry inward lyric. The essay's centrepiece is a comparison with "All I've Got To Do": the same five pentatonic notes rearranged around a different tonic produce a major-feeling song there and a deeply minor one here ().

Form. Two bridges with the usual verse arrangement plus a half-solo verse. The 4-bar intro is built from material that pre-states the bridge. The verse is 12 bars in three even phrases — blues-like in shape if not in style. The solo section is built like "From Me To You": the instrumental paraphrases the vocal melody closely, then the voice returns for the last phrase so it reads as a refrain.

Harmony. The v chord is minor, so it can't function as a dominant, and defining the key falls instead to VII and IV. The important twist is the major IV inside a minor mode — Dorian, not Aeolian (): George uses the minor iv inside the verse's stream-like first two phrases where it passes smoothly, and saves the Dorian major IV for the third phrase as the surprise. The bridge slows the harmonic rhythm to one change every two bars, which makes the verse's per-bar rate sound like an acceleration when it returns, with no tempo change at all.

Melody. Pentatonic throughout, missing the 2nd and 6th (), and how the missing degrees are spent is the lesson (). The 2nd is withheld until the climax of the bridge, where it's also the highest note in the song; the 6th is absent from the tune entirely, which is exactly what lets the harmony flip IV between minor and major without the melody objecting. Pollack's caveat: none of them read music, and doing this intuitively is more impressive, not less.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-don-t-let-me-down.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Don't Let Me Down
the-beatles-don-t-let-me-down.html:
Pollack's analysis

A slow, hard-driving screamer with John's structural fingerprints all over it: strictly symmetrical, with a one-off Alternate Verse occupying the exact keystone position at the centre, the instrumental break displaced to the outro, and a tune so pentatonic it never touches scale degree 7 in either form.

Form. A mirror around the middle section. The 2-bar intro is lifted from the last two bars of the verse, and the slow triplets declaiming the title start in the second half of bar 2 — where Buddy Holly banked slow triplets for a late climax, this song spends them in the first two bars as a warning. Refrain 8 bars AA; verse 8 bars AA with the bar preceding each phrase extended by one extra beat, one line of loose pentameter dropped into an otherwise four-square setting. The Alternate Verse is the only section not built on AA.

Harmony. Three chords stated — I, ii, V — plus a IV that is heavily implied and almost never actually played. Refrain and verse both start away from I and converge onto it; the Alternate Verse breaks the mould by starting and ending on the tonic. The subdominant is a phantom: where you think you hear IV you're usually hearing the tune's extensions over V, which stacks 7, 9, 11 and 13 to produce the effect of IV superimposed on V ().

Melody. Pentatonic in the strict sense (); degree 4 appears only in the backing vocal shadowing the tune in parallel thirds. The refrain contour drives downward, and the verse opens as if a broad upward arch is coming and delivers the same descent instead. The Alternate Verse is the only place a complete arch is permitted.

Arrangement. Live and impromptu, of a piece with its single's A-side; the only obvious retouch is a short stretch of double-tracked lead in the Alternate Verse. That section also carries a counterpoint line in octaves shared by bass and lead guitar, one of the more unusual instrumental ideas in the catalogue.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-don-t-pass-me-by.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Don't Pass Me By
the-beatles-don-t-pass-me-by.html:
Pollack's analysis

Three chords, one per four bars, no modulation anywhere — which makes this a case study in rescuing a harmonically inert song with phrase lengths and arrangement. Ringo's first released original, though it existed at least in part four years earlier, when a BBC broadcast suggests it was headed for a bluesy up-tempo treatment rather than the country arrangement it eventually got.

Form. Deliberately oversized sections (). The verse runs 19 bars — a prime number — in four lyric phrases, the last of which takes seven bars; the third is also a bar short against the pattern. The refrain runs 24 bars in six even phrases, and the final refrain adds one extra bar at the end of its third phrase, echoing the verse's missing bar in the same position. An interlude stops the beat dead for a couple of seconds. That silence exists because the song ends with two refrains back to back, a boredom risk; the surviving alternative version drops a verse reprise in between instead, and it drags.

Harmony. I, IV and V, changing once every four bars. The harmonic rhythm is slow enough to be a liability, and the asymmetric seven-bar phrase at the end of the verse is what keeps the song moving (). The outro's apparent plagal cadence is better heard as a double appoggiatura resolving into the tonic than as a cadence in its own right ().

Melody. Verse and refrain both drop a bluesy ♭3 near the end of the section () — the same placement in both, which makes it a structural signature rather than an ornament. In the refrain the vocal lines get shorter and more interjectory as the section runs, so the gaps get bigger and the fiddle obbligato takes over the space.

Arrangement. Thick to the point of muddy and unusually unvaried for a Beatles record; the country fiddle is the one inspired element, and both ends are bracketed by unstructured playing.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-drive-my-car.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Drive My Car
the-beatles-drive-my-car.html:
Pollack's analysis

The key of this song is decided by the melody, not the chords — a point Pollack revised his own designation over. Chords rooted on only five notes, an opening D chord, and a repeated D → G that on paper is an open-and-shut I → IV. But the vocal hammers G so insistently that the same two chords read equally well as V → I in G ().

Form. A flat folk-ballad shape: four verse/refrain pairs in a row with one verse handed to a guitar solo as the only relief. Rhythmic placement is deliberate and consistent — the verse enters late, after the downbeat; the refrain sits squarely on it; the coda winds up well ahead of it. The 2-bar intro is among the most disorienting they recorded: an eighth-note pickup, a syncopated guitar contour and an off-beat bass entrance make the meter genuinely hard to find (), and by the time the drum fill lands on the beat you've lost the trail.

Harmony. The verse's last chord sets up a pivot, but the target is deceptively deferred to bar 2 of the refrain, and before the new key can settle the music swings home and parks on a fat V that motivates the next verse — tonal mobility of a kind usually reserved for a bridge (). Only in the outro does the home key finally sound settled. The vi chord in the verse carries such a prominent ♭7 in the vocal that whether the chord's own third is in the mix at all is an open question, and that note is held through into the next chord for a straight major/minor clash.

Melody. Rap-like declamation rather than tune, shot through with ♭7s on top and 4–3 appoggiaturas underneath. The guitar solo is the one place D gets melodic emphasis — and for that stretch alone the progression finally sounds like I → IV.

Arrangement. The bass is unusually motivic, ornamenting roots with a triadic figure that free-associates with the refrain's top line. The electric piano's slow triplets run against a 4/4 backbeat that keeps going underneath them, which both cushions the rhythmic dissonance and rubs your nose in it ().

Production & Arrangement

Recorded on a fairly basic 4-track, in this order: Track 1 — Paul (rhythm guitar) + Ringo (drums) + John (tambourine), with George's live guide lead-guitar intro on the same track. Track 2 — George's re-recorded lead guitar overdub, done in the same pass as Ringo's cowbell. Track 3 — lead + harmony vocals. Track 4 — bass (Paul) + doubled backing vocals, recorded last, deliberately, to make the bass as loud as possible in the final mono mix — a conscious attempt to compete with the "Motown bass sound" coming out of America; bass-tracked-last is genuinely rare studio practice.

The 2026 stereo remix (Giles Martin) centers drums and vocals — respecting how the original mono mix would have carried them — and spreads the guitar tracks (George's overdub lead, Paul's rhythm guitar) across the stereo field, rather than hard-panning instruments to one side the way the original Capitol-style stereo pressing did.

Steal this

  • Track the bass last, on purpose, if you want it to dominate the final balance — most sessions build bass-up; doing the opposite forces every other part to make room for it rather than the reverse.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-eight-days-a-week.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Eight Days A Week
the-beatles-eight-days-a-week.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack's object lesson in false (cross) relation — a chromatic contradiction between two notes across adjacent chords. The whole song runs on one pair, G natural against G♯ in D major, the natural pulling down to F♯ and the sharp pulling up to A, with one instance in every phrase. The second thread is how long the V chord is withheld and how badly it behaves when it finally shows up.

Form. Double bridge with one verse between. The verse is a four-square 16 bars phrased AABA′ — A phrases harmonically closed, B phrase classically transitional. The bridge is 8 bars in four short phrases, so phrase lengths halve while the harmonic rhythm doubles in length: a two-sided contrast out of one decision.

Harmony. Six chords. The V chord is the tease — it never appears in the verse at all, even though V-of-V keeps setting it up (). Its first entrance is the downbeat of the bridge, where it resolves deceptively to vi (). The only ordinary V–I in the song is the bridge-to-verse return, which means the verses establish the key entirely by plagal IV–I (). The verse's cross relation is the subtle one: the sharp sits in a middle voice while the natural that contradicts it sits in the outer voices.

Melody. Confined to a sixth for the whole song. Individual phrases still get real contour out of that, but the narrowness may be what pushes attention onto the chord changes.

Arrangement. Texture change articulates the form (). The 4-bar intro is faded in over a pounded tonic pedal in rapid triplets heard nowhere else on the record (). Handclaps mark 2 and 4 in the A phrases and switch to a snapping dotted rhythm in the B phrase, where the kit drops out entirely; they sit the bridge out altogether. Changing what the handclaps do rather than whether they exist is the trick — nobody hears the plan, everybody hears the lift. The outro is musically the intro, but they refuse to make it symmetrical: no fade-in, no fade-out.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-eleanor-rigby.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Eleanor Rigby
the-beatles-eleanor-rigby.html:
Pollack's analysis

The whole song is one gesture — an anxious sigh, a sharp intake of breath let out in slow motion — and Pollack's point is that it operates at every level at once: foreground rhythm, harmonic rhythm, phrase lengths, melodic contour. The music is heavily syncopated but never bounces, because the syncopation enervates rather than propels. The string-quartet element and the bluesy, boxy pop element are not separable layers; they're fused past the point where you can pull them apart.

Form. Compact and cyclic. The intro is a great non-I opening — it starts on VI at what already sounds like peak tension, climbs a little further, then unwinds — and the bridge is simply that intro repeated. The verse is an odd 5 bars parsed 1 + 3 + 1, with off-beat vocal phrasing set against a march-beat accompaniment.

Harmony. Extremely spare: essentially i, VI and iv, with a major IV implied as a passing chord over the drone — the Dorian brightening inside a minor key (). The home key is asserted plagally and modally rather than by any dominant cadence, and the tonic gets so much drone-like airtime that "progression" is the wrong word for most of it (). The refrain is structurally one sustained tonic chord with a descending chromatic inner line doing all the work; sing that inner voice along with the record and it's obvious. Pollack is firm about not over-labelling — you could name a seventh here and an inversion there, but those are linear motion against a background, not structural chords ().

Melody. Dorian, an uncommon mode for them. The sighing shows up as contour: voice and accompaniment peak and unwind out of phase with each other. The register plan is strict () — the refrain's first phrase tops out lower than its second, and neither upstages the song's true ceiling, which sits in the intro.

Arrangement. Eight players but written in four real parts, each doubled. Short choppy down-bows near the frog, no vibrato, close-miked; the one softening move is retreating from stark quarter notes into eighths.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-every-little-thing.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Every Little Thing
the-beatles-every-little-thing.html:
Pollack's analysis

Generic early-Beatles pop on the surface, but Pollack's headline is an irregular harmonic rhythm deliberately used to underscore syncopation in the tune — a level of sophistication that separates this from "She Loves You".

Form. Neither the standard pop models nor strict folk alternation: three refrains alternating with double verses, with a single-verse guitar section breaking the pattern so it can't become mechanical. The 2-bar intro starts on beat 2 with nothing to tell you where beat 1 was, so the meter stays unmoored until the first verse lands. The verse is 6 bars in three 2-bar phrases; the refrain is 8, one 4-bar phrase twice.

Harmony. A frugal budget — I, IV, V, iv — with the only real colour being heavy ♭VII (). The syncopation is structural (): the verse's first two phrases both put their chord changes off the phrase's own downbeats, and the refrain does a slower version of the same thing by sustaining one chord across two bars. The verse's third phrase then drops into plain textbook motion, with the bass line rather than the harmony deciding an inversion — rare in the early catalogue, and it's what makes the phrase read as resolution.

Melody. Mixolydian rather than bluesy: ♭7 alongside the natural major third. The refrain runs counterbalancing appoggiaturas () — one downbeat dissonance resolves down, the next resolves up, so the section stops feeling like one gesture repeated.

Arrangement. Noisily strummed acoustic in the middle, bass heavy and doubled in the low octaves of a piano, punctuated by timpani played by Ringo — an early instance of them bringing an exotic instrument in and playing it themselves. The guitar solo tracks the verse's shape exactly: close paraphrase of the tune for the first half, then an improvised extension of the vocal's single slow triplet.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-everybody-s-got-something-to.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Everybody's Got Something To Hide Except For Me And My Monkey
the-beatles-everybody-s-got-something-to.html:
Pollack's analysis

A John rave-up whose whole design is extremely slow harmonic rhythm plus an invisible seam between verse and refrain, so the track reads as an improvisation sliced arbitrarily out of a longer take rather than a composed song. Pollack hears it as an early sketch of the primal-scream manner.

Form. Three verse/refrain cycles into a fade. The verse is 12 bars sitting on I and nothing else; the refrain is 24 bars where the changes finally start moving. Because the verse has no cadence to end on, you can't hear where it stops. The first refrain is eight bars short, entering only at the point where the chords reach IV — without that cut the song would spend an unbearable stretch on one chord (). The refrain's poetic pattern thins as it runs: two phrases that sound like more verse, two sung only in their first halves, two entirely instrumental. Words get sparser exactly as the chords speed up (). Two bars of 3/4 interrupt the last phrase.

Harmony. The core is I / IV / ♭VII, extended one further step around the flat side to ♭III (). Two cross-relations fall out of that: V against ♭VII, and I against ♭III. The final two phrases run the same three chords forwards then backwards, a small palindrome mirroring the inside/outside gag in the lyric.

Melody. Mostly chanted on a repeated pitch, closer to rapping than to a tune; it becomes an actual melody only at the title phrase and the guitar lick that follows. The meter shift lands on top of that lick, so the best guitar line and the biggest rhythmic jolt arrive together.

Arrangement. Thick pulsing backing from stacked guitar overdubs. The shaken bell only seems continuous — it's dropped and reintroduced deliberately. The outro strips the instruments out for four bars, leaving the vocal noise exposed, then resumes the one-chord vamp.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-fixing-a-hole.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Fixing a Hole
the-beatles-fixing-a-hole.html:
McCartney on harpsichord, George Martin plays a second harpsichord countermelody. Descending chromatic bass line anchors the verses. Harrison guitar solo opens the bridge. Recorded at Regent Sound — the first time the Beatles used a studio other than Abbey Road.

Chords

Key: F major (slipping to F minor) · the verse drifts toward C in the bridge

Verse: F – C+ – Fm7 – Fm6 → I – V+ – i7 – i6 (the C augmented and the slide into F minor create the woozy chromatic inner line)

"…really doesn't matter if I'm wrong": F – C – F → I – V – I

"See the people standing there": C – G – C – G – C → briefly tonicizes C (I – V – I, i.e. V – V/V of the home F)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-fixing-a-hole-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Sgt. Pepper — jazzy, harpsichord-led (McCartney), with a relaxed swing and a searching, chromatic harmony. One of the few Beatles tracks cut outside Abbey Road (Regent Sound).

Steal this

  • Harpsichord (Keyscape) for baroque-pop jazz color.
  • Chromatic, searching changes over a relaxed swing → Chord Progressions · Altered Chords.
  • Laid-back, spacious mix.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band · search "The Beatles — Fixing a Hole"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Fixing a Hole (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Fixing A Hole — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #110.

Form. A split stylistic personality by section: the verse a Gershwinesque jazz/blues hybrid in a mixed F minor, the bridge a harmonically clean major-mode torch-song march. The frame itself is an ordinary two-bridge model of the sub-type with two middle verses, the second instrumental. Intro is a strange two and a half bars — a brief harpsichord figure, then hi-hat. Verse 8 bars, parsed as one long 6-bar phrase plus a trailing 2-bar obbligato and derived directly from the intro's progression. Bridge 8 as 4+4. The outro is built on a verse and a half, with the fade well underway before its first eight bars are done.

Harmony. Intro: I – V+ | i7♭ – IV | (held), inner voices descending A – G♯ and F – E – E♭ – D · Verse: I – V+ | i | i7♭ | IV6/4 · i | IV | i | IV · Bridge: I – V ×3 · I · V – V-of-V ×3 · V. The rapid F major to F minor shift comes straight out of the intro, and the verse mode is a variety of F minor tinged by both the blues ♭7 and the Dorian raised 6 (), with a chromatic descent running through a middle voice throughout. He spells the augmented chord's fifth as G♯ rather than A♭, hearing it as V with a raised fifth.

Notable. The two sections' contours are as complementary as their harmony (): the verse spans an octave plus a third (F up to A♭) mixing steps and skips, the bridge restricts itself to a fifth and hammers a subset — and although the bridge sits higher it tops out a half step below the verse, so the verse keeps the song's melodic peak. The vocal plan is scheduled section by section, with backing voices withheld until the second bridge.

Against this page. The page reads F major slipping to F minor; Pollack inverts that emphasis — his heading is "F (Dorian minor and Major)," and his signature reading is the reverse of the familiar borrowing: a major IV inside a minor home key, which reads hard-boiled rather than sentimental ().

the-beatles-flying.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Flying
the-beatles-flying.html:
Pollack's analysis

A jam frame more than a composition — too choreographed to pass as real improvisation, and less developed than anything else they were writing by 1967. Pollack covers it largely because it's the rare mid-period trace of a habit that bookends the career: set a simple progression, usually a twelve-bar blues, and play over it until you're done. The 1960 Quarrymen tapes are full of it and so are the later session reels; the middle years show almost nothing.

Form. Three twelve-bar choruses and a fade. The intro is itself a complete twelve-bar frame — arguably a third verse, and parsed as an intro only because the tune hasn't shown up yet.

Harmony. A straight twelve-bar blues, in the variant where measure 12 takes a V chord rather than holding I over from measure 11 ().

Melody. The tune runs an AA'BA pattern across the first eight measures and then simply stops — the last four bars are left with no melody at all, the instrumental equivalent of scat-mumbling through a lyric you haven't finished writing.

Arrangement. The thick, heavily processed Mellotron mix of the period. The rhythm guitar works a 4–3 appoggiatura figure through the intro (). Verse 1's tune goes to English horn because an oboe can't reach its lowest note; verse 2 is all four of them in choral unison. The music stops dead at the end of verse 2 and the track runs on for roughly another thirty seconds of Mellotron noodling and tape noise — an available outtake carries a New Orleans jazz coda in that spot instead, dropped in favour of the effects version.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-for-no-one.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - For No One
the-beatles-for-no-one.html:
McCartney plays rented clavichord — no guitars on the track. Alan Civil of the Royal Philharmonia plays the iconic French horn solo. Lennon and Harrison did not contribute. Sparse and devastating.

Chords

Key: C major as played (capo 2 → sounds in B)

Verse: C – C/B – Am – C/G – F – B♭ – C → I – I/7 – vi – I/5 – IV – ♭VII – I (a descending bass C–B–A–G, then the B♭ borrowed ♭VII — the famous ache)

Chorus ("And in her eyes you see nothing"): Dm – A7 – Dm – A7 – Dm – Gsus4 – G → ii – V7/ii – ii … – V (the A7 tonicizes Dm; lands on G = V)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-for-no-one-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Chamber-pop at its sparsest — essentially McCartney solo: he plays clavichord and bass, Ringo light percussion, and the one guest is Alan Civil's French horn solo (George Martin scored it a note above the instrument's normal range for that plaintive strain). No other Beatles, no guitars.

  • The descending bass line (C–B–A–G) + the borrowed ♭VII (B♭) are the ache; the arrangement's emptiness is what lets them land.
  • Dry, close, intimate — a baroque miniature.

Steal this

  • Clavichord/harpsichord timbre for baroque-pop color (Keyscape has them) over a spare arrangement.
  • A single hero solo instrument (here French horn) scored slightly out of its comfort range for emotional strain — pick one unexpected lead voice.
  • Descending bass + ♭VII for the ache → Chromatic Bass Lines · Borrowed Chords.
  • Arrange with emptiness: the sparseness is the production.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Revolver · search "The Beatles — For No One"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - For No One (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — For No One — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #99.

Form. Paul borrowing from early-nineteenth-century art song, placed between "Eleanor Rigby" and "Michelle" on that axis. The form is completely cyclic — double verse plus bridge, three times through, with no intro, no outro and no interlude anywhere. Verse 8 bars in two 4-bar phrases, though the tune's rhythmic flow subdivides them unevenly so it never sits as square as the count implies; bridge 10 bars, an AA couplet plus a 2-bar tag that sets up the next verse, with a complete ending on its final appearance. B major is an unusual home key for the catalogue — he can only pair it with "One After 909."

Harmony. Verse: I (4 bars, bass walking B – A♯ – G♯ – F♯) | IV | ♭VII | I (2). He argues against assigning a fresh numeral to each of those first four bars — the ear follows one large motion from I to IV and hears the intervening sonorities as connective tissue. The section climaxes on the downbeat of bar 5 where a D♯ in the tune turns the chord into a major seventh; the move on to ♭VII, with a buried chromatic descent G♯ – G♮ – F♯, unwinds that and adds the nostalgic tint (). The verses establish the key with ♭VII instead of V, and V's only appearance in the whole song is inside the bridge's pivot home. Bridge (in C♯ minor): i | V | i (2), ×2 · i | V (6/4 → 5/3) — a textbook classical pivot modulation to ii (), whose last bar he reads entirely as V with a double appoggiatura rather than as I6/4 moving to V ().

Notable. The French horn solo is his recording riddle: he reconstructs it as played onto the off-pitch slowed vocal tape and then replayed at double speed, a full octave up — the brass analogue of the "In My Life" keyboard solo. The horn also enters inlaid, two beats before its verse and running into the following bridge.

Against this page. Agrees: his B major is this page's sounding pitch (capo 2 off C shapes).

the-beatles-for-you-blue.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - For You Blue
the-beatles-for-you-blue.html:
Harrison's 12-bar blues recorded live at Apple Studios. Lennon plays lap steel slide guitar. McCartney on piano, Ringo on drums. Joyful simplicity.

Chords

Key: D major — a 12-bar blues (played as A blues shapes, capo 5) · George Harrison

12-bar form: A7 – D7 – A7 – A7 – D7 – D7 – A7 – A7 – E7 – D7 – A7 – E7 → I7 – IV7 – I7 – I7 – IV7 – IV7 – I7 – I7 – V7 – IV7 – I7 – V7 (standard blues, relative to the capo'd A)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-for-you-blue-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Harrison's loose 12-bar blues from Let It Be, with Lennon on lap-steel slide and McCartney on a tacked-piano honky-tonk. Deliberately casual and rootsy.

Steal this

  • 12-bar blues as a genre exercise → Chord Progressions (all dom 7ths).
  • Slide/lap-steel for rootsy character (an amp-sim + slide, Morgan Amps Suite).
  • Prepared/tacked piano timbre for honky-tonk color.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — For You Blue"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - For You Blue (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — For You Blue — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #175.

Form. The plainest song on the album, and one of very few Beatles originals where every single section is a strict twelve-bar blues frame (). Six frames, a six-bar intro with a three-beat pickup, a tacked-on ending, and nothing else. George plays the intro alone; the band enters for the first verse; the two instrumental breaks sit back to back, slide first, piano second.

Harmony. I, IV and V plus one cameo of V-of-V in the intro. Intro (6): I – IV6/3 – V/V – V (2 bars) · Verse (12): I – IV – I – I · IV – IV – I – I · V – IV – I – V. George uses the quick-change variant, putting IV in bar 2 so the usually static opening phrase has somewhere to go (), and ends the frame on V rather than I so each section pushes into the next instead of closing. Bar 11 carries the standard chromatically rising bass D – F♯ – G – G♯ – A. Running IV straight into V-of-V in the intro exposes a cross relation the band usually spelled in the opposite order.

Notable. The tune is wide and jumpy — a tenth, F natural up to A — and saturated with blue thirds and sevenths (). Its signature move is a rising leap of a sixth in the first phrase, then followed through as triadic leaps that also span a sixth. The slide solo picks up the tune's jumpiness without quoting it; the piano solo opens with chopped chords descending the blues scale. Two things on the release aren't from the take: John's spoken introduction is flown in, and George's lead vocal was overdubbed a full year later, in January 1970.

Against this page. Pollack reads it in D major — which matches this page's own Chords section (A shapes, capo 5) but not the key: field, which says G major. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-free-as-a-bird.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Free As A Bird
the-beatles-free-as-a-bird.html:
Pollack's analysis

A slow, serious anthem assembled by creative derivation — the two-bridge model bent, the I–vi–IV–V cliché bent, and a key scheme playing A major against both its parallel minor and C major. Pollack reads that key scheme as narrative: the early verses reach toward C and get yanked back through A minor, the guitar solo finally arrives in C for real, and the ending returns to A major by a different route, so the same tonic doesn't mean what it meant at the start ().

Form. The verses are doubled up three separate times, which Pollack doesn't find in any earlier Beatles song. The guitar solo is placed so late that most songs would be winding down, and is shortened by two bars to make the pivot home work. The bridge's repeat is halved by cutting its most uncomfortable bars rather than trimming from the end, so the shortening means something.

Harmony. The engine is a single substitution: in I–vi–IV–V the third chord is consistently replaced by iv or ♭VI, both of which cross-relate with the vi chord immediately before them (). That one swap buys the pathos and an easy pivot into C. Bridge 1 is entered by a deceptive cadence () and is more honestly a rising chromatic bassline harmonised toward a key not yet decided — the proof being that the tonic chord ending its first phrase doesn't sound like a tonic at all. Bridge 2 is set up so it can be entered directly instead: same section, two emotional temperatures. The solo lands in C properly and then re-reads its own dominant as ♭VII of A to pivot straight home (), and that substitution replaces the old reach-and-fall gesture for the rest of the track — which is why the ending reads as acceptance rather than sadness.

Melody. Narrow, remembered by an opening phrase that occupies a tiny space and sustains its first note into the second bar. Re-harmonised in C for the guitar solo, the identical phrase feels like a different melody entirely — the late arrival is a reharmonisation, not new material.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-from-me-to-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - From Me To You
the-beatles-from-me-to-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

The third single, assembled almost entirely from techniques already in circulation — Pollack's framing is that a small fixed vocabulary still produced a first crop of originals that sound nothing like each other. Two things here are genuinely new: a pivot modulation in the bridge, among the first in their released catalogue, and an ending that lands on vi instead of I.

Form. Sprawling on paper — two bridges, two verses between, intro and outro — but tiny in time, because the verse is only 8 bars. Every section enters on a pickup. The solo verse is a semi-solo: an instrumental first half over the usual changes giving way to a verbatim sung return of the refrain half, a trick reused in "A Hard Day's Night". It doesn't exist in take 2, so it was presumably added because the song ran short.

Harmony. The verse is closed and stays inside the key; its one gratuitous chord is there purely for the bluesy bite. What lets verse 2 follow at all is the vi occupying the back half of the closing bar — take 2 held the tonic across the whole bar and the join is audibly worse. The bridge modulates on a chord already played: the previous verse's last chord is heard as I when struck, then retroactively re-read as V of the new key (). The common chord isn't required for a key change, but it's what makes this one seamless. The outro throws off an ambiguous augmented chord that could fall either way; the song takes the major, states the hook once more, then stops abruptly on the relative minor () — the hook's own finality covering for the fact that nothing resolved.

Melody. More chromatic than usual for them. The hook appears in two rhythmic settings with identical pitches — square in the intro and the solo verse, bouncy and syncopated in the verses () — and retreating to the square version is what makes the syncopated return feel bouncier ().

Arrangement. A duet essentially throughout, with no solo vocal anywhere. Paul's harmony crosses John's lead: above him in the verse's first phrase, below in the second.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-get-back.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Get Back
the-beatles-get-back.html:
Billy Preston on electric piano provides the track's signature groove. McCartney's hard riff and character-sketch lyrics. Performed live on the Apple rooftop.

Chords

Key: A major

Verse: A – A7 – D – A → I – I7 – IV – I

Chorus ("Get back to where you once belonged"): A – A7 – D – A – G – D → I – I7 – IV – I – ♭VII – IV (the G is the bluesy ♭VII)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-get-back-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Let It Be / the rooftop concert — the Beatles going back to a live-band R&B groove. Billy Preston's electric piano is the secret weapon (bright Rhodes-y stabs), the rhythm section is tight and dry, and it was tracked essentially live. Loose, funky, un-produced by design.

Steal this

  • Live-band tracking for feel (1 Electric Guitar Amp Track etc.) — the groove is four people locking in.
  • Guest keys as the hook: a bright electric-piano part (Keyscape Rhodes/Wurli) riffing over a simple progression.
  • Dry, un-produced mix — commit to the room and the take.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — Get Back"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Get Back (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Get Back — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #161.

Form. Stylized blues built out of one eight-bar phrase wearing four slightly different costumes. Every section is eight bars except the four-bar intro, and they only sort into three classes when you look at harmonic shape and accent placement — the composition is in the differentiation, not the material. Note that this is eight-bar blues, not twelve.

Harmony. Three chords: I, IV and ♭VII standing in for V (). Intro (4): I (3) – ♭VII–IV · Verse (8): [I (2) – IV – I] ×2 — closed, and deliberately unaccented · Refrain (8): [I (2) – IV – I–♭VII–IV] ×2 — open, cadencing so the next I lands · Refrain′ (8): I (2) – IV – I–♭VII–IV · I (3) – IV — the most open of the lot, three bars of I setting up a plagal cadence () then halting on IV for effect · Break (8): identical to Refrain. The break and the first refrain variant are the same chords; what separates them is where the accents fall. The ♭VII–IV pair in bar 4 is almost always played over an A pedal (), the only exception being the first phrase of the first guitar break; and the sharp ensemble accents on those chords are withheld on the first pass of a repeated phrase and hammered on the second, consistently enough that he rules out sloppiness.

Notable. The tune outlines A7 with the flat seventh on top, its centre of gravity on scale degree 5 — also its floor, a tenth below the ceiling — and the third degree never appears, which is why he calls the key Mixolydian rather than blues-inflected major. Played live with no overdubs; the refrain's syncopated arpeggio is led each time by whichever of guitar or piano is about to take the next solo. Both official releases are studio takes, not the rooftop.

Against this page. Same tonic (A). He specifies A Mixolydian where the page says A major, and reads the form as an eight-bar blues cycle rather than the I-V-C-V-C-S-V-C-O in structure:.

the-beatles-getting-better.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Getting Better
the-beatles-getting-better.html:
Pollack's analysis

A deliberate step down in intensity after the preceding track, and Pollack is explicit that its job is pacing the album side — relaxing tension between peaks without letting the pot go cold. The analytical interest is entirely in the arrangement and in a McCartney specialty: long phrases built over pedal points (). Tune and chords are pan-diatonic; nothing outside the key appears anywhere, and everything is treated as consonant with everything else.

Form. Elusive on purpose. Pollack parses the first refrain as slightly short and the later refrains as followed by a bridge, but you could as reasonably call the bridge an extension of the refrain — the dividing lines genuinely blur. The final verse inserts an extra bar between its two halves.

Harmony. C major with its centre of gravity pulled toward V by how much airtime the dominant gets. The intro is a plagal cadence () with a jazzy ninth produced by a sustained octave rather than by a chord choice. The verse sits on a G pedal, and Pollack's advice there is to stop transcribing verticals: the whole section is experienced as one elaborate V chord. Where a bass note sustains, the chords above it matter less than the envelope that bass note creates. The last chord sounded is I, but the octave chiming on into the fade implies an open ending on V, and the next track's intro exploits the ambiguity.

Arrangement. Thick with overdubs but texturally spare, and patterned by department (). The chiming octave is present in the intro, every refrain, both bridges and the outro, and absent from every verse — that is the entire rule, and it's what makes the verses feel different. Percussion accumulates by section: cymbal slashes on a syncopated half-beat, then four-in-the-bar, then handclaps, then tabla, with the outro running the layering in reverse until only the tabla is left. Verse 1 carries the most complicated vocal arrangement in the song and verse 2 deliberately does something simpler, because a literal repeat would have cost more than it gained.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-girl.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Girl
the-beatles-girl.html:
Greek-influenced descending chord changes. Intricate arpeggiated acoustic guitars. Close two-part harmonies. The 'tit-tit-tit' backing vocals were a deliberate inside joke.

Chords

Key: E minor (capo 8 on the recording)

Verse: Em – B7 – Em – Em7 – Am – C6 – G – B7 → i – V7 – i – i7 – iv – ♭VI – ♭III – V7

Chorus ("Ah, girl"): G – Bm – Am – D7 → ♭III – v – iv – ♭VII7 (or, heard in the relative G major: I – iii – ii – V7)

Bridge ("She's the kind of girl who puts you down"): Am – E → iv – V

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-girl-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Rubber Soul — Lennon's sighing minor-key ballad, famous for the sharp intake-of-breath sound on the hook (a percussive vocal gasp) and a Greek/sirtaki bouzouki-flavored bridge. Weary, intimate.

Steal this

  • Vocal as percussion: a sharp breath/gasp as a rhythmic hook (Hand Clap Studio-style layer, or record the breath).
  • Ethnic/modal bridge (bouzouki-style) for contrast → Scale Modes Reference.
  • Minor-key sighing melody, close double-tracked vocal (Artificial Double Tracking (ADT)).

Why I like it

Listen

  • Rubber Soul · search "The Beatles — Girl"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Girl (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Girl — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #84.

Form. The Beatles rarely modulated outright, which makes this one notable: it changes key at every section boundary, cycling minor / relative major / a second minor, and the key changes carry the emotional argument. No intro at all — it starts mid-scene, without even a cue for the opening pitch. Verse 8 bars in two parallel phrases, closed i to i, harmony varied on the second pass; refrain only 4 bars; bridge 8, built like the verse with its second phrase reharmonised to steer out. The only instrumental section is a verse placed very late.

Harmony. Verse (c minor): i – V – i – iv – ♭VI – V · i – V – i – iv – i — wholly minor, with the first phrase's ♭VI–V a feint at the relative major that the refrain makes good on. Refrain (E♭ major): I – iii6/4 – IV6/3 – V (×2) — the textbook reading is I–vi–IV–V, but the descending scalewise bass E♭–D–C–B♭ makes a second-inversion G minor with a 4–3 appoggiatura fit better; the last bar doubles as IV of F minor, which is how the bridge gets in. Bridge (f minor): i – V – i – V · i – V – i – ♭III, a real modulation down a fifth whose closing A♭ re-reads as IV in E♭ to hand back (, ). The chords are simple on purpose, to keep attention on the key scheme; and the switch to the "cheerful" major works against the phonemes sung over it, which is the reason for the modulation.

Notable. The tune sits high in John's range so the delivery strains on purpose, with augmented seconds available from the harmonic minor (). Two arrangement details he rates above the rest: surface rhythm as leitmotif (implied fast triplets everywhere except the bridge and final sung verse, which snap to dead-even eighths), and stacked counter-melodies — one added in verse 2, a second added in the instrumental verse.

Against this page. Agrees on C minor (this page's capo-8 note gives the same sounding key). He adds the relative E♭ major of the refrain and the F minor bridge, which the key: field does not carry.

the-beatles-glass-onion.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Glass Onion
