the-beatles-glass-onion.html:
Pollack's analysis

A short talking-blues patter song whose harmony never establishes a home key by cadence. A minor asserts itself, but there is no V–i and no iv–i anywhere; the only prop is the ♭VII–i implied at the top of each verse, which is thin evidence. Five chords total, and only two of them are diatonic to the key.

Form. Deliberately stick-figure: no intro, an unrelieved chain of verse/refrain pairs, immediate phrase repetition inside every section. The verse runs an unusual 9 bars in an AA-A'A'' pattern with the third phrase a bar longer than the rest; the refrain is 6 bars; the bridge is 10, eight of them static. The non-sequitur outro is what saves the song from complacency.

Harmony. The verse is a sustained lean toward the relative major that never arrives (), built from stacked secondary functions doing the work of a modulation that never happens (). The bridge is the clearest single device: eight bars of tonic pedal with a chromatically rising middle voice climbing over it (). The rise manufactures expectation and then declines to pay it off — nothing harmonic is happening behind the suspense. The outro's chromatic stream of dominant sevenths is a disguise rather than a non sequitur: it's the refrain's opening in altered dress, and the glissando delivery was already planted in the second halves of the verses, which is why it works on reflection rather than on impact.

Melody. Minor-key blues writing leaning hard on the flat fifth, which is also the top note of the song's most-used outside chord — so the tune's most characteristic pitch is supplied by the harmony rather than fighting it.

Arrangement. Heavily overdubbed and indistinct on the surface, but worth straining for: a bowed-string glissando on one specific chord change, a ghost falsetto as verse 2 closes, a moment of dead clean silence before the final verse, and a quoted recorder lick held back until the phrase after the lyric that names it.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-golden-slumbers.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Golden Slumbers
the-beatles-golden-slumbers.html:
McCartney couldn't read the original lullaby notation so wrote his own melody to the old text. George Martin's orchestral arrangement. Flows directly into 'Carry That Weight.'

Chords

Key: C major

Verse ("Once there was a way"): Am7 – Dm7 – G7 – C – E – Am – Dm9 – G7 – C → vi7 – ii7 – V7 – I – III7 (V/vi) – vi – ii9 – V7 – I

Chorus ("Golden slumbers fill your eyes"): C – Fadd9 – C – E – Am – Dm9 – G7 – C → I – IV – I – III7 – vi – ii9 – V7 – I

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-golden-slumbers-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Part of the Abbey Road medley — McCartney's piano ballad that swells, via George Martin's orchestra, straight into Carry That Weight. A lullaby verse detonating into a belted, orchestral chorus: maximum dynamic contrast in 90 seconds.

Steal this

  • Whisper-to-belt dynamics: a tender piano/vocal verse into a full orchestral, gang-vocal chorus — contrast is the payoff.
  • Segue by swell: let orchestration ramp one section into the next (Reverb Send Long, string pads).
  • Reuse a lullaby melody as an emotional anchor across a medley.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Golden Slumbers"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Golden Slumbers (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Golden Slumbers — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #189.

Form. Paul's anthem-meets-show-tune mode, and his hook is that the two most obvious things about the song are both misleading. Intro is two bars of piano vamping the a7 figure. Verse 21 bars, phrased 8 + 4 + 5 + 4; refrain 19 bars, phrased 6 + 4 + 5 + 4 — it sets up as an AA couplet of 6 + 6, but the second line elides into what is really a recap of the way the verses end. It earns the label refrain rather than bridge because the title phrase lives there, and both sections share the same 5 + 4 tail, which is what makes the recap land. Both counts are audible distortions of an ordinary four-square sixteen.

Harmony. Almost entirely diatonic, six chords, moving mostly around a short cycle of fifths. Verse: vi7 (4) – ii (4) | V (4) | I – iii – vi – ii9 (held) | V – I · Refrain: I – IV7 – I (6) | I – IV7 (4) | I – V-of-vi – vi – ii9 (held) | V – I. Harmonic rhythm is the real variable inside the section — leisurely across the first two phrases, radically faster in the third, a middle setting for the last (). The tart ii9 is set up by holding E natural through the entire phrase (): it belongs to every other chord there and only becomes a dissonance when the D chord arrives.

Notable. The opening a7 omits the E entirely — a bare C–G fifth trading off with a lone A underneath — which makes the chord hard to place; superimposing the tonic triad on its relative minor this way is a long-running Beatles device (). The tune is fully diatonic with the leap of a sixth recurring as a motif (), one of them disguised across a phrase boundary. Paul sings one unaccompanied track, no doubling, and shifts into a menacing third voice for the refrain, cast against the lullaby setting.

Against this page. Agrees the song lives in C. His heading is "a minor → C Major": the verse begins away from home and converges fast, and A minor is never actually made a tonal centre.

the-beatles-good-day-sunshine.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Good Day Sunshine
the-beatles-good-day-sunshine.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack's headline finding is that the refrain's famous meter change isn't there — the song is solid 4/4 until the very end, and what feels like a metric shift is a very slow 3 + 3 + 2 syncopation spread across eight beats (). Take a familiar fast accent cell and stretch it over two slow bars and it stops sounding like syncopation and starts sounding like a meter change, for free.

Form. Folk-ballad alternation of refrain and verse, pulled toward pop by an intro, outro and semi-instrumental middle verse. The 4-bar intro is really just an open fifth tapped mechanically four to the bar — its job is to lock the listener into the pulse before the refrain destabilises it, because disorientation only reads if there's a grid to lose. The refrain is 6 bars, open at both ends yet still converging on home; the verse is 8 squared-off bars, closed. The second verse's back half modulates and hands those four bars to a piano solo — a guitar solo in that slot is normal, a modulation plus a half-length solo is not. The one genuine metric break is a single three-beat bar near the end.

Harmony. Four chords total, every one major and adjacent on the cycle of fifths, so two are chromatic at home; the chain is stacked secondary dominants (). Note the direction — from V-of-V it moves backward to that chord's own dominant rather than forward toward the home V, which is approach avoidance, and until the verse arrives the key reads as the wrong one. The break is a textbook pivot (), and the outro bumps the harmony up a half step while the vocals refract into cascading echoes () — a golden-age cliché the Beatles use only three times, all McCartney songs.

Arrangement. Piano, drums and handclaps carry the track with almost no guitar. A snare triplet punctuates two bars of every refrain — but only from the second refrain onward — and handclaps arrive only in the third verse. Introducing a background figure on the second pass registers as development instead of furniture.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-good-morning-good-morning.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Good Morning, Good Morning
the-beatles-good-morning-good-morning.html:
Pollack's analysis

Frugal materials, radical surface. Four chords total and a tune built almost entirely out of one interval shape, wrapped around the most aggressive metric irregularity John had attempted to that point. Pollack's insistence is that for all the revolutionary gesturing the song sits on a completely classic pop/rock skeleton — the economy is the point, and he reads it as impatience.

Form. The 4-bar intro is square on paper, but its first and last chord changes land on a strongly syncopated offbeat, hinting at what's coming. The verse has four phrases — a traditional count at anti-traditional lengths of 10, 12, 9 and 14 beats. Draw the barlines however you like; the beat totals come out the same (). The bridge runs 5 measures, and both meter and chord rhythm regularise there, which the song badly needs by that point — the odd section length is the only irregularity left standing.

Harmony. The whole song uses I, IV, V and ♭VII. The recurring cross-relation between V and ♭VII is what makes so small a set sting () — four chords is plenty when two of them disagree about the same scale degree.

Melody. An uncanny number of phrases span a fourth subdivided into a third plus a second, in either order. One interval shape, permuted, is what holds a rhythmically chaotic verse together ().

Arrangement. The surviving backing track with a single-tracked lead exposes the build method with textbook clarity: backing vocals, brass and animal effects were each applied modularly on top of a plain outline. Set against "She Said She Said", the other extreme meter experiment: there the trouble is quarantined in the contrasting sections and comes off as passively wobbly, while here it lives in the main verse, gets far more airtime, and reads as active agitation.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-good-night.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Good Night
the-beatles-good-night.html:
Pollack's analysis

Schmaltz by design — the chords, tune and phrasing would already be sentimental before the arrangement pushes them over, and Pollack reads the whole thing as camp. The technically interesting parts are the verse, where the bass line chooses the chords instead of following them, and the bridge, which is nothing but an elaborate pedal point dressed as changes.

Form. Standard components made to feel longer and more complex than they are by three devices: the intro previews both bridge and verse material, the verses are doubled up, and the verse-into-bridge pairing happens three times. The one non-standard element is an instrumental special bridge inserted before the final verse. The outro plays the same half-verse twice — full scoring, then an octave up with thinner forces.

Harmony. Pan-diatonic, with sevenths and ninths used decoratively rather than functionally and chords moving in stepwise streams (). The verse's bass is the engine (): on its first pass the bass moves in bar 4, implying an inverted chord; every later pass holds instead, so the same melody sits over different harmony. Later the bass walks scalewise down and approaches the dominant through its third, so V arrives in first inversion before settling to root — a two-stage landing rather than a thud. The bridge is plainly a pedal point (): the tonic held underneath while three upper voices alternate their neighbours, so the "chords" are an artifact of oscillation. The special bridge makes a fake pass at the subdominant key — enough of a diversion to relieve an untroubled home key and motivate the last verse, but never a real modulation ().

Melody. The verse tune is full of wide leaps, but strip them away and the skeleton is a plain descending scale.

Arrangement. George Martin scores a string section small even by Mozart-era standards plus thin winds and a small choir, and gets a cast-of-hundreds sound out of it. The choir takes turns doubling the lead and trailing it, which removes any need for double-tracking.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-got-to-get-you-into-my-life.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Got To Get You Into My Life
the-beatles-got-to-get-you-into-my-life.html:
Pollack's analysis

Paul synthesising big-band pop, blues and modal rock into something that refuses a genre label. Formally, the notable thing is that the vamping, potentially endless coda grows out of an extra repeat of the refrain rather than being tacked on as a new section. Analytically the meat is the verse, which is a study in three consecutive strategies for a bass line.

Form. A 4-bar instrumental intro vamping on I, already carrying the stacked upper extensions that will characterise the verse. The verse is a squared-off 16 bars but internally phrased in unequal lengths. The refrain is 6 bars, extended from an expected four because one chord is sustained across two of them — syncopation operating on harmonic rhythm rather than in the foreground (). The outro runs over twelve bars on I before the fade, implying a jam that continues past the end of the tape.

Harmony. The verse's A phrases are a sustained tonic with 7–9–11–13 stacked on it; call it an extended I or call it ♭VII and IV superimposed, it's experientially identical. The key is established by pedal-point insistence, not by any cadence (). The B phrases hold a chord above a bass walking down chromatically until the sonority becomes an implicit half-diminished seventh pointing hard at the relative minor — but the resolution is deliberately deferred to the middle of the next phrase. The C phrase then descends diatonically and finally lands the key unequivocally. Sing the bass line alone and the section reads as three tries at the same climb. The refrain is plain but bluesy in delivery, with ♭3 and ♭7 rubbing against the chords ().

Melody. Spiky in the verse, wide leaps across a wide range. The refrain tune is fragmentary but elides seamlessly into the instrumental rejoinder answering it — a hocket that reads back as one continuous line when you hum the song.

Arrangement. A big brassy stage band recorded close enough to distort on purpose; the mix is genuinely dirty, partly tape limits and partly the intended aesthetic. The pulse is fast, but the thrust comes from relentless triplets filling the beats plus constant syncopation.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-happiness-is-a-warm-gun.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Happiness Is a Warm Gun
the-beatles-happiness-is-a-warm-gun.html:
Three distinct sections spliced by Lennon, described as 'three songs stuck together.' Complex shifting time signatures throughout. 95 takes to complete. Each section references a different era of rock history.

Chords

Key: shifts between A minor and C major · famously changing time signatures (4/4, 3/4, 9/8…)

Part 1 ("She's not a girl who misses much"): Am7 – Am – Em – Am – Dm – Am → i7 – i – v – i – iv – i (A minor)

"Mother Superior jump the gun": Am – C – Am – G7 → i – ♭III – i – ♭VII7

Chorus ("Happiness is a warm gun"): C – Am – F – G – G7 – C → I – vi – IV – V – V7 – I — a straight ’50s doo-wop turnaround (now in C major) under the shifting meter.

A suite of stitched-together fragments. From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-happiness-is-a-warm-gun-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A suite — three unrelated song fragments stitched into one ~2:45 track — and a masterclass in making stitched sections feel inevitable. The band reportedly ran ~70 takes to nail the tight ensemble through the constantly shifting time signatures (the "Mother Superior" section is famously hard to count).

  • Ends in a 50s doo-wop pastiche ("bang bang, shoot shoot") — a sudden genre shift that resolves all the tension.
  • Tight, dry band performance; the complexity is in the arrangement/meter, not the mix.

Steal this

  • Suite form: stitch 2–3 unrelated fragments into one song; use tempo/feel/genre contrast as the "sections."
  • Shifting meters for unease, then a simple pastiche section (doo-wop) to release it.
  • Rehearse the ensemble tight (or comp meticulously) so a complex arrangement still grooves.

Why I like it

Listen

  • The Beatles (White Album) · search "The Beatles — Happiness Is a Warm Gun"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Happiness Is a Warm Gun (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Happiness Is A Warm Gun — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #136.

Form. His term for it is a "teleological medley" — a run of non-recurring fragments that reads as one piece because the sequence is engineered to escalate. It is the first Beatles track built this way; the Abbey Road medley is the mature version, the difference being that those sections could each stand alone whereas these lean on immediate repetition to feel like sections at all. He counts four parts, not three (Lewisohn says three). Part 1 has two sub-sections, the second a quatrain of iv–i phrases running 5, 4, 4 and 4½ bars — the two identical middle phrases sit at positions 2 and 3, the one placement that destroys symmetry (). Part 2 is an eleven-bar phrase stated twice, internally 3 + 4 + 4. Part 3 is three phrase pairs, the second of each running one beat longer. Part 4 is the only part with an ordinary full progression. What binds them is a rising intensity curve plus meter change as the recurring motif in place of any recurring tune.

Harmony. Part 1a: i (Am7) – v (Em), ×2 · Part 1b: iv – i, ×4 (uneven) · Part 3: i – III · i – ♭VII · Part 4: I – vi – IV – V (repeated) · iv (≈4 bars) · I – vi – IV – V (×2). Three parts drone in A minor in modal rather than functional terms, then it lands in C for the finish — and the opening Am7 contains both the A-minor and C-major triads at once, so the destination is embedded in bar 1 (). The doo-wop finale's one deviation is a minor iv held about four bars before the last two loops ().

Notable. Part 3 runs a hemiola in the first bar of every phrase (); part 2 puts a quarter-tone-flat blues bend on several E naturals; the riffs repeatedly outline both triads together, which is why the arrival in C doesn't sound arbitrary. At the very end the engineer pushed the faders up as the last chord died.

Against this page. The key: field here says A major. Pollack reads C major, converged upon from A minor — close to this page's own Chords line ("shifts between A minor and C major"). Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-hello-goodbye.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Hello Goodbye
the-beatles-hello-goodbye.html:
Pollack's analysis

A song built on withholding V–I. The lyric's approach-avoidance gets an exact harmonic mirror: the music flirts constantly with a full authentic cadence and then actually cadences plagally or deceptively nearly every time.

Form. No intro at all. Verse and refrain strictly alternate four times, then two outros — a first with a complete ending and a second that fades. The verse is an unusual 17 measures, its last arguably overlapping the start of the refrain; the refrain is a true 16. The second outro is a four-measure vamp played six full times before the fade begins: 46 seconds of a 3:31 record.

Harmony. A non-I opening — theorists split on how to label the first chord, but either reading makes the arrival on the tonic a plagal cadence (). The verse then plays V twice and resolves it deceptively to vi both times (); the third V finally gets its I, but only after a five-measure pedal-point build (). The refrain then does the thing actually worth learning: V is excluded from it entirely, because the verse has already saturated the ear with it, so both its cadences use substitutes — ♭VI as a plagal substitute and ♭VII as a laid-back dominant substitute (). Put a real V in either slot and the song goes flat.

Melody. Almost nothing but arpeggio fragments — Pollack's standing challenge is to find two consecutive steps anywhere in the lead vocal that aren't broken by a leap or a change of direction.

Arrangement. A running scale motif unifies the whole record (): the bass descends in both verse and refrain, balanced by an ascending line in the refrain's background, and in the refrain the descent runs four times slower than in the verse. The backing vocals are the case study in scheduling — used sparingly through the body precisely so their full participation in the second outro reads as an arrival. Absent from the body entirely, that entrance would be arbitrary; exposed more, it would already be stale.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-help.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Help!
the-beatles-help.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack's central claim is that the song is unusually static and closed, and that this is the point — slow unvarying harmonic rhythm, one key throughout with no excursion anywhere, and a flat folk-ballad verse/refrain alternation with no story line to carry it. The closure underscores the single-mindedness of the lyric. The other headline: ♭VII doing two completely different jobs in the same song.

Form. The intro is an eight-bar compressed version of the refrain, and the refrain is the same design stretched to sixteen bars by doubling every chord's length () — which reveals a slow build the fast intro version conceals entirely. Write the section once, make the intro from it at half the harmonic rhythm, and the compressed version is a hook while the stretched version is a build.

Harmony. Six diatonic chords plus ♭VII, which plays two roles (). In the verse it makes an Aeolian cadence, standing in for V to close onto I. In the intro and refrain it isn't a dominant surrogate at all but a filler chord pleated between ii and V, and what makes it work is purely contrapuntal — the bass walks down while the top voice climbs chromatically. That intro progression also starts the song in the wrong key on purpose: heard one chord at a time it supports three different readings, and you aren't certain until the verse begins. The outro's payoff is a deceptive cadence () landing on vi before the following phrase puts it right.

Melody. Confined to a fifth, built mostly from triadic figures and short descending scale fragments — which is exactly what makes the one exception land: the upward leap of a sixth in screaming falsetto at each refrain's climax ().

Arrangement. Parts are assigned by section () — the lead guitar has no part in the verses at all. The best detail: near the end of the verse's first line the backing singers take the lead's own five-note figure, trailing a few beats, jumping above him in range, and accenting a different note of it. Not a harmony, not a response — a shadow.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-helter-skelter.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Helter Skelter
the-beatles-helter-skelter.html:
Pollack's analysis

A blues with no 12-bar frame and no V chord anywhere — the blues content lives entirely in the vocal's blue third and a nearly pure pentatonic tune, not in the changes. Pollack's point is that nothing in the form or harmony explains why the track is frightening; the effect comes from the lyric's compulsive circling, the vocal, and a mix printed deliberately into the red.

Form. Verse/refrain three times, with the intro returning midstream and a double fade-out. Verse 1 is a four-square 16 bars; verses 2 and 3 run 14, reaching ♭III two bars early, which tightens the pace but leaves the section lopsided. The same trimming is applied to the refrain's vamp after the instrumental pass. The outro runs six distinct stages across roughly 40% of the track's running time.

Harmony. Total vocabulary is I, ♭III and IV plus one ♭VI in the intro, and nothing else — no dominant at any point (). I against ♭III is a permanent cross-relation, the same collision the vocal makes melodically. The chords change slowly enough that harmony reads as texture rather than motion, and a chromatic line falls through the intro, marking the descent before a word is sung.

Melody. Essentially 100% pentatonic () with a single appoggiatura exception. The blues feel comes almost entirely from the blue third sung as a quarter-tone smear (, ) — get the blues from the melody, not the changes.

Arrangement. The vocal is loud throughout but varied inside that: yelling, screaming, sputtering, laughing. The backing track is metallic and mechanical, tracked hot and mastered close for impact; the quieter early take keeps the lyric and vocal and has none of the brutality. The outro halts the rhythm entirely, restarts it, fades to silence and then fades back in — a structural event, not a mistake, and it buys a second ending for free.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-her-majesty.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Her Majesty
the-beatles-her-majesty.html:
23-second hidden track. McCartney's tongue-in-cheek ode to the Queen. Originally cut from between 'Mean Mr. Mustard' and 'Polythene Pam' and accidentally left at the end of the master tape.

Chords

Key: D major · solo acoustic, ~20 seconds

Main line: D – D/C♯ – D/B – Asus4 – E7 – A – D → I – I/7 – I/6 – V – V7/V – V – I (a descending bass D–C♯–B; the E7 tonicizes A)

"I wanna tell her…": Bm – Bsus2 – D7 – G … G – G6 – D – B7 – Em7 – A – D → vi … I7 – IV … IV – I – V7/ii – ii7 – V – I

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-her-majesty-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A 23-second solo-acoustic McCartney fragment — the first-ever hidden track. It was snipped out of the Abbey Road medley, tossed onto the end of the reel by an engineer (instructed never to throw anything away), and the accidental placement stuck.

Steal this

  • Hidden track / accidental placement: a tiny fragment tacked after silence as an Easter egg.
  • Keep the offcuts: an idea cut from one song can become its own moment.
  • Solo acoustic + voice, seconds long — brevity as charm.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Her Majesty"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Her Majesty (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Her Majesty — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #193.

Form. A fragment deliberately placed to sound accidental — one crashing D chord (the discarded final chord of "Mean Mr Mustard," slightly out of tune against what follows) and then a single verse, cut off mid-cadence. The verse is more carefully made than the joke implies: an unusual 18 bars, a four-square 16-bar quatrain phrased AA′BA″ plus a 2-bar petit reprise of the last phrase. Phrase by phrase the harmonic shape runs closed · open to V · starting at vi and finishing at IV (a real harmonic misadventure at this scale) · convergent on home.

Harmony. I (walking bass) – V-of-V – V – I | I – V-of-V – V | vi – V-of-IV – IV | ♯ii°(4/2) – I – V-of-ii – ii – V – I – V-of-ii | ii – V – I (cut) — secondary dominants pointing three different directions (). The first two bars of each opening phrase are what he calls a harmonic envelope: the D chord is genuinely sustained while the bass walks D–C♯–B–A underneath, and every half-bar does not need relabelling as a new chord. Harmonic rhythm follows no fixed pattern and then noticeably accelerates for the final phrase (). The F♯ sitting high in the tune is what turns the E chords into E9s and the A chords into A13s. The diminished seventh opening the fourth phrase is the same chord as in "The End"; the chromatic voice leading forces an E♯ root rather than the tempting D.

Notable. The master ends on an A on beat 2 of the last bar and the two beats of D that should follow are simply gone — a clean demonstration of how thoroughly a V conditions the ear to expect its I, and how much the absence stings (). The simplest recording in the catalogue: acoustic guitar and a single-tracked vocal, no claps, no taps, no click.

Against this page. Agrees on D major.

the-beatles-here-comes-the-sun.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Here Comes The Sun
the-beatles-here-comes-the-sun.html:
Pollack's analysis

George's pastoral, and the one Beatles track where metrical sleight-of-hand is the main event: a folk-shaped run of verse/refrain pairs wrapped around a bridge built from a three-bar phrase in 11/8 + 4/4 + 7/8, repeated six times. Pollack's angle is that the odd meters aren't decoration but a tempo illusion — eighth-note groupings that make the beat appear to stretch and snap back while the underlying pulse never moves.

Form. The intro is the four-bar verse phrase played twice, instrumental, so the tune isn't given away early. The refrain is an odd 9 bars parsed 5 + 4, closed in shape but ending on V, with its final bar in 7/8. The bridge repeats its three-bar phrase six times, then drops the 7/8 on the last pass and holds V for four bars of 4/4 to load the final verse.

The meter trick. In the refrain, even eighths are accented in groups of three against the 4/4 backbeat and the count balances exactly — twelve plus four is sixteen eighths, two bars — so the disorientation resolves on schedule (). The bridge runs the same idea and refuses to let it balance: 11/8 heard as a wobbly four-beat bar where three beats run half again as long and the fourth snaps back, the 4/4 re-establishing the original tempo, the 7/8 stretching again. Metric modulation, not just an odd bar count.

Harmony. Plain material deployed so cadences pile up. The bridge is the "Hey Jude" double plagal pushed one more fourth around the circle into a triple plagal approach (), open at both ends — which is why six repeats never sound finished.

Melody. Verse and refrain sit almost entirely inside one pentatonic set (). Monotony is dodged by reharmonising repeated fragments rather than varying them — the title phrase carries different chords across its first two appearances.

Arrangement. Guitar, Moog, bass, drums in order of entry, with entrances staggered on purpose. Vocal density is the second dial: single-tracked, then overdubbed, then harmonised across successive verses.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-here-there-and-everywhere.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Here There and Everywhere
the-beatles-here-there-and-everywhere.html:
McCartney's ballad partly inspired by Pet Sounds. All four Beatles snapped fingers on a separate track. Lush three-part vocal harmonies. One of McCartney's personal favorites.

Chords

Key: G major

Intro: G – Bm – B♭ – Am7 – D7 → I – iii – ♭iii – ii7 – V7 (the B♭ is a chromatic passing chord sliding iii→ii)

Verse: G – Am – Bm – C … F♯m7 – B7 – Em – Am – Am7 – D7 → I – ii – iii – IV (a stepwise climb) … V7/vi → vi → ii7 – V7

Middle 8 ("I want her everywhere"): F – B♭ – Gm – Cm – D7 – Gm → modulates to G minor (the parallel minor of G major) before sliding back home — the darkening that makes the return to major feel like sunlight. The verse also uses V7/vi (B7 → Em), a secondary dominant.

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-here-there-and-everywhere-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Revolver (1966) — McCartney wrote it right after hearing Pet Sounds, and it shows in the vocal craft:

  • The varispeed vocal trick: the lead was recorded with the tape sped up, so on normal-speed playback McCartney's voice sits slightly slower/softer/more tender than he actually sang — the secret behind its floating, fragile quality.
  • Lush close three-part harmony — stacked, blended, arranged as a single instrument (Pet Sounds / Beach Boys lineage).
  • Finger snaps (all four Beatles, on a separate track) as the only percussion for much of it — texture instead of a kit.
  • Gentle, clean guitars, restrained bass, no drama in the mix — the arrangement stays soft so the harmony and vocal carry everything.

Steal this

  • Varispeed the vocal: track (or pitch) the lead a touch sped-up so playback is softer/more intimate — Little AlterBoy / kHs Pitch Shifter for the modern version. The Beatles' softness trick.
  • Parallel-minor bridge: drop to the parallel minor for the middle 8 so the return to major feels like relief → Parallel Minor · Borrowed Chords.
  • Percussion as texture, not kit: finger snaps/claps (Hand Clap Studio) instead of drums on a gentle song.
  • Harmony as one instrument: arrange close 3-part stacks and blend them tight → 1 Harmony Vocal Track / 2 Ensemble Stack Group.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Revolver (album) · search "The Beatles — Here, There and Everywhere"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Here There and Everywhere (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Here, There, And Everywhere — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #96.

Form. A classic two-bridge model with one verse between the bridges, no instrumental break, opened by one of their rare ad-lib intros. Intro 4 bars; verse 8 as 2 + 2 + 4 (AAB), where the B is itself a miniature AAB at half the durations (1 + 1 + 2); bridge strictly 6 bars, but the melody and lyric elide into the next verse by repeating the back half of its first phrase, so the section boundary is hard to locate; outro is the first half of the verse with a new melody set to the title words.

Harmony. Intro: I – ♭III – ii – V · Verse: I – IV · I – IV(=VI of e) · ii°ø – V-of-e · ii°ø – V-of-e · vi – ii · IV – V · Bridge (B♭): I – vi – ii · (g minor) iv – V – i – iv – V · Outro: … I – IV – I. Home is G, but the song also visits its relative minor, its parallel minor, and the relative major of that parallel minor — none of them full modulations, all furtive sidesteps, and the restlessness under a placid surface is the whole design. The second chord of the song gives the game away: B♭ against the preceding G, a chromatic-mediant cross-relation that pre-announces the bridge (). Two deceptive cadences do the emotional work (, ) — into B♭ to open the bridge, the slip to G minor, then back into the parallel major at the top of the next verse. The ending is a plagal I–IV–I (); substitute V and the difference is immediate.

Notable. By strict reckoning G major isn't formally established until the verse's final bar, and the chord on F♯ in bars 5–6 is a half-diminished seventh he could not find anywhere else in the catalogue. Paul's lead was recorded low and slow and sped up on playback; the lead vocal and the bridge guitar licks are selectively double-tracked rather than shadowed throughout.

Against this page. Agrees on G major.

the-beatles-hey-bulldog.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Hey Bulldog
the-beatles-hey-bulldog.html:
Pollack's analysis

Arranged and recorded start to finish in a single day, and it shows in the best possible way. The structural oddity worth leading with: the title phrase never appears until the outro, and the section everyone would call the bridge functions as a refrain — on the evidence of the music alone you'd have guessed a different title. The whole track runs on one riff and one rhythmic idea.

Form. Nominally the two-bridge model with the ends chopped about. There is no final verse: the second refrain runs straight into the extended outro, which repeats the ostinato twelve times and is the point of the song rather than an afterthought. The intro exposes the riff three times over staggered instrument entrances, a standing Beatles habit.

Harmony. The home key mode flips section by section — minor for intro, refrains and outro, Mixolydian-inflected major for the verses — with blues colour over the top of both, so even the "major" verses are full of ♭3 and ♭7 (). That pushes the chords to the flat side: a naturally occurring ♭VII and a v that appears minor rather than major (). The minor v doesn't destroy the tonic but props it up far more weakly than a major V would. The refrain lays a rising chromatic line in an inner voice over static i–iv harmony — dramatic, and deliberately not grammatical, since the line doesn't change the chords underneath it.

Melody. The riff is the melodic engine () — it opens the song, closes the refrain, colours the refrain tune, and is finally developed over a chord change in the outro. Rhythm is where the writing lives (): the refrain states one phrase three times with different scansion each time, with two repeats sharing an identical rhythm but starting in opposite halves of the bar.

Arrangement. Small band — piano, bass, drums, lead guitar — and the two success factors are relentless eighth-note piano chords and a bassline that never sits still. The stereo build is unusually deliberate and worth A/B-ing the channels. The outro's payoff is set up early: background chatter under the guitar solo, and the first bark landing during the last refrain, before the outro has even started.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-hey-jude.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Hey Jude
the-beatles-hey-jude.html:
Slow ballad written by Paul McCartney for Julian Lennon; builds from a quiet verse into a long, anthemic "na-na-na" outro.

Chords

Key: F major throughout — a deceptively simple harmonic frame for a 7-minute song.

Verse: F – C – Bb – F – C – F → I – V – IV – I – V – I, plain root-position diatonic triads (occasionally colored as C7) — almost all of the verse's emotional weight comes from the vocal melody and the slow arrangement build, not from harmonic complexity.

Bridge ("And any time you feel the pain..."): Bb – F – C – Eb → IV – I – V – ♭VII, a brief added color: that E♭ is borrowed from F Mixolydian, sitting outside the plain major-scale palette before the verse returns → Borrowed Chords

Coda ("Na-na-na-na"): F – Eb – Bb – F, looped for the entire four-minute outro → I – ♭VII – IV – I. Beatles scholar Alan W. Pollack singles this loop out directly in his canonical analysis of the song: the flat-VII chord gives the whole coda "a decidedly modal, Mixolydian flavor," distinct from the plain-major verse — a static, orchestrally-stacked vamp rather than a progression that resolves anywhere, which is exactly what lets it ride that long without wearing out its welcome → Borrowed Chords

None of the vault's controlled-vocabulary progression tags fit cleanly here — the verse is a plain I-IV-V (not a turnaround, not axis, not the doo-wop loop), and the coda's I-♭VII-IV-I is a modal vamp built on four chords rather than the one/two-chord shape the modal-vamp tag is defined around — so progressions is left empty above rather than stretched.

Production & Arrangement

Famous for its four-minute coda — the "na-na-na" outro is longer than the actual song, with a 36-piece orchestra doubling the chords and clapping/singing along, building through repetition to a euphoric, communal fade. At 7+ minutes it broke the "singles must be short" rule.

  • Arrangement as a slow build: solo piano+vocal → band → tambourine → orchestra → mass singalong. Each pass adds one layer.
  • Warm, intimate verse; huge, roomy coda — dynamics from addition.

Steal this

  • Build by addition: start with one element (piano+voice) and add exactly one layer per section until the payoff — the Vienna lesson at scale.
  • A long communal coda: ride a simple loop and stack claps/gang vocals/orchestra for a euphoric fade (Hand Clap Studio, 2 Ensemble Stack Group).
  • Break the length rule if the build earns it.

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Hey Jude — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #14.

Form. His subject is not the length but the means of sustaining it: an unusual binary form — a fully composed, hymn-like song followed by a mantra-like jam on a four-bar loop, the two halves built from very plain material and complementing each other by contrasting in kind. Charted out, the section durations divide the running time into roughly golden-mean proportions, with the jam the longer half. The song half is the standard two-bridge model with one verse between and no intro at all; every section has different words, rare for this band. Verse 8 bars, four through-composed phrases with no internal repeat, plus one bar added rhetorically when a verse leads into a bridge. Bridge 11½ bars despite surface AA phrasing — the first phrase stretched to five so its handoff mimics the verse-to-bridge lead-in, the second halving the F7 bar and tacking on a two-bar "na-na" tag that both returns to the verse and foreshadows the jam (). Jam: 18½ repeats of a closed four-bar phrase, fading mid-repeat.

Harmony. Purely diatonic F major in the song half — I, ii, IV, V, all root position, one chord per bar. Verse: I – V (2 bars) – I · IV – I – V – I → I7; the shape is closed, but the final tonic mutates into F7, V-of-IV, which is the entire mechanism for getting into the bridge (). Bridge: IV – ii – V – I → I7 (×2) · V7, open at both ends over a Bach-ish walking bass. The jam is I – ♭VII – IV – I, a double plagal cadence () whose ♭VII throws the whole second half into Mixolydian () — and that modal colour, more than the repetition, is the real contrast.

Notable. Every appoggiatura and escape note in the first half resolves; in the jam the na-na melody's peak F sits as an unresolved 9th against the E♭ chord. The orchestral doubling is layered across repeats, and the fade begins at repeat 10 with two full minutes still to run.

Against this page. Agrees on F major throughout.

the-beatles-hold-me-tight.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Hold Me Tight
the-beatles-hold-me-tight.html:
Pollack's analysis

A standard two-bridge, no-solo layout in an odd key choice for them. Pollack's angle is that the song's mixed reputation has nothing to do with its construction: chromatic inner-voice line clichés run through most of the chord changes as a structural device rather than decoration, and an arpeggiated ostinato figure, transposed to fit each chord, holds the rhythm track together in bass and guitar.

Form. A 2-bar intro that establishes the key, exposes the ostinato and plants a tag that becomes a hook. The verse is 16 bars phrased 4 + 4 + 8, the long third phrase balancing the opening couplet and carrying an arch to a clear climax on the downbeat of bar 13. The bridge is an unusual 7 bars whose sub-phrases don't parse neatly — though a metric elision at the end of verse 2 lets you hear it as 8 if you count the pivot bar in. The outro is a fake third bridge that grinds to a halt, with the ritardando starting three bars early.

Harmony. Seven chords, three of them borrowed: V-of-V, minor iv and ♭III (, ). ♭III is the rare one — the relative major of the parallel minor, which stops looking remote once you imagine the song in minor, and against I it produces an audible wavering between major and minor third. The line clichés are directional and sequenced for effect: the verse's first phrase rises, its third phrase falls, so the coaxing opening turns grim before the climax; the bridge's line snakes, which is where its suspense comes from. Harmonic rhythm is load-bearing — the root changes slow from every bar to every other bar on approach to the climax () — and the minor iv arrives immediately after that climax, denying the release the major IV would have given.

Melody. Narrow and repetitive by design. The first four bars of the long phrase hammer the same two notes, which is what makes the long-delayed high note land; the syncopation agitating the previous bars cuts out at the same moment.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-honey-pie.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Honey Pie
the-beatles-honey-pie.html:
Pollack's analysis

Pollack has little patience for Paul's period pastiches but rates this one on craft: the harmonic vocabulary is genuinely that of twenties and early-thirties show and dance tunes rather than a cartoon of it — ♭VI, minor iv in a major key, secondary dominants and a tertiary dominant all inside an eight-bar verse. The period tell is a slow, separate-tempo intro whose words and music appear nowhere else, something the Beatles otherwise barely attempted.

Form. An extended two-bridge model: long intro, three verses stacked between the bridges, then two more to close, with three verse sections mostly instrumental standing in for the dance breaks the genre expects. The song has no outro — it simply stops on the downbeat where another verse would have begun. The 12-bar intro is AAB, the pattern camouflaged by the half-spoken delivery of its second A. Verse and bridge are both 8 bars, but the verse is four short phrases and the bridge is two long ones.

Harmony. The ♭VI chord works in both directions inside one verse: rising, as an appoggiatura chord shoving up into the tonic; falling, as the approach to V (). Same chord, two functions, no extra material. The middle of the verse is a four-step walk around the circle of fifths, period cliché used on purpose (). The bridge is a bassline exercise (): the line puts most of the chords in inversion and gives the section an unusually high centre of gravity — play it in root position and it collapses. Where a verse leads into a bridge, its last bar is rewritten so a single chromatic voice stitches the two sections together and the seam disappears.

Melody. Wide range, worked in a jumpy triadic style that flatters the voice rather than a stepwise crooner line.

Arrangement. A stylised stage-band fox-trot pushed far enough to read as surreal. Saxophones enter tight and high, spend most of the song on background wash or answering phrases, and only get the actual tune in the final verse. The intro's second phrase runs through a megaphone/worn-78 effect — obvious now, technically adventurous in 1968.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-am-the-walrus.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Am the Walrus
the-beatles-i-am-the-walrus.html:
Intentionally nonsensical lyrics written to confuse literary analysts. Mike Sammes Singers provide the 'oompah' vocal parts. A BBC radio broadcast of King Lear fades in during the outro. George Martin's orchestration.

Chords

Key: A major, but built on parallel major triads marching up and down the scale

Verse: A – C – D – E – A → I – ♭III – IV – V – I (Lennon climbs through chromatic major triads, not diatonic chords)

"I am the eggman / walrus": C – D – E → ♭III – IV – V

Intro / outro riff: root-position major triads sliding by step — B–A–G–F–E descending, A–B–C–D–E ascending (II – I – ♭VII – ♭VI – V / I – II – ♭III – IV – V).

Deliberately resists a single key. From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-i-am-the-walrus-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A chaotic orchestral collage — one of the great "throw everything in" productions. George Martin's dense strings + brass, the Mike Sammes Singers chanting nonsense ("oompah, everybody's got one," rising "ho-ho-ho"), and — most famously — a live BBC radio broadcast of King Lear tuned in on the spot and recorded straight into the fade (pure chance/aleatoric; it's different every time it was mixed).

  • Lennon's vocal is heavily compressed/distorted through a cheap mic for the detached, sneering tone.
  • The harmony slides chromatically (the ascending "sitting in an English garden" line) — restless, unresolved, matching the collage.

Full from-scratch recreation, instrument by instrument (David Bennett Music Theory) — a copyright-safe rebuild for use in analysis videos, useful as a virtual-instrument matching reference: Pianet (the original's early Hohner electric piano) approximated via a Keyscape pianet patch. Horns: BBC Symphony Orchestra doubled with Session Horns Pro for extra bite. Violin: no dedicated violin instrument owned, so BBC Symphony Orchestra doubled with Spitfire Solo Cello for texture (a cello isn't a violin, but layering it in thickened the sound usefully). Cello (the arrangement's key harmonic-space instrument, playing almost throughout): BBC Symphony Orchestra layered under Spitfire Solo Cello as the main voice — prioritized for realism since it's so exposed. Strings/horns transcribed by ear into MuseScore, then exported as MIDI and imported into the DAW rather than programmed directly — useful workflow for matching an orchestral arrangement precisely. Drums: Abbey Road 60s Drummer (a period-correct kit/mic emulation). The King Lear radio broadcast: recreated literally, by tuning an actual AM radio (bought secondhand) live and capturing whatever happened to be broadcasting, rather than sourcing/simulating old BBC audio — same aleatoric spirit as the original. Backing vocals: recreated solo via pitch-shifting a single performance into a mock-choir, standing in for the original's 16-voice Mike Sammes Singers arrangement. → Layering and Stacking (the doubled-library technique used on horns/violin/cello) — David Bennett Music Theory, I recreated "I Am The Walrus" from scratch

Steal this

  • Print chance audio: record a live radio/TV/random source into the mix and commit to whatever lands (kHs Frequency Shifter/tape it) — aleatoric texture you can't plan.
  • Choral nonsense oohs/chants as a textural pad (Hand Clap Studio-adjacent vocal stacks / a vocal synth) under a dense arrangement.
  • Chromatic sliding harmony for restless, unresolved motion → Modulation · Chord Progressions.
  • Distort the lead vocal for detachment (Decapitator).

Why I like it

Listen

  • Magical Mystery Tour · search "The Beatles — I Am the Walrus"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Am the Walrus (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I Am The Walrus — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #121.

Form. Underneath the outrage, a talking blues — patter declamation, phrases grouped in threes, and an exposed V–IV–I inside a song whose harmony is otherwise nowhere near a key. Two structural moves have Lennon precedents: verses followed by refrains are subtly different from verses followed by other verses, and the intro comes back mid-song. Intro 7½ bars, with a perfectly traditional AABB melodic phrasing hiding inside the strangeness; first verse 6 bars, its second appearance extended by five; second verse melodically the same but harmonically rewritten to travel halfway to V; refrain only 3 bars, the third taking one extra that establishes the precedent for how the outro grows. The radio interlude is exactly one measure in tempo, which is nothing like what it sounds.

Harmony. Verse 1: I (G in bass) – ♭III – IV – I · ♭III – IV – I · Verse 2: I (G) – vi – ♭VI – ♭VII – I · ♭VI – V/V (2) · Refrain: ♭VI-of-V – ♭VII-of-V – V · Outro loop: I – ♭VII – ♭VI – V7 – IV9 – ♭III11 – v – I. Nominally A major, but V-of-V is given tonal focus and V the sense of arrival, so the refrain reads less as a half cadence than as an outright modulation to the key of V (, , ). Two passages honestly refuse Roman numerals: the intro chords exist because bass and top voice walk down together in parallel tenths, and the outro is a Möbius strip where contrary motion generates the chords rather than the other way round () — the loop resets on its eighth move against four-bar phrases, so a different chord lands on the downbeat of every third phrase, which is what makes it feel limitless.

Notable. The first verse establishes the tonic without ever using V. Verse 2's block slide f♯m – F – G – A, then the tritone leap F to B, is the harmonic signature. The tune has two modes only — hammering one pitch, or bluesy licks on ♭3 and ♭7 — and the radio is withheld until half the song has gone by, then allowed to dominate the last forty seconds.

Against this page. Agrees on A major as the nominal key, and on the parallel-triad reading in the Chords section.

the-beatles-i-call-your-name.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Call Your Name
the-beatles-i-call-your-name.html:
Pollack's analysis

The stylistic odd-one-out among the harder rockers around it — bluesy in flavour but not in form, closer to pop or jazz. The interest comes from a small budget spent oddly: seven chords total, three of them non-diatonic, including a V-of-V-of-V with no precedent earlier in the catalogue. The result is continual restless motion with no modulation anywhere.

Form. Full two-bridge form with two verses — one instrumental — between the bridges. Every verse after the first uses a variant, so the opening pair reads as one longer couplet-like unit while the later standalone variants sound slightly truncated. Verse and bridge are both 8 bars, parsing into four 2-bar phrases.

Harmony. Three of the seven chords are altered or borrowed (, ). The verse runs three dominant sevenths in a row and ends wide open; the verse variant instead cadences through IV rather than V, even though the preceding V-of-V has just built the expectation of a dominant () — answering a V-of-V with IV is a device they kept using for years. The bridge avoids the tonic completely, so it floats without a clear key. Harmonic rhythm is relaxed at roughly one chord every two bars, and the non-diatonic chords carry the entire sense of motion.

Melody. Pentatonic underneath, with the hook phrase outlining 1–3–5–6 and the fourth degree kept out entirely (). The appoggiatura over the V-of-V gets extra weight precisely because it's the melody's first non-pentatonic note.

Arrangement. The guitar-solo section switches to a jazzy ska feel at constant tempo — the drums trade even eighths for a limping dotted rhythm and the bass trades roots for a stepwise walk — so when the original beat returns it registers as another change. Probably the first appearance of a trick John reused for the rest of his career.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-don-t-want-to-spoil-the-pa.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Don't Want To Spoil The Party
the-beatles-i-don-t-want-to-spoil-the-pa.html:
Pollack's analysis

Another hybrid: acoustic guitars and country-flavoured vocal harmony as a facade over chord vocabulary and melodic style that are straight urban pop-rock. Unusually many chords for the period — five diatonic triads plus ♭VII and two secondary dominants.

Form. The 8-bar intro's material never returns in the body of the song, which is close to unique in their catalogue; it comes back only as the outro, now scored for the full band, so the two sections bookend everything. Symmetry without repetition. The verse is 16 bars, four equal phrases, AABA. The bridge is 12 bars built from a 6-bar phrase twice () — it could have been squeezed into a standard four by doubling the harmonic rhythm, and leaving it stretched, with the melodic rhythm drawing out, is what gives the section its rhetorical weight.

Harmony. The verse's third phrase is where it happens: the harmonic rhythm speeds up and the V-of-vi is left hanging as a non sequitur, splitting the phrase in two (). The ♭VII is deployed backwards from the usual habit () — normally it substitutes for V or alternates with it, but here V has been so thoroughly established that a late ♭VII reads as a shrug where a V9 was expected. The bridge runs the album's recurring trick, V-of-V reaching V by way of IV, cross relation included; and where the verse is harmonically closed, the bridge is left open to motivate the verse's return.

Melody. Purely major, no modal shading. The peak is managed across the whole song (): the verse tops out one note lower than the bridge, which owns the song's unique high point. The guitar solo is the irony — choppier and more dissonant than the sung tune, yet tracking its abstract outline more closely than it sounds like it does.

Arrangement. Vocals are staged phrase by phrase inside a single verse: close harmony, then wordless pads behind a solo lead, then the folksy texture back — which is what makes the AABA shape audible.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-feel-fine.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Feel Fine
the-beatles-i-feel-fine.html:
Pollack's analysis

Four chords, one key, and a form that comes out bulky because every section is short — including three verses in a row in the middle, one of them the guitar solo. The famous item is the opening feedback, and Pollack's correction to the folklore is worth keeping: it isn't random noise but the deliberate isolation of a natural harmonic sounding an octave above the plucked string, and the note plucked was chosen, not stumbled onto.

Form. An 8-bar intro after the out-of-tempo feedback, quoted almost verbatim later in the back half of the solo section. The verse is 10 bars, splitting 6 + 4 by the rhetoric of the lyric and tune rather than by the harmony — asymmetric, but the dramatic shape stays arch-like and closed. The bridge is 8 bars, the same phrase twice, left open so it hands off cleanly.

Harmony. Firmly in one key throughout, four chords total. The verses get by on I, IV and V; iii is the only addition and appears only in the bridges, used as the step from I to IV where it would normally head for vi — the cheapest unusual-sounding chord available in a four-chord song. The verse's entire first phrase sits static on the tonic.

Melody. Trademark noodling on two or three notes inside a narrow range. Blue-note placement is scheduled rather than scattered: ♭7s early in the verse, and the ♭3 withheld until near its end (), so the section escalates without any new material.

Arrangement. The lead guitar is a secondary hook in its own right — licks in the intro and between the verse phrases keep it lurking constantly, so the solo doesn't arrive out of nowhere. Absence is scheduled throughout (): the band is held out until late in the intro, and the backing vocals join across the back half of the verse but reinforce the front of each bridge phrase before retreating — same parts, and the two sections stop sounding alike. John's lead sits below the other two voices, which is where the tang comes from.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-me-mine.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Me Mine
the-beatles-i-me-mine.html:
Harrison's song about the ego. Alternates between a slow waltz and a faster hard-rock feel. Extended with Phil Spector overdubs for the Let It Be album — Lennon had already left the band by the time overdubs were recorded.

Chords

Key: G minor verse (3/4 waltz) → G major chorus (4/4) · capo 2 on the recording

Verse (waltz): Gm – C – F – D – Gm … Cm – D – Gm – B♭ – E♭ → i – IV – ♭VII – V – i … iv – V – i – ♭III – ♭VI (the major C (IV) gives a Dorian lift)

Chorus ("I-me-me mine"): G7 – C7 – G7 – D7 → I7 – IV7 – I7 – V7 (flips to a bluesy G major)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-i-me-mine-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Harrison's waltz-verse-into-rock-chorus — notable as the last thing the Beatles recorded together (Jan 1970), later padded out with Spector strings. A 3/4 lament that snaps to 4/4 heaviness.

Steal this

  • Meter flip for contrast: a 3/4 verse crashing into a 4/4 chorus → Chord Progressions.
  • Minor-key lament + bluesy chorus.
  • Strings to inflate a short song to length (Spector's move).

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — I Me Mine"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Me Mine (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I Me Mine — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #170.

Form. A folk/blues hybrid over a hard waltz, and the technically remarkable thing is the metric modulation between the 3/4 verse and the 4/4 refrain, which is arithmetically exact rather than approximate. In numbers: the verse runs one 3/4 bar per second (180 bpm); divide each bar into two dotted quarters and you get 120, which becomes the refrain's quarter note; coming back, split the 4/4 bar into two halves of two beats and you are back at the original bar rate. Against that precision everything else is left unresolved — both sections open out from i, there is no outro, and the track simply stops. Intro is the verse opening foreshortened to 6 bars by eliding into verse 1; verse an unusually long 32 bars, AA′BA″; refrain 10 bars — it wants to be a 12-bar blues frame and is cut short by the transition back ().

Harmony. Verse (32): i – IV – ♭VII – V7 – i (×2, 8 bars each) · iv (4) – V9 (4) · i over a chromatic bass A–G♯–G♮–F♯ – F7 = VI (4+4) · Refrain (10): i (4) · iv (2) – i (2) · V (2). The verse plays the three minor scales against each other — a major IV in a minor key, and ♭VII moving to V, which puts the natural minor's G♮ against the harmonic minor's G♯ (, ). Steering the verse to VI7 as its open target is genuinely unusual next to a refrain that ends conventionally on V.

Notable. The tune does little more than alternate scale degrees 5 and 6 at the structural level, which reinforces the unfinished quality. Paul's bass is the most composed element (): on any chord lasting two or more bars he jumps a third from the root to the chord's middle note, and the final phrase carries a fully exposed chromatic descent. The piano is withheld until the refrain.

Against this page. The key: field here says A major. Pollack reads the song in A minor — the same sounding pitch as this page's "G minor verse, capo 2," but he treats the minor as the home key rather than the major refrain. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-i-need-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Need You
the-beatles-i-need-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

George's second writing credit, read here as a folk-modal tune wearing pop-rock clothes. The structural hook is a negative one: the V chord is withheld from the entire verse and doesn't appear until the bridge — and the melody's missing fourth degree arrives at exactly the same moment ().

Form. Two-bridge model with a single verse between the bridges. The verse is an odd 14 bars in four phrases, the fourth running half as long as the first three; the asymmetry reads as free verse rather than as a mistake. The bridge is 9 bars of two unequal phrases and stretches exactly where the verse compressed. The 8-bar coda grows out of the final verse, starting where that truncated fourth phrase would otherwise sit.

Harmony. Seven chords, nothing more exotic than V-of-V. The verse establishes home by indirect routes — IV→I, and the even weaker stepwise ii→I — rather than by dominant motion. The bridge is the only place the key is pinned down, and it does it with V and V-of-V back to back: the reverse of the usual layout, where the verses hammer the tonic and the bridge wanders off. The coda is the I–vi–IV cliché with the V deleted, consistent with a song that treats the dominant as a rationed resource.

Melody. The verse tune is pentatonic () with one exception, a ♭7 at the end of the second phrase — and that single out-of-scale note carries the whole modal impression. Appoggiaturas are dense, and several are left dangling at phrase ends, hanging unresolved against the tonic chord ().

Arrangement. Acoustic rhythm guitar against an electric pedal-tone guitar that reads almost as a keyboard. A turn figure introduced in the two-bar intro returns at the end of three of the four verse phrases, overlapping the vocal's last two notes — and its second half is what resolves those hanging vocal appoggiaturas. Real tension, no loose end.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-saw-her-standing-there.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Saw Her Standing There
the-beatles-i-saw-her-standing-there.html:
Pollack's analysis

Their first genuinely fast, hard rocker and the lead-off track on the first album — Pollack treats it less as a milestone than as a specimen jar, the one early song running nearly every 1963 trademark at once: boogie bass, pickup entries, tight non-parallel two-part harmony, falsetto as a structural event, blue notes against major chords.

Form. The fully expanded two-bridge model with two verses between the bridges, the second being the guitar solo. Every section enters on a pickup, starting with the bass note between the count-in and bar 1 — forward lean with no change to the material. The verse is 16 bars in four even phrases (establish, reinforce, climb, resolve); the bridge is 10 bars phrased 2+2+6 rather than the expected 8.

Harmony. Almost pure I–IV–V with slow changes, which is most of why a song that isn't a blues sounds like one. The one reharmonised bar reads at first as ♭VI but is actually the minor iv in first inversion, borrowed into the major key () — the cross-relation is timed to the falsetto whoop, and it's the verse's peak. The bridge parks on IV for six bars, reaches V, and instead of stopping at eight resolves V deceptively to IV before the tonic (); the delay drains tension while the phrase extension and falsetto leap push the other way ().

Melody. Wide range, stepwise motion interrupted by large leaps — the octave jump up at the peak prepared by a nearly equal drop earlier. Stuffed with flat thirds and sevenths in a four-sharp key ().

Arrangement. The two-part vocal writing uses open fourths and fifths, some in parallel, deliberately unlike Everly-style thirds and sixths, and in the bridge John holds a note under Paul and then vaults an octave above him — so the top line switches singers mid-phrase. The solo verse quietly changes two chords back to plain ones, because both edits remove emphasis points that only work when words are landing on them.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-should-have-known-better.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Should Have Known Better
the-beatles-i-should-have-known-better.html:
Pollack's analysis

Looks like the plain one on the album and isn't. Two things carry it: the verse exists in two versions — closed and 10 bars when another verse follows, open and 8 bars when a bridge follows — and a syncopated accent on the last eighth of the bar runs through the whole song, always foiled by a backing track that never syncopates at all ().

Form. A strange take on the two-bridge model: three verses in a row between the bridges (the middle one instrumental), and the second bridge running straight into the outro with no verse between. The bridge is an unusually long and developed 16 bars in four distinct phrases.

Harmony. Few chords, all ordinary; the only real event is the trip to the relative minor for the bridges (), pivoting back on the chord that is VI in the minor and IV at home. Harmonic rhythm does structural work in the verse: it slows midway to add ballast, then the I–V oscillation returns for symmetry (). One bar is a rarity for the genre — a chord held in inversion while the bass walks down to its root. The bridge teases once more by dipping back to the minor just as you think the corner has been turned.

Melody. The verse covers a sixth, mostly noodling on its top four notes, but still reads as an ascent; its signature is a long sustained open vowel followed immediately by fast syllabic setting. The bridge answers with a clean arch across a tenth, climaxing on a falsetto flip. At the end of the guitar solo the leading tone refuses to resolve upward and an added-sixth chord arrives instead.

Arrangement. The harmonica feels omnipresent but isn't — outside the solo verse its main job is announcing each verse, two bars at a time, and it makes a piquant 9th and a flat cross-relation against the chord it enters on. Scarcity is what makes its one continuous pass land. The electric guitar enters one bar before the section it belongs to, to hide the seam. John is double-tracked everywhere except the second bridge, which drops to a single track — with the double restored for exactly the falsetto flip. Reserving one production element for one moment is a bigger event than any layer you could add.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-wanna-be-your-man.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Wanna Be Your Man
the-beatles-i-wanna-be-your-man.html:
Pollack's analysis

A one-chord jam with a refrain bolted on. Pollack's verdict is blunt — style carrying almost no content, a song that could plausibly have been written in an afternoon (it was handed to the Stones). What's formally worth noting is the bridge-shaped refrain and the improvisatory instrumental break.

Form. The verse is 17 bars: two 8-bar couplets plus one extra. That bar isn't required and it makes the meter lopsided, but drop it and the long pickup into the title phrase gets crammed into bar 16 — asymmetry was the lesser evil, and an odd bar count is a cheaper problem than a garbled hook. The refrain is 8 bars in four 2-bar phrases, each declaiming the title; the break is 12 bars, again over a single chord. Live and BBC versions add four bars of vamping before the vocal, turn the break into an explicit 12-bar blues frame, and take the song to a real ending instead of a fade.

Harmony. The verse is one chord and nothing else, with a brief hint of V late in each couplet. The refrain never leaves the home key either, but packs in functional changes whose roots move by fifths, so it sounds like it's hunting for something (). That's the transferable idea: hold one chord for a whole section, then answer it with dense circle-of-fifths motion that never actually modulates — it reads as a key change and costs nothing.

Melody. The verse tune supplies the harmonic motion the chords don't, colouring the static tonic from above with heavy emphasis on the sixth and the ♭7 (). The refrain's contrast is stylistic as much as harmonic — its cornball chromatic-scale guitar riffs are pointedly not bluesy.

Arrangement. Ringo on lead, John and Paul joining for the refrain. Texture is overstuffed with double tracking, overdubbed organ and a lot of screaming; the guitar break is a string of disconnected licks with none of the shape of the "I Saw Her Standing There" solo. The live arrangements drop the organ and are better for it.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-want-to-hold-your-hand.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Want To Hold Your Hand
the-beatles-i-want-to-hold-your-hand.html:
Pollack's analysis

Standard two-bridge form, mostly even phrase lengths, a backbeat closer to conservative pop than rock — and packed inside it, nearly every early-Beatles device at once. Two things carry it structurally: the verse repeatedly walks up to the V-of-vi and abandons it, and the bridge is a real pivot modulation that ends up 11 bars long because the returning intro collides with its last bar.

Form. Only one verse separates the two bridges, and there's no solo. The 4-bar intro opens a bar and a half ahead of the first downbeat. The verse is 12 bars and pointedly not a blues frame: two identical 4-bar phrases plus a 4-bar hook phrase.

Harmony. The intro hammers IV–V in syncopation and converges on a big V that spills into the verse — opening on IV and staging the climax this early is unusual, and it's what seizes attention. Both opening verse phrases head for the relative minor and stop on its dominant; the first time that V-of-vi is simply left dangling, the next phrase restarting on I as though nothing happened (), and the second time it resolves deceptively to IV instead (). The third phrase double-times the harmonic rhythm and cashes the accumulated tension as the title hook. The bridge is a genuine pivot modulation into IV rather than a tonicization (), relatively rare in the catalogue, with the drum part changed for extra contrast. The last surprise is in the outro: slow triplets, and two extra bars of IV wedged between V and its resolution.

Melody. Centred on the octave from the tonic. The two couplet phrases are melodically identical apart from their endings — one drops, the other climbs to the same note an octave higher. The real point of no return isn't the arch's top but the syncopated falsetto leap just before it.

Arrangement. No solo vocal anywhere — they duet the entire song, mostly in unison, opening into two-part harmony for roughly three bars per verse, and that restraint is what makes it register. The syncopation is established before the meter is: the intro's accents fall after beats 3 and 4, and only a plain four-in-the-bar guitar orients you ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-want-you-she-s-so-heavy.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Want You (She's So Heavy)
the-beatles-i-want-you-she-s-so-heavy.html:
Lennon's obsessive, repetitive refrain over a crushing groove. Second section builds with white noise generated by the Moog synthesizer. Ends with an abrupt mid-phrase tape cut — one of the heaviest Beatles recordings.

Chords

Key: A minor (D minor in the heavy riff sections)

Verse ("I want you so bad"): Am7 – C – D – F – G – E7/G♯ – Am7 → i7 – ♭III – IV – ♭VI – ♭VII – V7 – i (a climbing line capped by the E7 dominant)

Riff / "It's driving me mad": Dm – Dm/F – E7♭9 – C5 – B5 – B♭7 – Aaug → a chromatic descent (D–C–B–B♭–A) over the famous heavy guitar figure, landing on the E7♭9 dominant.

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-i-want-you-shes-so-heavy-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Hypnotic and minimal — 14 words of lyric over nearly 8 minutes, built entirely on repetition + dynamics. A massive layered white-noise/wind crescendo (multiple Moog + tape noise passes) builds for minutes until the track cuts off dead mid-note — Lennon's famous "cut it there" edit, one of the most abrupt endings in pop.

  • Heavy, bluesy, Leslie/tremolo-drenched guitars; the arrangement swells and contracts rather than "developing."
  • The abrupt tape cut replaces a fade — silence as a shock.

Steal this

  • Tension through repetition: ride one riff/loop and build with layers + dynamics, not new parts.
  • Growing noise bed: stack white-noise/riser passes (ValhallaSupermassive / noise + automation) into a wall, then...
  • Hard cut ending: end dead on a downbeat, no fade — the silence is the hook.
  • Minimal lyric as mantra — a few repeated words can carry a long track.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — I Want You (She's So Heavy)"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Want You (She's So Heavy) (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I Want You (She's So Heavy) — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #182.

Form. Not a medley — two separate songs cross-cut cinematically. One supplies the verses; the other supplies the intro, the refrains and the enormous outro. The separation is engineered on three independent axes: meter (squared-off 4/4 with a jazzy backbeat in the verses, slow cranking 6/8 everywhere else), texture (full ensemble behind a lead vocal versus a bass ostinato with slow guitar arpeggios), and lyric perspective (the verses address her directly, the refrains talk about her in the third person). The intro is five bars and every non-repeated appearance ends with a grand pause, so it plays closer to six; the refrains are AA doublings of it, ten bars; the verse reads as ABA′B′ but parses into deliberately unequal phrases of 8½ + 2 + 8½ + 6, the limping half-bar a Lennon signature. The outro runs just under fourteen consecutive iterations of the intro phrase.

Harmony. Intro (5): i (2) – V/V (E9) – VI (B♭7) – V+ (A augmented) · Verse, first half [in A minor]: i (6) · i – III – VII6/4 – IV – V (half bar) · i – I (= V of D) · Verse, second half [in D minor]: i (6) · i – III – VII – VI – chromatic climb · V/V (E9, held 6). The intro lands on another augmented V, echoing "Oh! Darling" two tracks earlier, and its five-bar length plus a V-of-V whose resolution is deferred () is exactly what lets the phrase loop fourteen times without closing. An F natural sustained as a common tone runs straight through the chord changes, and he hears the bass figure as a ground bass in the passacaglia sense rather than a rock riff.

Notable. The tune is minor pentatonic () with the alternate phrases leaning on flatted fifth and seventh (). He sets the track against "Hey Jude": both split in golden-section proportion, but here the coda material is exposed from bar 1 and already heard twice as a refrain, and the weight sits on the first half — which is the only thing keeping the riff from overexposure.

Against this page. A real disagreement. Pollack reads the home key as D minor, with the verses starting in A minor (v) and converging home from there. This page reads A minor with D minor in the heavy sections — the inverse. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-i-want-to-tell-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Want to Tell You
the-beatles-i-want-to-tell-you.html:
Harrison's song about the frustration of ideas not translating into speech. The piano deliberately plays a clashing note against the main chord to create harmonic tension that mirrors the lyrical theme.

Chords

Key: A major · George Harrison

Verse: A – B – E7 – A → I – II7 – V7 – I (the B major is a bright secondary dominant — V/V — instead of a diatonic Bm)

"But if I seem to act unkind": Bm – Dm6 – A – B7 – Bm – Dm6 – A → ii – iv6 – I – II7 – ii – iv6 – I (the dissonant Dm6 is the "confusing things" tension Harrison wrote in on purpose)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-i-want-to-tell-you-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Harrison, Revolver — opens with a guitar fade-in and rides a deliberately dissonant piano stab (a clashing E7♭9-ish note) to musically depict 'I can't get my thoughts out.' Harmony as lyric.

Steal this

  • Dissonance as meaning: use a clashing chord/note deliberately to express tension → Altered Chords.
  • Fade-in intro for an unusual entrance.
  • Repetitive, hypnotic groove under an anxious vocal.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Revolver · search "The Beatles — I Want to Tell You"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Want to Tell You (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I Want To Tell You — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #101.

Form. A standard two-bridge model whose sections resist being counted. The intro is a fade-in, their first since "Eight Days A Week" — you become aware of the ostinato already running on the guitar's low strings, three complete iterations with staggered entrances. Verse 11 bars, hard to parse for a second reason too: its four vocal phrases are unequal and are declaimed across barlines rather than into them, with a sneak reprise of the ostinato filling the gap between verses. Bridge 8 bars, much closer to square and badly needed as contrast by that point, though its three short phrases also hang over the barlines. Outro is half a varied reprise of the intro, half a counted-off fade.

Harmony. A major on a frugal budget. Verse: I (3½ bars) | V-of-V (entering mid-bar 4) | V (4 bars) | I (2) — the chord change in the middle of bar 4 is the sophisticated move. The guitar ostinato has I – ♭VII – IV – I embedded in it, which is where the modal tint comes from. The bridge sits on B in the bass under everything (): Bm | B°(with B beneath) | A | B major · Bm | B° | A, and his non-obvious call is to hear that diminished chord as vii° rooted on G♯, a V surrogate, despite the B underneath — he argues against assigning distinct numerals to those bars at all, since the real content is creeping chromatic motion in the inner voices.

Notable. The anxiety of the lyric is written into the fabric as literal dissonance: harmonic, in the piano's mechanical harping on an E minor ninth, and rhythmic, in the slow triplets of the bass ostinato grinding against the 4/4 backbeat (). The ostinato is a saw-tooth shape rather than an arch, starting just before the downbeat. The bridge vocal is full of 9–8 appoggiaturas echoing the piano's (), and backing vocals are used for emphasis on the even-numbered phrases — the same 2-and-4 logic as the beat.

Against this page. Agrees on A major.

the-beatles-i-will.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Will
the-beatles-i-will.html:
McCartney hummed the bass line rather than playing bass guitar. Drums played with brushes only. Took 67 takes. Among the most tender and sparse Beatles recordings.

Chords

Key: F major (McCartney played E-shapes capo 1, or C-shapes capo 5)

Verse: F – Dm – Gm7 – C7 – F – Dm – Am → I – vi – ii7 – V7 – I – vi – iii

Middle: Bb – C – Dm – B♭m – F/C – Fdim → IV – V – vi – iv – I – i° (the B♭m (iv) and passing diminished are the bittersweet color)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-i-will-chords.pdf (chart gives the C-shape / capo-5 voicings; numerals here are in the sounding key of F).

Production & Arrangement

McCartney's warm little love song (White Album) — famously he sang the bass line vocally (a mouth-bass 'boom') instead of playing bass, over gentle acoustic and light percussion. Intimate, simple, perfectly voiced.

Steal this

  • Vocal/mouth bass: sing the bass line for a soft, round low end when a real bass would be too heavy.
  • Small and warm: acoustic + light perc + close vocal; simplicity as the craft.
  • Sweet secondary-dominant color in a simple frame.

Why I like it

Listen

  • The Beatles (White Album) · search "The Beatles — I Will"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I Will (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I Will — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #144.

Form. A tiny song on one of pop's most worn progressions whose interest is concentrated almost entirely in the outro, which he rates the most sophisticated thing in it. Three structural oddities for something this short: no intro at all, an outro long in proportion to the whole, and different lyrics in every verse, so a two-minute song still tells a story. Verse 1 is 9 bars — a square eight elided with a two-bar interlude that separates it from verse 2; verse 2 is exactly 8, with the tonic sustained through the whole eighth bar; bridge 8; the outro is grown out of a morphed final verse and is itself a morph of the bridge.
