Harmony. Verse (two chords per bar): I – vi · ii7 – V · I – vi · iii – I7 · IV – V · vi – I · IV – V · I – vi · [interlude] ii – V. Stock material, deliberately. The move that matters is the added seventh on the tonic, which converts a resting I into V-of-IV and pulls the phrase forward instead of letting it settle () — mid-verse, and again on the held chord ending verse 2. Bridge: IV – iii · vi · ii – V · I (as V-of-IV) · IV – iii · vi · V-of-V · V: the verses are harmonically closed, the bridge the opposite in both directions, starting away from I and ending wide open on V via its own V-of-V. Outro: IV – V · vi – vii° – I (×2) · IV – V · vi · ii – V · ♭VI (≈3 bars) · I · IV – iii · vi · ii – V · I — the last verse deforms at bar 6 into a three-strikes rhetorical loop, and the third statement stretches into a long phrase arriving on ♭VI, the harmonic climax and the only genuinely foreign chord in the song ().

Notable. The verse tune is disjunct with clean arches and upward octave leaps; the bridge answers with far more stepwise motion, which is most of why it reads as contrast despite sharing the chord vocabulary. There is no bass guitar — Paul scat-sings the bassline, recorded very close, and the vocal staging runs single → parallel thirds at the bridge → unison → thirds again in the outro.

Against this page. Agrees on F major.

the-beatles-i-ll-be-back.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'll Be Back
the-beatles-i-ll-be-back.html:
Pollack's analysis

The song is built on one device: constant alternation between the major and parallel minor tonic (). The two-bar intro exists almost entirely so its major chord sets a trap for a verse that starts minor; the fade-out then loops the same alternation so the song ends unresolved by design rather than by convention.

Form. Three bridge sections, not two — bridge 1 appears twice and a different bridge 2 sits in the middle, though the two are cousins: the last two and a half bars of bridge 1 are repeated verbatim in bridge 2. Two deliberate irregularities (): bridge 1 is 6½ bars, with a half-measure in the middle, which in a world of 4-, 6- and 8-bar phrases is what makes the section stick; and the final verse is cut to half length, because with three verses and three bridges already banked a full one would overstay.

Harmony. The verse is a descending stream drawn from natural minor (), one chord per bar over a bass walking down and back. Despite that pull the section is harmonically closed, and Pollack refuses to notate the passing second-inversion sonority as a chord change because the bass never moves under it. Bridge 1 leans toward the relative minor and immediately bails back to V. Bridge 2 is more open still, on the prowl for a key for five or six bars without ever actually leaving home, and carries a descending chromatic inner line plus a cross relation between adjacent chords.

Melody. Narrow range, thick with appoggiaturas (). The verses hinge on the major/minor third switch. Bridge 1 stacks three appoggiaturas in close order on the same two pitches, each under different harmony.

Arrangement. Percussive acoustic rhythm guitars with light maraca-like drumming. Relief comes from the vocals: parallel thirds in the verses with John on the bottom part and Paul on top, yet John's is the voice you hear as the melody — a recurring illusion in their catalogue. Surviving takes document the arrangement being found: an early one is in 3/4, with electric rhythm guitar and no intro at all.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-ll-cry-instead.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'll Cry Instead
the-beatles-i-ll-cry-instead.html:
Pollack's analysis

Standard two-bridge model with no solo, no double verse and no outro — it simply stops at the end of the last verse. The analytical interest is the split between sections: the verses are bluesy in both melody and chords (I, IV, V only), while the bridge is a short-lived but real modulation to V with none of the blues in it.

Form. Two bars of intro vamping on I, a 16-bar verse in four equal phrases, an 8-bar bridge in two, and a complete halt at the end. (For the film's running-and-jumping scene this was originally meant to run instead of "Can't Buy Me Love"; to fix the timing an alternate version was spliced with the first verse repeated at the end, which is what appears on the United Artists album.)

Harmony. Harmonic rhythm is close to plodding for most of the verse, and the speed-up in the final phrase is what makes the section feel closed (). The intro's guitar hints at a chord on the offbeat, but those are neighbour tones filling between two tonics rather than a change of root. The bridge's pivot is deliberately clumsy (): the first move signals nothing on its own, the next tells you something is happening without telling you what, and you don't get a clear key again until the new tonic is nailed down by its own ii–V–I near the end — at which point the song scampers straight home in the final bar, the fastest harmonic rhythm anywhere in it.

Melody. Bluesy in the verses only, and not consistently even there: the tune keeps alternating the natural and flat third, and that wobble is most of its character (). The phrase over the IV chord is the specimen, carrying both the flat seventh and flat third while riding roughshod over the chord underneath.

Arrangement. John's is the only voice, double-tracked and unusually tightly synced. The overall sound is countryish — strummed rhythm guitar, a chordal obbligato lead part, prominent tambourine, and a recurring habit of zooming up into chords from the note below. In the two verses that follow a bridge, the penultimate phrase strips out to walking bass plus tambourine only, which links the sections without needing a transition.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-ll-follow-the-sun.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'll Follow the Sun
the-beatles-i-ll-follow-the-sun.html:
Early McCartney ballad written as a teenager. Ringo plays brushes on his own knees — no kit used. Sparse and delicate, with a bittersweet lyric about leaving before things go wrong.

Chords

Key: C major

Verse: G – F7 – C – D – C – Em/B – D7 – G7 → V – IV7 – I – II7 – I – iii – V7/V – V7 (the D and D7 are secondary dominants pulling toward G)

Middle ("And now the time has come"): Dm – Fm6 – C – C7 → ii – iv6 – I – I7 (the Fm6 borrowed minor-iv — classic McCartney)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-ill-follow-the-sun-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

One of McCartney's earliest songs (written as a teenager, cut for Beatles for Sale, 1964) — a gentle, bright acoustic ballad. Notably Ringo played light percussion by slapping his knees / a packing case rather than a full kit, keeping it soft and intimate. Simple major-key warmth with a sweet descending melodic turn.

Steal this

  • Soft-percussion substitute: knee-slaps / boxes / brushes (Hand Clap Studio, light perc) instead of a kit on a gentle song.
  • Bright, simple acoustic + close vocal — early-McCartney warmth, minimal processing.
  • A tender secondary-dominant lift in a plain frame.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Beatles for Sale · search "The Beatles — I'll Follow the Sun"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'll Follow the Sun (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I'll Follow The Sun — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #60.

Form. The acoustic surface says folk song; the chords and the tune are not remotely folk. He reads it as the same blending trick they had been running with blues, with folk elements substituted in, and hears the verse harmony as carrying a deliberate or at least unfixed awkwardness — a 1960 Quarrymen tape has the same form in G with the melody sitting badly on the chords, and the released version reharmonises heavily without fully smoothing it out. Textbook two-bridge model. The intro is 2 bars, and turns out to be nothing but the last two bars of the verse pre-announced — the same two bars serve as the outro. Verse 8 bars, scanning as two 4-bar phrases metrically but melodically a single long phrase; bridge 8, two genuinely parallel phrases.

Harmony. Intro / verse tail: I – V – IV – I · Verse: V – IV7 – I – V-of-V · I – iii(6/4) – V-of-V – V – I – V – IV – I · Bridge: ii – iv – I – V-of-IV ‖ ii – iv – I – ii. Three curveballs in the verse: an F7 that never resolves to B♭ (a dominant seventh used for colour, not function), a V-of-V whose resolution is deferred (), and iii turning up in 6/4. Both verse and bridge start away from the tonic and converge on it; the bridge then closes on ii, exactly what the following verse needs since the verse opens on V.

Notable. What holds the verse together is a concealed chromatic line cliché in an inner voice — D – E♭ – E – F♯ — implied purely by voice leading rather than played out loud, plus a speed-up in harmonic rhythm across the second half. The bridge answers with the same device made explicit, a descending A – A♭ – G carried by John's vocal counterpoint, which is what produces the minor iv (), rare in a Paul song of this period. The verse tune is a series of upward leaps of a fourth across an unusually wide arch (), and there is no percussion part at all.

Against this page. Agrees on C major.

the-beatles-i-ll-get-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'll Get You
the-beatles-i-ll-get-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

A rushed B-side Pollack rates as plain by essentially every compositional measure — which is exactly what makes it useful. With form and harmony offering nothing unusual, what's left is a set of ingredients already unmistakably theirs. The one forward-looking move is a minor v chord in a major key.

Form. The short single-bridge model. Every section enters on a pickup, ahead of its downbeat. Verse lyrics run ABA and all three verses close with the same refrain-like tag — the hook that the 4-bar intro exists to plant. The outro grows straight out of the last verse, repeating its final phrase three times with the harmonica left ringing after everything else stops.

Harmony. Unrelievedly in one key, roughly half a dozen chords, but an unusual number of them arrive embellished: added sixth on I, major seventh on IV, a 7/9 on the V-of-V. The minor v is why the essay earns keeping — a minor dominant inside a major home key, tilting the phrase modal and bluesy where the ear expects major (). The bridge doesn't modulate at all; it just starts away from home and converges, with a deliberately drawn-out approach to V.

Melody. Centred inside a single octave, with the verse tags opening space below it and the bridge opening space above. The tune is thick with appoggiaturas, and those leaning notes are precisely why so many chords read as embellished () — write the leaning tones first and let them name the chords, and the added sixths and ninths sound motivated rather than decorative. The bridge is a clean textbook case of harmony recolouring a fixed melodic figure: the same three-note descent is sung three times over three different chords and lands differently each time.

Arrangement. A nondescript backing track carrying a lot of fussy detail. The harmonica plays no hook phrase but runs almost continuously, resting only through the bridge — necessarily an overdub, since John sings throughout. Handclaps appear only in the intro as stand-in percussion, and the drums don't enter until a single fill at its end.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-m-a-loser.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm A Loser
the-beatles-i-m-a-loser.html:
Pollack's analysis

The most folk-leaning thing they'd recorded to that point, and Pollack builds the case structurally rather than by pointing at the acoustic guitars: strict verse/refrain alternation, different lyrics each verse telling a narrative in second person, a proverb for an ending, a tiny chord vocabulary and zero modulation. He also flags it as the real turning point in John's writing usually credited to "You've Got To Hide Your Love Away".

Form. Verse/refrain alternation throughout, no bridge. The unusual move is the instrumental break: a hybrid of the verse's first eight bars plus a complete refrain. Neither piece works alone — the verse is too static to carry a solo, and a refrain-only break would have to either follow a sung refrain or replace one. The 4-bar intro is ad-lib and out of tempo, with the full band holding off until its last beats rather than entering at the a-tempo downbeat.

Harmony. Everything stays in one key. Heavy ♭VII makes the harmony modal rather than bluesy (), and the repeated juxtaposition of ♭VII against V produces a cross relation that is the song's harmonic signature. The verse is static and closed — the same four-bar progression four times — while the refrain contrasts by starting off the tonic and ending on V, which is what motivates the section that follows. The refrain's last bar is the only place in the whole song where the harmonic rhythm goes faster than one chord per bar.

Melody. Mixolydian rather than blues: major 3rd and ♭7 run consistently through the verses, while the natural 7th and the 6th degree are withheld entirely from the verses and appear only in the refrain () — the refrain sounds like a different place with no chord change required. The tune repeatedly puts notes against chords they don't belong to (), which reads as deliberate primitivism.

Arrangement. Contrast between sections is engineered on every axis at once (): single-tracked solo vocal in the verse against double-tracked plus harmony in the refrain, oompah bass against walking bass, restrained drums against sizzling ones. Ringo plays exactly one fill in the entire song.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-m-down.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm Down
the-beatles-i-m-down.html:
Pollack's analysis

A deliberately regressive fifties R&B rave-up on a B-side, where the tone of the shouting matters more than the words and sounding improvised on the spot is part of the aesthetic. What makes it worth studying anyway: underneath the thrown-together surface the blues frames are carefully varied — the verse runs a distorted 14 bars while the breaks and refrains run genuine twelves.

Form. Verse, verse, guitar-solo break, verse, organ-solo break, then three refrains fading out. No bridge and no relief section — the entire song is blues frames in alternation.

Harmony. Strictly I, IV and V. The 14-bar verse is a standard twelve-bar frame with its middle phrase stretched by one extra statement of the title phrase; cut two bars out of the middle and the textbook form is sitting right there (). Extending one phrase and leaving everything else alone is what makes the lopsidedness read as energy rather than error. The first break holds V through bar 10 where the later ones move to IV.

Melody. Saturated with ♭3s and ♭7s throughout. Verse 1 opens with Paul completely unaccompanied — no bass note, no drum, nothing to locate either key or downbeat — and it retains the power to startle no matter how familiar the record is.

Arrangement. The first and last phrases of every verse carry sudden syncopated accents followed by an abrupt rest in the backbeat (). That gives the verse bookend symmetry, sets it against the bouncy texture used everywhere else, and imposes a slow periodic rhythm across the whole composition. The two breaks are staged to escalate over identical harmony by varying only the stops: the first keeps the verse's dramatic pauses, the second drops them, which loosens the section and sets up the jam-session feel for the rest of the record without anyone actually playing looser.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-m-happy-just-to-dance-with.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm Happy Just To Dance With You
the-beatles-i-m-happy-just-to-dance-with.html:
Pollack's analysis

A short song with a paradoxically long form — brisk tempo, small sections, a refrain heard three times plus its second half doing duty as the intro. Analytically the interest is the major/minor pairing: the relative keys keep swapping the role of home, with the verse always clearly major, the intro and refrains always starting minor, and the outro turning that duality into an actual fight before the major wins ().

Form. Intro and refrain share a plan of four 2-bar phrases, the first four bars instrumental and the last four turning out to be the refrain's back half. The verse is also 8 bars in four 2-bar phrases: a parallel couplet, then two phrases heard as one long balancing phrase. The outro is 7 bars, elided with the last bar of the final verse.

Harmony. Chord selection is plain except for an augmented V substituting for the ordinary major one. The verse gets a jazzy touch from putting iii between I and ii where vi would have been the obvious choice — that parallel chord-stream motion is the whole flavour. The outro is the payoff, entered by a deceptive cadence off the augmented chord (): you expect the tonic and get vi instead, which flips the key reading back to minor. Their standard trick would be a triple rote repeat of the final phrase; here they pull the deceptive cadence twice and only play it straight the third time. The ending is on an added-sixth chord — I and vi superimposed, the major prevailing with the bitter-sweet vi still embedded in it.

Melody. The refrain tune is markedly pentatonic with downward gestures dominating; the verse tune is unrestricted in pitch content and shaped as an arch. That contrast, plus the key contrast, is what separates sections that are otherwise formally identical.

Arrangement. George's double-tracked lead. The apparently throwaway reverberated backing part is actually what carries the song's rhythmic hook: its move always lands with a heavy syncopation on the "two-and", punctuated by a drum fill in the intro and first refrain. Backing-vocal entries are staged rather than repeated — later on they enter a phrase earlier than they did the first time.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-m-looking-through-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm Looking Through You
the-beatles-i-m-looking-through-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

Folk rock with a light blues coating, and the analytical interest is almost entirely rhythmic-metric: the words are scanned off-centre against four-square phrasing, and the verse is a genuine puzzle — Pollack cannot settle where the downbeat of each phrase falls, and lays out both parses with their costs. Parsing the downbeat just before the first word gives clean AABA' poetry and sensible chords at the cost of an awkward meta-syncopation; parsing that bar as a pickup removes the syncopation but starts every phrase on an odd chord and worsens the final elision. Neither is free.

Form. Textbook layout — two bridges with one verse between them. A 2-bar intro cell played three times plus a tag; four sung verse phrases in AABA′ with the last eliding into a vamping connector that reuses the intro cell; a clean 4 + 4 bridge; and an outro on the same vamp.

Harmony. An unusual key for them, likely written a few frets down and capo'd up. Two things carry it: the deceptive move to vi at the start of the third phrase (), the major key wilting into its relative minor, which is the monotony-breaker; and a harmonic rhythm unusually elastic for the Beatles at this point (), which is part of why the metric parse is hard. 4–3 suspensions unify the song () — quick and buried at the end of the first two verse phrases, huge and exposed at the end of the bridge. The intro's opening six-four is the same idea in disguise: better heard as a dual appoggiatura on the V chord than as a root-position tonic.

Melody. Diatonic major almost throughout, decorated with appoggiaturas; the only chromatic colour is bluesy ♭3 at each verse climax and ♭7 in the riffs trailing it. A fixed bass lick recurs under every I–IV–ii, descending against a rising tune — once you hear it, it works as a subliminal hook.

Arrangement. No drum kit; percussion is thigh slaps and handclaps plus tambourine, and the tambourine part is scheduled, not sprayed — deliberately silent under all four sung verse phrases. The lead is double-tracked everywhere except the outro, and dropping to single-tracking there buys a late jump in intimacy for nothing.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-i-m-only-sleeping.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm Only Sleeping
the-beatles-i-m-only-sleeping.html:
Harrison recorded a guitar solo which was then played backwards and overdubbed. Lennon captured the half-awake sensation in the arrangement as well as the lyrics. Deliberately drowsy tempo and feel.

Chords

Key: E minor (relative G major)

Verse: Em – Am – G – C – G – B7 → i – iv – ♭III – ♭VI – ♭III – V7 (the B7 is the harmonic-minor dominant pulling back to Em)

"Please don't wake me": G – Am – Bm – Am – Cmaj7 → ♭III – iv – v – iv – ♭VImaj7 (or in the relative G: I – ii – iii – ii – IVmaj7)

"Keeping an eye on the world": Dm – E7 – Am – Am7 → a brief modal sidestep tonicizing Am.

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-im-only-sleeping-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Revolver (1966). The first Beatles use of a backwards lead guitar — Harrison worked out a solo, then Martin/Emerick recorded it note-for-note reversed onto tape for that unmistakable sucking, dreamlike swell. The drowsy vocal is lightly vari-sped for a heavy-lidded droop.

Steal this

  • Backwards guitar/instrument: write a part, reverse the audio (kHs Reverser / reverse-render) for a dreamlike sucking swell.
  • Vari-speed the vocal down slightly for a drowsy, heavy feel (Little AlterBoy).
  • Languid, behind-the-beat feel = the arrangement's mood.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Revolver · search "The Beatles — I'm Only Sleeping"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm Only Sleeping (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I'm Only Sleeping — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #94.

Form. A song where gesture outranks content — his own distinction: content is the care spent on tune, chords and form; gesture is the disorienting effect of jamming recognisable clichés together and coating them in studio processing. Here that is a boozy jazz ride-beat, a patter-song tune, cooing forties backing vocals and a backwards guitar in one room. The structural feature is an elision: the bridge runs into the following verse so smoothly that the verse's first phrase is initially heard as the bridge's second phrase, which retroactively makes the bridge feel like a fragment rather than a section. Verse an odd 9 bars despite clean AA′ phrasing (); refrain 6 bars and not remotely binary inside; refrains before each bridge get two extra bars of a time-stopping i-chord vamp; the guitar solo fills only the 5-bar A′ half of a verse.

Harmony. Verse: i – iv – III – VI – III – V · i – iv – III – VI (2) – iv · Refrain: III – iv – v – iv – VI(maj7, 2) · i (2) · Bridge: vii – V-of-iv → (in a minor) iv – V – i – VI. Both verse phrases end open but differently — phrase 1 stops on V, which asks for a repeat; phrase 2 ends VI → iv, which asks for something new. The refrain runs a chord stream (stepwise root motion III–iv–v–iv) they had not used since the early singles, and that plus the fat major seventh is where the jazzy air comes from. Harmonically the song is all feint and no commitment (): it gestures toward the relative major without completing a modulation, and the bridge's tentative move to A minor is what pays for the elision.

Notable. The backing track was cut normally and slowed on playback while John's vocal was sped up. The backwards guitar does not appear until verse 2. Two tiny bass passing notes — a B between C and A minor, a G between A minor and F — quietly unify the track.

Against this page. He reads the record in E-flat minor, because backing track and vocal were varispeeded in opposite directions, and then discusses everything in E minor for legibility — which is the key this page uses. Same analysis, different reference pitch.

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I'm So Tired (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I'm So Tired — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #138.

Form. A song that swings between exhaustion and agitation, and does it with two clichés — I–vi–IV–V in the verse, I–IV–V in the refrain — with exactly two non-cliché chords dropped into the verse to break them. Verse-heavy with a refrain that functions as an outburst, then a complete ending rather than a fade. Verse 12 bars, AAB, blues-shaped, harmonically open — every verse begins on I and ends on V or IV, never at rest. Refrain also 12 bars but in short phrases in an AABBC pattern, and harmonically closed, a full circle back to I. Outro is the refrain's last phrase repeated three times. The ascending bassline pickup that opens the track also restarts verse 3 straight out of the refrain, as if the outburst had not happened.

Harmony. Verse: I – ♯V/III – IV – V · I – vi – IV – V · I – ♯Vaug – vi – iv. Two deliberate cliché-busters: the G♯ major in bar 2 of the opening phrase where the second phrase puts F♯ minor — so the two "identical" phrases are not, and the G♯→D that follows is root motion by tritone, close to unheard of in pop and specific to John's songs — and the augmented triad in bar 2 of the third phrase, which he says should not get a Roman numeral at all, being voice leading between the chords on either side (). The phrase then lands on minor iv, set up by a preceding chord that forces an F♮ cross-relation (). Refrain: I (4 bars) – V (4) – IV (2) – I (2) — three chords, four bars each, a drastically slower harmonic rhythm than the verse's one-per-bar. That, plus a different drum pattern, is the entire mechanism behind the apparent tempo lift (); the tempo never changes.

Notable. The outro is worth studying as an energy curve (): the closing phrase runs three times, the first two heavy with drums and organ glissandos, the third pulled back to muttering — the peak is not the last thing you hear.

Against this page. Agrees on A major. He calls the second section a refrain, where this page's structure: reads it as a bridge.

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I've Got a Feeling (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I've Got A Feeling — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #173.

Form. A loose bluesy groove hiding a genuinely unusual formal experiment: two separate songs, alternated and then stacked on top of each other. He files it under quodlibet rather than medley and reaches for two Broadway precedents, partly to note that both do it better — his verdict is that the idea outruns the material, because Paul's half and John's half don't contrast enough for the superimposition to pay off. The 24-bar verse is laid out as six four-bar units but words and tune cut across that into an 8 + 12 + 4 phrasing, and that asymmetry is what keeps a very static section from feeling like a loop. The bridge is a compressed, rhetorical 10 bars. The stacked section runs only 16 bars, not 24 — his stated principle in miniature: when a section has already been heard many times, condense the late repeats.

Harmony. Four chords plus a chromatic device. Intro / verse vamp: I with IV6/4 decoration, alternating bars · Verse (24): [vamp ×4] · I7 – I7 – V–♭VII – IV · I – IV – I – IV · Verse′ (24): I – IV – I – IV, ×6 · Bridge (10): V (2) – ♭VII (2) · IV–IV6/3 – ♭VII–G♯dim7 · I (4) · Outro (8): I – Bdim–Cdim – C♯dim – Cdim–Bdim · [vamp ×4]. He insists the alternating IV6/4 in the vamp is decoration inside a harmonic envelope on I, not real root motion — the same call he makes for the slinking diminished chords over their pedal () — and the V → ♭VII move used in both verse and bridge drags a cross relation along with it ().

Notable. The most instructive small thing: Paul is precise about where he breaks the pedal, dropping the actual root under the IV chord only at chosen spots, so the vamp reads as static while the bass is being edited underneath. Entrances are staged across a long span — two guitars only through bar 8, drums at bar 9, bass not until bar 17, piano at bar 20 ().

Against this page. Agrees on A major.

the-beatles-i-ve-just-seen-a-face.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - I've Just Seen a Face
the-beatles-i-ve-just-seen-a-face.html:

Verse: G – Em – C – D – G → I – vi – IV – V – I

Chorus ("Falling, yes I am falling"): D – C – G – C – G → V – IV – I – IV – I

Production & Arrangement

Steal this

  • Bassless acoustic arrangement: let fast strummed acoustics + the vocal carry it — the lack of low end makes it float.
  • Breathless, tumbling melody with no gaps for a headlong rush.
  • Country/folk flatpicking energy.

Why I like it

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - I've Just Seen a Face (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — I've Just Seen A Face — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #74.

Form. Four chords deployed two ways — the pop-rock cliché I – vi – IV – V in the verses, the bluesy V – IV – I in the refrains — and everything else is structural sleight of hand. The layout borrows a different genre's habits in each of its three stretches: two verses back to back at the top is pop-rock, the strict verse/refrain alternation in the second half is folk, and closing on the refrain three times over is an R&B rave-up habit. Intro 10 bars, fully instrumental, three phrases with the last foreshortened so the first verse arrives early (). Verse 12 bars in three phrases with slow harmonic rhythm — the blues frame carrying distinctly non-blues harmony (). Refrain 8 bars, AAB. The tempo never actually changes: the intro's slow triplet pulse against the verse's four-square beat produces an illusion of acceleration.

Harmony. Verse: I (4 bars) · vi (4) · IV (2) – V – I · Refrain: V (2) – IV (2) – I – IV – I. The intro is the interesting passage — it opens on vi under an unaccompanied bass note of the tonic and stays unmoored until its final bars, moving vi → IV (with a 9/6/4 and then a 7th stacked on by passing tones) → V → I, with the V voiced with an appoggiatura in the bass instead of the root.

Notable. The intro's long scalar bassline spans a full octave and has the song's D – C♯ – B – A – G♯ – A hook phrase embedded in its tail, so the hook is introduced as a bass line before it is ever a vocal one. In the verse, bars 3–5 put the tune in parallel tenths with the bass and the identical gesture at bars 7–9 comes out as parallel fifths. The song's only melodic minor third appears in the refrain, which is why that section reads bluesier. Wire brushes rather than sticks; maracas overdubbed onto refrains and solo only.

Against this page. Agrees — his A major is this page's sounding pitch (G shapes, capo 2).

the-beatles-if-i-fell.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - If I Fell
the-beatles-if-i-fell.html:
Lennon's complex intro modulates from a different key into the main verse. Close two-part harmonies between Lennon and McCartney throughout. One of the most harmonically sophisticated early Beatles songs.

Chords

Key: D major (the intro floats in from E♭ minor before settling)

Intro: E♭m – D – D♭ – B♭m – E♭m – D – Em – A → a chromatic descent that resolves onto ii – V (Em – A) of D.

Verse: D – Em – F♯m – Fdim7 – Em – A → I – ii – iii – ♭iii° – ii – V (the Fdim7 is a chromatic passing chord between F♯m and Em)

Bridge ("…cause I couldn't stand the pain"): D9 – G – Gm – D – A7 → I – IV – iv – I – V7 (the Gm borrowed minor-iv is the heartbreak chord)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-if-i-fell-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A Hard Day's Night — an intricate two-part close-harmony ballad (Lennon & McCartney sharing one intertwined melody), with a chromatic intro that sidesteps into the main key. Fragile and precise.

Steal this

  • Chromatic intro into the key as a fragile setup → Modulation.
  • Tender, exposed vocal — minimal backing.

Why I like it

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - If I Fell (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — If I Fell — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #50.

Form. The intro is in a different key from the song — eight bars in D♭ major, during which a D major chord passes by looking incidental, and on the repeat that same D chord is reinterpreted as I of the actual home key. He rates the pivot among their cleverest and most daring. The other oddity is that there is no discrete bridge or refrain at all: contrast comes from an extension that grows out of the middle two verses. Intro 8 bars, two parallel phrases, fully developed as its own section with material used nowhere else and its own backing texture. Verse (original) 10 bars — two parallel 4-bar phrases plus a 2-bar connector into the next verse; verse + extension keeps the first 8 and substitutes an asymmetric 7-bar extension for the connector.

Harmony. Intro: [D♭] ii – ♭II – I – vi · ii – ♭II – [D] I – ii – V · Verse: I – ii – iii – ♭iii° – ii7 – V (×2) · I – iv – V · Extension: I → V/IV (2 bars) – IV – iv (2) – I – V7. You assume the opening E♭ minor is i of the home key; the free-fall through D and down to D♭ leaves you genuinely lost for a couple of bars, and only the return to E♭ minor in bar 5 resets it as ii of D♭ (). After an opening that disorienting, the rest of the song never modulates at all. Stepwise motion is the unifying idea and runs in the harmony as much as the tune; the bittersweetness comes from the minor iv, which enters quietly in the verse connector and then recurs everywhere (). The ♭iii° is not functional — it is the incidental product of three lines moving between the chords on either side ().

Notable. Both sung verse phrases, the connector and the extension all end on V, which is how a ballad with no bridge keeps circulating. John harmonises below Paul in genuine two-part counterpoint — no George vocal at all — and the tell is the open fourths and fifths dropped in where you would expect thirds.

Against this page. Agrees on D major. A refinement: this page says the intro floats in from E♭ minor; Pollack reads the intro as being in D♭ major, with that E♭ minor as its ii.

the-beatles-if-i-needed-someone.html:
Harrison's raga-influenced riff built around a D chord with added open strings. Jangly jangle influenced by The Byrds. Tight Lennon/McCartney harmonies in the chorus.

Verse: A – G – A → I – ♭VII – I (the A↔G drone is the whole hook — Mixolydian, no leading tone)

Bridge ("Had you come some other day"): Em – F♯ – Bm – E → v – V/ii – ii – V (the F♯ major tonicizes the Bm)

Steal this

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - If I Needed Someone (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — If I Needed Someone — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #88.

Form. The verse has almost no harmonic motion at all — the key is asserted by a drone, not by a progression — which makes this an early, plain instance of the sustained-pedal writing that becomes George's default in his Indian period. His useful side-observation is that the device may descend as much from John's habit of sitting on the I chord for four-plus bars ("Ticket To Ride," "Day Tripper") as from Indian classical drone. Two-bridge model with an odd twist: three consecutive verses between the bridges, the middle one instrumental. Intro 4 bars, a 2-bar solo-guitar ostinato played twice, previewing the tune's pitch content, range and off-beat syncopation without giving the melody away. Verse 8 bars but parsed 2 + 3 + 3, very unusual. Outro is 2 bars of I-chord vamp using the exact original ostinato rather than a variation, then a final chord voiced as bare open fifths.

Harmony. Verse: I (4 bars) · ♭VII/I sus (2) · I (2) — the ♭VII superimposed over a held I (, ). Bridge (b minor): iv – V – (V) – i · iv – V – i(=ii of A) – V of A, a textbook pivot modulation () whose return trip is the instructive half: the B minor in bar 7 is heard as i until the E major arrives and the ear retroactively rewrites it as ii. The home key only gets a proper V–I at the very end of the bridge — and that E major chord is the single place in the whole song where G♯ appears, everywhere else it is G natural ().

Notable. The verse tune is straight Mixolydian in a very constricted range, using exactly five pitches; the bridge tune is straight minor. Entrances are staggered across the intro and the first two verses, not just the intro, and inside the harmony phrases the voicing moves from parallel 5/3 chords to a 6/3 inversion at the melodic apex.

Against this page. Pollack reads it in A major — which matches this page's Chords section ("A major, Mixolydian") but not the key: field, which says G major. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-in-my-life.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - In My Life
the-beatles-in-my-life.html:
George Martin recorded the baroque piano solo at half speed, giving it a harpsichord-like timbre when played back at normal speed. Lennon's most personal early lyric, evoking specific Liverpool memories.

Chords

Key: A major

Verse: A – E – F♯m – A7/G – D – Dm – A → I – V – vi – I7/♭7 – IV – iv – I (the D → Dm, IV sliding to minor-iv, is the song's signature heart-tug; the A7/G is a descending bass)

Bridge ("All these places had their moments"): F♯m – D – G – A – F♯m – B – Dm – A → vi – IV – ♭VII – I – vi – II7 – iv – I (the B is a secondary dominant, the Dm the borrowed iv again)

The baroque piano solo (George Martin, recorded half-speed) sits over the verse changes. From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-in-my-life-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Restrained, reflective band arrangement whose one famous flourish is George Martin's baroque piano solo — recorded at half speed, so on normal-speed playback it sounds double-tempo, bright, and harpsichord-like (and physically un-playable by hand). The rest is understated: clean guitars, gentle rhythm section, double-tracked vocal.

Newly discovered during the 2026 archival remix: before landing on the piano solo, George Martin's FIRST attempt at filling the 4th-track "hole" was an organ part — probably a Hammond or Lowrey (unconfirmed from the recording itself), played in a rock-and-roll style. Giles Martin (his son) says this take had never surfaced before this project; his father would have written/scored the counterpoint mentally first, realized it wasn't playable live at tempo by hand, and only then moved to the half-speed piano solution. The 4th track was routinely left as a deliberate "hole" for a late solo overdub on Beatles 4-tracks, since the record was being made for mono and didn't need the solo isolated from the rest of the band.

Tracking detail: guitar, bass and a "ghosted" guide vocal from an early take share one track; the released lead vocal is a replacement — John sang live to the existing backing track and the earlier guide vocal was wiped and re-sung on take 3, standard practice at this session, before Ken Townsend's Artificial Double Tracking existed at Abbey Road. The doubled harmony vocals on the bridge are two genuinely separate live takes of the same part, not an ADT double.

  • The IV → iv (D → Dm) borrowed-minor slide is the harmonic heart-tug (Borrowed Chords); the production stays out of its way.
  • Warm, close, intimate — a storytelling mix, nothing loud.

Steal this

  • Half-speed the solo: record a keyboard/guitar solo with the session slowed, so playback is faster/brighter than you could play — a harpsichord-ish sparkle (Melodyne/warp or literally track at half tempo).
  • IV → iv under a held vocal for instant nostalgia → Borrowed Chords.
  • Understated arrangement: let one flourish be the moment; keep everything else restrained.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Rubber Soul · search "The Beatles — In My Life"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - In My Life (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — In My Life — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #86.

Form. The warmth is real, but his reading is that it sits on top of a persistent unease built into the harmony and the melody's relationship to it — the tune is loaded with free dissonance and rides roughshod over the chords, and the harmony systematically dodges clear V–I closure. Rote alternation of verse and bridge, folk-ballad style, but with a bridge instead of a refrain and with the intro motif reused inconsistently as a spacer between sections, which blurs the folk association. Intro 4 bars, a 2-bar cell stated twice; verse 8, an AA couplet on one 4-bar phrase; bridge 8, a pseudo-AA′ couplet whose two phrases share a melody but are harmonised very differently; outro is spacer, then a short reprise of the bridge's last phrase, then the spacer again modified into a full ending.

Harmony. Intro / spacer: I – V (×2) · Verse: I – V – vi – V-of-IV · IV – iv – I (×2) · Bridge: vi – IV – ♭VII – I · vi – V-of-V – iv – I. Simple chords, indirect syntax. V is scarce and never resolves normally — it appears once in the verse and is answered deceptively by vi (), and in the bridge it does not appear at all. That avoidance is the source of the song's reticence. The verse's minor iv is John's signature, driven by a chromatic descent in an implied inner voice (), and the bridge's second phrase stacks three surprises: V-of-V that is never followed by V (), the F♯/F♮ cross-relation from the minor iv, and the deadpan fact that the melody over all of it is unchanged from the first phrase.

Notable. A rising sixth is the song's motto, opening the intro and closing both verse and bridge. The tune stays rigidly pentatonic until the bridge, where degree 4 enters for the first time on "lovers"; degree 7 never appears in the sung melody at all (). Against that, an unusual load of appoggiaturas, escape tones and unprepared sevenths and ninths () whose cumulative effect reads as weariness. The keyboard solo was played an octave down at half speed and sped up — two payoffs, the impossible velocity and the mangled attack that makes an electric piano read as harpsichord.

Against this page. Agrees on A major.

Why I like it

Listen

  • With the Beatles · search "The Beatles — It Won't Be Long"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - It Won't Be Long (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — It Won't Be Long — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #10.

Form. An album opener whose real interest is that the form refuses to parse. Three two-line couplets recur as X Y X Z Y X Z Y X, and depending on how you cluster them you get a refrain plus a bridge, a compound verse with a bridge, or a compound verse with a refrain — he lays out all three and does not fully commit. It reduces to the two-bridge model with one verse between, but only if you parse the second half of the verse as a mini-refrain that also serves as the intro. Two oddities survive: the verse is not doubled first time round, and its non-refrain half is seven bars, one short of balanced, because the last bar of the first phrase elides into the first bar of its repeat (). Intro/mini-refrain 8 bars as 2 + 2 + 4, starting on vi and converging on I; verse 15; bridge a square 8, harmonically open.

Harmony. Refrain: vi (2) – I (2) – vi (2) – IV·♯ii°7 – I (2) · Verse first half: I – ♭VI – I ‖ I – ♭VI – I – I · Bridge: I – B+ – Bm – C♯7 (V/II) – IV – V – V/V – V. vi acts as a pseudo-dominant to open the refrain, and ♭VI as a dominant substitute in the verse, borrowed from the parallel minor () — his nickname for it is the Buddy Holly chord. The bridge is genuinely open at the end because it exits through V-of-V voiced as a ninth ().

Notable. The rest is a study in chords that are byproducts of voice leading rather than choices. In refrain bar 6 the outer voices hold while the inner two move chromatically, producing a diminished seventh on ♯ii over a static bass — and it lands where the harmonic rhythm quickens, which is why it bites. In the bridge the bass descends chromatically under a held B and the augmented and minor chords falling out of that motion get no Roman numerals at all. The outro cadence uses a barbershop stream of chromatically descending dominant sevenths. The antiphonal "yeah"s are the trick worth studying: John is mixed forward and sings his on the offbeat against the others.

Against this page. Agrees on E major.

the-beatles-it-s-all-too-much.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - It's All Too Much
the-beatles-it-s-all-too-much.html:
Pollack's analysis

George welds an Indian-style harmonic drone to a modal tune and a pop-rock backbeat, then hangs a long improvisatory intro and outro off either end. The analytical punchline: verse and refrain are nearly indistinguishable as music — both 8 bars, both AA' — so any formal parse comes from the words, not from the sound. The track works by sheer length and repetition rather than by content.

Form. The intro runs a bit over a minute in two phases: a high sustained chord and feedback, then one refrain phrase scored for organ alone with no percussion, then a whole instrumental refrain adding guitar, bass, kit and surrealistically wide-panned handclaps, then one more with the title phrase sung. A one-bar spacer is appended to any refrain immediately followed by a verse — punctuation for a form the harmony can't punctuate. The outro runs roughly 2:45, deliberately balanced against the intro and longer than a fair number of complete Beatles songs.

Harmony. There effectively isn't any, and that's the design — the bass holds one note under the entire song (). Chord charts for the refrain print changes on various downbeats; Pollack's firm position is that no root motion occurs anywhere in the section. What sounds like changes is neighbour-tone motion in the inner voices sitting on top of the pedal () — the drone survives and the ear still hears harmony.

Melody. Modal in shape: the tune puts off-kilter weight on scale degrees 2 and 7 while avoiding 4 entirely. Worth setting beside "Within You Without You" for the same kind of scale-degree bias.

Arrangement. Organ, drums and lead guitar underneath, with trumpets and bass clarinet on top. The restraint is in the scheduling: the trumpets are held out until the second instrumental break, then rationed across the final refrains and selected stretches of the outro. A late first entrance is worth more than an early one.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-it-s-only-love.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - It's Only Love
the-beatles-it-s-only-love.html:
Pollack's analysis

A short, soft-focus John song whose whole harmonic character comes from chromatic voice leading, with cross-relations, a transient augmented triad and an odd root succession all falling out of it as side effects. The organising trick: the same ♭VII chord is used twice with two different meanings, changed only by what approaches it.

Form. Verse and refrain twice, plus intro and outro. The boundary between them is deliberately soft — the verse ends so open that the two arguably function as one long combined unit. The verse is 12 bars in AAB, matching the blues phrase pattern with neither blues harmony nor blues style; the refrain is 8 bars in two roughly parallel phrases, each launched by the same route.

Harmony. The verse opening is generated by a descending chromatic bass, which forces an odd root succession from I through iii to ♭VII. Putting that iii chord in second inversion and letting the bassline's logic carry it is what keeps it from sounding arbitrary — in root position the same progression is much stranger, and some analysts would decline to call it a chord at all. The ♭VII is borrowed both times (, ) but functions differently: in the verse it lands as IV-of-IV, arrived at chromatically from above; in the refrain it's approached from vi, where you'd expect IV or ii, and acts as a subdominant leading directly to V, setting up a cross-relation. Low-grade dissonance runs continuously () — some resolving properly, some left as pure colour. Both verse phrases open out to an augmented V which then declines to resolve and backs off to IV instead; the refusal is the emotional content.

Melody. The hooks are all built on a sighing 6–5 appoggiatura — the guitar lick descending through intro and outro, and the vocal's peak moments in both verse and refrain.

Arrangement. Guitar-dominated with almost no percussion, which should read as Byrds-style folk rock except the hazy final mix pulls against it. John is single-tracked in the verses and doubled in the refrains, and the double drifts far enough out of sync to raise the question of whether one pass is a surviving guide vocal.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-julia.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Julia
the-beatles-julia.html:
Pollack's analysis

A fingerpicked acoustic song whose harmony is the least folk-like thing about it: strong chord colours over deliberately weak root motion, with dissonances that arrive unprepared and leave unresolved. Pollack's phrase is free dissonance, and this is the best single case of it in the catalogue — there's enough V–I to keep the key in place, and almost nothing else behaves.

Form. The section labels are genuinely arguable; what settles them is the title being repeated mantra-like in the refrain regardless of which other words change. The verse is 9 bars as 4 + 5, the refrain 13 as 4 + 4 + 5, and both elide forward into whatever follows; the bridge is 10 bars scanning 4 + 2 + 4 after a two-bar wind-down.

Harmony. The vi7 is the model case of free dissonance — the seventh exists only because one note is held across the whole phrase, and it does no harmonic or contrapuntal work (). Root motion is intentionally slack: vi→iii is a fourth down, passive like a plagal move rather than driving like V–I, and iii→V is weaker still because the two triads share two of their three notes. The refrain is where the real work happens: vi into a minor v in a major key, then a chord that reads as V-of-ii and retroactively recasts what preceded it as a pivot () — and the promised modulation is then simply refused, the next chord being the Lennon-standard minor iv (), which throws off a double cross-relation and withholds its own root until beat 3. That root-delay is systematic: the picking pattern often postpones the root until the middle of the bar in which the chord nominally changes, so for two beats you can't name it. The bridge modulates to the relative minor () and does it weakly on purpose.

Melody. Confined to a sixth, which is where the held-back quality comes from. Exactly two escapes from that box, and both are saved for late.

Arrangement. Fingerpicked acoustic, sung sotto voce, recorded at a level so low that playing it audibly makes everything else on the album too loud. The lead is single-tracked and deliberately flat in delivery, doubled only for the last phrase of each section. In the outro John drops the iii chord from the penultimate pass and restores it for the very last one — its absence is what tells you it had been carrying the song's yearning all along.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-lady-madonna.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Lady Madonna
the-beatles-lady-madonna.html:
Pollack's analysis

A slice-of-life character sketch welded onto a hard-driving semi-blues, and by 1968 the hardest-rocking thing the band had released in a while. The fast tempo and very short verse mean the song racks up a lot of sections for an ordinary running time, and an unusually large share of them are instrumental.

Form. Verses arrive in pairs everywhere except the very last one, so the eight-bar unit reads as sixteen; counting the intro — a complete instrumental run-through of the verse — the opening block is effectively a verse stated three times over. The bridge is 16 bars in four phrases, ABAC.

Harmony. A small vocabulary used pointedly. The ♭VI–♭VII–I cadence is the whole harmonic idea — neither of those chords contains any of the home key's sharps, so the approach to the tonic is a wash of cross-relations (), and that clash is the sound rather than an error to fix. The actual V chord is withheld from the verse entirely and appears only at the end of each bridge. Because the home key is already soaked in the blue ♭3, the bridge can slip to the ♭III key through the parallel minor (), converge there, and swerve back at the last moment onto a dominant deliberately ambiguous between major and minor — which is exactly what makes the major verse feel earned when it returns. Harmonic rhythm is structural (): steady through the verse with a small acceleration into the cadence, then half speed through the bridge.

Melody. The tune leans on ♭3 and ♭7 () while the verse simultaneously stresses the diatonic major 6th against a bassline running ♭6 underneath — friction audible long before it's explicable. The bass riff's third note is a notation puzzle Pollack leaves open, and his answer is that the ear takes it both ways at once.

Arrangement. Piano, drums and bass with the exotic layer supplied by vocalising into cupped hands to fake a brass section, joined by real saxophones. The bassline competes with the tune for attention and is then promoted to lead in the instrumental verses instead of a solo being written. The intro is piano and drums alone, and the outro hands the track back to that same reduced trio, so everything between reads as accumulation rather than clutter.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-let-it-be.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Let It Be
the-beatles-let-it-be.html:
Pollack's analysis

The whole song runs on four chords and a five-note scale and never once leaves the home key — one passing chromatic note in the coda is the only non-diatonic pitch in the record. Everything that makes it sound larger than that is ornamentation and voice leading. Pollack treats it as the diatonic-Paul counterpart to "Hey Jude", and uses the bootlegged Get Back mix as his reference text because it's the least worked-over of the three.

Form. The verse is built directly on the intro's eight bars, so the intro pre-loads the harmony without giving away the tune — the listener arrives at the vocal already oriented and still surprised. The refrain is a plain AB pair of four-bar phrases; the coda is convergent, and on its first appearance is doubled.

Harmony. Four chords and nothing else. The modal flavour is a cadence habit, not a chord choice: despite V appearing constantly, resolution is nearly always plagal (), and where V does move it tends to slide to IV (blues style) or to vi (a classical deceptive move) rather than home (). Starve V of its resolution and an entirely ordinary diatonic set turns modal. The refrain's first phrase is a symmetrical root progression — a falling fourth twice — deliberately camouflaged by a stepwise bass and parallel tenths above it, and two spots stay productively ambiguous between two chord labels depending on which appoggiatura you privilege.

Melody. Almost entirely pentatonic (), including the guitar solo; the fourth degree appears essentially once, as a neighbour tone. Verse and refrain each span a ninth but the refrain sits a third higher, and the two sections end with the identical phrase, which reads differently each time — near the top of the arch in the verse, part of its descent in the refrain ().

Arrangement. A textbook energy ramp: piano alone, then cymbals, then bass in verse 2, full kit for the refrains and solo, percussion pulled back for the final verse, everything restored for the finish. The octave vocal flips are held back until after the guitar solo, and the outro plays the coda phrase once where the earlier coda played it twice — halving a returning section on its last appearance avoids a pompous ending.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-little-child.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Little Child
the-beatles-little-child.html:
Pollack's analysis

Four chords, no minor or altered harmony at all, and Pollack rates it the weakest of the five consecutive originals opening the album's side one — while arguing it works anyway as an unembarrassed rocker. Two features are worth the study: a form that parses differently depending on whether you follow the music or the lyrics, and a genuine instrumental break in strict 12-bar blues, which is rare this early.

Form. Musically it reads as the standard model. Follow the lyrics instead and it inverts — the "verse" repeats its words unchanged four times (so it's really a refrain) while only the "bridge" varies (so it's really the verse). Pollack keeps the musical reading but flags the ambiguity, and notes that "It Won't Be Long", written around the same time, poses the same puzzle. The 4-bar intro is in strict tempo despite sounding ad lib; a piano glissando is what lets your ear place the barline, and that moment of orientation is itself a hook. The bridge is 6 bars in three even 2-bar phrases — a poetic triplet against the verse's quatrains, and the odd count reads as relief rather than error.

Harmony. Only four chords, all major: I, IV, V and V-of-V (). The absence of anything minor, diminished, augmented or altered is what keeps the emotional tone flat and untroubled. The second verse is a small rewrite of the first purely to close its second phrase on I instead of leaving it open — one bar is the whole cost of a smooth handoff. The break is a pure 12-bar blues except that its last two chords are replaced with the verse's own tag (), which is what stitches an imported form into the song.

Melody. Facile and simple by design, with almost none of the appoggiaturas that fill something like "I'll Get You". The one exception is a sharp dissonance on a bridge downbeat.

Arrangement. Heavily overdubbed for such a plain track, muddy even in the original mix. The harmonica's spicy ninth in the intro comes back as the major ninth chords running through the verses and much of the break.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-long-long-long.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Long, Long, Long
the-beatles-long-long-long.html:
Pollack's analysis

A George song in which nearly every section refuses to begin on the tonic, and several refuse to end on it either — an approach-avoidance pattern in the harmony mirroring the lyric's inability to face its subject head-on. The style is a three-way blend of jazz waltz, folk and period psychedelia: ternary meter, ninth chords, acoustic backing, sitar, and an outro belonging to no other part of the song.

Form. Refrain and verse in rotating pairs, one bridge, and an outro grown out of the last verse. Phrases are consistently stretched a bar or more past where they need to end, which is where the exhausted quality comes from () — the verse is 13 bars as 6 + 7, the bridge 15 as 6 + 9, and the refrain a single four-bar phrase plus a two-bar sitar riff.

Harmony. Unambiguously major, but the tonic almost never sits at a section boundary, so the key feels asserted rather than felt. The verse's second phrase starts where the first phrase's third bar started, which lets the chord ending phrase 1 do double duty as phrase 2's opening — the seam disappears, and the section stops sounding like blocks. The bridge is where the harmony finally has a goal, and Pollack extracts a specific craft lesson: phrase 1 closes on ii, holds it an extra bar, and never gets its V — you have to go back and take the whole phrase again to earn the resolution, and on that second pass the wait is only two bars. Shortening the delay on the repeat is what makes it a climax () — the contraction, not the volume.

Melody. Local motion is almost all stepwise, yet the song covers a wide range; the breadth is engineered by assigning each section its own band of the register rather than by writing leaps ().

Arrangement. Strummed acoustic, an organ mastered with absurdly deep flutter, and sitar used as a psychedelic lead-guitar substitute rather than for anything Indian. Dynamics live at the extremes, and the only quiet percussion on the track is the brushwork in one refrain/verse pair. The ending is a small event of its own — a rattling wine bottle, off-key falsetto chanting, and a last drum hit after the track appears to be over.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-love-me-do.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Love Me Do
the-beatles-love-me-do.html:
Pollack's analysis

The first single, and Pollack's case is that the primitive surface hides real compositional idiosyncrasy: a thirteen-bar verse whose phrase lengths follow the lyric scansion, a tonic established with no dominant anywhere until the bridge, and vocal harmony built on open fifths instead of thirds. Whether that originality was intended or a by-product of imperfectly copying their influences is a question he leaves standing.

Form. The stock two-bridge layout with one verse dividing the bridges. What's unusual is the instrumental solo sitting inside a repeated bridge rather than a verse. The verse is an odd 13 bars phrased AAAB as 2 + 2 + 2 + 7, following the lyric rather than any metrical template. Every section starts squarely on the downbeat, which contributes to the clunky impression.

Harmony. Three chords in the entire song, and two of them do all the work: the tonic is established by I–IV–I with no dominant at all (), and V doesn't arrive until the downbeat of the bridge — where its first appearance becomes an event on its own. The bridge tune then alternates the natural and flat seventh continuously, so even the one place the major mode asserts itself stays contested. The verse's regular harmonic rhythm breaks at the point of greatest lyric stretch, which is what makes the irregular phrasing read as expressive rather than lost.

Melody. Mixolydian in effect — heavy ♭7s and no leading tone until the bridge, with the flat seventh doing the mode-defining work () — plus bent blue thirds sitting directly on top of major chords containing the natural third (). The hook is the harmonica's descending four-note figure, and because it also closes every verse it saturates the record ().

Arrangement. About as unadorned as a Beatles recording gets. Two vocal details became house style: open fifths instead of thirds on the title phrase, which melds the two voices into a single colour rather than stacking them, and holding one note in the upper part while the lower moves stepwise. Texture cycles deliberately across a verse — harmonica alone, then vocal duet, then a solo voice with the hook figure behind it.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-love-you-to.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Love You To
the-beatles-love-you-to.html:
Pollack's analysis

This goes well past the era's standard-issue add-a-sitar gesture: mode, melodic construction, rhythm and instrumentation are all handled in genuinely Indian terms, and even the boxy rock form preserves the Indian convention of a free-tempo improvised slow introduction. Pollack, who studied the tradition formally, is warm about the authenticity and blunt about the failure — the Western and Indian elements sit side by side rather than fusing, and the imported studio players comprehensively upstage George.

Harmony. A drone, with occasional implied oscillation toward ♭VII, and nothing else (). The drone is voiced as an open fifth so it never states the third, which leaves the home chord's major/minor identity formally undecided even though the sitar leans hard on the minor third (). This is the Indian aesthetic doing what harmony normally does in Western music: no teleology, no progress, elaboration over a fixed centre.

Melody. Dorian in Western terms, but a raga is more than a mode — it also carries characteristic riffs and a division of the scale into two registral halves, and the song honours both, with recurrent riffs staying within one half or the other. If static harmony is going to hold interest, that registral structure is what has to carry it.

Rhythm. Trickier than the "sixteen beats" instruction in the session literature suggests. A 3/4 bar is hidden in the lead-in to the refrain, and you don't notice because the same sitar hook fills a normal 4/4 bar a couple of bars later — the ear matches the figure and never audits the bar. Another 3/4 sits inside the refrain, filled the same way. The verse plods in even quarters and then breaks into a syncopated melisma that loosens your grip on the downbeat, with the drums dropping out for the two bars where that happens. The solo resists the analysis entirely, partly because the sitar declaims in irrational groupings against the steady pulse.

Arrangement. Effectively George plus hired Indian studio musicians, with tambourine added in verse 2 and a fuzz-toned embellishment on the ♭VII. The refrain is a call-and-response between voice and sitar, and the solo is the peak of the record.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-lovely-rita.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Lovely Rita
the-beatles-lovely-rita.html:
Pollack's analysis

The first properly rock-shaped thing on the album in a long while, placed as relief after the Indian, vaudeville and music-hall detours. The analytical interest is that root motion by fourths and fifths does nearly all the work: the verse runs the "Hey Jude" progression, and the bridge sets off down an actual non-diatonic circle of fifths, stretching the key almost to breaking before abandoning it.

Form. Pollack flags the section labels as arguable rather than the boundaries — what he calls the verse could be a refrain, and what he calls the bridge could be the verse. The intro is 8 measures thickened by staggered entrances; the bridge runs 14 measures where 16 is what you expect; the outro takes roughly a third of the record.

Harmony. The intro converges on I; both verse phrases converge on V instead, and that change of target is what separates the sections despite a shared vocabulary. The bridge is the real event: a diatonic circle of fifths would stay inside the key and return home in seven chords, while the non-diatonic version ignores the key signature, makes every chord major, and needs twelve. The bridge starts down that road, bails out at ♭III, jumps back to I, and leaves chromatic false relations in its wake (, ) — three or four chords out is enough to unmoor the key, and the abrupt snap home is the effect. Two spots are prolongations rather than progressions: the verse before the piano solo is an envelope around V dressed in ninths, elevenths and thirteenths that don't change its function, and the outro's long vamp boils down to i–iv–i in the relative minor, so the song ends in a key it never established ().

Arrangement. Conservative on paper and then covered wall to wall in effects: ADT set so the lead vocal reads as a peculiar single rather than a normal double, stray spoken remarks left on the backing track, an electronically altered kazoo, distant pristine backing vocals. Maracas are held back until the second phrase of each bridge — one percussion colour reserved for half a section rather than a new part written. The piano solo is very likely George Martin using the "In My Life" method, played an octave down at half speed.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-lucy-in-the-sky-with-diamond.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Lucy In The Sky With Diamonds
the-beatles-lucy-in-the-sky-with-diamond.html:
Pollack's analysis

Cut from the same cloth as "Tomorrow Never Knows" and "Strawberry Fields Forever" — less subtle than either, no less ingenious. The shifting key structure and the alternation of 3/4 and 4/4 do to the music what the imagery does to the words. Pollack's real claim is that beneath the surface chaos the song runs on one closed loop built from root motion by thirds, a Möbius strip in which every station is re-heard in the next key (). Each third-move throws off a cross relation for free ().

Form. Verse, bridge, refrain three times through, except that the bridge is dropped before the final pair. The 4-bar intro ostinato contains the complete design of the verse inside it. The verse's two long vocal phrases lie across a limping accompaniment quatrain of 4 / 5 / 4 / 6 bars. The bridge should be 16 bars and starts out that way, but where its fourth phrase would begin it's foreshortened by the switch to 4/4, the quarter note of the 3/4 bars becoming an eighth — a section cut short without sounding cut. The refrain is an unusual 7 bars.

Harmony. Each section has its own key and profile. The verse is essentially a chromatic filling-in of the tonic chord over a descending bass, whose last step implies ♭VI () and eventually gets its head as V of the bridge's key. The bridge's key looks remote and isn't — it's the parallel major of the relative minor of the one before. The refrain is deliberately the ballast, plain I–IV–V three times, ending on a chord that pivots to hand back to the verse; in the outro that same chord is left hanging unresolved instead.

Melody. Kept exceedingly thin given what it's riding on — hum it unaccompanied and there's very little there, which is the point. The bridge is stuck almost monotonously on one repeated note that rides roughshod over the chords beneath it, making a gratuitous ninth on one and a thirteenth on the next; it reads as enervation. The thirds motif governs the melody as well as the harmony: triadic outlining in the verse, a minor-third slide in the bridge, and parallel thirds harmonising the refrain. A song can be unified by an interval instead of a theme.

Arrangement. The opening ostinato is an organ on a celeste-like stop, Baroque in construction — one line implying a complete four-part texture. Paul's bass is the standout and its density is scheduled section by section: downbeats only in the verses, every beat in the bridges, running eighths in the refrains.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-magical-mystery-tour.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Magical Mystery Tour
the-beatles-magical-mystery-tour.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (6) · Verse (16, a vamp) · Refrain (8) · Verse · Refrain · instrumental Bridge (10) · Verse · Refrain · Refrain · fade. The whole back half of the record runs at roughly half the tempo of the front half.

An overture whose one real trick stays visible rather than buried: the song begins and ends in D, but most of it sounds like E. The intro's D–A–E reads either as I–V–V/V in D or as ♭VII–IV–I in E (, ), and the verse then argues for E by sheer repetition while pointedly withholding the V chord that would settle the question. The refrain finally closes it with a complete V–I in D, set up by a stepwise descending bass that gives every step its own chord (), including a minor iv borrowed from the parallel minor. The next verse starts on E and the ambiguity resets.

The bridge is where the withheld E-major V finally arrives, and it runs a slow/fast harmonic-rhythm shift () that fakes an acceleration — right before the real tempo halves. Rhythm carries the form throughout: dotted and on 1-and-3 in the intro, hard four with 2-and-4 accents in the verse, undotted again in the refrain. The arrangement is a deliberate collision of folk-rock strumming, pomposo trumpets and cocktail-lounge piano, with block vocals cut slow so they play back high and strident.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-martha-my-dear.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Martha My Dear
the-beatles-martha-my-dear.html:
McCartney's piano showcase — no guitars present. Unexpected key changes throughout. George Martin's orchestral arrangement. Possibly written about McCartney's sheepdog Martha or girlfriend Jane Asher.

Chords

Key: played in C shapes with capo 3 → sounds in E♭ · the bridge modulates

Verse (C shapes): C – C6 – Em – Dsus4/D – G – F – G7 → I – I6 – iii – II7 (V/V) – V – IV – V7

"Hold your head up, you silly girl": Bm – Em – D – A – Em – A – F♯m – Bm → a modulating passage tonicizing the Em/D area before circling back.

Harmonically restless (a piano étude McCartney wrote to stretch his playing). From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-martha-my-dear-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

McCartney solo-ish showpiece (White Album) built on a tricky, leaping piano part with brass + strings (George Martin) answering it. Ragtime-y, major-key bounce; the piano is the whole engine.

Steal this

  • Piano as the arrangement: a busy, leaping left/right-hand part carries harmony + rhythm (Keyscape grand).
  • Brass/string call-and-response answering the piano phrases.
  • Ragtime bounce + unexpected key moves → Modulation.

Why I like it

Listen

  • The Beatles (White Album) · search "The Beatles — Martha My Dear"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Martha My Dear (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Martha My Dear — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #137.

Form. The polite parlour-song surface hides a 14½-bar verse, a chain of secondary dominants, and a bridge that lurches into a key a whole tone up without preparation — and none of it announces itself. An unusually large share of the running time is instrumental, and that drives the whole layout: the intro is a complete verse section played without a vocal, which means only one sung verse can precede the first bridge, and the mid-song instrumental verse leaves the closing verse as the only other sung one. Two sung verses in the entire song. There are two bridges, but the extension appears after the first only. The verse's 14½ bars run in four phrases with the first cut short by six beats (), and the cause is melodic — the opening fragment repeats itself in a Charleston-style syncopation that pushes two extra beats into the first line. The bridge is a square 16, paying the verse's metrical debt; the extension goes back to irregularity with three-bar phrases.

Harmony. Verse (E♭): I – I – I / V-of-iii · iii – V-of-V-of-V – V-of-V – V-of-V · V – IV9 – V7 – IV7 · V7 – IV7 – V7. That second phrase is a descending chain of secondary dominants () aimed so hard at B♭ that the section's centre of gravity sits there rather than on E♭ — and B♭ is only retroactively confirmed as V, not I. Bridge (F): vi7 – ii7 · I(add6) held 4 · ii – V – ii – V / V-of-vi [over a C pedal] · vi – ii7 — a real key change made to feel more remote than a whole step by being entered and left with no transition at all (), with a bass pedal on C through the third phrase (). The way home is a root move down a major third, G minor to E♭, functioning as iii→I.

Notable. A jazzy, blues-tinged E♭ where the A♭ chords all arrive as 9ths and 7ths that never resolve as suspensions would. The arrangement is strictly additive over a dry, close-miked, un-pedalled piano, and the one structural surprise is that drums enter at the bridge extension — a passage that occurs exactly once.

Against this page. Agrees on E♭ major (this page's capo-3 C shapes).

the-beatles-maxwell-s-silver-hammer.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Maxwell's Silver Hammer
the-beatles-maxwell-s-silver-hammer.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (20) · Refrain (8) · Interlude (4), three times over, with the interlude phrase set to words for the only time as the outro. There is no intro at all — the first verse simply starts, even though the interlude would have made an ideal one.

Music-hall Paul with straight-faced serial-killer comedy over the top. What is technically worth the visit is a song that never modulates once yet spends an unusually dense budget of applied dominants — V-of-ii, V-of-V and V-of-vi do all the travelling (). The refrain comes in two versions of the same eight bars: one closed, ending on I, which appears three times (sung once, instrumental twice), and one open, ending on V, which heads the later refrains.

The bass is the real feature. It descends stepwise from the verse's first bar, fills bar 4 with a descending scale and bar 8 with a rising one, and answers the tune's rising scale in the connector. The interlude sounds like it roams and is in fact fully closed — the line just walks D down to G and back, with the intervening chords in inversion to keep it smooth ().

The melodic ceiling is staged in three steps (): the verse arches to C♯, the connector nudges it to D, and only the refrain reaches the high E. Best small detail in the essay — the anvil hits beats 1 and 2 all song, then moves to beats 2 and 3 in the final bar, and that shift is what seals the ending.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-mean-mr-mustard.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Mean Mr Mustard
the-beatles-mean-mr-mustard.html:
Brief Abbey Road interlude — under two minutes. Lennon's character portrait written in India. Flows without a break directly into 'Polythene Pam.'

Chords

Key: E major

Verse: E – Esus4 – E → I (rocking on the tonic with a sus4)

"Sleeps in a hole in the road": B7 – C7 – C♯7 – D7 (and back down) → V7 – chromatic passing dominants climbing then descending

"Such a mean old man": E – C – B7 – E → I – ♭VI – V7 – I (the C borrowed ♭VI is the sneer)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-mean-mr-mustard-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A short Lennon fragment in the Abbey Road medley, segueing directly into Polythene Pam. Character-sketch lyric, punchy and brief — an example of the medley's 'fragments as movements' approach.

Steal this

  • Fragment as a movement: a 60-second character sketch can be a section of a larger suite.
  • Hard segue into the next fragment (shared key/tempo).
  • Fuzz bass color.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Mean Mr Mustard"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Mean Mr Mustard (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Mean Mr Mustard — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #186.

Form. A deliberate fragment — intro plus two verses, no chorus, no ending — and his argument is that this is form serving function: after two substantial self-contained songs the medley needs its pace back, so this one couples tightly at both ends and gets out. Even at throwaway length it finds room for a 14-bar verse structured 4 + 6 + 4: the first phrase composed straight through over a sequenced motif, the middle phrase tiled A–B–A, the last tiled C–C. Verse′ is musically identical apart from a meter shift in its third phrase. There is barely an intro — two beats of snare with a grace-note roll, borrowed from the back half of the last bar of "Sun King," so the two tracks join without a gap.

Harmony. Four chords only: I (4 bars) · V – ♭VII – V (6 bars) · I – ♭VI – V (×2). Both ♭VI and ♭VII are borrowed from the parallel natural minor (). In the middle phrase the bass makes a syncopated chromatic climb and descent — B–C–C♯–D up, D–C♯–C–B back — that lands the D and B chords just before their downbeats, spotlighting the cross relations rather than smoothing them; the third phrase pushes the same idea further with ♭VI. The exit is the tightest transition on the album: the chromatic bass lick lands on D, which becomes the ♭VII of the double plagal opening "Polythene Pam."

Notable. The tempo is essentially identical to "Sun King" and you cannot hear it, because the backbeat changes from lazy flow to a lumbering march. In verse′ the eighth-note pulse is held constant while the meter shifts from 4/4 to 6/8 for the final four bars, so chords now change every three eighths instead of four () — a local acceleration that becomes the new half-bar for the following track. The melody is almost entirely one motif, a step down followed by a third down (), sequenced downward and then relaunched from higher scale positions.

Against this page. Agrees on E major.

the-beatles-michelle.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Michelle
the-beatles-michelle.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4) · Verse (6) · Verse · Bridge (10) · Verse · Bridge · Verse (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse · Outro. The four-bar intro doubles as the back half of every bridge and returns again in the outro — one idea covering three structural jobs.

Every verse opens on an F major chord, but the song's centre of gravity is F minor: the major triad is bracketed by minor material on both sides and lands as a small surprise each time. The intro is best heard as one sustained F minor chord with a chromatic inner line (F–E–E♭–D) moving against it — a prolongation, not a new chord per beat. Play the same scale four times faster and the effect vanishes; the slow rate is what makes it work.

The verse's I → iv7 turn inside two bars is the hook, parallel-minor borrowing where \"Yesterday\" used the relative (). The iv → ♭VII opening looks set to walk the minor circle of fifths and gets cut off by a diminished seventh, and that vii°-of-V gets unusual airtime (), dragging an augmented second into the tune with it.

The melody leaps far more than McCartney usually writes, and the leaps trace chord outlines so the tune keeps pointing at the harmony.
