The climax is bar 1 of the bridge, where the withheld high notes are finally spent over a 9–8 appoggiatura (). The solo sits in the baritone range of the electric guitar, deliberately not sounding like the Beatles.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-misery.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Misery
the-beatles-misery.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4) · Verse (8) · Verse · Bridge (8, slower harmonic rhythm) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro (the verse's last two bars looped to a fade). Standard two-bridge model with no instrumental verse — the verses are so closed and chord-poor that a solo chorus would have felt airless.

A four-chord song (IV, V, I, vi) that gets its variety from how one chord is used: the vi works as subdominant, as dominant substitute, and as plain relative minor at different points (). The intro starts away from the tonic and converges fast, pre-stating almost everything — unison singing opening into harmony, decorative piano, the I–vi–V cell.

The verse's best move is rhythmic: the IV is held across the bar 4–5 divide so the chord change straddles the phrase boundary instead of marking it, which is harmonic-rhythm syncopation wrung out of a progression with nothing else going on (). One formula worth noting — the verse's last bar goes to vi when another verse follows, and stays on I when a bridge follows.

The verse tune is short, jumpy and pentatonic in its first half, with the remaining scale degrees held back for the second; the bridge inverts that with a stepwise descent through a full octave (). The piano edit pieces are the first outside performance dropped onto a Beatles track to supply something the band could not play. John's unaccompanied outro ad-libs land because they are the first solo voice in the song.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-mother-nature-s-son.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Mother Nature's Son
the-beatles-mother-nature-s-son.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (an ad-lib figure, then 8 bars vamping on I) · Verse (16, as 4+4+8) · spacer · Verse · Bridge (15, with one bar elided) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro. The verse's final phrase is repeated alone as a spacer between the two opening verses, and the same gesture returns at the end as the outro.

A folk-hymn built on almost no root motion at all. Verse and bridge both sit on a D pedal, and what the ear takes for chord changes is two stepwise inner voices — Pollack declines to name the resulting 6/4 sonorities as chords at all, calling them by-products of neighbour motion (, ). Only the V-of-V in the verse and the V-of-IV in the bridge are genuine chromatic root events ().

Two effects worth stealing. The neighbour figures double in speed in the verse's third phrase, faking an acceleration of harmonic rhythm that a pedal makes impossible (). And the bridge holds its C♮ an extra bar, pushing the phrasing off centre; the song then ends on a D7 rather than a triad, which is why the close reads as unsettled rather than resolved.

The arrangement schedules its entrances tightly: acoustic guitar alone, then brass arriving during the spacer rather than on the downbeat of the verse it belongs to, with percussive tapping and bass drum coming and going section by section — and two stray drum beats planted in the intro that mean nothing yet.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-no-reply.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - No Reply
the-beatles-no-reply.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (16, shaped AA′BA″) · Verse · Bridge (a full 16, the same length as a verse) · Verse · Outro. Only one bridge, and only one verse after it; the verse lyrics run ABB rather than ABA, because the title phrase already returns inside the bridge.

Everything in the song points at the third phrase of the verse. It is the one place the harmonic rhythm doubles — every other phrase changes chord on each of its first three bars and holds through the fourth, while the B phrase changes every bar, on the eighth before each downbeat (). It is also where the syncopation turns violent and where the arrangement opens up.

The harmony keeps backing down while the lyric confronts, and that mismatch is the song. The verse opens on a ii⁶₅ that sounds like ii and IV superimposed; the B phrase runs vi → iii, then the IV7 arrives with the melody's E sustained over it and the expected forward move never comes — it slides back to iii. The bridge's E major into A major briefly suggests a real key change before resolving into V-of-ii and dropping straight home ().

Loud-versus-quiet is scheduled, not incidental (): acoustic guitar, bass and drums with no cymbals for verse phrases 1, 2 and 4; cymbals, piano and electric guitar added only for phrase 3 and the bridge. The peak phrase is then recycled as the coda rather than replaced.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-norwegian-wood.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Norwegian Wood
the-beatles-norwegian-wood.html:
Harrison's first use of sitar on a Beatles record — one of the first in Western pop. Lennon's ambiguous story of a possible affair ends with possible arson. 12/8 time gives it a Scandinavian folk lilt.

Chords

Key: D major / Mixolydian (capo 2 → sounds in E) · 3/4 lilt

Verse: D – C – G – D → I – ♭VII – IV – I (the C is the Mixolydian ♭VII — that modal, folky drone)

"She asked me to stay": Dm – G – Dm – Em – A → i – IV – i – ii – V (shifts to D minor/Dorian for the contrasting phrase)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-norwegian-wood-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

The first Beatles record with sitar (Harrison), and a landmark for bringing Indian instrumentation into Western pop. A 3/4 folk lilt, intimate and dry — acoustic guitar + sitar doubling the melody, close double-tracked vocal, minimal rhythm section.

  • The Mixolydian ♭VII (C) drone gives it the modal, folky, slightly-Eastern flavor; the shift to D minor/Dorian for "she asked me to stay" darkens it.
  • Recorded close and warm — the exoticism is in the instrument choice and mode, not effects.

Steal this

  • One unexpected doubled instrument (sitar here) tracking the vocal melody = instant signature — pick a timbre outside the genre.
  • Mixolydian ♭VII drone for a modal, folk-rock flavor without leaving the key → Borrowed Chords · Scale Modes Reference.
  • 3/4 lilt to make a simple folk song feel timeless.
  • Dry, close acoustic recording — character from the source, not the chain.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Rubber Soul · search "The Beatles — Norwegian Wood"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Norwegian Wood (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown) — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #78.

Form. Extreme economy: everything except the bridges is the same eight-bar hook motif, repeated over a static I-chord drone. In other hands that much unvaried repetition with that little harmonic movement would die on the page; here it buys cohesion. The 16-bar instrumental intro is really two statements of the verse's hook phrase — solo acoustic first, then sitar taking the melody with bass entering underneath — and every verse follows that model. The bridge is also 16 bars. The outro gives the hook one repeat where the song's established pattern would call for two: a rule broken deliberately at the last possible moment.

Harmony. The hook stretches across eight bars inside a single harmonic envelope on I — a drone rather than a progression () — and whether implied changes exist under it is, in his view, arguable and not worth arguing. Bridge: i (4 bars) – IV (4) – i (4) – ii – V (4). The bridge drops to the parallel minor and finally releases some harmonic motion, and its key device is the major IV inside a minor key — modal and antique-sounding, the exact inverse of the band's usual minor iv in a major key (). It rhymes with the melodic ♭7 in the verse hook ().

Notable. The hook is a textbook case of the downward spiral paradigm as distinct from the arch (): a full octave descent from the fifth degree that starts as a plain descending scale turning around its upper neighbour, then develops that idea twice via a subfigure dropping twice and climbing once, the leaps widening each pass. The underrated arrangement detail is the hard pick on the 12-string — the percussive noise it generates is what makes the sitar's buzz sit naturally in the track. This is one of their rare ternary-meter songs, lilting rather than waltz-like.

Against this page. Agrees — his E major is this page's sounding pitch (D shapes, capo 2), and both read the verse's modal ♭7.

the-beatles-not-a-second-time.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Not A Second Time
the-beatles-not-a-second-time.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (an odd 7 bars, 2+2+3) · Verse (variant) · Refrain (10, in short uneven phrases) · Refrain (guitar solo) · Verse · Verse (variant) · Refrain · fade. No intro — the drums only enter at bar 5 of the first verse, which makes the opening half-verse feel retroactively like one.

Nominally G major, but the song keeps tipping toward E minor, and Pollack reads that as programmatic: the lyric claims unbendable resolve and the harmony does not believe it. The middle section is a refrain, not a bridge — it carries the hook and fulfils the verse rather than contrasting with it.

The best lesson here is how much work one chord in one bar does. The two verse versions are identical except for bar 6: with I there the verse feels closed at six bars and bar 7's V is an appendix; swap that bar to ii and the V stays open, so the last three bars build an expectation the refrain then satisfies.

No V chord appears in the refrain at all. vii° stands in for it, and because a diminished triad spells as vii of G or of E minor, it smooths the when E minor lands in bar 9 where G was expected — and, unusually, the deception is never corrected. The persistent I → vi motion in the verses is the same ambiguity at lower intensity. The tune is heavily pentatonic, with F♯ used as a 9–8 appoggiatura over the vi chord (). John is double-tracked with no other backing voice at all, and the outro simply vamps I → vi into the fade.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-nowhere-man.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Nowhere Man
the-beatles-nowhere-man.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (8, three phrases where the third equals the first two combined) · Verse · Bridge (8) · Verse (guitar solo) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro. Three bridges — no other song in the series to this point repeats a bridge a third time.

A major-mode surface with a flat sixth pushing up through it. The C natural sits prominently in the backing vocals and effectively forces a minor iv into a major key, one of Lennon's favourite chords (, ). The other oddity is the bridge's iii → IV, last seen in "I Feel Fine".

Sustaining the A chord through bridge bar 7 gives the harmonic rhythm a subtly slow syncopation, and the bridge tune keeps dwelling on notes belonging to the chord before or after the current one. Those two lags combine to produce the illusion of a 4–3 suspension closing the section when no suspension is there at all.

The verse tune traverses a descending octave from the tonic and is deliberately plainer — melodically and rhythmically — than the octave descent in "Norwegian Wood", which runs from the fifth (). That blandness is what frees attention for the little guitar riff trailing every verse, the song's real hook, which descends an octave from the fifth with fanfare-like arpeggiation. The vocals are the event: one of their most ambitious three-part outings, opening a cappella, chorale-style in the verses and switching to lead-plus-la-las in the bridges as the lyric moves from description to direct address.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-ob-la-di-ob-la-da.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da
the-beatles-ob-la-di-ob-la-da.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (an unusual 5 bars — one bar of piano fanfare, then a 4-bar vamp, with the real downbeat at bar 2) · Verse (8, ABA′B′) · Refrain (8) · Verse · Refrain · Bridge (8) · Verse · Refrain · Bridge · Verse · Refrain · Outro. Take verse and refrain as one unit and the whole song reduces to the short two-bridge model.

Four diatonic chords — I, IV, V, vi — even phrase lengths, a deliberately childlike harmonic plan. The only relief is the refrain's deceptive cadence to vi (), and it is not decoration: repeating that same deception is what launches the outro and buys the extra bars needed to land the title phrase. The bridge is the one section that opens up, starting on IV and building to a big V.

The craft is in the verse tune, whose four phrases have plain surface contours but whose higher-level motion walks up the scale (): odd phrases nudge the ceiling up (3̂→2̂, then 5̂→6̂), even phrases fall through the whole range back to the bottom.

Two things separate the released take from the Anthology 3 version, and both come down to how much is left to chance (). The released bass limps — arpeggios phrased "one, two-and, three, four-and" — where the earlier take runs even eighths; that limp is the actual hook. And the overdubs are placed almost perversely at random, where the earlier take applied the same details in neat, consistent patterns.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-octopus-s-garden.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Octopus's Garden
the-beatles-octopus-s-garden.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (8) · Verse (a huge 32 bars, four even phrases, AABA′) · Verse · instrumental break (16, transposed to IV) · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. The verse is effectively a whole verse/verse/bridge/verse module folded inside one section.

The entire song is one four-chord cliché — I, vi, IV, V — played at home and then transposed wholesale to IV for the break (). Pollack calls it naive in the painterly sense and means it partly as praise: he flags barely-hidden parallel fifths and octaves between tune and bass, and is disappointed that the modulating section introduces no new material at all.

What keeps 32 bars of four chords standing up is that the harmonic rhythm is staged across the section — steady through the first two phrases, halved in the first half of phrase 3, then accelerated to close phrase 4. Phrase 3 begins on vi as the result of a , and the outro parlays that same deception into a three-times-and-out ending. The break is a complete textbook pivot to IV.

Tune and guitar riffs are almost purely pentatonic () and mostly patter without much contour; the section gets an arch at all simply because phrase 3 sits a register higher. The verse layering changes exactly one variable per phrase — vocal doubling, piano entering, drum pattern — which is the whole arrangement plan.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-oh-darling.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Oh Darling
the-beatles-oh-darling.html:
McCartney arrived each morning for a week and screamed the vocal to get the appropriately raw, ragged sound he wanted. Old-school R&B feel. Harrison guitar solo. No overdubbed vocals.

Chords

Key: A major · 12/8 doo-wop ballad

Verse: E7♯5 – A – E – F♯m – D – Bm7 – E7 – A → V7+ – I – V – vi – IV – ii7 – V7 – I (the E7♯5 intro chord sets the bluesy tension)

Chorus ("When you told me you didn't need me"): D – F7 – A – B7 – E7 – F7 – E7 – E7♯5 → IV – ♭VI7 – I – II7 – V7 – ♭VI7 – V7 (the F7 borrowed ♭VI7 is the dramatic gut-punch)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-oh-darling-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

A 50s doo-wop/R&B ballad pastiche, and a famous performance-capture story: McCartney came in early each morning for about a week and sang it once, fresh, deliberately wearing his voice down to get that raw, cracked, screaming quality — he wanted it to sound like he'd been performing it on stage for weeks. The lesson is that the performance is the production.

  • Heavily compressed, roomy, vintage-voiced mix to match the pastiche.
  • Restrained band under a huge lead vocal.

Steal this

  • Wear the voice in: to get a raw/worn lead, re-sing it fresh over multiple days rather than comping a rested take — capture fatigue on purpose.
  • Genre-pastiche production: commit fully to an era's mix (heavy comp, room, vintage EQ — UAD UA 1176LN, Kramer Tape).
  • Performance over perfection: a cracked, committed take beats a clean one.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Oh! Darling"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Oh Darling (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Oh! Darling — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #180.

Form. A hybrid: the emotional weight of slow heavy blues grafted onto the form and chord vocabulary of a wall-climbing doo-wop ballad. For all the blues surface the architecture is the standard pop two-bridge model with one verse between, and not one section matches a twelve-bar frame. Slow ternary meter is genuinely rare in their catalogue (). Effectively no intro and no outro — both are a single gesture. Inside the eight-bar verse the lyric scans 4 + 1 + 3, cutting across an otherwise four-square section; the bridge is a plain 2 × 4.

Harmony. Intro: V+ (E augmented, entering on beat 3) · Verse (8): I – V – vi – IV · ii–V · ii–V – I–IV – I–V · Bridge (8): IV – ♭VI – I (2) · V/V (2) – V–♭VI – V · Outro: … ♭II7 – I7. Spell the intro chord E – G♯ – B♯, not with an E♭ — the B♯ is there to push up into the C♯ of the A chord. Both sections accelerate their harmonic rhythm toward the end, and the transitions are handled two different ways: verse 1 ends on V to motivate the repeat, while verses running into a bridge sustain the A chord and let I re-read as V-of-IV. The chord worth the price of admission is the bridge's "F7": written with D♯ on top rather than E♭ it becomes a German augmented sixth, which he derives as an altered IV rather than a ♭VI () — both outer voices resolve chromatically outward onto the same note.

Notable. Blues colour comes from heavy stress on ♭3 and ♭7, and scale degree 4 is almost banished — absent from the verse entirely. The best study material is one two-note leaning figure, F♯ → E, introduced in bar 1 and reused over four different chords so it reads as a different dissonance each time (). The detail worth writing down: the backing vocals use similar material in all four verses but enter on a different bar each time — 4, then 2, then 3, then 1.

Against this page. Agrees on A major and on the 12/8 doo-wop feel.

the-beatles-old-brown-shoe.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Old Brown Shoe
the-beatles-old-brown-shoe.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4-bar vamp on I7) · Verse (16) · Verse · Bridge (12, AAB) · Verse (instrumental) · Bridge · Verse · Outro (a single reprise of the verse's last phrase, then 20-plus bars of I7 vamping to the fade). The two-bridge model with an instrumental middle verse is a shape Pollack cannot find anywhere else in the official catalogue.

Nominally C major, but the verse habitually slides into the relative minor and has to be hauled back: its last phrase reads in A minor as VI – V – i, a pivot that dies too quickly to really call a modulation (). Harmonic rhythm starts very slow and accelerates across the final two phrases ().

The ♭VI gets unusual prominence and makes a hard cross-relation with the A naturals in the IV chords on either side of it () — Harrison's habitual wilting-downward gesture, as in "If I Needed Someone" and "While My Guitar Gently Weeps". The bridge revolves entirely around V, and that is what asserts C major as home at all.

The sharpest detail: a C is held as a pedal point in the treble rather than the bass across the verse (), and that pedal is the reason the E chord has to be augmented — the C occupies the slot where a conventional B would sit. Jangle piano, organ, lead guitar and a very heavy bass make an uncanny composite at an extreme up-tempo full of triplets.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-one-after-909.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - One After 909
the-beatles-one-after-909.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4) · Verse (16, AABA′) · Verse · Bridge (16, a single 8-bar unit played twice) · Verse · Verse (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. As boxy as it gets — every section is an even number of four-bar phrases and the solo simply runs over a verse.

Written in the late fifties, taped by the Quarrymen around 1960, cut at EMI in 1963, shelved for six years, and finally released from the rooftop performance. It is compositionally the simplest thing they ever put out: four chords — I, IV, V and V-of-V — made to look worse than they are by a five-sharp key signature. That C♯ is the only chromatic chord in the song and it is the bridge's entire engine ().

The formal work is done by one asymmetry: the verse is closed at both ends (starts and finishes on I) while the bridge is open at both ends, beginning on IV and stranded on V. Inside the verse the harmonic rhythm goes from completely frozen for eight bars to a chord every two. The bluesiness arrives without a blues form — ten bars of stationary I plus a melody that keeps laying minor inflections over major chords ().

Come-as-you-are rooftop playing, closer to Dixieland collective improvisation than to an arrangement. John leads with Paul in parallel thirds above him on the verses, Everly Brothers style, while the bridges are John alone. The Let It Be and Get Back mixes of the same take differ sharply in panning, balance and edits.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-only-a-northern-song.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Only A Northern Song
the-beatles-only-a-northern-song.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro · Verse (19 bars) · Verse · Refrain (15 bars, 4+6+5) · Verse (instrumental) · Refrain · Verse · Refrain (instrumental) · Outro (fade). Pollack parses the whole thing in 2/4 just to make the uneven phrasing notatable; the refrain's third phrase opens with an interpolated bar of 3/4, the same trick as "Strawberry Fields Forever".

The lyric's complaint about chords going wrong is painted obviously by the noise layer on top, but the erratic harmonic rhythm and constantly shifting phrase lengths do the same job underneath, which is the more interesting half. The verse is glacial — eight bars on a single chord — and its only body English is the last line's chord change arriving a full bar early (). Shape-wise it opens toward V and then backs off to IV, a cadence set up and declined.

The refrain does the opposite, changing chords every bar or two and making a genuine, forced modulation to ii (B minor) rather than a passing tonicisation (), carried across by a functional pivot and by the note B held in common through all four chords of that phrase.

Over an organ/bass/drums base sits a stylised noise track — trumpets, metallic percussion, piano doodling — that probably never stops once it starts and is simply ridden on the fader. The rule is worth internalising: it is faded down at the start of sections and up at their ends ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-p-s-i-love-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - P.S. I Love You
the-beatles-p-s-i-love-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro · Verse (10 bars, phrased 3 + 2 + 2½ + 2½) · Verse · Bridge (a strict 8) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. Two bridges, one verse between, no instrumental verse — and the intro is a disguised variant of the bridge.

D major with Aeolian colouring: beyond the diatonic set it borrows ♭VI and ♭VII from parallel D minor (). The oddest chord is the C♯7 in the intro standing in for V — the diatonic chord there is a diminished seventh, already a rootless V⁷, and turning it into a dominant seventh sets up a resolution to F♯ that instead lands on I by pure stepwise voice leading in every part.

Two progression types run against normal directed root motion. Chord streams with stepwise roots (I–ii–I, ♭VI–♭VII–I) read as languid, out of Impressionism and jazz. And deceptive resolution used repeatedly — V to vi, later V to ♭VI, and even the eventual arrival at I reached sideways through ♭VII (). The verse's phrasing is articulated almost entirely by where those evasions land (); the bridge is the contrast, I–IV–V only, square 4+4.

Not a rock record — tempo and percussion put it nearer lounge-pop or Latin dance. The best arrangement detail: in every verse but the last the backing voices sing only on isolated words, functioning like italics, and in the final verse they abandon that and sing straight through.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-penny-lane.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Penny Lane
the-beatles-penny-lane.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (8, AA′B as 2+2+4) · Verse · Refrain (8, AA′) · Verse · Verse (solo) · Refrain · Verse · Verse · Refrain · Refrain/Outro with a written ending instead of a fade. Completely cyclical — no bridge, and the solo section is just another verse. There is no real intro: the vocal enters with about an eighth note of backing ahead of it.

The single most unusual thing in the song is that the refrain is in the key of ♭VII — verses in B, refrain in A () — which Pollack flags as something he cannot find another example of, and which is also why the final refrain's move up reads as earned rather than as the fifties last-chorus key bump. The pivot leans on F♯ major, not diatonic to A, so the raised third does the work: a real change of key, not a tonicisation ().

The verse opens with a textbook descending walking bass under I, then puts a minor seventh on the tonic in bar 4 and slides into jazzy, impressionist territory before closing with a classical 4–3 over V. Its skeleton is just I – ♭VI – V, with ♭VI borrowed from the parallel minor (), blurred because the voices move at different rates. That parallel-minor shadow is the ominous undertow under a sunny lyric.

A thick wall-of-sound mix closer to Pet Sounds than to Spector. The piccolo trumpet arrives in four graded doses — solo section, one isolated note, obbligato, closing lick — the same staging used for the horn in "For No One".

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-piggies.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Piggies
the-beatles-piggies.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4) · Verse (12, three equal phrases, AA′B) · Intro · Verse · Intro′ · Bridge (14, phrased 8+6) · Verse (instrumental) · Intro · Verse · Outro with a complete ending.

A run of classical mannerisms bolted to a snide lyric, and the structural item on that list is the one worth stealing: a short instrumental intro placed before every verse — a nineteenth-century art-song habit that makes a 2:04 track feel considerably longer than it is.

Everything stays anchored in A despite two feints away. The verse harps on I and V for six straight bars, which is exactly what makes the ii – V-of-V in the second phrase land (); that same pair then recurs at the opposite end of the following phrase, which is the section's rhetorical trick. The verse's last two bars slow the harmonic rhythm and fill the space with two inner voices rising in parallel tenths — four apparent chords, one actual function, a prolongation of V ().

The altered intro before the bridge is textbook motivic transformation (): the same four bars with the last chord swapped from V to V-of-vi, which reads as a modulation about to happen — and four bars into the bridge you are still at home. The ending is deliberately ambiguous, two broad chords hearable as I–V in A or as a plagal IV–I in E. Harpsichord, bowed cellos and a late operatic male chorus carry the period costume.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-please-please-me.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Please Please Me
the-beatles-please-please-me.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4 bars over a static I, entering on beat 4) · Verse (16, four even phrases grouped 2+2) · Verse · Bridge (10 bars, phrased 4+3+3) · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. Compact single-bridge model, the same economy as "No Reply" and "Day Tripper" — and the cold ending matters, because a fade would have implied endless begging rather than a decision.

Pollack reads the song as one gesture repeated at every scale: push forward, then catch yourself and back off. Mostly I–IV–V with ii and vi, plus the two imports that give it bite — ♭III and ♭VI borrowed from parallel E minor (). The verse's first phrase speeds the harmonic rhythm up on an offbeat, three major chords stepping upward, the first of them foreign — a G against a field of G♯s () — and phrase 2 restores order by being nearly identical but closing on I. Phrase 3, the one with hard syncopation on every 2-and, is ironically the only phrase where the harmony sits still for four bars: the agitation is purely rhythmic ().

The bridge's second phrase drops its expected fourth bar and runs straight into the third (). The outro is the payoff for that planted G — I – V/♭VI – ♭VI – V – I; play it with the diatonic chords instead and it collapses into squareness. In verse phrase 3 lead and backing vocals interlock so their fragments assemble into one continuous line.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-polythene-pam.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Polythene Pam
the-beatles-polythene-pam.html:
Lennon's character sketch written in India. The 12-string acoustic gives it a jangly, relentless drive. Recorded with a thick Liverpool accent. Flows directly into 'She Came In Through the Bathroom Window.'

Chords

Key: E major (A-Mixolydian flavor)

Verse: D – A – E → ♭VII – IV – I (driving Mixolydian rock)

"Well you should see her in drag": G – B7 → ♭III – V7

"Yes you should see Polythene Pam": C – D – E → ♭VI – ♭VII – I

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-polythene-pam-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Abbey Road medley — a raucous Lennon rocker sung in an exaggerated Scouse accent over a jangly 12-string acoustic, segueing straight into 'She Came In Through the Bathroom Window.'

Steal this

  • Accent/character vocal as a stylistic choice.
  • 12-string acoustic drive for a bright rhythmic bed.
  • Hard segue between medley fragments → Modulation.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — Polythene Pam"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Polythene Pam (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Polythene Pam — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #187.

Form. Sibling track to "Mean Mr Mustard" — same key, nearly the same chord set, opposite harmonic behaviour. Mustard starts on I and opens out to V; Pam never starts on I and converges on it every time. Intro is a 2-bar instrumental tile stated twice, recurring essentially unchanged three times and also supplying the outro material. The verse is an odd 10 bars — a quatrain AABA′ plus a spacer phrase — and the three groupings deliberately fall out of register with each other: the phrase tiling runs AABCC, while the harmonic shape reads AABA′A′. The outro is 22 bars, roughly 40% of the track: eight passes of the double plagal phrase, this time with each chord's own root in the bass, then six bars building on I, the last four carrying a descending bass scale that re-hears the E chord as V of A and delivers "... Bathroom Window."

Harmony. Intro: ♭VII – IV – I over an E pedal for the entire phrase (), so the double plagal sits on top of the tonic instead of travelling to it. Verse: ♭VII – IV – I (×2) | V-of-♭VI – V | ♭VI – ♭VII – I (×2). The one chord Mustard does not have is G — on paper ♭III, in the ear a delayed dominant into the C major a bar later. And since V always goes to ♭VI, every real arrival on I comes from ♭VII: V is demoted to a deceptive resolution () and cadence duty is handed to the double plagal (, ).

Notable. The tune is pattering, even more than in Mustard, its contour coming almost entirely from transposing simple descending motifs up and down the scale. The backbeat contrast with Mustard is a syncopation choice — Mustard marches and drops hard syncopations on the eighth before the downbeat; Pam swings on less syncopation, a faster tempo, and a motif accenting the last three eighths in the first half of the bar.

Against this page. Pollack reads it in E major — which matches this page's Chords section but not the key: field, which says A major. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-real-love.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Real Love
the-beatles-real-love.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4, in E minor) · Verse (8) · Verse · Refrain (8, AA′BB′) · Intro · Verse · Refrain · Break (unsquare, extended to 5 bars, in F♯ minor) · Verse · Refrain, with the refrain's second half repeated seven times into the fade. The returning intro is a Lennon habit going back to "Thank You Girl".

The intro's i – V6/3 is doing real work: the first-inversion dominant makes the phrase relaxed rather than transitive and hands the verse a bassline to descend from. Play it with V in root position and both effects vanish. The verse then shifts straight to the parallel major, and its opening bars resist Roman numerals altogether — a lazily voice-led filling of the distance from I to V, with one gratuitous augmented chord in bar 4. In the last two bars the bass holds E so the change above it is neighbour motion between two E major chords rather than a chord change at all ().

The refrain's peak chord is a half-diminished F♯ in 6/5, an ordinary ii6/5 altered for sentiment; its second half is then the I – vi – IV – V cliché completely unvarnished, and the three local oddities are what balance that predictability.

The tune is almost purely pentatonic () — Lennon's standing melodic mode — and runs roughshod over the chords with neighbour tones that are never resolved. The clearest case is the G♯ in bar 4 of the refrain: people supply the missing resolution themselves when singing it from memory.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-revolution-1.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Revolution 1
the-beatles-revolution-1.html:
Slower, more ambivalent version than the 'Revolution' single. Extended 'shooby-doo-wop' outro with Yoko Ono vocal improvisations. Lennon's political statement hedging on whether to support revolutionary violence.

Chords

Key: A major · shuffle blues feel

Verse: A – D/A – A – D/A – E/B → I – IV – I – IV – V

Pre-chorus ("But when you talk about destruction"): Bm – E/B – Bm – G – A – F♯ – E → ii – V – ii – ♭VII – I – VI – V (chromatic slide down to the dominant)

Chorus ("Don't you know it's gonna be all right"): E/B – A – D/A → V – I – IV

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-revolution-1-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

The slow, bluesy acoustic version (White Album) — distinct from the fast, distorted single. Lennon reportedly sang lying on his back for a relaxed tone; doo-wop 'shoo-bee-doo-wah' backing vocals and driven, distorted acoustic guitars.

Steal this

  • Reharmonize/re-tempo a song: the same tune as a laid-back shuffle vs. a hard rocker — pick the version per mood.
  • Distorted acoustic (Decapitator on an acoustic DI) for grit.
  • Doo-wop backing vocals as vintage color.

Why I like it

Listen

  • The Beatles (White Album) · search "The Beatles — Revolution 1"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Revolution 1 (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Revolution and Revolution 1 — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #129.

Form. One essay covering both cuts, and his verdict is that the single is the real song and the slower, brassy album version reads as a parody of its own remake — the ranting delivery of the single fits the words in a way the nightclub treatment does not. Musically this is heavily stylized blues: nothing obeys a twelve-bar, but the chord choices and bent notes carry the genre anyway. Intro 4 bars of manic guitar triplets; verse phrased ABAB′CC′ with unequal lengths and interpolated half-bars () — lopsided enough that it can be parsed as a verse and bridge fused into one section; refrain 8 bars, even AAA-plus-rest phrasing, deliberately square as a counterweight; break an abridged verse reprise then four bars piling up on V; outro grows straight out of the last refrain.

Harmony. Almost entirely I – IV – V. Intro: I (3 bars) – IV V · Verse: I (2½) · IV – I · I (2½) · IV – V · ii6/4 – V · ii6/4 – ♭VII/VI – V · Refrain: I – IV – I – IV · I – IV – V. That final verse phrase is the one exception and lands on the metrically strangest moment in the track — the only half-bar falling mid-phrase instead of at a phrase end, with the chords syncopated hard against the beat. Read locally in the relative-of-ii minor it runs i – ♭VII – V, and he calls it an unconsummated modulation to ii, a pivot set up and never completed (), which suits the lyric's mood. Underneath the verse there is a recurring 5–6–5 figure in the inner voice just above the bass — readable as I alternating with IV in second inversion, but structurally a neighbour tone with expensive furniture ().

Notable. About as close as the Beatles came to a grunge aesthetic. The odder treatment is the lead vocal dubbing, alternating plain single-track with ADT and punctuated by bursts of triple-tracking whose edits are too clumsy to be anything but deliberate.

Against this page. His Roman numerals are written for the single, in B major; "Revolution 1" is the same song down a tone in A major — the key this page uses — cleanly recorded, with brass, "shoo-be-doo-wop" backing vocals, no break section, a fade instead of a full ending, and the extra affirmative in the first verse.

the-beatles-revolution-9.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Revolution 9
the-beatles-revolution-9.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Pollack's own answer is Beginning · Middle · End, with a fade. This is the one track in the series that defeats his method outright — no sections, no progressions, no phrases, no tune to measure — so he abandons bar-by-bar analysis and writes about the listening experience instead. His framing: the piece is radical in what it withholds and surprisingly conservative in what it is actually made of.

Everything in it is a found object. Nothing is synthesised; the raw material is pre-existing musical and spoken recordings plus real-world noise, with the musical clips weighted heavily toward classical sources. Post-processing is deliberately limited to three operations — speed changes, reversed tape, and heavy crosscutting. Pollack rates that low-tech restraint as the piece's saving grace, and sets it against Stockhausen's Gesang der Jünglinge, far more technically arcane in how it handles vocal material.

Despite the anti-narrative surface, several sources recur as motifs without persisting across the whole piece: the title phrase, a soft slow piano passage in a Chopin manner, orchestral and choral snippets, spoken recitation. They surface the way a familiar face does in a crowd. His guess is that the assembly was stream of consciousness rather than genuine aleatoric procedure.

The claim worth keeping is about listening rather than composition: sustained ambiguity of content pushes the listener to project a continuity that is not in the material, the way a sleeping mind absorbs an outside noise into a dream. And context is part of the work — the track is inseparable from the album it sits on.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-rocky-raccoon.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Rocky Raccoon
the-beatles-rocky-raccoon.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Four bars of solo strummed acoustic on a tonally ambiguous Am7, then the same eight-bar loop seventeen times, then an implied four bars of held I where loop 18 would have started.

The single fact that matters: the entire three-and-a-half-minute track is one eight-bar progression looped seventeen times. Nothing in the harmony ever changes. Everything that makes it feel like a song with verses, refrains, a climax and an ending is done with vocal delivery, rhyme scheme and instrumentation — the same trick Chuck Berry and Little Richard run on the twelve-bar blues (). The loops are grouped in pairs, and one unpaired ninth pass is the whole design in miniature: after four paired statements, a single pass reads as an event.

The progression is vi⁷ – V-of-V – V – I, two bars each. Two internal lines do the work the chords do not: an inner voice descends chromatically G–F♯–F♮–E across the loop, audible once the backing vocals arrive, and in bar 8 the bass drops to B under the sustained C — a passing note, not a chord change (). The tune is almost entirely pentatonic () with a chromatically filled descent running through it.

Strummed acoustic runs the whole way; everything else arrives and leaves on schedule, and the subtractions are as structural as the additions — dropping the tack piano is what marks loops 12–13 as a return rather than a continuation ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-run-for-your-life.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Run For Your Life
the-beatles-run-for-your-life.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (6 bars on one chord) · Verse/Refrain (a fused 16-bar compound section) · Verse/Refrain · Break (a real 12-bar blues) · Verse/Refrain · Verse/Refrain · Outro (fade). The acoustic guitar enters just before the downbeat and is accented so that the beat is genuinely unlocatable until the rest of the band arrives.

The nominal key is D major but the song's centre of gravity is B minor — every verse veers off to cadence there, and the tune stripped of its chords points at B minor far more than D. The I–vi cliché was early-Beatles staple vocabulary and had all but vanished by this period; here it does structural work rather than colour, tilting the whole song toward the relative minor ().

The refrain is a ready/set/surprise: vi goes to V-of-V twice and then, on the third pass, to ii instead — in first inversion, carrying a G♯/G♮ cross-relation against the two E major chords before it (). Repeating V-of-V while withholding V for most of the song is a standing Beatles device; the break is the only place V appears at all, and it is a textbook except that V repeats in bars 9–10 instead of moving to IV. A rising chromatic bass lick hauls B minor back to D — and is pointedly absent after the break, which ended in D.

Vocals are fussily staged: single-tracked and exposed in the verses, apparently double-tracked with each track panned to its own channel in the refrains.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-savoy-truffle.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Savoy Truffle
the-beatles-savoy-truffle.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (a drum fill, then 2 bars vamping on E) · Verse (12 bars, three roughly parallel phrases) · Refrain (a single 4-bar phrase) · Intro′ · Verse · Refrain · Bridge (8, AA) · Verse (instrumental) · Refrain · Bridge · Verse · Refrain · Outro with a complete ending. Every section is harmonically open — verse and bridge both end on V — which is why nothing settles.

The song is filed in G major only because that is where it stops. It actually lives in the parallel pair E major / E minor, and the swing to G at the end of the refrain is close to a non sequitur (). Under the exotic surface, I–IV–V is still the skeleton of both verse and bridge; the F♯ and G chords are helpers, neither native to E major, and each is entered by whole-tone root motion — up to F♯, down to G. The signature colour is root movement by a major or minor third between non-diatonic chords, with chromatic scale riffs as connective tissue ().

The refrain is the pivot machinery: home shifts to the parallel minor, which makes the relative major an easy step away, and G is then confirmed only by a plagal cadence — deliberately weak, which is why the new key never feels earned (). Blues content comes from the near-minor third sung against the major I (). Best detail: beat 4 of the last bar has carried a pickup all song, and this time it is left silent.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-sexy-sadie.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Sexy Sadie
the-beatles-sexy-sadie.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (a single 6-bar phrase open at both ends, and note for note the verse's third phrase) · Verse (14 bars, 4+4+6) · Verse · Bridge (12, AAB) · Verse · Verse · Bridge · Outro (fade). The longer two-bridge model, but with two sung verses in the middle rather than one.

The analytic hook is a single two-chord gesture — I moving to V-of-iii — used as the song's signature and given three different continuations, so the same progression means something different every time it appears. Resolving to iii it behaves functionally; moving to ♭VII it produces a tritone root motion the ear excuses only because the phrases either side are rhetorically parallel; elsewhere it stops being a dominant at all and becomes one step in a chromatic descent ().

I, IV and V hold the key, but iii, V-of-iii and ♭VII do real work rather than decorate (). The ♭VII → V move is a textbook cross-relation (), the same trick as "I'm A Loser" and in the same key. In the bridge a rising diatonic stream I–ii–iii–IV is answered by four chromatic chords descending, with a C/C♯ cross-relation at the hinge — ascent and collapse balancing exactly, which is Pollack's reading of the whole song: an uphill struggle against something that keeps shoving you back down.

Style is deliberately mismatched — cutting lyrics over doo-wop backing vocals and a near-Classical piano part drowned in unnaturally heavy reverb.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-sgt-pepper-s-lonely-hearts-c.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
the-beatles-sgt-pepper-s-lonely-hearts-c.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: an arch, with both a bridge and a refrain in symmetry: Intro (4, intruding over ten seconds of hall ambience) · Verse (8, AAB) · instrumental Bridge (5, two uneven phrases) · Refrain (12, AA′B) · Bridge · Verse · Outro (2 bars on IV over a descending bass, segueing straight into the next track). Intros on a non-tonic chord are common in the catalogue; an outro on IV is not.

The harmonic engine is the archetypal Beatles progression I – V-of-V – IV – I, in use since "Eight Days A Week", whose entire character comes from a cross relation: the C♯ inside V-of-V immediately followed by the C♮ inside IV, which reads as deferred gratification (). Because you assume the opening chord is I, the intro's shift from V-of-V to IV lands as genuinely strange.

The sharpest lesson is in the two bridges, which use the same four chords and differ only by which one carries the seventh (). C7–F–C–D reads in F, a relatively distant excursion; C–F7–C–D reads in C, with the seventh as bluesy colour rather than a structural dominant. Both are then re-heard as IV and V at home.

The refrain — the arch's keystone, and nothing but this section twice is the Side 2 "Reprise" — runs a major/minor switch on I, the minor version in first inversion (). The tune is barely a notch above talking-blues patter, and that is the design: it leaves attention free for the production.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-she-came-in-through-the-bath.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - She Came In Through the Bathroom Window
the-beatles-she-came-in-through-the-bath.html:
McCartney wrote it after a fan literally climbed through his bathroom window. Syncopated rhythmic feel with an off-kilter groove. Part of the Abbey Road medley, flowing from 'Polythene Pam.'

Chords

Key: A major

Verse: A – D – A – D → I – IV

"Didn't anybody tell her?": A – Dm → I – iv (the Dm borrowed minor-iv darkens it)

"Sunday's on the phone to Monday": G7 – C – G7 – C – A → ♭VII7 – ♭III – ♭VII7 – ♭III – I (a bluesy sidestep before snapping back)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-she-came-in-through-the-bathroom-w.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Abbey Road medley — a tight McCartney rocker with punchy horns/organ and a driving groove; part of the seamless medley flow (from Polythene Pam).

Steal this

  • Punchy mid-tempo rock as a medley segment — momentum between ballad sections.
  • Tight rhythm + organ/horn stabs for drive.
  • Seamless segue in/out → Modulation.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — She Came In Through the Bathroom Window"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - She Came In Through the Bathroom Window (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — She Came In Through The Bathroom Window — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #188.

Form. The nearest thing to a conventional song form anywhere in the medley, and it plays much bigger than it is because the two fragments ahead of it act as a foil. The formal wrinkle is that a lone verse sits out front and the pair of verses falls between the two bridges, reversing the usual distribution. The intro is not the song's own material: it is the last four bars of "Polythene Pam"'s outro, and the E resolving to A on the verse downbeat is the payoff for that entire build. Verse 16 bars, four equal phrases, poetic pattern AAAB; bridge an unusual 15 bars, one short of the sixteen it seems to want, best parsed as overlapping the verse's last two bars so it begins before the verse has finished. The verse is rhythmically lopsided on purpose — the first three lines dodge the phrase downbeat and shift weight onto bar 3, the fourth lands on the downbeat for the first time.

Harmony. Very few chords. Verse: I7 – IV7 (×3) · IV – I. The bridge modulates to ♭III, giving the medley another head-on A-versus-C confrontation: I – iv | I – iv (pivot: iv = ii in C) | V – I | V – I → A. The exit uses the minor iv in a major key as an unmistakable pivot (, ), and the return has essentially no preparation — the A chord lands on the section's very last beat, which makes the next verse enter crooked the first time and is the punchline at the end.

Notable. The tune leans hard on ♭3 and ♭7 (), and that emphasis is what converts the chords into dominant sevenths — non-functional ones, since I7 can be rationalised as V-of-IV but IV7 has no such excuse (). Two descending scalar basslines in the bridge, the second playing its changes out in the 3+3+2 grouping that also drives "Here Comes The Sun" and "Because." The Get Back-era take used a I – vi – IV verse; the release strips it to the starker I – IV.

Against this page. Agrees on A major.

the-beatles-she-loves-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - She Loves You
the-beatles-she-loves-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (8, phrased 2+2+4, itself a variation of the refrain) · Verse (16, four equal phrases, harmonically open — starts on I, ends on V) · Verse · Refrain (8, converging on the tonic) · Verse · Refrain · Outro. Unusually, no verse comes between the last refrain and the outro — the song simply exits from the refrain.

Structurally this is the least adventurous thing in the early run: four-square phrasing, one key throughout, chords changing every two bars as a rule. What carries it is vocabulary. The verse's closing V never resolves to I — it hands off to the vi that opens the refrain, a deceptive resolution doing the work of relieving an otherwise flat scheme (), and the only complete V–I cadence in the song sits at the end of the refrain.

The colour is a minor iv borrowed from the parallel minor (), approached the hard way both times: jumped into from vi in the verse, forcing an E♮/E♭ cross relation, and landing right after V-of-V in the refrain, forcing two at once (). Set up conventionally from major IV the same chord reads as sentimental barbershop.

The added sixth on the final chord — the one George Martin argued against — works because the descending three-note hook has already been sung over vi and V-of-V, chords where that E belongs, before arriving over a I chord where it does not. The open fifths and fourths in the two-part vocal, rather than the expected thirds, are the actual signature of the early sound.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-she-said-she-said.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - She Said She Said
the-beatles-she-said-she-said.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (3 bars on I) · Verse (10 — an 8-bar verse plus a 2-bar instrumental reprise of its last two bars) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Bridge · Verse · fade. In the bridge the meter goes fluid: beats per bar run 4 + 4 · 3 + 3 + 3 · 6 + 3 · 6 + 3, and Pollack reads the long bars as single 6-beat bars because that is where the chord changes fall.

The famous feature is that collapsing meter, but the real lesson is a compositional rule: when you push one parameter to the limit, hold the others still. All that turbulence sits inside a textbook two-bridge form over four chords total, one of which does not arrive until the bridge's climax.

It is also his cleanest specimen of pure Mixolydian harmony with no leakage into ordinary major. The v is minor and cannot make a working dominant, so IV and ♭VII carry the key (), and the verse's ♭VII–IV–I tail is the double-plagal move. The bridge is a real modulation (): F minor, heard for the first time at the climax, is re-read as ii in E♭. The paradox worth holding onto is that in this mode the tonic makes a stronger V-of-IV than the minor v makes a V-of-I.

The tune is locked inside a fifth for nearly the whole song — the hard ceiling produces the trapped, circular quality. In the bridge, drums and bass give up syncopation entirely and mark even eighths so the shifting meter stays readable ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-she-s-a-woman.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - She's A Woman
the-beatles-she-s-a-woman.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (8) · Verse (24 bars) · Verse · Bridge (a scant 4 bars) · Verse · Break (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse · fade. The bridge is so short that the following verse is heard as a continuation of it.

The most blues-like thing in the catalogue to this point, as writing and as performance. The structural trick is that the verse is a twelve-bar blues stretched to 24 bars (), disguised further by IV chords jabbing into bars that would otherwise be plain tonic — and then the solo break and the outro drop the disguise entirely and play a straight twelve. I, IV and V and nothing else, apart from the bridges.

The bridge (iii – vi – iii – IV – V) is a neat counterpoint to "I Feel Fine", where iii went to IV: here the same chord is answered by both of its likely targets inside four bars, and it doubles as a compact reharmonisation demonstration — one identical two-bar melodic phrase stated twice under different chords ().

The hook is the lick opening the verse: a leap up of a minor sixth followed by a craggy descent, carrying its own implied cross-relation between an early C♯ and a later C♮ (). It sits at the very top of Paul's comfortable range, and the audible strain is part of the record — he transposed the song down a fourth to sing it decades later (). Overdubbed piano sits out the entire first verse before staying in for the rest.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-she-s-leaving-home.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - She's Leaving Home
the-beatles-she-s-leaving-home.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: barred as a slow-spun 12/8, where one long measure absorbs four bars of what would otherwise read as fast 3/4. Intro (a single measure of arpeggiation over I) · Verse (4 measures, phrased ABB) · Verse · Refrain (4 measures plus a truncated quarter-measure, so it ends short) · Verse · Verse · Refrain · Verse · Refrain · Outro, which restores the missing quarter measure.

Paul in mimicry mode rather than blend mode — a stylised send-up of turn-of-the-century drawing-room semi-classical, pointed at the parents. Pollack's defence is technical rather than sentimental: the modal ♭VII and the minor v are deliberate tells that mark it as parody (), and the harmony under the strings-and-harp gloss is stranger than the surface suggests.

Sevenths and ninths run nearly wall to wall, which is where the overlush quality comes from. The harmonic rhythm decelerates across every verse (), dense at the top and parked by the end — and the parked dominant is embellished with an appoggiatura and a ninth simultaneously, the most extreme single-chord elaboration Pollack can name in the catalogue to that point. The refrain's closing V-of-V resolves straight into the next verse's I with no V intervening (), and the outro's plagal IV–I () has a churchy sentimentality that is plainly the joke.

Strings and harp were scored by Mike Leander, not George Martin, and are more restrained for it. The stereo master sits a half step lower and slower than the mono.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-something.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Something
the-beatles-something.html:
Harrison's most celebrated song. George Martin's lush string arrangement. McCartney plays one of his most melodic bass lines on the album. Frank Sinatra called it the greatest love song of the 20th century.

Chords

Key: C major (middle 8 lifts to A major) · George Harrison

Intro lick: F – E♭ – G/D → IV – ♭III – V (the descending guitar figure)

Verse ("Something in the way she moves"): C – Cmaj7 – C7 – F – F/E – D9 – G → I – Imaj7 – I7 – IV – IV/3 – II9 – V (a chromatic descending bass C–B–B♭–A — the song's beating heart). The I → Imaj7 → I7 line-cliché (Seventh Chords) is that bass walk harmonized. The D9 is a secondary dominant (V9/V) pushing to G.

Middle 8 ("You're asking me will my love grow"): A – C♯m/G♯ – F♯m7 – D – G – A → modulates to A major (I – iii – vi – … – V) before sliding home to C.

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-something-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Abbey Road (1969) — George Martin's most restrained-but-lush production. The arrangement is a masterclass in parts that sing independently:

  • McCartney's bass is a second melody: it never just follows roots — it counter-melodizes constantly (one of his most celebrated lines). It's the model for melodic bass, not a low-end anchor. Why it reads as a conversation, not just a busy counter-line: McCartney's most active bass moments land specifically when the vocal is resting — creating a genuine call-and-response with Harrison's voice rather than the bass running dense underneath it regardless of what the vocal is doing. → Slap Bass Dynamics — Contrast, Force, and Restraint tool #4 (the same ensemble-restraint mechanism, applied to voice instead of a horn/other instrument) — BassBuzz, 10 Songs that Taught Me Bass (Easy to Effin’ Hard)
  • George Martin's strings lift the choruses/solo without turning it saccharine — they enter late and swell, arrangement dynamics again.
  • Harrison's guitar solo is composed and singable — doubled, warm (Leslie/compressed), it's a melodic statement you can hum, not a shred.
  • Ringo plays for the song: restrained, tom-forward fills that answer the vocal phrases.
  • Recorded warm and close; the space is intimate, the low end (that bass) is the star.

Steal this

  • Bass as counter-melody: write the bass as a second tune that moves against the vocal, not root-following → 1 Electric Bass DI Track / 1 Digital Bass Track. This is the Beatles bass lesson.
  • Chromatic descending bass under static harmony (the C–B–B♭–A line cliché) for instant emotional depth → Chromatic Bass Lines · Seventh Chords.
  • Compose the solo: make the lead a hummable melody (double it, warm it) rather than improvised runs.
  • Arrange in dynamics: strings/parts enter to lift, not to fill — silence and restraint first.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road (album) · search "The Beatles — Something"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Something (Guitar)
  • Also #46 on BassBuzz's First 50 Songs You Should Play on Bass repertoire list.
  • Song 6 in BassBuzz's 10 Songs that Taught Me Bass (Easy to Effin’ Hard) — the "how to play with a singer" lesson, sourced above.

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Something — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #178.

Form. The song's emotional position is built into a standing conflict between one rising hook and a constant falling undertow — the three-bar hook that opens the track, closes every verse and closes the record is affirmative and ascending, while the bass and the tune spend the rest of their time descending. And the hook is never given lyrics, which he reads as the point rather than an oversight. The verse divides into 12 bars of verse proper plus a 6-bar refrain-like tail, the back half of which is the intro hook again; the bridge is a four-square 8 in AA′. The structural signature is elision — the last bar of nearly every section lands on the downbeat of the next, so the hook phrase never gets its full two bars until the outro, the only place it stands alone.

Harmony. Intro (3): IV – ♭III – V6/4 – I · Verse (18): I – Imaj7 – V/IV – IV · V/V – V · vi – [A♭] – G – V/V · IV – ♭III–V6/4 – I · Bridge (8, in A): [I – (G♯) – vi – (E) · IV – ♭VII – I] ×2, the last unit re-read in C as V/V – V – I. The intro gets away with its cross relations because the outer voices move stepwise in contrary motion, which is also what forces V into second inversion. Inside the verse the V resolves deceptively to vi at the start of the tail () before the phrase converges home. The bridge is a real pivot modulation to A (, ); on paper the pivot is clean, and what makes it sound abrupt is the proximity of the E♭ and A chords, a tritone apart at the root.

Notable. The harmonic rhythm is punishingly slow, and the D→G root motion of bars 9–12 restates the C→F motion of bars 1–8 in half the time. The middle chords of the tail get no Roman numerals on purpose — they exist only as a consequence of harmonising the bass descent. The outro feints at repeating the bridge modulation and then cancels it; he hears two Beethoven coda gambits at once.

Against this page. Agrees on C major with the middle 8 in A.

the-beatles-strawberry-fields-forever.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Strawberry Fields Forever
the-beatles-strawberry-fields-forever.html:
Two recordings in different keys and tempos were spliced together — one sped up, one slowed down — so the join at 1:00 goes unnoticed. Indian swarmandal adds shimmer. Avant-garde coda fades out and then fades back in.

Chords

Key: A major as played (capo 1 → sounds in B♭)

Chorus ("Let me take you down"): A – Em7 – F♯7 – D – F♯7 – Dmaj7 – A → I – v7 – VI7 – IV – VI7 – IVmaj7 – I (the F♯7 is a dreamy secondary dominant pulling at the Bm region)

Verse: E – Emaj7 – E7 – F♯m – E – D – A → V – Vmaj7 – V7 – vi – V – IV – I (a descending inner line under the E chords)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-strawberry-fields-forever-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

The single most influential studio-as-instrument record ever made. Famously, the final master is two completely different takes — in different keys AND tempos — spliced together (~1:00 in); George Martin varisped one down and the other up until they almost matched, and the seam is audible if you listen (it's part of the magic).

  • Mellotron flute intro (the wobbly, unstable tape-sampled flutes) — the sound of the whole record.
  • Vari-speed everything: the vocal was slowed for the dreamy, detached quality; instruments pitched to make the splice work.
  • Backwards tapes, reversed cymbals, Indian swarmandal, timpani, and heavy tape manipulation throughout — texture over "band."
  • The F♯7 dreamy secondary dominant + the descending inner lines give the harmony the same unstable, floating quality as the production.

Steal this

  • Comp two different takes into one: record versions at different tempos/keys, then time-stretch/pitch them to splice the best of each (Melodyne / warp) — commit to a Frankenstein master.
  • Mellotron/unstable-sample texture: a slightly-detuned, wobbly sampled instrument (Cassette wow/flutter on a flute/pad sample) as the signature hook.
  • Vari-speed the vocal for a detached, dreamy lead (Little AlterBoy / kHs Pitch Shifter).
  • Reverse + backwards cymbals/tapes (kHs Reverser / reverse the audio) for psychedelic bloom.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Magical Mystery Tour · search "The Beatles — Strawberry Fields Forever"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Strawberry Fields Forever (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Strawberry Fields Forever — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #105.

Form. Underneath the effects it is a conservative folk-ballad shape with one late pop gesture: refrain-first, then strict refrain/verse alternation, no bridge and no instrumental solo, with all three verses carrying different words. That is folk practice, not pop practice. The pop move arrives only at the end, where the last refrain is repeated to the point of elision with the outro. Intro four bars, except the last carries two extra beats. The refrain is metrically slippery — a foreshortened half-measure at one point, a single bar of 6/8 at another, with the eighth-note pulse held constant across both, and the vocal entering mid-bar so the felt downbeat is really bar 2. The verse is the stable section: a plain 8 bars in four even 2-bar phrases with noticeably faster harmonic rhythm. The outro fades out, fades back in, and fades out again — novel in 1967.

Harmony. The governing device is cadence avoidance: V is set up repeatedly and almost never allowed to resolve, and the song settles for IV–I plagal closes instead (). Intro: F (V) · Cm – A° · B♭ – F · E♭ – B♭ over a stepwise descending bass. On paper that is tame; by ear the opening chord does not sound like V and you expect F to be home until the forced 6/4→5/3 plagal turn corrects it. Refrain: I (2) · v minor (2) · vii°-of-IV · IV – V · V-of-ii · [6/8] IV – I — minor v in a major key, a diminished chord that could be aiming at either IV or ii, an approach to ii that never lands (). Verse: V · V7 – vii°/vi · vi · IV · IV – V · I – vi · IV – V · IV – I, whose opening V resolves deceptively to vi ().

Notable. The released master is two different recordings spliced at 1:00: take 7 (cut in A) sped up and take 26 (cut in B) slowed down, both landing near B♭ — near enough that the opening reads slightly off against a tuning fork. His angle is that almost nothing here is technically new; it is the Revolver toolkit run all at once and pushed much further.

Against this page. Agrees — his "B-flat (more or less)" is this page's sounding pitch (A shapes, capo 1).

the-beatles-sun-king.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Sun King
the-beatles-sun-king.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: a bonsai medley inside the medley — a small self-contained song (refrain, bridge, refrain′) wrapped in verse-like material on both sides that could not stand alone. Intro (4 bars, two identical 2-bar tiles) · Verse (the intro tile with a convergent tile bolted to the front, stated three times) · Refrain · Bridge · Refrain′ · final Verse, with a complete ending. John assembles the track from short phrases repeated and re-sequenced like mosaic tiles rather than writing anything through.

The key scheme is E → C → E, a third relation rather than a fifth one (), which is exactly where the cross relations come from: four sharps against none. The move into the refrain has no pivot at all — two bars of G11, then an abrupt cut to C major with rhythmic activity stopped dead (). The chord looks like F stacked on G and functions unmistakably as V.

The refrain then targets a V-of-V-of-V, an odd destination in its own right (), whose resolution the bridge delays by inserting IV. Coming home, refrain′ lands on F and re-reads it as ♭II of E — a Neapolitan pivot, the same gambit as "You're Going To Lose That Girl". Chords are heavily embellished, added sixths especially, which produces the lounge-jazz luxury and the unbothered affect at once.

The melody is secondary throughout: the lead line does not carry a section, the block "ah" vocals do.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-taxman.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Taxman
the-beatles-taxman.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (a fake spliced count-off, then 2 bars vamping the bass ostinato) · Verse/Refrain (13 bars — an 8-bar couplet balanced against a lopsided 5-bar phrase, ) · Bridge (9 bars, the second phrase stretched by one) · the pair twice more, with a guitar solo occupying the verse portion of an otherwise ordinary pass · Outro (fade).

There is no V chord in this song. The harmony is I, ♭VII and IV () with one late ♭III, and the mode is deliberately undecidable: the third degree is simply absent from the tune (), so Mixolydian and Dorian are both live readings while the guitars keep supplying a major/minor I. The tune itself is pentatonic and mantra-like, circling a few motifs in a narrow range ().

The ♭III arrives once, late, purely to signal the end is coming, its two sustained bars filled by a descending bass counterpoint. Despite the asymmetry the verse reads as blues-adjacent — AAB rhetoric, obbligato-filled gaps, and a ♭VII→IV that paraphrases the blues V→IV.

The whole track is one long crescendo of density, staged verse by verse in those gaps: guitar chops and cymbal slashes, then tambourine, then cowbell and falsetto rejoinders, then a three-part shout. Paul's bass ostinato is one bar long with a saw-tooth contour — tense and tightly wound where "Day Tripper" and "Paperback Writer" use two-bar arches — and after taking the solo he stays in, doubling that ostinato an octave up.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-tell-me-what-you-see.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Tell Me What You See
the-beatles-tell-me-what-you-see.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (2 bars vamping on I) · Verse (16 bars — an 8-bar verse-like couplet, then an 8-bar refrain-like couplet with slower harmonic rhythm) · Verse · Bridge (8, of which the second phrase is entirely instrumental) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro (a compressed variant of the bridge's first phrase, hummed wordlessly, to a full ending).

A modest song with one instructive lesson: the harmony is only I, IV and V, and every formal boundary is articulated by changes in harmonic rhythm rather than by chord choice (). Two chords per bar in the verse's first couplet, one per bar in the second, one every two bars in the bridge — the deceleration alone tells you where you are in the form. The chord opening the bridge functions as V-of-IV because of the F natural in the tune above it, but it is still the same triad either way ().

The tune opens with a dramatic upward octave leap and is loaded with appoggiaturas (); contour-wise it gets stuck circling the fifth degree, and — a genuine oddity — the seventh degree never appears anywhere in it.

It is also the most Latin-flavoured original the band had written to that point: assorted hand percussion stands in for the kit through most of the song, and the complete kit does not appear until the bridge (). Two voices alternate between harmony and unison from phrase to phrase, which given the lyric reads as almost programmatic.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-tell-me-why.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Tell Me Why
the-beatles-tell-me-why.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4) · Refrain (12 — two parallel 6-bar phrases, each a 4-bar main phrase plus a 2-bar connector) · Verse (8) · Refrain · Verse · Refrain · Bridge (10) · Refrain · Outro (4). Odd twice over: the song opens with a refrain, and the lone bridge is held back until very near the end.

Almost the whole song is one cliché — I–vi–ii–V — used for both refrain and verse, so the interest is in how much differentiation you can get without changing the chords (). Most of the progression lies along the circle of fifths, and it is tonally open: every phrase of every section ends on V. The refrain's connector restates the whole four-bar progression in harmonic double time (); the bridge does the opposite and drags each chord across two bars.

The differentiation comes from melody and bass. The refrain tune is pentatonic-major and rhythmically stretched with a walking bass under it faking faster harmonic motion; the verse leans on the bluesy minor third, is chattier and jumpier, and sits over a stable bass. The bridge is set up by simply sustaining I at the end of the preceding refrain until it ripens into V-of-IV ().

Because everything circles back to V forever, stopping the song takes a genuinely foreign progression: the outro is entered as a to vi and then goes to ♭VI, a 4–3 over V, and finally I.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-thank-you-girl.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Thank You Girl
the-beatles-thank-you-girl.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4, and it returns intact as a full section before the final verse) · Verse/Refrain · Verse/Refrain · Bridge/Refrain · Intro · Verse/Refrain · Outro (6+4+4, the first phrase quoting the intro verbatim). Verse 8, refrain 4, bridge 8; lyrics across the three verses run ABA.

Three chords for better than 90% of its length, and the twists are not in the chord chart. The intro is V – IV – V – IV → I — four bars that never state the tonic, so the key is genuinely open and could as easily be read a fifth up until bar 5 confirms it. The refrain is four bars that never resolve, which is exactly why it has to follow a bridge that closes firmly on I. The vi and ii of that bridge are the only two chords outside I/IV/V in the entire song.

The real device is harmonic rhythm: one chord per bar in intro and refrain, two per bar in the verse. The verse feels faster and more driven without the tempo moving an inch ().

The vocal method is the payoff. Sing a phrase in unison, then on its repeat keep that exact line as the lower voice and write a new upper part against it. What comes out is fourths, fifths and the occasional sixth rather than thirds — dissonant on paper, motivated in the ear because the bottom line is already familiar. Three texture changes happen inside the 4-bar intro alone, including offbeat neighbour-tone embellishments ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-ballad-of-john-and-yoko.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Ballad Of John And Yoko
the-beatles-the-ballad-of-john-and-yoko.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (2 bars vamping on I — the extreme brevity sets a hurried tone for everything after) · Verse/Refrain ×3 · Bridge (8 bars plus two extra beats) · Verse/Refrain ×2 · Outro (the three-times-out gambit on the refrain's second half). Verse and refrain are best parsed as one unit; neither is self-sufficient.

Cut on impulse in a single April 1969 session with only John and Paul present, the two of them covering every instrument by overdub — and the record gives no hint of it. A stylised blues that keeps the flavour of the idiom while carefully avoiding any suggestion of twelve-bar form.

Chords are rooted only on I, IV and V. The verse vamps four bars on I and then flattens its seventh, so the second half retroactively becomes a four-bar dominant preparation for the refrain's opening IV (). The V chord is repeatedly coloured by a simultaneous major/minor third cross-relation — the blues rub applied to the dominant rather than to the tonic — and the tune leans hard on ♭7 with lighter use of ♭3 ().

The vocal arrangement escalates in three steps rather than two: John alone for three passes, Paul entering tentatively on the last word of each verse line in the fourth, then singing the fifth all the way through. Three closing signatures — slow triplets in the lead guitar, an added-sixth final chord, and a trailing drum fill that lands after you have already assumed the track is over.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-continuing-story-of-bung.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Continuing Story Of Bungalow Bill
the-beatles-the-continuing-story-of-bung.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Refrain (11 bars, ABA′B′, the odd length coming from a truncated second phrase) · Verse (12 bars, slower tempo, AAB, blues-shaped without being a blues) · Refrain · Refrain · Outro (roughly 4.8 refrain cycles, cut off by the lead-in to the next track). Refrain-first and refrain-heavy, which is what makes it read as a room full of people rather than a studio take.

A folk-ballad singalong whose surface is childishly simple and whose key scheme is anything but: three keys — C major, A major and A minor — locked together because A minor is the relative minor of one and the parallel minor of the other (). The refrain alone contains two of them; the G ending its second phrase is the hinge, V at home and ♭VII in A, which makes the move up readable as a pivot rather than a bare jump ().

Minor iv in a major key is the recurring device, a fifties rock cliché Lennon kept using: sour on first appearance, and in the third phrase the thing that opens the door to the minor mode (). The verse's last two bars re-read as vi – iv in C, which is how it hands back to the refrain, and its E-to-G move produces the standing Beatles G♯/G♮ cross-relation.

Best arrangement lesson: the bassoon that carries the song out is already inside the ensemble from the second outro repeat, well before it is exposed.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-end.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The End
the-beatles-the-end.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: three parts, roughly 34s / 55s / 35s, which produces an ABA symmetry even though the outer parts share no material. Part 1 — an 8-bar phrase instrumental, a 4-bar drum solo, the phrase again with a screaming double-tracked lead, then a 16-bar drum solo. Part 2 — fourteen passes of a 4-bar frame carrying the round-robin duelling guitar solos. Part 3 — one unusually long phrase: four bars of piano alone, eight of vocal, four of 3/4, then a final stretch of slow 4/4.

The home key migrates, A major for most of it and C only in the second half of part 3 — a third relation (). Part 1's opening A is far more a dominant pointing at D than a tonic, so the phrase behaves as convergent rather than closed (). Part 2 is a plagal I – IV frame and nothing else. Part 3 sits over a static A with a G major chord stacked in the treble against it — a pedal point, not a root change () — then holds the two inner voices while soprano and bass descend in parallel sixths, and the F that results is the pivot: ♭VI at home, IV in C.

Rhythmically it runs two metric modulations back to back: to 3/4 with the quarter held constant, then back to 4/4 with the new quarter equal to a whole bar of that 3/4 — a written-in slowdown rather than a played ritard. The syncopation motif threads all three parts (), down to the final "make" sung just ahead of its downbeat.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-fool-on-the-hill.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Fool On The Hill
the-beatles-the-fool-on-the-hill.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: completely flat — Intro (one measure) · (Verse · Refrain) ×4, the last two verses instrumental, then a fade. No bridge, no interruption of the pattern; the ballad shape shared by folk and by Schubert's song cycles. The verse is an unusual 7 measures, its final phrase truncated so it elides into the refrain; the refrain is only 4, with one solitary extra measure tacked on to get back. Both surviving outtakes had a four-measure intro that exposed the song's gambit immediately — the released version withholds it.

One harmonic event carries the whole song: verse in D major, refrain in D minor. Everything in the refrain comes from the parallel minor — i, iv, ♭VI, ♭VII () — and the two crossings are deliberately asymmetric: minor arrives with no warning at all, while the return to major gets a whole measure of runway. Pollack's historical point is that the classical models overwhelmingly run minor to major; this one inverts the direction, and he ties that to the difference between bittersweet love and oblivious foolishness.

The verse's first four measures are harmony suspended over a pedal, Bach-prelude fashion (); when the pedal releases, the harmonic rhythm doubles for the rest of the section ().

Both sections are melodic arches, and the refrain tops out on F natural while the verse goes slightly higher to F♯ — the two peaks differ by exactly the note that defines the mode. Three appoggiatura figures are named in the essay (), including an échappée that escapes downward before resolving up.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-inner-light.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Inner Light
the-beatles-the-inner-light.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (ad-lib drone plus a harpsichord pickup, then 10 bars in tempo) · Verse (an odd 13 bars, short phrases as AA′A′A′BCC′) · Break · Verse · Break′, extended to a full ending. The two breaks are built on the intro's foundation and their backing tracks are close to identical takes of the same material.

The purest of Harrison's three Indian records — backing cut entirely in Bombay, lyric inward-facing, form alternating almost mechanically between instrumental and sung blocks.
