Harmonically it is about as close to a drone as you can get while still using more than one chord: Mixolydian in name, but the mode's calling card never shows up, because there is no dominant function anywhere — no V, and not even ♭VII. The vocabulary is I against ii or IV and nothing else, with everything else carried by the drone (). The one cadential gesture is the lead instrument's upward run to scale degree 5 at the end of every section, which sets the sense of home unusually high in the register.

The backing material is regimented into descending four-note scale fragments, each answered by a three-note ascent; the sung tune is deliberately the opposite, moving in thirds, fourths and one fifth.

Texture articulates the form as reliably as chords would (): the breaks carry a deep drone, percussion and oboe leads, while the verses drop the low drone and the tambourine, add flutes, and hold the oboe back until the last phrase. Pollack's aside is worth keeping: perceived length tracks formal complexity, not duration.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-long-and-winding-road.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Long and Winding Road
the-beatles-the-long-and-winding-road.html:
McCartney's piano ballad about loss and longing. Phil Spector controversially added full orchestral and choral overdubs without McCartney's knowledge or approval for the Let It Be album — a source of lasting bitterness.

Chords

Key: D major as played (capo 1 → sounds in E♭)

Verse: Bm – Gsus2/A – D – D7 – G – Gmaj7 – G – F♯m – Bm – Em – A – D → vi – IV – I – I7 – IV – iii – vi – ii – V – I (a long, descending ballad arc — vi to I)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-the-long-and-winding-road-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

McCartney's piano ballad, famously drowned in Phil Spector's lush orchestra + choir overdub (added without McCartney's blessing — a big reason for the 'Let It Be… Naked' redo). The lesson is a cautionary one: over-production vs. the bare demo.

Steal this

  • Know when NOT to add: compare a sparse piano/vocal against a lush orchestral version — sometimes bare wins (the Naked lesson).
  • Lush orchestral pad if you do go big: strings + choir under a piano ballad (Reverb Send Long).
  • Descending, resolving changes for a 'closing' feel → Chord Progressions.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — The Long and Winding Road"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Long and Winding Road (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — The Long And Winding Road — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #175.

Form. A torch song whose surface sentimentality is bought back by genuinely sophisticated structure. The engine is a major/minor tug of war: the relative minor, C, spends the entire verse trying to unseat E♭ and never quite manages it, which is the harmonic image of the lyric's thwarted-but-still-hopeful want. A second, subtler device: the title phrase turns up in positions that make its formal job ambiguous — intro, verse opening, or bridge tail, depending where you are standing. The verse is a leisurely 24 bars in six even four-bar phrases, but the lyric groups them AB / CD / C′D′, which is why it can be that long without sagging. The song opens mid-stream with no intro. The bridge is a short 8, phrased AA, harmonically open, and elides straight back into the verse.

Harmony. Verse (24): vi (2) – V9/11 (2) · I7 (2) – IV (2) · IV – iii – vi (2) · ii7 – V – I7 (2) · IV – iii – vi (2) · ii – V – I (2) · Bridge (8): [I – IV – I6/3 – ii–V] ×2 · Outro: ii – V – I (2) · V7/11 (2) – I. The key never actually changes — C minor is tonicised repeatedly without ever modulating () — and his reason why is the sharpest thing in the essay: C minor is only ever served with a minor v, never a major V, so it is denied the leading tone it would need to establish itself (). Watch the A♭ chord pivoting: IV in the major reading, VI in the minor (). At the bridge's elision back into the verse, V → vi is a textbook deceptive cadence — one more chance for C minor to intercept the resolution ().

Notable. The whole verse is a fight to land structurally on the high E♭: it appears on the very first downbeat over a C minor chord, and only at the end of phrase 6 does it arrive as a goal, by way of a plain 6 – 7 – 8. Each four-bar phrase delivers its text in a burst landing on the downbeat of bar 3 and leaves the rest empty. Spector removed Paul's vocal from the second bridge and replaced it with the arching violin line — and trimmed a stage-whisper piano coda that would have reopened the minor question after an apparently conclusive ending.

Against this page. Agrees on E♭ major (this page's capo-1 D shapes).

the-beatles-the-night-before.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Night Before
the-beatles-the-night-before.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: the long two-bridge model — Intro (a single 8-bar phrase) · Verse (16, four equal phrases, AABC) · Verse · Bridge (8) · Verse · Verse (half solo) · Bridge · Verse · Outro (a petit reprise of the verse's last phrase plus the returning guitar fanfare lick).

A bluesy foreground over a pop chassis. Half of the eight chords are foreign to the key — ♭III, minor iv, ♭VII and V-of-V alongside I, IV, V and vi () — and this may be the first time they put ♭VII between I and IV (). The narrative is harmonic: the first two phrases open wide to V, the third refuses to resolve and introduces the ominous minor iv, and only the fourth restores I. In verses that lead to another verse, the ending is forced away from I at the last moment so the next verse's downbeat has something to arrive from.

The chromatic ♭3/♮3 pair runs at three scales at once (): melodically, with the blue third clashing against the major chords beneath; harmonically, in the vi/iv alternation; and ornamentally, in the bridge's noodling. Range is tightly managed for one payoff — the verse repeatedly caps at G and the song's only high A arrives at the very end of the bridge ().

The vocal arrangement is the standout: what sounds like call and response is really one melodic line split hocket-style between double-tracked lead and backing voices, with the backers dropping out entirely for the final phrase.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-the-word.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - The Word
the-beatles-the-word.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro · Verse (a straight 12-bar blues frame) · Bridge (4 bars only) · Verse · Bridge (instrumental) · Verse (partly instrumental) · Outro (a repeat of the instrumental bridge, rapid fade). Underneath a loud, inventive production sits a twelve-bar blues and a four-bar tag — that is the whole song, and the direct structural ancestor of "All You Need Is Love".

The labels break down in a useful way: what functions as the verse behaves like a refrain, because the same lyric closes every one of them, which starts to make the bridge sound like the real verse. The verse is I, IV and V only, with appoggiaturas and an arpeggiated bass decorating the V→IV move in bars 9–10 (). The bridge runs I – ♭VII – ♭III – IV, where the ♭VII functions as V-of-♭III — odd only because home is major; in the parallel minor it would be ordinary ().

The best device is in that bridge: a four-note ostinato under fuzz guitar runs through every bar while the chords move beneath it, so each note's consonance is rewritten chord by chord — a free seventh over one, a 9–8 appoggiatura over the next, the most consonant support over the third, the most dissonant over the fourth ().

The outro hides its own downbeat: the harmonium sustains through bars 1–2 of the final verse so the vocal re-entry lands on bar 3 and reads as some new section. It isn't.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-there-s-a-place.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - There's A Place
the-beatles-there-s-a-place.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: the small single-bridge model. Intro (5 bars) · Verse (15) · Verse variant (rewritten to hand off to the bridge) · Bridge (10) · Verse · Outro (the final verse, one bar shorter, into an antiphonal fade). Every irregular section length comes from the same cause: a stretched vocal pickup into the next section ().

The music contradicts the lyric — a confident claim over harmony that never finds its footing. The signature sonority is the major seventh landing on the very first downbeat, and the key is established by I–IV oscillation rather than by any cadence. Bars 7–8 sit on two full bars of V and leave it unresolved, veering toward the relative minor in what sounds like a modulation the next verse simply ignores (); the variant verse re-opens on V and hands it to a into vi at the bridge.

The bridge is the clearest case. Its first three chords set up a textbook pivot modulation to B major — and B never comes; a G♯ major chord aborts it and yanks the music back to C♯ minor. Pollack half-blames inexperience and half-argues the groping quality is exactly right.

Two competing hooks fight all song: the wailing harmonica motif on the anxious side and the rising figure carrying the title phrase on the reassuring side. The harmonica hook is then folded into the backing vocal in bars 9–12 (), and the outro simply alternates the two.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-things-we-said-today.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Things We Said Today
the-beatles-things-we-said-today.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: the standard two-bridge model with one verse between and no instrumental solo. Intro (2) · Verse (16, four even phrases) · Verse · Bridge (8) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro (a reprise of the intro material into a fade). Verses 2 and 3 end on A major instead of the expected minor, and the bridge's noisier texture starts in their final bar.

One of the earliest big harmonic stunts in the catalogue: a ♭II (Neapolitan) resolved directly to i, skipping the V that classical practice requires, used in both verse and bridge and reused later in "You're Going To Lose That Girl". It is also one of very few early originals pervasively in a minor key — natural minor, using minor v7 rather than a functional major V (), with the bridges shifting to the parallel major ().

The verse's third phrase is where the mood turns: you know immediately it is leaving home, you do not know where it is going, and at peak uncertainty the ♭II drops straight back to i. The bridge develops the same gambit — two phrases with an identical melodic backbone, the second substituting ♭II for the dominant, which is the source of their irony. That ♭II implies Phrygian throughout (), running in the inner voices even though the figure never appears in the top-voice melody.

Only Paul, on every vocal part, and the variation is in the tracking: single-tracked verse 1 except for a parallel-thirds phrase and a sudden switch to double-tracking mid-phrase, with the title line harmonised in open fourths.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-think-for-yourself.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Think For Yourself
the-beatles-think-for-yourself.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (2 bars of I-chord vamp that quietly declare the whole song) · Verse (12 bars as two parallel 6-bar phrases, not three fours) · Refrain (8 bars) · Refrain · Outro (two more refrains plus a petit reprise, complete ending). The seams are smoothed over deliberately: the verse's vocal-against-bass-lick byplay carries straight through the refrain, and the refrain loops back into the next verse with no join.

The distinguishing move is that Harrison blends the parallel major and minor rather than switching between them (). The I chord is bi-modal, carrying B natural in an inner voice against a B♭ in the melody (), and minor v, ♭III and ♭VI belong only to the minor. Never quite major, never quite minor, which is exactly the lyric's posture.

Home arrives late and by a wandering route — the verse opens on ii, and only at the end of the first six-bar phrase does G register as home at all; the second phrase is identical until its last bar, where landing on ii erodes whatever arrival you just got. In the refrain the harmony parses two phrases while the tune parses three, which is what makes the section loop.

Tambourine and maracas go four-in-the-bar in cheerful contradiction of the slow triplets everything else plays (), and the "fuzz bass" panned right does not carry the bass part at all — it selectively doubles the real bass an octave up.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-this-boy.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - This Boy
the-beatles-this-boy.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (5½ bars — three bare guitar chords, the first landing mid-bar, functioning as a stretched pickup into a 4-bar intro proper) · Verse (16) · Verse · Bridge (16, two neat equal phrases) · Verse · fade. Unusually for them, all three verses carry different lyrics, and the form runs short because the bridge is too intense to repeat.

The sharpest structural observation is that the voices and the band are on different grids: the backing loops a four-bar cliché four times while the vocal lays three unequal phrases across it that start in the wrong places — phrase 2 entering on a long anacrusis in the middle of bar 7, phrase 3 finishing early enough to leave two bars of filler.

The verse progression is I – vi – ii – V, and the point is the ii rather than IV: it lines the final three chords up as descending fifths, so the loop gains an inevitability the IV version does not have (). In the bridge the harmonic rhythm drops to one chord every two bars while the chords themselves get more restless — a high density of secondary dominants that never actually leaves the key (, ).

Appoggiaturas turn nearly every chord into a seventh or ninth and characteristically resolve late, after the harmony has already moved () — that delayed resolution is the source of the song's ache. One of only three sustained three-part-harmony vehicles in the catalogue, and the ostensible lead is the bottom voice, which is why the climb above the other two in the bridge lands so hard.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-ticket-to-ride.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Ticket To Ride
the-beatles-ticket-to-ride.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: two-bridge model, one verse in the middle, no instrumental section. Verse is 16 bars in four equal phrases, but the real split is 8 + 8 — an expository half opening out to V, then a refrain-like half heading back toward I. Bridge is 8 bars, one 4-bar phrase stated twice.

Ordinary form, ordinary chord vocabulary; everything interesting happens in texture, rhythm and dissonance. What keeps it from going flat is an exceedingly slow harmonic rhythm — four bars of nothing but I to open the verse — which creates suspense the chords themselves do not ().

The novel bit is a three-way pivot off vi: the same chord is answered first by IV, then by ♭VII (), and finally by V, which after the first two feels like the only functional move left on the board. The bridge provides contrast without modulating at all — it simply refuses to touch I for eight bars.

Free melodic dissonance is the main spice (), climaxing over the ♭VII chord where the sung line has no note in common with the chord underneath.

The ostinato does structural work far beyond where it actually plays — hear it at the start and end of a section and you assume it ran through the middle, which it often does not. And the payoff detail: Ringo's syncopated verse pattern, derived from the guitar figure, is quietly retired after the second verse for even eighths, so the two drift apart and the listener feels a release without locating it ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-tomorrow-never-knows.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Tomorrow Never Knows
the-beatles-tomorrow-never-knows.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (6 bars, built as 2 bars each of three entering elements — tamboura drone, hard-rock rhythm track, seagull loop) · Verse (a straightforward 8, repeated mantra-like seven times) · Instrumental (16 bars, divided 6 + 10 instead of 8 + 8) · Verse × several · Outro, ending in disintegration rather than a true fade.

A kitchen-sink collage — Indian drone, modal tune, tape loops, ADT, vocal through revolving Leslie speakers, distorted close miking — that somehow does not scatter. The structural reason it can afford all that is that the harmony essentially never moves: the whole track sits on a C pedal (), with an implied vacillation toward ♭VII in the second half of virtually every verse (). That is the entire harmonic content of the song.

The tune is equal parts triadic bugle call and bluesy lick leaning on ♭7, and its first half is deliberately simplistic — the archetypal case of keeping one parameter plain while the rest go to extremes. The instrumental's two halves split the modal question between them: the first emphasises the major third, the second the bent minor third, both over the flat seventh ().

Despite the thickness, the fabric is made of discrete elements each with its own timbre and its own rhythmic identity, which is what keeps it parseable — and mapping which element appears where shows the orchestration is carefully scheduled, not free-wheeling ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-two-of-us.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Two of Us
the-beatles-two-of-us.html:
McCartney wrote it about his relationship with Linda. Two strummed acoustic guitars throughout — no electric guitars. Lennon and McCartney harmonize on a song that feels like a celebratory road trip.

Chords

Key: G major as played (capo 3 → sounds in B♭)

Verse: G – Cadd9 – G/B – Am7 – G → I – IV – I/3 – ii7 – I

"On our way back home": Cadd9 – G – G/B – Cadd9 – D → IV – I – I/3 – IV – V

Bright, two-guitar strum. From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-two-of-us-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Let It Be — an intimate acoustic duet (Lennon & McCartney trading and blending), capo'd folk changes, gentle brushed rhythm. A back-to-basics reaction to the studio maximalism of the prior records.

Steal this

  • Two-voice blend: track two leads sharing the melody in close harmony (1 Harmony Vocal Track).
  • Capo folk simplicity — let the acoustic + vocals be the whole thing.
  • Warm, close, minimal processing.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Let It Be · search "The Beatles — Two of Us"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Two of Us (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Two Of Us — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #167.

Form. A pseudo-folk love song that would be too sweet to survive on its own terms; uneven phrase lengths, mid-verse meter changes and one modal swerve are what keep it edible. The verse's metric shifts are among the most extreme in the catalogue. The classic two-bridge variant with a single verse between the bridges and no instrumental solo, except that the intro returns between the first two verses. Intro 4 bars, all I, with a staggered entrance. Verse phrased AB / AB, C C C′, harmonically closed but metrically anything but — bar lengths run 4 4 2 4 4 | 3 3 3 3 | 3 2 4 4 (). The metric bookkeeping is the good part: phrase A ends half a bar short, the switch to 3/4 keeps the deficit running, and the lone 2/4 bar at the end of C′ pays back exactly the two beats that went missing.

Harmony. Verse: I (held) – IV – ii · I – V/IV | I – V/IV (3/4 bars) · I – IV – I · Bridge (in G minor): ♭III – v – i – ii (held 2) – V. The verse's chord list is small and ordinary, and his point is about function, not vocabulary: IV → ii moves from one subdominant to another, so nothing progresses, and that inertia is the idyllic feel (). The bridge simply switches to the parallel minor, flattening 3, 6 and 7 in the tune and dragging the chords with it () — the same device Paul used in "Here, There And Everywhere," in the same key. The difference: here the only V in the bridge leads straight back to major, so the minor is implied and never confirmed, and cross-relations pile up as a result.

Notable. The tune opens with a textbook pentatonic lick and then admits the 4th for the rest of the verse (). George is scored in tenor range and kept low, but gets one recurring scale figure that marks each metric shift in the verse's back half. The fade is a fabrication — the studio performance had a full ending. He rates the Let It Be take the definitive version, rare for that album.

Against this page. Agrees on G major, which is this page's as-played key; the record sounds in B♭ with the capo, and he analyses at the played pitch.

the-beatles-wait.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Wait
the-beatles-wait.html:
Recorded during the Help! sessions but held back for Rubber Soul. Tambourine and maracas add rhythmic texture. A straightforward mid-tempo track with tight harmonies.

Chords

Key: E minor as played (capo 2 → sounds in F♯m)

Verse: Em – Am – Em – B7 – Em → i – iv – i – V7 – i

"Wait till I come back to your side": G – Cmaj7 – G – B7 – Em → ♭III – ♭VImaj7 – ♭III – V7 – i (lifts to the relative G major before the B7 yanks it back to Em)

"I feel as though you ought to know": Em – Am – D – G → i – iv – ♭VII – ♭III

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-wait-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

Rubber Soul — built on volume-pedal / tremolo guitar swells and stop-start dynamics (the band cutting out and back in on the hook). Tension from the arrangement's gaps.

Steal this

  • Volume-swell guitar (no pick attack) for a soft, welling texture (LFOTool/volume automation, or a slow attack).
  • Stop-start arrangement: cut the band out and slam back in on the hook — silence as a hook.
  • Tremolo motion (PanMan/Tremolator).

Why I like it

Listen

  • Rubber Soul · search "The Beatles — Wait"

Learning

  • 🎵 THE BEATLES - Wait (Guitar)

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — Wait — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #87.

Form. An orphan from the Help! sessions pulled back out to fill Rubber Soul, and his argument is that you cannot actually hear the seam — itself an argument against treating those two albums as separated by a great divide. Formally it is dense for a filler track. It opens on an off-beat vocal pickup with no intro and no instrumental downbeat to cue the singer, and it has no real outro either — it just rhetorically stops, the last verse's final phrase dropping into slow motion. The main section is a 14-bar verse/refrain hybrid, splitting into a 6-bar "verse" (3 + 3) and an 8-bar "refrain" (4 + 4); he says it is tempting to call these two separate sections but that over-reads what you actually hear. The bridge runs two roughly parallel phrases differing in instrumentation and final chord.

Harmony. Verse (f♯ minor): i7 – B6/4 – b6/4 – i · V – i (×2) — but the Roman numerals are misleading, because F♯ is held as a pedal under all four chords with a descending inner line E – D♯ – D♮ – C♯ above it, so the ear hears one stretched i-to-V move rather than a progression (). Refrain (A major): I – IV · I – V-of-f♯ → i — an abrupt, unhedged modulation to the relative major, then a clean pivot home (). Bridge: ii – V – I – vi · ii – V – I(=♭III of f♯) – V(4–3), whose key is genuinely undecidable and better left that way (): read it in A and the B minor is ii; read it in F♯ minor and the E major becomes V-of-♭III. The ambiguity is the effect.

Notable. Syncopated throughout, sharpened by the non-square 3 + 3 phrasing and a harmonic rhythm that lands off the beat almost constantly (); against all that motion the lyric layout is rigidly symmetrical, ABCACBA. The percussion is staged phrase by phrase — tambourine, then maracas in even eighths, then the full kit on a drum roll with the tambourine switching to match.

Against this page. Pollack reads it in F♯ minor, which is this page's sounding pitch (E minor shapes, capo 2). That does not match the key: field here, which says C major. Nothing above has been changed.

the-beatles-we-can-work-it-out.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - We Can Work It Out
the-beatles-we-can-work-it-out.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro with a complete ending — the double-bridge model with no intro at all and a full ending rather than a fade, both unusual for it. The verse is 16 bars phrased 6 + 6 + 4 rather than four fours, which is why it scans like free verse over a steady 4/4. The bridge is 24 bars: a 12-bar unit of three 4-bar phrases, stated twice.

Nothing chromatic, no remote modulation — all the innovation is in phrasing and dissonance handling. The home key is established by ♭VII instead of V (); the actual dominant does not turn up until the very last bar of the verse, and when it does it is not resolved — the verse spills into the bridge by to vi. That left-hanging dominant is exactly why the song needs its little outro to tie itself off.

The melody is appoggiatura-driven throughout (), and the showcase instance holds a ninth unresolved across the bar line, by which time its own resolution note has become a dissonance against the new chord. The idea is carried into the backing too: the harmonium in the bridge holds a B natural through one chord change where it belongs and on through the next, where it does not.

The bridge's third phrase shifts to a slow-triplet oom-pah-pah feel — three beats per bar where there were four, at the same tempo — so the returning verse sounds faster without being faster ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-what-goes-on.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - What Goes On?
the-beatles-what-goes-on.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (a 3-beat pickup plus 4 bars) · Refrain (20 bars as five equal phrases, AB-AB-C) · Verse (14, asymmetrical AABC with the last phrase foreshortened to 2 bars) · Refrain (solo) · Verse · Refrain · Outro. Strict folksy alternation, no development, and fast enough that 2/2 describes it better than 4/4.

The most useful essay in the batch as a negative example — Pollack spends most of it diagnosing why the song has no forward drive, which makes it a working checklist of drag mechanisms. A five-line stanza needs compensating momentum and gets the opposite: every refrain phrase is short and followed by nearly two bars of dead air, so nothing accumulates, and the low point is the moment the ear registers that bars 1–8 are about to repeat verbatim. His test is to delete that repeat and play the remaining twelve bars, which flow.

I, IV and V and almost nothing else, at a slow harmonic rhythm that compounds the phrase-length problem (). The 4–3 suspension over V at each refrain climax is the only intensification and arrives far too late; the minor iv is the one borrowed colour ().

The one thing pushing forward is the verse's foreshortened final phrase — round it out to four bars and the section sags (). The solo refrain worsens matters by entering on phrase 2, so its start reads as a new section.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-what-you-re-doing.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - What You're Doing
the-beatles-what-you-re-doing.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (8 bars in two layered halves — four bars of solo drums playing a marching fanfare, a first for them, then the band entering with the ostinato twice) · Verse (8, or 9 when another verse follows, with a two-bar ostinato restatement overlapping the last bar) · Verse · Bridge (8, parsed 2+2+4) · Verse · Verse (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse · Outro (a triple petit reprise, then the intro replayed in reverse layering).

Standard form, five chords, and yet what the essay keeps returning to is the sheer volume of melodic dissonance — appoggiaturas, suspensions and free non-resolving sevenths and ninths, enough to turn most of those plain triads into added-sixth and extended sonorities (). That is what makes the song read jazzy rather than hymn-like.

The home key is established entirely by I and IV. Apart from vi, no other chord appears at all until the bridge, and V is withheld right to the end of it — which then stops wide open on that dominant, set up by V-of-V, so the section's whole job is to motivate the verse's return (). Both sections lean on alternating vi and IV, the device Paul would push further in "Drive My Car".

The tune leans hard on the bluesy ♭3, which cross-relates with the major third inside the tonic chords every time the hook lands (). One subtle distinction worth having: the ostinato enters syncopated from the previous bar's "four-and" while the tune starts squarely on the downbeat — same material, two identities.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-when-i-get-home.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - When I Get Home
the-beatles-when-i-get-home.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: refrain-first, and it also has a bridge — compare "Tell Me Why". Refrain 8 bars (two parallel 2-bar phrases balanced by one 4-bar phrase) · Verse 8 · Refrain · Verse · Refrain · Bridge (10 bars, the only non-square section, five 2-bar phrases grouping 2 + 3) · Verse · Refrain · Outro.

The key scheme is the event. A Hard Day's Night is full of songs using either a relative or a parallel major/minor shift; this is the only one that uses both. The refrain starts in A major and ends in A minor, and that A minor is then the relative minor of the C major that owns the verses and bridge (, ). The hinge is a chord that puns: G is ♭VII at home and V of C (), so the pivot is inaudible as machinery. Harmonic rhythm is deliberately uneventful for the first half of the refrain so those moves land as events.

All of it runs on barely six chords, and the sense of where home is never settles — enough that Pollack thinks the hard ending on C sounds forced and a fade would have served better. The verse's second chord is written IV but is more properly a ii⁶₅, a first-inversion D7 with the melody holding D♮ against a double-stopped bass fifth.

The refrain's rhythmic hook is a hard syncopation on the last eighth of the bar with no demarcation of the next downbeat at all, which is what makes it wrench ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-when-i-m-sixty-four.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - When I'm Sixty-Four
the-beatles-when-i-m-sixty-four.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: a perfect arch — Intro · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro, symmetrical end to end. No section doubles up, there is no separate refrain, and the outro is the intro again. The verse is a four-square 16 phrased ABA′C; the bridge is an unusual 17, a square 16 with one extra measure tacked on. The intro's four measures plus a two-measure vamp — the band waiting on the singer — is a convention of the style, not an accident.

The harmony sounds clunky on purpose while actually running secondary dominants, added-note chords and harmonised chromatic basslines underneath. The reason a busy progression still sits still is that every phrase opens on the chord the previous phrase closed on, with the harmonic rhythm accelerating toward the end of the verse ().

Two chromatic rising basslines carry phrases 2 and 4, and Pollack's distinction between them is the transferable part (): the first is contrapuntal filling inside one sustained dominant, the second earns a Roman numeral per step because each bass note lasts twice as long and there is real root motion underneath. The diminished seventh in the last verse phrase is a first for the catalogue — a subdominant diminished seventh built on ♯2 rather than the usual VII-based dominant substitute ().

The two bridges tease the vocal differently — the first withholds the singer for a whole phrase so you start assuming it is instrumental.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-while-my-guitar-gently-weeps.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - While My Guitar Gently Weeps
the-beatles-while-my-guitar-gently-weeps.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: two-bridge model with verses between, one of them the guitar solo, but with the usual opening double verse deliberately missing — the verse is already an internal double couplet, so a second one back to back would be a repeat of a repeat. Intro 8 bars (the first half of the verse, instrumental, ending on V so the vocal entry is motivated) · Verse 16 · Bridge 16 (one 8-bar phrase stated twice, and unusually the two bridges carry different lyrics) · Outro, nearly two full verse cycles into a fade.

The sadness lives in the notes, not the production: the heavy official take and the acoustic Anthology 3 outtake share melody, chords and phrasing. The verse holds one A-minor chord for three bars while the bass walks down chromatically — on the fretboard that looks like a new chord every bar, analytically it is one harmonic event and the odd sonorities are byproducts of the bass (, ).

The bridge answers the verse's closing E with A major, not A minor (), then leans toward C♯ minor and never establishes it — it is reached through its IV, not by I–V–I. That is the pattern for the whole song: three keys touched and abandoned before any takes hold ().

The solo is the structural peak. Clapton ignores the couplet and plays two eight-bar phrases across the sixteen, and the high A at its top is the only place an upward gesture wins.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-why-don-t-we-do-it-in-the-ro.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Why Don't We Do It In The Road?
the-beatles-why-don-t-we-do-it-in-the-ro.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (8 bars — three percussion layers stacking across the first six, the stuttered title question filling the last two) plus the same 24-bar chorus three times, with a complete ending. Two passes would be thin, four would outstay it.

One of Paul's "bonsai tree" songs in Pollack's taxonomy: minimal material, stick-figure form, and no interest whatsoever in disguising either. The instructive comparison is with "Rocky Raccoon" two tracks earlier, which builds a convincing song form out of one repeated frame; this one makes no such attempt and is the better for it.

The chorus is a 12-bar blues with every unit doubled () — eight bars of I, four of IV, four of I, then two/two/four. The tempo is fast and the harmonic rhythm is not, one change every two to eight bars, and the gap between the two is most of what gives the track its lumbering weight ().

The ending is a loud ringing cymbal crash on a downbeat, with the final word of the lyric placed on the beat just before it, syncopated so it lands weakly — the crash takes the emphasis the word was supposed to have.

Almost entirely self-played. Two elements are staged rather than constant: the guitar is withheld until bar 13 of the second chorus and then stays, and the bass thumps unvaried roots until switching to jumpy melodic riffing for the final chorus.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-wild-honey-pie.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Wild Honey Pie
the-beatles-wild-honey-pie.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Break (7 bars) + Refrain (4 bars), three times through, then an outro with a complete ending. A miniature rather than a fragment — it has a complete form on a minimal definition, plus a real written ending. The seven-bar break is an odd length nobody had to bother with on a throwaway, and it is the reason the section registers at all. It also works as an entr'acte between the two songs around it, which is a use of the album as a medium rather than filler; the first of Paul's one-man-band tracks.

The vocabulary is essentially a semi-chromatic stream of dominant sevenths with just enough root motion to establish G as home (). The mechanism is audible in the harpsichord's right hand, which walks a descending parallel set of tritones. Bluesiness comes from the tonic carrying its own flat seventh and from an implied major-against-minor clash on the tonic, sharpest right at the close ().

The final cadence uses an altered V that resists naming: the bass moves G–F–G, which tempts a ♭VII reading, but D persists as a melodic pedal, so the chord is better spelled from D with both third and fifth flattened, in first inversion.

There is also a cross-track effect worth hearing: B natural sits on top of the opening chord, and B was the tonic of the song you just heard — same pitch, new function.

Why I like it

the-beatles-with-a-little-help-from-my-f.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - With A Little Help From My Friends
the-beatles-with-a-little-help-from-my-f.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4, which in album context reads as sitting on the boundary with the title track — only its return as the outro reveals which song owns it) · Verse (8) · Refrain (8 the first time, and later refrains drop its two voiceless balancing bars) · Verse · Refrain · Bridge (8) · Verse · Refrain · Bridge · Refrain · Outro. Verse and refrain almost merge into a single 16-bar section; they are kept separate only because the last refrain has to stand alone after the second bridge.

Deliberately over-simplified vocabulary in the "Yellow Submarine" manner, minus the effects and plus a far more advanced antiphonal vocal arrangement. Verse and bridge are straightforward E major; the intro, refrain and outro carry all the modal contrast — ♭VI and ♭VII, contrast without leaving home (, ). The bridge hints at a modulation to V purely to relieve how tightly the song is tethered to E, then leaves its V-of-V begging.

Verse and refrain stay inside a five-note range; the bridge finally opens the top half of the octave (), but the answering part keeps returning to the other sections' melodic floor, so the register gain reads as an event rather than a new normal.

The real work is the vocal arrangement: one melodic line split between soloist and group, escalating across the form — chorus asks, solo answers — yet written so you hum it back as a single tune without noticing the seam.

Filed under the song's full title; Pollack's essay heading drops the "My".

Why I like it

the-beatles-within-you-without-you.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Within You Without You
the-beatles-within-you-without-you.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: a sprawling ABA conceived in three large blocks — two vocal sections around a central instrumental. Intro (drone fades in, dilruba lays out the main arch riff) · regular Verse (AAB, the parallel phrases six measures each, the third rhythmically free) · extended Verse (identical opening, third phrase stretched so it feeds the refrain — a trick lifted from their ordinary pop songs) · Refrain (freer still; the beat count per measure changes about as often as it would in Stravinsky or Bartók) · Instrumental (two free variations on the extended verse) · Intro · extended Verse · Refrain.

There is one chord for the entire song. A tamboura drone holds I throughout (), so every structural event has to be carried by melody and meter alone — which makes this the cleanest available demonstration of how much a tune can do without harmony.

The scale is essentially Mixolydian, but a raga is not a mode: Western modes map one scale to one name, ragas map one scale to many, distinguished by which degrees carry emphasis and which riffs characterise them (). Verses keep the melodic floor on 3 and hold the octave back until late; refrains push 2, 4 and 6 and leave the tune hanging on 2 for the dilruba to answer.

The best move is in the extended verse, which breaks its own scale with a ♭3 by transposing the verse motif's interval pattern onto scale degree 1 (). And the floating meter is faked — Indian practice fixes a tala; here the meter itself simply changes.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-yellow-submarine.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Yellow Submarine
the-beatles-yellow-submarine.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse (8, parsed 4+4, harmonically open) · Verse · Refrain (8, closed) · Verse · Refrain · Verse (instrumental) · Verse · Refrain. It uses a refrain, not a bridge; three verses run back to back in the middle, which is rare; and it starts in medias res on an unaccompanied vocal pickup.

The music is deliberately plain so the sound collage has something solid to stand on — five ordinary diatonic chords and a tune with a hole in it. What actually tells the sections apart is harmonic rhythm (): verse changes straddle the barline, landing on beat 4 and holding through the downbeat, while refrain changes sit square on the beats. Root motion falls by fifths almost throughout, which is what makes one chord in verse bar 3 a genuine puzzle — the pattern wants ii, but there is a C in the bass.

The tune is pentatonic in the Lennon manner (): scale degree 7 never appears at all, and degree 4 shows up only as a passing note. Narrow range, chant-shaped, pitched for a non-singer.

Variation is scheduled by section rather than written into the music, and the effects are counted as instruments in that scheme: guitar and maracas, then water, then party noise plus a sloppy brass band whose chords clash with the backing track, then submarine machinery, then Lennon echoing Ringo like a captain on a squawk box, then widened backing vocals.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-yer-blues.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Yer Blues
the-beatles-yer-blues.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Verse-A ×2 · Verse-B ×3 · Verse-C (guitar solo) ×2 · Outro (a Verse-A) into a fade. Every section in the track is the same twelve-bar frame (), and all the variety comes from re-parsing and re-feeling it in the foreground — which puts it in surprising company with "Rocky Raccoon".

The device is splitting the same twelve bars two different ways: Verse-A as 8 + 4, Verse-B as 4 + 8, with the opening phrase declaimed over dramatic pauses. The joke is that the same music fills the second and third phrases of every section regardless — the structure changes purely from where you cut it.

Harmonically it is the blues trio plus ♭III, sitting where the approach to V would normally be (); the tune is genuinely blues, ♭3 and ♭7 throughout, with no stylisation there.

Pollack parses the meter as 6/8, which contradicts the numbers Ringo counts in but is what makes the form come out right (). Two metric games run on top: most sections carry one deliberately spastic extra beat in bar 10, and the last Verse-B drops it, which is what lets the backbeat shift while the bar lengths stay put; and the instrumental sections run their eighth-note triplets at double speed, flipping the feel from ternary to four-square with no tempo change. The counterweight comes late, in a deliberately rough splice.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-yes-it-is.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Yes It Is
the-beatles-yes-it-is.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (2 bars) · Verse (15 bars the first time — two 4-bar phrases, a 6-bar closing phrase, then one bar of breathing space) · Verse · Bridge (10, split 4 + 6) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. Verses 2 and 3 extend to 16 by repeating the closing hook, and that extra sustained tonic is exactly what makes the pivot into the bridge possible.

The mature rewrite of "This Boy": same three-part-harmony ballad genre, richer palette, a real if short-lived modulation. ♭VII appears twice inside one verse and behaves differently each time () — first as a surprise substitute for the ii that filled the same slot in the previous phrase, then, considerably stranger, resolving to vi. That late swerve to the relative minor is a in a song otherwise plainly major, and it leaves the home key faintly ambiguous.

The sustained tonic ending verses 2 and 3 puns as I at home and V in the bridge's key, which buys a genuine modulation with no setup bar () — though it is not consummated until the bridge's third bar.

Free dissonances are everywhere, and they resolve late, after the root beneath has already changed () — several never resolve at all. The best instance is a note that wants to rise across a bar line and never gets the chance: the voices drop out, leaving the resolution implied rather than sung.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-yesterday.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Yesterday
the-beatles-yesterday.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: the shorter two-bridge model at an uncharacteristically slow tempo. Intro (2 bars of guitar on an open fifth, no third, so major or minor is withheld from the start) · Verse (7 bars, three phrases grouped 3 + 2 + 2) · Verse · Bridge (8 on paper) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro (one reprise of the final phrase, hummed). The bridge does not sound like its notation: each phrase is heard as starting on the notated second bar, with the first functioning as a wind-up tacked onto the previous phrase.

Under the over-familiarity is a genuinely asymmetrical song whose engine is a home key that keeps sliding toward its relative minor (). The music retreats to D minor before F is ever properly established — the vi chord in bar 3 is the first moment anything feels grounded. Secondary dominants carry that pull: V-of-vi at the top of both verse and bridge, V-of-V near the verse's end () — and that V-of-V then hands off to IV rather than V, softened by a descending chromatic inner line.

The only clean V–I cadences in the song are the bridge phrase endings (), and because the bridge starts from the relative minor's point of view they land more like a modulation arriving than a return home.

Layering discipline: the bowed strings do not enter until verse 2, and no section ever gets an identical quartet part twice. The cello's E♭ in the bridge is the only flat seventh in the entire song.

Why I like it

the-beatles-you-can-t-do-that.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Can't Do That
the-beatles-you-can-t-do-that.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4 bars of I, ostinato running, bass and percussion held back until bar 3) · Verse (a 12-bar blues frame) · Verse · Bridge (8) · Verse · Verse (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse · Outro (2 bars, abrupt, ostinato only, ending on a teasing sustained F♯). The last bar of the verse is the tell: verses leading into another verse move to V, verses leading into a bridge just sustain I.

A song with a split stylistic personality. The verse is a twelve-bar frame on I, IV and V () whose tune is composed straight through with almost no parallelism between phrases. The bridge breaks that diet and stages a fake modulation to E minor — a tonicisation that never commits () — and then turns home by ii → iii → I where the textbook would put V.

The verse works ♭7 with blues consistency, which puts it in direct collision with the major third inside the IV chord, and both thirds of the tonic are in play, so the mode reads bi-modal (). The bridge tune drops every blue note in favour of a strict major third and major seventh.

The unifying hook is an ostinato oscillating between the major and minor third, played wherever the tonic sits still. The rhythmic hook is a hard syncopation on the eighth before the downbeat () — and Ringo spells out "and-four-and-one" in even eighths after the last verse line so the ear can locate the displaced beat.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-you-know-my-name-look-up-the.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Know My Name (Look Up The Number)
the-beatles-you-know-my-name-look-up-the.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: four takes of the same fragment, end to end — hard rock, lounge/samba, Goon Show, jazz club — each Intro · Verse · Refrain with local variations. Better described as a fragmentary song delivered as a medley of four alternate takes of itself than as character variations on a theme. The verse is an odd 7 bars, the asymmetry manufactured by the harmonic rhythm briefly doubling in bar 5 ().

Each take alters the actual material, not just the mood: take 2 replaces the pedal-point bars with percussion, take 3 drops the two-bar opening entirely and swaps the iii chords for a first-inversion tonic, take 4 fills the old pedal bars with a jazz piano figure.

The verse shape is peculiar — it starts on IV and ends on V, and the tonic makes one furtive appearance in bar 5 as the only chord in the section not on a downbeat. The V-of-V is made to wait through an intervening chord change before resolving, a trademark going back to "Eight Days A Week" (); strip the camouflage and the verse is a circle of fifths. The first take's tune is three notes.

The backbeat is the primary device separating the four settings (), and the joins are engineered as carefully as the takes — take 2 has no final chord at all, only the tail of a spoken line running past where the music stopped. Pollack's lesson: a joke track still needs a properly built chart under it.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-you-like-me-too-much.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Like Me Too Much
the-beatles-you-like-me-too-much.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (6 bars, one drawn-out phrase that only sounds out of tempo because there is no backbeat under it) · Verse (16, four equal phrases) · Verse · Bridge (8) · Verse · Break (a 12-bar instrumental blues frame with the sung title hook grafted onto the end) · Bridge · Verse · Outro with a complete ending. Verse and bridge elide in both directions — the lyric runs straight through the seam and the harmony refuses to close there either.

The analytical payload is root motion. Where the standard pop/rock verse is driven by circle-of-fifths motion toward I or V, this one moves by step and by third, sets up its goals indirectly, and backs away from resolution every time it gets close (). ii→IV and iii→V are the weak, indirect approaches that create the sense of avoidance, and the verse is open at both ends despite being full of tonic chords.

Opening on ♭III in intro bar 3 is already unusual (), and its F natural sustained into the following major chord is the bluesiest instant in the song. The bridge piles applied dominants up to a V-of-V-of-V () and ends as a wind-up on V whose resolution the next verse defers again by entering on ii.

The entire tune lives inside six notes; the bridge does not break that ceiling, taking its contrast from broadening out rhythmically instead.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-you-never-give-me-your-money.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Never Give Me Your Money
the-beatles-you-never-give-me-your-money.html:
Opens the Abbey Road medley. Three distinct sections: piano ballad, boogie-woogie groove, and a nursery-rhyme coda ('one two three four five six seven, all good children go to heaven'). McCartney's commentary on Apple Corps financial disputes.

Chords

Key: A minor verse → C major boogie section (the suite's first movement)

Verse: Am7 – Am – Dm7 – Dm – G – C – Fmaj7 – Dm – E – Am → i7 – i – iv7 – iv – ♭VII – ♭III – ♭VImaj7 – iv – V7 – i (a circle-of-fifths descent through A minor)

"Out of college, money spent": C – E7 – Am – C7 – F – G – C – C7 → I – V7/vi – vi – V7/IV – IV – V – I – I7 (modulates to C major for the rolling boogie)

From your chart: Songs/Files/the-beatles-you-never-give-me-your-money-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

The opening of the Abbey Road medley and a suite in miniature — several unrelated fragments (a piano ballad → a boogie "out of college" section → a dreamy "one sweet dream" → the "1-2-3-4-5-6-7" nursery coda) segued into one, then flowing straight into the rest of the medley. A masterclass in transitions.

  • Each section has its own key/feel/tempo; the segues (tape edits, key pivots, sound-effect crossfades — crickets into "Sun King") are the art.
  • Rich 7th-chord piano harmony.

Steal this

  • Medley/suite transitions: write fragments and focus on the joins — pivot chords, tempo ramps, sound-effect crossfades → Modulation (Key Change) · /setlist flow thinking.
  • Segue with a sound effect (crickets, noise) to bridge two unrelated sections.
  • 7th-chord piano for a bittersweet, sophisticated bed → Seventh Chords.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Abbey Road · search "The Beatles — You Never Give Me Your Money"

Learning

Pollack's analysis

Extracted from AWP — You Never Give Me Your Money — Alan W. Pollack, "Notes On…" #13.

Form. The clearest Beatles example of a teleological medley rather than a cyclical song form — three sections (X, Y, Z) that never return, each in its own key, each fragmentary enough to sound like the opening of a different song. What holds it together, he argues, is two things: a single ordinary syncopation recurring across unrelated material, and a key plan tracing an arch — A minor → C major → A major. In place of a return, every section repeats one short phrase several times immediately; that substitution is the song's whole formal argument. X is three passes of an 8-bar phrase, the first an unusually generous instrumental intro that gives away the entire verse. Y splits in two — YA is two passes of a 4-bar phrase, YB is five passes of a 3-bar phrase, a prime number of repeats of an asymmetrical unit. Z also splits: ZA is an 8-bar instrumental intro plus a seven-and-a-half-bar verse, ZB a 2-bar phrase run fourteen times to the fade.

Harmony. X (A minor) is a complete diatonic circle of fifths, i – iv – ♭VII – ♭III – ♭VI – ii° – V – i, every chord in root position and none converted into a secondary dominant — placid and propulsive at once, because even harmonic rhythm holds it still while fifth motion pushes it along (). YA (C major) is I – V-of-vi – vi – V-of-IV – IV – V – I, the same fifth-driven motion but harder, because the fifths are now secondary dominants (). YB flips C major to C Mixolydian for a double plagal ♭VII – IV – I (). ZA cycles in minor thirds, bass and upper voice each outlining diminished sevenths, which gives clanging chromatic cross relations plus a few bars of genuine keylessness — the "Rhapsody in Blue" device, unique in their work. ZB is ♭III – ♭VII – I in A, the song's entire key arch compressed into two bars.

Notable. The connective tissue is an accented eighth falling between beats 2 and 3 — ordinary for the genre, which is exactly why it works as glue rather than as a motif.

Against this page. Agrees: A minor into a C major boogie section, and then out into A major.

the-beatles-you-won-t-see-me.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You Won't See Me
the-beatles-you-won-t-see-me.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: two-bridge model, one verse between the bridges, no solo. Verse is an unusual 18 bars — four 4-bar phrases in AABA′ plus a 2-bar petit reprise — and every phrase is harmonically closed, starting and ending on I. The bridge is a true middle eight, open at both ends, which is the relief after four claustrophobically closed verse phrases. The outro plays the verse without the lead vocal and fades fast.

The unifying device is invisible: four-note descending chromatic fragments tucked into an inner voice in every section — piano at first, then the backing vocals. Chromatically altered chords, above all the secondary dominant, are what let a chromatic line be knitted into an otherwise diatonic fabric (), and one phrase borrows iv from the parallel minor to supply its own (). The bridge carries a six-note descent that lands its resolution on the next verse's first downbeat, and its chord changes fall in bars 1, 2 and 4 rather than 1, 3 and 4 — an ultra-slow syncopation. The proof it is all deliberate: at the end of the verse the backing voices invert the fragment and sing it upward.

Paul's double-tracked lead is almost entirely anticipatory syncopation (); the single place he sings on the downbeat is the one place the backing track itself syncopates. And the instrumental texture never changes at all — the entire energy curve is built from vocal layers alone ().

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-you-re-going-to-lose-that-gi.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You're Going To Lose That Girl
the-beatles-you-re-going-to-lose-that-gi.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (4 bars — call it phrase A; it is also the verse's third phrase and the title hook, so it works as intro and mini-refrain at once) · Verse (12, three even phrases as BBA) · Verse′ (14, extended by a two-bar half phrase that pivots into the bridge) · Bridge (7 bars, two parallel but unequal phrases) · Verse′ (guitar solo) · Bridge · Verse′ · Outro. Run the song from the top through verse 2 and the phrase order is a palindrome.

The series' showcase for pivot modulation into a key that shares no chords with home. E major goes to G major for the bridge — a genuine interlude, not a flirtation — and both the trip out and the trip back are engineered on borrowed chords (). G is reachable only as the relative major of the parallel minor ().

Going out, the ♭VII is re-heard as the dominant of ♭III () — grammatically clean, still a surprise. Coming back, G's own ♭VII is re-read as ♭II of E, the Neapolitan, dropping straight onto I in root position with no dominant in between. The outro then closes a song built almost entirely on I→V motion with a double plagal cadence ().

Shortening the bridge by one bar exactly where the harmonic trick happens is what throws weight onto it; squaring it up would make it tidier and duller.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-you-ve-got-to-hide-your-love.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - You've Got To Hide Your Love Away
the-beatles-you-ve-got-to-hide-your-love.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: a cross between the two-bridge pop model and the folk verse/refrain ballad — a central unit of two verses plus a refrain, twice, with a scanty intro and, unusually, a closing instrumental verse that ends the song rather than a solo placed mid-song. Almost every section length is irregular (): the primary verse is 18 bars as 4+4+4+6, the verse′ is 20 as 4+4+4+8, and the refrain is 12 bars, AA as 6 + 6. All four sung verses have different lyrics, which pushes it toward ballad rather than pop.

Four chords — no modulation anywhere. Pollack uses it as his set piece on ♭VII (), a Beatles habit that suddenly explodes on this album, and calls the style "almost modal" rather than modal because the V chord stays major where a pure modal reading would want a minor v. The spicy by-product is a repeated cross relation between the major third inside V and the flat seventh inside ♭VII — substitute IV for ♭VII wherever V precedes it and the clash disappears, along with everything interesting about the song. The instrumental verse closes with a double plagal cadence ().

This is the first ternary meter in the series, and every section starts squarely on the downbeat, which suits the flattened mood. The contrast between sections is nearly all in range (), and the percussion accumulates section by section and never resets.

Why I like it

-

the-beatles-your-mother-should-know.title: 🎵 THE BEATLES - Your Mother Should Know
the-beatles-your-mother-should-know.html:
Pollack's analysis

Form: Intro (two vamping measures in the relative minor) · Verse (an unusual 11 measures, three phrases, the middle one a measure short) · Verse · Bridge (a single long instrumental phrase of 6 measures, sitting where a sung refrain would normally go) · Verse · Bridge · Verse · Outro. The second verse's final measure is stretched by a limping half measure as it feeds the bridge — a trick whose only Beatles precedents are Lennon's ().

More music-hall nostalgia, and against the surface impression less four-square than "When I'm Sixty-Four". Verse and bridge share one plan: start in A minor, converge slowly and steadily on the relative major, then flip straight back to the minor at the last moment (). Pollack's comparison is "And I Love Her", where the same gambit produces anxious bittersweetness; here the minor is a foil whose only job is to make the major sound cheerier.

The engine is a run of three dominants back to back in measures 7 through 9 () spelling a descending chromatic fragment, answered by an upward chromatic push in the backing vocals. The first verse's bass walks down the scale, putting one chord into second inversion ().

The sing-it-again tag appears only after the first verse and the second bridge, though it would have fit everywhere. Using it everywhere would have cost it everything.

Why I like it

-

victor-young-stella-by-starlight.title: 🎵 VICTOR YOUNG - Stella By Starlight
victor-young-stella-by-starlight.html:
A jazz standard famous for sounding harmonically "mysterious" — it doesn't reach its own home key (B♭ major) until bar 9, and its opening move (a chord that seems to resolve nowhere sensible) is one of the most commonly reharmonized passages in the standard repertoire. Jens Larsen's full harmonic breakdown demystifies it: almost the entire tune is a chain of secondary/auxiliary dominants, backdoor cadences, and one reharmonized diminished chord, all still inside a single key — with only one genuine modulation in the whole form. Full worked breakdown: Analyzing a Standard - Stella By Starlight - Functional Harmony in Jazz - Jazz Guitar Lesson.

Form and key map

Section Bars (approx.) What happens
Opening statement ~16 Develops/expands rather than repeating a fixed 8-bar block; wanders through a chain of secondary/auxiliary cadences before B♭ major is finally confirmed at bar 9; a brief true modulation up to F major (the tune's fifth degree) happens near the end of this section, just before the bridge
Bridge 8 Moves to the subdominant (ii, Cm, treated as a plain subdominant not part of a ii-V); harmonic rhythm and melodic pacing shift from the rest of the tune — the two cues used to identify it as a bridge even though the form isn't a clean, literal AABA
Return ("A3") remainder Restates the opening statement's idea but "turns into something else" rather than a literal repeat; closes with a descending ii-V sequence and a final cadence borrowed wholesale from the parallel minor (B♭ minor)

The opening — reharmonized diminished, not a broken cadence

The tune's famous opening (Em7♭5–A7 resolving into Cm7–F7) looks non-functional — there's no real dominant-to-target relationship between A7 and Cm7 on paper. It's actually a reharmonization of a ♯4° diminished chord (E° in the key of B♭), the same "♯4°/subdominant diminished, reharmonized as a ii-V" device documented at length on Diminished Chords — Larsen names this exact tune there as one of the standards sharing the device, alongside "I Remember You" (identical cadence, identical melody-scale-degree: the leading tone of the key sitting in the melody). Practical improvising fix: don't chase the theory while soloing — target the notes A7 naturally resolves to (D or F; F also happens to be the tune's own melody note over the following Cm7).

Chords

Chord-function map, as analyzed — roman numerals in B♭.

Opening statement (auxiliary-cadence chain, never really leaving B♭ despite sounding unmoored): Em7♭5–A7 (♯4° reharmonized, cadences "in D minor") → Cm7 (ii) – F7 (V) → Fm7–B♭7 (auxiliary ii-V into IV, decorating an already-diatonic chord) → E♭maj7 (IV) – A♭7 (backdoor dominant, ♭VII7) → B♭maj7 (I, finally arrives at bar 9) – Dm7 (iii) → [repeat of the opening ♯4° device] → Cm7♭5 (ii, borrowed half-diminished from the parallel minor) – F7 (V)

The one real modulation, just before the bridge: Fm (iv) → B♭m7 (heard as iv of the visiting key) → E♭7 → F major (brief true tonic, up a 5th from B♭) — falls back toward B♭/D minor almost immediately after arriving.

Bridge: G7 (looks augmented on the chart, but the melody's natural 5th confirms it's a plain auxiliary dominant to ii, not whole-tone) → Cm7 (ii, plain subdominant, not part of a ii-V) → E♭m6/A♭7 (iv-minor "backdoor," the way home from a bare subdominant)

Closing sequence (last A): Em7♭5–A7 → Dø7–D7 → Cm7♭5–F7 (a single ii-V shape restated as a descending sequence before the true resolution) → Cm7♭5–F7♭9 (final cadence, both chords borrowed from the parallel minor, B♭ minor) → B♭maj7 (I)

Chord-scale map for soloing (from the video, B♭-major reading)

Chord / device Scale
Opening ♯4° cadence (Em7♭5–A7) D harmonic minor
Plain ii-V-I in B♭ B♭ major
ii-V into E♭maj7 (IV) E♭ major
A♭7 backdoor / IV-minor (E♭m) E♭ melodic minor (≅ A♭ Lydian dominant)
Secondary ♯4°-family cadences elsewhere in the form Harmonic minor of the local cadence target
Brief modulation to F major F major, straightforward
Bridge's G7 → Cm C harmonic minor, 2 bars
Final ii-V (borrowed from parallel minor) B♭ harmonic minor

Steal this

  • When the melody's own final note doesn't confirm the key, fall back on the key signature + final chord — Stella is one of the rare standards whose melody doesn't end on the tonic note, so the key has to be confirmed from the last chord (B♭maj7) and the key signature instead. Extends the "confirm key from the ending" method already on 🎵 JEROME KERN - All The Things You Are one step further. → Keys, Cadences
  • A tune can sound harmonically "busy" and mysterious purely from stacked secondary/auxiliary dominants, without ever actually leaving its home key. Before concluding a tune "has no key," check whether an unfamiliar chord is a real modulation or just a decorated approach to a diatonic chord you already know. → Secondary Dominants, Chord Progressions
  • The sharp-4 diminished device isn't just a passing chord here — it also works as a genuine modulation tool, cadencing up a major 3rd into a new key. Cited elsewhere doing exactly that: "I'm Old Fashioned," "I Love You" (Cole Porter). → Modulation (Key Change), Diminished Chords
  • A iv-minor chord can pivot a brief modulation up to the fifth degree — an unusual but real device (B♭ → F major here), also used in "My Foolish Heart." → Modulation (Key Change)
  • Don't trust an "augmented"-looking chord symbol on sight — check the melody before reaching for whole-tone. The bridge's G7 looks written for a whole-tone/altered treatment, but the melody's plain natural 5th confirms it's just a secondary dominant into a minor ii chord, soloed with harmonic minor instead. → Scale Modes Reference, Secondary Dominants
  • Turn a single ii-V into a descending sequence to prolong the arrival before resolving — reusable in original writing/reharmonization. → Chord Progressions

Why I like it

Listen

Learning

Full chord-by-chord and bar-by-bar breakdown (the opening's reharmonized-diminished device, the auxiliary-cadence chain, the one true modulation, the bridge's disguised secondary dominant, the closing sequence, and the full chord-scale map) → Analyzing a Standard - Stella By Starlight - Functional Harmony in Jazz - Jazz Guitar Lesson. Tie into Song Practice if/when queued for active learning (not auto-queued by this enrichment pass).

wayne-shorter-footprints.title: 🎵 WAYNE SHORTER - Footprints
wayne-shorter-footprints.html:
No prior entry existed for this tune. Captured from a real 1-on-1 comping lesson (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared, filmed with a returning student, Alex) focused entirely on comping vocabulary and voicing variety over the tune's vamp and turnaround — not a soloing breakdown. → Private Jazz Guitar Comping Lesson Over Footprints by Wayne Shorter

Chords (as taught in this lesson)

Tonic vamp: written on the chart as Cm11, played by the student as Cm7 → Dm7 (passing) → back to Cm7, occasionally substituting Cm6. Jared's reframing: all of this is just C Dorian — Dm7 is the iii of the same B♭-major parent scale a whole step up from C, and Cm6 uses the same Dorian natural-6 — so none of it needs separate justification, it's one mode throughout. Because the vamp is genuinely modal rather than a fixed tertian chord, any diatonic chord from B♭ major works as a substitute voicing over the same vamp (named but not fully worked in the lesson: B♭maj7, E♭maj7 and their inversions). → Diatonic Modes, Jazz Comping

Turnaround (as played by the student, roughly the last stretch of the form): F half-diminished (F♯ø7 as voiced) → F7♯9 → E7♯9 → A7♯5. Practiced as a single memorized "string" of four linked voicings rather than reharmonized chord-by-chord. → Turnarounds

Fm chord (elsewhere in the form): same quartal comping shape used on the Cm vamp, relocated wholesale up to F — the shape tracks the tune's own root motion rather than being rebuilt from scratch. → Quartal Chord Voicings

Comping concepts (Jared's breakdown)

  • Voicing-multiplication by top note — 3–4 inversions of the same Cm7/Cm11, differing mainly in which chord tone (root/5th/3rd/♭7) sits on top, "doubles" then "triples" the perceived variety of a static vamp with minimal new theory.
  • A quartal "hub" shape (stacked 4ths, strings 4–2, off the 3rd fret) grooved as a repeating whole-step/half-step figure over the Cm vamp, relocated to F for the Fm chord.
  • Turnaround vocabulary chunking — memorize the whole 4-chord turnaround as one linked unit; build 2–4 total alternate "strings" rather than freely reharmonizing live.
  • Half-step-away approach chords as a function-agnostic passing color anywhere in the form.
  • Full technique breakdown, generalized beyond this tune → Jazz Comping.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Wayne Shorter — Adam's Apple (1966)
  • Miles Davis Quintet — Miles Smiles (1967), a markedly more abstract, tempo-shifting arrangement of the same tune

wes-montgomery-d-natural-blues.title: 🎵 WES MONTGOMERY - D Natural Blues
wes-montgomery-d-natural-blues.html:
A 12-bar jazz blues in D from Wes Montgomery's 1960 album The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery. Jack Ruch uses a short stretch of Wes's solo — all falling over the I chord (D7) or IV chord (G7) — as a worked example of transcribing → naming the harmonic device → building an original line from the same "recipe," the same method documented in full on Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction. For the tune's full jazz-blues chord progression (not just the I/IV passages analyzed here), see The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues, which cites this same recording as its jazz-blues example.

Chords

Key: D — a 12-bar jazz blues, cited directly on The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues as the jazz-blues example (alongside Grant Green) contrasted with a plain 1-4-5 blues. A jazz blues keeps the same 12-bar skeleton (I in bars 1-4, IV in bar 5) but plays the tonic bars as major 7, not dominant, and closes with a 1-6-2-5 turnaround rather than a static or dominant-cycled tonic. Transposed to D, that standard jazz-blues form reads:

Dmaj7 (I) – G7 (IV) – Dmaj7 (I) – B7 (VI7) – Em7 (ii) – A7 (V7) – (back to Dmaj7)

→ I – IV – I – VI7 – ii – V7 – I, the same 1-6-2-5 turnaround worked in B♭ on The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues and documented generally on Turnarounds. Only the I (D7) and IV (G7) portions are what the source video below actually transcribes solo lines over — the full turnaround above is the vault's standard jazz-blues form applied to this key, not a bar-by-bar transcription of Wes's own comping.

Solo concepts by passage (Jack Ruch's analysis)

Four short passages, each reduced to a reusable concept and immediately re-played by Ruch as his own line — see Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction for the general method.

  • Over D7 (I), passage 1: D7 scale (D Mixolydian: D major with a ♭7) → on the change to G7 (IV), target chord tones directly (3rd → root → ♭7). → Blues Scales and Blue Notes, Chord-Tone Soloing
  • Over D7 (I), passage 1 continued: a chromatic walk-down from the 5th to the 3rd of D7, into a D7♭9 arpeggio, then chord-tone targeting of G7 again on the change — the single device Ruch calls out as what "makes this solo special." → Chord-Tone Soloing, Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
  • Over G7 (IV), passage 2: chord tones + chromatic passing tones, followed by the D tonic diminished scale (whole-half/half-whole diminished, starting on C♯) used as a connector to bring the line back from G7 into D7. → Scale Modes Reference, Diminished Chords
  • Over D7 (I), passage 3: a C major 7 arpeggio played over D7 — gives ♭7-9-11-13, the chord's full upper-extension stack, from one familiar shape a whole step below the root — followed by D minor pentatonic as a bluesy cadential move into the IV chord. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Blues Scales and Blue Notes, Extended Chords
  • Over D7 (I), passage 4: an A minor 7 ("five minor") arpeggio over D7 — gives the 5th, ♭7th, 9th and 11th from one shape — decorated with chromatic connective notes. → Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes, Chord-Tone Soloing

Steal this

  • C major 7 over a dominant a whole step below as a one-shape way to grab ♭7/9/11/13 all at once — reusable over any dominant 7 chord, not just D7.
  • Minor pentatonic on the I as a cadential move into the IV, rather than as changes-outlining vocabulary — a bluesy "punctuation mark" use of the pentatonic distinct from running it through the whole form.
  • Whole-half diminished scale as connective tissue between IV and I, not a static "correct scale for the IV chord" — framed as a bridge, the same way Secondary Dominants and approach-chord material gets used elsewhere in this vault's jazz strand.
  • v-minor (A minor 7 over D7) arpeggio as a quick way to imply the 5-♭7-9-11 stack over a dominant chord — the minor-7-off-the-5th trick, distinct from the C-major-7-off-the-♭7 trick above.

Why I like it

Listen

  • Search "Wes Montgomery — D Natural Blues," The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery (1960)

Learning

  • Wes Montgomery Blues Lesson D Natural Blues (Jack Ruch's passage-by-passage breakdown + his own variations)

whitney-no-woman.title: 🎵 WHITNEY - No Woman
whitney-no-woman.html:
From Light Upon the Lake (2016), the debut album by Whitney (Julien Ehrlich & Max Kakacek).

Chords

Key: D major (E-Dorian feel) · 112 BPM · 4/4. Chords: Em · A6 · A · Gmaj7 · D.

  • Intro: Em
  • Verse / Pre-chorus: Em – A6 – A – Gmaj7
  • Chorus ("No Woman"): Em – D – Em – D
  • Bridge / Solo: Em – D – Em – D
  • Outro: Em – A6 – A – Gmaj7 (verse)

Roman numerals (in D major): Em = ii · A/A6 = V · Gmaj7 = IV · D = I. In E Dorian the verse reads i – IV – ♭III — the major IV (A, with its C#) over the minor tonic is the dreamy modal signature; the 6th/maj7 extensions add the haze.

Full chart: !<span class="xlink xlink-vault" data-note="Whitney - No Woman - Chords.pdf" title="Vault note — not in this page">Whitney - No Woman - Chords.pdf</span>

Production & Arrangement

Light Upon the Lake (2016) — Chicago indie-folk-soul: a drummer-sung falsetto lead, warm analog recording, gentle horns, and a nostalgic, sun-faded palette. Live-band intimacy with a country-soul lilt.

wings-silly-love-songs.title: 🎵 WINGS - Silly Love Songs
wings-silly-love-songs.html:
McCartney's pointed response to critics — especially Lennon — who dismissed his sentimental writing. Multi-layered counterpoint with multiple vocal lines running simultaneously. The funk bass groove is the backbone of the entire track.

Chords

Key: C major · ~125 BPM

Verse / Chorus ("I love you, I love you"): C – Em7 – Fmaj7 → I – iii7 – IVmaj7 — the whole song floats on this one three-chord loop

Pre-chorus ("what's wrong with that?"): Em7 – Fmaj7 – G → iii7 – IVmaj7 – V

Bridge ("Love doesn't come in a minute"): Em – Fmaj7 → iii – IVmaj7

From your chart: Songs/Files/wings-silly-love-songs-chords.pdf.

Production & Arrangement

1976 — McCartney's disco-inflected pop, famous for its interlocking melodic bass line (a counter-melody hook in its own right) and the stacked multi-melody outro where three separate vocal lines sing different words at once in counterpoint.

Steal this

  • Bass as a lead counter-melody (the McCartney signature, disco edition) → 1 Electric Bass DI Track · Chromatic Bass Lines.
  • Contrapuntal outro: stack 2–3 different vocal melodies singing simultaneously → 2 Ensemble Stack Group.
  • Four-on-the-floor + horns disco-pop groove.
