yes-roundabout.title: 🎵 YES - Roundabout
yes-roundabout.html:
Fragile (1971). This note is a bass-focused breakdown of Chris Squire's part — ghost notes, a commonly-missed 16th-note syncopation, an anticipation/push device, a genuinely rule-breaking drum-and-bass conversational section, whole-song use of space, and a buried melody-doubling bass line in the bridge — as taught by BassBuzz. Framed by the video as the direct influence behind Geddy Lee, John Entwistle, Steve Harris, and Les Claypool's own playing.

Chords

This is an 8-plus-minute prog epic with real tempo and meter shifts across sections, so this covers only the two sections underneath the bass part broken down below — the main verse-ish riff section and the "I'll be the roundabout" chorus — not the harmonics-only intro, the "in and around the lake" bridge, or the extended closing guitar-solo section. Chord transcriptions for this song genuinely disagree more between sources than most tunes on this page (different capos, different enharmonic spellings, different section boundaries), consistent with how harmonically restless the writing is — treat the below as "as commonly transcribed," not a definitive chart.

Verse-ish riff section, roughly in G major: G – Em – G – Em – G – A – C – A – Bm – A – G → I – vi – I – vi – I – II – IV – II – iii – II – I. That "A" (a major II chord, not the diatonic Am) is a non-diatonic borrowed color — Yes leaning on chromatic-mediant-adjacent harmony well outside a plain major scale → Chromatic Mediants and Pop Modulation

Chorus ("I'll be the roundabout"): G – C – G – F – Bb – G – C – G – F – Bb – G – Em – G → I – IV – I – ♭VII – ♭III – I – IV – I – ♭VII – ♭III – I – vi – I. The F (♭VII) and B♭ (♭III) are both borrowed from G's parallel minor / Mixolydian world — the kind of chromatic-mediant color that makes Yes's harmony feel bigger than a plain diatonic pop chorus while still resolving home to G each time → Chromatic Mediants and Pop Modulation · Borrowed Chords

No controlled-vocabulary progression tag fits this cleanly (not ii-V-I, not axis, not a turnaround) — the borrowed ♭VII/♭III chorus movement is genuinely its own thing, so progressions is left empty above.

The main riff: ghost notes for contrast

The riff is full of ghost notes — cover the string(s) with the fretting hand, then pick/pluck for a thumpy, unpitched, percussive sound (marked X in tab). Playing every note clean instead loses contrast and fills up the sonic space, leaving less room for the rest of the band to cut through — ghost notes deliberately break the riff into a mix of pitched notes and percussive thumps. Full technique, cross-genre examples (Chuck Rainey, Kim Deal, Mark King), and a practice drill → Ghost Notes (Slap Bass).

The main riff: a syncopation most players miss

Notes mostly land on the beat, but there's an off-beat emphasis later in the riff that gets missed often enough that BassBuzz calls it out directly (and admits playing it wrong himself before listening closely). 16th-note count: "1 e and a, 2 e and a, 3 e and a, 4 e and a." The riff plays "1 e and, 2 e and a, 3 e and—" then starts its next note group early, on the "and" of 3 — that's the syncopation. The common mistake: starting that note squarely on beat 4 instead — a 16th note late. The end-of-riff shape is otherwise a common one (scale degrees 4–5–7 of the minor pentatonic) — the syncopation, not the notes, is what sets this apart from an unsyncopated cousin like "Paranoid" (Black Sabbath, same notes, straight quarters) or the Tenacious D "Tribute" guitar riff. Full device (with the strong/weak-beat framework and the "and"/"e"/"a" weight hierarchy) → Syncopation and Metric Displacement.

The main riff: anticipation (the push)

The riff normally starts squarely on beat 1 — except the first time it's heard (and a few times after), where the first note lands early, on the "and" of the previous beat 4. Named directly as anticipation, also called a push — it adds excitement and pulls the listener toward the next section. Important detail: pushes are usually played by multiple instruments together (bass + drums here) — from just one instrument, the same early note reads as a timing mistake, not a device. A second worked instance later in the track pairs the push with a drum fill leading into it. Full device (and why it's distinct from harmonic "anticipation" in Non-Harmonic Tones) → Syncopation and Metric Displacement.

The chorus-ish section: drum-and-bass conversation, rule broken on purpose

BassBuzz's own baseline advice elsewhere: as a safe default, play the bass in the kick drum's rhythm. This section of Roundabout breaks that rule deliberately — bass and drums share the same 8th-note grid but bounce/ping-pong off each other rather than locking, and drummer Bill Bruford swaps the snare in for spots the kick would normally hold. Snare, kick, and bass sometimes line up, sometimes don't — that disagreement is what pulls listener attention, and there's room for it because the hi-hat plays plain quarter notes and the vocal has big gaps here. A direct A/B demo shows the section sounds noticeably flatter if the bass lines up 100% with the drums instead. Guardrail from the video: this isn't a rule to apply by default — test conversational bass/drum rhythm with a real drummer before committing, and don't reach for a busy counter-kick-drum part on a simple pop song where it isn't earned. Extends the "lock to the pocket, not the kick map" method step and gets its own worked example → Bassline Writing.

Whole song: use of space as arrangement contrast

Zoomed out, the bass track has long blank stretches where it isn't playing at all — presence/absence itself is a contrast device. Density then swings hard between the sections that ARE playing: the main riff is dense even with ghost notes thinning it → the chorus riff is much sparser → the closing guitar solos invert that completely, with the bass hitting every 16th note. General lesson: view a song from a bird's-eye verse/chorus/bridge level and ask whether there's contrast — when the vibe shifts and the bass part doesn't, the two simplest levers are fewer notes ↔ more notes, or short notes ↔ long sustained notes. Full note, more worked examples → Bassline Writing.

The bridge: doubling the buried organ melody

The bridge's obvious bass part is the one you'd play live. On the record, Chris is simultaneously doubling the keyboard/organ melody on bass, in the same register as that main bass part — two real bass parts' worth of material at once, described as "freaking mayhem," demonstrated by playing both together against the drums. Read as a direct line back to earlier melodic bassists — Paul McCartney, Jack Bruce, and John Entwistle are named explicitly — and pointed at more of the same across Yes's catalog and Squire's 1975 solo album Fish Out of Water. A second 70s-melodic-bass worked example (Marvin Gaye's "Your Precious Love," bass doubled note-for-note by guitar) lives on → Bassline Writing.

Tone and gear: the recipe, plus a no-Rickenbacker fallback

Squire's tone: clicky, growly, notes audibly buzzing as they sustain. Real gear: a 1964 Rickenbacker, both pickups engaged, into two separate amplifiers — described as unreplicable exactly (a P-bass with flatwounds won't get there, and even the official signature reissue reportedly didn't sound like the original). Four achievable steps toward it on any bass:

  1. Strings — bright stainless-steel round wounds, specifically Roto Sound Swing 66 (what Chris used).
  2. Pick — gray Herco heavy picks, plasticky and bright.
  3. Position — pluck/pick near the bridge for more edge.
  4. Attack — play hard and nasty.

No Rickenbacker or no pick? Use Geddy Lee's version instead. Geddy plays this exact riff fingerstyle on a Jazz bass: engage both pickups, turn the bass's tone up, crank treble/high-mids (bass or amp). Two plucking-hand options named: clacky downward plucks (Geddy's default a lot of the time, also covered for Steve Harris), or, specifically for this riff, a back-and-forth strum with the index finger rather than string-by-string alternating plucks. Full tone-chain framing and cross-references → Bass Tone Chain Priority; pick-vs-fingers decision framework → Pick vs. Fingers on Bass — Tone and Technique Tradeoffs; bridge-position plucking → Playing Fast on Bass — Efficient Technique, Setup, and Bridge Plucking; the strum technique → String Crossing and Plucking Patterns.

Steal this

  • Ghost-note a dense riff on purpose to open up sonic space for the rest of the band, not just for percussive flavor. → Ghost Notes (Slap Bass)
  • A note that arrives early on the "and" of the previous beat 4, played together with the drums, is a push — exciting when locked with another instrument, sloppy-sounding alone.
  • Deliberately let the bass NOT lock to the kick in a section that has room for it (sparse hi-hat, gapped vocal) — test with a real drummer before trusting it on a real song.
  • Chart a song's felt density verse-to-chorus-to-bridge and make sure the bass part actually tracks it — fewer/more notes or shorter/longer notes are the two cheapest levers.
  • A second, buried bass part doubling the keyboard melody is a real (if mayhem-inducing) arranging move, not just a live simplification of "the" bass part.
  • String + pick + plucking-position + attack is a portable tone recipe even without the exact original instrument — and there's always a fingerstyle fallback path.

Why I like it

-

Listen

  • Yes — "Roundabout," Fragile (1971) · search "Yes Roundabout"

Learning

keys.title: Keys
keys.html:
Part of Music Theory. A key = the pitch that feels like "home" in a song, plus the scale built on it (major or minor). Play the same melody's scale degrees from a different key's scale and you've transposed it.

What makes a song sound "in a key"

A song is in C when it gives the listener these clues:

  • Phrases start/end on the C (or Cm) chord
  • Chord motion follows tonic → subdominant → dominant patterns (Chord Progressions)
  • Most notes come from the C major (or minor) scale
  • The melody emphasizes C at important points

Real songs weaken some of these on purpose — remove too many and the key feeling dissolves.

Relative major & minor

  • Pairs that share the exact same pitches (and the same key signature): C major ↔ A minor, G ↔ Em, D ↔ Bm, A ↔ F♯m, E ↔ C♯m, B ↔ G♯m, F♯ ↔ D♯m, G♭ ↔ E♭m, D♭ ↔ B♭m, A♭ ↔ Fm, E♭ ↔ Cm, B♭ ↔ Gm, F ↔ Dm
  • Relative minor = 2 scale degrees DOWN from the major tonic; relative major = 2 degrees UP
  • Songs commonly drift between relative keys section-to-section (they share all diatonic chords — see Chords by Key); the VIm chord as temporary home = instant relative-minor feel

Parallel major & minor

  • Same tonic, different scale: C major vs C minor
  • Mixed by borrowing chords: a ♭III (E♭) appearing in a C-major song is borrowed from C minor. Common borrowed chords: ♭III, ♭VI, ♭VII, IVm
  • See Chord Progressions for how borrowed chords function

Identifying / choosing keys

  • Key Signatures narrows it to a major/minor pair; the actual chords + melody decide which
  • Circle of Fifths shows how closely two keys are related (neighbors share 6 of 7 notes)
  • Full chord menu per key: Chords by Key
  • By ear: find the tonic (imagine the music resolving to one note, or find the bass note of the tonic chord), then test major vs. minor by feel or by playing the minor/major 3rd above the tonic against the track — full method, common mistakes (relative-key confusion, assuming first/last chord = tonic) on Transcribing and Playing by Ear. — Max Konyi, Find the Key of Any Song in 30 Seconds (By Ear)
secs: What makes a song sound "in a key"

wavetable.title: Wavetable
wavetable.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's modern wavetable synth with two wavetable oscillators, a dedicated modulation oscillator, effects section, and a large built-in wavetable library plus scanning/warping controls.

What it's used for

Modern electronic leads, basses, pads, and evolving textures — Live's answer to Serum/Massive-style wavetable sound design for EDM, trap, and pop production.

FX chain notes

As the instrument source; commonly followed by FabFilter Saturn or Ableton Saturator for harmonic reinforcement, then a limiter/EQ on the bus.

chord-tone-soloing.title: Chord-Tone Soloing
chord-tone-soloing.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony — the improvisation-practice complement to the strand's melodic-language notes: Bebop Vocabulary supplies the decoration (enclosures, approach notes, passing tones), Guide Tones supplies the theory of which notes matter most, and this note is the practice ladder that turns both into something a hand can actually do over a real, fast-moving progression. Built around a worked example — a 1–6–2–5 turnaround at two beats per chord (Dmaj7 Bm7 Em7 A7, the I–vi–ii–V loop that also forms the Rhythm Changes A section) — but the ladder generalizes to any chord-tone-dense progression, jazz or not.

The core question: do you have to target every chord?

No — but practicing as if you do is what earns you the freedom to not. Outlining every chord tone on every chord isn't the end goal; it's a conditioning exercise that gets the internal ear and the hand used to what the harmony is actually doing, so that later you can target things only if and when you want to and still land convincingly. Treat the whole ladder below as "learn it, then forget it" — the mechanical drilling is temporary scaffolding, not the finished sound.

Step 1 — Treat the whole progression as one chord (the tonic)

Before touching the changes at all, play the tonic's scale/arpeggio (major pentatonic, then full chord tones) over the entire loop, ignoring the other three chords completely — over Dmaj7 Bm7 Em7 A7, that means playing D major pentatonic / D major-7 chord tones the whole way through. This sounds "wrong" against the underlying harmony in theory but works in practice because a fast turnaround like this genuinely functions as a prolonged tonic — it's the seed of the prolongation idea below, introduced early so the ear has already heard it once by the time it's named. (general starting point: any I–vi–ii–V or similar turnaround at ≤2 chords/bar will tolerate this — try it before assuming you need to chase every chord.)
secs: The core question: do you have to target every chord?
Step 1 — Treat the whole progression as one chord (the tonic)

operator.title: Operator
operator.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's FM/subtractive hybrid synth with four operators, each switchable between multiple oscillator algorithms, plus a filter and modulation section.

What it's used for

FM basses, electric-piano and bell tones, aggressive leads, and classic FM-style sound design without needing a dedicated FM synth like Native Instruments FM8.

FX chain notes

As the instrument source, often followed by an EQ to control harsh FM overtones and a chorus/delay send to add width.

serum-2.title: Serum 2
serum-2.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Xfer Records

What it is

Xfer's flagship wavetable synthesizer, one of the most widely used modern synths for EDM, trap, pop, and sound design, with an intuitive wavetable editor.

What it's used for

Modern electronic sound design across basses, leads, plucks, and pads — an industry-standard modern wavetable synth.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, often followed by saturation, EQ, and a limiter to manage its dense harmonic content.

arpeggio-shapes-for-playing-over-changes.title: Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes
arpeggio-shapes-for-playing-over-changes.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and the guitar side of Chord Voicings — a system for outlining a non-diatonic or fast-moving chord progression in a solo, built around CAGED bar-chord shapes rather than a single scale stretched across the whole progression. Pairs directly with Secondary Dominants and The ii-V-I: the harmonic analysis those pages describe (spotting a secondary dominant or a 251 inside a scary chart) is what tells you which arpeggio shape to reach for at each chord; this page is the physical, on-the-neck half of that same skill.

The core idea: arpeggiate each chord in position, not scale over the whole progression

When a progression isn't cleanly diatonic to one key — it's full of secondary dominants and borrowed ii-V units — a single parent scale won't outline the changes convincingly. Instead, address each chord individually with its own arpeggio (root-3rd-5th-♭7, in whatever order the position gives you), chosen from whichever CAGED bar-chord shape sits physically closest to the shape used for the previous chord, so the hand barely moves between chords instead of jumping to a fresh spot on the neck for every change.

Picking the shape: closest CAGED grip, not the "textbook" one

Worked example targeting C7 → E7 → Am7, all found within a few frets of each other:

  • C7 — root-position arpeggio off a C-shaped bar chord. Ascending pattern from the root: root – 3rd – 5th – ♭7 – root – 3rd – 5th – ♭7 – root.
  • E7 — not a fresh E-shape from scratch, but the closest E-shaped bar chord to the C shape just used. Because of where that shape sits, the lowest available note in the position is the 5th (B), not the root, so the arpeggio pattern shifts to start there: 5th – ♭7 – root – 3rd – 5th – ♭7 – root – 3rd – 5th.
  • Am7 — played as a D-minor CAGED shape moved up the neck (the relative-minor trick: reuse the CAGED minor shape rather than inventing a new fingering for the minor chord). Lowest note is the ♭3 (C), so the pattern starts there: ♭3 – 5th – ♭7 – root – ♭3 – 5th – ♭7 – root – ♭3.

Same logic continues through any chunk of the progression — e.g. Gm7 → C7 (or C13) → Fmaj7 (a major ii-V-I) and Bm7♭5 → E7 → Am7 (a minor ii-V-i): each chord gets the CAGED-family shape that's already closest to hand, not the "default" open-position grip for that chord.
secs: The core idea: arpeggiate each chord in position, not scale over the whole progression
Picking the shape: closest CAGED grip, not the "textbook" one

analog.title: Analog
analog.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's virtual analog modeling synth, built around a dual-oscillator subtractive architecture modeled on classic analog synth circuitry (including component drift/imperfection modeling).

What it's used for

Warm analog-style bass, pads, and leads without loading a heavier third-party synth; good for quick sketching and for sounds that don't need modern wavetable complexity.

FX chain notes

Used as a sound source at the start of an instrument chain; often followed by Ableton's own Saturator/Amp or a third-party drive plugin to add grit, then EQ Eight to carve space in the mix.

Techniques

  • Pitch envelope + Pitch Wrap for a laser SFX layer — an analog-style laser/zap texture built from a pitch envelope (fast downward sweep at note-on) combined with Analog's Pitch Wrap behavior (pitch that folds/wraps rather than just sliding linearly) — the same laser-design goal as Operator's Laser SFX recipe, done on Analog's simpler subtractive engine instead of FM. → Operator (Laser SFX recipe) — Eli derp, How To Make Insanely Phat Basses with @eliderp_

sub-slot.title: SUB Slot
sub-slot.html:
Physical weight; felt more than heard. The mix's anchor — everything else is balanced against it.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • 808 — Serum 2 808 recipe; tuned to song key, glide for slides
  • Sub sine — Omnisphere sub recipe · Analog quick sine
  • Bass guitar fundamental — when the bass gtr is deep enough, it is the sub; don't add another
  • Kick tail — in some genres (house/techno) the kick's tail owns this slot

Mix rules

  • Mono. Always. No reverb, no chorus, no widener below 100 Hz — ever.
  • One occupant, ever — never stack two subs; the second one only makes mud and phase.
  • Level: set it against the kick first, the vocal second; check on small speakers that the harmonics (BASS slot) carry the note.
  • Standard processing: see FX Chain System bass chains; saturation adds audible harmonics, not level.

When it's the hook

808-driven trap: the 808 pattern is the hook — push it, HPF everything else at 100–120 Hz, and let slides/glide carry melody. Vocal dips slightly for the 808's attack.

When it competes

  • vs Kick (TRANSIENT Slot): sidechain the sub to the kick, offset the 808 to avoid stacking hits, or make the 808 the kick.
  • vs everything else: nothing else belongs down here — HPF all BED/MIDS/AIR sources ≥100 Hz (Masking and Carving).

Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

  • The kit's high-pass ladder starts here. Every drum gets filtered out of the sub except the kick: kick low cut 40–60 Hz (remove rumble) — and even the kick only keeps this slot when no 808 is present; in a trap/808 context the kick HPFs at 40–60 Hz and the 808 owns the sub outright. Toms 60–200 Hz, snare 100–200 Hz, hats 200–300 Hz — nothing else in the kit reaches down here at all. → EQ, Kick Design, Masking and Carving — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

Neighbors: BASS Slot above. Index: Sound Palette.
secs: Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

bass-scale-shapes-major-minor-pentatonic.title: Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues
bass-scale-shapes-major-minor-pentatonic.html: From BassBuzz's beginner "7 Days to Learning Bass Scales" routine — five movable fretboard shapes (major, major pentatonic, minor, minor pentatonic, blues) taught with a running spice-cabinet metaphor: a scale is a subset of the 12-note chromatic alphabet guaranteed to sound coherent together, and a shape is just a memorized finger pattern that locates that subset relative to a root note — movable to any starting fret, so "C major scale" and "F major scale" are the exact same shape, just anchored to a different root. Each shape below is drilled first as a bare scale, then internalized by playing a real riff/melody built from it — melodies use more of the scale's notes than a typical bassline does, which is why riffs (not basslines) are the internalization tool here. The freeform half of internalization — improvising over a drone instead of copying a fixed riff — lives on its own page: Improvising Over a Drone Track.

reverb-send-long.title: Reverb Send Long
reverb-send-long.html:
Role: The "big moment" space — plate/hall tails for hooks, vocal features, ballad moments. Where Reverb Send Room is invisible glue, this one is audible as an effect.

Signal chain

1. ValhallaPlate — The tail

  • Mix 100% (②) · Decay 2.4 s (③ — 1.8–3.0 window) · Pre-delay 35 ms (④ — longer than the room: big spaces have late first reflections, and the longer gap keeps the lyric intelligible under a long tail)
  • Plate for vocals (dense, bright, no early-reflection clutter) — swap ValhallaVintageVerb hall for orchestral/ballad size.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter

  • HPF 250–350 Hz · LPF 6–8 kHz (slightly brighter than the room — plate sparkle is the point) — same band-limiting logic as the room send.
  • 🎬 From video (clarity): a narrow dip around 1.5–3.5 kHz on top of the HPF/LPF keeps a long, audible tail from burying the lyric — pair with pre-delay in the 10–50 ms range (this send already runs 35 ms) so the transient clears before the tail arrives — Sage Audio, Reverb Masterclass

3. Pro-C 2 — Duck the tail (sidechain from lead vocal)

  • 2:1 · 2–3 dB GR keyed from the dry lead · slow release
  • Why: The pro trick for big-but-clear: the tail tucks while the singer sings and blooms in the gaps between phrases. You get cathedral size with dry-vocal intelligibility.
  • 🎬 From video (creative sends): the George Michael trick — invert a de-esser and use it to drive this send, so only the S's trigger the reverb (sibilance as a crash cymbal) — Disclosure, Higher Than Ever Before. And reverse-reverb "dream" swells — print a part full-wet, reverse the audio → a rising wash into a hit — Disclosure, You've Got To Let Go. (These often live as track inserts, not just this send.)

keyscape.title: Keyscape
keyscape.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Spectrasonics

What it is

Spectrasonics' deeply-sampled keyboard instrument covering acoustic and electric pianos, Rhodes, Wurlitzers, and rare vintage keyboards.

What it's used for

Studio-quality acoustic and electric piano/keys sounds across pop, hip hop, and R&B production.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, typically followed by light compression and EQ to fit the keys into the mix.

Techniques

  • The "Creative" preset category as a chord-instrument source beyond the standard piano/EP patches — a deep sub-library ("so much good stuff") used for a jazzy half-diminished chord vamp (F♯ø7 → Fm6 → C9/E) in a lofi hip-hop context, distinct from reaching for a plain Rhodes/Wurli patch. → Neo-Soul - Lo-fi — Max Konyi, Jazzy LoFi Hip-Hop - Beat Breakdown
  • Sustain-layer under a pluck — same chords as the lead pluck but sustained, tucked underneath so the pluck carries attack and Keyscape carries body; two patches reading as one instrument — Lophiile, Paradise breakdown
  • "Greg Phillinganes" electric-piano hits for a UK-garage flip — the go-to Keyscape EP patch for chopped-soul garage chords; pairs with deliberately-loud lo-fi hats + a bedroom MPC saturation over the loop. → Saturation and Distortion, House - EDM, BED Slot — Disclosure, Writing U.K. Garage in the Studio!

Manual

  • 📄 Local PDF (294 pp, compressed) · Official web reference guide

High-level points:

  • 36 deeply-sampled keyboard instruments; each patch exposes custom controls specific to that instrument (a Rhodes gets bark/bell/tremolo, a piano gets lid/pedal-noise/velocity curve) — the controls page changes per patch, so always look.
  • The per-patch EQ, drive, and FX knobs are modeled for that instrument and genuinely good — shape there before reaching for Ableton devices.
  • Velocity curve matters more than any knob: match it to your controller or every patch feels wrong.
  • Mechanical/pedal/release noises are separately mixable — they're the "realness" layer; too loud reads as noise, off reads as fake.
  • Keyscape patches load inside Omnisphere as a satellite — layerable with pads, filterable, arpeggiable.
  • House rule: internal reverb OFF, sends do space (see Instrument Preset Map for the per-job patch table).

drift.title: Drift
drift.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's dual-oscillator analog-modeled synth introduced in Live 12, combining classic subtractive synthesis with drift/character modeling and a built-in modulation matrix.

What it's used for

General-purpose analog-style synth duty — basses, leads, pads — as Live's modern default alongside Analog and Wavetable.

FX chain notes

Used as an instrument source; pair with Ableton's Saturator for extra harmonics and a chorus/ensemble effect to widen mono patches.

Techniques

  • LFO Wander mode + Key-modulated rate for natural pitch drift — set the modulation LFO to Wander mode and route it to Pitch so the pitch meanders instead of cycling on a fixed shape; then, in the Mod section, have Key (which note is being played) modulate the LFO's Rate — every note wanders at a slightly different speed instead of all notes drifting identically, a more natural/human result than one fixed Wander rate across the whole part. → Randomized Rack Design — dnksaus, Expressive Chords Trick - Live 12.2

Used in my chains

An instrument source (not an FX slot) — the warm analog option for synthwave/indie:

  • Digital Bass Track — analog-style synth bass → dedicated patch Drift — Analog Synth Bass.
  • Synth Bed Track — evolving/motion pads (Shape/position modulation that OTT loves).
  • Synth Lead Track — warm analog mono lead (vs. Massive growl / Omnisphere texture).

bass-slot.title: BASS Slot
bass-slot.html:
The groove's pitch and the mix's warmth. Where the note of the low end actually reads.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Bass guitar — the band feel; FX Chain System bass chains
  • Juno/analog synth bass — Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer (square+sub, unison)
  • Reese / growl low end — Serum 2 growl recipe (sub split out to SUB Slot)
  • 808 harmonics — the audible top of an 808 lives here even when its body is SUB
  • Piano left hand — Keyscape; on sparse ballads the LH is the bass

Mix rules

  • Mono-ish below ~120 Hz; width only in the upper octave.
  • Don't HPF a bass guitar past its ~100 Hz fundamental (house rule from Production System Report).
  • Octave discipline vs SUB Slot: if both are occupied, they need different octaves or the sub yields.
  • Compression: consistent bass = consistent mix; this slot takes heavier leveling than any other melodic slot.

When it's the hook

The McCartney lane: melodic bassline as the hook (Beatles core taste) — push +1.5–2 dB, brighten 700 Hz–1.5 kHz so the melody reads on phones, and dip BED low-mids around it.

When it competes

  • vs BED (BED Slot): HPF beds/keys at 120–150 Hz; dynamic dip 200–350 Hz in the bed keyed by the bass (Masking and Carving, Soothe2 sidechain).
  • vs Kick: classic pocket problem — sidechain or arrangement offset, same as SUB.
  • vs Vocal warmth (200–350 Hz overlap): the vocal wins; static 1–2 dB dip in the bass there if the vocal sounds thin.
  • vs a hip-hop/trap percussion loop sharing this territory with an 808: cede the loop's low end to the 808 outright (cut it, don't just duck it) and reclaim its cut-through higher up — Jaycen Joshua: "you're taking a little bit of the low end off because obviously the 808 is taking, or occupying, all of that. And you're adding a little bit of what you need — that upper high-mid that just lets that cut through." → Pro-Q 4, Masking and Carving, SUB Slot — Mix with the Masters (Jaycen Joshua), Jaycen Joshua on creative drum mixing

how-to-get-so-good-at-guitar-it-feels-il.title: How to get SO GOOD at guitar it feels ILLEGAL (Using Neuroscience)
how-to-get-so-good-at-guitar-it-feels-il.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A "how to practice" video rather than a technique/song lesson — Daniel Seriff (25,000+ lessons taught) argues that 10,000 hours of undirected repetition ("massed practice" — drilling one thing over and over until your brain checks out) doesn't work, and lays out a full replacement system built on named deliberate-practice/learning-science concepts, each tied back to a concrete guitar drill: interleaved practice (rotating between several short blocks instead of one long grind) run from a forward-planned practice journal, 15–20 minute session caps enforced with a physical kitchen timer, the "additive approach" (Anders Ericsson's chunking, worked on a chord progression one chord at a time), practicing hands separately (fretting-hand shape alone, then muted picking pattern alone, then air-strum plus fretting before finally playing it), going directly to the trouble spot instead of restarting from the top when something breaks down, deliberately practicing at the edge of ability (Daniel Coyle's "deep practice"/myelin framing), catching the "illusion of knowing" (recognizing a concept intellectually isn't the same as being able to play it cold), and building strong mental models/audiation (hearing, seeing, and singing a phrase before playing it). He name-checks several learning-science books throughout (Make It Stick, Peak by Anders Ericsson, The Musician's Way — misheard/garbled by auto-captions as "Jeroen Klijsen" but the described author-and-teacher bio matches Gerald Klickstein, whom Seriff also separately credits by name later for the hands-separate method, so this is very likely one person referred to two ways by the transcript — The Talent Code by Daniel Coyle, The Art of Learning, The Inner Game of Music) as the intellectual scaffolding, but the video is dense with actual step-by-step drills, not just narrative — this page and the routed notes below extract those drills concretely rather than just the neuroscience framing.

pro-q-4.title: Pro-Q 4
pro-q-4.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: FabFilter

What it is

The latest version of FabFilter's Pro-Q EQ, adding new dynamic EQ behavior, spectral grab tools, and workflow refinements over Pro-Q 3.

What it's used for

Same corrective and tonal EQ role as Pro-Q 3, with newer dynamic-EQ and spectral-editing tools.

FX chain notes

Same placement as Pro-Q 3 — pre- and post-compression EQ stages, or as a dynamic EQ substitute for narrow problem frequencies.

sound-palette.title: Sound Palette
sound-palette.html:
Pick sounds by slot, not by instrument. Every sound in a mix occupies a frequency/role slot; sounds in the same slot are interchangeable (an e-piano and a synth bed are the same arrangement object — warm sustained low-mid harmony), and two sounds fighting for one slot is where mud comes from. Fill each slot once, on purpose, and the mix balances itself before any EQ (Masking and Carving is the repair shop; this page is how you avoid needing it).

Rules of thumb

  • One main occupant per slot per section. A second occupant enters only when the first leaves (verse Rhodes → chorus pad = a swap, not a stack).
  • A sound's slot = where its energy lives, not its note range (an 808's harmonics reach the BASS slot; a bright pad is BED + AIR).
  • Arrangement contrast = changing which slots are filled, not adding more sounds to filled ones.
  • Every recipe/patch in the instrument notes is tagged with its slot (see Serum 2 / Omnisphere Patch Recipes).

ott.title: OTT
ott.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Xfer Records

What it is

Xfer's free multiband upward/downward compressor, famous for its extreme, 'over-the-top' dynamic-leveling character.

What it's used for

Aggressive multiband dynamic leveling for a dense, in-your-face EDM/trap-style loudness and energy.

FX chain notes

Used on individual tracks or a bus for heavy dynamic leveling, often blended in parallel to taste.

model-84-polyphonic-synthesizer.title: Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer
model-84-polyphonic-synthesizer.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Softube

What it is

Softube's emulation of the Roland Juno-106 (1984 — hence the name), faithfully replicating its six-voice structure, DCO-based oscillator section, and the famous onboard chorus.

What it's used for

Classic analog polysynth sounds — lush pads, brass stabs, and vintage-style leads.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, often followed by chorus/ensemble and tape saturation for extra vintage character.

10-years-of-bass-advice-in-10-minutes.title: 10 Years of Bass Advice in 10 Minutes

guitar-positions.title: Guitar Positions
guitar-positions.html:
A position is the 4-fret span the fretting hand sits in on the guitar neck — the index finger anchors the lowest fret, middle/ring/pinky cover the next three. This set covers positions 1 through 12 across the whole neck, in standard tuning (E A D G B E, low string 6 → high string 1). Each page maps every note available in that position — as a lookup table and an ASCII fretboard diagram — notes the finger assignment and the reachable stretches just outside the position, and leaves stub sections for chord shapes, scales, and arpeggios to be mapped in later. This mirrors and generalizes the first-position structure of the Berklee Modern Method for Guitar (Book 1) across the full neck.

Enharmonic key

Sharps are used throughout these pages. Flat equivalents: F# = Gb · G# = Ab · A# = Bb · C# = Db · D# = Eb

Positions

Position Frets Index finger Page
1 open–4 fret 1 Position 01
2 2–5 fret 2 Position 02
3 3–6 fret 3 Position 03
4 4–7 fret 4 Position 04
5 5–8 fret 5 Position 05
6 6–9 fret 6 Position 06
7 7–10 fret 7 Position 07
8 8–11 fret 8 Position 08
9 9–12 fret 9 Position 09
10 10–13 fret 10 Position 10
11 11–14 fret 11 Position 11
12 12–15 fret 12 Position 12

Extensibility

Each position page has empty Chord shapes, Scales, and Arpeggios sections — populating those is future work (relates to idea #22 Scales and Modes by Box and String, idea #15 Arpeggios). Progress-tracking through the Berklee book itself is a separate idea, out of scope here.

Related training method — reading, not soloing

The position map above is built for scale/arpeggio/chord vocabulary. For sight-reading melodies specifically, there's a narrower, faster-to-fluency alternative: instead of learning to read across all positions, freeze one fret/string spot per written note name in a single register and drill until it's automatic — see Reading Notation on Guitar §7a, from Shortcut to Reading Sheet Music for Guitar - Read Guitar Lead Sheets. Complementary, not competing: the one-spot drill gets you reading fluently fast in one zone; the full position map (this page) is still what you want for soloing/vocabulary that needs to move around the whole neck.

width-and-stereo.title: Width and Stereo
width-and-stereo.html:
What it is: the left-right dimension — real width (two different performances), psychoacoustic width (micro-pitch/delay tricks), and M/S width (processing the sides separately from the center).

The width hierarchy (best to cheapest)

  1. Double-track it. Two real performances panned L/R is width no plugin matches (Electric Guitar Amp Track, Double Vocal Track). Stacks in fours, hard-panned as you track, first take checked in mono before the pan spreads it (Kuk Harrell, Creating vocal stacks with Kuk Harrell).
  2. Micro-pitch (MicroShift): detuned L/R copies under a mono center — width and focus (Width Send). This is the modern form of Artificial Double Tracking (ADT) — the Beatles/Lennon "fake a double from one take" trick (invented at Abbey Road, 1966).
  3. Chorus/ensemble (Chorus-Ensemble, kHs Chorus): modulated-delay width — vintage, audible motion.
  4. Haas/delay offset (kHs Haas, EchoBoy L/R offset): free but the most mono-fragile.
  5. M/S widening (S1 Imager, Ozone 9 Imager, Wider): boosts the side channel — use in single dBs; it can't create sides that don't exist.

The rules that keep width safe

  • Mono-check everything (Utility mono flip / Stereo Tool): a widened element should get quieter in mono, never vanish or comb. If it disappears, reduce the effect or raise its crossover.
  • Low end mono, always (<100–120 Hz — Utility Bass Mono, Imager band 1 to zero): stereo lows phase-cancel on clubs/vinyl/phones.
  • Width is relative. The sides only feel wide against a solid center (lead vocal, kick, snare, bass stay centered) and a narrow verse makes a wide chorus bloom — automate width per section.
  • Where width is cheap and safe: hats/percussion group, pads, backup stacks, piano/keys sides. Where it's dangerous: anything low, anything that must survive mono, the lead vocal's dry center.
  • Widening also cleans the center — pushing keys/pads outward is a masking fix as much as an aesthetic one (Masking and Carving, the M/S carve).
secs: The rules that keep width safe

transient-slot.title: TRANSIENT Slot
transient-slot.html:
The rhythm skeleton. Drums and percussion don't occupy one frequency slot — each piece straddles the melodic slots, which is exactly why they collide with everything.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Kick — straddles SUB Slot + BASS Slot; Drums Group chain
  • Snare/clap — straddles MIDS Slot + LEAD Slot presence
  • Hats/shakers — live in AIR Slot (see that page)
  • Percussion/toms — BASS through MIDS depending on tuning
  • AnalogKick-style synthesized hits — AnalogKick.amxd
  • Foley hits — clicks, snaps, stomps replacing traditional drums

Mix rules

  • Transients win by being first, not loudest — a clean 5 ms attack cuts through a wall.
  • The kick/808 relationship is the mix's foundation: sidechain, offset, or merge (SUB Slot rules).
  • Parallel compression (Parallel Comp Send) adds density without killing attacks.
  • Drum bus glue: Drums Group chain; OTT in moderation on top loops.

When it's the hook

Beat-switch moments, drum fills, the trap hat-roll, the iconic break: percussion as hook = push the pattern, strip melodic slots for its bars (the carve is arrangement, not EQ).

When it competes

  • Snare vs vocal (LEAD Slot): the 2–4 kHz crack pokes the vocal's home — tuck the snare's presence when the vocal is on, or write around it.
  • Kick vs bass: pick who owns the low attack; sidechain the loser (BASS Slot).
  • Hats vs vocal air: AIR Slot rules.
  • Cymbal wash masking everything: Soothe2 on the drum bus, sides-only.

Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

  • The four-lane EQ map for kick/snare/hats/toms — which band makes each hit read as a transient: kick snap 2–4 kHz (+ a click band at 8–10 kHz, printed as a "notch" but almost certainly a boost — see Kick Design) · snare crack 5–7 kHz · toms stick attack 5–10 kHz · hat sizzle high-shelf 7–10 kHz+. Body counterparts, set first: kick 80–100 Hz, snare 200–300 Hz, toms 100–300 Hz. Every lane also gets a high-pass, ascending down the kit (kick 40–60 · toms 60–200 · snare 100–200 · hats 200–300) — that ladder is the kit's internal lane assignment. → EQ, Pro-Q 4, Masking and Carving, 2 Drums Group — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
secs: Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

pro-c-2.title: Pro-C 2
pro-c-2.html:
FabFilter's current Pro-C UI (Pro-C 3 shown — Pro-C 2's interface is nearly identical).

Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: FabFilter

What it is

FabFilter's flagship compressor — eight compression styles (Clean, Classic, Opto, Vocal, Mastering, Bus, Punch, Pumping), a sidechain filter, and a detailed gain-reduction display.

What it's used for

FX chain notes

triads-as-a-fretboard-map.title: Triads as a Fretboard Map
triads-as-a-fretboard-map.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. Where Chord Voicings and Chord Inversions use close-position triad shapes to comp through a progression, this page uses the same underlying triad shapes as a soloing map — landmarks for finding where an equivalent phrase lives when you move it to a different part of the neck. The core problem it solves: a lick learned by ear off a record usually only lives in the one spot/string-set/key you learned it in — this is a way to generalize it across the whole fretboard on purpose.

The core idea: three triad shapes = three usable neck positions

Any major triad (root, 3rd, 5th) repeats across the neck in three close-position shapes, and each shape anchors a playable 4–5 fret zone. Worked in E major (E, G♯, B): on the high E string alone, the three notes fall at open (root), fret 4 (3rd), fret 7 (5th), then the pattern repeats an octave up starting at fret 12 — that ladder is the skeleton. Applied across a full string set instead of one string, the same three notes reshuffle into different inversions (3rd-5th-root, 5th-root-3rd, root-3rd-5th) depending on where on the neck you grab them, and those inversion points cluster into three usable zones:

Zone Roughly Maps to
Open-position triads frets 0–4 Position 1 (open)
5th-fret triads frets 5–8 Position 5
9th-fret triads frets 9–12 Position 9

Each zone is one physical grip of the E-G♯-B triad in a different inversion/string-set — the same three notes, relocated. Knowing where those three shapes sit turns "the fretboard" into three known landmarks instead of an undifferentiated grid.
secs: The core idea: three triad shapes = three usable neck positions

fretting-hand-strength-stretch-stamina-a.title: Fretting-Hand Strength, Stretch, Stamina, and Finger Control
fretting-hand-strength-stretch-stamina-a.html: BassBuzz's four-exercise beginner routine for the fretting hand — a companion, hand-flipped counterpart to String Crossing and Plucking Patterns (which drills the plucking hand). Each exercise targets a distinct beginner failure mode — a rattly, thin tone; a hand that can't reach wide interval spans; fretting/plucking muscles that give out mid-song; and exaggerated "flying finger" flails that waste motion and cost speed — and they're built to be run in order, each one leaning on the exercise before it (stretch needs strength's pressure/lift-off control already in place; stamina reuses stretch's exact note pattern; finger control assumes the first three are solid). BassBuzz frames it as (general starting point): 10 minutes/day for a couple of weeks, done with attention to technique rather than mindlessly running the tabs, since sloppy reps mostly waste the practice time. A free PDF (tabs + play-along tracks) is offered in the source video's description but not captured here — this note documents the technique itself.

dune-3.title: DUNE 3
dune-3.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Synapse Audio

What it is

Synapse Audio's wavetable/virtual-analog hybrid synthesizer known for a rich unison engine and powerful modulation system.

What it's used for

Modern EDM and electronic leads, basses, and pads with a distinctive thick unison character.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, often followed by saturation and EQ to manage its dense harmonic content.

Techniques

  • Dawn FM synth-pop pad recipe: two waveforms tuned to an interval (not unison), then Chorus → Reverb → Overdrive, then two LFOs in two different cycle modes. From-scratch build reverse-engineered from The Weeknd's Dawn FM: (1) blend a saw and a square wave, mix ~70% toward the saw — Osc 1 VA saw, Osc 2 VA pulse; (2) tune Osc 2 to a major-key interval above Osc 1 instead of unison-detuning it — an interval (not detune) is what makes the patch read "big," maps to DUNE 3's Osc B semitone/fine-tune offset; (3) effects in this exact order: Chorus first (widens the raw blend), Reverb second (spatializes the now-wide signal), Overdrive last (colors the already-spatialized sound rather than distorting dry) — route via the effect bus/insert FX in that sequence; (4) modulation is two separate LFOs with two different cycle modes, not one LFO doing double duty: LFO2 → filter (Cutoff, ⑥) cutoff, synced to quarter notes, cycle mode set to Single (one-shot per-note sweep, not looping) for a filter-opening motion on every note; LFO3 → the effect bus's Reverb dry/wet amount, cycle mode set to Cycle (continuous loop) specifically to fill the space between chord hits with breathing reverb wetness. → BED Slot, Chorus-Ensemble, Overdrive, Modulation (Effects), Reverb (Effects), Synth Bed Track — loner, the production secrets behind the weeknd's evolving sound!?

granulator-3.title: Granulator 3
granulator-3.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

Ableton's redesigned single-device granular sampler (free in the Live 12 Suite — Packs tab), replacing the split Granulator II / GranulatorInput II / GranulatorFollow II trio with one instrument: load a sample, and it plays back overlapping/looping/stacked grains from it with built-in position, grain-size, LFO, and per-key modulation controls, no companion device needed for live-input capture or follow-modulation.

What it's used for

Granular synthesis on any sample — vocals, sound-design sessions, drum-kit textures — for pads, chorused/stereo-spread grain washes, glitchy stuttering slices, and evolving ambient textures.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source; often followed by a multiband glue compressor and/or reverb send to extend the granular texture, or resampled to a new audio/MIDI track once a good variation is found.

eq.title: EQ
eq.html:
General best practice for equalization — corrective and tonal — independent of the plugin. Specific moves live on Pro-Q 4, EQ Eight, Pro-MB (dynamic/multiband); reusable lessons here. See also Masking and Carving, De-essing.

What it is

Shaping tone and carving space by boosting/cutting frequency bands — the most-reached-for tool in the mix, and the one most worth doing subtractively first.

Owned (first-call)

Pro-Q 4 (surgical + dynamic) · EQ Eight (Ableton) · Pro-MB (dynamic/multiband) · Ozone 9 Equalizer · EQ Three

From books

  • The four-lane drum EQ map: every drum gets a high-pass, and the ascending order of those high-passes IS the lane assignment. Kick low-cut 40–60 Hz (rumble) → snare low-cut 100–200 Hz → toms low-cut 60–200 Hz (per drum: floor toms low, racks high) → hats low-cut 200–300 Hz ("or more, use ears"). Then the paired rule that runs through the whole chart: cut below the fundamental, boost at it — kick shelf 80–100 Hz (thump), snare shelf 200–300 Hz (umph), toms boost 100–300 Hz (low-end power). Presence side: kick 2–4 kHz (snap), snare 5–7 kHz (crisp), toms 5–10 kHz (high-end punch), hats high-shelf 7–10 kHz+ (sizzle); tom boxiness cut 300–800 Hz. No Q/gain/slope given anywhere — ranges only, and the card's own footer says "always use your ears." Read its two "remove harsh freq" high-cuts (snare 15–20 kHz, hats 18–20 kHz) skeptically — real harshness is 2–5 kHz / 5–12 kHz and is better handled dynamically (Soothe2, De-essing). → Masking and Carving, Kick Design, Snare Design, SUB Slot, BASS Slot, BED Slot, MIDS Slot, LEAD Slot, AIR Slot, TRANSIENT Slot — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

bass-fretboard-note-memorization-system.title: Bass Fretboard Note Memorization System
bass-fretboard-note-memorization-system.html: BassBuzz's five-step system for learning every note name on the bass neck without brute-force memorizing all 84 (or more) frets at once. The core idea: memorize a small, high-value anchor set first (the "money notes" — the plain letter names most basslines actually use), then layer on three tools that let you derive any other note from the nearest anchor instead of memorizing it directly — the musical-alphabet walk (Say and Play), two movable relocation shapes (octave and unison), and a mnemonic-driven map of the dot-marker frets. A fifth step (Bass GPS) is the test/drill that proves the map actually works under recall pressure. Framed throughout with a "lost in the forest" metaphor: money notes = the safe home base, the other tools = ways to navigate out from it and back.

transcribing-licks-and-making-them-your-.title: Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own
transcribing-licks-and-making-them-your-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch teaches the process of transcribing, not just the vocabulary that comes out of it — this is the methodology companion to How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues (same channel, same two Grant Green tunes — "Miss Ann's Tempo" and "Number One Green Street," both jazz blues in B♭), and the direct headline case study for Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction's thesis that "it's not enough to just simply learn a solo by ear, you've got to get under the hood." Ruch's stated warning up front: transcribing is one of the best ways to improve ear training, phrasing, and vocabulary, but only if you don't stop at learning someone else's lines verbatim — you have to break them down, analyze what's actually happening against the chord underneath, and then rebuild your own line from the same raw material. He works three short phrases from Grant Green solos (over the same B♭ jazz-blues 6-2-5-1 form as the companion video, plus a third tune, "Blues for Willarine," not covered there), explains the harmonic reasoning behind each one, then explicitly plays his own reworked version of each — demonstrating the "make it your own" step live rather than just asserting it. The most concrete, reusable device in the video is one not documented elsewhere in the vault yet: transposing a fragment by a fixed interval (a half step or a minor third) to fit a related chord, which Ruch identifies as a genuine recurring habit in Green's own phrasing, not just a teaching trick.

part-writing.title: Part-Writing
part-writing.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chord Progressions. Part-writing is writing music in the four-voice (SATB) style reverse-engineered from J.S. Bach's ~200 chorale harmonizations — the standard textbook corpus for common-practice "rules," because chorales have fast harmonic rhythm and huge, consistent sample size. Not really "rules" so much as patterns Bach and his contemporaries consistently followed because they sounded good; each style has its own rulebook.

Vertical rules (one chord, four voices)

  • Soprano↔alto and alto↔tenor must each stay within an octave; tenor↔bass can be any distance.
  • Voices stay in their proper order (tenor shouldn't sit above alto — Bach occasionally broke this for melodic shape, but it's the exception).
  • With 4 voices and only 3 notes in a triad, one note must be doubled. Root-position triads default to doubling the root unless another rule forces otherwise (see doubling-in-inversion below).
  • Each voice has a real singable range (amateur congregational singers, not virtuosos).

Horizontal rules (voice leading)

  • Move each voice the shortest distance to the nearest chord tone in the next chord.
  • Keep the common tone across a chord change whenever one exists — always a safe, good move.
  • The bass typically moves in contrary motion to the upper three voices — preserves voice independence.
  • Never write parallel perfect octaves, parallel perfect 5ths, or parallel perfect unisons between any two voices — this is the defining rule of counterpoint (no two voices doing the exact same melodic thing = independence).
  • An outer-voice (soprano or bass) leading tone must resolve to tonic.
  • Never move any single voice by an augmented 2nd or augmented 4th.
  • The 3-move safety net that avoids all of the above automatically: (1) keep the common tone, (2) move to the nearest chord tone, (3) use contrary motion.

decapitator.title: Decapitator
decapitator.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Soundtoys

What it is

Soundtoys' analog saturation plugin modeling several classic analog circuit types (tube and transformer-based) for harmonic distortion.

What it's used for

Adding punchy analog-style saturation and harmonic drive to drums, bass, vocals, and mix busses.

FX chain notes

A go-to coloration stage, often used per-track and again lightly on the mix bus.

Used in my chains

  • Saturation Send — slot 1, "the dirt": the primary home. Style E, Drive 6.0, Low Cut 150 Hz, High Cut 10 kHz, Mix 100% — parallel grit blended under vocals / bass / drums.
  • Guitar Bus — variation: swap Kramer Tape → Decapitator (Style A, Mix ~20%) for a rock-forward grit instead of tape gloss.
  • Synth Lead Track — creative move: Punish ~9–10 for a hero raspy-lead moment (MS-20 → 303 acid).
  • Main Vocal Track — lo-fi lane: Shure SM57 → 1176 slammed → Decapitator for a crushed section vocal.
  • Also an attitude/texture option in the vocal stack: Harmony, Backup, Ensemble Stack Group, Vocal Bus.

simpler.title: Simpler
simpler.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's lightweight one-sample-at-a-time sampler with slicing, warp, filter, and envelope controls — the fast, simple counterpart to Sampler.

What it's used for

Turning any audio sample or loop into a playable instrument quickly — chopping breaks, playing one-shots melodically, quick sample-based sketching.

little-alterboy.title: Little AlterBoy
little-alterboy.html:
Category: Pitch/Vocal Vendor: Soundtoys

What it is

What it's used for

FX chain notes

Used as a creative vocal effect insert, separate from a transparent pitch-correction tool like Auto-Tune.

string-crossing-and-plucking-patterns.title: String Crossing and Plucking Patterns
string-crossing-and-plucking-patterns.html:
A BassBuzz coach's live-coaching fix for a bassist whose self-diagnosed weakness was finger speed/accuracy when improvising fast 16th-note lines — specifically fumbling which string to hit next, not fretting-hand errors. The root-cause framing: stumbling happens when a fast line pulls the plucking hand outside a pattern it has actually rehearsed, so the fingers hesitate ("wait, which finger goes now?"). The fix is to pre-drill a small set of string-crossing patterns in isolation so that, when improvising, the hand is drawing on rehearsed muscle memory more of the time instead of guessing live.

The core method: break improvisation into rehearsable chunks

Fast improvised playing is too complex to drill directly — break it into simpler, isolatable pieces first ("that's working... now this is working... now this is working"), get each piece solid on its own, then let them recombine into the complex skill. The specific pieces to isolate here are how many plucks you play per string before crossing to the next one, and which picking-hand fingering you use across the crossing.
secs: The core method: break improvisation into rehearsable chunks

20th-century-harmony.title: 20th-Century Harmony
20th-century-harmony.html:
Part of Music Theory. Two early-20th-century movements that broke from common-practice harmony in opposite directions — impressionism toward color/mood over function, neoclassicism toward a deliberate return to Classical-era order (filtered through very different techniques depending on the composer).

Impressionism

Debussy (with Ravel, Satie, Griffes, Respighi, Sibelius, Hanson) drew a deliberate parallel to visual Impressionist painting (Monet) — broad strokes and mood/light over fine detail.

Technique What it is
Planing Parallel 5ths/octaves moving as whole chord-blocks — a common-practice no-no, used deliberately here
Whole-tone scale All whole steps, no half-steps — avoids traditional dissonance entirely
Non-functional harmony Chords juxtaposed chromatically, defying Roman-numeral analysis
Augmented triads Less tonally "loaded" than diminished triads — used for color, not tension
Chords with added 2nds/4ths/6ths Color without harsh dissonance
Uneven harmonic rhythm Chords change unpredictably rather than on a regular grid
Pentatonic scale Specifically the anhemitonic (no-half-step) 5-note pentatonic
Extended harmonies 7ths/9ths/13ths used for color regardless of function — this vocabulary fed heavily into early jazz

Neoclassicism

A return to Classical-era restraint after Romantic-era intensity — but the two poster composers demonstrate opposite favored techniques:

Hindemith's toolkit:

  • Pantriadicism — juxtapose major/minor triads with zero traditional functional logic between them.
  • 20th-century counterpoint — dissonance treated freely; melodic/rhythmic independence prioritized over strict Palestrina-style rules (contrast Species Counterpoint's much stricter dissonance handling).
  • Pandiatonicism — combine diatonic melodic lines in multiple voices with no regard for the resulting vertical harmony.

Stravinsky's toolkit:

  • Polytonality — genuinely different keys sounding simultaneously (not just borrowed color — actual key conflict).
  • Quartal harmony — chords stacked in 4ths/5ths instead of 3rds (see Chords's tertial-vs-quartal-vs-quintal-vs-secundal breakdown; fretboard shapes and the canonical So What example on Quartal Chord Voicings).
  • Rhythmic primitivism — intense, unpredictable accents; complex meters (see Time Signatures & Note Values); even polymeters (conflicting simultaneous meters).

rap-subgenres.title: Rap Subgenres
rap-subgenres.html:
Companion to Hip Hop - Trap — the quick-identity card for each rap lane: tempo, the defining element, the technique that gets you there, and examples to reference. Core rules (808/kick lanes, hats-as-melody, dry upfront vocal) carry across; each subgenre bends them.

Boom Bap — 85–95 BPM

  • Identity: chopped soul/jazz samples over dusty swung drums — the MPC feel; rapping is rhythmic, vocals barely effected.
  • Techniques: sample flip (Serato Sample chop, pitch ±2–4) · drums layered from vinyl breaks, Decimort 2/RC-20 Retro Color 12-bit crunch · swing 54–62% · bass = simple sub following the sample's root · vocal: Main Vocal Track minus tune, compressed hard, mono room only.
  • Examples: Nas — N.Y. State of Mind · Wu-Tang — C.R.E.A.M. · Joey Bada$$ — Paper Trail$ · Griselda (modern revival) — Westside Gunn 327.

Trap (core/modern) — 130–160 BPM halftime

  • Identity: the Hip Hop - Trap playbook itself — 808 melody, rolled hats, snare on 3, hard-tune.
  • Examples: Future — Mask Off · Migos — Bad and Boujee · Metro Boomin — Superhero · Young Thug — Hot.

mids-slot.title: MIDS Slot
mids-slot.html:
Rhythmic harmony, comping, riffs — the mix's density and drive. Articulation lives here.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Comping keys — Keyscape Wurli 200A pop bark, tight Rhodes comps
  • Clavinet — Keyscape Clavinet C + auto-wah (Envelope Follower) for funk
  • Muted/rhythmic guitar riffs — the funk/indie engine
  • Plucks — Serum 2 pluck recipe
  • Stabs — Omnisphere poly stab recipe · Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer brass stabs
  • Vocal chops — chopped hooks functioning as an instrument

Mix rules

  • Pan off-center — this slot loves 30–60% L/R; the center belongs to vocal + bass + kick.
  • Short > long: this slot is rhythmic; long tails push it into BED territory.
  • Saturation reads as energy here more than anywhere; light drive > level.
  • Standard chains: FX Chain System keys/guitar chains.

When it's the hook

Riff-driven songs (funk clav line, the indie guitar riff): push it toward center, +presence 2–4 kHz, and dip the BED's top so the riff articulates. Vocal-less sections hand this slot the wheel by default.

When it competes

  • vs Vocal presence (LEAD Slot 1–2.5 kHz overlap): the vocal wins — dynamic dip keyed by vocal, or arrange the comp between vocal phrases (the best fix is a writing fix).
  • vs BED (BED Slot): LP the bed ~2 kHz, keep this slot HPF'd ~300 Hz so they interlock instead of overlap.
  • vs Snare (TRANSIENT Slot): transient collision — nudge the comp's timing or shorten its attack hits.

Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

  • Kick snap begins here. Kick boost 2–4 kHz for beater snap runs from the top of this slot into LEAD Slot — worth knowing because it collides directly with comping keys/guitar riffs living in this slot; if the kick's snap and the comp fight, move the comp rather than the kick (the kick's snap is what makes it read on small speakers). Hats also get a 2–4 kHz cut if clanky (1 Drums Hat Track) — the same band, opposite direction. → EQ, Kick Design, Masking and Carving — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
secs: Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

ambient-texture-and-field-recording.title: Ambient Texture and Field Recording
ambient-texture-and-field-recording.html:
Using low-level ambience — field recordings, vinyl/tape noise, room tone, granular pads — as glue and mood, not content. It fills the TEXTURE Slot (full-band, low level) and gives a record a place and an era. A core Disclosure/Burial move. Companions: Sound Palette, TEXTURE Slot, RC-20 Retro Color.

Why

  • Kills dead silence. A baseline of hiss/crackle/room makes it "feel like play is pressed" — absolute digital silence feels unnatural (grew up on vinyl/CD noise floors).
  • Sets place + time. A street/road recording under a track reads as nighttime-city-with-headphones; rainforest/cafe noise puts you somewhere specific.
  • Era + glue. Vinyl crackle and tape hiss tie disparate elements into one "record."

How (general starting points)

  • Source: own recordings (a phone works) or libraries; the Burial trick is lifting just the ambient soundscape you love from a reference, not the music.
  • Level: low — felt more than heard. Automate it up in breakdowns/intros, duck it under dense sections so it doesn't crowd the AIR Slot.
  • Tone: high-pass so it doesn't muddy SUB Slot/BASS Slot; roll off harsh top if it fights vocal air.
  • Tools: RC-20 Retro Color (noise + wobble), granular textures from Omnisphere, vinyl-crackle samples, a plate/room verb tail as its own texture.
