upper-structure-triads-from-seventh-chor.title: Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords
upper-structure-triads-from-seventh-chor.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony and Seventh Chords. Distinct from — but related to — Upper Structure Chords: that page's "upper structure" is a different chord dropped over a foreign bass note (a reharmonization/polychord device). This page's upper structure is narrower and more literal: the triad already sitting inside a seventh chord's own 3rd, 5th, and 7th, extracted and played as a substitute/simplification for the full four-note chord. Same word, two different jazz devices — don't conflate them.

The derivation

Any seventh chord = a root-3rd-5th triad plus a 7th stacked on top. Instead of reading the chord as root+triad+7th, read the top three notes (3rd, 5th, 7th) as their own triad — that triad is playable on its own, on a completely different part of the neck from the root, as a lighter-weight stand-in for the full seventh chord. Worked example: C minor 7 = C-E♭-G-B♭; the 3-5-7 stack (E♭-G-B♭) is an E♭ major triad — so any E♭ major triad shape already known on the fretboard is fair game to play over Cm7, comping or soloing, with no need to grip the full four-note chord.

The four chord-quality rules

Each seventh-chord quality produces a fixed upper-structure triad quality, independent of key — learn these four once and they transfer to any tune, any key:

Seventh-chord quality Upper structure triad Relationship to root
Minor 7 Major triad Minor 3rd above the root
Dominant 7 Diminished triad Major 3rd above the root
Major 7 Minor triad Major 3rd above the root
Minor 7♭5 (half-diminished) Minor triad Minor 3rd above the root

(general note: not stated as a formal rule in the source video, but implied by all four worked examples — the pattern holds because the upper-structure triad is built from exactly the two notes that define seventh-chord quality, the 3rd and 7th, plus the 5th; cross-reference Guide Tones.)

harmonized-scale-triads-for-soloing.title: Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing
harmonized-scale-triads-for-soloing.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Diatonic Modes. A third distinct triad-soloing device alongside the vault's other two: Triads as a Fretboard Map takes one triad (the tonic) and finds its three close-position zones across the neck; Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords extracts a triad from inside a single seventh chord's 3rd-5th-7th; this page instead harmonizes the whole parent scale into seven triads (one per scale degree, skip-a-note/tertian stacking) and uses each one, in sequence up the neck, as a self-contained lick-starting motif. Worked in A Mixolydian over an A7 vamp. See also Triad Pairs — a fourth device that takes this page's same harmonized-triad table but combines two adjacent triads at once rather than using them one at a time.

Deriving the seven triads (skip-a-note method)

Build the parent scale first: A7 scale = A major with a ♭7 = A Mixolydian: A B C♯ D E F♯ G. Stack a triad on each degree by playing every other note of the scale from that starting point (skip one, play one, skip one, play one): starting on A, skip B, play C♯, skip D, play E → A C♯ E = A major. Move the same skip-a-note pattern up one scale step at a time and the qualities cycle through the whole scale:

Degree Triad Quality
I A major
ii B minor
iii C♯ diminished
IV D major
v E minor
vi F♯ minor
♭VII G major

(general note, not stated as a formal rule in the source video but implied by the derivation: this is Mixolydian's own harmonized-triad sequence — I–ii–iii°–IV–v–vi–♭VII — and it differs from the parent major scale's harmonization in exactly one triad: Mixolydian's flattened 7th moves the diminished triad from the major scale's vii° down to Mixolydian's iii°, and turns the major scale's vii° into a plain major ♭VII instead. Cross-reference Diatonic Modes's "only one degree in each key carries a dominant 7th, and it's the Mixolydian degree" note — same fact, seen from the chord-quality side.)

guitar-practice-how-to-be-your-own-teach.title: Guitar Practice - How To Be Your Own Teacher
guitar-practice-how-to-be-your-own-teach.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen lays out a complete self-diagnosis method built around recording yourself practicing — the substitute for "what you pay a teacher to do," namely listen to your playing, identify what to work on, and evaluate whether it's improving over time. The video moves through why recording works (you can't objectively hear yourself while you're busy performing), practical how-to (gear, metronome-vs-backing-track), the psychological obstacle almost everyone hits (nobody likes hearing their own recorded playing, even famous players), and finally three disciplines for actually getting value out of the recordings once you have them: don't get distracted from the one thing you're evaluating, be specific rather than vague about what's wrong, and keep sessions short and archived so you can measure progress over time. This is a genuinely different, self-contained self-teaching process rather than a technique or vocabulary lesson — it slots directly alongside the practice-methodology material already in the vault (recording-based self-diagnosis is a gap the existing The Five Pillars of Jazz Guitar Practice framework doesn't cover) rather than the tune/theory/vocabulary content most guitar lesson videos carry.

instrument-preset-map.title: Instrument Preset Map
instrument-preset-map.html:
Where to go inside each instrument plugin — the go-to patches/categories per musical job, so sound selection takes 2 minutes instead of 40. Companion to the Step 1a sections in the chain notes. Rule: browse by job, audition ≤5, commit — preset surfing is the great time thief.

Keyscape (pianos + EPs — the crown jewel)

Job Patch
Flagship studio grand LA Custom C7 (+ its "Cinematic"/softer sub-variants for ballads)
Character/vintage piano Wing Upright, Wing Tack (honky-tonk lane)
Neo-soul/hip hop Rhodes Rhodes LA Custom E, Classic Mark I (kill patch tremolo if using PanMan)
Wurli grit Wurlitzer 140B (tube/warm) · 200A (pop/rock bark)
Funk comping Clavinet C (add auto-wah via Envelope Follower)
Beatles tine Pianet M
80s ballad digital MKS-20 patches (the "human nature" lane)
- Every patch: internal reverb OFF (sends do space), velocity curve to your controller, the built-in EQ/drive knobs are genuinely good — tweak there before Ableton.
- Hidden superpower: Keyscape patches load inside Omnisphere as a satellite — layerable with pads, filterable, arpeggiable. Verify it's active.

Omnisphere (pads/atmospheres/hybrid)

  • Browse by category, not name: Pads + Strings for beds · Atmospheres for intros/textures · Keyboards for hybrid keys · ARP + BPM for pulsing beds (Psych-Pop (Tame Impala) pulse).
  • The move: layer A (dark/wide) + layer B (airy/thin) in one multi, balance to taste (Synth Bed Track).
  • Search terms that consistently deliver: "analog", "juno", "tape", "choir", "glass".

Serum 2 (modern leads/bass design)

  • Factory: Leads → start from a plain saw/unison patch and shape (per Synth Lead Track recipe) rather than a finished flashy preset — finished presets rarely sit in a mix.
  • Bass → the growl/reese starting points (EDM Subgenres DnB/future bass); keep the sub osc clean.
  • Its FX rack: strip reverb/delay from any preset you keep (sends do space).

Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer (the Juno)

  • This one you play, not browse: saw (+ sub osc) → Chorus II → slow filter = the entire bedroom-pop/synthwave/psych pad food group in 30 seconds. Chorus I = subtler, II = wider/wobblier, I+II = broken-lush.

granulator-ii.title: Granulator II
granulator-ii.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

Ableton's official Max for Live granular sampler, playing back a loaded sample as a cloud of overlapping grains with position, size, and pitch controls.

What it's used for

Granular synthesis — turning samples into evolving pads, textures, and glitch instruments.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source; often followed by reverb/delay sends to extend the granular texture.

Techniques

  • Granulate two different resampled sources separately, then layer them, for a denser "atmosphere" texture — rather than granulating one already-combined mix, resample each source individually (a string part, a piano part) to its own audio track, run each through its own Granulator II instance (Grain size + Spray for randomized grain variation), and layer the two granulated results together — the layered pair reads as richer/more atmospheric than granulating either alone. Raise the device's own amp envelope Attack for a slow ease-in rather than an abrupt grain onset, and follow with a convolution reverb to further space the result out. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording — You Suck at Producing, Part 2 of my video with Ableton!

Key Parameters

image: Images/Granulator II.jpeg
coords: Images/Granulator II.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique
① Sample display The loaded sample or LIVE-INPUT buffer; Grab/Write captures incoming audio Load a note/texture, or Grab live input to granulate it
② Grain Grain rate/density (grains per second) Low for a stuttery texture; high for a smooth pad
③ FilePos / Spray Playback position in the sample + spray (random scatter of the grains) Freeze FilePos on a vowel; add Spray for a wider, blurred texture
④ Scan (Time / Curve) Automatically moves the read position through the sample Slow Scan for an evolving pad that drifts across the sample
⑤ LFO Modulation LFO (Cycle + waveform) animating the grains Slow sine LFO into position/pitch for movement
⑥ AM Amplitude modulation of the grains Add for tremolo/ring-mod-style texture
⑦ Volume / Voices Output level and grain voice count (polyphony) More voices for a denser, thicker granular wash

air-slot.title: AIR Slot
air-slot.html:
Sheen, openness, "expensive." The slot listeners don't notice until it's missing.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Hats/shakers — Drums Hat Track chain; usually the main occupant
  • Shimmer reverb — ValhallaShimmer on a send
  • Vocal air/breath — Fresh Air or a high shelf on the vocal chain
  • Pad harmonics — a bright bed's top end reaching up (bed does double duty)
  • Sparkle layers — bells, tambourine, vinyl-crackle brightness (RC-20 Retro Color)

Mix rules

  • Additive slot: multiple quiet occupants coexist better here than anywhere — but each needs its own rhythm or register.
  • Brightness is relative: one bright element makes the mix bright; three make it harsh.
  • Fresh Air/shelf boosts on one element per mix; the rest earn air by arrangement.
  • Lo-fi genres deliberately empty this slot (LP the mix ~10 kHz) — absence of AIR is the aesthetic (Bedroom Pop - Indie).

When it's the hook

Rarely alone — but a signature hat pattern or shimmer swell can be the section's identity (trap hat rolls are AIR-slot hooks). Push the pattern, keep everything else's top rolled.

When it competes

  • vs Vocal sibilance (LEAD Slot): de-ess the vocal; don't dull the hats.
  • vs itself (hats vs shimmer vs sparkle): pick one dominant texture per section; LP the others ~10 kHz.
  • Harshness anywhere up here: Soothe2 sides-only on the bus tames wash without dulling the center.

Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

  • Hat sizzle is a shelf, not a peak, and the "harsh" high cuts up here are mostly headroom hygiene. Hats: high shelf 7–10 kHz+ for sizzle. Snare crisp 5–7 kHz and tom punch 5–10 kHz reach in from LEAD Slot. The source's "remove harsh freq" high cuts (snare 15–20 kHz, hats 18–20 kHz) are worth treating as headroom moves only — genuine harshness is a 2–5 kHz (snare) / 5–12 kHz (hats) problem, better handled dynamically with Soothe2 as the rules above already say. Vocal air still beats hat sparkle when they collide. → EQ, De-essing, 1 Drums Hat Track — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide

Neighbors: LEAD Slot below. Index: Sound Palette.
secs: Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

1-digital-bass-track.title: 1 Digital Bass Track
1-digital-bass-track.html:
Role: 808s, synth bass, sub bass — the programmed low end. Treated like an instrument per the process: same stages a recorded bass gets, with UAD plugin equivalents standing in for the hardware pass.

Chain philosophy: tone EQ → saturation → control comp → sidechain duck → mono. Saturation before the compressor here (unlike the recorded chains) because on an 808 the saturator is generating the tone — you want the comp to level the harmonics it creates.

clipping-and-loudness.title: Clipping and Loudness
clipping-and-loudness.html:
What it is: the modern loudness recipe — density stages → clipper → limiter, each doing the part it's transparent at, instead of one limiter doing everything and pumping.

Hard vs soft clipping

  • Hard clip: shears everything above the ceiling, touches nothing below. Odd harmonics, only on the shaved samples. Micro-transients (a few ms) are inaudible to remove — pure free headroom. Use for: peak control before a limiter (Gold Clip, Gold Clip Track).
  • Soft clip: a knee that rounds into the ceiling — audible warmth/saturation and rounded transients. It's a tone, not a headroom tool (kHs Clipper flavors, tape stages behave like this).

The loudness stack (as used in Master Chain / Drums Bus)

  1. Density first (Oxford Inflator): perceived loudness with zero GR — psychoacoustic, not dynamic. Effect 100% + ride input to the clip lights, level-match the output (the only honest way to judge it).
  2. Clip the peaks (Gold Clip): shave 1–2 dB of micro-transient.
  3. Limit last (Ozone 9 Maximizer): 2–3 dB GR max on the loudest section, ceiling −1.0 dBTP. Each stage hands the next a smaller job; that division is why loud modern masters still sound open.

Traps

  • Oversampling in clippers can recreate overs on the way back down and silently eat the headroom you just made. Gold Clip's algorithm holds true sample peak — most others don't. Verify with a sample-peak meter, don't trust the label.
  • Aliasing fear is overblown for transient clipping — transients mask it completely.
  • Clip earlier too: kick/snare tracks (Gold Clip Track) so the drum bus and master barely work.

Loudness targets (honest version)

  • Streaming normalization (−14 LUFS) is not a mixing target — louder masters just get turned down; the only crime is smashed dynamics.
  • Competitive: pop/trap ≈ −9 to −7 LUFS-I · band/organic ≈ −10 to −12 · ballads ≈ −11 to −12.
  • Judge by ear at matched loudness against 2–3 reference tracks; push until it sounds worse, then back off.
secs: The loudness stack (as used in Master Chain / Drums Bus)

1-main-vocal-track.title: 1 Main Vocal Track
1-main-vocal-track.html:
Role: The lead. Center, loudest vocal element — everything else in the vocal stack supports it.

Chain philosophy: tune → corrective EQ → leveling comp → resonance tame → color → tone EQ → de-ess → air. Corrective before compression, saturation after compression, de-ess near the end (sibilance is shaped by everything before it).

kramer-tape.title: Kramer Tape
kramer-tape.html:
Waves' current UI (Kramer Master Tape shown — Kramer Tape's interface is nearly identical).

Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Waves

What it is

Waves' tape saturation plugin modeled on engineer Eddie Kramer's tape machine settings, capturing analog tape warmth and compression.

What it's used for

Analog tape warmth, glue, and gentle compression character on tracks or busses.

FX chain notes

A coloration stage, often used per-track and again lightly on the mix bus.

teeter-totter-slap-pop-technique.title: Teeter-Totter Slap-Pop Technique
teeter-totter-slap-pop-technique.html:
BassBuzz's fix for slap-and-pop playing that's technically correct but slow and wasteful: a single continuous forearm motion — down for the slap, up for the pop — instead of two separate up-and-down trips. Named "teeter-totter" for the seesaw-like single arc; the video's own line is blunt about the alternative: "you must teeter-totter, or else you're a teeter-noter."

The problem it fixes

The naive way to slap-and-pop looks correct in isolation but has a hard speed ceiling: rotate the forearm down to slap, rotate all the way back up, then come back down to grab the pop, then back up again — a down-up-down-up, four-part motion just to get one slap and one pop. It works, but "there's just no way in hell to play fast like that" — the wasted travel between the slap and the pop is the bottleneck, not finger speed or coordination.

The fix — one continuous cycle

Slap the string, and without twisting the forearm back up first, get the thumb off the string — either by letting it bounce off naturally or by striking through the string — then hook the pop finger under the target string on the way past, and twist back up with the forearm to execute the pop. The whole slap-then-pop sequence becomes one down/up cycle instead of two round trips, which is what actually unlocks speed over time.

  • Either exit style off the string works — bouncing off it or striking through it — the technique doesn't require one specific hand shape, just that the thumb doesn't reverse direction and travel back up before the pop happens.
  • The pop finger gets positioned under the string during the same upward half of the cycle that lifts out of the slap — it isn't a separate motion tacked on after.

Practicing it — string difficulty and rhythm discipline

  • BassBuzz's paired drill pattern to test this directly: slap–mute–slap–slap–pop, repeated, watching for wasted motion creeping back in.
  • Harder variant: pop finger moves from the G string to the D string — flagged as trickier specifically because the finger has to tuck further in to get under the D string, so accuracy (not just the teeter-totter motion itself) needs extra attention on that string.
  • Keep listening to the drums (especially the kick) for rhythm while drilling this — the motion-efficiency fix doesn't replace the general rhythm discipline from Slap Thumb Technique — Angle, Anchoring, and Muting's and Bass Note Muting Technique's underlying accuracy/muting/note-length work; teeter-totter only fixes the pop half of the equation.
secs: Practicing it — string difficulty and rhythm discipline

bass-note-muting-technique.title: Bass Note Muting Technique
bass-note-muting-technique.html:
BassBuzz's "Mute Master" exercise — a deceptively simple-looking F major scale line that isn't actually about the notes at all; it's about controlling the silence between the notes with deliberate muting, so basslines stop ringing/rumbling unwantedly. Framed as the third exercise of a beginner three-exercise routine (see Fretting-Hand Finger Independence Drill for exercise one, String Crossing and Plucking Patterns for exercise two) and specifically targets: unwanted ringing strings, notes that come out the wrong length, and mutes that don't line up rhythmically with the plucks. Adjacent right-hand/left-hand muting concept, different instrument: Classical Guitar Expression & Muting (guitar's thumb-hop and fretting-hand string-damping techniques solve the same "unwanted ringing" problem with different specific moves).

The core distinction: two muting tools, and when to reach for each

  • Fretting-hand muting — release fretting pressure and/or touch the string with a fretting finger to kill the note. Natural choice right after a fretted note, since the fretting finger is already on the string.
  • Plucking-hand muting — touch/rest a plucking-hand finger on the string to kill the note. Natural choice for an open string (nothing is fretted, so there's no fretting finger positioned to damp it) or when the fretting hand is already busy moving to the next shape.
  • Choose whichever hand is comfortable for a given note — the exercise deliberately mixes both so the player builds fluency with either, rather than defaulting to one hand exclusively.
secs: The core distinction: two muting tools, and when to reach for each

blues-lead-phrasing-and-touch.title: Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch
blues-lead-phrasing-and-touch.html: Part of Music Theory → Blues Scales and Blue Notes (the note-choice half) and Blues Form and Harmony (the form the phrasing sits inside). This note covers the guitar-specific delivery side of blues soloing — the physical/phrasing moves that turn "the right scale" into "the right sound": where a phrase lands relative to the beat, how vibrato and pick position shape touch, and the chord-tone-targeting/chromatic-connector vocabulary that gets you from box to box. A close cousin, covered in its own section below: lead-fill accompaniment — phrasing that answers a separate vocal/melody line rather than carrying one, the B.B. King / Albert King call-and-response half of the same skill set.

harmonic-minor-modes.title: Harmonic Minor Modes
harmonic-minor-modes.html:
Part of Music Theory → Scales. The 7 modes generated by starting the harmonic minor scale on each of its own scale degrees — same construction logic as Diatonic Modes, applied to harmonic minor instead of the major scale. For melodic-minor modes, see Scale Modes Reference.

Building harmonic minor

Harmonic minor = natural minor with the 7th raised back to natural (i.e. major scale with ♭3 and ♭6 only — the 7th stays unflattened). Worked from A: A major (no accidentals) → A natural minor (♭3 ♭6 ♭7 → C, F, G natural) → A harmonic minor (♭3 ♭6, 7th raised back to G♯). One key produces a double-sharp when raised: G♯ harmonic minor's 7th is F♯ raised to F𝄪 (F double-sharp), the only harmonic minor scale that needs one.

The seven modes (built from A harmonic minor)

# Mode Starts on (of A harm. min) Formula vs. major Alt. names
1 Harmonic minor (Aeolian ♮7) A 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 7 —
2 Locrian ♮6 B 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 ♭5 6 ♭7 Locrian ♯6
3 Ionian ♯5 C 1 2 3 4 ♯5 6 7 —
4 Dorian ♯4 D 1 2 ♭3 ♯4 5 6 ♭7 Ukrainian Dorian (close cousin, not identical)
5 Phrygian dominant E 1 ♭2 3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 Spanish Phrygian
6 Lydian ♯2 F 1 ♯2 3 ♯4 5 6 7 —
7 Super Locrian 𝄫7 (altered dominant ♭♭7) G♯ 1 ♭2 ♭3 ♭4 ♭5 ♭6 𝄫7 Ultralocrian

Same relative-approach logic as Diatonic Modes: each mode is the identical 7-note collection, only the starting note (and therefore which note reads as "home") changes.

Five shapes, not seven

Although there are seven modes, they reduce to five distinct fretboard shapes for practice purposes (the same "modes vs. shapes" simplification Diatonic Modes doesn't need to make, since harmonic minor's shapes overlap differently) — practice the five shapes, and any of the seven modes is a relabeling of one of them starting from a different root within it.
secs: The seven modes (built from A harmonic minor)

transcribing-music-by-ear-in-real-time-e.title: Transcribing Music by Ear in Real-Time Ep.01
transcribing-music-by-ear-in-real-time-e.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The first episode of Max Konyi's real-time transcription series — he picks random songs cold from Spotify playlists (never heard before) and narrates, out loud, the entire internal process of working out chords and melody as the song plays for the first time. The explicit goal is to de-mystify what looks like "magic" by making the internal calculation, guesswork, and pattern-matching fully explicit, take by take. This episode covers a country track, two pop tracks, and a deep-house track — genre chosen specifically to range from harmonically simple to production-obscured. This is the origin video of the "abstracted key-center map" framing and the "no-perfect-pitch" tonic trick that recur across the whole Transcribing and Playing by Ear series (Ep.02, Ep.03).

transcribing-complex-music-by-ear-in-rea.title: Transcribing Complex Music by Ear in Real-Time Ep.02
transcribing-complex-music-by-ear-in-rea.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Episode 2 of Max Konyi's real-time transcription series steps up the harmonic difficulty from Ep.01's pop/country material into jazz-fusion, video-game orchestral, and K-pop territory — songs with fast chord changes, extended/altered chords, and genuinely ambiguous major/minor resolutions. Three tracks: "Yellow Jacket" by Sean Martin, the Genshin Impact soundtrack, and "Star" by Heize (K-pop). The through-line is that the same core toolkit from Ep.01 (bass-motion tracking, the no-perfect-pitch tonic trick, chord-position feeling recognition) scales up to handle real harmonic complexity — it doesn't need new tools, just faster/deeper application of the same ones plus a bigger trained vocabulary.

corpus.title: Corpus
corpus.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock physical-modeling resonator (Suite) — excites an incoming signal against a modeled resonant body (beam, marimba, membrane, plate, pipe, string, or tube) to impose tuned, ringing resonant character, distinct from a filter or EQ.

What it's used for

Adding a physically-modeled resonant texture layer to drums, percussion, and sound-design elements — a stock alternative in the same territory as kHs Resonator.

FX chain notes

Inserted on a texture/layering track, usually macro-mapped as a rack so its resonant character can be dialed in fast; often layered under an existing drum hit rather than run as the whole sound.

Techniques

  • Tune the resonator to the played note for sub-bass reinforcement, not texture — a distinct role from the drum-texture use below: on a bass patch (Operator/Serum/Wavetable), tune Corpus's resonance to the same fundamental frequency the bass note is playing (e.g. ~156 Hz for D♯) so its physically-modeled resonance reinforces the sub rather than adding an unrelated ringing pitch — paired with two or three Saturator instances each tuned to the note (fundamental, then an octave up) for a "thick bass" starting point. A free, pre-tuned rack version of this exact recipe (every note already tuned) is available as a free download from the source video. → Bass Design, Saturator, SUB Slot, BASS Slot — dnksaus, Tighten Your Sub Bass with CORPUS (Not Clickbait) [I Swear]
  • Macro-map most controls except Width/L-R/Spread; keep Dry/Wet mapped — for UK-style drum-pattern sound design, map nearly every relevant Corpus parameter to rack macros, skip the stereo-positioning controls (Width, left/right position, Spread), but do map Dry/Wet so the resonance can be blended in. An LFO on a mapped parameter adds a "splinky" modulated character; cap the Decay so a layered-in resonance doesn't ring out long enough to become annoying under the main hit. → Snare Design — dnksaus, craft UNIQUE snares

lead-slot.title: LEAD Slot
lead-slot.html:
The thing the listener is listening to. Mix priority #1 by default — every other slot yields to this one.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Lead vocal — the default occupant; FX Chain System vocal chains (Auto-Tune Pro first)
  • Lead synth — Serum 2 supersaw/trap lead recipes · Synth Lead Track chain
  • Bell/whistle hook — Omnisphere Mike Dean lane
  • Lead guitar — solos and melodic hooks
  • Top-line vocal chop — a chop promoted from MIDS to carry the hook

Mix rules

  • Only one occupant at a time. Non-negotiable. Lead vocal in? The synth lead waits its turn.
  • Center, upfront, dry-ish: predelay on its reverb (20–40 ms, ValhallaVintageVerb) keeps it in front of its own tail.
  • Presence 3–5 kHz is its home — that band belongs to this slot in every competing track's EQ.
  • De-harsh here, don't dull: Soothe2 over static high cuts.

When it's the hook

It always is — that's the definition. Hook-focus workflow: decide per section what the hook is (vocal, riff promoted from MIDS Slot, 808 pattern from SUB Slot) — whatever it is becomes the LEAD occupant for that section, gets pushed high in the mix, and every competing track gets carved around it (dynamic dips keyed by the hook, Masking and Carving).

When it competes

  • It doesn't — it wins. Everything overlapping 2.5–6 kHz gets a dynamic dip keyed by this slot (Soothe2 sidechain on guitars/keys = automatic vocal pocket).
  • vs AIR sibilance (AIR Slot): the one fight it can lose — de-ess the vocal rather than dulling the hats.
  • Two hook candidates in one section is an arrangement bug, not a mix problem: demote one to MIDS Slot or move it to another section.

Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

  • Drum presence/crack lives across 2.5–6 kHz — and this is the slot the vocal wants. Kick snap 2–4 kHz · snare crisp/crack 5–7 kHz · toms stick punch 5–10 kHz (both running up into AIR Slot). Three drum lanes boosting into the vocal's presence range at once is the most common reason a mix's drums and lead vocal fight; stagger them (kick low in the range, snare/toms high) rather than boosting all three at the same frequency. → EQ, Masking and Carving, Snare Design — Whipped Cream Sounds, Drum Mixing EQ Guide
secs: Drum lanes in this slot (from books)

ian-kirkpatrick-the-production-secret-be.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - The Production Secret Behind Huge Pop Hits
ian-kirkpatrick-the-production-secret-be.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The clearest statement of Ian's production philosophy: the complexity of great pop is not the track count — it's knowing when to perfect something and when to leave it alone. The hardest, most "complex" decisions are the ones where you don't fix something. Illustrated with three hits he admires for a single committed imperfect choice.

What's taught (philosophy)

  • Don't interfere with the songwriting / don't distract from the story. The biggest advice he gives: production should never pull the ear off the vocal and the story. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Arrangement and Song Form
  • "Perfection" can mean leaving something alone. The most complex decision is often "you know what, I'm gonna leave the kick like that" — committing instead of fixing. → Arrangement and Song Form
  • Sia — "Chandelier": the last line of the verse ("throw them back till I lose count") is suddenly hard-tuned a gajillion percent — probably a demo vocal someone chose to keep. Ian's instinct would've been "re-record that," but someone decided no, leave it. → Auto-Tune Pro, Pitch and Formant
  • Adele — "Hello": all the drums are muffled / low-pass filtered and kept that way, which helps the vocal stand out. A committed tone choice, not a fix. → EQ, Kick Design
  • Kanye — "All of the Lights": the snare is "so like a tone" — a sound Ian says he'd have thrown out if he'd started with it, but Kanye committed and it's iconic. Confidence over preciousness. → Sound Selection Guide
  • The takeaway: pop's complexity = when to perfect and when not to. Be confident, commit, don't be precious. → Ian Kirkpatrick - New Rules (25 Big Tips in 13 Min) (the "rate of information" companion idea)

Routed to

  • Arrangement and Song Form — commit / don't-fix philosophy (From videos)
  • Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — serve the story, not the flex
  • Auto-Tune Pro — hard-tune-as-a-choice (Sia example)

saturator.title: Saturator
saturator.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock saturation/waveshaping device with multiple curve types (analog clip, soft sine, medium curve, hard curve, sinoid fold, digital clip) plus a built-in pre-EQ.

What it's used for

Adding harmonic warmth, grit, or aggressive distortion to any track — from subtle analog-style warming to full-on digital destruction.

FX chain notes

Commonly placed after EQ and before or blended in parallel with compression to add harmonic density without losing punch.

width-send.title: Width Send
width-send.html:
Role: Parallel stereo thickener — the classic "pitch-shift widener" (a.k.a. the H3000 micro-pitch trick on every pop vocal since the 80s). Splits the signal to L/R copies detuned a few cents apart with tiny delays, creating width that doesn't exist in the mono source.

Signal chain

1. MicroShift — The widener

  • Style I (① — the classic H3000 recipe) · Detune & Delay at 100% default (②/③ — push toward 200% only for deliberately phasey/crazy moments) · Mix 100% (⑤ — return)
  • Focus knob (④): set the crossover ~100–200 Hz — everything below stays mono inside the plugin, so the widening never touches the low end
  • Audition all three styles per source — same trick, subtly different phase behavior
  • Why a send: at 100% wet on an insert, micro-pitch makes the source blurry; as a blend under the dry center image, the dry keeps the focus and the shifted copies pure width. Focus + size simultaneously.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Keep it out of the way

  • HPF 250–400 Hz (belt-and-suspenders on top of the focus knob) · LPF ~10 kHz.

Usage

  • Lead vocal hooks: automate the send up in choruses — verse stays intimate/mono-ish, chorus blooms wide. The cheapest "chorus lift" in pop.
  • 🎬 From video (mono→wide drop): make a chorus feel bigger without turning it up — keep the verse mono, then on the drop fade this send (or a chorus/rotary) up so it opens to full width; the fastest one-knob version is the RC-20 Retro Color "Whip" control, or just switch on a flanger/chorus/phaser for the drop — Disclosure, Talk.
  • Mono synths/guitars that need to feel doubled without re-recording.
  • 🎬 From video: direct confirmation of the exact hardware this send's "H3000 micro-pitch trick" is modeling — a real Eventide H3000 set to ±4 cents split L/R as a guitar-solo widener, run alongside a second H3000 on a subtle custom flange for character. Full technique on MicroShift — Chris Lord-Alge (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Muse Guitars - Chris Lord-Alge.
  • Never on bass, kick, or anything whose mono low end matters.

Mono-compatibility check: flip the master to mono (Utility) — the widened element should get quieter but not disappear or comb-filter. If it vanishes, drop the send or raise the return's HPF.

Variations

  • Subtle tape-chorus flavor: Chorus-Ensemble on the return instead — more vintage motion, less surgical width.
  • Extreme trap vocal width: MicroShift Style II + higher send, panned doubles on top.

pitch-and-formant.title: Pitch and Formant

omnisphere.html:

Spectrasonics' flagship hybrid synthesizer combining sample-based and synthesized sound sources with deep modulation and granular capabilities.

Wide-ranging synth duty — pads, atmospheres, basses, and leads — often the deepest sound-design synth in a producer's toolkit.

Used as the instrument source, followed by whatever mix-bus processing the patch's role in the arrangement needs.

rootless-voicings-wow.title: Rootless Voicings - WOW!
rootless-voicings-wow.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Episode 22 of Jared Borkowski's "chord theory and chord techniques" series (soundguitarlessons.com, Seattle) — a theory-first lesson on rootless voicings: the idea that any chord shape's root doesn't have to be a note you're actually fretting, and that a single physical shape can therefore be re-labeled as several different chords depending on where you decide the (unplayed) root is. Jared works three progressively bigger derivation examples (triads as the upper 3 notes of a 7th chord, 7th chords as the upper 4 notes of a 9 chord, and directly replacing a root with the 9th above or the 7th below), then spends the back half on the video's real payoff — the half-diminished chord shape used as a "favorite example" of a single grip supporting six different chord identities depending on assumed root — worked into a full chord progression and a pop-songwriting example. Closes with a caveat concept (ambiguous chords that resist any single root/label) and a practical ear-training exercise. This is a theory-heavy but fully guitar-fretboard-worked lesson — same "root droppable, one shape many identities" territory the vault already documents extensively via Jack Ruch, Jens Larsen, and Nathan Borton (see Related below), but Jared's own contribution is the replace-the-root-with-a-neighbor-tone mechanical trick and the unusually rich six-way half-diminished-shape example, both new to this vault's coverage. Same channel/series as several existing notes (Check out how these two chords are related! (chord substitution trick), Drop Chords Guitar Lesson - Drop 2 & Drop 3 voicings explained for guitarists, Neo Soul Chords on Guitar - 14 incredible voicings for ONE chord!); not the same video as the similarly-titled Rootless Voicings - Part 1 - Triads (that one is Jens Larsen, a different channel, a narrower triads-only lesson).

directional-alternate-picking-system.title: Directional Alternate Picking System
directional-alternate-picking-system.html:
Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons) core picking-hand default: a backdrop picking rule you fall back on whenever you're not deliberately doing something else, plus seven progressive exercises that drill it into automatic use. Distinct from Angular Reach Exercise (same channel, a reach/relaxation-under-tension drill on a fixed angular fret pattern, part of the Warm-up & Technique "always item" rotation on The Practice Priority Pyramid) — this note is a picking-direction rulebook + exercise ladder, not a reach drill, and the source video doesn't reference the Practice Priority Pyramid system at all. Genuinely separate material from the same teacher, not a duplicate.

The core rule: directional alternate picking

  • Not the same thing as "strict" alternate picking. Strict alternate picking = literally alternate every stroke (down after up, up after down), no matter where the beat falls. Directional alternate picking = pick direction is locked to the beat position, independent of whether you're actually plucking a note there.
  • The rule: downbeats (1, 2, 3, 4) get a downstroke; offbeats/upbeats ("and") get an upstroke.
  • The picking hand keeps moving through rests and slurred notes even when it isn't plucking — on a beat you don't pluck, the hand still travels the "right" direction for that beat position (down on a downbeat, up on an upbeat) so the motion stays continuous and the next real pluck is already moving the correct way. Framed with a strumming analogy: constant fluid motion (always moving, only striking the strings when you want sound) beats a jolting stop-start motion where you consciously reposition the hand before every strike.
  • Why it matters: it's meant as a default/backdrop mode — something intuitive enough that you stop spending cognitive energy on pick direction, which matters most once slurs (hammer-ons/pull-offs/slides) start skipping strokes in real playing (scale runs, licks). You're free to break the rule on purpose (deliberate runs of downstrokes, etc.) — it's a fallback, not an absolute rule.
  • Positioned against economy picking — Jared calls economy picking "a whole different ballgame," a deliberate alternative technique to reach for later; directional alternate picking is presented as the default you return to when nothing else is called for.
secs: The core rule: directional alternate picking

slap-thumb-technique-angle-anchoring-and.title: Slap Thumb Technique — Angle, Anchoring, and Muting
slap-thumb-technique-angle-anchoring-and.html:
A BassBuzz live-coaching fix (Josh coaching guest bassist Matt, from Source Audio) for the specific flavor of "sloppy" slap playing that isn't a groove problem — the player's quarter-note feel and consistency were already solid — but a hand-mechanics problem: hitting the wrong string, unwanted ringing from adjacent strings, and a general lack of confidence/efficiency in the left-hand/right-hand connection. Three concrete mechanical fixes, in the order the coach introduced them, plus one drill to lock them in.

Fix 1 — thumb angle: get closer to parallel to the strings

The root cause of hitting an adjacent string: a thumb angled too steeply down (or up) relative to the strings has a wide hit box — at that angle, striking the target string also catches the neighboring string (e.g. aiming for the A string but also clipping the D string). The fix isn't a single "correct" angle — whether the thumb ends up pointing slightly below or slightly above the string doesn't matter — what matters is bringing the angle closer to parallel with the strings so the hit box narrows to roughly one string's width instead of two. (General principle from the video: closer to parallel = narrower strike zone, not a specific degree number — none was given.)

Fix 2 — lock the thumb's position relative to the hand; move the whole arm assembly

Symptom: the thumb "hunts" for the target string while the hand itself stays static — this breaks muscle memory because the thumb's position isn't fixed relative to anything, so the hand can't reliably predict where the thumb will land. The fix: keep the hand's shape locked (the thumb stays in the same relative position within the hand), and move the whole hand/arm assembly to reach each string rather than reaching with just the thumb. The motion that crosses strings is described as coming from the shoulder and elbow (coming down and up), not from independent thumb movement. The hand can and should stay relaxed — this isn't about tensing up, it's about the thumb's position within the hand being consistent trip to trip.
secs: Fix 1 — thumb angle: get closer to parallel to the strings
Fix 2 — lock the thumb's position relative to the hand; move the whole arm assembly

piece-no-6-of-7-easy-classical-guitar-so.title: Piece No. 6 of 7 Easy Classical Guitar Songs for Beginners — With sheet music & classical guitar tabs
piece-no-6-of-7-easy-classical-guitar-so.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Piece #6 of Jared's ("Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared") 7-part beginner classical guitar series, teaching a short piece called "Waltz," attributed by Jared to "Ferdinando Kuli" — almost certainly a caption mis-transcription of Ferdinando Carulli (1770–1841), the early Romantic-era Italian guitarist-composer whose description ("late classical, early Romantic era guitarist and composer") matches exactly; flagged here as a low-confidence name, not corrected in the transcript itself. As with the rest of the series, the format is: full performance demo, sheet-music walkthrough, a set of extraction exercises, one featured "element of expression" for the piece (here: staccato vs. legato), a bonus tip, a harmonic analysis, and a slow play-along demonstration. This is the most substantive lesson entry from this channel enriched so far — unlike the channel's meta "Practice Log" vlog entry (This might ruin my channel Practice Log No. 1), this is real teaching content, and it transcribed cleanly apart from a handful of garbled music-terminology words (composer name, "D.C. al Fine" → "capo aline"/"deapo," "3/8 time" → "38 times," "sheet music" → "Sheep music") that context makes unambiguous. The two most valuable, clearly reusable ideas — a backward-chaining practice order borrowed from a David Russell masterclass, and a token-based deliberate-practice method for certifying a chunk before moving on — are general-purpose and not specific to this piece or even to guitar.

how-i-organize-my-guitar-practice-so-i-n.title: How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop)
how-i-organize-my-guitar-practice-so-i-n.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared's deepest practice-log entry yet — the next entry after Practice Log #2 in the same from-scratch rebuild, now with the philosophy layer named — a screen-share tour of the personal practice-tracking spreadsheet he's been rebuilding from scratch since the start of the year, plus the top-level philosophy behind it. This is the payoff video that Practice Log #1 previewed and Practice Log #5 partially demonstrated (the Vocabulary/scale category) — here he walks the whole system end to end: the philosophy (a five-stage "practice priority pyramid" and a three-part operating mechanic he calls "milestones, rotation, and variation"), the spreadsheet's category structure (Warm-up & Technique, Vocals, Guitar Vocabulary, Ear Training, Transcription, Classical Guitar Repertoire), and two fully worked exercise examples (the angular reach/alternate-picking exercise and a snake/economy-picking exercise), plus his stretch routine and nail-care update. He's explicit throughout that the spreadsheet itself is not the point — any tracking method (paper, pencil-and-checkbox, a notebook) works as long as it gives the same effect: showing up, knowing exactly what to do, and being able to instantly resume any thread exactly where it was left off. Genuinely the most systematic, structurally complete practice-methodology video from this channel to date — worth treating as the connective spine for the channel's other practice-methodology notes already in the vault.

practice-this-daily-10-min-technique-fix.title: Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix)
practice-this-daily-10-min-technique-fix.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's "blunder buster" exercise: rather than five separate drills for five separate technique problems (which the video argues bloats a practice routine into a boring, hours-long mess that people quit within a week or two), it's one single riff that progresses through five levels, each level specifically dialed to expose and fix one of five named beginner bass-technique failure modes — flying fingers, fretting too hard, uneven alternate plucking, "duck wrist" on octaves, and technique breakdown at speed. Each blunder gets a short before/after demo (including footage of the presenter's own younger, worse technique) and a bare-minimum prep drill to do before attempting that level of the exercise, rather than a full separate practice routine per problem — the whole point being to keep the daily fix down to 10 minutes. The video closes with a genuine field test: BassBuzz forum students ran the exercise for two weeks and their before/after clips are shown, which is a nice bit of accountability most technique-fix videos skip. A free companion PDF (fingerings + practice-routine suggestions) is referenced repeatedly but not capturable from the transcript — noted here for completeness, not extracted. Solid, concrete, and genuinely differentiated from BassBuzz's other beginner-routine videos already in the vault (see Routed to) by focusing on failure-mode diagnosis first, prep-drill second, exercise-level third — rather than leading with the exercise.

how-to-get-better-at-guitar-the-science-.title: How to Get Better at Guitar - The science of getting past a plateau
how-to-get-better-at-guitar-the-science-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons) steps back from a specific exercise or tune to make the research case for why plateaus happen at all and what to do about them — built almost entirely around direct quotes from Anders Ericsson's book Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise. The structural arc: why plateaus happen (challenge stops → progress stops, because the brain is wired to conserve effort once something reaches "good enough"), a doctor-performance study and a memory-athlete case study as evidence, then Jared's own distilled practice method — "repetition with manipulation" plus parameter-locked exercise design — as the guitar-specific application of the research. This is the theoretical/citation-backed companion to two notes already in the vault: Technique Is Part of the Path (The Red-Flag Repair Loop) (Jared's own "go to the exact spot" method, which this video supplies the Ericsson research grounding for) and Interleaved Practice, Chunking, and Deliberate-Practice Drills (Daniel Seriff's toolkit, which independently cites the same Peak source and the same "target the trouble spot directly" principle). Most valuable if you already buy the practice methods on those notes and want the actual research citations behind them, plus one genuinely new named technique: repetition with manipulation.

how-using-the-teleport-can-improve-your-.title: How using the TELEPORT can IMPROVE your PRACTICE routine!
how-using-the-teleport-can-improve-your-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A hybrid gear-review-plus-practice-routine video. Jack Ruch demos the Teleport, a new looper pedal from his friend Michael Palmazano that records tracks to jam along with and shares them via a companion app, then uses it as a springboard to walk through how he actually uses a looper in his own daily practice — not a deep feature-by-feature tutorial (he defers that to Michael's own channel), but a highlight of what he likes about this looper specifically and, more valuably, a full worked demonstration of his loop-based woodshedding routine. He picks an eighth-note-rock drum groove at 86 BPM, records a short part with the built-in drum machine and one-measure count-in for reference, then switches to a slower 128-ballad-feel groove and works through a longer, more harmonically involved progression — a Ray Charles-style gospel changes sequence — breaking it into small chunks (starting with E♭maj→G7→Cm, then a secondary ii–V into the ♭IV, B♭m7→E♭9→A♭7), looping each chunk, working out arpeggio-based lines against it out of time first and then in time, and gradually tying the chunks together into a full solo over the whole progression. The most valuable material isn't the pedal review itself but the transferable practice methodology: loop small, harmonically tricky chunks with a drum groove under them so phrasing gets tested against a real rhythmic/harmonic bed instead of played free, then expand outward once each piece is comfortable. He closes by naming what he likes best about the Teleport specifically (dedicated, no-latency record button; built-in drum machine; count-in) while noting he personally now mostly practices against DAW backing tracks day to day rather than a pedal looper.

bass-playing-position-setup-and-tuning-b.title: Bass Playing Position, Setup, and Tuning Basics
bass-playing-position-setup-and-tuning-b.html: BassBuzz's literal day-one fundamentals — getting plugged in with a usable sound, sitting/standing in a position that won't hurt you or fight your technique, and getting in tune — from the channel's actual "Lesson #1" video. Genuinely the floor everything else in 20 Music/Bass/ sits on top of: no prior note in this vault covered playing posture, bass/amp knob basics, or tuning fundamentals at all, despite the roadmap (The BassBuzz 55-Step Bass Learning Roadmap) having had empty "—" cells at exactly these steps (Level 0, steps 2–3; Level 1, step 5) since it was built. This note fills those cells. Not a tone-optimization or troubleshooting page — for that, see Bass Tone Chain Priority (which this note's gear-setup section defers to for the deeper version of Links 5 and 8).

how-grant-green-played-jazz-blues.title: How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues
how-grant-green-played-jazz-blues.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch transcribes and analyzes two Grant Green blues-solo excerpts — the opening chorus of "Miss Ann's Tempo" and the first chorus of his solo on "Number One Green Street," both swing/jazz blues in B♭ — to extract reusable jazz-blues vocabulary rather than just admire the playing. A second Jack Ruch video, Transcribing Licks And Making Them Your Own, revisits an overlapping stretch of the same two solos plus a third tune ("Blues for Willarine") with a methodology focus — how to rework a transcribed lick into your own, including a minor-third/half-step transposition device not covered here. This is a direct companion to The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues (same channel, same B♭ jazz-blues form, same 6-2-5-1 turnaround, and that video names Grant Green as one of its two headline jazz-blues players alongside Wes Montgomery) — where that video builds one worked line from scratch, this one reverse-engineers Green's actual recorded vocabulary over the identical harmonic terrain and finds the same core devices independently: hit the ♭9 over the VI7 chord for the altered/bebop color, and chromatically approach the tonic's chord tone to close the turnaround. The most valuable transferable idea isn't a single lick but the method stated at both the start and the end: learn a handful of these vocabulary phrases, and over time — through repetition and by tying fragments together in different combinations rather than replaying them verbatim — they blend into your own playing and start appearing on their own in improvisation. Ruch also states a concrete on-ramp for anyone newer to this: learn the arpeggios of the underlying chords first, and the licks in this video will turn up naturally inside those chord tones.

connecting-licks-into-longer-lines.title: Connecting Licks Into Longer Lines
connecting-licks-into-longer-lines.html:
Part of Bebop Vocabulary's vocabulary-acquisition material and a cousin of Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes's "lick-splicing across shapes" section — but where that page splices fragments of arpeggio shapes, this note is about splicing whole memorized licks/vocabulary phrases (transcribed from a real solo) into new combinations. Distinct from Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction, which reduces a transcribed solo to a named reusable concept; this method keeps the actual licks intact as raw material and focuses on the mechanics of gluing two or more of them together into one flowing line.

The setup: map each lick to a 2-5-1 role first

Before connecting anything, sort memorized licks by which chord function they work over: minor language → the ii chord, dominant language → the V chord, resolving/tag phrases → the I chord. This sorting step is a prerequisite, not optional — you can't usefully connect two licks until you know which chord each one belongs on. → The ii-V-I
secs: The setup: map each lick to a 2-5-1 role first

1-harmony-vocal-track.title: 1 Harmony Vocal Track
1-harmony-vocal-track.html:
Role: Harmony parts around the lead (3rds/5ths/6ths), pushed further back in the depth field. Harmonies carry pitch information, not tone — strip everything that isn't the note.

Chain philosophy: tune → tightest EQ of the stack → compress flat → de-ess → wide + wet.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Same setup as Main Vocal Track §1: Neumann TLM 102, ghost latency track.
  • Sung softer than the lead, same mic position as the lead session for fused timbre.

2 — Tracking Best Practice

  • Pan L/R pairs at ~35–42 L/R (Live's 0–50 scale) — just inside hard-panned doubles so layers don't stack on the same spot (no doubles in the section? harmonies can take the outside). Block harmonies come in fours (L/R per note), each note balanced to the chord.
  • Time-align to the lead, keep their own pitch — harmonies match timing (manually or VocAlign Ultra AU) but never pitch-match to the lead's notes.
  • 🎬 Blend later stack layers down in level for balance, rather than matching the first pair at full strength. After the first two stacks are level-matched and mono-checked while tracking (see 1 Double Vocal Track), a third/fourth note gets pulled down slightly — "this particular note is blended down just a little bit because [they] have to be balanced properly" — the level-matching discipline is for judging the blend honestly, not for the final print level of every layer — Kuk Harrell (Mix with the Masters), Creating vocal stacks with Kuk Harrell.
  • 🎬 Fifthy/medieval harmonies are a flavor — Khalid's "very fifthy, quite medieval-sounding" stacks; parallel fifths break the rules and sound modern — Disclosure, Making Beats + Talk.
  • 🎬 Consider more tune on harmonies than the main when the singer is reaching (Smino logic) — Kenny Beats, Auto-Tune Process.

3 — Source → Ableton (UAD Console)

Same console pass as Main Vocal Track §3, printed conservatively.

2-ensemble-stack-group.title: 2 Ensemble Stack Group
2-ensemble-stack-group.html:
Role: Sums a self-stacked vocal ensemble — however many layers you built — into one cohesive element, and holds the arrangement (which layer-roles are present) plus the glue, cohesion, shared space, and width treatments. The per-layer prep already locked pitch/time/level on Ensemble Stack Track; the group makes the layers read as one. Distinct from Main Vocal Group (which balances a lead against its layers) — here the stack is the instrument.

Two ways to run it (choose per song)

  • Fused ensemble (no lead) — every core layer level-matched so nothing wins; one shared space; tightest fusion. Bon Iver "Holocene", Imogen Heap, gospel self-stacks.
  • Lead + support stack — a front vocal with the other roles tucked underneath (doubles just under, octaves ~−8 to −12 dB, harmonies below the lead); the standard pop stack. Same building blocks either way — only the level relationship changes. Everything below applies to both.
secs: Two ways to run it (choose per song)

hand-clap-studio.title: Hand Clap Studio
hand-clap-studio.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Robotic Bean

What it is

Robotic Bean's dedicated hand-clap synthesis/sound-design instrument.

What it's used for

Building custom, layered hand-clap sounds for beats without relying on sampled claps.

FX chain notes

Used as a drum-voice instrument, typically feeding a drum bus alongside kick/snare.

Techniques

  • "Underneath claps" + the early clap — layered under the main clap for thickness, plus a dry clap placed slightly AHEAD of the beat in the step sequencer — Disclosure, Remix Stems Stream

Used in my chains

A realistic clap instrument (source, not an FX slot) — built from real hand-clap samples (4 clap types, 5 velocities, round-robins, ~700 samples). The magic is modeling many people clapping slightly out of sync:

  • Drums Snare-Clap Track — "underneath claps": layered under the main clap for thickness (Disclosure's move). Set Clappers to 4–8, a little Looseness for a human group feel, Spread for width, and Close-mic'd (dry) so it reinforces the main clap without adding space.

Key Parameters

image: Images/Hand Clap Studio.jpg
coords: Images/Hand Clap Studio.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique Artist / record example
