neapolitan-sixth.title: Neapolitan Sixth
neapolitan-sixth.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords / Altered Chords. The Neapolitan chord is a major triad built on the lowered 2nd scale degree. Despite the naming pattern of other altered-root chords (♭III, ♭VI), it isn't actually borrowed from the parallel minor — it's usable in both major and minor keys.

Why "sixth"

The chord is almost exclusively used in first inversion — root position is rare, second inversion rarer still. That's why it's called the Neapolitan 6th (N6), not "the Neapolitan sixth chord" (as if six modified "chord"). In the rare root-position case it's simply "the Neapolitan chord"; in the rare 2nd-inversion case it's the "Neapolitan six-four."

Function

  • Functions as a subdominant/pre-dominant chord despite being built on the supertonic (♭II) — it commonly resolves toward dominant-function harmony.
  • Common resolutions: to a dominant seventh in third inversion, or to a cadential 6/4 (Part-Writing).
  • Grouped with the predominant family alongside the other subdominant-function chords (ii, IV) rather than treated as its own category.

Origin

Named for "from Naples" — associated with the operas of Neapolitan composers like Alessandro Scarlatti, though the chord isn't actually native to Naples and was already common well before Scarlatti's time, in music far from Italy.

artificial-double-tracking-adt.title: Artificial Double Tracking (ADT)
artificial-double-tracking-adt.html:
What it is: a studio process that fakes a second take from a single performance — the signature Beatles/Lennon vocal-doubling sound. One vocal reads as two slightly-different voices without singing it twice.

The origin (log this)

  • Invented by Abbey Road engineer Ken Townsend in April 1966, expressly because John Lennon hated the tedium of manually double-tracking his vocals and asked for a shortcut. First used across Revolver, then on nearly every Lennon vocal (and many instruments) from 1966 on.
  • How the original worked: the recorded signal was tapped from one tape machine and fed to a second tape machine to delay it; the delay time was wavered by driving that machine's capstan with a variable-frequency (varispeed) oscillator, then the delayed copy was recombined with the original. Two machines → one wandering, slightly-detuned copy.
  • Lennon called it "Ken's flanger"; McCartney famously fobbed him off with a nonsense explanation about a "double-bifurcated sploshing flange" — which is where the word flanging comes from. ADT and flanging are cousins (both = signal + short modulated delay); flanging uses shorter delays + feedback for the jet-swoosh, ADT uses a slightly longer, subtler wander.

Why it works

  • A static short delay is just a slap/comb. The modulation (the varispeed wobble) is the whole trick — it makes the copy drift in time and pitch like a real second performance would, so the ear hears "two takes," not "one take + echo."
  • Typical feel: ~7–25 ms delay + a slow, shallow pitch/time wander (a few cents). Pan the copy opposite the dry for width, or keep it centered for thickness.

How to do it in the box (owned tools)

The modern equivalent is a micro-pitch/modulated-delay doubler — pick by flavor:

  • MicroShift / Little MicroShift — the cleanest modern ADT (Eventide H3000 micro-pitch): detuned + delayed L/R copies. Style I, Detune/Delay ~100%, Focus ~120 Hz, Mix 100% on a width return. Best for a wide, invisible double.
  • Doubler2 / Doubler4 — literally a modeled ADT: set Detune ~8–15 cents, Delay ~10–20 ms, Modulation (Rate/Depth) ON so the voices wander, Dry/Wet ~20–30%. This is the closest to the tape behavior.
  • Chorus-Ensemble / kHs Chorus — more audible modulation (a "wider" wander) when you want vintage motion, not an invisible double.
  • EchoBoy / kHs Delay — a single ~15 ms delay with wow/flutter or a modulated time for a mono ADT-thickening in one channel.
secs: How to do it in the box (owned tools)

drum-notation.title: Drum Notation
drum-notation.html:
Part of Music Theory and the percussion branch of Notation. How a drum kit is written down — the neutral clef, which staff position and notehead shape means which piece of the kit, the articulation marks that are the difference between four different snare sounds, and how a written bar maps onto a DAW grid.

The general symbol system (note values, rests, ties, dots, repeats, dynamics) is in Notation and Time Signatures & Note Values and is not repeated here. What follows is only what changes when the staff stops encoding pitch and starts encoding which drum.

1. The drum (neutral) clef

Drum parts use the percussion / neutral clef — two thick vertical bars (𝄥) — not treble or bass. It carries no pitch information at all. Its only job is to announce: the vertical axis on this staff is kit position, by convention, not frequency.

Consequences worth internalising:

  • There is no absolute standard. The layout below is the common modern convention (and the one the vault's cheat-sheet poster uses), but charts vary — a well-engraved part prints its own key at the top. Read the key before the notes.
  • Ledger lines above and below are in constant use — cymbals sit above the staff, the feet sit below it. Unlike pitched notation, that's normal here, not an extreme register.
  • The horizontal axis is unchanged: time, read left to right, in the printed meter.

bed-slot.title: BED Slot
bed-slot.html:
Warm sustained harmony; the emotional floor of the song. The biggest swap list in the palette — and the #1 source of mud when double-booked.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Synth bed/pad — Omnisphere bed recipe · Serum 2 bed recipe · Synth Bed Track chain
  • E-piano / Rhodes — Keyscape Rhodes LA Custom E / Classic Mark I (neo-soul, hip hop)
  • Wurlitzer — Keyscape 140B/200A (warmer/barkier flavor of the same object)
  • Juno pad — Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer (saw+sub → Chorus II; bedroom-pop/psych lane)
  • Organ — sustained harmony with more grit
  • Rhythm guitar (open/chorused) — the Bedroom Pop - Indie bed
  • Acoustic piano (sustained) — Acoustic Piano Track · Keyscape LA Custom C7
  • Drift/Wavetable stock pads — Drift Pad folder, Wavetable Pads

Mix rules

  • Sits behind the vocal: wide sides, soft center (M/S — high-shelf the sides, dip the mid; Pro-Q 4 per-band M/S).
  • HPF 120–150 Hz always — the warmth illusion lives at 250–500 Hz, not below.
  • One bed at a time; verse Rhodes → chorus pad is a swap, not a stack.
  • Movement beats level: slow filter/WT motion keeps a quiet bed interesting.

When it's the hook

Intros, breakdowns, and post-chorus moments where the vocal exits: open the bed's high end (+shelf 8 kHz), widen, let internal movement carry it. The Tame Impala pulse lane (Psych-Pop (Tame Impala)) is a bed-as-hook genre.

When it competes

  • vs Vocal (the classic 200–500 Hz mud): dynamic dip in the bed keyed by the vocal — Soothe2 external sidechain or Pro-Q 4 dynamic bands = automatic vocal pocket.
  • vs BASS (BASS Slot): HPF harder; if it still fights, the bed loses low-mids, not the bass.
  • vs MIDS/COMP (MIDS Slot): thin the bed's top (LP ~2 kHz) so comping/riffs own the articulation range.

plugin-wishlist.title: Plugin Wishlist
plugin-wishlist.html:
Gaps identified while building the FX Chain System — the collection (302 plugins) covers nearly everything; these are the few holes where a purchase would actually change results, ranked by impact. (Rule of thumb before buying anything: the Production System Report first-call table probably already covers the job.)

High impact (real workflow gaps)

  1. Melodyne (Studio or Editor) — the one genuine hole. Manual, note-level pitch/timing editing is the documented method for the natural lanes (Frank Ocean Vocal Chain, Finneas comping) and for fixing stack notes Auto-Tune can't isolate. Auto-Tune Pro is a style; Melodyne is surgery. → Used in: every vocal chain's prep step. Reinforced by an instrumental use-case, not just vocals: Melodyning a bounced-and-pitched-down sample to extract its own bass notes (found B♭–C–B♭–C–A♭) before writing a new bass part against it, pitching the whole sample up 2–3 semitones first when the extracted notes read too low — see Sampling and Sound Selection, PARTYNEXTDOOR Jazz Sample Chain — loner, how to make moody vintage r&b samples for partynextdoor (sounds like a real jazz sample)
  2. VocAlign (Synchro Arts, Standard is enough) — automatic time (+pitch in Pro) alignment of doubles/stacks to the lead. The research was unanimous that alignment beats all stack processing (Double Vocal Track); doing it by hand works but costs 20 min/song. → Used in: every hook stack.
  3. Youlean Loudness Meter 2 (FREE) — proper LUFS-I/short-term + true peak on the master. The Ozone Maximizer shows some of this; a dedicated meter is clearer. Zero-cost fix for Clipping and Loudness targets — just install it.

1-drums-snare-clap-track.title: 1 Drums Snare-Clap Track
1-drums-snare-clap-track.html:
Role: The backbeat. Snares/claps are the loudest transient in most modern mixes — crack + body + a tail that sets the mix's sense of space.

Chain philosophy: shape EQ → transient → color → level. Body-vs-crack balance first, dynamics after.

1 — Sound Selection

  • A snare that already crunches through raw needs almost no chain; a weak/airy one can't be EQ'd into hardness. Audition in XO against the beat's intent — hard trap = crunchy digital, boom bap = live/dusty — before reaching for a single plugin.
  • 🎬 No sample fits? Build the snare from scratch — Operator body oscillator (fixed frequency ~160–250 Hz + pitch envelope) + noise tail + texture layers (Shifter/Corpus/Grain Delay), grouped and saved as a reusable "snare starter" rack — see Snare Design for the full recipe — dnksaus, craft UNIQUE snares.
  • 🎬 Match transients across a loop — one snare with a bad transient/pop gets chopped and replaced so it matches the rest — Disclosure, Never Enough.
  • 🎬 Hand Clap Studio "underneath claps" — layered under the main clap for thickness (Clappers 4–8, a little Looseness for a human group, Close-mic'd/dry and fairly narrow so it reinforces without adding space) — Disclosure, Remix Stems Stream.

depth-and-space.title: Depth and Space
depth-and-space.html:
What it is: placing elements front-to-back (depth) and giving the record a coherent acoustic world (space). Width gets all the attention; depth is what makes a mix three-dimensional.

The four depth cues (how the ear judges distance)

  1. Level — closer = louder. The fader is a depth knob.
  2. High-frequency content — air absorbs highs; darker = further. LPF a repeat/element and it recedes ("your phone bouncing away down the street"). This is why returns are always filtered duller than their source.
  3. Transient sharpness — close sounds snap. Transient attack up = toward your face; down = backed off. A Transient Master is a depth knob that doesn't touch the fader.
  4. Wet/dry ratio + pre-delay — more reverb relative to dry = further away. Long pre-delay (20–40 ms) keeps a wet element close (big room, singer near you); zero pre-delay pushes it into the wall.

Building the depth field (this template)

  • Front: lead vocal, kick, snare — dry-ish, bright, transient-intact, slap delay rather than reverb.
  • Middle: guitars, keys, backups — room send, moderate filtering.
  • Back: pads, harmonies, textures — darker EQ, more send, softened transients.
  • One shared room (Reverb Send Room) = everyone in the same world; the long tail (Reverb Send Long) is the "big moment" space, ducked under the dry vocal so size never costs intelligibility.

Space discipline

  • Returns run 100% wet, band-limited (HPF 200–300, LPF 4–8 kHz) — space without spectral cost (Masking and Carving).
  • Delay before reverb (echoes then enter the room, like reality).
  • Low end gets no reverb, no widening, and lives in mono <100–120 Hz.
  • Contrast is the tool: a dry verse makes a wet chorus enormous. Automate sends per section instead of finding one static setting.
secs: The four depth cues (how the ear judges distance)

1-electric-bass-di-track.title: 1 Electric Bass DI Track
1-electric-bass-di-track.html:
Role: DI'd Hofner B-Bass H-Series — the low-end foundation. Current working chain, kept as the default with starting points.

Chain philosophy: cut-EQ → compress → tube color → broad tone → carve-EQ. EQ on both sides of the dynamics/color block — cut before so the comp doesn't chase rumble, carve after so the kick relationship is set on the finished tone.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Bass: Hofner B-Bass H-Series, DI into the Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII Hi-Z — no amp needed. With flatwounds this IS the Dahi lane: "flatwounds just got a tone — sounds old school but got pocket," tracked straight in with nothing on it. Trust the dry take — SZA "Used" breakdown.
  • Playing technique is the tone:
  • Modern hip hop thick bass: bass pickup solo'd, play lightly with the thumb above the neck pickup — the Hofner goes lower/thicker than a Fender; a legit 808-alternative.
  • Beatles palm-mute: the classic "Hofner sound" is really palm muting — short thumpy notes, tone rolled down.
  • 🎬 From video: the same "technique over gear" diagnosis from the tracking-engineer side of the glass: a boomy bass sound is almost always the bass/player's tone, not a mic-placement or processing problem — "most good bass players get a good tight sound," and a boomy one doesn't get fixed by leaning on a compressor ("the Summit doesn't help that much in controlling it"). Applies just as much to a DI signal as a mic'd one: if the DI reads boomy, check the instrument/technique before reaching for more EQ/comp. → Sound Selection Guide — Al Schmitt (Mix with the Masters), Recording techniques with Al Schmitt
  • 🎬 From video: a blind-test teardown of the full bass tone chain rated fingers/plucking-hand technique as the single most important link — ahead of every piece of gear, including strings, pickups, and amp: push with the pad of the finger (not near the nail) for a strong tone, dig in for growl vs. wispy/light plucking for a weak thin tone, and always fix technique first when a tone problem shows up before reaching for gear. Full ranked chain: Bass Tone Chain Priority. → BassBuzz, How to Fix Your Sh*tty Bass Tone
  • Levels: peaks −12 dBFS, ~−18 average — bass has the widest level swings of any DI source (Gain Staging).

how-i-approach-practicing.title: How I Approach Practicing
how-i-approach-practicing.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch lays out his current practice philosophy: learning a solo by ear is necessary but not sufficient — real growth comes from getting "under the hood" and analyzing why the vocabulary works over the harmony, then reducing each idea to a reusable "concept" that becomes a template for your own lines. He demonstrates the whole method on a real transcription — a bluesy jazz solo over Delilah, an AABA tune in F♯ minor originally recorded by Clifford Brown and Max Roach. He breaks the solo into chunks, names the harmonic concept behind each chunk (a blues phrase, a relative-major arpeggio, an upper-structure diminished arpeggio, several melodic-minor-family substitutions), then plays two full passes of his own solo over the same changes using those concepts rather than the original licks — proving the point that a concept, not a memorized lick, is the actual payoff of transcription. The most valuable part of the video isn't any single scale choice but the repeatable process: transcribe → chunk → analyze against the chord → name the concept → template a new solo from the concept set. Full extraction of that process is on Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction; the tune-specific chord-by-chord concept map is on the Delilah song note.

ghost-notes-slap-bass.title: Ghost Notes (Slap Bass)
ghost-notes-slap-bass.html:
BassBuzz's level-3 addition to the 5-level slap exercise (see Slap Bass 5-Level Daily Drill): muted, unfretted slaps and pops used deliberately, both for percussive texture and — the more important argument in the video — as a rhythmic anchor that helps the rest of the line stay locked in time.

What a ghost note is, mechanically

A ghost note is a muted slap or pop — the fretting hand covers the string(s) being struck without fretting an actual note, so the strike produces a percussive "thwacky" sound instead of a pitch. Marked as X in tab/notation. The strike itself is the exact same physical motion as an un-muted slap that misses its mute — the only difference from a mistake is that it's now deliberate and placed on purpose.

Why it matters beyond texture: a rhythmic anchor

The video's real case for ghost notes isn't just "it sounds cool" — it's timekeeping. The analogy given: it's easier to stay locked to a metronome that clicks frequently than one with big gaps between clicks. Ghost notes work the same way for a slap line — keeping the thumb moving in a semi-regular pulse (even on strikes that don't sound a pitch) gives the ear and the hand a denser rhythmic grid to lock against than sparse "real" notes alone would provide.

  • Not a rule to always fill every gap — sometimes a real musical phrase needs the space, and the video is explicit that you shouldn't ghost mechanically over every rest.
  • But even pros lean on it as a default habit. Reference example: Marcus Miller ("one of the ancient Greek gods of slap") — watch his thumb on a groove and it's bouncing on almost every eighth note in the bar, whether or not each strike sounds a pitch. He doesn't need the crutch to play with good rhythm, but organizes lines so the thumb keeps moving anyway. BassBuzz's own framing, from 20 years of playing: keeping the thumb ghosting away like that "just feels good."

Practicing it

  • BassBuzz's exercise pattern for level 3 layers ghost notes onto the level-1/level-2 slap-and-pop pattern, marked as X in the tab — play the slap/pop motion exactly as normal but with the fretting hand covering the string instead of fretting a note, so no pitch sounds.
  • Same underlying mechanical skill as covering unplayed strings for muting (see Slap Thumb Technique — Angle, Anchoring, and Muting) — a ghost note is that same "cover the string with the fretting hand" motion, just applied to the string being struck instead of to the neighboring strings.
secs: What a ghost note is, mechanically
Why it matters beyond texture: a rhythmic anchor

using-space-and-pauses-in-phrasing.title: Using Space and Pauses in Phrasing
using-space-and-pauses-in-phrasing.html: Part of Music Theory — a companion to Singing Along With Your Playing (Phrasing) (a different training method aimed at the same four-element phrasing target), Phrasing Blueprints (a close cousin: also a fixed-rhythm/free-pitch phrase drill from the same channel, but built around letter-form repetition — A A' B, A A A B, etc. — rather than rests), Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch (note-choice/touch vocabulary within a phrase), and Solo Dynamics and Arc (the macro shape of a whole solo). This note is Jared's "phrasing exercise #1" from the same "Nail the Changes" course — a specific, leveled drill for building rests/space into an improvised line by controlling only rhythm, with note choice left completely free.

pentatonic-scale-harmonized-in-thirds.title: Pentatonic Scale Harmonized in Thirds
pentatonic-scale-harmonized-in-thirds.html: Stack the pentatonic scale's own notes in 3rds (skip one scale tone, not one chromatic note) instead of pulling chords from the full parent major scale, and cycle the resulting shape through every degree of the scale to get a full set of usable, pentatonic-flavored chord voicings and arpeggio patterns from a single physical grip. This is the tertian (3rds) counterpart to Quartal Chord Voicings's stacked-4ths pentatonic harmonization — that page names "harmonizing pentatonic scales instead of the full major/melodic-minor scale" as an extension flagged for later; this note is that extension, worked in 3rds rather than 4ths. Because the pentatonic scale skips the 4th and 7th degrees, stacking "thirds" within it doesn't produce plain triads the way harmonizing a full major scale does — some of the resulting intervals land wider than a diatonic 3rd, which is exactly what gives the shapes their open, non-tertian-sounding character even though the construction method is nominally tertian.

never-ending-scale-exercise.title: Never-Ending Scale Exercise
never-ending-scale-exercise.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Jazz Harmony — Kurt Rosenwinkel's own stated practice method (relayed by Jens Larsen from master classes he attended as a student), for building the skill of a melodic idea that survives a chord change instead of resetting direction at every barline. Adjacent to, but distinct from, Continuous Scale Exercise (Jared Borkowski's drill for tunes that change keys often): that exercise trains finding the physically closest correct note the instant the harmony changes and moving by step only; this one deliberately decouples the scale-change moment from the actual chord-change moment — you keep a line going as if the progression were static, then swap scale on your own schedule (roughly every 8 notes), not the harmony's. The goal in both cases is melodic freedom across changes, but Rosenwinkel's version trains pre-planning ahead of the harmony rather than reacting instantly to it.

Transcript note: the source captions render Rosenwinkel's name for this as "the never-ending scale of cosines" — almost certainly a mishearing/mistranscription of the actual term (possibly "concepts"). Kept here verbatim as heard rather than guessed at; the mechanics below are unambiguous regardless of the exact name.

The core idea

Take a chord progression and keep a scale (or other harmonic unit) running continuously as if the progression were static/"in time" — i.e. don't stop and re-derive the correct scale/arpeggio the instant a new chord arrives. Instead:

  1. Play roughly eight notes through the harmony (Rosenwinkel's worked example: a turnaround with altered dominants), thinking of the line as a continuous run rather than one scale-choice-per-chord.
  2. Change scale whenever you've played about eight notes — on your own note-count schedule, not necessarily synced to the actual chord boundary. The chord may already have changed underneath you by the time you swap; that's the point.
  3. The practice target is thinking ahead — pre-planning the next scale/unit before you need it, and keeping the melodic movement going, rather than stopping to solve "what's the right scale for this chord" reactively at each change.

the-key-to-understanding-a-jazz-blues.title: The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues
the-key-to-understanding-a-jazz-blues.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch's short, focused lesson on the single chord sequence that separates a jazz blues from a plain 1-4-5 blues: the 1-6-2-5 turnaround that replaces (or gets inserted into) the tonic bars of a standard 12-bar form. Rather than teaching the whole form at once, Ruch isolates just the 1-6-2-5 section, builds one worked melodic line over it phrase by phrase (chord by chord, explaining the reasoning behind every note choice), and then drops that line into a full 12-bar solo over a B♭ blues so it's heard in context. The teaching approach itself is the most reusable thing here as much as the specific line: isolate the hard four-bar section of a longer form, build vocabulary over just that, then reintegrate. Harmonically the video is a compact, concrete worked example of ideas the vault's Theory strand already has pages for — the VI7 turnaround, diatonic I→iii substitution, and guide-tone/chord-tone targeting — which is why most of this enrichment lands as sourced examples on those existing notes rather than as new pages.

modulation.title: Modulation
modulation.html:
Effect-sense modulation — chorus / flanger / phaser / rotary. For changing key see Modulation (Key Change) in 20 Music/Theory/.

General best practice for chorus / flanger / phaser / rotary and stereo movement. Specific tools: Chorus-Ensemble, TAL-Chorus-LX, kHs Flanger, kHs Phaser. See also Width and Stereo, Delay.

What it is

Time/pitch-varying effects that widen, thicken, and animate — from subtle stereo detune to full rotary swirl.

Owned (first-call)

Chorus-Ensemble (Ableton, "Logic chorus"-style width) · TAL-Chorus-LX · kHs Chorus · kHs Flanger · kHs Phaser · Spectral Resonator (Ableton, MIDI-drivable resonant/vocoder-like texture)

georgia-on-my-mind-fingerstyle-guitar-tu.title: Georgia on My Mind Fingerstyle Guitar Tutorial (With Sheet Music & Tab)
georgia-on-my-mind-fingerstyle-guitar-tu.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) walks measure-by-measure through his own solo fingerstyle arrangement of "Georgia on My Mind," transposed to the key of C, teaching it "as if we're sitting in a room together" — notation/tab call-outs plus fretboard-level fingering commentary. It's a from-scratch chord-melody arrangement (melody on top, harmony and a moving bass filled in underneath, one guitarist covering all three parts), and Jared repeatedly narrates the why behind each choice, not just the what: which finger to leave up so it's free for the next reach, when to sacrifice a harmony note versus the melody, how to mute a bass note cleanly, how to shift position smoothly without an audible bump. He explicitly withholds the chord symbols from the printed sheet music ("it would just muck up the sheet music too much") and instead points listeners to a companion video — "Georgia on My Mind Chords (Guitar Lesson)" (same channel) — to learn the harmony on its own first. The tune's own origin story as his arrangement is folded in at the end: he transposed it to C, learned the chords, sang the melody over them, and the fingerstyle arrangement "came to life on its own" from that process — offered as a general song-internalization strategy, not just a one-off anecdote. Free sheet music/tab is available via his site (not fetched here — external resource). No production/mixing content — pure solo-guitar arranging and execution technique.

shortcut-to-reading-sheet-music-for-guit.title: Shortcut to Reading Sheet Music for Guitar - Read Guitar Lead Sheets
shortcut-to-reading-sheet-music-for-guit.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borkowski (soundguitarlessons.com) answers a student's question — "what's a good way to start reading jazz lead sheets out of the real book?" — with one specific, unconventional shortcut he built for himself: pick exactly one fretboard spot per written pitch, in one register, and drill until the mapping is automatic. The framing is a direct comparison to piano: a pianist has exactly one key per written pitch, so sight-reading pitch recognition is a solved problem before you even touch rhythm; a guitarist has that same pitch playable in four to six different places, and that — not note-naming — is the actual source of guitar reading's reputation for being uniquely hard. Rather than teaching a full position system top to bottom (the conventional method-book approach, which he says can take years to reach the point of reading fluently around the whole neck), he deliberately narrows the problem: freeze one location per note in a single working register, ignore rhythm completely at first, and just drill "jump to the note" against real lead-sheet melodies (he demos on Pat Metheny's "Bright Size Life," a second unnamed tune, and "What a Wonderful World"). This is a companion piece to Reading Notation on Guitar rather than a replacement for the position system taught there — it's a specific training method for building fluency once (or instead of) working through the full CAGED/position map, and it's aimed squarely at "I know some theory, I want to start actually reading real book melodies" rather than at beginners.

roland-tr-808.title: Roland TR-808
roland-tr-808.html:
What it is

Roland's TR-808 Rhythm Composer is the most influential drum machine ever made — a fully analog, 16-step programmable box that flopped commercially (~12,000 units, discontinued after three years) because it sounded nothing like real drums, then conquered the world precisely because it sounded nothing like real drums. It is the sonic foundation of hip hop, trap, electro, Miami bass, and half of modern pop's low end.

What makes the sound

  • Every voice is an analog circuit, not a sample — bridged-T oscillators, filtered noise, and VCAs, which is why 808 sounds are so tweakable and so clean at the bottom.
  • The kick is a self-oscillating bridged-T resonant circuit: a trigger pings the filter, which rings down as a decaying sine. Long decay + high resonance = a pitched sub bass note, not a drum hit — the entire "808 bass" concept (the SUB Slot as an instrument) comes from this one circuit. Tune it and it's your bassline → Kick Design.
  • Snare = two bridged-T oscillators (~180/330 Hz "snappy" body) + filtered white noise; claves/cowbell = square-wave oscillators through band-passes (the cowbell's two detuned squares are why it's so iconic); hats/cymbal = six detuned square oscillators mixed and band-passed — metallic but obviously synthetic.
  • Character comes from imperfection: Roland used out-of-spec, noisy 2SC828 transistors for the sizzle; when supplies ran out, the 808 couldn't be built the same way again.
  • Accent + per-voice decay/tone knobs made it performable — long-decay kick + snappy snare + tick hats is a mix that arrives pre-carved.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Kick 3 (synthesize/tune 808-style kicks per key), Serum 2 (808 recipe — see Sound Palette), Operator (sine + pitch-envelope 808 from scratch), Analog, Microtonic (analog-style drum synthesis), Drum Rack/Impulse for the thousand free 808 sample packs, Ramzoid 808 Cooker for saturating/tuning 808 samples into modern trap weight.
  • Paid: Roland Cloud TR-808 (official ACB model), D16 Nepheton 2, Softube Heartbeat, 808 Studio / 808 Studio 2 (deep parametric 808-synthesis plugin — many independent envelope parameters per voice, favored specifically over the "find a sample, pitch it" workflow, see Plugin Wishlist); Behringer RD-8 in hardware.
  • Free: sample packs everywhere (the 808 is the most-sampled instrument on earth); AudioThing things aside, honestly samples + Ramzoid 808 Cooker cover the modern use case.

sound-selection-guide.title: Sound Selection Guide
sound-selection-guide.html:
