delay.title: Delay
delay.html:
General best practice for delay — throws, movement, and using echoes as arrangement. Specific tools: EchoBoy, Echo (Ableton), the delay sends. See also Reverb, Depth and Space.

What it is

Repeats — for depth, rhythmic interest, width, and dramatic tape/feedback throws.

Owned (first-call)

EchoBoy · Echo (Ableton) · Delay (Ableton, basic stock delay) · Grain Delay (Ableton, granular) · Spectral Time (Ableton, frequency-bin spectral delay) · Note Echo · ValhallaDelay

house-edm.title: House - EDM
house-edm.html: What makes it the genre: the groove engine — four-on-floor kick as the clock, everything breathing around it via sidechain, arrangement as energy management (build → drop → breakdown), and sound design carrying the identity a lyric would carry elsewhere.

hip-hop-trap.title: Hip Hop - Trap
hip-hop-trap.html: What makes it the genre: the low end IS the song — 808 + kick carry melody and groove simultaneously; everything else is negative space. Halftime feel (~130–160 BPM, snare on 3), hats as a lead instrument, hard-tuned vocal as texture, dry and upfront presentation (space comes from throws, not reverb).

2-drums-group.title: 2 Drums Group
2-drums-group.html:
Role: The kit summed (kick, snare, hats group, percussion). This is your current working drums chain (Step 1 Drums export), kept as the default — it's a solid EQ → comp → saturate → transient structure.

Source note — all drums come from packs/loops (no live kit): XO to browse/audition one-shots by similarity, Drum Rack/Simpler to play them, Serato Sample for chops. That means: (1) sound selection replaces mic technique as "Step 1 — Record" — swap samples before reaching for plugins; (2) samples arrive pre-processed, so track chains stay light; (3) full loops: split stems or slice into the Drum Rack when possible so kick/snare/hats can hit their own chains — an unsplit loop gets treated on this group directly (RC-20 Retro Color texture + the chain below).

Chain overview

Corrective EQ → kit compression → color → punch restore. The Transient Master at the end is the clever part of your chain: it restores the attack that compression and saturation soften.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Kit balance

  • Broad moves on the summed kit: low-mid mud cut 250–400 Hz · any whole-kit tilt
  • Per-drum EQ already happened on tracks — this is about the kit as one instrument.

2. Pro-C 2 — Kit compression

  • Punch style · 4:1 · attack 20–30 ms (transients pass) · release 100–150 ms or auto — time it to "breathe" with the tempo · 2–3 dB GR
  • Why: Compressing the kit together is what makes separate samples sound like a band's drummer — they start moving each other's levels, which reads as cohesion.

3. Saturn 2 — Kit color

  • Tape, single band or gentle multiband · low drive
  • Why: Rounds the digital edges of the whole kit uniformly — shared harmonics are shared identity.

4. Transient Master — Punch restore

  • Attack +5–15%
  • Why: Both previous stages shave transients slightly; adding attack back after them gives you compression's glue AND the punch — order is the trick.

Variations

  • Harder hip hop: raise Pro-C 2 GR to 3–4 dB and lean on Parallel Comp Send blended under for size.
  • Live-feel/Beatles: swap Saturn for Kramer Tape pushed harder, slow the Pro-C release, let it pump musically.

harmonic-ear-training.title: Harmonic Ear Training
harmonic-ear-training.html:
Part of Music Theory → Intervals. The harmonic counterpart to Scale Degree Ear Training — where that note trains hearing sequential, tonally-contextualized notes (scale degrees relative to a tonic), this one trains hearing simultaneous notes: pulling one note out of a chord, or separating two-or-more notes sounding at once. Jared (Sound Guitar Lessons) draws the line explicitly: harmonic ear training = identifying a specific sound among many happening at once; melodic ear training = hearing the structure/distance of single notes happening one after another. Both matter and are trained differently.

Why guitar specifically underdevelops this

Guitar's frets let you find/verify any note by looking at your hand instead of listening for it — you tune once, then navigate by sight for the rest of the session. Fretless/bowed string players (violin, cello, upright bass) have no such shortcut: from the first lesson, every note has to be intonated by ear, so the skill is forced rather than optional. This is a structural fact about the instrument, not a talent gap — a guitarist who also plays a fretless instrument (or switches to one) typically reports a sudden, forced jump in harmonic-ear ability, because for the first time listening isn't optional. — Jared, Important Ear Training Exercise for Guitarists (we need this!)

texture-slot.title: TEXTURE Slot
texture-slot.html:
Ambience, era, "air in the room." Glue, not content — the listener should feel it leave, not hear it play.

Swap list (interchangeable occupants)

  • Vinyl/tape noise — RC-20 Retro Color noise module (ducked = reads as real media)
  • Real tape/cassette hiss — print through Sony TC-630 (hardware) or Cassette (Wavesfactory, its Static/Dynamic noise controls) for a genuinely captured noise floor rather than a synthesized one
  • Granular atmosphere — Omnisphere texture recipe
  • Room tone / field recordings — rain, street, crowd, amp hum
  • Reverb bed — a 100%-wet long tail (ValhallaSupermassive) fed quietly by the bed
  • Foley loops — vinyl run-out, tape start/stop, breath

Mix rules

  • Level: –18 to –25 dB under the mix — the mute test is the level test (mute it: the mix should feel smaller, not quieter).
  • One texture per song usually; per section at most.
  • Full-band but not full-time: drop it in choruses so they open, return it in verses (texture = intimacy).
  • Mono is fine — often better (a wide texture eats the bed's width contrast).

When it's the hook

Intros/outros/transitions: the texture exposed (vinyl crackle alone before the beat drops) is a classic hook moment — the one time it comes up in level. Also the Bedroom Pop - Indie "one wrong sound per song" candidate.

When it competes

  • It shouldn't be loud enough to compete. If it masks anything, it's 6+ dB too hot.
  • vs AIR (AIR Slot): crackle brightness vs hats — LP the texture ~8 kHz.
  • Cumulative mud: HPF textures ~100 Hz like everything else (SUB Slot stays clean).

Overlay across all slots. Index: Sound Palette.

multiband-dynamics.title: Multiband Dynamics
multiband-dynamics.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock three-band compressor/expander, splitting the signal into low/mid/high bands with independent upward and downward compression per band, plus a soft-clip stage.

What it's used for

Frequency-specific dynamic control — gluing a busy sound source together, taming one band without touching the others, or (via its factory presets) a gentler multiband glue alternative to a full up-and-down unit like OTT.

FX chain notes

Placed at the end of a texture/instrument chain as a glue stage, or on a bus where one frequency band needs independent control from the rest.

1-drums-kick-track.title: 1 Drums Kick Track
1-drums-kick-track.html:
Role: The kick — anchor of the groove. Sample selection is 80% of the job; the chain sharpens what the sample already is.

Chain philosophy: EQ → transient → comp → clip. Transient shaping before compression (shape the hit, then level it); clipper last to shave the peak for loudness.

1 — Sound Selection

  • Selection IS the recording step — audition in XO until it knocks raw. If the kick needs heavy processing to hit, swap the sample: pick crunchy, don't manufacture crunch.
  • 🎬 Or synthesize it — Disclosure build kicks from a kick-synth (Ultrabeat / BigKick / Kick 2) and tune the fundamental to the song key — full method in Kick Design — Latch / Waterfall.
  • 🎬 The "all-knock" kick — energy ~100 Hz, "nothing at 50 Hz" (old UK garage) — for when a bendy sub or 808 already owns the SUB Slot and the kick only needs to knock through the BASS Slot — Disclosure, NO CAP.
  • 🎬 LinnDrum click layered low on a dead kick — "use it for the click, not very loud" — attack layer only — Disclosure, Making Beats + Talk.
  • 🎬 Or skip the kick entirely — modern trap often runs an 808 with enough front-end attack alone; audition a harder 808 before adding kick + duck — Kenny Beats, 808 & Kick.
  • 🎬 A live-tracking-stage version of "layer two": a physically distinct 28" marching band bass drum set up in front of the main kit kick and damped with blankets over the top, for character — mic'd with an NS10 monitor driver (reversed as a mic) + D12 on the front head for the tonal split, then a subtle sample layer blended in on top via a Logic drum-replacement plugin ("Trigger" per the transcript, name uncertain — Plugin Wishlist). Full mic/damping detail on Drum Mic Technique. → Drum Mic Technique, Kick Design, Layering and Stacking — Mix with the Masters (Paul Epworth), Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"

glue-compressor.title: Glue Compressor
glue-compressor.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's bus-style compressor modeled on classic VCA console/SSL-bus compressor behavior, with a program-dependent auto-release and a Range control for makeup gain limiting.

What it's used for

Bus and master glue compression — pulling a drum bus, mix bus, or group together with a cohesive, musical compression character.

FX chain notes

Sits at the end of a group/bus chain (drum bus, mix bus) after individual track processing, usually with light gain reduction (1-3 dB) for cohesion.

Used in my chains

My default group/bus glue — slot 2 on almost every group, and the stereo glue on the master. Pattern: 2:1 + 30 ms + Auto release + ~1.5 dB GR for gentle "move as one section" glue; 4:1 and firmer when a bus can take real compression.

  • Master Chain — slot 3, the glue: 2:1, Attack 30 ms, Auto, 1.5 dB GR on the beat, Soft Clip OFF. The SSL-bus move that makes buses sound like a record.
  • Bass Bus — 2:1, Attack 30 ms, Release 0.2 s, ~1.5 dB GR — glues bass sources without squashing sub/transient.
  • Guitar Group / Inst-Synth Group — 2:1, 30 ms, Auto, ~1.5 dB GR — section moves as one, pick/note attack intact.
  • Drums Hats Group — 2:1, Attack 1 ms (no transient to protect), ~1.5 dB GR — hat + shaker + perc breathe as one.
  • Backup Vocals Group — firmer 4:1, Attack 20 ms, ~3 dB GR — fuses multiple backing takes into one block.
  • FX Bus — 4:1, Attack 10 ms, ~2.5 dB GR — keeps unpredictable FX throws civilized.

kickstart-2.title: Kickstart 2
kickstart-2.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Nicky Romero

What it is

A sidechain-pumping plugin by Nicky Romero/Cableguys that applies rhythmic volume ducking synced to the host tempo, simulating classic sidechain compression pumping.

What it's used for

Classic EDM/house sidechain 'pump' effect on pads, bass, and synths without routing an actual sidechain compressor.

FX chain notes

Inserted directly on the track to be pumped — no sidechain routing required, since the ducking pattern is drawn/tempo-synced internally.

delay-send-other.title: Delay Send Other
delay-send-other.html:
Role: The rhythmic/synced delay — dotted-8th and quarter-note repeats, ping-pong, ad-lib throws. Where slap adds size, this adds motion and energy (synced repeats push the groove; reverb just smears it).

Signal chain

1. EchoBoy — Synced repeats

  • Echo Type: Ping-Pong (①/⑧ — bounces L↔R) · Time: dotted 1/8 (③ — the pop/U2 default; 1/4 for a slower throw) · Feedback 22% (④ — 2–4 audible repeats) · Style: analog/tape character on (② · ⑨) · Low Cut 200 Hz / High Cut 8 kHz on the feedback (⑥ — repeats sit behind the dry) · Mix 100% (⑦ — it's a return)
  • Why dotted-8th: it lands off the main beats, so repeats fill the pockets between the vocal phrases instead of stacking on them.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter

  • HPF 300–500 Hz · LPF 4–6 kHz — repeats always duller than the source.

3. Pro-C 2 — Duck (sidechain from dry vocal)

  • 2–3 dB GR keyed from the lead · medium release
  • Simpler alt: Ableton's stock Echo has built-in ducking (one knob + threshold) — use it when this return runs Echo instead of EchoBoy.
  • Why: Repeats hide while the line is sung and answer in the gaps — you can run a hot send level and never lose a lyric. Same trick as the long reverb.

1-synth-bed-track.title: 1 Synth Bed Track
1-synth-bed-track.html:
Role: Pads, beds, atmosphere — the glue layer the listener feels but never notices. The whole chain is about making room: a pad fills space until something more important needs it.

Chain philosophy: aggressive framing → even the wash → width/level → duck.

lfo-tool.title: LFO Tool
lfo-tool.html:
Category: Volume/Filter LFO Shaper Vendor: Xfer Records

What it is

Xfer's LFO-driven volume/filter/pan shaper — draw a custom curve and it modulates the signal in sync with the tempo. The standard tool for rhythmic sidechain ducking without a compressor, and Ian Kirkpatrick's self-described favorite plugin. (Ableton equivalents exist via a shaped envelope / the stock LFO on a Utility, but LFO Tool's drawn curves are the workflow.)

What it's used for

Pumping/ducking, rhythmic gating, and creative volume shaping — from a subtle groove duck to chopping a vocal into slivers.

2-inst-synth-group.title: 2 Inst-Synth Group
2-inst-synth-group.html:
Role: All keys + synths summed — the harmonic middle of the record. This group's enemy is cumulative low-mid buildup: every keyboard part adds 200–500 Hz, and together they swamp a mix that soloed fine.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Sum carve

  • Cut the summed low-mids 200–400 Hz −1 to −3 dB (the buildup only exists on the sum — this can't be done on tracks)
  • Collision-detection workflow (Pro-Q's killer diagnostic): put a Pro-Q on the vocal bus, another here; on this one, set the analyzer's sidechain to the vocal-bus instance — the display highlights the exact colliding frequencies in red while both play. Cut the red zones here (music yields to vocal), by ear, until the vocal opens up. No more guessing where the masking is.
  • Broad dip in the vocal presence zone if the section still masks the singer
  • Alt (often better): Soothe2 sidechained from the lead vocal (soft mode, mid-channel, pre-emphasis in the vocal's range) — clears the vocal's lane dynamically and exactly, the modern unmasking move for dense synth beds vs vocals
  • 🎬 From video: a more surgical alternative to the Soothe2 route above — build multiple bands on this group centered on the exact frequencies colliding with the vocal, set each Dynamic, and point each band's external sidechain at the vocal so the threshold measures the vocal's level instead of this group's own; only those targeted frequencies duck, and only while the vocal is actually singing. Push further with per-band Stereo Placement — one dynamic band ducking the mid image, another the side image — combining the frequency-specific duck with a stereo-imaging decision in the same move — Sage Audio, EQ Masterclass
  • Why: Step 4 of your process at its purest — EQ decisions that only make sense against the other groups.

2. Glue Compressor — Section glue

  • Ratio 2:1 (②) · Attack 30 ms (③) · Release Auto (④) · Threshold for ~1.5 dB GR (①) · Makeup to unity (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦) — the section moves as one.
  • Why: Same gentle section glue as the other groups — enough to fuse keys + pads + synths into one layer, light enough that no single part's dynamics get flattened.

1-acoustic-piano-track.title: 1 Acoustic Piano Track
1-acoustic-piano-track.html:
Role: Piano VST — usually a supporting harmonic instrument that must not fight the vocal (piano covers the entire spectrum, so it's the #1 masking offender).

Chain philosophy: carve → even → sweeten → width check.

1 — Sound Selection

  • Keyscape — the default. LA Custom C7 flagship grand (pop/ballad centerpiece), Wing Upright/Wing Tack for character/vintage, duo patches for hybrid color. In-patch: internal reverb OFF (space comes from sends), velocity curve to taste. → Keyscape — LA Custom C7 Grand / Keyscape — Wing Upright & Tack Piano
  • Kontakt 7 libraries for felt/intimate or cinematic flavors.
  • Nexus for instant pop "stacked piano" (already produced — bypass most of the chain below). → Nexus — Stacked Pop Piano
  • Rule: choose the patch that already IS the sound — patch-switching beats EQ-rescuing. 🎬 Pre-highlight favorites before a writing session (Disclosure star their D-50 patches ahead of time — "less messing about") — Making Beats + Talk → Sound Palette.

2 — Programming Best Practice

  • Play at performance energy, commit to audio when dialed (FX Chain System bounce-in-place — Disclosure record synths/keys in as audio: "the MIDI isn't the sound").
  • Cut the low junk from the part itself: if the left hand doubles the bassline's register, thin the voicing — arrangement beats EQ (Masking and Carving).
  • HPF discipline applies to keys too — sub-100 Hz belongs to kick/808; the piano's low octave stays only when piano is the star — Kenny Beats, 808 & Kick.

3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

The "recorded through a console" pass that keeps software instruments on the same footing as recorded ones — printed when dialed:

1. UAD Neve 1073 — Preamp plugin — barely driven, ~0 VU

2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A (Silver) — 1–2 dB gentle leveling

3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — +1 @ 12 kHz air max

parallel-comp-send.title: Parallel Comp Send
parallel-comp-send.html:
Role: The "New York" crush bus — a destroyed copy of the drums blended under the clean ones. Adds weight, sustain, and room excitement while the dry signal keeps all its transients. Parallel = you can crush without consequences.

Theory: serial compression trades transients for control. Parallel compression sidesteps the trade: the dry path keeps the punch, the crushed path brings up all the quiet detail (ghost notes, room, decay), and you mix in just enough of the wreckage.

Signal chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Pre-EQ (the "NY" part, optional)

  • Smiley: +2–3 dB lows (~100 Hz) and highs (~8 kHz) before the comp
  • Why: The compressor slams the boosted extremes hardest, exaggerating the thick-bottom/crispy-top character of the classic NYC drum sound.

2. UAD UA 1176LN — The crush

  • All-buttons-in mode (push all 4 ratio buttons) · attack FAST (7) · release FAST (7) · input cranked for 10–20 dB GR — pin the needle, it cannot be too much here
  • Why all-buttons: the ratio goes nonlinear and program-dependent, adding explosive harmonic excitement — famous on drum busses for 50 years. The fast release creates the pumping that drags up room sound and sustain.
  • Alt flavors: Devil-Loc Deluxe (even more destroyed) · FETish (same 1176 trick, native).
  • 🎬 From video: on a film/game percussion stem, this exact fast-1176-into-EQ shape gets reused lighter — a Chris Lord-Alge-style 1176 blended (not slammed) with a Pultec-style EQ pushing top end, aimed at "snap" rather than NYC-style crush; framed as necessary because media delivery is separate stems, not one locked mix, so the whole stem gets parallel-compressed as a unit instead of the finished mix Andrew Scheps-style. → UAD Pultec EQP-1A, Parallel Processing, TRANSIENT Slot — Mix with the Masters (Alan Meyerson), Adding impact to percussions with Alan Meyerson

3. Pro-Q 4 — Post-tame (optional)

  • HPF 40 Hz · shave any harsh 3–5 kHz the crush created.
  • 🎬 From video: an alternate top-end stage in this same slot — Pultec-style EQ pushing "top end" for snap, positioned as an addition to the crush rather than a tame — worth trying instead of/alongside the HPF+shave move above when the goal is more snap, not less harshness. → UAD Pultec EQP-1A — Mix with the Masters (Alan Meyerson), Adding impact to percussions with Alan Meyerson

edm-subgenres.title: EDM Subgenres
edm-subgenres.html:
Companion to House - EDM — the quick-identity card for each electronic lane: tempo, the one element that defines it, and the technique that gets you there. The core rules (pump, mono low end, energy arrangement) apply to all of them.

Deep House — 118–124 BPM

  • Identity: warm, rolling, understated — jazzy 7th/9th chord stabs, sub-heavy round bass, shuffled hats, sparse soul vocal chops.
  • Key techniques: lazy sidechain curve (shallow, late ramp) · Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer/Drift filtered stab chords (LPF ~2–4 kHz, short amp release) · vocal chops pitched −2 to −5 semis, LPF'd · swing 55–60%.

Tech House — 124–128 BPM

  • Identity: stripped and percussive — one rubbery bass hook, minimal chords, big dumb drop that's mostly groove.
  • Key techniques: bass = mono synth, heavy Ghz Vulf Compressor 3-style pump, plays with the duck · percussion loops layered thin (Drums Hats Group wide) · vocal one-liners as rhythmic objects (delay throws, filter automation).

Future Bass — 130–150 BPM (half-time drops)

  • Identity: the detuned supersaw chord stab with sidechained wobble — bright, emotional, vocal-chop hooks.
  • Key techniques: Serum 2 7-voice unison saw chords → OTT at real depth (30–50% — this genre is why OTT exists) → volume-LFO wobble (Kickstart 2 triggered per-8th) · pitch-bent vocal chops as the lead · white-noise risers everywhere (FX Bus).

committing-and-printing.title: Committing and Printing
committing-and-printing.html:
Deliberately removing your own ability to keep tweaking something — printing a processed take, bussing multiple tracks together onto tape or a single audio track, or otherwise locking a decision in — so a mix reaches "done" instead of staying endlessly revisable. Source: Zach Scholz's tape-workflow videos, built around a genuinely surprising A/B result — an all-digital mix of his read as more characterful than a tape-printed version of the same song. His conclusion: most of what people credit to tape as "warmth" is actually decided during mixing, before tape ever enters the chain. Tape still does something real, but the workflow discipline it forces is the bigger prize.

Why commit

  • Unlimited undo/redo/punch-in access breeds second-guessing — deciding something is "done" and moving on beats endless revision, which reads back as a felt sense of dissatisfaction with over-tweaked mixes when the alternative is tried.
  • Track-count discipline (a self-imposed ≤16-track full-song challenge) forces deliberate sound choices instead of stacking layers to compensate for a part that isn't quite right — e.g. thickening a thin synth-bass part with a single piano layer underneath instead of adding more synth basses on top.
  • Committing to a tone before recording — locking EQ/compression/level decisions ahead of pressing record rather than "fixing it in the mix" — is a skill worth practicing even outside a hard-tape workflow; see the ear-training exercise below.

Ear-training exercise (no tape or hardware required)

Practice EQ moves on a simple, feature-limited EQ instead of a full surgical/dynamic one — a 3-band Neve-1073-style plugin (a free replica works fine) with no spectrum/numeric visual feedback. The point isn't that EQ's sound, it's removing your ability to make endless tiny adjustments and forcing a decision by ear — the skill transfers back to sharper moves on precise modern EQs afterward.
secs: Ear-training exercise (no tape or hardware required)

ozone-9-maximizer.title: Ozone 9 Maximizer
ozone-9-maximizer.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: iZotope

What it is

Ozone 9's loudness maximizer/limiter, with multiple limiting algorithms (IRC), true-peak limiting, and a transient-preserving mode.

What it's used for

Final loudness maximization on a master to competitive streaming/commercial loudness levels.

FX chain notes

The last device in the Ozone master chain.

pro-mb.title: Pro-MB
pro-mb.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: FabFilter

What it is

FabFilter's multiband dynamics processor, combining up to six bands of independent compression/expansion with FabFilter's visual band-editing interface.

What it's used for

Frequency-specific dynamics control — taming boomy low end, harsh mids, or sibilant highs independently on a mix bus or individual track.

FX chain notes

Used on a mix or master bus after broad-strokes EQ, before the final limiter.

neumann-tlm-102.title: Neumann TLM 102
neumann-tlm-102.html:
Category: Microphone (large-diaphragm condenser, cardioid) Vendor: Neumann Ballpark value (used, 2026): $450–600

What it is

Neumann's compact large-diaphragm cardioid condenser — transformerless (TLM) circuit, 144 dB max SPL, and a gentle presence lift above ~6 kHz designed for close vocal work.

What it's used for

The vocal mic: lead vocals, acoustic guitar, and anything that needs detail and air without harshness.

Signal chain notes

Into the interface preamp with a pop filter ~4" out; its gain-friendly output and high SPL handling also make it usable on the Fender Blues Junior cab or percussion.

Manual

  • 📄 Local PDF · Official product/docs page

High-level points:

  • Fixed cardioid, no pad, no HPF switch — all shaping happens by placement and in the DAW; the mic itself is deliberately simple.
  • 144 dB max SPL — it will take a guitar amp, drums, or a screamed vocal without a pad.
  • The slight rise above 6 kHz is the built-in "air" — plan vocal EQ around it (you rarely need to add top).
  • TLM = transformerless: very low self-noise (11.5 dB-A) and clean low end — quiet sources (fingerpicked FG730S, soft vocals) stay noise-free.
  • Very compact body changes placement geometry vs a big-body LDC — the grille sits closer to where you point it than you think.
  • Needs 48V phantom; shock mount recommended (small body transmits stand rumble).

shure-sm57.title: Shure SM57
shure-sm57.html:
Category: Microphone (dynamic, cardioid) Vendor: Shure Ballpark value (used, 2026): $70–90

What it is

The most-used instrument microphone ever made — cardioid dynamic with a midrange presence peak, effectively indestructible, and the reference sound for snare and guitar cab.

What it's used for

Guitar amps and snare first; also horns, percussion, gritty character vocals, and anything loud.

Signal chain notes

On the Fender Blues Junior grille; needs real preamp gain (dynamic, no phantom required).

Manual

  • 📄 Local PDF · Official user guide

High-level points:

  • The sound is the frequency response: presence bump ~5–6 kHz, rolled-off lows and top — sources come back "pre-mixed" toward the midrange.
  • Placement is the EQ. On a cab, an inch of movement across the speaker cone changes tone more than any plugin.
  • Handles absurd SPL — there is no amp too loud for it.
  • Strong proximity effect: right on the grille = thick lows; a hand-width back = leaner and roomier.
  • No pad, no switches, no phantom needed; it works forever.

chord-voicings-guitar-lesson-unlimited-c.title: Chord voicings guitar lesson - Unlimited Chord Options!
chord-voicings-guitar-lesson-unlimited-c.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Episode 12 of Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) guitar-chords-and-theory series, and — despite the "unlimited chord options" title suggesting a broad survey — actually a narrow, single-idea lesson: a deliberately unsystematic, exploratory method for generating new voicings of any chord shape you already know, by moving individual notes up or down an octave one at a time and seeing what turns up. It leans on a prior episode in the series (not yet in the vault) that teaches finding the same note in other fretboard locations via octave/unison interval shapes — this lesson assumes that skill and applies it specifically to chord tones. Before the method itself, Jared draws out a three-way terminology distinction that the rest of the vault's Chord Voicings page uses constantly but has never stated explicitly as its own thing: a chord (the abstract pitch collection, e.g. "C major"), a voicing (the specific order/interval spacing those pitches are arranged in), and a shape (the specific physical fretboard fingering used to play a given voicing) are three genuinely separate concepts — the same voicing can be played as different shapes in different fretboard positions, or even on a different instrument entirely (a piano player can play the identical voicing with zero relationship to any guitar shape), and the same shape moved to a new root becomes a different chord while remaining the same voicing. He then works the octave-shift method through three open chord shapes (A major, B7, D minor 7) from his own "Chords with Color" chart, turning up several usable inversions per chord, three of which he ties to real songs.

bossa-nova-jo-o-gilberto.title: Bossa Nova (João Gilberto)
bossa-nova-jo-o-gilberto.html: What makes it the genre: samba's percussion section compressed onto one nylon-string guitar, under cool-jazz harmony, played quietly. Born late-1950s Rio — João Gilberto invented the guitar style (classical fingerstyle technique + tamborim rhythm), Jobim supplied the songbook, Getz/Gilberto (1964) took it worldwide. The identity is intimacy: soft dynamics, close mics, straight 8ths, and a two-bar sway built on anticipation — nothing is loud, nothing is swung, everything breathes.

hub-latching-approach.title: Hub-Latching Approach
hub-latching-approach.html:
A memorization/comping-practice method for internalizing every inversion of a single chord voicing — Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) named strategy from his "Jazz Comping Mastery" course. It answers the same underlying problem Chord Voicings and Guide Tones already frame theoretically (many possible voicings per chord, guide tones defining which notes matter) with a concrete drill order for getting them under the fingers on one physical position of the neck.

The core idea

Pick one familiar root-position voicing and treat it as the "hub" — the home base every other voicing is measured against and returned to. Instead of practicing inversions by walking a single scale tone up the neck (staying anchored to a moving root), the hub-latching approach works all the inversions of one chord in roughly one hand position, jumping out to a voicing rooted on a different chord tone and back to the hub, over and over — closer to how comping actually happens in real playing than a straight-line inversion drill is.

melodic-harmonic-blending-comping-while-.title: Melodic-Harmonic Blending (Comping While Soloing)
melodic-harmonic-blending-comping-while-.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony and the guitar side of Chord Voicings — how to get a pianistic, self-accompanied fullness out of a single guitar line by continuously deciding, in real time, how much harmony the moment needs and filling it in yourself rather than relying on a rhythm section. Distinct from Chord Melody Arranging: that page's method is for arranging a fixed, known melody ahead of time (or reading one off a lead sheet); this page is for improvised soloing where the "melody" doesn't exist yet and the harmonic support has to be invented on the fly, in the moment, as part of the line itself. Also distinct from Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline, which is comping behind another soloist; this is comping behind your own solo, as you play it. Adding Chords to Single-Note Lines is the earlier-stage, more structured on-ramp to this same idea — chords placed deliberately at phrase-ending target notes, drilled on one static chord, before the alternation dissolves into the continuous blend described below.

The governing question: how active does the harmony need to be right now?

The whole technique reduces to one continuously-asked question: is the harmony active enough in the space right now, or does it need more support? When a melodic line alone feels sufficient, keep soloing single-note. The moment it feels like it needs support — more harmonic information, more fullness — stop the line and fill out the harmony with a chord, then either hold it or launch back into a line. There's no fixed rule for when to switch; it's a continuous read of the musical space, re-decided constantly rather than planned in advance. (This is the same underlying judgment call as Chord Melody Arranging's "don't harmonize every note" section — both pages land on "space, not density, is the goal" — but that page applies it to a known melody being arranged, this one to an improvised line being built in the moment.)
secs: The governing question: how active does the harmony need to be right now?

this-might-ruin-my-channel-practice-log-.title: This might ruin my channel Practice Log No. 1
this-might-ruin-my-channel-practice-log-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Not a lesson in the usual sense from this channel — this is Jared (Sound Guitar Lessons, teaching professionally since ~19, ~6 years on YouTube posting weekly evergreen lessons) launching a new, deliberately looser weekly format he's calling a "practice log" (he wanted to call it a "blog," his wife vetoed it). The premise: his regular lesson videos are built to be timeless, prescriptive, one-stop tutorials; this new series is the opposite — recorded and posted same-day, no rehearsed teacherly framing, just "here's what I'm actually working on this week," admittedly risking that it clashes with his channel's usual algorithmic lane (hence the title). Most of the video (~20 of 25 min) is meta — why he's doing this, how it differs from his lesson content, his philosophy that he thinks of himself as a student sharing what works rather than a teacher instructing from above. Two genuinely useful, concrete threads run through the framing: (1) a real update on fixing chipped classical/fingerstyle nails without giving up his return to nails after years of playing without them, and (2) a walkthrough of the practice-system screen he uses to structure a 2:30 daily practice window, including a "finish designing it, then actually practice it" discipline he's imposed on himself. No guitar is played on camera in this video — he's explicit that's coming in future entries.

how-much-should-i-practice-guitar-the-su.title: "how much should i practice guitar?" (the surprising answer that will keep you going)
how-much-should-i-practice-guitar-the-su.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Full transcript: "how much should i practice guitar?" (the surprising answer that will keep you going) (transcript)

Synopsis

A talking-head/mindset episode (a new once-a-month format Jared is testing, distinct from his usual deep technical drill videos) answering a viewer question from "Pat" (David Patrick, a repeat commenter): how do you actually pick and stick to a daily practice time window? Jared reads Pat's comment on-screen, then gives a three-part answer he'd already posted in reply, elaborating on each part. The video is explicitly framed as a companion/prequel to The Practice Priority Pyramid — Jared opens by restating that consistency is the first and most important stage, before any question of what or how hard to practice even matters, then spends the rest of the video on the specific tactic that makes consistency achievable: deliberately committing to half of the amount you think you want to practice. That halving rule is the "surprising answer" of the title. He closes with his own current routine (1 hour/day jazz guitar, calendar + habit-tracker, a missed-day "quota" make-up system, and a fixed daily warm-up) and a closing perspective-shift ("it's all a construct — expect to fall off, diagnose why, and adjust rather than repeat the same broken plan").

angular-reach-exercise.title: Angular Reach Exercise
angular-reach-exercise.html:
A daily "always item" technique exercise from Jared's (Sound Guitar Lessons) Warm-up & Technique category, part of the broader system documented on The Practice Priority Pyramid and demonstrated on How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop). Purpose stated directly: it's a reach and relaxation-under-tension drill built on alternate picking, deliberately angular (jumping between string groups at a fixed fret pattern) rather than a straight scale run — plus chord and sweep-picking variants of the same underlying shape.

The base pattern

  • Click = quarter notes on the offbeat, not the downbeat — same offbeat-click convention Jared uses elsewhere (see Circle-of-Fourths One-Position Scale Drill).
  • Play 16th notes starting on the 9th fret.
  • Angle up, then back down, across the bottom four strings, then repeat the same up-and-down angle shape on the middle four strings, then the top four strings, then back to the middle four, then the bottom four again.
  • Shift position, then repeat the whole sequence starting from the other direction — i.e. run it a second time starting from the pinky side rather than the pattern's original starting finger.
  • Alternate picking throughout, crossing a string on every note — this is what makes it "excellent for alternate picking" specifically (as opposed to a same-string run).

What it's for (stated purpose)

  • Reach — the angular string-group jumps stretch the fretting hand beyond what a straight scale run demands.
  • Relaxation under tension — Jared names staying relaxed through the pattern as an explicit focus alongside the notes themselves, not just a side effect.
  • Alternate-picking fluency across string changes — every note crosses a string, so the picking hand can't fall into a same-string groove.

Variations (same shape, different execution)

  • Chord version — the same angular shapes played as chords rather than single notes, jumping between the shapes the way the single-note version jumps between string groups. Stated benefit: direct carryover to chord creation — internalizing how those same reach/angle shapes work as voicings, not just as a picking drill.
  • Sweep-picking version — the same shape executed with a sweep-picking motion instead of alternate picking, given as a third, separate variation to rotate into once the base and chord versions are checked off.

circle-of-fourths-one-position-scale-dri.title: Circle-of-Fourths One-Position Scale Drill
circle-of-fourths-one-position-scale-dri.html:
Part of Guitar Positions — Jared Borkowski's own scale/mode mastery-check drill, part of the "Vocabulary" category of his personal practice-tracking system (previewed on Practice Log #1, demonstrated in full on The Scale Practice Method That Forces You to Really Know Your Fretboard). Unlike Continuous Scale Exercise (same channel — training the reactive skill of finding the nearest correct note when a tune's actual key changes) or Never-Ending Scale Exercise (Rosenwinkel/Jens Larsen — decoupling scale-swap timing from the harmony on purpose), this drill isn't about a tune at all: it's a pure vocabulary-mastery gate for one scale or mode at a time — proof you can execute it, clean, in every key, without a chord progression involved.

The core idea

Take one scale or one mode. Stay in roughly one fretboard position/area (small shifts as the shape moves are fine — same spirit as One-Position Fretboard Overview Drill's "don't be rigid about a strict box"). Play it through all 12 keys back to back, in the circle of fourths, in one continuous take, with zero mistakes. That single clean pass is the mastery gate — it's what earns the checkmark in a scale/mode tracking list.

Two axes of scale practice (pick one per pass)

  1. Same root, all positions — play all five scale-forms/shapes off one root note, walking the shape up the neck.
  2. Same position, all roots — stay in one fretboard area and cycle through all 12 keys (this is the axis this drill uses). Both are worth drilling; they build different fluency (shape-recall vs. key-recall).
secs: Two axes of scale practice (pick one per pass)

what-to-learn-on-bass-in-order.title: What to Learn on Bass (in Order)
what-to-learn-on-bass-in-order.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's master curriculum video — the "what order to learn everything on bass" companion piece that Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments and How to Start Learning Bass - Self Taught! both point at and leave for later (their Commandment 6 closer names it directly as a way to keep short-term practice goals fresh over a 6–12 month horizon). This video is that promised curriculum: 55 numbered steps grouped into five levels (Level 0 through Level 5), each step a self-contained thing to learn, roughly in the order BassBuzz recommends learning it, from "buy a bass" all the way to jazz-fusion-shredder-level theory and technique. It's explicitly framed as an index, not a tutorial — "you could technically learn all of these things in like an hour but it'll take weeks or months to actually learn good technique," and the video itself is a curriculum map, not a lesson, with a companion free PDF (linked in the video's description, not accessible from the transcript) providing resources/exercises per step and a "mega playlist" ordering BassBuzz's own catalog to match. The load-bearing psychological frame, repeated at every level transition: learning bass is, in part, a fight against "the resistance" — a term borrowed explicitly from Steven Pressfield (author, The War of Art), personified here as an internal voice that "urges you to give up, forget about it, think you're not good enough." Each level's song-list section closes with the same beat: crushing a level's assigned songs is ammunition against the resistance, and — named as its own explicit step (Step 21, "notice your progress") — most self-taught players (and even some teachers) never do this without being prompted, so it has to be a deliberate practice, not an assumption. This reframes the whole roadmap as goal-tiered in the same spirit as Goal-Tiered Practice and the Self-Taught Bass Commandments's long/medium/short-term ladder, just laddered by skill level (0–5) instead of by a player's personal goal — the two frameworks are meant to be read together: this video answers "what's next," Goal-Tiered Practice answers "how to structure showing up for it."

bass-shapes-the-chunking-principle.title: Bass Shapes — The Chunking Principle
bass-shapes-the-chunking-principle.html:
BassBuzz's foundational "shapes" video — the psychology-grounded case for why movable fretboard shapes are the core mental model for playing bass at all, plus five starter shapes (root-fifth, octave, major triad, minor triad, and "supershapes" layering/switching between them) and a reusable 3-step process for learning any future shape. This is the prerequisite video two already-enriched sibling BassBuzz notes point back to without being able to link it: Root-Fifth Bass Lines and the 3-Step Style Rhythm Formula's companion video opens with "if you've seen my shapes video, then you're already familiar with the root fifth shape" and that note's own page flagged it as "an earlier 'shapes' video... not yet a page in this vault" — filled now. Fill gap: the vault had individual shapes (root-fifth, octave-via-Jamerson, the fill-specific "triangle") but nothing documenting the meta-concept — shapes as a chunking device, why bass specifically is suited to it, or the major/minor triad shapes as a plain 1-3-5 arpeggio pattern (distinct from the fill-writing triangle shape).

The chunking principle — why shapes work

  • A shape is a visual/finger pattern on the neck representing a fixed set of pitch relationships, not a fixed set of pitches — because it's movable to any root, the same shape reproduces the same music starting on a different note every time.
  • Grounded in psychologist George Miller's concept of chunking: combining many small, hard-to-remember bits of information into one larger, easier-to-remember chunk. Demoed with a random letter sequence (hard to memorize) rearranged into recognizable words (the identical letters, suddenly easy) — the same letters, chunked differently.
  • Applied to bass: instead of frantically recalling individual note names and theory in real time, a bassist who's internalized a shape treats the whole shape as one pre-computed decision — "find the root, imagine the magic dots, plant your fingers" — freeing attention for everything else happening in the song.
  • Proof the ear tracks relationships, not absolute pitches — the "Another One Bites the Dust" demo: two completely different sets of notes both read unmistakably as the same bassline, because the distances between the notes (the shape) are identical in both — the pitches themselves are irrelevant to recognition, only the relationships are.
secs: The chunking principle — why shapes work

bass-chords-and-double-stops.title: Bass Chords and Double Stops
bass-chords-and-double-stops.html:
Playing two or more notes together on bass — pulling the instrument out of its usual single-root-note role and into a melodic/harmonic one — via two distinct mechanisms: a fretted chord shape (register-gated, see below) or an open-string pedal tone under a melodic line (root-note-gated, see the open-string section).

The core mechanic: register makes or breaks it

Bass chords played down low sound muddy and gross; the same voicing played higher up the neck sounds clean and "guitar-ly." This is the whole technique in one line — the chord shape itself isn't the hard part, the register choice is. Low strings/low frets have too much fundamental energy and not enough separation between the chord tones for a stacked voicing to read clearly; moving the same shape up the neck (into a register closer to a guitar's normal range) gives the notes enough separation to sound intentional rather than smeared.
secs: The core mechanic: register makes or breaks it

jamerson-s-root-fifth-octave-exercise.title: Jamerson's Root-Fifth-Octave Exercise
jamerson-s-root-fifth-octave-exercise.html:
James Jamerson (Motown's uncredited house bassist, the Funk Brothers, Rock and Roll Hall of Fame) taught this exercise one-on-one to Ron Brown (bassist on later West Coast Motown sessions) as a way to drill his own chromatic approach to bass playing; it's documented in the Standing in the Shadows of Motown book, though that book only writes it out in a handful of keys. It's not just a finger-warmup — it's a compressed formula for how Jamerson generated hit basslines on the fly, and BassBuzz reverse-engineers it into three combinable ingredients: root-fifth-octave as the harmonic skeleton, chromatic approach walks as the connective tissue, and syncopation as the rhythmic engine. Fill gap: this is the vault's first dedicated note for Jamerson's formula and the step-39 ("Roots, fifths, and octaves") entry on The BassBuzz 55-Step Bass Learning Roadmap had no linked note until this one.

The exercise itself

Played over a static C: root-fifth-octave (C, G, C) as the skeleton, then a chromatic walk starting three frets below the target, working up chromatically into the fifth, and the same walk-up into the octave — Jamerson deliberately re-inserts the fifth in between the walk-up notes to "hammer home" the target rather than just running straight chromatic scale tones. Rhythmically it's played in swing eighths (offbeat notes land two-thirds of the way past the beat rather than the even halfway point of straight eighths) — noted as sounding "kind of lumpy" compared to a straight-eighths read, and worth learning in all 12 keys, not just C, so the shape is recognizable by ear in any song's key rather than only in the one key it was first learned in. (general starting point for the walk: three chromatic notes leading into each target — adjust the walk's length to fit however many beats are available before the target lands.)

bass-fill-writing-the-3-step-rhythm-and-.title: Bass Fill Writing — The 3-Step Rhythm-and-Shape Method
bass-fill-writing-the-3-step-rhythm-and-.html:
BassBuzz's dedicated answer to "what do I actually play for a bass fill" — a repeatable pick rhythm → pick shape → combine process that deliberately front-loads rhythm over note choice ("even if the notes you play are garbage, if you sell the rhythm it'll still kind of work"). This is the vault's first note built specifically around fill-writing as its own skill (as opposed to the connective-tissue chromatic-walk fills on Bass Walkup and Walkdown Fills, or the harmonic-skeleton material on Jamerson's Root-Fifth-Octave Exercise and Root-Fifth Bass Lines and the 3-Step Style Rhythm Formula) and it introduces a genuinely new shape to the vault — the major/minor "triangle" shape — alongside a fill-specific usage of the already-documented root-fifth-octave shape. Full worked source: 3 Steps to Killer Bass Fills (for Beginners).

Step 1 — Pick a rhythm

Three questions, in order, before any note is chosen:

  1. Where does the fill go? The end of a musical unit — typically the end of a 4-bar phrase, or the end of a larger section (verse → chorus). Fills are lead-ins/transitions, not decorations dropped mid-phrase.
  2. How much space? 2 or 4 beats is the typical fill length.
  3. What subdivision? Start simple: two quarter notes, eighth-eighth-quarter, or four eighth notes. (general starting point: pick whichever of the three feels most natural to count first — none is "more correct," they're just increasing note-density options for the same space.)

Leveling up: for a more complex/intense fill rhythm, imagine a drum fill in that spot and copy its rhythm onto the bass, then plug shape-notes into it. The rhythm is what reads as "intense," independent of which notes you choose on top of it — proven in the source video with an A/B of the same borrowed rhythm played with two different note sets.

pentatonic-superimposition-and-side-slip.title: Pentatonic Superimposition and Side-Slipping
pentatonic-superimposition-and-side-slip.html: Three escalating ways to get more mileage out of one pentatonic scale than "play it over its own tonic": play it wholesale over chords it isn't diatonic to (comparison-by-ear substitution), stack a second pentatonic scale on top of the first (interval-based mixing), and slide the whole scale a half step off and back (side-slipping). Grounded in Joe Henderson and McCoy Tyner's jazz vocabulary (named source records: In 'N Out and The Real McCoy). Sits a level up from Single-Note Pentatonic Substitutions Over Changes (which edits one note at a time to track a changing progression) and Diagonal Pentatonic Blues Soloing (one shape, one edited note, one transposition across a I-IV-V) — the techniques here instead keep the whole, unedited pentatonic scale in place and reinterpret it against different harmonic backdrops.

triad-pairs.title: Triad Pairs
triad-pairs.html:
A fourth distinct triad-soloing device alongside the vault's other three: Triads as a Fretboard Map takes one triad and maps its three close-position zones; Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords extracts one triad from inside a single seventh chord's 3rd-5th-7th; Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing harmonizes a whole scale into seven separate triads used one at a time. This page instead combines two triads at once — a "triad pair" — played together as a compound source of line material over a single chord, associated with modern/modal jazz phrasing. Worked entirely over a C minor blues.

Finding a triad pair (the mechanics)

  1. Harmonize the parent scale into seven triads, one per scale degree (skip-a-note/tertian stacking, same derivation as Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing). Worked here on C melodic minor: C minor, D minor, E♭ augmented, F major, G major, A half-diminished, B diminished.
  2. A triad pair = any two of those triads that share no common notes. In a 7-note diatonic scale this constraint always resolves to one specific relationship: the two triads must sit next to each other in the scale (adjacent scale degrees) — confirmed as true for every pair used in the source video without exception.
  3. Fast derivation shortcut, stated directly: decide which single scale note you don't want to play over the target chord, remove it from the 7-note scale, and the remaining six notes split cleanly into two adjacent triads — that's the pair. Faster than deriving and scanning the full harmonized-triad table each time.
  4. The pair as a compound sound, not two separate ideas. Because the two triads are scale-adjacent, together they spell out an extended chord sound in one breath — see the worked chord-by-chord mapping below for what each specific pair adds harmonically (7ths, 9ths, 11ths, 13ths) on top of the underlying chord.

sweep-picking-arpeggio-shapes.title: Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes
sweep-picking-arpeggio-shapes.html:
A small set of movable arpeggio shapes, played with sweep picking (one continuous pick stroke through several strings, "just like playing a chord," rather than alternate-picking each note) instead of a complex picking system, as the actual mechanism behind Barney Kessel's fast, fluid lines. Complements Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes — that page's CAGED-adjacency system is about where on the neck to find the next chord's arpeggio; this page is about how the pick hand executes an arpeggio shape once you're there, plus a distinct core idea: treat each shape as a flexible visual pattern, not fixed to the one chord it was first learned over.

The four shapes

  • Shape 1 — minor 9 arpeggio, bidirectional. Ascending: up–down–down–down–down–up (the core minor-9 shape with an added note before/after it). Descending (reverse): down–up–up–up–up–down.
  • Shape 2 — minor 7 arpeggio, bidirectional. Ascending: down–up–up–up. Descending: down–down–down–up.
  • Shape 3 — descending only.
  • Shape 4 — ascending only.
  • All four appear together within a single Barney Kessel phrase (his solo on "Mean to Me," from the Poll Winners' debut record).
  • One note per string throughout — the sweep motion is a single continuous pick stroke, not alternate picking, exactly the motion used to strum a chord but applied one note at a time.

Getting the motion under the fingers

  1. Isolate the shape and the pick motion first, before trying to use it musically — practice each shape slowly, ascending and descending, focused purely on a smooth, connected sound through the sweep (general starting point — no metronome number given in the source).
  2. Only once the picking motion is comfortable, move to the applications below.
secs: Getting the motion under the fingers

legato-and-picking-technique-mixing.title: Legato and Picking Technique Mixing
legato-and-picking-technique-mixing.html:
Part of Music Theory. Covers why and how to combine legato (hammer-on/pull-off), slides, alternate picking, and small economy-picking sweeps within a single line, as distinct from Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes (full-shape sweep-picking mechanics) and Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch (blues-specific touch vocabulary). The core idea: real playing mixes several techniques inside a two-bar line, so technique choice is really two decisions at once — a mechanical one (what's easiest/fastest to execute here) and a musical one (which notes should pop and which should recede). Complements Solo Dynamics and Arc's "hammer-on/pull-off drilling → controlled dismount" point — that page covers arc-level dynamics; this page is the same legato-is-softer mechanism applied note-by-note.

Why mix techniques

  • Isolated technique drilling under-prepares you for real playing. A transcription of a good player's line typically shows several different techniques (legato, slides, picking, small sweeps) inside a single two-bar phrase, not one technical idea run straight through — so an exercise built around only one technique at a time doesn't reflect how it actually gets used.
  • The end state is not thinking about technique while playing — technique is drilled and internalized separately in the practice room; while actually soloing, attention should go to the music (what's being played, what the band is doing), not to which technique comes next. Combined-technique drilling (below) is what makes that automatic integration possible.

inside-outside-picking-and-pick-slanting.title: Inside-Outside Picking and Pick Slanting
inside-outside-picking-and-pick-slanting.html:
Brandon D'Eon's two picking-mechanics rules for fast multi-string alternate-picked lines — small physical details that materially affect achievable speed independent of raw hand speed. Complements Directional Alternate Picking System (a beat-locked default picking rule) and Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes (the sweep alternative to alternate picking entirely).

Inside vs. outside picking (2 notes per string)

  • Inside picking: each pick stroke moves toward the next string you're about to cross to.
  • Outside picking: each stroke moves away from it, requiring an extra "hop" back over the string just left before the next stroke lands.
  • Ascending 2-notes-per-string lines (e.g. pentatonic scales): start with an upstroke to stay on inside picking — the following downstroke then naturally moves toward the next higher string.
  • Descending 2-notes-per-string lines: the rule flips — start with a downstroke to stay on inside picking.
  • Net effect: picking-stroke direction relative to the string-crossing direction, not raw alternation speed, is what limits achievable tempo on these lines.

Pick slanting (uneven note groupings per string)

  • Even note-count per string (groups of 4, 6, etc.): hold the pick at a consistent downward slant — it clears the next string without a separate hop, and the slant angle never needs to change since the same picking-direction pattern repeats identically on every string.
  • Odd note-count per string (3 notes per string is the common case): the required slant flips every string crossing — one crossing needs the downward slant, the next needs an upward slant — which is inherently less efficient than the even-grouping case, since the hand has to keep switching slant angle mid-line.
  • Practical read: pick slanting is a genuine speed unlock for even-numbered groupings, but doesn't pay off as cleanly for 3-notes-per-string material without constant slant-switching.

Picking approach is a deliberate choice, not a fixed rule to always alternate-pick

When a fast line resists clean execution even after real practice time, the fix isn't always more repetition of the same picking pattern — it can be switching part of the line to a different picking approach entirely (sweep picking, economy picking) that fits the line's actual shape better. Worked example: a line that resisted full alternate picking for 7 weeks of dedicated practice was solved by sweep-picking part of it instead.
secs: Inside vs. outside picking (2 notes per string)
Pick slanting (uneven note groupings per string)
Picking approach is a deliberate choice, not a fixed rule to always alternate-pick

diatonic-modes-practice-ladder.title: Diatonic Modes Practice Ladder
diatonic-modes-practice-ladder.html:
Brandon D'Eon's leveled drill progression for internalizing the major scale's seven diatonic modes on guitar — the major-scale counterpart to Harmonic Minor Scale Practice Ladder, sharing most of its drill shapes. See Diatonic Modes for the underlying theory (mode construction, character, chord-per-degree table) this ladder drills.

The ladder

  1. One major scale shape, memorized and transposable to any root.
  2. Per-mode drilling across all 12 keys. Random-key generator + stopwatch + metronome: generate a random key, play the one mode currently being drilled in that key, repeat across all 12 keys before moving to the next mode. Trains the mode's shape, interval knowledge (relating notes back to the key), and fretboard knowledge simultaneously. Same method as Routine 1 in The Five-Category Practice Method.
  3. All seven modes of one key, played as one continuous octave-spanning pass. Random key generated, then walk through all seven modes back to the starting mode an octave up, starting as low on the neck as possible without open strings — timed with a stopwatch as the progress metric.
  4. Musical application: improvise over backing tracks using everything drilled in levels 1–3. The explicit checkpoint that isolated scale-running isn't the end goal.
  5. Fixed position, cycling key — the inverse of a position-per-key drill. Pick one fixed fretboard position and, across all 12 randomly-generated keys, find and play whichever mode's shape sits in that position for each key. Contrast with Positional CAGED Soloing with Matched Modes and Arpeggios and Harmonic Minor Scale Practice Ladder's Level 7, which fix the key and walk multiple positions — this drill fixes the position and walks all 12 keys instead.
  6. Three-notes-per-string, all 12 keys, ~130 BPM. Same three-notes-per-string mechanic as the harmonic minor ladder's Levels 5–6.
  7. The chain exercise (capstone). Pick a random key, improvise continuously across the whole fretboard without stopping, in a subdivision matched to actual skill level. Rated the single hardest and most effective scale-internalization method — a real test of key knowledge rather than a fun improvising exercise (that's Level 4's role).

augmented-sixth-chords.title: Augmented Sixth Chords
augmented-sixth-chords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chords / Altered Chords. A family of predominant chords built to approach the dominant with maximum half-step tension — named for the augmented 6th interval between their top and bottom notes.

Construction

Start from a doubled root of a V chord; approach the upper note of that octave with a half-step below, and the lower note with a half-step above; add the tonic as a third note. The interval between the resulting top and bottom notes is an augmented 6th.

The three flavors

Type Symbol Built by
Italian It.6 3 notes only, doubled tonic
French Fr.6 adds the 2nd scale degree instead of doubling the tonic
German Ger.6 adds the lowered 3rd scale degree instead

Resolution

  • Normally resolve to a dominant triad — not a dominant 7th, because the doubled roots present in a dominant triad would otherwise create parallel-motion problems.
  • Also commonly resolve to a tonic chord in 2nd inversion (which itself has a doubled 5th scale degree, avoiding the same problem).
  • Rarely, an augmented 6th chord is found transposed down a perfect 5th ("on ♭2"), used to approach a root-position tonic chord instead.
  • Resolving a German 6th → V creates textbook-illegal parallel 5ths — but it's accepted as idiomatic anyway ("Mozart did it all the time").
  • A Romantic-era-specific variant resolves the Ger.6 to a dominant seventh instead of a plain triad, which makes the augmented-6th interval resolve obliquely rather than outward to the octave.

Enharmonic pivot trick

A German 6th is enharmonically identical to a dominant 7th chord (respell the augmented 6th as a minor 7th). This makes it a ready-made pivot chord for enharmonic modulation — approach it like a Ger.6 in the old key, resolve it like a V7 (or a secondary dominant) in the new key, or vice versa. Beethoven used this move.

this-simple-process-creates-successful-s.title: THIS Simple Process Creates Successful Solo Guitar Playing
this-simple-process-creates-successful-s.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A condensed, step-by-step build order for turning a bare melody into a solo jazz-guitar chord-melody arrangement, using the standard "All of Me" as the worked example throughout. Rather than presenting isolated tricks, Nathan Borton lays out the process as an explicit sequence — pick the melody, learn it correctly (by ear, from a period vocal/film recording, not off a lead sheet by eye), lock it to a metronome with a groove, layer in chord roots at the phrase pauses, upgrade roots to full chords, add chromatic passing chords, harmonize the melody itself by matching voicings to their top note, then stitch connective lines between phrases — and finishes by playing the fully-assembled arrangement of "All of Me" straight through. The value here isn't any single device (each one — chromatic passing chords, top-note voicing lookup, enclosure-to-third connective lines — is already documented in more depth elsewhere in the vault, principally Chord Melody Arranging) but the ordering: this is the practice-room sequence for building an arrangement from scratch, one layer at a time, each layer played in time before the next is added, rather than trying to assemble a full arrangement in one pass.

george-benson-this-is-the-best-jazz-blue.title: George Benson - This is The Best Jazz Blues Solo I know
george-benson-this-is-the-best-jazz-blue.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen picks apart what he calls his favorite jazz blues solo — George Benson's solo on "Billie's Bounce" (a 12-bar blues in F, misheard by the auto-captions as "Billy bounds"), the first track/first solo on the first George Benson CD Larsen ever owned. The through-line of the video is why this particular solo is more interesting than most jazz blues playing, broken into three named ingredients: (1) Benson constantly mixes bebop and blues vocabulary inside a single line rather than picking one lane, (2) he has a favorite device on dominant chords — an arpeggio built from the chord's own 3rd (functionally a half-diminished shape) — that recurs across the whole solo, and (3) on at least one turnaround he thinks in plain triads plus chromatic leading (approach) notes rather than a parent scale, which is what produces the wide, "unexpected but still correct" interval skips that make his lines sound more sophisticated than scale-noodling. Larsen walks four passages chunk-by-chunk (matching the same transcribe → chunk → name-the-device → replay-your-own-version method documented on Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction), naming the underlying device at each stop rather than just teaching the notes verbatim. Transcript confidence note: the auto-captions garble jazz terminology heavily (e.g. "apeto"/"pet"/"aeto" for "arpeggio," "Trad" for "triad," "cord" for "chord," "Jos Benson" for "George Benson," "bbob" for "bebop") — settings/qualitative descriptions below are read through that garbling rather than treated as verbatim; no numeric bar/beat counts are invented that the transcript didn't actually support.

Debuting a prototype "circle visualizer" tool (tuned to a key, showing which scale degree is currently sounding as Konyi plays around it), the video drone-drills all 7 degrees of natural minor with particular focus on the 3 degrees that differ from major (♭3, ♭6, ♭7), and lays out the circle-of-fifths arrangement as a predictive tool for which degrees get confused with which. mode-derivation-and-polychords.title: Mode Derivation and Polychords
mode-derivation-and-polychords.html:
Part of Music Theory → Scale Modes Reference. That page (and the Guitar Grimoire book page behind it) is the mode-by-mode catalog — formulas, names, compatible chords for 27 scales, looked up. This page is the method behind that catalog: how to derive any mode's formula from scratch by hand, how to find its parent scale by chart instead of counting, and how to build a polychord substitute for any big chord on a 6-string instrument — a reusable technique, not more data to memorize. Sourced from the book's own front-matter method section, p.1–14.

1. The building blocks (p.2–4)

Everything below leans on one piece of vocabulary. There are 12 equal chromatic "blocks" a half-step apart. Intervals split into two families:

  • Majors — 2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th
  • Perfects — 1st (unison), 4th, 5th, 8th (octave)

Flat a major → minor. Flat a minor → diminished. Sharp a major or a perfect → augmented. Flat a perfect → diminished. There's no such thing as a diminished unison. Count blocks to name any interval directly — e.g. 4 blocks = minor 3rd = 1½ steps.

2. What a mode actually is (p.5–7)

A mode is the same 7 tones, renumbered from a different starting degree — no new pitches, just a new "1." The major scale's 2nd degree becomes the II mode's 1, its 3rd degree becomes the III mode's 2, and so on. Worked out against the major scale (1 2 3 4 5 6 7):

Mode Renumbering rule Result
II (Dorian) 2→1, 3→2, 4→3... 1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 ♭7
III (Phrygian) 3→1, 4→2, 5→3... 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7
IV (Lydian) 4→1, 5→2, 6→3... 1 2 3 ♯4 5 6 7
V (Mixolydian) 5→1, 6→2, 7→3... 1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7
VI (Aeolian) 6→1, 7→2, 1→3... 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7
VII (Locrian) 7→1, 1→2, 2→3... 1 ♭2 ♭3 4 ♭5 ♭6 ♭7

The book's own reframing is worth keeping: "there is actually only 1 scale, the Major scale and its modes. All other scales can be thought of as derived modes which also have modes" (p.6) — every one of the 27 scales in the full catalog is built by running this exact renumbering process on a different parent, not by a fundamentally different method.

phase-alignment.title: Phase Alignment
phase-alignment.html:
What it is: when two mics (or a mic + DI) capture one source, sound arrives at each at different times. Summed, the time offset comb-filters — frequencies cancel and reinforce in a pattern no EQ can fix. Alignment makes multi-mic captures sum fuller, not thinner.

Prevention (at the source)

  • Equal distance rule: capsules the same distance from the source can't disagree about arrival time.
  • 3:1 rule (spaced pairs): mics ≥3× as far from each other as from the source — the late arrival lands low enough in level that the combing is inaudible (Acoustic Guitar Track).
  • Polarity flip test, every setup: flip ø on one mic; keep whichever way has more low end (bass frequencies cancel first — the low end is your phase meter).
  • 🎬 From video: on a multi-mic source (a whole drum kit especially), interrogate every mic pairing independently rather than applying one universal polarity setting — rack tom vs. floor tom, overheads vs. front/room mic, and stereo pair vs. close mics are each their own relationship and each can prefer a different answer session to session; there's no absolute-right polarity, only what sums fullest for that pairing, that day — Steve Albini, Optimizing phase relationships with Steve Albini.

The pink-noise method (Dan Austin — the pro cab move)

  1. Play pink noise through the amp.
  2. Place mic 1 by ear (headphones in front of the cab).
  3. Flip mic 2's polarity and physically move it until the summed pair cancels hardest — a thin, windy near-silence. Maximum cancellation out-of-phase = perfect alignment in-phase.
  4. Flip mic 2 back. The pair is now phase-locked; blend freely. Repeat per extra mic. (Electric Guitar Amp Track.)

In the box

  • Align Delay: nudge sample-level delay on the later mic until the low end is fullest. For mic + DI, the DI always arrives first — delay the DI to the amp mic.
  • Zoom in: the waveforms show the offset directly; slide the late track back.
  • Also a creative control: deliberately-not-quite-aligned distant mics = size and room. Alignment is a dial, not a law — but know where zero is before you leave it.
secs: The pink-noise method (Dan Austin — the pro cab move)

referencing-and-translation.title: Referencing and Translation
referencing-and-translation.html:
What it is: the discipline that keeps a mix honest — comparing against professional records at matched loudness, and checking that the mix survives every playback system (phone, car, earbuds, club, mono).

Referencing (the honest A/B)

  • 2–3 reference tracks per project, chosen before mixing: same genre, similar arrangement density, a sound you'd sign. Keep them on a muted track in the set.
  • Loudness-match or the test is rigged — louder always wins. Gain the references down to your mix bus level (or use a Utility trim you toggle). Compare sections (their chorus vs yours), not whole songs.
  • What to listen for, one at a time: low-end weight → vocal level → brightness/air → width → density. One property per pass; "does mine sound worse?" is too vague to act on.
  • Reference early (first hour, per the Modern Pop recipe), not as a final grade — early references steer decisions; late ones just cause despair.

Translation (the playback gauntlet)

  • Mono check (Utility flip / Stereo Tool): elements may get quieter, nothing may vanish. Catches width and phase sins (Phase Alignment, Width and Stereo).
  • Phone speaker: does the bass read (via its mids — the "heard vs felt" model in Electric Bass DI Track)? Is the vocal still the loudest thing? Is the hook still a hook?
  • Car / earbuds / quiet listen: the quiet listen is underrated — at whisper volume, only balance survives; if the vocal or kick disappears, the balance is wrong, not the EQ.
  • Fix at the source chain, not with master EQ: phone says no bass → drive the bass mids (Saturation Send); car says harsh → find the 2–5 kHz offender track, don't dip the master.

Meters that matter

  • VU (~0 = −18 dBFS) for gain staging (Gain Staging) · sample-peak around clippers (Clipping and Loudness) · LUFS-I only at export time · correlation meter if mono keeps surprising you.
  • Ears first, meters as tiebreakers. If the meter disagrees with a level-matched ear judgment, trust the ears.

The reset ritual

Ears calibrate to whatever they hear for 20 minutes. Before big decisions: 5 minutes of silence, then the reference, then your mix. Never EQ after an hour of loud listening.

gain-staging.title: Gain Staging
gain-staging.html:
What it is: managing signal level at every handoff — interface → track → each plugin → group → bus → master — so each stage receives the level it was designed for.

Why it matters in a 32-bit world

Live's float engine can't clip internally, so gain staging isn't about digital overs anymore. It's about two things:

  1. Analog-modeled plugins are calibrated to hardware sweet spots. UAD, Decapitator, Kramer, API-2500 expect ≈ −18 dBFS average (hardware "0 VU"). Feed them 10 dB hotter and their modeled nonlinearity turns to choke; 10 dB colder and they're asleep.
  2. The louder-is-better illusion. Any un-level-matched A/B is rigged — louder always wins. Unity through every device is what keeps your ears honest on every knob.

The house convention (from the working chains)

  • Meter sandwich: Utility (gain in) + mvMeter2nogpu (VU) at the chain head · Utility (trim) + meter at the tail · extra meters between sections of long chains (Swiss Army Meter alternates).
  • Target ~0 VU (≈ −18 dBFS RMS) into everything. Peaky sources (drums): average 0 with peaks flying above. Background elements: looser is fine.
  • Unity out of every device: set each plugin's output so bypassing it changes nothing but the effect. The 1176's input/output pair, Inflator's output fader, Kramer's linked record/playback all exist for this.
  • Clip-gain first: pull raw recordings to ~0 VU average by hand (per phrase for vocals) before any plugin — the compressor should meet a signal that's already musically level (see Main Vocal Track Step 0.5).

Downstream

  • Groups/buses also want ~0 VU at their heads — if every track obeys, sums land close automatically.
  • Mix into the master with peaks ≈ −8 to −6 dBFS before the loudness stages (the Disclosure habit — headroom to "mix into the limiter").
  • The fader is for balance; the Utility gain is for calibration. Don't fix calibration with faders.
secs: Why it matters in a 32-bit world

vocal-production-for-billie-eilish-by-fi.title: Vocal production for Billie Eilish by Finneas
vocal-production-for-billie-eilish-by-fi.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

An 8-minute Mix with the Masters clip of Finneas walking through the origin and build of one Billie Eilish song (unnamed on-screen — the writing session predates "when the party's over"/"bad guy"-era releases; the hook line quoted is "I'm not your friend... I think therefore I am"), told mostly as a songwriting-and-process story rather than a settings-by-settings mix breakdown. It's short on plugin names and numeric parameters compared to other Mix with the Masters episodes in this vault, but it's dense with concrete, transferable production decisions: a scratch vocal sung through Auto-Tune specifically for its atypical texture that became a keeper hook; Billie tracking a verse vocal into a handheld Neumann TLM 103 at a house in Highland Park; a naturally quiet ad-lib laugh gained up +27 dB in the mix specifically to make it pop; treating a repeated chorus as a "double" where only ONE new element (a clap) gets reintroduced the second time through rather than layering more; a non-sample, hand-programmed "cowbell-type" clacky percussive layer working in rhythmic relationship to the kick; an understated bass sweep substituted for the drums' "the one" hit in part of the chorus; and — the video's real headline lesson — a sparse Spectrasonics Trilian synth-bass patch introduced on the second verse that completely reset the song's rhythmic feel and, in turn, pulled an entirely different vocal melody/rhythm out of Billie that a piano-first writing session never would have reached. Finneas frames that last point explicitly as a maturing production philosophy: "what you're capable of writing over what" — starting from a track's rhythmic components (rather than piano or acoustic guitar) can generate songwriting that literally couldn't exist any other way. The song itself took 7–8 months to finish in short, spaced-out sessions rather than his and Billie's usual day-or-two writing sprint.
