body-and-soul-guitar-lesson-chords-tab-s.title: BODY AND SOUL Guitar Lesson (chords, tab, scales, melody) No. 18 of Top 25 Jazz Standards for Guitar
body-and-soul-guitar-lesson-chords-tab-s.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Video #18 in Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) top-25-jazz-standards series, covering "Body and Soul" — Johnny Green's 1929 ballad, one of the most-recorded jazz songs ever (~3,000 versions), landmark-ized by Coleman Hawkins' 1939 recording, which largely abandoned the written melody in favor of extended improvisation over the tune's dense harmony and helped establish the tenor sax as a leading jazz voice. The lesson is dense specifically because the tune is dense: frequent 2-5-1s, a key change in the bridge, and a lead sheet full of altered-dominant symbols that reward a strong default interpretation rather than agonizing over "the one correct" reading. Two ideas anchor the video and generalize well beyond this tune: a plain-language walkthrough of tritone substitution (any dominant a half-step above a target can resolve into it, and you can freely insert one in front of any chord as decoration, understood or not), and a "default to harmonic minor with implied ♭9/♭13" habit for any dominant resolving to a minor chord, applied even when the lead sheet doesn't spell it out. A comping tip demonstrates that walking-chords idea live across a real passage, and a voicing-reuse observation in the bridge (a rootless Dmaj9 shape and an Em7 shape being physically identical) continues the "same shape, different chord identity" theme already documented from earlier videos in this channel.

someday-my-prince-will-come-guitar-lesso.title: SOMEDAY MY PRINCE WILL COME Guitar Lesson (tab, chords, scales) Top Jazz Standards for Guitar No. 17
someday-my-prince-will-come-guitar-lesso.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Video #17 in Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) top-25-jazz-standards series, covering "Someday My Prince Will Come" — Frank Churchill and Larry Morey's 1937 waltz from Disney's "Snow White," canonized as a jazz standard largely through Miles Davis's 1961 recording. Two things make this entry distinctive within the series: it's a 3/4 waltz (an unusual, valuable time-feel against a catalog otherwise dominated by 4/4), and its 2nd chord is a dominant 7♯5 — described as the tune's signature sound and reason enough on its own to learn it. The lesson's two standout technical moments are a superimposition trick (any inversion of a half-diminished shape doubles as a rootless dominant-7♭9♭13 voicing a major third above its root — meaning fretboard work on half-diminished shapes pays double duty) and a concrete, no-nonsense jazz-waltz comping backdrop (bass-note-then-two-chord-stabs on "1, and-of-2, 3") that solves the specific problem of 3/4 feeling unfamiliar after a career mostly spent in 4/4. The melody analysis also introduces a genuine classical-theory term — the appoggiatura — precisely and with a worked example, rather than the looser "passing tone" language used elsewhere in the series.

9th-and-13th-chord-voicings-for-blues-rh.title: 9th and 13th Chord Voicings for Blues Rhythm
9th-and-13th-chord-voicings-for-blues-rh.html: Part of Guitar Positions. A small vocabulary of rootless 9th- and 13th-chord grips for blues rhythm guitar — four-note shapes on the middle four strings, each movable to any I-IV-V key by sliding whole steps — plus two concrete rhythmic fills for turning plain chord jabs into a fuller-sounding comping part. Where L-Shape Root Map for Blues Chords solves "where does my hand go from I to IV to V" for shell voicings, this page is the "what do I actually grab once I'm there" layer, one step up in color from a shell (root-3rd-♭7) toward the 9th/13th extensions Chord Voicings names as the next thing to add after guide tones. Different content from Layering Rhythm Guitar Parts with Triads (same channel) — that page stacks three separate triad-based parts; this one is a single comping part built from bigger extended-chord grips, with fills woven into the same part rather than layered as a second part.

pivot-tone-lines.title: Pivot Tone Lines
pivot-tone-lines.html:
Part of Bebop Vocabulary (§3 Approach notes) and Chord-Tone Soloing — a fourth device in the enclosure/approach family, distinct from the three already documented (Enclosures Through the Scale's scale-mechanical sizing, Downbeat and Upbeat Enclosures's beat-driven sizing, and §2's four static enclosure shapes). Where those all frame or approach a single target note, a pivot tone repeats ("pedals") one note and uses it as a launch point to chromatically approach a second note — a two-note unit, not a single-note ornament. Also covers two spin-off devices from the same lesson: half-step approaches walked through an arpeggio, and the same approach vocabulary applied to chord shapes when comping.

The core device: pedal a tone, chromatically approach the next

  1. Pick a pivot tone (a chord tone you return to / repeat).
  2. From the pivot, move by half step to a second, target tone. That's the whole mechanism — a repeated note doing double duty as both a stable anchor and the approach note's launchpad.

On minor chords — 5th pivots to the 6th

Worked example: pedal the 5th of a minor chord, chromatically approach the 6th from below. Set up as a 2-5-1: that chromatically-approached 6th of the ii chord becomes the 3rd of the V7 chord a beat later, so the same pivot-tone shape that started as decoration on the ii chord resolves directly into V7's most important guide tone. Finish the phrase into the I chord using scales + enclosures (Enclosures Through the Scale / Bebop Vocabulary §2) for a complete worked 2-5-1 line. (general starting point: over Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, pedal A (5th of Dm7), chromatically approach B from below — B then reads as the 3rd of G7 the instant the chord changes underneath it.)

On major and dominant chords — root pivots to the 5th (both directions)

For major/dominant chords the pivot tone is usually the root, not the 5th:

  • Root → 5th, approached from the 3rd. Pivot on the root, then chromatically walk up from the chord's 3rd to its 5th. Worked in a blues line context — described as "quintessential" for the sound of jazz language.
  • The reverse: start on the 5th, walk down to the root (through the same territory the first shape covers ascending). Works over both blues (dominant) and major 2-5-1 contexts.

Both directions land the same core sound — treat them as one device played two ways, choose whichever direction fits the phrase's melodic contour in the moment.

scale-sequences-in-thirds.title: Scale Sequences in Thirds
scale-sequences-in-thirds.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Diatonic Modes. A classic diatonic-thirds ("broken thirds") scale sequence, taught by Daniel Seriff as a fix for the single most common intermediate-player problem: learning a scale and then only ever playing it straight up and down, which "doesn't sound like music." Skipping notes in a fixed pattern breaks the stepwise habit and is the on-ramp to sounding less scalar and more like real phrasing.

The pattern

Instead of running the scale 1-2-3-4-5-6-7, play it in overlapping broken thirds: land on a degree, skip up to the degree a third above it, then step back down to the note in between, then skip up a third from there, and so on — "skip a note, back a note, skip a note, back a note." Framed with scale-degree numbers so it transposes to any scale/key instantly (here, E Dorian: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 6 ♭7): ascending broken thirds run roughly 1→2→♭3, back to 2→4, ♭3→5, 4→6, 5→♭7, 6→(octave)1, ♭7→2… continuing the same skip/step-back shape up through the scale, then the same shape in reverse coming back down. (The exact number call-out in the transcript garbles partway through — auto-captions on rapid spoken numbers — but the shape is unambiguous and a tab is shown on-screen in the original video for the precise fingering.)

How to use it (the actual lesson, not just the drill)

  • Practice the mechanical sequence first to get it under your fingers — a few minutes is enough, don't over-drill it, because playing it straight through for a long stretch "starts to sound dull" by design.
  • Then immediately stop playing it verbatim. The real lesson (credited to teacher Tom Quayle): drilling a sequence exercise straight up-and-down doesn't transfer to real improvising if that's all you ever do with it — "you can't practice learning how to improvise better if you don't actually practice musical things." A scale sequence is a musical concept, but only if you practice it musically.
  • Grab small fragments of the pattern rather than the whole run — pull 3–5 notes out of the broken-thirds shape and drop them into a phrase in the groove/pocket over the backing track, instead of playing the complete ascending-then-descending sequence. This is where it stops sounding like an exercise and starts sounding like a solo.
  • Progression: isolate → drill for 1–5 minutes → immediately work it into material you already play. Treat the sequence as raw vocabulary to fold into existing licks/repertoire, not a standalone party trick.
secs: How to use it (the actual lesson, not just the drill)

hard-yet-effective-way-to-learn-the-fret.title: Hard, Yet Effective Way To Learn The fretboard
hard-yet-effective-way-to-learn-the-fret.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A demanding but high-payoff fretboard-mapping drill: climb the entire neck playing every diatonic triad of one key, low to high, as arpeggios starting on the 3rd, using two different shape families depending on which string carries the bass note.

Techniques

  • Prerequisite: know the key's diatonic chord-quality order (major-minor-minor-major-major-minor-diminished).
  • The drill: starting as low on the neck as possible without open strings, play the diatonic triads of one key in order, all the way up the fretboard as high as possible — as arpeggios (root-3rd-5th), specifically starting from the 3rd of each triad.
  • Two shape families: one set of major/minor/diminished shapes when the triad's bass note lands on the E, A, D, or B string; a different set when it lands on the G string.
  • Cadence: one key per day, all 12 keys, for 30 consecutive days.
  • Beginner entry point: run the drill in a single key (G recommended) until confident before adding more keys.
  • Instrument-agnostic: framed as applicable to any instrument, not guitar-specific.

Routed to

  • Triads as a Fretboard Map — added a ## From videos bullet describing this as a distinct full-neck triad-climbing drill, alongside the page's existing lick-relocation method.

cage-system-scale-shapes.title: CAGE System Scale Shapes
cage-system-scale-shapes.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. The CAGE system finds one chord in five places on the neck using the five open chord shapes C – A – G – E – D as movable/barred grips (e.g. a C chord fingered as a C-shape, then as an A-shape barre, then a G-shape barre, then an E-shape barre, then a D-shape barre, walking up the neck). This page is the scale layer on top of that chord map: instead of using the five CAGE grips to outline chord tones for fast-moving changes (that's Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes's job), it uses them as fixed anchor points for a pentatonic scale and a major scale, so a soloist can navigate the whole fretboard over one static key/chord rather than memorizing five disconnected scale boxes with no relationship to each other.

Finding the pentatonic scale from a CAGE root

Relative-minor-pentatonic shortcut: the major pentatonic scale over a chord is identical in pitch content to the minor pentatonic scale starting 3 frets below the major root on the low E string — e.g. C major pentatonic = A minor pentatonic (same five notes), so C major pentatonic can be played by finding the A minor pentatonic box shape 3 frets down from the C root. This is the standard relative-minor relationship, stated here as a fast on-the-fly way to locate the shape rather than counting scale degrees.

Technique 1 — map the pentatonic scale onto all five CAGE positions

For a given chord (worked example: C), find the pentatonic scale shape that sits at each of the five CAGE root positions (C-shape, A-shape, G-shape, E-shape, D-shape) — five pentatonic box shapes, each anchored to a different CAGE grip, covering the full neck. Practice sequence: drill each of the five shapes individually first, then start soloing within one position at a time, then work on connecting the five positions into one continuous line rather than treating them as isolated boxes — a solo built from stringing the five CAGE-anchored pentatonic positions together end to end. (general starting point: work through the shapes slowly at first — the demonstrated C-shape and A-shape positions are described as "a little bit tricky" — before soloing over them.)
secs: Finding the pentatonic scale from a CAGE root
Technique 1 — map the pentatonic scale onto all five CAGE positions

fretting-hand-finger-independence-drill.title: Fretting-Hand Finger Independence Drill
fretting-hand-finger-independence-drill.html:
BassBuzz's "Finger Fixer" exercise — a two-bar fretting-hand pattern built on the B minor scale shape, aimed squarely at beginner fretting-hand weak points: mixed-up notes, a weak ring finger, an even weaker pinky, and a fretting hand that "looks like a lost and undecided spider" from uncoordinated finger choices. Framed as the jump-start exercise of a three-exercise beginner routine (see String Crossing and Plucking Patterns for exercise two, Bass Note Muting Technique for exercise three) — this one builds finger strength/coordination to a level solid enough to tackle common beginner songs, and doubles as a plucking-hand wake-up since every fretted note still has to be plucked.

The pattern

Assumes the B minor scale shape is already known (taught in BassBuzz's own beginner course) — most of the fingerings below reuse fretting patterns from that shape rather than introducing new ones, so the exercise is really about coordination and strength, not new note-finding. See Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues for the general movable minor-scale shape and fingering this exercise draws on.

  • Bar 1: ring–pinky–index–ring–pinky–ring–middle–pinky.
  • Bar 2: ring–pinky–index–ring–pinky–index–ring (the "weird one" — an intentionally less-natural finger order than bar 1, there specifically to break rote-pattern autopilot).
  • Keep fingers low to the frets throughout — the fix that actually delivers the strength/accuracy payoff; fingers hovering high above the fretboard is the beginner default this exercise is designed to correct.
  • Bar 2's ring-finger curl-back is flagged as the hard part: the ring finger has to curl back rather than reach straight down, a motion most beginners haven't built yet. Isolate and slow down specifically at that finger if the rest of the bar is fine.

How to practice it

  • Slow the tempo to 50–75% of target speed, or isolate one bar at a time, before attempting the pattern at full speed and as a whole — don't force full-speed, both-bars playthroughs before the ring-finger curl and the finger order are separately solid.
  • Count-in 1-2-3-4 and play through; the exercise is short enough (two bars) to loop repeatedly inside a 10-minute session.

groove-and-microtiming.title: Groove and Microtiming
groove-and-microtiming.html:
Part of Music Theory → Rhythm and Groove. What the research actually says about why a beat makes people move — as opposed to what producer folklore says, which on two of these points is measurably wrong.

Written 2026-08-09 to back the RHY strand, which was the vault's thinnest theory subject relative to how central hip hop, trap and EDM are here. Every claim below is cited; where the evidence is contested, that's stated rather than smoothed over.

1. Groove peaks at medium syncopation — it's an inverted U

The single most actionable finding in the literature.

Witek et al. (2014) played listeners funk drum breaks across a range of syncopation levels and measured both wanting to move and pleasure. Both rise as syncopation increases — but only to a point. Past the optimum, more syncopation makes people want to move less and enjoy it less.

"Medium degrees of syncopation elicited the most desire to move and the most pleasure, particularly for participants who enjoy dancing to music."

The proposed mechanism is predictive: a fully straight pattern gives the brain nothing to fill in, and a wildly syncopated one gives it no stable meter to fill in against. Groove lives in the gap between the pulse you infer and the pattern you hear — big enough to be interesting, small enough that the pulse survives.

What this means at the desk:

  • If a beat feels stiff, the fix is more syncopation. If it feels busy and unmoving, the fix is less. Both are the same dial, and you're looking for the middle of it — not the maximum.
  • The dial is per-instrument. A straight kick under a syncopated hat pattern still lands mid-scale overall; that's why the combination works.
  • "Too syncopated to dance to" is a real, measurable phenomenon, not a taste complaint.
secs: 1. Groove peaks at medium syncopation — it's an inverted U

bass-pentatonic-riff-writing-recipe.title: Bass Pentatonic Riff-Writing Recipe
bass-pentatonic-riff-writing-recipe.html: BassBuzz's answer to a gap Bass Scale Shapes — Major, Minor, Pentatonic & Blues deliberately leaves open: that note teaches the five scale shapes (where the notes live on the neck), but knowing a shape doesn't automatically make someone able to write a good riff with it — running the analogy hard, learning the shapes is "buying a bunch of meat and veg with no recipe and expecting to be the Iron Chef." This note is the recipe half: a small, repeatable set of composition rules for turning five pentatonic notes into a riff that actually sounds intentional, plus the companion choice of which hand shape to play them in. Taught entirely through worked examples — a real riff first, then the same recipe steps used to fix a deliberately bad improvised riff on the spot, twice (once for minor pentatonic, once for major pentatonic).

root-fifth-bass-lines-and-the-3-step-sty.title: Root-Fifth Bass Lines and the 3-Step Style Rhythm Formula
root-fifth-bass-lines-and-the-3-step-sty.html: Root and fifth — no octave, no chromaticism — are, in BassBuzz's own framing, "the two most awesome notes on bass," and this note is the vault's dedicated home for why that's true (frequency-ratio physics, not just convention) plus a reusable three-step rhythm generator for making the same two notes sound like country, bossa nova, soul, or rock just by changing what rhythm they're played in. This is the prerequisite half of a two-video BassBuzz pair — Jamerson's Root-Fifth-Octave Exercise is the note for the fuller root-fifth-octave formula (plus chromatic approach walks and syncopation layered on top), and that video literally points back to this one ("check out my root-fifth video in the description"). Fill gap: the vault had root-fifth-octave (via Jamerson) and pentatonic riff-writing, but nothing distilling the plain two-note root-fifth interval on its own — its acoustic justification, or a style-adaptation method independent of any specific exercise.

pick-vs-fingers-on-bass-tone-and-techniq.title: Pick vs. Fingers on Bass — Tone and Technique Tradeoffs
pick-vs-fingers-on-bass-tone-and-techniq.html: There's no universal "punk uses a pick, jazz uses fingers" rule — the choice trades off tone character against technical ease on a riff-by-riff basis, illustrated across three worked examples pulled from one video's song-by-song commentary rather than stated as an abstract rule.

hammer-ons-and-pull-offs-bass.title: Hammer-Ons and Pull-Offs (Bass)
hammer-ons-and-pull-offs-bass.html:
Using the fretting hand alone to sound a note change, without a matching pluck from the picking hand — taught via a Green Day-style (Mike Dirnt) hooky bassline as the concrete example of why it's worth learning, not just how to execute it.

The mechanics

  • Hammer-on: strike the string firmly with a fretting-hand finger to sound a higher note than the one currently ringing, without plucking again.
  • Pull-off: as a fretting finger lifts off the string, pluck/flick it slightly on the way off so the lower note (an open string, or a finger still holding a lower fret) sounds — the release itself does the plucking, not the picking hand.
  • Net effect: the picking hand is freed from having to strike every single note change, which matters most in fast runs where alternating plucking can't physically keep pace with the note density.

Why bother — the tonal-variety argument, not just the speed argument

The video's actual pitch for this technique isn't "it's faster" (though it can be) — it's that hammered/pulled notes carry a slightly different tonal flavor than picked notes. A line that's 100% picked reads as more uniform/flat; mixing in hammer-ons and pull-offs against picked notes gives the line more textural variety. Concrete before/after demonstrated in the source video: the same riff played with only picked notes sounds noticeably plainer than the same riff with the hammer-ons/pull-offs restored — described as "it just sounds cooler, and it flows a lot better." Worth doing your own before/after A-B on a riff you're learning to hear this for yourself, the same ear-training move the video uses.

When it shows up

Common wherever a bassline needs to move quickly between adjacent or nearby frets without the picking hand's help — punk basslines built for speed and drive lean on it heavily (the source example is squarely in that pocket), but the technique isn't punk-specific; it's a general fretting-hand articulation tool anywhere a line needs more notes than the picking hand can cleanly strike, or needs deliberate tonal contrast between phrases.
secs: Why bother — the tonal-variety argument, not just the speed argument

improvisation-difficulty-ladder-pentaton.title: Improvisation Difficulty Ladder — Pentatonic to Coltrane Changes
improvisation-difficulty-ladder-pentaton.html:
A practice-sequencing framework: six stages of soloing harmony, each isolating exactly one new harmonic tool over a deliberately simple vamp before moving on. The ladder is organized by which harmonic tool unlocks the level, not by tempo or technical difficulty — a genuinely different axis from Positional CAGED Soloing with Matched Modes and Arpeggios (which is about neck coverage within one harmonic context) or 10 Hidden Soloing Mistakes and Constraint-Based Fixes (about phrasing constraints).

The ladder

Level Tool unlocked Vamp (worked example, key of B) Why this vamp
1 Minor pentatonic, one box shape only i–♭III (Bm–D) Bm and D share 2 of 3 tones — near-substitutes, so the harmony stays effectively static
2 Blues scale (pentatonic + ♭5), moved across positions i–iv (Bm–Em) The 1 and 4 chords of the key — blues progressions typically run 1–4–5
3 Major scale modes, applied modally i–♭VI (Bm–G) Bm/G again function as substitutes — a modal (one-chord-feel), not functional, progression
4 Mid-solo modulation ("bimodal harmony") i–♭VI shape shifted down a whole step mid-phrase (B→A) Forces a real key change inside one improvised line, not just between takes
5 Jazz changes — ii–V–I, m7♭5 A tune's real changes (worked over "Black Orpheus," transposed to Bm) Functional harmony with real cadential motion, swung 8ths
6 (bonus) Rapid, widely-spaced key changes "Giant Steps"-style changes, key center shifting roughly every 4 beats The extreme end — minimal overlapping notes between adjacent keys

How to use it

Each level should be practiced as its own isolated vamp before combining — the point is that levels 1–3 deliberately hold the harmony still (via substitute-chord vamps) so the only variable changing is the scale/mode being applied, then levels 4–6 introduce actual harmonic motion on top of an already-comfortable scale toolkit. Skipping straight to level 5 or 6 without having drilled the scale vocabulary in isolation first (levels 1–3) is the likely failure mode — same principle as Positional CAGED Soloing with Matched Modes and Arpeggios's point that new positions don't fix a chord-tone-targeting gap, more scales alone don't fix an unfamiliarity with functional harmony.

chord-quality-cycle-exercise.title: Chord Quality Cycle Exercise
chord-quality-cycle-exercise.html:
A single-root drill for internalizing how 7th-chord qualities relate to and transform into each other, and for training the ear to hear exactly which chord tone changes between neighboring qualities — distinct from practicing chords in the context of a key (see Chords by Key for that complementary approach).

The cycle

Six chord qualities, each one half-step-moving note away from its neighbor:

Major triad → Major 7 → Dominant 7 → Minor 7 → Half-diminished (m7♭5) → Fully diminished 7 — then reversed back down through the same sequence.

Each step moves exactly one note by exactly one half step:

  • Triad → maj7: root moves down a half step (to the major 7th)
  • maj7 → dom7: that same note moves down another half step (to the ♭7)
  • dom7 → m7: the 3rd moves down a half step (major 3rd → minor 3rd)
  • m7 → half-diminished: the 5th moves down a half step (natural 5 → ♭5)
  • half-diminished → dim7: the (already-flat) 7th moves down one more half step (♭7 → 𝄫7)

How to practice it

  1. Pick a root and a template shape — a major triad voicing rooted on the 6th, 5th, or 4th string (see Chord Voicings for the underlying shapes).
  2. Walk the cycle up, moving one note at a time between each chord quality, keeping every other note fixed.
  3. Walk it back down through the same sequence in reverse — deliberately harder, since the "which note moves" logic isn't as automatic in reverse.
  4. Repeat off all three string-root templates (6th, 5th, 4th string) for the same root.
  5. Repeat off every root, moved through the circle of fourths (C → F → B♭ → E♭ → A♭ → D♭ → G♭ → B → E → A → D → G) — full 12-key coverage.

Skip a shape entirely rather than forcing an uncomfortable stretch (especially relevant high on the neck or on instruments with less upper-fret reach) — there are three templates specifically so a cramped shape in one position can be dropped without losing key coverage.

Why it works

Practicing chords that exist together diatonically within a key (the complementary drill) doesn't put chord qualities directly next to each other for comparison — you don't have to locate which specific chord tone differs between two chords. Cycling through qualities off a single shared root forces exactly that: "minor 7 has to have a flat 3rd — where is that on this shape?" It's an ear-training and fretboard-relationship drill, not a harmony-in-context drill, and works best as a targeted tool for those specific goals rather than a daily-practice default.

drum-rack.title: Drum Rack
drum-rack.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's dedicated container/instrument rack for building drum kits, mapping one sample or instrument chain per MIDI note with per-pad routing, choke groups, and macros.

What it's used for

The standard way to build and play a multi-sample drum kit in Live — assembling kicks, snares, hats, and one-shots into a single playable instrument.

FX chain notes

Each pad is typically its own mini chain (sample/Simpler > EQ > compression); the whole rack often feeds a shared drum bus with glue compression and parallel saturation.

solo-dynamics-and-arc.title: Solo Dynamics and Arc
solo-dynamics-and-arc.html:
Part of Music Theory — the shape a solo travels over time, as distinct from Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch (note choice, touch, and phrasing vocabulary within a phrase) and Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction (how to extract reusable concepts from a transcribed solo). This note covers the arc-level decisions: when to climb, when to hold back, and how to land the plane at the end — the macro structure that makes a solo read as a story rather than a string of licks.

Building the arc — save the peak for the peak

  • Use a very wide range inside a single short phrase as a deliberate identity trait, not just a slow arc-level build. Distinct from the "slowly expand register" arc-level advice below — this is register used within one or two bars for its own sake: e.g. starting on a low root and climbing to a high note within the same bar, then repeating that wide-range move across several phrases in a solo, which reads as an immediately recognizable stylistic signature rather than a one-off effect. → 🎵 KURT ROSENWINKEL - Nefertiti (Ballad Session)
  • Slowly expand register rather than jumping straight to the highest note available. Walking up to a mid-register target (e.g. the 10th fret of the B string) first, then continuing to climb over subsequent phrases, tells a story of ascent — jumping immediately to the highest note in the position "shows your cards" too early and leaves nowhere further to go. (general starting point: treat register like a dynamic — spend it gradually, not all at once)
  • The high root note is a special-occasion note — save it for the actual climax of the solo, not an early phrase. If a position only offers one note that high (the octave-up root, in this case), hitting it early spends the solo's single biggest "wow" moment before the arc has built toward it. Reserve it for the last phrase or two, where it reads as the payoff rather than a preview.
  • "Getting into fifth and sixth gears" — deliberately keep something in reserve through the early/mid solo so there's a visible/audible gear change left for the end. Framed as the main thing separating a solo that "continues to engage" from one that peaks and plateaus.
  • Once you've peaked, don't come back down into the same register — after building into the higher frets, the instruction was explicit: transition up and stay there, rather than climbing and then immediately backing off, which undercuts the arc that was just built.
secs: Building the arc — save the peak for the peak

kurt-rosenwinkel-this-is-what-makes-his-.title: Kurt Rosenwinkel - This Is What Makes His Style Unique
kurt-rosenwinkel-this-is-what-makes-his-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen breaks down what makes Kurt Rosenwinkel's melodic language distinct, using four short excerpts from Rosenwinkel's guitar solo on "Nefertiti" (Wayne Shorter), taken from Mark Turner's album Ballad Session. Larsen frames the video around Rosenwinkel's melodic language specifically — not licks or vocabulary in isolation, but how the lines are constructed and how they relate to (or deliberately ignore) the underlying harmony — and folds in things Rosenwinkel himself said about practicing this in master classes Larsen attended as a student. Nefertiti is chosen deliberately: as a Wayne Shorter composition its chords are strongly melodic/atmospheric but not functionally connected in the standard ii-V-I sense, so a soloist can't lean on "the changes" the way you can over a functional tune — melody has to be its own organizing principle. The four excerpts each surface a different facet of the same underlying approach: (1) very wide range used inside a short phrase, (2) a melodic idea that keeps moving in one direction through a chord change rather than resetting at the barline, (3) large-interval, non-sequential lines built from stacked/adjacent arpeggios and diatonic triads rather than a single scale, and (4) tightly restrained motivic development — building a whole passage from a small pool of notes (an arpeggio) without it reading as an obvious "motif." The most valuable single idea in the video, and the one Larsen explicitly ties back to Rosenwinkel's own stated practice method, is the melody-first, changes-second mindset: decide the shape/direction the line wants to take, and treat moving through the chord changes as a constraint to solve underneath that shape rather than the thing generating the notes in the first place.

learn-charlie-parker-s-phrasing-secrets-.title: Learn Charlie Parker's Phrasing Secrets... with CONFIRMATION!
learn-charlie-parker-s-phrasing-secrets-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton's phrase-by-phrase deconstruction of Charlie Parker's head melody to "Confirmation" — a follow-up to an earlier Parker-melody video (not yet in the vault). Borton walks the A section and B section of the tune roughly in order, pulling out named, reusable devices from each phrase rather than treating the melody as a fixed thing to memorize: the 6th interval as a Parker signature, a minor ii–V lick built from a triad plus the 6th, blues language layered directly into bebop lines, guide-tone connective lines (♭9-down-to-root, 4th-resolving-to-3rd), a 4th→3rd tension-and-release device that then jumps to an altered tone, CESH (chromatic embellishment of static harmony) in the B section, and a couple of "closer" phrases Parker (and Borton) reach for to end a line. The video closes on a practice-methodology point that's as valuable as the licks themselves: build a "lick journal," categorize every extracted phrase by type (5–1 phrases, CESH phrases, altered phrases, etc.), and "plug and chug" them over different changes rather than leaving them tied to this one tune — plus a reminder that Parker's edge is as much about rhythm (not playing straight consistent eighth notes) as it is about note choice. Borton performs two short written etudes built from the lesson's own material — one over the first half of the A section partway through, one full chorus over the whole tune at the end — modeling the "write your own etude from the vocabulary" step he asks the viewer to do. Companion piece to Borton's other Parker-melody breakdowns and rhythm-changes/lick-connecting videos already in the vault (see Routed to).

continuous-scale-exercise.title: Continuous Scale Exercise
continuous-scale-exercise.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Modulation (Key Change) — a drilled improvisation method for tunes that change keys often (jazz standards especially): keep a scale running continuously and, right at the moment the harmony changes, find the physically closest correct note in the new key's scale and keep going in the same direction. The point isn't playing scales — it's rehearsing the split-second decision at each key change until it's reflexive, so real improvising over moving changes stops being a memorized path and becomes a live, in-the-moment choice.

Demonstrated over "Solar" (Miles Davis), worked out as five scale/key zones mapped as close together as possible in one fretboard position: 2 measures C melodic minor → 4 measures F major → 3 measures E♭ major → 2 measures D♭ major → 1 measure C harmonic minor (12 bars total, then the cycle repeats). The method generalizes to any tune with a known chord-scale map — Solar is just the vehicle. → 🎵 MILES DAVIS - Solar

Prerequisites (mapped out before this drill starts)

  1. Know the melody at a "service level" first — enough to recognize it and hum it, not a full transcription yet. Coming back to the melody after this drill (see Exercise 10 below) is where it clicks.
  2. Determine the scale for each chord/zone of the tune (sometimes more than one scale option exists for a chord — pick one).
  3. Position-map all the zones as close together as possible on the fretboard, ideally within a single 4-fret position, so changing key means finding the nearest note rather than jumping to a memorized shape somewhere else on the neck. On Solar, four of the five zones (C melodic minor, F major, E♭ major, C harmonic minor) sit in the same position; only D♭ major needs a small shift.
  4. Play each scale up and down in time, flawlessly, 10 times in a row, one at a time — a mastery gate before combining them. Skipping this and going straight to the key-change drilling below just papers over a shaky scale.
  5. Play the scales back-to-back in the tune's actual zone order (still out of time) to start hearing/feeling the progression's shape before adding the real-time constraint.
secs: Prerequisites (mapped out before this drill starts)

cassette.title: Cassette
cassette.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Wavesfactory

What it is

Wavesfactory's vintage cassette tape simulator — four modelled cassettes, Pro/Home/Micro deck characters, and six degradation knobs: erasures (HF loss from re-recording), spread (stereo→mono), stability (wow/flutter speed fluctuation), static and dynamic noise, and artifacts (HF dips + dropouts).

What it's used for

Adding lo-fi cassette warmth, saturation, and tape imperfection character to drums, vocals, bass, or a full mix bus.

FX chain notes

Used as a coloration/character stage, typically after the main mix chain when a deliberately degraded/vintage texture is wanted.

tonic-minor-soloing.title: Tonic Minor Soloing
tonic-minor-soloing.html:
Imply a momentary V7–i resolution inside a single static minor chord, instead of parking on minor pentatonic for the whole bar. A bebop-flavored alternative for any minor tune or minor-blues vamp — the Blues Form and Harmony § Minor blues rule that "the V frequently stays a dominant" gives the harmonic reason this works: a minor tonic and its own V7 are close enough in sound (they share the tonic-minor sixth-chord family below) that you can hint at both without the rhythm section ever playing the V chord.

The core sound: minor 6 / minor-major 7 as "tonic minor"

A static minor chord (i) can be voiced or implied as a minor 6 or minor-major 7 (m(maj7)) chord — both of these contain both the i chord and its own V7 chord's guide tones stacked together. That shared-tone relationship is what "tonic minor" means here: soloing lines that outline a minor 6/mM7 sound over the plain minor chord automatically flirt with the V7-of-i resolution without anyone changing the harmony.

  • B♭m6 = B♭ D♭ F G — contains G, which reads as the major 3rd of F7 (V7 of B♭ minor).
  • B♭ minor-major 7 = B♭ D♭ F A — contains A, the same F7 major-3rd relationship from a different extension.

Device 1 — a single outside note implying a quick 5–1

The cheapest version: land on one note foreign to the plain minor scale that happens to be the 3rd of the chord's own V7, then resolve it down a half step into a chord tone. The ear hears a compressed V7→i cadence even though nothing but the i chord is sounding.

  • Over E♭ minor, play D natural → E♭. D is not in E♭ minor (natural or harmonic), but it is the major 3rd of B♭7, the V7 of E♭ minor — so the ear hears an implied B♭7→E♭m resolution compressed into two notes.
  • Over B♭ minor, play A natural → B♭, by the identical logic: A is the major 3rd of F7, the V7 of B♭ minor.
  • General recipe, any minor key: find the major 3rd of the key's own V7 (a half step below the tonic) and resolve it down into the root (or another chord tone) — instant implied 5–1 over a chord that never actually moves.
secs: The core sound: minor 6 / minor-major 7 as "tonic minor"
Device 1 — a single outside note implying a quick 5–1

autumn-leaves-chords-5-useful-ways-to-un.title: Autumn Leaves Chords - 5 Useful ways to unlock Extensions
autumn-leaves-chords-5-useful-ways-to-un.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen builds a single teaching arc out of one 8-bar phrase — the first eight bars of Autumn Leaves (G minor: Cm7 – F7 – B♭maj7 – E♭maj7 – Aø7 – D7 – Gm(tonic) – G7) — playing it five times in a row, each pass adding more color than the last, so the same worked example doubles as a live demonstration of how to add extensions and alterations rather than just a list of finished voicings. Pass 1 is bare Drop 2 voicings on the top string set with zero extensions or alterations, establishing the "basics" everyone should have under their fingers before decorating anything. Passes 2–4 progressively add extensions by substituting root and/or 5th for a 9th/11th/13th while always keeping the 3rd and 7th intact (the guide tones that define quality and function), moving from one substituted note per chord to two. Pass 5 abandons functional voice-leading almost entirely in favor of a modal, sound-first approach — treating each chord as its own color to be maximized rather than a step in a progression that has to keep announcing itself — including inserting an extra ii-V that doesn't belong to the tune's own harmony and substituting a chord (Am9 for Aø7) that "really doesn't belong in G minor," on purpose. Larsen is explicit throughout about why each substitution works (which scale degree becomes which extension, why a given extension was avoided because it clashes with the tune's own melody or functional cadence), and repeatedly ties choices back to the parent scale each chord is drawn from (the tune's own G minor/G harmonic-minor material, or an altered/diminished scale layered on top for color). The video ends on the explicit point of the whole exercise: understanding the mechanics well enough to freely choose, on a chord-by-chord basis, how far to push a static harmony's color without losing the song underneath it — and knowing that Autumn Leaves stays recognizable even under heavy alteration, which is why he picked it as the demo tune.

soloing-over-changes-in-3-levels.title: Soloing Over Changes in 3 LEVELS!
soloing-over-changes-in-3-levels.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch plays a weekly organ-trio gig in Nashville and uses the band's regular tune — Ray Charles's slow blues "Hard Times" — as the vehicle for a layered teaching demo: three complete solos over the same progression, each one adding a harder layer of theory on top of the last, so the viewer can hear exactly what changes (and what stays the same) as the harmonic sophistication increases. Level 1 is a pentatonic-blues solo built entirely around phrasing/touch/dynamics rather than theory — mostly E♭ major pentatonic with deliberate dips into E♭ minor pentatonic at specific harmonic pressure points. Level 2 switches to full chord-tone/arpeggio outlining, using CAGED-adjacent arpeggio shapes kept in one small neck position and stitched together with chromatic connecting tones — explicitly presented as "chunk it, then connect the chunks." Level 3 layers in the altered scale (melodic minor's 7th mode) over three functioning-dominant spots in the form, taught from first principles (built as a dominant 7 shell — root/3rd/♭7 — plus four altered extensions: ♭9, ♯9, ♯11, ♭13) and always resolved onto a chord tone of the next chord. The most valuable framing is structural rather than any single lick: the same tune, the same solo skeleton, three levels of vocabulary — a genuinely reusable practice template for approaching any new tune first simply, then with chord-tone precision, then with outside color. Ruch flags a new tiered-solo-approach course coming with Brett Papa built on exactly this method, and the lesson's tabs/notation/backing track are Patreon-gated.

half-step-pentatonic-shift-over-moving-c.title: Half-Step Pentatonic Shift Over Moving Changes
half-step-pentatonic-shift-over-moving-c.html:
A lighter-weight sibling to Single-Note Pentatonic Substitutions Over Changes — that page swaps one note within a static pentatonic box as the chord changes; this page instead slides the whole box (or arpeggio shape) up a half step, timed to land exactly when the harmony itself moves up a half step. Worked over the Lady Bird changes, where — per Jens Larsen — "a lot of the harmony tends to move up" a half step repeatedly through the form, which is what makes the device recur so often in this particular tune.

The core move: pick the "color" pentatonic specifically because its relative sits one fret from where you're headed

Over Cmaj7, E minor pentatonic is a common "10th line" color choice (built off the major 7th's — or more precisely a third above the root's — relative minor). The reason it's chosen here, specifically, isn't just that it sounds good over the tonic: its relative, F minor pentatonic, sits exactly a half step up on the fretboard — which happens to be the next chord (Fm7). So the same movable pentatonic shape just slides one fret when the chord changes; there's no new box to learn, no arpeggio to switch to mid-phrase. The line keeps moving in its own logic (a half step up) rather than tracking the chord change note-for-note, which reads as a mild counterpoint against the bass — it doesn't sound like the melody is "just laying there" restating the harmony.

Generalizes beyond pentatonic boxes: half-step-planed arpeggios

The same device shows up in the source video as a half-step-up arpeggio plane, not just a pentatonic shift: over a B♭7-to-Cmaj7 move, playing a D♭ major 7 arpeggio (a half step above the target Cmaj7) resolves down cleanly onto the real chord. The stated mental model matters: even while playing notes that spell a D♭maj7 shape over a chord that isn't D♭, the player is still hearing/tracking the real underlying chord the whole time — the half-step-up shape is a melodic observation (an interval relationship that happens to produce good target notes), not a conscious reharmonization. This distinction is worth keeping explicit: you're not "thinking in D♭," you're borrowing D♭'s shape as a source of notes that resolve well.
secs: The core move: pick the "color" pentatonic specifically because its relative sits one fret from where you're headed

khs-reverser.title: kHs Reverser
khs-reverser.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Kilohearts

What it is

An audio-reversing snap-in that plays back a buffered chunk of audio backwards in real time.

What it's used for

Reverse-swell and reverse-crash effects (classic reverse cymbal/riser technique).

FX chain notes

Stacked in a Snap Heap chain, often combined with reverb for reverse-reverb swells.

Techniques

  • Reverse EVERY duplicated layer of a texture stack differently, not identically, so the copies read as distinct elements rather than one reversed sound repeated. Building a multi-layer metallic texture ("metal two"), five-plus duplicates of the same source each get reversed with a different point/length per layer ("different reverse puppies... just mess them up") — alongside one layer left phase-inverted and another patched with a pasted-in section — so no two duplicates sound alike going into the pitch-shifting pass. set-theory.title: Set Theory
set-theory.html:
Part of Music Theory → Twelve-Tone & Serialism. Roman-numeral analysis works great for tertial tonal harmony, but breaks down for atonal/serial music where chords aren't built from stacked 3rds and don't have functional roots. Set theory analyzes ANY combination of notes by their raw interval content instead.

Pitch-class set

Convert pitches to integers (C = 0, chromatically up through 11), strip duplicates and ignore octave (enharmonics and octaves don't matter), list what's left in brackets: e.g. [1,2,8].

Inversion

Flip a set upside-down mathematically: subtract each non-zero member from 12. [1,2,8] inverts to [11,10,4] → reduced/reordered, [4,10,11].

Normal form

The most compact ordering of a set — the rotation with the smallest total span, found by testing each rotation around a 12-pitch circle and picking the one that "wraps" the tightest.

Prime form

Take the more compact of (a) the set's own normal form, or (b) its inversion's normal form, then transpose it to start on 0. This is the canonical label for "what interval content does this set have" — independent of the actual pitches used, analogous to how a chord symbol is independent of which inversion is voiced.

Hanson analysis

Howard Hanson's system: order the six basic interval types from consonance to dissonance — P (perfect 4th/5th), M (major 3rd/minor 6th), N (major 2nd/minor 7th), S (minor 3rd/major 6th), D (minor 2nd/major 7th), T (tritone) — then list which appear in a set, with superscripts for duplicates. Example: [0,3,4,7] = PM²N²D.

Interval vector

A 6-slot count of how many of each interval class a set contains, in the fixed order (m2/M7, M2/m7, m3/M6, M3/m6, P4/P5, tritone). Example: [0,1,2,6] → interval vector (100011).

Forte numbers

Allen Forte catalogued every possible prime form with a unique ID (e.g. "3-5" — 3 notes, 5th unique 3-note prime form in his catalog). Sets that share an interval vector but have different prime forms get a "Z" suffix — e.g. 4-Z15 and 4-Z29 are both 4-note "all-interval tetrachords" sharing interval vector (1,1,1,1,1,1) despite being distinct sets.

chord-progressions-beginner-s-guide-part.title: Chord Progressions - Beginner's Guide - Part 4 (The Diatonic Secret)
chord-progressions-beginner-s-guide-part.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The payoff video of the series: builds the diatonic triads of a major scale by stacking every scale degree in 3rds (root, +1 scale step, +1 scale step) and shows the result is six usable chords plus one oddball (the vii° diminished chord, set aside for later). Names the qualities-per-degree pattern as a memorizable chant — Ma-mi-mi-Ma-Ma-mi-dim — and frames a chord progression as simply reordering those six diatonic chords. Content-wise this duplicates the "Major keys — the pattern" table on Chords by Key exactly, but the chant format is a genuinely useful memory device the vault didn't have in prose form, so it's worth adding as a quick-recall line.

What's taught

  • Build the diatonic triads of a scale by stacking every scale degree: take chord I (root, +4+3 half steps = major), then shift every note up to the next scale tone to get chord II, and so on through all 7 degrees. In C major: C Dm Em F G Am B°.
  • The universal major-key chord-quality pattern, as a chant: "Ma-mi-mi-Ma-Ma-mi-dim" — major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished, scale degrees I–VII, true in every major key with no exceptions. The I, IV, and V chords are always major; ii, iii, vi are always minor; vii is always diminished.
  • The vii° (diminished) chord is set aside deliberately as a "chord we'll come back to" — beginner framing to avoid overwhelming a first pass at diatonic harmony; it's covered properly in Diminished Chords already.
  • Chord progressions = reordering the six diatonic chords — no new theory beyond permutation; the video demos several manual reorderings (F–D–E–C, D–C–D–G, A–G–F–G) as examples of "just try an order and use your ear."

Routed to

  • Chords by Key — added the "Ma-mi-mi-Ma-Ma-mi-dim" mnemonic chant to the "Major keys — the pattern" section, next to the existing I·ii·iii·IV·V·vi·vii° table, as a quick-recall memory aid for the same information already tabulated there.

kenny-beats-making-trap-drums-more-inter.title: Kenny Beats - Making Trap Drums More Interesting
kenny-beats-making-trap-drums-more-inter.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Rapid-fire answers on dynamic trap drums: freakier/off-grid patterns, weirder percussion, multiple beat-sections (Sicko Mode), panning the auxiliary percussion, drum-drop arrangement, multiple bass sections per song — and the humbling artist-simplicity lesson (Lil Baby reacting to 5–7 sounds).

Techniques

  • Swing it, break the grid — freakier patterns, move hits off-grid, weirder perc sounds; "try stuff that's against the rules — sounds you'd assume won't work." → Hip Hop - Trap, Drums Group
  • Multiple sections, not one loop — Sicko Mode is "three different beats in one of the biggest songs of our generation"; give the drums sections that do different things. → Arrangement and Song Form
  • Pan the auxiliary percussion — keep trap kick/snare/808 center, but extra hi-hat rolls, open hats and percussion belong off-center; "a lot of people don't pan their drums — everything's right in the middle." → Width and Stereo, Drums Hats Group
  • Drum drops as arrangement — drop the claps for a section, drop kick+808 for a section, drop ALL drums at the end of a bar; programming interest = scheduled absence. → Arrangement and Song Form, Automation
  • Multiple BASS sections in one song — a "Mike Dean section" (big synth/Reese/live bass) vs an 808 section, or live bass playing between the 808 hits; the bass doesn't have to be one thing per song. → Digital Bass Track, Electric Bass DI Track, Hip Hop - Trap
  • Artists are the simplicity referee — Lil Baby reacted to just 5–7 sounds ("Smack the Baby"/"Toes" sessions stopped early); the extra perc layer matters less than you think when someone's waiting to perform. "Too busy is a relative term" — the performer is the best common denominator. → Hip Hop - Trap, session craft

Routed to

  • Hip Hop - Trap — patterns/sections/simplicity (From videos)
  • Arrangement and Song Form — sections + drum drops
  • Width and Stereo — aux-percussion panning
  • Drums Hats Group — pan/off-grid hats note

you-suck-at-drums-no-5-how-to-make-sick-.title: You Suck at Drums No. 5: How to make SICK House Drum Beats
you-suck-at-drums-no-5-how-to-make-sick-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Fifth lesson in the "You Suck at Drums" course, delivered entirely in-character as a parody frat-party DJ ("pre-game," "turn-up," "rage mode," "after-party" instead of Intro/A/B/Outro) — the comedic wrapper sits over the same energy-tier drum-loop method from episodes 2–4, applied to house. Underneath the bit, the actual demo is a clean example of building a four-section drum arrangement purely by layering in one new percussion element per section and progressively gating/shortening each new layer to control density, plus a passing mention of multiband compression as a drum-bus loudness/glue tool.

Techniques

  • House-genre application of the Intro→A→B→Outro energy-tier method — "pre-game" (Intro), "turn-up" (A), "rage mode" (B), and "after-party" (Outro) map directly onto the same 4-tier structure from earlier episodes: each section adds exactly one new percussion layer, building density progressively rather than jumping straight to a busy pattern. → Arrangement and Song Form (new bullet added this pass)
  • Gate/shorten each new layer as it's introduced, rather than leaving every hit at full length — several of the added percussion layers get switched to a shorter/gated envelope specifically when they're first layered in, so the density ramp reads as a build rather than everything just getting louder at once.
  • The outro should drop the harshest/newest layers first, not reset to the intro — the final section keeps a couple of the track's now-familiar core layers but removes the densest/most recently added ones, so it reads as a comedown from peak energy rather than a full return to the sparse opening.
  • Multiband compression on the full drum pattern as a loudness/glue tool — mentioned in passing as a way to make the stacked drum layers read louder and more cohesive together; no specific settings given (band splits, ratios, or crossover points), so this is a name-drop-with-a-stated-reason rather than a fully concrete recipe — noted here but not routed to a dedicated destination note since there's nothing settings-specific to capture.

Routed to

  • Arrangement and Song Form — house-genre application of the energy-tier method (new bullet added this pass).

drum-rudiments.title: Drum Rudiments
drum-rudiments.html:
The sticking vocabulary a real drummer builds fills and grooves out of — and, for a producer who never picks up sticks, the reason a programmed fill sounds programmed. A rudiment is a fixed pattern of which hand hits when; the rhythm is often unremarkable, and all the character comes from the hand order and the accents it forces.

Companion to Drum Notation (how these are written), Genre Drum Patterns (what genre plays what) and Rhythm and Groove (humanisation and ghost notes). The 18 rudiments below are the set printed on the vault's cheat-sheet poster — a working selection, not the full 40 PAS rudiments (the flam-drag family — flamacue, flam paradiddle, ratamacue, lesson 25 — is absent).

The one rule the poster teaches by layout

Every rudiment on the sheet is printed twice — once right-hand-lead, once left-hand-lead. That's the instruction: a rudiment you can only start with your strong hand is half-learned. The programming equivalent is that a fill should not always resolve with the same hand/sample landing on the downbeat — alternate which layer lands on the accent and the repetition stops reading as a loop.
secs: The one rule the poster teaches by layout

mosty-mixing-a-reggaeton-track.title: Mosty mixing a reggaeton track
mosty-mixing-a-reggaeton-track.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short Mix with the Masters screen-recording of reggaeton mixer/producer Mosty walking through his session-build order on a reggaeton track, focused almost entirely on the low end: why he starts every mix with the bass, how he tames a sine-wave bass's uneven note-to-note loudness with heavy compression, and — the video's real centerpiece — how he builds the dembow rhythm's "click" layer out of several generic, commonly-available percussion samples combined into a texture that reads as unique even though none of the individual sounds are. He closes with a parallel-kick-boost technique he says he learned years ago from another video: duplicate the kick channel, drive it hard through an aggressive plugin printed without dry/wet blending, boost around 60 Hz, double it for extra body, and fix the resulting phase clash between the layers. A brief closing aside notes a collaborator ("Sky") loosening the dembow pattern's strict grid feel using FL Studio's swing function.

Transcript confidence: low. The captions read as an auto-generated Spanish→English machine translation, not clean English — "sine wave" comes through as "Sainz Wave," "FL Studio" as "Fruit and Loops," and several plugin/technique references (an "Arabic" harmonics tool, "involution") are unrecoverable garble. No exact plugin names, dB, or Hz figures survive intact anywhere in the video; every setting below is described qualitatively per the depth standard's guidance for garbled transcripts, not quoted as a number.

break-plus-cadence-programming.title: Break-Plus-Cadence Programming
break-plus-cadence-programming.html:
Build one base break, then keep a small library of interchangeable one-bar endings for it — close each phrase with whichever ending fits the transition, instead of programming (or looping) one fixed break start to finish. This is the Hybrid Breaks technique from Pocket Operations (p.51–52): a "Hybrid Kick" base pattern printed once, followed by six alternate "ending" bars, each explicitly marked ↳ FOLLOW WITH… — play the base for however many bars the phrase needs, then land on any one of the six endings to punctuate it. Two more base+ending pairs (Hybrid 7, Hybrid 8) repeat the same idea in miniature, one base and one ending each.

It's the same "same loop, swap the tail" logic as the section-transition fills in Arrangement and Song Form, just packaged as a small reusable component library rather than a one-off fill you write fresh each time. The payoff is variation without extra composition: the base bar stays boring and repeatable (so the groove reads as consistent), and all the ear-interest comes from which tail you dock onto it.

Why this beats looping one break

A single break repeated for 8 or 16 bars gets predictable fast — the ear locks onto the pattern and stops paying attention. The usual fixes are either (a) hand-program a new fill every few bars, which is slow and inconsistent, or (b) rely on a break's own internal A/B/C/D lettered variants (like the Pocket Operations Amen Break A–D) and rotate through those. The Hybrid Breaks technique is a third option: decouple the base from the ending entirely, so you're not constrained to variants of one pattern — you can swap in whichever ending matches how hard the next section needs to hit, and reuse the same small ending library across completely different base breaks and different songs.

Practically, this also lowers the cost of arranging a section transition. Instead of asking "what fill do I write here," you're asking "which of my 6 pre-built endings fits" — a selection problem instead of a composition problem, which is faster mid-session and easier to keep consistent across a project.
secs: Why this beats looping one break

classic-breaks-reference.title: Classic Breaks Reference
classic-breaks-reference.html:
Four more real, widely-sampled breaks worth knowing by name and by pattern — not vocabulary to practise, just vocabulary to recognize, sample, or interpolate. These sit alongside the bigger-name breaks already documented on Genre Drum Patterns (Amen, Funky Drummer, When the Levee Breaks, Cold Sweat, Synthetic Substitution, Cissy Strut, Boom Bap, Planet Rock, Son Clave) — this note covers the four that were transcribed in Pocket Operations's curated table but not yet written up on their own. Step patterns below are verified against the book's actual page images (not just its text layer), one correction found and applied (see The Big Beat, below).

Every pattern is one bar, 16-step grid, given in raw step numbers (1–16) and in 16th-note beat position (1 e & a etc.), per the vault's usual counting convention (see Rhythm and Groove).

Impeach the President — The Honey Drippers (1973)

Pattern (Pocket Operations p.20 / PDF p.24): BD 1, 8, 9, 15 · SN 5, 13 · CH 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 13, 15 · OH 11.

In beat position: kick on 1, 2-a, 3, 4-and; snare on the standard 2 and 4; closed hat plays a steady 8th-note pattern (downbeat + "and" of every beat) but drops the "and" of 3 and picks up an extra push on the "a" of 2 instead. The open hat fills exactly the hole the closed hat leaves — it lands alone on the "and" of 3, right before the snare answers on 4. That hand-off from closed to open on the last upbeat before the backbeat is the pattern's signature move — a small hi-hat swing that gives the whole bar its bounce.

Origin. Released in 1973, the single is credited to "The Honey Drippers" but was really Roy C. Hammond (Roy C) working with a group of students from Jamaica High School in Queens, NY. The song's lyric target was Nixon during Watergate — a protest single, not a dance record, and it went nowhere commercially on release.

Why it recurs. The break itself — tight, hi-hat-forward, built around that late-bar open-hat lift — got a second life once early hip-hop DJs and compilers (it's a staple of the Ultimate Breaks & Beats series) started digging it out. Marley Marl is credited with cracking it open for hip-hop via MC Shan's "The Bridge" (1985), after which it became one of the most reused breaks in the genre — reporting varies, but it's commonly cited at 800+ tracks, with some estimates putting it as high as one in five hip-hop records containing it somewhere. LL Cool J, Ice Cube, 2Pac, Prince, Wu-Tang Clan and Janet Jackson are among the artists who've used it.
secs: Impeach the President — The Honey Drippers (1973)

60s-beatles.title: 60s - Beatles
60s-beatles.html: What makes it the genre: performance-forward recording with committed sounds — few mics, tape compression doing the glue, hard-panned mixes, harmony as arrangement, and every "effect" printed at the source. The limitations were the aesthetic; recreate the limitations, not just the EQ curve.

the-secret-of-ear-training.title: The Secret of Ear Training
the-secret-of-ear-training.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The earliest video in this batch (2022) and the origin point of Max Konyi's whole feeling-state ear-training philosophy — the seed that A Guided Tour of Musical Feeling, Essential Ear Training - Feeling the Minor Scale, and everything downstream of them build on. The central claim, stated as plainly as it ever gets across the channel: ear training isn't learning to recognize a note, chord, or scale as an abstract concept — it's learning to recognize the subjective feeling state that comes attached to it, and attaching a label (a number, a chord name) to that feeling after the fact. This video narrows to just one feeling state — the tonic — and lays out three escalating levels of practice for recognizing it, ending with two real-music drills using Konyi's own copyright-free production-stream tracks.

inverted-guitar-chords-guitar-chord-inve.title: Inverted Guitar Chords - Guitar chord inversions explained
inverted-guitar-chords-guitar-chord-inve.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A 2021 entry in Jared's ongoing "theory of harmony and chords on guitar" series, focused on a single distinction most guitar-inversion content skips: a chord shape that's technically an inversion (some chord tone other than the root under your fingers) is not automatically a functional inversion — that only happens when the bass note actually sounding underneath the whole piece of music is that chord tone. Play an "inverted" D shape while the bass player holds the root, and nothing has actually inverted; it's just a rootless-sounding voicing. The video works this distinction through six real-song/etude examples (Bob Dylan, Randy Newman/"You've Got a Friend in Me," The Beatles' "In My Life," a Stairway-style progression, "My Funny Valentine," and Carcassi's Etude in A), each demonstrated both with and without the inverted bass note so the ear can hear what the inversion actually buys — smoother, more singable, stepwise bass motion instead of chord-to-chord root jumps. Closes with the "neighbor IV chord" idea (keep the key's root under the bass when moving to IV) and an explicit reframe: guitarists mostly practice inversions as fingering shapes (jumping between a chord's inversion voicings while the bass, if any, ignores it), which is a genuinely different — and equally worthwhile — skill from writing/hearing functional inversions in real music.

find-the-key-of-any-song-in-30-seconds-b.title: Find the Key of Any Song in 30 Seconds (By Ear)
find-the-key-of-any-song-in-30-seconds-b.html:
