the-perfect-ear-training-routine.title: The Perfect Ear Training Routine
the-perfect-ear-training-routine.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Max Konyi lays out a complete, structured daily ear-training routine that touches all four core recognition skills in a single session, rather than drilling them in isolation. Where Scale Degree Ear Training and A Guided Tour of Musical Feeling teach what the feeling states are, this video is the practical how-to-practice companion — a repeatable sequence any session can follow, built around a chosen chord progression (own or borrowed) run through five escalating drills. This is the routine Transcribing and Playing by Ear's "daily practice routine" section is built directly from.

shifter.title: Shifter
shifter.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock pitch/frequency-shifting device, combining harmonic Pitch mode (musical, formant-preserving-ish octave/interval shifts) and inharmonic Frequency mode (a flat-Hz shift that detunes overtones — the classic "frequency shifter" metallic/dissonant character) in one device.

What it's used for

In Pitch mode, harmonizing/octave doubling; in Frequency mode, the dissonant, robotic, or spacey texture character that a true frequency shifter (as opposed to a pitch shifter) is known for.

FX chain notes

Inserted on a texture layer needing pitch-center movement without full pitch-correction; Frequency mode in particular reads as an atmosphere/texture tool rather than a tuning tool.

neo-soul-lo-fi.title: Neo-Soul - Lo-fi
neo-soul-lo-fi.html: What makes it the genre: human time-feel (behind-the-beat everything), warm degraded texture, extended harmony (7ths/9ths/11ths as the default), and the Rhodes as the harmonic center. Perfection is the enemy — the drag and the dirt ARE the style.

jazzy-lofi-hip-hop-beat-breakdown.title: Jazzy LoFi Hip-Hop - Beat Breakdown
jazzy-lofi-hip-hop-beat-breakdown.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Max Konyi's first-ever attempt at writing a lofi hip-hop beat (made in Studio One; all techniques below are DAW-agnostic and map onto Ableton), narrated as a genuine experiment rather than a formula — he'd never made one before, likes the genre as a listener, and wanted to see if he could land the feel from scratch. The result is one of the most concrete, plugin-specific breakdowns in this batch: a full RC-20 lofi-preset build module by module, a half-diminished-centered jazzy chord loop, a "fake harp" ornament technique (play a random gesture, conform the notes afterward), a Lydian-dominant decorative run, mod-wheel-driven clarinet realism, and a genuinely clever chord-tail crossfade trick for hiding a mid-ring chord change behind a kick hit. Strongly complementary to this vault's existing Neo-Soul - Lo-fi genre page — same pillars (loose drums, half-diminished/extended jazz harmony, RC-20 texture, sidechain-everything), extended here with concrete preset-level detail.

ian-kirkpatrick-new-rules-25-big-tips-in.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - New Rules (25 Big Tips in 13 Min)
ian-kirkpatrick-new-rules-25-big-tips-in.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The single densest New Rules session breakdown — Ian opens the actual Cubase project and walks every stem: the half-speed vocal trick, the layered percussion built from tapping a guitar and desk with the room-talk left in, the 8-layer main synth that starts life as a pitched 808 tom, the two-layer snare, the vocal chain (Auto-Tune-to-track then Melodyne everything), reverse-reverb hits, the pitched drumline fill, and the mix moves that went to the mixer. Threaded through it is his real thesis: pay attention to the reason behind each decision, not the settings, and manage the "rate of information" so you never over-feed the listener. This page is the master record; the individual moves fan out to the plugin/effect/technique/chain notes below.

ian-kirkpatrick-make-your-kick-stand-out.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Make Your Kick Stand Out
ian-kirkpatrick-make-your-kick-stand-out.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Short stream clip on why he splits the kick into separate layers (body vs transient): late in a dense song, when the transient stops poking through, you can raise just the transient to keep the kick present — instead of turning the whole kick up and unbalancing the low end.

Techniques

  • Split the kick into body + transient layers — with the transient on its own track, you can push its level independently. → Layering and Stacking, Kick Design, TRANSIENT Slot
  • Late-song move: raise the transient, not the kick — in a busy outro the transient gets buried; nudging just the transient layer up restores the kick's presence without adding low-end energy that would swamp the mix. → TRANSIENT Slot, Masking and Carving
  • Why it works — the ear locates the kick by its attack; preserving the transient keeps it "there" even when the sub is masked. → TRANSIENT Slot, SUB Slot

Routed to

  • Kick Design — split-kick / raise-the-transient (From videos)
  • Layering and Stacking — multi-layer kick
  • 1 Drums Kick Track — transient-layer level move

ian-kirkpatrick-new-rules-plucks-and-syn.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - New Rules Plucks and Synths Layers
ian-kirkpatrick-new-rules-plucks-and-syn.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Ian opens the New Rules project to show that the huge chorus synth is actually many separate synth layers printed and combined into one stem, and that his workflow is to print each synth and move on (so there's no live instance to recall). Names the sources (a "massive preset" that's just Brass, Sylenth, Kontakt-labelled prints) and re-confirms the "each layer has a job" principle — the bottom layer adds sustain/presence, and losing the attack layer bums him out.

Techniques

  • Print every synth, then reach for another — "I'd do a synth of something and then print it — I don't want to have an instance of that synth." Commit to audio, keep moving; this is why a final-project stem hides what was really done. → Layering and Stacking, Sampling and Sound Selection
  • The chorus synth = many layers combined to one stem — several synths (one sounds like Sylenth, one a "massive preset" that's just Brass, others he mislabeled "Kontakt") printed and merged. The listener hears one synth. → Layering and Stacking, BED Slot, LEAD Slot
  • Each layer's job: a bottom layer adds sustain / makes the notes more present; removing it loses the percussive attack and presence ("I'm bummed we lost that attack"). One layer's volume is automated. → Layering and Stacking, Automation, SUB Slot
  • Sylenth is still a go-to — "almost vintage software," still awesome; a recommended synth source. → Sound Selection Guide
  • The stem's processing: OTT (zero upward — "there was some purpose"), an image/width plugin (maybe from automating width once), LFO Tool at 65%, a brickwall limiter he doesn't remember adding. Audit-your-chain lesson again. → OTT, LFO Tool, Width and Stereo
  • The New Rules vocal chop is Emily & Caroline — the chopped vocal texture is his collaborators' voices (the same background-talkers gated into the percussion). → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths

Routed to

  • Layering and Stacking — print-each-synth, combine-to-one-stem, each-layer-a-job (From videos)
  • Sound Selection Guide — Sylenth as a go-to synth
  • OTT, LFO Tool — stem processing on the layered synth

ian-kirkpatrick-don-t-start-now-bassline.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Don't Start Now Bassline
ian-kirkpatrick-don-t-start-now-bassline.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

How the "Don't Start Now" bass — the song's disco engine — is actually built from three layers: a simple printed NI Scarbee bass patch (main note, but light on low end), a sine sub mixed under it for weight, and a separate "slap" layer from Trilian's Atmosphere patch. In the pre-chorus he swaps in a "big and clicky" Trilian sound to pull away from the pure-disco feel for a moment.

Techniques

  • Main bass = NI Scarbee (printed), but it lacks low end — the finger-bass character/note source, committed to audio; on its own it's thin. → Sound Selection Guide, 1 Electric Bass DI Track
  • Add a sine sub underneath for the low end — a plain sine layer tuned to the bass note fills SUB Slot that Scarbee doesn't cover. → SUB Slot, Bassline Writing, Layering and Stacking
  • The "slaps" are a separate patch — Trilian "Atmosphere" — the percussive slap articulation comes from a different Trilian patch layered in, not the main bass. → Sound Selection Guide, TRANSIENT Slot
  • Pre-chorus: a "big and clicky" Trilian sound to leave the disco — deliberately swap timbre in the pre to "go somewhere else" before the disco chorus returns. → Arrangement and Song Form

Routed to

  • Bassline Writing — layered disco bass (main + sine sub + slap)
  • Layering and Stacking — three-source bass
  • Sound Selection Guide — NI Scarbee / Trilian Atmosphere as bass sources
  • Plugin Wishlist — Spectrasonics Trilian, NI Scarbee (to vet)

stereo-field.title: Stereo Field
stereo-field.html:
Sound Palette is the vertical axis (frequency); this page is the horizontal (pan/width) and depth (front/back) axes. Layout and routing live on Session Layout. House workflow: mix in mono first — levels and phase get decided in mono; stereo is a reveal, not a crutch.

The mono-first workflow

  1. Utility → Mono on the master (or Stereo Tool for a correlation meter) from the first level balance.
  2. In mono, set all levels and fix all masking (Masking and Carving) — if the mix reads in mono, panning makes it better; if it doesn't, panning is hiding a problem.
  3. Phase pass in mono: anything doubled, layered, parallel-processed, or multi-mic'd gets checked here (below).
  4. Flip to stereo → pan per the slot map → width moves last, and every width move gets re-checked against the mono fold.
  5. The test forever after: A/B mono constantly. Elements that vanish in mono = phase problem, not a level problem.

Pan map (by Sound Palette slot)

Slot Pan/width rule
SUB Slot / BASS Slot Dead center, mono. No exceptions below ~120 Hz.
Kick + snare (TRANSIENT Slot) Center. Hats/percussion spread 20–50%, mirrored.
LEAD Slot (vocal/hook) Center. Its doubles/harmonies pan out (30–70%), never the lead itself.
BED Slot The widest thing in the mix — sides-heavy, soft center (double-track L/R or M/S shelf on sides).
MIDS Slot 30–60% off-center, opposing pairs (keys 40L ↔ gtr 40R) so the center stays clear for the vocal.
AIR Slot Wide but additive; shimmer/air can be 100% sides.
TEXTURE Slot Anywhere — mono texture off to one side reads "real"; wide texture eats the bed's contrast.
  • LCR bias: when unsure, hard-left / center / hard-right beats timid 15% pans — commitment reads as intent.
  • Arrangement first: two parts fighting for one pan position is the stereo version of a slot collision — move one.

kontakt-7.title: Kontakt 7
kontakt-7.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Native Instruments

What it is

The current version of Native Instruments' Kontakt sampler, with updated browsing, a modernized interface, and expanded scripting capabilities over older versions.

What it's used for

Same sampled-instrument playback role as Kontakt, with newer library compatibility.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source in a track's chain.

lophiile-how-i-made-paradise-by-bts-behi.title: Lophiile - How I Made Paradise by BTS (Behind the Beat)
lophiile-how-i-made-paradise-by-bts-behi.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Full track-by-track breakdown of BTS's "Paradise": started on a plane using the Suggester iOS app to build a chord progression (inspired by Ariana Grande's "True Love") and export MIDI, sped up + half-step up on MNEK's advice, topline written by MNEK, picked up by BTS a year later. The production lesson is layering: a custom Serum pluck ("Dusty" — character comes from the noise osc) doubled by sustained Keyscape chords, a two-layer bass (clicky "How About Now" tone + sub), Omnisphere organ with an opening filter, and a chorus built from deliberately weird Massive noise patches. Also a candid "old habits" segment on how his process changed.

sampler.title: Sampler
sampler.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's full-featured multi-sample instrument with layered zones, modulation, filters, and a dedicated built-in effects/LFO section — the deep-editing counterpart to Simpler.

What it's used for

Building velocity-layered and round-robin instruments from multi-sampled recordings (pianos, orchestral instruments, custom multisamples).

FX chain notes

Used as the primary instrument source when a patch needs zone/velocity layering that Simpler can't do; typically followed by standard mix-bus processing.

the-secrets-behind-oz-s-her-loss-product.title: the secrets behind OZ's 'her loss' production!?
the-secrets-behind-oz-s-her-loss-product.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short breakdown of the dark-synth trap style Ozzy (with Elias) uses on Drake & 21 Savage's Her Loss — analyzed through "No BS" but referencing "pop star" and "Rich Flex"/"3am on Glenwood" — followed by a from-scratch soulful-sample build and two ways to flip that sample into different beats. Two distinct halves: (1) recreating Ozzy's dark synth-melody + drum recipe, and (2) building and chopping a vintage-sounding sample the way you'd need to for the label's Soulful/boom-bap-leaning cuts. Auto-generated captions are reasonably clean for the spoken narration but garble a couple of plugin/preset names (flagged inline below) — treat those as low confidence.

eq-eight.title: EQ Eight
eq-eight.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's flagship 8-band parametric EQ with per-band filter types, a real-time spectrum analyzer, and mid/side or L/R channel processing.

What it's used for

General-purpose tonal shaping and surgical cuts on any track — the default first-call EQ in a stock Ableton mixing workflow before reaching for a third-party EQ.

FX chain notes

Usually the first EQ move on a channel (cutting mud/resonance) before compression, with a second EQ Eight instance post-compression for tonal balancing.

vocoder.title: Vocoder
vocoder.html:
Category: Pitch/Vocal Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock vocoder — a bank of tuned band-pass filters ("bands") that impose one signal's spectral envelope (the Modulator — internal noise, or an External carrier's audio) onto another, with Formant, Bandwidth, Depth, Release, and per-band Range controls, plus a Carrier section that can add a pitch-tracking oscillator underneath whatever's playing.

What it's used for

Far more than the classic "robot voice": a genuinely versatile texture and cleanup tool — subtle enhancement/de-washing on an already-decent sound, a pitch-tracking color oscillator, noise-into-texture design on drums/cymbals, external-carrier chord-driven "watery" pads and rhythms, and narrow-bandwidth "bloopy" modulator-mode sound design. The routing recipe (mute-bus send as carrier/modulator input) is what unlocks the chord-driven and drum-bus uses below.

FX chain notes

Insert directly on the signal being shaped (drums, a texture layer, a synth pad); for the chord-driven "watery" and constant-level-pad uses, route a pre-fader send to a muted bus as the External carrier/modulator input rather than trying to side-chain a track that's also being heard normally — see the routing recipe below.

duck-buddy.title: Duck_Buddy
duck-buddy.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live sidechain-ducking utility that applies gain reduction to a signal in response to a trigger source, without needing a full compressor.

What it's used for

Simple sidechain pumping effects (e.g. bass or pad ducking under the kick) without configuring a full compressor's sidechain routing.

FX chain notes

Inserted on the track to be ducked, triggered by a chosen source track.

Techniques

  • A "pumper" (sidechain-style ducking) run purely for vibe/breathing character on a background vocal texture layer, not for masking or level control. On a re-purposed background "effects vocal" part running throughout "Dancing With A Stranger": "we added a little pumper to it to give it a vibe, but it's verbed out... add a little pumper behind it, just added a little vibe to the song" — one stage of a chain also running channel-strip character (Scheps, unowned — see Plugin Wishlist), Solid Bus Comp, and reverb, each A/B'd against bypass. (qualitative only — no depth/length settings given, and the pump's trigger source isn't specified) → Solid Bus Comp, Vocal Stacks and Ad-libs, Sidechaining — Kevin Davis (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Vocals from 'Dancing With A Stranger' with Kevin Davis

Used in my chains

A MIDI-triggered ducking utility (Slynk, Max for Live) — draws a custom gain-reduction shape triggered by a MIDI note (not audio detection), so the duck is perfectly repeatable and clickless:

  • Digital Bass Track — the real-triggering alternative to Kickstart 2's tempo-sync: feed it the kick's MIDI so the bass ducks exactly on each kick, even when the pattern varies (vs. Kickstart's fixed sync, or Pro-C 2 external sidechain).

2-backup-vocals-group.title: 2 Backup Vocals Group
2-backup-vocals-group.html:
Role: Sums all backup/ad-lib tracks into one wide, controlled element that never steps on the lead.

Chain overview

Carve → glue harder than the main group → widen slightly → duck under the lead.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Carve

  • HPF the summed group again (150–200 Hz) · dip the lead's presence band (3–5 kHz) −1 to −2 dB.

2. Glue Compressor — Glue

  • Ratio 4:1 (②) · Attack 20 ms (③) · Release Auto (④) · Threshold set for 3 dB GR (① — read the GR meter, not the number) · Range 8 dB safety cap (⑥) · Makeup to match bypassed level (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦)
  • Why: Backups can take real bus compression (harder than the lead) — it fuses multiple takes into one solid block. 4:1 + 20 ms is firm enough to glue without killing consonant transients.

3. S1 Imager — Width

  • Width +15% (①) — slight increase; check mono compatibility (⑤)
  • Why: Backups live at the sides; the lead owns the center.

4. Pro-C 2 — Duck (sidechain from lead vocal)

  • External sidechain keyed from Main Vocal Track · 2:1 · 1–2 dB GR only when the lead sings · slow release
  • Why: Automatic priority — backups bloom in the gaps and tuck when the lead speaks.

Send FX

  • Backups feed the same shared vocal send bank as the mains (dialed on Main Vocal Group) — one delay/reverb space for every vocal lane. Backups typically run the delay hotter than the lead (throws + wetter tails are on-brand), sidechain-ducked to the lead → Sidechaining.
  • Ad-lib word throws are inserts, not sends — a dedicated throw track (loud EchoBoy, high-end cut, subdivision), per Backup Vocal Track §6. Cohesion → shared group send · moment → insert.

Variations

  • Call-and-response arrangements: skip the duck — the parts already alternate.
  • Huge hook stacks: swap S1 Imager push for Width Send so the width is blendable.

3-fx-bus.title: 3 FX Bus
3-fx-bus.html:
Role: Sums the sound-effect elements (Drums FX Track, risers, impacts, transitions, foley). Distinct from the send returns (Reverb Send Room etc.), which are shared spaces — this bus is for elements that ARE effects.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Containment

  • HPF 100–200 Hz and LPF ~12 kHz on the sum — FX get the mid window, the spectral edges belong to the music.

2. Glue Compressor — Tame

  • Ratio 4:1 (②) · Attack 10 ms (③ — fast-ish, grabs unpredictable spikes) · Release Auto (④) · Threshold for ~2.5 dB GR (①) · Makeup to unity (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦)
  • Why: FX elements (delays, risers, one-shots) are unpredictable by nature; a firm 4:1 with a fast attack keeps their collective level civilized so no single throw jumps out of the mix.

3. Pro-C 2 — Duck vs lead vocal

  • External sidechain from the lead vocal · 1–2 dB
  • Why: Ear candy should never cost a lyric. Ducking the whole FX lane under the vocal means you can be generous with candy and never mask the money.

Variations

  • Instrumental/EDM: re-key the duck from the lead synth instead.

fx-chain-system.title: FX Chain System
fx-chain-system.html:
The master reference for every FX chain in the template — the routing model, the theory behind chain order, the conventions every chain note follows, and the index of all chains. Built around the actual rig: Apollo MkII + UAD Console (Unison), Ableton Live Suite, the Plugin Index collection, Neumann TLM 102 + Shure SM57, Strat / Yamaha acoustic / Hofner bass.

The routing model

TRACK ──→ GROUP ──→ BUS ──→ MASTER
  │          │        │
  └──────── sends ────┘──→ RETURNS ─┬─ dedicated to one family ──→ that family's BUS
                                    └─ shared / mix-wide ───────→ MASTER

Division of labor — each level exists to answer a different question:

  • Track — "what does this sound like?" Corrective + character work on one source. The only level where surgery belongs.
  • Group — "how do these tracks relate to each other and to the other groups?" Carving, internal balance, section glue. (Steps 4–5 of the process.)
  • Bus — "what's the finish on this section?" Broad, gentle, analog-flavored: glue comp, tape, density. If you reach for surgery at bus level, the fix belongs upstream.
  • Returns/sends — shared spaces and parallel treatments (reverbs, delays, crush, dirt, width). Shared = coherent: everyone in the same room, one dirt flavor, blendable per-track via send levels.
  • Return routing rule: a return that serves ONE family routes into that family's bus (Delay Send Slap, Delay Send Other, Reverb Send Long → Vocal Bus) — the bus glue melts wet into dry, and a bus fader ride carries the space with the voice. A return shared mix-wide (Reverb Send Room, Saturation Send, Width Send, Parallel Comp Send) stays → master — folding it into any one bus would drag every other sender through that bus's chain. Handle shared returns at the return (band-limit, duck); the Master Chain is the only processing they pass through, and that's correct.
  • Master — the final 10%. ±1–2 dB moves only; two modes (mix-into-it vs export loudness) — see Master Chain.

clipgain.title: ClipGain
clipgain.html:

What it is

What it's used for

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

jo-oscilloscope.title: jo.Oscilloscope
jo-oscilloscope.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live metering device (by Max/MSP developer 'jo') that displays a real-time oscilloscope view of the audio waveform.

What it's used for

Visually inspecting waveform shape, clipping, and phase behavior during mixing.

FX chain notes

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

Key Parameters

image: Images/jo.Oscilloscope.jpg
coords: Images/jo.Oscilloscope.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

2-guitar-group.title: 2 Guitar Group
2-guitar-group.html:
Role: All guitars summed. The group stage decides how the guitar section sits against vocals, keys, and drums — per-guitar tone is already done on the tracks.

Chain overview

Carve → light glue. The most important guitar-group move is a cut for the vocal, not anything additive.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Section carve

  • Dip 2–4 kHz −1.5 to −3 dB where the lead vocal lives — use a dynamic node sidechained from the vocal so guitars only duck spectrally while the vocal is present
  • HPF the summed group 80–100 Hz — guitars don't need what the bass owns
  • Why: Guitars and vocals fight over the same midrange. Dynamic carving keeps full-bodied guitars in instrumental sections and clears the lane automatically when the singing starts.
  • Alt (often better): Soothe2 on this group, external sidechain = the lead vocal, soft mode, boost its band selection in the vocal's midrange — it dynamically ducks only the exact frequencies the vocal occupies moment-to-moment, and only in the mid channel if you set it that way. More surgical than one static/dynamic EQ node.

2. Glue Compressor — Section glue

  • Ratio 2:1 (②) · Attack 30 ms (③) · Release Auto (④) · Threshold for ~1.5 dB GR (①) · Makeup to unity (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦)
  • Why: Slow-attack, low-ratio bus compression makes separate guitar parts move as one section without killing strum transients — 30 ms leaves the pick attack intact so the section still sounds played, not pumped.

Diagnosis moves (before touching EQ)

  • The mute test: play the mix, mute the guitar group. Whatever suddenly gets clearer is what the guitars are masking — cut the guitars there. Bring them back louder than normal: whatever they bury tells you the other direction.
  • Spread the boosts: if multiple guitar layers all got the same "magic" boost (1k / 2.5k / 5k), they're fighting each other and the vocal — give each layer a different lane.
  • Pro trick: sidechain a touch of the snare's fundamental into the guitar group (1–2 dB, subtle) — the backbeat punches through a wall of guitars without anyone hearing the duck.

Variations

  • Guitar-driven song (guitars ARE the hook): skip the vocal dip, give guitars the presence lane, and carve the synths instead.
  • Panned wall (L/R doubles): check the group in mono — if the center collapses, back off any wideners on the tracks.

utility.title: Utility
utility.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock gain-staging and stereo-management device — width control, mono-below-frequency, phase invert, and DC offset removal in one simple utility.

What it's used for

Gain staging before/after other devices, correcting stereo width or phase issues, and mono-ing low end on bass and kick tracks.

FX chain notes

Commonly the first device on a channel (gain trim) and/or the last device before a bus (width/phase correction) — essentially a mix-hygiene tool, not a creative effect.

modern-pop.title: Modern Pop
modern-pop.html:
What makes it the genre: the lead vocal is the product — everything else is furniture arranged around it. Immaculate vocal chain, stacked hooks vs intimate verses, contrast as the master arrangement tool (every 8 bars something changes), and a polished loudness that still breathes.

The pillars

1. The vocal hierarchy (where the budget goes)

  • Lead: the full Main Vocal Track → Vocal Bus treatment, tuned invisible (retune 35–50, Humanize 100), compressed in stages, always the loudest thing.
  • Verse = intimate, chorus = enormous: verses mono-ish and dry, choruses bloom — doubles hard-panned in fours, harmonies inside them, Width Send automated up, long verb ducked under the dry voice. The chorus lift IS this contrast, not level.
  • Stacks tuned/timed tighter than the lead (Double Vocal Track editing rules); ad-lib answers panned wide.

2. Drums — punchy, tight, small-count

  • Few elements, each perfect: one kick, one snare/clap stack, one hat lane, maybe percs. Pop kicks are tight (sustain down), snares are layered (body + clap slap).
  • Four-on-floor for dance-pop (kick ducks everything — Kickstart 2 gentle); halftime borrowed from trap for urban-pop.
  • The 80s lane (Weeknd): gated-verb snare (Reverb Send Room send high + gate), analog synth bass instead of 808.

3. Bass — supportive, never competing

  • Synth bass or Hofner-clean: locked to the kick pocket, mids controlled, sub mono. Melodic fills only in vocal gaps (the McCartney rule).

4. Music — hooks in every register

  • Chords: diatonic + one borrowed chord for the "lift" · keys/synth beds M/S-carved out of the vocal's lane (Synth Bed Track) · one countermelody max at a time — pop is disciplined about who speaks when (Masking and Carving hierarchy strictly enforced).
  • Ear candy budget: risers/impacts/sweeps into every section (FX Bus, ducked under the vocal), one "signature sound" per song that recurs.

5. Mix presentation

  • Clean top (vocal air wins over hats), controlled low mids, wide sides/solid center (Width and Stereo).
  • Master −9 to −10 LUFS, limiter transparent, dynamics preserved between sections even when loud within them (Master Chain).

travis-scott-vocal-chain.title: Travis Scott Vocal Chain
travis-scott-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: hard-tuned voice as a synthesizer, drowned in space — the tune locked to zero, the voice dark and hooded, huge hall/plate behind it, delay throws and pitched ad-lib layers everywhere. Psychedelic rap: the effects are the arrangement. Signal source: U87-class condenser in his sessions — Neumann TLM 102. Delivery: melodic mumble, ad-libs performed with full commitment (they're half the record).

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — a little drive; his vocal reads warm-dark, not crisp
  2. UAD 1176LN — 4:1 fast, 3–4 dB (rap phrasing spikes hard)
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — low ATTEN @ 100 Hz, no air boost (dark on purpose)

Chain overview

Hard tune → dark EQ → heavy comp → saturate → the space. The intelligibility rules get inverted: the blur is the aesthetic; the dry/wet balance and the throws carry the drama.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Auto-Tune Pro — THE effect

  • Retune 0–10, Humanize 0, key set carefully (a wrong key note = full robot warble) · Classic mode algorithm for the harder snap
  • Flip Formant/Throat on ad-lib layers for character spread.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Dark shape

  • HPF 90–110 Hz · shelf DOWN the top slightly (−1–2 dB above 8–10 kHz) — the hooded quality; presence lives 2–4 kHz, not in air · cut 400–600 boxiness.

3. Pro-C 2 — Flatten

  • 4:1–6:1 · 4–6 dB GR — modern rap density; dynamics come from arrangement, not the voice.

4. Saturn 2 or Decapitator — Density

  • Tube, medium drive, mix ~30–40% — thickens the tuned tone into that synthy sustain.

5. Pro-DS — De-ess firm.

Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is the Travis part)

  • The big verb: ValhallaVintageVerb or ValhallaPlate — decay 2.5–4.5 s, pre-delay 20–40 ms, send/return (never insert), HPF'd return, ducked hard from the dry vocal — huge behind him, clear when he speaks.
  • Throws: Delay Send Other 1/4 (and 1/4T) ping-pong, automated onto line-end words, feedback 30–50% — throws answer in the reverb, so they smear into the hall.
  • Ad-lib layers: Little AlterBoy pitch/formant shifted (±3–5 semis, or octave), panned wide, drenched wetter than the lead — the crowd of hims ("it's lit!" energy).
  • Width Send on hook stacks · Reverb Send Room barely used — this aesthetic skips "natural."
secs: Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is the Travis part)

charli-xcx-vocal-chain.title: Charli XCX Vocal Chain
charli-xcx-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: the voice as plastic — hard Auto-Tune worn as jewelry ("I drink and I smoke and I use Auto-Tune"), distortion for attitude, formant shifting as an expressive tool (A.G. Cook shifts formants to make lines read younger/older without pitch change), all presented bone-dry and abrasively upfront over minimalist club production punctuated by abrupt silences. Signal source: Neumann TLM 102 close and confident — delivery is spoken-bratty as much as sung; attitude over accuracy (Auto-Tune will handle accuracy anyway).

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — driven a little (the edge starts here)
  2. UAD 1176LN — 4:1 fast, 3–4 dB
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — bypass

Chain overview

Hard tune → formant play → crush → distort → dry presentation. Brat-era vocals are more processed than Travis but less spacious — the effects are on the voice itself, not the room around it.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Auto-Tune Pro — Jewelry-grade tune

  • Retune 0, Humanize 0, Classic algorithm — the snap is celebrated. Automate key/scale changes for deliberate warble moments.

2. Little AlterBoy — Formant character (the A.G. Cook move)

  • Formant ±2–4 (pitch untouched): up = brattier/younger, down = darker/detached — automate it per section or per line ("Everything is romantic" style). Print bold choices as separate takes/layers.

3. Pro-C 2 — Flatten hard

  • 6:1, 5–8 dB — zero dynamics; the voice becomes a synth stab.

4. Decapitator — The attitude

  • Style E, Drive 4–6, Mix 40–60%, Punish for the shouted lines — audible, unapologetic distortion (this is an insert, not a send — the dirt IS the tone).

5. Pro-Q 4 — Bright plastic finish

  • HPF 100–120 · presence 3–5 kHz forward · air up — hyperpop vocals are bright to the point of glassy (opposite of the Travis hood).

Step 3 — Effects (dry, then extreme — no middle)

  • Default state: dry, center, loud. The minimalism (A.G. Cook mutes everything, leaves silences) makes the dry voice enormous.
  • The extremes, automated in for single words/bars: pitch-throw an entire line ±12 (Little AlterBoy), Delay Send Other feedback spikes into self-oscillation as transitions, one sudden cavernous Reverb Send Long word, stutter/retrigger edits (chop the audio itself).
  • Stacks: unison clones (same take duplicated with different formant/distortion settings) rather than re-sung doubles — the clone aesthetic, deliberately inhuman.
secs: Step 3 — Effects (dry, then extreme — no middle)

dance-pop-dua-lipa-charli-xcx.title: Dance Pop (Dua Lipa, Charli XCX)
dance-pop-dua-lipa-charli-xcx.html:
What makes it the genre: pop songwriting welded to club engineering — a four-on-floor (or electro) engine under radio structure, the vocal as a rhythm instrument, and production that's danceable at 2 AM but hooky in the car. Two poles: nu-disco polish (Dua) and brat-club abrasion (Charli); most tracks live on the line between them.

Pole A — Nu-Disco / Disco-Pop (the Dua lane)

  1. The rhythm section is 1979 with 2020s low end: four-on-floor kick + real-feel disco groove — octave-bouncing bassline (live-played or Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer), tight funk guitar chanks (Electric Guitar DI Track clean-funk variation, panned, dry), strings/brass stabs as hooks.
  2. The pocket is played, not just ducked: the bass avoids the kick (offbeat octave pattern) so sidechain stays light (Kickstart 2 shallow) — bounce over pump.
  3. Percussion layers: open hat on the offbeat (the disco engine), congas/tambourine loops low in the mix, big clap+snare stack (Drums Hats Group doing real work).
  4. Vocal: Dua Lipa Vocal Chain — smooth opto power, low-mids soothed, rhythmic consonants, chorus stacks hard-panned. Everything serves the groove grid.
  5. Arrangement: pre-chorus lifts (filter opens, stack widens), post-chorus instrumental hook (the "Don't Start Now" bass moment), disco strings answering vocal lines.
  6. Mix: bright, punchy, controlled — Modern Pop presentation over House - EDM energy management. Master −8 to −9 LUFS.
secs: Pole A — Nu-Disco / Disco-Pop (the Dua lane)

psych-pop-tame-impala.title: Psych-Pop (Tame Impala)
psych-pop-tame-impala.html: What makes it the genre: everything is slightly wrong on purpose — pumping over-compression, tape wobble, effects in the "wrong" order, brutal instruments under a soft, buried voice. Kevin Parker's formula: 60s psych sonics + modern pop/hip-hop rhythm section + one-man-band layering. The dreaminess is engineered, not vibes.

1-drums-fx-track.title: 1 Drums FX Track
1-drums-fx-track.html:
Role: Sweeps, impacts, risers, reverses, foley percussion — drum-adjacent ear candy. Routes to the FX Bus, not the drums bus: these are texture, not groove — they shouldn't hit the drum-bus compressor and make it pump.

Chain philosophy: fit → character → tame.

1 — Sound Selection

  • Selection IS the recording step — audition in XO / pack browser. Human-touch sources beat stock sweeps: 🎬 Disclosure use Splice acapella vocal shouts + a white-noise sweep as impact tools, and self-recorded tambourines at different speeds (varispeed) that lock when pitched together — Never Enough → Sampling and Sound Selection.
  • 🎬 Layer many small risers instead of one Splice riser — a freq-mod build + delay build + filtered clap-verb + two tambourines drifting in early, all cresting together — Disclosure, Never Enough.

2 — Programming Best Practice

  • FX earn their place at section boundaries — risers into drops, impacts on downbeats, reverses as pre-echoes. One per transition; more = noise.
  • 🎬 "Sneaky stuff": heavily distorted, near-silent accent layers under loud kick/snare, pumped hard by the sidechain so you never consciously hear them — "all they do is bring out the hi-hat." Texture you feel, not hear — Disclosure, Making Beats + Talk → TEXTURE Slot.

3 — Source → Ableton (UAD front end)

Rarely needed — texture wants character, not fidelity. If a sample is sterile: UAD Neve 1073 driven harder than usual → print. (The Sony TC-630 loop is the better sterile-fix for this lane.)

4 — Ableton Initial Processing

1. Pro-Q 4 — Fit

  • HPF aggressively (usually 100–300 Hz — FX rarely deserve low end) · LPF if the element fights vocal air
  • Why: Ear candy earns its place at the spectral edges; full-range FX mask the money elements.

2. RC-20 Retro Color — Character

  • Any flavor that separates it from the clean kit — texture is the point. (Hardware lane: Sony TC-630; Kenny's Generation Loss pedal is this same job — Guitar Recording Process.)

3. Pro-C 2 — Tame

  • Fast catch of unpredictable peaks (impacts/risers vary wildly) · 2–4 dB GR.

ian-kirkpatrick-hiding-synths-in-vocals.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals
ian-kirkpatrick-hiding-synths-in-vocals.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

30-second clip of Ian's current obsession: hiding synths behind vocals to make a single word stand out. He wanted one word to pop; his first instinct was a reverb throw, but instead he put a synth playing the same note behind the word, mixed loud enough to feel but low enough that "you don't even know." The signature move behind a lot of his pop candy.

Techniques

  • Synth-behind-the-word instead of a reverb throw — to make a lyric word stand out, layer a synth on that note underneath it; loud enough to register subconsciously, hidden enough that the listener can't name it. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals (pt 2)
  • He deliberately rejected the reverb throw — "that sounded cool, but what if I put a synth behind it" — the hidden synth reads as excitement without the wash of a throw pulling the word back in space. → Reverb, Depth and Space

Routed to

  • Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — the hidden-synth technique (created, primary home)

ian-kirkpatrick-hiding-synths-in-vocals-.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals (pt 2)
ian-kirkpatrick-hiding-synths-in-vocals-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Part 2 of the hidden-synth idea, with the actual method: build the synth patch out of the vocal word itself. He drags the word "move" into PadShop (the granular synth) and makes a patch so the pad sounds like the "ooh" of move; then does the same for "me." The synth is literally the vowel of the word, so it fuses invisibly under the vocal.

Techniques

  • Make a PadShop patch from the vocal word — drag the sung word ("move," "me") into PadShop's granular engine, build a pad from it, and play the note under the word. Because the patch is the vowel, it accentuates the word without sounding like a separate synth. → PadShop, Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Pitch and Formant
  • A fun way to accentuate specific words — pick the one or two words you want to lift and hide a matched-timbre synth under each. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Ian Kirkpatrick - Hiding Synths In Vocals

Routed to

  • Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — PadShop-from-the-word method
  • PadShop — plugin technique (wishlist/owned check)

padshop.title: PadShop
padshop.html:
Category: Granular / Wavetable Synth Vendor: Steinberg

What it is

Steinberg's granular synthesizer. Loads any sample and plays it back as clouds of grains — you control grain length, count, position, and randomization to turn a sound into an evolving, playable instrument. Runs as a VST outside Cubase (confirmed available in Ableton), which matters because it's the engine behind several of Ian Kirkpatrick's signature moves.

What it's used for

The go-to for hiding synths in vocals and for granular ear-candy — turning a spoken word, an acapella, or a percussion hit into a pad, a crash, or a subliminal texture that fuses with the vocal.

Techniques

  • Hide a synth behind a vocal word — make the patch from the word — drag the sung word ("move," "me") into PadShop and build a pad from it; the pad becomes the vowel ("ooh"/"ee"), so playing the note under the word accentuates it without sounding like a separate synth. Record PadShop's live output (don't print a patch) so every key gives different random grains — "10 minutes of noodling → a quarter-second I use." → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — Ian Kirkpatrick, Hiding Synths pt 2 / Charli Vocal FX
  • The "explosion" crash — drop an acapella in, grab a ~32 ms grain; 0% random loops that spot; duration stacks 2/3/4 loops; turn random up and after each loop it jumps to a new position, fanning into a stereo cloud "explosion of all the vocals." A cymbal/impact replacement. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Stereo Field — Ian Kirkpatrick, Ear Candy Adventures
  • Playable instrument from percussion — load percussive/drum samples; randomized grain + spread + a slight glide makes each key an interesting new sound. → Sampling and Sound Selection — Ian Kirkpatrick, Produce a Track pt2
  • Rhythmic tempo-agitator — a PadShop layer fed by a vocal adds rhythm/motion to a slow half-time track. → Arrangement and Song Form — Ian Kirkpatrick, Move Me Synths

ian-kirkpatrick-creating-vocal-fx-vocals.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Creating Vocal FX (VocalSynth 2)
ian-kirkpatrick-creating-vocal-fx-vocals.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

One-minute Splice clip: Ian's favorite "unorthodox" use of iZotope VocalSynth 2 — sidechain mode, where an external signal modulates the vocal. He sends a synth loop into VocalSynth's sidechain input so the synth's spectrum shapes the vocal, producing "combinations of sounds that don't exist anywhere."

Techniques

  • VocalSynth 2 sidechain mode — instead of the vocal driving the effect, route a separate synth (or drum) loop into VocalSynth's sidechain so it modulates the vocal. Talk-box / vocoder-adjacent territory but far weirder. → Ear Candy and Hiding Synths, Modulation
  • Pick a synth loop with strong character — the modulator's timbre defines the result; he found a synth loop he liked first, then fed it in. → Sound Selection Guide
  • VocalSynth is unowned in Ableton land — the behavior (external-signal-modulates-vocal) can be approximated with Ableton Vocoder (external modulator) or a talk-box style rack; the specific plugin goes to the wishlist. → Plugin Wishlist

Routed to

  • Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — sidechain-mode vocal modulation
  • Plugin Wishlist — iZotope VocalSynth 2 (to vet)

ian-kirkpatrick-pitch-shifted-vocals-voc.title: Ian Kirkpatrick - Pitch Shifted Vocals (VocalSynth 2)
ian-kirkpatrick-pitch-shifted-vocals-voc.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Splice clip: using VocalSynth 2 to add a lower octave to a vocal. Ian drops VocalSynth on a vocal, sets it to auto mode, and turns on Compuvox to generate an octave-down layer — a fast way to fatten a vocal or reach notes the singer can't hit. He also names Polyvox / Biovox for the low or high octave.

Techniques

  • Add a lower octave with Compuvox (auto mode) — instant octave-down doubling to thicken a thin vocal, or to imply a low note the vocalist didn't sing. → Pitch and Formant, Ear Candy and Hiding Synths
  • Polyvox / Biovox for the octave layers — reach for these VocalSynth modules when you want a low octave for weight or a high octave for shimmer. → Pitch and Formant
  • Use it as a "twist," not the whole vocal — a supporting octave to add interest on a section, blended under the real take. → Layering and Stacking
  • Ableton equivalent — an octave-down double can be done with a Pitch/Shifter rack or Little AlterBoy (formant + pitch) since VocalSynth isn't owned. → Little AlterBoy, Plugin Wishlist

Routed to

  • Pitch and Formant — octave-doubling a vocal (From videos)
  • Ear Candy and Hiding Synths — octave-layer twist

reverb.title: Reverb
reverb.html:
General best practice for reverb — space, depth, and creative sends. Specific tools: the ValhallaVintageVerb family, Reverb (Ableton), Ozone 9 tools. See also Depth and Space, Delay.

What it is

Putting sounds in a room — or in an impossible space — to set depth, glue, and mood.

Owned (first-call)

ValhallaVintageVerb · ValhallaRoom · ValhallaPlate · ValhallaShimmer · Reverb (Ableton) · Hybrid Reverb (Ableton, convolution + algorithmic) · Spectral Blur (Ableton Creative Extensions, clear ambient freeze) · Ozone 9 Low End Focus (for tightening verb lows via EQ)

collision.title: Collision
collision.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's physical modeling synth for mallet, string, and membrane percussion instruments (a Native Instruments Reaktor-derived engine licensed to Ableton).

What it's used for

Bells, mallets, plucked/struck percussive tones, and hybrid percussive instruments — often layered under drum samples or used melodically for tuned percussion.

FX chain notes

Sits at the top of an instrument chain; commonly routed through a short reverb/delay send and a transient-shaping compressor when used as a drum layer.

massive.title: Massive
massive.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: Native Instruments

What it is

Native Instruments' classic wavetable synthesizer, known for aggressive, modern EDM/dubstep-style bass and lead sounds.

What it's used for

Growling basses, aggressive leads, and classic 2010s-EDM-style wavetable sound design.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, often followed by saturation and multiband processing to control its aggressive harmonic content.

Techniques

  • One-osc/one-filter bed patch recipe — smooth square wavetable with bend +/- for an old-school analog-ish saw → low-pass with an opening envelope → unison stack in the Voicing tab (Restart via Gate on) → white noise low for hiss → copy the filter envelope onto the amp → subtle LFO on pitch for drift. His philosophy: complexity comes from the chords, not the patch — Lophiile, Sound Design With a Musical Mindset
  • Combo-macro patches ("RnB Twinkles") — build one macro that opens the filter AND raises reverb together, then automate just that macro over a simple line for an expressive bridge layer; also his "machine plucks" = simple patch + harsh noise layer for deliberate weirdness in a chorus stack — Lophiile, How I Made Paradise by BTS

limiter.title: Limiter
limiter.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's brickwall peak limiter, used to catch transients and prevent clipping without complex mastering controls.

What it's used for

Final safety limiting on a track or the master bus, and quick loudness maximization during mixing/rough mastering.

FX chain notes

Always the last device in a chain — placed after all EQ, compression, and saturation to catch peaks before output.

Techniques

  • A dry kick+808 print with only a stock Limiter on top can beat sidechain, EQ, or phase-alignment for resolving their clash — compared head-to-head against five other kick/808-clash fixes, the plain-limiter-only version was the preferred result: no ducking or carving at all, the limiter alone absorbs the collision. Worth trying before reaching for a dedicated sidechain chain. → Sidechaining, Kick Design — Oliver (Sol State), Oliver ENDS The "Sidechain Your 808" Debate

Used in my chains

Ableton's stock brickwall limiter — a transparent peak ceiling (vs. kHs Clipper's transient shave or Pro-L 2's deeper control):

  • Digital Bass Track — long sliding 808s (trap): at the end of the chain to pin the 808's sustain to a fixed ceiling (glide lives on the instrument, not the chain).

Key Parameters

② Ceiling Maximum output level (the brickwall) Set to your headroom target (−0.3 to −1 dBTP for masters) —

ghz-faraday-limiter-3.title: Ghz Faraday Limiter 3
ghz-faraday-limiter-3.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: Goodhertz

What it is

Goodhertz's Faraday Limiter, a transparent brickwall limiter designed for clean, artifact-free peak control.

What it's used for

Clean peak limiting on tracks, busses, or masters where a neutral limiting character is wanted.

FX chain notes

The last device in a chain, catching peaks after all other processing.

saturation-send.title: Saturation Send
saturation-send.html:
Role: Parallel dirt — a filthy copy blended under clean sources for density and attitude. Same parallel logic as Parallel Comp Send: keep the clean signal intact, add controlled wreckage underneath.

Why parallel instead of insert saturation: an insert saturator has one drive knob per source; a saturation send gives every track a blendable dirt knob (the send level) into one consistent flavor — and the dirt can be EQ'd separately from the source.

Signal chain

1. Decapitator — The dirt

  • Style E (① — Chandler/EMI TG, aggressive but keeps low-end weight + airy top; the parallel-attitude default) · Drive 6.0 (② — genuinely dirty; subtle defeats the purpose on a parallel path) · Low Cut 150 Hz (⑥ — keep flabby lows out of the saturation circuit) · Tone slightly Bright, ~1 o'clock (⑦) · High Cut 10 kHz (⑧ — tame fizz at the source) · Thump off · Steep off · Auto on (⑩ — output stays level-matched) · Mix 100% (⑪ — the send level is the parallel blend, so the plugin runs full wet)
  • Punish (③): off by default — punch it in for a hook / rap-verse attitude moment, then print the result. Alt Style P (Culture Vulture pentode) for thicker, odd-harmonic grit.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Shape the dirt

  • HPF 200–300 Hz (saturated lows = instant mud) · LPF 6–8 kHz (fizz control)
  • Why: Mid-focused distortion is what reads as "attitude"; full-range distortion reads as "broken."

Usage

  • Lead vocal: blend under for hooks/rap verses — density that EQ can't buy.
  • Bass: parallel grit lets the Hofner keep its clean low end while the mids snarl.
  • Snare/full drums: an alternative flavor to the 1176 crush — try both, pick per song.

Variations

  • Lo-fi flavor: swap Decapitator for RC-20 Retro Color (adds wobble/noise, not just drive).
  • Tape flavor: Kramer Tape slammed (input hot) — softer, rounder dirt for the Beatles lane.

ozone-9-vintage-compressor.html:

Ozone 9's vintage-modeled bus compressor, emulating classic analog compressor character for mastering-bus glue.

What it's used for

FX chain notes

Used mid-chain in the Ozone mastering rack, after EQ and before the maximizer.

roar.title: Roar
roar.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's Live 12 stock multi-stage saturation/distortion device — the first audio effect (alongside the instruments Wavetable and Meld) to get its own expanded device view. Two saturation stages can be routed serially, in parallel, multiband, or mid/side, plus a self-contained feedback mode, with three LFOs, an envelope follower, and a Shaper section feeding its own modulation matrix.

What it's used for

Multi-stage drive/distortion duty on anything from a single track to a whole bus — dnksaus frames it as "a bus of buses," the same relationship a drum bus has to a further drum bus, i.e. a saturation stage meant to sit at a summing point, not just on one source.

FX chain notes

Works as a track-level saturator/distortion or as a bus-level glue/color stage; the routing choice (single/serial/parallel/multiband/mid-side/feedback) should match the role — parallel or multiband for a gentler bus-glue use, feedback mode for a self-oscillating sound-design texture.

decimort-2.title: Decimort 2
decimort-2.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: D16 Group Audio Software

What it is

A bit-depth and sample-rate reduction (decimation) plugin from D16 Group modeling the character of vintage samplers and lo-fi digital hardware.

What it's used for

Classic lo-fi/bitcrushed textures on drums, vocals, and synths — emulating old sampler grit (SP-1200/MPC-style character) rather than harsh digital distortion.

FX chain notes

Placed on an individual track or a drum bus, often before saturation/EQ to shape the resulting lo-fi tone.

Techniques

  • Owned best-match for a "Lo-Fi" bitcrush/downsample stage added to a thin, weak percussion loop purely to give it WEIGHT — not brightness, not vintage color, just heft. Jaycen Joshua, on a "ticky, poofy" tambora loop: "so I just dirty it up a little bit with the Lo-Fi — I love this plugin, you're adding the distortion and saturation that gives it the weight that it needs." Positioned right after a CLA-76-style compressor and before an EQ pass that cedes low end to the 808 — see UAD UA 1176LN, Pro-Q 4. → UAD UA 1176LN, Pro-Q 4, Saturation and Distortion, Masking and Carving — Mix with the Masters (Jaycen Joshua), Jaycen Joshua on creative drum mixing
  • Fake "drums baked into an old sample" by dropping a plain boom-bap kick+snare pattern through a sample-rate reduction stage — since real vintage soul samples always have their original drums smeared into the recording, program a simple kick/snare pattern and lower its sample rate (source video used FL Studio's Edison; Decimort 2's Sample Rate control is the direct owned equivalent) for the same washed-out/filtered vintage character, rather than trying to EQ/reverb a clean modern kit into sounding old. → Sampling and Sound Selection — loner, the secrets behind OZ's 'her loss' production!?

3-vocal-bus.title: 3 Vocal Bus
3-vocal-bus.html:
Role: Final polish on all vocals summed — the "vocal master." This is your current working chain, kept as the default with researched starting points.

Vocal FX returns feed this bus — Delay Send Slap, Delay Send Other, Reverb Send Long output here (not master), so the glue melts tails into the dry voice and a bus fader ride moves voice + space together. Safe because the GR here is gentle (1–3 dB — heavy bus compression would pump the tails). Mix-wide returns (Reverb Send Room, Width Send, Saturation Send) stay → master. If a hook wash ever turns murky, the Decapitator/Inflator densifying the tails is the suspect — trim the return level, don't re-route.

🎬 From video: the reason THIS bus exists as a separate, dedicated bus rather than sitting inside a general vocal group — with the lead routed here and every OTHER instrument (including backing vocals/doubles/harmonies) summed into a separate instrumental bus, LUFS meters on both buses let you measure and match the two: in the majority of popular mixes the lead vocal reads at roughly the SAME loudness as the instrumental. Once matched, push the vocal slightly below that reading to sit "in" the mix, or slightly above to sit "on top of" it. → Master Chain, Referencing and Translation — Sage Audio, The 5 MOST IMPORTANT Vocal Mixing Tips

Chain overview

Slow leveler → saturation → broad tone → density → de-ess → resonance cleanup. The logic: glue the level first so every later stage sees a steady signal; add color; then the last three stages clean up what the color added. De-ess and soothe sit at the end because saturation and Inflator both regenerate harshness.

Bus philosophy: by the time audio hits a bus, moves should be broad and gentle — 1–3 dB, wide Qs, low mix knobs. If you're reaching for surgery here, the fix belongs on a track or group.

lala.title: LALA
lala.html:
Category: Compressor/Limiter Vendor: AnalogObsession

What it is

A freeware optical leveling-amplifier compressor plugin by Analog Obsession modeled on the classic LA-2A-style opto compressor circuit.

What it's used for

Smooth, musical vocal and bass leveling with the gentle, program-dependent character of an opto compressor.

FX chain notes

Often the first compression stage on vocals for smooth leveling, followed by a faster compressor for peak control.

Used in my chains

My opto leveler (the owned LA-2A) — slow, program-dependent gain riding that melts things together without audible pumping. Used for gentle glue/level-ride, 1–3 dB GR, never as a peak grabber:

  • Main Vocal Group — slot 2, layer glue: ~1.5 dB GR, gentle — melts the vocal layers into one voice (real leveling already happened per-track).
  • Electric Piano Track — slot 2, leveling: 2–3 dB GR — opto is what a Rhodes historically ran into (an LA-2A in every 70s studio); smooth sustain without killing the bark.
  • Bass Group — slot 2, level ride: 1–2 dB GR, slow — smooths section-to-section bass (verse fingerstyle vs. chorus 808) so low-end energy stays constant.
  • Acoustic Guitar Track — slot 4, gentle or none: bypass on exposed parts (~90% sound better with EQ and no comp); 2–3 dB GR + Mix 100% only when it's a bed in a dense mix.

uad-neve-1073.title: UAD Neve 1073
uad-neve-1073.html:
Category: Preamp & EQ (Unison) Vendor: Universal Audio — owned (paid add-on, confirmed 2026-07-16); stock-bundle sibling is UAD UA 610-B

What it is

Emulation of the Neve 1073 console module — the most recorded preamp/EQ in history. Class-A transformer "iron" that adds weight and sheen; Unison version models the input stage on the Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII.

What it's used for

Body + silk on anything: vocals, acoustic/electric guitar, bass DI. Drive the red gain for thick harmonic push, keep it low for clean weight.

Key settings

  • Mic gain: lowest position that reaches level (condensers run hot); output trim to ~−18 dBFS average.
  • EQ on the way in: high shelf +1–2 dB @ 12 kHz max, HPF off — sweeten lightly, never carve (carving happens in Ableton where it's undoable).
  • Ultimatum tip: Disclosure's tracking chain is 1073 (treble boost, roll a little bass) → LA-2A → air EQ — see Disclosure - Ultimatum Breakdown + Breakbeat.

FX chain notes

Primary Unison preamp in uad_console chains — the 1073's gentle iron adds body to acoustics and weight to vocals; swap to UAD UA 610-B for a rounder tube flavor. See Acoustic Guitar Track.

billie-eilish-vocal-chain.title: Billie Eilish Vocal Chain
billie-eilish-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: ASMR-close whisper singing over enormous negative space — the quietest vocal presented the loudest. The technique is 80% capture + editing: sing genuinely soft inches from the mic, comp obsessively, crossfade between every word to kill the noise floor, then stack quiet harmonies until the whisper becomes a choir. Signal source: Neumann TLM 102 (her mic is the TLM 103 — same family), often handheld, 1–3" away. Bedroom, not booth.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — clean, generous gain (whispers need it; watch the noise floor)
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 1–2 dB
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — bypass - The real step 1 is takes + comping: many full takes, something usable in each; Finneas: "crossfade into silence between every word she sings" — the between-word editing IS the noise-floor control. (Main Vocal Track Step 1.5 discipline, doubled.)

Chain overview

Comp/edit → de-pop the proximity → gentle level → de-ess soft → intimate space. Every stage tiny — the whisper must never sound processed, only impossibly close.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Pro-Q 4 — Proximity manage

  • HPF 60–80 · tame the proximity boom 150–250 Hz dynamically (handheld distance varies) · zero air boost — her top end is breath already.

2. Pro-C 2 — Even the whisper

  • Vocal style, 3–4 dB, slow-ish release — whispers have tiny dynamics; this is about consistency, not control.

3. Pro-DS — Soft-S

  • Whisper sibilance is huge relative to tone — range 6–8 dB but listen: S's are part of the ASMR aesthetic; tame, don't remove.

4. Saturn 2 — Warmth

  • Warm tape, mix 10–20% — body for a voice with almost no chest.

Step 3 — Effects (sends)

  • Space as an instrument, per song: dead dry ("bad guy") vs cathedral ("when the party's over" — Reverb Send Long hot, ducked). Pick one identity per song, don't blend.
  • Harmony stacks are the sound: quiet 3–5 part harmonies (Harmony Vocal Track rules but softer than the lead), sometimes pitched layers (Little AlterBoy octave-down whisper tucked).
  • Delay Send Slap rarely; Width Send on stack blooms.

the-32-thaats-32-modes.title: The 32 Thaats (32 Modes)
the-32-thaats-32-modes.html:
Part of Music Theory. Thirty-two seven-note modes generated by one rule, taken from the Hindustani thaat system and presented in Western terms. Every scale the vault already knows — plus about twenty it doesn't — falls out of a single closed piece of combinatorics.

Why this widens the library rather than repeating it. Every other modes note here derives modes downward from a parent scale — Diatonic Modes from major, Harmonic Minor Modes from harmonic minor, Scale Modes Reference from melodic minor and harmonic major, and the world-scale table there from a book's catalogue. All of that is derivative thinking, and it can only ever produce scales that already have a parent. This system is generative and closed: it states the rules a mode must satisfy, then produces the complete list — which turns out to include nine modes that are nobody's mode of anything. See ; this is the strongest argument in the library for the parallel side of that split.

ensemble-listening-and-comping-restraint.title: Ensemble Listening and Comping Restraint
ensemble-listening-and-comping-restraint.html:
Part of Music Theory — the sideman/accompanist skillset: what to do (and, more often, what not to do) while someone else is soloing. Distinct from Jazz Comping — Rhythmic Motif and Walking Bassline (a specific rhythmic comping pattern to play) and Solo Dynamics and Arc (shaping your own solo) — this note is about listening, balance, and restraint as a comper, the largely-untaught skill of supporting rather than playing.

Connect to the rhythm section, not just the changes

  • A comping instrument's rhythmic connection point in a jazz context is the drummer's snare — a piece of secondhand-but-repeated advice: "your chords have to connect with the snare drum," meaning the rhythmic placement of a comped chord should lock to what the drummer's snare is doing, not just land wherever feels natural against the harmony. (general starting point: listen to snare comping/kicks for a chorus before you start comping, and place your first few hits directly on ones you hear.)
  • The bass player's equivalent connection point in a jazz feel is the hi-hat (vs. the kick drum in a more pop/rock feel) — the same "lock to a specific drum voice" logic applied to the bass chair. Relevant when comping alongside a bassist, or when a guitarist is covering the bass role: know which drum voice the genre's groove actually organizes around before trying to "connect with the drums" in the abstract.
  • Listen for what the soloist's intention actually is before reacting to it — and know you don't have to follow it; you can also deliberately pull the music in another direction and see what happens. Both are valid responses; the failure mode is neither following nor contrasting, just comping on autopilot without reference to what's happening around you.
secs: Connect to the rhythm section, not just the changes

chord-melody-arranging-is-miserable-unti.title: Chord Melody Arranging is Miserable (Until You Do It This Way)
chord-melody-arranging-is-miserable-unti.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) walks through the full arranging process he teaches inside his paid course, Chord Melody Magic, building a real chord-melody arrangement of the jazz standard "What Is This Thing Called Love" from its lead sheet, chord by chord, on screen. Where Chord Melody Made Simple (Part 5): Modes of the C Major Scale (already in the vault) teaches the live, real-time method — renumbering the melody note against whichever chord/mode is currently sounding and reaching for a memorized go-to shape — this video is the complementary slow, deliberate, working-it-out-on-paper method: a repeatable four-step process (root of the chord → letter name of the melody note → chord-tone number of the melody note → look up/build a voicing with that note on top) applied lead-sheet-line by lead-sheet-line, plus a chord-tone dictionary organized by which guitar string the melody note falls on. The video closes with what's genuinely the most useful transferable idea for playing (not just arranging) chord melody: you don't have to harmonize every note with a full chord grab — deliberately choosing when to play a single melody note versus a full voicing is both easier to execute and sounds better, because it creates space instead of a wall of chords. Several concrete jazz-guitar voicing moves come out of the worked example: a rootless diminished-seventh shape standing in for a dominant 7♭9, a one-note-moves-a-half-step voice-leading link between a half-diminished ii chord and its rootless V7♭9 (a "piano left-hand comping" effect), and rootless altered-dominant (G7alt) shapes built from guide tones plus color tones.

passing-chords-and-how-to-sound-amazing-.title: Passing Chords And How To Sound Amazing With Them
passing-chords-and-how-to-sound-amazing-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen works through the same four-way passing-chord taxonomy already documented on Passing Chords (diatonic, chromatic, diminished, dominant) but this time keeps everything anchored to one single skeleton — a plain 2-5-1 in C major (Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7) — so every technique is directly comparable against the same two bars rather than scattered across different turnarounds. He's explicit that the point isn't naming the theory correctly, it's having options and knowing how they sound; the video is built as a sequence of worked examples, not a lecture. Two things here aren't already on the vault's Passing Chords page: a same-root diminished neighbor-tone move (embellish a static chord with the diminished chord built on its OWN root, not a half step below the next chord) demonstrated on both a major chord and a dominant chord, and a guitar-specific voicing equivalence — Larsen's usual "Cmaj7" comping shape is literally an Em7 shape played over a C bass (Em7 = the 3rd-5th-7th-9th of Cmaj9 with no root), explained visually rather than by spelling out note names. Transcript confidence: medium — auto-generated (non-manual) English captions with heavy ASR mangling ("atonic passing costs" for "diatonic passing chords," "C-terminus" for "C sharp diminished," "true cause" for "chords") — decipherable from musical context and cross-checked against the companion video Jazz Chords: Every Type of Passing Chord You Need To Know, which covers the same taxonomy with cleaner captions, but every specific chord/example below was verified against this video's own audio-implied content, not assumed from the other video.

jens-larsen-how-to-use-diatonic-passing-.title: Jens Larsen - How To Use Diatonic Passing Chords With Easy Practical Examples
jens-larsen-how-to-use-diatonic-passing-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, dense Jens Larsen jazz-guitar theory lesson that works out diatonic passing chords entirely through one worked example: a basic 1-6-2-5 in C major (Cmaj7 – Am7 – Dm7 – G7). Larsen explicitly frames this as a follow-up answering questions from an earlier video on using passing chords in improvised solo lines — his point being there's barely any theory to it: a diatonic passing chord is just any chord already sitting in the parent scale (here, the seven diatonic chords of C major: Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bø7) placed on the weak beat between two chords of the real progression to add stepwise motion and color, while the strong-beat chord stays the harmonic anchor so the original progression is still audible underneath. He walks through every transition in the 1-6-2-5 (C→Am, Am→Dm, Dm→G7, G7→C) giving 2-4 concrete passing-chord options per transition — approach from below, approach from above, full stepwise walk-ups, and full stepwise walk-downs — plus one non-diatonic-in-the-strict-sense bonus (a triad-over-bass inversion, G/B). The whole video is a comping-focused companion to a prior solo-line-oriented video, and Larsen is explicit that the same vocabulary applies to both: play it as chords first to test whether it makes musical sense, then move it into single-note lines.

delayed-resolution-a-gorgeous-reharmoniz.title: Delayed Resolution - A Gorgeous Reharmonization Technique (10 Examples)
delayed-resolution-a-gorgeous-reharmoniz.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) gives delayed resolution its own dedicated, systematic treatment — the exact device his Georgia on My Mind chords lesson pointed to but didn't teach ("references a separate video of his on the theory of delayed resolution — not yet in the vault" — this is that video). Defined directly: instead of resolving to the expected tonic chord at the end of a progression, substitute an unexpected chord that still contains the melody's tonic note, leaving the tension hanging longer before finally arriving home. The whole lesson works one fixed setup — a ii–V–I in C major with the melody landing on the tonic note C — and reharmonizes that final C ten different ways by treating it as a different chord tone (root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, ♭7, 9th) each time, both as single substitute chords and as full delaying progressions, closing with a bonus tip on applying the same idea to single-note lead lines rather than full harmony. Highly concrete and example-driven — exact chord names and voicing logic throughout, not vague theory-speak — a strong direct feed for Reharmonization technique #1 (Change the chord's function under a held note), which this video expands into a fully worked-out, named device.

enclosures-through-the-scale.title: Enclosures Through the Scale
enclosures-through-the-scale.html:
Part of Bebop Vocabulary (§2 Enclosures) and Jazz Harmony — a scale-degree, chord-tone-independent drill for the enclosure device. Where Chord-Tone Soloing's three enclosure shapes are targeted at chord tones and depend on knowing the chord's function (dominant/Dorian/Aeolian) to pick the right note above the target, this drill strips that out entirely: it applies one fixed mechanical rule to every note of a scale form in turn, descending from the top all the way to the bottom, without regard to which notes happen to be chord tones. A good on-ramp before or alongside the chord-tone-targeted material — same core device (surround a target note, then land on it), simpler decision tree.

The core rule

Always descending. Starting on the highest note of whatever scale form/box you're working in:

  1. Pick your target = the next scale tone down from where you are.
  2. Descend note by note (through the scale) until you land exactly one half step above the target.
  3. From there, skip down PAST the target to the next note that is actually IN THE SCALE — never skip to a chromatic note, it has to be a diatonic scale tone below the target.
  4. Walk chromatically UP from that scale tone through however many half steps sit between it and the target, landing on the target.
  5. The target you just landed on becomes the new starting point — repeat from step 1 on the next scale tone down.
  6. Continue until you reach the bottom of the scale form.

(general starting point for reading this as note names: over a C major scale form, descending from the top, each "target" is successively B, A, G, F, E, D, C — the descent through the scale itself supplies the "half step above" position for a run of targets naturally, since a fixed rule of "skip to the scale tone below, walk up chromatically" is being reapplied at every stop.)

Why the enclosure length varies — not a separate case

How many chromatic notes land between the skipped-to scale tone and the target falls straight out of the rule, it isn't a second rule to memorize: where two adjacent scale tones are already a half step apart (e.g. the 3rd–4th or 7th–root gap in a major scale), step 4's "walk up chromatically" collapses to zero filler notes — you land on the target directly off the skip. Where a whole step or more separates them, one or more chromatic passing notes fill the gap. Same mechanism throughout; the shape just gets longer or shorter depending on where you are in the scale.
secs: Why the enclosure length varies — not a separate case

downbeat-and-upbeat-enclosures.title: Downbeat and Upbeat Enclosures
downbeat-and-upbeat-enclosures.html:
Part of Bebop Vocabulary (§2 Enclosures) and Chord-Tone Soloing — a third enclosure-sizing rule, distinct from both. Enclosures Through the Scale fixes the enclosure's length mechanically off the scale's own half-step gaps (Jared's descending drill); Chord-Tone Soloing's Shape 3 fixes it off the chord's function (Mixolydian/Dorian/Aeolian). This one fixes the enclosure's note-count (2 vs 3) purely off which beat the target lands on — a downbeat target gets a two-note enclosure, an upbeat target gets a three-note enclosure — and then uses that single rule to (a) drill every diatonic arpeggio in a key and (b) build connective lines between chords of a ii–V.

The core rule

Target a note. Check which beat it lands on:

  • Downbeat → two-note enclosure — approach from below or above by one note.
  • Upbeat → three-note enclosure — adds rhythmic tension; either two notes below or above, or one note below and one above (the reverse also works).

This is the rhythmic complement to Bebop Vocabulary §2's four enclosure shapes (chromatic above/below, diatonic above + chromatic below, etc.) — those tables describe what notes to use; this rule decides how many, driven entirely by where the target sits in the bar. (general starting point: the underlying logic is the same reason a bebop scale adds a passing tone — Bebop Vocabulary §1 — extra notes exist to keep strong tones landing on strong beats; here the enclosure's own length is what absorbs the offset instead of a scale passing-tone.)

Drill 1 — Enclose the first note of every diatonic arpeggio

Take a diatonic 7th-chord arpeggio (worked example: C major 7 — C E G B) and enclose just its first note (the root) with either a two- or three-note enclosure. Repeat through every chord of the C major scale in turn (Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bm7♭5) until the enclosure shape is automatic under the fingers and the ear recognizes it on sight. Builds the same "small fragments of information" vocabulary Bebop Vocabulary §5's digital patterns describe, but sourced from enclosures rather than scale-degree numbers.
secs: Drill 1 — Enclose the first note of every diatonic arpeggio

best-beginner-sweeping-exercise-master-s.title: Best Beginner Sweeping Exercise - Master Sweep Picking TODAY!
best-beginner-sweeping-exercise-master-s.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A beginner sweep-picking exercise on a single worked Cmaj7 arpeggio shape, paired with the core mental-model shift BERNTH considers the real obstacle: reusing the "strumming a chord" motor pattern instead of the "picking individual notes" one.

Techniques

  • Worked shape: Cmaj7 arpeggio — root C (10th fret, D string), major 3rd E (9th fret, G string), perfect 5th G (8th fret, B string), major 7th B (7th fret, high E string).
  • The core mental-model reframe: sweep picking borrows the chord-strum motor pattern, not the individual-note-picking pattern. Most players' hands already have two separate motor connections — "arpeggiate/solo mode" (pick each note individually, e.g. alternate picking) and "chord/strum mode" (one continuous motion across strings) — and default to the first one for an arpeggio, which caps out at a wall as tempo rises. Sweep picking requires deliberately tearing apart that default association and re-routing arpeggio-playing onto the strum-mode motion instead. Framed as the single biggest mental obstacle for most beginner sweepers, more than any physical difficulty.
  • Practiced very slowly first, watching for zero individual string attacks — one continuous motion across the strings, banked into muscle memory before any speed work.

Routed to

Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes

sweep-picking-for-beginners-the-5-best-e.title: SWEEP PICKING for Beginners - The 5 BEST Exercises!
sweep-picking-for-beginners-the-5-best-e.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A beginner sweep-picking lesson framed around BERNTH's own honest early history — years of "faking" sweep arpeggios as dead-note rakes before deliberately fixing the technique — leading into two concrete, still-relevant beginner methods and a Paganini Caprice arrangement as motivating repertoire.

Techniques

  • Anchor the first and last note of the arpeggio to the metronome. Rather than trying to place every note correctly at once, lock in the lowest (first) note and the highest (last) note precisely on the click; the notes in between reliably fall into place rhythmically around those two anchors over time. Direct fix for the classic beginner "confusing mess of dead notes in the middle" sound.
  • Two-phase daily routine: slow-and-perfect, then deliberately too-fast-and-sloppy. Most students over-index on perfection at a slow tempo and never leave it; BERNTH's own breakthrough came from also including a fast, sloppy, no-stakes pass at the end of each sweep session — not aiming for cleanliness at that point, just breaking the individual-string-attack habit at speed. Framed as more effective than a strict linear BPM climb (+2–4 BPM/day).
  • Motivation-driven repertoire choice. Learning sweep picking purely because it's technically hard (a "flex") tends to stall; picking a specific piece/lick that's genuinely inspiring sustains practice better. Worked example: the opening section of Paganini's Caprice No. 5 (a well-known neoclassical shred arrangement), which is deliberately beginner-accessible because it sweeps in one direction only (upward) and connects just two common arpeggio shapes via slides — the intermediate continuation section adds a second direction and more shapes.
  • A named failure mode to recognize in your own or others' playing: attacking every string individually (down/up strokes per string, like alternate picking) instead of one continuous sweeping motion — works at slow tempos but caps out hard as tempo rises, and is the single most common beginner sweep-picking problem BERNTH sees.
