Sweep Picking Arpeggio Shapes

practice-this-daily-10-mins.title: Practice THIS Daily (10 Mins)
practice-this-daily-10-mins.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's answer to "what should I practice with only 10 minutes a day" — not a menu of separate drills, but one riff pushed through five progressive levels, each level layering a new skill onto the same underlying pattern (fingering → flying-fingers fix → plucking hand → theory → moving-root variations). The pitch is that the single exercise scales from true beginner to advanced player, since the ceiling lives in the BPM target and the level-5 variations rather than in a harder pattern. Before getting into the levels, the video makes a genuinely useful side point: most bassists think in four-fret chunks because they have four fretting fingers, but the bass's fourths tuning means a real "position" spans five frets — and this exercise is deliberately built across a five-fret span to train that awareness. The five levels: basic pattern + tempo target, fixing flying fretting fingers, fixing the plucking hand (alternate vs. rake), root-fifth-octave theory with three chromatic/scale walking patterns, and finally applying all of it to moving root notes (chord changes) at an intermediate and advanced level. Concrete and well-sequenced throughout — light on the channel's usual Lord of the Rings bit, heavy on actual technique. This is BassBuzz's second "Practice THIS Daily" video in the vault — distinct from both Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix) (a five-blunder diagnostic format, different riff, different failure modes) and Slap... Practice THIS Daily (10 Mins) (slap-specific) — same daily-10-minute framing and five-level structure as a recurring BassBuzz format, but a genuinely different exercise and skill set each time.

positional-caged-soloing-with-matched-mo.title: Positional CAGED Soloing with Matched Modes and Arpeggios
positional-caged-soloing-with-matched-mo.html:
Brandon D'Eon's method for covering the whole neck over a static diatonic progression by walking through the five CAGED positions, and at each one working out the matching mode, pentatonic shape, and chord-tone arpeggios for every chord in the progression. Complements Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes (that page's method is for fast-moving, non-diatonic progressions — closest-CAGED-shape-per-chord-change; this page is for a single diatonic progression held in one key, walked position by position across the whole neck) and CAGE System Scale Shapes (the underlying position/shape system this method is built on).

The core reframe, and the actual point of the video: most players who feel "stuck in the box" haven't mastered chord-tone targeting even in the one box position they already know — escaping to new positions doesn't fix that gap, it just gives you more positions to be equally unfocused in. Master chord-tone targeting in one position first.

The five-position map (worked example: Em–G–D–C, key of E minor)

Position Mode Pentatonic (CAGED shape)
3rd (frets ~2–7) G Ionian (major) G major pentatonic
5th (frets ~5–8) A Dorian D-shape pentatonic
7th (frets ~7–10) B Phrygian C-shape pentatonic
10th (frets ~10–13) D Mixolydian A-shape pentatonic
12th (the "box") E Aeolian (minor) G-shape pentatonic (standard minor pentatonic box)

The five positions fall out of walking the parent major scale's own pentatonic notes (here, G major pentatonic's degrees land at frets 3, 5, 7, 10, 12) — the 15th position is skipped as redundant, since it repeats the 3rd position's shapes one octave up.

At every position: locate the chord tones, not just the scale shape

For each chord in the progression, physically find and target its chord tones within that position, rather than defaulting to running the scale or pentatonic shape regardless of which chord is currently sounding. This is named as the real differentiator between amateur and advanced improvisers — amateurs play the same scale shape through every chord change; advanced players shift emphasis to the current chord's tones using the same fixed hand position.

Chord tones aren't limited to a compact barre-chord grip's fretted notes. A chord's full tone set (e.g. Em = E, G, B) usually appears in more places within a given position than the handful of notes in its barre-chord voicing — those extra instances are still legitimate soloing targets even though they're not part of the compact chord shape.
secs: The five-position map (worked example: Em–G–D–C, key of E minor)

Everything from slapback to ambient reverse washes; the looper doubles as a writing scratchpad.

music-theory-for-bass.title: Music Theory for Bass
music-theory-for-bass.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A "mega dump" survey of essentially the whole beginner/intermediate theory curriculum, taught explicitly through the lens of "use it immediately on the bass or it doesn't count" — the host frames his own college theory classes as a cautionary tale (classmates who memorized rules like figured bass and cadence names without ever applying them never actually learned the material) and states his method up front: every new concept gets picked up and played on the instrument the moment it's introduced. The video moves fast through notes/pitches → the musical alphabet and fretboard navigation → generic vs. specific intervals → scales → chords/triads and arpeggios → chord progressions and diatonic numbering → rhythm (beat/tempo/time signature/note values) → song form, consistently translating each abstract concept into "what shape does this make on the bass neck." Nothing here is deep on any single topic by design (the host repeatedly defers depth to a paid course and a free PDF), and every topic already has a dedicated, much deeper reference page in this vault's Music Theory library — the video's real value-add is the bass-first framing: intervals become fretboard shapes ("box shapes") you can navigate without knowing interval names, chords become arpeggios you outline one note at a time instead of full grips, and the musical alphabet becomes a literal fret-by-fret map starting from the four open strings. Good orientation video for a bass beginner; low new-information density for anyone who has already read the theory library, but the bass-specific translations are worth capturing since nothing in the vault currently documents them.

bass-setup-truss-rod-action-intonation-a.title: Bass Setup — Truss Rod, Action, Intonation, and Pickup Height
bass-setup-truss-rod-action-intonation-a.html:
A DIY basic-bass-setup procedure from BassBuzz — five ordered steps (truss rod → bridge saddle action → nut check → intonation → pickup height) that fix most of what makes a cheap bass feel and sound bad: buzzing/rattling notes, strings too far off the fretboard, out-of-tune fretted notes, and weak or distorted amp tone. Order matters — each step subtly affects the measurements for the ones after it (truss rod affects action, and truss rod + action + nut all affect intonation), so doing them out of order means re-doing earlier ones. Tools needed: a ruler, a screwdriver, a couple of Allen wrenches, a tuner, and a business card. The video's own blind test (see below) is the argument for bothering with this at all: a properly set-up cheap bass can beat an un-set-up expensive one in a blind feel/sound test with an experienced player.

Step 1 — Truss rod (sets the neck's forward bow)

The truss rod is a metal rod inside the neck that counteracts string tension. Set wrong, it causes either buzzing (too straight) or strings sitting too far off the neck (too much forward bow).

The truss rod test trifecta (do this before touching anything):

  1. Press the E string down right behind the 1st fret (capo, or wedge in a pick/ruler).
  2. Press the E string down past the 12th fret with your plucking hand.
  3. Measure the gap at the 7th fret with a business card. Can't slide it in at all → neck too straight, loosen the rod. More than 1–2 business cards of clearance → too much forward bow, tighten the rod. 1–2 cards of clearance → correct, leave it. - Alternate check: tap the E string against the 7th fret — a small click = correct; no click = too straight (loosen); lots of click/travel = too much bow (tighten).

Adjusting: find the truss rod adjuster (headstock, body-end/heel, or — on a vintage-style neck — you may have to pull the neck to reach it). Use the correctly-fitting thicker Allen wrench (no wiggle, to avoid stripping it). Start any adjustment with an 1/8 turn to de-stick it, then return to start. Tighten clockwise (too much bow → straightens the neck), loosen counterclockwise (too straight → lets it bow forward), 1/8 turn at a time — firm pressure is normal, forcing it or big turns is not. Retune and re-run the trifecta after each adjustment, always in playing position (not flat on a bench), always in tune first. Truss rod changes take hours to fully settle — make small moves and re-check later rather than chasing the measurement in one sitting.
secs: Step 1 — Truss rod (sets the neck's forward bow)

5-string-vs-4-string-bass-why-beginners-.html: BassBuzz's gear-choice argument for beginners: the low B string that makes a five-string bass look appealing (more range, more notes, "more bass") compounds the difficulty of every single skill a beginner is already learning on four string, without adding anything a beginner is ready to use yet. Every one of the seven reasons below is a skill-acquisition or ergonomics tax, not a claim that five-strings are bad instruments; the video's own closing line is that all seven problems are fixable, they just add load to a curve that's already steep for a beginner. how-to-read-sheet-music-the-biggest-mist.title: How to Read Sheet Music — The BIGGEST Mistake Everyone Makes Part 4
how-to-read-sheet-music-the-biggest-mist.html:
https://youtube.com/shorts/ZWL-9Wmb9sU?si=XNMKJwvw0uXGTgkz

👤 Musiah AI Piano Lessons 🔗 Watch video

Summary

The video explains the evolution of musical notation from an 11-line staff to the modern grand staff, highlighting how these changes made sheet music easier to read. It discusses the purpose and function of ledger lines and clefs (treble and bass), clarifies common misconceptions about reading piano music, and offers tips for efficient music reading. The video also promotes AI-based piano lessons for further skill development.

Key points

  • Early sheet music used a single 11-line staff, with the middle C marked specially, which made reading difficult.
  • The introduction of ledger lines split the staff into two five-line staves, improving readability.
  • Treble (G-clef) and bass (F-clef) indicate high and low notes, and their symbols mark specific lines on the staff.
  • Middle C sometimes causes confusion about hand usage, which was addressed by spacing staves apart.
  • The original 11-line staff concept survives in the modern "grand staff," with the treble and bass staves joined by a vertical line.
  • A common but inefficient habit among students is reading right and left hand notes separately; instead, one should read both together in a single vertical eye movement.
  • Misconceptions about the left hand being harder to read are unfounded.
  • The video encourages viewers to check out advanced AI piano lesson resources.

Technical terms

  • Clef: A symbol placed at the beginning of the staff to indicate the pitch of written notes; common types include treble (G-clef) and bass (F-clef).
  • Ledger line: A short line used to notate pitches above or below the regular lines of the staff.
  • Grand staff: The combination of the treble and bass staves, traditionally used for piano music, joined by a vertical line and encompassing a wide range of pitches.
  • Treble clef (G-clef): A clef that designates the second line as G above middle C.
  • Bass clef (F-clef): A clef that designates the fourth line as F below middle C.

bass-walkup-and-walkdown-fills.title: Bass Walkup and Walkdown Fills
bass-walkup-and-walkdown-fills.html:
BassBuzz's no-theory-required version of the chromatic connective-tissue device also covered (from the theory side) on Chromatic Bass Lines and (from Jamerson's specific three-fret formula) on Jamerson's Root-Fifth-Octave Exercise: a short chromatic run that leads INTO a target root note rather than landing on it cold. The pitch is deliberately beginner-friendly — "count two frets and walk this way," no scale/key knowledge required — which makes it the right first stop for someone who isn't ready for Jamerson's three-fret/root-fifth-octave version yet. Fill gap: this is the vault's first note built specifically around this two-fret, rhythm-placed version of the device, worked on three real, fully-named recorded basslines rather than a single exercise; The BassBuzz 55-Step Bass Learning Roadmap step 40 ("Walk-ups and walk-downs") previously pointed only at Chromatic Bass Lines, which covers the harmony/reharmonization side of chromatic bass motion, not this melodic-approach-fill version — now updated to point here too.

The two-fret rule

  1. Find your target (root) note — the note you need to land on to follow the current chord.
  2. Walkup: start two frets below the target and step up chromatically, one fret at a time, landing on the target. Example: target = D (5th fret, A string) → start on the 3rd fret, walk 3rd → 4th → 5th.
  3. Walkdown: start two frets above the target and step down chromatically into it. Example: target = C (3rd fret, A string) → start on the 5th fret, walk 5th → 4th → 3rd.
  4. That's the entire theory requirement — count two frets, walk one direction, land on the root. No scale or key awareness needed to execute it (though Chromatic Bass Lines and Non-Harmonic Tones cover why it works harmonically, for when that's wanted).
  5. You don't have to walk into every target. Real basslines skip the walk on some chord changes and use it on others (see "Gold Dust Woman" below) — it's a decoration to place deliberately, not a rule to apply every time a chord changes.

→ BASS Slot (this is a low-end melodic-fill device, not a harmonic one) · Bassline Writing step "chromatic walk-up/walk-down connects one phrase to the next, regardless of scale" is the production-side statement of the same device.

the-10-rules-of-bass-playing-that-pros-b.title: The 10 Rules of Bass Playing (That Pros Break)
the-10-rules-of-bass-playing-that-pros-b.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's Josh runs a "rules of bass" format (explicitly credited as inspired by Mike at Art of Guitar's "10 rules guitarists break" video) — ten standard beginner-teacher rules, each paired with a named pro bassist who breaks it, followed by an honest verdict on whether breaking it actually helps or hurts. The format is consistently even-handed rather than "rules are dumb, break them all": every rule gets the reason it exists stated plainly, then the specific, narrow condition under which the named pro's exception works — and one rule (pinky fretting, Chris Squire) is flagged directly as the one genuine rule of the ten, where even the counter-example probably shouldn't be fully copied. The ten rules span technique (plucking force, one- vs. two-finger plucking, pinky use, thumb-over-neck, fingertip vs. flat-finger fretting), setup/posture (strap height), and musical judgment (staying in the low "money note" register vs. playing melodically higher, tone brightness/thinness, whether theory is required, and playing on vs. around beat one). Ten named pros anchor the ten rules: Geddy Lee (Rush), James Jamerson (Motown), Chris Squire (Yes), Louis Johnson ("Billie Jean"), Rocco Prestia (Tower of Power), Robert Trujillo (Metallica), Peter Hook (Joy Division/New Order), Victor Wooten, Billy Sheehan, and Sting (The Police). Runs light on production/gear content and heavy on right-hand/left-hand technique judgment calls plus a couple of musical-decision rules (register choice, theory necessity, rhythmic placement) — a companion piece, by format and level, to the vault's other BassBuzz rule-of-thumb compilations.

whole-note-chord-tone-targeting-with-sca.title: Whole-Note Chord-Tone Targeting with Scalar Resolve
whole-note-chord-tone-targeting-with-sca.html:
Brandon D'Eon's two-stage drill for building confident chord-tone targeting, deliberately unglamorous (sustained whole notes) so the ear and hand fully register each chord's sound before any scalar material is layered on top. Compare Chord-Tone Soloing (Jared's jazz-vocabulary practice ladder, built around a fast turnaround and chromatic approach tones) — this drill is a simpler, slower on-ramp aimed at basic chord-tone confidence rather than bebop decoration, and works well as a prerequisite before that page's ladder.

Stage 1 — Whole-note thirds

Over a chosen chord progression (worked example: Am–C–Em–D), play only the 3rd of each chord as a sustained whole note through that chord's full bar. Thirds specifically, not roots — most beginner improvisers default to roots by habit, so targeting thirds forces genuinely new territory and builds a fuller picture of each chord's color. This stage is a hard gate: don't move to Stage 2 until it's reliable without fail.

Stage 2 — Chord-tone-then-scalar, resolving back

Once Stage 1 is solid, halve the chord-tone duration: hold the chord tone for 2 beats, then fill the remaining 2 beats of the bar with scalar movement (whichever scale/mode fits the chord — e.g. Dorian or the matching minor pentatonic). The scalar material must resolve back to a chord tone at the end of its 2 beats — it isn't free noodling, it's controlled motion away from and back to a known-good landing point.

Notes on scope

The full version of this drill repeats both stages across every root (not just thirds — roots and fifths too) and in every fretboard position, not the single worked example above. Treated properly, it's a real time investment (the source estimates roughly a month per drill done thoroughly) rather than a one-session exercise.

string-bending-technique.html: The mechanics of a clean, in-tune, professional-sounding bend — finger support, pitch accuracy at both ends, and stopping the note cleanly. 10-levels-of-shred-guitar-beginner-to-pr.title: 10 LEVELS OF SHRED GUITAR - (beginner to pro)
10-levels-of-shred-guitar-beginner-to-pr.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A genuine beginner-to-advanced shred curriculum ladder, each level explicitly building on the one before rather than being a standalone trick — useful as a reference progression, not just a single workout.

Techniques

  • Level 1 — alternate picking basics to a metronome, hands synchronized, groups of 4 notes.
  • Level 2 — same idea, explicitly contrasted against the anti-pattern of just picking as fast as possible and hoping the fretting hand keeps up (unsynchronized "pushing" is called out directly as not a shortcut to clean speed).
  • Level 3 — transition every 2 notes instead of 4, less thinking time per group but "easier than it looks"; picking hand stays relaxed, minimal motion.
  • Level 4 — sync every single picking stroke to a different note. Named as the actual key unlock for shredding and the first real technique wall — up to this point the fretting hand could mostly "chill" while the picking hand did the work; from here everything must lock together. Worth spending real time here rather than rushing past it.
  • Level 5 — clean string transitions (2-string, e.g. B→E) with the goal of the transition being inaudible to a listener — no stuck pick, no unwanted noise at the string change.
  • Level 6 — full 6-string ascending scale, same clean-transition goal scaled up; minimize both picking- and fretting-hand movement, keep the fretting wrist still for consistency.
  • Level 7 — combine mixed note values, odd time signatures, string skipping, and 4-notes-per-string phrases — framed as recombining the existing foundation, not new material.
  • Level 8 — blend legato, alternate picking, and sweep picking within one passage while deliberately preserving each technique's distinct tonal character (alternate = fast/aggressive, sweep = cascading, legato = fluid/effortless) rather than smoothing them into one uniform sound.
  • Level 9 — advanced techniques used musically, not as flash: multi-finger/double tapping, sweep-picking finger rolls for arpeggios — explicit framing that these should serve real musical lines, not just "chromatic nonsense" eye candy.

Routed to

Directional Alternate Picking System (Level 4's "every stroke synced" unlock) · Legato and Picking Technique Mixing (Level 8's preserve-distinct-character blending principle)

caged-chord-shapes-by-string-shift.title: CAGED Chord Shapes by String-Shift
caged-chord-shapes-by-string-shift.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. Standard CAGED teaching (see CAGE System Scale Shapes) explains the five shapes as the same chord walked up and down the neck — headstock to body. This page documents a different derivation Daniel Seriff calls out as rarely taught: instead of moving a shape up the neck, push it sideways, one string at a time, toward the floor (thick strings → thin strings), and the E/A/D shapes (and, separately, the G/C/F shapes) fall out of each other mechanically, with one repeatable fix for the guitar's one tuning irregularity. The payoff isn't a new shape to learn — it's realizing the E, A, and D shapes are literally the same interval skeleton with one string cut off each time, so there is nothing new to memorize once you've built the first shape.

The core mechanism: slide down a string, then fix the B string

  1. Take a chord shape you already know (say the open/barre E shape).
  2. Copy the exact same fretting pattern down one string — shift every fretted note from its string to the next thinner string, one string over. The string that used to carry the lowest note (originally the low E) falls off the bottom and is no longer played.
  3. Standard tuning is all perfect 4ths except the G→B string pair, which is a major 3rd. Any note that lands on the B string after the shift is therefore a half step flat of what the shape "expects." Fix: raise only that one note, on the B string, up one fret (one half step). Nothing else in the shape changes.
  4. Repeat the same slide-and-fix move again and a third shape falls out.

This one rule — slide a string, then bump the B string up a fret — is the entire system. Applied to E it generates A then D. Applied to G it generates C then F.
secs: The core mechanism: slide down a string, then fix the B string

modal-interchange.title: Modal Interchange
modal-interchange.html:
Part of Music Theory → Chord Progressions. Also called modal mixture. Keeping the tonal center (the tonic note) fixed, while borrowing chords from a different scale built on that same tonic — most commonly, borrowing from the parallel minor into a major key, or vice versa.

The idea

"The tonic note stays the same... but which flavor of that tonic — major, minor, Mixolydian... — is changing." A chord borrowed this way doesn't belong to the song's main diatonic key, but reads as related rather than foreign because it shares the tonic.

Why it can pass as consonant rather than clashing: the borrowed chord's "wrong" note (e.g., a ♭3 in an otherwise major-key song) only clashes if the melody actually lands on the conflicting natural-scale note at the same moment. In practice, songwriters often keep the melody diatonic to the main key throughout and simply avoid singing the one note that would collide with the borrowed chord's altered tone — letting the harmony and melody each stay internally consistent while still blending two "flavors" of the same tonic.

The most common single instance — the borrowed minor iv

Replacing a major key's normally-major IV chord with its minor version (Fm instead of F, in C major) is the single most common modal-interchange move in pop/rock — see Cadences for the minor plagal cadence (iv→I) this produces, and the common IV→iv→I extended form.
secs: The most common single instance — the borrowed minor iv

the-dorian-pentatonic-scale-combining-mo.title: The Dorian Pentatonic Scale - Combining Modes With Pentatonics Part 2
the-dorian-pentatonic-scale-combining-mo.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Part 2 of a two-part series (part 1 combined Lydian with major pentatonic — not yet in the vault). This time: combine the minor pentatonic scale with Dorian by adding exactly one note, the major 6th. Same "just change one note" logic BERNTH uses across the whole modes series — Aeolian → Dorian is F → F♯ in every position of the A natural minor scale.

What's taught

  • Dorian = natural minor (Aeolian) + one raised note, the major 6th. Demonstrated in A: A natural minor has F natural; A Dorian has F♯. Framed explicitly as "don't learn Dorian as a separate scale — learn where the one changed note falls in every position of the scale you already know."
  • Applying that to the pentatonic box: starting from the classic A minor pentatonic (2 notes per string, no 2nd, no 6th), add the major 6th (F♯) at specific spots to get the "Dorian pentatonic" — a 6-note hybrid, not the full 7-note mode.
  • C Lydian and A Dorian share the same key signature/notes — both are built from raising the same scale degree (the 4th in C major → C Lydian; the 6th in A natural minor → A Dorian) and F♯ is the characteristic note in both. Stated as a practice shortcut with a caveat: you can substitute "play C Lydian" for "play A Dorian" since the notes match, but you then lose track of exactly where the characteristic color note falls relative to the A root, so you can't deliberately accent it.
  • Why Dorian over Phrygian for this pairing: Phrygian (♭2) is "the metal scale" and BERNTH's own preferred fingering for it is the 3-note-per-string pattern, not this 2-note-per-string pentatonic-hybrid approach — Dorian's added major 6th fits the pentatonic-hybrid framing better and shows up naturally in blues/jazz/fusion riffs and chords (e.g. alternating perfect 5th/major 6th vamps).
  • Practice suggestion: loop a backing track, switch between plain minor pentatonic and the Dorian-hybrid (added 6th) without leaving the 2-note-per-string fingering system, so the ear learns to place the color note as a deliberate accent rather than incidentally.

Routed to

  • Dorian from the Minor Pentatonic Box — added a ## From videos bullet: the Aeolian→Dorian "one note raised" framing plus the C Lydian/A Dorian shared-note relationship, as a second independent source for the page's core "add the 6th" technique.

What's taught

word-painting.title: Word Painting

Ranges from the obvious (a high note on the word "high") to genuinely subtle, structural choices.

bass-runs-and-target-notes.title: Bass Runs and Target Notes
bass-runs-and-target-notes.html:
BassBuzz's method for writing a bass run — "just another word for a bass fill": cool transition notes layered onto an otherwise-plain bassline at a chord change, aimed at making an on-its-own-not-very-interesting rock/pop bassline read as melodic and forward-moving. Distinct from Bass Walkup and Walkdown Fills (a fixed two-fret chromatic approach into a single target) and Bass Pentatonic Riff-Writing Recipe (composing a repeating riff inside one scale shape) — this note covers the more general case: a scale-based melodic run connecting two or more chords, including runs that deliberately span more than one bar. Fill gap: the vault had no note on this device before this pass, despite "fills"/"runs" showing up loosely across Bassline Writing's "From videos" log.

What a bass run is for

A bass run replaces a flat chord-to-chord handoff with a melodic connector. Two weaker default options, both worth naming so the run's value is obvious by contrast:

  1. Jump straight to the new root — technically correct, reads as abrupt/static.
  2. Sit on the current root until the section changes — safe, but adds no forward motion.

A run instead walks a scale between the two roots, arriving at the new chord's root exactly on time but with real melodic movement along the way. It doesn't need to use every scale degree in order — a run built from scale degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, then 6 (skipping the 4th) still reads as a smooth, connected line, not merely "any notes from the scale."

A run can also borrow its rhythm from somewhere else in the arrangement — mimicking the vocal line's rhythm at a transition point (rather than inventing a new rhythmic idea) is a legitimate, cohesive source for a fill's rhythm, distinct from mimicking the guitar/chord rhythm the rest of the band is already outlining.
secs: What a bass run is for
