rootless-9th-chords-and-chromatic-moveme.title: Rootless 9th Chords and Chromatic Movement in Blues Rhythm Guitar
rootless-9th-chords-and-chromatic-moveme.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Jazz Harmony — a blues rhythm-guitar comping vocabulary, the T-Bone Walker/Robin Ford lineage, built almost entirely from one small rootless dominant-9 shape moved chromatically and reharmonized with inserted ii–V–I's. Where L-Shape Root Map for Blues Chords answers "where does my hand go for I/IV/V" and Chord Voicings documents shell-voicing shapes generally, this page is about what to do with your hand once it's there — the fills, chromatic slides, and functional substitutions that turn a static I-IV-V into sophisticated rhythm playing. This is the comping-side counterpart to The ii-V-I's existing "insert a 2-5-1 into the blues's I→IV pivot" soloing material (worked there as single-note lines in If Your Blues Solos Feel Stale, Try This!) — same device, played here as chords instead of lines.

The base shape: rootless dominant 9

Four notes: major 3rd, ♭7, 9th, 5th — no root. This is the vocabulary's entire raw material; every move below is either a relocation, a chromatic slide, or a reharmonization of this one grip.

Move 1 — the major-6 fill (T-Bone Walker's signature move)

From the rootless-9 shape, slide the two inner notes (the ♭7 and 9th) up a whole step — the grip stops sounding like a dominant 9 and starts sounding like a major 6 chord (root-3rd-6th once the root is added back in with the 1st finger). Named directly as a T-Bone Walker rhythm-guitar signature. Use case: a passing fill that sits neatly between solo lines or vocal phrases — not a chord to hold, a decoration that moves the harmony forward for a beat.

Drill: take the rootless-9 shape on the I chord of a 12-bar blues, do the whole-step-slide-to-major-6 fill, then relocate the identical fill (same shape, same fingering) to the IV and V chords — the video works it moving G9 → C9 → D9, i.e. play the fill on every chord of the form as it goes by, not just the I chord. Vary the rhythmic placement of the fill (on the "and" of 2, right on beat 4, etc.) once the shape itself is comfortable — the video notes there are "all kinds of variations" possible in the phrasing.
secs: Move 1 — the major-6 fill (T-Bone Walker's signature move)

silent-night-jazz-guitar-chord-melody.title: Silent Night Jazz Guitar Chord Melody
silent-night-jazz-guitar-chord-melody.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A solo-guitar chord-melody arrangement of "Silent Night" walked through measure-group by measure-group, with the harmonic reasoning behind every reharmonization spelled out rather than just shown. Nathan Borton takes a plain I–V–I carol progression and dresses nearly every phrase with a jazz device: inserted ii chords ahead of the V, walkdowns connecting IV back to ii, dominant chords approached chromatically from a half step above, diminished chords substituted in for dominant color, a delayed-resolution ♭II major 7 voicing, diminished-arpeggio-derived melody notes harmonized with matching diminished (and "major-diminished") voicings, a quick inserted ii–V, a tritone sub, and a closing ♯IV chromatic triad walkdown into a big open-string B♭maj9♯11 final chord. What makes this valuable beyond "here's a cool voicing" is the why: almost every substitution is justified by naming which melody note is sounding and which chord tone of the new harmony it becomes (drop-2 harmonization philosophy — see Chord Melody Arranging), and the diminished-substitution logic is stated as a fully generalizable rule (any diminished chord built off the 3rd, 5th, ♭7, or 𝄫7 of a dominant chord gives that dominant a richer "dominant 7♭9" sound), not a one-off trick for this tune. Full PDF/tab and chord analysis are gated behind the creator's Patreon; this transcript captures the spoken theory only, no notation.

how-to-add-bebop-jazz-vocabulary-to-the-.title: How to Add Bebop Jazz Vocabulary to the Blues
how-to-add-bebop-jazz-vocabulary-to-the-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch teaches three specific bebop saxophone lines — one each from Cannonball Adderley ("Spontaneous Combustion," off Live in San Francisco, 1959), Charlie Parker ("Billy's Bounce"), and Jimmy Forrest (the title track of Black Forest) — transposed from their original horn recordings onto guitar, each mapped to a different structural chunk of a jazz-blues 12-bar form (transposed to the key of C for the lesson): the I→IV transition at the top of the form (Adderley), the IV chord sliding back to I and on into the VI7 (Parker), and the VI7–ii–V–I turnaround (Forrest). He then stitches all three together into one continuous 12-bar chorus, closing the loop between isolated vocabulary and a real solo. This is the same channel and the same underlying jazz-blues form already documented from The Key To Understanding A Jazz Blues (a single Ruch-composed line over the 1-6-2-5) and How I Approach Practicing (the "transcribe → chunk → name the concept → build your own solo" method) — this video sits between the two: unlike the concept-extraction method, these three licks are taught essentially verbatim (transcribed from real horn recordings, not reduced to a reusable "concept"), and the pedagogical point is explicitly the practice of "transcribe different players, then pull the solos apart and combine them with other things you know" — using borrowed vocabulary as raw material for a personal solo rather than analyzing it down to an abstraction first. The most valuable transferable material: horn players lean much harder on the major 7th as a chromatic color inside a blues than guitarists typically do, on downward chromatic runs through altered tensions to resolve a dominant chord, and on superimposing a simple triad (relative to the underlying dominant chord) to generate extensions without thinking in scale-degree numbers.

wes-montgomery-blues-lesson-d-natural-bl.title: Wes Montgomery Blues Lesson D Natural Blues
wes-montgomery-blues-lesson-d-natural-bl.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch transcribes and breaks down a short stretch of Wes Montgomery's guitar solo on "D Natural Blues" (from the 1960 album The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery), applying the same chunk-analyze-template method he lays out in full on How I Approach Practicing — but this time the vehicle is a real jazz guitar icon's playing rather than his own transcription-derived variation. He isolates four short passages, all falling over the tune's I chord (D7) or IV chord (G7), and names the harmonic device behind each: a plain D7 (Mixolydian) scale into chord-tone targeting on the IV, a chromatic walk-down into a D7♭9 arpeggio, a whole-half (tonic) diminished scale used as a connector back from IV to I, a C major 7 arpeggio played over D7 for its upper extensions followed by a D minor pentatonic blues cadence into the IV, and a v-minor (A minor 7) arpeggio over D7 decorated with chromatic notes. After naming each device he immediately plays his own line built from the same "recipe" — the identical concept-not-lick framing from Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction. Short (7 minutes) and dense — almost every sentence maps to a concrete, reusable arpeggio/scale choice over one of two chords, making it a compact companion piece to the longer Delilah breakdown.

how-to-use-chord-extensions-in-your-solo.title: How To Use Chord Extensions In Your Solos!
how-to-use-chord-extensions-in-your-solo.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, dense jazz-guitar lesson from Nathan Borton built entirely around a single short Wes Montgomery guitar solo from Nat Adderley's 1960 album Work Song (in the key of A♭). Rather than teaching scales, Borton reduces the solo to three reusable devices for getting "buttery," melodic chord extensions (9ths, 11ths, 13ths) into a solo: (1) playing a whole chord's arpeggio on top of a different chord — an A♭ major 7 arpeggio over an F minor 7 reads as an F minor 9 sound (and the relationship reverses too — an F minor 9 arpeggio over A♭ major 7 gives a major 13 sound), because A♭ is F minor's relative major and shares nearly all the same notes; (2) the same "play a chord on top of a chord" idea applied to a dominant resolution, where a shape that "shouldn't" work over the V chord functions anyway once one note is treated as a passing tone rather than a chord tone; (3) a movable four-note guitar shape (C-B♭-G-F) that Wes shares with Grant Green, playable in octaves up and down the neck and reusable over any diatonic chord in a key for an instant extension flavor. It's a compact, single-idea-per-example lesson — closer to a "steal this shape" video than a full harmonic-analysis breakdown — and closes by pointing the viewer at the parts of the solo it deliberately didn't cover (Wes's rhythm/articulation and his use of octaves) as further study.

john-mclaughlin-this-is-not-like-other-a.title: John McLaughlin - This Is Not Like Other Approaches
john-mclaughlin-this-is-not-like-other-a.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen analyzes John McLaughlin's solo on "Take the Coltrane" (F blues, from the album with Joe DeFrancesco and Elvin Jones), focused on McLaughlin's atypical approach: minimal arpeggio use, heavy chromaticism, and lines that are sometimes deliberately harmony-ambiguous rather than chord-tone-anchored — described as thinking in "a larger picture" (attributed partly to McLaughlin's Indian-classical-music influence) rather than scale-per-chord.

What's taught

  • Chromatic sliding minor-3rds as a connective device, used repeatedly across the solo to move between target notes rather than diatonic scale steps — creates deliberate melodic ambiguity/tension independent of the underlying chord.
  • Harmonic "pull-ahead" — playing content that belongs to the next chord before the bar line actually arrives (e.g. treating an F7 bar as already G7, playing a Lydian-dominant-flavored line early) — offered as an alternate analysis to "this note doesn't fit the current chord," reframing an apparently-outside note as an anticipated resolution instead.
  • Triad substitution for a sus sound: playing an F major triad over a G7 chord, or a B♭ major triad over C7, both effectively spelling the 7sus4 sound of that root without naming it that way.
  • Held outside notes as pure melodic tension, not harmonic: a note that doesn't belong to the current chord/key (e.g. the ♭6 over an F blues) is picked deliberately and held rather than passed through quickly, then resolved later — argued to be a melodic choice (tension-and-resolution shape) rather than an attempt at a "correct" alternate scale.
  • Minimal arpeggio use as a stylistic signature — most phrases are built from scale fragments, chord-tone landing points, and chromatic connectors rather than full arpeggios; when arpeggios do appear, they're used sparingly and often stacked as triads-over-a-different-root rather than run as lines.
  • Motif displacement within a bar — restating the same short melodic motif but shifted to start on a different beat than its first statement, creating rhythmic variation from identical melodic material.
  • Tritone-substitution reading of a ii-V: an F♯7→B7 pair analyzed as the tritone-substitute ii-V resolving to B♭, rather than naming the chords in F.

kenny-burrell-how-to-make-the-blues-soun.title: Kenny Burrell - How to Make the Blues Sound Outside
kenny-burrell-how-to-make-the-blues-soun.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen analyzes Kenny Burrell's guitar solo on "Blackbird" from the Jimmy Smith album Standards. The through-line: Burrell uses blues language — not altered dominants, reharmonization, or diminished substitutions — as his primary "outside" tension device over straight-ahead jazz changes, deliberately clashing blue notes against clean chord tones and resolving back into the changes. A second, independent tension axis is rhythmic: contrasting straight eighth-note swing against a much harder/sharper swing feel within the same phrase, without changing note choice at all.

is-your-improvisation-practice-a-waste-o.title: Is Your Improvisation Practice a Waste of Time? (And How to Fix That)
is-your-improvisation-practice-a-waste-o.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen's answer to a specific practice-room failure mode: scales-and-exercises practice is easy to structure into a routine with visible progress, but soloing practice is often just unstructured noodling with no goal and no way to tell if you're actually getting better. His fix, demonstrated by playing two full solos back-to-back over the same tune (the jazz standard "I Want to Be Happy," a tonic-diminished-turnaround form he'd never played before, learned on the spot from a bandstand call), is to give soloing practice an explicit, nameable goal — melodicism, specifically motivic development — instead of "play more licks." The first solo is deliberately the unstructured baseline: connect the harmony competently with arpeggios and target notes, staying in one position, but with no larger melodic thread — musical, but reading as "a bunch of licks next to each other," not a solo. The second solo is the fix in action: one melodic idea (a 2–3 note motif) is stated, then developed continuously through the A section by changing its rhythm, its ending, and its starting position on the neck, rather than restarting from scratch on each chord. Larsen narrates both solos bar-by-bar, naming exactly which arpeggio/target-note device is happening on each chord and, in the second solo, exactly how the motif is being varied and why a fresh idea is introduced at the bridge. The most transferable single idea in the video is procedural rather than theoretical: after every phrase you play, listen to what you just played and ask "what should come next" — thinking in terms of the sound/shape you want to hear, not in note names or scale choices — which is what actually produces continuity between phrases instead of a new lick per chord.

octave-technique-split-finger-fretting-a.title: Octave Technique — Split-Finger Fretting and Duck-Wrist Prevention
octave-technique-split-finger-fretting-a.html:
BassBuzz's fix for the specific failure mode octaves expose that flatter fretboard patterns don't: jumping quickly between an octave's low note and high note (adjacent strings, two frets apart) tends to bend the fretting wrist sharply — nicknamed "duck wrist" ("quack, quack, quack") — which hurts, and which also throws off the plucking hand, which ends up scrambling to keep pace with a fretting hand that's fighting its own position. Named as a beginner blind spot specifically because it "sneaks up on you" — technique can look and feel solid on simpler patterns right up until an octave line exposes it. Two separate fixes are given: an ergonomic setup fix for the wrist bend itself, and a fretting-hand mechanic (split-finger technique) for the speed/stumbling problem underneath it.

Duck-wrist fix — ergonomic setup

Explicitly stated to work even with small hands — this is a setup adjustment, not a stretch you have to grow into:

  • Raise the strap so the neck isn't hanging too low — a too-low neck forces the wrist into a sharper bend to reach the fretboard at all.
  • Tilt the neck up further, beyond just raising the strap, for the same reason.
  • Add a bit more curl/bend in the fingers themselves so the wrist can stay straighter overall — trading finger curl for wrist angle, rather than eliminating the bend entirely.

Case study: a BassBuzz forum student ("Sarah") is shown with visibly reduced wrist bend after a couple of weeks of practicing with this setup, compared to a clearly-bent "before" clip — offered as evidence the fix is trainable, not just a one-time equipment tweak. (Practice slow motion through the octave shapes first, without worrying about plucking speed, to confirm the wrist itself is no longer bending sharply before adding the split-finger technique below on top.)

playing-fast-on-bass-efficient-technique.title: Playing Fast on Bass — Efficient Technique, Setup, and Bridge Plucking
playing-fast-on-bass-efficient-technique.html:
BassBuzz's three named levers for raising a bassist's playable speed ceiling, framed directly against the idea that speed is a talent you either have or don't — the video is explicit that no shortcut substitutes for years of deliberate practice (using Thundercat's shredding as the reference point), but names three concrete, trainable/settable things that get a player closer faster than raw reps alone. None of the three is about finger strength — they're about removing wasted motion and wasted resistance from the system, three different links in the chain (fretting-hand motion, instrument setup, plucking-hand position).

Lever 1 — relaxed, efficient fretting-hand technique

Minimize how far the fretting hand has to move to reach each note, rather than reaching with big, loose motions. The video doesn't break this down into a specific drill, but the underlying failure mode it's describing is the same one named explicitly in Fretting-Hand Strength, Stretch, Stamina, and Finger Control's Exercise 4 (the "flying fingers" fix — the "cup of tea" pinky flail and "flip the bird" middle-finger flail): any finger that lifts higher/wider off the fretboard than the next note requires is wasted travel, and wasted travel is what puts a hard ceiling on how fast a line can be played, not raw finger speed. Treat this lever as "go run Exercise 4" rather than a separate drill — same mechanism, same fix.

Lever 2 — set the bass up with low-to-medium action

Action = the height of the strings above the fingerboard. Lower action means the fretting hand needs less vertical travel to fully seat a note (smaller, more efficient movements) and the string offers less resistance to the plucking hand, so both hands do less physical work per note — which raises how fast the whole system can move before technique breaks down. This is a one-time setup change (or a tech's job), not a practice-session drill, and it's the one lever of the three that touches the instrument rather than technique. Deliberately in tension with Jamerson's Root-Fifth-Octave Exercise/Bassline Writing's Motown tone recipe, which calls for the opposite — high action — as part of James Jamerson's signature Funk Brothers tone; that's a genre/tone tradeoff (higher action = firmer, more resistant string = part of that thick, dug-in P-bass sound) working against this lever's speed goal, not a contradiction — pick the setup for what the part needs, tone or speed.
secs: Lever 2 — set the bass up with low-to-medium action

1-double-vocal-track.title: 1 Double Vocal Track
1-double-vocal-track.html:
Role: Unison double(s) of the lead — thickness, not a second voice. Band-limit dramatically, compress flat, mix in until you only notice it when you mute it (tucked −6 to −10 dB under the lead).

Chain philosophy: tune tight → bandpass hard → crush → de-ess → tuck.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Same setup as Main Vocal Track §1: Neumann TLM 102, same room/latency discipline, ghost latency track armed.
  • Performance note: sing doubles slightly softer than the lead — a softer unison layers in as sweetness instead of competing.

3-reasons-this-bon-jovi-bass-line-kicks-.title: 3 Reasons This Bon Jovi Bass Line Kicks Ass (+Full Song Tab)
3-reasons-this-bon-jovi-bass-line-kicks-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz breakdown of the bass part on Bon Jovi's "Livin' on a Prayer" (Slippery When Wet, 1986) — explicitly credited to "either Alec John Such or Hugh McDonald," flagged as a genuinely disputed/controversial credit rather than picking one. Modeled directly on Rick Beato's "What Makes This Song Great" format (named and linked as the inspiration for the video). Three transferable devices get pulled out of one arena-rock bassline that, on its face, "is not that interesting" the way a busy funk or prog line is: pedal point on the main riff (the bass holding one note while the keys change chords above it), bass runs/fills as melodic connective tissue between chords (with a full worked "playing over the bar line" example using target notes), and matching the bassline's busyness to the song's overall intensity arc (first chorus vs. last chorus as the A/B). Each device gets a "how to apply this yourself" pass, not just a spot-the-technique tour — the video's real center of gravity is the target-note method for writing your own over-the-bar-line run, worked twice with different filler-note choices over the same three targets.

how-to-solo-over-bolivia-cedar-walton.title: How To SOLO Over Bolivia! (Cedar Walton)
how-to-solo-over-bolivia-cedar-walton.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton walks through the chord changes to Cedar Walton's "Bolivia" section by section, purely as an improvisation vehicle — melody is deliberately skipped (stated reason: YouTube copyright), so this is a chord-scale/vocabulary lesson, not a chart or arrangement. His method throughout is reduction: instead of treating each chord as its own harmonic event to be handled individually, he collapses the tune's four sections down to a small handful of already-known "sound buckets" — a 5-1 (dominant-to-tonic), a tritone-sub 5-1, a long stretch that's almost entirely a single static B-minor sound (including a half-diminished chord reached via melodic minor off its ♭3), and a closing run of short 2-5s. The payoff move, saved for the tune's trickiest spot (the A7-to-G7 turnback before the tune's framing G7 vamp), is recognizing that a ii chord and its V are functionally the same sound (Dm7 ≈ G7, since Dm7 is G7's related ii in the key of C) — which lets him reinterpret A7→G7 as A7→Dm7's "5-1," folding an otherwise-awkward transition into vocabulary he already has. He closes by generalizing this into a practice philosophy: sort every jazz lick/line you transcribe into one of three buckets (5-1, 2-5-1, static-minor) rather than memorizing licks tune-by-tune, so a whole tune like this one ends up being "just 5-1 lines and static minor sounds" instead of four unrelated hard sections. Short (under 9 minutes), spoken clearly, captions clean/high-confidence — the only garble worth flagging is the ASR mishearing "tritone sub" as "trionee sub" throughout, corrected in the transcript and here.

how-to-improve-your-bebop-lines-and-phra.title: How To Improve Your BEBOP LINES and Phrases with DONNA LEE - The Ultimate Bebop Guide...
how-to-improve-your-bebop-lines-and-phra.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton teaches the head melody of Charlie Parker's bebop contrafact "Donna Lee," then takes it apart to extract the four devices Parker leans on throughout: arpeggios (sometimes decorated with extensions), chromaticism, the major bebop scale, and line closers — a device with no prior home in the vault. This is a companion piece to an earlier-enriched Borton video on the same tune (THIS Song Turns Students Into BEBOP Pros...), which broke down Donna Lee's own harmony (the non-diatonic B♭7, the backdoor G♭7→D♭maj7 move); this one stays on the melodic-line-construction side instead — how Parker actually builds phrases out of the harmony, not what the harmony itself is doing. The most valuable new material is the line-closer concept itself: a short, largely memorized cadential tail that either ends a phrase (paired with an ascending arpeggio, the textbook 5–1 bebop shape) or — flipped — opens one, turning the same fixed phrase into a way to generate tonic-dominant (non-resolving) language instead. Both the melody-teaching and the line-building material are consolidated onto a new song-ref page, 🎵 CHARLIE PARKER - Donna Lee, alongside the harmonic analysis already logged from the companion video.

chorus-ensemble.title: Chorus-Ensemble
chorus-ensemble.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's modulation effect combining classic chorus and multi-voice ensemble modes for thickening and widening a signal.

What it's used for

Widening mono synths, guitars, and vocals, and adding classic chorus movement to pads and leads.

FX chain notes

Placed after EQ/compression on an instrument chain, often as a subtle send-based width effect rather than a heavy insert.

how-to-play-feel-good-inc-on-bass.title: How to Play Feel Good Inc. on Bass
how-to-play-feel-good-inc-on-bass.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's Josh teaches the "Feel Good Inc." (Gorillaz) bassline as a five-challenge progression, each challenge adding one new layer of difficulty on top of the same short riff rather than teaching it all at once: (1) right notes with a fretting/plucking fingering system explicitly not synced to each other, (2) the same notes with correct syncopated rhythm, (3) the same notes with correct note length/muting, (4) the riff's signature slide, and (5) the short bass solo that recombines everything. The video is genuinely well-built pedagogically — each challenge is playable and gradeable on its own before the next difficulty layer is added — and it's unusually well-sourced for a BassBuzz video: it pulls in an actual voice-note quote from Shay Adelican, Gorillaz's current touring/session bassist, on both the feel of the syncopation and the real-world E♭ tuning, plus a reference to Murdoc's (the band's fictional bassist/frontman) DVD commentary on why the riff itself was written the way it was. The most broadly reusable teaching device in the video is the "finger syncing" myth-bust in challenge one — treating fretting-hand and plucking-hand fingerings as two fully independent systems rather than mirroring one to the other — plus the "beat ruler + hum the drum part" method for internalizing syncopated rhythm in challenge two. Confidence note: manual (non-auto) captions, high confidence for content, but the caption track carries no timestamps and the riff's exact rhythmic subdivisions (challenge two's "on, off, on, off, off, off, 3-and-4-and-1-2-and-3-and-4-and-1-and-2-3-4" count) come through the transcript somewhat garbled — treat that specific count as approximate, not a verified rhythm chart.

first-50-songs-you-should-play-on-bass.title: First 50 Songs You Should Play on Bass
first-50-songs-you-should-play-on-bass.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A repertoire-selection video, not a technique lesson: BassBuzz plays a rapid-fire montage of ~50 iconic bass riffs (roughly 14 seconds each, back-to-back, almost no spoken narration) as a curated "songs to build your skills on" list for beginner-to-intermediate bassists. The description frames the throughline explicitly — these 50 riffs, collectively, will teach syncopation, plucking speed and endurance, different time signatures, major/minor/blues scales, shifting, hammer-ons and pull-offs, bass slides, locking in with the kick drum, and "extreme bass face mastery" — but the video itself doesn't narrate which riff teaches which skill; that mapping isn't stated anywhere in the source. Because it's a montage with almost no host speech, the captions mostly transcribe the sung lyrics of each song clip rather than instruction, and they're heavily garbled the way music-heavy auto-captioning always is (see the transcript note below) — a handful of phrases are clean enough to identify the song playing at that moment, but most aren't. The actual value of this video is the song list itself: BassBuzz links a companion PDF in the description (bassbuzz.com/go/50-first) that names all 50 songs in order with artist and year, and flags which ones have a free full bass tab and/or dedicated BassBuzz lesson video — that PDF is the real "what's taught" content here and is reproduced in full below, cross-referenced against the vault's existing bass/library notes. Six of the 50 songs already have real coverage elsewhere in the vault (two get full technique breakdowns in a sibling BassBuzz video, two have their own 20 Music/Library/ song-ref notes, and two have their own dedicated lesson-video notes) — those overlaps are called out inline.

unlock-jazz-improv-with-one-grant-green-.title: Unlock Jazz Improv with ONE Grant Green Solo?! Honestly, Yes.
unlock-jazz-improv-with-one-grant-green-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton reverse-engineers Grant Green's solo on "Cool Blues" (from the album Born to Be Blue, a B♭ jazz blues) into three named "essential sounds" he argues every jazz improviser must have, framed as a complete master-class-in-miniature rather than a lick catalog: 5-to-1 ideas (single-note lines that outline a V→I pull, including strongly altered versions using 9/♭9/♯9), 2-equals-5 / 5-equals-2 (soloing over any dominant 7th chord using the melodic language of its related ii minor chord, and vice versa), and tonic dominant (treating a dominant 7th as a stable home sound rather than a tension needing resolution, via a major-7-arpeggio-off-the-♭7 trick and the dominant bebop scale). A fourth umbrella, blues language, adds three further devices: chromatic walk-ups/walk-downs between chord tones, classic movable blues-opening vocabulary usable over any chord in the form, and a named five-note Kansas City blues scale. This is the third Grant Green solo-breakdown video now in the vault (alongside How Grant Green Played Jazz Blues by Jack Ruch and Borton's own Why Grant Green's Minor Blues Soloing Is PERFECT (Jazz 101)) and it's the most abstract of the three — Borton names and generalizes each device explicitly ("this will work over any chord in the jazz genre") rather than staying tied to this one tune, which is the most valuable thing about it: these read as reusable soloing tools, not just annotations on one solo. The video is a Patreon funnel (a written etude/PDF is gated there), so the free content here is the concept-naming and one demonstrated example per device — exact fretboard positions and full multi-bar transcription aren't in the free captions.

how-to-solo-over-grant-s-tune-grant-gree.title: How To Solo Over Grant's Tune! (Grant Green)
how-to-solo-over-grant-s-tune-grant-gree.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton breaks down how to solo over "Grant's Tune," a Grant Green original off the album Solid, picked by audience poll (tied with a promised follow-up blues video). The whole lesson is a reduction exercise, same method as his "Bolivia" breakdown: the tune looks tricky at a glance but collapses to a small number of already-known sound-buckets once the harmony is renamed correctly. The A section's two-chord vamp (Cm7–D♭7) is really just a 1-5-1 in disguise — D♭7 is the tritone sub of G7 — so every option for soloing over a plain minor-to-its-dominant applies directly, and he lays out four parallel systems (C blues scale, C Dorian + A♭ melodic minor, C "minor diminished," or just parking on G7♭9 the whole time) rather than picking one as correct. The A-section tag (E♭ major) and the B section (a set of slash chords over an E♭ pedal that turn out to be ordinary E♭ major/minor7/major/sus9 shapes once fingered with E♭ in the bass) get the same treatment — play them modally chord-by-chord, or blend E♭ blues with a major/minor 3rd swap keyed to each chord's quality. He closes by naming the tune's real lesson: the ability to sit on one sound over a long static stretch (the vamp) AND the ability to move one sound fluently across many different chords (the B section) are two different skills, and this tune is built to drill both in the same eight bars. Short (8:27), spoken clearly, captions clean/high-confidence — the only garble worth flagging is the ASR mishearing "tritone sub" as "trionee sub," corrected here and in the transcript, and a couple of spots where the spoken example licks aren't transcribable from captions alone (no words, just playing).

why-grant-green-s-minor-blues-soloing-is.title: Why Grant Green's Minor Blues Soloing Is PERFECT (Jazz 101)
why-grant-green-s-minor-blues-soloing-is.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton pulls four concrete, transferable concepts out of a single Grant Green solo — the minor blues chorus over Green's own tune "Trace and Tracy" (B♭ minor) — arguing that Green's minor-blues vocabulary is under-discussed compared to his major/jazz-blues playing and deserves the same close-reading treatment. The video is explicitly framed as a blueprint that generalizes to any minor jazz situation, not just this one tune. Four devices, in the order taught: (1) tonic minor soloing — implying a momentary V7-to-i resolution inside a static minor chord by borrowing from the minor-6/minor-major-7 "tonic minor" sound, first as a single outside note resolving down a half step, then as a full 5-1 line played straight over the unmoving chord; (2) color tones — deliberately landing on the 9th, 11th, and natural 13th of the minor chord as a melodic feature, not incidental color; (3) the "dilla rhythm" — a named syncopated embellishment cell Green uses to break up straight eighth-note lines while moving through scale or arpeggio tones, demonstrated over both a scalar walk-down and a minor-6 arpeggio; and (4) blues language — small one-octave blues boxes moved around the neck, plus the blues scale played vertically up and down the neck rather than boxed horizontally. The most valuable material is the tonic-minor device (a genuinely underdocumented bebop-over-static-minor trick) and the naming of the dilla rhythm as a reusable rhythmic vocabulary item, since most minor-blues instruction stops at "use the minor pentatonic or blues scale."

diagonal-pentatonic-blues-soloing.title: Diagonal Pentatonic Blues Soloing
diagonal-pentatonic-blues-soloing.html:
One diagonal fretboard shape, one altered note, one transposition — a low-overhead alternative to tracking a separate arpeggio per chord over a I7-IV7-V7 blues. Contrasts directly with Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes's CAGED-arpeggio-per-chord method: instead of re-fingering a fresh arpeggio at every chord change, this technique keeps one continuous pentatonic shape running and moves only what has to move. Worked in the key of A over exactly the I7-IV7-V7 progression (A7-D7-E7) documented on Blues Form and Harmony, and grounded in the same note-choice logic as Blues Scales and Blue Notes — a direct guitar-fretboard application of that page's "one scale over all three chords" vs. "following the changes" practical notes, landing on a hybrid: mostly one shape, with a single deliberate note swap where the changes actually demand it.

The diagonal shape

A "diagonal 3-2 major pentatonic" — a two-notes-per-string fingering that climbs diagonally across the neck (fret gaps alternating roughly 3 then 2 frets per string, with an irregularity on the B string) rather than sitting in one vertical box position. Starts on the root at the 5th fret (A, low E string). (The source names the pattern directly as "diagonal 3-2 major pentatonic" and calls out the B-string fingering as the one spot that breaks the regular 3-2 alternation, but doesn't give the complete fret-by-fret map on all six strings in the transcript — treat the exact fingering as best confirmed against the source's free diagram download, referenced in the video description, rather than fully reconstructed here.) The pitch content is plain A major pentatonic: A B C♯ E F♯ — the shape's value is that it's playable diagonally across the whole neck rather than boxed into one position, which is what lets the same physical logic keep working as the chord changes (below).

Step 1 — I7 (A7): straight major pentatonic

A major pentatonic (A B C♯ E F♯) over A7, the I chord — inspired directly by BB King's use of major pentatonic (not just minor/blues scale) over the tonic dominant. The C♯ is the chord's major 3rd, so it "lines up with the chord perfectly." Same idea as Blues Scales and Blue Notes § What to play over the I7 — Mixolydian-leaning material (major 3rd intact) reads as the "sweet" end of that page's blend, here delivered as a fixed fretboard shape rather than a scale-degree list.

georgia-on-my-mind-chords-guitar-lesson-.title: Georgia on My Mind Chords (Guitar Lesson) - Easiest way to play the REAL chords
georgia-on-my-mind-chords-guitar-lesson-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borowski (Sound Guitar Lessons) teaches a full chord-by-chord arrangement of "Georgia on My Mind" — the chords-first companion to his own fingerstyle tutorial on the same tune (his recommended order: this video, then the fingerstyle arrangement) — using only open-position chord shapes in the key of C — explicitly designed so any guitarist with basic open chords can play it, while still capturing "the REAL chords" (the jazz-informed harmony, not a dumbed-down 3-chord version). The lesson is built around choice: for nearly every chord he gives a preferred shape plus one or more alternates that trade simplicity for jazzier color, and explains why each alternate works (passing chords, chromatic alteration, delayed resolution, melody-note-in-the-chord logic) so the viewer can build their own arrangement rather than just copy his. He frames the song in its home key (F, most common on sheet music) and Ray Charles' recorded key (G), and shows how a capo (5th fret for F, 7th fret for G) lets the same open-C shapes work in either. Two bonus segments close the video: a free "8 movable shapes" system for reading any jazz lead sheet, and a short lesson on walking chromatic bass notes between chord changes (building on the slash-chord bass motion already written into the arrangement). This is a strong "REAL chords, easy hands" teaching approach — worth mining for its reharmonization logic (delayed resolution, chord-in-front-of-a-chord insertion, melody-note substitution rule) as much as for the Georgia on My Mind chart itself.

slap-pop-bass-bad-vs-good-technique-begi.title: Slap & Pop Bass - Bad vs Good Technique (Beginner - Intermediate)
slap-pop-bass-bad-vs-good-technique-begi.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz technique breakdown focused specifically on the popping half of slap-and-pop — thumb-up vs. thumb-down popping hand shape, two named artist variations, an explicit anti-pattern, and a "minimum viable pressure" framework for not shredding a beginner's pop finger — bookended by a compressed recap of slap fundamentals and a full teaching pass on the teeter-totter technique that connects slap and pop into one efficient motion. The video opens by naming its own three-part structure: the core popping essentials, how beginners wreck their popping with bad technique, and the teeter-totter technique itself. It briefly recaps slap technique (forearm rotation, relaxed bouncing thumb) as already covered in an earlier BassBuzz video, then spends its middle section on popping mechanics in real depth — thumb-up style (Larry Graham, Victor Wooten, Rhonda Smith, Les Claypool lineage), thumb-down style (a different artist lineage, one name garbled beyond recognition in the auto-captions), Flea's middle-finger variation with the specific reason to use it, and Louis Johnson's arm-assisted pop variation. It calls out isolated-finger and wrist-flex popping as things not to do, and introduces "minimum viable pressure" (MVP) as the amount of finger tension needed for a clean pop and no more, tying pressure directly to action height with a concrete ~5 mm quick-check. The back half re-teaches the teeter-totter technique (the single continuous forearm cycle that connects a slap to its pop without extra up/down trips, already the subject of its own vault note from three earlier videos) with a dedicated open-string drill and explicit tempo ladder, then applies the whole system to a real riff — the intro to Jamiroquai's "Emergency on Planet Earth" (bassist Stuart Zender). Short (11:28), technique-dense, entirely a right-hand-mechanics lesson — no production, no gear signal chain beyond the one action-height aside.

jens-larsen-all-the-things-you-are-harmo.title: Jens Larsen - All The Things You Are - Harmonic Analysis
jens-larsen-all-the-things-you-are-harmo.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A full chord-by-chord harmonic analysis of the Jerome Kern jazz standard "All The Things You Are," walked through in Jens Larsen's usual method: figure out the form from the melody first (before touching the chords), then work out the key centers and modulations, then the chord-scale/soloing choices, closing with a short discussion of Kern's own voicing choices in the original sheet music and why they matter. The tune is chosen specifically because it modulates far more than a typical standard — four separate key centers across a 36-bar AABA-ish form — which makes it Larsen's worked example for how to find and name a pivot chord, and for the recurring "modulate up a major 3rd" device that shows up across a lot of the American songbook. The back half covers a full bar-by-bar chord-scale map for soloing (harmonic minor, Lydian, melodic minor, Dorian-over-a-diminished-substitute), a detailed dissection of the ♭3°/♯4° (subdominant diminished) chord that closes the form, and a closing note on why Kern wrote the last A section in bare triads rather than fully spelled chords — a deliberate ambiguity device. Density is high throughout; almost no bar goes undiscussed.

the-jazz-standard-that-turns-students-in.title: The Jazz Standard That Turns Students Into Pro Players
the-jazz-standard-that-turns-students-in.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Nathan Borton frames Jerome Kern's "Nobody Else But Me" as a single, unusually dense practice vehicle — one standard that happens to contain seven distinct, commonly-recurring jazz harmonic devices, so drilling this one tune functions as a compressed survey of most of what a student will run into across the wider standards repertoire. He comps through the tune once for ear reference, then walks each device in turn with a guitar voicing/lick example: 5–1 motion into multiple key centers, a "dominant two chord" (the ii chord made dominant instead of minor, treated as a static lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant color rather than a functioning V), passing diminished chords (two solving methods — reading as a rootless dominant, or as triads pulled from the diminished scale when the chord resolves downward), a backdoor dominant (♭VII7→I, treated with the same lydian-dominant/tonic-dominant sound as the dominant-two chord), a chord walkup progression at the tune's end (offered three ways: play the literal changes, substitute a long ii–V across the whole passage, or ignore the chords entirely and outline the key center), the Tadd Dameron turnaround (a dense chromatic-root turnaround simplified two ways — C minor pentatonic over the whole thing, or the "Coltrane pattern" of 1-2-3-5 chord tones per chord), and non-functional changes (a passage that exists purely because Kern is reharmonizing the melody, not moving through real function — solved either by targeting the melody note directly or by treating each chord as its own local sound/scale). Most valuable parts: the two-method passing-diminished-chord split (dominant read vs. triad-from-diminished-scale read, chosen by which way the chord resolves), and the three-tier "how much do you actually need to track" approach to the walkup and Tadd Dameron sections, which generalizes well beyond this one tune.

this-is-how-joe-pass-plays-amazing-solos.title: This is How Joe Pass Plays Amazing Solos
this-is-how-joe-pass-plays-amazing-solos.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen transcribes and breaks down the opening of Joe Pass's chord-melody arrangement of "Little Darlin'" from Pass's Intercontinental album (Larsen: "probably one of his best albums if not his best"), working through roughly the first 16 bars bar-by-bar. Larsen's stated focus isn't just how Pass harmonizes the melody with block chords (a chord under every melody note) but specifically what Pass plays in the gaps between phrases — the song's structure gives a two-bar melodic phrase followed by a sustained note, and Pass fills that sustained-note space with short melodic fills built directly out of chord voicings rather than scale runs. Larsen credits studying Pass's chord solos as foundational to his own chord vocabulary and to learning how to harmonize a melodic statement in real time. Two reusable devices recur across the whole breakdown: (1) turning fills into arpeggiated chord voicings — "using your chord voicings as melodic structures," a direct callback to a chord-melody-fills video Larsen names as published the week before — and (2) a stated Joe Pass trademark: reharmonizing a diatonic minor chord (most often the iii) as its own dominant seventh for extra forward pull, deployed "at random" across tunes and even inside blues turnarounds, not just at this one spot. Caption-quality flag: the pulled English track is garbled throughout in an auto-generated/auto-translated way despite being labeled a plain "en" track (e.g. "Jens Larsen" → "Jen's Larsson," "chord solos" → "core/call solos," "melodic fills" → "Mirotic fills," "sharp line" → "shop line") — treated as low-to-medium confidence; the extraction below reconstructs Larsen's actual jazz terminology from context and cross-checks against his vocabulary on other enriched videos rather than trusting the caption text's literal wording for chord names. Numbers/chord symbols below are the best-supported reading, not verbatim captions.

jazz-comping-jazz-chords-and-approaches-.title: Jazz Comping - Jazz Chords and Approaches - Just Friends - Jazz Guitar Lesson
jazz-comping-jazz-chords-and-approaches-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Full transcript: Jazz Comping - Jazz Chords and Approaches - Just Friends - Jazz Guitar Lesson (transcript)

Synopsis

A long-form (~59 min), deliberately less-scripted Jens Larsen lesson that steps back from "here's a drop-2 voicing for a B♭maj7" to address comping as a whole skill — because, as he opens with, a working jazz guitarist spends far more time comping than soloing but almost nobody makes lesson content specifically about it. He picks "Just Friends" as the vehicle: first a full harmonic analysis of the tune (key of F, 32-bar AABA-ish form with nearly-identical A sections, functional breakdown chord by chord, including the ♯IV° diminished and its two derivable "one-note-changed" scale options), then two full comped choruses over a backing track demonstrating his two main voicing families — drop-2 and triads — narrated chord by chord, then a third, more "open" chorus that layers in triad-arpeggiation, sustained-note-plus-moving-inner-melody, and riff-based comping. The back half of the video pulls back further into the philosophy of comping behind a soloist: giving room vs. pushing energy, locking to the rhythm section, style-dependent density (Wes Montgomery/hard-bop busy-but-not-in-the-way vs. Bill Frisell's Paul Motian/Charlie Hayden trio "On Broadway" records, where almost nothing is played and the harmony is just laid down and left open), and named reference recordings to study (Herbie Hancock/Tony Williams behind Miles Davis, Wynton Kelly, John Scofield's "So Near, So Far" with Joe Henderson). Larsen is explicit that this is intentionally not a "here's the exact voicing" video — the value is in the reasoning and the listening habits, not a transcript to copy note for note. Most valuable material: the tonic-diminished harmonic-major derivation for the ♯IV° chord (a genuinely new angle vs. the vault's existing harmonic-minor-only diminished-scale coverage), the "reduce a chord run to one word" learning habit applied concretely to Just Friends' structure, the riff-comping practice method as the on-ramp to truly open/free comping, and the sideman-listening material (which reinforces and extends Ensemble Listening and Comping Restraint with new named reference recordings and a "leaning on energy vs. leaning on groove" framing that note didn't yet have).

slow-dancing-in-a-burning-room-chords-un.title: Slow Dancing in a Burning Room Chords - Unique John Mayer Guitar Lesson
slow-dancing-in-a-burning-room-chords-un.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borkowski isolates one small, recurring moment from John Mayer's "Slow Dancing in a Burning Room" — the IV→I (A→E) triad move with its signature hammer-on ornament — and uses it as a full worked example of his "go deep on one small thing" method: name the harmony (plagal cadence, IV→I in the key of E), analyze the voice leading (closest possible triad-to-triad motion, one note per voice moving the smallest distance), locate every instance of that same A→E voice-leading move across three different string sets on the neck, add John Mayer's specific 2→3 hammer-on embellishment to each one, then package the whole thing into a timed, in-tempo self-test exercise. This is not a full song walkthrough — it's a magnifying-glass lesson on a single 2-chord fragment, chosen because it's the exact spot students keep asking Jared to explain. Clean, high-confidence spoken lesson audio; the standard yt-transcript.cjs pull returned an empty transcript for this video (words: 1, known drop issue on this channel's manually-uploaded captions) — worked around with a manual pinned-yt-dlp VTT pull.

triad-melodic-devices-for-jazz-soloing.title: Triad Melodic Devices for Jazz Soloing
triad-melodic-devices-for-jazz-soloing.html: Part of Jazz Harmony and Bebop Vocabulary. A fourth distinct triad-soloing angle alongside the vault's other three: Triads as a Fretboard Map relocates one triad shape across three neck zones; Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords extracts a triad from inside a single seventh chord; Harmonized Scale Triads for Soloing harmonizes a whole parent scale into seven triads used in sequence up the neck. This page instead treats triads as melodic raw material to be varied — superimposing diatonic triads onto changes, reordering a triad's notes into different inversions, reshuffling the note order into patterns (3-1-5 instead of 1-3-5), and stacking a triad into a wide spread/open voicing — all worked over jazz ii-V-I and turnaround changes rather than a single vamp.

upper-structure-triads-for-comping-and-s.title: Upper structure triads for comping and soloing
upper-structure-triads-for-comping-and-s.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, dense jazz-guitar lesson from Jack Ruch on deriving upper structure triads — the triad hiding inside a seventh chord's 3rd, 5th, and 7th — and using those triads both to simplify comping over a moving jazz progression and as a target-note map for soloing. The whole lesson is worked over the seven chords of Autumn Leaves (C minor 7, F dominant 7, B♭ major 7, E♭ major 7, A minor 7 flat 5, D7, G minor 7), which conveniently touches all four common seventh-chord qualities, so it functions as a mini-reference for "which triad quality sits on the 3-5-7 of each seventh-chord type." The pedagogical throughline connects directly to Ruch's separate "triads as a fretboard map" lesson (already in the vault as Triads as a Fretboard Map): the payoff of learning the upper-structure triad for a chord is worthless without already knowing that triad's shape in all three fretboard zones, so the two lessons are meant to be used together — this video supplies the harmonic what, the fretboard-map lesson supplies the physical where. Comping and soloing are treated as the same skill at two different speeds: comping strings the shapes together as chords on one string set, soloing uses the same shapes' individual notes as a target map for single-note lines.

a-classic-tune-for-learning-about-second.title: A Classic Tune for Learning About Secondary Dominants
a-classic-tune-for-learning-about-second.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch teaches a single tune — Ray Charles's arrangement of "You Don't Know Me," in the key of E♭ major — end to end, using it as a vehicle for one specific soloing device: a movable diminished-7 arpeggio lick for outlining functioning dominant chords, both the primary V7 (B♭7) and every secondary dominant in the progression (E♭7 → A♭, C7 → Fm, G7 → Cm). He plays the tune down first with chord names on screen so it can be learned by ear/eye, then names and locates every functioning dominant in it, teaches one diminished-arpeggio lick built off the chord's own 3rd, and drills moving that single lick across all four dominant spots plus a diminished passing chord (A♭ → A°). The back half of the lesson is about integration, not just vocabulary: he plays a plain E♭ major pentatonic solo through the changes as a template, then rebuilds it substituting the diminished lick in one dominant spot at a time (C7→Fm, then G7→Cm, then E♭7→A♭), before playing a full solo blending pentatonic, bluesy minor phrasing, and the diminished lick together — a concrete demonstration of how a single harmonic-analysis device becomes usable, musical vocabulary rather than a party trick played over its own backing track in isolation. Most valuable here: naming the general principle ("be on the lookout for where functioning dominant chords appear in other songs") while grounding every step in one real, specific tune rather than an abstract example — the same "identify → drill in isolation → blend into a solo template" arc Jack Ruch uses across his catalog (see Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes).

analysis-and-jazz-guitar-solo-ideas-for-.title: Analysis and Jazz Guitar Solo ideas for a Jazz Standard - Lady Bird - Pentatonic, Lydian Dominant
analysis-and-jazz-guitar-solo-ideas-for-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A two-part Jens Larsen lesson on Tadd Dameron's "Lady Bird" (captions render the composer as "Ted Cameron" — resolved from context): first a chord-by-chord harmonic analysis of the 16-bar form (key of C), then an extended pass at soloing vocabulary chord-by-chord over the changes, closing with a worked line over the tune's signature turnaround. The analysis half is short and functional — establish the tonic, name the ii-V's, flag the one spot he treats as genuinely ambiguous (whether the cadence to A♭maj7 is a real modulation or just a borrowed chord), and point out that the turnaround's descending-major-third motion is a compact, low-stakes way to internalize the same interval cycle that drives Coltrane's "Giant Steps" — worth knowing this tune as a stepping stone before tackling that one. The solo-ideas half is the bulk of the video and moves chord-by-chord through the form, demonstrating a specific vocabulary device on nearly every chord: half-step-shifted pentatonic boxes, Lydian dominant and altered-scale color on the dominants, triad pairs and half-step-planed arpeggios for connecting adjacent chords, and diminished-family sounds leaned on throughout because (his framing) the tune's own turnaround already has a diminished/half-step-up character baked into it. Runs almost an hour; dense, and the auto-captions garble jazz terminology heavily (see transcript note) so several specific chord/scale names below are read from context rather than quoted directly — flagged inline where that applies.

uad-ua-1176ln.title: UAD UA 1176LN
uad-ua-1176ln.html:
Category: FET Compressor Vendor: Universal Audio — SE/Legacy version in the Apollo stock bundle (Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII)

What it is

Emulation of the 1176 FET limiting amplifier — the fastest attack in the business (20–800 microseconds). Where the UAD Teletronix LA-2A rides, the 1176 grabs.

What it's used for

Peak control and attitude: drums, aggressive vocals, strummed acoustic when the pick transients spike. Also the classic serial partner (1176 catches peaks → LA-2A levels).

Key settings (tracking)

  • Ratio: 4:1.
  • Attack: 3–4 (medium-slow for the 1176 — lets the pick/consonant through). Counter-intuitive: higher number = faster on an 1176.
  • Release: 6–7 (fast, ~50 ms — resets before the next strum).
  • Input: drive to 2–4 dB GR on peaks only; Output to unity.
  • Never "all-buttons" on the way in — that's a mix decision.

FX chain notes

Alternative to the UAD Teletronix LA-2A in uad_console chains when the part is percussive rather than smooth — see Acoustic Guitar Track.

melodyne.title: Melodyne
melodyne.html:
Category: Pitch/Vocal Vendor: Celemony

What it is

Celemony's audio-to-MIDI pitch and time editor, using DNA (Direct Note Access) technology to isolate and edit individual notes within polyphonic and monophonic audio.

What it's used for

Deep pitch and timing correction on vocals and instruments — far more surgical than real-time pitch correction, plus note-level formant, vibrato, and timing edits.

FX chain notes

Used offline/pre-mix as a corrective editing pass, typically before the vocal chain's EQ, compression, and de-essing.

Techniques

  • Switch off Polyphonic detection specifically to make manual note-dragging easier, then move a whole detected note by hand as a creative sound-design edit, not a correction — and accept some loss of the note's original character as part of the result. Building a metallic texture layer, the algorithm gets switched away from polyphonic ("it's trying to go polyphonic, but it's much easier to manipulate this stage in") before dragging a whole detected note (read as starting around F3, target A2) down by hand; some of the original note's detail gets lost in the drag and is deliberately kept rather than undone — "I start losing some of the note on this one, right here... at this point it's just kind of, you're just kind of being creative and designing however you want it." (qualitative — thin, demonstrative transcript; no exact semitone value confirmed) → Layering and Stacking — Shawn Everett (Mix with the Masters), Digital Audio Manipulation with Shawn Everett
  • Resynthesize mode used deliberately for its "digital and futuristic" character, not for pitch correction. "We used Melodyne a lot, so of course it's a tool made to fix vocals tuning and everything. And we used the Resynthesize part of the plugin. And what we love about it is that it gives things like a very digital and futuristic texture. And we wanted things to sound a bit unnatural on this record. Not unnatural, but supernatural." Justice run vocals, synths, and pianos through Resynthesize specifically for the artifact character it introduces — a corrective tool repurposed as a texture/sound-design source. → Pitch and Formant — Justice x Kevin Parker (Mix with the Masters), Behind the Track｜'Neverender' by Justice & Tame Impala

10-songs-that-taught-me-bass-easy-to-eff.title: 10 Songs that Taught Me Bass (Easy to Effin’ Hard)

Song IDs below are reconstructed from three sources: the official YouTube description's riddle-style artist hints, cross-references inside this same transcript (song 6 is later named directly — "after learning songs like Something and I'll Take You There" — confirming song 6 and giving strong context for song 5), and two proper nouns the auto-captions did pick up correctly (Cliff Williams, song 3; Nikolai, song 7). analyzing-a-standard-stella-by-starlight.title: Analyzing a Standard - Stella By Starlight - Functional Harmony in Jazz -  Jazz Guitar Lesson
analyzing-a-standard-stella-by-starlight.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen's own functional-harmony analysis of "Stella By Starlight" (Victor Young), the tune he explicitly cites — one video later, in this vault's own "All The Things You Are - Harmonic Analysis" note — as the counter-example of a tune that looks harmonically busy and mysterious but barely modulates at all, in contrast to All The Things You Are's four real key centers. This is that video. Larsen's core thesis: Stella is famously confusing to players because it wanders through a long chain of chords before ever landing on its home key (it doesn't touch B♭ major until bar 9), and several of its chords look non-functional at a glance (an A7 resolving to Cm7, a G7 that seems to want a whole-tone scale) — but almost every one of those chords is explainable as a secondary/auxiliary dominant, a backdoor dominant, or a reharmonized diminished chord, all still inside the single key of B♭, with only one genuine modulation in the whole 32-ish-bar form (a brief, unusual pivot up to F major just before the bridge). The video works section by section: confirm the key from the ending, work out a loose/asymmetric AABA-ish form, assign Roman numerals to the parts that are unambiguous, then tackle the tune's two hardest passages — the famous opening (Em7♭5–A7–Cm7–F7) and the pivot into F major before the bridge — as reharmonized/borrowed devices rather than mysteries. It closes with a full bar-by-bar chord-scale recap for soloing, and flags the exact same ♯4°-diminished opening device this vault already has extensively documented from the All The Things You Are page (Larsen even names Stella there as one of the tunes that shares it). Transcript quality is medium — a dense, screen-capture-narrated theory lecture (no visible chord chart in the audio-only transcript), with a number of chord letters and proper nouns garbled by auto-captions (flagged inline below where it affects a specific claim); the underlying reasoning transcribes cleanly.

📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz breakdown of Chris Squire's bass part on Yes's "Roundabout" (Fragile, 1971) — framed explicitly as decoding why Squire's playing influenced Geddy Lee, John Entwistle (named as "john," the reference is The Who's Entwistle rather than a typo), Steve Harris, and Les Claypool, not just a note-for-note tab walkthrough. Six distinct devices get pulled out of one riff/song, each with a real, transferable lesson rather than trivia: ghost notes as a contrast/texture device (with real cross-genre examples beyond rock), a 16th-note syncopation the video says most players get wrong, a rhythmic "push"/anticipation device, a genuinely rule-breaking drum-and-bass conversational rhythm, whole-song use of space as an arrangement tool, and Squire doubling a buried organ melody on bass in the bridge. The tone/gear section is the most concrete "steal this" segment: a specific string, a specific pick, a specific plucking position, and — notably — an explicit fallback path for anyone without a Rickenbacker or without pick technique (Geddy Lee's own fingerstyle approach to the same riff). The whole video reads as a "here's the toolkit, here's how to use it even if you're not Chris Squire" lesson, closing the gap between "listen to how cool this is" and "here's what to actually practice."

dynamics-articulations.title: Dynamics & Articulations
dynamics-articulations.html:
Part of Music Theory → Notation. Reference glossary for the symbols that shape how a note is played, beyond just pitch and rhythm.

Dynamics (how loud)

Full ladder, loudest to softest: fff (very very loud) → ff (very loud) → f (loud) → mf (medium loud) → mp (medium soft) → p (soft) → pp (very soft) → ppp (very very soft) → n (niente, inaudible).

  • Hairpins (< / >) or the terms crescendo/diminuendo show gradual volume change.
  • Placement: below the staff for instrumental parts, above the staff for vocal parts (stays clear of the lyrics — see Writing for Voice).
  • Specific interpretation (exactly how loud is "f"?) is left to the performer — notation only shows relative volume.

Articulations (how a note is treated)

Symbol Name Meaning
> Accent with additional emphasis
. Staccato short and detached — originally meant "half the written value" (a literal durational instruction), drifted over time to mean "detached" generally rather than strictly short
– (line) Tenuto emphasized, held for full value (properly "legato" in older usage, implying connection into the next note)
^ Marcato ("marked") short and accented
Marcato + extra stress Marcatissimo heavily/more emphatically accented than plain marcato
(bow-heavy accent) Martelé bowed-strings-specific: a very heavy accent from heavy bow pressure on a down-bow
▼ Staccatissimo very short and forceful
sfz Sforzando suddenly loud and accented
fermata (bird's-eye) Fermata hold longer than indicated
≠ (slashes) Tremolo rapidly alternate between two notes
V Up bow (bowed strings) start at tip of bow
⊓ Down bow (bowed strings) start at frog of bow
tr Trill rapidly alternate two adjacent notes
arpeggio wavy line Arpeggio "roll" the chord, notes added separately

Symbols affecting groups of notes

  • 8va (ottava) — play an octave higher (or lower, depending on placement); 15ma = two octaves; 22ma = three octaves.
  • Slur — most commonly groups notes to be played smoothly/connected; in vocal parts, a slur over multiple notes on one syllable is a melisma; can also serve as a phrase marking over a larger group, showing the music's overall shape.
  • Pedaling marks — show when the piano's damper pedal should be held down/released; older scores use different symbols for down vs. up than modern notation.

transposing-instruments.title: Transposing Instruments
transposing-instruments.html:
Part of Music Theory → Notation. Some instruments sound a different pitch than what's written on their part — a transposing instrument. Relevant if arranging or writing parts for horns/woodwinds beyond Ableton MIDI (session players, notated charts).

Why they exist

  • Woodwinds come in different sizes to cover a wider combined range without forcing players to learn new fingerings per size — one fingering system works across the whole family (soprano/alto/tenor/baritone sax, etc. all finger the same way).
  • Brass instruments were historically built in many different keys, especially before valves (when they could only play the harmonic overtones of a single fundamental note) — so music was written so fingerings/slide positions stayed consistent across instruments in different keys. Certain keys became preferred for timbre/range and stuck around even after valves made the original constraint obsolete.

Common transpositions (written → sounds)

Instrument Sounds relative to written
Piccolo one octave higher
Flute, oboe, bassoon as written (non-transposing)
B♭ clarinet, B♭ trumpet, soprano sax major 2nd lower
Bass clarinet major 2nd + 1 octave lower
Alto sax major 6th lower
Tenor sax major 2nd + 1 octave lower
Baritone sax major 6th + 1 octave lower
F horn (French horn) perfect 5th lower
English horn perfect 5th lower
Contrabassoon one octave lower

(Table condensed from the source's full chart, which also covers cello/viola/trombone/violin/glockenspiel as non-transposing or specific-interval cases — see the enrichment page for the complete visual reference.)

How to use it

To write for a transposing instrument, figure out the sounding pitch you want first, then transpose it by the opposite direction/amount before writing it into that instrument's part (e.g. want a written-C-actual-pitch on B♭ clarinet → write a D, since the clarinet sounds a major 2nd lower than written). Most modern notation software automates this once the instrument is set correctly.

Genuinely one of BassBuzz's more theory-dense beginner videos — three of the five riffs get a full rhythmic-notation breakdown (16th-note counting, quarter-note-triplet math) rather than "just feel it by ear."

songs-that-use-5-4-time.title: Songs that use 5-4 time
songs-that-use-5-4-time.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The densest of the odd-time-signature survey videos in this batch — a wide catalog of 5/4 songs across grouping styles (3+2 vs. long-long-short-short), a real notation-choice case study (5/4 vs. 10/8), several genuine polymeters built on top of 5/4, and a practical guide to when to notate the same rhythm as 5/4 vs. 5/8.

songs-that-use-6-4-time.title: Songs that use 6-4 time
songs-that-use-6-4-time.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A survey of 6/4 songs (a rarer choice than 5/4 or 7/4) that turns into a genuinely deep point about time-signature notation itself: 6/4 vs. two bars of 3/4 have the identical beat count, so the real choice between them is about accent fit — and for recorded (not hand-notated) music, that choice can be a real, unresolvable ambiguity rather than an objective fact waiting to be discovered.

Techniques

  • 6/4 often feels like alternating 4/4-then-2/4 bars rather than 6 equal beats, giving forward momentum ("Galvanize," Chemical Brothers; "Enough Space," Foo Fighters — both could be notated as alternating 4/4+2/4, but a single 6/4 signature reads more simply).
  • The same fixed beat count can genuinely change felt meter depending on where the accent lands: Alice in Chains' "Down in a Hole" has a 12-beat guitar phrase that reads as 2 bars of 6/4 while the riff repeats alone, then re-reads as 3 bars of 4/4 once the vocal enters and the guitar stops enforcing the 6/4 feel — identical 12 beats, different meter, purely from accent placement.
  • 6/4 vs. two bars of 3/4 — mathematically the same, chosen by accent fit, not arithmetic: any 6/4 piece could be forcibly transcribed as 3/4, but if the natural strong-beat accents don't land where 3/4 would put them, that's a bad-fit choice regardless of being technically valid ("Schism," Tool, as the clean case).
  • Some songs genuinely sit on the boundary and get published different ways by different people: "Take Me to Church" (Hozier verse) heard as 64bpm 6/4 by this analyst, published as 63bpm 3/4 on official sheet music — same recording, different chosen pulse; "Electric Feel" (MGMT) similarly gets described as either.
  • The deepest point: time-signature ambiguity is a specifically MODERN problem. Classical composers hand-wrote their own time signature as a deliberate authorial choice onto the manuscript itself (Chopin's Nocturne Op. 9 No. 1 could have been notated 3/4 but he specifically chose 6/4 for its particular feel) — no ambiguity is possible because the composer's intent is literally on the page. Modern songwriters release recordings; any sheet-music transcription is usually made after the fact by a copyist guessing at the best-fit signature, not by the songwriter — meaning "what time signature is this song really in" can be a genuinely unresolvable question for recorded music in a way it never was for notated music.

midi-generate-and-transform-tools.title: MIDI Generate and Transform Tools
midi-generate-and-transform-tools.html:
Live 12's piano roll added a Generate menu (creates new MIDI from scratch — rhythms, note clouds, melodic shapes, chord stacks) and a Transform menu (reshapes MIDI that already exists — arpeggiate, fill gaps, add ornaments, quantize, shuffle, adjust note-ends, warp time) — a genuinely new layer of the piano roll, distinct from MPE Piano Roll Tools (which covers the MPE tab's per-note expression generators, Glissando and the MPE LFO) and from Randomized Rack Design (device/macro-level randomization rather than MIDI-note generation). A sensible order to work in: Generate → Transform → Pitch and Time (the last for humanizing/extending/adding scale intervals). Companion to Chord and Scale (the Stacks generator overlaps their territory but works directly inside the piano roll rather than as a rack device), Arpeggiator (the Arpeggiate transform mirrors the stock device), and Ableton Extensions and MIDI Tools.

Generate

  • Rhythm — generates a rhythmic pattern for a chosen sample/pitch; Split adds double-time in places. Layering several Rhythm-generated parts (different sample, different generated pattern, panned apart, velocity variance with adjustable accent placement) builds a full hi-hat pattern fast — finish with a reverb send and a sample selector.
  • Notes — generates a cloud of notes across a set pitch range, with controls for note-length range, velocity range, max simultaneous voices, and a Density knob controlling how much randomness shows up. Follow with the Pitch and Time section to humanize the result.
  • Shape — a sequencer-like melody generator: set a rate, add random variation, control the density of that randomness, or start from a preset shape. A genuinely useful way to generate melodic ideas, not just rhythmic ones.
  • Stacks — the piano roll's own chord generator: choose a root note and inversion (shown as a chord name plus a constellation-style diagram), add further chord shapes, and offset each chord to start at a different time. Needs tweaking to sound musical, but a strong idea-starter. → Chord, Scale
  • Max for Live generators — a stock M4L generator ships by default, with room for community-built ones — opens the Generate menu up beyond Ableton's own presets.

free-rate-arpeggiator-resampling-rack.title: Free-Rate Arpeggiator Resampling Rack
free-rate-arpeggiator-resampling-rack.html:
Reference/vibe: rhythms that stretch and compress "like a rubber band" instead of sitting on a fixed BPM grid — the entry point of asd's five-part "Exponential Rhythms" series, and its most straightforward method. The sibling chains reach related territory a different way: Exponential Groove Drum Rack (part 2) uses Simpler's percentage-based Length parameter across a whole Drum Rack; Texture Mode (part 3) uses clip-level warp settings. This chain instead decouples Arpeggiator's Rate from BPM-synced time divisions entirely, then — the technique's real power move — resamples the arpeggiator's live MIDI output onto a new track so the result becomes permanent, editable rhythm material rather than a one-off performance.

Signal source: built entirely from stock Ableton devices (Arpeggiator, Random, Scale, instrument-internal LFO, optionally Corpus/Grain Delay) — nothing here needs an unowned plugin, see Plugin Wishlist (nothing added from this video).

exponential-groove-drum-rack.title: Exponential Groove Drum Rack
exponential-groove-drum-rack.html:
Reference/vibe: an evolving, self-mutating drum groove built from a completely ordinary drum pattern — the pattern itself never changes, but a single macro rides every pad's sample-loop length at once, so the groove constantly stretches, compresses, and drifts into audio-rate texture while the underlying beat stays recognizable. Part of asd's five-part "Exponential Rhythms" series; the sibling clip-level technique (Texture warp mode, no instrument needed) is Texture Mode. The through-line across the whole series: use a percentage-based (not fixed-time) parameter as the modulation target, so the same automation/macro produces genuinely different, evolving results rather than a locked-in repeat.

Signal source: built entirely from stock Ableton devices (Drum Rack, Simpler ×N, Reverb, Compressor) — nothing here needs an unowned plugin, see Plugin Wishlist (nothing added from this video).

grain-delay.title: Grain Delay
grain-delay.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock granular delay — instead of repeating the incoming signal whole like a normal delay, it samples small snippets ("grains") of it, with the grain size set by its Frequency knob, and can randomize the timing/pitch of those grains as they repeat.

What it's used for

Turning a delay into a granular texture/pitch-shift tool rather than a plain echo — metallic, glitchy, or randomized repeats distinct from Echo/EchoBoy's rhythmic-repeat role.

FX chain notes

Inserted on a texture or drum-layering track; often run with Time near zero (so it isn't producing an audible discrete echo) purely for the grain-texture character.

kilohearts-spiff.title: Kilohearts Spiff
kilohearts-spiff.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: "Kilohearts"

What it is

A transient/spectral shaper snapin with a Delta listen mode (hear only what's being boosted vs. dry).

What it's used for

FX chain notes

2-bass-group.title: 2 Bass Group
2-bass-group.html:
Role: All bass sources summed. Usually only one bass plays at a time, so this group is mostly about a consistent low-end lane regardless of which source is active.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Lane consistency

  • Match the electric and digital bass into the same spectral footprint (their track chains differ; the mix shouldn't notice a handoff between them)
  • The kick-pocket dip lives on the tracks — only repeat it here if both basses layer simultaneously.

2. LALA — Level ride

  • Peak Reduction for ~1.5 dB GR (① — slow) · Comp mode (③) · HPF engaged (④ — so the sub doesn't pump it) · Gain to unity (②)
  • Why: An opto leveler smooths section-to-section bass level (verse fingerstyle vs chorus 808) so the low-end energy of the song stays constant — the thing listeners feel as "solid."

Variations

  • 🎬 From video: found bass presence in the 700 Hz–1 kHz tone/string-noise range rather than adding low end that was already excessive. Andrew Scheps: "there's more than enough low-end, but a lot of these sort of tone and string noise will be down in this 700 to 1k range, so I'm gonna try adding a little bit of this — just sounds a little more present." → EQ, Masking and Carving — Andrew Scheps (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Guitars & Bass - Andrew Scheps
  • Live bass + 808 layered (pop-trap hybrid): split duties with EQ — 808 owns below ~120 Hz, Hofner owns 120 Hz+ (HPF the Hofner hard) — two basses only work when they don't share an octave.

7-stupidly-simple-methods-for-killer-bas.title: 7 Stupidly Simple Methods for Killer Bass Lines
7-stupidly-simple-methods-for-killer-bas.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz frames "great artists steal, but they don't copy" as the whole video's thesis, then spends nineteen minutes building out seven named, escalating-in-risk methods for turning a bass line you already love into something that reads as your own — not a vague "get inspired" pep talk but a genuinely reusable ideation toolkit, each method demonstrated on 2-4 real song pairs (and one art-history pair, Van Gogh's Starry Night borrowing its composition from Hokusai's The Great Wave) so the line between "inspired by" and "lawsuit" stays concrete rather than abstract. The methods are explicitly ordered by how much of the original material survives: method one keeps a whole half of a riff verbatim; method seven only borrows a genre's vocabulary. The video closes by stacking multiple methods on a single source riff (Megadeth's "Peace Sells") to show they combine rather than compete — the most practically useful demo in the video, since it's the one move a viewer can copy directly into their own writing process. Two songwriting-law cautionary tales anchor the risk gradient: the Led Zeppelin "Stairway to Heaven" / Spirit "Taurus" lawsuit (Zeppelin won) and the Ray Parker Jr. "Ghostbusters" / Huey Lewis "I Want a New Drug" dispute (Parker settled) — both used as "here's what happens when you undercook the transformation" warnings rather than legal advice. Confidence: manual (non-auto) captions, high confidence for content; no per-line timestamps in the caption track, so timing below is sequence-order only. One example (the method-four "rearranged" pop song, framed as "not meant as a diss to Rod Temperton") is deliberately left unnamed in the video itself — likely a rights-avoidance choice — so it's captured here as a named technique without inventing the specific comparison song.
