bass-tone-chain-priority.title: Bass Tone Chain Priority
bass-tone-chain-priority.html:
A BassBuzz blind-test teardown of the full bass signal chain — fingers → strings → tone wood → pickups → electronics → cable → pedals → amp → speaker cabinet → room/band/PA — built to answer a concrete question: which links actually deserve troubleshooting time when a bass tone sounds bad, and which are internet-forum obsessions with little real payoff? Method: same bass/riff/mic position held constant per link, a blind A/B (or A/B/C) comparison played for two working professional bassists who don't know what changed, then a verdict. The headline finding cuts against where most players spend their attention: fingers/technique tests out as the single most important link, ahead of every piece of gear, while several commonly-fussed-over links (tone wood, same-type pickup upgrades, electronics/wiring swaps, cable) tested as marginal-to-placebo when the existing gear is functional.

Use this as a troubleshooting priority order, not just trivia

When a bass tone isn't working, check links in this order rather than reaching for gear first — it matches where the video's own blind tests found the actual leverage:

  1. Fingers/technique first, always. Before touching any gear, check hand position and attack — this is the highest-leverage, zero-cost link in the whole chain (below).
  2. String type, if technique checks out — round wound vs. flat wound is a real, deliberate tonal choice (brighter/modern vs. warmer/deader), not a brand/gauge rabbit hole.
  3. Pickup type and position, if the bass itself is the suspect — this is what makes a P-Bass, Jazz bass, and Stingray sound fundamentally different from each other; a same-type pickup upgrade inside a working bass is not this and rarely moves the needle.
  4. Amp and speaker cabinet, for anyone running through an amp rather than DI'ing — both tested as genuinely important, not just "flavor."
  5. Pedals, only when a specific effect is actually wanted — not a default reach for a flat/bad baseline tone.
  6. Everything else (tone wood, electronics/wiring parts, cable) is a low-leverage place to spend troubleshooting time if the existing parts are functional — skip straight past these unless something is actually broken.
  7. Room/band/PA is the biggest wildcard of all and outside player control entirely — see below.
secs: Use this as a troubleshooting priority order, not just trivia

reverb-send-room.title: Reverb Send Room
reverb-send-room.html:
Role: The mix's shared "room" — the default space most elements send to. One room for everyone is what makes separate recordings sound like they happened in the same place.

Send/return theory: returns run 100% wet; the send knob is the dry/wet control. One reverb shared by ten tracks beats ten inserted reverbs — cheaper, and more importantly coherent: every element sits in the same acoustic space.

Signal chain

1. ValhallaRoom — The room

  • Mix 100% (②) · Decay 1.0 s (③ — 0.8–1.2 window) · Pre-delay 20 ms (④ — 15–25) · High Cut ~5–6 kHz (⑦)
  • The controls that matter, in order: Mix, Decay, High Cut (then pre-delay, then everything else). Workflow: set Early Size first (it defines the room's perceived size/attack), then fine-tune Late Size (default ~15 is fine); Depth balances early-vs-late character.
  • Mode picks: Large Room / Bright Room = the do-everything modes (Bright Room even works on bass) · Dark Room/Dark Chamber = washier, more chorused · Nostromo/Narcissus = great on keys.
  • Low Mult below 1.0 to tighten the reverb's low end at the source (on top of the return HPF).
  • Why pre-delay matters: 0 ms glues the reverb onto the dry signal and blurs it; 15–25 ms separates the dry transient from the tail — the source stays upfront and sounds placed. The #1 amateur reverb fix. (Fast rhythmic sources like busy bass lines want it shorter, ~10 ms, or the timing smears.)

2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter the return

  • HPF 200–300 Hz · LPF 4–6 kHz
  • Why: Low reverb energy = mud, high reverb energy = harsh sizzle that fights vocal air. The "Abbey Road filter" trick: a band-limited reverb adds space without adding frequency content — you can run more of it before the mix notices.
  • 🎬 From video (clarity): on a vocal fighting to stay clear through this send, add a narrow dip around 1.5–3.5 kHz on top of the HPF/LPF — a general clarity move, separate from the wide-band filtering above — Sage Audio, Reverb Masterclass

Usage

  • Snare is the main customer (its tail defines the space) · vocals low send · guitars/keys to place them · never send bass, kick, or 808s (low end + reverb = mud, always).

Variations

  • Drier modern trap: decay down to 0.5–0.7 s — a "small booth" flavor just for glue.

echoboy.title: EchoBoy
echoboy.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Soundtoys

What it is

Soundtoys' flagship delay plugin modeling dozens of classic echo unit types (tape, analog, digital, and more) in one plugin.

What it's used for

The primary creative delay across a huge range of styles — from clean digital slap-back to warped tape echo.

FX chain notes

Used on a send/return, or inserted for a dedicated delay effect on vocals, guitars, and synths.

master-chain.title: Master Chain
master-chain.html:
Role: The final 10%. If the buses did their jobs, every move here is ±1–2 dB. Two modes: mix-into-it (the tonal/glue stages live on the master from early in the mix, so you're always hearing "the record" — the Disclosure/SSL-Fusion habit) and final loudness (the last three stages, engaged at export time).

Chain overview

Corrective EQ → adaptive clarity → glue → tape → imaging → density → clip → limit. Corrective before compression (the comp should react to a balanced signal); limiter dead last, always.

xo.title: XO
xo.html:
Category: Instrument Vendor: XLN Audio

What it is

XLN Audio's AI-assisted drum sample browser and playback instrument, using machine tagging to organize huge sample libraries by sonic characteristics.

What it's used for

Fast browsing and auditioning of one-shot drum samples (kicks, snares, hats) tagged by AI for quick kit-building.

Techniques

  • Percussion loop pulled straight from XO's browser and dropped in unprocessed as a texture/bounce layer under an ambient synth pad. On an underwater-sounding R&B synth-pad build, a perc loop sourced from XO is layered in alongside a rain-noise texture with no further processing mentioned — it "sounded really good as it is." Auto-captioned "this perk loop from x y," a near-certain caption garble of "XO." (Flagged uncertain — the source could instead be a same-sounding third-party pack name; logged here as the closest owned match.) → Ambient Texture and Field Recording, Sampling and Sound Selection — loner, how to make melodic r&b beats for tory lanez & chris brown (underwater synth/vocal sample)

FX chain notes

Used as the drum instrument source when assembling a kit from one-shot samples.

2-drums-hats-group.title: 2 Drums Hats Group
2-drums-hats-group.html:
Role: Hats + shakers + top percussion summed — the mix's "top layer" treated as one texture.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Sum cleanup

  • HPF the whole group 300+ Hz · one broad tilt decision: how bright is the top layer vs the vocal air?
  • Why: Hats and vocal air share 8–12 kHz — decide who owns it (usually vocal, in your genres) and shelf the hats accordingly.

2. Glue Compressor — Texture glue

  • Ratio 2:1 (②) · Attack 1 ms (③ — fast; hats have no transient worth protecting at group level) · Release Auto (④) · Threshold for ~1.5 dB GR (①) · Makeup to unity (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦)
  • Why: Makes hat + shaker + perc breathe as one instrument instead of three competing tickers. A fast attack is fine here — clamping the tick fronts evens the texture rather than dulling it.

3. S1 Imager — Width

  • Width +15% (①) — top percussion is where width is cheap and safe (no mono-compat risk like low end).

Variations

  • Trap: skip the imager, keep hats fairly centered and dry — modern trap tops are narrow and upfront.
  • 🎬 From video: Southside signature exception to "dry" trap hats — reverb specifically on the hats (named example: Married to the Game), as either the hats' own insert or a dedicated hi-hat send depending on the session. → Reverb — loner, the secret samplemaker behind Southside's best beats!?

1-synth-lead-track.title: 1 Synth Lead Track
1-synth-lead-track.html:
Role: Melodic synth lines — the "second vocal." Gets vocal-style treatment: present, controlled, carved against the actual vocal.

Chain philosophy: carve → multiband control → edge → width → seat.

1 — Sound Selection

  • Serum 2 — the modern default (pop/trap/EDM). Patch recipe: 1–2 osc, unison 3–7, detune 0.10–0.20, LPF 24 dB with a touch of envelope, mono + legato + glide 40–80 ms for expressive lines. → Serum 2 — Modern Lead
  • DUNE 3 — festival supersaws (the unison engine is the point, 8–16 voices). → DUNE 3 — Festival Supersaw Lead
  • Massive — growly 2010s character. · Drift / Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer — warm analog mono (synthwave/indie; Model 84 chorus = instant vintage width). · Omnisphere — hybrid/organic texture leads.
  • Universal patch rules: vibrato via mod-wheel LFO (not baked in), attack 0–10 ms, release short enough not to smear, kill sub content below ~100 Hz at the patch.
  • 🎬 No VST for the target hardware? Substitute a one-shot sample kit and keep it unquantized — Mike Dean's Moog Matriarch leads (no VST exists) sourced from a producer one-shot kit instead, played back completely off the grid on purpose. → Sound Selection Guide, Sampling and Sound Selection, Rhythm and Groove — loner, mike dean's secret 'astroworld' synth techniques!?
  • 🎬 Pick oscillators whose harmonic content fits the key — a major-harmonic voice sits where a clashing square wouldn't — Disclosure, Higher Than Ever Before. Pre-highlight favorite patches before the session (Sound Palette).

bedroom-pop-indie.title: Bedroom Pop - Indie
bedroom-pop-indie.html: What makes it the genre: intimacy and charm over polish — one person's taste audible in every decision, imperfections kept as identity, small sounds presented close instead of big sounds presented far away. This is the home-studio-native genre: the "limitation aesthetic" (Steve Lacy cut Dark Red vocals through an SM58 into an iPhone) is a choice you now make deliberately with better gear. This is your default lane — the other playbooks are trips; this is home.

echo.title: Echo
echo.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's flagship delay device modeling analog and tape-style echo units, with dual delay lines, modulation, filtering, and a noise/character section.

What it's used for

Rhythmic delay effects, tape-echo character, and dub-style repeats — Live's deep, modern delay replacing the older Simple/Ping Pong Delay devices.

FX chain notes

Used on a send/return for shared delay throws, or inserted directly for a dedicated rhythmic delay effect on vocals, leads, or guitars.

uad-pultec-eqp-1a.title: UAD Pultec EQP-1A
uad-pultec-eqp-1a.html:
Category: Passive Tube Program EQ Vendor: Universal Audio — Legacy version in the Apollo stock bundle (Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII)

What it is

Emulation of the Pultec EQP-1A passive program EQ. Broad, musical curves that are nearly impossible to make sound bad; the tube make-up stage colors even at flat settings.

What it's used for

Gentle tone-shaping on the way in, and the famous low-end trick (boost + atten at the same low frequency = tight lows with a scooped mud notch) on bass/kick.

Key settings (tracking, acoustic guitar)

  • Low ATTEN: 2–3 @ 60 CPS — takes out rumble/boom before it hits the converters.
  • Low BOOST: 0 (the boost/atten trick is for bass/kick, not acoustics).
  • High BOOST: 0–2 @ 12 KCS max, bandwidth broad — save real sweetening for Pro-Q 4 in Ableton where it's undoable.
  • ATTEN SEL: 10 KCS, 0 — leave it.

FX chain notes

Third device in uad_console chains, after the compressor — see Acoustic Guitar Track. Note the desk-order lesson from Disclosure - SSL SIX Mixing Al Green Stems: EQ after compression on the way in.

1-acoustic-guitar-track.title: 1 Acoustic Guitar Track
1-acoustic-guitar-track.html:
Role: Mic'd Yamaha FG730S — strummed beds or fingerpicked features.

Chain philosophy: phase-align → de-noise → subtractive EQ → gentle leveling → resonance tame → sweeten. Acoustic guitar is a subtractive instrument in a mix — it covers the entire spectrum, so the job is removing what fights everything else, not adding character.

pro-ds.title: Pro-DS
pro-ds.html:
Category: Pitch/Vocal Vendor: FabFilter

What it is

FabFilter's de-esser, using an adaptive, wideband or split-band detection algorithm to target sibilance without engaging on transients or plosives.

What it's used for

Controlling harsh 's', 'sh', and 't' sounds on vocal recordings.

FX chain notes

Placed after the main vocal compressor and before final EQ, so it reacts to the already-leveled signal.

valhallaplate.title: ValhallaPlate
valhallaplate.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Valhalla DSP

What it is

Valhalla's plate reverb emulation, modeling the dense, bright character of classic studio plate reverb units.

What it's used for

Classic plate reverb character on vocals, drums, and instruments.

FX chain notes

Used on a send/return for a vintage-style reverb tail.

Used in my chains

My plate reverb — dense, bright, no early-reflection clutter; the classic vocal-tail plate:

  • Reverb Send Long — slot 1, the tail: Mix 100%, Decay 1.8–3.0 s, Predelay 30–40 ms (longer than the room — keeps the lyric intelligible under a long tail). Plate for vocals; swap ValhallaVintageVerb hall for orchestral/ballad size.

Key Parameters

image: Images/ValhallaPlate.jpg
coords: Images/ValhallaPlate.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique Artist / record example
① Mode The plate algorithm/character (Chrome, etc.) Dense/bright plate modes for vocals — no early-reflection clutter —
② Mix Dry/wet (100% on a send) 100% on the return; send level sets amount —
③ Decay Tail length 1.8–3.0 s for a lush vocal tail —
④ Predelay Gap before the plate blooms 30–40 ms — longer than a room; keeps the dry lyric clear under a long tail —
⑤ Size Perceived plate size Larger for orchestral scale; smaller for a tight vocal sheen —
⑥ Width Stereo width of the plate 100% for a wide vocal sheen; narrow to keep it centered —
⑦ EQ (Low/High Freq + Gain) Shelf EQ shaping the tail's tone Pull HighGain down a few dB so the bright plate doesn't sizzle; trim LowGain to keep it off the sub —
⑧ Mod (Rate / Depth) Chorusing of the tail Subtle to keep the plate lush and moving —

khs-chorus.title: kHs Chorus
khs-chorus.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: Kilohearts

What it is

A classic modulated-delay chorus snap-in for thickening and widening a signal.

What it's used for

Widening synths, guitars, and vocals with classic chorus movement.

FX chain notes

Stacked in a Snap Heap chain, typically post-EQ.

Key Parameters

image: Images/kHs Chorus.png
coords: Images/kHs Chorus.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique
① Delay Base delay time of the chorus voices Short for tight shimmer; longer for a doubling/slap feel
② Depth Modulation depth Low for subtle width; high for obvious chorus
③ Rate Speed of the modulation LFO Slow for lush drift; fast for warble
④ Taps Number of chorus voices (2 / 3) More taps for a thicker, denser ensemble
⑤ Spread Stereo spread of the voices Widen for a big stereo image; narrow to keep it centered
⑥ Mix Dry/wet blend ~30–50% for width without smear

stereo-tool.title: Stereo Tool
stereo-tool.html:
Category: Pan/Imaging Vendor: Mensia

What it is

Mensia Technologies' stereo image analysis and correction plugin, checking mono compatibility and adjusting stereo width.

What it's used for

Verifying and correcting a mix's stereo/mono compatibility before delivery.

FX chain notes

Used on the master bus late in the mixing/mastering process.

Techniques

  • Mid/side saturation via the Mid Sat / Side Sat controls: drive Mid Sat for a more centered low end, drive Side Sat for expanded stereo highs. A native-plugin route to a technique the source video otherwise built by hand (duplicate-channel routing + a saturator per image): push ③ Mid Sat to emphasize/thicken the mid image's lows so the center reads more anchored, push ③ Side Sat to emphasize the side image's highs for a stereo-highs expansion — same underlying "harmonics as an imaging tool" mechanism as the ③ Mid Sat/Side Sat entry already below, applied with a frequency-emphasis intent rather than just edge-softening. → Saturation and Distortion, Width and Stereo, Roar — Sage Audio, Mid Side Masterclass

Used in my chains

Ableton's stock width/pan/mono utility — a lightweight alternative to Utility for width and mono-below control:

  • Width/mono duty on instrument and synth tracks where a quick spread or a mono-below-X-Hz is all that's needed (keeps the low end centered; mono-check with it too).

envelope-follower.title: Envelope Follower
envelope-follower.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live device that tracks the amplitude envelope of an incoming audio signal and converts it into a control signal (e.g. for Max mapping).

What it's used for

Driving other parameters (filter cutoff, effect mix) dynamically from a track's amplitude — classic envelope-follower sound design.

FX chain notes

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

Techniques

  • The unowned "Wave LFO" alternative — bipolar, sample-derived, no live audio needed — dnksaus's own Max for Live device drops any audio file straight in and generates its modulation curve from that file's waveform (Scale/Zoom/Offset/Smooth/Phase shape it), which differs from Envelope Follower in two ways worth knowing even without owning it: it's bipolar (real peaks and troughs around center) where Envelope Follower is unipolar (rises from a floor only), and it can be scrubbed/auditioned by reading the file directly, without routing a live audio track through it first. → LFO, Plugin Wishlist — dnksaus, I Dropped a Max for Live Device...
  • Make a texture layer follow the melody's dynamics — map an Envelope Follower reading a drum loop or lead line to a volume-raising Utility on a separate texture track, so the texture swells and recedes with the source's own dynamics instead of sitting at a static level. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording — dnksaus, Texturing Your Tracks in Ableton

2-main-vocal-group.title: 2 Main Vocal Group
2-main-vocal-group.html:
Role: Sums the lead + its layers (high, doubles, harmonies) into one balanced element. Group-stage work is about the relationship between the layers and carving against the rest of the mix — the heavy lifting already happened on the tracks, and the Vocal Bus does the final polish. Keep this lean.

Chain overview

Carve EQ → gentle glue. Balance between layers is faders/automation, not more processing.

Chain

1. Pro-Q 4 — Group carve

  • EQ against the other groups: find where the vocal masks or is masked (usually 1–5 kHz vs guitars/synths, 200–400 Hz vs everything)
  • Cut the offending band in the other group's chain first — boost here only if the vocal still needs it
  • Dynamic node dip on this group only if a layer resonance pokes out when the stack is summed
  • Why: Step 4 of the process — pick what stands out, EQ the interference out of the other tracks so the vocal wins its lane without being boosted into harshness.

2. LALA — Layer glue

  • Peak Reduction for ~1.5 dB GR (① — slow/gentle) · Comp mode (③) · HPF engaged (④) · Mix 100% (⑤) · Gain to unity (②)
  • Why: An LA-2A-style leveler melts the layers into one voice without audible pumping; the real leveling already happened per-track.

universal-audio-apollo-twin-mkii.title: Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII
universal-audio-apollo-twin-mkii.html:
Category: Audio Interface (2-in/6-out, Thunderbolt, UAD-2 DUO DSP) Vendor: Universal Audio Ballpark value (used, 2026): $500–650 (DUO)

What it is

UA's desktop Thunderbolt interface with Unison mic preamps (impedance-modeling preamp emulations) and onboard UAD-2 DSP for near-zero-latency tracking through UAD plugins.

What it's used for

The studio hub: Neumann TLM 102/Shure SM57 go in through Unison preamps, monitors out to the Yamaha HS8 pair; Console app handles low-latency tracking with effects printed or monitored.

  • A small Apollo is the anchor of a deliberately bare-bones mobile writing rig — Myles Smith / Peter Fenn: desk + a small Apollo + a vocal mic + guitars + a MIDI controller + speakers, chosen specifically to feel like a living room rather than a studio (low-pressure creative environment); paired with UAD Spark (unowned, needs only an internet connection, no Apollo DSP) so the same plugin chains travel from the anchor studio to any Airbnb/hotel room. → Creative Process and Idea Capture — Myles Smith / Peter Fenn (Tape Notes), TN 184 Myles Smith & Peter Fenn - Full Video Episode

Signal chain notes

Unison preamp emulations (610, Neve-style, API-style) change the input character — pick per source before touching plugins. Line outs can also feed the Sony TC-630 for the tape-print loop.

tal-chorus-lx.title: TAL-Chorus-LX
tal-chorus-lx.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: TAL-Togu Audio Line

What it is

TAL's chorus plugin modeled on the classic Juno-60-style analog chorus circuit.

What it's used for

Classic analog-style chorus thickening on synths, guitars, and vocals.

FX chain notes

Used as an insert effect, post-EQ, for width and movement.

sony-tc-630.title: Sony TC-630
sony-tc-630.html:
Category: Reel-to-Reel Tape Machine (~1970, 3-head, 7") Vendor: Sony Ballpark value (used, 2026): $150–375 (working; serviced units fetch $500+)

What it is

Sony's early-70s consumer/prosumer reel-to-reel — 3 heads (so it can monitor off tape while recording), built-in amps and speakers, 7½/3¾ ips.

What it's used for

Not for playback — it's a tape-color processor: guitar or synths get run through it to print real wow/flutter, head-bump warmth, and tape compression, then recorded back into Ableton. The hardware version of RC-20 Retro Color — and it lands anywhere from subtle glue to full TEXTURE Slot character.

Signal chain notes

Line/aux out of the interface → TC-630 input, record while monitoring off the playback head (3-head = real-time tape return, slightly delayed) → line out back into a new Ableton track. Slower speed (3¾ ips) = more warble/less fidelity; hotter input level = more tape compression. Print it — don't try to monitor through it live in the arrangement (the head-gap delay).

uad-teletronix-la-2a.title: UAD Teletronix LA-2A
uad-teletronix-la-2a.html:
Category: Optical Compressor Vendor: Universal Audio — Legacy version in the Apollo stock bundle (Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII)

What it is

Emulation of the Teletronix LA-2A tube opto leveler. Program-dependent attack (~10 ms) and release (~60 ms then slow tail) — it rides the signal rather than clamping it. Two knobs, no wrong answers.

What it's used for

Gentle leveling on the way in: vocals, acoustic guitar, bass. Disclosure's "one-LA" rule: threshold + gain are the only controls — the harder you hit it, the higher the effective ratio (Disclosure - Ultimatum Breakdown + Breakbeat). Their reach-for on tracked vocals/guitar "for shine."

Key settings

  • Peak Reduction: ≤3 dB GR on the loudest phrases while tracking — printed compression is forever; add more later in the box, never less.
  • Gain: makeup to unity (bypass A/B at equal loudness).
  • Comp/Limit switch: Comp (4:1-ish) always for tracking.
  • Emphasis (rear-panel R37): leave stock.

FX chain notes

Second device in uad_console chains, after the Unison preamp — see Acoustic Guitar Track. In-the-box equivalent for later stages: LALA.

fender-blues-junior.title: Fender Blues Junior
fender-blues-junior.html:
Category: Tube Amp (15W, 1×12) Vendor: Fender Ballpark value (used, 2026): $400–600 (mods may add — document them)

Modified — document what the mods are (speaker swap? bias/cap job? tube change?) so the manual/parameters section can account for them.

What it is

Fender's 15-watt EL84 tube combo — spring reverb, "Fat" switch, the small-venue/home-studio classic that breaks up at recordable volumes.

What it's used for

Clean-to-edge-of-breakup Fender tone for the Fender Stratocaster and Hofner B-Bass H-Series; the pedal platform for the board.

Signal chain notes

Mic'd with the Shure SM57 (dust-cap edge, ~1" off grille); Master low + Volume high = earlier tube grit at bedroom levels.

🎬 From video: a third source confirms the small-clean-Fender-as-pedal-platform lane this amp occupies — "all these old Fender amps have a great balanced, clean tone and are a really nice starting place for adding pedals," demoed on a vintage Princeton Reverb (volume ≈3–4) for studio work and a bigger Pro Reverb for more headroom live with a louder drummer. New, reusable dial-in tip for this amp's own pedal platform: amp volume changes the whole downstream pedal calculation — at a quiet studio volume, boost/overdrive pedal settings can be more assertive; pushed toward the live end of this amp's own Volume 5–7 "edge of breakup" range (see ① below), the amp's own tubes/speaker are already compressing on their own, so pedal-side volume/boost settings need to come back down from wherever they sat at bedroom volume. Re-tune the pedalboard any time this amp's own Volume/Master setting changes, rather than assuming one pedal dial-in transfers across a quiet mix session and a loud live set. → Electric Guitar Amp Track — Jack Ruch, Dial In Your Amps and Pedals for Great Clean and Overdriven TONES!

delay-send-slap.title: Delay Send Slap
delay-send-slap.html:
Role: Single short echo (80–140 ms) — the "thickener" delay. Reads as size and attitude, not as an audible echo. THE hip hop and rock'n'roll vocal effect (and the sound of every 50s Elvis record).

Signal chain

1. EchoBoy — The slap

  • Echo Type: Studio Tape (①, Slapback style ②) · Time 110 ms, unsynced (③ — slap is a physical size cue, not rhythmic; syncing to tempo usually makes it worse) · Feedback 5% (④ — ONE repeat) · Wow & Flutter on for tape character (⑤) · High Cut ~6 kHz on the repeat (⑥) · Mix 100% (⑦ — it's a return)
  • Why: One fast, slightly-degraded repeat fools the ear into hearing a bigger performance rather than an effect — thickness without the pitch-wobble of chorus or the wash of reverb.
  • 🎬 From video: Disclosure reach for slapback (+ a short "toilet"-sized room verb) to put a vocal in a space rather than flood a cathedral — reads as "mic in a room," more natural/human; and on a chorus bus a slapback keeps it present/"right there" while other sections use long verbs (a very Lennon/Beatles move) — Disclosure, Deeper / Waterfall. Often run as a track insert, not just this send.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Filter

  • HPF 250–400 Hz · LPF 3–5 kHz — the repeat should always be smaller than the source (duller + narrower = sits behind). EchoBoy note: its low cut sits before the delay circuit, high cut after — use the high cut for taming, and remember darker repeats read as moving away (free depth).
  • Stereo control: EchoBoy's tweak panel has a L/R offset (~25 = repeats spread off-center; 0 = mono slap dead behind the voice — both are valid looks).

Combine, don't choose: slap + Delay Send Other's 1/8 running together is the standard pro vocal setup — slap does thickness, the synced delay does motion.

Usage

  • Lead vocal (rap verses especially — slap instead of reverb keeps it dry-but-big) · ad-libs · lead guitar stabs.

Variations

  • Doubling effect: pull time down to 60–90 ms and pan the return slightly off-center — fake double.
  • 50s/Beatles slap: more EchoBoy wobble + saturation, time ~120–140 ms.

scale.title: Scale
scale.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock MIDI effect that snaps incoming notes to a defined scale — reads the global song scale (set top-left in Live) when its own scale-aware toggle is on.

What it's used for

Force-fitting MIDI input (a keyboard performance, a generated/random pattern) into the song's key so nothing plays outside the scale — the backbone device behind most of the scale-aware sound-design tricks used across this channel.

FX chain notes

Sits early in a MIDI chain, before chord/arpeggiator/instrument devices, so everything downstream only ever receives in-scale notes.

jaycen-joshua-on-creative-drum-mixing.title: Jaycen Joshua on creative drum mixing
jaycen-joshua-on-creative-drum-mixing.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jaycen Joshua breaks down his hip-hop/trap drum-loop processing on a tambora/percussion loop, then zooms out to the drum bus's four parallel aux sends — the real substance of the video, and directly relevant to Nate's hip-hop/trap production. The loop chain is a straight subtractive-then-additive move: a CLA-76-style FET compressor for control, a Lo-Fi/bitcrush stage for weight, an EQ cut that deliberately cedes low-end territory to the 808 while boosting upper-high-mids for cut-through, and — the most unusual move — a noise suppressor run backwards, as a deliberate fidelity-destroying lo-fi effect rather than a cleanup tool. He states his overarching mix philosophy directly: strip a sound down to what it actually needs, then rebuild only what heavy bus compression/limiting took away via dedicated parallel aux sends, each doing one specific job (transient "spark," a front-to-back attention effect, and a Fruity-Loops-style blown-out kick character) — so nothing has to sound "perfect" in isolation, only correct in its frequency pocket next to everything else.

position-01.title: Position 01
position-01.html:
Overview

  • Fret range: open strings + frets 1–4
  • Fingers: 1 → fret 1, 2 → fret 2, 3 → fret 3, 4 → fret 4 (open strings played with no finger).
  • Lowest note: E (string 6, open) · Highest note: G# (string 1, fret 4)
  • Interval span (lowest to highest note): 2 octaves + a major 3rd

Note map

String Open 1 2 3 4
1 (E) E F F# G G#
2 (B) B C C# D D#
3 (G) G G# A A# B
4 (D) D D# E F F#
5 (A) A A# B C C#
6 (E) E F F# G G#

Fretboard

        Open     1     2     3     4
  e  |-E-----F-----F#----G-----G#---
  B  |-B-----C-----C#----D-----D#---
  G  |-G-----G#----A-----A#----B----
  D  |-D-----D#----E-----F-----F#---
  A  |-A-----A#----B-----C-----C#---
  E  |-E-----F-----F#----G-----G#---
       nut

Stretches

  • Pinky stretch (fret 5, one above the pinky): 1 (E): A · 2 (B): E · 3 (G): C · 4 (D): G · 5 (A): D · 6 (E): A
  • Index stretch: none below the nut — the open strings (already shown in the Open column) are as low as this position goes.

Chord shapes in this position

  • Open ('cowboy') chords: E, Em, E7 · A, Am, A7 · D, Dm, D7 · G, G7 · C, C7 · Am7, Em7, Dsus.
  • Barre shapes anchored at fret 1: F (E-shape barre) · B♭ (A-shape barre) — the first movable barre positions.
  • These are the foundation chords; everything higher up is a movable version of the E/A/C/G/D (CAGED) shapes seen here. See Chords · Chords by Key · Seventh Chords.

Scales in this position

  • Open-position major scales: C, G, D, A, E all lie naturally in open position (the Berklee Book 1 reading zone).
  • Pentatonic: E minor pentatonic and A minor pentatonic sit in open position (roots on the open 6th/5th strings).
  • Read melodies here first, then move the same shapes up the neck. See Scales · Scale Modes Reference · Circle of Fifths.

Arpeggios in this position

  • Open triad arpeggios: E, A, D, G, C major · Em, Am, Dm minor — the chord tones of the open chords above.
  • Practice arpeggiating each open chord to hear its 1–3–5. See Chords · Chord Inversions · Seventh Chords.
  • Soloing use: this zone is the first of three E major triad "positions" (open, 5th fret, 9th fret) used as a fretboard map for transposing blues lines — see Triads as a Fretboard Map — Jack Ruch, Triads! The Secret To Learning The Fretboard.

↩ Guitar Positions

Chord shapes in this position

Barre at fret 5 (the index-finger fret of this position):

creating-vocal-stacks-with-kuk-harrell.title: Creating vocal stacks with Kuk Harrell
creating-vocal-stacks-with-kuk-harrell.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A Mix with the Masters walkthrough of Grammy-winning vocal producer Kuk Harrell (Justin Bieber, Rihanna, Beyoncé, Chris Brown) building a stacked background-vocal section live, working from a real second-verse example. Harrell narrates the session step by step — panning the first stack immediately as it's tracked so he can judge it in mono, keeping every stack's level identical to the one before it so he can honestly compare the blend, the "always four, never two" stacking rule, and a specific soft-delivery direction ("give it to me sexy") for a unison layer sitting under an already-powerful lead. He also lays out his simplicity philosophy for FX — one reverb/delay/doubler/EQ/compressor/"driver" chain reused across the entire record's stacks rather than reinvented per line — and closes with the vocal-producer judgment side of the job: harmonies created live and by feel rather than written out, needing both a "toolbox of audio colors" and real music-theory knowledge, and the discipline to know when a record needs elaborate stacks versus none at all (he cites most Rihanna records as staying single-lead). Short and dense — a companion piece to the channel's separate 5:32 Harrell breakdown (Radio-ready vocal effects with Kuk Harrell), which covers the lead-vocal tracking chain rather than the stack-building process this video documents.

valhallashimmer.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Valhalla DSP

What it is

Valhalla's pitch-shifting shimmer reverb, adding octave-up (or other interval) pitched reflections to the reverb tail for an ethereal, ambient texture.

What it's used for

Ambient, ethereal shimmer-reverb pads and atmospheric textures on vocals and instruments.

FX chain notes

Used on a dedicated send/return for a shimmer texture layered under the dry signal.

Techniques

  • Bright Hall algorithm, Center width, on a guitar arpeggio for an ethereal wash — Valhalla Shimmer's Bright Hall mode set to Center width turns a plucky/arpeggiated clean guitar part into a beautiful, ethereal shimmer wash — the go-to when a source needs to read as dreamy/emo/ambient rather than just "reverberant." Pair with BLEASS Granulizer's pitched-delay mode (see Plugin Wishlist) for even more ethereal depth on top. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording — You Suck at Producing (Underbelly), How To Make EDM (Emo Dance Music)
  • First-call reverb for turning a plain/dry source into a lush ambient soundscape, with Supermassive as the free fallback — for a fast lush-pad/wash effect, ValhallaShimmer is the first reach; if the $50 isn't worth it yet, Valhalla's free Supermassive gets close, especially starting from one of its own reverb presets rather than dialing from scratch. Chain it early in a soundscape-building signal path — before granular/tape/pitch layers stack on top. → Grain Delay — You Suck at Producing, The best FX for creating LUSH Soundscapes

Used in my chains

My pitch-shifted (shimmer) reverb — feeds the tail through a pitch shifter so it blooms into an angelic, evolving pad (an effect, not a room):

Chain overview

Glue comp → tape → density → color → peak catch. Compressor first so everything downstream saturates a steady signal; limiter last purely as a peak net.

electro-funk-hop.title: Electro Funk-Hop
electro-funk-hop.html: What makes it the genre: a funk rhythmic backbone (syncopated bass, tight drum programming) fused with 8-bit/chiptune sound sources and a bright, "video-gamey" character — cool and groovy but energetic and slightly retro-digital rather than warm/vintage like Neo-Soul - Lo-fi. Composition carries almost the whole identity; the genre tolerates (even rewards) a near-bare mixing chain because the sound design is already doing the work.

beat-breakdown-groovy-electro-funk-hop-o.title: Beat Breakdown - Groovy Electro Funk-Hop (one of my favourites!)
beat-breakdown-groovy-electro-funk-hop-o.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Max Konyi breaks down the trailer music he wrote for his own "Musical Warp Drive" course (made in Studio One; every technique below is DAW-agnostic and maps directly onto Ableton) — a short, dense "electro funk-hop" cue built to be cool and video-gamey without being distracting under spoken narration. It's a genuinely rich lesson precisely because it's SHORT: with almost no processing budget to hide behind (his own summary — "the amount of inserts on here is nothing"), the entire track's identity comes from composition and sound choice alone. Highlights: harmonizing three monophonic synth voices instead of playing block chords (a classical/orchestral way of thinking about harmony), a Lydian-intro-to-relative-Dorian-verse modulation that's really the same 7 notes reframed, a deliberately non-diatonic "magical" chord dropped into an otherwise-minor progression, a polyphonic bass patch that plays its own harmony line against the root, a bass fill used instead of a drum fill at a transition, and a minimal-processing mixing philosophy (sound design does the work, not inserts). Genuinely useful as a case study in getting maximum musical mileage from minimum production budget.

drum-mic-technique.title: Drum Mic Technique
drum-mic-technique.html:
The part of a live drum sound that's decided before any plugin loads. Mic choice, position, and how the mics are checked/blended against each other — the tracking-stage counterpart to Vocal Mic Technique. This vault's own drum chains currently run entirely from samples/loops (see the source note on Drums Group) — this note captures the tracking-stage discipline as reference, for the day a real kit gets mic'd, and because the mic-position lessons (proximity effect especially) transfer directly to mic'd overdubs and sample-source recording either way.

The core split: direct mics get the heat, ambient mics stay alone

Kick and snare (direct/close mics) are where EQ and dynamics processing belongs; overheads and room mics mostly shouldn't be touched. Stated as the whole philosophy in one line: "the important thing about cutting drums is the direct mics — the kick and snare — that's where you're gonna put some heat and EQ'ing... the room tracks and the [overheads] — they're so good you're not gonna EQ those, so it's easy, left for later." A good overhead/room pair already captures the kit's real balance and space; processing it risks undoing what the mic placement already got right. Spend the EQ/comp budget where the mics are closest and least representative of the whole kit (kick, snare), and leave the mics that already sound like "the record" alone. → EQ, Drums Group

"Never be shy with EQ" on the direct mics — the flip side of the rule above: once you've decided a mic needs correcting (a snare read too dark/deep on first listen), commit to the move rather than under-correcting it. Tentative EQ on a direct mic wastes the one place in the chain where aggressive correction is actually the job. → EQ
secs: The core split: direct mics get the heat, ambient mics stay alone

adding-impact-to-percussions-with-alan-m.title: Adding impact to percussions with Alan Meyerson
adding-impact-to-percussions-with-alan-m.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Alan Meyerson (score mixer, also behind Using reverb to create space with Alan Meyerson) takes an already-solid percussion stem from the Gears of War cue "Raid Action" and walks through a short, concrete before/after pass to squeeze more impact out of it. The video is compact (under 8 minutes) but structurally dense: it opens with a genuinely useful piece of theory borrowed from Andrew Scheps — pop mixing can get away with compressing the whole mix instead of individual elements, but film/game scoring can't, because the deliverable is separate stems rather than a finished mix, so a single mix-bus compressor would react to material that isn't present in every stem. The workaround is to run parallel compression per stem (here, the whole percussion stem treated as one unit) rather than per element or per finished mix — a middle ground between the two extremes. From there it's two concrete processing moves: (1) build a parallel percussion bus using a Chris Lord-Alge-style 1176 plus a Puig Tec-style EQ for top-end snap, with PSP Vintage Warmer 2 auditioned as an alternate/additional color source; (2) revisit an aux bus the percussion was already routed through, which carries a restrained compressor and a Sonnox Oxford Envolution transient designer, nudging the transient designer's attack up and sustain down slightly and blending only a small amount back in. It closes with a quick critical-listening pass across individual elements, catching a specific frequency that's dulling the new snap — flagged as a fix but not executed on screen. No exact numbers are given anywhere in the transcript; every setting is qualitative ("a little bit," "a tiny bit," "over the top then dial back"), consistent with a quick demo video rather than a full walkthrough.

single-note-pentatonic-substitutions-ove.title: Single-Note Pentatonic Substitutions Over Changes
single-note-pentatonic-substitutions-ove.html:
Part of Guitar Positions, and a lighter-weight sibling to Chord-Tone Soloing and Arpeggio Shapes for Playing Over Changes: instead of outlining every chord's own arpeggio or scale, stay on one pentatonic box the whole way through a progression and swap or add exactly one note at the moment each chord changes. Uses the same movable diagonal pentatonic fingering system as that page, but the goal here isn't building toward a mode — it's the minimum viable move that makes a static box sound like it's actually tracking the changes. Worked over a C minor 12-bar blues (Cm7–Fm7–Ab7–G7), the same form documented on Blues Form and Harmony.

The core idea: one box, one note change per chord

Most of a chord progression's pentatonic-compatible notes overlap from chord to chord — usually only one note in the box actually clashes with the next chord. Find that one note, swap it (or add a neighbor) exactly on the downbeat of the chord change, and leave everything else in the box alone. The payoff: it sounds like you're "playing the changes" — deliberately targeting each new harmony — while the physical vocabulary stays almost entirely the same box shape throughout. Framed directly against full re-scaling per chord: "you don't have to arpeggiate some crazy arpeggio or even play a whole new scale shape, just simply add the [one note] when the chord comes along."

Setup: why the minor pentatonic is the right base at all

Cm7 (the i chord) is built from C – E♭ – G – B♭ (1, ♭3, 5, ♭7) — exactly the four notes of C minor pentatonic (C E♭ F G B♭), plus the pentatonic's extra note, F (the 11/4), which is "super colorful" and safe to hit as much as you want over the i chord. So the whole exercise starts from a scale that's already 100% consonant with the tonic chord, and the per-chord moves below are deviations from that safe home base, not a new scale per chord.

Fingering used: the diagonal (movable) C minor pentatonic — same string-pair system as Dorian from the Minor Pentatonic Box's Fingering 2, here worked on the D and G strings: a two-note set at frets 8, 10 on the D string, then a three-note set at frets 8, 11, 12 on the G string. (Transcript numbers are consistent but unconfirmed against video footage — verify fret-by-fret before drilling; the relational logic below holds regardless of the exact frets.)

Setup: why the minor pentatonic is the right base at all

harmonic-minor-scale-practice-ladder.title: Harmonic Minor Scale Practice Ladder
harmonic-minor-scale-practice-ladder.html:
Brandon D'Eon's leveled, seven-stage system for internalizing the harmonic minor scale on guitar, from raw scale memorization through to free improvisation. See Harmonic Minor Modes for the underlying theory (mode construction, the five-shapes-not-seven simplification, the per-mode chord table) this ladder is built on.

The ladder

  1. Theory + the two-octave shape. Understand harmonic minor as natural minor with a raised 7th; memorize one two-octave fretboard shape and be able to transpose it to any root.
  2. The seven modes, by name and order. Harmonic minor (Aeolian ♮7) → Locrian ♮6 → Ionian ♯5 → Dorian ♯4 → Phrygian dominant → Lydian ♯2 → Super Locrian. Understand that all seven share one note collection, reduced to five practicable fretboard shapes.
  3. Eighth notes at 100 BPM, through all keys. Drill the five mode shapes across every key at a moderate, steady subdivision before adding speed or complexity.
  4. Chord construction from each mode. Build the triad and 7th chord native to each of the seven modes (see the table in Harmonic Minor Modes); understand the borrowed-chord convention (writing in the relative natural-minor key, borrowing the harmonic-minor major V/V7 for cadential strength).
  5. Three-notes-per-string, 16th notes, 80 BPM, all 12 keys — E strings only. Ascend on the low E string's version of the shape, descend on the high E string's version, cycling through all 12 keys at this fixed subdivision/tempo.
  6. Same three-notes-per-string drill, but rotate the starting string. Repeat Level 5's drill starting from the A string (12 keys), then the B string, then the D string, then the G string — not just the E strings — so the shapes get internalized independent of which string you started memorizing them on.
  7. Free improvisation over a backing track, mapped by position. Over a track in a chosen key (e.g. C minor, using the C harmonic minor scale — remember there's no true "key of harmonic minor," see Harmonic Minor Modes), work through five fretboard positions, identifying which harmonic minor mode is native to each position before improvising in it. Goal: full-fretboard improvisational freedom once every position is comfortable.

synthwave.title: Synthwave
synthwave.html: What makes it the genre: the imagined 1980s, rebuilt with reverence — Juno chorus on everything harmonic, LinnDrum-family drums with gated reverb, a relentless 16th-note synth bass, and neon brightness as an emotional statement. It's nostalgia engineering: period-correct sound sources, but mixed with modern low end and loudness. Nearly always minor-key, mid-tempo, cinematic.

l-shape-root-map-for-blues-chords.title: L-Shape Root Map for Blues Chords
l-shape-root-map-for-blues-chords.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. A movable-shape system for finding the IV and V (and, for the minor blues, ♭VI) chord roots of a 12-bar blues purely by counting strings and frets from the I chord — no separate memorized chord shape per key, no scanning the neck for the next root. Where Blues Form and Harmony documents the harmony of the 12-bar form and Chord Voicings documents shell-voicing shapes in general, this page is the missing piece between them: where your hand physically goes once you've grabbed the I chord. The root layout it produces looks like a small "L" on the fretboard — that's the whole mnemonic.

The core idea

Once you know where the I chord's root sits, the IV and V roots are a fixed number of strings and frets away — the same offset in every key, because it's a relative (movable) shape, not a fixed-position chord. Two versions exist depending on which string the I chord's root falls on.

Dominant blues (I7-IV7-V7) — root on the low E string

Worked in A (A7-D7-E7), but the offsets are key-independent.

  1. I chord (A7): root on the low E string. Play any dominant-7 shape off that root — a full E-shaped bar chord, or a smaller shell voicing (root-3rd-♭7 only) for a band context or to dodge a full bar-chord grip. Matches the E-string-root shell already documented on Chord Voicings § From videos (Seriff's own maj7→dominant7→minor7→dim7 shell-shifting shape).
  2. IV chord (D7): move down one string (E string → A string), same fret. Play the same shape family there (bar chord = classic A-shaped bar chord; shell = the shell shape relocated).
  3. V chord (E7): from the IV chord, move up two frets, same string.

Root layout: I → (down a string, same fret) → IV → (same string, up two frets) → V. Traces a small L.

Dominant blues (I7-IV7-V7) — root on the A string

Same three chords, mirrored, for when the tonic falls on the A string instead (worked from A at the 12th fret of the A string).

  1. I chord: shell voicing (root-3rd-♭7) or full bar chord, root on the A string.
  2. IV chord: move to the low E string, down two frets (toward the headstock).
  3. V chord: from the IV chord, up two frets (back toward the body), same string.

Same L shape, mirrored — confirms the mnemonic generalizes to "one string over, ± a fret count," not to one specific starting string.

digital-audio-manipulation-with-shawn-ev.title: Digital Audio Manipulation with Shawn Everett
digital-audio-manipulation-with-shawn-ev.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, screen-recorded Mix with the Masters segment of Shawn Everett live-editing a session, building out a metallic texture layer ("metal two") from scratch. It's dense with concrete moves but thin on narration — Everett talks through what he's clicking almost in shorthand ("let's go like that," "that one could be inverted, who knows"), so most of the value here is in the process, not quotable numbers. Two distinct techniques get demonstrated back to back: (1) a duplicate-and-mangle sound-design recipe — take one source, make five-plus copies, apply a different manipulation to each (reverse, phase invert, splice in a pasted section, pitch-shift by a different rough amount), crossfade the edit points, then mute/arrange the results across the timeline to follow the track's dynamic build; and (2) a Melodyne pitch-editing pass — switching off polyphonic detection to make manual note-dragging easier, then moving a whole detected note by hand and deliberately accepting some loss of the original note's character as part of the creative result rather than something to fix. A small workflow habit bookends the clip: color-coding edits red (old) vs. green (new) to track edit generations at a glance.

twelve-tone-serialism.title: Twelve-Tone & Serialism
twelve-tone-serialism.html:
Part of Music Theory → 20th-Century Harmony. Atonality is the complete absence of a tonal center — the logical endpoint of the Romantic era's steadily increasing chromaticism. Arnold Schoenberg engineered a systematic way to guarantee it mathematically: twelve-tone technique.

The twelve-tone row

  • Every composition begins with a sequence of all 12 chromatic pitches, each used exactly once — the row.
  • Avoid anything that suggests tonality while building it: triad fragments, familiar-scale bits.
  • A complete row is a short, "pure" atonal composition on its own.

The twelve-tone matrix

A 12×12 grid used to generate related rows from one original ("Prime," labeled P-1):

  1. Place the original row across the top row.
  2. Fill the left column with the row's inversion — flip it upside-down (a rising interval in the original becomes the same-size falling interval in the inversion).
  3. Transpose the original row to start on each of the 12 pitches to fill in the rest of the top row, producing P-2 through P-12.
  4. Doing the same transposition down each column produces the inversion rows I-1 through I-12.
  5. Reading any row backward gives its retrograde (R).
  6. Reading backward down a column gives retrograde inversion (RI).

Composition rules

You CAN You CAN'T
Use any row, any time Use a partial row
Restrike a note before moving to the next one Change the order of notes within a row
Combine adjacent row-notes into chords Bend the material toward tonality
Pass rows between voices, overlap rows —

Convention: start a piece with P-1, so an analyst can reconstruct the matrix.

a-guided-tour-of-musical-feeling.title: A Guided Tour of Musical Feeling
a-guided-tour-of-musical-feeling.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Max Konyi's foundational ear-training video — a 50-minute walkthrough of all 12 scale degrees of the chromatic scale, each played against a sustained tonic drone and described purely in terms of its subjective "feeling state" rather than its pitch or interval name. The premise: tonal music organizes every note as a relationship to a home note (the tonic), and that relationship produces a distinct, learnable, non-verbal quality — a "vibe" — independent of octave, instrument, or absolute pitch. Konyi walks degree by degree (1, 5, 4, 3, 2, 6, 7, ♯4, ♭7, ♭3, ♭6, ♭2), for each one: describing its feeling in his own words, contrasting it against its most commonly confused neighbors on a "feeling-circle" (not the circle of fifths — a circle arranged by which degrees people actually mistake for each other), and playing short melodic examples that isolate it. This is the master reference for the whole feeling-state ear-training method that the three "Answering Your Ear Training Questions" videos build on — the most valuable video in this batch for anyone starting the method from zero, since it's the only one that actually walks through and demonstrates all 12 degrees rather than just discussing the training process abstractly.

dua-lipa-vocal-chain.title: Dua Lipa Vocal Chain
dua-lipa-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: the disco-pop powerhouse — a naturally dark, low-mid-rich alto kept punchy and rhythmic over a busy dance floor. The documented chain (Ian Kirkpatrick, "Don't Start Now") is instructive: many of her vocals are cut on a handheld Shure SM7B — close cousin of your Shure SM57 — with the character coming from smooth opto compression and taming her prominent low mids so the voice cuts without shouting. Signal source: Shure SM57 handheld (yes, really — the movement/energy in the performance beats mic technique here), or TLM for the balladry.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — solid gain (a dynamic needs it), clean
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 2–3 dB smooth (the LA-3A in Kirkpatrick's chain is this family — opto glue)
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — low ATTEN @ 60–100 Hz (handheld rumble), nothing else

Chain overview

Sweep the subs → smooth opto → soothe the low mids → tune tight-ish → bright rhythmic finish. The dance-pop insight: the vocal is a rhythm instrument — consonants land on the grid, dynamics flattened enough to ride the groove.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Pro-Q 4 — Clean sweep

  • HPF ~30–40 Hz first (the documented first move — the comp shouldn't react to sub junk), then a real HPF ~90 · check 200–400 Hz but don't gut it yet (next stage handles it dynamically).

2. LALA — The smooth engine

  • 3–5 dB GR constant — the LA-3A-style always-on silk that keeps power without edge.

3. Soothe2 — The documented trick

  • Pre-emphasis centered on the LOW MIDS (200–500 Hz), soft mode — her body/power lives there and overpowers the track; soothe ducks it only when it blooms. (Most vocal soothe targets 2–6 kHz — this is the opposite move, and it's the Dua-specific one.)

4. Auto-Tune Pro — Tight pop

  • Retune 20–35, Humanize 50 — locked enough to be rhythmic, not robotic.

5. Pro-C 2 — Rhythm flatten

  • 4:1, 2–4 dB — dance vocals sit still on top of a pumping track.

6. Pro-Q 4 — Finish

  • Presence +1–2 @ 3–4 kHz · air +1–2 @ 12 kHz · the low mids are already handled — resist cutting them statically.

uad-ua-610-b.title: UAD UA 610-B
uad-ua-610-b.html:
Category: Tube Preamp / Channel Strip (Unison) Vendor: Universal Audio — stock Realtime Analog Classics bundle on the Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII

What it is

Emulation of the UA 610 tube console preamp — the desk Sinatra and the Beach Boys were cut on. As a Unison plugin it physically reconfigures the Apollo's preamp impedance/gain staging to behave like the hardware, not just process after the fact.

What it's used for

Warm, round tube color on the way in. The go-to Unison pick for acoustic guitar and vocals when "flattering, not flat" is the goal.

Key settings

  • Gain (tube stage): LOW setting for condensers — the Neumann TLM 102 runs hot. Drive higher only when you want audible tube thickening.
  • Level: trim so the DAW sees ~−18 dBFS average, peaks −12 (see Gain Staging).
  • HPF: off at the preamp — do surgical cuts in Ableton where they're undoable.
  • Impedance: 2.0k default for mics; changing it audibly shifts brightness/body — sweep by ear.

FX chain notes

Rounder-tube alternative to the UAD Neve 1073 as the first device in uad_console chains — see Acoustic Guitar Track. Neutral alternative: no Unison plugin at all (clean Apollo preamp).

Used in my chains

My rounder tube preamp (Unison) — the warmer, tube-forward alternative to the Neve 1073 on the way in; especially good where tube input flatters the source. ~0 VU, printed conservatively:

  • Electric Piano Track — slot 1: driven slightly harder than a piano (EPs love tube input), ~0 VU.
  • Electric Bass DI / Digital Bass — slot 1, Unison preamp: tube weight on the bass DI.
  • Synth Bed — slot 1: barely on, ~0 VU.
  • Alt to the 1073 for round tube warmth on soft/ballad vocals.

chord.title: Chord
chord.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock MIDI chord device — a preset browser of chord voicings with a Learn mode (play a chord, every subsequent key plays that same voicing), plus Strum, Tension, and Crescendo controls for arpeggiating the chord's notes, and (Live 12.2, marketed as "Expressive Chords") Invert/Reverse/Quantize articulation controls plus an Import Chords from Clip button that lifts an entire progression straight out of any MIDI clip. Distinct from the Max for Live Chord Generator pack device, which builds voicings from an extension/inversion/disposition grid instead of a preset browser.

What it's used for

Turning single-note MIDI input into full chord voicings — either by teaching it a chord via Learn, or by browsing its preset library — with built-in strum/timing/velocity shaping on top.

FX chain notes

Sits before the instrument in a MIDI chain, generating the notes the instrument then plays; commonly racked with several Chord instances (each on a different preset) selected via a chain-selector macro for on-the-fly voicing changes.

ableton-sound-design-exponential-rhythms.title: ableton sound design - EXPONENTIAL RHYTHMS 3-5 Texture Mode
ableton-sound-design-exponential-rhythms.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Third entry in a five-part series on building "exponential rhythms" — evolving, self-varying rhythmic patterns rather than static loops — this installment covers the method built entirely on Ableton's Texture audio-warp mode, one of Live's six warp algorithms (Beats/Tones/Texture/Complex/Complex Pro/Repitch). Unlike the series' first two methods (arpeggiator/Simpler repetition, referenced but not detailed here), the texture-warp method needs no instrument or extra device at all — it's a pure clip-level technique: stretch an audio clip's segment BPM far past the project BPM, drop it into Texture warp mode, and the resulting grain-based playback naturally evolves in pitch/timbre/rhythm as it follows the source's original contour. The video is dense but short (904 words / ~15 min with demos) and teaches exactly two new parameters — grain size (grain length → controls the resulting rhythm's rate) and flux (random per-grain length jitter → rhythmic chaos amount) — plus the one non-obvious Ableton mechanic that makes them musically controllable: automating them requires the clip's own Envelopes tab (not a track automation lane), and that automation is percentage-of-current-max, not an absolute value, which is why the standard move is to set grain size and flux to their maximum in the Audio tab first, then carve the actual range down inside the Envelopes tab. Demonstrated across a percussive one-shot, a drum loop, a click/percussive sample, and a kick, plus a callout to try reversed samples and to layer further audio effects on top. Most valuable: the grain-size/flux/transpose interdependence (small grain + high flux = noisy-but-transient-preserving; large grain + flux + pitched-up = smoothed/spread textural drone) as a compact recipe space, and the Envelopes-tab/percentage-based-automation mechanic, which generalizes to warp-mode automation on any clip, not just Texture mode.

5-beginner-bass-riffs-you-can-t-f-up.title: 5 Beginner Bass Riffs (You Can’t F*** Up)
5-beginner-bass-riffs-you-can-t-f-up.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz beginner-repertoire video that solves a specific first-song problem — pick something too hard and you get discouraged, pick something too easy and it's boring — by curating five real, recognizable riffs, each one deliberately chosen to drill a different skill rather than just being five isolated tabs to memorize. The five, in order of skill targeted: I Love Rock and Roll (Joan Jett, bass by Gary Ryan) for alternating plucking and simple root-note restraint; Seven Nation Army (The White Stripes) for hand-shifting via a "look ahead with your eyes" trick; Something in the Way (Nirvana, bass by Krist Novoselic) for micro-shifting through an awkward stretch plus note-length/sustain control, and — uniquely among the five — a riff that covers the entire song, not just a chorus excerpt; Zombie (The Cranberries, bass by Mike Hogan) for stamina/endurance via non-stop chugging that also mixes open strings with fretted notes; and Under Pressure (Queen & David Bowie, bass by John Deacon) for a "rhythm mnemonic" hack — inventing a nonsense phrase whose natural speech rhythm matches a syncopated riff — as a way to feel a hard rhythm correctly before you can count it formally. Each riff gets real artist/song context (who actually played it, why the choice works as a bassline, any tuning quirks) rather than being presented as a bare tab. A "Beginner to Badass" paid-course plug appears once mid-video but gates nothing — every riff, fingering, and technique taught is complete in the free video.

drift-analog-synth-bass.title: Drift — Analog Synth Bass
drift-analog-synth-bass.html:
Instrument: Drift · Slot: BASS Slot · Used by: Digital Bass Track

What it's for

Indie/synthwave analog-style synth bass — a Moog-ish saw/square with a filter-envelope pluck, not a sub-focused patch. Reach for it when the part wants a played, articulated bassline rather than a static 808.

Settings

  • Adapted from Drift — Bass / sub: Voice Mode Mono
  • Osc 1: Saw or Square (the recipe's default is Sine/Triangle for a clean sub — swap the waveform here for the Moog-ish harmonic content this chain note wants); Osc 2 off or an octave down for weight
  • ③ Filter: MS2 24 dB, moderate–high resonance
  • Filter envelope: fast attack, short-medium decay, low sustain — the pluck shape
  • ⑦ Detune: 0 — stays mono and clean despite the more aggressive waveform choice
  • ⑩ Glide legato for slides
  • FX: none pre-bus — keep it dry into the mix bus

In context

  • Same BASS-slot indie/synthwave lane as Model 84 — Juno Bass — pick Drift for a cleaner modern voice, Model 84 for the real Juno chorus/circuit character.
  • Filter-envelope pluck is the defining move here — without it this collapses into a plain sub patch.

position-02.html:
Overview

  • Fret range: frets 2–5
  • Fingers: 1 → fret 2, 2 → fret 3, 3 → fret 4, 4 → fret 5.
  • Lowest note: F# (string 6, fret 2) · Highest note: A (string 1, fret 5)
  • Interval span (lowest to highest note): 2 octaves + a minor 3rd

2 (B) C# D D# E
3 (G) A A# B C

Stretches

  • Pinky stretch (fret 6, one above the pinky): 1 (E): A# · 2 (B): F · 3 (G): C# · 4 (D): G# · 5 (A): D# · 6 (E): A#
  • Index stretch (fret 1, one below the index finger): 1 (E): F · 2 (B): C · 3 (G): G# · 4 (D): D# · 5 (A): A# · 6 (E): F

Chord shapes in this position

Barre at fret 2 (the index-finger fret of this position):

  • E-shape barre → F# major / F# minor (root on string 6, fret 2). Add the ♭7 for F#7 / F#m7.
  • A-shape barre → B major / B minor (root on string 5, fret 2). Add the ♭7 for B7 / Bm7.
  • The 4-fret span also contains fragments of the C, G, and D CAGED shapes; the two barres above are the workhorses. See Chords · Chords by Key · Seventh Chords.

Scales in this position

  • Roots in this position: F# on string 6 (fret 2) and B on string 5 (fret 2) — anchor the F# major and B major scales (and their relative minors) as movable patterns here.
  • Pentatonic box: F# minor pentatonic with its root on string 6, fret 2 (the box-1 shape movable to any key).
  • Any scale is playable in this span — it's the same shapes as open position, shifted up. See Scales · Scale Modes Reference · Circle of Fifths.

Arpeggios in this position

  • Triad + 7th arpeggios for the barre roots above: F# and B major/minor (and dom7/min7/maj7), played within frets 2–5.
  • Arpeggiate each barre shape to internalize its 1–3–5–7. See Chords · Chord Inversions · Seventh Chords.

What it is

A Haas-effect snap-in creating stereo width via short (sub-40ms) delay offsets between channels.

ozone-9-imager.title: Ozone 9 Imager
ozone-9-imager.html:
Category: Pan/Imaging Vendor: iZotope

What it is

Ozone 9's stereo imaging module, offering multiband stereo width control and a vectorscope/phase display.

What it's used for

Adjusting a master's stereo width by frequency band and checking mono compatibility.

FX chain notes

Used on the master bus, typically after EQ and dynamics, before the final limiter.

Techniques

  • Mono Maker named directly and used on a drum bus (not just a master): set the crossover at ~61 Hz to collapse everything below it to mono/center. "It's called the mono maker… taking all your low-end signal from wherever you set the cross point — 61 hertz and below — and putting it right in your middle." Stated as taste rather than a hard rule ("sometimes you want a stereo low end, sometimes you want some crazy stuff") but his default preference: a centered low end reads better, "period, point blank." Directly matches this plugin's own Band Width/crossover controls — set the low crossover ~61 Hz and Band 1 width to 0. → Drums Bus, Width and Stereo — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), Jaycen Joshua's drum bus
  • Reach for it on individual elements (a shaker, a tambourine, even a reverb return), not just at mastering — used as a general-purpose per-track widener on Mode 2, pushed hard whenever a small element needs to sound bigger/wider or have its highs lifted — treated as a normal mix-stage tool rather than a rare mastering-only device. → Disclosure, 11 Best Music Tips from "In My Arms"
  • Widen the highs, keep the bass mono, on an individual riddim-bass patch (not just the master) — the same multiband-width logic as the master-chain use below, applied directly on a bass instrument's own FX chain: open up the top-band width for an airier high end while leaving the low band collapsed to mono, so a heavily-processed dubstep/riddim bass stays club/mono-safe without sacrificing perceived width up top. → BASS Slot, Width and Stereo — You Suck at Producing (Underbelly ft. San Holo), How To Make WHOLESOME RIDDIM with San Holo

Used in my chains

My multiband stereo imager — width per frequency band, so the low end stays mono while the top opens up:

  • Master Chain — slot 5, imaging: Band 1 (<120 Hz) width DOWN to 0 (mono low end — punch + vinyl/club safety); top band +5–10% width max if the mix needs it.

wider.title: Wider
wider.html:
Category: Pan/Imaging Vendor: Polyverse Music

What it is

Polyverse's stereo widening plugin using spectral processing to widen a signal without the phase issues of simple Haas-based widening.

What it's used for

Widening mono or narrow-stereo synths, guitars, and vocals for a bigger stereo image.

FX chain notes

Used late in a track's chain, after EQ/compression, for final stereo-width shaping.

Used in my chains

My one-knob, phase-coherent widener — mono-compatible spread that stays solid in the center (no hollow phase-flip collapse):

  • Synth Lead Track — slot 4, width: subtle, mono-compatible — big without leaving the center.

Key Parameters

image: Images/Wider.png
coords: Images/Wider.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique Artist / record example
① Width The main width amount, shown as a percentage above the knob (100% = unprocessed). Spreads the signal while preserving mono compatibility. Keep it subtle; the whole point is width that survives a mono fold-down. Past ~130% the centre starts to feel hollow even though it stays mono-safe. —
② Low Bypass Frequency below which widening is not applied — everything under it stays centred. Shown in Hz on the knob face. Set it around 300–400 Hz so bass and kick stay mono and locked while the top half widens. This is the control that keeps a widener from wrecking your low end — see Stereo Field. —
③ Mono Collapses the output to mono — a built-in mono-check button. Use it as the A/B: hit Mono and confirm nothing disappears. Faster than reaching for a Utility just to check. —

overdrive.title: Overdrive
overdrive.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock overdrive/distortion effect with a resonant filter and dry/wet control, geared toward classic tube/pedal-style overdrive tones.

What it's used for

Guitar and synth overdrive, adding edge to basses and leads, or general lo-fi character on drum/instrument busses.

FX chain notes

Placed early in an instrument's effects chain (before EQ) so the tonal shaping downstream can tame the added harmonics.

Techniques

  • A very light touch (~5% dry/wet) for subtle warmth, not obvious distortion — a much stronger setting was tried first and rejected as too much for a sensitive/delicate part; pulled back to roughly 5% wet it adds just a touch of crunch/warmth without reading as a distortion effect. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording — You Suck at Producing, Warmth
  • Built-in notch/resonant filter adds crunch on top of plain drive — Overdrive's Filter Band section is called out specifically for making a sound (an 808 in this case) "nice and crunchy" beyond what the Drive knob alone gives you — dial in the filter band's frequency/width to target where that extra crunch bites. — You Suck at Producing, How to use Distortion

Key Parameters

image: Images/Overdrive.jpg
coords: Images/Overdrive.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique
① Filter Band The band the distortion focuses on — drag the circle for frequency (1.25 kHz) and width (Q) Narrow onto a range so only that band drives
② Drive Distortion amount Edge-of-breakup → full overdrive
③ Tone Output brightness after the drive Brighten to cut; darken to sit back
④ Dynamics How the drive responds to input level More dynamics = more touch-sensitive
⑤ Dry/Wet Parallel blend Blend for controlled grit

ozone-9-equalizer.title: Ozone 9 Equalizer
ozone-9-equalizer.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: iZotope

What it is

The standalone EQ module from iZotope's Ozone 9 mastering suite, offering digital and analog-modeled EQ curves with a spectrum display.

What it's used for

Mastering-grade broad tonal shaping and surgical correction on a final mix bus.

FX chain notes

Used on the master bus, typically before Ozone's dynamics/EQ modules in the mastering chain.

Techniques

  • A genuinely light-touch stereo-bus EQ pass, useful as a literal numeric floor for "barely anything": +0.3 dB ~80 Hz, +0.8 dB ~8 kHz. Framed explicitly as a discipline — "I'm never a heavy EQer unless I know that it needs it... just light little touches" — run on the 2-bus after an (unowned) Waves L2 Ultramaximizer's first pass (Threshold −2.6 — see Plugin Wishlist) and before Ozone 9 Maximizer, only when listening first confirms the bus needs anything at all — never a default step. → Ozone 9 Maximizer, Master Chain, Critical Listening for Mastering — Neal Pogue (Mix with the Masters), Understanding Kaytranada's vision with Neal Pogue
  • Switch a band to Digital mode specifically for narrow, surgical fixes — sibilance or a harsh resonance confined to a narrow frequency range — and reach for Analog mode instead for broad, tonal moves. The decision is about the kind of change needed, not one mode being generally better: broadband/tonal → analog-modeled curves (this plugin's ③ Analog/Digital toggle, or see Ozone 9 Vintage EQ for the dedicated analog-emulation module); narrow/precise → digital. This module's built-in per-band Analog/Digital switch makes it the single owned tool that covers both halves of the decision without swapping plugins. → EQ, Master Chain — Sage Audio, How to EQ Your Master

eq-three.title: EQ Three

Category: EQ Vendor: "Ableton (stock)"

What it is

Ableton's stock 3-band EQ (Low/Mid/High with per-band kill switches), used for quick tonal shaping and band-kill moves.

What it's used for

Techniques

  • Standing role as the go-to "surgical EQ" in a deliberately small, memorized plugin toolkit — reached for on problem-solving cuts specifically because it's known well, not because it's the most powerful option. Andrew Scheps: "I use a really small sampling of plugins, and I actually do work this way... if I need a surgical EQ, the EQ Three, I'm done; if I need a musical EQ, usually [a character-style channel EQ]... I'm done." → EQ, Session Templates — Andrew Scheps (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Guitars & Bass - Andrew Scheps
  • Sweep EQ Three's Freq Lo / Freq Hi split points across a kick without touching any gain knob — it still audibly changes the transient. Discovered by accident (reaching for EQ Eight, grabbing EQ Three instead): with all three band gains left flat, just sliding the Freq Lo and Freq Hi crossover-point knobs across a kick changes how its transient reads, because moving the crossover split itself reshapes the signal even with zero boost/cut applied. A fast way to reshape a kick's attack character without committing to an EQ cut. → Kick Design — Habstrakt (Sol State), How Habstrakt makes his SIGNATURE KICK

FX chain notes

3-guitar-bus.title: 3 Guitar Bus
3-guitar-bus.html:
Role: Final color pass on the guitar section. In your routing, groups handle relationships and buses handle finish — broad tone + analog glue, nothing surgical.

Chain overview

Musical EQ → tape → density. All gentle: the bus should be almost removable without the mix falling apart.

Chain

1. Sie-Q — Musical tone

  • Broad strokes only: a dB of top (Höhen) if the section is dull, a dB off the low-mids if thick
  • Why: A character EQ makes "vibe" moves that a surgical EQ makes clinical — buses want musical, not corrective.
  • 🎬 From video: a single shared guitar-bus EQ move used to replace duplicating the same correction on every individual guitar track — "why use twelve EQs when you can use one?" Andrew Scheps builds a dedicated guitar aux specifically for one overall mid-range presence lift, on top of (not instead of) any per-track EQ. → EQ, EQ Three — Andrew Scheps (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Guitars & Bass - Andrew Scheps
  • 🎬 From video (clicky guitar): Disclosure's guitar-bus recipe on "Talk" — overdrive → a note-following EQ (Surfer EQ) → a small EQ to boost the click, on a Telecaster tracked clean through a Neve (light drive) → DBX 160 ("the best comp for clicky guitar; I'd track through one"). Note-following EQ tracks the played note so one moving band does the work of five fixed ones. → Sound Selection Guide, wishlist: Surfer EQ / DBX 160 — Disclosure, Talk.

2. Kramer Tape — Tape glue

  • 15 ips (④) · Flux low, to taste (①) · Record low (②) · Playback to unity (③ — watch output)
  • Why: Tape compression + harmonics is the classic "guitars glued to the record" finish — subtle rounding of transients that makes parts feel produced, not just summed.
  • 🎬 From video: hardware validation of this exact stage — bussing several guitar parts (a strummed lead, a doubling tremolo part, a harmony line) out to a physical tape deck together and consolidating them to a stereo pass produced glue he credited directly to "tape's compression and saturation." → Sony TC-630 — Zach Scholz, Using Analog Tape to Glue a Mix Together

3. Oxford Inflator — Density (optional)

  • Effect 15–25%
  • Why: A touch of perceived loudness so the section holds up against the drums bus without pushing faders.

classical-guitar-expression-muting.title: Classical Guitar Expression & Muting
classical-guitar-expression-muting.html:
Right-hand and left-hand execution techniques for cleaning up and shaping a classical/fingerstyle guitar performance — keeping unwanted notes from ringing, and shaping repeated notes/sections so a piece doesn't sound mechanically identical on every pass.

Bass-note and string muting

Unwanted ringing is one of the hardest things to fully ingrain — a genuinely simple piece can take days of dedicated attention to get every mute exactly right.

  • Thumb-hop bass muting. When a bass note isn't part of the chord currently sounding (e.g. an open low string left ringing from the previous chord), hop the picking-hand thumb onto that string preemptively — right after playing it, or just ahead of the next chord where it isn't wanted — so it damps rather than bleeds into harmony that doesn't want it. Described as "bass note muting 101": not easy, but foundational — worth working on as soon as you're ready even though a piece will still sound fine without it.
  • Fretting-hand finger-muting for a ringing top string. When an open high string (e.g. high E) keeps ringing over a chord where it isn't wanted, mute it with a fretting-hand finger rather than the thumb (the thumb is busy on the bass side) — same principle, opposite hand, for whichever string is actually ringing.
  • Expect a lot of hopping around. Muting multiple strings in sequence (e.g. the low A then immediately the high E right after) feels "weird" and effortful at first — like any new physical habit, it becomes automatic with repetition and stops feeling hard.
  • Which notes need muting is determined by harmony: mute any open string that isn't a chord tone of the harmony currently sounding (cross-reference the piece's harmonic analysis to know which notes are safe to let ring vs. which need damping).

— Jared, Piece #6 of 7 Easy Classical Guitar Songs for Beginners
