mixing-muse-guitars-chris-lord-alge.title: Mixing Muse Guitars - Chris Lord-Alge
mixing-muse-guitars-chris-lord-alge.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A Mix with the Masters session walkthrough with Chris Lord-Alge working a Muse guitar session. Two guitar situations get built up in front of the camera: a guitar solo, and the six-plus tracks that make up the song's main "one guitar sound." On the solo, after basic rumble-removal and a midrange bump ("bark it up"), CLA layers a dual delay (an eighth-note repeat and a longer quarter-note repeat) with a touch of reverb behind it, then adds a dedicated pair of Eventide H3000 harmonizers — one set to a classic micro pitch-shift widener (roughly ±4 cents split left/right), the other running a custom program he calls "Death Flange," used subtly to add a "supernatural" quality rather than an obvious sweep. On the main guitar sound, he shows the six tracks that make up ONE guitar tone across the song: several room-mic'd amp tracks plus a separate DI fuzz track of unclear pedal origin, with the DI track specifically checked and flipped for phase against the mic'd signal (audibly restoring lost low end once corrected) and credited with adding real "heat" to the overall blend. He also notes, in passing, that the same six-ish fader strips cover three different roles across the song — rhythm guitar in one section, the solo in another, piano in a third — so despite eating up a lot of physical channels, they're rarely all active at once.

check-out-how-these-two-chords-are-relat.title: Check out how these two chords are related! (chord substitution trick)
check-out-how-these-two-chords-are-relat.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A single-topic Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) deep-dive into the dominant-7/diminished-7 relationship, built as a from-scratch guitar-shape derivation rather than a soloing-vocabulary lesson. Jared derives the mechanism twice, in both directions: (1) take any voicing of a dominant 7th chord anywhere on the neck, raise the root a half step, and the shape you're left with is always a diminished-7 shape — demonstrated on four different physical voicings (root position, and three different inversions across the top-four-string, middle-four-string, and 6th-string-rooted voicing families) to prove it's a universal property of dominant-7 chords, not a one-off coincidence. He explains why every one of those raised shapes ends up identical: diminished-7 is a symmetric chord (built entirely of stacked minor 3rds), so it inverts to itself every three frets. (2) He then inverts the whole process: starting from a known diminished-7 voicing, lower any one of its four notes a half step and you get a voicing of dominant 7 — used explicitly as a voicing-discovery tool ("you're gonna find some voicings you may have never played before"), demonstrated by lowering each of the four notes of one diminished shape in turn to generate all four inversions of dominant 7 from a single known grip. The lesson's payoff is the practical conclusion: because a dominant 7 chord's diminished-shape-off-any-non-root-tone gives you a dominant 7♭9 sound (the diminished chord IS the dominant 7 with the root swapped for a ♭9), you can superimpose diminished-7 shapes over any dominant 7th chord to get instant, movable 7♭9 voicings — worked concretely on a live A7 → D minor progression, playing diminished shapes off the 3rd, 5th, and ♭7 of A7 and resolving into D minor. Confidence: high — clean, spoken theory lesson, transcribes cleanly (recovered from raw VTT after yt-transcript.cjs returned an empty transcript despite captionType: "captions" — known drop bug on this channel).

drop-chords-guitar-lesson-drop-2-drop-3-.title: Drop Chords Guitar Lesson - Drop 2 & Drop 3 voicings explained for guitarists
drop-chords-guitar-lesson-drop-2-drop-3-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared Borkowski demystifies "drop 2" and "drop 3" chord terminology for guitarists specifically — the labels come naturally from a piano/stacked-thirds view of a chord, but on guitar the derivation isn't obvious, so he works it fretboard-first: build a close-position seventh chord (all four notes stacked in thirds, spanning less than an octave), then derive drop 2 and drop 3 by physically dropping a specific chord tone — counted from the top down — an octave lower. He worked two build-from-scratch examples (Cmaj7 → drop 2, Gmaj7 → drop 3) and, more usefully, a general diagnostic trick: given any seventh-chord shape you already know (no construction history required), move its bottom note up an octave and count down from the new top note to find where the moved note lands — 2nd from the top means the original shape was a drop-2 voicing, 3rd from the top means drop-3. This is a companion/derivation video to the vault's existing Chord Voicings page, which already documents the drop-2/drop-3 family (string sets, "workhorse" framing) without showing the construction — this video is the missing "why it's called that" piece, worked slowly and concretely on the fretboard. Short (12:43), tightly focused, spoken clearly throughout — high transcript confidence once manually pulled (see Source).

neo-soul-chords-on-guitar-14-incredible-.title: Neo Soul Chords on Guitar - 14 incredible voicings for ONE chord!
neo-soul-chords-on-guitar-14-incredible-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A minor-chord sequel to an earlier video in the same series (7 voicings over E♭maj7, referenced directly but not yet a page in this vault). Jared plays through 14 distinct guitar voicings of a single chord — Cm7 — one at a time, naming every note in scale-degree terms as he goes, then plays the whole set through again as a small composed arrangement. The organizing idea, stated explicitly and repeatedly: only the ♭3 and ♭7 are non-negotiable — every other note (root, 5th) is fair game to swap out for a 9th or 11th when a voicing wants more color. Two voicings also carry embellishments (a slurred/trailed top note, a doubled-11-drop-♭3 hit) that Jared deliberately does not count toward the 14, on the grounds that they're ornaments layered on a fixed shape rather than new chord shapes — and he calls that slur/trail-on-top habit "a quintessential element of the neo-soul guitar sound." Jared's own working definition of "neo-soul," given directly in the video: rich, extended jazz chord voicings (the harmony) played in a groove/beat-based genre rather than swung jazz (lo-fi hip-hop, R&B), with those top-note ornaments as the genre-marking flavor on top. Ends with a plug for his "Any Jazz Chord" booklet (a shell-voicing-based method for accessing any jazz chord from as few as 8 shapes, two places on the neck) — noted here for context, not something to route anywhere since it's a paid resource outside the transcript's own content.

rootless-voicings-part-1-triads.title: Rootless Voicings - Part 1 - Triads
rootless-voicings-part-1-triads.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen's practical, non-theoretical take on rootless voicings: instead of deriving them from scratch, take chord shapes you already know, strip the root, and you're left with a triad — and that triad is what you actually practice, move around, and decorate. The whole lesson is one system built from a single 2-5-1 in C (Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7): drop the root from each of the three voicings and you get an F major triad (2nd inversion, for Dm7), a B diminished triad (root position, for G7), and an E minor triad (1st inversion, for Cmaj7). Larsen then shows the same triad shape covers every inversion of the underlying chord (root position, 1st inversion, 2nd inversion are all "the same trick" applied to different starting voicings), walks each triad diatonically through the C major scale as a fretboard-mapping drill, adds a melodic "suspend the top note" ornament that turns the exercise into a mini-melody generator, and closes with three worked example progressions (major 2-5-1 in C, minor 2-5-1 in A minor with harmonic-minor extensions ♭9/♭13 on the V, and a 3-6-2-5-1 in C). Deliberately framed as the practical companion to his earlier, more theoretical "Jazz Chord Essentials — Triads" lesson: this one assumes you already know some jazz voicings and shows what to actually do with them once you drop the root, rather than deriving triad-substitution theory from first principles. Directly overlaps with — and is a guitar-fingering-first companion to — the vault's existing Upper Structure Triads from Seventh Chords note (same 3-5-7-of-a-seventh-chord derivation, worked from a different starting angle: known voicing → strip root, rather than seventh-chord quality → triad-quality rule) and reinforces Chord Voicings's existing "rootless = 3rd+7th+extensions, root droppable" material with concrete drop-2/drop-3-derived fretboard shapes.

the-ultimate-practice-system-is-coming-t.title: The ultimate practice system is coming together (how I'm tracking progress)
the-ultimate-practice-system-is-coming-t.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared's (Sound Guitar Lessons) second "practice log" entry — the direct sequel to Practice Log #1, which first previewed this format and his practice categories. Where #1 was mostly meta (why the series exists), this one delivers the concrete payoff it promised: a real walkthrough of the spreadsheet he uses to both plan and track his guitar practice, plus his explicit philosophy on what to track and why. Framing detours: two book quotes on embracing difficulty in creative work (Creativity, Inc. by Ed Catmull; The War of Art by Steven Pressfield, "the Resistance"), a running poll on what to call the series (plog/slog/sound log), and answers to two viewer questions (Paulo, on feeling like he's not progressing despite tracking time; Brad, on whether the planning sheet is the same as the tracking record — yes). The core teaching, though, is precise and directly actionable: how he structures a milestone-tracking spreadsheet for arpeggio/scale vocabulary, and a hard philosophical stance against practice journaling in favor of milestone-gated tracking. This is the same underlying tracking mechanic later demonstrated in full for scales on The Scale Practice Method That Forces You to Really Know Your Fretboard — that video shows the drill live on guitar; this one shows the spreadsheet design and reasoning behind it, and applies the same mechanic to arpeggio/chord-tone vocabulary rather than scales.

1-ensemble-stack-track.title: 1 Ensemble Stack Track
1-ensemble-stack-track.html:
Role: The per-layer prep for a self-stacked vocal ensemble — the tune/align/band-limit/level work applied to each individual layer you record, whatever its role in the stack. There is no fixed take count: you build the ensemble from a menu of layer-roles (core, doubles, octave anchor, air, harmonies…) and add blocks as the section needs. The arrangement/roles and the glue live on Ensemble Stack Group; this note is what makes any single layer sit right.

This is distinct from Double Vocal Track (one lead + one double) and Backup Vocal Track (elements that answer the lead). A stack can be run two ways — decide per song (see the group note): a fused ensemble (no single lead, everything level-matched into one source — Bon Iver/Imogen Heap) or a lead + support stack (a front vocal with doubles/octaves/harmonies underneath — standard pop). The building blocks are the same; only the balance differs.

Chain philosophy: tune → align → band-limit → level-match (per layer) ▸ EQ → glue → saturate → de-ess → shared space (on the group). Unify per-layer, glue on the group. What fuses a stack is consistency of tuning, timing, and space — not per-layer processing. Keep the performance differences you tracked on purpose (a soft approach vs a full one, ahead vs behind, vowel shape), but lock pitch and time and match tone. In a fused ensemble, level-match ruthlessly so no layer becomes an accidental lead; in a lead+support stack, the support layers deliberately sit lower.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Same mic for every layer — Neumann TLM 102, shock mount, pop filter ~4" out, 48V on. One consistent source is half of what fuses a self-stack; don't swap mics between layers the way you would for contrast on backups.
  • Consistent distance and position per layer-role. Keep mic distance identical across a role (esp. whisper/air layers, which expose distance changes). Step back slightly and sing softer for gang/choir layers to keep peaks controlled.
  • Same room/latency discipline as Main Vocal Track §1 (phone silenced, HVAC off, track through the UAD Console to sidestep latency).

⑧ Dry/Wet Balance of the four voices vs. the original 30%+ for obvious width; the point of Doubler4 (vs 2) is more spread —

What it's used for

Rhythmic delay effects on vocals, synths, and drums within a modular chain.

Stacked in a Snap Heap chain, often paired with a filter snap-in to shape the repeats.

frank-ocean-vocal-chain.title: Frank Ocean Vocal Chain
frank-ocean-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: bone-dry, dead-center, breathing — the anti-Travis. Dynamics kept (whispers stay whispers, belts stay belts), pitch edited by hand not snapped, and the production interest comes from many differently-treated voice layers placed in 3D rather than effects on one voice. Garage-recorded intimacy with the confidence to be nearly naked. Signal source: Neumann TLM 102 close (3–5"), a real room but not a dead booth. Performance-first: comp for emotion, not accuracy — the best crack wins.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — clean, low gain
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 1–2 dB only (the dynamics ARE the record)
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — bypass or hair of 12 kHz

Chain overview

Hand-tune → light shape → gentle 2:1 → placement layers. Less chain than any other style note — restraint is the technique.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Manual pitch (Melodyne-style — his documented tool)

  • Hand-correct only the notes that distract; leave drift that carries feeling. No Auto-Tune Pro on the natural lane. (For the "Nikes" pitched voice: Little AlterBoy pitch +3–5 or formant-shifted, printed as its own track — a character, not a correction.)

2. Pro-Q 4 — Light shape

  • HPF 70–90 · small mud cut ~300 · presence untouched (closeness comes from the mic distance, not 4 kHz).

3. Pro-C 2 — Preserve

  • 2:1, slow attack, 1–3 dB on peaks only — the documented "let it breathe" setting. Automate clip-gain per phrase instead of compressing deeper.

4. Saturn 2 — Barely

  • Tape, mix ~15% — analog rounding, nothing audible.

Step 3 — Effects (placement, not wash)

  • Dry lead, dead center — often literally no reverb send. Space comes from other layers:
  • Harmony layers panned wide with different treatments each (one dark + roomy, one pitched-up + dry, one whispered + close) — the Blonde signature 3D stack
  • A distant double: same line re-sung soft, 2–3 ft off mic, tucked −12 dB (real depth beats reverb)
  • Delay Send Slap mono, low, for select phrases · Reverb Send Long only as an event on a single line, automated in and out.

partynextdoor-jazz-sample-chain.title: PARTYNEXTDOOR Jazz Sample Chain
partynextdoor-jazz-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch vintage jazzy R&B instrumental built to chase the mood of PARTYNEXTDOOR's "Joy" (off P3) — real jazz harmony (minor 9ths, minor 7ths, an inverted major 9th), an unusual 6/8 time signature identified by ear from the drums, and an arrangement built entirely by subtracting elements rather than adding new ones. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, how to make moody vintage r&b samples for partynextdoor (sounds like a real jazz sample). Companion build to Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain and Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain — same vintage-sample-flip lineage, jazz-forward voicings instead of soul/trap.

Chain overview

Five elements (piano, guitar, bass, brass, drums) build a single instrumental sample, then the whole thing gets bounced, pitched, and flipped as a second-pass demo. The two biggest reusable ideas: identify an odd time signature (6/8) by ear from the drums, not the melody, and arrange by subtraction across four 8-bar sections rather than writing new material per section — bass and guitar are toggled off/on and brass drops out for the final section, explicitly reasoned to leave room for whoever eventually flips the sample.

0. Time signature — set before writing anything

  • Identify 6/8 by ear from the drums: "Joy" counts in groups of three (one-two-three, one-two-three) rather than four — the tell for 6/8 over 4/4.
  • Owned-lane equivalent of the FL Studio numerator/denominator field: Ableton's time signature, set alongside tempo at the top of Arrangement/Session View (or per-clip in Session View).
  • 🎬 From video: the same chords in 6/8 vs. 4/4 read as a genuinely different bounce against a metronome click — 6/8 changes the feel, not just the count.
secs: 0. Time signature — set before writing anything

recording-techniques-with-al-schmitt.title: Recording techniques with Al Schmitt
recording-techniques-with-al-schmitt.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, dense Mix with the Masters two-part masterclass with the late Al Schmitt (26x Grammy-winning engineer — Sinatra, Steely Dan, Diana Krall, Ray Charles) walking through his actual tracking setups for upright bass and lead vocal, filmed live in session. Part one covers double-micing an upright bass (two Neumann M149s, one at the f-hole and one near the plucking hand) into a Neve preamp and a Summit tube compressor tapped for barely a dB — used purely for color, never for control — plus how his isolation strategy scales with the ensemble (tight and close for a jazz trio, a full iso booth for a big band). Part two covers his vocal chain, built around a Neumann U-47 (Sinatra/Nat Cole/Dean Martin's mic) into a Neve preamp with almost no compression, because the singer's own mic technique — leaning in and backing off — is already doing the compressor's job. The through-line across both halves is the same philosophy stated twice in different words: the mic and the room reveal a good performer's sound, they don't manufacture one. A boomy bass is a bass problem, not a mic-placement problem; a vocalist with real mic discipline needs almost no gain reduction. Schmitt also draws a clean line between problems worth chasing at the source (mic choice, distance, isolation) and problems he now just fixes afterward in Pro Tools (light sibilance, plosive pops) — a tape-era engineer explicitly naming what's changed for him in the DAW era.

singing-along-with-your-playing-phrasing.title: Singing Along With Your Playing (Phrasing)
singing-along-with-your-playing-phrasing.html:
Part of Music Theory — a practice method for developing phrasing, distinct from Blues Lead Phrasing and Touch (note-choice/touch vocabulary within a phrase) and Solo Dynamics and Arc (the macro shape of a whole solo). This note is about how to train the instinct that produces good phrasing in the first place, by literally singing/vocalizing along with your own improvising — a specific 4-step method, not a vague "sing more" suggestion.

The four elements that make phrasing sound good

Named directly as the target: any phrase that hits these four reads as strong phrasing, regardless of note choice.

  1. Strong, concrete rhythm — not ambiguous timing. The rhythmic shape has to be decisive, not smeared.
  2. Repetition — either purely rhythmic repetition, or pitch/note repetition (repeating the actual notes), or both.
  3. Ideas reacting to / building on what was just played — a phrase should sound like a response to the previous one, not a disconnected new idea.
  4. Conclusions — ideas need to actually resolve/finish, not just trail off or run out.

The claim (and the reason this method works): singing along with your own playing pushes all four of these automatically, because you physically can't sing the way you can shred — you have to breathe (forces pauses/space), you naturally gravitate to simpler/catchier material (forces repetition), and there's a felt desire to resolve a vocal phrase (forces conclusions). Cited as a documented habit of Keith Jarrett, Kurt Rosenwinkel, and Glenn Gould — all known for audibly singing/humming along while they play/improvise.
secs: The four elements that make phrasing sound good

phrasing-blueprints.title: Phrasing Blueprints
phrasing-blueprints.html:
Part of Music Theory — four fixed rhythmic/structural forms for practicing phrasing, distinct from Singing Along With Your Playing (Phrasing) (training the phrasing instinct directly, by vocalizing) and Solo Dynamics and Arc (the macro shape of a whole solo). This note is the first of the "three broad ways to work on phrasing" referenced but not yet detailed in Singing Along With Your Playing (Phrasing): deliberately choose a letter-form (A, A', B, C…), commit to it strictly for a fixed number of measures, and use the constraint to force yourself to react to what you just played instead of just moving on to a new idea. All four blueprints below share the same underlying skill — repeat, react, conclude — with a different amount of freedom in what "repeat" means (exact pitches, exact rhythm only, or a fixed measure-count/rest structure).

The core mechanic (applies to all four)

  • A = whatever you play first — you don't plan it. You're improvising; the constraint only kicks in after you've played the first idea, forcing you to react to your own material rather than to a pre-picked lick.
  • A' ("A-prime") = repeat A, change only the very last note (or few final notes) to strict-at-first. Loosen later — let the prime mean several different possible endings — but start with one changed note so the repeat is unmistakably a repeat.
  • Every blueprint below ends with a genuinely contrasting idea (B or C) that "wraps it up" — the whole point is finishing off complete ideas before switching things up, not trailing off.
  • Works over any scale, key, or vocabulary — demoed in A minor pentatonic and, for blueprint 3, plain major scale, explicitly to show the structure is genre/scale-agnostic (works equally well with blues bends, jazz vocabulary, or plain scale tones). Also usable as a songwriting-structure tool, not just an improv drill.
  • Practice a single idea can span 4, 8, or 16 bars depending on how long each lettered phrase runs.
secs: The core mechanic (applies to all four)

spectral-resonator.title: Spectral Resonator
spectral-resonator.html:
Category: Modulation Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock spectral resonator (Live 11 Suite) — resonates the incoming signal at a tunable frequency/note, with control over harmonic spacing (stretch/compress) and pitch-shifting, plus a MIDI input path so an external track's notes/chords can drive which pitches it resonates at.

What it's used for

A "robotic vocoder that isn't a vocoder" — tonal, resonant textures on vocals, samples, or full tracks; MIDI-driven harmonic/chordal coloring when fed notes from another track.

FX chain notes

Used as an insert/texture device on a vocal, sample, or lead layer; when MIDI-driven, needs a MIDI-from-track routing set up (source track + Poly mode) rather than sitting purely as an audio effect.

spectral-time.title: Spectral Time
spectral-time.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock spectral delay (Live 11 Suite) — splits the incoming signal into frequency bins and delays them independently rather than repeating the whole signal at once, with a built-in harmonic freezer alongside the delay section.

What it's used for

Turning a delay into a frequency-aware texture/transition tool — smeared "laser," watery, or metallic repeats distinct from Echo/EchoBoy's whole-signal echo, plus instant frozen-harmonic pads via its Freeze section.

FX chain notes

Inserted on a lead, pad, or vocal layer for a texture/transition effect rather than a rhythmic echo; often driven hard (Time + Dry/Wet maxed) so the spectral smear is the whole point rather than a subtle blend.

important-ear-training-exercise-for-guit.title: Important Ear Training Exercise for Guitarists (we need this!)
important-ear-training-exercise-for-guit.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

An older (2020-01-07), more foundational entry in Jared's ear-training material than Guitar Ear Training Essentials - The Missing Link for Guitarists and Amazing Guitar Ear Training Exercises (hearing & singing modes of the major scale) — this one opens with the why (guitarists specifically have underdeveloped ears because frets let you find notes by sight instead of by ear) before teaching two distinct exercises: an unstructured harmonic ear-training test (pick one note out of a strummed chord, by ear, and sing it back) and a structured, methodical interval-drilling system (two notes at a time, every interval type in order from half-step to octave, sung and verified with a 10-in-a-row streak gate). Where the sibling videos are about singing scale degrees/solfège against a known reference (melodic, tonal-context-first), this one is squarely harmonic ear training — pulling individual notes out of simultaneous sound, the skill Jared says guitar's fretted, look-don't-listen design actively suppresses relative to fretless/bowed instruments. Includes a good personal anecdote (a bar chord missing its supposed-to-be-there note, unnoticed until arpeggiated) that motivates why this matters beyond the abstract.

linndrum.title: LinnDrum
linndrum.html:
What it is

The LM-2, sold as "LinnDrum" — Roger Linn's cheaper ($2,995), more successful follow-up to the Linn LM-1 (~5,000 units). This is the drum machine you're hearing on a huge share of mid-80s radio pop: tight sampled kit, huge gated-reverb-friendly snare, crisp hats. If a track sounds like a neon jacket, it's probably a LinnDrum.

What makes the sound

  • 8-bit drum samples on EPROMs like the LM-1, but with real hi-hats and crash/ride added (hats even respond to a decay knob via VCA — a sampled hat with analog envelope control).
  • The snare is the star: fat, mid-forward, slightly crunchy — and it became the 80s gated reverb snare once producers slammed it through an AMS RMX16 or SSL talkback compression → the Synthwave playbook's snare recipe.
  • Tunable voices (clock-rate repitch) but tighter/cleaner overall than the LM-1 — less funk grit, more pop gloss.
  • Linn swing/quantize again — patterns sit perfectly, which is the "drum machine pop" feel of the era; the stiffness is the aesthetic.
  • Individual outputs per voice → per-drum console processing → that produced, layered 80s drum mix.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Drum Rack / Simpler with LinnDrum samples (the standard synthwave starting kit); RC-20 Retro Color for vintage sheen; gated-verb the snare with Ghz Megaverb 3 or ValhallaVintageVerb (NonLin mode) to complete the 80s move.
  • Paid: UVI Beat Box Anthology 2, Samples From Mars "Linn From Mars", Wave Alchemy Revolution.
  • Free: LinnDrum sample packs are ubiquitous — the whole machine is ~28 sounds.

Used on

  • a-ha — "Take On Me" (1985): LinnDrum pattern under the arpeggio, the canonical example.
  • Tears for Fears — "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" (1985): LinnDrum groove (with live overdubs), that shuffled 12/8 feel is Linn swing.
  • Hall & Oates — "Maneater" (1982) and the H2O era: LinnDrum as the pop-radio backbone.
  • Genre/era: mid-80s pop/synthpop/R&B wholesale; the entire modern synthwave revival (Synthwave) builds kits from LinnDrum samples.

paul-epworth-opens-up-the-session-for-ad.title: Paul Epworth opens up the session for Adele's "Rolling In The Deep"
paul-epworth-opens-up-the-session-for-ad.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short Mix with the Masters session walkthrough: Paul Epworth (writer/producer of Adele's "Rolling in the Deep," and separately its co-writer) opens his Pro Tools session for the final East Coast Studios recording and narrates, section by section, what got re-tracked versus kept from the original Logic demo. The throughline is a deliberate hybrid of demo and re-record — re-tracking drums, piano, and acoustic guitar for a better performance/sound while consciously preserving specific demo elements (the stomp/clap layer, the MIDI piano-bass part) that already worked, rather than treating "re-record" as an all-or-nothing decision. Three concrete techniques stand out as reusable beyond this one song: a physical second kick drum (a 28" marching band bass drum) set up in front of the main kit kick and damped with blankets for character, blended with a subtle sample-replacement layer via a Logic drum-replacement plug-in; a binaural head used twice for very different jobs — capturing the whole kit's stereo image, and later switching the acoustic guitar to a noticeably wider recording specifically at the pre-chorus as a structural width-automation move; and a clap reverb send with its pre-delay used as a groove tool, deliberately pushed to add "swing and timing" to the rhythm track rather than just space. A companion piano mic'ing habit (a pair of small-diaphragm condensers, "K86s," strapped directly to the piano's soundboard — attributed to Abbey Road) and an offhand, hedged mention of a hardware stereo bus compressor ("may well have been a 1178") round out the tracking-stage detail. This is a companion piece to Tom Elmhirst breaks down his mix of 'Rolling in the Deep' by Adele — Elmhirst's video covers the mix stage of the same record; this one covers the tracking stage that fed it. The captions cut off mid-sentence at the very end (Epworth mid-thought about the acoustic guitar performance) — everything captions provided is captured below.

3-bass-bus.title: 3 Bass Bus
3-bass-bus.html:
Role: Final pass on the low-end lane. Light — most bass work already happened at track/group.

Chain

1. Ghz Tupe 3 — Warmth

  • Tube 15% (① — very low drive) · Tilt neutral (②) · Mix 100% (④) · Output matched (⑤)
  • Why: one more coat of harmonics helps the whole low end translate; the bus is the right place because it catches whichever bass source is active.

2. Glue Compressor — Glue

  • Ratio 2:1 (②) · Attack 30 ms (③ — lets the note attack/pluck through before clamping) · Release 0.2 s (④ — or Auto) · Threshold for ~1.5 dB GR (①) · Range 6 dB (⑥) · Makeup to unity (⑤) · Dry/Wet 100% (⑦)
  • Why: Gentle 2:1 with a slow attack fuses whichever bass source is active without squashing the sub or dulling the transient — the bus glues, it doesn't level.

3. Utility — Mono guarantee

  • Bass Mono ~100 Hz — the final insurance under everything (harmless if the tracks already did it).
  • 🎬 From video: when a synth bass has lots of built-in chorus/sides, a touch of OTT before this (upward, "a push not a squash") tightens the mono low end so the SUB Slot reads punchy — Disclosure, Deeper.

Variations

  • If the bass lane feels over-compressed: bypass Glue here — three comps (track, group, bus) can be one too many; the track comp is the load-bearing one.

keyscape-la-custom-c7-grand.title: Keyscape — LA Custom C7 Grand
keyscape-la-custom-c7-grand.html:
Instrument: Keyscape · Slot: BED Slot · Used by: Acoustic Piano Track

What it's for

The flagship studio grand — the default pop/ballad centerpiece piano. Keyscape's duo patches (layering the C7 with a second instrument, e.g. a pad or second piano) are a fast route to instant hybrid color when a plain grand feels thin; browse those from the same patch list rather than building the layer by hand.

Settings

  • ⑥ LA Custom C7, main lid/mic position (not a "Cinematic" sub-variant — those are for ballad-specific darker/wider mixes, see Instrument Preset Map)
  • ⑧ Internal FX: reverb OFF always — space comes from the chain's sends, not the patch
  • ① Velocity curve: set once per controller, saved as default (fixes soft-playing response, not a per-song setting)
  • ⑤ Drive/EQ knob: touch only if the patch needs it — Keyscape's modeled tone stage responds like the real piano's action, so small moves go a long way
  • ④ Mechanical/pedal noise: default level for a pop mix; push it up only for an intimate ballad ("musician in the room" effect)

In context

  • Patch-switching beats EQ-rescuing — if the part wants brighter/warmer, change patch before reaching for EQ downstream.
  • Piano LH content can double as BASS-slot support in a sparse arrangement (per Sound Palette) — watch for masking against a bass instrument in that case.

keyscape-wing-upright-tack-piano.title: Keyscape — Wing Upright & Tack Piano
keyscape-wing-upright-tack-piano.html:
Instrument: Keyscape · Slot: BED Slot · Used by: Acoustic Piano Track

What it's for

Character/vintage piano — Wing Upright for an intimate, boxy, band-in-a-room sound; Wing Tack for the muted, percussive "tack piano" color (thumbtacks-on-hammers timbre). Reach for either when the C7 flagship grand (Keyscape — LA Custom C7 Grand) is too polished for the part.

Settings

  • ⑥ Patch: Wing Upright (warmer, boxier) or Wing Tack (brighter, more percussive/muted) — the two live in the same browse list, audition both
  • ⑧ Internal FX: reverb OFF always
  • ④ Mechanical/pedal noise: keep it audible on the Upright — the room/mechanism noise is part of the vintage character, don't gate it out
  • ① Velocity curve: standard per-controller default
  • ⑤ Drive/EQ knob: light touch on the Upright for extra grit if the part is exposed; leave the Tack patch untouched — its character is already baked into the sample

In context

  • Tack piano sits further toward MIDS in practice (percussive, less sustain) even though it's filed as a BED-slot piano — check against comping keys/plucks in the same section.
  • Swappable with a Kontakt felt-piano library for an even more intimate/lo-fi version of the same idea (library-dependent — no single settings recipe, browse and commit).

nexus.title: Nexus
nexus.html:
reFX's current Nexus UI (Nexus 5 shown).

Category: Instrument Vendor: reFX

What it is

reFX's rompler-style workstation synth built around a massive library of preset-based sounds spanning EDM, pop, and hip hop genres.

What it's used for

Fast access to production-ready synth, pad, and lead sounds across mainstream electronic and pop genres.

FX chain notes

Used as the instrument source, typically followed by EQ and light compression to fit presets into a mix.

Techniques

  • "Tippy top" sparkle layer — a bright Nexus patch as the last thin layer on a chorus stack; lesson learned when his Nexus install broke: print/bounce irreplaceable plugin layers to audio while they still load — Lophiile, Paradise breakdown

Used in my chains

A preset ROMpler (instrument source) — already-produced sounds, so it usually bypasses most of the track chain below it:

  • Acoustic Piano Track — instant pop "stacked piano" (produced/layered already) → Nexus — Stacked Pop Piano.
  • Synth Bed Track — instant produced pads (vs. Omnisphere/Wavetable where you build the motion yourself).

Key Parameters

image: Images/Nexus.png
coords: Images/Nexus.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

Mostly preset-driven; the editable layer is light on purpose:

# Parameter What it is / does Technique Artist / record example
① Preset / Library The loaded produced sound (the 90% decision) Pick the preset that's already finished — Nexus's value is not sound-designing —
② Filter (Cutoff / Res) Tone-shapes the preset Small cutoff moves to seat it; that's usually all the shaping needed —
③ Amp Envelope (A/D/S/R) Shapes level over the note Shorten release so produced pads don't wash into the next chord —
④ Insert FX Nexus's built-in effect slots (already baked into presets) Leave as the preset sets them — they're part of the "produced" sound —

adding-chords-to-single-note-lines.title: Adding Chords to Single-Note Lines
adding-chords-to-single-note-lines.html:
Part of Jazz Harmony and the guitar side of Chord Voicings — a structured method for punctuating an improvised single-note solo line with a chord voicing, so a solo line reads as harmonically self-supporting rather than bare. Distinct from Melodic-Harmonic Blending (Comping While Soloing): that page's method is a continuous, in-the-moment read of how much harmony a phrase needs, blending melody and chord into one texture; this page's method is narrower and more mechanical — chords land specifically at phrase endings / target notes, worked as a drill on a single static chord before it's ever applied to a moving progression. Treat this as the earlier-stage, more structured on-ramp; Melodic-Harmonic Blending is the more advanced, freer version of a related idea. Complements Chord-Tone Soloing (which drills outlining a moving progression) by drilling the opposite half — stopping the line and stating the harmony directly.

Why add chords to a solo line at all

Three distinct payoffs, all from the same move:

  • Clarifies vague/extension-heavy playing. A line built mostly from upper extensions can sound ambiguous against the underlying chord on its own; stacking the underlying chord tones under it (as a voicing) makes clear "this vague-sounding line really is meant to be heard against this chord," without changing the line itself.
  • Fills space between phrases. Whenever there's a break in an improvised line, a chord placed in the gap fills the silence and can add a sense of groove/rhythm — an alternative to just sustaining or resting.
  • Emphasizes a specific note. Adding a chord under one melody note makes that note louder simply because more notes are sounding at once — a way to make a note "stand out" without changing dynamics or technique.
secs: Why add chords to a solo line at all

how-to-start-learning-bass-self-taught.title: How to Start Learning Bass - Self Taught!
how-to-start-learning-bass-self-taught.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz practice-philosophy video, built as a comedy sketch (a self-serious, faux-biblical "bass ghost" narrator handing down "six commandments of self-teaching") wrapped around a genuinely concrete framework for structuring self-taught bass practice with no teacher to guide it. It opens with three escalating cautionary examples — a player stuck after a year, one who's "barely progressed beyond 6 months" after two years, and one who still can't play a single full song after 14 years — to establish the video's real thesis: the failure mode isn't lack of effort or lack of material, it's picking the wrong material with no way to check whether it's useful. The fix is a three-tier goal ladder (long-term destination, medium-term process commitment, short-term day-to-day material derived from the long-term goal) plus four coverage categories to check that derivation against — songs, technique, fretboard knowledge, and theory — closing with a quickfire list of chronic self-taught pitfalls and a final point that patience, not routine perfection, is the actual highest-leverage factor. It's a companion piece, in both content and structure, to BassBuzz's other beginner videos already in the vault (7 Days to Learning Bass Scales (Beginner Lesson), The PERFECT Bass Practice Morning Routine For Beginners, Bass Exercises for Beginners (Strength, Stamina, Flexibility, Control)) — this one is the organizing layer that explains why/when to reach for those, rather than another drill set itself. One soft course plug (BassBuzz's "Beginner to Badass") appears mid-video but is explicitly framed as optional — the DIY path is treated as fully viable throughout, which is the video's entire premise.

3-steps-to-killer-bass-fills-for-beginne.title: 3 Steps to Killer Bass Fills (for Beginners)
3-steps-to-killer-bass-fills-for-beginne.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Josh (BassBuzz) tackles the "epic bass fill" panic-moment beginners hit — the urge to play something impressive at the end of a phrase with no idea what notes to use — by breaking fill-writing into a repeatable three-step process: pick a rhythm, pick a shape, combine them. The pitch throughout is deliberately anti-theory: you don't need to know scale degrees or even whether a chord is major or minor to build a solid fill, because the rhythm alone carries most of the "this sounds intentional" weight ("even if the notes you play are garbage, if you sell the rhythm it'll still kind of work"). The video introduces two note-shapes for fills — the already-documented root-fifth-octave shape (works blind, major or minor) and a new-to-this-video three-note "triangle" shape that requires knowing the chord's quality but rewards it with a distinctly Motown-flavored, more melodic fill. Both shapes get worked live over play-along tracks, first over a straightforward G–Em–D progression and then over a minor-key Gm–E♭–Cm–Gm progression, so the same formula is demonstrated on both a major-ending and a minor-ending phrase. The most valuable structural idea, stated almost in passing at the very end, is that fill-writing is as much about restraint as vocabulary: "sometimes there will be a big glorious space in the music for your awesome bass fill, sometimes there might be another fill in the way" — knowing when NOT to fill is named as the next-level skill once the mechanics here are solid.

sparkle-texture-rack.title: Sparkle Texture Rack
sparkle-texture-rack.html:
Reference/vibe: a fully-wet, 6-stage "one or two knob pedal" built from stock/owned plugins to replicate the character of chased-after hardware guitar pedals (Chase Bliss Thermae, Hologram Microcosm, Chase Bliss Blooper, Cooper FX Arcades — pure name-drops in the source, no settings given) without the rarity/cost/learning-curve tax of hunting real hardware down. Built in FL Studio's Patcher (a routing/container plugin hosting a chain of other plugins with a custom macro-knob surface); the direct Ableton equivalent is an Audio Effect Rack with Macro knobs — see EffectRack for the same "save FX-rack chains as reusable sounds" lesson from a different video, and Randomized Rack Design for the general macro-mapping mechanics. Saved and named "Sparkle" in the source, then dragged onto a fresh 130 BPM perc loop on a new mixer track to prove instant recall.

Signal source: built from a mix of stock and owned tools plus two unowned Waves plugins swapped for owned equivalents below — nothing here blocks an owned-tools build.

  • Reverb/delay opening stage → owned lane: ValhallaDelay (Tape/BBD mode) or EchoBoy/Kramer Tape feeding Echo.
  • Pitch shift → source names "Waves SoundShifter" (unowned, Plugin Wishlist); owned lane kHs Pitch Shifter (±12 semitones covers the octave move).
  • Texture stage → Portal (owned).
  • Chorus stage → owned lane TAL-Chorus-LX or kHs Chorus (source plugin name garbled in captions, "Clever" — unconfirmed, medium confidence).
  • Half-time stage → Cableguys HalfTime (unowned, Plugin Wishlist) — already the established owned-adjacent gap for every other half-time chain on this vault (see Little AlterBoy, Phaser-Flanger).

align-delay.title: Align Delay
align-delay.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live utility device that delays a signal by a precise, adjustable amount (samples or ms) to correct phase/timing alignment between tracks.

What it's used for

Time-aligning mic'd sources (e.g. DI vs amp, close vs room mic) so they sum without phase cancellation.

FX chain notes

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

Techniques

  • Owned best-match for the Eventide Precision Time Align used to recreate analog tape flanging — automate the Delay parameter sweeping a couple of milliseconds back and forth around zero on a duplicate of the exact same audio. Tom Lord-Alge's modern recreation of classic half-inch tape varispeed flanging: duplicate a track to two identical copies, insert a delay-compensation plugin on one (he names the Eventide Precision Time Align specifically because it can push delay in either direction around zero, not just add positive delay), set it to zero delay, then automate the delay value sweeping by a couple of ms either side of zero — the flange "jet engine" sweep appears purely from that automated near-zero modulation between two otherwise-identical signals: "you just automate the movement — tape flange in a DAW, solved." This plugin's own Delay parameter (in ms, not samples) is the direct owned mechanism; the one gap is whether it can express negative/pre-delay the way the named unit does — check before relying on it for the exact pre/post-delay flip TLA demonstrates, and fall back to a send/return trick (advance one copy instead of delaying the other) if it can't. → Modulation, Automation, Tape Flanging Emulation, Plugin Wishlist — Mix with the Masters (Tom Lord-Alge), Tom Lord-Alge's secret mixing techniques

Used in my chains

Always slot 1 on a two-mic source — align before anything else, because every downstream move assumes a phase-coherent signal.

  • Acoustic Guitar Track — on the Shure SM57 body mic vs. the condenser: units = samples, ~13 to start, null-tuned per take.
  • Electric Guitar Amp Track — on the TLM track if spaced from the 57: samples, nudge until the low end is fullest.

Only needed when two mics capture one source; skip on DI-only / single-mic takes.

jazz-fusion.title: Jazz Fusion
jazz-fusion.html: What makes it the genre: jazz harmony and improvisation played with the instrumentation and production of a band record. The two things that separate it from straight jazz are contrast — sections that genuinely change character rather than one groove with solos over it — and realism, since most of it is now written into a DAW with virtual instruments and has to sound like humans in a room.

mvmeter2nogpu.title: mvMeter2nogpu
mvmeter2nogpu.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: TBProAudio

What it is

TBProAudio's loudness/true-peak metering plugin (non-GPU-accelerated build), offering LUFS and true-peak measurement to broadcast/streaming standards.

What it's used for

Loudness and true-peak metering during mixing and mastering to meet streaming platform targets.

FX chain notes

Used as an analysis-only tool, typically on the master bus.

Manual

  • 📄 Local PDF · Official manual

High-level points:

  • mvMeter2 isn't a true-peak/LUFS-only meter — it's several classic meter behaviors (VU, PPM, RMS, RMS+3dB, EBU R128) rebuilt in one plugin, each with correct ballistics for that standard (VU's slow analog swing vs. PPM's fast-attack/slow-release).
  • EBU R128 mode reads Momentary Loudness (ML) and Short-term Loudness (SL) — this is the actual loudness-standard mode, not a separate "LUFS meter" — reference level defaults to -23 dBFS (EBU spec).
  • Reference Level is mode-specific and matters more than it looks: VU's standard reference is -18 dBFS, so 0 VU ≠ 0 dBFS — miscalibrating this makes the needle lie.
  • Gain Match auto-sets Pre-Gain so the current Max reading lands on the mode's reference level — the fast way to calibrate a signal to a target loudness without doing mental dB math.
  • Dual meter mode (L/R or M/S side-by-side) is how to catch mono-incompatible content — a wide stereo source will show the two needles disagreeing.
  • The "nogpu" build in this vault exists for CPU-only rendering environments — functionally identical metering to the GPU build, just without hardware-accelerated graphics.

Used in my chains

A metering/reference tool (no audio processing, no settings to dial into a chain) — the 0 VU calibration reference for the meter-sandwich/gain-staging convention used across the FX Chain System. Drop it to check that each stage sits around 0 VU / −18 dBFS average before and after coloration devices; it doesn't change the sound.

10-hidden-soloing-mistakes-and-constrain.title: 10 Hidden Soloing Mistakes and Constraint-Based Fixes

session-layout.title: Session Layout
session-layout.html:
How Sound Palette's slots show up in an actual Live Set. Arrangement View workflow. Companion to Stereo Field (pan map per slot) and FX Chain System (what goes on each tier).

Group vs Return — the difference

  • Group track = a bus. The tracks' actual audio flows through it. Everything downstream of it hears it.
  • Return track = an effect. It receives a copy, dialed in with the send knob. The dry track still goes to its group.
  • Rule: families are Groups. Effects are Returns. A "Vocal Return" is a mistake — that's a Group.

The hierarchy

  1. Tracks — individual sources.
  2. Groups (by family) — Vocals · Drums · Bass · Keys/Synths · Guitars · FX/Risers.
  3. Buses (by family) — same six, one tier up. Only add this tier if a family actually needs it; most songs, the Group is the bus.
  4. Mix Bus — one Group holding all of the above.
  5. Master — the final 10% (Master Chain).

Returns sit off to the side, not in that chain: Reverb Room · Reverb Long · Delay Slap · Delay Other · Saturation · Width · Parallel Comp · Air/Shimmer. They feed the Mix Bus.

Buses go by family, not by frequency. Slots change every section (verse Rhodes → chorus pad), so they can't carry routing. Family never changes. Slots decide the sends — which return, how wet — not the wiring.

Track order — low to high, at both scales

Scanning down the Arrangement should always go low → high.

Group order, top to bottom:

  1. Drums
  2. Bass
  3. Keys / Synths
  4. Guitars
  5. Vocals
  6. FX / Texture

Within each group, same rule:

  • Drums → kick · snare · toms · hats (this is the ascending HPF ladder, in track order)
  • Keys → pad · Rhodes · comping clav
  • Guitars → open rhythm (BED) · muted riff (MIDS) · lead
  • Vocals → lead · doubles · harmonies · ad-libs

Why: two things sharing a slot end up as adjacent lanes instead of twenty rows apart.

1-electric-guitar-di-track.title: 1 Electric Guitar DI Track
1-electric-guitar-di-track.html:
Role: DI'd Fender Stratocaster — the flexible lane (re-ampable forever, no mic bleed, silent tracking). Two sub-lanes: amp-sim (Archetype does the amp's job) and no-amp-sim (preamp character in, EQ in the box — Kenny's current default).

Chain philosophy: amp sim → corrective EQ → color → tone → comp. Identical logic to Electric Guitar Amp Track once the "amp" exists — the sim replaces amp+mic+room, everything after treats it like a mic'd source.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Clean signal in > expensive guitar — "a really cheap guitar with a really, really clean signal — processing it and making it sound great doesn't even matter." Fresh-ish strings, tune BEFORE the effects, direct into the Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII Hi-Z input — Kenny Beats, How to Make a Guitar Sample.
  • Pedals-into-DI is a legit lane: comp pedal first (Dyna Comp-style squash, "very slept on") → dirt → straight into the preamp. Fuzz straight DI, no amp — a Big Muff-family fuzz (Big Muff Pi) direct into the preamp "sounds amazing" — Guitar Recording Process.
  • Latency: buffer ~128 while tracking; if monitoring through the sim in Ableton, arm a ghost latency track (Latency-Free Tracking).
  • Levels: peaks −12 dBFS, ~−18 average (Gain Staging).

2 — Tracking Best Practice

  • Record the clean DI even when monitoring through a sim — re-amp forever; no comp/EQ printed (the sim wants raw dynamics).
  • Stack immediately for width: same part twice, panned opposite (35–50 L/R), then a contrasting layer on a different patch/color — Kenny's guitar-sample move. Never copy-paste a take.
  • Treat the finished loop like a SAMPLE — pitch it, chop it, "f*** it up"; recording your own guitar loop = sample-flip freedom with zero clearance — How to Make a Guitar Sample → Sampling and Sound Selection. This is the comp-tool lane.
  • Mono per take; width comes from the stacked takes, not wideners.

hybrid-reverb.title: Hybrid Reverb
hybrid-reverb.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock reverb that blends two engines in one device: a Convolution side (loads any sample as a real impulse response) and an Algorithmic side (five distinct synthetic algorithms), crossfaded or blended together.

What it's used for

Everything from a straightforward vocal/pad space to using arbitrary samples (drum hits, whole loops, chord bounces) as impulse responses for tonal, rhythmic, or texture-driven reverb effects — well beyond a normal room/hall/plate reverb.

FX chain notes

Used as a send for shared space, or as a direct insert for sound-design moves (freezing, convolution-as-resynthesis, drop-FX creation) — several of the techniques below specifically want it inserted rather than sent.

spectral-blur.title: Spectral Blur
spectral-blur.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Ableton

What it is

A spectral smearing/freeze effect that ships free in Ableton's Creative Extensions pack (installed separately from the base Suite install, but free for Suite owners) — described by dnksaus as "half stock" for that reason. Functions like Spectral Time's Freeze section, but reads clearer/less smeared.

What it's used for

Turning a vocal or any sustained source into an instant ambient texture layer — freeze at any point and it keeps sustaining as its own atmospheric bed, distinct from Spectral Time's freeze in being noticeably cleaner/more defined.

FX chain notes

Used as an insert on a vocal or lead layer specifically to generate a frozen atmosphere bed; the frozen result can sit under the dry source as its own texture layer rather than replacing it.

Techniques

  • Freeze a vocal anywhere for an instant, clear atmosphere layer — similar in principle to Spectral Time's Freeze, but reads noticeably clearer; freeze at any point in a vocal take and it becomes a standalone atmospheric bed under the mix, still sustaining after the freeze is triggered. → Ambient Texture and Field Recording — dnksaus, The Underrated Spectral Stock Plugins in Ableton

disclosure-ultimatum-breakdown-breakbeat.title: Disclosure - Ultimatum Breakdown + Breakbeat
disclosure-ultimatum-breakdown-breakbeat.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

A 4-hr stream: a deep breakdown of "Ultimatum" (ENERGY's first single, ft. Fatoumata Diawara), then a casual Splice-breakbeat jam. This is the batch's richest mixing / mastering / gear reference: the definitive Disclosure master-bus procedure ("since Ultimatum"), a 500-series vocal-tracking chain, the Gem Dopamine "Dolby Trick," running a whole vocal (and drums/claps) through a vintage vocoder, 808 + pitch-envelope kicks, the comp→saturation transient-limiting order, and gain-staging by getting the drums to ~−8 dB. Whisper transcript (no captions) — high confidence; long, with chat asides.

slap-practice-this-daily-10-mins.title: Slap... Practice THIS Daily (10 Mins)
slap-practice-this-daily-10-mins.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's dedicated slap entry in the "Practice THIS Daily" format (companion to the general Practice THIS Daily (10 Min Technique Fix)): one single exercise, five progressive levels, forum-tested by BassBuzz students (the video opens on real students' day-one struggles and closes with a two-week follow-up on how they progressed). The pitch is explicit — don't skip ahead to cool-sounding slap riffs before the fundamentals are locked, or the playing will "sound super sketchy." Levels 1–4 are gated as noob-to-intermediate and meant to be mastered in order before level 5 (the advanced level, mentioned up front but the deep-dive content in this video tops out building toward it). Level 1 isolates the four ingredients of a clean slap (accuracy, muting, note length, rhythm) with no pops yet. Level 2 introduces the Teeter-Totter technique — a single continuous down/up forearm motion that gets both a slap and a pop out of one cycle, which is what actually enables speed (the two-motion "down-up-down-up" approach is explicitly shown as a speed dead-end). Level 3 adds ghost notes — muted, unfretted slaps/pops for texture and, more importantly, as a rhythmic anchor (the video draws a direct analogy to Marcus Miller's thumb bouncing on nearly every eighth note). Level 4 adds hammer-ons into the slap line via a simple "two-fret-below" rule that works without scale knowledge, plus the specific risk hammer-ons introduce (the fretting hand, not the plucking/slapping hand, now controls rhythm — a common source of rushing for players new to the technique). Level 5 addresses why disco-octave slap lines stop being satisfying once the basics are down, and gives a concrete fix (mixing in close-together, non-jumpy "singable" notes) grounded in why melody perception ties to the human vocal range. Dense, exercise-first, and squarely aimed at giving Nate one repeatable daily slap drill rather than a grab-bag of riffs.

big-muff-pi.title: Big Muff Pi
big-muff-pi.html:
Category: Pedal (fuzz/distortion) Vendor: Electro-Harmonix Ballpark value (used, 2026): $60–90

What it is

EHX's legendary four-stage fuzz — huge sustain, scooped mids, violin-like saturation. Three knobs: Volume, Tone, Sustain.

What it's used for

Wall-of-fuzz rhythm and singing lead sustain; the shoegaze/psych/grunge food group (Psych-Pop (Tame Impala) adjacency).

Signal chain notes

After Wah Pedal, before Line 6 DL4; the mid-scoop can vanish in a band mix — stack the Boss DS-2 or push amp mids to compensate.

🎬 From video: a second source's board runs a fuzz before the overdrive rather than after — "oftentimes I'll stack it just in front of my overdrive sound" (a Yard Box fuzz into a King of Tone overdrive) — the same fuzz+dirt stacking family as this pedal stacked with Boss DS-2, just reversed order. Worth A/B'ing fuzz-first vs. fuzz-second rather than assuming one fixed sequence. — Jack Ruch, My Home Recording Setup for Guitar

boss-ds-2.title: Boss DS-2
boss-ds-2.html:
Category: Pedal (distortion) Vendor: Boss Ballpark value (used, 2026): $60–90

What it is

Boss's Turbo Distortion — the DS-1 lineage with a second "Turbo" mode adding mid-boosted, thicker gain; remote-switchable between modes.

What it's used for

Tighter, mid-forward distortion that cuts where the Big Muff Pi scoops; grunge/garage rhythm and solo boost (Turbo II).

Signal chain notes

After Wah Pedal; Turbo I = DS-1-ish rhythm, Turbo II = fat lead. Famously a Kurt Cobain staple (In Utero era) and John Frusciante's long-time drive.

🎬 From video: a boost-into-overdrive stacking order worth trying ahead of this pedal — a low-gain clean-boost stage (Roger Mayer Voodoo 1: "I set it kind of like a boost. It adds a little bit of hair... it honestly in a track still kind of reads as clean") feeding a more obvious overdrive: "you get more of that low-end body from the [boost] and... a little bit of extra push of that boost going into the [overdrive]" — extra push and low-end body, not just more gain. Maps onto this pedal's own "more obvious"/mid-forward dirt role, same Big Muff Pi-adjacent "cuts where the Muff scoops" lane. — Jack Ruch, My Home Recording Setup for Guitar

🎬 From video: a concrete volume-dial-in method for any dirt pedal with its own volume/level control, including this one — set gain to taste, but push the pedal's own volume higher than feels necessary solo, to compensate for the perceived volume loss caused by the pedal's own compression. Demoed on a two-in-one overdrive+clean-boost pedal (Analog Man King of Tone / an Apollo Approved "Vertical"-style pedal): "it might sound loud when you're playing by yourself, but as soon as a band comes in and drums and cymbals, you're going to notice that perceived volume loss with the compression of an overdrive." Also: overdrive's main job isn't just grit — it adds compression (sustain, "squishier" feel) and typically cuts some high end, taming a bright clean guitar/amp combo, which is worth remembering when A/B'ing this pedal against a cleaner rhythm tone. Set the pedal's own volume slightly louder than clean rhythm volume, then re-check in a full-band context, not alone. → Electric Guitar Amp Track — Jack Ruch, Dial In Your Amps and Pedals for Great Clean and Overdriven TONES!

dorian-from-the-minor-pentatonic-box.title: Dorian from the Minor Pentatonic Box
dorian-from-the-minor-pentatonic-box.html:
Part of Guitar Positions and Diatonic Modes. The core idea: don't learn Dorian as a new seven-note shape — start from the minor pentatonic box you already know and add exactly two notes (the 2 and the major 6th) onto it. Two fingerings are given below: the classic box shape (fixed low-string position) and a movable "diagonal" shape that copy-pastes to any root/string-set. Both worked in D minor (D Dorian).

The two notes that turn minor pentatonic into Dorian

D minor pentatonic is D (1) F (♭3) G (4) A (5) C (♭7) — no 2, no 6. Dorian adds:

  • The 2 (E natural) — an easy, safe color note; "you can land on it almost any time and it's going to sound great."
  • The major 6 (B natural) — the note that actually defines Dorian. This is "the sound of Dorian" and the single highest-value target once you're past plain pentatonic soloing. → the character difference vs. Aeolian (natural minor, which has ♭6 instead) comes entirely from this one note — demonstrated as a direct A/B in NO ONE is teaching Dorian LIKE THIS! (Daniel Seriff).

Optional stopping point: the hexatonic scale. Pentatonic + just the 2 (six notes total, no 6th) is a legitimate, complete-in-itself sound some players lean on rather than pushing to the full seven-note mode — cited players: Derek Trucks, Jimmy Herring. Useful permission to think of "add the 2" and "add the 6" as two separable steps, not an all-or-nothing jump to the full mode.

Fingering 1 — the classic box (fixed position)

Built on the familiar D minor pentatonic box (root at the 10th fret, low E string):

  • Add the 2 (E) at three spots around the box: 12th fret, low E string · 12th fret, high E string · 9th fret, G string.
  • Add the major 6 (B) at: 12th fret, B string · 9th fret, D string.
  • Practice habit: center your improv on the plain D minor pentatonic first; don't reach for the 2 or the 6 right away — save them for later in the phrase so they read as deliberate color choices, not just extra notes. Demoed over a D minor 7 → G7, ~80 BPM funky backing track.
secs: The two notes that turn minor pentatonic into Dorian

lfo.title: LFO
lfo.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

Ableton's official Max for Live modulation device — a flexible LFO that can target almost any device parameter via Live's mapping system.

What it's used for

Adding rhythmic or free-running modulation to filter cutoffs, volume, pan, or nearly any mapped parameter.

FX chain notes

Inserted on the track/device chain and mapped to a target parameter; a foundational Live modulation building block.

expression-control.title: Expression Control
expression-control.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live MIDI utility for managing MPE/expression data (pressure, timbre, pitch-bend) routing between controller and instrument.

What it's used for

Fine-tuning MPE controller expression mapping into synths that support per-note modulation.

FX chain notes

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

shaper.title: Shaper
shaper.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Max for Live

What it is

A Max for Live modulation device that generates a drawn/custom modulation shape to control mapped parameters over time.

What it's used for

Custom modulation curves for parameters that need a shape LFO/step modulators can't produce.

FX chain notes

Runs inline in the signal/MIDI chain at the point it's inserted; combines with whatever device follows.

looper.title: Looper
looper.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock live-looping/overdub device — records incoming audio into a buffer that plays back in a continuous loop, with overdubbing, speed (including reverse and octave-shift), and feedback-decay controls, plus the ability to insert other devices directly into its own feedback path.

What it's used for

Usually framed as a live-performance/beat-jamming tool, but equally useful as a sound-design engine — layering overdubs while continuously varying speed, direction, and decay builds evolving ambient beds and glitch textures that are hard to get any other way.

FX chain notes

Runs inline on a track; audio routed to its own track with output set to Insert Looper (instead of Post Mixer) feeds back into Looper's own buffer rather than the main mix — anything on that insert track processes and re-processes the looped content every pass.

if-your-blues-solos-feel-stale-try-this.title: If Your Blues Solos Feel Stale, Try This!
if-your-blues-solos-feel-stale-try-this.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch teaches how to break a stale blues solo out of its box by inserting a jazz-style ii–V–I (2-5-1) at the point in a 12-bar blues where the I chord resolves to the IV chord (bar 4 of the form). Worked entirely in the key of G, targeting C (the IV chord) as the "1" of a Dm7 → G7 → C insertion — the same major ii-V-I shape as The ii-V-I's own worked example, applied specifically to the blues's I→IV pivot. Ruch is explicit that this substitution is a soloist's private reharmonization: it works "even if the rhythm section isn't playing this harmony underneath" — you can hear/imply the Dm7-G7-C motion in your line while the band just holds the plain blues changes. Four increasingly decorated example lines are built from the same chord-tone/arpeggio foundation, the last one lifted from a Joe Pass line (from the tune "Bluesology," originally in F, transposed up to G here). Reference listening named directly: T-Bone Walker, early B.B. King (Live at the Regal), Ray Charles for how this vocabulary sits inside "jump blues" and swing-blues playing without taking it out of style, plus Joe Pass and Wes Montgomery for the jazzier end of the same vocabulary. Full tab/notation is gated behind Ruch's Patreon — no tab data survives in the transcript, only spoken note names/degrees, so the fingering/position detail below is reconstructed from those verbal descriptions.

10-songs-that-taught-me-punk-easy-to-eff.title: 10 Songs That Taught Me Punk (Easy to Effin’ Hard)
10-songs-that-taught-me-punk-easy-to-eff.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

BassBuzz's Josh runs a personal, chronological "how I learned punk bass" countdown — ten songs ordered easy-to-brutally-hard, each one picked because it taught him a specific real skill, not because it's a generic genre landmark. The throughline is explicitly anti-dogmatic: punk bass is framed repeatedly as "no rules" — weird note choices that ignore scale theory, fingerstyle tone that's "wrong for the style" on purpose, chords played where a bassist "shouldn't," a singer who (per the video) just noodled a riff until it sounded right instead of consulting a mode chart. Difficulty escalates from The Ramones' three-note-but-blazing-fast simplicity up to Matt Freeman's (Rancid) borderline-unplayable "Maxwell Murder" solo, which Josh visibly struggles through live on camera at the end — an unusually candid "I'm not sure I can do this" moment for the channel. Each song contributes one concrete, transferable technique (hammer-ons/pull-offs, pick-vs-fingers tone, bass chords, melodic walking-quarter-note fills, blues-derived fills) rather than a full tab — this is a highlights/commentary video, not a note-for-note tutorial, so no song gets a complete chart. Confidence flag: the caption track carries no on-screen text overlays, so several song titles are inferred from context (release year, album, "recorded near where I grew up") rather than stated aloud — flagged individually below wherever inferred rather than confirmed.
