10-songs-that-taught-me-slap-easy-to-eff.title: 10 Songs That Taught Me SLAP (Easy to Effin’ Hard)
10-songs-that-taught-me-slap-easy-to-eff.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

The slap-specific entry in BassBuzz's "10 Songs That Taught Me [style]" series (sibling to the vault's already-enriched 10 Songs That Taught Me Punk (Easy to Effin’ Hard) and 10 Songs That Taught Me Metal (Easy to Effin’ Hard)) — Josh runs a personal, chronological countdown of the ten songs that actually built his slap technique, ordered easy-to-brutally-hard, each contributing one specific "aha moment" rather than a full note-for-note tutorial. Unlike the punk/metal entries, which are mostly mindset/arrangement commentary, this video is dense with transferable slap-hand mechanics — it's effectively a second, song-anchored curriculum for the same skill BassBuzz's dedicated exercise videos (Slap... Practice THIS Daily (10 Mins), Fix Your Slap in 5 Minutes) already teach in isolation, but here each technique is tied to a specific bassist, riff, and "why it clicked" story: Flea's 12/8 triplet feel, Les Claypool's thumb-hammer pattern for melody, Larry Graham's whole-song dynamic contrast, Louis Johnson's hit-harder tone control, Nate Phillips's slap-to-fingers switching, Marcus Miller's ensemble restraint, Mark King's start-slow speed advice, a Squarepusher speed benchmark, and Victor Wooten's thumb-hammer-pluck technique from "Classical Thump." The throughline across all ten: slap isn't just a hand-speed technique, it's a vocabulary of contrast (space vs. density, soft vs. hard, fingers vs. slap, restraint vs. showcase) that has to be arranged across a song, not just executed cleanly in isolation. Confidence note: this is a commentary/highlights video — Josh plays snippets of each song and narrates the lesson, but doesn't teach a full note-for-note tab for any of them, so no complete chart exists for any of the ten songs here (same call as the punk/metal siblings). Manual/auto captions transcribed cleanly (spoken narration throughout, no on-screen text overlays for song titles) — a few song titles below are inferred from context (album year, artist named, or a distinctive detail) rather than stated aloud, flagged individually.

writing-for-voice.title: Writing for Voice
writing-for-voice.html:
Part of Music Theory. Setting words to music — distinct from Vocal Harmony, which is about choosing intervals for harmony parts; this page is about fitting a melody to lyric text in the first place.

Scansion

Scansion = identifying accented vs. unaccented syllables in the text before writing melody. It's usually easier to write words first, then set them to music — but some great songs came from music and lyrics together, or even music first, so don't treat the order as a hard rule.

  • Long notes and downbeats are for accented syllables.
  • A rhythm that matches scansion exactly can still feel dull — adding rhythmic variety (an unaccented syllable landing on a long note, a rest for a breath — singers love to breathe) keeps it interesting without breaking the underlying scansion.

Melody

  • Good vocal melodies are predominantly stepwise, with occasional leaps — especially leaping into an accented syllable.
  • The range and shape of the melody should reflect the tone of the text.

Notation specifics for vocal parts

  • Dynamics go ABOVE the staff for vocal parts (opposite of instrumental convention, where they go below) — keeps them clear of the lyrics.
  • Melisma — a single syllable sung over more than one note, shown with a slur.
  • Word extension line — when a melisma's last syllable falls on a long held note, extend it with a line so the syllable's duration is clear.
  • Separate syllables within a word using a single centered hyphen.
  • Don't draw barlines between staves on vocal parts — makes the lyrics harder to read.

Accompaniment

  • Give the vocal part room to breathe — if the melody goes high, have the accompaniment go low.
  • Avoid doubling the vocal line outright in the accompaniment — move in parallel 3rds or 6ths, or in counterpoint, instead.
  • Add accompaniment motion during the voice's long notes or rests — keeps momentum going when the voice is holding still.

mpe-piano-roll-tools.title: MPE Piano Roll Tools
mpe-piano-roll-tools.html:
Live's piano roll has an MPE tab (per-note expression lanes — Pitch Bend, Slide, Pressure) that lets you shape an individual note's pitch/timbre independently even while other notes are sounding at the same time — true polyphonic per-note control, not one shared pitch-bend lane for the whole clip. Live 12.1 added two "mini tools" inside that tab that generate per-note MPE data automatically instead of hand-drawing every note's curve: Glissando (auto pitch-glide between chord voicings) and the MPE LFO (an auto-generating per-note modulator). Companion to Expression Control (the Max for Live device that does per-note randomization on mapped Ableton parameters more generally) and Ableton Extensions and MIDI Tools (the broader productivity-shortcut family).

Glissando — auto pitch-glide between chord voicings

  • Connects matching notes across a chord progression — e.g. the top note of each chord automatically pitch-glides into the top note of the next chord. If the chord voicings have different note counts from one chord to the next, Glissando shows which note in the next chord each current note connects to.
  • Timing and slope are both adjustable — control when the glide starts relative to the chord change and how curved (vs. linear) the glide is.
  • Use for voice-leading tension between chords — a fast way to add glide/tension into a chord progression's top line without manually drawing pitch-bend on every note. → Chord
secs: Glissando — auto pitch-glide between chord voicings

ableton-extensions-and-midi-tools.title: Ableton Extensions and MIDI Tools
ableton-extensions-and-midi-tools.html: Live's Extensions ecosystem (the extensions-SDK add-ons, distinct from stock devices and third-party plugins) collapses several manual production steps — programming a drum fill, re-voicing a chord, chopping a vocal, designing a glitch transition — into a few clicks, while still leaving room for manual override so the result doesn't sound generic. Reach for these when you want fast idea generation or drop/transition material without leaving Live for a dedicated MIDI-generation or glitch plugin. See also MPE Piano Roll Tools for the native piano-roll (not Extensions-menu) auto-generating per-note tools added in Live 12.1.

random.title: Random
random.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock MIDI effect that randomly transposes incoming notes by a defined interval — a Chance-of-being-applied device with an Interval amount and a Sign (Add/Sub) direction, distinct from Expression Control's Random mode (a continuous random modulation source) and from dnksaus's own "Random Generator" macro-randomizer utility rack (see Randomized Rack Design).

What it's used for

Adding occasional octave (or other interval) jumps to a melodic line at random, rather than a fixed, predictable transposition on every note.

FX chain notes

Sits in a MIDI chain after the main note-generating devices (arpeggiator, chord rack) so it randomly re-transposes the notes those devices already produced.

Techniques

  • Chained after Arpeggiator, feeding a Scale device, for a generative-but-in-key melody — placed directly after Arpeggiator (Rate Mode = Free), Random re-transposes each arpeggiated hit; a Scale device chained after that quantizes the randomized result back into a chosen scale/set of pitches — turns a fixed arpeggio into a self-generating melodic line for tonal/harmonic instruments, distinct from the octave-jump use below (interval/direction on a normal melodic line rather than a generative arp chain). → Arpeggiator, Scale, Melody Writing — asd, EXPONENTIAL RHYTHMS [1/5] Free Rate Arpeggiator
  • Occasional random octave jumps — set Interval to 12 (an octave) and Sign to Add so some notes get randomly bumped up an octave (flip Sign to Sub for random octave-downs instead) — a lighter-touch, note-level alternative to fully re-randomizing pitch, good for adding unpredictable accents to an otherwise-generated melody line. → Randomized Rack Design — dnksaus, generating music using our BRAINS (+ controlled randomness)

mixing-guitars-bass-andrew-scheps.title: Mixing Guitars & Bass - Andrew Scheps
mixing-guitars-bass-andrew-scheps.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Andrew Scheps walks a guitar-and-bass mix pass built entirely around a deliberately small plugin toolkit used the same way every time, favoring speed and familiarity over hunting: EQ Three for surgical cuts, a Helios-style channel EQ for musical/character moves (and previously an API 550/560 chain before that), applied both per-track and again as a single overall guitar-bus EQ instead of duplicating the same move twelve times. Two concrete moves stand out — using a Helios-style EQ's low-frequency circuit-switch resonance (60 Hz / 120 Hz) as a "bump" even with no boost dialed in, and finding bass presence in the 700 Hz–1 kHz range rather than reaching for the low end that was already out of control.

smooth-r-b-6-8-chain.title: Smooth R&B 6-8 Chain
smooth-r-b-6-8-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch "smooth/sexy R&B in 6/8" beat build, reverse-engineered from loner's own breakdown, making a smooth/sexy rnb beat in 6/8 time signature. Not a specific record recreation — the target is a genre/feel (name-checked as "Kehlani/Ty Dolla $ign"-adjacent) built around a single structural lever: the whole project runs in 6/8 instead of 4/4, which reshapes the chords, the drum programming, and the guitar's processing depth. The guitar chain here (9 stages) is the deepest single processing chain logged from this channel to date — most of the "reusable" value in this chain lives in that ordered device list.

Chain overview

Kontakt guitar (4-chord harmonic-minor progression) carries the harmonic/melodic weight through a 9-stage FX chain. A simple root-following bass gets one widening move. Piano thickens the bed. Kontakt Session Horns and Spitfire Studio Strings (demo) are reserved for the hook only — the verse runs on guitar + bass alone to leave room for a vocalist. Drums are the other half of the "6/8-ness": same physical snare placement as a 4/4 beat, reinterpreted entirely by counting in 3s instead of 4s.

1. Foundation — project time signature

  • Options → Project → General Settings → Signature → 6/8 (3/4 named as the alternative). Set BEFORE writing any parts — every subsequent chord/drum decision is built around counting in 3s. → Rhythm and Groove

little-plate.title: Little Plate
little-plate.html:
Category: Reverb/Delay Vendor: Soundtoys

What it is

Soundtoys' simplified plate reverb emulation, offering classic plate-reverb tone with a reduced control set.

What it's used for

Quick, classic plate reverb character on vocals and drums.

FX chain notes

Used on a send/return for a vintage-style reverb tail.

2000s-r-b-piano-sample-chain.title: 2000s R&B Piano Sample Chain
2000s-r-b-piano-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch sample deliberately styled on the 2000s R&B era — reference tracks named on-screen are Ne-Yo's "So Sick" and T-Pain/Chris Brown's "Best Love Song" — then flipped into a modern-day R&B trap beat aimed at a Tory Lanez/Bryson Tiller lane. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, how to make a 2000's r&b sample & flip it into a beat for tory lanez/bryson tiller. Distinct from Tory Lanez Underwater Synth Chain (a minimal two-melodic-element build) and Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain (heavily vintage/worn processing) — this chain's defining move is restraint: because the 2000s reference material "isn't too vintage," no tape/wear stage is added anywhere, keeping the piano and vocal comparatively clean while still reading as period-appropriate.

Chain overview

Four melodic sources stack around a piano bed (piano, counter-melody, chopped string loop, second string layer for a vocal-free section), plus a full lead-and-harmony vocal — then the whole finished sample gets a 3-stage lo-fi push (EQ → reverb → stretch/tempo-drop) before a compact drum pattern (snap, rim shot, hi-hat roll, switch-up bass) turns it into a beat. The reusable core idea: genre-appropriate restraint is itself a production decision — skip the default aging/vintage stage when the reference material doesn't call for it — paired with a simple, repeatable "flip a finished sample" recipe (EQ → reverb → stretch) that works on the whole sample rather than per-layer.

1. Piano — Kontakt "Gentleman"

  • Instrument: Kontakt's "Gentleman" patch — "super clean, super simple." → Kontakt 7
  • Chords: built entirely from the A minor scale (all white keys) — "a great way to instantly get a more melodic sound" without hunting for voicings by ear. → Melody Writing, Chord Progressions
  • Voicing detail: top-line notes double as both the part's bounce AND its melody.
  • Chain: Compressor ("tighten the sound up, make it super together") → small room plate reverb (Little Plate) → Pro-Q 3 (low-end cut + a Make Dynamic threshold-gated carve — "almost like compression").
  • Deliberately no tape/vintage stage — "these types of songs often have really clean sounds... not too vintage." → Sampling and Sound Selection
  • 🎬 From video: try a single diatonic scale (all-white-keys) as a shortcut to guaranteed-melodic chords before reaching for more complex voicings. → Melody Writing

soulful-sample-stacking-chain.title: Soulful Sample Stacking Chain
soulful-sample-stacking-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a Rhodes-led "soulful sample" built in two clean stages — first a six-element instrumental bed (electric piano, bass, two synth textures, an accent synth, a second piano), each processed with its own small effects chain that leans on spring reverb as the vintage-color constant across every layer; then a "sample stacking" finishing pass that reaches for outside Splice samples (a perc loop, strings, a "wire guitar," brass) layered on top of the finished bed for accents/melodies/textures the bed itself can't easily produce. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, use this easy technique to take your samples to the next level!? (making a soulful sample). The reusable idea distinguishing this chain from Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain and Afro Sample Chain: sample stacking as a named, deliberate workflow — don't force every element from a VST when a real recorded performance (violin, guitar, brass) is one Splice search away; source it, then shape it around what you've already written rather than composing and processing it yourself.

Chain overview

Ten elements total: six written/programmed (electric piano, bass, two synth textures, an accent synth, a second piano), then four sample-stacked on top (a perc loop, a strings sample, a guitar sample, a brass sample). The bed elements share a consistent processing language — spring reverb + a compressor + EQ + delay, at varying intensities per element's role (sustained chord bed vs. single-note accent) — while the stacked samples share a consistent SOURCING language (Splice search → chop → reverse where useful → confirm key → time-stretch → shape with reverb/EQ/delay to sit in the mix, usually pushed toward mono for its own pocket).

the-ultimate-jazz-chord-guide-12-most-im.title: The Ultimate Jazz Chord Guide - 12 Most Important Voicing Types
the-ultimate-jazz-chord-guide-12-most-im.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jens Larsen's systematic walk through 12 jazz chord voicing families, organized around one core idea: almost every voicing type in the video is built by adding or removing a single note from a shell voicing (root-3rd-7th), so the twelve types aren't twelve things to memorize independently — they're one thing (the shell) plus a small set of add/remove/drop operations. This exact video is the source article already cited in Chord Voicings (jenslarsen.nl/the-ultimate-jazz-chord-guide-12-most-important-voicing-types) — that page's "named voicing families" table and its shell/drop-2/drop-3/rootless/quartal framing come directly from this content, so most of the theory here is already in the vault. This page exists as the master record and fills in the construction sequence Larsen teaches (which type leads to which) more explicitly than the reference table does.

root-to-root-scale-form-mapping-method.title: Root-to-Root Scale-Form Mapping Method
root-to-root-scale-form-mapping-method.html: Part of Guitar Positions. Jared Borkowski's (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared) standard method for internalizing any scale's five positional shapes across the neck — he states he applies this identical method to every scale type in his channel's ongoing position-mapping series (major scale, natural minor, pentatonic, blues scales, harmonic minor, and an announced upcoming melodic minor entry), so this page is the reusable method extracted once rather than re-documented per scale. Distinct system from this vault's own fret-span Position 01–12 pages — Jared's "five scale forms/positions" are five shapes anchored to a scale's own recurring root pattern (loosely related to, but not identified by him as, the CAGED system — see caveat below), not the vault's 12 fixed fret-span zones; also distinct from CAGE System Scale Shapes's five chord-shape-anchored positions (C-A-G-E-D grips). Three different position-numbering conventions can all describe the same stretch of fretboard — check which system a given note/video is using before cross-referencing.

make-your-rhythm-guitar-sound-like-a-rec.title: Make Your Rhythm Guitar Sound Like A Record
make-your-rhythm-guitar-sound-like-a-rec.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch's third note in this vault (29 videos) — despite the title reading like a mixing/production breakdown, this is an arranging lesson, not a signal-chain one: no gear, mics, or plugins are discussed at all. Over a simple four-chord backing track (A major–E major–F♯ minor–D major, a I–V–vi–IV progression in A), Ruch builds up three separate rhythm-guitar parts layered on top of each other, and the whole video is a demonstration of how a small set of closed-position triad shapes on three adjacent strings — reused across a handful of neck positions and string groupings — generates all three parts without ever needing a different chord vocabulary. The throughline connecting this to Triads as a Fretboard Map (Ruch's other triad-zone video already in the vault): both lessons treat triad shapes as a small, memorizable set of physical "landmarks" that get relocated around the neck for different purposes — soloing there, multi-part comping/arranging here. The most transferable idea for a home recordist layering guitar parts: each layer gets deliberately separated by pickup selection and effect, not by writing genuinely different material — same triads, different tone, so the parts sit in their own space when stacked rather than needing separation to be built afterward in the mix.

guitar-nail-care.title: Guitar Nail Care
guitar-nail-care.html:
Maintenance for players who use their right-hand nails for tone — classical/nylon-string and fingerstyle playing — where a cracked or chipped nail mid-project is a real problem, not just cosmetic.

Fixing a chip or crack without wrecking the nail

  • Daily use is what prevents chips in the first place. Since starting a strict daily-practice rebuild at the beginning of the year, Jared reports zero nail issues — the mechanism, per him, is simply playing (and polishing) every single day rather than intermittently; he keeps both a classical and an electric guitar within reach so both hands stay in daily use, and consistent wear avoids the small imperfections that build up when nails go days between sessions. Superglue-the-dead-part remains the fallback for when a chip does happen. — Jared, How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop)
  • Superglue only the dead part, never the flesh. The white free edge of the nail is dead tissue; only glue that part — never let glue touch the live nail bed/cuticle underneath, which is the actual health risk people warn about with nail products. — Jared, Practice Log #1
  • Only works on a partial crack. The technique only holds a chip/split that hasn't fully broken off — a beginning slice or an overlapping crack you could still peel back, not a nail that's already snapped clean through. — Jared, Practice Log #1
  • Buff with 500-grit classical guitar nail paper. After the glue sets, polish the repaired tip with nail paper at 500 grit (sold specifically as classical-guitar nail paper) — smooths the glue bump, and the reinforced tip ends up sounding thicker/fuller than the bare nail, not just repaired. — Jared, Practice Log #1
  • Nightly cuticle oil for the next nail, not the current one. "Healthy Hoof" cuticle product, worked in around the cuticle every night before bed — the logic is it feeds the nail bed so nail that's still growing in comes out stronger; it takes weeks to show since it's not affecting the nail you already have. Unverified/anecdotal (Jared calls it possibly "snake oil" but is trying it). — Jared, Practice Log #1
secs: Fixing a chip or crack without wrecking the nail

keyscape-clavinet-c.title: Keyscape — Clavinet C
keyscape-clavinet-c.html:
Instrument: Keyscape · Slot: MIDS Slot · Used by: Electric Piano Track

What it's for

Funk comping — the Clavinet's percussive, filtered-pluck character. Unlike the Rhodes/Wurli entries here, this one lives in the MIDS Slot (rhythmic comping, not sustained harmony) per Sound Palette.

Settings

secondary-dominants-what-you-want-to-kno.title: Secondary Dominants - What You Want To Know
secondary-dominants-what-you-want-to-kno.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A concise jazz-guitar theory lesson from Jens Larsen walking through secondary dominants from three angles: what they are, how to find them inside a real standard, and how to use them in comping and soloing. He opens from first principles — in C major, the only diatonic dominant is G7 and it only resolves to the tonic, so a secondary dominant "borrows" a dominant 7th for any other scale degree (V7/vi = E7 → Am, V7/IV = C7 → F). The middle section is a full worked analysis of the first half of "There'll Never Be Another You" (key of E♭ major): find every dominant-quality chord in the chart, then test each one against whether it actually resolves down a fifth to determine which are secondary dominants versus decorative/non-functional dominant-quality chords. He explicitly frames this as the general method for learning any standard — spot the secondary dominants first, and the rest of the chart usually reduces to plain diatonic chords. Two practical payoffs get real depth: (1) a clean two-case rule for which scale to solo over a secondary dominant with (major target → that key's major scale; minor target → harmonic minor built off the target), plus a third case (V7/V, "the dominant of the dominant") that gets its own Lydian dominant treatment; and (2) two comping/soling patterns for inserting secondary dominants that aren't already written into a chart — as a passing chord right before a target chord in an existing progression, and as an embellishment dropped into a long static vamp. Efficient, well-sequenced lesson with real chord-chart numbers throughout, not just abstract theory-speak — a strong companion to the vault's more example-dense secondary-dominant videos.

jens-larsen-learn-jazz-standards-get-the.title: Jens Larsen - Learn Jazz Standards - Get The Most of What You Already Know
jens-larsen-learn-jazz-standards-get-the.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A methodology lesson rather than a licks-and-voicings video — Jens Larsen steps away from his usual format to argue for two habits that make learning jazz repertoire dramatically faster. First: learn the songs, quoting Peter Bernstein directly ("learn the songs") as the single piece of advice he values most — repertoire depth is what actually makes someone a better improviser, because it stocks a library of real progressions to draw on. Second, and the video's real payload: learn a song's form before its chords, and think in chord functions/small progressions rather than individual chords. He demonstrates both by analyzing five 32-bar standards back to back — "All The Things You Are," "It Could Happen to You," "But Not for Me," "Out of Nowhere," and "Just Friends" — three of them deliberately chosen in the same key (E♭ major) specifically to remove the transposition step and let the shape of the form become obvious on repeat exposure. The payoff is a small set of recurring structural devices (a secondary ii–V to vi, a secondary ii–V to IV, a "IV → IV-minor → I" cadence, a "dominant of the dominant" V7/V near the end of the first half) that show up in the same slot of the form across unrelated tunes by different composers — once you can recognize the slot, a new standard stops looking like 32 bars of arbitrary chords and starts looking like a known shape with a few tune-specific variations. Caption-quality note: this transcript is a music-heavy spoken lesson with sung/played chord names, and YouTube's auto-captioner garbles a large fraction of the chord-letter vocabulary badly (see Source below for the specific substitution pattern) — the functional/conceptual teaching (which is the actual point of the video) survives cleanly, but individual chord-letter spellings in the worked analyses below are reconstructed carefully from context and flagged as lower-confidence where the garbling is severe. Nothing below was invented from general knowledge of these standards' published changes — only used to help interpret an otherwise-unreadable caption artifact.

mixing-dua-lipa-s-vocals-with-josh-gudwi.title: Mixing Dua Lipa's vocals with Josh Gudwin
mixing-dua-lipa-s-vocals-with-josh-gudwi.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A Mix with the Masters screen-share of Josh Gudwin (Dua Lipa, Justin Bieber) mixing "Electricity," working directly in an Ableton-style session at 118 BPM. This is a stem-handoff mix, not a from-scratch build — Josh is explicit throughout that the producer (Mark, unnamed surname but referred to respectfully as "one of the OGs") sent him a track that already sounded good, and his stated approach is to build off that mix rather than replace it: keep sends and plugins the producer's team already had in place when they're working ("I kept those on because the reverb actually sounded pretty cool"), only add processing where something is genuinely uneven, and stay out of the way of a good source. The most detailed material is the lead-vocal chain — a deep, mostly-subtractive stack (EQ → EQ → compressor → light multiband resonance suppression → more EQ → narrow multiband cuts → LA-2A → C6-style subtractive multiband EQ/de-essing) applied per-track rather than as a blanket vocal-bus move, because the original vocal was delivered as one combined track and Josh's habit is to split every performance out and tailor each individually. The video's standout reusable trick is a parallel "girth" aux — duplicate the vocal's master aux, run a default/aggressive EQ + 1176-style compression on the duplicate, and blend it back in at roughly −33 dB for fullness without turning up the fader. Beyond vocals he covers piano (subtle mid/side + kick-sidechain mono-narrowing), guitars (an unlinked-stereo compression fix for a right-heavy signal, plus a harder-driven outro-guitar bus), bass (light-touch blend-first philosophy, Trash/Clip Control character, kick-sidechain on the drop), and drums (left almost entirely alone because the source sounds already sounded good, with Decapitator and Transient Master kept on standby for individual hits). He closes with a genuinely useful "delay throw as feel, not clarity" layering technique (tucked quarter-note + audible filtered reverb + a "half-verb blast," all dialed in then turned down further) and an automated spring-reverb swell used once, deliberately, at the bridge. Auto-captions garble a couple of product names (a reverb Josh calls "Clear" doesn't match anything sonically plausible and is logged as unidentified rather than force-matched to the owned Supertone Clear vocal-clarity tool, which does a completely different job).

pentatonic-mastery-practice-routine.title: Pentatonic Mastery Practice Routine
pentatonic-mastery-practice-routine.html:
Part of Guitar Positions. A three-stage practice progression for breaking a pentatonic scale out of "box shape noodling" and into musical, ear-led playing — each stage restricts the scale further (fewer strings, then reordered note groupings, then a single string) so the fretting hand can't lean on memorized box shapes and the ear has to do the navigating instead. Built on the A minor pentatonic, worked across all five movable box positions, and explicitly stated to transpose to any key by moving the same five shapes to a new anchor fret. Compare String-Group Pentatonic Bursts (a related but distinct two-string-fragment drill that stays inside one box, layering fragments together) and the "two strings at a time" baby-step variant in Continuous Scale Exercise — this routine instead sweeps the same narrow string set across all five positions to connect them, rather than fragmenting a single position.

Prerequisite — map all five positions

Before any of the three exercises: be able to play the A minor pentatonic scale through all five movable box shapes, position to position up the neck, starting from the familiar first box as the anchor. Same notes throughout, five different shapes/fingerings. Skipping this and jumping straight to the exercises defeats the point — the exercises all depend on knowing where each of the five shapes sits. See Guitar Positions for the general fretboard-position framework this slots into.

finneas-drum-sampling-chain.title: Finneas Drum Sampling Chain
finneas-drum-sampling-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-Finneas-himself breakdown of one song's build, reverse-engineered from Creative drum sampling with Finneas (Mix with the Masters, 2021). Unlike the fuller multi-take vocal-chain breakdowns elsewhere in this vault, this one is short and the value is concentrated in process and philosophy rather than exact numeric settings: a solo drum-programming session as the song's literal starting point, a stated belief that any raw sound is only a starting place ("dress it up until it's kind of unrecognizable"), and a direct compositional lesson pulled from writing "bad guy" (make the bass line itself singable). Treat every device setting below as qualitative — the video shows the signal path and reasoning, not exact parameter values.

Chain overview

Two chain-shaped elements plus a build-order lesson: (1) a drum kit built from sound-first layering (Battery → PanMan on one layer, a two-kick pattern, and a chorus-gated character tom), and (2) a five-effect "dress it up until unrecognizable" processing stack turning a plain Output Analog Strings patch into cinematic, aged-sounding strings. A separate 808 Studio bass stage rounds out the low end. The reusable core idea: a raw starting sound (sampled, patched, or purchased) is a beginning, not a ceiling — the payoff is in how far you're willing to process it, and a drum kit's real job is how it locks with the bassline's pocket, not how it sounds solo.

1. Drum foundation — the song's actual starting point

  • Source: the very first piece of the song, written alone, became "the main percussion element" before anything else existed.
  • Kit build: primary kick chosen for its own sound first, then how it layers with the rest — a sparse "one and one" (downbeat-only) kick plus a second kick pattern hitting 1-and-3. Claps layered directly onto the 2-and-4 backbeat snare as one composite hit; a second snare doubled with a deliberately "crappy"-toned tom, reserved for a specific section (named as chorus) — described as reading like "20th Century Fox or something."
  • 🎬 From video: a stated minimalism preference governs the whole kit — "I love minimalism, I love simplicity, anything that's just a wonderful foundation for other things to develop is really exciting to me." → Layering and Stacking, Kick Design, Snare Design, Arrangement and Song Form

creative-drum-sampling-with-finneas.title: Creative drum sampling with Finneas
creative-drum-sampling-with-finneas.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short Mix with the Masters breakdown of Finneas walking through one song's drum-and-sample build, start to finish: the track began with him alone, programming a drum beat that became the song's core percussion, then grew outward — a heavily-processed "old sounding" string patch, an 808 built inside a deep parametric 808 synth, and a kick/snare/clap/tom kit built around finding good individual sounds and layering them. The most valuable thing in the video isn't any single setting, it's the stated philosophy that runs through the whole thing: a raw starting sound (a self-played patch, a purchased sample) is only ever a starting place, and the satisfying part of production is dressing that raw sound up until it's "kind of unrecognizable." He also names a direct compositional lesson pulled from writing "bad guy" — make the bass line itself singable, not just the vocal — and describes how the drum kit's real job is to coexist with that bassline's pocket rather than stand alone. Tool-wise it's a useful snapshot of a working producer's engine migrating over time: Battery was his primary sampler when this song was written; by the time of the interview he'd moved to Logic Pro's then-new Drum Machine Designer/Quick Sampler update instead.

sza-r-b-guitar-chain.title: SZA R&B Guitar Chain
sza-r-b-guitar-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a nostalgic, ambient R&B guitar sound built from two layers of the same guitar part — a dry, tightly processed signal chain, plus a second reamped pass through a hardware pedal that detunes/delays the signal out of time, layered on top as a wash. Recreated (not a confirmed session breakdown) by loner from Blind, on SZA's SOS — the secrets behind sza's 'sos' production!?. Signal source: a clean electric guitar, arpeggiated chord progression, for a nostalgic feel. Works over Electric Guitar DI Track.

Chain overview

Layer 1 (dry) sets the main tone: EQ → compressor → spring reverb → short slap delay → flanger → shaper box. Layer 2 (texture) re-runs the same performance through a Montreal Assembly Count to 5 hardware pedal (set to detune/delay the signal out of time), then shaper box → EQ → reverb → pan, and sits underneath/behind Layer 1 as an ambient wash rather than replacing it. The two layers are meant to be heard together — Layer 1 carries the part, Layer 2 blurs it.

ozone-9-vintage-eq.title: Ozone 9 Vintage EQ
ozone-9-vintage-eq.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: iZotope

What it is

Ozone 9's vintage-modeled EQ, emulating the character of classic analog EQ hardware (broader, musical curves) rather than clinical digital EQ.

What it's used for

Musical, characterful tonal shaping on a master when a clean digital EQ feels too surgical.

FX chain notes

Used as an alternative or complement to the standard Ozone Equalizer module.

Techniques

  • This is the owned stand-in for the boutique analog-emulation curve behavior a video demos on the (unowned) Maag EQ4 — reach for it when a broad, tonal move needs to sound analog-modeled rather than digital-clean. The lesson: broadband/tonal changes call for an analog-emulation EQ over a digital one, because the character comes from how closely the curve is modeled off real hardware, not from a display hiding what's changing (a frequency/curve analyzer on the Maag EQ4 showed its curves are mostly reproducible on a typical digital EQ — the one genuine exception being its reach into supersonic frequencies most digital EQs don't model). This module's own low-shelf/mid/high-shelf-with-Q layout (①–③) is the same broad-curve, musical-shaping approach — use it for overall tone, not a specific narrow fix (see Ozone 9 Equalizer for that half of the decision). Most analog-emulation EQs, this one included, default to natural phase. → EQ, Master Chain, Plugin Wishlist — Sage Audio, How to EQ Your Master

kendrick-lamar-soul-sample-chain.title: Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain
kendrick-lamar-soul-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch "vintage soul sample" built to sound like a genuine Kendrick Lamar-style piano-led flip (inspired by the piano-forward tracks on the Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers era) rather than a chopped real record. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, how to make the most realistic vintage soul samples for kendrick lamar!?. Unlike Beatles Psych-Rock Sample Chain (real-gear research into owned/replica hardware), this build leans on VST sources with no owned equivalents — see Plugin Wishlist for every unresolved plugin.

Chain overview

Five elements stack into one sample: a piano chord bed, a mallet counter-layer, two synth texture layers, and a 3-take vocal harmony stack — finished by bouncing the piano+vocal portion into a slicer for a chop/pitch/micro-timing pass. The build's two biggest reusable ideas: spread/low-velocity chord voicing on the piano (theory-level "vintage" before any processing touches it) and a 3-take vocal stack sharing one base chain, each take earning exactly one distinguishing extra stage (not three fully separate chains, not a plain doubled take).

1. Piano — Cinesamples Blue

  • Instrument: Cinesamples Blue (Contact bank) — "probably my favorite piano vst." No owned equivalent, see Plugin Wishlist.
  • Chords: VI–III–v–VII in B natural minor — Gmaj9 → Dmaj9 → F♯m → Amaj7 (spoken on-screen as "6-3-5-7"). Full theory writeup: Chord Progressions.
  • Voicing: root low, then the rest of each chord (including the 7th/9th) spread up a full octave — "helps to create such a different vibe... much more emotion out of your chords." The second chord (Dmaj9) repeats the exact same major-9 shape but is re-voiced slightly differently (F♯ brought up) purely for variety between two structurally identical chords. → Chord Inversions
  • Velocity: dropped to near-zero on every note, deliberately — "the texture sounds better doing this... when the velocity is super high the notes can be a bit too harsh."
  • 🎬 From video: try a whole chord part at very low velocity before reaching for EQ/compression on a harsh-sounding source — a general lesson worth applying beyond this chain.

future-style-vintage-sample-chain.title: Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain
future-style-vintage-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch "vintage sample" built to sound like a genuinely old chopped record, then flipped into a hard, dark trap beat for Future. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, this is how frank dukes & cubeatz make vintage samples in 2022!? — despite the title, this is loner's own build, not an actual Frank Dukes/CUBEATZ session. Nine layered elements stack into one sample before the whole thing is bounced and chopped. Unlike Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain (piano-centric, 3-part vocal harmony stack), this build's centerpiece ideas are semitone-close chord voicing for tension, room-preset reverb on real-instrument samples, and giving each vocal layer in a stack its own distinct processing chain rather than one copied chain. See Plugin Wishlist for every unresolved instrument/plugin name in this chain.

Chain overview

Nine elements — a Rhodes-style chord bed, a doubled vintage-upright piano, a bass, an accent hit, a violin melody, a texture layer, two perc loops, two differently-processed vocal loops, and a reversed/chopped guitar — are built up individually, then the whole mix is bounced into a beat-slicer, pitched down 9 semitones, and chopped by ear into a beat, finished with a simple programmed drum layer. The two biggest reusable ideas: voice a repeating chord shape so only the top note moves, always by a semitone, and treat "give every vocal/instrument layer its own distinguishing chain" as a rule, not an accident — no two layers in this build share an identical processing chain.

1. Chords — Arturia Wurli V2 ("funky cat" preset)

  • Instrument: Arturia Wurli V2, "funky cat" preset (heard/captioned "Whirly V2" — see Plugin Wishlist).
  • Voicing: all three chords are the same D♯m shape (the last a G♯m), only the top note changes each time — bar 1–4 the top line walks up, bar 5–8 it walks back down. Every top-line move lands a semitone from an adjacent chord tone, which is where the "creepy, eerie, mysterious" tension comes from. → Chord Inversions
  • 🎬 From video: "these two notes are only a semitone apart... it's just creating real tension and mystery" — a reusable voicing principle independent of the specific chord.
secs: 1. Chords — Arturia Wurli V2 ("funky cat" preset)

ozone-9-match-eq.title: Ozone 9 Match EQ
ozone-9-match-eq.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: iZotope

What it is

Ozone 9's reference-matching EQ, analyzing a reference track's spectral curve and applying a matching EQ curve to the current master.

What it's used for

Matching a master's tonal balance to a reference commercial track.

FX chain notes

Used early in the mastering chain to establish a target tonal balance before further manual EQ.

Techniques

  • Reference-match a vocal against a specific ARTIST's captured tonal signature, not just a generic reference track — build a small preset library per artist, per role. A working match-EQ setup with multiple saved reference snapshots, each captured from a different target artist's vocal and applied by role in the chain: two presets (one per artist) for the main vocal-EQ stage, and a separate pair for a later "air"-EQ stage. The mechanism is this note's own reference-snapshot-then-match workflow — the new information is treating "artist" as the organizing unit for a preset library (several saved snapshots, picked by which artist's tonal signature the vocal should lean toward) rather than one generic reference track re-captured per song. Paired in the same chain with a distinct pre-compressor "pushpull" EQ stage (parametric bands nudging toward a level indicator rather than shaping tone) — see EQ (effect) for that half. → EQ — Jaycen Joshua (Mix with the Masters), Mixing Summits with Jaycen Joshua
  • Track-level use, not just mastering: match-EQ a tape-returned (or otherwise reprocessed) signal back toward a pre-processing balance you already liked — when a physical tape print (or any hardware/character stage) shifts a part's tone more than you want, snapshot the pre-stage tone as the reference and pull the post-stage signal back toward it, so you keep the glue/character without losing a balance that was already working. A legitimate earlier-stage use of the same reference-matching idea this note otherwise documents at mastering. — Zach Scholz, Recording Vintage Acoustic Guitar Tones

serum-2-modern-lead.title: Serum 2 — Modern Lead
serum-2-modern-lead.html:
Instrument: Serum 2 · Slot: LEAD Slot · Used by: Synth Lead Track

What it's for

The pop/trap/EDM default single-line lead — modern, mono, expressive. Reach for it when the part is played (not chorded) and needs to sit forward without a supersaw's width eating the mix. Replaces a live lead instrument when speed matters.

Settings

  • Derived from Serum 2 — Supersaw lead, narrowed for mono use: Osc A saw/supersaw wavetable, ③ unison 3–7 voices, detune 0.10–0.20 (down from the recipe's 7-voice/0.12–0.18 width, which fights a mono voicing)
  • ⑥ Filter: LPF ~24 dB, cutoff open with a touch of envelope amount (fast attack, short decay) for pluck-forward motion
  • ⑦ Amp env: fast attack (0–10 ms), release short enough to not smear the line
  • ⑩ Mono + legato + glide 40–80 ms (poly only for chord-stab variants — that's a voicing switch, not a different patch)
  • Kill sub content below ~100 Hz at the patch (HPF or osc-level) — leads never need it
  • Vibrato via mod-wheel LFO, not baked into the patch
  • FX: chorus off — unison ③ already does the width job

In context

  • Sits after the chain's saturation/OTT stage on Synth Lead Track — keep the patch's own output clean, let the chain add grit.
  • Mono at the source; width comes from the chain's stereo tools, not this patch (Stereo Field).

Settings

  • ⑨ Unison: 8–16 voices (wide end of DUNE 3's range — the recipe's default 2–4 is too tight for this use), moderate–wide Detune and Spread
  • Filter Env → ⑥ Cutoff, fast decay for pluck shape at the front of each note
  • Amp Env: fast attack, medium decay
  • Kill content below ~100 Hz at the patch — sub stays with the bass/808

In context

creative-process-and-idea-capture.title: Creative Process and Idea Capture
creative-process-and-idea-capture.html:
How to deliberately set up conditions for inspiration to arrive, and what to do the moment it does — distinct from arrangement/mixing technique, this is about the writing process itself.

Set the parameter, then let it go

Michael Jackson's own described method (recounted by his engineer, on writing "Billie Jean" and "Beat It"): consciously state the specific creative goal to yourself — "I have to write a song with a driving, hooky bassline," or "this one needs a rock edge" — then deliberately stop thinking about it and let it sit in the back of the mind rather than actively working the problem. Over-rehearsing a goal in conscious thought is described as producing tension that blocks the spontaneous result ("you get locked... it doesn't flow"); the parameter-setting step is what points the subconscious at the right target, but the actual idea has to arrive on its own.

Capture the idea the instant it arrives

Quincy Jones's rule for a spontaneous idea, regardless of when it strikes: write it down or record it immediately, because the window closes fast — "if I don't, it's going next door to Hank" (Henry Mancini, his neighbor). The moment of inspiration is treated as fragile and non-negotiable to act on right away, not something to trust yourself to remember later.

Don't discard "gibberish" placeholder lyrics too quickly

When writing a melody by singing nonsense syllables or half-formed words before real lyrics exist, specific words that surface during that process aren't always random — they can be a buried signal of what the song is actually about. "Annie, are you OK?" (Michael Jackson's "Smooth Criminal") reportedly surfaced this way, sourced from a CPR-class catchphrase lodged in memory, and became the hook a full narrative was then built around. Treat an unexpectedly specific phrase in a scratch vocal as worth investigating before rewriting it away.

A reference sets the ENERGY, not the content

When a creative brief points at another song ("we need something with that My Sharona energy"), the brief is naming a feeling/spirit to hit, not a template to copy — Michael Jackson's "Beat It" was written in response to exactly that kind of brief and shares none of the referenced song's actual content, only its crossover pop-rock intensity. See also Steve Porcaro In-Studio - Writing Human Nature and Unreleased MJ Songs Part 1 for the same discipline applied to a sonic (not songwriting) reference: a reference sound is a starting point that still has to be tailored to the actual song.
secs: Set the parameter, then let it go
Capture the idea the instant it arrives
Don't discard "gibberish" placeholder lyrics too quickly
A reference sets the ENERGY, not the content

triads-the-secret-to-learning-the-fretbo.title: Triads! The Secret To Learning The Fretboard
triads-the-secret-to-learning-the-fretbo.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jack Ruch's lesson on using triad shapes as a map for moving blues soloing vocabulary around the entire guitar neck. The setup: play the same basic blues solo — a 12-bar blues shuffle in the key of E — three times, in three different neck positions, then show how those three positions connect into one continuous fretboard. The reason three positions specifically: an E major triad (E, G♯, B) repeats across the neck in three close-position inversions/string-set groupings, roughly centered on open position, the 5th fret, and the 9th fret, and those three triad zones are exactly the three spots the solo gets relocated to. The pedagogical point isn't "here are three solos to memorize" — it's a general method: take a short phrase built from ear-picked-up blues vocabulary (not derived from running a scale), and deliberately relearn it in relative terms (same scale degrees, same rhythm) starting from each triad zone in turn, so a lick that started out locked to one spot on the neck becomes playable anywhere. Ruch frames this against his own early learning experience — picking up isolated Freddie King/Albert Collins/Albert King licks that only worked in the one position/key/string-set he learned them in — and the video closes by demonstrating a full 3-chorus solo that ascends through the three zones (low to high) rather than sitting in one spot for the whole form. Tabs/notation/backing tracks are gated behind the creator's Patreon (external, not something to route further here).

A short Mix with the Masters breakdown of Grammy-winning vocal producer/engineer Kuk Harrell's (Justin Bieber, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Chris Brown) go-to tracking-vocal effects chain, demoed live on a real session. The throughline is deliberate simplicity: the same short signal chain — EQ, a touch of compression, RVox, then reverb/delay/doubler sends — on every singer, dialed in by ear and feel rather than technical frequency knowledge ("I'm not going on tech, I'm going on emotion"). He closes on a mix-handoff philosophy: keep routing dead simple (three sends only — reverb, delay, doubler/"chorus" — nothing daisy-chained through "a thousand aux"), so the session that reaches the mix engineer needs no cleanup and leaves them room to do more with it. using-reverb-to-create-space-with-alan-m.title: Using reverb to create space with Alan Meyerson
using-reverb-to-create-space-with-alan-m.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Alan Meyerson (score mixer — the video references pitching a scoring approach directly to Trent Reznor, Atticus Ross, and David Fincher, i.e. this is a Mank-era session) walks through the exact problem every dry-tracked orchestral score has: every section was recorded separately, close-miked, "in someone's bedroom" — no shared room, no shared acoustic identity. His fix is Vienna Symphonic Library's MIR Pro convolution-acoustics software, used not as a normal reverb send but as a full virtual scoring stage that every instrument group is placed INTO together, so the whole orchestra reads as one consistent room instead of a pile of dry, individually-mic'd parts glued only by shared mic type (ribbons). The most valuable idea here isn't "add reverb" — it's that MIR repurposes each instrument's own pan control into a position-in-the-room control (narrow/wide, off-center, and even rotation, which changes the mic's implied distance and therefore its high-frequency content), and that a shared convolution engine with per-instrument EQ/reverb-time feeding into it is what makes disparate dry recordings sound like one performance in one hall. Short video (under 6 minutes) but dense — a genuinely different mental model for "space" than a normal reverb-send workflow, even though the specific tool (MIR Pro) is unowned and specific to large-ensemble/film scoring rather than Nate's usual production context.

critical-listening-for-mastering.title: Critical Listening for Mastering
critical-listening-for-mastering.html:
What it is: the specific listening discipline mastering asks for beyond running tools correctly — five things to judge on every pass (Dynamics, Loudness, Timbre, Width, Depth), genre-aware processing judgment (the same move is right for one genre and wrong for another), and the ability to imagine the target sound before touching a device. Complements Referencing and Translation (the A/B/playback-check discipline) rather than replacing it — this note is about what to listen for, that one is about how to check it honestly.

The five categories

  1. Dynamics — the ratio/relationship between quiet and loud passages. Too dynamic → quieter details get lost on most consumer playback systems; too compressed → the listening experience gets fatiguing fast. Compression, Compression Staging, Ozone 9 Maximizer, kHs Clipper all act here.
  2. Loudness — the overall track level, inherently tied to Dynamics: two mixes with identical peak values but different dynamic range — the less dynamic one has to run louder to read the same. See Clipping and Loudness for the concrete LUFS targets and stack.
  3. Timbre — the track's overall tonal character: frequency response plus the ADSR (mainly attack/decay of transients) plus harmonic/disharmonic distortion. Compressors, EQs, and exciters/saturators do the most work here — EQ, Saturation and Distortion.
  4. Width — the ratio of centered vs. distinctly-left/right signal: identical L/R reads centered, differing L/R reads wide. Typically shaped with mid-side EQ/compression/saturation and stereo imagers (which also add psychoacoustic width tricks on top of straight M/S routing) — full toolkit on Width and Stereo. Too wide costs mono compatibility and reads unfocused; too centered reads closed-in and lacking a natural sense of space — a downside Width and Stereo doesn't otherwise call out explicitly, since that note's own "rules that keep width safe" section is mostly written from the too-wide side.
  5. Depth — the ratio of perceived background to foreground (dry vs. wet) signal. The most complex category: on the surface it's just the dry/wet relationship, but perception of it is tied into Dynamics, Loudness, Width, and EQ all at once — see Depth and Space for the fuller four-cue breakdown (level, HF content, transient sharpness, wet/dry+pre-delay); this category is the umbrella those four cues live under.

understanding-kaytranada-s-vision-with-n.title: Understanding Kaytranada's vision with Neal Pogue
understanding-kaytranada-s-vision-with-n.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, mix-philosophy-heavy breakdown from Neal Pogue (mix engineer for Kaytranada, OutKast, TLC, and others) walking through his mix of a Kaytranada/Kali Uchis track. Unusually light on plugin-chain detail compared to most Mix with the Masters entries — at 9:39 and ~1,000 words, it's really three ideas stretched across the runtime: (1) respect what an artist has already printed into a demo rather than reverse-engineering or replacing it, (2) an ears-first, reactive workflow — never reach for EQ or a compressor before actually listening to decide whether it's needed, and (3) a concrete, deliberately minimal 2-bus/Stereo Bus routine when he does reach for something: an unowned Waves L2 Ultramaximizer followed by Ozone 9's EQ and Maximizer, both barely engaged. What's most valuable here isn't a chain to copy move-for-move — it's the restraint discipline itself, backed by two named, concrete data points (the L2 threshold, the Ozone EQ gains) that make "light touch" measurable rather than just a vibe.

session-templates.title: Session Templates
session-templates.html:
Building one reusable "starting point" Live Set — instruments pre-created and pre-routed but powered off, buses wired, default device chains parked and disabled — so a new song starts from zero setup friction instead of rebuilding routing every time. Companion to Session View Workflow (drafting within a session) and Gain Staging (the levels discipline a template should already encode).

Why it exists

A template isn't just a saved tempo/key — it's every decision you'd otherwise make fresh each session (which synths, how they're routed, what the buses are, what a default insert chain looks like) captured once so composing starts immediately instead of after twenty minutes of setup. The habit compounds: each session you build without a template is unpaid research for the next template revision.

guitar-ear-training-essentials-the-missi.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Lesson 2.9 of Jared's own guitar course — explicitly the first lesson in his "Ear Training" category, i.e. the foundational, singing-based entry point that sits underneath the more advanced "Learning to Listen" interval/chord app-drilling system he demonstrates later in How I Organize My Guitar Practice (So I Never Want to Stop) (category 4 of that video's spreadsheet tour). Where that later system trains splitting apart stacked chord voicings with a metronome and streak targets, this lesson is the prerequisite underneath it: can you sing a scale degree or solfège syllable back accurately at all. Jared's framing is personal and direct — he played guitar 10 years before anyone told him he should be listening and singing, calls it "the most life-changing practice" of everything he's worked on (ahead of reading, improvising, or theory), and is candid that it's still one of his weaker spots even after deliberate work. The core diagnosis: guitar's frets let you find the right note by looking at your hand instead of your ear, so guitarists specifically (more than other instrumentalists) can go years without ever being forced to identify a sound. The fix he teaches is a singing curriculum, not a listening app: sing the major scale up and down with scale-degree numbers, then again with solfège, then apply both systems to real, known melodies (a generic ascending/descending pattern, "Row Row Row Your Boat," "Three Blind Mice"). No good vocal tone required — the only bar is "am I thinking of the right note, and can I hear when I'm on it."

amazing-guitar-ear-training-exercises-he.title: Amazing Guitar Ear Training Exercises (hearing & singing modes of the major scale)
amazing-guitar-ear-training-exercises-he.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Jared's deep-dive on the single ear-training exercise he says "changed the game" for him personally: singing through all seven modes of the major scale, one at a time, over a sustained single-note drone on the root. This is a distinct, more advanced technique than Guitar Ear Training Essentials - The Missing Link for Guitarists (lesson 2.9, his singing-first foundation — scale-degree numbers/solfège on the plain major scale plus real melodies) — that video builds the raw "can I sing a scale degree back accurately" skill; this one applies that skill across every mode of the major scale, so the singer ends up producing and identifying every chromatic degree that can appear above a root (♭2, 2, ♭3, 3, 4, ♯4, 5, ♭6, 6, ♭7, 7) in the actual modal context each one belongs to, not as an isolated interval. The mechanism is the same "singing is the diagnostic test" philosophy as the Missing Link video and as Max Konyi's drone method on Scale Degree Ear Training, but the drilling structure is new and guitar-modes-specific: start on Lydian (the brightest mode) and walk down to Locrian (the darkest) by lowering exactly one scale degree a half-step at a time — the same bright-to-dark "color tones" ladder documented on Diatonic Modes, just sung instead of played. Jared is candid throughout that he's not a comfortable or trained singer and still misses intonation sometimes, which is part of the video's point — the bar is "am I singing the right note and can I hear it," not vocal polish. For a non-singer or someone who doesn't know the mode shapes yet, he gives an explicit guitar-first on-ramp: map the modes structurally on one string before trying to sing them.

linn-lm-1.title: Linn LM-1
linn-lm-1.html:
What it is

Roger Linn's LM-1 Drum Computer was the first drum machine built on samples of real drums — a $4,995 luxury item (~500 made) that instantly made every analog rhythm box sound like a toy to 1980 ears. It's also where quantization and programmable swing were invented. Its most famous owner reshaped pop with it: the LM-1 is the Prince drum sound.

What makes the sound

  • 8-bit samples of real drums (recorded from session drummer Art Wood's kit) stored on EPROM chips — real snare/kick/perc hits, but with the grainy, slightly crunchy edge of 8-bit companded encoding.
  • Per-voice tuning knobs change playback clock rate — pitching a sample down also darkens and lengthens it. Prince's signature moves live here: the pitched-down clap-rimshot and detuned toms that sound like no acoustic kit.
  • No cymbals/hi-hat crash memory constraints: no crash or ride (too much sample memory), so arrangements built on it feel tight and dry by construction.
  • Swing/shuffle ("timing humanize") invented here — Linn's quantize-with-swing is the groove template every MPC and DAW swing knob descends from → Akai MPC60.
  • Individual outs per voice meant each drum could be processed on its own console channel — part of why LM-1 records sound so produced.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Drum Rack / Simpler with LM-1 sample packs (pitch them down for the Prince trick — Simpler's classic mode repitches just like the hardware); RC-20 Retro Color or kHs Bitcrush to push the 8-bit grain harder; Cassette for era-glue.
  • Paid: UVI Beat Box Anthology 2 (covers LM-1 and most of this worklist), Samples From Mars "LM-1 From Mars".
  • Free: LM-1 sample packs circulate widely.

Used on

  • Prince — everywhere from Controversy through the 1999 / Purple Rain era; "When Doves Cry" is an LM-1 masterclass (that clap!). He bought one of the first units.
  • The Human League — Dare (1981), incl. "Don't You Want Me": British synthpop adopted the LM-1 immediately.
  • Genre/era: early-80s synthpop, boogie/post-disco, Minneapolis funk.

tom-elmhirst-breaks-down-his-mix-of-roll.title: Tom Elmhirst breaks down his mix of 'Rolling in the Deep' by Adele
tom-elmhirst-breaks-down-his-mix-of-roll.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, dense Mix with the Masters solo-in-the-room breakdown: Tom Elmhirst (Adele, Amy Winehouse, Beck) walks through four stages of his session for Adele's "Rolling in the Deep" — drum sample reinforcement, an outro-chorus parallel-compression lift, a two-piano arrangement with a spring-reverb chorus entrance, and the full analog vocal chain plus its three-return effects architecture. The real headline isn't any single plugin — it's how deliberately every processing and effects decision is staged to the song's structure: the snare sample only exists in the chorus (the verse is a bare stomp with no snare hit at all), the parallel drum compression is held back until the outro-chorus lift, the high piano and its spring reverb are chorus-only, and the vocal's entire effects budget builds in three discrete steps across the song (dry + tape delay in the verse → add reverb at the bridge → add two delays at the chorus). Elmhirst also drops a compact mixing-philosophy line worth remembering: when the multitrack, arrangement, and production already do the work, the mix engineer's job is "just not to [mess] up" — restraint as the whole brief on a record this strong. Settings given are mostly qualitative (console channel/send numbers, not plugin parameters) since this predates his in-the-box rebuild, but the routing/arrangement logic transfers directly.

ghz-tupe-3.title: Ghz Tupe 3
ghz-tupe-3.html:
Category: Drive/Color Vendor: Goodhertz

What it is

Goodhertz's tape-emulation plugin (Tupe), modeling analog tape saturation, wow/flutter, and compression character.

What it's used for

Adding analog tape warmth and gentle compression/saturation to tracks or busses.

FX chain notes

A coloration stage, often near the end of a bus chain to 'glue' the sound with tape-style character.

Used in my chains

My tube-warmth stage — restores "pushed amp / analog" harmonics that clean DIs and VST sources miss. Always low-ish drive, placed before the compressor so the comp glues the colored tone:

  • Bass Bus — slot 1, warmth: Tube 15%, Tilt neutral, Mix 100% — one coat of harmonics so the low end translates on small speakers.
  • Electric Piano Track — slot 3, tube drive: Tube 30% (push to 50% for bark on funky parts) — a Rhodes' character comes from overdriving its amp.
  • Electric Guitar Amp Track — slot 4, tube color: Tube 30%, output matched to input — restores pushed-amp harmonics after corrective cleanup.
  • Electric Guitar DI Track — slot 3, tube glue: Tube 20% — the owned "CLA Guitars" first-aid for thin DIs (this + 1073 drive).

7-days-to-learning-bass-scales-beginner-.title: 7 Days to Learning Bass Scales (Beginner Lesson)
7-days-to-learning-bass-scales-beginner-.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A beginner-focused BassBuzz lesson that packages five essential bass scale shapes — major, major pentatonic, minor, minor pentatonic, and blues — into a single 7-day practice routine, one shape (or one improv session) per day. The framing device runs the whole video: the 12-note chromatic alphabet is a spice cabinet, and a scale is a pre-mixed subset of spices guaranteed to taste coherent together, so learning a scale means learning both what notes it contains and a fretboard shape that finds them. Rather than teaching five isolated topics, the lesson deliberately builds each new shape as a small modification of the previous one (pentatonic = full scale minus two notes; blues = minor pentatonic plus one note) so viewers are never really learning from scratch after day one. Every shape gets the same three-step treatment: (1) the bare scale shape with exact fingering, (2) a short, well-known riff or melody built from that scale to internalize it as music rather than a pattern, and (3) on two of the seven days, a freeform improvisation session against a sustained drone track instead of a written riff — explicitly framed as the deepest of the three internalization methods, because it forces a genuine ear-to-finger connection rather than shape recall or pattern-copying. The riffs chosen are all recognizable classic-rock/soul cuts (Lord of the Rings' Shire theme, My Girl, Crazy Train, Knock on Wood, Sunshine of Your Love), each picked specifically because it's simple enough to teach in a few minutes while still using most of the notes in that day's scale. A paid course plug (BassBuzz's "Beginner to Badass") appears twice but doesn't gate any of the free content — every shape, fingering, and riff taught in the video is complete on its own.

the-perfect-bass-practice-morning-routin.title: The PERFECT Bass Practice Morning Routine For Beginners
the-perfect-bass-practice-morning-routin.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz beginner routine built from three short, named exercises meant to fit inside a 10-minute daily session — the "morning" framing is explicitly a consistency hack (getting practice in before the day's distractions show up), not a claim that the exercises only work in the morning. The video's real content is the three exercises themselves, each targeting a distinct beginner weak point: Finger Fixer (fretting-hand strength/coordination, including the pinky, via a two-bar B-minor-scale-based pattern), String Crossing Crusher (plucking-hand pattern vocabulary — four ways to pluck any string-crossing line, plus a pinky finger-roll technique for root-fifth-octave shapes), and Mute Master (fretting-hand vs. plucking-hand muting, long mutes vs. short/staccato mutes, over an F-major-scale-shaped line that's really about the muted silences, not the notes). BassBuzz frames the routine as cumulative — early sessions might spend all 10 minutes on one exercise, later sessions rotate through all three — and closes by pointing to a separate play-along workout video and a "5 beginner bass riffs" video for applying the exercises to real songs. Coaching value is in the how, not just the tab: each exercise's practice notes (slow-it-down, isolate a bar, watch this specific finger) are what turn the drill into an actual habit-fixer rather than "mindlessly wiggling your fingers," which the video explicitly calls out as the wrong way to use it.

bass-exercises-for-beginners-strength-st.title: Bass Exercises for Beginners (Strength, Stamina, Flexibility, Control)
bass-exercises-for-beginners-strength-st.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A BassBuzz beginner-technique lesson built around a relatable cold open — the host flubbing "Californication" with buzzing, unreachable frets and "stupid dumb fingers" — before laying out four short, targeted fretting-hand exercises meant to fix exactly that class of problem: rattly/thin tone, limited reach, fading stamina mid-song, and wasteful "flying finger" flails. Each exercise is diagnosed first (what specifically goes wrong and why, at a mechanical level — string pressure, fret proximity, release speed, hand relearning how to move, muscle tire-and-recover cycles, wasted motion) and then drilled with a simple, count-in-able pattern, in a deliberate order where each exercise's pattern or skill feeds the next one. BassBuzz cites forum testers who improved strength/coordination, stretch/stamina, and flying-finger control and then carried it into actual songs — with the explicit warning that mindlessly running the tabs without the stated technique focus mostly wastes the practice time. The video is short and beginner-pitched but genuinely mechanical rather than motivational filler: every exercise ties a named failure mode to a specific physical cause and a specific fix, in the same diagnose-then-drill mold as BassBuzz's other technique videos (Fix Your Plucking in 5 Minutes). A free PDF (tabs + play-along backing tracks) is offered in the video description but not available to this pipeline; the paid "Beginner to Badass" course gets a brief mid-video plug, not itself a technique.

effectrack.title: EffectRack
effectrack.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: Soundtoys

What it is

Soundtoys' container plugin that hosts multiple Soundtoys effects in one signal chain with shared routing and a single interface.

What it's used for

Combining several Soundtoys effects (e.g. Decapitator into EchoBoy into Crystallizer) in one manageable rack.

FX chain notes

Used as a container hosting a chain of other Soundtoys effects.

Techniques

  • The "1-2 knob custom pedal" design pattern: chain several devices, but expose only the 2-3 macros that actually matter for real-time use. FL Studio's Patcher (a routing/container plugin — the direct sibling of this device and Ableton's Audio Effect Rack) chains a reverb into a chorus into an EQ, but the design goal is explicit: "I want to make this kind of like a one or two knob pedal... this is the effect it's going to give you, but I want to let the person decide" — everything upstream (preset choice, pitch amount, internal chain order) stays baked-in and unmapped; only the 1-2 controls someone would actually want to ride live (e.g. a half-time mix, a low-pass cutoff) get a macro. Framed as the general fix for the guitar-pedal-envy problem (rare/expensive/hard-to-learn hardware) — replicate the character with owned plugins, then package it exactly like a real pedal's simple front panel. Full worked chain: Sparkle Texture Rack. → Randomized Rack Design, ValhallaVintageVerb, Portal — loner, this secret plugin will change the way you process your melodies!?
  • Save FX-rack chains as reusable "sounds" — the feature that converted him to Ableton: hours of sound design saved as an audio-effect-rack chain becomes a recallable instrument in your palette; build a library of signature chains, not just presets — Lophiile, Help Me Devvon interview

phaser-flanger.title: Phaser-Flanger

Category: Modulation Vendor: Ableton

What it is

Ableton's stock combined phaser/flanger device — the flanger side is functionally a very short (~0.1–20 ms) modulated delay, paired with a phaser stage, plus a built-in envelope follower and LFO section that can drive the device's own parameters from the incoming signal.

What it's used for

Classic sweeping phaser/flanger movement on guitars, keys, and synths; the built-in envelope follower additionally makes it a lightweight audio-reactive modulation source for other parameters, without wiring up a separate Envelope Follower device.

FX chain notes

Insert on the source track needing the sweep/flange movement; when used purely as an envelope-follower-driven auto-modulator (feedback/rate reacting to the input), it can sit ahead of a following delay-family device to make that device's own character respond to dynamics.

tape-flanging-emulation.title: Tape Flanging Emulation
tape-flanging-emulation.html:
Classic analog flanging comes from playing two copies of the same audio back nearly in sync and physically wobbling the speed of one tape machine so the two drift a couple of milliseconds apart and back — the resulting comb-filter sweep is the "jet engine" flange sound. Source: Tom Lord-Alge's own 2000s-era analog session and his modern DAW recreation of the identical effect. This note documents both the original hardware mechanism and the in-the-box method that reproduces it exactly, without a half-inch tape machine.

The hardware mechanism

  1. Print (bounce) the exact piece of mix you want to flange to half-inch analog tape — with generous pre-roll, since dialing in the sweep by hand takes time (TLA's own example ran ~32 bars before the sweep landed where he wanted it).
  2. Fly that tape back into the multitrack alongside the original, unprinted signal.
  3. Manually varispeed the tape machine — slow it down, speed it up — while listening for the moment the two signals drift into and out of near-unison. The comb-filter sweep ("the flange") appears specifically in that couple-of-millisecond drift window.
  4. Ride the varispeed control live until the sweep lands exactly where the arrangement needs it, then use only the region you actually need — the rest of the pre-roll was just runway to catch the timing.

The in-DAW recreation

  1. Duplicate the audio you want to flange onto a second, identical track — the effect requires two copies of the same signal, not two different sounds.
  2. Insert a delay-compensation-style plugin on one of the two tracks — one that can push delay in either direction around zero (both positive delay and negative/pre-delay), not just add positive delay. TLA names the Eventide Precision Time Align specifically for this; the owned lane is Align Delay (Max for Live) — verify it can express negative delay before relying on it for the full pre/post-delay range the named unit covers.
  3. Set the delay to zero as the starting point — the two copies are now identical and in phase.
  4. Automate the delay value sweeping back and forth by a couple of milliseconds around zero. The flange sweep is produced entirely by that automated near-zero modulation between two otherwise-identical signals — no dedicated flanger plugin required.
  5. Print/commit the automated result rather than leaving it live, the same commit-and-move-on discipline documented in Committing and Printing.

tom-lord-alge-s-secret-mixing-techniques.title: Tom Lord-Alge's secret mixing techniques
tom-lord-alge-s-secret-mixing-techniques.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Tom Lord-Alge revisits his own 18-year-old analog mix (multiple singers on the verse vocals, spread across seven or eight tape channels) and translates each analog-era move into a modern-DAW equivalent: driving a console channel's line input for saturation, committing (printing) processed comps to tape rather than leaving them open-ended, a snare reverb that's actually an emulation of a specific vintage hardware unit, and a filtered slapback delay used as a hook effect. The back half is a single extended demonstration and the clear centerpiece of the video: recreating classic analog tape flanging — normally done by physically varispeeding a half-inch tape machine back and forth by hand to sweep the flange — using a modern delay-compensation plugin (the Eventide Precision Time Align) automated to sweep a couple of milliseconds around zero delay. He walks through both the original 2000s tape method and the live in-the-box recreation, explicitly framing it as "tape flange in a DAW, solved."

clariphonic-dsp-mkii.title: Clariphonic DSP MKII
clariphonic-dsp-mkii.html:
Category: EQ Vendor: Kush Audio

What it is

Kush Audio's parallel-EQ plugin, modeled on the classic passive/parallel EQ technique for adding 'air' and presence without harshness.

What it's used for

Adding smooth top-end lift and vocal/instrument presence using a parallel-EQ approach rather than standard subtractive/additive EQ.

FX chain notes

Used in parallel (blended in) after the main EQ pass, for final polish on vocals and mix busses.

Techniques

  • Run LAST in a vocal chain, explicitly as a restoration move rather than a first-pass brightening decision. "After that I'm doing a bit of Clariphonic to then make up for overall Shimmer where I might have lost it along the way" — placed after a de-ess → drive → EQ → Soothe → proximity-fix → parallel-comp → de-ess → cross-vocalist sidechain-duck stack, specifically to top up whatever top-end got dulled by everything upstream. A useful placement rule generally: treat this plugin as the corrective final stage of a busy chain, not the tone-shaping starting point. → EQ, AIR Slot, James Blake Vocal Chain — Mix with the Masters, MSM Mixing James Blake's Vocals

Used in my chains

The broad "seat it" tone stage — a hi-fi tilt/shelf EQ used late to sit a source against the vocal, not to carve surgically (that's Pro-Q 4's job):

  • Electric Bass DI Track — slot 4, broad seat: darker (Bass +1.5, Treble −1) for Motown support, brighter (Treble +1.5) for melodic/McCartney lines.
  • Electric Guitar Amp Track — slot 5, broad tone: Treble −1.5 dB with a low Treble Slope so the darkening is broad rather than shelf-y, and Master Air −20 to −30% to push the guitar back behind the vocal — guitars give up 2–5 kHz where the vocal lives (Masking and Carving).
  • Electric Guitar DI Track — slot 4, broad seat: darker/brighter to carve the DI lane apart from the mic'd guitar when both are in the song.

latency-free-tracking.title: Latency-Free Tracking
latency-free-tracking.html:
Getting Ableton to record on the grid while the performer hears a fully-produced monitor mix. Two layers: the settings (fix most of it) and the ghost latency track (fix all of it). Source: Kenny Beats' template workflow, used on ~150 released songs. Note: tracking through the Apollo's UAD Console (DSP monitoring) sidesteps most of this — this page is for when monitoring runs through Ableton plugins instead.

Layer 1 — The settings (do these once)

  1. Options → Reduced Latency When Monitoring: ON. The first switch to flip.
  2. Buffer size 128 while tracking (64 if the machine allows), never 1024 — Preferences → Audio. Kenny's demo: ~26 ms → ~6 ms overall latency just from this. Big buffers are for mixing sessions, small for recording. Under ~3 ms is unnoticeable to most performers.
  3. Driver Error Compensation to ~0 ms — after setting the buffer, trim the compensation field until the overall-latency readout reads as close to zero as possible (6 ms → 0.05 ms in his demo).
  4. Track vocals in a separate session from the beat — bounce the beat to a 2-track first: CPU stays fast at low buffer, and the bounce commits you ("imperfections you were gonna fix end up making the song").
  5. Simple plugins while tracking — CPU-heavy chains re-add latency; run Pro-Q 4 in Zero Latency mode while tracking, Natural Phase when mixing, and keep zero-latency processors (Pro-DS wideband) in the monitor chain.
