no-one-is-teaching-dorian-like-this-dani.title: NO ONE is teaching Dorian LIKE THIS! (Daniel Seriff)
no-one-is-teaching-dorian-like-this-dani.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A guitar-specific angle on the Dorian mode from Daniel Seriff: rather than teaching Dorian as a new seven-note scale shape to memorize from scratch, the whole lesson is built on the premise that most players already own the hard part — the minor pentatonic box — and Dorian is just that box plus two notes. Worked entirely in the key of D minor (the classic 10th-fret box), the lesson first adds the notes one at a time onto the familiar pentatonic shape, explicitly naming the optional "hexatonic" stopping point along the way (pentatonic + the 2, without going all the way to the full mode), then re-teaches the same two added notes inside a second, movable "diagonal pentatonic" fingering that Seriff frames as his preferred practical system because it copy-pastes to any root/string-set on the neck. The most useful theory nugget is a direct, ear-first A/B: Dorian and Aeolian (natural minor) are separated by exactly one note (the 6th, natural vs. flat), demonstrated back-to-back so the character difference is heard, not just read off a formula table — this matches Diatonic Modes's "one distinguishing degree" framing exactly but earns its own citation here for the concrete before/after audio demo. A sponsor read for Seriff's own paid course sits at the midpoint (11:49 total, ~1:20 of it ad); everything either side is genuinely actionable fretboard content, not just a theory table restated on guitar strings.

fix-your-slap-in-5-minutes.title: Fix Your Slap in 5 Minutes
fix-your-slap-in-5-minutes.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Another entry in BassBuzz's short live-coaching format (companion to Fix Your Plucking in 5 Minutes): Josh coaches a guest bassist, Matt from Source Audio, on slap technique in five minutes. Matt self-diagnoses the problem up front — he's aiming for one string (e.g. the A string) and often catches a neighbor (the E string), his hands feel "unwieldy," and he wants more efficiency and confidence in the left-hand/right-hand connection specifically for slap, which feels like a different action from his regular fingerstyle playing. Josh's read is telling: the groove and quarter-note feel are already genuinely solid — the "sloppy" feeling is coming entirely from hand mechanics, not timing or musicality. He isolates three mechanical fixes in order — thumb angle (narrowing the strike zone so it's not catching two strings at once), locking the thumb's position relative to the hand so the whole arm assembly moves to cross strings instead of the thumb hunting independently, and a small forward wrist bend that opens a gap behind the string so the thumb doesn't immediately re-mute what it just struck. A stripped-down E-A-D-G slap-mute drill (no musical content, pure string isolation) reinforces the first two fixes, and the session closes with Matt replaying his original riff purely as an accuracy exercise, reporting audibly less unwanted string ringing by the end. Short, dense, and immediately practice-able, in the same mold as the plucking-hand companion video — no filler, no theory tangents, just mechanics.

tory-lanez-underwater-synth-chain.title: Tory Lanez Underwater Synth Chain
tory-lanez-underwater-synth-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a from-scratch "underwater synth + vocal chop" melodic R&B beat, reverse-engineered from Tory Lanez's "Take Care," name-checking Chris Brown and Drake as the same stylistic lane. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, how to make melodic r&b beats for tory lanez & chris brown (underwater synth/vocal sample). Unlike the richer multi-take builds in Kendrick Lamar Soul Sample Chain or Future-Style Vintage Sample Chain, this beat is deliberately minimal — only two melodic elements (the synth pad and the vocal chop) for almost the entire runtime, with a flute added only to salvage a weak hook late in the build.

Chain overview

A single reversed one-shot, hand-trimmed and driven by a repeating 4-chord progression, is processed into a submerged-sounding pad; a Splice vocal chop gets a parallel heavy-processing treatment; two low-level texture layers sit underneath both; a 3-layer hi-hat kit plus a bounce-varied kick and long 808 carry the drums; a flute is bolted on late purely to strengthen the hook. The reusable core idea: reverse + hand-trim a one-shot for pulse, then bury the result under progressively heavier filtering/reverb until it stops reading as a clean synth — the "underwater" character is entirely a processing choice, not a special patch.

1. Synth pad — reversed/trimmed one-shot

  • Source: an ambient/synthy one-shot from the producer's own ("Nami's") one-shot kit, chosen because it matched the "watered down synth" heard in the Tory Lanez reference.
  • Reverse + trim: reverse the one-shot, then hand-adjust its start point and length until the reversed tail's natural swell pulses in and out on its own — no LFO/modulation device involved.
  • Chords, D minor tonal center, one per bar: Dm7 → D♯maj7 (♭II7 borrowing) → Gm7 (top two notes dropped an octave) → Fmaj (C dropped an octave). Full theory: Chord Progressions.
  • Rhythmic pattern: each chord hit four times per bar — combines with the reversed-tail swell to produce the track's signature pulse.
  • 🎬 From video: reverse-and-hand-trim is a zero-extra-plugin way to generate rhythmic pulse before reaching for a dedicated modulation device. → Sampling and Sound Selection

afro-sample-chain.title: Afro Sample Chain
afro-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: the exact 3-element sample loner built and sent out that ended up placed on an unnamed song with over a million streams — reverse-engineered from his own breakdown, how i made the sample that got a 1 million stream placement (it's easier than you think!?). Unlike most other chains on this page (a specific artist's record being copied), this one is loner's own confirmed working sample, built specifically as an "afro sample" for another producer to develop. The processing across all three elements is deliberately plain (EQ, reverb, chorus, delay — nothing exotic); the real lesson of this chain is what got LEFT OUT (a perc loop and a horn layer, both built then cut) so the sample stayed open for a collaborator to build on. See Sampling and Sound Selection and Arrangement and Song Form for the restraint argument in full.

Chain overview

Two AAS Lounge Lizard EP-3 layers (a dry chord bed and a heavily-processed pad built from the same chord progression) plus one Kontakt "Evolution Strawberry" guitar counter-melody. A perc loop and a horn layer were built and then deliberately removed before the sample was sent out. The whole finished mix gets pitched down 2 semitones on the master as the last step.

1. Chord bed — Lounge Lizard "blues comp" preset

  • Instrument: AAS Lounge Lizard EP-3, "blues comp" preset. No owned electric-piano VST equivalent tracked — see Plugin Wishlist.
  • Chords: F major → G major (C passing note) → A minor → D passing note → E minor (pitched up an octave to match the preceding chord). Two majors then two minors, a deliberate melodic→emotional arc. → Melody Writing
  • Feel: strummed (not block-triggered) for a natural feel, with deliberate gaps left between chord hits — the simplicity is what makes the gaps stand out, giving the part "bounce" before drums are even added. → Rhythm and Groove, Pocket and Microtiming
  • FX: EQ Eight cutting low end + some mid-range, then a light spring reverb (owned lane: ValhallaVintageVerb spring-modeled algorithm, or UAD RealVerb-Pro). (general starting point — no specific frequencies given) → EQ, Reverb
secs: 1. Chord bed — Lounge Lizard "blues comp" preset

roland-juno-106.title: Roland Juno-106
roland-juno-106.html:
What it is

Roland's affordable 6-voice polysynth — one DCO per voice, one envelope, one filter, and the most beloved chorus circuit ever built. It was the "starter polysynth" of the 80s and has never left fashion since: house stabs, synthwave beds, dream-pop pads, and half of modern bedroom production speak Juno.

What makes the sound

  • DCOs (digitally-clocked analog oscillators) — rock-stable tuning, unlike a drifting Jupiter/Prophet. Why: all 6 voices share one common clock and stay perfectly phase-locked to each other — play the same note on all 6 voices and there's zero beating between them, unlike a true free-running analog oscillator design (Prophet-5) where identical notes across voices drift slightly and beat. One oscillator per voice should sound thin, which is why…
  • …the Bucket-brigade chorus (I/II/I+II) is the actual instrument. The famously noisy BBD stereo chorus splits and detunes the mono voice into a wide, glassy ensemble. Juno pad = simple saw + chorus. That hiss is authentic → TAL-Chorus-LX exists purely to clone it.
  • A single very musical analog lowpass (self-resonant, with that specific squelchy sweep) + HPF slider for instantly cleaning boom out of pads — the "Juno bass to bed" workflow is built into the panel → BED Slot, BASS Slot.
  • PWM on the DCO gives shimmering motion without tuning chaos; sub-oscillator slider adds one-knob weight.
  • Six voices force economical writing: stabs, pads, and basses, all committed and mix-ready.
  • The filter is a Roland IR3109 chip — the same chip used in the Jupiter-8 and Juno-6/60, which is why all four synths share a family-recognizable low-pass character despite different oscillator sections. Single shared envelope generator drives both VCA and VCF (a deliberate simplification vs. the Prophet-5's per-section envelopes) — fewer knobs, but any envelope change affects amp and filter together. HPF is a stepped (not continuous/voltage-controllable) global control, and its "0" position is actually a slight bass boost rather than true bypass.
  • Digital pitch bend is exact — bends a precise octave up/down, unlike the earlier all-analog Juno-6/60 bender, which drifts unpredictably. One of the concrete upgrades the 106 made over its own siblings, alongside added MIDI and refined patch management.

akai-mpc60.title: Akai MPC60
akai-mpc60.html:
What it is

The MIDI Production Center — Roger Linn's post-Linn-Electronics design for Akai, fusing a 12-bit sampler, a 99-track MIDI sequencer, and the now-universal 4×4 velocity pad grid into one box. The MPC turned sampling into an instrument you play, and its sequencer timing became the feel of hip hop. Every pad controller and every DAW drum grid descends from this machine.

What makes the sound

  • 12-bit / 40 kHz sampling with Akai's converters + filtering — grittier than modern digital but brighter and cleaner than the E-mu SP-1200; "punchy" is the usual word.
  • The swing and timing are the real instrument. Linn's quantize/swing (54–58% is the classic pocket) plus the machine's slightly loose internal timing produce the head-nod feel; MPC swing is arguably the most copied groove in music software → Ableton's groove pool, Group Humanizer.
  • Pads + note-repeat made programming physical — velocity-layered hats, drum rolls, and chopped-sample performances that sound played, not drawn.
  • 16 levels / tuning per pad and quick chop-assign workflow → the chop-a-loop-across-pads vocabulary of hip hop production → Sampling and Sound Selection.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Drum Rack + Simpler/Sampler replicate the chop workflow (slice-to-drum-rack is the MPC move in Ableton); Ableton's MPC-style groove files for the swing; Decimort 2 for the 12-bit converter character; Group Humanizer for pocket.
  • Paid: Akai MPC Software / MPC hardware line (direct descendants), XLN XO for a modern take on the workflow.
  • Free: Akai MPC Beats (free version of the modern MPC software); MPC60-processed drum kits circulate widely.

Used on

  • DJ Shadow — Endtroducing..... (1996): built almost entirely on an MPC60 + records, documented and celebrated.
  • DJ Premier — Gang Starr-era productions on MPC60: the boom-bap swing standard.
  • Genre/era: late-80s→90s hip hop production wholesale; the MPC3000 successor carried it on (J Dilla's machine — his note will cover the drunk-swing evolution).

gorillaz-vocal-chain.title: Gorillaz Vocal Chain
gorillaz-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: 2D's lead vocal — lo-fi, band-limited, tape-warped, slightly detached and unpolished on purpose. The character comes from narrowing the vocal's frequency window and degrading it, not from cleaning it up. Signal source: Dry lead vocal, already comped/edited, no processing yet.

Chain overview

Tune → band-limit → level → degrade (the core ingredient) → tame new harshness → subtle wobble/width → dub-style delay → boxed reverb. The whole chain works against "clean" — every stage after compression is there to remove fidelity, not add polish.

dijon-vocal-chain.title: Dijon Vocal Chain
dijon-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: cracked, desperate, performed — a voice breaking up at the edges with the whole room bleeding in. The character is mostly capture, not plugins: omni mic in an untreated room, monitors blasting, take-one energy kept. What sounds like "processing" on Absolutely is largely bleed — the entire song coming back through the vocal mic ("It's literally just his voice… you're hearing the entire song coming through" — Tommy King). Signal source: a raw, committed take. Comp lightly — imperfections are the genre.

Step 1 — Record (this chain lives or dies here)

  • Mic: Neumann TLM 102 in omni if available — otherwise back off the mic 1–3 ft in an untreated room. His album chain was an AKG 414 (omni) → Neve 1073 — yours: UAD Neve 1073 (Unison), driven harder than a clean pop vocal (the 1073 pushed = the first distortion stage).
  • Record with the speakers ON (moderate, or one small speaker) — the bleed is the glue. Or the Shure SM57 handheld with monitors up for the aggressive lane.
  • Sing it like a take, not a comp — punch full phrases, keep cracks, breaths, mic handling. No UAD 1176LN needed on the way in unless peaks are wild (2 dB max); UAD Pultec EQP-1A bypass.

Chain overview

Level → drive → band-shape → break up → real-room space. Everything pushes toward "performance in a room," away from "vocal on a track."

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. LALA — Leveling

  • 3–6 dB GR, pushed harder than tasteful — the constant opto squeeze keeps the quiet cracked phrases as loud as the shouts (that suffocating closeness).

2. Decapitator — The break-up

  • Style N or E · Drive 4–6 · Punish on for the peaks moments · Mix 50–70% — this is a lead effect, not seasoning
  • Why: The signature — the voice audibly distorting when he pushes. Automate Drive/Mix up on the emotional peaks so the breakup follows the performance.

3. Pro-Q 4 — Rough shape

  • Gentle HPF ~80 Hz (keep chest — don't clean it) · tame 2.5–4 kHz only if the distortion gets spiky · no air shelf — polish is the enemy.

4. RC-20 Retro Color — Texture

  • Tape/Lo-Fi · wobble 10–20% · noise 10% · Mix ~30% — the take sounds found, not produced.

5. Soothe2 — Only if needed

  • Light, 2–5 kHz — rescue listenability without sanding the grit.
secs: Step 1 — Record (this chain lives or dies here)

sequential-prophet-5.title: Sequential Prophet-5
sequential-prophet-5.html:
What it is

Dave Smith's masterpiece — the first fully programmable polyphonic synth, the instrument that defined what "a polysynth" is. Five voices, two oscillators each, patch memory that actually worked, and a sound so complete that studios have never stopped booking it. The first microcontroller-based synth, full stop — Smith repurposed a Z80 chip (the same class used in home computers of the era) to scan the keyboard/panel, assign voices, and generate control voltages, replacing the CS-80's room of discrete analog logic with a single digital "brain." One genuinely novel capability that came with it: the Prophet-5 could tune its own oscillators (hold two specific keys simultaneously to trigger auto-calibration) — a first; the CS-80 and other pre-microcontroller synths required a tech to manually calibrate drift by hand. Tradeoff for going microcontroller-first this early: no velocity, no aftertouch — keys are on/off only, dynamics have to come from elsewhere in the signal chain.

simmons-sds-v.title: Simmons SDS-V
simmons-sds-v.html:
What it is

Not a drum machine but a drum synthesizer — an analog brain triggered by Simmons' iconic hexagonal pads, played by an actual drummer. The SDS-V (SDS-5) is the "80s electronic tom" incarnate: the descending doooom fill that stamps a record with its decade in half a second.

What makes the sound

  • Per-voice analog synthesis, not samples: a swept oscillator (the pitch-drop envelope is the sound), a noise source, and a click/attack component, each with its own filter and envelope — kick, snare, and three toms as five little synthesizers on cards.
  • The tom voice = triangle/sine swept downward with resonance — huge, hollow, synthetic; run through a hall reverb (or gated verb) it becomes the canonical 80s fill → pure TRANSIENT Slot drama.
  • Velocity-ish dynamics from real playing — pads feed playing dynamics into the circuits, so it phrases like a drummer, unlike any step-programmed box of its era.
  • The snare's noise/tone crack cuts like a rifle shot; the whole kit is mix-ready loud, no low-end mud.

Digital versions

  • Owned: DS Tom — Ableton's DS drum synths are literally this architecture (swept osc + noise + click); DS Kick/DS Snare for the rest of the kit; Microtonic for a full synthesized-kit approach; gate a ValhallaVintageVerb/Ghz Megaverb 3 tail to complete the cliché.
  • Paid: UVI Beat Box Anthology 2 (Simmons kits), assorted SDS sample libraries.
  • Free: SDS-V one-shots are in every 80s sample archive; the DS Tom recipe costs nothing.

Used on

  • Duran Duran — mid-80s records/tours ("The Wild Boys" era), Roger Taylor's hybrid kit.
  • Rush — Neil Peart's mid-80s electronic-kit phase (Grace Under Pressure era) ran Simmons pads.
  • Genre/era: 1982–87 pop/rock/R&B wholesale — the electronic tom fill, the Synthwave revival's favorite drum cliché to quote.

roland-tr-909.title: Roland TR-909
roland-tr-909.html:
What it is

The TR-808's successor and the drum machine of dance music. Another commercial failure in its day (~10,000 units, killed within two years by the sample-based LinnDrum/DMX wave), the 909 got dumped into pawn shops cheap — which is exactly how Chicago house and Detroit techno producers got hold of them. Its kick, clap, and open hat are the rhythmic DNA of house, techno, and basically every four-on-the-floor genre since.

What makes the sound

  • Hybrid architecture — the key fact: kick, snare, toms, clap are analog synthesis; hi-hats and cymbals are 6-bit samples clocked through analog VCAs. That crunchy, gritty 909 hat sizzle is literally low-bit-rate digital audio — lo-fi by necessity, iconic by accident.
  • The kick is a triangle-wave VCO shaped toward sine with a fast pitch envelope and a click transient circuit on top — punchier, more mid-forward and shorter than the 808's sub ring. It's a dance-floor thump (energy ~60–100 Hz) where the 808 is a bass note → Kick Design, TRANSIENT Slot.
  • The clap = filtered noise retriggered through a multi-tap envelope (the "several people clapping" flam) + a reverb-ish noise tail — the house-music clap.
  • The open hat's 6-bit crunch + accent structure defined the offbeat "tsss" of house; shuffle/flam and per-step accent gave 909 patterns their swing.
  • MIDI (it was one of the first drum machines with it) + the 16-step X0X sequencer made it the live techno instrument.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Microtonic (nails analog-style 909 kicks/percussion), Kick 3 (909-style kick synthesis), Drum Rack/Impulse with 909 sample packs, kHs Bitcrush to fake the 6-bit hat crunch on any noise/cymbal source.
  • Paid: Roland Cloud TR-909 (official ACB), D16 Drumazon 2; Behringer RD-9 in hardware.
  • Free: high-quality 909 sample packs are everywhere (Samples From Mars 909 etc. often on sale/free).

Used on

  • Chicago house from the mid-80s on — Frankie Knuckles famously bought one of Derrick May's 909s, wiring the Detroit↔Chicago origin story into one machine.
  • Daft Punk — "Revolution 909" (1997): a homage in the title; French house runs on 909 kits.
  • Jeff Mills — "The Bells" and his live three-deck-plus-909 sets: the 909 as a performance instrument in techno.
  • Genre/era: Chicago house, Detroit techno, acid house (with the TB-303), 90s rave/hardcore, French house — see House - EDM, EDM Subgenres.

roland-tb-303.title: Roland TB-303
roland-tb-303.html:
What it is

The Bass Line — a silver box meant to give practicing guitarists a fake bassist (Roland TR-606 was its drummer). It failed completely at that job, hit pawn shops for pennies, and was then misused into acid house: the single most famous case of a machine's flop becoming a genre. The 303 doesn't imitate bass; it IS a sound.

What makes the sound

  • One VCO (saw or square) into an 18 dB/oct diode-ladder lowpass — a filter topology unlike Moog's or Roland's own synth lines: raspy, vocal, squelchy, with a resonance that squeals instead of blooming.
  • Accent is the magic circuit: accented steps goose VCA level and filter envelope together (with resonance interplay), so a pattern breathes and barks — the "acid" articulation is accent + resonance + envelope-mod knobs ridden live.
  • Slide (glide between tied steps) gives the drunken legato swoops; the famously awkward step sequencer produced happy-accident patterns nobody would play on a keyboard.
  • Crank resonance, ride cutoff, run it into distortion → the acid scream → Saturation and Distortion.

Digital versions

  • Owned: no dedicated 303 in the collection — closest paths: the MS-20-style trick already in the Sound Selection Guide (drive a resonant filter's peak into distortion), Analog/Serum 2 mono saw into kHs Nonlinear Filter or Volcano 3 with high resonance + Saturator; automate cutoff per-step.
  • Paid: D16 Phoscyon 2 (the standard), AudioRealism ABL3, Roland Cloud TB-303; Behringer TD-3 in hardware (~$150).
  • Free: Open303/JC303 (open-source, surprisingly good).

roland-tr-505.title: Roland TR-505
roland-tr-505.html:
What it is

The bottom rung of the TR ladder — a ~$300 plastic PCM box with the 707's brain, a smaller speaker-grade kit, and a rack of latin percussion borrowed from the TR-727's world. It was the drum machine you could actually afford in 1986, which made it the bedroom machine of early house, techno, and countless demos.

What makes the sound

  • Even shorter, cheaper companded PCM samples than the 707 — thin, papery kick and snare, chirpy toms, plus timbale/conga/cowbell latin voices that give it a distinct flavor the 707 lacks.
  • No individual outs, no tuning — one stereo pair, take the kit or leave it; the flat, boxy print through its converters is the sound.
  • Full X0X-style step programming + MIDI at a toy price — the point was access, and the patterns kids wrote on it seeded scenes.
  • Its cheap-and-cheerful character has made it a lo-fi/indie cult box today — the "honest little drum machine" aesthetic → Bedroom Pop - Indie.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Drum Rack / Impulse with 505 samples; Cassette / RC-20 Retro Color lean into the budget-plastic vibe.
  • Paid: UVI Beat Box Anthology 2; Samples From Mars and similar vintage-archive packs.
  • Free: 505 kits circulate in every free drum-machine sample archive.

Used on

  • Genre/era: late-80s bedroom house/techno demos, UK bleep-era budget productions, and the modern lo-fi indie/bedroom lane that reaches for it precisely because it sounds cheap — credits are largely undocumented at the record level, so this one stays genre-level on purpose.

roland-juno-6-juno-60.title: Roland Juno-6 - Juno-60
roland-juno-6-juno-60.html:
What it is

The original Junos — Roland's first affordable polysynths and the Roland Juno-106's slightly wilder parents. Same one-DCO-plus-chorus recipe, but with an arpeggiator, punchier envelopes, and a filter many players swear is sweeter than the 106's. The Juno-60 (patch memory, DCB interface) is the studio darling that never went out of style.

What makes the sound

  • Same DNA as the 106: rock-stable DCO, sub-osc slider, PWM, the BBD chorus that turns one oscillator into an ensemble — see Roland Juno-106 for the full anatomy.
  • What's different and why people care: a hair more filter character (earlier IR3109 voicing driven harder), snappier envelopes, and the onboard arpeggiator — the up/down octave arp through that chorus is its own genre sound.
  • No MIDI (Juno-6 has nothing, Juno-60 has DCB — modern retrofits abound) and no velocity: everything lands at one confident dynamic, which reads as committed in a track.
  • The 60's patch memory made it the giggable one; the 6's pure-panel immediacy makes it the jam machine.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Model 84 Polyphonic Synthesizer (Juno-family emulation — covers this sound; add Ableton's arpeggiator MIDI effect for the 6/60 arp), TAL-Chorus-LX (the chorus, free), Analog/Drift for stock approximations.
  • Paid: Arturia Jun-6 V (models this generation specifically), TAL-U-NO-LX, Roland Cloud Juno-60.
  • Free: TAL-Chorus-LX; TAL-U-NO-62.

Used on

  • Overmono — in their studio gear list (no specific technique given). → TN 187 Overmono - Gear List — Tape Notes
  • Cyndi Lauper — "Time After Time" (1983): Rob Hyman's Juno-60 carries the intro/bed (widely documented).
  • Genre/era: 80s synthpop and Italo, 90s house, and the modern indie/bedroom-pop studio staple lane — the 60 is arguably the most re-bought vintage poly of the 2010s revival → Bedroom Pop - Indie, Synthwave.

roland-sh-101.title: Roland SH-101
roland-sh-101.html:
What it is

A cheap plastic monosynth (came in red and blue, with an optional keytar grip) that sold poorly, then became the bass synth of dance music — probably the most-recorded analog bassline machine of the 90s rave/techno era and still a first-call sound.

What makes the sound

  • One VCO, mixed waveforms: saw + square/PWM + sub-oscillator sliders blend into a single fat mono voice — the mixer-of-waves design is why 101 basses sound dense despite one oscillator.
  • The Roland 24 dB filter driven by a snappy one-shot envelope — instant rubbery attack, quick close; acid-adjacent squelch when resonance rises, warm round thump when it doesn't → BASS Slot archetype.
  • The onboard step sequencer (plus arp) locks tight, hypnotic 16th-note bass patterns — the Synthwave "16th-note bass engine" and 90s techno's pulse both live here.
  • Noise source + white-simple architecture: commit fast, tweak live, no menu anywhere.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Analog (mono patch: saw+square+sub into the 24 dB filter — very close), Serum 2/DUNE 3 one-osc-plus-sub recipes, kHs Ladder Filter to Roland-ify any bass.
  • Paid: TAL BassLine-101 (the reference emulation), Roland Cloud SH-101, D16 LuSH-2; Behringer MS-1 in hardware.
  • Free: the Analog recipe above covers it in stock Ableton.

Used on

  • Genre/era: 90s techno/rave/big beat basslines wholesale, UK acid/electro, and the modern synthwave bass engine — cited constantly across that era's artist interviews (Aphex Twin's early rig among the best-documented 101 fanbases), with individual track credits rarely pinned; largely genre-level per the rule.

e-mu-sp-1200.title: E-mu SP-1200
e-mu-sp-1200.html:
What it is

E-mu's SP-1200 sampling drum machine is the sound of golden-era hip hop — 10 seconds of total sample time, 12-bit resolution, and a workflow so limited it forced an aesthetic. Producers chopped records into it for a decade after better specs existed, because "better" didn't sound like that.

What makes the sound

  • 12-bit / 26.04 kHz sampling — immediate loss of top end and added quantization grit; the "dusty" sound is literal information loss.
  • SSM2044 analog low-pass filters on the outputs — after the crunchy digital conversion, everything passes through warm analog filtering. Digital dirt + analog rounding is the signature combo → same principle as running kHs Bitcrush into a dark filter.
  • The 33/45 trick: 10 seconds was nothing, so producers sampled vinyl at 45 rpm (or pitched up) and played it back pitched down, stretching sample time — and the repitch artifacts (darkened, grainy, slightly warbly loops) became the boom-bap texture → Sampling and Sound Selection.
  • Coarse pitch steps and chunky pad-bank workflow made chops percussive and confident — the machine pushes you toward loops-as-drums.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Decimort 2 (D16's vintage-sampler emulation — has SP-1200 mode: bit depth, sample rate, and filter character in one plugin; put it on any Drum Rack or Sampler chop chain), RC-20 Retro Color for the vinyl/dust layer, kHs Bitcrush for a quick version.
  • Paid: Inphonik RX950/RX1200 (dedicated SP-1200 plugin), Rossum Electro-Music SP-1200 reissue (hardware, by the original designer).
  • Free: the Decimort/bitcrush recipe above covers it; SP-1200-processed drum packs are common.

Used on

  • Public Enemy — Bomb Squad productions (It Takes a Nation of Millions...): SP-1200 collage chaos.
  • Pete Rock, Large Professor, EPMD — the boom-bap canon; the SP-1200 (often paired with an Akai S950 for longer samples) is that era's texture.
  • Daft Punk — "Da Funk" (1995): that beat is an SP-1200, documented by the band — the crunch works outside hip hop too.
  • Genre/era: golden-era/boom-bap hip hop 1987–1995 (Rap Subgenres boom bap card), early French house.

akai-mpc2000.title: Akai MPC2000
akai-mpc2000.html:
What it is

The MPC democratized — Akai's post-Linn, mass-market MPC (especially the 2000XL revision) that put the pads-and-swing workflow in every bedroom and project studio of the late 90s and 2000s. If the Akai MPC60 built hip hop's grammar and the Akai MPC3000 perfected it, the 2000/2000XL is the machine a whole generation actually learned on.

What makes the sound

  • 16-bit / 44.1 kHz sampling with Akai's house converter character — slightly rounded, punchy, forgiving; cleaner than the 12-bit ancestors but still recognizably "MPC" rather than DAW-flat.
  • The same swing/quantize/note-repeat vocabulary inherited from the Linn-designed machines — the pocket is the product → Group Humanizer.
  • XL added the chop-shop workflow conveniences (auto-chop, time stretch with its famously crunchy artifacts) — the 2000XL time-stretch grain is its one genuinely unique sonic fingerprint, still sought after for lo-fi textures.
  • Zone/slice sampling + effects board options made it a self-contained beat studio — the "one machine, one producer" archetype of 2000s beat culture.

Digital versions

  • Owned: Drum Rack + Simpler/Sampler (slice-to-drum-rack = the XL chop workflow); MPC groove files for the swing; RC-20 Retro Color/kHs Pitch Shifter abuse approximates the time-stretch crunch.
  • Paid: Akai MPC Software / MPC Live-era hardware (lineage), XLN XO for a modern chop workflow.
  • Free: Akai MPC Beats (the free modern descendant).

Used on

  • Genre/era: the backbone of late-90s/2000s underground and mainstream hip hop production and the 2000s beat-scene culture that followed — ubiquity again beats clean documentation, so credits stay genre-level; the marquee-name MPC credits in this library attach to the 60 and 3000.

fix-your-plucking-in-5-minutes.title: Fix Your Plucking in 5 Minutes
fix-your-plucking-in-5-minutes.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short live-coaching format from BassBuzz: a bassist who self-diagnoses "sloppy finger speed and accuracy" — specifically hitting the wrong string when improvising fast 16th-note lines — plays a before riff, gets coached through a five-minute fix, then replays the same riff after. The coach's diagnosis: the stumbling isn't a raw-speed problem, it's that improvised fast lines pull the plucking hand outside patterns it has actually rehearsed, so the fingers hesitate mid-line. The fix is a small, drillable set of string-crossing exercises — a fixed number of plucks per string walked up and down the strings (2, 3, 4, then 1 per string, since most real playing needs two, three, or four notes per string before moving on) — plus, critically, deciding in advance whether a direction change rakes (repeats the same finger across the string change) or alternates (keeps strictly alternating fingers through it), since indecision at that exact fork is what causes the flub. A metronome-driven accuracy threshold rounds it out: find the tempo you nail 100% clean, then creep it up until you're missing roughly 10% of the time, and drill there rather than either the too-easy tempo or full speed. Short video, but genuinely concrete and immediately practice-able — no filler.

rx-music-rebalance.title: RX Music Rebalance
rx-music-rebalance.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: iZotope

What it is

An RX module using AI source separation to independently adjust the level of vocals, bass, drums, and other elements within a finished mix. Owned in both the RX 10 and RX 11 suites.

What it's used for

Rebalancing an already-mixed stereo file (e.g. remix stems recovery, karaoke creation, fixing a buried vocal in a bounced reference).

FX chain notes

Used as a corrective/creative tool on a finished stereo file rather than during the original mix.

Techniques

  • Phase-cancel the separated stems against the source before trusting them. Giles Martin's QA discipline for the Beatles "demixing" remixes (a bespoke, higher-end cousin of this same AI source-separation category): after splitting a mix into stems, sum the stems back together and phase-invert against the original source — a correct separation cancels to silence. "I don't want the process to add anything or take away anything from what we have... it's important that we start from a raw format" before any further EQ/processing. Applies directly to any stem split pulled from this plugin: before rebalancing a vocal/bass/drum level or exporting a stem split, sum the separated stems and phase-cancel them against the source stereo file to confirm the AI split didn't silently color or lose anything. → Ozone 9 Master Rebalance, Phase Alignment — Tape Notes (Giles Martin), TN 190 The Beatles (Giles Martin) - Full Video Episode

Key Parameters

image: Images/RX Music Rebalance.png
coords: Images/RX Music Rebalance.coords.json

Tap a numbered circle for what that control does, the technique, and any artist example.

# Parameter What it is / does Technique
① Stem faders (Vocals / Bass / Drums / Other) AI level control of each separated stem (Mute/Solo per stem) Bring a vocal up or drums down in a finished mix
② Sensitivity (per stem) How aggressively that stem is separated Small moves keep artifacts low
③ Quality Separation quality (Best / …) Best for a final render; lower while auditioning
④ Stem split / Render Export the separated stems, or render the rebalanced mix Stem split to pull a rough acapella/instrumental

3-inst-synth-bus.title: 3 Inst-Synth Bus
3-inst-synth-bus.html:
Role: Finish coat on the harmonic section. Lightest bus in the template — keys/synths arrive already polished (VSTs are pre-produced sounds).

Chain

1. Sie-Q — Musical tilt

  • A dB brighter or darker to seat the whole section behind the vocal.

2. Kramer Tape — Analog unify

  • 15 ips (④) · Flux low (①) · Record low (②) · Playback to unity (③)
  • Why: running every digital instrument through the same tape stage gives sample-based and synthesized parts one shared "recorded" texture — the cheapest cohesion available.

3. Bus glue for presence, not squash — a UA 33609 alternative

  • 🎬 From video: Marcella Araica adds a UA 33609 here (an "All Music" bus carrying samples, transitional risers, AND guitars together) deliberately light: "I don't want it compressing too much, I want it to breathe. It's not about really over-compressing it, just allowing it to give it more presence without it feeling like it's being [squashed]." Rode the gain by ear against the mix and pulled the guitars down slightly in the same pass — a light-glue-for-presence move, not a leveling/control move. Unowned — see Plugin Wishlist; owned stand-in for the same light-touch role is this chain's own Sie-Q/Kramer Tape pairing, or Solid Bus Comp barely engaged. Contrast with the SAME plugin dialed much harder on the drum bus in the same session — see Drums Bus and Compression Staging. → Committing and Printing, Compression Staging, Drums Bus, Guitar Bus — Mix with the Masters (Marcella Araica), Printing stems through analog equipment with Marcella Araica

4. Duck the section off the vocal (add when there's a lead)

  • 🎬 From video: Disclosure make room for a soft lead by ducking the whole synth section off the vocal — a compressor keyed off the vocal (via a muted empty bus), or Soothe2 / Pro-MB in dynamic/sidechain mode so the synths give up exactly the frequencies the vocal occupies (sharper than a wideband ducker like Trackspacer). Slow release so it flows. → Sidechaining, LEAD Slot — Disclosure, Looking For Love / Higher Than Ever Before / Help Me Lose My Mind.

Variations

  • If this bus feels redundant: it often is for sparse arrangements — bypass and let the group feed the master. Buses earn their place in dense mixes.

beatles-psych-rock-sample-chain.title: Beatles Psych-Rock Sample Chain
beatles-psych-rock-sample-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: a full period-accurate psych-rock "sample" built from scratch (not sourced from a real record) — a Fender Stratocaster guitar and a Höfner violin-bass replica processed to sound like a genuine 1960s/70s recording, using real research into the actual gear the Beatles and their contemporaries used rather than a generic "vintage" preset. Reverse-engineered from a loner (YouTube) breakdown, these 1960's production secrets will change the way you make samples!?. Nate owns the two lead instruments this chain is built around: Fender Stratocaster and Hofner B-Bass H-Series.

Chain overview

Two parallel instrument chains (guitar, bass) built on real-gear research, finished with hard L/R panning to opposite sides so the two elements "fill both sides" of the stereo field rather than competing for the same space — the video's own stated first lesson from studying the era.

blending-melodies-with-marcella-araica.title: Blending melodies with Marcella Araica
blending-melodies-with-marcella-araica.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

A short, screen-recorded Pro Tools clip of Marcella Araica (Mix with the Masters) working two separate melodic elements of the same record: a doubled/harmonized string pair (a lower and a higher string line) and an 808 that Danja has placed twice in the same verse. On the strings, she demonstrates a sub-mix-first workflow — route the harmony pair through a shared, labeled Aux, EQ each part individually to carve them apart from each other and from the (not-yet-processed) bass, then glue the pair with a UA 33609 stereo compressor on the Aux itself. On the 808, the clip is a monitoring-and-color pass: she mixes 808 low end primarily on NS-10s (notoriously bad at translating sub content, which forces careful decisions) before confirming on the mains, adds distortion purely for grit and cut-through, and reaches for the Pultec EQP-1A as her go-to low-end EQ for its emulated-hardware "sense of bottom." The clip closes mid-thought, checking whether Danja's second 808 hit in the verse is a genuine duplicate of the first or a distinct sound. Light on hard numbers for the 808 stage (qualitative — "add distortion," "I love this EQ") but the string EQ carve gives three concrete frequency values, and the sub-mix-first routing habit and NS-10-primary monitoring choice are both concrete, transferable workflow moves.

steve-porcaro-in-studio-writing-human-na.title: Steve Porcaro In-Studio - Writing Human Nature and Unreleased MJ Songs Part 1
steve-porcaro-in-studio-writing-human-na.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

An in-studio conversation between Anthony Marinelli and Toto's Steve Porcaro (who wrote "Human Nature" and worked every Michael Jackson album from Off the Wall through HIStory in various capacities) about writing and recording with Jackson. Mostly biography and studio-culture anecdote — the "yatas" nickname story, the origin of the "Human Nature" demo, MJ's turntable-referencing habit — but several passages carry real, specific technique: the actual instrument breakdown behind "Human Nature," a keyboard-transition trick, and Porcaro's own filter/mix philosophy on string patches.

tn-184-myles-smith-peter-fenn-gear-list.title: TN 184 Myles Smith & Peter Fenn - Gear List
tn-184-myles-smith-peter-fenn-gear-list.html:
📎 View on Patreon

Synopsis

A Patreon-exclusive gear-list image post accompanying Tape Notes' Myles Smith / Peter Fenn episode (TN 184) — no video/audio, just a 7-page PDF spread of studio plugins and a handful of hardware/instrument pieces. Same shape as the other TN gear-list posts: one-line vendor-style "what it is" blurbs, no artist-specific settings or workflow given for any item — an inventory, not a technique breakdown.

tame-impala-vocal-chain.title: Tame Impala Vocal Chain
tame-impala-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: soft, dreamy, dissolved into the track — a falsetto-leaning voice layered until Parker "can't recognize the sound of his own voice," phased and echoed, sitting 2–4 dB lower than a pop vocal ("the instruments are brutal, the voice is really soft"). Another instrument, not the focus. Signal source: relaxed, breathy delivery — simple melodies, no runs. Parker tracks on a dynamic (MD-421); your Shure SM57 is the closer match, Neumann TLM 102 for the airier lane.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD UA 610-B (Unison) — soft tube, gentle level (the round choice over the 1073 here)
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 2–3 dB smooth
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — bypass - The real step 1 is takes: 4–8 unison layers of the same line, soft delivery — the blur between them IS the sound. Pitch-shifted doubles (octave/5th at low level) for thickness without "chipmunk."

Chain overview

Thin it → level it → color it → smear it. His voice reads thin on purpose — don't fatten it; the lushness comes from layers + effects, not body.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Pro-Q 4 — Thin and seat

  • HPF up to ~150 Hz (yes, that high) · scoop low mids −2 to −3 dB @ ~350 Hz · gentle presence, no aggressive air
  • Why: the vocal cuts by being narrow, floating above the brutal instruments rather than competing.

2. Pro-C 2 — Subtle level

  • 3:1 · 2–4 dB — even, unremarkable, invisible.

3. Saturn 2 — Warm blur

  • Tape, low drive, mix ~25% — softens consonants into the wash.

4. PhaserFlanger or ValhallaSpaceModulator — The psych movement

  • Slow phaser, low depth, ~20–30% mix — constant gentle sweep. Automate deeper per section/line ("Mind Mischief" moments).

Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is most of the sound)

  • Tape echo: EchoBoy Space Echo/Tape mode, 1/8 or dotted-1/8, feedback 25–40%, wobble/saturation ON, send generous — echoes louder relative to the dry than pop would allow.
  • Long modulated verb: ValhallaVintageVerb (70s mode, 2.5–4 s, modulation high) — the dissolve. Send hot; duck it under the dry only if lyrics vanish entirely.
  • Width Send on the layered stack; slap for the drier RnB-leaning cuts ("The Less I Know the Better" verses).
  • Automate the delay time knob for detune-warble transitions (the hardware move).
secs: Step 3 — Effects (sends — this is most of the sound)

the-weeknd-vocal-chain.title: The Weeknd Vocal Chain
the-weeknd-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: the modern pop-R&B gold standard — silky, breathy intimacy that can open into a huge 80s belt without ever getting harsh. Warmth at 200–300 Hz + extended air above 10 kHz + controlled mids (slight 1–2 kHz dip) — expensive-sounding restraint, tuned invisibly, stacked wide on hooks. Signal source: U87-class condenser in the references — your Neumann TLM 102 is the right family. Breath control IS the instrument; record close (3–6") for the intimacy proximity warmth.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD Neve 1073 (Unison) — clean-rich, minimal drive
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 2–3 dB smooth optical (the CL-1B-style silk in his documented chains; LA-2A is your equivalent)
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — +1–2 @ 12 kHz air, low ATTEN @ 60 Hz

Chain overview

Tune (subtle) → clean → two-stage comp → dynamic mids → color → de-ess → air. His documented mix chains run deep (Auto-Tune EFX → Pro-Q → Pro-MB → 1176 → doubler → MicroShift → plate) — the theme is many light touches.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. Auto-Tune Pro — Invisible tune

  • Retune 30–45, Humanize 100 — locked but human (the EFX-era pull is slightly rubbery; a touch faster than you'd expect for how natural it reads).

2. Pro-Q 4 — Sculpt

  • HPF 70–90 Hz · keep 200–300 Hz (his warmth — don't scoop it like a rap vocal) · dip 1–2 kHz −1 to −2 dB (the anti-harshness move) · air shelf +2 @ 10 kHz+.

3. Pro-C 2 → LALA — Two-stage

  • Pro-C 2 Vocal style 3–4 dB, then LALA 1–2 dB ride — glassy evenness for long sustained notes.

4. Pro-Q 4 (dynamic) or Soothe2 — Mid control

  • Dynamic dip 2–4 kHz on the belts only — how he gets loud without ever biting.

5. Little Radiator — Tube silk

  • Low drive (it's in his documented chain) — warmth that reads as "expensive," not "dirty."

6. Pro-DS — De-ess

  • Split-band, slightly firm — all that air makes S's expensive too.

Step 3 — Effects (sends)

  • Width Send (MicroShift — literally his documented plugin): hooks and stacked choruses wide, verses nearly dry-center.
  • Plate: ValhallaPlate 1.5–2.5 s, pre-delay 30 ms, ducked — the 80s bloom on "Blinding Lights"-style choruses.
  • Delay Send Slap subtle + 1/4 throws on phrase-ends · Doubler4 barely-on for the chorus thickener.
  • Stacks: octave-down whisper layer under big hooks (tucked), harmonies bright and wide per the pop rules (Harmony Vocal Track).

mac-demarco-vocal-chain.title: Mac DeMarco Vocal Chain
mac-demarco-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: the slacker croon — lazy, warm, slightly seasick. One voice, barely tuned, wrapped in tape slap and pitch wobble instead of reverb. The whole aesthetic is "expensive tape machine in a cheap bedroom": his records are tracked to actual tape with the vari-speed drifting. Signal source: Shure SM57 — a cheap dynamic suits the croon (his classic era was cheap dynamics anyway — an SM57 is more period-correct than an SM7B). Relaxed, low-effort delivery is the instrument.

Step 1 — Record (UAD Console)

  1. UAD UA 610-B (Unison) — tube, pushed a little (soft round drive)
  2. UAD Teletronix LA-2A — 2–3 dB lazy
  3. UAD Pultec EQP-1A — bypass

Chain overview

Level → warm → wobble → slap. Four moves; stopping early is the style.

Step 2 — Process (Ableton)

1. LALA — Croon leveler

  • 3–4 dB, constant gentle squeeze — flatters the lazy delivery into evenness.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Round it

  • HPF 80 · LPF or high-shelf down above ~10 kHz (no modern air — this voice is AM-radio warm) · small 3 kHz lift if the words blur.

3. Kramer Tape — The machine

  • 7.5 ips (darker) · flux medium · wow/flutter ON and audible (10–20%) · noise a touch
  • Why: this stage is the genre — the pitch instability reads as nostalgia/unease. His actual method is vari-speed tape; Kramer's wow/flutter is the plugin path. (RC-20 Retro Color wobble is the alternative flavor.)

4. Chorus-Ensemble — Seasick (optional, for the synthy cuts)

  • Slow vibrato-leaning setting, shallow, ~20% — the Chamber of Reflection queasiness (on that song the whole track wobbles, not just the vocal).

Step 3 — Effects (sends)

  • Delay Send Slap is the reverb: 100–140 ms, wobbly EchoBoy tape mode, feedback ~10%, send generous — the doo-wop slapback croon. Real reverb barely used (Reverb Send Room whisper at most).
  • Doubles: loose unison on hooks only, drift kept.

Vocal arrangement

Section Lead Behind it
Verse one voice, barely tuned, tape slap nothing
Chorus same voice, slap send pushed maybe one loose harmony, drifting
Outro talking, laughing, or the tape running on —

The move — the wobble is the width. No stacks, no widening. Vari-speed drift and tape slap do the job doubles would do elsewhere, which is why one voice never sounds thin here.

Don't tighten the double if you add one. Drift is the point — the alignment rules that apply to a pop stack are exactly backwards for this lane.

Stack count: 1, occasionally 2.

bitspeek.title: Bitspeek
bitspeek.html:
Category: Pitch/Vocal Vendor: Sonic Charge

What it is

Sonic Charge's vocoder-esque speech-synthesis effect that imposes robotic, low-bitrate speech-codec character on an input signal.

What it's used for

Robotic vocal effects and retro speech-synthesizer-style vocal processing.

FX chain notes

Used as a creative vocal effect insert, often blended in parallel with the dry vocal.

Techniques

  • A second, more-processed layer stacked behind an AlterBoy robot-mode static backing vocal, for an "even weirder" texture. On nonsense-syllable backing vocals already run through Little AlterBoy's robot mode (static, one-note, "not really harmonies"), a second layer runs through Bitspeek instead, pushing the texture further into robotic/vocoder territory as a contrast layer. → Little AlterBoy, Pitch and Formant — Charli XCX / A.G. Cook / Finn Keane (Tape Notes), TN 185 Charli XCX, A. G. Cook, Finn Keane - Full Video Episode

Key Parameters
