bryson-tiller-vocal-chain.title: Bryson Tiller Vocal Chain
bryson-tiller-vocal-chain.html:
Reference/vibe: present-but-filtered, moody, chopped-down R&B — the vocal stays up front in the mix (not buried the way a straight lo-fi vocal would be), but a lo-fi/filter pass at the end gives it a "muffled through something" character that's the genre's signature. Three lanes depending on era/song: a light-touch present + filtered lane (Exchange), a light-touch present, layered lane (Next to You), and a heavier chopped and screwed lane (Outside). Signal source: built from scratch in this breakdown rather than pulled from a real session — the general shape (pitch tool → space → time-based FX → a character/lo-fi finishing stage) is the reusable part, not exact settings.

Lane 1 — Present + filtered (Exchange, Trap Soul)

  1. Little AlterBoy — pitch shifted up a touch; kept subtle, this is not a full character/robot effect, just enough lift to sit the vocal in its slot.
  2. Reverb → EQ → Delay — standard placement/space stage (source didn't specify exact plugin per stage; on this vault, ValhallaRoom for the reverb and Pro-Q 4 for the EQ are the natural first calls).
  3. kHs Bitcrush — Quantize (sample-rate) reduction as the finishing stage. Bounce the whole processed vocal and drop the Quantize knob down until the top end reads as muffled/"filtered out" rather than clean-hi-fi, while staying present in the mix — this is the signature Exchange-era Tiller vocal texture. Source used Edison's sample-rate control; kHs Bitcrush's Quantize knob is the owned equivalent.

Why: the vocal is the main melodic element of the sample (per the source, "the most important part"), so it can't be washed out the way a background layer would be — the filtering has to land after everything else, as a final color pass, not as an upfront processing choice.

Lane 2 — Present, layered (Next to You, Anniversary)

  1. Little AlterBoy → Reverb → EQ → Delay — identical light-touch chain to Lane 1's steps 1–2, but no bitcrush/filter finishing stage this time — this song's vocal stays cleaner.
  2. A second vocal layer, chopped from a separate recording (not a duplicate/double of the lead take) — layered under/around the lead for texture and thickness, rather than a straight ADT double.
secs: Lane 2 — Present, layered (Next to You, Anniversary)

jeff-buckley-s-guitar-sound-with-andy-wa.title: Jeff Buckley's guitar sound with Andy Wallace
jeff-buckley-s-guitar-sound-with-andy-wa.html:
📺 Watch on YouTube

Synopsis

Andy Wallace, revisiting his own Jeff Buckley mix, isolates and A/B's three separate room/reverb returns he had printed on the guitar (a short "tiled room," a medium room, and a long hall/chamber), then live-recreates the printed guitar reverb from scratch using only stock reverb plugins as a demonstration of matching an existing analog reference sound with affordable modern tools. The most transferable lesson is procedural: layering multiple reverb lengths on one source rather than picking a single reverb, and where in the signal path to EQ a reverb return versus the dry/direct signal.

uad-tube-tech-cl-1b-mkii.title: UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII
uad-tube-tech-cl-1b-mkii.html:
Category: Optical (tube) Compressor Vendor: Universal Audio — emulation of the Tube-Tech / Lydkraft CL 1B mk II hardware. Owned.

What it is

Emulation of the Tube-Tech CL 1B — a tube-driven optical compressor famous for smooth, program-dependent gain reduction and silky tube warmth. Where the UAD UA 1176LN (FET) grabs transients, the CL 1B rides the whole phrase like a fader. The mkII adds a switchable sidechain HP filter and a wet/dry (parallel) mix control over the classic model.

What it's used for

The go-to opto leveler on the way in — lead and stacked vocals especially. Gentle 2–4 dB GR that glues level and prints tube silk without clamping peaks. Also great on bass and anything that wants smoothing rather than transient control.

Key settings (tracking)

  • Ratio: ~2:1–3:1 (soft, musical — not a peak grab).
  • Attack: fast (or the mkII's fixed setting) so it engages cleanly; Release: slow / auto so it decelerates like a fader.
  • Gain reduction: 2–4 dB — a ride, not a crush. Make-up gain to unity.
  • Sidechain HP filter (mkII): engage so low-end doesn't pump the gain.
  • Wet/dry: keep ~100% when printing on the way in — parallel is a mix-phase move.

FX chain notes

Console tracking compressor in the uad_console vocal chains — Main Vocal Track §3.2, and inherited by Harmony, Backup, Double, and Main Vocal High. Replaced the UAD UA 1176LN here (opto ride in, fast peak-precision now on Pro-C 2 mid-chain). Pairs with the UAD Teletronix LA-2A on the Vocal Bus — two smooth opto stages bracketing one fast stage (Compression Staging).

rx-guitar-de-noise.title: RX Guitar De-noise
rx-guitar-de-noise.html:
Category: Utility Vendor: iZotope

What it is

An RX module tuned specifically for removing amp hiss, hum, and noise floor from guitar recordings. Owned in both the RX 10 and RX 11 suites.

What it's used for

Cleaning up noisy DI or amp recordings of guitar and bass.

FX chain notes

Used early in an instrument cleanup pass, before amp-sim or EQ processing.

Techniques

  • Run a denoiser deliberately for its side-effect low-pass character, not its intended noise-removal job — closing stage of a vintage-sample-flip chain. Jake One's vintage-Rhodes sample chain (Percocet and Stripper Joint, Future) ends with a noise-reduction plugin (captioned "Bruce Free," near-certainly Brusfri by Klevgrand) whose noise reduction unintentionally rolls off the top end — treated as a feature, adding to the vintage vibe rather than something to correct for. Best-match owned trick: RX Guitar De-noise's Amp module reliably darkens a source's top end as a byproduct of hiss removal when Reduction is pushed past what's strictly needed for the noise floor — lean into that darkening on purpose instead of dialing it back for transparency. (general starting point — no exact Sensitivity/Reduction values given on screen) → UAD Tube-Tech CL 1B mkII, EQ Eight, UAD RealVerb-Pro, Sampling and Sound Selection — loner, the secret samplemaker behind Southside's best beats!?

expressive-controllers-and-cv-conversion.title: Expressive Controllers and CV Conversion
expressive-controllers-and-cv-conversion.html:
Controlling vintage analog synths — genuinely voltage-controlled, no MIDI input at all — with a per-note continuous expressive controller (Haken Continuum, Osmose) via a MIDI-to-CV converter, so each key/note carries independent, continuous pitch/pressure/position data into a real analog voice rather than the synth's own on/off keyboard gate. Source: a deep two-controller demo pairing a Haken Continuum and an Osmose with four ARP 2600s and a Moog Modular 3C, one voice per instrument.

MPE fundamentals this depends on

Every new note played opens its own MIDI channel (up to 15), carrying continuous, independent tracking of pressure, aftertouch, and pitch-bend per note — the mechanism MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression) is built on. A CVC (Control Voltage Converter) takes that per-channel MPE data and converts it into actual control-voltage signals a vintage analog synth's CV/gate inputs can use directly — multiple CVCs can be networked together (or a dedicated CVC Expander used) to drive more independent voices than one converter alone supports.

analog-vs-digital-workflow-philosophy.title: Analog vs Digital Workflow Philosophy
analog-vs-digital-workflow-philosophy.html:
Not a signal-chain technique — a set of working-philosophy positions on the analog/digital question, drawn from a conversation between Anthony Marinelli and Mark Barton (a working analog synth designer — co-designer of the Synthesis Technology Zeroscillator, the first commercially successful through-zero-FM Eurorack module, and formerly a speech-synthesis researcher at Apple — now a third-party developer for Cherry Audio). Barton's central technical claim and Marinelli's pushback on what that claim does and doesn't settle are both worth keeping, since they land on a genuinely useful working standard rather than a "team analog / team digital" argument.

The technical claim

Modern digital synthesis, run at 64-bit floating point (53 bits of accuracy), exceeds analog electronics' signal-to-noise ceiling (roughly 100 dB on a very good analog circuit) by hundreds of dB. The common "digital is stepped, analog is continuous" objection misses that a DAC's reconstruction filter mathematically reconnects the digital steps into a genuinely continuous waveform on the way out — so the "smoothness" argument for analog doesn't actually hold once the full signal chain (including reconstruction) is considered. Analog's continuity is real but noisy in transition; digital's reconstructed continuity is smoother.

The blind-test standard

Cherry Audio's actual development bar for a plugin emulation: A/B it blind (someone else switches between the original and the emulation without saying which is which, on single notes or short phrases) — if a listener genuinely can't tell them apart, ship it. Real anecdote proving how strong the sighted-bias effect is: users who believe they prefer the sound of the original vintage Synclavier over the "Regen" (the modern hardware reissue) turn out to be picking at chance (50/50) in a genuine blind test — knowing in advance which one is playing is itself the deciding factor, not the sound.

tempo-changes-and-rubato.title: Tempo Changes and Rubato
tempo-changes-and-rubato.html:
What it is: deliberately varying tempo within a song — a permanent shift up or down, a temporary detour and return, or a continuous free-floating rubato feel — as an expressive/arrangement tool most modern click-track production quietly forecloses.

Why it's underused

A grid-locked DAW workflow (Pro Tools/Logic/Ableton to a fixed click) makes editing easier but makes tempo a non-decision by default. A consistent tempo isn't wrong — it gives groove and stability — but treating tempo as fixed-by-default means skipping an entire expressive dimension without ever choosing to.

1-main-vocal-high-track.title: 1 Main Vocal High Track
1-main-vocal-high-track.html:
Role: High lead layer (octave-up or high harmony that reinforces the lead). Sits with the lead in the center — tucked under it, never competing. A support layer earns its place by being narrower and more controlled than the lead.

Chain philosophy: tune tighter → band-limit harder → compress flatter → de-ess.

1 — Recording Setup

  • Same setup as Main Vocal Track §1: Neumann TLM 102, ghost latency track, tempo/key locked.
  • Falsetto/octave-up parts sit closer to the mic's sweet spot at lower level — drop input gain ~3 dB so the thin register doesn't ride the preamp hot.

2 — Tracking Best Practice

  • Track it right after the lead take it supports, same mic position — matched timbre fuses; a different session's tone reads as a separate voice.
  • Sing softer than the lead; the layer is reinforcement, not a feature. 🎬 Set Auto-Tune Pro's input voice type to the register actually sung (Soprano for falsetto) or the tracking misreads — Kenny Beats, Auto-Tune Process.
  • Center, mono — width belongs to doubles/harmonies.

3 — Source → Ableton (UAD Console)

Same console pass as Main Vocal Track §3, printed conservatively.

4 — Ableton Initial Processing

1. Auto-Tune Pro — Pitch

  • Retune 22 (①) · Humanize 100% (③) · input voice type = register actually sung (④ — Soprano for falsetto) — tighter than the lead
  • Why: High layers expose pitch drift; tighter tune keeps it fused.

2. Pro-Q 4 — Band-limit

  • HPF up to 150–200 Hz · LPF/high-shelf cut above 10–12 kHz · dip the lead's presence zone (3–5 kHz) −1 to −2 dB
  • Why: The lead keeps the full range; this layer keeps a narrower window so they never fight.

3. Pro-C 2 — Flatten

  • 4:1 · attack 5–10 ms · release auto · 4–8 dB GR — more than the lead
  • Why: Support layers want near-zero dynamics so they sit still under the lead.

4. Pro-DS — De-ess

  • Harder than the lead (range 6–8 dB) — stacked S's multiply.

5 — Track FX (optional)

  • Nothing, usually — invisibility is the job.

ant-nio-carlos-jobim-the-girl-from-ipane.title: The Girl from Ipanema
ant-nio-carlos-jobim-the-girl-from-ipane.structure: 32-bar AABA (unusually long, harmonically dense B section)
ant-nio-carlos-jobim-the-girl-from-ipane.about: Composed 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim (Portuguese lyrics Vinícius de Moraes, English lyrics Norman Gimbel 1964). Global fame via the 1964 Getz/Gilberto recording (Stan Getz, João Gilberto, Astrud Gilberto) — Grammy Album of the Year 1965, Record of the Year for the song. Reportedly the second-most-recorded song in music history after 'Summertime.

baby-keem-16.about: Short, melodic cut from Baby Keem's debut studio album The Melodic Blue (2021).

bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.title: How Deep Is Your Love
bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.feel: soft ballad, falsetto lead vocal, lush strings and electric piano
bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.structure: verse–pre-chorus–chorus pop ballad form (no separate bridge; final chorus repeats to fade)
bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.cover_file: Bee Gees - Saturday Night Fever (Original Movie Soundtrack).jpg
bee-gees-how-deep-is-your-love.about: Written by Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb — reportedly written with Barbra Streisand in mind before the Bee Gees recorded it themselves. From the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack (1977).

billy-joel-vienna.title: Vienna
billy-joel-vienna.about: From The Stranger (1977), produced by Phil Ramone. A piano-driven, jazz-inflected ballad — the 'slow down, you crazy child' reflection on patience and mortality.

bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.title: Livin' on a Prayer
bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.key: E minor (main riff/verse), modulating up before the final chorus (source video says "G minor"; the commonly-cited change for this song is E minor to F# minor — flagged, auto-caption sourced)
bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.feel: driving arena rock, tension-and-release via pedal point, busyness escalating with the song's intensity
bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.structure: verse (pedal-point riff), pre-chorus (Em–C–D–Em), chorus (D–G–C), first chorus vs. final chorus contrasted for busyness — as covered by the source video, not a full arrangement chart
bon-jovi-livin-on-a-prayer.about: From Bon Jovi's *Slippery When Wet* (1986). This note documents the bass part — credited to either Alec John Such or Hugh McDonald (disputed) — as taught by BassBuzz: pedal point on the main riff, three worked bass-run/fill examples (including a target-note over-the-bar-line run connecting three chords), and the bassline's density tracking the song's overall intensity arc.

brockhampton-sugar.title: Sugar
brockhampton-sugar.about: Second track from BROCKHAMPTON's fifth studio album Ginger (2019), featuring Ryan Beatty; a hip hop/pop/R&B slow jam built on a looped acoustic-guitar figure with folk and funk textures under bubbling drum programming.

broken-bells-the-high-road.title: The High Road
broken-bells-the-high-road.about: Lead single (Dec 2009) off Broken Bells' self-titled 2010 debut album — a collaboration between James Mercer (The Shins) and Danger Mouse.
chart_files: Broken Bells - The High Road - Chords.pdf

cedar-walton-bolivia.title: Bolivia
cedar-walton-bolivia.key: multiple key centers (E♭ → D → G → B minor → F/B♭/D minor)
cedar-walton-bolivia.about: Cedar Walton original — a jazz standard whose changes move through several distinct key centers per section, framed by a G7 vamp at the top and bottom of the form. Melody not covered in the source video (YouTube copyright); this note documents the chord progression and improvisation approach only.

charlie-parker-confirmation.title: Confirmation
charlie-parker-confirmation.album: Now's the Time: the Quartet of Charlie Parker
charlie-parker-confirmation.cover_file: Charlie Parker - Now's the Time the Quartet of Charlie Parker.jpg
charlie-parker-confirmation.about: Charlie Parker's own head melody to "Confirmation," that Nathan Borton breaks down phrase by phrase as a study in bebop line-building and phrasing — 6th-interval leaps, a minor ii-V lick, blues mixed into bebop, guide-tone connective lines, a 4th-to-3rd-then-altered-tone device, CESH in the B section, and named closing phrases.

charlie-parker-donna-lee.title: Donna Lee
charlie-parker-donna-lee.about: A bebop contrafact (built over the changes of "Indiana," credited to Charlie Parker though sometimes attributed to Miles Davis) that Nathan Borton uses as a source melody to teach line-closer/arpeggio construction, chromatic enclosures, and the major bebop scale; the tune's own harmony (a non-diatonic B♭7 and a backdoor G♭7→D♭maj7 move) is separately broken down in a companion Borton video already logged on this page's harmony sources.

clifford-brown-max-roach-delilah.title: Delilah
clifford-brown-max-roach-delilah.cover_file: Clifford Brown & Max Roach - Clifford Brown and Max Roach.jpg
clifford-brown-max-roach-delilah.about: Old jazz standard (composer Victor Young, written for the film Samson and Delilah) covered by Clifford Brown & Max Roach — a bluesy AABA solo built around F♯ minor that Jack Ruch uses as a vehicle to teach [[Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction]].

djo-end-of-beginning.title: End of Beginning
djo-end-of-beginning.about: Sixth track from Joe Keery's (Djo) second album Decide (2022); reissued as a single in 2024 after going viral on TikTok, later hitting #6 on the Billboard Hot 100 following the Stranger Things series finale.

elani-karaindrou-eternity-and-a-day-ii-b.title: Eternity and a Day II. By The Sea 1
elani-karaindrou-eternity-and-a-day-ii-b.cover_file: Elani Karaindrou - Eternity and a Day.jpg
elani-karaindrou-eternity-and-a-day-ii-b.about: Film score for Theo Angelopoulos' 1998 Palme d'Or–winning film. Sparse and impressionistic. A recurring melodic motif builds and dissolves. Slow harmonic movement creates a timeless, suspended quality.
chart_files: Elani Karaindrou - Eternity and a Day II. By The Sea.pdf

erik-satie-3-gymnopedies.title: 3 Gymnopédies
erik-satie-3-gymnopedies.about: Three pieces in 3/4 time written in 1888. Gentle waltz bass patterns support sparse, floating melodies. Open, unresolved chords create a dreamlike ambiguity. Satie deliberately avoided conventional harmonic resolution.

erik-satie-gnossienne-no-1.title: Gnossienne No. 1
erik-satie-gnossienne-no-1.structure: free time — no time signature or bar lines in the original notation; additive/cyclical form (short motifs repeat and recombine, no fixed refrain)

erik-satie-gnossienne-no-2.title: Gnossienne No. 2
erik-satie-gnossienne-no-2.structure: free time — no time signature or bar lines in the original notation; additive/cyclical form (short motifs repeat and recombine, no fixed refrain)

erik-satie-gnossienne-no-3.title: Gnossienne No. 3
erik-satie-gnossienne-no-3.structure: free time — no time signature or bar lines in the original notation; additive/cyclical form (short motifs repeat and recombine, no fixed refrain)

erik-satie-gnossiennes.title: Gnossiennes
erik-satie-gnossiennes.about: Written without bar lines or time signatures — the performer sets the pace. Hauntingly modal melody over slow, sparse chords. Each piece carries unusual written instructions: 'with astonishment,' 'wonderingly,' 'from the tip of the thought.

erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-1.title: Gymnopédie No. 1
erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-1.structure: no classical form (no development/recapitulation) — three loosely related gestures grow from and return to the same ostinato bass and alternating maj7 chords

erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-2.title: Gymnopédie No. 2
erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-2.structure: no classical form (no development/recapitulation) — the same ostinato-and-maj7-pendulum approach as No. 1, in a related key

erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-3.title: Gymnopédie No. 3
erik-satie-gymnop-die-no-3.structure: no classical form (no development/recapitulation) — the same ostinato-and-maj7-pendulum approach as Nos. 1-2, in a related key

fats-waller-honeysuckle-rose.title: Honeysuckle Rose
fats-waller-honeysuckle-rose.about: Music by Thomas "Fats" Waller, lyrics by Andy Razaf. Written 1928, published 1929; introduced as a soft-shoe number in the Off-Broadway revue Load of Coal at Connie's Inn, Harlem. The only one of the five Montgomery-Ward standards with a clean, uncontested composer credit. Waller reportedly dashed the melody off casually and didn't much like it. His 1934 recording entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999.

frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.title: Someday My Prince Will Come
frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.album: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1961 Miles Davis recording on the album of the same name)
frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.cover_file: Frank Churchill - Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1961 Miles Davis recording on the album of the same name).jpg
frank-churchill-someday-my-prince-will-c.about: Written 1937 by Frank Churchill (music) and Larry Morey (lyrics) for Disney's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. Solidified as a jazz standard via Miles Davis's iconic 1961 recording, with John Coltrane, Hank Mobley, Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb.

frank-ocean-ivy.title: Ivy
frank-ocean-ivy.about: From Blonde (2016). Built around a detuned guitar riff, produced with Rostam Batmanglij and Om'Mas Keith.

frank-ocean-pink-white.title: Pink + White
frank-ocean-pink-white.about: From Blonde (2016), track 3. Features Beyoncé (uncredited backing vocals) and Kendrick Lamar (uncredited outro vocals).
chart_files: Frank Ocean - Pink Plus White - Chords.pdf

frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.title: Fly Me to the Moon
frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.album: It Might as Well Be Swing
frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.cover_file: Frank Sinatra - It Might as Well Be Swing.jpg
frank-sinatra-fly-me-to-the-moon.about: Written by Bart Howard in 1954 (originally "In Other Words"); most famous recording is Sinatra's 1964 version with the Count Basie Orchestra, arranged by Quincy Jones.

fr-d-ric-chopin-nocturne-op-9-no-1.title: Nocturne Op. 9 No. 1
fr-d-ric-chopin-nocturne-op-9-no-1.structure: ternary (ABA) form — primary theme, secondary theme from m.19, varied return of the primary theme from m.70; 85 measures, 6/4

george-benson-billie-s-bounce.title: Billie's Bounce
george-benson-billie-s-bounce.about: Charlie Parker original (1945); George Benson's solo on this recording is Jens Larsen's pick for the best jazz blues solo he knows, and the one analyzed in [[George Benson - This is The Best Jazz Blues Solo I know]] using the same chunk-analyze-name-the-device method as [[Solo Analysis and Concept Extraction]].

george-harrison-beware-of-darkness.title: Beware of Darkness
george-harrison-beware-of-darkness.cover_file: George Harrison - All Things Must Pass.jpg
george-harrison-beware-of-darkness.about: From All Things Must Pass (1970), produced by Phil Spector. Devotional warning against illusion, maya, and negative thought. Possibly Pete Drake on pedal steel. Slow, hymn-like progression.

gorillaz-feel-good-inc.title: Feel Good Inc.
gorillaz-feel-good-inc.key: E♭ minor (riff played in "open" E-family shapes, bass tuned down a half step — see tuning below)
gorillaz-feel-good-inc.structure: not fully documented — this note covers the main riff, its slide, and the short bass solo as taught by BassBuzz, not a full chord chart or arrangement
gorillaz-feel-good-inc.about: From Gorillaz's *Demon Days* (2005) — the album's lead single. This note documents the bass part (main riff, slide, and short solo) as taught by BassBuzz's Josh, cross-referenced against Gorillaz's own touring/session bassist Shay Adelican via a shared voice note, not a full chord/arrangement chart.

grant-green-blues-for-willarine.title: Blues for Willarine
grant-green-blues-for-willarine.about: A Grant Green jazz-blues tune Jack Ruch pulls a single 6-2-5-1 turnaround line from as a third worked example of transcription-and-recombination method — thinner documentation than the other two Green tunes since only this one line is transcribed, not a full chorus.

grant-green-cool-blues.title: Cool Blues
grant-green-cool-blues.cover_file: Grant Green - Born to Be Blue.jpg
grant-green-cool-blues.about: Grant Green's solo on "Cool Blues," from the album Born to Be Blue, that Nathan Borton breaks down as a master class covering three named improv sounds: 5-to-1 lines, 2-equals-5/5-equals-2 (soloing a dominant's related ii minor), and tonic dominant (extensions over a static dominant), plus a fourth umbrella of blues-language devices.

grant-green-grant-s-tune.title: Grant's Tune
grant-green-grant-s-tune.structure: AABA-adjacent (A-section vamp + tag, distinct B section)
grant-green-grant-s-tune.about: A Grant Green original from his album *Solid* — a two-chord A-section vamp (Cm7–D♭7, a disguised minor 1-5-1) with an E♭ major tag, plus a B section built from slash chords over a held E♭ bass that resolve to ordinary E♭ major/minor7/major/sus9 shapes. Nathan Borton frames it as a compact drill for two distinct soloing skills: sitting on one static sound over a long stretch, and moving one sound fluently across several chord qualities.

grant-green-miss-ann-s-tempo.title: Miss Ann's Tempo
grant-green-miss-ann-s-tempo.about: Grant Green original swing blues in B♭ that Jack Ruch transcribes the opening solo chorus of to teach jazz-blues vocabulary.

grant-green-number-one-green-street.title: Number One Green Street
grant-green-number-one-green-street.about: Grant Green original swing blues in B♭ that Jack Ruch transcribes the first chorus of Green's solo to, as a second worked example of his jazz-blues vocabulary.

grant-green-trace-and-tracy.title: Trace and Tracy
grant-green-trace-and-tracy.about: Grant Green original minor blues in B♭ minor that Nathan Borton breaks down for tonic-minor soloing, color-tone use, and rhythmic phrasing.

harry-warren-there-will-never-be-another.title: There Will Never Be Another You
harry-warren-there-will-never-be-another.structure: ABAC (32 bars — A 8, B 8, A 8, C 8); B and C share their first 3 bars
harry-warren-there-will-never-be-another.about: Music by Harry Warren, lyrics by Mack Gordon (1942, from the film *Iceland*); a jam-session staple used here as the teaching vehicle for a memorization-by-chunking method.

hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.title: Georgia on My Mind
hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.key: F major (sheet music) / G major (Ray Charles recording) — taught here as open-position C shapes
hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.structure: AABA-shaped, 32-ish bar standard with a distinct bridge ("the arms that reach out to me...") and a written turnaround
hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.cover_file: Hoagy Carmichael - The Genius Hits the Road.jpg
hoagy-carmichael-georgia-on-my-mind.about: Music by Hoagy Carmichael, lyrics by Stuart Gorrell (1930). Most famous recording is Ray Charles' 1960 version (key of G), which made it a #1 pop hit and later Georgia's official state song. Sheet music is most commonly published in the key of F.

jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.title: Emergency on Planet Earth
jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.key: not documented — this note covers only the intro riff as taught by BassBuzz, not a full chord chart
jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.structure: intro riff only, as covered by the source video — not a full arrangement chart
jamiroquai-emergency-on-planet-earth.about: Title track from Jamiroquai's debut album *Emergency on Planet Earth* (1993), bassist Stuart Zender. This note documents just the intro riff — a slap-and-pop roots-and-octaves pattern used by BassBuzz as a real-song application of the teeter-totter technique — not a full chord/arrangement chart.

jerome-kern-all-the-things-you-are.title: All The Things You Are
jerome-kern-all-the-things-you-are.structure: AABA-shaped (36 bars — A1 8, A2 8, Bridge 8, A3 12) with 4 distinct key centers
jerome-kern-all-the-things-you-are.about: Music by Jerome Kern, lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II (1939, from the musical *Very Warm for May*); one of the most-played jam-session standards, notable for modulating through four key centers in 36 bars — an unusually high modulation rate for the form.

jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.title: Nobody Else But Me
jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.album: Show Boat (1946 Broadway Revival Cast Recording)
jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.feel: standard jazz tempo (comped, not specified further by source)
jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.structure: not stated in full by the source video — analyzed bar-by-bar in fragments (measures 6-9, end-of-tune passing diminished run, measure 26, final 3 bars, closing turnaround, measures 9-12)
jerome-kern-nobody-else-but-me.about: Music by Jerome Kern (lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II) — Kern's last song, written for the 1946 Broadway revival of *Show Boat* (he died in November 1945, shortly before it opened); introduced by Jan Clayton as Magnolia. Not from *Very Warm for May* (1939) — that show produced "All The Things You Are," a different Kern/Hammerstein standard.

joe-pass-little-darlin.title: Little Darlin
joe-pass-little-darlin.about: Joe Pass's solo-guitar chord-melody arrangement of the standard 'Little Darlin'', from his album *Intercontinental* — analyzed opening-to-bridge by Jens Larsen as a teaching example of block-chord harmonization and chord-derived fills.

john-klenner-just-friends.title: Just Friends
john-klenner-just-friends.key: F major (also commonly played in G)
john-klenner-just-friends.structure: 32-bar, nearly-identical first and second halves — the only real difference is the first half leads back to the top (via the dominant) while the second half cadences fully home to the tonic
john-klenner-just-friends.cover_file: John Klenner - Charlie Parker with Strings.jpg
john-klenner-just-friends.about: Written 1931 by John Klenner (music) and Sam M. Lewis (lyrics); a jazz-standard staple, recorded widely across the bebop and post-bop eras.

john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.title: Slow Dancing in a Burning Room
john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.bpm: 73 (sheet music "slowly" marking; some algorithmic BPM trackers report ~134, almost certainly a double-time misread)
john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.structure: not fully documented — this note covers one recurring 2-chord fragment (IV-I), not a full chart
john-mayer-slow-dancing-in-a-burning-roo.about: From John Mayer's *Continuum* (2006). This note documents a single detail from the song's arrangement — the IV→I (A→E) plagal-cadence fragment with its signature hammer-on ornament — as taught by Jared Borkowski (Sound Guitar Lessons With Jared), not a full chord chart.

johnny-green-body-and-soul.title: Body and Soul
johnny-green-body-and-soul.about: Composed 1929 by Johnny Green (lyrics Edward Heyman/Robert Sour/Frank Eyton), written for Gertrude Lawrence. Coleman Hawkins' 1939 recording — largely improvised over the harmony rather than the written melody — is the landmark version, credited with helping establish the tenor sax as a leading jazz voice. One of the most-recorded jazz songs ever (~3,000 versions).

johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.title: Out of Nowhere
johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.album: Out of Nowhere" (single, Johnny Green and His Orchestra)
johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.structure: Two nearly-identical 16-bar halves; first half ends on a half cadence (to the dominant), second half's equivalent spot resolves to the tonic
johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.cover_file: Johnny Green - Out of Nowhere (single, Johnny Green and His Orchestra).jpg
johnny-green-out-of-nowhere.about: Music by Johnny Green, lyrics by Edward Heyman, written 1931 for the film *Dixiana*. A jazz standard since the bebop era, recorded widely (Charlie Parker, Clifford Brown, and many others); the version studied here is analyzed by Jens Larsen, inspired by a Jonathan Kreisberg recording.

joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.title: Autumn Leaves
joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.feel: swing / ballad / bossa nova (all common treatments)
joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.structure: AABC-shaped (32-bar form; first 8 bars = i-VII-... functionally a vi-ii-V-i-then-turnaround in G minor, i.e. the classic Cm7-F7-B♭maj7-E♭maj7-Aø7-D7-Gm(i)-G7 opening)
joseph-kosma-autumn-leaves.about: Music by Joseph Kosma, French lyrics by Jacques Prévert ("Les Feuilles Mortes," 1945); English lyrics by Johnny Mercer (1947). One of the most-recorded jazz standards ever, prized as a teaching vehicle because its first 8 bars touch all four common seventh-chord qualities (minor 7, dominant 7, major 7, half-diminished) in one compact phrase.

kendrick-lamar-pride.title: Pride
kendrick-lamar-pride.about: Track 6 on DAMN. (2017). Built around a sample from James Blake's "Element of Surprise." Kendrick's most confessional track on the album — a self-inventory of pride and personal flaw.

kurt-rosenwinkel-nefertiti-ballad-sessio.title: Nefertiti
kurt-rosenwinkel-nefertiti-ballad-sessio.artist: Kurt Rosenwinkel (soloist, on Mark Turner's album)
kurt-rosenwinkel-nefertiti-ballad-sessio.about: Wayne Shorter composition, most associated with the second Miles Davis Quintet (Davis/Shorter/Hancock/Carter/Williams); this page covers Kurt Rosenwinkel's guitar solo on Mark Turner's recording, analyzed by Jens Larsen as a study in Rosenwinkel's melodic language.

lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.title: Let The Light In
lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.album: Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd
lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.cover_file: Lana Del Rey - Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd.png
lana-del-rey-let-the-light-in.about: Duet with Father John Misty from Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd (2023); a warm, acoustic-leaning love song.
chart_files: Lana Del Rey - Let The Light In - Chords.pdf

lana-del-rey-paris-texas.title: Paris, Texas
lana-del-rey-paris-texas.album: Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd
lana-del-rey-paris-texas.cover_file: Lana Del Rey - Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd.png
lana-del-rey-paris-texas.about: Wistful ballad named after Wim Wenders' 1984 film. Strings build gradually over a sparse arrangement. Del Rey's breathy, detached vocal amplifies the melancholy. From Did You Know That There's a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd (2023).

lana-del-rey-video-games.title: Video Games
lana-del-rey-video-games.cover_file: Lana Del Rey - Born to Die.png
lana-del-rey-video-games.about: Breakout single from Lana Del Rey's major-label debut Born to Die (2012); a stripped, string-laden ballad built around a descending piano/harp figure.
chart_files: Lana Del Rey - Video Games - Chords.pdf

mac-miller-2009.about: Produced by Eric G using a sample chop with live drums, bass, and piano. Simple, melancholic loop drives the track. Reflective lyrics about youth, innocence, and the passage of time. One of Miller's most emotionally resonant productions.

mac-miller-cinderella.title: Cinderella
mac-miller-cinderella.about: From The Divine Feminine (2016); features Ty Dolla $ign. Lush, soulful production anchoring the album's love-themed arc.

miles-davis-solar.title: Solar
miles-davis-solar.about: Widely attributed to Miles Davis (first recorded 1954, *Walkin'*); moves through several key centers in a compact 12 bars, which is what makes it a favorite teaching vehicle for chord-scale/key-change practice.

nat-adderley-work-song.title: Work Song
nat-adderley-work-song.structure: short jazz solo chorus (12-bar-scale form, not analyzed in full)
nat-adderley-work-song.about: Nat Adderley original from his 1960 album Work Song; the source solo analyzed here is Wes Montgomery's short guitar improvisation on the tune, transcribed and broken down by Nathan Borton to teach chord-extension devices.

nathan-borton-all-of-me.title: All of Me
nathan-borton-all-of-me.structure: 32-bar AABA-family standard (opening A-section phrases covered here)
nathan-borton-all-of-me.about: Music and lyrics by Gerald Marks & Seymour Simons (1931); featured in the 1932 film *Careless Lady*; a widely-played jazz standard, used here as the worked example for a full solo-guitar chord-melody build process, arranged/taught by Nathan Borton.

paul-mccartney-every-night.title: Every Night
paul-mccartney-every-night.about: Simple acoustic ballad from Paul McCartney's 1970 solo debut, written a couple of years earlier around the Beatles' breakup — about wanting to stay in with a loved one instead of going out.

paul-mccartney-junk.title: Junk
paul-mccartney-junk.about: Tender fingerpicked ballad about abandoned objects finding new owners. Written during the Rishikesh retreat with the Maharishi. An instrumental version, 'Singalong Junk,' also appeared on McCartney (1970).

paul-mccartney-teddy-boy.title: TEDDY BOY
paul-mccartney-teddy-boy.about: Lighthearted story song about a boy caring for his widowed mother. Started during the Get Back sessions; Lennon famously improvised mockery over it during rehearsals. Released on McCartney (1970).
chart_files: Teddy Boy Official by Paul McCartneytabs @ Ultimate Guitar Archive.pdf

paul-mccartney-that-would-be-something.title: That Would Be Something
paul-mccartney-that-would-be-something.about: Loose, groove-driven rocker from McCartney (1970) — same album as Junk and Every Night. Built mostly around one chord vamp with a driving groove.

ray-charles-hard-times.title: Hard Times
ray-charles-hard-times.structure: 12-bar-family slow blues with a 1-6 move, a ii-V into the IV, a passing diminished chord, and a chromatically-walked VI7 turnaround
ray-charles-hard-times.cover_file: Ray Charles - The Genius Sings the Blues.jpg
ray-charles-hard-times.about: Ray Charles slow blues, played weekly by Jack Ruch's organ trio in Nashville; used as the teaching vehicle for a three-level soloing progression (pentatonic blues -> chord-tone/arpeggio outlining -> altered scale).

ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.title: You Don't Know Me
ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.album: Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music
ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.cover_file: Ray Charles - Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music.jpg
ray-charles-you-don-t-know-me.about: Written by Eddy Arnold & Cindy Walker (1955); Ray Charles's arrangement/recording is the version taught here, learned via Jack Ruch's [[A Classic Tune for Learning About Secondary Dominants]] as a vehicle for [[Secondary Dominants]] and a movable diminished-arpeggio soloing lick.

red-hot-chili-peppers-funky-monks.title: Funky Monks
red-hot-chili-peppers-funky-monks.cover_file: Red Hot Chili Peppers - Blood Sugar Sex Magik.jpg
red-hot-chili-peppers-funky-monks.about: Funk-rock cut from Blood Sugar Sex Magik. Good practice target for funk rhythm feel, blues phrasing, and hammer-on/pull-off technique.

sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.title: Softly As in a Morning Sunrise
sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.structure: AABA, A sections built almost entirely from a chained minor 2-5-1; bridge modulates to the relative major (E♭)
sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.cover_file: Sigmund Romberg - Django (Modern Jazz Quartet, recorded Dec 1954).jpg
sigmund-romberg-softly-as-in-a-morning-s.about: Written 1928 by Sigmund Romberg (music) and Oscar Hammerstein II (lyrics) for the operetta *The New Moon*; became a jazz standard after the Modern Jazz Quartet's 1954 swing recording. Recorded since by John Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, Chet Baker, Stan Getz, George Benson and many others.

steely-dan-deacon-blues.title: Deacon Blues
steely-dan-deacon-blues.about: Becker and Fagen's meditation on romantic losers and alternate lives. Pete Christlieb's saxophone solo is widely considered one of the greatest in rock. Extended multi-section structure over jazz harmony. From Aja (1977).

steely-dan-only-a-fool-would-say-that.title: Only a Fool Would Say That
steely-dan-only-a-fool-would-say-that.cover_file: Steely Dan - Can't Buy a Thrill.jpg
steely-dan-only-a-fool-would-say-that.about: From Steely Dan's debut Can't Buy a Thrill (1972); often read as a wry response to Lennon's 'Imagine.
chart_files: Steeley Dan - Only a fool would say that.pdf

tadd-dameron-lady-bird.title: Lady Bird
tadd-dameron-lady-bird.cover_file: Tadd Dameron - The Fabulous Fats Navarro, Vol. 2.jpg
tadd-dameron-lady-bird.about: Composed by Tadd Dameron; several differing lead-sheet melody versions circulate (Larsen notes the older Berklee "real book" version differs from others he's seen). Miles Davis's bebop contrafact "Half Nelson" is written over the same changes. Prized as an early-jazz-repertoire tune because every chord change moves to a harmonically distant/contrasting chord, making the form's location easy to track by ear, and because its turnaround's descending-major-third motion is a compact, low-stakes entry point into "Giant Steps"-style changes.

the-beatles-cry-baby-cry.title: Cry Baby Cry

the-beatles-dig-a-pony.title: Dig a Pony

the-beatles-fixing-a-hole.cover_file: The Beatles - Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band.jpg
the-beatles-fixing-a-hole.about: McCartney on harpsichord, George Martin plays a second harpsichord countermelody. Descending chromatic bass line anchors the verses. Harrison guitar solo opens the bridge. Recorded at Regent Sound — the first time the Beatles used a studio other than Abbey Road.

the-beatles-for-no-one.title: For No One
the-beatles-for-no-one.about: McCartney plays rented clavichord — no guitars on the track. Alan Civil of the Royal Philharmonia plays the iconic French horn solo. Lennon and Harrison did not contribute. Sparse and devastating.

the-beatles-for-you-blue.title: For You Blue
the-beatles-for-you-blue.about: Harrison's 12-bar blues recorded live at Apple Studios. Lennon plays lap steel slide guitar. McCartney on piano, Ringo on drums. Joyful simplicity.

the-beatles-girl.title: Girl

the-beatles-happiness-is-a-warm-gun.about: Three distinct sections spliced by Lennon, described as 'three songs stuck together.' Complex shifting time signatures throughout. 95 takes to complete. Each section references a different era of rock history.

the-beatles-her-majesty.about: 23-second hidden track. McCartney's tongue-in-cheek ode to the Queen. Originally cut from between 'Mean Mr. Mustard' and 'Polythene Pam' and accidentally left at the end of the master tape.

the-beatles-here-there-and-everywhere.title: Here There and Everywhere
the-beatles-here-there-and-everywhere.about: McCartney's ballad partly inspired by Pet Sounds. All four Beatles snapped fingers on a separate track. Lush three-part vocal harmonies. One of McCartney's personal favorites.

the-beatles-i-me-mine.about: Harrison's song about the ego. Alternates between a slow waltz and a faster hard-rock feel. Extended with Phil Spector overdubs for the Let It Be album — Lennon had already left the band by the time overdubs were recorded.

the-beatles-i-want-you-she-s-so-heavy.about: Lennon's obsessive, repetitive refrain over a crushing groove. Second section builds with white noise generated by the Moog synthesizer. Ends with an abrupt mid-phrase tape cut — one of the heaviest Beatles recordings.

the-beatles-i-want-to-tell-you.title: I Want to Tell You
the-beatles-i-want-to-tell-you.about: Harrison's song about the frustration of ideas not translating into speech. The piano deliberately plays a clashing note against the main chord to create harmonic tension that mirrors the lyrical theme.

the-beatles-i-will.title: I Will
the-beatles-i-will.about: McCartney hummed the bass line rather than playing bass guitar. Drums played with brushes only. Took 67 takes. Among the most tender and sparse Beatles recordings.

the-beatles-i-ll-follow-the-sun.title: I'll Follow the Sun
the-beatles-i-ll-follow-the-sun.about: Early McCartney ballad written as a teenager. Ringo plays brushes on his own knees — no kit used. Sparse and delicate, with a bittersweet lyric about leaving before things go wrong.

the-beatles-i-m-only-sleeping.title: I'm Only Sleeping
the-beatles-i-m-only-sleeping.about: Harrison recorded a guitar solo which was then played backwards and overdubbed. Lennon captured the half-awake sensation in the arrangement as well as the lyrics. Deliberately drowsy tempo and feel.

the-beatles-i-m-so-tired.title: I'm So Tired
the-beatles-i-m-so-tired.about: Lennon wrote it at 3am in Rishikesh, plagued by insomnia. Raw, urgent vocal delivery. Ends with a short mumbled backwards passage that sparked 'Paul is dead' rumours.

the-beatles-i-ve-got-a-feeling.title: I've Got a Feeling
the-beatles-i-ve-got-a-feeling.about: Two unfinished songs merged: McCartney's 'I've Got a Feeling' and Lennon's 'Everybody Had a Hard Year' play simultaneously in the final section. Billy Preston on electric piano. Rooftop performance energy.

the-beatles-i-ve-just-seen-a-face.title: I've Just Seen a Face
the-beatles-i-ve-just-seen-a-face.about: McCartney's breathless folk-country number. Double-tracked acoustic guitars. Running eighth notes give it a sense of momentum and excitement. One of McCartney's most purely joyful performances.

the-beatles-if-i-fell.title: If I Fell
the-beatles-if-i-fell.cover_file: The Beatles - A Hard Day's Night.jpg
the-beatles-if-i-fell.about: Lennon's complex intro modulates from a different key into the main verse. Close two-part harmonies between Lennon and McCartney throughout. One of the most harmonically sophisticated early Beatles songs.

the-beatles-if-i-needed-someone.title: If I Needed Someone
the-beatles-if-i-needed-someone.about: Harrison's raga-influenced riff built around a D chord with added open strings. Jangly jangle influenced by The Byrds. Tight Lennon/McCartney harmonies in the chorus.

the-beatles-in-my-life.title: In My Life
the-beatles-in-my-life.about: George Martin recorded the baroque piano solo at half speed, giving it a harpsichord-like timbre when played back at normal speed. Lennon's most personal early lyric, evoking specific Liverpool memories.

the-beatles-it-won-t-be-long.title: It Won't Be Long
the-beatles-it-won-t-be-long.about: Call-and-response 'yeah' vocals between Lennon and harmonies. Beatlemania-era energy. Tight, punchy arrangement with prominent harmonies in the chorus.

the-beatles-it-s-all-too-much.title: It's All Too Much

victor-young-stella-by-starlight.title: Stella By Starlight
victor-young-stella-by-starlight.feel: ballad ("Adam Levy term" per the source: "mysterious")
victor-young-stella-by-starlight.structure: loose/asymmetric AABA-ish (sections don't literally repeat; ~16-bar opening statement, an 8-bar bridge, a transformed return) — 32 bars overall, home key not reached until bar 9
victor-young-stella-by-starlight.about: Music by Victor Young, lyrics by Ned Washington (1944, written for the film *The Uninvited*); one of the most-analyzed jazz standards, notorious for opening on chords that seem to have no functional relationship to each other and not settling into its home key of B♭ major until bar 9.

wayne-shorter-footprints.title: Footprints
wayne-shorter-footprints.about: A Wayne Shorter original, first recorded on his 1966 album *Adam's Apple* and later given a more abstract, tempo-shifting treatment by the Miles Davis Quintet on *Miles Smiles* (1967). Structurally a 12-bar minor blues, but functions modally — the tonic Cm chord is really C Dorian-based quartal/modal harmony rather than a fixed tertian chord, which is what lets comping and soloing vocabulary borrow freely from the parent B♭ major scale over long static stretches.
